name: Acontext (memodb-io)
category: skill-file memory (server-backed context/memory platform with an LLM that writes Markdown "agent skill" files)
status: shipped. There is a hosted cloud (acontext.io, sk-ac API keys) and a self-hostable Apache-2.0 server, plus PyPI/npm SDKs and a Claude Code plugin. The repo is not archived, but it looks inactive: main's last commit is 2026-04-21, dev's is 2026-04-15, and no feature branch moved after April 2026, which I checked with git ls-remote and shallow fetches on 2026-10-02. ROADMAP.md still says "current version: v0.0" and component tags only reach about v0.1.x.
what_is_stored: Two layers. (1) Raw session records: messages (user/assistant only, with typed parts such as text, image, tool-call, tool-result, thinking and redacted_thinking), each with a parent_id, a task_id and a processing status, plus tasks extracted from the stream, session events, "disks" (a virtual filesystem made of artifacts) and sandbox logs. (2) Distilled "skill memory": Markdown agent-skill folders, each a SKILL.md with name/description frontmatter plus optional scripts/ and resources/. An LLM writes them after a task completes or fails, recording what worked, what failed and user preferences. Every learning space starts with two default skills: daily-logs (one file per day) and user-general-facts (one file per topic). Users can upload further skills whose SKILL.md sets the schema and layout the learner follows. The Claude Code plugin reads the transcript_path JSONL from its hooks and uploads the messages in Anthropic format.
where_stored: Server/cloud. The self-host docker-compose runs PostgreSQL 16 with pgvector (rows and metadata), SeaweedFS as S3-compatible object storage (message parts and skill files kept as Disk artifacts), Redis (locks and caching), RabbitMQ (async pipeline), Jaeger (tracing) and Traefik. The API layer is in Go and the "core" learner is Python/FastAPI. The Claude Code client mirrors skills one way into ~/.claude/skills/ (ACONTEXT_SKILLS_DIR) and keeps a local manifest plus sent-message state in a data dir. Nothing is stored in git. The README says "Git, grep, and mount to the sandbox", which only means the exported files can be put into git.
format_and_model: Relational model managed through GORM. agent_skills has id, project_id, user_id, a name that is not unique, description, disk_id and meta jsonb. The file index is computed at query time from the skill's Disk artifacts. artifacts is unique on (disk_id, path, filename) and holds asset metadata pointing to S3. learning_spaces has meta jsonb with a GIN index. learning_space_skills is the join table, and learning_space_sessions tracks a status per session (pending/queued/skill_writing/completed/failed). messages has session_id, parent_id (so a session is a message tree), role, meta jsonb, a parts asset in S3 and task_id. Skill content is plain Markdown with YAML frontmatter, and a whole skill exports as a ZIP. The learner edits skill files with tools: create_skill, create_skill_file, str_replace_skill_file, mv_skill_file and delete_skill_file. These overwrite in place. I found no per-file version history, but that is an inference from the model and grep, not a documented claim.
multi_writer_and_merge: Many sessions and agents can feed one learning space. Skill writes are serialised per learning space with a Redis SET NX EX lock named skill_learn.{learning_space_id}, which is renewed during the agent loop. If the lock is taken, the distilled payload is pushed to a pending list, the session is marked QUEUED, and the lock holder drains queued sessions afterwards. Merging is semantic: an LLM "Skill Agent" decides which existing skill or file to update and rewrites it. There is no textual or CRDT merge and no conflict record. Skill names can collide; the Claude Code sync detects collisions of sanitized names and skips every colliding skill. Client sync is one way, server to local. When a skill's updated_at changes, the plugin deletes the local skill directory (rm -rf) and downloads it again, so edits made directly in ~/.claude/skills are silently overwritten. "Editable" really means editing through the API or dashboard.
realtime: Near-real-time ingestion, asynchronous learning. The Claude Code plugin captures messages incrementally on PostToolUse, Notification and Stop hooks (30–60 s timeouts) and triggers learning on Stop once there are at least ACONTEXT_MIN_TURNS_FOR_LEARN turns (default 4). The server buffers messages until BUFFER_MAX_TURNS is reached or 8 s pass with no new message, then runs task extraction, distillation and the skill agent through RabbitMQ. Other agents only see the result when they next sync skills: on SessionStart, after learning, or on demand through MCP tools. There is no push or subscription channel to clients.
search_retrieval: Deliberately "progressive disclosure, not search". Agents call list_skills, get_skill and get_skill_file, and pick what to read by reasoning, with no semantic top-k. Disk tools offer grep_disk (regex) and glob_disk. The Claude Code MCP server has acontext_search_skills (keyword or regex over skill files), acontext_get_skill, acontext_session_history (summaries of recent tasks), acontext_stats and acontext_learn_now. Skills mirrored to ~/.claude/skills are auto-loaded by Claude Code's native skill mechanism. Server text search is turned off for projects with encryption enabled. Embedding search over sessions is still an unchecked roadmap item, although pgvector and embedding code are present.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Sessions are scoped by project, user identifier (ACONTEXT_USER_IDENTIFIER, default "claude_code") and learning space. I found no capture of cwd, repository, branch or commit in the Claude Code plugin; grepping hook-handler.ts and bridge.ts for cwd/git/branch/commit turned up only unrelated hits. Learned skills are free-text knowledge with no provenance link back to code. Within the server, messages link to the tasks extracted from them.
scale: No scale, throughput or latency claims in the README or docs. The only quantitative knobs are buffer sizes (8–32+ turns), the fixed 8 s idle flush and agent iteration limits. Adoption signal: about 3.7k GitHub stars, 334 forks and about 1,080 commits on main, as shown on the GitHub page.
privacy_security: Optional per-project "end-to-end encryption", which is really encryption at rest with the key held by the client. It uses envelope encryption with AES-256-GCM. The sk-ac API key embeds a 16-byte auth secret and a 40-byte master key (KEK) wrapped with RFC 3394 AES Key Wrap. Each object gets a server-generated DEK, which is stored wrapped. The server keeps only an HMAC/PHC hash of the key, so a lost key means unrecoverable data, and rotation re-wraps the same KEK. When encryption is on, text search and deduplication are disabled. Caveat: the server must unwrap the KEK from the API key on each request, and the LLM pipeline (distillation and skill agent, default gpt-4.1) reads plaintext, so the operator and the LLM provider see the content during processing. The core passes user_kek through the message queue and hard-fails rather than store plaintext when the KEK is invalid. I found no secret or PII redaction and no prompt-injection defence in the learner prompts; grepping llm/prompt for inject/untrusted/credential/password/sensitive returned nothing. Distilled skills are written straight into ~/.claude/skills and auto-loaded, which creates an automatic path from untrusted transcript and tool output to future model context. The client sends everything to api.acontext.app unless ACONTEXT_BASE_URL is pointed at a self-hosted server.
lesson_for_parinn: Acontext shows the main risk of turning learned memory into auto-loaded instruction files. An LLM summarises raw transcripts, including tool results, which may hold injected text or secrets. The output becomes a SKILL.md that Claude Code loads natively in every later session, and the client then overwrites local edits with an rm -rf and re-download. That is exactly the automatic untrusted-to-model channel ParleyInn's I2 forbids, with no audit of what was dropped or overwritten (I6). ParleyInn can take the useful parts: plain, inspectable Markdown; a user-defined schema; progressive disclosure through list/get tools rather than top-k embeddings; and per-scope serialised writers with a queue-and-drain fallback. It should reject the rest: any distilled or learned artifact must stay pull-only and enveloped unless a human promotes it to TrustedText, and writes should be append-only with history rather than in-place rewrites. Acontext's encryption also shows that client-held keys are only as strong as the server's need for plaintext. Server-side LLM processing defeats "zero-knowledge", so ParleyInn should do derivation locally and offline.
license: Apache-2.0

name: Agent Client Protocol (ACP) session/list and session/load
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Session metadata for discovery (session/list): sessionId (unique identifier), cwd (working directory), title (optional human-readable title), updatedAt (ISO 8601 timestamp of last activity), _meta (optional agent-specific metadata like message count). Full conversation history for restoration (session/load): complete message replay as user_message_chunk and agent_message_chunk notifications with optional messageId fields. No client-specified session storage in protocol; agents manage storage independently.
where_stored: Agent-side only. Protocol defines request/response surface but not storage substrate. Individual agents choose storage: in-memory registries, databases, file systems, cloud storage, etc. ACP does not standardize storage layer. Clients discover sessions via RPC query; agents replay history via notification stream during session/load.
format_and_model: JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (default) or HTTP/SSE transports. session/list request: optional cwd filter and cursor pagination token. session/list response: array of SessionInfo objects + optional nextCursor. SessionInfo: {sessionId (string), cwd (string), title (string, optional), updatedAt (string, optional ISO 8601), additionalDirectories (string[], optional), _meta (object, optional)}. session/load request: sessionId, cwd, optional additionalDirectories, mcpServers. session/load response: empty result object; history streamed as session/update notifications before response sent.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable to ACP core. Protocol is single-writer-per-session (one agent owns session state). No merge semantics. Agents are responsible for their own multi-session consistency. ACP provides no distributed consensus, locking, or merge resolution. Clients can list sessions across multiple agents but cannot merge histories.
realtime: session/list is synchronous pull-only (client-initiated query, agent responds). session/load replays history synchronously via agent-initiated session/update notifications; all history streamed before final response. Agents MAY push session_info_update notifications in real-time to notify clients of title/metadata changes without polling, but this is optional and outside session/load flow.
search_retrieval: Protocol provides cursor-based pagination in session/list (opaque token passed as continuation, agent returns nextCursor). Optional filtering by cwd (working directory) on request. No full-text search, tag search, or content search defined in v1. Search/filtering logic is agent-specific (some agents may implement search, some return all sessions). Agents SHOULD enforce reasonable page sizes but size limit is not standardized.
links_sessions_to_code: Sessions are keyed by cwd (working directory, absolute path). cwd is immutable after session setup and serves as primary workspace root. additionalDirectories (optional, since June 2026) expand effective root set for multi-root workspaces. sessionId is opaque identifier; no structural link to code artifacts. Agents typically generate titles from first user message but no standard for content-based linking to files or code entities.
privacy_security: Protocol assumes authenticated client-agent transport (credentials, TLS). No encryption specified for history at rest; per-agent. session/list enumerates sessions for authenticated client; no public listing. No redaction mechanism in ACP core; agents responsible for scrubbing sensitive data before replay. messageId fields in replay are opaque, agent-generated. _meta object carries agent-specific data (tags, costs, error flags); no standardized PII handling. Agents MUST ensure sessions only listed for authorized client (no cross-client leakage). No session-level access control or sharing defined in v1.
lesson_for_parinn: ACP session/list and session/load are discovery + restoration primitives, not a full context layer. They standardize the handshake between client and agent but leave history storage, indexing, and retrieval to agents. Unlike ParleyInn (append-only, hash-chained, immutable), ACP assumes agents control storage and accept that agents can lose, modify, or selectively replay history. For ParleyInn: (1) The RPC surface (list with pagination, load with streaming replay) is proven and broadly adopted; (2) But ACP's trust model differs—ParleyInn treats recalled content as untrusted and re-injects pinned constraints; ACP assumes agent honesty; (3) Cursor-based pagination scales better than offset for large histories; (4) Streaming replay via notifications is a clean pattern for large histories; (5) sessionId + cwd + title + updatedAt are the minimal session surface clients expect; agents often add custom _meta; (6) No search or filtering standard means agents fragment here—an opportunity for ParleyInn to offer federated search across agents + worktrees if storage is standardized downstream.
sources: https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/clients (100+ clients implement ACP: Zed, JetBrains, Cursor, Neovim, Obsidian, VS Code, Sublime, Qt Creator, and web/desktop frameworks)

https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/agents (50+ agents: Claude Code via adapter, Cursor, Cline, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Goose, OpenCode, DeepSeek Harness, Anthropic Agent SDK, GitHub Copilot in preview, many others)
https://github.com/zed-industries/agent-client-protocol/blob/main/schema/v1/meta.json (method registry showing session/list and session/load as agent methods)

name: Agent Client Protocol (ACP) — session/load and session/resume
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Session metadata (sessionId, cwd, title, updatedAt, additionalDirectories) and conversation history streamed as session/update notifications containing user messages, agent responses, tool calls, execution plans, and usage information. ContentBlock types (Text, Image, Audio, ResourceLink, EmbeddedResource) carry the actual message payloads.
where_stored: Protocol-agnostic; implementation-dependent. ACP defines message exchange format (JSON-RPC 2.0), not storage backend. Agents and clients independently decide persistence mechanism—Zed stores sessions locally, other implementations may use cloud storage or databases.
format_and_model: JSON-RPC 2.0 wire protocol with two message types: Methods (request-response) and Notifications (one-way). Sessions identified by sessionId string; metadata uses ISO 8601 timestamps. ContentBlocks are discriminated unions (type: 'text'|'image'|'audio'|'resource_link'|'resource'). Schema defined in v1 and v2 JSON Schema artifacts in schema/ directory.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not addressed by protocol. ACP assumes single-writer sessions (one agent-client pair controls a session at a time). Session operations (load, resume, delete, list, prompt) imply exclusive control. RFD for session forking proposed as future feature; no merge semantics defined. Distributed multi-agent scenarios not explicitly supported.
realtime: Yes. session/load streams entire history as sequential session/update notifications; agents replay conversation transparently. session/resume reconnects without replay, allowing immediate continuation. Active prompt turns send real-time progress via session/update (user_message_chunk, agent_message_chunk, agent_thought_chunk, tool_call, tool_call_update, plan, usage_update).
search_retrieval: Session search not in protocol. session/list method filters stored sessions by optional cwd parameter, returns SessionInfo array with pagination cursor. Agents implement their own discovery and indexing; ACP provides no query language or full-text search primitives.
links_sessions_to_code: Sessions store cwd (absolute path to working directory) and optional additionalDirectories for workspace roots. No explicit code-to-session linking. session/prompt turns may include file operations (fs/read_text_file, fs/write_text_file) and terminal operations that modify code, but session history does not prescribe diffs or code snapshots.
privacy_security: Authentication negotiated at initialization via authMethods; agent advertises available methods, client selects one. Protocol-driven or terminal-based flows supported. No encryption, redaction, or secrets handling prescribed by protocol—delegated to implementations. Logout supported via session/logout. After logout, clients should expect authentication errors on active sessions. No explicit data retention policies or crypto-shredding mechanisms in protocol.
lesson_for_parinn: ACP is a real-time, synchronous communication protocol, not a persistent session storage architecture. It optimizes for live agent-editor interaction where clients control sessions and agents replay/resume on demand. ParleyInn's core concern—hash-chained, append-only records with untrusted content at recall—is orthogonal: ACP has no notion of content provenance, redaction, or multi-agent sharing across machines/worktrees. Key differences: (1) ACP assumes client-initiated session control; ParleyInn must support agent-driven persistence. (2) ACP streams messages in real-time; ParleyInn rebuilds history from immutable records. (3) ACP provides no separation between trusted metadata and untrusted history; ParleyInn enforces TrustedText invariant (I2) to prevent injection from recalled content. (4) ACP session/list is agent-local; ParleyInn must support distributed session discovery. For ParleyInn, ACP suggests sessions should emit immutable update events (like session/update notifications) that can be appended to a record; but ParleyInn's storage, replay guarantees, and multi-agent invariants will differ fundamentally from ACP's design.

name: Agent Deck (asheshgoplani/agent-deck)
category: TUI agent session manager (tmux-based), with an optional cross-harness transcript index called "Recall"
status: shipped
license: MIT (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/LICENSE)
what_is_stored: Agent Deck stores two kinds of data. (1) An operational registry for each profile: session "instances" with id, title, project_path, group, tool, status, tmux_session, tmux_socket_name, parent_session_id, worktree_path/repo/branch, account, archived_at and a tool_data JSON column. Alongside it sit groups, process heartbeats, polling-ownership claims, recently deleted sessions, cost_events (token counts and cost in microdollars per model), and watchers/watcher_events (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/statedb/statedb.go). The same per-profile DB holds the "recall phase 1" tables, which keep human intent that cannot be rebuilt: session_hints (single-valued keys such as purpose, ticket, why, decision, outcome, note, parent; values capped at 8 KiB), session_tags, and session_links (which map a deck session to a harness's native conversation id, with authoritative and historical rows) (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/statedb/recall_hints.go, https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). (2) An opt-in derived index, recall.db, built from the harnesses' own transcripts (Claude JSONL first, then Codex, pi, Gemini, OpenCode, Hermes). It keeps user prompts and assistant text (each body zstd-compressed and clipped to 8 KiB by default, or full with text_tier="full"). It also keeps each tool_use with its name, timing, error flag and a 200-character argument digest, the files read, written or edited, token usage, interrupts, compactions, API errors, title, cwd, branch and model. Tool results, thinking, attachments and snapshots are never stored. Derived "cards" and rule-based artifacts (lost_time, session_kind, outcome) are stored on top (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). Agent Deck does not own conversation content: the harness (for example ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl) remains the source of truth, and forks rely on each tool's native fork (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#fork-sessions). It also keeps an event bus of NDJSON frames per profile (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/events.md).
where_stored: All storage is a local DB plus local files, with no git storage. The per-profile registry lives in SQLite at ~/.local/share/agent-deck/<profile>/state.db (legacy path ~/.agent-deck/<profile>/state.db) (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md). The machine-global, disposable recall.db sits in the agent-deck data dir with recall/sweep.lock and recall/queue.jsonl (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). Event-bus segments are at <data-dir>/bus/<profile>/active.ndjson and seg-<start>-<end>.ndjson (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/events.md). Config is in ~/.config/agent-deck/config.toml. Live processes run in tmux sessions named agentdeck_* (SessionPrefix in https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/tmux/tmux.go), optionally on an isolated server via `tmux -L agent-deck`.
format_and_model: The registry is a relational, mutable SQLite schema (SchemaVersion 13) using the pure-Go driver modernc.org/sqlite with WAL mode and busy_timeout 5000 (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/statedb/statedb.go). Rows are updated in place, not appended. Hints are UPSERTed by (scope_kind, scope_id, key), and each write bumps seq and records its source (cli_create, annotate, hook, conductor, fleet, derived), so a derived value never outranks a typed one. Schema changes are additive only (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS) and the version number is deliberately not bumped, because an older binary sharing the DB would rewrite it back (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). recall.db is a rebuildable projection. It has a contentless FTS5 body index (msg_fts, detail=none, contentless_delete=1, membership-only), a ranked card_fts that supports phrase queries and snippet(), and an ingest ledger keyed on (device, inode) with a byte cursor and a signature of the preceding 4 KiB per source, used for resumable tail parsing (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/recall/schema.go). Event-bus frames are canonical JSON {cursor, event_id, ts, kind, session_id, data}. The cursor is monotonic per profile. Segments seal at 8 MiB or 50,000 frames, and only the last 32 sealed segments are kept (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/events.md).
multi_writer_and_merge: Agent Deck supports multiple processes on one host, but has no cross-machine merge. On state.db, the TUI, CLI, notify-daemon and hooks write concurrently through WAL. busy_timeout is applied per connection, and a linear-backoff withBusyRetry handles SQLITE_BUSY. The code comments say the modernc driver still surfaces BUSY "under heavy multi-writer load" (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/statedb/statedb.go). A session_claims table assigns polling ownership through owner tokens, with heartbeat-stale takeover. The code also records data-loss incidents (2026-06-04, "the third of its class"), which led to ErrRefusingEmptySweep and a .bak copy taken before destructive sweeps (same file). recall.db has one writer connection and one flock shared by all profiles (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). When two transcript files carry the same conversation id (a fork, an import, or an account switch), the copy indexed first owns the session and the other is quarantined, never merged. The docs list this as a known limit: turns appended later to the quarantined original are never indexed (same doc). The event bus assigns cursors under a cross-process writer.lock, batching up to 256 frames per lock (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/events.md). Across machines, remote hints stay in the remote's own state.db and are "never copied locally" (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md).
realtime: Real-time only on the local machine. The TUI polls tmux panes and transcripts for status (running, waiting, idle, error). A Stop/SessionEnd hook and session events trigger a bounded inline recall sweep, and each search first runs a sweep capped at 150 ms and 32 MB. `agent-deck events follow --json --after <cursor>` streams NDJSON frames live. Resuming after a kill is tested to lose and duplicate nothing (TestResumeAfterKillLosesNothingAndDuplicatesNothing). Frames can be dropped when a queue is full or when the process crashes before a sync; drops are counted in drops.count (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/events.md). Remote hosts are polled over SSH, not pushed. A conductor gets a remote worker's completions only through a manual `agent-deck remote drain` (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#remote-instances). A web UI on 127.0.0.1:8420 streams terminals over WebSocket.
search_retrieval: Session search in the TUI: `/` fuzzy-searches session titles and filters by status; `G` runs global search across all Claude conversations (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#search). `agent-deck recall search` searches across every profile and harness and ranks sessions, not messages. A hit in the title, hints or tags (card_fts) always outranks body hits; body hits then rank by count and recency. Search supports AND/OR/NOT and prefix*, treats identifiers such as SB-412 as single terms, and caps candidates at 5,000 messages. `--phrase` checks the phrase against the decompressed bodies and reports "phrase unverified (clipped body)" rather than a false negative. Other read commands are `recall show` (tiers card, excerpt, raw), `recall timeline` and `recall follow`. `recall context --tier card|brief|excerpt --budget N --into <session>` turns history into a token-budgeted handoff. `agent-deck recall mcp` is a stdio MCP server exposing recall_search, recall_show and recall_context. Across machines, search is federated over SSH by default with nothing stored locally. Optional card sync (`remote_cards = true` on both ends) exports NDJSON with no bodies, offsets or paths (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). There is no embedding or vector search; the design says only FTS5 plus rules, and LLM enrichment is never run automatically (same doc).
links_sessions_to_code: Linking is indirect, through worktree and branch, never through commits. Each instance row records worktree_path, worktree_repo and worktree_branch. Quick fork (`f`) creates a new worktree and branch by default (prefix fork/) and carries the parent's uncommitted state; Jujutsu workspaces are also supported. `agent-deck worktree finish` merges the branch, removes the worktree and deletes the session (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#git-worktrees, https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#forking-sessions). recall.db records the cwd, branch and files touched by each tool call, and `recall show` and the brief tier print the touched files (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). A ticket hint (`--ticket SB-412`) adds a human-entered link to issue trackers. I found no git notes, commit trailers or commit-SHA linkage in the repo's docs or Go code (grep over the shallow clone at commit 035fd60).
scale: Measured on the author's machine: 3.4 GB of Claude transcripts in 1,809 files produced an index about 3.8% of input size (2.1x zstd compression on chat text, with no shared dictionary). Peak RSS was about 93 MB on the first backfill and 48 to 76 MB on later passes. A 100 MB transcript adds about 11 MB of heap. An unchanged-tree stat sweep over about 7,000 files takes about 50 ms (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). Backfill and sweep refuse to run while a session of the active profile is running or when loadavg exceeds 4.0 (`--force` overrides); the daemon backfill throttles instead of refusing (same doc). MCP socket pooling claims an 85-90% cut in MCP memory and about 3 s crash recovery (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md#mcp-socket-pool). The SESSION-PERSISTENCE spec describes an incident with 33+39 managed sessions on one host (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/SESSION-PERSISTENCE-SPEC.md). I could not verify the star count: the GitHub API was not available in this session.
privacy_security: Local-first. The data dir and lock are created with 0700 and 0600, and the pooled MCP Unix socket is chmod 0600 (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/mcppool/socket_proxy.go, https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/recall/store/store.go). There is no encryption at rest for state.db or recall.db, and no secret redaction of transcript text before indexing. The only redaction code I found covers the telemetry API key (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/internal/telemetry/posthog.go). Recalled context is labelled as data: the handoff text is harness-neutral and closes with a line saying it is recalled context, not an instruction. It is still delivered into the target session's prompt as keystrokes or over a messaging socket (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/docs/recall.md). Cross-machine exposure is minimized. Federated search moves results, not bodies. The card export is tested never to emit bodies, offsets, spans or paths (TestExport_NeverEmitsOffsetsSpansBodiesOrPaths). Imports are bound to a minted host_uid and refused on alias mismatch. Raw transcript fetch over SSH is deliberately not built, and a "remote transcript boundary" test walks every entry point that could resolve a transcript (same doc). The web UI takes a bearer token, with `--token-file` that must not be group- or world-readable, an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie and a Host allow-list (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/README.md). Telemetry is opt-in and off by default (PostHog EU, never prompts, paths or titles; DO_NOT_TRACK honored) (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/TELEMETRY.md). Copying gitignored files into forks is off by default because of .env secrets (README#forking-sessions). Releases carry SLSA provenance attestations; v1.10.9 through v1.10.11 are a known unattested gap (https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck/blob/main/SECURITY.md). Agent Deck does use the network itself: SSH remotes, a self-updater, Telegram/Slack conductor bridges, `gh` for feedback, and opt-in telemetry.
lesson_for_parinn: Split durability explicitly. Recall keeps the small set of human- or binding-authored facts that cannot be rebuilt (hints, tags, authoritative harness-to-session links) in a durable store. Everything derivable from transcripts goes in a disposable index, where deletion "costs a rebuild and nothing else". The index binds a transcript to a session only through an authoritative link, never by working directory. ParleyInn should do the same: the record carries the irreducible facts, and every index is a projection, which matches I10. ParleyInn should also bind transcripts only through explicit ids. Two of Agent Deck's choices ParleyInn should not copy. First, its in-place mutable SQLite registry has needed repeated data-loss safeguards (ErrRefusingEmptySweep, .bak copies before destructive sweeps). Second, "first copy wins, others quarantined" silently stops indexing when forked transcripts share an id. ParleyInn's append-only, hash-chained log should model forks as explicit parent-linked branches instead of collisions. Agent Deck's cross-machine design is also worth copying: federated query by default, opt-in sync of derived cards only, no bodies or paths crossing hosts, and imports bound to a host id. This shows a useful sharing tier that never moves raw history.

name: Agent Note (wasabeef/AgentNote; npm package "agent-note")
category: git-notes session transcripts: per-commit AI session summaries stored as git notes, plus a PR report and dashboard through a GitHub Action
status: shipped. v1.0.0 (first stable) came out 2026-05-11 and v1.0.8, the latest, on 2026-07-13 (GitHub Releases). The default branch's HEAD is the v1.0.8 version-bump commit bf51ac6, dated 2026-07-13, so no commits landed in the roughly 2.5 months before 2026-10-02. It is not archived. On 2026-10-02 the repo page showed 15 stars, 0 forks, 0 open issues and 601 commits. I could not cross-check those numbers because the GitHub REST API returned 403 to this session.
what_is_stored:
Git stores one JSON entry per AI-assisted commit. Each entry holds the schema version, agent name, agent session id, a timestamp and the model id. It then holds interactions[]: each one is a prompt, the full AI response (never truncated), files_touched, the edit tools used, optional display-only contexts[] excerpts and selection evidence (schema/source/signals). It also holds files[] ({path, by_ai, optional generated/ai_ratio_excluded}) and attribution ({ai_ratio 0-100, method line|file|none, lines {ai_added, total_added, deleted}}).

The entry is not a transcript. Only the prompts in a "commit-to-commit window" around the turns that produced the committed lines are kept. Planning and clarification turns in that window stay; earlier edit turns that no longer own lines are dropped. Before storage, prompts pass a sanitizer that strips leading <environment_context> blocks and drops standalone <system-reminder>, <task-notification> and <teammate-message> messages.

The commit message gets the trailer "Agentnote-Session: <uuid>".

Local temporary state, which is never pushed:
- session pointer
- per-session prompts.jsonl, changes.jsonl (files touched, with post-edit blob hash), pre_blobs.jsonl, events.jsonl, heartbeat, transcript_path, turn counter and rotated archives
- committed_pairs.jsonl

Before and after every AI edit, `git hash-object -w` writes a snapshot blob into the object store. These blobs are unreferenced and left for gc.

The full agent transcript stays in the agent's own data directory, which Agent Note only reads. The architecture doc's entire.io table says the note holds a transcript "reference only (pointer in note)". That conflicts with the schema, which has no transcript field and stores the full response text.
where_stored:
- **Permanent record:** git notes on the dedicated ref refs/notes/agentnote, one note per commit SHA. It is shared by `git push` through a generated pre-push hook and fetched through a refspec that `init` adds to remote.origin.fetch.
- **Commit message:** the Agentnote-Session trailer, in the commit itself.
- **Local temp:** .git/agentnote/ in the working git dir; in a linked worktree it lives under that worktree's git dir (.git/worktrees/<name>/agentnote), while notes are shared through the common git database.
- **Edit snapshots:** pre/post-edit blobs as loose objects in .git/objects.
- **Downstream copies (optional):** the PR description or a PR comment (GitHub Action), and for the dashboard, JSON files under gh-pages/dashboard/notes/*.json plus a GitHub Pages artifact.
- **Committed agent config:** hook configuration in .claude/settings.json, .codex/config.toml + .codex/hooks.json, .cursor/hooks.json or .gemini/settings.json. Git hooks (prepare-commit-msg, post-commit, pre-push) are installed per clone into the directory Git reports, respecting core.hooksPath, and chain to existing hooks.
format_and_model:
The note body is pretty-printed JSON with "v": 1, written by `git notes --ref=agentnote add -f -m <json> <sha>` (storage.ts). The data model is keyed by commit: commit SHA → note, plus a session-id trailer on the commit. Local buffers are append-only JSONL. A file is rotated at each new prompt (UserPromptSubmit); archives are kept within a turn so split commits still see them. If the process dies, only the last line can be torn.

Attribution uses a monotonic per-session "causal turn id" instead of timestamps. Line-level AI attribution is a 3-diff algorithm per file:
- diff1: parent blob → committed blob
- diff2: pre-edit blob → committed blob
- diff3: post-edit blob → committed blob
- AI lines = (diff2 ∩ diff1) \ diff3, unioned across turns

It falls back to file-count attribution when blob data is missing. Agents plug in through an AgentAdapter interface:
- **Claude Code:** full support, from hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Pre/PostToolUse, Stop) plus the transcript at ~/.claude/projects/...
- **Codex CLI:** driven by its transcript
- **Cursor:** afterFileEdit/afterTabFileEdit hooks plus transcripts
- **Gemini CLI:** preview, file-level attribution only

The CLI is TypeScript on Node 20+ with zero runtime dependencies and drives git only through execFile.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Each developer or agent writes notes locally at post-commit. Because notes are keyed by distinct commit SHAs, the authors say note conflicts are "rare".

Push conflicts are documented, but only manual recovery is offered: fetch the notes ref, run `git notes --ref=agentnote merge origin/notes/agentnote`, push. The CLI has no merge logic. push-notes runs `git push <remote> refs/notes/agentnote` with a 10 s timeout and swallows every failure, including a non-fast-forward rejection, without a warning. The hook warns only when no CLI resolver can start at all.

The auto-fetch refspec `init` installs is forced and maps straight onto the local ref: `+refs/notes/agentnote*:refs/notes/agentnote*` (constants.ts). If the remote notes ref has moved, a later fetch or pull can therefore overwrite local notes that were never pushed. That is my inference from the code; the docs do not discuss it.

Concurrency limits:
- Concurrent sessions in one worktree share a single active-session pointer, and the last writer wins. The docs admit this can put the wrong session id in a trailer.
- Per-session directories are isolated, and worktrees get separate temp state.

History rewriting:
- Rebase or amend orphans notes, since they are keyed by SHA. Setting notes.rewriteRef is still marked "planned" and `init` does not set it.
- GitHub squash-merge loses all per-commit notes, so the PR description becomes the surviving copy.
- The dashboard merges note state on gh-pages from Actions runs.
realtime: No. It works in batches at git boundaries: notes are written at post-commit and shared only when the user runs `git push`, where the pre-push hook pushes the notes ref first. Other machines see them after a fetch or pull. The PR Action retries its notes fetch to cover the race between the branch push and the notes push. There is no live streaming or cross-machine session sharing. Uncommitted session buffers never leave the clone.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by commit, not by content:
- `agent-note show [commit]` prints one note.
- `agent-note log [n]` lists commits with session id, AI ratio and prompt count.
- `agent-note why <file:line | range | GitHub URL | vscode:// URL>` runs git blame, finds the commit, reads its note and prints the matching interactions, with an honest "evidence level".
- Raw access: `git notes --ref=agentnote show <sha>`.
- `agent-note pr --json` emits structured data, and the Action exposes outputs such as overall_ai_ratio and a json report.
- An optional static Astro dashboard on GitHub Pages builds its note index at build time.

There is no full-text, semantic or cross-session search, and no API for an agent to recall history (no MCP server). The hidden "agentnote-reviewer-context" block in the PR body is aimed at AI review tools, which read it as intent.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, and it is the product's main purpose ("Link every git commit to the AI session that produced it"):
- **Session to commit:** the Agentnote-Session trailer, injected by the prepare-commit-msg hook when the session is fresh and has file evidence, or by Claude Code's PreToolUse Bash(git commit) hook through --trailer.
- **Commit to conversation:** the per-commit note.
- **Prompt to files:** files_touched on each interaction.
- **Line to conversation:** `why` through git blame.
- **Lines to AI vs human:** the 3-diff blob attribution.

There are guards against false links. Prompt-only sessions do not get trailers on plain git commits. A stale heartbeat falls back to recording only when a post-edit blob matches a committed blob. The environment fallback trusts only an adapter-provided session id (e.g. CODEX_THREAD_ID), validated as a canonical UUID.
scale: No quantitative claims, benchmarks or limits are published. Full responses are stored untruncated, justified only by "Git notes blobs are compressed and well within GitHub limits". Size is held down by keeping only the commit prompt window rather than the full session. The authors contrast this with Entire's full transcript copy per checkpoint, which they call "O(n²) bloat". Every AI edit writes two loose blobs into the object store; growth is left to `git gc`. Performance claims are limited to async agent hooks and lightweight git hooks, compared with Entire's reported "2min 44s commit".
privacy_security:
**Network and services:**
- Local-first: no hosted service, account, token or telemetry.
- Agent transcripts are read but never modified.

**No protection for content:**
- No automatic redaction of secrets or PII. The threat table says "Not automatically redacted. Users are responsible for reviewing notes before pushing them to public repos."
- No encryption and no signing. Anyone with write access can edit or delete notes; the docs say to "Treat them as advisory, not as audit trail."

**Exposure:**
- The pre-push hook auto-publishes prompts and responses on every push, which makes them public on public repos. The documented opt-out is --no-git-hooks.
- The dashboard republishes notes to gh-pages and GitHub Pages, with a warning to match Pages visibility to repo policy.

**Hardening:**
- Session ids from the environment are validated as UUIDs.
- transcript_path must lie under the agent's data directory such as ~/.claude/.
- Prompts are sanitized for injected runtime metadata.
- Existing hooks are chained, not overwritten.
- Text in the PR report is escaped, and "--" is neutralised inside the hidden reviewer-context comment.
- Fork PRs are steered away from pull_request_target.

**Supply chain:** agent hooks run `npx --yes agent-note hook`, a risk the docs acknowledge. Git hooks prefer the local binary.

**Trust model (opposite of ParleyInn's I2):** stored prompts are deliberately fed back to AI reviewers (Copilot, CodeRabbit, Devin, Greptile) as reviewer context. The docs say only "Treat git notes as trusted repository data; do not push untrusted prompt content to public notes."

**Vulnerability reporting:** SECURITY.md routes reports through GitHub Security Advisories, with acknowledgement within 48 h.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy the cheap link, not the storage key. A short session trailer on each commit, plus a hook that keeps plain `git commit` working, is a robust, agent-agnostic way to tie history to code; `why` then works by walking git blame → trailer → record.

Do not key the record itself by commit SHA, as Agent Note does. Its own docs list what that costs:
- rebase and amend orphan notes
- squash-merge erases them
- a forced `+refs/notes/agentnote*` fetch can clobber unpushed local notes
- non-fast-forward push failures are silently swallowed
- notes are unsigned ("advisory, not audit trail")

If ParleyInn uses git as a transport, it should:
- key its append-only, hash-chained session log by session and event hash, not by commit
- fetch into a non-forced remote-tracking namespace and merge as an append-only union, which the hash chain makes conflict-free and verifiable
- audit and count every failed or rejected push (I6)
- redact before anything leaves the machine

Never re-inject stored prompts into model-facing surfaces unenveloped, as Agent Note's PR reviewer-context block does (I2).
