format_and_model: An informal key/value token in the commit message. The examples use RFC-822-style trailer syntax "Key: value" with the value "<Name of Tool> <Version>" (https://www.apache.org/legal/generative-tooling.html). The ASF page does not say the token must be in the git trailer block, does not define a grammar, a controlled vocabulary for tool names, a version format, or an email field. It offers Co-authored-by as an equal alternative, which collides with GitHub's human co-author trailer (that trailer normally carries "Name <email>"). The data model is one flat assertion per commit: tool X version Y helped produce this commit. Related ASF material is all marked unofficial draft. The Responsible AI initiative's "Commit messages for AI-assisted code" uses "Generated-by: <tool-name>" with no version (e.g. "Generated-by: Claude-3.5-Sonnet", "Generated-by: GitHub Copilot") and says it is "a convention — it is not yet a formal, Foundation-wide requirement" (https://rai.apache.org/commit-messages.html). A separate draft page proposes authored-by, co-authored-by and "ai-assisted-by: <tool>" (https://rai.apache.org/authored-by-tags.html). Projects vary. For example, Apache Wayang's policy cites the ASF guidance and asks for a Generated-by token, but its own example is malformed ("Co-author by: GitHub Copilot") (https://wayang.apache.org/docs/community/ai-tooling-policy), so in practice the format is not uniform.
multi_writer_and_merge: Inherits git's model. Each commit carries its own token, set by whoever writes the message. The guidance says nothing about squash merges, rebases, cherry-picks or merge commits. Squash merges on GitHub concatenate or rewrite messages, so trailers can be duplicated or lost. That is a general git/GitHub behavior, and the ASF page does not address it. No conflict resolution is needed because the token is append-once metadata inside an immutable commit.
realtime: Not applicable. The token is written when the commit is made and seen when it is pushed. Nothing streams or syncs beyond normal git push/fetch.
search_retrieval: Only generic git tooling, e.g. `git log --grep` or `git interpret-trailers --parse` / `git log --format=%(trailers)`, and only when contributors used real trailer syntax. The ASF provides no index or query service. The proposed Tooling-Provenance file would be the retrieval artifact, but it is unbuilt or unverified (https://www.apache.org/legal/generative-tooling.html).
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, and at the tool level only. The token links a commit to a tool name and version, not to an agent session, a prompt, a transcript or a conversation ID. The guidance asks for no session identifier, and the RAI draft says nothing about prompts or session logs (https://rai.apache.org/commit-messages.html). Granularity is the whole commit, with no per-line or per-hunk attribution.
scale: No scale claims. The policy applies to all ASF projects (more than 300, though that number is not stated on the page). I did not find adoption metrics for Generated-by trailers.
privacy_security: There is no redaction, encryption or secrets handling, because only a tool name and version is recorded, and that is low-sensitivity by design. Commit messages are public and permanent once pushed to a public ASF repo. The main concern is legal provenance, not confidentiality. Contributors must make sure tool terms allow Apache-2.0 licensing, should use similarity detection or code scanning to rule out copied training data, and under ICLA s.8 must notify legal-private@apache.org if they later learn a representation was wrong (https://www.apache.org/legal/generative-tooling.html). The page does not tell contributors to keep prompts or sessions out of commits, and it does not tell them to include them either.
license: The page is Copyright 2026 The Apache Software Foundation, licensed under Apache-2.0 (footer of https://www.apache.org/legal/generative-tooling.html). The source is apache/www-site content/legal/generative-tooling.md.
lesson_for_parinn: Keep the commit side to a tiny, public, low-sensitivity pointer, and keep the history itself somewhere else. The ASF convention shows the ecosystem already expects a trailer naming the tool. Its weaknesses show what ParleyInn should add. It has no defined grammar (Generated-by and Co-authored-by are both allowed, versions are optional, projects write malformed variants), it says nothing about squash or rebase survival, and its promised machine-parsable Tooling-Provenance file was never built after three years (2023 to 2026). ParleyInn could emit an ASF-compatible "Generated-by: <tool> <version>" trailer plus one strictly specified, opaque trailer that carries no content, for example a session or record ID with a hash-chain head digest. The parser would be strict and validated by a fuzz target. Session content, prompts and transcripts would never go in the commit message. A public, immutable commit message is the wrong place for untrusted or sensitive history (I2/I8), and the ASF never asks for it there. ParleyInn should also generate the provenance file itself, deterministically from its record (I10), instead of counting on future release tooling. And it should say in its docs what happens to trailers on squash merges.

name: asciinema 3.0 / asciicast v3
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Terminal session event stream with relative timing: output (stdout/stderr), input (optional), markers, window resize events, and exit status. Each event has a time delta in seconds since the previous event. Session metadata in header: terminal size, type (e.g. xterm-256color), timestamp, title, and captured environment variables.
where_stored: Local .cast files (append-only NDJSON). Can be uploaded to asciinema.org (SaaS) or self-hosted asciinema servers. Live streaming via HTTP server (localhost/LAN) or WebSocket relay to asciinema servers. Format itself is file-based; transport is HTTP(S).
format_and_model: Newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON). Line 1: JSON object header with version (3), term.{cols, rows, type}, timestamp (Unix epoch), title, env, and optional other fields. Lines 2+: Events as 3-element JSON arrays: [interval_float_seconds, event_code_string, event_data_string]. Event codes: 'o' (output), 'i' (input), 'm' (marker), 'r' (resize), 'x' (exit). Highly compressible (8% of original size on average).
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer per session. The asciinema recorder (CLI process) captures one terminal session sequentially and writes to a single .cast file. File structure is append-only but does not support concurrent writes or merging of multiple recordings. Sessions are independent; no built-in branching or conflict resolution.
realtime: Yes. asciinema 3.0 (released 15 Sep 2025) added live streaming: (1) record to file + stream simultaneously, (2) stream-only to built-in HTTP server for LAN viewers, (3) stream via relay to remote asciinema server. WebSocket used for remote relay; HTTP for local server. Viewers see output in near-real-time.
search_retrieval: Not built into the format. asciinema.org (and self-hosted servers) provide web-based search and browsing of published recordings. File playback uses embedded player or terminal playback. No full-text search of event data in format spec. Players can seek within recordings but retrieval is manual navigation.
links_sessions_to_code: Not directly supported. Header can capture SHELL and other env vars; title can describe the session. No built-in git commit reference, PR link, or repository metadata. When uploaded to asciinema.org, recordings get a unique URL but no automatic linking to code repositories or version control systems.
privacy_security: No encryption, hashing, or redaction in the format spec. Recordings capture terminal output verbatim, including any secrets accidentally printed. asciinema.org uploads allow visibility control (public/unlisted/private). Self-hosting gives full control. No built-in crypto-shredding, log verification, or trust boundaries. Content is treated as public-by-default if not carefully managed.
lesson_for_parinn: Append-only, newline-delimited event log is efficient for storage and streaming (can stream while still recording). Relative timing (deltas) reduces encoding; players reconstruct absolute timing. No hash-chaining or cryptographic verification of history—each file is independent. Git integration would strengthen auditability; asciinema relies on external SaaS or self-hosted servers, creating network dependencies and single points of trust. For ParleyInn's security-first model, asciinema's lack of built-in tamper-evidence and crypto-shredding would require layering (e.g., sign recordings, encrypt before upload, integrate with git refs).

name: AT Protocol repositories (Merkle Search Tree repos + sync/firehose)
status: shipped. Public repos and Sync v1.1 run in production on the Bluesky network. Sync v1.1 relays launched in May 2025 (https://atproto.com/blog/relay-updates-sync-v1-1). The non-public extension "Atproto Spaces" (earlier called private data, then permissioned data, then buckets) has been an alpha since 20 Aug 2026, with breaking changes expected and a warning that it is not for production (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha).
what_is_stored: Each account (DID) has one repository holding its current set of records. Records are Lexicon-typed data at a path `<collection NSID>/<record-key>`. Blobs (media) are referenced by content hash but stored outside the repo. A signed commit object holds `did`, `version` (fixed at 3), `data` (the CID of the MST root), `rev` (a TID that only ever increases), `prev` (the CID of the previous commit; the field must be present but may be null, and the spec calls it "largely unused") and `sig` (https://atproto.com/specs/repository). The repo is a current-state snapshot, not a history: "Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or tombstone" (https://atproto.com/specs/repository).
where_stored: On a server/cloud: each account's Personal Data Server (PDS) hosts the repo. Relays used to mirror full repos. Since Sync v1.1 they are "non-archival": they keep only a rolling event backfill, about "a couple hundred GByte" for 24 hours (https://atproto.com/blog/relay-updates-sync-v1-1). Downstream AppViews and consumers keep their own derived indexes. Space data (alpha) lives in "per-space permissioned repos on the author's PDS", and no relay is involved (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha).
format_and_model: The data model is a content-addressed Merkle Search Tree. Keys are kept in sorted byte order. A key's depth is SHA-256(key), count the leading zero bits, divide by 2 and round down, which gives a fanout of 4. Because of this, the same set of records always produces the same root CID, whatever order the writes came in. Records, MST nodes and commits are encoded in DRISL CBOR (deterministic DAG-CBOR). To sign a commit, the unsigned commit is serialized, hashed with SHA-256, and the binary hash is signed with the account's signing key. Repos are exported and transferred as CAR v1 archives (https://atproto.com/specs/repository). Commit diffs travel as CAR slices inside firehose `#commit` events (https://atproto.com/specs/sync).
multi_writer_and_merge: There is one writer per repo: only the account's PDS, using the account's signing key, can commit, and `rev` must increase monotonically. There is no multi-writer merge or fork resolution inside a repo. Collaboration happens across repos: each user writes records into their own repo, and AppViews aggregate them. The spec warns that accounts fully control their own contents, so they can mine keys to unbalance the tree, and recommends capping entries per node (https://atproto.com/specs/repository). Spaces (alpha) gives a shared context that is split across members' PDSes and governed by a "space authority" DID that decides which DIDs have access (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha).
realtime:
Yes. `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos` is a WebSocket firehose, offered by PDSes and relays with compatible semantics. Event types are `#commit`, `#sync`, `#identity` and `#account`.
- `#commit` carries `rev`, `since`, `commit`, `blocks` (a CAR slice of at most 2 MB), `ops` (at most 200 per commit) and `prevData` (the previous MST root).
- Consumers store a `seq` cursor so they can resume. They check signatures against current identity data. They also apply each op in reverse to the new tree and check that the result equals `prevData`, which proves the diff is complete.
- If `since` or `prevData` does not match, the consumer marks the repo out-of-sync and fetches the whole repo again.
- Limits: frames up to 5 MB, records up to 1 MB (https://atproto.com/specs/sync).

Bluesky's relay checks signatures and does this reverse-apply check for every firehose message. It handles "thousands of messages per second" on about 2 vCPU, 12 GB RAM and 30 Mbps. At first it ran in a lenient mode that logs failures instead of rejecting them (https://atproto.com/blog/relay-updates-sync-v1-1). Spaces sync is a separate, lighter real-time protocol that goes straight from the PDS, with no relay (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha).
search_retrieval: The repo itself only supports lookup by path (collection/rkey), range scans over sorted keys, and full CAR export. Search and indexing are left to downstream AppViews and indexers. For backfill there is `com.atproto.sync.listReposByCollection`, which finds the repos that contain a given collection (https://atproto.com/specs/sync). The protocol has no full-text or semantic search.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. The protocol has no notion of agent sessions, prompts or commits to code. One related ecosystem project: Tangled (https://blog.tangled.org/intro) builds git collaboration on atproto. Git repos sit on self-hostable "knot" servers, and the social and collaboration layer uses atproto identity and records. Nothing found shows it stores agent-session history.
privacy_security:
Public repos are public by design. The spec says repos are "entirely public and verifiable" and has no encryption or redaction mechanism (https://atproto.com/specs/repository).
- Deletion: deleting a record removes it from the current tree without a tombstone. But firehose consumers and mirrors that already copied it keep it, so this is erasure from the source, not a retraction.
- Listed security concerns: key-mining attacks on tree shape, CBOR limits on size and recursion depth, dangling references in CAR imports, and data leaking across accounts on import. With key rotation, checking old commit signatures "can become ambiguous" (https://atproto.com/specs/repository).
- Spaces (alpha) explicitly gives "access control not confidentiality". Data is not encrypted and anyone or any app with access to the space can read it (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha).
- Nothing in the protocol detects secrets.
scale: The spec says repos are meant for "up to single-digit millions records" each and become "unwieldy" beyond that (https://atproto.com/specs/repository). Network-wide, the Sync v1.1 relay handles thousands of events per second on modest hardware. The new relays started their sequence numbers at 20 billion, while the old relay was at about 8.4 billion (https://atproto.com/blog/relay-updates-sync-v1-1). Spaces claims to scale from a single record up to billions of records (https://atproto.com/blog/atproto-spaces-alpha). I did not check current account counts for the whole network.
license: The specs are published openly at atproto.com. I did not check the license of the reference implementations (bluesky-social/atproto in TypeScript, indigo in Go) for this sheet. Treat it as unverified here.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy the shape of the sync message, not the trust model. Each atproto diff names the state it was applied to (`since` rev and `prevData` root), and a consumer can prove the diff is complete and correctly ordered without fetching the whole repo, by applying the ops in reverse and checking the signature. When anything does not match, the consumer falls back to a full CAR re-sync. ParleyInn could ship session-log deltas between worktrees, machines and sandboxes the same way. Each batch would carry the prior chain head plus a signature, receivers would refuse batches whose base does not match, and a gap would trigger a full re-fetch. That works over any carrier (git ref, file drop, relay), so the core never needs the network.

What not to copy: atproto repos are mutable current-state trees with deletion that leaves no tombstone and a `prev` link that is mostly unused. They are public and unencrypted, and even the private Spaces alpha gives access control without confidentiality. ParleyInn's append-only record, its need for audited redaction (I6) and its treatment of recalled content as untrusted (I2) all need explicit tombstones, encryption, and treating content as data. None of these come with this model.

name: Atlassian Rovo Dev (Bitbucket Cloud)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Rovo Dev stores agent session conversation history and metadata separately from code changes. Session data includes: (1) full conversation history with context, messages, tool calls, and results in session_context.json; (2) session metadata (title, workspace, fork relationships) in metadata.json. For Bitbucket Cloud integration, Rovo indexes repository metadata: repositories, pull requests, commits, and branches (last 12 months). Code content itself is NOT indexed. Agent outputs (generated code, reviews) can create pull requests and commits in Bitbucket, which are stored as normal repository objects. LLM inputs/outputs are processed in-memory with zero retention—neither OpenAI nor Anthropic models retain inputs to improve their services.
where_stored: Sessions in Rovo Dev CLI are stored locally at ~/.rovodev/sessions/ as JSON files (session_context.json and metadata.json). Bitbucket Cloud metadata (repositories, PRs, commits, branches) is indexed in Rovo's search backend—storage location not publicly documented but supports data residency in user-selected geographic regions. Agent-generated code changes are stored directly in Bitbucket Cloud as commits and pull requests. LLM provider processing occurs over SSL to third-party (OpenAI, Anthropic) servers under zero-retention agreements—no persistent storage there. MCP server connections are configured in ~/.rovodev/mcp.json (local CLI storage).
format_and_model: Session storage: JSON format (session_context.json with conversation history, metadata.json with session metadata). Data model: hierarchical sessions with parent-child fork relationships, message-based conversation history, and workspace scoping. LLM integration: Multi-model approach using OpenAI and Anthropic through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers with zero data retention agreements. Bitbucket metadata indexed into Rovo Search backend using semantic/keyword indexing (format not publicly specified). MCP transport: supports stdio, HTTP, and Server-Sent Events (SSE) connections.
multi_writer_and_merge: Limited multi-writer support. CLI sessions (~/.rovodev/sessions/) are single-writer per session with no built-in conflict resolution—serialized by workspace. Each session is independent with UUID-based identities. Rovo Dev supports session forking (/sessions fork [title]) creating child sessions linked to parents but no merge operation documented. For Bitbucket Cloud: Rovo creates PRs and commits which follow Bitbucket's native conflict resolution (Git merge strategies). MCP server architecture supports multiple concurrent clients but no documented concurrency control for session writes. Workspace-level serialization appears to be primary conflict prevention mechanism.
realtime: Not real-time. Typical interaction latency is 10-15 seconds per agent response. Asynchronous execution model supported for background tasks, allowing multi-step operations to run in parallel without blocking user. Session restoration supports both automatic and manual resumption (/sessions, /sessions restore). Bitbucket metadata indexing appears to be batch-indexed rather than live-streamed—last 12 months metadata available but update frequency not documented. Pull requests and commits created by agents are written synchronously to Bitbucket Cloud.
search_retrieval: Two search mechanisms: (1) Full conversation history retrieval from session files (session_context.json) with /sessions menu showing all sessions sorted by last activity, message count, creation date, token usage, and preview. (2) AI-powered semantic search across Bitbucket Cloud metadata (repositories, pull requests, commits, branches) integrated into Rovo Search. Search respects existing Bitbucket permissions—users can only retrieve metadata they already have authorization to view. Search is pull-only, initiated by user or agent request, not pushed.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, bidirectionally. Sessions link to code through: (1) Bitbucket MCP Server integration—agents read files, browse branches, view commit history, and search repositories. (2) Agent actions create code: agents can open pull requests, create commits, merge PRs, and post comments in Bitbucket. Session history is SEPARATE from code repository—conversations stored in ~/.rovodev/sessions/ as JSON, code changes stored in Bitbucket. No built-in tracing back from a commit to the session that created it (no session metadata embedded in commits). Agents can reference and understand code context but the linkage is unidirectional from sessions→code, not indexed back.
privacy_security: SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified. Zero data retention with LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic)—explicit contracts prevent model training on customer prompts/outputs. In-memory processing: inputs and outputs discarded immediately after LLM response. Permissions inherited from source systems: users can only access Atlassian, Bitbucket, Jira, Confluence, or third-party data they have authorization to view. Data residency: configurable geographic region for data at rest. Admin controls: content blocklists to restrict indexing of sensitive folders, audit logging of all user actions and admin changes. HIPAA partial support (Chat, Agents, Search certified; CLI, MCP server, mobile excluded). SSL encryption for external LLM provider connections. GDPR compliant.
lesson_for_parinn: Three concrete lessons: (1) **Session-code separation**: Storing agent conversations separately from code (~/. rovodev/sessions/ vs. Bitbucket) is clean and avoids committing sensitive conversation history. ParleyInn should store session records in a separate, append-only system from the code repository. (2) **Permission inheritance**: Rovo respects existing Bitbucket/Jira/Confluence permissions automatically without duplicating access control. ParleyInn's recall system should inherit agent-team permissions rather than recreating them, making trusted content a question of source permissions, not ParleyInn's own logic. (3) **Zero retention as contract**: Explicit zero-retention agreements with external LLMs (Anthropic, OpenAI) prevent model poisoning. If ParleyInn integrates external models, require contractual zero-retention guarantees rather than relying on promises. (4) **Session forking for branches**: Rovo Dev's /sessions fork feature creates child sessions linked to parents—useful for ParleyInn to track session lineage as agents fork execution (e.g., trying alternate plans). This provides audit trail without merging heterogeneous session histories.

name: Augment Cosmos: Sessions, Files/VFS, Artifacts, Memory
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
A Session is one conversation with an "Expert", which is a reusable agent configuration: instructions, model, capabilities and an environment. The Session owns every message, agent turn and tool call (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/sessions-overview.md, https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/getting-started.md). Prompts can carry attachments: up to 10 files (4 MB combined) and 10 images per message (sessions-overview). The conversation is "saved indefinitely" and never expires. Archiving a Session keeps the full conversation (sessions-overview).

Stored next to each Session are per-session "Artifacts" of four types: Pull request (the URL), Git branch, Linear issue, and Link, which is stored as `CUSTOM` (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/artifacts.md).

Separately, each org has a "Files" virtual filesystem (VFS) with User and Organization scopes. Experts write notes there, such as Markdown files and JSONL logs like `organization/incidents/log.jsonl`. It also holds Skills under `.augment/skills/` and Expert Memory as curated Markdown, plus an optional evidence log for the "noisy memory" model (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/understanding-files.md, https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/experts-memory.md).

Cosmos also stores every inbound trigger event (the events log) and per-Expert run history (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/automations.md). Expert and environment configurations are kept as immutable versions (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cli/cloud.md).

The Environment's workspace (`/workspace`) is not durable. The VM pauses when idle and runs at most 24h at a time. After a long pause it may restart clean and lose uncommitted changes (sessions-overview).
where_stored:
Augment's server/cloud control plane. The web UI, the `auggie cloud` CLI and Slack are all clients of the same API (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cli/cloud.md). Even with self-hosted daemons, where tools run on your own machine, the session is driven from the Cosmos control plane and LLM calls go to Augment. Messages sent while a daemon is offline are queued server-side until it reconnects (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/environments/daemons.md).

The Files VFS is a hosted, versioned store, synced from the VM at turn boundaries (understanding-files). Git is used only as the workspace substrate inside the VM: repos are cloned to `/workspace/{org}/{repo}`, and daemons can give each session its own isolated git worktree (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/environments/cloud.md, https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/environments/daemon-workspaces.md). The docs never say that session history is written to git.

The docs do not disclose the storage backend, data residency or retention controls beyond "indefinitely" (unverifiable).
format_and_model:
The docs give no public wire or storage format for transcripts. The documented model is a hierarchy:
- Org → Space → Expert (versioned config) → Session (messages / turns / tool calls; visibility Shared or Private; viewer ACLs).
- A Session holds an Artifact list (typed: PR / branch / Linear / CUSTOM) and Subscriptions.
- Worker sessions form a tree under a parent session (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/automations.md, https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/workers-subagents.md).

Files VFS:
- Path-addressed objects under `user/` or `organization/`.
- Limits: 1 MB per file, 10,000 files and 100 MB per filesystem.
- Every write creates an immutable version attributed to the writing agent, and deletes are tombstones.
- Old versions are thinned on a time-decayed schedule: all kept for 15 minutes, then at least one per week kept beyond 30 days (understanding-files). So file history is not lossless over time.

Config bundles export as YAML with `metadata.resourceVersion` (cli/cloud). Most list/get CLI commands give JSON output via `--json` (cli/cloud). I could not find a documented command that exports a session transcript (unverifiable).
multi_writer_and_merge:
The docs describe no merging of conversations: each Session is a single conversation. While the agent is working, a user's next message is queued until the current turn ends (sessions-overview). Teammates get viewer access through Share. The secrets page notes that "people who can contribute to one of your shared sessions" can cause it to use your personal secrets, which implies more than one human can write to a shared session (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/config-secrets.md).

Agents coordinate in three ways (workers-subagents):
- **Workers:** separate sessions with their own VMs.
- **Subagents:** helpers inside the same session.
- **Expert-to-Expert:** a shared external surface such as PR comments is the medium.

The docs themselves warn about data races and deadlocks in worker orchestration.

Files VFS: there is no merge. Changes are uploaded at turn end and history is kept as versions with tombstones. An Aug 2026 changelog fix says "outdated clients can no longer recreate deleted files", which suggests last-writer-wins sync with tombstone checks (https://www.augmentcode.com/changelog).

Code: daemon "Isolated Workspace" puts each session on its own git worktree, while "Shared Workspace" can overwrite or conflict (daemon-workspaces). Expert configs use optimistic concurrency through resourceVersion (cli/cloud).
realtime:
Yes, for observers inside the hosted product. You "watch it run and follow every turn" from the web, phone browser or Slack (sessions-overview). The Aug 2026 release notes mention:
- the sidebar refreshing in real time
- streaming file changes
- reliability work on transcripts, queued messages and reconnects
- Cmd+K searching "synchronized local data first", which implies a client-side replica (https://www.augmentcode.com/changelog)

Agents can create runtime subscriptions (`subscribe-event`) so that external events (GitHub, Linear, Slack, cron) are pushed into a live session. These subscriptions end with the session (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/automations.md). Files sync to other sessions only at turn boundaries, not continuously (understanding-files).
search_retrieval:
The Sessions page lists every session you can access; you can pin them and put them in folders (sessions-overview). The Cmd+K palette matches session names and artifact content: PR number or URL, branch name, Linear ID, link label. Results are scoped to the tenant (artifacts.md).

The docs do not document full-text search over transcript contents (unverifiable). Cosmos Advisor "reads the Session data" to diagnose a failed session, so an agent can read past transcripts on request (sessions-overview). For cross-session recall, the design leans on the Files VFS and Memory: Experts load the curated Markdown for their scope at the start of work (experts-memory). The docs show no semantic or vector recall of past sessions. Augment's Context Engine indexes code, not session history, and this is not documented for Cosmos sessions.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, but by reference in the hosted database, not in git. This corrects the discovery note: the Artifacts page does cover PR and branch links.
- **PR artifacts** attach automatically when the Expert opens a PR through its GitHub tool, or when a chat message contains a GitHub PR URL.
- **Branch artifacts** are "recorded automatically from the running VM's git context".
- You can search in reverse ("find the session that opened a specific pull request, branch, or Linear ticket") (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/artifacts.md).

The docs show no commit-SHA-level linking and no git notes or trailers. Nothing is written into the repository to point back at a session (unverifiable / not documented). PR comments serve as a coordination surface between Experts (workers-subagents).
scale:
No numeric scale claims for sessions. The documented limits are:
- **Session attachments:** 10 files at 4 MB combined, and 10 images up to 10 MB each, per message (sessions-overview).
- **Files VFS:** 1 MB per file, 10,000 files and 100 MB per filesystem (understanding-files).
- **Environment variables:** 64 KB (environments/cloud).
- **Environment runtime:** at most 24h at a time (sessions-overview).
- **Daemon container workspace:** up to 64 repos (daemon-workspaces).

Marketing says Cosmos "runs fleets of agents across your SDLC" (https://www.augmentcode.com/product/cosmos).
privacy_security:
Session visibility is Shared (org-wide) or Private. The default is Shared for sessions started by an org-shared Expert or by a trigger, and Private for sessions from a personal Expert. The owner can grant specific viewers and revoke them (sessions-overview). Resources use object-level access controls (OLAC) (environments/cloud).

Secrets are "encrypted on disk and stripped from logs", write-only (they cannot be read back), and injected as environment variables at VM boot (https://docs.augmentcode.com/cosmos/config-secrets.md). Environment variables are warned to appear in internal logs and session output and to be committed into the environment's version history, while "secrets are redacted automatically" (environments/cloud). Revoking a secret does not recall values already delivered to running sessions. The docs warn that collaborators on a shared session can make it use your personal secrets (config-secrets).

The docs describe no redaction of general transcript content: only Secrets-Manager values are stripped. Cloud VMs are egress-only (environments/cloud), and daemons must reach Augment for inference (daemons). Company-level claims, which are not Cosmos-specific: SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 42001, customer-managed encryption keys, and no training on customer code (https://www.augmentcode.com/security). The docs say nothing on how recalled memory or Files content is treated as untrusted. Memory is described as "evolving context, not an unquestionable rule", and the docs tell Experts to flag conflicts (experts-memory). There is no prompt-injection envelope.
lesson_for_parinn:
Cosmos keeps the transcript as its permanent record and treats the VM workspace as disposable. It ties sessions to code with a small typed "artifact" index: PR URL, branch auto-captured from the VM's git context, ticket ID, and link. That index is searchable both ways, from session to PR and from PR to session, without writing anything into git.

ParleyInn can copy this as derived, rebuildable projection rows (I10). A hook would capture repo, branch and HEAD from the local git context at each turn, and find PR or ticket URLs in tool output. ParleyInn would store these as typed references in the append-only record and offer the reverse lookup, "which sessions touched branch X / PR Y?".

ParleyInn should avoid two Cosmos choices:
- Shared files there are mutable, last-writer-wins and time-decay pruned, so they are not lossless. Shared notes and memory should be versioned events in ParleyInn's hash chain.
- Cosmos redacts only declared secrets and puts memory into context automatically. ParleyInn should keep recall pull-only and enveloped (I2), and redact before storing, not only in logs.
license: Proprietary hosted SaaS (closed source). The Auggie CLI and daemon are Augment's own client software. The docs reviewed do not state its license.

name: Autobase (holepunchto/autobase)
status: shipped
license: Apache-2.0 (package.json and the repo README: https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/package.json)
what_is_stored:
Autobase is a generic multi-writer event log. It stores whatever opaque byte or encoded values the application appends. Nothing is specific to agents, sessions or code. Each writer appends nodes to its own local core. A node is {heads: clock, batch, value}, where the clock is an array of (writerKey, length) checkouts naming the other writers' nodes it has seen (build.js 'node' and 'clock'/'checkout' schemas). Indexers also write checkpoints in their oplog messages: a 64-byte signature plus the signed length, for the system, encryption and user views (build.js 'index-checkpoint'/'checkpointer'). Null 'ack' nodes carry only causal references (README, base.ack()). Autobase also keeps three kinds of derived state:
- A '_system' core, a Hyperbee holding membership. It records members with isIndexer, isRemoved and length, plus indexers, pendingIndexers, heads, views, encryptionLength and entropy (lib/system.js; build.js 'info-v2' and 'member').
- An '_encryption' view.
- One or more application views built by a deterministic apply() reducer, most often a Hyperbee (README "Views").
Large payloads are meant to live outside the base, with only a pointer appended ('external pointer pattern', for example hyperblobs).
Sources: https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/build.js, https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/lib/system.js, https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/tree/main/examples/external-pointer-pattern
where_stored: A local DB on each peer, replicated peer to peer. Every writer core, the system core and every view is a Hypercore held in a Corestore. Corestore 7 and Hypercore 11 persist through hypercore-storage, which is built on RocksDB and supports cross-core atomic batches (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore-storage; Autobase depends on hypercore ^11.27.12 per https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/package.json). Per-peer secrets such as the encryption key and the local-writer-to-bootstrap link sit in Hypercore 'User Data', a local key-value store that is never replicated (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore README "User Data"). Cores replicate over Corestore replication streams, usually found through Hyperswarm topics keyed by base.discoveryKey (README base.replicate). Optional always-on 'blind peers' mirror the cores of an autobase through blind-peering's addAutobase() (https://github.com/holepunchto/blind-peering). Git and any central server are not involved.
format_and_model:
Each core is a Hypercore: an append-only log with a BLAKE2b Merkle tree whose roots are signed with Ed25519. Its manifest sets the signers and can 'link' other cores, as the system core links the encryption view (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore README manifest section).

Blocks are binary compact-encoding/hyperschema records. The current OplogMessage v2 is {node, checkpoint?, digest?, optimistic?, trace?}, and versions 0 and 1 remain decodable as legacy (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/build.js). MESSAGE.md is an older proposal and differs in detail: it names a 'clock'/'abi' field where the code has 'heads'/'batch' (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/MESSAGE.md).

The model is event sourcing over a causal DAG:
- Writers' nodes reference earlier nodes.
- A deterministic linearizer orders the DAG. A node never comes before anything it references, and concurrent branches are tie-broken by key comparison.
- The application's open()/apply() handlers fold the linearized nodes into views.
(https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/DESIGN.md)

View cores are signed jointly by the indexer set, as a multi-signer manifest with quorum = min(n, floor(n/2)+1) (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/lib/store.js, around line 573). base.hash() returns the system core's Merkle root hash (README). Implementation is JavaScript only, for Node and Bare. No Go implementation could be found or verified.
multi_writer_and_merge:
This is the core feature. Each writer owns a single-writer Hypercore, so no two parties ever write to the same log. Merging happens by deterministic linearization of the causal DAG (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/DESIGN.md).

- **Ordering is eventually consistent.** New causal information can reorder nodes already seen. Autobase then undoes the view changes and reapplies them, so apply() must be fully deterministic and may mutate only the view (README "Reordering"/"Views").
- **Finality comes from quorums of indexers.** A node is a quorum once a majority of indexers reference it, and the degree rises as majorities see majorities. Order is final up to a node once its quorum is two degrees above any competing quorum (DESIGN.md "Quorums", "Caveat").
- **That final point is published as signedLength.** Indexers sign checkpoints, and the system core's signedLength 'will not change'. This lets lagging peers fast-forward to a quorum-signed state (README signedLength, fastForward, the 'fast-forward' event; lib/apply-state.js maybeSigned()).
- **There are three writer roles** (DESIGN.md "Writer Roles"):
  - indexers, whose references count toward quorums;
  - non-indexing writers, whose entries are ordered but who cast no votes, e.g. a server as indexer with clients;
  - relayed writers, whose entries enter only when referenced.
- **Membership is itself an event inside apply().** host.addWriter(key, {indexer}), host.removeWriter(key) (the last indexer cannot be removed) and host.ackWriter(key). With 'optimistic' mode, non-members can append blocks, which apply() must verify before acking them (README AutobaseHostCalls and optimistic).
- **Convergence needs extra traffic.** Indexers append null 'ack' nodes to merge forks. The default ackInterval is 10 s and the ack threshold is 4 (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/index.js lines 43-44). A writer can be rotated with setLocal().
- **Known rough edges:** issue #359 (open) reports signedLength stuck at 0 in a single-writer, multi-indexer topology until extra null appends are made (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/issues/359). A test comment notes an edge case when many writers are added concurrently (test/apply.js line 373 in the repo).
realtime: Yes, live sparse replication. Hypercore verifies the signed Merkle tree in real time, and peers fetch only the blocks they need (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore README). Autobase emits 'update' after each apply() run, and base.update() pulls in available remote data (README). A wakeup protocol (protomux-wakeup) hints which writers are active (README 'wakeup' option). Peers find each other through Hyperswarm, which does DHT discovery and hole punching (README replicate example). Blind peers keep the data available while writers are offline (https://github.com/holepunchto/blind-peering). The view can change under the reader until signedLength catches up.
search_retrieval: Autobase has no search of its own. Retrieval goes through whatever view the app builds, usually Hyperbee. Hyperbee offers point get, sorted range streams (gt/gte/lt/lte), history and diff streams, and watch(). It has no full-text or semantic search (https://github.com/holepunchto/hyperbee). Raw nodes can be read by index from each writer core, and base.heads() exposes the current DAG heads (README). Full-text search would have to be another deterministic view or an index outside Autobase.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. Autobase is a general data structure with no notion of agent sessions, prompts, commits or files (README). Any link to git commits or worktrees would sit in the application's value schema.
scale:
Neither the README nor DESIGN.md nor the Pear docs make any scale claim; the docs say 'specific scaling characteristics aren't detailed' (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/autobase). Hints from the code and issues:
- The project recommends side-loading large data with pointers because writer data copied into views 'can slow down indexers' (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/tree/main/examples/external-pointer-pattern).
- 'bigBatches' trades responsiveness for throughput (README).
- Each new indexer adds a signer to every view manifest, and finality needs a majority of indexers to keep writing (DESIGN.md; lib/store.js).
- Open issues show operational fragility. In #374, an undecodable block in a writer core froze the writer silently and caused a 99% CPU busy-loop for 40 minutes in production (https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/issues/374). #359 covers delayed signedLength convergence.
I could not verify the number of writers per base in real deployments. The project is maintained: v7.28.2 was committed on 2026-09-08, per git log of the cloned repo and https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/autobase, which documents v7.28.2 as 'stable'.
privacy_security:
Integrity and authenticity: every writer core is Ed25519-signed with a BLAKE2b Merkle tree, and views are multi-signed by an indexer quorum (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore; https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/lib/store.js).

Confidentiality is optional (encryptionKey / encrypt / encrypted options in the README):
- The whole base uses one symmetric key shared by all members.
- Each block is encrypted with libsodium crypto_stream_xor (XSalsa20). The nonce comes from the block index, a key id and an 8-byte keyed BLAKE2b hash of the block.
- The block itself carries no per-block MAC; integrity rests on the Hypercore Merkle signatures over the stored bytes.
- Keys rotate through the '_encryption' view, which stores entropy and key ids.
(https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase/blob/main/lib/encryption.js)

Key storage: since January 2026 a 'blindEncryption' hook can encrypt the key at rest in local User Data (git log of the cloned repo: commits 1c7f8ae 'Allow encryption keys to be encrypted' and 7d868ac 'Rotate blind encryption'; lib/boot.js). Blind peers mirror the ciphertext (https://github.com/holepunchto/blind-peering).

Gaps:
- No per-reader access control. Anyone holding the key reads everything.
- No redaction or secret scanning.
- History is append-only. core.clear() only drops local copies and tells peers, and truncate() forks a single-writer core (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore README clear/truncate).
- Removed writers keep their history.

Untrusted-input caveat: optimistic blocks from non-members must be validated in apply(), 'otherwise any peer ... could attempt to inject values' (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/autobase). Replication needs network access (Hyperswarm), so it conflicts with an in-process, no-network core like ParleyInn's (I4).
lesson_for_parinn:
Take the shape, not the stack. Keep one single-writer, signed, hash-chained log per agent or sandbox as the only source of truth. Each entry carries a clock of (writerKey, length) for the other logs it has seen. The shared record is then a deterministic, rebuildable projection: a linearizer that reads no clock or randomness, which is exactly I10. It is not a jointly written log, so git-style merge conflicts never arise.

Two cautions from Autobase. First, its merged order can still reorder until a quorum-signed checkpoint. So ParleyInn should treat only checkpointed or signed prefixes as stable for anything that feeds restore blocks. Recall over the unfinalized tail should be labeled as provisional.

Second, issue #374 shows how this design fails silently. A writer with an undecodable block froze with no event and spun the CPU. ParleyInn's linearizer must audit and count decode or verify failures per writer, and fail open for the agent without wedging it (I6, I9).

The external-pointer pattern also carries over: keep large payloads out of the merged log and reference them by hash.

name: Automerge (core CRDT library) and automerge-repo (sync and storage layer)
status: shipped. Core Automerge 3 is stable: npm @automerge/automerge 3.5.0 was published 2026-09-16, and the Rust crate is at 0.12.0 (updated 2026-09-16, per the npm registry and crates.io API). automerge-repo is shipped but its current line is alpha: npm 'latest' is 2.6.0-alpha.3 and 'next' is 2.6.0-alpha.5 (2026-09-16). The sync server is at 0.3.0 (2026-09-30). Keyhive (E2EE and access control) and Subduction (the new sync protocol) are alpha or preview. The Go binding automerge-go is effectively stale: its only module version is a pseudo-version dated 2024-10-30, with no tags.
what_is_stored:
Automerge stores JSON-like documents: maps, lists, collaborative text and counters. It also keeps the document's full, never-discarded edit history as operations grouped into "changes" (commits). Each change records:
- its dependencies (the hashes of the changes it builds on)
- an actor ID
- a per-actor sequence number (1 for the actor's first change, then +1 each time)
- a start op counter
- a timestamp
- an optional commit message
- the operation columns (https://automerge.org/automerge-binary-format-spec/)

Changes are fine-grained: there is often one operation, or one commit, per keystroke (https://github.com/automerge/beelay/blob/main/docs/sedimentree.md). Losing values from concurrent writes are kept as conflicts, not dropped (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/documents/conflicts/).
where_stored:
Core Automerge is an in-memory library that saves to bytes. Where the bytes go is up to the application.

automerge-repo writes them through pluggable StorageAdapters, for example NodeFS on the filesystem or IndexedDB in the browser (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/). Storage keys take the form [documentId, 'snapshot'|'incremental', id] (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/under-the-hood/storage/).

The reference sync server persists documents to a filesystem directory set by DATA_DIR (https://github.com/automerge/automerge-repo-sync-server). Subduction's server recently moved from a filesystem backend to the redb embedded database (https://automerge.org/blog/2026-july/).

This is not git: it is a local DB or files plus an optional relay server.
format_and_model:
There are two binary chunk types:
- **Document chunk (0x00):** the whole change graph, compressed. It stores the heads (the terminal change hashes) in sorted order.
- **Change chunk (0x01):** one change.

Encoding details (https://automerge.org/automerge-binary-format-spec/):
- Change hash: "the 32-byte SHA-256 hash of the concatenation of the chunk type, chunk length and chunk contents".
- Checksum: the first 4 bytes of the same SHA-256.
- Operation data is columnar (all columns hold the same number of items), compressed with RLE and DEFLATE.

History is therefore a content-addressed hash DAG, Merkle-like and similar to git's commit graph (https://github.com/automerge/beelay/blob/main/docs/sedimentree.md).

automerge-repo stores two kinds of chunk:
- incremental chunks, keyed by change hash
- compacted snapshots, keyed by the document heads at the time of compaction

Because the heads uniquely identify the set of changes, two processes that write the same key write identical content (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/under-the-hood/storage/).

Automerge 3 kept the Automerge 2 file format (https://automerge.org/blog/automerge-3/). A new columnar engine, Hexane v1, reports 2 to 9 times faster operation (https://automerge.org/blog/2026-july/).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Automerge is designed for many writers. Every actor appends changes offline, and merges are deterministic and need no coordination.

Conflict rules:
- Concurrent writes to the same map key are resolved by a deterministic winner based on the operation ID (counter plus actorId), not wall-clock time. The losers stay retrievable through getConflicts (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/documents/conflicts/).
- Concurrent list and text inserts interleave in a consistent order on every node.

Sync between peers is a two-party protocol: exchange heads, summarize "have" sets with Bloom filters, then send the missing changes. False positives can cost extra rounds, and the protocol needs the whole commit graph in memory (https://github.com/automerge/beelay/blob/main/docs/sedimentree.md). Its basis is Kleppmann and Howard's Byzantine Eventual Consistency work (https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00472, cited from https://automerge.org/automerge/automerge/sync/index.html).

The storage layer tolerates several processes on one storage directory: on compaction, a process deletes only the incremental chunks it loaded itself (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/under-the-hood/storage/).
realtime:
Yes. automerge-repo pushes changes live over NetworkAdapters such as WebSocket, and DocHandles emit change events from remote peers (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/). The project supports peer-to-peer, client-server and file-based sync topologies (https://automerge.org/).

Subduction, the successor sync system, adds:
- WebSocket, HTTP long-poll and Iroh/QUIC transports
- incremental, sharded sync through Sedimentree

Its README says it is an "early release preview ... DO NOT use for production" (https://github.com/inkandswitch/subduction). Its stated performance target is Patchwork loading "low thousands" of documents (https://www.inkandswitch.com/newsletter/dispatch-014/, found via search, not fetched).
search_retrieval:
There is no built-in full-text or semantic search. Retrieval is by document ID or AutomergeUrl through the Repo (https://automerge.org/docs/reference/repositories/).

Inside a document, changes can be enumerated, current heads read, and individual changes examined. The Go binding exposes Changes(), Heads(), Fork(), and Change.Hash(), Message() and Timestamp() (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/automerge/automerge-go). The homepage advertises "complete version history" (https://automerge.org/).

Any index, such as BM25, has to be built by the application outside Automerge.
links_sessions_to_code:
Not applicable. Automerge is a general data-sync library. It has no concept of agent sessions, prompts, commits or source files.

The closest feature is per-change metadata: actor ID, timestamp and free-text message (https://automerge.org/automerge-binary-format-spec/). Work on author provenance is in progress under Keyhive (https://automerge.org/blog/2026-july/), and there is an npm 'authors' dist-tag, 2.7.0-authors.1 (npm registry).
scale:
Claims from the project:
- The homepage claims "compact storage supporting millions of changes" (https://automerge.org/).
- Automerge 3 cut memory use by more than 10 times. Moby Dick pasted as text went from 700 MB to 1.3 MB, and one document that "hadn't loaded after 17 hours" now loads in 9 seconds (https://automerge.org/blog/automerge-3/).
- The design doc admits that the current sync server is memory-intensive and that its performance is unpredictable over ciphertext (https://github.com/automerge/beelay/blob/main/docs/sedimentree.md).

History grows without bound. Truncating or deleting history has been requested repeatedly (issues #348 and #799, both closed; #588, "File format v3", open), and none of the pages read showed a supported way to do it (https://github.com/automerge/automerge/issues/348, https://github.com/automerge/automerge/issues/799). I could not verify an official maintainer position from those pages.
privacy_security:
Defaults are weak:
- The reference sync server is described as "unsecured" with no authentication (https://github.com/automerge/automerge-repo-sync-server).
- Plain automerge-repo servers see plaintext. The design doc notes that the server builds compressed documents from plaintext (https://github.com/automerge/beelay/blob/main/docs/sedimentree.md).

Keyhive/ARK (@automerge/automerge-repo-keyhive, alpha, "details will change") adds:
- end-to-end encryption
- Ed25519 identities
- relay, read, edit and admin access levels, plus groups
- revocation with key rotation

Sync servers get "relay" access and move ciphertext without decrypting it (https://automerge.org/docs/keyhive/ark-api-guide/). The BeeKEM group-key paper is a preprint (https://automerge.org/blog/2026-july/).

Redaction: there is no in-place redaction or secret scrubbing of history. The append-only hash DAG means a leaked secret persists in every replica (see the history-truncation issues above). An anonymizer tool was added in mid-2026, but it strips content only for producing debugging and performance repros, not for redacting live history (https://automerge.org/blog/2026-july/).

Integrity: SHA-256 change hashes and 4-byte checksums detect corruption, but changes are not signed in the core format (https://automerge.org/automerge-binary-format-spec/). Licenses are MIT (core, repo) and MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Subduction), per the npm registry.
lesson_for_parinn:
Automerge shows two things for ParleyInn.

What to copy: a content-addressed, per-writer hash DAG merges many offline writers without coordination. Each writer has its own actor ID and sequence chain, and each change lists its parent hashes. Storage keyed by content hash, with snapshots keyed by heads, makes concurrent writers and compaction safe without locks. ParleyInn can copy this for per-agent, per-worktree chains of its own record in Go, with no CRDT dependency. An append-only event log needs no CRDT merge semantics, only DAG union.

What to avoid:
- Automerge keeps history forever with no in-place redaction. ParleyInn must design a redact-before-append step, or a tombstone and re-key mechanism, before history replicates. Once a secret enters a replicated hash DAG it cannot be recalled.
- Encryption and auth bolted on later (Keyhive, Sedimentree) forced a sync-protocol redesign because relays could no longer see plaintext. ParleyInn should make transport ciphertext-only and relay-blind from day one.

Adopting Automerge directly would be a poor fit:
- The only Go path is a cgo wrapper last updated in October 2024.
- The new sync stack is network-bearing Rust that is explicitly not production-ready.
- That conflicts with I4 (no network) and with ParleyInn's dependency budget.
license: MIT for core Automerge, automerge-repo, automerge-go and the sync server. MIT OR Apache-2.0 for Subduction (npm registry license fields; https://github.com/inkandswitch/subduction).

name: AVCS (Agentic Version Control System), izagood/avcs, npm @izagood/avcs
category: Agent-native VCS that is deliberately not git-compatible, with a git bridge. Self-described as a research prototype, though it is far more built-out than the discovery note implies.
status: beta. Actively developed: the README badge says 'experimental' and the README says 'research prototype'. The last commit was 2026-10-01 (16d0ce8). npm @izagood/avcs runs 0.1.0 (2026-06-15) to 0.51.0 (2026-09-08), with an 'Unreleased' breaking merge change in RELEASES.md. Not archived. I could not get the star count: the GitHub API and HTML were blocked from this sandbox, so the 'about 1 star' figure is unverified.
what_is_stored:
Content-addressed, append-only objects. First-class objects: intent (goal, NL constraints, enforced constraintKinds, successCriteria, allowedScopes), session, operation, evidence, decision, checkpoint, view, policy, blob. Governance objects: lease, release, line, membership, protection, promotion, redaction, undo, override, approval, integration.
- Session = {intentOid, actor{kind human|ai_agent|ci_bot, id, model?, name?, email?}, baseViewOid, summary, openedEntities[], toolCalls[], startedAt}. Source comment: "Distilled, redaction-safe context. Raw transcripts live out of band."
- Operation = {sessionOid, intentOid, actor, target{entityKind, entityId}, body{put_file|edit_file|delete_file|rename_file|note, path, blobOid, baseBlobOid}, causalDeps[], declaredPurpose, effects{reads, changesBehavior, breaksPublicApi}, lamport, createdAt, confidence?, line?, workspace?}.
- Evidence = test/typecheck/lint/scan results bound to a treeHash, with a fromUntrustedRunner flag.
- Decision = signed conflict resolution plus rationale.
Raw prompts and transcripts are NOT stored. The docs mention a separate short-lived encrypted transcript store, but I found no implementation of it in src/.
where_stored:
A local store in <repo>/.avcs/: objects/<aa>/<oid> (sharded), refs/<name>, HEAD, config.json, an append-only 'oplog' (operations) and 'objlog' (all oids in arrival order), indexes/entity, packs, and a compaction snapshot. A git worktree gets a '.avcs' pointer file ('avcsdir: <path>'), like .git's gitdir file.
Transport:
- An optional HTTP hub (avcs serve / startHub, or the separate avcs-server). The core protocol is GET /have, GET /objects/:oid and POST /objects.
- Git, in two bridge modes. 'sidecar': .avcs is fully git-ignored. 'committed': objects/refs/HEAD/config are tracked in git, caches are ignored, and git union-merges the immutable object files. A post-merge hook runs 'avcs reindex' to rebuild the git-ignored oplog.
Signing keys live in the machine keystore ~/.avcs/private (0600).
format_and_model:
An object's id is `${type}_${first 32 hex of sha256(type + ' ' + canonicalJSON(payload minus oid/sig))}`. That is a 128-bit truncated SHA-256 with a type prefix. The id is not the full digest, which corrects the discovery note.
Bytes on disk are now canonical CBOR. Legacy canonical-JSON objects are still read (sniffed by first byte). The oid stays JSON-derived, so it does not depend on the storage format. Golden vectors are in spec/canonical-vectors.json, with a language-neutral canonicalization spec in docs/24.
Signatures are ed25519 over the oid and excluded from the hash. Large blobs are chunked into a manifest of chunk oids, with dedup.
The data model is a causal operation DAG (causalDeps + Lamport). The code tree is a projection: state = reduce(base, opDAG, decisions, policy, materializer). The projection is deterministic, and its treeHash is stamped with MATERIALIZER_VERSION/MERGE3_VERSION. Views replace branches, checkpoints replace commits, releases replace tags.
multi_writer_and_merge:
This is the core of the design. Many writers append ops concurrently, and replicas converge by object gossip (the set of oids is a grow-only set). The merge is a pure reduction, not text selection, and contention is graded:
- L0/L1: different entities, or disjoint line regions → auto-merge, via a language-neutral N-way line 3-way merge.
- L2: overlapping regions → automatic decision weighted by policy and trust, itself recorded.
- L3: a behavior change without trusted, non-author evidence → blocked.
- L4: a public-API break → a human decision routed to the owners.
The reducer never falls back to last-write-wins. Identical-effect heads count as agreement (#176).
Phase 14 added a server-side integration queue: a stale submission is re-reduced for the submitter. The verdict is always one of advanced, conflict (a repair packet), needs_evidence or queued, never 'pull first'. Ref advance on the hub uses finalize CAS, which rejects non-fast-forward.
Lines handle long-lived divergence, and workspaces are converging scopes mapped from git topic branches. Leases and contention checks are scoped by intent.
realtime:
Near-real-time. Phase 15 added GET /events?since=<objlogCursor>&timeoutMs=30000. It is a long-poll, not SSE, chosen for zero dependencies and proxy friendliness. Any successful mutation wakes waiters; waiters are capped at 256 by default (503 above that). It shares its cursor with GET /sync?since=N.
'avcs sync --watch' is a single-instance daemon with contention early warning when another actor's concurrent op or a lease touches your keys. MCP resources notify subscribed clients when the head moves.
search_retrieval:
Structured retrieval only. I found no full-text or semantic search. What exists:
- The entity index (keyed by 'file:<path>').
- blame and blame.lines (who and why), history/log, diff, and a deterministic bisect.
- materializeAt (time travel), object.show with line and byte limits.
- decision.recall by conflict key, plus 'learned policies'.
- avcs.context.build, a ContextPack: risks > decisions > policies > symbols > evidence > history > suggestedOps under a byte budget (default 8 KiB). Truncation is deterministic and recorded in budget.truncated. It holds no file content, only provenance and blob oids.
The MCP server exposes 39 tools; '--profile core' exposes 13 (≈3.5k vs ≈8.8k tokens, per the README).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, structurally and strongly. Every operation carries sessionOid and intentOid. A session points to its intent, actor and model id. Evidence binds to operations and a treeHash. Decisions bind to contending ops. Blame therefore answers who, with what intent, on what evidence. However, it links a distilled session summary and tool-call list, not prompts or transcripts. Agents write code only through avcs.operation.propose (MCP), so capture is explicit and agent-cooperative, not passive hook capture of Claude Code transcripts. 'avcs commit' and the git importer write operations for human or legacy changes.
scale: No numeric scale claims for repo size or number of agents. Scale features exist: an entity index, incremental reduce (on by default, with clean groups reused), packs/compaction, chunked large blobs with dedup, and an objlog cursor for incremental sync. Benchmarks live in bench/ (incremental and materialize), but the README publishes no results from them. The only headline numbers are token costs: landing after another PR on a 30 KB file costs 18,922 tokens with git vs 279 with AVCS, and the saving across the file sizes measured is 37–99%. Those numbers come from the separate avcs-demo harness. The README cites an 827-test contract suite.
privacy_security:
- Transcripts are kept out of the repo on purpose. docs/06 criticizes Entire for storing transcripts on a git branch that becomes public with a public repo, with only best-effort redaction. The planned 'separate encrypted store, short retention, no push by default' for raw transcripts is design-only: I found no encryption code in src/.
- The 'redaction' object is admin-signed and hub-authoritative. It evicts a blob's bytes on every replica and leaves a hash-preserving stub {blobOid, sha256, length, reason, by}, so oids, treeHash and causalDeps stay valid. A planned requireRedactionAck is meant to stop stale bytes surviving on replicas.
- Local 'undo --purge' handles a secret that was never shared, including a careful git-side rewrite where that is safe. It refuses once ops have been pushed.
- Evidence and decisions are signed with ed25519, and an author cannot vouch for its own op. Evidence from untrusted runners is excluded from the gate. Contributions from outsiders go to a quarantine tier until promoted.
- Hub requests are authenticated with an 'AVCS-Sig' ed25519 signature over method, path and body. A read-only bearer token (AVCS_HUB_TOKEN) is accepted for CI clones and cannot write. TLS/mTLS is left to a reverse proxy.
- The README claims zero runtime dependencies; the MCP SDK is an optionalDependency.
- I found no at-rest encryption. Recalled content is not treated as untrusted model input; no injection envelope was found.
lesson_for_parinn:
Its 'committed' git-bridge mode is a working proof of the git-as-transport pattern ParleyInn is weighing:
- Keep immutable, content-addressed object files in git, sharded by hash prefix.
- git union-merges them with no conflicts, because filenames never collide.
- Keep every derived index (the oplog/objlog arrival logs, the entity index, packs) git-ignored and rebuild it after a post-merge hook ('avcs reindex').
- Make worktrees share one store through a pointer file ('avcsdir:'), not per-worktree copies.
For real-time it uses a cheap HTTP long-poll keyed on an append-only arrival cursor, not git.

ParleyInn should borrow two more things:
- The hash-preserving redaction tombstone: evict the bytes, keep {oid, sha256, length, reason, by}, so the chain and references stay valid. This fits an append-only, hash-chained record better than history rewriting.
- The rule against storing raw transcripts in shared history.

ParleyInn should avoid three things:
- Truncating ids to 128 bits.
- Leaving transcript encryption as design-only.
- Relying on agents to cooperate through MCP to capture history. ParleyInn's hook-based capture keeps I6/I9 without depending on agent behaviour.

name: Backlog.md (MrLesk/Backlog.md)
category: kanban / task tracker for agents (Markdown-in-repo, git-as-transport)
status: shipped
license: MIT (LICENSE and package.json "license": "MIT"; https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/LICENSE)
what_is_stored: Work items, not agent sessions. Each task is one Markdown file holding the spec and the record of the work: title, status, assignees, labels, priority, milestone, dependencies, due date, ordinal, references, documentation links, and modifiedFiles (project-relative paths). The body holds a Description, Acceptance Criteria and Definition of Done checklists, an Implementation Plan, Implementation Notes, a Final Summary, and comments with an author and date. Agents write the plan, notes and summary into the task (README "three review checkpoints"; Task type in src/types/index.ts). The same folder also holds drafts, completed and archived tasks, docs, decisions, milestones and config.yml. Nothing records prompts, transcripts or tool calls. A per-task `onStatusChange` shell command can also live in the frontmatter (ADVANCED-CONFIG.md). Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/README.md , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/types/index.ts , example task https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/tree/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/backlog/tasks
where_stored: Working-tree files, committed with the code. The folder is project-local: backlog/, .backlog/, or a custom project-relative path set by backlog_directory in backlog.config.yml (README, ADVANCED-CONFIG.md). Git is optional: `backlog init --no-git` makes a filesystem-only project. Lifecycle is the directory a file sits in: tasks/, drafts/, completed/, archive/tasks/ (STATE_DIRECTORIES in src/core/task-loader.ts). Other branches and origin/* remote-tracking refs are read in place through git plumbing (ls-tree, log, show), with no checkout. Locks live in the shared git common dir at .git/backlog.md/locks, or at <backlog>/.locks without git (src/file-system/operations.ts getCreateLockTarget). There is no server or database. Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/ADVANCED-CONFIG.md , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/core/task-loader.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/file-system/operations.ts
format_and_model:
One file per task, named `<prefix>-<n> - <Title>.md` (e.g. `back-706 - Remove-redundant-tests....md`). YAML frontmatter holds id, title, status, assignee[], created_date, updated_date, labels[], dependencies[], type, ordinal, priority, milestone, references[], modifiedFiles[], and optionally onStatusChange. Dates are stored in UTC as 'yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm'. The Markdown body is split into machine-parsed sections by HTML-comment sentinels such as `<!-- SECTION:DESCRIPTION:BEGIN -->`, `<!-- AC:BEGIN -->`, `<!-- DOD:BEGIN -->`, `<!-- SECTION:PLAN:BEGIN -->` and `<!-- SECTION:NOTES:BEGIN -->`, with numbered `- [x] #1` checklist items. Records are mutable: every edit rewrites the file in place, and git history is the only history. There is no event log, hash chain or tombstone.

Task IDs are human-readable sequential integers with a configurable prefix. The manifesto rules out random IDs: "collision prevention must not replace them with opaque random identifiers." Status columns come from config; the defaults are To Do / In Progress / Done. The CLI emits stable, versioned JSON with `--json`.

Sources: sample task https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/tree/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/backlog/tasks , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/MANIFESTO.md (Design Principles item 7), https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/ADVANCED-CONFIG.md (Date/Time notes), https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/CLI-INSTRUCTIONS.md
multi_writer_and_merge:
It works on three levels.

(1) Same machine, many worktrees. Task creation takes a lockfile (proper-lockfile, with stale-lock recovery) in the git common dir, which every worktree shares. Each task's read-modify-write takes its own lock, which fails fast on contention instead of merging (src/file-system/operations.ts withCreateLock and the per-task lock). ID allocation also globs other worktrees' uncommitted tasks/ and completed/ files, because "same-repository worktrees share the task ID namespace" (src/core/backlog.ts getActiveAndCompletedTaskIds, around line 1607).

(2) Across branches and clones, this is a read-time view merge, not a write merge. With checkActiveBranches=true (the default), it lists refs/heads and refs/remotes/origin tips whose commits fall within activeBranchDays (default 30). It pins each tip to a commit SHA, builds an index with `git ls-tree` plus one `git log --name-only` pass that gives each file its last committer time, and hydrates only the winning files with `git show`. That runs at concurrency 4 for branches and 8 for files, with caches keyed by commit (src/core/task-loader.ts BranchTaskLoader; src/git/operations.ts getBranchLastModifiedMap and listRecentBranchTips). For each ID it shows exactly one whole record: the working copy wins; otherwise the default taskResolutionStrategy 'most_progressed' takes the highest index in the status list, then the latest committer timestamp, then a lexical tiebreak. Lifecycle (active, completed, archived) goes to the newest commit time, then a state rank (src/core/task-identity-index.ts selectTaskRecord and selectLifecycleRecord). Fields are never merged. Tasks from other branches are read-only: "Task X exists in branch Y and cannot be moved from the current branch. Switch to that branch to modify it." (src/core/backlog.ts crossBranchMoveReason).

(3) Real git merges of task files are ordinary line merges of Markdown. The repo has no custom merge driver, and the README's guidance is to avoid conflicts by keeping "one task per agent session, one PR per task." Sequential IDs can still collide across clones. Before allocating an ID it forces a fresh `git fetch origin --prune`; reads reuse a fetch for up to 60 s. The code says why: "an ID that looks free only because remote refs are up to a minute old is an ID another clone has already published" (src/core/backlog.ts around lines 162 and 719-775). That still cannot stop two unpushed clones from picking the same ID. Duplicates are repaired afterwards with `backlog doctor --fix`, which renames files atomically, rewrites the frontmatter IDs, and leaves ambiguous references for a human to review. Reads fail closed on ambiguous IDs.

Committing: autoCommit is off by default. When it is on, it commits only the selected paths, using a temporary index, `commit-tree` and `update-ref`. Hooks run unless bypassGitHooks is set, and commits are signed if commit.gpgSign is set (src/git/operations.ts commitFiles).

Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/core/task-identity-index.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/core/backlog.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/git/operations.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/CLI-INSTRUCTIONS.md (doctor)
realtime: Real time is local only. `backlog browser` serves a web UI on 127.0.0.1 (default port 6420). It pushes updates to open views over a WebSocket, driven by fs.watch watchers on tasks/, completed/, decisions/ and the config (src/server/index.ts; src/core/content-store.ts). `backlog task list --json --watch` (v1.52.0) prints a full replacement JSON list on each change. It uses fs watchers plus an interval stat-signature check (src/commands/watch-json.ts). Nothing pushes changes between machines: other agents' work appears only after they push and this clone fetches. On reads the fetch is opportunistic, at most once per 60 s, and it can be turned off with remoteOperations=false. Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/server/index.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/commands/watch-json.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/releases
search_retrieval: Fuzzy search runs in memory with Fuse.js over tasks, docs and decisions (src/core/search-service.ts). Filters cover status, priority, project and a reverse lookup by modified file (`backlog search --modified-file src/path.ts`). Output can be `--plain` for agents or `--json`, and v1.53.0 added paging with `--max-count`/`--skip`. There is no persistent index, BM25 or embeddings. Agents get workflow guidance from `backlog instructions overview`, or through optional MCP resources (backlog://workflow/...). The manifesto now calls MCP "a legacy, optional adapter" and makes the CLI canonical. Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/core/search-service.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/CLI-INSTRUCTIONS.md , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/MANIFESTO.md
links_sessions_to_code: Only by convention and co-location. It captures no session, transcript or prompt. The workflow is "one task = one context window = one PR," and the task file is committed in the same branch and PR as the code it describes, so git history ties them together (README). Tasks can record modifiedFiles (searchable in reverse), references, an implementation plan, notes and a final summary written by the agent, and agent-named assignees: the repo's own BACK-706 has assignee '@codex-test-pruning' and notes that point to local /tmp logs. No field stores a commit SHA, PR URL or session ID. The onStatusChange hook can launch an agent, e.g. `claude "Task $TASK_ID ..."` when a task enters In Progress (ADVANCED-CONFIG.md). Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/README.md , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/ADVANCED-CONFIG.md , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/tree/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/backlog/tasks
scale: There is no formal scale claim. The docs only warn that cross-branch checking "may impact performance on large repositories," and suggest lowering activeBranchDays or setting checkActiveBranches=false (ADVANCED-CONFIG.md). The author said on HN that it may be slow with many branches but works in typical cases (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44483530). v1.53.0 (Sept 24) added list paging and CPU fixes (https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/releases). The project uses its own tool: its backlog/ holds about 720 task files (about 94 active, 584 completed, 45 archived, plus drafts), IDs reach BACK-706, and the repo's own config sets active_branch_days 10 (counted from a clone at commit 69e7b15, 2026-09-27; https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/backlog/config.yml). Adoption: about 6.9k stars, 437 forks and 1,391 commits per the GitHub page (https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md); 254 points on HN in July 2025.
privacy_security:
It is local-first: "no server, no account, no telemetry" (README). The web UI binds 127.0.0.1 only (BROWSER_HOST in src/server/index.ts). In src/ (tests excluded) I found no redaction, secret scanning or encryption code, by grepping for secret, redact and encrypt. Tasks are plaintext and spread wherever the repo is pushed. Read-side git calls set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0. The tool shells out to the `git` binary through Bun.spawn, and by default runs `git fetch origin --prune` during ordinary reads (remoteOperations=true), so reading the board can touch the network.

Notable risk: `onStatusChange` runs through `sh -c` with the task's ID, statuses and title in the environment. A per-task value in a task file's frontmatter overrides the global config (src/utils/status-callback.ts; executeStatusChangeCallback in src/core/backlog.ts; ADVANCED-CONFIG.md). Task files arrive through git merges and PRs, so content written by any contributor can carry a command that runs on another user's machine when they change that task's status.
