I found no allow-list or confirmation step, and no public issue or advisory on this; that last point is unverified, because search tools were unavailable. Safety elements that do exist: atomic writes, failing closed on ambiguous identity, and preview-then-confirm for doctor repairs (MANIFESTO.md). Sources: https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/utils/status-callback.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/server/index.ts , https://github.com/MrLesk/Backlog.md/blob/69e7b15362337d6712783d9a685f6e4bb693fa9d/src/git/operations.ts
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy the read side, not the identity or merge model. Backlog.md shows that git can serve as a zero-infrastructure transport. It reads every recent branch and remote-tracking ref without a checkout, pins each tip to a commit SHA, indexes it with ls-tree and log, hydrates only what it needs, and caches by immutable commit. That gives agents in many worktrees and clones a shared view with no server.

Its weak points are the parts ParleyInn must design differently:
(a) Sequential human IDs collide across clones. It needs a forced network fetch before allocation and a `doctor` repair afterwards. ParleyInn records should be keyed by content hash or (session ID, sequence number), so concurrent appends cannot collide and merging is a set union of append-only chains.
(b) Picking a winner by committer timestamp or "most progressed" silently discards the losing version. That is acceptable for a kanban card and wrong for a lossless record (I6, I10).
(c) A synced data file can carry an executable `sh -c` hook. That is exactly the untrusted-content-to-execution path I2 forbids, so no field in a shared ParleyInn record should ever be interpreted as a command or instruction.
(d) It fetches and shells out to git during ordinary reads. Under I4, any git transport for ParleyInn has to live outside the core, in a separate opt-in sync tool or the user's own `git push`/`fetch`. The core would only read files already on disk.

name: Basic Memory (Basic Machines)
category: Markdown knowledge graph MCP server (local-first, optional paid cloud)
status: shipped. The OSS server is active; the README shows v0.23 as a pre-release that needs uv's --prerelease=allow. Basic Memory Cloud is in paid beta at $15/month. I could not get release dates: GitHub API access to this repo was denied in this session.
what_is_stored: Curated knowledge notes, not raw session transcripts. Each note is an "Entity": a Markdown document with YAML frontmatter (title, type, tags, a stable permalink, created/modified timestamps and custom fields). It holds "Observations", which are categorized facts written as `- [category] content #tag (context)`, and "Relations", which are typed wikilinks such as `- implements [[X]]` that may point at notes that do not exist yet. An agent writes these notes on purpose through MCP tools (write_note, edit_note, move_note, delete_note). Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/concepts/knowledge-format.md, https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory
where_stored: Local mode: plain Markdown files in project folders on disk. They are the source of truth. A local SQLite database is a rebuildable secondary index, and Postgres is an option for the index. Cloud mode: the README says it uses Neon Postgres, Tigris S3 object storage and WorkOS AuthKit. File history uses Tigris object versioning: "each save writes a new object version". Git is not built in. In local mode you can track the files with git or Syncthing yourself. Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/reference/technical-information.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/file-history.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/start-here/what-is-basic-memory, https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory
format_and_model: The design is file-first: "all knowledge is represented in standard Markdown files and the database serves as a secondary index". The sync pipeline detects a file change, parses it, upserts the entity, observations and relations into the DB, resolves forward references and refreshes the search index. Notes are addressed by permalink URLs (memory://slug) that survive file moves. A schema system (schema_infer, schema_validate) can infer and check note shapes. There is no append-only log, no hash chain, and no event or turn model: a note is mutable and edited in place. Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/reference/technical-information.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/concepts/knowledge-format.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/concepts/schema-system.md
multi_writer_and_merge: Locally, writers are whoever touches the folder: the MCP agent, an editor, or Obsidian. A file watcher reindexes changes. There is no merge logic beyond last write to the file. Cloud sync to personal workspaces uses rclone with a tenant-scoped remote; team workspaces use a permissioned WebDAV API. pull and push are additive and never delete; `sync` is a one-way mirror in which local is authoritative and missing files are deleted from the cloud. A "conflict guard" aborts when a file differs on both sides. You then pick fail (the default), keep-cloud, keep-local, or keep-both (renames one copy). Merging is at whole-file level, with no line-level or CRDT merge. Inside the cloud app, agents can leave CriticMarkup suggestions and attributed comments for a human to accept or reject instead of rewriting text. The docs do not say how two agents writing the same note at the same moment are resolved. Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/cloud-sync.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/ai-collaboration.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/cloud-guide.md
realtime: Locally, changes are reindexed close to real time by the file watcher. Sync between local and cloud is entirely manual, with no watch mode: the docs' workflow is "pull, edit locally, push when you're done", on the git push/pull model. The cloud web app streams agent edits live into notes, so you can "watch it write, and steer it", and edits show in an Activity view. Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/cloud-sync.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/ai-collaboration.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/reference/technical-information.md
search_retrieval: Hybrid search over observations, relations and content. Full-text search runs on the SQLite or Postgres index. Semantic and vector search use FastEmbed, with optional cross-encoder reranking. build_context walks the relation graph from a memory:// URL to gather connected notes for the model. The tools are pull-based, invoked by the agent through MCP. Sources: https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/reference/technical-information.md
links_sessions_to_code: No. Nothing ties notes to commits, files or code lines, and there is no capture of agent sessions or prompts. Notes are knowledge the agent or user chooses to write. A note could mention code by hand, but the primary docs I read show no hook-based transcript capture. I could not run a search for a Claude Code hooks integration because the session's search budget was used up.
scale: No numeric scale claims in the docs I read. Cloud folder import accepts ZIP uploads up to 100MB. The repo has about 4.1k GitHub stars (from the README page, not verified through the API). Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/cloud-guide.md, https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory
privacy_security: Local-first: "All data remains on your machine", "No Cloud Dependency". The cloud uses WorkOS AuthKit with OAuth, plus API keys, team roles and customer SSO pages. The README describes telemetry as minimal with no content tracking, and BASIC_MEMORY_NO_PROMOS turns off promos. I found no documented redaction or secret scrubbing, no client-side or E2E encryption, and no encryption-at-rest statement. The file-history page says nothing on encryption or retention. Nothing treats recalled notes as untrusted. Stored Markdown flows straight back to the model through read_note and build_context, so a poisoned note is a prompt-injection channel. Sources: https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/reference/technical-information.md, https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/file-history.md, https://docs.basicmemory.com/raw/cloud/api-keys.md
license: AGPL-3.0 (https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory). This is copyleft and not on a typical permissive allow-list, so ParleyInn should borrow ideas, not code.
lesson_for_parinn: Keep the human-readable files as the source of truth and treat the SQLite index as disposable, rebuilt by a watcher. This matches ParleyInn's I10, and it works well for transport: the files can go through git, rclone, Syncthing or S3 versioning without ParleyInn owning a network stack. Basic Memory also shows where that gets weak. Mutable in-place notes leave only whole-file conflict choices (keep-local, keep-cloud, keep-both) and a manual push/pull for multiple writers. Recalled notes go to the model unenveloped. ParleyInn should keep the file-first, rebuildable-index idea but write immutable, content-addressed, per-writer append-only segments, so no file is ever edited by two writers and merging is just a union. It should also keep recall enveloped as untrusted, not copy BM's raw note return. One more idea to borrow: BM's CriticMarkup suggestion flow, where agents propose and a human accepts, is a useful model for letting agents propose pinned constraints without writing them directly.
confidence: medium-high for storage format, index design and sync semantics, which come from the official docs. Medium for the cloud stack: the Neon and WorkOS claims rest only on the README, while Tigris is confirmed in the docs. Low for any session-capture or Claude Code hook features, which I could not search for.

name: Beads (bd)
category: agent memory in Dolt and git
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Issues (beads) with id, title, description, status, priority, issue_type, owner, created_at, created_by, updated_at, started_at, closed_at, closed_reason, dependency counts; ephemeral messages (wisps) with optional lifecycles; task relationships via typed dependency graph (blocks, depends-on, relates-to, duplicates, supersedes, replies-to, parent-child); project memories (durable facts for agent recall); Dolt commit history (every write creates a Dolt commit); comments with threading and mail delegation; labels and custom metadata as JSON objects
where_stored: Primary: Dolt SQL database in .beads/embeddeddolt/ (single-writer, embedded mode) or .beads/dolt/ (multi-writer, server mode). Export: .beads/issues.jsonl (JSONL format for interchange and viewers, NOT source of truth). Configuration: .beads/config.yaml (YAML). Dolt remotes can be git (refs/dolt/data on same origin), DoltHub, S3, GCS, or local file:// URL. Cross-machine sync via bd dolt push/pull against remotes (not git branches, separate refs/dolt/data namespace)
format_and_model: Dolt is a version-controlled SQL database with cell-level diffs. Core tables: issues (primary tracking), wisps (ephemeral subtable), dependencies, comments, labels. Schema versioned with migrations. Hash-based IDs (bd-a1b2) to prevent merge collisions. Hierarchical ID support for epics (bd-a3f8, bd-a3f8.1, bd-a3f8.1.1). Issues export as JSONL array with one record per line. Dolt stores full commit history and branching separate from git
multi_writer_and_merge: Embedded mode (default): single-writer with file-based locking (.beads/embeddeddolt/). Server mode (orchestrator): multiple concurrent writers via external dolt sql-server on localhost:3307 or Unix socket. Dolt native: cell-level 3-way merge, no line-based conflicts. Hash-based IDs prevent merge collision. Dolt branches independent of git branches. Shared server mode available for multi-project setups. Schema version guard prevents version skew (older binary reading newer schema fails with actionable error)
realtime: Not designed for real-time sync. Cross-machine sync explicit via bd dolt push/pull commands (not continuous). Within single workspace: embedded mode auto-commits per command (Dolt commit per write), server mode defaults auto-commit OFF to avoid 'database is read only' under concurrent load. Ephemeral messages (wisps) support optional lifecycle (e.g., message types). No webhooks documented. Federation (peer-to-peer Dolt sync) available but requires explicit bd federation add-peer/sync
search_retrieval: FTS5 full-text search on issue text. bd ready lists claimable tasks (status ready, no open blockers). bd show <id> retrieves single issue with full audit trail. GetReadyWork API detects hierarchical ready state. Search by status, priority, owner, issue_type. CountIssuesByGroup for aggregation. History viewer shows version-control diff per Dolt commit. SearchWispsPlane searches ephemeral only. IterEvents walks event journal for audit
links_sessions_to_code: Agents optionally store session ID in issue close reason (bd close <id> '<reason>'). Commit message convention: include issue ID in parentheses (git commit -m 'Fix auth bug (bd-abc)'). bd doctor detects orphaned issues (open issues mentioned in git history). Agent instructions in AGENTS.md guide bd usage (claim/close/update patterns). NOT a session recorder—Beads is task tracking for agents, not Claude Code session history storage. Sessions reference issues, not vice versa
scale: Designed for multi-agent coordination. Dolt server mode supports concurrent writers (production scale not quantified in docs). FTS5 full-text search handles moderate volumes. Hash IDs prevent collision-based scale limits. Known constraint: molecule-sized graphs (100+ edges) can exceed per-command transaction budgets; optimization available via SkipCycleCheck + whole-graph validation in single transaction. Benchmarks in BENCHMARKS.md (ingest, BM25 p95, expand p95 metrics per driver)
privacy_security: No built-in encryption at rest. Dolt server mode supports password (env var BEADS_DOLT_PASSWORD or credentials file ~/.config/beads/credentials with INI format [host:port] sections). Credentials file has mode 600 warning on Unix. Remotes support private git URLs (ssh, https with credentials). .beads/ directory excluded from git (.gitignore). No documentation of field-level encryption or secrets redaction. Dolt remotes can use S3/GCS with cloud credentials
lesson_for_parinn: Beads chose Dolt for cell-level versioning and native branching (separate from git), but couples tightly to that choice. Initially used SQLite; migration required schema rewrite. ParleyInn lesson: maintain clear storage backend interface (as Beads does with driver pattern) to allow future swaps. Second lesson: Beads' .beads/issues.jsonl export is explicitly NOT source of truth—it allows agent tooling without coupling to Dolt history. ParleyInn should separate durable canonical state (append-only record) from agent-facing interchange format (trusted text, JSONL export)
sources: go.mod and LICENSE file inspection in repository

name: bettermemory (0Mattias)
category: memory MCP server (Markdown files, single user, local first)
status: shipped. It is under very active development. PyPI shows 133 releases from 1.4.1 (2026-05-13) to 8.0.0 (2026-09-24), per https://pypi.org/pypi/bettermemory/json. The main branch had commits up to 2026-09-25, and the changelog's Unreleased section describes an 8.1.0 session-capture feature. Not archived.
what_is_stored: It stores curated, distilled facts ("memories") that a coding agent writes through the memory_write tool. It does not store raw session transcripts. Each memory is a short body plus YAML front matter. The always-present fields are schema_version, a ULID id, created, updated, scopes, confidence and source. Some fields appear only when they have a value: verification attestations (last_verified_at, verified_paths, verified_head commit), origin (repo, branch, worktree), typed links (supersedes, contradicts, extends, depends_on), category such as user-inference, and claims. Claims are structured assertions that the memory makes about the repo, written as `path`, `path::symbol`, `path::NAME=literal` or `!path`. Since 7.10.0, every write also records an actor: client and model are self-declared, and an OAuth principal is attested only on HTTP transports. Three other kinds of data sit beside the memories. Episodes are a per-session journal of run state under episodes/<session_id>/ with a 30-day TTL. Tombstones go to .tombstones/ and keep a removed_reason. An append-only JSONL event log, sharded by session, holds telemetry about writes, searches, verifications, pulls and use. Sources: https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/internals.md and https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/api.md. An unreleased 8.1.0 `bettermemory capture` command turns a Claude Code transcript into memories by running `claude -p`, and keeps the segments in host-local captures/<session>/ (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
where_stored: Working-tree files in a local directory. The location is $BETTERMEMORY_DIR if set, else ./.claude-memory/ if it exists, else ~/.claude-memory/. Next to the files sit a derived SQLite FTS5 index and some host-local sidecars (.quarantine.json, the event log, lockfiles). Config lives in ~/.config/bettermemory/config.toml (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/internals.md). Optional replication goes through a separate git repo: the store directory itself is the repo, pushed to a remote the user controls. There is no cloud service and no account (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory).
format_and_model: There is one Markdown file per memory, with YAML front matter parsed only through yaml.SafeLoader. The YAML region is capped at 64 KB and the file at 1 MiB. The Markdown files are canonical. The SQLite FTS5 index (index schema 11) is a cache you can delete and rebuild with `bettermemory reindex`. SCHEMA_VERSION is still 1 in 8.0.0. Removal is a soft delete into tombstones, and a restore re-checks the claims. Typed links between memories form a small graph. A provenance label (local, synced, untracked or unaccounted) is never read from the file: it is derived from the event log and from `git ls-files` in the sync repo on every rebuild. Each store write records the file's SHA-256 next to its index row, but this only detects tampering (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/internals.md, https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/SECURITY.md).
realtime: No. Sharing within one host goes through the shared directory and its locks. Sharing across hosts happens only when a user or a cron job runs `bettermemory sync`, which is batch git push/pull. There is no daemon, no push channel and no network listener. 5.0.0 removed the web UI, and the only transport is MCP stdio (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/SECURITY.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Partly, and only at the level of facts. Memories link to code through origin (repo, branch, worktree), through declared claims about paths, symbols and literal values that are re-checked against the working tree, and through the verified_head commit hash, which feeds commit-drift counting. Episodes and the event log are keyed by session_id, and memory_search can narrow results to the current session (since_prior_session). Memories are not linked to individual prompts or commits as a provenance trail. "Cause provenance", meaning what was in context when the agent wrote a memory, is explicitly called an open, unsolved problem. Sources: https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/internals.md#provenance and https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/api.md.
scale: Scaling past about 500 memories relies on the derived SQLite FTS5 index. Swarm throughput was measured at one point only: about 318 ops/s at 12 agents on a 12-core box, falling at 24 agents. The project deliberately makes no ceiling claim and has run no many-core test (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/docs/swarm-convergence-plan.md). The intended scale is one user and one store of hand-curated facts, not a full session history.
privacy_security:
The threat model is single-user and local-first, and access control is OS permissions: the directory is 0700 and the files are 0600. There is no encryption at rest (the docs recommend disk encryption), and clients are not authenticated.

Write gates:
- The credential gate refuses secret-shaped tokens such as API keys, PEM blocks, JWTs and password= assignments, unless the writer acknowledges it as an example. This same gate is the one hard check on sync admission.
- Further gates reject transient state, duplicates or tombstoned content, scope mismatches, and optionally text not grounded in the transcript.
- user-inference labelling keeps the model's inferences about the user separate from facts.

Event-log queries are stored by default as hash, 32-character preview and length, with sk-ant, sk, ghp, AKIA and similar shapes redacted. Credentials embedded in git remote URLs are masked in output. Provenance labels catch planted files (labelled unaccounted). Remote verification stamps are not trusted: a pulled memory reads as unverified until this host verifies it. The SHA-256 content evidence only detects tampering: there is no MAC or hash chain over the files or the event log, and a forged event line makes a planted file read as local.

Known gaps:
- a false but secret-free remote memory is admitted;
- git signatures and fsck are not verified;
- tombstones sync with no admission check.

The project also discloses a real leak. From 6.6.0 to 7.17.1, memory_search served quarantined memories with their bodies, fixed in 7.17.2 (2026-09-12) by commit 760c217. Injected instructions in bodies are handled by delivering bodies only through explicit tool calls, plus labels; no envelope or sanitizer is described. Source: https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/SECURITY.md.
lesson_for_parinn: Never derive trust from fields carried in a synced file. bettermemory learned this the hard way. Any memory file arriving over git is hostile until it passes an admission chain: size cap, then parser, then an id-alias/shadowing check, then the secret gate. A failed file is quarantined in a host-local, gitignored sidecar, not deleted, so the refusal does not spread to other hosts. Provenance comes from the local event log, not from the file. A remote 'verified' stamp counts as unverified until it is re-checked locally. For ParleyInn, if git carries session history, apply the same idea to records arriving from other machines and sandboxes. Admit and label them on ingest: local vs synced vs unaccounted, checked against ParleyInn's own hash chain. Never let a pulled record reach a restore block (I2). Add one structural test that lists every read path, since bettermemory's quarantine bypass came from a third read path that skipped the guard. Two more points. First, its git-merge-conflict sync gives no real-time sharing and no cross-host convergence; the project says so itself. That supports an append-only, per-writer log design, where merging is just set union, over shared mutable files. Second, its "deterministic lexical BM25, no embeddings" retrieval and its claim-anchored staleness checks (verified_head..HEAD commit drift on the cited paths) can be borrowed directly for ParleyInn's recall annotations, because neither needs network access or randomness (I4, I10).
license: MIT (https://github.com/0Mattias/bettermemory/blob/main/LICENSE; PyPI metadata https://pypi.org/pypi/bettermemory/json)

name: ByteRover CLI (brv), formerly Cipher
category: Versioned context tree for coding agents. It stores curated agent memory and is git-versioned through an embedded git library.
status: shipped. Latest npm release is byterover-cli 3.16.1, published 2026-07-05 (https://registry.npmjs.org/byterover-cli). The newest commit on main that I cloned is dated 2026-06-26. So the project was active as of mid-2026, but I saw no release or commit for about three months before early October 2026. I could not check activity after that because the GitHub API was blocked in this session. The Cipher name is superseded: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/campfirein/cipher/main/README.md now shows the "ByteRover CLI" README. Whether campfirein/cipher is formally archived could not be verified.
what_is_stored: It stores curated knowledge, not raw session history. Two paths create entries: the user runs `/curate "Auth uses JWT with 24h expiry" @src/middleware/auth.ts`, or brv's own LLM agent curates during its REPL tasks (README). The paper describes entries in a Domain > Topic > Subtopic > Entry hierarchy. Each entry has explicit relations, provenance and lifecycle metadata: importance score, maturity tier and recency decay, which the paper calls the "Adaptive Knowledge Lifecycle" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01599). The code also writes generated summaries, an index.html and a manifest (src/server/infra/context-tree/: summary-frontmatter.ts with fields such as evicted_importance, index-generator.ts, file-context-tree-manifest-service.ts). Separately, brv keeps its own REPL session metadata and a task/query log capped at 1000 entries per project (`taskHistory.maxEntries`) in the global XDG data dir. It does not capture Claude Code transcripts.
where_stored: Files in the working tree under `<project>/.brv/context-tree/` (constants BRV_DIR='.brv', CONTEXT_TREE_DIR='context-tree' in src/server/constants.ts). Project config is `.brv/config.json`. `brv vc init` creates a separate, nested git repository inside the context-tree directory: the code reads `<dir>/.git/MERGE_HEAD` (src/server/infra/git/isomorphic-git-service.ts). Remote sync goes to ByteRover Cloud's "CoGit" git server at `{BRV_COGIT_BASE_URL}/{team}/{space}.git` (src/server/infra/git/cogit-url.ts, src/server/config/environment.ts). Global settings and sessions live in `~/.local/share/brv` (README). Linked subdirectories get a `.brv` pointer file, modeled on git worktrees (README, "Worktrees and Knowledge Sources").
format_and_model: Human-readable Markdown files with YAML front matter, arranged as a hierarchical directory tree (paper; remark-frontmatter and js-yaml are dependencies in package.json). Correction to the discovery note: `brv vc` is not a custom VCS. It is ordinary git, implemented with the isomorphic-git library (isomorphic-git ^1.37.2 in package.json). It produces real commits, branches, merges and remotes over Git Smart HTTP v1/v2 (src/server/infra/git/git-http-wrapper.ts implements pktline/ls-refs). Branch names follow native git rules (isValidBranchName in cogit-url.ts). The older `brv push`/`brv pull` is a snapshot sync, now labelled "Legacy" in the README, that compares content hashes against a stored snapshot (file-context-tree-snapshot-service.ts). There is no hash-chained append-only log. Entries are mutable documents that the LLM rewrites, summarizes and evicts.
multi_writer_and_merge: vc path: git three-way merge through isomorphic-git. MergeConflictError is surfaced as bothModified/deleteByUs/deleteByTheirs, conflict markers are detected, and `abortMerge` is supported (isomorphic-git-service.ts). vc-handler.ts resolves an index.html conflict automatically by regenerating the derived file, and passes every other conflict to the user. Ahead/behind counting is capped at 500 commits. Legacy snapshot path: last-writer rules per file with conflict copies (file-context-tree-merger.ts): "Remote changed, local also changed → conflict... local copy saved to .brv/context-tree-conflicts/ and renamed _N.md; remote content written to the original path". A full backup is taken before each merge, with automatic rollback. Inside one machine, a daemon runs one agent process per project, with up to 5 concurrent curate/query tasks (agentPool settings in the README). Curate operations can be gated by a review queue (`brv review pending/approve/reject`).
realtime: No real-time multi-writer sync. Sharing is explicit: `brv vc push/pull/fetch` against ByteRover Cloud (README). Locally, a daemon serves the TUI, the web UI and MCP clients over socket.io (dependency in package.json). That is local IPC, not cross-machine streaming.
search_retrieval: No vector DB, graph DB or embeddings. The paper describes "a 5-tier progressive strategy that resolves most queries at sub-100 ms latency without LLM calls, escalating to agentic reasoning only for novel questions" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01599). Lexical tiers use MiniSearch (^7.2.0), an in-memory BM25-style index with title boost 2, fuzzy 0.2 and prefix matching, and fall back from AND to OR (src/agent/infra/swarm/adapters/local-markdown-adapter.ts and siblings). Adapters also exist for Obsidian vaults and "memory-wiki" sources. `brv source add` searches another project's tree read-only, and results are tagged with origin local or shared (README). Access is through `brv query`, the REPL, the web UI or the `brv mcp` server.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. A curate call can attach file references (`@src/middleware/auth.ts`), and entries carry provenance (README, paper). The context-tree git repo is separate from the project's code repo, so there is no commit-to-session linkage, no code SHA anchoring, and no capture of prompts or transcripts. The Claude Code integration installs a `UserPromptSubmit` hook in `.claude/settings.local.json` that runs `brv hook-prompt-submit`. That command only prints static "ByteRover workflow instructions" into the prompt context, and it fails silently (src/server/infra/connectors/hook/hook-connector-config.ts, src/oclif/commands/hook-prompt-submit.ts). Other integrations use MCP, rules files and skills (src/server/infra/connectors/{mcp,rules,skill}).
scale: Accuracy claims, all LLM-as-judge (README, paper): LoCoMo 96.1% (1,982 questions, 272 docs); LongMemEval-S 92.8% (500 questions, 23,867 docs). The paper claims sub-100 ms for most queries without LLM calls. I found no storage-volume, team-size or throughput claims. Built-in limits: 10 concurrent projects per daemon, 5 tasks per project, a 10-minute agent-loop budget per task (README settings table).
privacy_security: The README cites "SOC 2 Type II certified infrastructure with privacy mode" for ByteRover Cloud; I could not verify the details of privacy mode. Local trees stay local until pushed ("Everything works locally by default"). Push and pull authenticate with a ByteRover token sent as HTTP Basic auth (isomorphic-git-service.ts). I found no secret redaction or scrubbing of curated content: a grep for redact/secret in src/server matched only OAuth/provider credential code. I found no at-rest encryption of the context tree and no integrity chain. Recalled memory goes straight into the agent's context, and the brv agent itself can read and write files and execute code (README: "24 built-in agent tools (code exec, file ops...)"). The tool depends on network services by design: 20 LLM providers, cloud sync, a hub package registry. License: Elastic License 2.0 (LICENSE), which is source-available, not OSI open source.
lesson_for_parinn: ByteRover shows that git can be a sync format for agent memory without hosting the memory in the code repo. It keeps a separate repository inside `.brv/` and uses an embedded git library (isomorphic-git), so no git binary or subprocess is needed. That repo speaks standard Git Smart HTTP to a dedicated server, so ordinary branch, merge and push semantics work for "spaces" that teams share. For ParleyInn, a separate repo per project or space is a viable transport, and a pure-Go equivalent (go-git) would keep `os/exec` out of the shipped code under I4. But that network push has to live in a separate, opt-in transport process, outside the networkless core. The counter-lesson is just as concrete. ByteRover's tree is mutable, LLM-rewritten Markdown. Merge conflicts in it need humans or regeneration, and nothing in it is redacted or hash-chained. ParleyInn should commit only immutable, append-only segments: new files named by content hash or chain position. Then git merges are always conflict-free unions, and anything derived (summaries, indexes) is rebuilt locally and excluded from sync, as ByteRover already does for index.html with isExcludedFromSync (I10).
license: Elastic License 2.0 (source-available; restricts offering as a managed service). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/campfirein/byterover-cli/main/LICENSE
confidence: high for the storage layout, the git/isomorphic-git mechanics, merge behaviour, search and the hook integration, all read from source at main commit 1052ac1 (2026-06-26). medium for the paper-level architecture (5 tiers, lifecycle), taken from the arXiv abstract only. low for the cloud privacy-mode and SOC 2 details, and for whether campfirein/cipher is formally archived, since the GitHub API was unavailable.

name: C2SP transparency-log spec family: tlog-tiles, tlog-checkpoint, signed-note, tlog-witness (plus tlog-cosignature, tlog-proof, tlog-policy, tlog-mirror and https-bastion, which go with them)
status: shipped. Most of the family is stable, but tlog-tiles itself is still pre-1.0 and changing. Tagged stable versions in the C2SP repo (github.com/C2SP/C2SP): signed-note v1.0.0 and tlog-checkpoint v1.0.0 (both 2025-11-08); tlog-cosignature v1.0.1 (2026-03-28), with v1.1.0-rc.1 (2026-04-23) adding ML-DSA-44; tlog-witness v1.0.0 (2026-03-31). tlog-tiles has only one tag, v0.1.0 (2024-08-27, https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles@v0.1.0). Its editor's copy is under active edit: the "allow multiple URL prefixes" and "remove MUST for Ed25519" commits landed 2026-09-30, and the pruning/partial-tile clarifications landed 2026-10-01. tlog-proof, tlog-policy and tlog-mirror exist only as untagged editor's copies. Production implementations: Tessera v1.0.4 (tagged 2026-07-16, Apache-2.0, "generally available and production ready"); Sunlight, a static-ct-api log that runs the Tuscolo production instance (ISC); Sigstore Rekor v2 (rekor-tiles), whose public-good instance has a 99.5% SLO; and torchwood/litewitness (BSD). The Go checksum database is the design ancestor: it is in production but uses an older tile path layout. Superseded: transparency-dev/serverless-log, whose README says "should not be used for new logs" and points to Tessera's POSIX driver. The Witness Network is still a work in progress: its production log lists and witness tables say "Not available yet".
what_is_stored:
The log stores:
- Arbitrary opaque entries, which the application defines.
- The RFC 6962 SHA-256 Merkle tree over those entries, published as "tiles" of 256 consecutive hashes. Level-0 tiles hold leaf hashes; tiles at level 1 and above hold the hashes of full tiles at the level below.
- One signed "checkpoint" (signed tree head) for the current state: an origin line (the log identity, at most 255 bytes), the tree size, the base64 root hash, and optional extension lines, which the spec marks NOT RECOMMENDED because monitors cannot audit them.

Each entry is limited to 65,535 bytes because entry bundles use a big-endian uint16 length prefix (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles).

The specs carry no per-entry metadata such as author or timestamp. The only timestamps are inside witness cosignatures (a u64 POSIX time; https://c2sp.org/tlog-cosignature).

Other roles store less or more:
- A witness keeps only the latest checkpoint it has verified for each log origin (https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness).
- A mirror keeps a full copy of the log and cosigns that it has durably stored it (https://c2sp.org/tlog-mirror).
- tlog-proof defines a self-contained text proof: a checkpoint with cosignatures, the entry index, the inclusion-proof hashes, and an optional unauthenticated `extra` line. These files use the `.tlog-proof` extension and are called "spicy signatures" (https://c2sp.org/tlog-proof).
where_stored:
Static files under one or more URL prefixes, served from any HTTP file host, object store, CDN or POSIX directory (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles):
- `<prefix>/checkpoint`: mutable, served as text/plain.
- `<prefix>/tile/<L>/<N>[.p/<W>]`: immutable Merkle tiles.
- `<prefix>/tile/entries/<N>[.p/<W>]`: immutable entry bundles.

Redirects are forbidden. Since the 2026-09-30 edit, alternate prefixes act as replicas that must serve identical content.

Implementations store these files in different places:
- Tessera keeps them on GCP (Spanner plus GCS), on AWS (MySQL plus S3), or on POSIX with a `.state/` directory (https://github.com/transparency-dev/tessera, storage/posix/README.md).
- Sunlight writes to a POSIX filesystem or to S3-compatible storage. It keeps a separate small checkpoint database for its lock (https://github.com/FiloSottile/sunlight).
- Mirrors republish a log at `<monitoring prefix>/<sha256(origin)>` (https://c2sp.org/tlog-mirror).
- Witnesses persist one checkpoint per origin. litewitness uses SQLite (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood).

Git as a host has been tried. The now-superseded serverless-log showed a log kept in a GitHub repository: entries arrived by pull request into `leaves/pending/`, GitHub Actions ran sequencing and integration with the signing key held as a repository secret, and files were served through raw.githubusercontent.com. Its own docs mark this "experimental" (https://github.com/transparency-dev/serverless-log/blob/master/deploy/github/log/README.md).
format_and_model:
The data model is an append-only sequence addressed by index. Merkle hashing follows RFC 6962 with SHA-256.

Tiles (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles):
- A full tile is exactly 256 hashes, or 8,192 bytes. Levels run from 0 to 63.
- Tile indices are encoded as zero-padded 3-digit path elements, with every element but the last prefixed by `x`. For example, index 1234067 becomes `x001/x234/067`.
- Partial tiles of width 1–255 carry a `.p/<W>` suffix. They must not be hashed into the level above, and the log may delete them once the full tile exists.
- Entry bundles are concatenations of uint16-length-prefixed entries, and the spec says they SHOULD be gzip-compressed over HTTP.
- Pruning works through a "minimum index": the log denies requests for a prefix of the log while keeping indices and hashes unchanged. The spec recommends denying requests rather than deleting the files.

Signed note (https://c2sp.org/signed-note):
- The note is UTF-8 text with no control characters other than newline. A blank line separates it from the signature lines.
- Each signature line has the form `— <key name> base64(4-byte key ID || signature)`.
- Key ID = SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || signature-type byte || public key)[:4].
- Assigned signature types: 0x01 Ed25519, 0x02 ECDSA, 0x04 timestamped Ed25519 cosignature, 0x05 RFC 6962 tree-head signature, 0x06 ML-DSA-44 subtree cosignature.
- Public keys are written as text "vkeys": `name+hexID+base64(type||key)`.

Cosignatures (https://c2sp.org/tlog-cosignature):
- The Ed25519 type signs `cosignature/v1\ntime N\n` followed by the checkpoint body.
- The ML-DSA-44 type signs a binary `CosignedSubtree` structure: label, cosigner name, timestamp, origin, start, end and hash. It also supports cosigning subtrees.

Since editor's-copy changes on 2026-04-22/23, tlog-checkpoint and tlog-witness say logs and witnesses SHOULD use ML-DSA-44. Since 2026-10-01, canonical base64 is mandatory.

tlog-policy is a line-based text file with `log`, `witness`, k-of-n `group` and `quorum` lines (https://c2sp.org/tlog-policy).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no multi-writer merge. Each log is a single logical sequencer with one origin and one set of signing keys. "A log MUST not sign any checkpoint which is inconsistent with any checkpoint it previously signed" (https://c2sp.org/tlog-checkpoint). A fork is not a branch to reconcile. It is a split view, which counts as misbehaviour, and witnesses exist to catch it.

Many clients can submit, but one sequencer orders their entries:
- Tessera batches submissions in memory and assigns contiguous indices. Within a batch, the order of assigned indices is not guaranteed (Tessera README).
- Tessera's POSIX driver serialises concurrent writer processes with an advisory lock on `.state/treeState.lock` plus temp-file-and-rename writes. It was tested with several writers on ext4, ZFS and CephFS, and the docs warn that NFS and s3fs are "unlikely to result in long term happiness" (storage/posix/README.md).
- Sunlight uses a global lock backend (SQLite, DynamoDB, or S3 with ETag/If-Match) that holds the latest checkpoint with compare-and-swap semantics. Its README states that "the global lock backend is trusted: an attacker who can modify it can cause Sunlight to sign a split view", while the storage backend is "not trusted" and an attacker there "can at most cause Sunlight to stop working" (https://github.com/FiloSottile/sunlight).

Witness add-checkpoint is optimistic concurrency. The client sends `old <size>` and a consistency proof. If the old size does not match, the witness answers 409 with its current size. The check and the persist step must be atomic, or a race can roll the witness back (https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness).

Replication works through mirrors. A mirror is fed by add-checkpoint and then add-entries, which streams 256-aligned packages, each carrying a subtree consistency proof (https://c2sp.org/tlog-mirror).
realtime:
There is no push. Clients poll the `checkpoint` endpoint, whose headers SHOULD prevent caching beyond a few seconds, and then fetch the immutable tiles in parallel. The spec gives guidance for "tailing" a log that grows by more than 200 entries per checkpoint (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles).

Write-to-publish latency depends on the implementation:
- Sunlight flushes its pool every `period` milliseconds (200 in the example config; the README says not to exceed 1000). Its Skylight health check requires a valid checkpoint within the last 5 seconds (Sunlight README).
- Tessera publishes on a configurable checkpoint interval. Its benchmarks report observed time-to-integrate from about 0.6 s to 6.6 s (https://github.com/transparency-dev/tessera/blob/main/docs/performance.md).

Witness cosigning happens synchronously on each new checkpoint. The witness's read endpoint for monitors may lag by up to an hour so that it can sit behind a CDN (https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness).

For a witness that has no public address, https-bastion provides a reverse proxy it can connect out to (https://c2sp.org/https-bastion).
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by index only:
- A client fetches the tile or entry bundle that contains an index.
- Inclusion and consistency proofs are computed by the client from tiles. The server serves no proof endpoints (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles).

tlog-tiles has no lookup by key or hash and no full-text or content search. Applications build their own index. For example, the Go checksum database's separate dynamic lookup API sits outside the tiles. Sigsum also offers get-inclusion-proof by leaf hash, but through its own API, not tlog-tiles (https://git.glasklar.is/sigsum/project/documentation/-/blob/log.md-release-v1.0.1/log.md).

For offline verification, a `.tlog-proof` bundle plus a tlog-policy file is enough to check inclusion without network access (https://c2sp.org/tlog-proof, https://c2sp.org/tlog-policy).
links_sessions_to_code:
Not applicable. The specs carry opaque entries and model no agents, sessions, prompts or commits.

Ecosystems built on them do bind artifacts to log entries:
- Go module hashes in the checksum database.
- Sigstore signatures in Rekor v2.
- tlog-proof's "spicy signatures", a detached and offline-verifiable proof that some data was logged. Its `extra` line is explicitly unauthenticated (https://c2sp.org/tlog-proof).

Unverified suggestion, not a documented practice: ParleyInn could attach a `.tlog-proof` to a commit or pull request to show which session-log state the change came from.
privacy_security:
Integrity and anti-equivocation are strong:
- Signed checkpoints use Ed25519, or ML-DSA-44, which is now recommended because it resists quantum computers.
- Witness quorums, written as k-of-n groups in tlog-policy, defend against split views.
- Verifiers must ignore unknown keys, must reject a note when no known key's signature verifies, and SHOULD reject a note when a known key's signature fails.
- Note text "MUST be ignored unless the note is signed by a trusted key". The spec says notes suit operator-facing artifacts, not user-facing ones (https://c2sp.org/signed-note).
- Verifiers must accept at least 16 signatures and should cap the total.
- Witnesses authenticate requests only by the checkpoint signature (https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness).
- A bastion "is in the position of blocking, observing, and manipulating the backend's traffic" and should only carry self-authenticating protocols (https://c2sp.org/https-bastion).

Privacy is out of scope. Logs are built to be public. tlog-tiles, tlog-checkpoint and tlog-witness have no encryption, access control, redaction or secret handling. The only mention of encryption is that a mirror's opaque `ticket` MAY be encrypted (https://c2sp.org/tlog-mirror).

Pruning hides a prefix of the log by denying requests, and the spec recommends keeping the underlying files, so hashes and proofs survive (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles).

The privacy pattern the ecosystem uses is to log commitments rather than content. Sigsum leaves are a fixed 128 bytes: checksum = H(H(data)), signature and key hash. The data itself is not stored (https://git.glasklar.is/sigsum/project/documentation/-/blob/log.md-release-v1.0.1/log.md).

Key custody is the main operational risk. The serverless-log GitHub demo kept the log's private key in a GitHub Actions secret.
lesson_for_parinn:
Separate commitment from content, and never merge logs.

Make every ParleyInn writer (each agent, worktree, machine or sandbox) a single-writer log with its own origin and key. It writes C2SP-format checkpoints and tiles locally, inside the core, with no network access, so I4 holds. The Merkle leaves are commitments to events (Sigsum-style H(H(event)), or hashes of redacted or encrypted blobs), never raw transcripts. Raw transcripts would also break the 64 KiB entry limit and leak secrets.

Because the output is plain static files, a separate opt-in transport can carry them to any dumb host: a git branch, Forgejo, an object store or a CDN. That host can be untrusted, as Sunlight's storage is. Witnesses or mirrors (other ParleyInn peers, or the public witness network once it reaches production) then cosign the checkpoints to detect forks and rollbacks.

Only the per-log compare-and-swap checkpoint state needs to be trusted and local. Recalled content stays untrusted until it is checked with a tlog-proof against a tlog-policy.
license: The specifications are CC BY 4.0, and code and data in the C2SP repo are BSD 1-Clause (https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/.github/README.md). Implementations: Tessera Apache-2.0, Sunlight ISC, torchwood BSD-style (derived from the Go license), transparency-dev/witness Apache-2.0. The implementation licenses were read from each repo's LICENSE file.
scale:
The specs set these limits: tile levels 0–63, at most 63 consistency-proof lines per request, at least 16 signatures that verifiers must accept, and at most 65,535 bytes per entry (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles, https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness).

Measured or claimed scale:
- Go checksum database: sum.golang.org/latest reported tree size 66,338,891 when fetched on 2026-10-02. This log uses the older layout from which tlog-tiles was derived: `/tile/8/0/000` returns an 8,192-byte tile, while the tlog-tiles path `/tile/0/000` returns HTTP 400.
- Tessera claims CT-scale write throughput. Its POSIX driver sustained about 10,000 writes/s on NVMe with deduplication on, about 2,900 writes/s on SAS HDD without it, and more than 1,500 writes/s on a GCP e2-micro. On GCP, 100 Spanner processing units gave more than 3,000 qps (https://github.com/transparency-dev/tessera/blob/main/docs/performance.md). Reads scale through CDNs because tiles are immutable.
- Witness Network staging lists are sized "10qps-4klogs" and "100qps-40klogs"; production lists are not yet available (https://witness-network.org/log-lists/).
- Sigstore shards its Rekor v2 public instance roughly every 6 months (https://github.com/sigstore/rekor-tiles).

name: C3Sync (part of the C3 suite: C3 Mobile, C3 Desktop, C3 Bridge, C3Sync)
category: E2E encrypted multi-machine sync of native agent sessions and working-tree state, through a self-hosted NATS JetStream hub
status: beta. The newest release is C3Sync 1.0.0-beta.25, a GitHub pre-release published 27 July 2026 (https://github.com/ccc-app/ccc-releases/releases). The site says "Beta · Linux" and that macOS and Windows builds are untested previews (https://getc3.app/sync/docs). The July 2026 roadmap lists it as "AVAILABLE ... C3Sync beta.25". The independent security review is still pending (https://getc3.app/roadmap). I found no newer release by early October 2026.
what_is_stored:
Three kinds of encrypted event (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/security, https://getc3.app/sync/docs):
(1) Transcript or session events. These are each agent's own on-disk session data for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Pi. They are not exported transcripts: "C3Sync reads each agent's on-disk session format and writes it back natively on peers, so the agent's own resume command works on the next machine" (https://getc3.app/sync).
(2) File packs. These hold the git-visible working tree captured at each agent-turn boundary: tracked files, untracked files that git does not ignore, and .c3syncinclude entries. .c3syncignore exclusions are removed. The .git directory, .c3sync state and conflict sidecars are never synced (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/sync-semantics).
(3) Restore anchors. A restore anchor "binds the session position to the file state that existed when that turn completed" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/sync-semantics).
Git heads are also announced to peers so they can auto-pull (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/git-integration). Each device keeps local config in ~/.c3sync/config.json (handle, mode, nats_url, tls_pin, epoch, keystore, git_ssh_key, node_id) (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/cli).
where_stored:
Three places:
- Server you host. A NATS + JetStream hub, embedded in the c3sync binary or brought by you ("external" mode). It "provides routing, durable streams, and object storage" and stores only ciphertext (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/architecture, https://getc3.app/sync/docs/cli). There is no hosted C3 relay (https://getc3.app/privacy-policy).
- Each peer machine. Sessions are written back into the agent's own session store, and files into the working tree.
- Local restore points. These "generally follow git's object-pruning horizon, commonly around two weeks" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/safety). That suggests snapshots are kept as unreachable git objects in the local repo, but this is my inference and the docs do not confirm it.
Git and GitHub are not used to carry session history. Git is used only for project identity, stale-history detection, and fetch plus fast-forward from the project's real remote.
format_and_model:
Topology: each machine runs a daemon, c3syncd. It watches the agent session stores and the enabled working trees, turns changes into encrypted events, and consumes events from peers (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/architecture).
Session channel: agent adapters read and write each vendor's native format. "Session events form an append-only log ordered with hybrid logical clocks, so a peer can materialize the conversation in the format its local agent expects." node_id is the HLC tiebreak identity (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/cli).
File channel: files merge per path at turn boundaries.
Project identity: "Clones with the same origin and root commit join the same project identity even when their local paths differ" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/quickstart). Non-git folders sync transcripts only.
Wire format: NATS subjects and durable consumer names embed a scheme version. A breaking change needs a new scheme number. Readers must reject an unknown scheme or algorithm. Algorithm identifiers are authenticated (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/wire-compatibility).
No hash chain or tamper-evident log is documented. The exact envelope byte layout is not published.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Sessions: append-only merge with HLC ordering. "Two agents writing to the same session at the same time are unsupported. C3Sync detects concurrent writers and pauses materialization for that session instead of guessing." Moving a session from one machine to the next in turn is supported (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/sync-semantics, https://getc3.app/sync/docs/troubleshooting).
Files: changes to different paths merge on their own. If two machines edit one path at once, the result is chosen deterministically and the losing bytes go to a <name>.conflict sidecar, which is not synced onward. "A losing edit is written beside the file, never silently discarded" (https://getc3.app/sync). A device whose wall clock is far in the future can bias which version wins (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/troubleshooting).
Git awareness, backward: stale-history detection stops an older clone from reverting content that newer commits already protect.
Git awareness, forward: "commit-aware auto-pull" fetches with the user's own credentials, fast-forwards only, absorbs local changes that are byte-identical to the incoming commits, leaves unrelated uncommitted work alone, and blocks on real divergence. "C3Sync never pushes for you" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/git-integration).
Guards: a capture that would delete most of a project is held until c3sync sync --confirm-deletions (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/safety).
realtime: Near real time while peers are online. The daemon pushes events through NATS at agent-turn boundaries, after a capture debounce that c3sync sync bypasses. Poll and discovery intervals can be tuned with C3SYNC_POLL_INTERVAL and C3SYNC_DISCOVERY_INTERVAL (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/troubleshooting, https://getc3.app/sync/docs/cli). Offline catch-up is durable: "JetStream retains encrypted events, and a peer resumes its durable consumer when it reconnects" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/sync-semantics). No latency figures are published.
search_retrieval: No search over content is documented. Retrieval is by native resume in the agent itself, plus c3sync checkout --list and c3sync checkout <turn>. Checkout rewinds the working tree to a captured turn and prints an undo turn. c3sync conflicts list shows unresolved files and sessions that were edited on two machines (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/cli, https://getc3.app/sync/docs/safety).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, closely. That is its main feature. Every captured agent turn can carry a restore anchor that pairs the session position with the exact uncommitted working-tree state at the end of that turn, so you can rewind files to any turn (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/sync-semantics, https://getc3.app/sync). Projects are keyed by git origin plus root commit, not by path. It does not write commit trailers, git notes or prompt-to-commit attribution. Commits stay the user's own act, and C3Sync only fast-forwards to pushed history (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/git-integration).
scale: No scale claims are published. The hub is lightweight: "a Raspberry Pi is enough" (https://getc3.app/sync). The design targets one user's own machines, with one tenant and a few devices. It is not built for teams: every enrolled device is fully trusted and there is no per-project or read-only tier (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/security).
privacy_security:
Encryption: transcript events, file packs and restore anchors are sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305 under per-project content keys. These keys derive from a tenant secret held only by enrolled devices.

What the hub sees: the hub is "untrusted for confidentiality" but sees routing hashes, sizes, timing and activity patterns. The docs say plainly that E2EE does not hide traffic analysis (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/security).

Transport and enrollment: TLS uses certificate pinning with no insecure fallback, and each device gets its own NATS credentials minted from the account trust chain. A new device enrolls through a balanced P-256 PAKE with an enrolled device online to answer. The PAKE is rate-limited, uses two rounds of key confirmation, and a wrong passphrase leaves no orphaned credentials.

Secrets at rest: stored in the OS keyring, or in an encrypted-file backend that refuses to run without an explicit password.

Rotation and revocation:
- rekey rotates the tenant secret and passphrase and bumps the key epoch. Retired epoch secrets are kept so old history stays readable.
- revoke cuts the device's credentials at the hub, rotates the tenant secret and makes surviving devices re-enroll. The docs say "Treat all previously synchronized material as disclosed."
- Hub trust can be backed up offline as a sealed file. Restoring it rotates the CA and all credentials.

Account isolation: C3 Mobile control traffic uses a separate NATS account, C3_CONTROL, which "can never read synchronized project data" (https://getc3.app/sync/docs/security).

Gaps:
- No secret redaction or scanning of synced content is documented. .gitignore is honored, for example .env is shown as ignored (https://getc3.app/sync), but anything else visible to git, and the transcripts themselves, sync as-is.
- Recalled content is not treated as untrusted beyond the trust boundary between devices.
- The independent security review is still pending (https://getc3.app/roadmap).

Source and support: closed source as far as I can verify. The installer script names github.com/ccc-app/c3sync, but that URL returns 404 publicly. The public ccc-app org holds only ccc-releases, which has binaries and a README and no source (https://github.com/ccc-app, https://github.com/ccc-app/ccc-releases). The project is run by a solo developer with best-effort support (https://getc3.app/terms).
license: Cannot be verified. No source is public, and the GitHub org shows only a binaries repo with no license shown (https://github.com/ccc-app/ccc-releases). The terms say each component is "governed by the license published with that component's source or release" (https://getc3.app/terms). The site has refund and cancellation policies and mentions optional support payments (https://getc3.app/privacy-policy), but no pricing is published. The implementation language is not stated. It embeds a NATS server, which hints at Go, but that is unverified.
lesson_for_parinn:
C3Sync shows that an E2E-encrypted, offline-first transport can sit outside the core, with git used only for project identity. That fits I4: no network in shipped core code.

The pattern has four parts:
- A separate daemon (c3syncd) owns all network access to a hub you host.
- The hub is treated as untrusted for confidentiality and only stores sealed events (XChaCha20-Poly1305 under per-project keys derived from a tenant secret).
- Events are kept as JetStream durable streams, so offline peers and short-lived sandboxes replay from their consumer position.
- Projects are keyed by git origin plus root commit, so worktrees and clones at different paths map to one record.

ParleyInn can copy this as an optional sync process that ships sealed copies of its hash-chained records. Three of C3Sync's choices are worth adopting as written:
- Put a scheme version in every subject and authenticate algorithm identifiers.
- When two writers append to the same session at once, detect it and pause rather than merge. That keeps the per-session chain linear.
- Write the losing side to a sidecar instead of dropping it. That matches I6.

ParleyInn should also close the gaps C3Sync leaves:
- C3Sync has no tamper-evident chain, so a malicious enrolled peer can inject events.
- It does not redact or scan for secrets beyond .gitignore.
- It treats every enrolled device as fully trusted, with no read-only tier.

For ParleyInn, recalled peer events should stay untrusted (I2), and the chain should be signed per writer.
confidence: high for the architecture, merge behaviour and security model, which come from detailed official docs updated in July 2026. Low for the license, the implementation language and the on-disk restore-point format, which are not published.

name: cass (coding-agent-search), Dicklesworthstone/coding_agent_session_search
category: cross-agent session archive/search (local-first, single-user, multi-machine by pull-mirroring)
status: shipped (alpha badge; actively developed: v0.10.0 released 2026-10-01, v0.9.0 2026-09-25, v0.8.0 2026-09-10; last commit 2026-10-01)
what_is_stored: Normalized copies of conversations read from 32 local agent connectors. These include Claude Code ~/.claude/projects JSONL plus the macOS Desktop sidecars, Codex rollout JSONL, Cursor state.vscdb, Goose/Crush/Hermes/Devin/OpenCode SQLite, Aider Markdown, Kiro, Kimi, Grok and others. Each becomes a Conversation -> Message -> Snippet model. Messages carry role (normalized to user/assistant/system), content (tool calls flattened, e.g. "[Tool: Read] path=/foo/bar.rs"), timestamps, workspace, agent, token usage and title. Provenance fields are source_id, origin_kind (local/remote), origin_host and workspace_original. Also kept: a "raw mirror" holding byte-exact verbatim captures of the provider session files, for preservation when an agent prunes its own logs; derived BM25 lexical indexes; optional MiniLM vectors (.fsvi); analytics rollups; bookmarks; watch_state.json watermarks; and sources.toml config. cass never modifies the agent's own log files.
where_stored: Local DB plus local files under ~/.local/share/coding-agent-search (Linux default). Files there: agent_search.db (the canonical store, run on frankensqlite, a pure-Rust SQLite reimplementation, in WAL mode); index/v9-quill/ (lexical); vector_index/index-<embedder>.fsvi (vectors); raw-mirror/v1/ (content-addressed blobs); remotes/<source>/mirror/<path>_<fnv1a-hash>/ (rsync'd copies of remote machines' session dirs). Config lives at ~/.config/cass/sources.toml. Nothing goes in git. The optional `cass pages` command exports an encrypted static-site bundle that can be deployed to GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages. That is a publishing path, not storage.
format_and_model: Canonical store: a normalized SQLite schema (conversations, messages, agents, meta, _schema_migrations; fresh DBs record schema versions 13-21). Conversations have UNIQUE(source_id, agent_id, external_id); messages have UNIQUE(conversation_id, idx). Growth is mostly insert-only, but conversation rows are updated as they grow. Codebuff messages are updated in place by native ID, and dedup, forget and purge delete rows, so the store is not strictly append-only. No hash chain or tamper-evident log appears in the README or docs I read (not verified in source). Lexical and vector indexes are explicitly derived and are rebuilt from SQLite when missing, stale or incompatible; each lexical generation carries a schema_hash.json fingerprint. Raw mirror: whole blobs, or 4 MiB content-addressed chunks for large mutable sources, so growing JSONL files and SQLite files reuse unchanged chunks and every snapshot stays byte-exact. Portable logical backup: `cass archive export` writes a cass.logical_archive JSONL file. Export runs in one read-only transaction and the file is reread through a verifier before no-clobber publication. Backups can be searched (literal substring) and viewed by message_id plus a mandatory content_sha256, without restoring.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single-writer by design. One index-run.lock admits a single indexer. cass enables BEGIN CONCURRENT in frankensqlite, but indexing is still serialized; a parallel persist path is experimental and off by default. Multi-machine works as a pull-based star, not true multi-writer: the controller pulls each configured remote's session directories over SSH into a per-source mirror namespace. rsync is tried first, then WSL rsync, scp, then SFTP. Merge conflicts are avoided structurally: every remote has its own source_id and directory, and the identity key is (source_id, agent_id, external_id). Syncs are additive-only (rsync without --delete), so a remote deletion never propagates. The local mirror always follows the remote (-a without -u); a newer local copy is overwritten. --partial can leave a truncated file until the next sync. Identical content from different sources stays as separate results, and search-time dedup collapses only exact key tuples. No CRDT, no shared server, and no remote write-back. Gap states (remote_source_pruned, local_archive_ahead_of_remote, etc.) are reported as preservation signals.
realtime: Local only, near-real-time. `cass index --watch` uses filesystem notify watchers with a 2 s debounce and a 5 s maximum wait. It re-scans a whole changed file, relying on unique keys rather than per-message filtering, and watches SQLite WAL/SHM sidecars. The TUI does not start a watcher itself. A stale-on-read catch-up spawns a detached, niced background index when the index is more than 30 min stale, at most once per 5 min. Cross-machine is not real time: sync runs manually (`cass sources sync`) or on a manual/hourly/daily schedule through `cass schedule install` jobs.
search_retrieval: Three modes. Lexical: BM25 via the Quill engine in frankensearch, with edge n-gram prefixes (2-20 chars) on titles and the first 4 KiB of each message, code-aware tokenization, wildcards, and auto-fuzzy fallback on small indexes. Semantic: local MiniLM (all-minilm-l6-v2, or multilingual) embeddings in memory-mappable FSVI files, exact brute force by default and HNSW only with --approximate. The model is downloaded from Hugging Face only on explicit `cass models install`, SHA-256 verified, and can be installed air-gapped. Hybrid is the default: RRF with K=60, failing open to lexical when vectors are absent. The engine query is claimed under 60 ms, but a one-shot CLI call spends about 1 s on archive open and preflight for a ~10 GB archive. Agent-facing robot mode offers JSON/JSONL output, cursors, aggregations, `expand` context around a line, `timeline` and `related`. `pack` builds token-budgeted, cited, extractive evidence bundles for handoff to another agent, with freshness policies; injected skill payloads are excluded by default. `serve --stdio [--mcp]` is a persistent read-only search service with per-request deadlines and memory caps. Each hit can carry an advisory `trust` block: tier trusted/likely/unverified/stale/failed, confidence, provenance_refs and stale_reason. It never changes ranking.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly and explicitly. Sessions are tied to workspace paths; path mappings rewrite remote paths to local ones and keep workspace_original. The trust verdict links a hit to code only when the hit's own indexed text names an identifier (`commit:<sha>` or `bead:<id>`). That identifier is joined against the current project's local git history and beads, and the containing release is resolved from git. Temporal or workspace coincidence is never enough to link. A linked commit stays `proof_debt` and cannot reach `trusted` from this correlation alone. Off-project hits report workspace_mismatch. cass does not write anything into git (no notes, refs or trailers).
scale: Claims from the docs: tested limits run from 10 MB / 1k conversations / 10k messages (search under 1 s) to 1 GB+ / 100k+ conversations / 1M+ messages ("may require increased timeouts"). Practical limit is about 10,000 messages per conversation; messages over 1 MB are indexed fully. The README cites a ~10 GB archive, an A/B ingest test on a 2.1-million-message archive (53,155 messages committed in 10 CPU-minutes after the redaction fix), and a 593 MiB / 3.1M-string redaction benchmark (261-284 MiB/s prefilter). All are self-reported; I found no independent verification.
privacy_security: Redaction: CASS_INDEX_REDACTION=full is the default. 13 regex families (AWS, GitHub, OpenAI and Anthropic keys, Bearer tokens, JWTs, PEM/SSH/PGP private keys, DB URLs, generic password/api_key assignments, Slack, Stripe) plus redaction by JSON field name are applied before data reaches SQLite or the lexical index. The README says plainly that this protects queryable surfaces only: original session files and raw-mirror blobs keep raw text unencrypted on the same disk, so there is no at-rest encryption of the archive. Exports: HTML export can be password-encrypted (AES-256-GCM, PBKDF2 at 600k iterations). `pages` bundles are encrypted with LUKS-style key slots, use share profiles (public/team/personal) that redact PII, and fail closed on a staged secret scan rather than publishing a rewritten credential. Connectors whose stores also hold credentials (Shelley, Grok Bot) disable raw mirroring and remote ingestion. SSH uses BatchMode and StrictHostKeyChecking=yes. Network: unlike ParleyInn's I4, cass does talk to the network. The TUI checks GitHub releases hourly, models download on request, sources sync over SSH, and HTML exports load Prism.js from jsdelivr with SRI. Diagnostics (doctor/health/status/triage) are local-only. Recalled content is labelled with advisory trust metadata but is not enveloped as untrusted against prompt injection. License: "MIT with OpenAI/Anthropic Rider". This is not an OSI license: it grants no rights to OpenAI, Anthropic, their affiliates or anyone acting for them, and it bars indexing or benchmarking by them. It is therefore off any normal allow-list, and ParleyInn should not take cass as a dependency or vendor its code.
lesson_for_parinn: For multiple machines, give each source its own namespace and merge by copying additively, not by merging contents. Each remote's sessions land under their own source_id, and the identity key is (source_id, agent_id, external_id). Syncs never propagate deletes. Because only one writer ever touches a namespace, merges cannot conflict. Keep one canonical store and treat every index as rebuildable. Also keep byte-exact, content-addressed chunked snapshots of provider transcripts, because agents prune their own logs. ParleyInn's hash-chained per-source logs fit this shape directly, whether carried by git refs or by rsync. ParleyInn should close two gaps cass leaves open. First, cass redacts only the queryable surfaces, so the raw mirror still holds secrets in plaintext on disk; ParleyInn should redact or encrypt before persisting the raw copy as well. Second, cass labels recall with advisory trust tiers but does not envelope it; ParleyInn should wrap recalled content as untrusted rather than rely on metadata.
license: MIT with an OpenAI/Anthropic rider (non-OSI). It grants no rights to OpenAI, Anthropic, their affiliates or anyone acting on their behalf, and its definition of use covers indexing, benchmarking and training. Unsuitable as a ParleyInn dependency.

name: CCManager (kbwo/ccmanager)
category: Multi-agent session manager on git worktrees: a local TUI built on PTYs, written in TypeScript and run with Bun or Node. It handles Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Cursor Agent, Copilot CLI, Cline, OpenCode, Kimi and MiniMax MCode. It is not a history store: it orchestrates the agent CLIs and leaves their transcripts where the agents write them.
status: shipped. The project is active and not archived. npm version 4.4.4 was cut on 2026-09-27 (commit ee0af83, "let worktree creation continue in the background", #337). The repo page showed about 1.3k stars, 93 forks and 4 open issues when fetched on 2026-10-02. Two relevant features: session-data copying arrived in PR #39 (merged 2025-07-18, released in v1.4.0), and session restore arrived in #333 (2026-09-05).
license: MIT (Copyright 2025 Kodai Kabasawa)
what_is_stored:
CCManager does not persist any conversation content or terminal output itself. Its own state:
(1) config.json, the global config. It holds shortcuts, command presets (command, args, fallback args, detection strategy), status hooks, worktree hooks, worktree settings (including the copySessionData default and the auto-directory pattern), merge config and auto-approval config.
(2) .ccmanager.json, an optional per-repo config at the git root, merged field-wise over the global config.
(3) sessions.json, the restore record (format v1). Each session entry holds id, projectPath, worktreePath, presetId?, sessionName?, devcontainerConfig?, ownerPid and createdAt. The source says terminal output and the conversation inside the CLI are deliberately not stored. Restore re-runs the launch command; it does not resume the conversation.
(4) recent-projects.json, used in multi-project mode.
(5) A rotating log, ccmanager.log (5 MB, 3 rotated files).
(6) A per-worktree git config key, ccmanager.parentBranch, written when extensions.worktreeConfig is enabled.
In memory only: each session's PTY is mirrored into a headless xterm with 5000 lines of scrollback.
The 'Session Data Copying' feature is optional and runs at worktree creation. It recursively copies Claude Code's own directory ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-source-path> to ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-target-path>, honouring CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR. Those are the JSONL transcripts and project state. The encoding takes the absolute path and replaces '/', '\' and '.' with '-'. Only Claude Code data is copied, not data from the other agents.
where_stored:
Local filesystem only.
- CCManager state: ~/.config/ccmanager/ (%APPDATA%\ccmanager on Windows), holding config.json, sessions.json and recent-projects.json.
- Logs: $XDG_STATE_HOME/ccmanager/ccmanager.log, else ~/.local/state/ccmanager/ on Linux or ~/Library/Logs/ccmanager/ on macOS.
- Per-project config: .ccmanager.json in the working tree. It is user-authored and may be committed.
- Parent branch: per-worktree git config (config.worktree), under the key ccmanager.parentBranch.
- Transcripts: they stay in Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects/. CCManager only duplicates directories there.
No server, no git refs, notes or branches for history, and no sync.
format_and_model:
Pretty-printed JSON files throughout.
- sessions.json is {version: 1, sessions: SessionRecord[]}. It is a mutable snapshot of the sessions currently open, keyed by the in-memory session id. It is not an event log: records are removed when a session is killed or exits on its own.
- The copy model duplicates the whole directory with fs.cp (recursive, force:true, errorOnExist:false, preserveTimestamps:true). Nothing is rewritten.
- Claude Code's JSONL records carry cwd, gitBranch, sessionId, uuid and parentUuid. I saw this in local transcripts in this environment; neither CCManager nor its README documents it.
- So, by inference from the code, a copy leaves records that still name the source worktree's path and branch, and the same sessionIds then exist under two project directories. The result is a fork with no new identity and no lineage record.
- Restore is 'run preset X in worktree Y again under name Z', not a replay of state.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Built for one user on one machine. Several CCManager processes may share sessions.json.
- Each mutation (record, forget, rename) re-reads the file, filters or replaces entries, writes sessions.json.<pid>.tmp, then renames it over the original. The replace is atomic and crash-safe.
- There is no cross-process file lock, though. The Mutex class in the repo works within one process only and the store does not use it. So two processes doing read-modify-write at the same moment can still lose an update in the window between read and rename. This is my inference from the code; the project does not document it.
- Ownership: each record carries ownerPid. On restore, records whose owner is still alive (checked with process.kill(pid, 0)) are skipped, so a session is not started twice. A reused PID could misclassify a record (inference).
- Config merging: .ccmanager.json fields override global fields. In multi-project mode only the global config is used.
- Session copying has no merge. It is a one-shot fork at worktree creation, and force:true overwrites same-named files in the target. The two copies then diverge for good: no copy-back and no reconciliation.
- Nothing works across machines or users.
realtime:
Real time only on the local machine, and by screen scraping.
- Each agent runs in a PTY that is mirrored into @xterm/headless.
- A per-agent state detector polls every 100 ms. It parses screen text (spinner '…ing…' lines, the token-stats line, the prompt box) to classify the session as idle, busy or waiting_input. For Claude, the move to idle waits 1500 ms of unchanged output.
- On each state change, status hooks run shell commands with CCMANAGER_OLD_STATE, CCMANAGER_NEW_STATE, CCMANAGER_WORKTREE_PATH, CCMANAGER_WORKTREE_DIR, CCMANAGER_WORKTREE_BRANCH and CCMANAGER_SESSION_ID. The docs show sending these to Slack with curl, so any outbound push is up to the user.
- sessions.json is written synchronously as sessions come and go.
- There is no shared or remote live view.
search_retrieval:
No search over history or content.
- In the menu, '/' filters projects, worktrees and session display names vi-style, and Tab/Shift+Tab filters sessions by state.
- Getting a conversation back is left to the agent itself, for example a command preset with '--resume'.
- The background-restore fix (#317) rebuilds the host terminal's scrollback from the in-memory session buffer. Nothing is indexed.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak, by location only.
- A session is tied to a worktree path, and the path to a branch.
- With git's worktreeConfig extension enabled, CCManager stores ccmanager.parentBranch per worktree. The menu then shows +/- line counts and commits ahead/behind the parent.
- Nothing ties a session to a commit: no trailers, no notes, and nothing written into commits.
- The only provenance in the transcripts is Claude Code's own cwd and gitBranch fields, and a session-data copy leaves them stale (inference, see format_and_model).
scale: The project makes no scale claims. Fixed limits in the code: 5000 lines of scrollback per session in memory, and log rotation at 5 MB with 3 files kept. The session-data copy was made asynchronous because 'session histories can be large'. Multi-project mode recursively finds git repos under CCMANAGER_MULTI_PROJECT_ROOT. Adoption signal: about 1.3k stars and 93 forks.
privacy_security:
No encryption and no redaction of stored or copied data.
- Copying session data duplicates full transcripts, including any secrets that were pasted or echoed, to a second path with no filtering.
- The log directory is created with mode 0700. The JSON state files are written with default permissions; the code sets no mode.
- The logger's header promises 'Sensitive information filtering on console output', but the implementation just formats and appends. I found no filter, so that claim is unverified in the code.
- Hook commands are logged in plaintext. A webhook URL inside a hook command therefore lands in the log.
- .worktreeinclude deliberately copies gitignored secrets (.env, certificates) into new worktrees. A file is copied only if it matches a pattern and is actually gitignored.
- Notable risk: a repo-root .ccmanager.json can define statusHooks, worktreeHooks and commandPresets, which run through spawn(..., {shell: true}), and its fields override the global config. I found no trust prompt or consent gate. A cloned repo's config can therefore choose which commands run (inference from the code).
