name: claude-session-management (deemkeen)
category: git-native session store (Claude Code plugin, a single prompt-only slash command)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: A snapshot of the current session that the model writes from what is in its context window. It is not the raw transcript. The command prompt says: "Create a timestamped export of the current session, using the current context" (commands/session-snapshot.md). The last commit, c6cf154 on 2025-11-12, replaced the earlier wording "using Claude's internal export command" with that phrase. So the snapshot is model-authored and lossy: whatever survives in the context window after compaction, written out however the model chooses. It is not the full record. Claude Code keeps that record itself at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl ("every message, tool call, and tool result", per the claude-directory docs), and the plugin never reads it. There is no session ID, no metadata header, and no tool-call structure. The plugin offers three operations: save (write and commit a snapshot), load (paste a chosen snapshot back into the conversation) and delete (remove the file and commit the deletion). It has no hooks, so nothing is captured unless the user runs /session-snapshot by hand. The whole repo is 7 files (README, LICENSE, .gitignore, plugin.json, marketplace.json, commands/session-snapshot.md, scripts/sanitize-session.sh), all read in full from a clone.
where_stored: Working-tree files in ./saved-sessions/, relative to Claude's current working directory in the user's project. The directory is created if missing. The model is told to commit each snapshot to git, which puts it on whatever branch is checked out in the project repo. There is no dedicated ref or branch, no separate repo, no push, no remote sync and no local database.
format_and_model: One free-form plain-text file per snapshot, named YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-session-snapshot.txt (README example: 20250112-143022-session-snapshot.txt). The timezone is not specified. There is no schema, no event model, no per-message records, no content hash and no chain. The filename timestamp is the only ordering key. Versioning is just git history on the files. Deletes are ordinary git deletions, so a snapshot stays reachable in history unless someone rewrites it.
multi_writer_and_merge: No explicit design. Merges are git's default behaviour, applied to add-only, uniquely named files. Two machines or worktrees saving at different seconds create different paths, so merging their branches is conflict-free. Saves in the same second with the same name would collide, because the name has no machine, user or session component. Snapshot commits go onto whatever branch is checked out, so they mix with code commits and travel with feature branches and PRs. Nothing pulls, pushes or reconciles. The command does not limit what goes into the commit (it just says "Commit the snapshot to git with a descriptive message"), so whether other staged changes get swept in depends on the git commands the model picks. That could not be verified.
realtime: None. Snapshots happen only when the user runs /session-snapshot and picks Save in an AskUserQuestion dialog. The plugin ships no hooks/hooks.json and no monitors, and it never syncs between machines.
search_retrieval: Minimal. For load and delete, the model scans ./saved-sessions/ and shows the files sorted by date, newest first, for the user to choose from. There is no index, no full-text or semantic search, and no filtering beyond that list. Load says to "Clear the current context" and then "Load the selected snapshot content into the conversation", meaning the whole file is pasted back as context. The prompt names no mechanism for the clearing step. Per the Claude Code commands docs, /clear is a user-typed command, and no evidence was found that the model can trigger it, so whether context is really cleared is unverified.
links_sessions_to_code: Only by accident. Snapshot commits sit in the same repo and branch history as the code, so git log shows them next to code commits. Nothing records a commit SHA, branch name, changed files, session ID or commit trailer, and code commits do not point back at snapshots.
scale: No scale claims. Each snapshot is one text file about the size of a context window, committed into the project repo. Nothing bounds repo growth (no LFS, no retention policy).
privacy_security:
Weak, and partly not hooked up.

1. The sanitizer is never called. The README promises removal of home paths, working directories, usernames and hostnames, and scripts/sanitize-session.sh exists. But the command prompt never names the script or ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, which the plugin docs say command content must use to reach bundled files. Whether it runs depends on the model finding it.

2. When it does run, it is six chained sed substitutions on $HOME, $(pwd), $(whoami), $(hostname), /home/*/ and /Users/*/. The variables go into the regex unescaped. A test run in an isolated HOME showed three problems:
   - The CWD rule never fires when the project is under $HOME, because the HOME rule has already rewritten the path, so the project directory name leaks.
   - Usernames and hostnames are replaced as substrings anywhere: with user root, "chrooted" became "chusered", and a short hostname like "vm" would hit every word containing it.
   - There is no secret redaction at all. A sample AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY value and a ghp_ GitHub token came through unchanged.

3. No encryption, no secret scanning and no audit trail of what was redacted. The snapshots are committed into the project repo, so they reach any remote the user pushes to.

4. Load pastes committed text straight into the model's context with no envelope, which makes it a prompt-injection path. Anyone who can land a file in saved-sessions/, through a PR, a fork or a compromised collaborator, has text that gets loaded as trusted context next time.

Aside: under current docs, plugin names starting with "claude-" make `claude plugin validate` report a reserved-name error, though Claude Code still installs such plugins.
lesson_for_parinn:
Git works fine as a dumb carrier for uniquely named, add-only files: snapshots from different machines merge with no conflicts. Everything that goes wrong in this plugin sits around git, and each failure has a matching ParleyInn rule:

- The model writes the record. That makes it lossy and impossible to check. ParleyInn should capture hook events byte-for-byte (I10, losslessness).
- Redaction is a free-text sed pass that is never called and catches no secrets. ParleyInn needs deterministic, tested secret redaction that is audited and counted before anything leaves the machine (I6).
- History lands on code branches. ParleyInn should use a dedicated ref.
- Load pastes repo-committed text straight back into context, so anyone with push access gets a prompt-injection channel. If ParleyInn uses git transport, everything fetched from a remote must be treated as untrusted, offered only through enveloped, pull-only recall, and never auto-restored (I2). Per-writer unique paths, or a per-writer chain, give conflict-free merges.
license: MIT (LICENSE file and plugin.json; GitHub API reports spdx_id MIT)

name: claude-session-tracker (ej31)
status: shipped. Actively maintained: npm package v2.9.7, last commit 2026-08-18 (merge of PR #47), not archived. Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/package.json and https://registry.npmjs.org/claude-session-tracker/latest. I could not reach the GitHub API from this session, so I did not check the star count (about 46) or the repo creation date myself.
what_is_stored:
Each Claude Code session becomes one GitHub Issue. The issue body holds the session_id, start timestamp, local IP address, absolute cwd and the local transcript_path (hooks/cst_session_start.py, lines 182-191). Comments on the issue then hold:
- every user prompt (UserPromptSubmit hook);
- the last assistant text message of each turn (Stop hook, using the payload's last_assistant_message and falling back to parsing the transcript JSONL);
- AskUserQuestion answers (PostToolUse hook).

It does not store tool calls, tool outputs, thinking blocks, intermediate assistant messages or diffs. It also skips system-generated turns such as <task-notification>, <system-reminder> and <command-name>.

A GitHub Projects v2 item tracks status (Registered, Responding, Waiting, Closed) plus 'Session Created' and 'Last Active' date fields. The issue title is overwritten with the latest prompt (first 80 characters). A label carries the workspace's GitHub remote 'owner/repo'.

Install, pause and resume actions write Projects status updates that hold the session ID, workspace path, issue URL, timestamp and local IP.

Locally it keeps per-session JSON state in ~/.claude/hooks/state/<session_id>.json (issue number, item id, prev_hash, timer pid) plus hooks.log.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md, https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_prompt_to_github_projects.py, https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_session_stop.py, https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_post_tool_use.py
where_stored:
On a forge server, as GitHub Issues, issue comments and a Projects v2 board in a private 'notes' repository (NOTES_REPO, by default <user>/claude-session-storage) that the installer creates. Nothing goes into git objects: no commits, notes or refs. Local per-session state is kept as JSON files under ~/.claude/hooks/state.

All writes go through the gh CLI (REST plus GraphQL), and installation needs the 'repo' and 'project' token scopes. GitHub is the only backend; there is no Forgejo or GitLab support.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md (Configuration, Under the Hood), https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_github_utils.py (STATE_DIR line 69; add_issue_comment around line 464)
format_and_model:
The model is one session = one Issue, one turn-half = one Markdown comment.

Each comment body has the form '<!-- integrity: {sha256} | prev: {prev_sha256} -->\n<!-- meta: {timestamp} {label} -->\n{raw text}'. The hash is SHA-256(prev_hash || content) over the raw text only. Timestamp and label are left out of the hash, and the genesis value is 64 zeros. The current chain head (prev_hash) lives only in the local state file. The hash chain was added in PR #32 on 2026-03-15.

A verify_chain() function exists, but the shipped hooks and CLI never call it, so integrity is never checked automatically. Because timestamps and roles sit outside the hash, they can be edited without breaking the chain. Anyone with write access can edit or delete a comment, and GitHub keeps no tamper-evident anchor.

Status and dates live as Projects v2 single-select and date fields.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_hash_chain.py and https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/commit/e7158ea
multi_writer_and_merge:
This is a single-writer design with no merge logic. Each developer installs under their own GitHub account with their own private repo and board. Team sharing means inviting collaborators to the Project.

Several sessions write to separate issues. Within one session, the prompt, Stop and PostToolUse hooks all run with async: true. Each one does an unlocked read-modify-write of state/<session_id>.json (prev_hash) and posts a comment through gh. Two hooks that overlap can therefore post comments out of order or fork the hash chain. This is my reading of the code; there is no locking or fcntl anywhere.

Resume (claude --resume) reuses the same issue, found through the state file or the cwd. A second machine has no local state, so it would open a new issue. Hosting is centralized (GitHub), so nothing like CRDTs or git merges is involved.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/bin/index.mjs (mergeHooks around lines 916-934, async: true) and https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_github_utils.py (load_state/save_state)
realtime:
Near real time and push-based. Every prompt and every response is posted as a comment within seconds, through async hooks with a 10-15 s timeout. Anyone with access to the private repo or Project sees updates live in the GitHub UI and can get notifications.

An idle timer process (cst_mark_done.py, default DONE_TIMEOUT_SECS=1800) moves the item to Closed after 30 minutes of inactivity.

Remote control is a kill switch: setting the Project status update to INACTIVE in the web UI makes every hook stop logging. Each hook therefore makes a GraphQL round-trip per event to check board status. Failures are only logged to hooks.log; nothing is retried or queued, so comments are lost while offline.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md (How It Works, Pause/resume) and https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_github_utils.py (check_project_board_status)
search_retrieval:
Search relies entirely on GitHub: issue and comment search, plus Projects board filters by label (workspace repo), status and date fields. The tool adds no search index, no recall API and no MCP server. Nothing is ever re-injected into the agent automatically, apart from a tracking-URL notice described under privacy. Retrieval means a human reading the issue on the web, or 'gh issue view'.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md (Use Cases, Key features)
links_sessions_to_code:
The link is weak and limited to repo level. The workspace's git remote origin (GitHub only) becomes an 'owner/repo' label on the session issue, or optionally a title prefix. The cwd path is recorded in the issue body. There is no link to commit SHAs, branches, diffs or PRs, and no trailer or note is written into the code repo.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_github_utils.py (get_git_repo around line 545, get_context_repo) and https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md (Repository label)
privacy_security:
Privacy rests on visibility alone. Before each session it checks that NOTES_REPO and the Project are private, and if not it refuses to log. On re-running the installer, a repo that was made public is set back to private and archived, and a new private repo is created. A public board is closed and replaced (README, Privacy protection).

There is no redaction, secret scanning or encryption. Prompts and responses go to GitHub verbatim, even though the README admits they may contain API keys. Data rests on GitHub's servers in plaintext, readable by anyone with repo access and by GitHub. The local IP, absolute paths and transcript path are published in the issue body and in status updates.

The hooks use the network directly: gh, an npm registry update check through urllib, and a UDP connect to 8.8.8.8 to find the local IP. The token comes from gh auth or GITHUB_TOKEN, and --token-stdin is offered to keep the PAT out of process listings.

The UserPromptSubmit hook prints an instruction to stdout ('Please inform the user of this tracking URL...'). Claude Code injects that output into model context, so the hook is itself a tool-to-model text channel.

The hash chain gives no real tamper evidence. It is never verified, and since it is unsigned and the head is kept locally, anyone with write access can rewrite comments and recompute the hashes.

Sources: https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/README.md, https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_session_start.py (get_local_ip, the visibility check), https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_prompt_to_github_projects.py, https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/hooks/cst_hash_chain.py
lesson_for_parinn:
The forge's issue and comment layer is an attractive real-time transport. It gives push, notifications, access control and a UI with zero infrastructure. This project shows what goes wrong when it is used as the record itself:
- **Lossy record:** only prompts and final replies are kept, with no tool I/O.
- **Writes can be lost or reordered:** fire-and-forget hooks post comments that can arrive out of order and are dropped when offline.
- **Integrity is never checked:** the hash chain covers content but not timestamps or roles, keeps its head off-record and is never verified.
- **Plaintext secrets:** everything rests verbatim on a third-party server, with privacy left to a visibility flag.

For ParleyInn:
- Keep the authoritative append-only chain local, where it is written in order, cross-process locked, hash-chained over the full event including timestamp, role and sequence number, and verified on read.
- Treat any forge (an issue thread, a git ref, Forgejo) only as an optional, separate export or sync transport that ships already-redacted and ideally encrypted segments. Name the chain head in the export so a receiver can verify it.
- Never let the transport hold the only copy, and never let it skip I6 audit counting on failure.

Also note the anti-pattern of a hook printing instructions into model context. ParleyInn's restore output must stay TrustedText-only (I2).
license: MIT (https://github.com/ej31/claude-session-tracker/blob/main/LICENSE, package.json "license": "MIT")
confidence: high (based on reading the source at commit 03c7d14, 2026-08-18). The star count and repo creation date could not be checked from this session.

name: claude-sync (tawanorg)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: A per-file mirror of the Claude Code home directory, not a session log of its own. In the default 'full' scope it syncs ~/.claude/projects/ (session JSONL transcripts and auto-memory), plans/, tasks/, history.jsonl, agents/, skills/, plugins/, rules/, settings.json, settings.local.json and CLAUDE.md. The 'sessions' scope keeps only projects/, history.jsonl, tasks/ and plans/ (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md, 'What Gets Synced'). It also writes an encrypted manifest of file mtimes to _metadata/manifest.json.age, and MCP server configs from ~/.claude.json to _external/mcp-servers.json.age (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/sync/sync.go, https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/config/config.go). Locally it keeps ~/.claude-sync/config.yaml (storage credentials), age-key.txt (the derived secret key) and state.json (per-file SHA-256, size, mtime, upload time and a hostname DeviceID) (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/docs/architecture.md).
where_stored: Server/cloud object storage owned by the user: Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, any S3-compatible service (Backblaze B2, MinIO, Wasabi, Ceph) or WebDAV (Nextcloud, ownCloud). The bucket is one flat namespace per user, plus local state files under ~/.claude-sync (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md). Git is not involved.
format_and_model: Each local file becomes one object. On upload a file is (1) path-normalised: the home directory and any configured path_map prefixes are replaced with tokens such as ${HOME} or ${WORK}, both in the object key and inside session transcript content; (2) gzip-compressed; (3) age-encrypted to an X25519 recipient; and (4) uploaded whole under the key '<normalised relative path>.age' (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/sync/sync.go, uploadFile/remoteKey; https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md, 'Cross-Device Path Mapping'). There is no event, record or chunk model, no versioning and no hash chain. A JSONL transcript that grows by appends is re-uploaded in full on each push. The storage interface is just Upload/Download/Delete/List/Head/BucketExists on byte blobs (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/docs/architecture.md). A single download is capped at 100 MB (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/storage/storage.go).
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple devices share one bucket, with no locking and no conditional writes: a grep of the storage adapters finds no If-Match or precondition use (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/tree/main/internal/storage). Push looks only at local changes against state.json and overwrites remote objects without checking them first, so a push is last-writer-wins (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/sync/sync.go, Push). Pull detects conflicts by timestamp: a file is in conflict when the remote LastModified is after the local 'Uploaded' time and the local hash also differs from the recorded hash. In that case the local file is kept and the remote copy is written as '<file>.conflict.<timestamp>', and the user resolves it with 'claude-sync conflicts' (keep local, keep remote, diff, skip) (same file, Pull/handleConflict; README 'Conflict Resolution'). The README itself says history.jsonl is last-writer-wins and loses entries across devices. Its fix is 'rebuild-history', which rebuilds the prompt history from the per-session files, because 'session files sync cleanly (one file per session)' (README 'Rebuilding Prompt History'). MCP configs get a per-server-key three-way JSON merge (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/sync/mcp.go). A design spec proposes 'sync packs' for OpenClaw/Bifrost, with a three-way JSON merge and SQLite snapshots (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/docs/specs/openclaw-bifrost-sync.md). I found no sign it has shipped.
realtime: No. Sync runs only on the manual push and pull commands. The README suggests shell hooks, a background 'pull -q' when a shell starts and 'push -q' on shell EXIT. The repo also ships a Claude Code plugin with hooks and /sync-* slash commands (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md 'Shell Integration'; https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/tree/main/claude-code-plugin). The OpenClaw spec lists auto-sync triggers as a deferred phase (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/docs/specs/openclaw-bifrost-sync.md).
search_retrieval: None beyond listing files. Commands are status, diff, conflicts and 'pull --dry-run'. Retrieval means restoring the files so that Claude Code's own 'claude --resume' finds them. The bucket holds only ciphertext, so it cannot be queried on the server side (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Only indirectly, through Claude Code's own layout. Sessions sit under projects/<path-encoded project dir>/, and claude-sync rewrites those absolute paths to portable tokens so a session resumes on another machine where the checkout is somewhere else. It does not link to commits, branches or repositories (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/README.md 'Cross-Device Path Mapping').
scale: The README claims 'Claude sessions typically use < 50MB' and that syncing is effectively free on provider free tiers (README 'Cost'). Single objects are capped at 100 MB (internal/storage/storage.go). It is aimed at one user's few devices, with no multi-user or team model. The repo has a ~5.8k-line sync package and release v1.17.1, dated 2026-07-26 (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), and is published on npm as @tawandotorg/claude-sync (https://registry.npmjs.org/@tawandotorg/claude-sync/latest). The 287-star count comes from the discovery note: the GitHub API returned 403 from this sandbox, so I could not check it.
privacy_security: Client-side gzip, then age encryption (X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305) before upload, so the provider sees only ciphertext blobs (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/docs/security.md). Keys come from a passphrase via Argon2id (64 MB, 3 iterations, 4 threads) with a deliberately fixed global salt, SHA256('claude-sync-v1'), so the same passphrase gives the same key on any device. The project's own docs and audit say this enables rainbow-table attacks across all users. The minimum passphrase length is 12 characters. A random-key mode is also offered (https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/internal/crypto/encrypt.go; https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/SECURITY-AUDIT.md M4/M5). Every file is encrypted to the one shared identity: there are no per-device or per-user recipients and no way to revoke a device short of 'reset --remote' and re-keying. Object keys are plaintext normalised paths, for example projects/-${HOME}-my-app/<session>.jsonl.age, so project directory names and file counts and sizes leak to the provider. This follows from remoteKey in internal/sync/sync.go; it is my inference from the code, and the docs do not state it. Integrity comes only from age's AEAD on each file: nothing stops a bucket writer from deleting, rolling back or swapping whole objects. There is no redaction or secret scrubbing of transcripts, so secrets in sessions are synced as they are, only encrypted. Storage credentials sit in plaintext config.yaml with 0600 permissions (SECURITY-AUDIT.md M1). The self-update path now checks SHA-256 checksums (README 'Security'). The audit dated 2026-03-08 is labelled as done by an 'AI Security Agent' (SECURITY-AUDIT.md).
lesson_for_parinn: Encrypting each file and mirroring it whole to a bucket gives confidentiality but no history and no integrity. Concurrent pushes are last-writer-wins, conflicts are guessed from timestamps, and the shared history.jsonl loses entries, which the project patches with 'rebuild-history'. Only the one-file-per-session data 'syncs cleanly'. For ParleyInn this argues that any transport, whether S3, WebDAV or git, should carry immutable, content-addressed, append-only segments named by hash, with a per-session, per-writer layout so writers never contend for one object. The hash chain and signatures should provide integrity against rollback and deletion, which AEAD on single files cannot. Two pitfalls to avoid: plaintext object keys that leak project paths, and a single shared fixed-salt key with no per-device recipients or revocation. One idea worth borrowing: tokenising home and checkout paths (${HOME}, path_map) so a session resolves on another machine or sandbox.
license: MIT (README badge and package.json "license": "MIT"; https://github.com/tawanorg/claude-sync/blob/main/package.json). No LICENSE file was found in the shallow clone of main.

name: claude-tap (liaohch3/claude-tap)
category: API traffic capture: a local MITM proxy plus trace viewer for AI coding-agent CLIs
status: shipped. Python package claude-tap on PyPI. The latest release is 0.1.145, uploaded 2026-08-16 (https://pypi.org/pypi/claude-tap/json). The main branch is active: the last commit, 4cc867d, landed 2026-09-22 (feat(viewer) #444). pyproject.toml classifies it as "Development Status :: 4 - Beta". It is not archived. I could not check the 3.3k star count because the GitHub API was blocked from this session.
what_is_stored: It stores the actual HTTP and WebSocket exchanges between an agent CLI and its model API. It does not store the agent's on-disk transcript. Each request/response pair becomes one record with these fields: timestamp, request_id, turn, duration_ms, request {method, path, headers (filtered), body}, response {status, headers (filtered), body}, optional upstream_base_url, and a capture metadata object (client, proxy_mode). The body holds the full system prompt, messages, tool schemas, tool calls and results, and the streamed response put back together, plus token usage (proxy.py build record, trace.py). Raw SSE and WebSocket event arrays are left out unless --tap-store-stream-events is set. Two more things are stored: per-session proxy log lines, and a session summary with API call count, input, output and cache tokens, models used, has_error, trace_storage_errors and dropped_trace_records. Cursor is the exception. It is transcript-only: claude-tap watches ~/.cursor/projects/*/agent-transcripts/*.jsonl and does not MITM Cursor's API (README).
where_stored: A local SQLite database. The default path is ~/.local/share/claude-tap/traces.sqlite3. It honours $XDG_DATA_HOME and can be overridden with CLOUDTAP_DB (trace_store.py resolve_db_path). Older versions wrote JSONL files under ./.traces. The --tap-output-dir flag is now only a "legacy trace directory to import once" (cli.py). The README still calls it the trace output directory, so the README is partly out of date. The MITM CA certificate and key live in ~/.claude-tap/ (certs.py). Exports are user-chosen files: a self-contained HTML viewer, JSONL, or a compact .ctap.json bundle. Nothing goes to git or to a server.
format_and_model:
SQLite in WAL mode, schema version 4, with these tables:
- sessions: id (a UUID4), started_at, updated_at, date_key, client, proxy_mode, status (active, complete, error or empty), record_count, summary_json.
- records: primary key (session_id, record_index), plus turn, timestamp and payload_json.
- proxy_logs.
- record_blobs: primary key (session_id, hash), plus kind, payload_json and size_bytes.
- migration_state.
Records are stored in a "compact" form. Large repeated JSON subtrees (request.body.instructions and tools, plus messages and input items) are replaced by references keyed on SHA-256 hashes into record_blobs. Only subtrees of at least 512 bytes are replaced, and the dedup is per session (compact_trace.py, trace_store.py _store_json_blob). The portable export bundle uses the same json-blob-ref encoding and carries an inline blob dictionary. Records are appended in record_index order, but nothing is truly append-only: replace_record_payloads() rewrites stored payloads to backfill fields, sessions are deleted for retention, and there is no hash chain or signature.
multi_writer_and_merge: The only multi-writer support is local, on one machine. Several claude-tap processes, one per agent, write to the same SQLite file. Writes are serialized by a thread lock plus an exclusive advisory lock file, traces.sqlite3.write.lock (fcntl.flock on POSIX, msvcrt.locking on Windows). The lock times out after 1 s, and SQLite's busy_timeout is 1000 ms (trace_store.py _process_write_lock). If storage fails, the record is dropped and counted in dropped_trace_records. A warning goes to stderr, and the proxy keeps forwarding so the agent is never blocked (trace.py; changelog #385 "prevent SQLite locks from blocking clients"). Nothing syncs or merges across machines. Sessions are separate UUIDs, so you could carry exported bundles around, but there is no merge semantics.
realtime: Yes, locally. The live viewer is on by default since v0.1.75. TraceWriter.write() stores each record and then broadcasts it to the browser over Server-Sent Events (/events and /dashboard/events in live.py). A shared dashboard service (claude-tap dashboard) runs on one fixed local port and lists sessions from every process writing to the database. Streams pass through to the client chunk by chunk. Nothing is shared in real time across machines.
search_retrieval: There is no FTS index. The session list search is a case-insensitive SQL LIKE '%term%' scan over session fields, summary_json, records.payload_json and record_blobs.payload_json (trace_store.py, the query builder). The viewer adds client-side full-text search across messages, tools, prompts and responses, plus filters by path and model, model grouping, and a structural diff between adjacent requests (README Viewer Features). An HTTP API on the local viewer lists sessions and records and exports JSONL, compact or HTML per session (live.py routes). There is no semantic search and no recall interface for agents.
links_sessions_to_code: No. The schema stores no repo, cwd, branch or commit. Session metadata covers only client and proxy_mode (cli.py trace_metadata; sessions table). Any file paths or git output appear only incidentally, inside prompt and tool-result bodies.
scale: The project makes no throughput or size claims. Retention defaults to the 50 most recent sessions (--tap-max-traces 50, where 0 means unlimited). The oldest sessions that are not active are pruned. Active sessions count as stale after 24 h, or after 15 min if they have no records (trace_store.py cleanup_old_sessions). Storage size is reduced by per-session dedup of prompt and tool blobs. Recent commits address viewer performance, for example lazy loading, tests/test_perf_viewer.py, and #444, which flags very large tool results.
privacy_security:
Everything stays local, with no hosted dashboard (README, docs/guides/agent-trace-viewer.md).

Redaction at write time covers header values only:
- authorization and x-api-key are cut to their first 12 characters plus "...".
- cookie, set-cookie, x-amz-security-token and the Qoder cosy-* identity headers become "***" (proxy.py SENSITIVE_HEADER_KEYS).
- Request and response bodies (prompts, code, tool output) are stored verbatim.

A second redaction pass runs only when the dashboard serves data. It masks JSON keys such as token, secret, password, apikey and refreshtoken, along with URL query strings and form values (dashboard.py _redact_sensitive_value). This pass does not change what sits on disk.

The database file is not encrypted, and the code does not chmod it. Only the CA private key is set to 0600 (certs.py).

MITM mode generates a local RSA-2048 CA and per-host certificates. On macOS it may add that CA to the user's login keychain (trust-ca; automatic for agy and codexapp).

The proxy binds 127.0.0.1 by default but 0.0.0.0 in --tap-no-launch mode (README CLI options). The dashboard's quit endpoint requires a trusted localhost Host and Origin plus a random token (live.py).

The macOS menu app temporarily rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/config.toml and restores them byte for byte afterwards.

SECURITY.md warns that trace files still hold prompts, paths and private context even with keys redacted. Recalled content is shown to humans, never re-injected into a model, so it has no prompt-injection channel of its own.
lesson_for_parinn:
What the API sees is not what the transcript says. claude-tap exists because the payload actually sent to the model (the full system prompt, injected reminders, tool schemas, what is left after compaction) differs from Claude Code's on-disk JSONL. Two lessons follow for ParleyInn's record:
- ParleyInn's provenance should say which source each event came from (hook, transcript, or wire) and not treat the transcript as ground truth. An optional, opt-in wire capture lane could check ParleyInn's "pinned constraints were re-injected verbatim" claim against the bytes actually sent. It would have to be an out-of-process, user-run proxy so ParleyInn's own core stays network-free under I4.
- Avoid claude-tap's weak points. Its store is mutable, with no hash chain, rewritten payloads and pruning. Secrets are redacted only in headers and only at the display layer for bodies, so raw secrets in prompts persist on disk unencrypted. Its multi-writer story is one SQLite file plus flock, with records silently dropped (only counted) on lock timeout. ParleyInn should keep its append-only hash chain, redact before persisting, and audit every drop (I6). Content-addressed dedup of repeated system prompts and tool schemas is worth copying, because it shrinks history a lot and is easy to make rebuildable.

confidence: high. These facts come from reading the source at commit 4cc867d (2026-09-22) and the PyPI metadata. Star count and fork count are unverified because the GitHub API was blocked.

name: claude-trace (apps/claude-trace in badlogic/lemmy; npm @mariozechner/claude-trace)
category: API traffic capture (local wire-level recorder for Claude Code)
status: shipped, but stale. npm 1.0.9 (13 Aug 2025) is the latest release. The last commit to apps/claude-trace is also 13 Aug 2025 ("Add --log parameter"). Issue #48, open since Oct 2025, says it no longer works with Claude Code's native (Bun-bundled) binary installs. Issue #59 (Feb 2026) reports the same for Homebrew/Bun builds. I saw no maintainer reply. I did not confirm through the API whether the repo is archived, because gh access was denied. The repo page shows no archived banner.
what_is_stored: Every HTTP request/response pair Claude Code sends to api.anthropic.com, at the raw API level. Request: timestamp, method, URL, headers and the parsed JSON body. The body holds the full system prompt, tool definitions, the whole messages array (user prompts, tool results such as file contents and command output, thinking blocks) and the model. Response: timestamp, status_code, headers, and either the parsed JSON body or body_raw for SSE streams, which the viewer reassembles. Each pair also gets a logged_at ISO time. By default it logs only /v1/messages calls whose conversation has more than 2 messages; --include-all-requests logs every api.anthropic.com call. A July 2025 commit added interception of custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL endpoints. Optional --index writes summary-*.json files with AI-generated titles and summaries per conversation, plus a master index.html. Sources: README https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/lemmy/main/apps/claude-trace/README.md and interceptor.ts https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/lemmy/main/apps/claude-trace/src/interceptor.ts
where_stored: Working-tree files in the current directory: .claude-trace/log-YYYY-MM-DD-HH-MM-SS.jsonl plus a matching .html. The base name can be changed with --log or CLAUDE_TRACE_LOG_NAME. --index adds .claude-trace/summary-*.json and .claude-trace/index.html. There is no server, cloud or git integration. The tool writes no .gitignore entry, so whether the folder gets committed is left to the user. I inferred this from the source and found no gitignore handling.
format_and_model: Append-only JSONL with one RawPair object per line: {request:{timestamp, method, url, headers, body}, response:{timestamp, status_code, headers, body | body_raw}, logged_at}. Pairs are written with fs.appendFileSync when a response completes. On exit, requests still pending are flushed without a response. Each session is one flat file. There is no session id, no parent links, no hash chain and no schema version. Conversation structure (threads, compaction, subagents) is rebuilt after the fact by a shared conversation processor that runs in both the CLI and the HTML frontend. The HTML is a self-contained single page: the bundled JS/CSS plus the full pair list, base64-encoded and embedded inline (html-generator.ts https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/lemmy/main/apps/claude-trace/src/html-generator.ts). Capture works by running node --require interceptor-loader.js on Claude Code's JS entry point, which patches global.fetch and the Node http module (cli.ts https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/lemmy/main/apps/claude-trace/src/cli.ts; https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/2/claude-trace/). That design breaks once Claude Code ships as a Bun single-file binary (https://github.com/badlogic/lemmy/issues/48).
multi_writer_and_merge: Not supported. Each process gets its own timestamp-named file. Two runs started in the same second, or two runs given the same --log name, would collide, because the constructor truncates the file with writeFileSync(logFile, "") (interceptor.ts). Nothing merges data across files, worktrees or machines. --index only scans the local .claude-trace/ folder and lists the files in time order.
realtime: The JSONL is appended as soon as each response completes. With enableRealTimeHTML (on by default), the whole HTML file is regenerated from all in-memory pairs after every call, so cost grows as O(n) per call. Nothing is streamed or shared off the machine. The browser opens the finished HTML on exit unless --no-open is given (interceptor.ts; commit history https://github.com/badlogic/lemmy/commits/main/apps/claude-trace).
search_retrieval: The HTML viewer is for browsing only. It has a conversation view with tool visualisation, model filtering, a raw HTTP pairs view and a JSON debug view. There is no full-text index. --index runs Claude itself (spawn("claude", ["-p", prompt])) to write a title and summary for each non-compacted conversation with more than 2 messages, then builds a chronological index.html that links to each session's HTML. This costs extra tokens, and issue #46 reports that it can hang (README; index-generator.ts https://raw.githubusercontent.com/badlogic/lemmy/main/apps/claude-trace/src/index-generator.ts; https://github.com/badlogic/lemmy/issues?q=is%3Aissue+claude-trace). It has no recall API or MCP server, so nothing feeds traces back to the running agent.
links_sessions_to_code: Only implicitly. Logs land in .claude-trace/ under the directory where you launched it, and the payloads contain whatever file contents and tool calls Claude saw. Nothing records a commit SHA, branch, worktree or diff, and nothing links a pair to the code it changed.
scale: The project makes no scale claims. The design implies limits: one file per session, every pair kept in memory, the whole self-contained HTML rewritten after each call, and the full message history re-logged in every request body. Long sessions therefore produce large, highly redundant files (the same prompt prefix repeats in every line). The default filter exists "to reduce log file size" (README). I found no published benchmarks.
privacy_security: Weak; this is a debugging tool. Header redaction only: headers whose names contain authorization, x-api-key, x-auth-token, cookie, set-cookie, x-session-token, x-access-token, bearer or proxy-authorization are masked, but values longer than 14 characters keep their first 10 and last 4 characters (redactSensitiveHeaders in interceptor.ts). Request and response bodies are stored in full and unredacted, so any secret Claude read, such as .env files, tool output or pasted keys, ends up in plaintext JSONL and in base64 inside the HTML. The files are not encrypted, and the code sets no file permissions. Write errors are swallowed silently ("Silent error handling during runtime"). A separate --extract-token mode deliberately captures the Claude Code OAuth token. The --index feature sends recorded transcripts back through the model, which is an automatic path from stored, untrusted history to the model. Sources: interceptor.ts, index-generator.ts and the README linked above.
license: MIT, per the npm registry metadata (https://registry.npmjs.org/@mariozechner/claude-trace)
lesson_for_parinn: Do not build on patching the client's HTTP stack. claude-trace stopped working once Claude Code moved from a Node JS entry point to a Bun single-file binary (issue #48 is still open), so capture tied to runtime internals is fragile. ParleyInn should take its record from stable, documented surfaces: hooks and the session transcript files. It should also do what claude-trace does not: redact secrets in bodies before persisting, not only in headers, and never keep 14 characters of a token. Store each prompt prefix once with content-addressing instead of re-logging the full message array per call. Count and audit every write failure instead of swallowing it (I6). Never route stored traces back into a model automatically, as claude-trace's --index summariser does (I2).

name: claudereview (CLI `ccshare`, npm packages `claudereview` and `claudereview-mcp`)
category: Session sharing linked to PRs. It is a one-shot snapshot share with a hosted viewer. It does not store history.
status: Shipped, but dormant. Not archived. On 2026-10-02 the live site answered https://claudereview.com/health with {"status":"ok"}. The response header `server: railway-hikari` shows it runs on Railway. The last npm releases came out 2026-01-09: claudereview 0.1.3 and claudereview-mcp 0.1.5 (https://registry.npmjs.org/claudereview, https://registry.npmjs.org/claudereview-mcp). The repository has 60 commits, all by the author, between 2025-12-25 and 2026-01-08. The last is 0e02433, "Add Gemini CLI session support". This comes from cloning https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview. One outside pull request (#2, 2026-03-09, a Codex lookup speed-up) has not been merged (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/pull/2). One issue is open: #1, "Option to self host or store in git" (2026-01-08). It has no body and no maintainer reply (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/issues/1). The GitHub page showed about 15 stars and 6 forks, read with a fetch tool. npm counted 24 downloads of `claudereview` in September 2026 (https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-month/claudereview). The Show HN post on 2025-12-26 got 1 point (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46394091).
what_is_stored:
Each share stores one encrypted snapshot of one local session. The payload is not the raw transcript. It is a JSON object `{html, session:{id,title,metadata}}`, where `html` is a complete self-contained viewer page (CSS and JS inline) rendered by the CLI (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/cli.ts#L241-L255).

- **Not lossless.** The parser drops `thinking` blocks (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/parser.ts#L114-L115).
- **Plaintext metadata.** Next to the blob, the server keeps the title, message count, tool count and duration in plaintext. This applies to every share, password-protected ones included. The title is the session summary, or else the first human message cut to 100 characters (parser.ts L25-L49; server.ts L626-L642). The privacy page admits it: "Metadata is stored but only visible to you (the owner)" (https://claudereview.com/privacy).
- **Other server data.** The server also keeps the IV, the PBKDF2 salt (private shares only) and an optional `owner_key`. For signed-in public shares, `owner_key` is the AES key in plaintext. It also keeps a view count, `session_views` rows, GitHub user rows, and SHA-256 hashes of API keys (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/db/schema.ts#L13-L56).
- **Git context.** The remote URL, branch and HEAD commit are rendered into the encrypted HTML header (src/session.ts L444-L500).

Inputs come from three places: Claude Code JSONL in `~/.claude/projects/`, Codex in `~/.codex/sessions/`, and Gemini in `~/.gemini/tmp/*/chats/` (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/README.md).
where_stored:
On a server, in a cloud database. One PostgreSQL `sessions` table holds the ciphertext as a base64 TEXT column, up to 100 MB per upload. The server is a Bun/Hono app, deployed to Railway with a Dockerfile (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/server.ts#L25, schema.ts L21, railway.toml).

- **Login sessions** live in an in-memory Map in the server process (server.ts L28). They are lost on restart, and the server cannot scale past one instance without changes.
- **Self-hosting** means running the same server with your own `DATABASE_URL`/`BASE_URL` and pointing the CLI at it with `CCSHARE_API_URL` (README "Environment Variables").
- **Nothing is written to git.** The shared URL is pasted into a PR by hand. Issue #1 asks for git storage and has had no response (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/issues/1).
- **Local export.** `ccshare export` writes a self-contained HTML file to disk instead (README).
format_and_model:
**Upload.** The CLI sends one JSON body to `POST /api/upload`: `{encryptedBlob, iv, salt?, ownerKey?, visibility: public|private, metadata:{title, messageCount, toolCount, durationSeconds}}`. It is checked with zod (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/server.ts#L570-L645).

**Encryption.** AES-256-GCM with a 12-byte IV. The 16-byte auth tag is appended to the ciphertext and the whole thing is base64url-encoded (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/crypto.ts).

**Keys.**
- Public shares use a random 32-byte key, carried in the URL fragment: `/s/{nanoid(12)}#key=<b64url>`.
- Private shares use PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations and a 16-byte random salt. PLAN.md planned Argon2id. The code switched to PBKDF2 to match browser Web Crypto (commit 53a1968, "use PBKDF2 on server to match browser").

**Data model.** A flat table of immutable snapshot rows, one row per share. There is no event log, no hashes, no chaining and no versioning. The decrypted plaintext is a pre-rendered HTML document, not structured events. Messages carry sequential anchors `msg-0`, `msg-1`, and so on (parser.ts L84-L160; renderer.ts L348-L442).

**Deep links.** A message link looks like `/s/{id}#msg-N`. One bug, found by reading the code and not tested live: the per-message copy-link button builds `href.split('#')[0] + '#' + id`. That drops `#key=`, so a copied deep link into a public share cannot be decrypted unless the owner opens it (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/renderer.ts#L2344-L2352). The deep-link scroll is also skipped whenever the fragment contains `key=` (renderer.ts L2446).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Does not apply. Each share is a single-writer, write-once snapshot with a fresh nanoid ID. Sharing the same session again creates a new, separate row. Nothing is appended, deduplicated or merged, and two machines or agents never touch the same record (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/server.ts#L585-L645).

The only change allowed after upload is through the owner dashboard: edit the title, flip visibility, or delete. A visibility change re-encrypts the blob on the server (server.ts L281-L370). Anonymous shares cannot be deleted at all: "Anonymous sessions cannot be deleted (you don't own them)" (https://claudereview.com/privacy).
realtime: None. A share is a point-in-time snapshot made by an explicit `ccshare share`, the `/share` slash command, or the MCP tool `share_session`. A session that keeps running is not updated at the link. There is no streaming, watching, websocket or sync (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/README.md, https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/mcp/README.md).
search_retrieval:
Search only works inside one session, after it is decrypted. The viewer has a client-side full-text overlay opened with Cmd+F, plus tool navigation, collapsible outputs and a "Key Moments" summary of files touched and commands run (README "Viewer"; renderer.ts search code around L2354).

The server cannot search content, because it only holds ciphertext. There is no search across sessions. The dashboard lists a user's shares by their plaintext title and counts (`GET /api/my-sessions`, https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/server.ts#L229-L255).

Retrieval for agents is limited to the local MCP tools `list_sessions`, `share_session` and `copy_session`. `copy_session` returns a local session as Markdown. Nothing reads shared sessions back from the server (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/mcp/README.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Only loosely, and by hand.

- **Git context.** When you share, the CLI runs `git remote get-url origin`, `git branch --show-current` and `git rev-parse HEAD` in the session's project directory and renders them as repo/branch/commit links in the viewer (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/session.ts#L444-L500).
- **The commit is from share time.** It is HEAD when you share, not the commit the agent worked on. The code says so for Codex: "we'll override with fresh data". So the link can point at the wrong commit if HEAD has moved.
- **PR link.** The PR side is a URL the user pastes into the PR description. There is no GitHub App, no PR comment bot, no check run, and nothing in commit trailers or notes. PLAN.md lists "PR/commit linking" under post-MVP Phase 3, and it was never built (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/PLAN.md).
- **Diffs.** The viewer shows diff views of file edits taken from the transcript's tool calls (src/diff.ts, README "Diff View").
privacy_security:
**Encryption.** Content is encrypted on the client before upload, with AES-256-GCM (crypto.ts).

**Server access depends on the share mode:**
- **Anonymous public share:** the key sits only in the URL fragment, so the server cannot read the content.
- **Password share:** the server cannot read it at rest.
- **Signed-in public share:** the CLI sends the AES key to the server as `ownerKey` so the dashboard can open the session. The server stores it in plaintext. The privacy page says "Technically yes" claudereview can read these (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/cli.ts#L298, https://claudereview.com/privacy).

**Problems found by reading the code at 0e02433 (not tested against the live site):**
1. **Passwords reach the server.** Changing visibility from the dashboard sends `currentPassword` and the new `password` to `PATCH /api/sessions/:id`, and the server decrypts and re-encrypts there (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/src/server.ts#L281-L370). That contradicts the privacy page's claim that the key "never leaves your machine".
2. **Shared content runs as code.** The decrypted payload is HTML written by the uploader. The viewer injects its body into the claudereview.com origin and re-creates its `<script>` elements so they execute (server.ts L5150-L5170). No Content-Security-Policy header was seen on 2026-10-02, only HSTS and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (server.ts L52-L57, plus a curl of the live site). So a hostile share could run same-origin JS in a signed-in viewer's browser. That script could call cookie-authenticated endpoints such as `/api/my-sessions`, which returns that viewer's ownerKeys. I inferred this from the code and did not exploit it.
3. **Plaintext metadata.** Titles, which may be the first prompt, are stored in plaintext even for password shares (see what_is_stored).
4. **Password on the command line.** The password is passed as a CLI argument (`--private "secret"`), so it can end up in shell history or the process list (README).

**Also missing:** there is no secret or PII redaction anywhere. Grepping for redact/secret/sanitize found nothing.

**Other details:**
- API keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes.
- Login cookies are HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax.
- The view counter leaves country and city null.
- Retention is "indefinitely unless you delete them" (https://claudereview.com/privacy).
scale:
No scale claims are made. Hard limits in the code:
- Up to 100 MB per upload, stored as base64 TEXT in Postgres (server.ts L25).
- Up to 100,000 messages and 100,000 tool calls in metadata.
- Duration up to 10 days (server.ts L570-L582).

Login sessions are held in memory in one process (server.ts L28). Real use looks small: 24 npm downloads in September 2026 (https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-month/claudereview).
license: The README, package.json and the npm registry all declare MIT. A GitHub page summary read with a fetch tool also reported MIT, but at commit 0e02433 the repository tree contains no LICENSE file (`git ls-tree` found none). So MIT is declared, but no license text ships with the code (https://github.com/vignesh07/claudereview/blob/0e0243302de26770d4aa88d19c99efd05ef0d7f6/package.json, https://registry.npmjs.org/claudereview).

name: Cline Checkpoints and Task History
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Complete file state snapshots after each tool use (file edits, commands, etc.), capturing both tracked and untracked files. Checkpoint metadata includes: git ref SHA, creation timestamp, run count number, and kind (stash or commit). Session history persists across editor sessions. Conversation context (messages) is separate but can be restored alongside file state.
where_stored: Shadow git repository separate from the project's main git history. Checkpoints stored as git refs under refs/cline/checkpoints/{sessionId}/{runCount}. Persistent git index for untracked file detection at ~/.cline/checkpoint-scratch/{sha256_hash_of_cwd_and_sessionId}. Session metadata containing checkpoint history stored in session records (location varies by host: VS Code extensions, desktop app, CLI each store differently).
format_and_model: Git commit objects using two or three-parent merge commits. Two-parent stashes store (base commit, index state). Three-parent stashes add a third parent for untracked files. Metadata stored as JSON: CheckpointEntry {ref: string, createdAt: number (ms), runCount: number, kind?: 'stash' | 'commit'} and CheckpointMetadata {latest: CheckpointEntry, history: CheckpointEntry[]}. Snapshot creation uses git stash create with custom merge structure for untracked support.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer per session. No support for concurrent checkpoints within a session. Session ID namespaces prevent collisions across sessions (refs/cline/checkpoints/{sessionId}/). No merge logic; checkpoints are write-once sequential history. Each run creates at most one checkpoint, appended to history without modification of prior entries.
realtime: Checkpoints created synchronously after each tool use via beforeModel hook. Captured during agent run lifecycle before model invocation. Fire-and-forget reaping of stale scratch directories (14+ day idle sessions). Snapshots block the turn if git operations fail; degradation to HEAD commit checkpoint available if full snapshot fails.
search_retrieval: Retrieval by run count number to find checkpoint at or before a given run. History is linear list ordered by runCount. UI provides point-in-time diff view comparing latest checkpoint to current working tree. Restoration options: (1) restore files only, (2) restore task/messages only, (3) restore both. No full-text search or time-based queries; purely run-number indexed.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Session ID encoded in checkpoint ref namespace and stash message (message format: 'cline checkpoint session={sessionId} run={runCount}'). Checkpoint history stored in session metadata keyed by sessionId. Restoration plan includes session record lookup. Code state tied to specific session run count, enabling per-session state recovery.
privacy_security: Checkpoints stored only locally on the user's machine; never transmitted to network. Can be deleted via deleteCheckpointRefs which removes refs and scratch dirs. No encryption at rest. Untracked file index stored in scratch directory with 0700 permissions (user-only on Unix). Private ref namespace (refs/cline/) keeps snapshots invisible to user's normal git stash list. No redaction of file contents or paths in stored snapshots.
lesson_for_parinn: Original shadow-git checkpoint pattern. Cline pioneered this approach: storing agent-generated snapshots in a separate git repo/namespace parallel to the user's project, enabling per-run recovery without touching user commits. Stash vs commit choice optimizes for both tracked and untracked files. Three-parent merge captures complete worktree state. Key invariant: agent commits never pollute user history. Key limitation: scaling concern for very large repos; no built-in compression. Foundational design that has been forked by Roo and Kilo.

name: Cloudflare Agents SDK (Durable Objects SQLite state, State and Sessions capabilities)
status: shipped. The npm package `agents` is at 0.24.0 (latest dist-tag, published 2026-09-18), and 0.23.0 was published 2026-09-11 (https://registry.npmjs.org/agents). The repo is active and not archived: the main branch HEAD is e780214, committed 2026-10-01 (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents). The conversation store `agents/sessions` is marked "experimental". It arrived in 0.23.0, which also removed the earlier experimental memory stack, including the Postgres providers (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/agents/CHANGELOG.md). The public docs page still documents the superseded `agents/experimental/memory/session` path, so the published docs lag the code (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/sessions/).
what_is_stored: Each agent instance holds everything for one agent identity: (1) a typed state object for the agent; (2) conversation messages, kept as a tree with branches, compaction summaries, attachments and per-session config; (3) operational tables for schedules, the job queue, workflows, fibers, tool runs, MCP server registrations, resumable stream blocks and context blocks (frozen system prompt, skills); (4) any tables the app creates through `this.sql`. The SDK creates these tables itself: cf_agents_state, cf_agents_session_messages, cf_agents_session_message_chunks, cf_agents_session_compactions, cf_agents_session_config, cf_agents_session_attachment_{meta,chunks,refs}, cf_agents_session_fts, cf_agents_streams, cf_agents_stream_blocks, cf_agents_jobs, cf_agents_mcp_servers, cf_agents_context_blocks and others (CREATE TABLE statements in https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/tree/main/packages/agents/src). The docs say "Each Agent instance has an embedded SQLite database accessed via this.sql" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/agents-api/). State "Automatically saves to SQLite, survives restarts and hibernation" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/store-and-sync-state/). Sessions "stores messages. It is not a file store". Large files are expected to go to a file store such as R2: Think's Workspace spills to R2 at 1,500,000 bytes (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/sessions.md).
where_stored: server/cloud. Data sits in the private embedded SQLite database of one Cloudflare Durable Object per agent instance. Queries run synchronously in the same thread as the object. Durability comes from the Storage Relay Service, which streams the SQLite WAL to 5 followers in other data centers and confirms a write once 3 have acknowledged it. It also batches the log to object storage every 10 s or 16 MB and takes periodic snapshots (https://blog.cloudflare.com/sqlite-in-durable-objects/, Sept 26 2024). An object is placed near its first `get()` caller and "do[es] not currently change locations after they are created" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/data-location/). There is no local or offline mode. Point-in-time recovery is "not supported in local development" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/storage-api/).
format_and_model:
Relational SQLite tables plus JSON text.

State: one row in `cf_agents_state(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, state TEXT)`. The whole state object is stored as `JSON.stringify` output and written with `INSERT OR REPLACE` (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/agents/src/state/index.ts).

Sessions: `cf_agents_session_messages(session_id, id, seq, parent_id, type, role, content JSON, content_chunks, token_estimate, created_at, content_hash)`. All Sessions tables are WITHOUT ROWID, use composite primary keys and have no secondary indexes. Messages form a tree through `parent_id`, and the active leaf is the row with the highest `seq` (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/agents/src/sessions/core.ts, https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/sessions.md).
- Messages larger than the 1.5 MiB row budget are split on UTF-8 byte boundaries into continuation rows. The design states "There is no size ceiling" and "Sessions never truncates".
- Non-text media parts are moved to a content-addressed store. In the message, the payload is replaced by an `attachment:sha256:<hex>` pointer.
- `content_hash` is a SHA-256 of the stored JSON. It lets an update detect "unchanged" without a read. It is not a hash chain (core.ts).
- Compaction is "an overlay that replaces a span at read time. Original rows are never deleted" (design/sessions.md).

The store is NOT append-only: `updateMessage`, `deleteMessages` and `clearMessages` exist (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/agents/src/sessions/handle.ts). AIChatAgent keeps "destructive regeneration" and `maxPersistedMessages` retention (design/sessions.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writes never merge. Each agent is a single-writer actor: "Durable Objects are single-threaded and cooperatively multi-tasked" and globally unique by name (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/what-are-durable-objects/). Every writer (WebSocket clients, RPC callers, the agent's own code) is serialized through that one instance, and input/output gates prevent storage races (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/storage-api/).

- State: a client or the server replaces the whole JSON object, so the last writer wins. `validateStateChange()` runs synchronously before persistence and can reject an update. `onStateChanged` receives `source` ("server" or the Connection) (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/store-and-sync-state/). Readonly connections are enforced inside `setState()` (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/readonly-connections.md).
- Chat: overlapping user submits follow a `messageConcurrency` strategy: queue (default), latest, merge (collapses messages into one), drop or debounce (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/chat-agents.md). `reconcileMessages` maps optimistic client-minted IDs onto server IDs to avoid duplicate orphan rows (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/chat-shared-layer.md).
- Workspace files: last-write-wins with no locking (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/workspace.md).
- Multi-conversation: the accepted topology is one per-user hub Durable Object (catalog) plus one Durable Object per chat (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/rfc-user-chat-durable-objects.md). Moving data between objects uses `importMessage` (design/sessions.md).

There is no cross-object transaction, replication between agents, or offline fork/merge.
realtime: Yes, for clients connected to the same agent instance. `setState()` "Saves to SQLite (persistent), Broadcasts to all connected clients", then triggers `onStateChanged()`. Changes are "broadcast to all connected WebSocket clients instantly", and reads are "Immediately consistent - Read your own writes". The docs advise "Keep state small" because the full state goes to every client on every change (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/store-and-sync-state/). AIChatAgent has built-in message persistence and "Automatic resumable streaming" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/agents-api/). It uses a full-transcript client protocol (design/sessions.md). Sessions emits an in-process change feed after commit (design/sessions.md). Since 0.24.0, a Cap'n Web transport is available alongside the hibernating WebSocket (CHANGELOG.md). Real-time sync stops at the object boundary: different agents or conversations do not sync with each other except through app code or RPC.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is plain SQL through `this.sql` (template-literal queries; FTS5, JSON and math extensions are available) (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/).

Sessions search: `session.search()` uses an FTS5 virtual table with `tokenize='porter unicode61'`. The index is built lazily on the first search, backfilled from the stored message JSON, and then maintained on every write (core.ts; https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/api-reference/sessions/).

Sessions history reads:
- One recursive CTE over IDs and parents, capped at 10,000 rows. Content is then fetched in windows bounded by 50 rows and 4 MiB.
- `getRecentHistory(maxBytes)` charges each row its full stored size, including continuations and attachments.
- `getBranches()` lists alternative branches, and `getHistory({ leafId })` selects one path (design/sessions.md).

`agents/context` adds `AgentSearchProvider` and context blocks for prompt assembly (CHANGELOG.md). No built-in vector or semantic search was found in the docs read; Vectorize would be a separate Cloudflare product, which these sources do not cover.
links_sessions_to_code: Not natively. Sessions stores chat messages with no commit, branch or diff fields. `@cloudflare/shell` wraps isomorphic-git (clone, status, add, commit, push, log) over a virtual SQLite/R2 filesystem inside the agent (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/shell/src/git/index.ts), but nothing ties a commit to a message. A coding-agent RFC (Status: proposed, not shipped) would drive Claude Code inside a Cloudflare Sandbox. Under it, a per-user hub would keep a userland session table with `repo/branch/status/lastDiff` columns. Authority would be persisted in the Durable Object (the CLI session id plus a workspace checkpoint), and state would be reconciled on wake. The RFC also notes that `claude -p --resume` "cannot resume a killed turn" (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/rfc-coding-agent.md).
scale:
Marketing claim: "scaling to tens of millions of instances" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/). Per SQLite-backed Durable Object (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits/):
- 10 GB storage on the Paid plan; account storage unlimited on Paid, 5 GB on Free
- key plus value at most 2 MB
- SQL statements at most 100 KB; 100 columns; 100 bound parameters
- soft limit of 1,000 requests/s
- received WebSocket messages up to 32 MiB
- 30 s CPU per request by default, configurable to 5 min

Point-in-time recovery reaches back 30 days (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/). Sessions design figures:
- a row write costs about 1000x a row read, so a text append bills exactly one row
- history path capped at 10,000 rows
- Think hydrates 32 MiB by default
- in real transcripts, Claude Code's largest message across 82,902 messages was 481 KB (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/design/sessions.md)

Repo: about 5.7k stars and 748 forks, MIT license (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents). I found no independent benchmarks.
privacy_security:
At rest, data is encrypted with "AES-256" using LUKS. Encryption is automatic, with "Encryption keys ... managed by Cloudflare". No customer-managed keys are mentioned. Traffic uses TLS in transit (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/data-security/). Jurisdictions eu, us and fedramp restrict where an object runs and stores data, but logs leave the jurisdiction "for billing and debugging purposes" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/data-location/).

Access controls:
- Readonly connections and synchronous `validateStateChange` gate client writes (design/readonly-connections.md; store-and-sync-state docs).
- `appendMessage(msg, { source: "client" })` "sanitizes provider metadata and strips reserved metadata keys — it does not limit size". It strips ephemeral provider fields such as OpenAI `reasoningEncryptedContent` (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/sessions.md, packages/agents/src/sessions/sanitize.ts).

Missing pieces, from the sources read:
- No secret redaction and no audit of what was dropped.
- No tamper evidence: there is no hash chain or signatures.
- Recalled history is not treated as untrusted. Stored messages and context blocks are fed back to the model as-is, with no envelope.
- Point-in-time recovery means deleted data stays restorable for up to 30 days.
- The runtime is a cloud service operated by Cloudflare, so data leaves the developer's machine by design.
lesson_for_parinn: Copy the design split and the topology, not the platform. Cloudflare draws a line: "Sessions stays lossless; context shapes". Compaction is a read-time overlay over rows that are never deleted. Lossy caps live only on the read path, "where a cap can change without having destroyed the stored bytes". Media moves to a content-addressed `sha256` store before persist (design/context.md, design/sessions.md). That matches ParleyInn's I10, where projections are rebuildable from the record. Their one-actor-per-conversation layout, a single-writer Durable Object behind a per-user hub catalog (rfc-user-chat-durable-objects.md), shows that merges disappear when each session log has exactly one writer. Only the catalog has to be shared or synced. ParleyInn can get the same thing without a network: one append-only, hash-chained log per session per machine, plus a separate mergeable index. Where ParleyInn must go further: the Cloudflare store is mutable (`updateMessage`/`deleteMessages`, destructive regeneration), has no tamper chain, and puts recalled history back into prompts unenveloped. ParleyInn's I2/I6 guarantees have no counterpart there.
license: MIT (https://github.com/cloudflare/agents). The runtime it depends on (Cloudflare Workers/Durable Objects) is a proprietary hosted service. Storage billing for SQLite-backed objects begins January 2026, per https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/.

name: Cloudflare Artifacts
status: beta. Open (public) beta since 2026-10-01, Workers Paid plan only, billing from 2026-10-14. It slipped from the "early May" public-beta target in the launch post; private beta began 2026-04-16 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/platform/changelog/, https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-10-01-artifacts-open-beta/)
what_is_stored: Plain git repositories: blobs, trees, commits, refs and git notes. Cloudflare calls it "versioned storage that speaks Git" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/). The launch post says Cloudflare's own agents keep "the current state of the filesystem *and* the session history in a per-session Artifacts repo", so both prompt state and file state can be rewound "irrespective of whether there were commits" (https://blog.cloudflare.com/artifacts-git-for-agents-beta/). The post does not say how session history is encoded. Notes are the documented place for "prompts, agent attribution and other metadata"; the best-practices page adds model outputs and execution context (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/concepts/best-practices/). Auth tokens are kept separately, in KV (blog).
where_stored: On Cloudflare's servers. Each repo is one Durable Object, and git objects sit in that object's SQLite store (the sync KV API on SQLite), chunked across rows because of the 2MB row limit. Snapshots go to R2 and tokens to Workers KV (blog). The docs say repo data is replicated "synchronously across multiple data centers" and copied "asynchronously to object storage and snapshots" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/concepts/how-artifacts-works/). Since 2026-08-13 data can be pinned to the EU or the US (changelog).
format_and_model:
Standard git object model, served over smart HTTP, protocol v1 and v2. Supported features include ls-refs, shallow clones (deepen, deepen-since, deepen-relative) and have/want incremental fetch. The protocol engine is a roughly 100KB Wasm binary written in Zig with no dependencies. It implements SHA-1, zlib, delta encoding, pack parsing and smart HTTP, and calls 11 host-imported storage functions plus one streaming function. Forks keep raw deltas and base hashes beside the resolved objects (blog). The hierarchy is namespace (created implicitly) > repo; repo names are unique within a namespace (how-artifacts-works). Ways in:
- Workers binding: create, get, list, import, delete; on a repo handle info, createToken, listTokens, revokeToken, fork, log, readCommit, readTree, readBlob, readFile (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/api/workers-binding/).
- REST API: namespace, repo, fork, import, log, commit, tree, blob, file, raw and token routes (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/api/rest-api/).

Writes go through git push. No commit-write, diff, merge or notes API is documented in either the binding or REST pages, although the product page advertises diffs and search (https://www.cloudflare.com/products/artifacts/). Limits: 1 GB per repo, 32 MB per blob, 1 TB per account (can be raised), unlimited repos, and 2,000 requests per 10 s per namespace and per artifact (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/platform/limits/). A third-party write-up quotes 10 GB per repo, which conflicts with the docs (https://flaviocopes.com/cloudflare-artifacts/).
multi_writer_and_merge: The recommended pattern avoids sharing: "Create one repo for each unit of autonomous work. If you have 10,000 agents, create 10,000 repos", with names like ${agentName}-${sessionId}-${repoName}, each forked from a reviewed baseline repo (best-practices). Merging means ordinary git branch/fork plus merge done client-side; the docs mention "parallel exploration with branching and merging" (docs index), and ArtifactFS supports git merge locally (https://github.com/cloudflare/artifact-fs). Each repo is a single Durable Object, so writes to one repo are serialised. The docs say nothing about atomic ref updates, rejection of non-fast-forward pushes, or behaviour under concurrent pushes. I could not verify any of these, nor any server-side merge or conflict handling.
realtime: Nothing is live-synced. Event subscriptions arrived 2026-05-19: account-level repo.created, deleted, forked and imported, plus repo-level pushed, cloned and fetched. They are delivered to a Cloudflare Queue and consumed by a Worker or an HTTP pull consumer (https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/guides/event-subscriptions/, https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-05-19-event-subscriptions/). Latency figures are not published. Updates are push/fetch-granular, not streamed.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by git object: log (ref, limit, offset), readCommit, readTree, readBlob, and readFile by ref and path (workers-binding page). The product page lists "search" (https://www.cloudflare.com/products/artifacts/) and the launch post called search APIs "coming", but no search endpoint is documented in the REST or binding API as of 2026-10 (rest-api page). I could not verify that content or notes search exists. ArtifactFS (Go, Apache-2.0, FUSE, beta) does blobless mounts that fetch file content on demand with copy-on-write writes. Its goal is a 10-15 s start where a full clone took about 2 min (blog, https://github.com/cloudflare/artifact-fs).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, by convention rather than schema. The intended model is one repo per agent session, holding both filesystem state and session history (blog). Prompts, model outputs, attribution and execution context go into git notes on commits, which leaves the commit and working tree untouched (best-practices, blog). No notes schema, notes API, or format for the session-history record is published, so I could not verify the exact linkage format.
privacy_security: Each repo has its own bearer tokens of the form art_v1_<hex>?expires=<unix>, scoped read or write. Write is the default scope, so callers must ask for read explicitly. TTL is optional and tokens can be revoked (workers-binding, rest-api). Git remotes carry the token in the URL, e.g. https://x:${TOKEN}@<id>.artifacts.cloudflare.net/git/<repo>.git (blog). The control plane uses a separate Cloudflare API token. Guidance is short-lived tokens per agent session and read-only wherever possible (best-practices). Data can be localised to EU or US (changelog, 2026-08-13).
