- File-content search with regex (https://www.conductor.build/changelog/0.87.0-search-across-files-opencode-2-0).
- Chat summaries can be attached to new chats or forks (https://www.conductor.build/changelog/0.22.6-conversation-summaries-codex-diffs-and-custom-review-models).
Cloud:
- POST /v0/sql (and the MCP tool run_sql) runs one read-only SELECT against session_transcripts_view only. Matching is substring-based, e.g. ILIKE. There is no documented full-text, BM25 or vector search.
- Limits: 500 rows (with a truncated flag), 5 s timeout, 10,000-character query. Semicolon chaining, writes, U& escapes and any query containing "set_config" are rejected.
- Scope is the caller's org: workspaces shared with the org plus private ones shared with the caller (https://api.conductor.build/v0/openapi.json, https://www.conductor.build/docs/api/mcp).
- Exact per-message retrieval is available through GET /v0/sessions/{id}/messages and GET /v0/messages/{id}.
- The docs' own "Daily Report" recipe has an agent pull every org transcript from the last 24 h and summarize them (https://www.conductor.build/docs/api).
links_sessions_to_code:
Linkage is structural, not in commit metadata. Workspace = branch = worktree, and "Chats, diffs, PR state, and archive actions stay attached to the same workspace" (https://www.conductor.build/docs/concepts/git-worktrees).
- Per turn: a checkpoint ref captures the branch state before each agent reply, so each user turn maps to a code snapshot that can be reverted (https://www.conductor.build/docs/reference/checkpoints). Each AI response also lists the files it changed (0.25.0 changelog).
- Authorship: "The agent's commits are attributed to you." The workspace git identity defaults to the API caller's account (https://www.conductor.build/docs/api).
- What is missing: no commit trailers, git notes or session IDs in commits are documented. The public API Workspace object carries repoUrl but no branch or commit SHA. The SQL view has repo_url but no branch or commit (https://api.conductor.build/v0/openapi.json).
- Checkpoints are local-only. Whether cloud workspaces have them is not documented.
- CONDUCTOR_SESSION_ID can be sent as an X-Conductor-Session-Id header to attribute API calls to a session (https://www.conductor.build/docs/reference/environment-variables).
scale:
Vendor claims:
- "10x" user growth since January 2026, a $22M Series A, and "dozens of engineers" each at Google, Meta, Amazon, Spotify, Datadog and others (https://www.conductor.build/blog/series-a). The jobs page says $24M raised (https://www.conductor.build/markdown/join-us).
Documented limits:
- Each cloud sandbox has 8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and 32 GB of ephemeral NVMe (https://www.conductor.build/docs/cloud/cloud-computer). The 0.82.0 changelog says disk was doubled to 64 GB (https://www.conductor.build/changelog/0.82.0-conductor-mcp). Docs and changelog disagree here.
- Up to 50 GitHub repos per Cloud Computer (https://www.conductor.build/docs/cloud/cloud-computer).
- Pro allows live collaboration with up to 5 Pro users; Teams allows any size (https://www.conductor.build/markdown/pricing).
- SQL is capped at 500 rows and 5 s (OpenAPI).
No figures on transcript volume or retention size are published. The Terms allow storage-time and size limits, with automatic deletion of data beyond them (https://www.conductor.build/markdown/terms).
privacy_security:
Local:
- "For local workspaces, we don't access your chats." Model traffic goes straight to the provider (https://www.conductor.build/docs/reference/privacy).
- Local chat data "can be accessed by people and processes that can access your Mac user account". Local encryption at rest is not stated.
- Agents run unsandboxed with full user permissions. "Workspace isolation is development isolation, not a security boundary" (https://www.conductor.build/docs/faq, https://www.conductor.build/docs/concepts/git-worktrees).
- Analytics go to PostHog, including error messages, stack traces, OS and IP address (privacy page).
- An "Enterprise data privacy" switch (user setting or enterprise_data_privacy in .conductor/settings.toml) disables features that call external AI providers, such as AI chat titles and custom MCP servers. It blocks Cloud entirely (privacy page, 0.77.0 changelog).
Cloud:
- Conductor stores session inputs and outputs. Stored data "is encrypted", with no details on algorithm or key management (privacy page).
- SOC 2 Type II, with reports available via trust.conductor.build (https://www.conductor.build/markdown/pricing).
- Org secrets are injected as environment variables and hidden in the settings UI. The only safeguard against secrets reaching transcripts is the advice "don't ask an agent to print secrets into chat, build logs, or command output" (https://www.conductor.build/docs/cloud/cloud-computer). No transcript redaction or secret scanning is documented.
- New machine-launched cloud workspaces receive a workspace-scoped CONDUCTOR_API_TOKEN by default. An agent can therefore create workspaces, drive other sessions and SQL-query org transcripts. This can be opted out per user (https://www.conductor.build/docs/api).
- A routine's webhook URL is its "only credential" (https://www.conductor.build/docs/api).
- MCP OAuth uses DCR and PKCE and is scoped to mcp:tools plus one org (https://www.conductor.build/docs/api/mcp).
- Conductor injects its own system prompts (https://www.conductor.build/docs/faq).
Recent security fixes:
- Crafted Markdown could run code inside the app (https://www.conductor.build/changelog/0.85.0-sections-routines-and-a-new-model-picker).
- Shell injection via crafted branch names, clone URLs and file names. Shared cloud setup scripts used to auto-run on collaborators' Macs (https://www.conductor.build/changelog/0.87.0-search-across-files-opencode-2-0).
No untrusted-content marking of recalled transcripts is described.
lesson_for_parinn:
Conductor is a well-used product that deliberately keeps agent history out of git:
- Code moves on a branch per worktree.
- Per-turn state lives in a private local git ref, which is the code-to-turn link.
- Handoffs go in an uncommitted .context directory.
- Anything shared across machines or teammates, live, needs a hosted Postgres-backed service. Its read path for agents is an auto-injected workspace token plus a SQL view over every org transcript, with no untrusted-content envelope, redaction or integrity guarantee. Transcripts can also be destructively truncated on checkpoint revert.
Concrete lesson: keep git as the code plane and, at most, a turn-to-commit index (private refs or notes keyed by session/turn). Put the shared history record in a separate transport.
Conductor's design shows the anti-pattern ParleyInn's I2 and I6 exist to prevent. A sandboxed agent that can query and summarize other agents' transcripts by default is an automatic cross-agent injection path. ParleyInn's recall should stay pull-only, enveloped and scoped per project. Revert should append a tombstone rather than delete history.
sources: UNREACHABLE (not verified): https://blog.conductor.build/checkpointing/ (DNS no longer resolves; Wayback unreachable from this environment)
confidence: high for the documented behaviour: workspace and worktree model, .context, the cloud/local split, the API, SQL view and data model, privacy statements. Low for anything undocumented: the local on-disk format under com.conductor.app, the checkpoint ref names and mechanics, the cloud database beyond the Postgres hints in /v0/sql, and the encryption and retention specifics.

name: container-use (Dagger)
category: Sandboxed agent environments, git-backed (an MCP server and CLI that gives each coding agent a Dagger container plus its own git branch)
status: beta
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/dagger/container-use)
what_is_stored:
Status first. The README carries an "Experimental" badge and says the project is "in early development". The repo had 4.1k stars, 210 forks and was not archived when fetched (https://github.com/dagger/container-use). The latest release is v0.4.2: the releases page dates it Aug 19, and the tag's commit is dated 2025-08-15, so the year is 2025 (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/releases). There has been no release since. Main has unreleased commits up to 2026-08-12 (commit 2e43e62, https://github.com/dagger/container-use/commit/2e43e625e95216b719ec9338f4034fd3a0be2734), with long quiet gaps between Oct 2025, Feb 2026, Jun 2026 and Aug 2026.

What it stores, read from the source:

(1) Code history. Each environment is a branch named with a petname, such as "fancy-mallard". Its first commit is an empty one titled "Create environment <id>: <title>". After that, each tool call that changes something makes one commit: run_cmd, file_write, file_edit, file_delete, config and add_service. The commit message is the agent's one-sentence "explanation" argument. Only some files get committed: non-binary files under 10 MB. It skips archives, images, media, office documents, node_modules, .git, venv/.venv, env/.env, target/build/dist/.next, and *.log/*.tmp/*.cache (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/git.go).

(2) Command log, in refs/notes/container-use. This is free text appended with `git notes append` to the environment's HEAD commit. Each entry is "$ <cmd>", then "exit N" if the exit code is nonzero, then stdout and "stderr: ...". It also records "Write/Edit/Delete <file>", "Add service <name>" with the explanation, and the output of setup and install commands (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/note.go, https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/environment.go).

(3) Environment state, in refs/notes/container-use-state. This is indented JSON with these fields: created_at, updated_at, config, container, title, submodule_paths. The config holds workdir, base_image, setup and install commands, env values in plaintext, secret references and services. The container field is an opaque Dagger ContainerID, which the environment README calls the container's "LLB definition" (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/state.go, https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/README.md).

(4) Project config in .container-use/environment.json inside the user's repo, which can be checked in (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/config.go).

Not stored: I found no code that records prompts, model replies, transcripts, agent or Claude Code session ids, or file reads.
where_stored:
A separate local bare git repo, plus custom notes refs that are mirrored into the user's own repo.

- The fork is `git init --bare` at ~/.config/container-use/repos/<origin host/path>. If there is no origin, the path comes from the repo's absolute path. On Windows it lives under %APPDATA%\container-use (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/repository.go, normalizeForkPath in https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/git.go).
- Each environment's checkout is a git worktree at ~/.config/container-use/worktrees/<id>. That worktree is copied into the container at /workdir.
- The user's repo gets a remote named "container-use" that points at the local fork path. After every update, the environment's branch and both notes refs are fetched into the user's repo (propagateToGit and propagateGitNotes in git.go).
- Container layers and filesystem live in the local Dagger engine cache.
- The only push goes to the local container-use remote. The tool never pushes branches or notes to GitHub or Forgejo (every push and fetch call is in git.go).
format_and_model:
Plain git objects. The model is one branch per environment and one commit per mutating tool call. Notes are keyed by the SHA of the annotated commit.

- The log note is unstructured text. Entries are concatenated, with no per-entry timestamp or id.
- The state note is a full JSON snapshot, force-written (`notes add -f`) on HEAD at each update. That gives a state history per commit (saveState in https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/git.go).
- The notes refs are themselves git commit chains. Integrity comes only from git's object hashing; container-use adds no chain or checksum of its own.
- Commits are deliberately unsigned: the fork sets commit.gpgsign=false. They are authored under the user's identity, because the fork's config includes the user repo's .git/config through include.path (setupConfigInclude in https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/repository.go).
- A legacy state format, an array of revisions, is migrated on read (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/state.go).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Designed for many agents on one host. Each environment has its own branch and worktree. Every environment of a project shares one fork and its two global notes refs.

**Collisions and races it has hit**
- Because notes are keyed by commit, environments created from the same commit overwrote each other's state (issue https://github.com/dagger/container-use/issues/174). The fix gives every environment its own empty initial commit (PR https://github.com/dagger/container-use/pull/240; createInitialCommit in git.go).
- Parallel servers produced "cannot lock ref 'refs/notes/container-use-state'" and "unexpected end of JSON input" (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/issues/251). The fix adds gofrs/flock file locks in $TMPDIR/container-use-locks, of three types: user-repo, fork-repo and notes (PR https://github.com/dagger/container-use/pull/257; https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/flock.go). These locks only work within one host.

**How divergence is resolved**
- On the user side, notes are fetched with a non-forced refspec. If the fetch is "[rejected]", the code deletes the user's notes ref and fetches again. That is last-writer-wins, and divergent local notes are thrown away (propagateGitNotes in git.go).

**Getting work back into the user's branch**
- `merge` runs `git merge --no-ff --autostash` with hooks disabled through core.hooksPath=/dev/null, so the agent's commits and their notes survive.
- `apply` runs `git merge --squash`, which makes a fresh commit. My inference is that the notes are not carried over to it (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/repository.go).

**Gaps**
- There is no cross-machine merge, no configured notes merge strategy, and no pushing of notes.
- Possible race, inferred from the source but not tested: the lock is keyed by the user repo's path, but the fork is keyed by the origin URL. So two clones or worktrees of the same origin on one host would share a fork without sharing locks.
realtime:
Local and near-real-time only. After each mutating tool call, the commit and both notes refs are fetched into the user's repo (git.go). `container-use watch` re-runs `git log --remotes=container-use --graph` every 1 second (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/cmd/container-use/watch_unix.go). This is what backs the README's "Real-time Visibility" claim (https://github.com/dagger/container-use).

Changes made by background commands are not committed (run_cmd in https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/mcpserver/tools.go). There is no network sync, push, or subscription across machines or sandboxes. History in an ephemeral sandbox dies with ~/.config unless someone pushes it by hand.
search_retrieval:
There is no index and no search; retrieval is plain git.

- `container-use log <env>` runs `git log --notes=container-use <merge-base>..container-use/<env>`, with an optional --patch.
- `diff` runs `git diff` over the same range.
- `list` reads every branch's state note in parallel (up to 8 workers) and sorts by updated_at.
- When no environment is named, it picks one by checking ancestry with `merge-base --is-ancestor` (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/repository.go).
- Since commit 0d87ad6 (2026-08-11), the MCP tools environment_log and environment_diff return the same text to the agent (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/mcpserver/tools.go).
- Anything else depends on the user's own git log --grep or git grep.
links_sessions_to_code:
It links agent actions to code well, but does not link sessions.

- Each commit carries the agent's per-call "explanation" as its message. The command output from that call is a note on the same commit.
- The environment's title is in its initial commit (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/mcpserver/args.go, https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/repository/git.go).
- The unit is an environment, not a chat session. Any session can reopen an environment by id.
- No prompt, transcript, model or Claude Code session id is recorded.
- The link survives `merge`. It is lost with `apply` (squash) and when pushing to origin, because git does not push refs/notes/* by default and the tool never pushes them (inference from git defaults and the push calls in git.go).
scale:
I found no scale claims or benchmarks in the README, the docs or the releases (https://github.com/dagger/container-use, https://container-use.com/environment-workflow).

Structural limits, from the source:
- Every mutating call runs many git subprocesses and fetches into the user's repo.
- All notes writes for a project are serialized by one host-local lock.
- `list` opens the state note of every branch.
- `prune` deletes branches and worktrees older than 1 week by default (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/cmd/container-use/prune.go). It does not touch the notes refs, so pruned environments presumably leave dangling notes (inference).
privacy_security:
**Isolation**
- Agent commands run inside Dagger containers.
- The agent rules tell the model never to run git itself (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/rules/agent.md).

**Secrets**
- Config stores only references: op://, env://, vault:// and file://. They are resolved at run time into Dagger secret environment variables (containerWithEnvAndSecrets in https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/environment/environment.go).
- The docs claim secrets are "stripped from logs and command outputs" (https://container-use.com/secrets).
- container-use has no redaction code of its own; a grep for scrub, redact, mask and encrypt finds nothing. It relies on the Dagger engine's safeguards (https://docs.dagger.io/features/secrets).
- That scrubbing covers stdout and stderr. Files the agent writes into the workdir are committed with no redaction, though paths named env or .env and *.log files are skipped (shouldSkipFile in git.go).
- Non-secret env values sit in plaintext in the state note.

**Integrity and identity**
- There is no encryption at rest.
- Commits are unsigned (gpgsign forced off) and authored under the user's identity, so they do not show agent provenance.
- The user's git hooks are disabled for container-use's own git operations.

**Leakage on disk**
- Every git command line, including note text (that is, command output) and commit messages, is logged at INFO to $TMPDIR/container-use.debug.stderr.log with mode 0600 (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/cmd/container-use/logger.go; RunGitCommand in git.go).
- saveState writes the state JSON to $TMPDIR/.container-use-git-notes-* and never removes the file (inferred from git.go).

**Recall as an injection channel**
- environment_log returns stored raw stdout and stderr to the model without any envelope or trust marking. Stored history is therefore a direct injection channel (https://github.com/dagger/container-use/blob/main/mcpserver/tools.go).

**Recent hardening**
- A path-traversal fix in single-file export (issue #337, commit 2e43e62).
- Validation of ref and branch names (git.go).
lesson_for_parinn:
Don't use one shared, mutable git ref as the log that many writers append to. container-use sends every environment's log and state into two global notes refs keyed by code-commit SHA. That cost it three things:
- An empty commit per environment to stop notes colliding (#174, #240).
- Host-local file locks to stop ref-lock races and truncated JSON (#251, #257).
- On the user side, divergence is settled by deleting and re-fetching the ref, so the last writer wins.

None of this extends past one machine. ParleyInn should give each writer (session, agent or machine) its own append-only, hash-chained stream in its own namespace, keyed by ParleyInn's own event ids rather than by code commits. Streams should be merged by union at read time, never reconciled by deletion. A link to code should be an attribute of an event, not the key that stores it.

A second lesson: its environment_log tool replays raw command output to the model with no envelope. That is exactly the I2 hazard ParleyInn's recall envelope exists to close.

name: Context Portal MCP (ConPort), by GreatScottyMac
status: shipped. Latest release is v0.3.13, published 2025-12-31 on GitHub and PyPI. The newest commit on main is a Dependabot merge dated 2026-01-19. As of 2026-10-02 there has been no release for about 9 months, so treat it as maintained but slowing. It is not archived, but I could not check that through the GitHub API (no access), and I could not get star or issue counts.
what_is_stored:
Project context that the agent chooses to write. It does not record sessions. The tables are:
- product_context and active_context: one JSON blob each (id=1).
- product_context_history and active_context_history: on every update, the previous blob is copied in with a version number, a timestamp and a change_source string.
- decisions: summary, rationale, implementation_details and tags.
- progress_entries: status, description, and a parent_id that forms a tree.
- system_patterns: name, description, tags.
- custom_data: category and key with a JSON value. A ProjectGlossary category gets its own search tool.
- context_links: typed edges (source type/id, target type/id, relationship_type, description). These are the 'knowledge graph'.

Embeddings of decisions, progress, patterns and custom data are kept alongside. The agent writes all of this through MCP tools (log_decision, log_progress, update_active_context, and so on), driven by system prompts pasted from conport-custom-instructions/. Raw prompts, transcripts and tool calls are never captured.
where_stored:
A local DB inside the project's working tree.
- SQLite: <workspace>/context_portal/context.db by default. It can be moved with a custom DB path, or with a base path that puts per-workspace subfolders in a central directory.
- Alembic scaffolding is written into the same folder: alembic.ini and alembic/versions/2025_06_17_initial_schema.py.
- ChromaDB vector store: <workspace>/context_portal/conport_vector_data/.
- The repo's own .gitignore ignores /context_portal/, and the project gives no guidance on committing the DB to git.
- Markdown export/import (default ./conport_export/) is the only file-based way to carry data elsewhere.
format_and_model:
Relational SQLite tables, created by an Alembic migration that the server writes out and runs (upgrade to head) on first connection. Context blobs are JSON text. Tags are stored as a text column. The graph is a plain edge table with string item ids; there is no graph engine.

The model is mutable CRUD, not append-only:
- Decisions, progress, patterns and custom data can be updated in place (custom_data upserts on a unique (category, key)), and delete_*_by_id tools exist.
- Only product and active context keep version history, as pre-update snapshots.
- There is no hash chain and no content addressing. Ids are SQLite autoincrement integers, so they are local to one DB.

Embeddings are ChromaDB collections ('conport_semantic_store') made with the sentence-transformers model all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Not designed for multiple writers.
- Each server process caches one sqlite3 connection per workspace in a module-level dict. WAL is not set and no busy timeout is configured, so concurrent processes (for example two IDE agents on one workspace) depend on SQLite's default rollback-journal locking.
- There is no sync, replication or merge. Autoincrement ids would collide if two DBs were combined.
- The deep-dive document lists 'permissions and access control if data is shared' and 'real-time updates/notifications if a multi-user model were adopted' as future work. It also mentions possible 'cloud synchronization options' and a 'DatabaseID' remote-storage model as ideas, not features.
- Worktrees each get their own context_portal/ folder unless a shared base path is configured. With a shared path they share one SQLite file on the same machine, with no coordination beyond file locking.
realtime: None. It answers MCP tool calls on request, over STDIO by default or over HTTP (FastAPI/Uvicorn, /mcp, default bind 127.0.0.1:8000). There are no change notifications or subscriptions. The deep dive lists real-time multi-user updates as a future consideration.
search_retrieval:
Three ways to find things:
1. SQLite FTS5 (external-content tables kept in sync by triggers), via search_decisions_fts, search_custom_data_value_fts and search_project_glossary_fts. The mem4sprint docs list the column prefixes the FTS queries accept.
2. Semantic search over ChromaDB with MiniLM embeddings (semantic_search_conport). Indexing is best-effort and done in the handler: embedding failures are only logged, and updating a progress entry skips re-embedding (a logged warning), so the vector index can drift from the DB.
3. Structured getters (tag filters, status, a recent-activity summary, item history by version or timestamp) and graph traversal with get_linked_items.

Results go straight back to the model as tool output. They are not enveloped or marked as untrusted.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only weakly, and only by hand.
- No session ids, no prompt capture, no commit SHA or file/line anchors.
- Items link only to other ConPort items, through context_links or the progress linked_item_type/id fields.
- Code references exist only if the agent writes them into free text.
- workspace_id is the project's absolute path, found by auto-detection that looks for .git, go.mod and similar markers. That ties the DB to a directory, not to a git revision.
scale: No scale claims or benchmarks were found. It is built for one developer and one workspace on a local SQLite file.
privacy_security:
Minimal.
- No redaction, no secret scanning, no encryption at rest. SQLite and Chroma files are plaintext in the project folder.
- SECURITY.md is an unfilled template: the contact is literally [YOUR_EMAIL_ADDRESS].
- The security work in the release notes is dependency bumps: mcp>=1.23.0 for a DNS-rebinding fix, and filelock>=3.16.2 for CVE-2024-53981. v0.3.13 added MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint).
- ChromaDB runs with anonymized_telemetry=False.
- Loading SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2') by name normally downloads the model from the Hugging Face Hub on first use. That is standard sentence-transformers behaviour; I inferred it and did not observe it being run here. So the core is not network-free.
- Stored text goes back to the LLM unfiltered. The strategy prompts also tell the agent to read projectBrief.md and offer to import it, so there is a path from untrusted content to the model.
- HTTP mode binds to localhost by default.
lesson_for_parinn:
ConPort shows why a per-workspace SQLite file is not a sharing format. The DB sits in a gitignored folder inside the project, so it does not follow a project across worktrees, machines or sandboxes. Its rows can be changed and deleted, and their autoincrement ids are local to one file, so two copies cannot be merged. The only way to carry data elsewhere is a lossy Markdown export/import.

ConPort also lets its derived vector index drift. Embedding failures are only logged, and re-embedding on update is skipped. That breaks the 'rebuildable from the record' property.

For ParleyInn this means:
- Use SQLite only as a local, rebuildable projection (FTS5 kept in sync by triggers is fine), never as the thing that is transported.
- Transport and merge an append-only, content-addressed event log whose ids are globally unique (hash-based, not autoincrement), so copies from different worktrees or machines can be combined without conflicts.
- Rebuild FTS and vector indexes deterministically from that log, and audit any indexing failure (I6, I10) instead of only logging it.
- Ship any embedding model with ParleyInn or make it opt-in, because a lazy model download would break I4.

name: Corrosion
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Distributed mutable state for service discovery across global clusters. Each node runs a SQLite database with CR-SQLite CRDT extensions. Stores application tables, internal CRDT metadata (crsql_changes virtual table with column versions, db versions, causal length), and subscriptions state. Can propagate state from Consul services into the cluster. Data model is normalized SQL schema defined via CREATE TABLE/INDEX statements with optional CRDT backing per table.
where_stored: Each node maintains its own SQLite database file (configurable path, default /var/lib/corrosion/db.sqlite). Per-subscription state stored in separate SQLite databases under a subscriptions directory (default /var/lib/corrosion/subscriptions/). No centralized storage; gossip-based replication propagates changes. Data persists locally on disk; no encryption at rest implemented.
format_and_model: SQLite 3 with CR-SQLite extension (https://github.com/vlcn-io/cr-sqlite) for CRDTs. Uses two CRDT strategies: Causal-Length and Last-Write-Wins (LWW). Each change tracked in crsql_changes table with: table name, primary key, column ID, value, col_version (per-column increment), db_version (per-transaction), site_id (actor/node ID), sequence ordering. Rows can be marked CRDT-backed via crsql_as_crr() function on a per-table basis.
multi_writer_and_merge: Automatic multi-writer support via CR-SQLite. Conflict resolution uses deterministic 'largest write wins': (1) col_version comparison first, (2) lexicographic value comparison if versions tie, (3) site_id as tiebreaker. All writes route through Corrosion HTTP API to ensure CRDT invariants. No manual conflict resolution required. Merges are automatic on change ingestion via crsql_changes INSERT.
realtime: Real-time via HTTP streaming subscriptions. POST /v1/subscriptions accepts SQL query, returns Newline Delimited JSON stream of: {columns}, {row} events, {eoq} (end of query marker with change_id), and {change} events (insert/update/delete with row_id). Clients can resume from change_id parameter. GET /v1/subscriptions/{id} re-subscribes to existing query. Changes streamed to subscribers immediately as they propagate through cluster.
search_retrieval: Standard SQL query API via HTTP POST /v1/queries with JSON body containing SQL statement and optional parameters. PostgreSQL wire protocol (v3) compatible for read-only access. SQLite full capabilities available (WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, JOINs, subqueries). FTS5 full-text search available via SQLite extension but not explicitly documented. Query results paginated via NDJSON events. No built-in search indexing or specialized retrieval beyond SQL.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Corrosion is designed for distributed service discovery and general state management on Fly.io infrastructure. No concept of agent sessions, prompts, code snapshots, or session linking. Could theoretically be used as a backend IF application code manages session-to-code mappings, but no native support.
privacy_security: Peer-to-peer QUIC encryption (UDP-based) between cluster nodes using TLS with configurable CA, server cert, key. Optional mutual TLS (mTLS) for client authorization. Plaintext mode available for development/wrapped transport. No encryption at rest on disk. No built-in data redaction, masking, or secrets handling. TLS supports both IPv4/IPv6 mixed clusters. No audit logging of data access.
lesson_for_parinn: CR-SQLite's automatic Last-Write-Wins merge with column versioning is elegant for distributed mutable state but fundamentally mismatched to ParleyInn's needs. ParleyInn requires append-only immutable records to prevent untrusted content (I2) and enable exact historical recall (I8); Corrosion trades away history for eventual consistency. The per-node local database pattern is good (fast reads <1ms locally vs 300ms remote), but Corrosion resolves conflicts destructively (smaller updates lose), while ParleyInn must preserve every decision. The streaming subscription model with resumable change IDs is valuable—ParleyInn could learn from that pattern for re-injecting recall blocks after compaction. Key difference: Corrosion mutates state in-place; ParleyInn appends immutably.

name: Crush (Charm)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Full agent conversation state per project. Sessions: id (UUID), parent_session_id (sub-agent and child sessions), title, message_count, prompt/completion tokens, cost, summary_message_id, todos, channel, timestamps. Messages: id, session_id, role, parts (a JSON array of typed parts: text, reasoning, image URL, binary, tool_call, tool_result, finish, shell command), model/provider, is_summary_message, timestamps. A files table holds full-content snapshots of every file the agent touched, versioned per (path, session, version). A read_files table records which paths each session read and when. There are also MCP enabled/disabled tables. A global projects.json lists every project path with its data_dir and last_accessed time. Sources: initial migration and later migrations in internal/db/migrations, internal/message/content.go, internal/projects/projects.go, all checked at main commit 92aab5e (2 Oct 2026).
where_stored: A local SQLite DB at <project>/.crush/crush.db. The data_directory option overrides the path, and Crush looks for the closest existing .crush within the project boundary. A crush.lock flock file sits next to the DB. The global projects.json registry is in the global data dir (e.g. ~/.local/share/crush or $CRUSH_GLOBAL_DATA). Crush writes a .gitignore with '*' (re-including only skills/) into .crush, so session history is deliberately kept out of git. No server or cloud copy. Sources: internal/db/connect.go, internal/config/config.go (defaultDataDirectory=".crush"), internal/cmd/gitignore/default, the codeburn provider doc.
format_and_model: Relational SQLite in WAL mode (synchronous=NORMAL, foreign_keys=ON, secure_delete=ON, busy_timeout=30s). Schema migrations use goose; queries are generated by sqlc. Rows are mutable: UpdateMessage overwrites a message's parts JSON in place while it streams, and sessions/messages are deletable with ON DELETE CASCADE. Triggers keep updated_at and message_count current. Timestamps are Unix seconds, so ordering within one second is ambiguous; the code itself notes this in ListMessagesBySessionFromSummary. Compaction does not destroy history: it inserts a summary message, sets sessions.summary_message_id, and later prompts send only messages from the summary onward. Session IDs are UUIDs, shown to users as an xxh3 hash prefix (git-style short ids). There is no hashing or chaining for integrity. Sources: internal/db/connect.go, internal/db/sql/messages.sql, internal/session/session.go.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer per database. Inside one process, every access goes through one shared, refcounted connection. The code comment says this is because interleaved pool connections under concurrent sub-agents caused 'WAL/header desync'. Across processes, the server path takes an exclusive non-blocking flock on .crush/crush.lock and refuses a second crush process with ErrDataDirLocked. Local mode does not take the lock by default, until client/server becomes the default. There is no merge, sync or replication between machines or worktrees: each checkout or data dir is its own island. projects.json is a JSON file rewritten under a process-local mutex. Sources: internal/db/connect.go, internal/db/datadirlock.go, internal/projects/projects.go.
realtime: Yes, on one machine, through an opt-in client/server mode. With CRUSH_CLIENT_SERVER=1, the TUI auto-starts a detached 'crush server' process (the command is 'server', not 'serve'). It listens by default on a per-user Unix socket ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/crush-<uid>.sock, or a named pipe on Windows); TCP is also accepted. Multiple clients that open the same path share one deduplicated workspace and one DB. They read sessions and history over an HTTP/2 REST API (/v1/workspaces/{id}/sessions, .../history, .../messages) and get live updates from an SSE stream (/v1/workspaces/{id}/events), which carries pubsub events for sessions, messages, permissions and files. The server shuts down after an idle linger. Nothing crosses machines unless you expose TCP yourself. Sources: internal/cmd/root.go (useClientServer), internal/server/server.go, internal/server/endpoints.go, internal/backend/backend.go.
search_retrieval: Minimal. The SQL layer has list and get queries only: messages by session, from the latest summary on, user messages, the last assistant message, and usage stats by day, model, hour and tool. There is no FTS5 and no LIKE search over content. The CLI offers 'crush session list/show/last/delete/rename' with --json, addressed by UUID, full hash or hash prefix. Agents can also read Crush's own logs through a crush_logs tool. I found no semantic or vector recall. Sources: internal/db/sql/*.sql, internal/cmd/session.go.
links_sessions_to_code: Indirectly, and only locally. The DB lives inside the project directory. The files table stores per-session versioned snapshots of the contents of files the agent edited, and read_files records which paths each session read. The server exposes the current git branch (/v1/workspaces/{id}/git/branch). I found no record of commit SHAs, no git notes or trailers, and no link from a commit back to a session. Because .crush is gitignored, the history never travels with the code. Sources: internal/history/file.go, the read_files migration, internal/server/endpoints.go, internal/cmd/gitignore/default.
scale: No scale claims for session storage. The README's 'powering 25k+ applications' refers to the wider Charm ecosystem, not to Crush storage. The design is one SQLite file per project with one connection, and storing full file snapshots per version suggests growth tied to how much the agent edits. Unverified: GitHub API access was blocked in this session, so I could not get star or release metadata. The repo is active, with its latest commit on 2026-10-02.
privacy_security: Local only, with no encryption at rest: plain SQLite, and the data dir is created 0700. secure_delete=ON overwrites deleted content in the DB file. Prompts, tool outputs and full file contents are stored verbatim with no redaction. Redaction exists only in the crush_logs tool, which masks sensitive keys in logs shown to the agent. Keeping .crush gitignored stops accidental commits of history. The server's Unix socket is per-uid in the user runtime dir. I saw no authentication on the HTTP API, so a TCP listener would be unauthenticated (inferred from server.go; not confirmed in docs). Recalled history is fed back to the model as trusted context; there is no untrusted-content envelope. License: FSL-1.1-MIT, a source-available license that converts to MIT after two years, not OSI open source. Sources: internal/db/connect.go, internal/agent/tools/crush_logs.go, internal/server/server.go, LICENSE.md.
lesson_for_parinn: A per-repo SQLite with one serialized writer, plus a local daemon fanning out over SSE, is enough for live sharing between agents on one machine. ParleyInn should copy two pieces of it: the flock-guarded single-writer DB (Crush hit WAL corruption when sub-agents wrote through multiple connections) and the summary-pointer compaction that keeps everything. It should avoid Crush's mutable rows and seconds-resolution timestamps. Messages are rewritten in place during streaming, and ordering inside one second is ambiguous, so neither the record nor its order can be checked after the fact. ParleyInn should instead append immutable, sequence-numbered, hash-chained events, and keep the 'gitignore the store' default: the store stays local, and anything shared across machines goes out only as an explicit, signed export.
license: FSL-1.1-MIT (Functional Source License 1.1, MIT Future License)

name: Crystal (stravu/crystal), deprecated and replaced by Nimbalyst
category: Parallel agent session manager. It is an Electron desktop app that runs Claude Code and Codex CLI sessions in separate git worktrees.
status: archived
what_is_stored:
Everything is kept per project and per session in one local SQLite database, on a single machine. The tables are:
- projects: path, name, custom prompt, run script.
- sessions: name, initial prompt, worktree_name, worktree_path, status, pid, exit_code, the agent's own resume id (claude_session_id), archived flag.
- session_outputs: every raw JSON message streamed by the agent CLI, stored as-is, plus stdout and stderr.
- conversation_messages: user and assistant turns.
- prompt_markers: each prompt's text, its position in the output, and start and finish times.
- execution_diffs: per prompt run, the full git diff, files changed, line stats, before and after commit hashes, and the commit message.
- tool_panels and claude_panel_settings: per-panel JSON state, including the Claude resume id and the Codex agentSessionId.
- migrations.
Source for the table list: https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/docs/DATABASE_DOCUMENTATION.md. Source for the base schema: https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/database/schema.sql. Panel and diff migrations live under https://github.com/stravu/crystal/tree/main/main/src/database/migrations (003_add_tool_panels.sql, 004_claude_panels.sql, add_execution_diffs.sql, add_commit_message_to_execution_diffs.sql).
App settings go in config.json, including anthropicApiKey and the analytics settings (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/services/configManager.ts). Logs go to ~/.crystal/logs (main/src/index.ts line 705). The agent CLIs also keep their own transcripts, for example under ~/.claude. Crystal stores only the resume id and calls `claude --resume <id>` (main/src/services/panels/claude/claudeCodeManager.ts lines 107-118).
where_stored:
A local database file, plus checkpoint commits in the working tree.
- The database is ~/.crystal/sessions.db, a SQLite file opened with better-sqlite3. CRYSTAL_DIR or a programmatic override can move it, and dev builds use ~/.crystal_dev (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/utils/crystalDirectory.ts, https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/services/database.ts).
- The docs disagree with the code. DATABASE_DOCUMENTATION.md says ~/.crystal/crystal.db; the code opens sessions.db.
- config.json sits in the same directory.
- Code changes stay in ordinary git worktrees, by default at <project>/worktrees/<name> or at an absolute folder you configure (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/services/worktreeManager.ts lines 45-60). In checkpoint mode they become ordinary commits on the session branch (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/services/commitManager.ts).
- No session history goes into git: no notes, no custom refs, no separate repo. No session history goes to a server either.
format_and_model:
The data model is relational SQLite. A project has many sessions. A session has many panels, outputs, conversation messages, prompt markers and execution diffs. Child rows carry session_id and, after migration 004, panel_id; deleting a session cascades to its rows.
- Agent output is kept as raw JSON or text in TEXT columns. Formatting is applied when the output is read, never when it is stored (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/docs/SESSION_OUTPUT_SYSTEM.md).
- Panel state is a JSON string column.
- Schema changes are ad-hoc SQL migration files, tracked in a migrations table.
- The record has no hashing, no signing, and no append-only guarantee. Rows are mutable and are deleted by cascade.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is one writer: one Electron main process on one machine owns the database through synchronous better-sqlite3 calls. The code sets no WAL or busy_timeout pragma; a grep found none in main/src.
- Parallel agents are separated at the code level, not the history level. Each session gets its own worktree and branch. Since 0.3.4, several agents can share one worktree (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
- Code is merged with plain git operations from the UI: rebase from main, squash with `reset --soft` and commit, and "merge and archive" (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/docs/CRYSTAL_ARCHITECTURE.md, CHANGELOG 0.3.4).
- Session history itself is never merged or synced across machines or users.
realtime: Agent stdout JSON is written to SQLite as soon as it arrives. It is streamed to the renderer over IPC in two forms, formatted and raw. The database stays the single source of truth, and switching sessions reloads from it (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/docs/SESSION_OUTPUT_SYSTEM.md). The doc itself warns that this path is "complex and fragile", prone to duplicate or disappearing messages. Real-time behaviour is local UI only; nothing is shared between machines or people.
search_retrieval: There is no full-text or semantic search over history: no FTS5 table appears in the schema or migrations. Retrieval works by session_id and panel_id through B-tree indexes (session_id, timestamp, execution_sequence). prompt_markers let the UI jump to a prompt inside a long output. The model resumes its context only through the agent's own resume id (`claude --resume`, or the stored Codex session id); Crystal does not re-inject anything itself.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, partly.
- execution_diffs links each prompt (prompt_marker_id) to the git diff it produced, with before_commit_hash and after_commit_hash (add_execution_diffs.sql).
- In "checkpoint" commit mode, the worktree is committed after every prompt with `git add -A`. The message is "checkpoint: " plus the prompt text cut to 50 characters, and by default a footer is added: "Built using Crystal" plus "Co-Authored-By: Crystal <crystal@stravu.com>" (commitManager.ts lines 86-110, main/src/utils/shellEscape.ts).
- So the link from session to code lives in the local database. Git sees only a truncated prompt and a trailer, with no pointer back to a session id.
privacy_security:
Crystal does almost nothing to protect stored history.
- Not encrypted at rest: full prompts, agent outputs and diffs sit in plain SQLite.
- No redaction: a grep for redact or sanitize in main/src found nothing.
- No integrity protection.
- The API key may be in plain text. DATABASE_DOCUMENTATION.md says the anthropicApiKey in the config store is "encrypted", but the configManager code writes it to config.json with JSON.stringify, and I found no safeStorage call. I could not confirm that it is encrypted.
- Checkpoint commits run `git add -A` and pass `--no-verify`, which skips pre-commit hooks such as secret scanners. Anything the agent writes to the worktree, secrets included, can end up in a commit.
- Isolation is only at the worktree and process level (CRYSTAL_ARCHITECTURE.md, "Security & Isolation").
- Analytics are PostHog, opt-in (default false), and send hashed session ids (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/main/src/services/analyticsManager.ts, configManager.ts line 211, https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/docs/FEATURE_USAGE_TRACKING_INTEGRATION.md).
- Recalled content is not treated as untrusted. It is only shown in the UI and is not re-injected.
scale: The project makes no scale claims. Its design limits it to one user on one machine with one SQLite file. The GitHub page shows about 3.1k stars (https://github.com/stravu/crystal, fetched 2026-10-02).
license: MIT (https://github.com/stravu/crystal/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn:
Crystal is the plain baseline: a private SQLite record per machine, plus per-prompt checkpoint commits. It shows two traps.
1. The link from session to code lives only in the local database. Git gets a truncated prompt and a vendor trailer with no stable session id, so the history cannot follow the code to another worktree, machine or sandbox. ParleyInn should give every commit a content-addressed session or event id, for example a trailer or a note that points into ParleyInn's hash-chained record, so the link survives any transport.
2. Auto-committing agent output with `git add -A --no-verify` sends unredacted content, possibly secrets, into a channel that is pushed and shared. ParleyInn must redact and audit before anything leaves the local record (I6), and must never skip the user's hooks.
A smaller point: Crystal's docs and code disagree on the database file name and on whether the API key is encrypted. That is the kind of drift ParleyInn's drift tests are meant to catch.

name: ctx (ctxrs/ctx)
category: Local session index plus commit blame. It also ships a code graph (ctx graph), a tool-output compactor (ctx sift), and, since 2026-09-30, an opt-in beta server for sharing history.
status: shipped. Actively developed and not archived. HEAD d0885f4 is dated 2026-10-01, Cargo.toml says version 2.2.6, and the newest changelog entry is 2.2.3 (2026-09-30). The hosted sharing server is beta: it arrived in 2.2.0 on 2026-09-30.
what_is_stored:
Normalized copies of transcripts that coding agents already wrote. Covered agents include Claude Code (~/.claude), Codex (~/.codex), Cursor, Gemini CLI, Pi, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Factory Droid and many more. ctx converts each provider's JSONL, document/tree or SQLite format into common records: sessions, messages/events, tool calls with complete decoded JSON arguments and results ("activity"), parent/subagent/fork relationships, and repository/file/VCS evidence. Every session and event gets a stable ctx ID (ses_/evt_) and keeps its source identity. Derived stores sit beside the records:
- optional local embeddings (flat-F32 vectors with no plaintext chunks)
- a Blame attribution index holding repository facts plus citations into Core, not a second transcript copy
- content-free daily usage counts in usage.sqlite
- for ctx graph, a SQLite code graph at .graf/index.db in the project

ctx never writes to provider history or to source repositories. It has no hooks inside the agent process. It writes nothing to git: no notes and no trailers (I grepped the source).

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/storage.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs-content/concepts/how-it-works.mdx
where_stored:
A local DB/index under the ctx data root: ${CTX_DATA_ROOT:-~/.ctx}, with search/lexical (Tantivy), search/semantic, search/attribution, usage.sqlite and config.toml. Provider files stay where they are and act only as read-only sources. Optional extras:
- portable archive exports, which you back up with restic or similar
- a self-hosted ctx server (beta) with its own directory: SQLite for permissions and accepted uploads, immutable files for retained history, and a Tantivy index for search. The default listen address is 127.0.0.1:7332, meant to sit behind your own HTTPS reverse proxy.

Git is not used to store or transport anything. (https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/storage.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/hosted-history.md)
format_and_model:
The index is the store. Instead of loading data into SQLite first, parallel workers write complete normalized records straight into Tantivy, which keeps full stored records next to a BM25 inverted index. The project claims this indexes 16x faster than its earlier SQLite pipeline (9.65 s vs 155 s cold).

Data is published as immutable, verified "Core generations". An update is fully built, checked against a manifest and integrity receipts, and then switched in atomically, so readers never see half an index. Readers pin one generation. ctx keeps the active generation plus one previous one, merges Tantivy segments after 16 comparable segments, and expunges a segment once more than 25% of its documents are deleted.

Core is treated as disposable derived data. When the format changes, ctx rebuilds from the provider sources and does not migrate. The semantic and attribution indexes are tied to a Core generation and can lag behind it.

Per event, body plus structured content plus activity share a 16 MiB budget. Anything too large gets an explicit "omitted" state rather than being truncated.

The model is mutable in one respect: when a provider file is rewritten, the old documents are marked deleted and replaced. That makes it a snapshot index of whatever the providers' logs currently say, not an append-only or hash-chained log.

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/storage.md
multi_writer_and_merge:
Locally there is one writer: the daemon or an explicit import publishes generations under a native writer lock, while query processes only read and may send a content-free wake to the daemon. The threat model assumes no other process running as the same OS user tampers with the data root.

Several machines or people can only combine history through the opt-in beta server:
- Each device publishes sessions it has been told to share into a collection. The default "reviewed" mode allows only the exact current revisions; "automatic" mode can include future ones. Uploads queue offline.
- Collections carry separate read, publish and manage rights.
- A corrected session replaces the current searchable version. Earlier citations stay readable until the publication is explicitly withdrawn.

There is no CRDT and no merge of concurrent edits. Each publisher's sessions remain separate provenance-tagged revisions. The docs say there is no multi-node replication and no zero-data-loss guarantee, and that restoring a checkpoint does not reconcile later changes. (https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/hosted-history.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/threat-model.md)
realtime:
Near-real-time on one machine, but not streaming:
- A daemon (systemd user unit, launchd agent or Windows scheduled task) runs by default, follows provider history as it changes and publishes new generations.
- Search defaults to --refresh background: it answers from the active generation and lets the daemon catch up. --refresh wait forces a foreground refresh.
- The docs give no latency figure for local refresh.

For sharing, the daemon picks up a saved share policy within 30 seconds and retries offline uploads. There is no push or subscription across machines. (https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs-content/concepts/how-it-works.mdx ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/hosted-history.md)
search_retrieval:
- **Lexical search:** BM25 is the default. It takes multiple --term flags plus filters such as --file, --session, source root and source group.
- **Semantic search (optional):** an embedding model runs locally on ONNX Runtime and needs no API key or vector DB. You can configure an external semantic executor instead, which sends text to that endpoint.
- **Retrieval:** search returns ctx IDs and snippets. `ctx show event <id> --window N` and `ctx show session <id>` fetch exact stored records, and `ctx locate` returns where a record came from. None of these reopen the provider files.
- **Self-indexing exclusion:** records that consist only of ctx's own retrieval output are kept for show but left out of ranking.
- **Interfaces:** an MCP server, SDKs (TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, JVM, Swift, .NET) and an agent skill.
- **Token claim:** about 917 tokens per search vs 45,734 for raw transcript grep, which the project describes as roughly 50x.

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/storage.md
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, and this is the standout feature: `ctx blame file <path> --lines A:B`, `ctx blame commit <sha>` and `ctx blame pr <url>`, also exposed as an MCP blame tool.

The link is derived after the fact from the transcript alone. Nothing is recorded at commit time.
- **Commit IDs:** ctx's repository-evidence code reads the agent's recorded `git commit`, merge and cherry-pick tool results. For example, it takes the `[branch abc1234] subject` line and keeps a candidate only when exactly one is unambiguous. Amend and rebase mappings are carried over when the tool-call evidence supports them.
- **Repository identity:** it comes from cwd, tool workdir, file activity and remotes, and is then certified against local git objects. SHA-1 and SHA-256 repos and linked or moved worktrees are handled.
- **Abstentions:** typed reasons such as Ambiguous, DynamicPath, HistoryRewriteUnlinked, ConcurrentDrift and GitProbeFailed.
- **Result classes:** proven production, possible attribution, conflicting records, and missing evidence. A session that merely mentions a commit or PR does not count as producing it. If a teammate's session is not on your machine, ctx says it cannot prove the attribution.
- **No forge access:** a PR URL is only a selector and is never fetched.

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/blame.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/crates/ctx-repository-evidence/README.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/crates/ctx-repository-evidence/src/outcome.rs
scale:
From the project's own claims, not independently verified:
- Cold indexing in 9.65 s with Tantivy vs 155.09 s with its previous SQLite pipeline, corpus not specified.
- About 50x fewer tokens than raw transcript search.
- ctx graph on the 19,036-file VS Code repo: 13 ms search vs 13.26 s for Graphify, on an M1 Mac mini.
- Sift adds at most 1.35 ms of overhead and cuts tool output by 43% (v0.4.0 benchmark).

Documented storage bounds: worst-case peak storage is about 3.67x to 5x the deletion-free index footprint while compacting, and manifests and pages are capped at 16 MiB each.

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/storage.md
privacy_security:
Search content is local by default: "No session text, prompts, or transcripts leave this machine by default", and an optional local-only security mode turns off network use.

**There is no redaction.** The README says transcript text is preserved rather than automatically redacted. The threat model lists secrets in indexed prompts and output as a risk and mitigates it only by telling users to treat output as private.

**There is no encryption at rest.** The local indexes, the attribution index, server storage and checkpoints are plaintext. The docs point to encrypted disks and restic.

Measures that do exist:
- owner-private files with no-follow and non-symlink checks
- the supervisor environment file is mode 0600
- provider SQLite is opened only as short read-only snapshots
- unknown provider formats are rejected
- bounded, non-executing static parsing of shell commands
- duplicate-key-rejecting JSON parsing
- remote evidence is treated as "untrusted historical content" that cannot authorize commands, path reads or new sharing
- the server has per-collection rights, single-use invitations that expire in 15 minutes, revocation and withdrawal

**The discovery note's "everything stays local" needs qualifying.**
- CLI product analytics are on by default. They are content-free and allowlisted, and are sent to https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v1/analytics. Raw telemetry is currently not auto-deleted. Opt out with `[analytics] enabled=false` or `CTX_ANALYTICS_ENABLED=false`.
- Auto-upgrade is on by default.
- There are optional network features: an external semantic executor, the Jev selector in sift, and the hosted server.

Sources: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/SECURITY.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/threat-model.md ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs-content/legal/privacy-policy.mdx ; https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/docs/hosted-history.md
lesson_for_parinn:
Link sessions to code from evidence the record already holds, never by writing to git, and abstain with a typed reason when the proof is incomplete. ctx shows that blame for commits, line ranges and PRs works with no hooks, notes or trailers. It reads the commit OID from the recorded `git commit` tool result, certifies it against local git objects, and reports "cannot prove" as a reason code rather than guessing, which fits ParleyInn's I6.

ParleyInn can do better on trust:
- ctx scrapes `[branch sha] subject` out of tool output, which is untrusted text that an agent or the command itself could forge.
- ParleyInn's hooks can capture the HEAD OID before and after each tool call into a trusted, hash-chained field. Blame then becomes a lookup in the record.
- Any linkage parsed from content would stay untrusted and enveloped.

ctx also gets no git transport for free. Its cross-machine story is a separate opt-in HTTP server, and its index is a mutable snapshot of provider logs, not an append-only chain. That suggests git and forges are a poor fit as ParleyInn's transport too, and that ParleyInn's append-only record is a real point of difference.
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/LICENSE ; Cargo.toml license = "Apache-2.0"). The GitHub page shows about 1.1k stars and 72 forks as of 2026-10-02 (https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx).

name: ctxmem
category: in-repo git-native memory (Python CLI + MCP server)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Hand-written or agent-written memory records, not transcripts. Each record has a type: note, decision, session, todo, or map. `ctxmem map` adds a map record holding the repo structure and its Python import map. Each record carries id, ts, type, branch, commit, path, file_hash, title, content, tags and supersedes (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/src/ctxmem/cli.py, cmd_remember; https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/src/ctxmem/mcp_server.py, remember). The derived index also holds code symbols (functions and classes) taken from the working tree (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2-4). A "session" record is a free-text summary that someone chooses to save. Nothing captures prompts or transcripts automatically. Saving relies on an instruction block that tells the agent to remember. The guide says this makes saving "reliable, not guaranteed" (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/GUIDE.md, "Reality check").
where_stored: In the working tree. `.ctxmem/memory.jsonl` and `.ctxmem/config.json` are committed to git and are the source of truth. `.ctxmem/index.db` (SQLite FTS5 plus an optional sqlite-vec table) and `.ctxmem/emb_cache.db` are gitignored, local and rebuildable (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2). No server, no git notes, no custom refs. Git is the only transport: "No server: nothing to host, nothing to sync — git *is* the transport" (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/GUIDE.md, Sharing with your team).
format_and_model: JSONL: one JSON object per line, appended with `json.dumps` (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/src/ctxmem/store.py, append_jsonl). The id is the first 12 hex characters of a uuid4. ts is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp. branch and commit come from `git rev-parse` at write time. file_hash is the SHA-256 of the file in `path` at save time (store.py file_hash; gitinfo.py). Corrections are append-only: a new record names the old id in `supersedes`. Recall then demotes the old record and flags it "⚠ SUPERSEDED". Nothing is edited in place (store.py supersede_index). Staleness is computed at read time, never stored. A record is flagged STALE when its `path` is missing, unreadable, or has different bytes from the saved fingerprint (fingerprinting arrived in v2.1.0, commit "check stale memory based on code", https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/commit/2939efb; https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/GUIDE.md, "Detecting changes to a memory's source file"). The format has no hash chain, no author or agent identity field, no signature and no schema version. The index is a single FTS5 virtual table `mem`. A sync rebuilds it by replaying the JSONL and rescanning the code (store.py init_schema).
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple writers are handled entirely by git's ordinary text merge. The repo ships no merge driver and no `.gitattributes` `merge=union` rule; the tree contains no `.gitattributes` file. The guide claims "append-only lines merge cleanly; conflicts are rare" (GUIDE.md). I tested git's default 3-way merge locally: two branches that each append one line to the end of the same JSONL file produced "CONFLICT (content)". So in practice concurrent writers conflict at end-of-file, and someone has to resolve it by hand (keep both sides). Within one checkout there is no file locking around the append (store.py append_jsonl opens the file in "a" mode). Records are branch-aware: each branch carries its own lines, and switching branch changes what recall sees (GUIDE.md). Because ids are random, merged branches do not collide on ids. If two branches each supersede the same id, both successors survive, and supersede_index keeps whichever it reads last as "superseded_by".
realtime: None. Teammates see memory only after commit, push and pull. A post-commit hook (`ctxmem hook install`, which writes .git/hooks/post-commit) rebuilds only the local index after each commit (GUIDE.md "Auto-sync with a git hook"; cli.py cmd_hook). Nothing streams between agents, worktrees or machines.
search_retrieval:
There are three modes (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5):
- `keyword` is the default: SQLite FTS5 with every query token quoted, OR'd together and ranked by bm25 (store.py _fts_query and search).
- `semantic` uses local Ollama embeddings (nomic-embed-text) with sqlite-vec KNN. Embeddings are cached by the SHA-256 of their content.
- `hybrid` merges the two. If Ollama is unavailable it falls back to keyword automatically.

The commands built on this are:
- `ask` returns a HIT, WEAK or MISS verdict. A keyword HIT needs at least 50% overlap with the meaningful query tokens (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/src/ctxmem/retrieval.py).
- `context --budget N` (v2.1.0, https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/commit/f6c0a61) packs whole records under a token budget. Active decisions come first, then other memories, then code and maps, then stale records. Superseded records are excluded, and records are never truncated or summarized (GUIDE.md "Context within a token budget").

Agents reach all of this through MCP tools recall, ask, context, remember and memory_status over stdio (mcp_server.py), or through a CLI protocol block that `agent-init` writes. agent-init targets Copilot (.github/copilot-instructions.md) and Codex (AGENTS.md). It has no Claude Code-specific target, though any MCP client can use the server (README).
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, and only by metadata. Each record stores the branch and short commit hash at write time, plus an optional repo-relative `path` with its SHA-256 fingerprint. That fingerprint drives the STALE check (cli.py cmd_remember; GUIDE.md). Records do not link to a specific prompt, tool call or transcript. Nothing links a commit back to the memory or session that produced it.
scale: The project claims a benchmark on the Django tree: about 2,900 Python files and about 45k indexed symbols. With 13 answerable questions, context tokens fell from 272,354 to 14,028 (19.4x) and premium requests from 49 to 13 (3.8x), measured with tiktoken cl100k_base (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §7). The FAQ says the keyword index is "fine for large repos" and that semantic sync is incremental (README FAQ). These are self-reported and I did not reproduce them. They measure code retrieval, not scale of the memory log. The project's own memory.jsonl has 39 lines. I found no claims about many writers or large logs.
privacy_security: It is local-only, with no network calls except to a local Ollama endpoint the user configures. The MCP server uses stdio and opens no socket (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/SECURITY.md, Threat model). It has no redaction, no secret scanning and no encryption. SECURITY.md leaves this to the user: "Never store secrets, credentials, tokens, or personal data in a memory — the JSONL is committed to git", and lists secrets a user stored on purpose as out of scope. SECURITY.md says to "Treat memory content coming from an untrusted repository as untrusted input." The code does not do that. Recalled text goes back to the agent without a trust envelope, and the injected protocol tells the agent "If the memory is right and your context was stale, trust the memory" (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/AGENTS.md; cli.py protocol text). So any contributor's committed JSONL line is a prompt-injection channel. FTS query tokens are quoted to stop FTS5 syntax injection (store.py _fts_query). The supported-versions table in SECURITY.md still says 1.3.x even though 2.1.0 is current, so the document is out of date.
license: MIT (https://github.com/DoppiaG93/ctxmem/blob/main/LICENSE, copyright 2026 Giuseppe Gillini; PyPI metadata https://pypi.org/pypi/ctxmem/json)
lesson_for_parinn:
ctxmem shows the model is sound: commit a canonical, human-readable log, keep the index derived and gitignored, and make corrections append-only (`supersedes`). That matches ParleyInn's I10 rebuildability. Its gaps are exactly what ParleyInn has to fix:
1. A plain JSONL file appended to on every branch conflicts at EOF under git's default merge, which I reproduced. If ParleyInn puts history in git, it should use per-writer or per-session segment files (or a union or custom merge driver), not one shared file. A hash chain also needs a defined merge rule for forked chains.
2. Tagging records with commit and fingerprint gives a cheap, deterministic STALE signal at read time, and ParleyInn could adopt it for recalled facts.
3. ctxmem's protocol tells agents to "trust the memory". Its own SECURITY.md calls repo memory untrusted, yet any committer can inject instructions. ParleyInn's enveloped, pull-only recall (I2) and redaction-before-commit are the needed difference if git is the transport.

name: Cursor Blame (with the Cursor AI Code Tracking API and the "Made with Cursor" commit trailer)
status: shipped. Cursor Blame went out in Cursor 2.4, announced on the Cursor forum on 2026-01-22, and is Enterprise-only (https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-2-4-cursor-blame/149405, https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md). The AI Code Tracking API it builds on is still labelled "Alpha (response shapes and fields may change)". Its per-commit blame endpoint is in "limited alpha and only available to select users" (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). None of it is archived or superseded as of October 2026.
what_is_stored: Four kinds of data. (1) On the device: a log of the "signature of every AI line (Tab or Agent) that is suggested to the user during their chat session" (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). (2) On Cursor's servers, per commit: commitHash, userId, userEmail, repoName, branchName, isPrimaryBranch, commitSource (ide|cli|cloud), and total, tab, composer and non-AI lines added and deleted. It also keeps the commit message, commitTs and the ingestion time createdAt (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). (3) Per accepted AI change: a deterministic changeId, source (TAB|COMPOSER), model, line counts, and per-file metadata (fileName, fileExtension, linesAdded, linesDeleted). In privacy mode fileName may be left out (same URL). (4) For blame: rangeAnnotations per commit and file, each a set of groups of {conversationId, model, operationType, ranges[{start,end}]}. Each conversation carries a title, tldr, overview and summaryBullets (same URL). The docs say Blame shows conversation summaries, "brief descriptions rather than full conversation history" (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md). Nothing indicates that code text or full transcripts are stored for attribution, but the docs neither confirm nor deny it.
where_stored: Mostly on Cursor's servers, with a local cache and on-device signatures. "When you view files and commits, data is fetched from Cursor's servers", and "Cursor Blame caches attribution data locally for performance" (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md). The AI line signatures stay on the device: "Code signatures are stored on-device", which is why CLI commits "must be scored on the same machine where the code was authored" (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). Attribution is not stored in git: no notes, refs or files. The only thing that reaches git is an optional `Made with Cursor` trailer on Agent-created commits and PRs. It is on by default, users can turn it off, and Enterprise admins can turn it off for everyone (https://cursor.com/help/integrations/git.md).
format_and_model: The client works out attribution by matching signatures. Cursor logs signatures of suggested AI lines, and these "are later compared to the signatures of each line in subsequent git commits that were written by the same author". Any matching added or deleted line is counted as AI (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). The signature algorithm is not published, and I could not confirm whether it is a hash. Counting is per action, not per final line. A line accepted from Tab and then edited by hand counts as a Tab change and as a user change: "The same line can be modified by tab, user and AI in a sequence and count as a change for each" (Cursor staff, https://forum.cursor.com/t/details-on-ai-code-tracking-api/128253). Non-AI lines are derived as max(0, totalLines - AI lines). The server model is keyed by commit hash, with line ranges grouped by conversationId and model, and served as JSON or streaming CSV over a REST API with Basic auth (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). The blame view shows three classes, Tab, Agent with model, and Human, plus a percentage split per commit (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md).
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no merge model. Each developer's client scores its own commits, keyed by user and commit hash, so many writers just means many rows. The docs flag several weak spots. "Commit hashes are not unique or unchangeable", so an amended commit can appear twice, while "Commit timestamps will remain unchanged even if the commit is amended" (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). Automatic formatting can invalidate diff signatures, and CLI commits must be scored on the machine that wrote the code (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). Only the top-level repo of the workspace is tracked; multi-root workspaces are unsupported (API docs, plus forum reports at https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-2-4-cursor-blame/149405). In 2025 staff said only commits made inside Cursor are seen, "not from other IDEs or GUIs" (https://forum.cursor.com/t/details-on-ai-code-tracking-api/128253). commitSource now also covers "cli" and "cloud". PR tracking was a feature request as of August 2025. How rebases, squashes and cherry-picks are handled is not documented. Commits made by other agents such as Claude Code are invisible.
realtime: Near-real-time ingestion, with no live sharing. In the example, createdAt is about 27 seconds after commitTs, which suggests the client uploads at commit time (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). The blame view fetches on demand and caches locally. Staff said blame data "should be retroactive for the last few months" when it launched (https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-2-4-cursor-blame/149405). There is no push or subscribe channel between agents.
search_retrieval: Lookup only, no search. The IDE has hover, file-blame and commit views (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md). The API filters by date range (ISO date, "now" or "7d"), by user, by commit hash or a comma list, and by branch. It pages up to 1000 rows, and the CSV export streams in pages of 10,000 (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). The docs describe no full-text or semantic search over conversations or summaries.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, the link is the main point of the product. Each blame range group carries a conversationId and model, and the conversations array gives that conversation's title, tldr, overview and summaryBullets (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). Hovering a line in the IDE shows the conversation summary, and the commit view lists related conversations (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md). The link stops at a summary. Full prompts and transcripts are not shown, and users have reported empty "Agent Conversation" summaries even when model attribution is present (https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-2-4-cursor-blame/149405). The link lives only on Cursor's servers, so it is lost once a repo leaves Cursor's tenant.
privacy_security: On privacy, the analytics docs claim "All the AI detection is done on device, and never leaves the user's computer. We store the line counts as metadata" (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). However, the Commit Details endpoint serves line ranges per file path with conversation IDs, model names and conversation summaries from Cursor's servers. So more than counts leaves the device: at least paths, line ranges, commit messages, emails and summaries (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/ai-code-tracking-api.md). With client privacy mode on, fileName and some other fields may be left out (same URL). Blame is off by default at team level and an admin turns it on. Users can hide the decorations with `cursorBlame.editorDecoration.enabled: false` (https://cursor.com/docs/integrations/cursor-blame.md, https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-2-4-cursor-blame/149405). The related Conversation Insights feature says it classifies on device with "default classifiers" that keep PII from leaving the machine (https://cursor.com/docs/account/teams/analytics.md). The docs say nothing about encryption at rest, retention, secret redaction in summaries, or tamper evidence, so none of these can be verified. Attribution data is not signed or chained, and git holds no check against it. Proprietary product.
lesson_for_parinn: ParleyInn should link sessions to code with content signatures computed on the device and matched to commits by the same author, and it should not rely on commit hashes. Cursor documents that commit hashes get rewritten (amend, and implicitly rebase and squash) and that formatters break signatures. Its link also lives only in a vendor server, so it disappears outside the vendor and covers no other agent. For ParleyInn this means: (a) store the session-to-code link inside ParleyInn's own append-only record, as range signatures with session and event ids, so it can be rebuilt (I10) and does not depend on a server (I4). (b) Make signatures robust to formatting, for example by normalising whitespace before hashing, and re-match after rewrites instead of trusting SHAs. (c) Treat any summary shown in a blame-like view as untrusted, enveloped recall (I2), never as auto-injected text.
