Writes for one user are serialized in three places: a per-user `threading.Lock` in the inline executor (single process only; https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/executor/inline.py), a Hatchet concurrency key `input.user_id` with `max_runs=1` (https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/executor/hatchet_workflows.py), and a PID-based lockfile `.diffmem/consolidator.lock` with a 30-minute stale reclaim (consolidator_agent/lock.py). Semantic "merges" are LLM rewrites, not git merges: the dedupe tool merges two entity files and keeps the loser's name as an alias (README). The GitHub mirror pushes `user/x:user/x` without force, so a diverged remote is rejected; the error is logged and swallowed, and the next tick retries (github_backup.py L105-118, https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/storage/github_backup.py). The pull side force-fetches `user/x:user/x` and then hard-resets the worktree to the remote SHA. The code comments "Only fast-forward" but runs no ancestry check (L120-156). Our reproduction with git 2.43 (scratch repo, same refspec, branch checked out in a worktree) got `fatal: refusing to fetch into branch ... checked out at ...`. DiffMem calls the pull only after mounting the worktree, so on modern git the advertised "remote pull at mount time" probably always fails and only logs a warning. This is a local reproduction of the git command, not a run of DiffMem itself. "Collaborative Memories ... merge requests for memory reconciliation" is listed only under Future Vision (README).
realtime: No. A write runs 60-600 s of LLM and git work. It is synchronous by default, or async with `?sync=false` returning a job id; a `callback_url` webhook is best-effort (README "Known limitations" and API). Replication works like this: a managed post-commit hook curls the service's own `/memory/{user}/webhook/post-commit`, which pushes that branch to GitHub in the background, and a periodic backup runs every 30 minutes by default (local_storage.py L167-229; README "Enabling GitHub backup"). Readers on other machines see changes only after a service restart remounts the worktree, and the reproduction above suggests even that pull is refused by git. There are no subscriptions, streaming or live fan-out.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is agentic and uses no index. The current README says "No vector databases, no embeddings, no BM25 — just git and an LLM". The discovery note's BM25 claim is stale: BM25 (rank-bm25) belonged to the August 2025 PoC (HN thread https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44969622) and was replaced by the "git based retrieval" agent in commit c4fe4a3 (2026-03-18, v0.3). A multi-turn LLM (default 4-6 turns, 30 s timeout) gets one `run(command)` tool. It reads `index.md`, greps, and runs `git log/diff/blame/show`, then emits a JSON retrieval plan of file, file-section and git-command pointers. A resolver loads those pointers within a token budget, and on failure it falls back to a baseline of user entity plus recent timeline (https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/retrieval_agent/agent.py ; resolver.py). Temporal questions are answered from git diffs and logs. The README says retrieval quality is model-dependent.
links_sessions_to_code: No. It does not link sessions to source code. The only provenance is session-to-memory: the commit message carries the caller-supplied `session_id`, so `git log`/`git show` maps a session to the memory diff it caused, and the raw transcript sits at `sessions/{date}_{session_id}.txt` (agent.py L1216-1279). There is no notion of a code repo, commit, file or prompt-to-diff attribution. The product targets a chat persona, not coding agents (README).
privacy_security: Weak, and several problems were confirmed. (a) Auth is off by default: `REQUIRE_AUTH=false`, one shared bearer `API_KEY` compared with `!=`, and CORS `*` (server.py L30-41, https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/server.py). If `REQUIRE_AUTH=true` but no key is set, auth is silently disabled (L54-58). (b) The retrieval "sandbox" checks only the first token of each pipe segment against a whitelist (cat, grep, awk, sed, find, git log/show/...) and then runs the whole string with `shell=True` (command_router.py L22-26, L221-272, https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/src/diffmem/retrieval_agent/command_router.py). Running that module locally on a scratch directory, we confirmed four bypasses: `cat $(echo ...)`, a newline-separated second command, `awk 'BEGIN{system(...)}'` and `>` redirection writing a file. The same router is exposed directly at `POST /memory/{user_id}/run-command` (server.py L482-496). Stored memory and the live conversation both feed the LLM that writes these commands, so this is a prompt-injection-to-command-execution path. The resolver also runs any LLM-supplied `git_cmd` that starts with `git ` under `shell=True`, and reads `worktree / pointer.path` without a containment check (resolver.py L22-79; code reading, not run). (c) Tenants are isolated only by orphan branches in one repo. Worktrees share refs and objects, so from alice's worktree the whitelisted `git show user/bob:bob.md` and `git log --all` return bob's data; we confirmed this through the router in a scratch repo. (d) There is no redaction, PII handling or encryption at rest; a grep of src/ and docs found none. Raw transcripts are committed and mirrored to GitHub, and all content goes to OpenRouter (docs/api-surface.md). (e) Credential handling is mixed. Good: the GitHub PAT reaches git through a `GIT_ASKPASS` script and an env var, never `.git/config` (github_backup.py L1-83). Bad: the service `API_KEY` is written in plaintext into the post-commit hook file on the volume (local_storage.py L187). (f) Right-to-be-forgotten is partial. `wipe_user` deletes the local worktree and branch, but the GitHub backend defines no `delete_user`, so the mirrored branch remains, and no HTTP endpoint calls wipe at HEAD (repo_manager.py L84-93; grep).
scale: Claims only; none are benchmarked here. The README says it powers Annabelle "across thousands of conversations on WhatsApp and Messenger" and that "an e2-small / 1 vCPU VPS is plenty for thousands of conversations". The Hatchet guide puts "Annabelle-scale" at about 6,000 runs a month and suggests a CX22 with 2 vCPU and 4 GB (https://github.com/Growth-Kinetics/DiffMem/blob/48ecbb61e7fedca40d1b41bdfb217a5f80432b20/docs/deployment-hatchet.md). Costs are $0.005-0.05 per write at GPT-4o-mini, with writes taking 60-600 s and reads 5-30 s (docs/api-surface.md). The August 2025 PoC claimed "100MB RAM with sub-second retrieval" for a year of conversations, but that was the superseded BM25 design (HN 44969622). The roadmap admits the indexing strategy is "too memory intensive". Repo traction: 906 stars, 61 forks, 57 commits from 2025-08-20 to 2026-08-28; not archived (GitHub page, fetched 2026-10-02; local clone). The README FAQ says `pip install diffmem`, but PyPI returns 404 (https://pypi.org/pypi/diffmem/json). The pyproject says 0.4.0 while the README badge says 0.5.0.
license: MIT (README badge and footer; pyproject classifier)
lesson_for_parinn: A branch is a namespace, not a security boundary. DiffMem shows this exactly where git would be tempting for ParleyInn. It isolates tenants as orphan branches in one repo with shared worktrees. Any read-only git command reachable from recall (`git show user/<other>:file`, `git log --all`) crosses tenants, and one PAT with `repo` scope covers every tenant on the mirror. Its "read-only" retrieval also runs LLM-composed strings through `shell=True` behind a first-token whitelist, which we confirmed can be bypassed. If ParleyInn uses git to hold or transport history, each trust domain (project, org, OSS repo) needs its own object database: a separate repo or bundle with its own credentials, never a ref prefix. Recall must also stay a fixed, typed query path with no shell or general-purpose git porcelain (I2, I4). Two smaller lessons. First, a best-effort mirror that logs and swallows push and pull failures leaves divergence unresolved forever; DiffMem's pull is refused by git in our reproduction. ParleyInn's I6 should audit and count every failed sync. Second, archiving raw input and tagging repair commits apart from ingest commits is worth copying. LLM-written, clock-dependent derived files are not, because they break I10 rebuildability.

name: Diversion (cloud VCS) + Diversion Claude Code plugin ("Diversion Ask", sold as "Diversion Trajectory")
category: agent-native cloud VCS (proprietary SaaS, YC S22) with a Claude Code hook plugin that captures sessions and links them to commits
status: beta
what_is_stored:
Status: the VCS itself is a paid, generally available product (https://www.diversion.dev/pricing). The session-capture plugin is labelled "EARLY ACCESS" on its product page, which also says it "can be installed and used ... today" (https://www.diversion.dev/diversion-claude-code-plugin). It is at v0.5.2 and its public repo was last committed on 2026-05-25 (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json). It was announced in May 2026 (https://www.diversion.dev/blog/diversion-product-updates-may-highlights-05-26). GitHub Mirroring is still an early-access waitlist (https://www.diversion.dev/github-mirroring).

What is stored, in four parts:
(1) Claude Code's own raw transcript JSONL. Before every Edit, Write, MultiEdit or Bash call, the plugin records a checkpoint "covering the new transcript bytes" (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/README.md).
(2) "Agent session" records. Each holds a task, an agent_type (claude-code, cursor or codex), a branch id and a status.
(3) Checkpoints over a transcript line and byte range. Each carries prompt_text (the user prompt that started the turn), files_modified, tokens_in, tokens_out, tokens_cache, api_calls and the model. Parts (2) and (3) come from the hidden `dv agent-session` command spec embedded in the dv client binary of 2026-10-01 (https://dv-binaries.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/linux_x86_64/dv; I read its strings without running it).
(4) A link from each commit to a checkpoint id. In addition, the verbatim text of each /diversion:ask query is logged server-side ("logged to Mongo"), and completion analytics go to Mixpanel (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/agents/ask-analyst.md).

Local state: a per-session file `.diversion/diversion-claude/state-<session_id>.json` holds agent_session_id, transcript_lines, last_checkpoint_id, last_transcript_bytes and updated_at (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/commands/checkpoint-status.md). There is also a local cache of fetched trajectories, which SessionEnd wipes (dv binary command spec).

Not documented: any summaries, embeddings or index. The page says the data is "indexed in real time", and that claim cannot be verified.
where_stored:
Server/cloud: Diversion's proprietary backend, reached over its REST API. The binary shows the endpoints /agent-sessions, /checkpoints/repos/, /transcript/repos/, get_git_commit_transcript and ask_queries, plus a transcript_url field on reads (dv binary strings). Transcripts are not working-tree files, git notes or refs. The marketing phrase "stored alongside your repo" (https://www.diversion.dev/diversion-claude-code-plugin) means the same Diversion cloud repository, not files in the checkout.

Infrastructure, per a founder in Jan 2024: "S3 storage, lambda and ECS compute, and serverless DBs" (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39088551). Private-cloud and on-prem deployment exist for Enterprise customers (https://www.diversion.dev/security-hub). The client keeps only a state file and a short-lived cache of fetched transcript slices.
format_and_model:
Each session is an append-only transcript of raw Claude Code JSONL bytes. The CLI base64-encodes them for upload. `transcript-append <session_id> --start-line --end-line` requires start-line to "equal the session's current transcript_lines", with end-line exclusive. The server returns 409 Conflict on a mismatch (dv binary command spec; AppendTranscriptConflict type).

A checkpoint is a [transcript_start_line, transcript_end_line) range, also stored as start and end byte offsets, plus metadata. A commit carries a checkpoint id. Diversion commit ids are sequential (`dv.commit.<digits>`) (ask-analyst.md).

fetch-trajectory returns metadata (checkpoint_id, agent_session_id, agent_type, task, transcript_start_line, transcript_end_line, files_modified, prompt_text). The cached JSONL it returns runs "from session start (line 0) through the commit point", not just the checkpoint's delta (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/agents/ask-analyst.md).

No hash chain, signatures or content addressing of transcripts is documented. The binary reports a server-side transcript size limit (transcript_size_limit_exceeded, after which a transcript_upload_stopped flag is set), but its value is not published.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The VCS is centralized. "Commits go through an API that handles conflicts on the server side, so there's no retry loop on the client. If two people commit at the same time, they both go through" (https://www.diversion.dev/blog/30-vs-300-benchmarking-github-against-diversion).

- **Workspaces:** work in progress syncs continuously to a cloud copy of each workspace. Auto-Update merges new branch commits into it. Workspaces belong to one user and are tied to one machine (https://docs.diversion.dev/concepts/repo-branch-workspace, https://docs.diversion.dev/concepts/syncing).
- **Conflicts:** a sync conflict writes a `.dv-conflict` backup file and overwrites the original with the incoming contents. Merge conflicts are "stored outside your workspace in the cloud" for resolution (https://docs.diversion.dev/concepts/conflicts).
- **Agents:** Diversion recommends one branch and one workspace per agent (`dv clone <repo> <path> --new-workspace --ref <branch>`), because agents sharing a branch "can conflict" (https://docs.diversion.dev/agent-quickstart).
- **Transcripts:** they are never merged. Each Claude session is its own record. The expected-line precondition makes appends single-writer per session and safe to retry.
- **Git repos:** git commits are linked by a trailer. "Multi-commit ops (cherry-pick, rebase, merge, pull, revert) are out of scope for trailer machinery and proceed unchanged" (session-start text in the dv binary). Rewritten history can therefore lose its links; this is my inference.
realtime:
For the VCS: "Every commit replicates to the cloud and to teammates automatically. There is no dv push or dv pull" (https://docs.diversion.dev/agent-quickstart). Work in progress syncs "in real time (even before a commit)" (founder, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39088551). GitHub Mirroring is "near real time" and runs "asynchronously after GitHub acknowledges your push" (https://www.diversion.dev/github-mirroring).

For transcripts: upload happens synchronously inside the PreToolUse hook (matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash, 20 s timeout). Turns made only of reads therefore wait until the next mutating call. The hook fails open "(no dv on PATH, not in a Diversion repo, server unreachable)" (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/hooks/hooks.json, README). There is no live streaming to other viewers. The "indexed in real time" claim is not explained anywhere.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval starts from blame, not from search. `/diversion:ask <query>` first records the verbatim query. It then spawns an `ask-analyst` sub-agent, which uses the same model, has only the Bash, Read, Grep and Glob tools, and may run only allowlisted read-only dv commands. The sub-agent's steps:
1. Classify the query: commit ids, paths, line ranges, time windows.
2. Glob or Grep to find files when the query names none.
3. `dv annotate <path> -L a,b` (blame).
4. `dv log --since/--until`.
5. `dv show`.
6. Rank and keep at most 5 commits.
7. `dv claude-hook fetch-trajectory -- <commit>` for each one.
8. Read the cached JSONL.
9. Synthesize an answer of 250 words or fewer, ending with a coverage line.
(https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/agents/ask-analyst.md, https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/plugins/diversion/commands/ask.md)

Follow-up questions go back to the same warm sub-agent through SendMessage. A PostToolUse hook nudges Claude toward /diversion:ask when a Bash history command surfaces a commit id (dv binary spec). The marketing page says Ask is "Available from your agent, CLI, or web UI" (https://www.diversion.dev/diversion-claude-code-plugin). I found no documented full-text or semantic search over transcripts.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, this is the core feature.

- **Diversion repos:** the PreToolUse hook rewrites `dv commit` to attach the latest checkpoint id, "so the commit is permanently linked to the conversation that produced it" (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude/blob/master/README.md).
- **Git repos:** the current dv binary (2026-10-01) also handles `.git/` checkouts that are synced to Diversion. Its injected context says "The plugin automatically attaches a `Diversion-Checkpoint-Id` trailer to every `git commit` you run". It then reconciles the git SHA to the checkpoint server-side (TrajectoryGitReconcileGitSha; `dv git-detect` maps the git remote to a Diversion repo). I inferred this from binary strings; it is not in the public docs or the plugin README.
- **Lookup path:** line range → `dv annotate` → commit → checkpoint → transcript slice from session start to the commit.

Uncommitted lines and lines blame cannot resolve cannot be linked (ask-analyst.md).
privacy_security:
- **Encryption and certification:** "All data in Diversion is encrypted both at rest and in transit". The same page states a "SOC 2 Type I audit" (https://www.diversion.dev/security-hub). The mirroring FAQ instead says "SOC 2 Type II. End-to-end encrypted." (https://www.diversion.dev/github-mirroring). That conflicts with the founder's 2024 statement that end-to-end encryption would prevent cloud merges and CI (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39088551), and with server-side indexing of transcripts. Treat the end-to-end claim as unverified marketing; the provider can read the data.
- **Redaction:** none documented. Raw transcript JSONL, including tool outputs that may contain secrets, is uploaded verbatim (README, ask-analyst.md).
- **Prompt injection:** the only mitigation is context isolation. "The raw transcripts only live inside the sub-agent's context", and that sub-agent is restricted to read-only commands (commands/ask.md). Its summary still flows into the main session with no trust envelope.
- **Telemetry:** verbatim queries are logged server-side and analytics go to Mixpanel (ask-analyst.md).
- **Install:** the installer is `curl | bash`, fetching an unsigned binary from S3 with no checksum check (https://get.diversion.dev/unix). On macOS it also registers a launchd background agent.
- **Deletion:** Obliterate permanently deletes file blobs (https://docs.diversion.dev/advanced/obliterate). A `/obliterate/transcript` path exists in the binary but is undocumented.
- **Access:** governed by repo permissions. API tokens need the Pro plan; SAML SSO is Enterprise-only (https://www.diversion.dev/security-hub).
- **Settings:** the plugin's /diversion:setup-permissions command edits `~/.claude/settings.json`.
scale:
All figures are the vendor's own and unaudited:
- "fleets of thousands of AI agents working in parallel", "10s of millions of files in one repo", "100s of TB", "1,000+ commits/min" (https://www.diversion.dev).
- A vendor benchmark reached about 300 commits/min at 100 concurrent users, where GitHub plateaued at about 30 (https://www.diversion.dev/blog/30-vs-300-benchmarking-github-against-diversion).

No scale figures are published for the transcript store. Ask reads at most 5 trajectories per query by default, and an unpublished per-session transcript size limit exists. Each per-agent workspace is still a full clone, and code-only cloning from the CLI is "on the roadmap" (https://docs.diversion.dev/agent-quickstart).
license: Proprietary and cloud-hosted. The dv client is a closed-source Go binary (module DiversionCompany/client). The plugin repo is public but has no LICENSE file, so no open-source licence is granted (https://github.com/DiversionCompany/diversion-claude). The 2024 plan to open-source the VCS (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39088551) had not happened as far as I could see by Oct 2026. Pricing: Pro $25 and Studio $35 per user per month, Indie free for the first 5 users, Enterprise for on-prem (https://www.diversion.dev/pricing).
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy Diversion's linking model, which needs no server: an append-only per-session transcript, appends that must state the expected line offset (rejected on mismatch), a checkpoint id minted in PreToolUse just before a commit and covering a [start,end) range, and a commit trailer such as `ParleyInn-Checkpoint:` that carries the id to the code. This works over git or GitHub mirroring without a server.

Fix three things Diversion leaves open:
1. Its trailer links break on rebase, cherry-pick and merge, so make the link recoverable from ParleyInn's own record.
2. It uploads raw JSONL without redaction, so ParleyInn must redact before anything leaves the machine.
3. Its ask-analyst passes transcript-derived summaries into the main agent without an envelope. ParleyInn should keep blame → commit → checkpoint → slice as a pull-only recall path and envelope its output as untrusted (I2).

name: Dolt
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Dolt stores complete SQL relational databases with full version control history. Core data: tables with rows/columns, schemas, constraints (foreign keys, check constraints, indexes). Version control metadata: commits with committer/date/message, branch pointers, merge history, diff records. Each table is stored as a Prolly Tree (a content-addressed B+ tree variant) within the Noms Block Store. All writes are immutable and append-only: no update/delete operations directly; instead, new versions are committed and addressed by content hash.
where_stored: Local storage: NBS (Noms Block Store) on local filesystem, storing content-addressed chunks as files, organized by hash. Each chunk is a serialized node addressed by 20-byte SHA-like hash. Remote storage: Git-like protocol to DoltHub (hosted), self-hosted DoltLab, or Hosted Dolt. AWS backend: S3 holds immutable chunk data; DynamoDB holds the manifest (single root pointer). Multi-agent scenario: branches can be local to a machine or pushed to remotes; each agent/session typically operates on its own branch.
format_and_model: Prolly Tree (Probabilistically Balanced Tree) for table storage: immutable, content-addressed B+ tree with structural sharing—siblings share unchanged subtrees. Serialization: FlatBuffer messages (defined in /proto) for compact, schema-evolved encoding. NBS layer: content-addressed DAG of nodes, root pointer stored in manifest. Commit graph: directed acyclic graph of commit objects, each referencing tree roots and prior commits. SQL interface: MySQL 5.7-compatible protocol and dialect via Vitess engine integration. System tables (dolt_log, dolt_commits, dolt_diff_<table>, dolt_status, dolt_branches, dolt_conflicts_<table>) expose version control operations as queryable metadata.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple writers supported via optimistic locking at the file level (NBS). Writes are serialized to a manifest—multiple goroutines can write concurrently; NBS detects and drops duplicate chunks. Merging: Git-style three-way merge. CLI and SQL both expose `dolt merge <branch>`. Merge algorithm: structural—compares table rows by primary key, detecting row-level conflicts. Conflict resolution: CLI `dolt conflicts` commands and SQL system table `dolt_conflicts_<table>` show rows with conflicts; user can resolve via `dolt conflicts resolve --ours/--theirs`. No automatic conflict-free merge guarantees across concurrent branches; conflicts must be explicitly resolved. Row-level granularity: only rows differing on the same primary key cause conflicts; schema-level conflicts are also detected (e.g., incompatible column additions).
realtime: Partial. Dolt ships a MySQL-compatible SQL server (`dolt sql-server`). Clients connect via TCP/socket and issue live SQL queries. Multiple concurrent connections are supported; each connection maintains its own active branch (via `CALL dolt_checkout('<branch>')` or CLI `dolt --branch <branch> sql`). Writes are synchronous: SQL INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE execute immediately and require explicit `CALL dolt_commit()` or `CALL dolt_add()` + `dolt_commit()` to create a version. Autocommit mode can tie every SQL transaction to a Dolt commit (system variable `@@dolt_transaction_commit`). No streaming or watch-for-changes mechanism; polling required to detect commits from other branches. Branches are isolated until merged; live collaboration requires explicit merges and conflict resolution.
search_retrieval: Full SQL query language (MySQL 5.7 compatible) with WHERE clauses, JOINs (up to 12 tables), subqueries, aggregate functions. Secondary indexes supported; can create indexes on table columns for query optimization. System tables for version control queries: SELECT from dolt_log (commit history), dolt_diff_<table> (row-level changes), dolt_status (staged/unstaged), dolt_branches (branch list), dolt_commits (commit metadata). No full-text search (FTS) built-in (though Dolt internally uses SQLite with FTS5 for some features, FTS is not exposed to users as of documented versions). Filtering/sorting: standard SQL WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT. Git-style log filtering: `dolt log --oneline`, `dolt log --decorate`, etc.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, by design. Dolt's primary marketed use case for agents is per-agent session memory via branching (Beads project, mentioned in README). README states: 'Dolt is the best database for agent memory, especially as you move up the ladder to multi-agent and multi-machine workflows.' AGENT.md (in codebase) provides explicit guidance: agents should create feature branches (e.g., `dolt checkout -b feature/agent-changes`), commit changes per session, then merge back. Each agent session can maintain isolated branch; commit hashes and messages are used for session traceability. Commits record author (committer email) and timestamp, linking data changes to agent execution. No built-in link to code files (prompts, weights, models), but schema design is agent-agnostic and can include references to external code systems.
privacy_security: Authentication: root user with optional password (via `DOLT_ROOT_PASSWORD` env var); localhost-only by default for security. User constraints: foreign keys, check constraints prevent invalid data. No built-in row-level security or cell-level encryption. No automatic data redaction or secrets management. Network: runs as a process; relies on OS and network layer for confidentiality (no TLS by default, though can be added via reverse proxy). When deployed on AWS via S3/DynamoDB: data at rest in S3 (can be encrypted by S3 settings), in transit via HTTPS to AWS. Branch isolation: different branches are logically isolated (one agent sees only its branch) until merged, but no cryptographic isolation—someone with filesystem access can read all committed data. Version control history is immutable and append-only; once committed, data cannot be deleted (only garbage collected), providing audit trail but no crypto-shredding.
lesson_for_parinn: Content-addressed immutable storage (NBS) provides tamper-evidence: each chunk's hash depends on its contents, so silent corruption is unlikely (hash mismatch detects it). Append-only commit log ensures full audit trail and prevents retroactive rewrites—similar to ParleyInn's goal of lossless session history. Git-style merging shows multi-agent branching pattern: agents work on separate branches without blocking, resolving conflicts during merge. However, Dolt's SQL query model allows full-table scans and joins across all data—there is no inherent boundary preventing an untrusted agent from reading another agent's session data once merged or from the same branch. For ParleyInn, this suggests: (1) use content addressing for integrity, (2) isolate agent sessions by branch/partition (per-agent namespace), (3) but recognize that SQL's data accessibility model differs from ParleyInn's I2 requirement (untrusted recall must be pull-only and enveloped). Dolt's strength is structured history; ParleyInn's additional challenge is untrusted-content containment during query/recall.

name: Durable Streams (Electric / durable-streams org)
status: beta. The README badge says "status-beta". The protocol document is still headed "DRAFT ... Version 1.0" (https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md). It is actively maintained: the last commit on main I checked out was 2026-09-10. Ownership has changed. Electric announced on 2026-08-11 that it is joining Databricks (Neon group). Its own words: "Everything Electric has previously open sourced stays open source: Postgres Sync, PGlite, TanStack DB, Durable Streams" and "Electric Cloud is winding down" (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/08/11/electric-joining-databricks.md; also https://techstrong.ai/articles/databricks-buys-electric-to-provide-postgres-for-ai-agents/). So the protocol and code are alive, but the managed hosting is being withdrawn. The electric.ax homepage still markets "Electric Cloud" with usage-based pricing (https://electric.ax/), which conflicts with the wind-down notice. No sunset date is published. I could not verify how long-term maintenance will be funded after the acquisition.
what_is_stored:
A stream is "a URL-addressable, append-only byte stream", and data cannot change once written: "Bytes at a given offset never change" (PROTOCOL.md sections 2 and 4, https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md).

- **Content:** the protocol does not care what the bytes are. Each stream has one MIME type, fixed when it is created.
- **JSON mode:** `application/json` streams store each JSON value as one message, and POSTed arrays are flattened into separate messages (PROTOCOL.md section 9.1).
- **Stream metadata:** content type, TTL or Expires-At, a durable "closed" (EOF) flag, the last Stream-Seq, idempotent-producer state, and fork lineage (forkedFrom, forkOffset, refcount, soft-delete).
- **Session data:** for agent sessions, Electric's "Durable Sessions" pattern puts several kinds of data in one stream. It holds whole messages, token chunks for active generations (messageId, actorId, role, content), presence and agent-registration state, CRDTs for typing indicators, and binary frames (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/01/12/durable-sessions-for-collaborative-ai).
- **Layers built on top:** the State Protocol (insert, update and delete events materialized client-side), StreamDB, StreamFS, a Yjs provider, and AI SDK transports (README, https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams).
where_stored:
On a server you run yourself or one that is hosted. The protocol is HTTP, and clients only hold offsets.

- **Node reference server** (`@durable-streams/server`, for dev and test): in-memory by default, or file-backed with "log files and LMDB for metadata" (docs/deployment.md in the repo).
- **Go Caddy v2 plugin** (production server): the README says "In-memory and file-backed (LMDB)". The code actually uses bbolt (`go.etcd.io/bbolt`) for metadata, plus one length-prefixed segment file per stream (`data.seg`), fsynced on append (packages/caddy-plugin/store/bbolt.go, segment.go, file_store.go at commit 461b402).
- **Cloudflare variant:** one SQLite-backed Durable Object per stream (packages/server-cloudflare/src/store.ts).
- **Electric Cloud:** hosted, now winding down (see status).

Nothing is stored in git.
format_and_model:
The data model is one ordered, append-only log per URL. Positions are opaque offsets that sort lexicographically, are unique, and strictly increase. Clients must not interpret them. `-1` (start) and `now` (tail) are reserved sentinel values (PROTOCOL.md section 8).

- **Offset format in the Go server:** `%016d_%016d` (read-seq_byte-offset) (store/offset.go).
- **On-disk record:** `[4-byte big-endian length][data]`, with a 64 MB maximum message size. There is no CRC, hash or hash-chain over records. A grep for crc, sha256 or checksum in the store package finds nothing (store/segment.go).
- **Operations:** PUT creates a stream, or forks one when `Stream-Forked-From` and `Stream-Fork-Offset` are set. POST appends, optionally with `Stream-Closed: true` for an atomic final append. GET reads in catch-up, long-poll or SSE mode. HEAD returns metadata and DELETE removes the stream.
- **Forks:** a fork inherits the source's data up to the fork offset without copying it, and uses the same offset space. Deleting the source soft-deletes it, with refcounted garbage collection (PROTOCOL.md section 4.2; docs/fork.md).
- **Retention:** servers may enforce TTL and retention policies.
- **Subscriptions:** reserved APIs for webhooks and pull-wake claim/ack/release, with generation fencing (PROTOCOL.md sections 6 and 7).

Licensing is inconsistent across sources. The repo LICENSE is MIT, but the Dec 2025 announcement says Apache 2.0 (https://electric.ax/blog/2025/12/09/announcing-durable-streams), and the Cloudflare store cites "Apache-2.0" for the ported reference code.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writes are serialized by a single server per stream. Branches can be forked but are never merged back.

- **Multiple writers:** many writers can POST to the same stream, and the server decides the order.
- **Optional `Stream-Seq`:** a lexicographic per-writer sequence. Sending a value at or below the last one gets 409, which protects against out-of-order writes.
- **Kafka-style idempotent producers:**
  - Headers: `Producer-Id`, `Producer-Epoch` and `Producer-Seq`.
  - Retries: a retried duplicate gets a 204 and is not appended again.
  - Gaps and stale writers: a sequence gap gets 409 with the expected seq. A stale epoch gets 403, which fences off "zombie" writers.
  - Ephemeral producers: they can "auto-claim" by bumping the epoch.
  - Server duties: it must serialize validate-and-append per (stream, producerId), and should commit producer state and the log append atomically. A non-atomic store downgrades delivery to at-least-once across crashes (PROTOCOL.md section 5.2.1).
- **No merge:** forks diverge permanently, and the spec has no merge or reconciliation operation. Cross-server forking is not supported (section 4.2).
- **Concurrent state:** the spec leaves this to higher layers, such as CRDTs or Yjs over a stream, or State Protocol last-write semantics (README, Durable Sessions post).
realtime:
Yes, real-time delivery is the core purpose.

- **Live tailing:** long-poll (default timeout 30s) or SSE. `offset=now` subscribes to future data in a single request (PROTOCOL.md sections 5.7, 5.8 and 8).
- **Resuming:** clients resume from their saved `Stream-Next-Offset` after a disconnect, a tab refresh or a device switch.
- **CDN-friendly:** request collapsing uses cursor intervals (section 10).
- **Electric's own scale claims:** "millions of concurrent clients subscribed to a single stream", and end-to-end sync latency under 15 ms for its Postgres sync (https://electric.ax/blog/2025/12/09/announcing-durable-streams).
- **Benchmark targets:** under 10 ms of protocol overhead per round-trip, and 100+ msgs/s for small messages (docs/benchmarking.md).
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by position only: read from an offset, or fork at an offset. Neither the protocol nor the servers offer full-text, semantic or field search. Clients materialize state themselves. For example, StreamDB/TanStack DB live queries group chunks by messageId (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/01/12/durable-sessions-for-collaborative-ai). Any index would have to be built by a consumer.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Nothing in the protocol or the docs ties a stream to a git commit, branch, worktree or file. The agent-session framing is about chat, tokens, tool output and presence for collaborative AI apps (https://electric.ax/; https://electric.ax/blog/2026/01/12/durable-sessions-for-collaborative-ai). A consumer could put a commit SHA in its own messages, but that is not specified anywhere.
scale:
These are vendor claims and were not independently verified.

- **README:** "one origin can serve millions of concurrent viewers" through CDN fan-out, "based on 1.5 years of production use at Electric ... reliably delivering millions of state changes every day" (https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams).
- **electric.ax homepage:** "1M+ concurrent readers", "99% CDN cache hit rate", "DB load stays flat" (https://electric.ax/).

Server limits:

- **Message size:** at most 64 MB in the Go server (store/segment.go).
- **Storage layout:** one segment file per stream. A ReadSeq field exists "for future log rotation support" but is not used yet (store/offset.go).
privacy_security:
The spec explicitly leaves authentication and authorization out of scope. Implementations "MUST provide appropriate access controls", and the docs say to put auth in your app or proxy (PROTOCOL.md sections 11.2 and 12.1).

What the spec does require or recommend:

- **Untrusted content:** "Clients MUST treat stream contents as untrusted input and MUST NOT evaluate or execute stream data", and it names log injection as a concern (section 12.3).
- **Server hygiene:**
  - TLS is required in production.
  - Appended content types must match the stream's type, to prevent type confusion.
  - Rate limiting should be applied (429).
  - Path-traversal sanitizing, and access control even behind shared caches when URLs are guessable.
  - Browser headers: `nosniff` and CORP. `Cache-Control: no-store` for sensitive streams, because CDN caching of public reads is the default scaling path.
- **Webhooks:** SSRF validation, HMAC-signed tokens in the Authorization header, and JWKS-verified signatures with a replay window (sections 12.7 to 12.10).

What it lacks:

- No redaction, no secret scanning and no at-rest encryption. A grep for encrypt in the Go store finds nothing.
- No tamper-evidence such as hashes or signatures on records.

A forked stream shares its source's bytes, so deleting a source only soft-deletes it while forks exist. Its data stays on the server (section 4.2).
lesson_for_parinn:
Durable Streams could carry ParleyInn's records for replication (the spec has no merge), but it cannot be where they are stored. The protocol to copy for multi-machine and sandbox replication is the Kafka-style idempotent-producer scheme:

- Each writer has its own (Producer-Id, epoch, seq).
- Duplicates are answered 204 and never appended twice.
- A seq gap gets 409 with the expected seq.
- A stale epoch gets 403, which fences off zombie writers.
- An ephemeral producer re-claims its id by bumping the epoch.

This fits ParleyInn's ephemeral sandboxes, which retry and get killed mid-write.

ParleyInn should also copy two more ideas:

- Opaque, server-minted, strictly increasing offsets as resume cursors.
- Fork-at-offset without copying, for branching a session.

The limits are why it must stay a transport:

- The store has no integrity: its records are `[len][bytes]` with no CRC or hash chain.
- It has no auth, redaction or encryption, and CDN caching is on by default.
- Upstream hosting is in flux (Electric Cloud is winding down after the Databricks deal).

The hash chain, trust envelope and audit must stay in ParleyInn's local core. Any Durable Streams sync belongs in a separate opt-in sidecar process, because I4 bans net/http in the core. The official Go client has zero dependencies (go.mod lists none), so it would suit that sidecar. The sidecar would ship already-chained, redacted records and verify the chain on the receiving end.
license: The repository LICENSE file is MIT ("Copyright (c) 2025 durable-stream"). The Dec 2025 announcement said Apache 2.0, and the Cloudflare server's store.ts cites Apache-2.0 for code ported from the reference server. The LICENSE file in the repo is the authoritative one today, but the sources conflict.

name: E2B Sandbox Persistence and Snapshots
status: shipped
what_is_stored: E2B persistence stores both filesystem state (all files) and memory state (running processes, loaded variables, and in-memory data). Snapshots capture a complete point-in-time state of a running sandbox. Each paused sandbox includes all filesystem contents and all process memory at the moment of pause.
where_stored: E2B stores paused sandboxes in its cloud infrastructure. The platform supports multiple deployment models: managed cloud (E2B-hosted), BYOC (Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS/GCP/Azure), and self-hosted (E2B Embed on Linux machines). The documentation does not specify the underlying storage backend (e.g., whether using object storage, block storage, or database).
format_and_model: The documentation does not specify the exact data format or binary layout. E2B captures snapshots at a VM/process level using Firecracker microVM snapshots. Snapshots are accessed by immutable snapshot IDs. The data model treats each snapshot as a discrete, immutable point-in-time capture that can seed new sandboxes.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable. E2B sandboxes are isolated execution environments with no explicit multi-writer coordination. One-to-many fork model: a single snapshot can create many new sandboxes, each starting from the identical snapshot state. No merge operations are documented; each sandbox is independent.
realtime: Pause operation takes approximately 4 seconds per 1 GB of RAM. Resume/connect takes approximately 1 second. During snapshot creation, the original sandbox briefly pauses, then automatically resumes running with the same ID, allowing transparent checkpointing of live runtime state.
search_retrieval: No search functionality is documented. Snapshots and paused sandboxes are retrieved by explicit ID via API calls. The SDK provides connect(sandboxId) to resume a paused sandbox and list operations to enumerate available sandboxes and snapshots.
links_sessions_to_code: E2B is purpose-built for executing AI-generated code in isolated sandboxes. Each sandbox has a unique ID. Code execution context (scripts, terminal commands, interpreter state) is captured within snapshot/pause state. No explicit session history log or agent session linking is documented; snapshots serve as discrete checkpoints rather than a continuous audit trail.
privacy_security: E2B provides hardware isolation via Firecracker microVM (per-sandbox isolated kernel, not shared-kernel containers). SOC 2 Type II compliance. Secrets are injected at the egress proxy to prevent values from entering sandboxes. Network controls include CIDR/hostname-based egress filtering. Paused sandboxes persist indefinitely until explicitly killed via API—no automatic expiration. Documentation does not mention encryption at rest or in transit (egress proxy likely uses TLS). No redaction or data minimization strategies are mentioned.
lesson_for_parinn: E2B's model differs fundamentally from ParleyInn's invariants: (1) E2B stores state monolithically (filesystem + memory together), not as an append-only audit log; (2) E2B treats restored snapshots as trusted execution contexts, whereas ParleyInn (I2) treats all restored content as untrusted until explicitly pinned by human; (3) E2B provides execution isolation via hardware (Firecracker), while ParleyInn must handle history isolation via content security and audit; (4) E2B's indefinite retention of paused sandboxes creates operational liability (requires manual cleanup), whereas ParleyInn's lossless append-only model provides durability by design without manual intervention. For agent context persistence, ParleyInn's approach of separate, versioned history snapshots (keyed by session ID) is preferable to E2B's monolithic sandbox persistence because it enables history retrieval, replay, and merging across multiple agents without implying trust in the restored context.
verification_notes: Information sourced from official E2B documentation at docs.e2b.dev and e2b.dev. The documentation does not provide exhaustive technical details on data formats, storage backends, or low-level infrastructure, so some fields note 'not specified' or 'not documented.' The task description mentioned a '30-day' retention period; however, official documentation states paused sandboxes are 'kept indefinitely' until explicitly killed. This discrepancy could indicate a change in E2B's service terms or a misremembered detail.

name: Electric (Electric Sync / Electric Streams = Durable Streams / Electric Agents), by ElectricSQL
category: sync-engine (Postgres read-path sync) plus an HTTP append-only stream protocol and an agent runtime built on it
status: beta. The Postgres sync engine is shipped and in production use. Durable Streams is labelled "DRAFT" v1.0 in its protocol spec and "beta" in its repo README. Electric Agents is at 0.6 (June 2026), self-hosted only: the desktop and mobile apps are canary builds and managed Agents servers on Electric Cloud are "coming soon". The project is not archived. electric-sql.com now redirects to electric.ax.
what_is_stored:
Electric Sync: it stores no history of its own. It streams "Shapes" (subsets of Postgres tables) from Postgres to clients over HTTP/JSON. It is read-path only, so writes go through your own API back into Postgres (https://electric.ax/docs/sync/guides/security.md, https://electric.ax/llms.txt).

Electric Agents: each agent is an "entity", described as "an addressable, schema-typed unit of state at /{type}/{id}", whose "session and state live on a durable Electric Stream of events", one stream per entity (https://electric.ax/docs/agents.md). The runtime fills 20 built-in collections, each a distinct event type: runs, steps (LLM calls), texts, textDeltas, toolCalls, reasoning, reasoningDeltas, errors, inbox (incoming messages), wakes, entityCreated, entityStopped, signals, childStatus, tags, slashCommands, manifests, contextInserted, contextRemoved and replayWatermarks. User-defined typed collections can be added (https://electric.ax/docs/agents/reference/built-in-collections.md).

So an agent's full transcript is stored: token deltas, reasoning, tool calls and context-window changes. Attachments (files, images) are supported too (https://electric.ax/docs/agents/usage/attachments.md, listed in llms.txt).

The April 2026 launch post describes a built-in "coder" entity that "wraps a Claude Code or Codex session" and can "import an existing local coding session" (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/04/29/introducing-electric-agents). However, the source file that post links to (packages/agents/src/agents/coding-session.ts) returns 404 on main, and packages/agents/src/agents now holds only horton.ts and worker.ts (https://github.com/electric-sql/electric/tree/main/packages/agents/src/agents). I could not verify whether the coder entity still ships or how it captures a Claude Code session (JSONL import, hooks or SDK).
where_stored:
On a server.

- **Durable Streams server:** a self-hosted single binary or Electric Cloud (https://electric.ax/streams.md). The current server is written in Rust. It stores "bytes on disk in the format they are sent over the wire" in an append-only log, behind a sharded write-ahead log with group commit and fsync. Sealed chunks are immutable and CDN-cacheable. It runs on one node today; a multi-node server for high availability is planned (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/06/26/durable-streams-at-kernel-speed).
- **Agents runtime:** a separate agents-server (TypeScript) that you self-host. Managed hosting is announced but not yet available (https://www.electric.ax/blog/2026/06/16/electric-agents-0-6-from-runtime-to-app).
- **Postgres Sync:** the source of truth is your Postgres. Clients can hold local copies in TanStack DB or PGlite.

None of it uses git or working-tree files.
format_and_model:
Durable Streams protocol (https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md):
- A stream is "an append-only sequence of bytes" at a URL.
- PUT creates a stream and POST appends to it. GET reads from an offset as a catch-up read, a long-poll or SSE.
- Offsets are opaque and sort lexicographically. Each append returns a `Stream-Next-Offset` header.
- Streams carry a content type. In JSON mode (application/json) message boundaries are preserved and reads return a JSON array.
- Streams can be closed (EOF), can have a sliding TTL (`Stream-TTL`) or an absolute expiry (`Stream-Expires-At`), and can be soft-deleted.
- Forking is native: `PUT` with `Stream-Forked-From` and `Stream-Fork-Offset` creates a new stream that inherits the source's data up to that offset. Forks have their own lifetimes.

On top sits the State Protocol ("Durable State"): JSON change events `{type, key, value, old_value?, headers:{operation: insert|update|delete, txid?, timestamp?}}` plus control messages for snapshot boundaries and resets. Clients materialise state by applying events in order (https://electric.ax/docs/streams/durable-state.md).

StreamDB (typed reactive collections queried through TanStack DB) and StreamFS (a shared filesystem) are built on that layer. Electric Agents entity state is StreamDB collections over one stream per entity.

The model is event sourcing: "The agent is the durable stream. Everything else is a projection or a subscriber" (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/04/29/introducing-electric-agents). There is no hash chain and no content addressing.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writes to a stream are serialised by the server in append order. Coordination works as follows.

**Stream level** (https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md):
- **Optional `Stream-Seq`:** a per-writer sequence that only goes up. A regression gets 409.
- **Kafka-style idempotent producer:** `Producer-Id`, `Producer-Epoch` and `Producer-Seq` headers give exactly-once retries. A stale epoch gets 403, which fences off "zombie" writers.
- **Forks:** a fork does not inherit producer state.

**State level:** no CRDT or merge semantics are defined. Events apply in order, so the effective rule is last write wins by stream position; `old_value` is offered "useful for conflict detection" (https://electric.ax/docs/streams/durable-state.md).

**Agents:** agents coordinate by writing to each other's inbox streams and to shared-state streams (a "blackboard" pattern) rather than by merging (https://electric.ax/docs/agents/usage/shared-state.md, https://electric.ax/blog/2026/04/29/introducing-electric-agents). Divergence is modelled as an explicit fork, never merged back. The docs describe no merge of forks.

**CRDTs:** for documents that need them, Electric points to Yjs over Durable Streams with server-side compaction (https://electric.ax/llms.txt).

**Postgres Sync:** conflicts are left to the app's write path into Postgres (https://electric.ax/docs/sync/guides/security.md).
realtime:
Real time is the core feature.

- **Streams:** live tailing over long-poll or SSE. Clients resume with "everything after offset X". SSE fan-out latency is about 1 ms at small fan-out and about 4 ms at 1,000 subscribers (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/06/26/durable-streams-at-kernel-speed).
- **Agents:** sessions can be "observed in real time by any number of users and entities", and agents wake when their inbox or an observed stream changes (https://electric.ax/docs/agents.md).
- **Postgres Sync:** about 6 ms write-to-client latency (3 ms Postgres plus 3 ms Electric), flat as the number of shapes grows (https://electric.ax/docs/sync/reference/benchmarks.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Weak and not verified. The launch post's coder entity takes `agent: "claude"` and a `cwd` (the target repo), plus free-form tags such as `project`, and gives the session a stable URL such as /coder/landing-page-build (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/04/29/introducing-electric-agents). I found no link to commits, branches, diffs or file hashes, and no git integration in the docs I read. The coder source file the post links to is missing from main (https://github.com/electric-sql/electric/tree/main/packages/agents/src/agents), so its current behaviour cannot be verified. Electric Agents otherwise treats sessions as data, independent of any code repository.
privacy_security:
**Durable Streams protocol (§12):**
- Authentication and authorisation are "explicitly out of scope". Implementations must still provide access control.
- TLS is required in production.
- SSRF checks apply to webhook URLs.
- Callback and claim tokens are HMAC-signed and sent in the Authorization header.
- `Cache-Control: no-store` is recommended for sensitive streams.
- Notably: "Clients MUST treat stream contents as untrusted input and MUST NOT evaluate or execute stream data without appropriate validation... log injection attacks are a concern" (https://github.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/blob/main/PROTOCOL.md).

**Electric Agents:**
- Principals are sent in an `Electric-Principal: <kind>:<id>` header, with kinds user, agent, service and system.
- Type-level grants are spawn and manage. Entity-level grants are read, write, delete, signal, fork, schedule, spawn and manage, and can propagate to descendants.
- Some low-level writes need claim-scoped write tokens.
- The built-in Horton and Worker types grant every user principal spawn and manage by default (https://electric.ax/docs/agents/usage/permissions-and-principals).
- Tool execution goes through sandbox profiles (local, Docker, or a remote E2B VM) with network policy allow-all, allowlist or deny-all. Allowlist is incomplete under Docker. The host's process.env is not forwarded to shell commands (https://electric.ax/docs/agents/usage/sandboxing.md).

**Postgres Sync:** the HTTP API is "public by default" and exposes everything the database user can read. It must sit behind an authorising proxy, an API token or network rules. Electric "syncs ciphertext as well as it syncs plaintext": end-to-end encryption is done in the client or middleware, and Electric prescribes no key management (https://electric.ax/docs/sync/guides/security.md).

**Gaps:** I found no secret redaction, no encryption at rest in the stream server, and no tamper evidence such as hashes or signatures over the log in the docs I read.
scale:
- **Durable Streams (Rust):** about 860,000 appends/s at 100k streams, catch-up replay up to about 2.0 GB/s in aggregate, and a median of about 515 MB memory for 100,000 streams, on a single node (https://electric.ax/blog/2026/06/26/durable-streams-at-kernel-speed).
- **Postgres Sync:** the homepage claims 1M+ concurrent readers with 99% CDN cache hit rates and flat database load (https://electric.ax/). The benchmarks page shows one Electric server behind a CDN serving 100k to 1M concurrent users at 960 transactions per minute (https://electric.ax/docs/sync/reference/benchmarks.md).
- **Production history:** the protocol is "based on 1.5 years of production use at Electric for real-time Postgres sync, reliably delivering millions of state changes every day" (https://electric-sql.com/blog/2025/12/09/announcing-durable-streams).

These are vendor benchmarks; I did not verify them independently.
license: The Electric monorepo (sync-service, agents, agents-server, durable-streams-rust and others) is Apache-2.0 and requires a CLA (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electric-sql/electric/main/LICENSE, https://github.com/electric-sql/electric). The durable-streams/durable-streams spec and reference repo carries an MIT LICENSE file (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/durable-streams/durable-streams/main/LICENSE), even though the announcement says "fully open under Apache 2.0" (https://electric-sql.com/blog/2025/12/09/announcing-durable-streams). This is a discrepancy, but either license is permissive.
confidence: high for Durable Streams protocol semantics, the Agents data model, permissions and licensing (read from the primary spec and docs); medium for status and scale (vendor claims); low for how the coder entity captures Claude Code sessions (its linked source is 404 on main)

name: Emdash (generalaction/emdash)
category: agentic development environment (worktrees): an Electron desktop orchestrator plus a remote Node daemon over SSH
status: shipped. The repo is active and not archived. v1.2.7 was released 2026-09-27 and v1.2.6 on 2026-09-21 (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/releases). The last commit in my shallow clone is a39d9c8, dated 2026-10-01. The README says YC W26 (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash). About 5.9k stars when fetched. I could not cross-check that through the GitHub API, because API access to the repo was refused in this session.
what_is_stored:
Emdash stores orchestration metadata. It does not store agent transcripts. The desktop SQLite schema has these tables: ssh_connections, projects, project_remotes, project_settings, app_settings, notifications, tasks, workspaces, pull_requests (plus their users, labels, assignees and checks), automations, automation_runs, conversations, terminals, kv, provider_accounts and app_secrets (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/apps/emdash-desktop/src/core/services/app-db/node/schema.ts).

A conversations row holds title, provider, cwd, workspacePath, config, status fields and a deletion tombstone. It also holds providerSessionId, which the schema comments call a 'last-observed provider resume handle — a pointer, never the record's identity'. There is no message or transcript column (same schema.ts).

Transcripts come from the provider. The runtime gets history back through provider replay (ACP load/resume). 'Parsed transcript and raw ACP log exports are live-activation reads', and the raw log is activation-local (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/acp-runtime.md).

The host side persists a few more things:
- A versioned, allowlisted session 'intent': provider/session identity, cwd, desired model/mode/effort, and a bounded non-secret presentation snapshot.
- Queued Prompt payloads, kept only until dispatch.
- Command receipts holding metadata only, with no Prompt content.
- Attachments (acp-runtime.md; https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/CONTEXT.md).

Workspaces carry what the docs call Provenance (the creation config) and host Observations (observed git state, last outcomes, script outcomes) (schema.ts; CONTEXT.md).
where_stored:
Desktop data goes in a local SQLite file, emdash4.db (previously emdash3.db). It lives in the userData directory: ~/Library/Application Support/emdash on macOS, %APPDATA%/emdash on Windows, and $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/emdash on Linux. EMDASH_DB_FILE overrides the location (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/apps/emdash-desktop/src/main/db/default-path.ts; https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/risky-areas/database.md). A sibling '<db>-file-search.db' holds the file-search index (apps/emdash-desktop/src/main/core/file-search/database-path.ts).

On remote hosts, the workspace-server daemon installs under ~/.emdash/workspace-server/. Its runtime state sits under its state directory. That covers automation and file-search databases, session intents, ACP attachments, and JSON-file key-value stores (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/workspace-server.md).

Remote worktrees default to <remote-project>/.emdash/worktrees. A project can optionally share config through .emdash.json (https://emdash.com/docs/remote-projects).

Transcripts stay wherever each agent CLI keeps them, for example Claude Code's own session store. That last point is my inference from the provider-pointer design; Emdash's docs do not name provider storage paths.

Git holds code only: worktrees and branches. Emdash puts no session data in git. I found no git notes, custom refs or commit trailers in the source tree (my grep of the source).
format_and_model:
The desktop uses SQLite in WAL mode (db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL') in apps/emdash-desktop/src/main/db/drizzleClient.ts), accessed through Drizzle ORM and better-sqlite3. Migrations are generated by drizzle-kit and tested against committed fixture DBs. Evolving structured fields are stored as 'versioned JSON columns' (text) that run an upgrade chain on read (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/risky-areas/database.md).

The domain model is written up as a glossary in CONTEXT.md (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/CONTEXT.md):
- **Host, Repository, Worktree, Workspace:** where the work lives.
- **Session:** a process that dies with its workspace.
- **Conversation:** the durable record, identified by Emdash's own id. The provider session id is only a pointer.
- **Prompt:** immutable.
- **Prompt attempt:** immutable, with its own acceptance order.
- **Generation fences:** a Session generation, a Provider connection generation and an Owner generation.
- **Command receipt:** metadata only.

Attachments are a directory per attachment holding metadata.json plus content. They are published with one atomic rename out of a staging directory, and there is no separate index (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/acp-runtime.md).

The record is mutable state, not append-only. History is kept as per-step 'durable last-outcomes on host records (lastCreateOutcome, lastRemovalAttempt, per-script outcomes) — no event list' (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/docs/adr/0006-tombstone-and-reconcile-deletion.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Every resource has exactly one writer. The state-ownership doc says: 'Use one writer per resource. Convergence happens through live models and snapshot sync, not by merging concurrently-written state' (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/state-ownership.md).

**Host authority.** The host is authoritative for what exists. The desktop keeps a mirror (the 'Registry') plus its own annotations. Kubernetes-style spec/status convergence was explicitly rejected, because 'multi-writer desired state is incoherent' (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-host-authoritative-workspaces.md).

**Single writer per table.** One module owns all writes to the workspaces table, through named verbs (register, adopt, refresh, untrack, purge, …). Raw writes from anywhere else are banned by lint (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/docs/adr/0002-registry-single-writer.md).

**Mutations.** Mutations are fail-fast RPCs, serialized on the host with a keyed mutex. Deletion is the only mutation that survives an unreachable host. It does so as a durable tombstone on the mirror row, swept idempotently by a reconcile loop. The earlier outbox and operation log were retired (ADR 0006).

**Multiple desktops.** Several desktops can write to one Host Conversation. Each is a 'Desktop writer' with an attribution-only identity. A total 'Prompt acceptance order' is kept separately from a revisioned, shared 'Prompt queue order' (CONTEXT.md).

**Future sync.** A client-to-client CRDT sync plane is mentioned only as planned. ADR 0006 calls tombstones 'the future multi-client sync unit… the planned remove-wins CRDT tombstone'. I found no CRDT library in the repo, so this is announced, not shipped.
realtime:
Within one installation, updates are live. The host pushes registry snapshots and live models to desktops over the @emdash/wire protocol, through an SSH-forwarded Unix socket. Snapshots are delivered on subscribe, and stale observations are shown as stale rather than hidden (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/workspace-server.md; https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/CONTEXT.md).

Transcripts stream live from the active ACP session. After a reconnect, the desktop refetches committed history pages, which are fenced by generation and revision (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/acp-runtime.md).

There is no sharing between users or across machines through an Emdash server. 'Emdash does not send your code or chats to Emdash servers' (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash). With tmux, remote agent sessions survive Emdash restarts and SSH reconnects (https://emdash.com/docs/remote-projects).
search_retrieval:
The command palette searches actions, tasks, projects, conversations and files, with @kind prefixes to narrow it (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/CONTEXT.md). Conversation search runs fuzzy matching over title and subtitle metadata (apps/emdash-desktop/src/core/features/conversations/contributions/browser/conversation-palette-source.ts).

File content search uses a separate SQLite index, '<db>-file-search.db', on the desktop and on the host (workspace-server.md; apps/emdash-desktop/src/main/core/file-search/database-path.ts).

I found no full-text or semantic search over transcript content, which fits the fact that transcripts are never stored. Agents get no recall API.
links_sessions_to_code:
The link to code is structural and coarse:
- A Task links to a Workspace, which is a worktree on its own branch.
- Conversations link to a Task and Project, plus cwd and workspacePath.
- Workspace Provenance records what Emdash asked for at creation.
- PRs are cached with head and base ref names and OIDs (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/apps/emdash-desktop/src/core/services/app-db/node/schema.ts).

PR rows have no foreign key to tasks. I infer they join on the branch.

There is no per-commit or per-line attribution to prompts or sessions. I found no trailers, git notes or provenance refs in the source. The link from a branch to a conversation exists only in the local SQLite file, not in the repository.
scale: The project makes no quantitative scale claims. The design scales across many parallel agents, each in its own worktree, on local and SSH hosts (README: https://github.com/generalaction/emdash). Supported agent CLIs include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Amp, Devin, Qwen Code, Droid and Copilot (same README). Remote Windows hosts are rejected as unsupported (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/workspace-server.md).
privacy_security:
**Local-first.** Emdash sends no code or chats to its own servers, but agent CLIs may send data to their providers (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash).

**Telemetry.** Telemetry goes to PostHog and can be switched off in Settings or with TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false. It excludes code, prompts and messages, user input, and file paths or repo names as standard properties. Properties pass through an allowlist before they are sent (https://emdash.com/docs/telemetry).

**Secrets.** Secrets in app_secrets are encrypted with Electron safeStorage, which uses the OS keychain. Emdash refuses to store them when Linux falls back to the 'basic_text' backend (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/apps/emdash-desktop/src/main/host/secrets/encrypted-app-secrets-store.ts). SSH credentials are kept in the OS keychain (README). On the host, 'Provider environment, MCP credentials, runtime endpoints, and unknown descriptor fields are never persisted', and session intents are explicitly allowlisted (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/agents/architecture/acp-runtime.md).

**Secret delivery.** The design names a Desktop Secret Authority and a Host Secret Runtime that grant and deliver secrets to Git, agents and scripts, with an audit history (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash/blob/main/CONTEXT.md).

**Gaps.**
- The SQLite database itself is not encrypted. I found no SQLCipher.
- I found no redaction of transcript content, which Emdash does not store anyway.
- I found no treatment of recalled history as untrusted, or of prompt injection.

**Remote installs.** The installer verifies a SHA-256 sidecar for the remote daemon artifact (workspace-server.md).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/generalaction/emdash)
lesson_for_parinn:
Separate the durable identity of a conversation from the provider's session handle. Emdash treats the Claude Code session id as a 'last-observed pointer', and fences every live incarnation with generation counters, so late events from an old process can never change current state. ParleyInn's record should key everything on its own conversation and attempt ids, and store the provider session id as an attribute that can be re-pointed.

Emdash also shows the cost of not keeping its own record. It depends on provider replay for history, so history reads can come back 'unavailable' or 'outcome unknown' and need explicit uncertainty states (acp-runtime.md). ParleyInn's append-only log removes that failure mode, which supports ParleyInn owning the transcript bytes rather than pointing at CLI-owned files.

Two more patterns are worth borrowing:
- Emdash's 'positive-assertion invariant': a failed or partial scan writes nothing, and is never taken as 'nothing exists'.
- Tombstones as the only cross-host mutation that survives an unreachable host.

Both map directly onto ParleyInn's I6 (no silent failures) and I10 (everything derived is rebuildable from the record). Emdash keeps its task-to-branch-to-conversation links only in local SQLite, never in git. That means another machine or a sandbox cannot recover provenance. If ParleyInn wants provenance that works across machines, it must carry it in a transport of its own, such as refs or a log.

name: Engram (Gentleman-Programming)
category: memory MCP server with git sync
status: shipped
license: MIT for the code. The Engram name and logos are trademarks of Alan Buscaglia (README, TRADEMARKS.md).
what_is_stored:
Engram stores curated memories, not transcripts. The README says to treat it "as a curated project memory, not a transcript sink." DOCS.md says it does "not record a firehose of raw tool calls." It has these tables:
- sessions: id, project, directory, started_at/ended_at, summary.
- observations: type (decision, architecture, bugfix, pattern, config, discovery, learning), title, content in What/Why/Where/Learned form, scope (project, personal or global), topic_key for upserting a topic as it evolves, normalized_hash for dedup, revision_count, pinned, review_after/expires_at, optional embedding columns, and soft deletes.
- user_prompts: what the user asked, with prompt tombstones.
- memory_relations: supersedes or conflicts verdicts from mem_judge.
- Sync bookkeeping: sync_chunks, sync_state, an ordered sync_mutations queue, delete tombstones, and deferred applies.
Session summaries follow the Goal/Instructions/Discoveries/Accomplished/Next Steps/Relevant Files template. Sources: DOCS.md "Database Schema", "No Raw Tool-Call Auto-Capture" and "mem_session_summary".
where_stored:
Three places:
- Authoritative store: one local SQLite file at ~/.engram/engram.db, overridable with ENGRAM_DATA_DIR. Engram refuses to start on NFS or SMB data directories because WAL is unsafe there.
- Git sync: `engram sync` writes .engram/manifest.json plus .engram/chunks/<id>.jsonl.gz into the repo working tree. Users commit these and move them with git or any file transport. The working DB is gitignored.
- Optional Engram Cloud: a self-hosted `engram cloud serve` backed by Postgres (image ghcr.io/gentleman-programming/engram). Clients push and pull mutations per explicitly enrolled project.
Project identity is kept in a private, untracked "binding" in the repo's shared git metadata (git common dir). Linked worktrees share it; clones and forks each get a fresh opaque id (DOCS.md "MCP Project Resolution"; internal/project/detect.go uses `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`).
format_and_model:
Local DB: SQLite in WAL mode with synchronous NORMAL and foreign keys on, through pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite. FTS5 virtual tables over observations and prompts are kept in sync by triggers.

Git sync format, from internal/sync/sync.go:
- manifest.json is {version, chunks:[{id, created_by, created_at, sessions, memories, prompts}]}, pretty-printed and rewritten whole on each sync (transport.go WriteManifest uses os.WriteFile).
- Each chunk is gzipped JSON containing {sessions[], observations[], prompts[], mutations[]}.
- The chunk id is an 8-hex-char prefix of the content's SHA-256. That is only 32 bits, so collisions are a theoretical risk in very large teams; this is my inference.
- Hard deletes travel as canonical delete mutations. Child deletes precede their session so replay is safe.

Rows carry a sync_id for identity across machines. Cloud push uses a versioned `application/vnd.engram.sync+gzip; version=1` envelope with an 8 MiB default limit (configurable). It is a mutable relational model with soft deletes and tombstones, not a hash-chained log. There are no signatures and no chaining (sources: DOCS.md, docs/engram-cloud/README.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Each `engram sync` creates a new immutable chunk, so chunk files never conflict. The docs claim "No merge conflicts: each dev creates independent chunks, git just adds files." Import is idempotent: imported chunk ids are tracked per target in sync_chunks.

manifest.json is shared mutable state, though. It is one JSON array rewritten whole, so two branches that both sync will both append at the array's tail. I infer from transport.go that this produces an ordinary git textual conflict, despite the docs calling it "git-mergeable". I found no documented custom merge driver, and the conflict could not be confirmed against a public issue.

Logical conflicts:
- Exact duplicate saves are deduplicated in a rolling time window (normalized hash + project + scope + type + title).
- topic_key saves upsert the latest observation with the same project, scope and topic_key.
- mem_judge and mem_compare record "supersedes" or "conflicts" relations. Conflict scans can shell out to the `claude` or `opencode` CLI (internal/llm, ENGRAM_AGENT_CLI).
- Pulled upserts pass a tombstone guard against hard deletes.
- Pulled mutations missing an FK dependency are deferred and retried up to 5 times, then marked dead.

Engram does not resolve conflicts by CRDT or vector clock; the latest writer wins for each topic_key.
realtime: Git sync is manual or batch: you run `engram sync` and `engram sync --import`. Cloud autosync is opt-in (ENGRAM_CLOUD_AUTOSYNC=1 plus a token and server URL). It runs a background push/pull loop that never blocks local writes, with phases such as healthy, push_failed and backoff, and reason codes such as transport_failed and auth_required. Docs describe polling cycles, not push notifications; I could not verify any streaming or websocket channel. Scheduled cloud sync wrapper scripts are also provided (DOCS.md "Cloud Autosync", "Scheduled Explicit Cloud Sync Wrappers").
search_retrieval:
Search is SQLite FTS5 over title, content, tool_name, type, project and topic_key. Each query word is quoted to avoid FTS5 syntax errors. Filters cover type, project, scope and limit, and `all_projects` searches across projects.

Retrieval is in three layers ("progressive disclosure"):
1. mem_search returns previews.
2. mem_timeline shows the chronological neighbourhood.
3. mem_get_observation returns full content.

mem_context recovers recent session history. The Claude Code plugin can inject prior context at session start; bare MCP does not. Results are annotated with supersedes, superseded_by and conflicts relations.

The design choice was "SQLite + FTS5 over vector DB — FTS5 covers 95% of use cases." The schema has embedding columns, but I did not verify any semantic search path. FTS5 is not multilingual, so the team docs advise one lingua franca for shared memories (DOCS.md "Features", "Design Decisions"; docs/TEAM-USAGE.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Only weakly. A session records its project and its directory, normalized to the worktree root. Project identity comes from .engram/config.json, the git origin remote name, or the git root basename, held stable by the private git-common-dir binding across renames and linked worktrees. Observations carry a free-text "Where" field (file paths) and session summaries a "Relevant Files" section. mem_save can attach the user prompt that triggered the save.

I found no commit SHA, branch, diff or file-hash linkage in the schema, and no git notes or trailers. The docs say "Shell history and git provide the raw audit trail" (DOCS.md "Database Schema", "MCP Project Resolution", "No Raw Tool-Call Auto-Capture").
scale:
There are no throughput or corpus-size benchmarks in the docs. The only figure: "a chunk with 8 sessions + 10 observations = ~2KB" compressed. Cloud push and pull payloads default to 8 MiB (ENGRAM_CLOUD_MAX_PUSH_BYTES). SQLite runs with WAL and a 5000 ms busy timeout. Child-repo scanning is capped at depth 1, 20 entries and 200 ms.

Project activity is high: 12 v2.0.0 release candidates, then v2.1.0, v2.2.0 and v2.2.1 (2026-09-25), and v3.0.0. The v3.0.0 tag is dated 2026-10-02 00:27 +0200 and the Go module path is now .../engram/v3. This comes from `git ls-remote`, tag metadata and go.mod. The discovery note's "latest is v2.0.0-rc.4 (2026-09-02)" is outdated: rc.4 was tagged that day but has since been superseded.

The README still says Homebrew stays on stable v1.20.0 (tagged 2026-07-20). The GitHub Releases API was not reachable here, so I could not check whether v3.0.0 is marked stable or prerelease.
privacy_security:
Redaction is opt-in and manual. Text inside `<private>...</private>` tags is replaced with [REDACTED] twice: in the TypeScript plugin and in the Go store (stripPrivateTags in AddObservation and AddPrompt; regex `(?is)<private>.*?</private>`). There is no automatic secret or pattern detection; I found none in internal/store.

Scope is "a search and filter signal, not a privacy boundary." Personal-scope observations are still exported by both git sync and cloud sync for the project (docs/TEAM-USAGE.md).

There is no encryption at rest and no encryption of the git chunks. The cloud gzip envelope "is not encryption and does not provide confidentiality."

Cloud auth:
- Bearer tokens, with a required non-default ENGRAM_JWT_SECRET.
- Managed principals and tokens hashed with ENGRAM_CLOUD_TOKEN_PEPPER; raw tokens are printed once.
- Per-project grants or allowlists and an auth audit log.
- The local admin HTTP routes take ENGRAM_HTTP_TOKEN.

Recalled memories get no untrusted-content envelope; the plugin injects them straight into agent context, and no docs mention prompt injection. SECURITY.md scope lists "injection in MCP/HTTP API inputs". Only the latest stable release gets security fixes; RCs are not guaranteed. Engram also shells out to the claude or opencode CLI for conflict judging.
lesson_for_parinn:
Engram shows that git transport works when every unit is an immutable, content-addressed file that git only ever adds: no merge driver is needed, and import is idempotent by chunk id.
