Its weak spot is the one mutable shared index, manifest.json, a whole-file JSON array rewrite that two branches will both append to. ParleyInn should take the immutable-segment idea but drop the shared index. Two ways to do that: name segments by full content hash under per-writer directories, for example .parinn/log/<writer-id>/<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl.gz, and derive the manifest by listing the directory; or keep segments under a custom ref so the index is the tree itself. Then concurrent agents across worktrees and sandboxes never touch the same path, and the hash chain lives inside each writer's segments.

Engram also shows what to avoid:
- 32-bit chunk ids.
- Scope labels that look like privacy but sync anyway.
- Injecting recalled memories with no untrusted envelope.
ParleyInn's I2 envelope and automatic redaction should stay non-negotiable.

name: Entire CLI
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Session transcripts (prompts, responses, tool calls), checkpoint metadata (summary stats, timestamps), token usage (input, cache creation, cache read, output, API calls, nested subagent tokens), code snapshots (file changes at commit time), task records (subagent work with transcript and files), session state (ID, branch, worktree, timestamps, phase). Transcripts are JSONL format; metadata is JSON. One or more sessions per checkpoint. Subagent task records materialized at condensation with agent transcript and task metadata.
where_stored: Git object store as commits under either (1) git-refs backend: refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id> where <shard> is last 2 chars of ID; each ref points to commit whose tree is the checkpoint contents (metadata.json, 0/, 1/, 2/, tasks/); or (2) git-branch backend (legacy): entire/checkpoints/v1 branch with subtree sharding <id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/. Temporary session state in .git/entire-sessions/<session-id>.json (git common dir, shared across worktrees). Shadow branches entire/<commit[:7]>-<worktreeHash[:6]> hold full snapshot + metadata during active session. Push queue in entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl (per-checkpoint refs awaiting push). No separate server or database; transport via elected checkpoint sync remote (origin, fork, or configured target).
format_and_model: Checkpoint metadata: metadata.json (CheckpointSummary with aggregated stats). Per-session transcripts: full.jsonl (sanitized + redacted agent transcript), transcript.jsonl (compacted), prompt.txt (checkpoint-scoped user prompts), content_hash.txt (sha256 dedup). Task records: tasks/<tool-use-id>/agent-<agent-id>.jsonl (subagent transcript), task.json (metadata). Session state: .git/entire-sessions/<session-id>.json with session ID, description, branch, worktree, phase, timestamps, files touched, task records. Checkpoint IDs: 26-char ULIDs under git-refs (Crockford base32, lexicographically time-sortable, minted on first write), or 12-char hex legacy (git-branch). Commit trailers: Entire-Checkpoint: <id>. No explicit JSON schema version mentioned; all text UTF-8.
multi_writer_and_merge: Independent per-checkpoint refs eliminate shared tip contention. Concurrent sessions interleave on same shadow branch. Worktree-matched set (every session with pending content in worktree) plus identity-matched session (process ancestry of committing agent) determine checkpoint linking per commit. Multiple sessions per checkpoint supported via 0/, 1/, 2/ indexing. Divergence when same checkpoint written on two machines: fetch-and-replay (fetch remote ref, rebase local-only commits on top, retry fast-forward) rather than force push. Commit merges remain unlinked by design; squash commits inherit Entire-Checkpoint trailers from SQUASH_MSG; redone commits (git reset scenario) inherit trailers if staged files match dropped commit exactly. Background sweep finalizes zombie sessions (non-ended with exited agent process) and stale sessions (24h+ uncondensed after end); sweep throttled to one spawn per repo per window. No explicit conflict resolution for transcript contents; duplicates handled by shadow-branch interleaving or checkpoint immutability.
realtime: Shadow-branch capture as session progresses (per agent turn or tool use). Session condensed to persistent checkpoint at user commit time (fast-path when ACTIVE, defer + doctor when IDLE or exited agent). Transcript sanitization and redaction run at Stop (before full.jsonl written) and Post-commit condensation. Image externalization optional, runs only on committed paths (condensation/finalize), not shadow-branch. Pre-push hook drains push-discovery queue, batch-pushes checkpoint refs to elected remote (stable fast-forward-only). On-demand fetch for refs written on other machines (lazy hydration on first read). Remote discovery via git ls-remote (names only, no object transfer) for user-facing enumeration (explicit `entire checkpoint list`, not per-turn hook). Per-turn hook is network-free (local-only, best-effort push enqueue). Session state updates via MutateSessionState closure (atomic, flock-protected).
search_retrieval: `entire checkpoint list` enumerates checkpoints on current branch (with --session filter by session ID); `entire checkpoint explain <id>` shows full tree (metadata, transcripts, token counts, files); optional AI-generated summaries via configured agent (Claude, Codex, Pi, etc.) at commit or on-demand via `--generate`. `entire session list` shows active sessions; `entire session resume [branch]` restores latest session metadata. Remote discovery via git ls-remote for refs written on other machines (hydrated lazily on read). No built-in full-text search of transcript contents mentioned; user would `git show <ref>` or `git log` with custom filtering. Session identity (agent process ancestry) enables fast lookup of session by committing process. Per-session indexing via worktree + session ID + branch.
links_sessions_to_code: Commits carry Entire-Checkpoint: <id> trailer in message (zero or more per commit, ordered by condensation). Session metadata in .git/entire-sessions/<session-id>.json names the branch and worktree the session belongs to. Checkpoint-to-code linkage resolved at commit time via worktree matching (exact WorktreePath first, then sibling worktree if unambiguous, prefer sessions interacting within 15 min) or agent-process identity matching (process ancestry using proclive, skipped on Windows). Multiple sessions per checkpoint via 0/, 1/, 2/ indexing when parallel sessions commit same code. SessionState.Owner captures agent process identity (hostname, boot-id, start-time) so a session commits link to its agent in any worktree without bookkeeping. Squash and redo commits inherit trailers from previous commits (only if staged content matches exactly).
privacy_security: Six always-on redaction layers: (1) entropy scoring (Shannon entropy > 4.5), (2) pattern matching (Betterleaks default on + configurable goredact), (3) provider token prefixes (e.g. Supabase sb_secret_), (4) credentialed URIs (scheme://user:password@host), (5) database connection strings (JDBC, Postgres, SQL Server, ODBC), (6) bounded credential key/value (DB_PASSWORD=...). Optional (7) custom secret patterns, (8) PII redaction (email, phone, US addresses, custom), (9) OpenAI Privacy Filter (1.5B token-classification model, names/emails/phones/addresses/URLs/account-numbers/secrets, runs at push only). Fail-closed: at least one scanner (Betterleaks or goredact) always enabled; setting both false is rejected. Transcript sanitization before redaction removes agent-specific encrypted payloads and compaction blobs (Codex). Image externalization optional (redaction-safe assets/ folder or unredacted inline base64); no OCR or vision scanning. Shadow-branch copies never pushed (local-only). Code-file snapshots written as raw blobs without redaction (so hardcoded secrets visible; git-ignore filters .env). Redaction happens at Stop (before shadow-branch write) and pre-push (OPF re-redaction per ref before remote push). Pre-push OPF fails closed on per-ref push (git-branch aborts, git-refs withholds refs and lets git push through).
lesson_for_parinn: Append-only per-ID history (one commit per write to a checkpoint) prevents silent loss of concurrent writes while keeping local fast-forward-only semantics. Independent per-checkpoint refs (rather than one shared branch tip) eliminate contention and allow on-demand fetch of exactly the data needed. Lazy hydration via opt-in remote discovery decouples fast local listing (no network) from eventual-consistency (names fetched later). Process-ancestry-based session identity matching (proclive) is remarkably reliable for routing agent intent into the right session across worktrees and process trees without needing explicit bookkeeping. Sanitization-before-redaction pipeline (remove encrypted/temp, externalize images, then redact) avoids wasting cycles on data that won't survive. Fail-closed redaction defaults (at least one scanner always on, both-disabled is an error) prevent silent leaks from misconfiguration. Shadow-branch + commit-time condensation keeps the permanent record clean while allowing streaming capture. Fast-forward-only with fetch-and-replay for divergence (never force-push) preserves concurrent writes across machines without losing either side.

name: episodic-memory (obra / Jesse Vincent)
category: Session archive and search plugin: a local semantic memory over coding-agent transcripts, packaged as a Claude Code, Codex and opencode plugin plus a CLI and an MCP server
status: shipped
license: MIT (LICENSE: "Copyright (c) 2025 Jesse Vincent"; package.json "license": "MIT"). https://github.com/obra/episodic-memory/blob/main/LICENSE
what_is_stored:
Three kinds of data.

(1) An archive of verbatim copies of each harness's own transcript files, subagent "sidechain" files included. Sources are ~/.claude/projects, ~/.claude/transcripts, ~/.codex/sessions, ~/.cursor/projects and ~/.omp/agent/sessions. opencode sessions are first exported from opencode.db into generated JSONL. Legacy Cursor chats are exported from state.vscdb (src/paths.ts getConversationSourceDirs; README "Commands").

(2) A "<name>-summary.txt" file next to each archived conversation. It holds an LLM-written summary, or an empty or error placeholder file (src/sync.ts). The README says summaries are "display-only… never embedded or searched".

(3) A SQLite index with three tables (docs/SCHEMA.md, src/db.ts):
- `exchanges`: one row per user/assistant message pair, holding both messages, project, archive_path, line_start/line_end, timestamp, session_id, parent_uuid, is_sidechain, harness, cwd, git_branch, claude/agent version, model, model_provider, thinking metadata and embedding_version.
- `tool_calls`: tool name, JSON input, result text and is_error.
- `vec_exchanges`: 384-dimensional float embeddings.

Two filters apply:
- Conversations that contain the marker `<INSTRUCTIONS-TO-EPISODIC-MEMORY>DO NOT INDEX THIS CHAT</INSTRUCTIONS-TO-EPISODIC-MEMORY>` are archived but not indexed.
- Single messages over 256 KB (EPISODIC_MEMORY_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES) are dropped from the index (README; CHANGELOG 1.6.0).
where_stored:
Local disk only, as plain files plus a local SQLite database. There is no git, server or peer-to-peer component.
- Archive: ~/.config/superpowers/conversation-archive/<project>/...jsonl
- Index: ~/.config/superpowers/conversation-index/db.sqlite
- Exclusion list: conversation-index/exclude.txt
- Logs: ~/.config/superpowers/logs/episodic-memory.log

The root can be moved with EPISODIC_MEMORY_CONFIG_DIR, PERSONAL_SUPERPOWERS_DIR or XDG_CONFIG_HOME, and the database with EPISODIC_MEMORY_DB_PATH (src/paths.ts).

The launch post names the archive folder "conversations-archive". The code says "conversation-archive" (https://blog.fsck.com/2025/10/23/episodic-memory/).
format_and_model:
Archive:
- Each file is a byte-for-byte copy of the source harness's native JSONL. Nothing is normalised and there is no hash chain or signature.
- The copy is written to a temp file and renamed into place, and the source mtime is kept.
- The archive copy is overwritten whenever the source file's mtime is newer (src/sync.ts copyIfNewer, L135). It is therefore a mirror with no versions. Its value is surviving the source's deletion; the launch post says Claude Code deletes transcripts after 30 days.

Index:
- better-sqlite3 in WAL mode, plus a sqlite-vec `vec0` virtual table of FLOAT[384] (src/db.ts L122, L175).
- Exchange id = md5 of "archivePath:userLine-lastAssistantLine" (src/parser.ts L189). The id depends on the local path and is not content-addressed. Tool-call ids are random UUIDs.
- Rows are written with INSERT OR REPLACE (src/db.ts L222).
- Schema changes are idempotent ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN migrations. An embedding_version column drives background re-embedding, 500 rows per sync by default (CHANGELOG 1.2.0).

Embeddings:
- Model: Xenova/bge-small-en-v1.5, q8 quantisation, run locally through Transformers.js.
- Input: "User: …\n\nAssistant: …\n\nTools: …", cut to 2000 characters, mean-pooled and normalised. Queries get the BGE retrieval prefix (src/embeddings.ts L15, L121).

The index can be rebuilt from the archive (`index --cleanup/--verify/--repair`). The summaries cannot be regenerated identically, because an LLM writes them.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Built for one user on one machine.

Within one machine:
- Several sessions or worktrees each fire `sync --background` from SessionStart.
- A proper-lockfile lock (atomic mkdir, 10-minute stale timeout) lets only one sync or index worker run. Others log "sync already running (pid X); skipping" and exit (src/file-lock.ts; src/sync-cli.ts L187; CHANGELOG 1.4.2 #97 and 1.5.0 #156).
- SQLite WAL plus busy_timeout=5000 lets the MCP readers run alongside the writer (src/db.ts).

Incremental indexing:
- Each archive file has a high-water mark, MAX(line_end). This assumes transcripts are append-only (src/sync.ts L303; CHANGELOG 1.1.0 #84, 1.6.0 #152).
- For Oh My Pi's branching JSONL, only the active leaf-to-root path is indexed (README).

Across machines: there is no replication, no sync protocol, no CRDT or merge logic, and no documented way to share one archive between machines or people. Neither the README nor the CHANGELOG mentions one. A GitHub issue search for "machines" turned up only an unrelated process-spawn bug (#89).

Inference, not tested: exchange ids hash the absolute archive path, so two machines' databases would not de-duplicate if merged.
realtime:
Not real-time. Sync is a batch job.
- The shipped hooks.json runs `episodic-memory.js sync --background` on SessionStart (matcher "startup|resume|clear") as a detached process. In effect, a session is indexed when the next session starts.
- The README still says it indexes "at the end of each session". The code and the launch post both say "on startup".
- A session that is still running gets indexed in part, and its tail is picked up at a later sync through the high-water mark.
- Summaries are capped at 10 per sync run.
- EPISODIC_MEMORY_DISABLE_AUTO_SYNC=1 turns off the hook-driven sync so it can run from cron instead (README; CHANGELOG 1.6.0).
- Nothing is pushed to other agents or sessions. Recall only works by query.
search_retrieval:
An MCP stdio server exposes two read-only tools (src/mcp-server.ts).

(a) `search`:
- Modes vector, text or both (default both). Passing an array of 2–5 concepts gives an AND search across concepts.
- Filters: after/before (YYYY-MM-DD), project, session_id, git_branch.
- include_sidechains defaults to true; sidechain rows get a 0.05 L2 distance penalty.
- limit 1–50; output as markdown or json.

(b) `read`: renders an archived JSONL file as markdown, with startLine/endLine paging.

How the search runs:
- Vector mode is a sqlite-vec KNN query with k = 3×limit, so date and metadata filters still leave enough results (CHANGELOG 1.5.0 #126).
- Text mode is an AND of per-token LIKE patterns over the user and assistant messages (src/search.ts L87). There is no FTS5 or BM25 ranking.
- The README still describes text mode as one whole-query substring match, which is out of date (CHANGELOG 1.5.0 #127/#144 fixed it).

Prompting:
- The `remembering-conversations` skill tells the agent to search before saying "I don't know".
- In Claude Code, the skill dispatches a Haiku subagent, `search-conversations`. It searches, reads the top 2–5 results and returns a synthesis of at most 1000 words. The project claims this "saves 50-100x context" (skills/remembering-conversations/SKILL.md; agents/search-conversations.md).

Quality claim: on a 17,000-exchange test, bge-small puts the right answer first 53% of the time versus 47% for MiniLM, and in the top ten 75% versus 68% (CHANGELOG 1.2.0).
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak, and only from session to code.
- Each exchange records cwd and git_branch from the transcript metadata, and tool calls keep their inputs and results, including Bash git commands and file paths (docs/SCHEMA.md).
- The MCP search can filter by project and git_branch. A commit SHA is findable only by text search over tool output; the README's example prompt is "Git commit SHA for the routing refactor".

Missing: there is no column for a commit or SHA, no git notes or commit trailers, and no link from a commit back to a session. The only worktree identity is the cwd or the project folder name.
privacy_security:
At rest:
- Everything is stored in plaintext under ~/.config/superpowers, with no encryption.
- There is no secret or PII redaction. A grep of src/ for redact, secret, scrub and sanitize finds nothing; the only scrubber is scripts/scrub-fixtures.sh, for test fixtures.

Opt-out controls:
- The DO NOT INDEX marker. Since 1.6.0 its scan fails closed: an unreadable file is skipped, not indexed (src/sync.ts L26–45).
- Excluding projects by folder name via exclude.txt or CONVERSATION_SEARCH_EXCLUDE_PROJECTS.

Network egress — "local, offline" covers only embedding and search:
- The ~34 MB embedding model is downloaded on the first sync (CHANGELOG 1.2.0).
- The summarizer sends conversation content to Claude through the Claude Agent SDK by resuming the session. It can instead use a custom endpoint or AWS Bedrock, or Codex app-server for Codex sessions. That is up to 10 calls per sync; EPISODIC_MEMORY_SKIP_SUMMARIES=1 turns it off (README).
- The MCP wrapper may run `npm install` at runtime (cli/install-runner.js).

Security fixes on record:
- 1.5.0: the background summarizer had resumed live sessions with the user's tools, MCP servers and settings loaded. In one report it "commit[ted] to a working repo". It now runs with tools: [], settingSources: [], no user MCP servers and persistSession:false (CHANGELOG 1.5.0; src/summarizer.ts L337–370).
- 1.1.2: a recursive SessionStart→summarize→SessionStart cascade spawned hundreds of processes. A guard environment variable now stops it.

Recall handling:
- Recall is pull-only through MCP, but recalled text is returned raw as tool output, with no marker telling the model it is untrusted. The only buffer is the Haiku subagent's synthesis, which the launch post frames as a context-size measure, not a security one.
- Observed in the code: `read` opens any absolute path that exists. Nothing confines it to the archive folder (src/mcp-server.ts L285–294).
- SQL filters use bound parameters, and Codex HTML rendering escapes raw HTML (CHANGELOG 1.1.0, 1.3.0).
scale:
- Retrieval benchmark: a 17,000-exchange corpus (CHANGELOG 1.2.0).
- The migration example log shows 29,569 stale rows in one user's index. Re-embedding 5,000 rows takes about a minute on a recent Mac (CHANGELOG 1.2.0).
- One user's index reached 3 GB, 97% of it oversized pasted-transcript "messages". That led to the 256 KB per-message cap (CHANGELOG 1.6.0 #139).
- Sync re-embedded whole files on every run until 1.6.0 (#152).
- No limits on corpus size or concurrency are published.
- Adoption, as shown on the GitHub page when fetched on 2026-10-02: about 483 stars, 143 forks, 16 open issues, 12 open PRs, not archived.
- Release history: latest release v1.6.0 on 2026-09-08; last commit 2026-09-10; v1.0.0 on 2025-10-14.
lesson_for_parinn:
Main lesson: anything that re-processes stored history must run with zero authority and outside the user's live configuration.

episodic-memory's summarizer resumed archived sessions with the user's tools, MCP servers and settings loaded. In one reported case it acted on that old session and committed to a working repo. Version 1.5.0 fixed this with tools: [] and settingSources: [], and 1.1.2 fixed a separate recursive hook cascade.

For ParleyInn, derived views (summaries, restore blocks, indexes) should be pure functions of the record (I10). They should never resume or replay a session, and never call a model or tool from inside a hook (I2, I4). Every derived artifact should also carry an untrusted-content envelope, which episodic-memory's raw MCP output lacks.

Secondary lesson: an archive that mirrors by mtime, with ids derived from local paths, cannot be merged across machines or prove its own integrity. ParleyInn's content-addressed, hash-chained events are the right base for multi-machine sharing. The SessionStart batch sync behind a single-instance lock is a simple, robust pattern for capture that never blocks the agent (I9).

name: Evolu
status: shipped
license: MIT
what_is_stored: User application data in typed SQLite tables with system metadata (createdAt, updatedAt, isDeleted, ownerId). Changes include CRDT causality information for conflict-free replication. Each table row belongs to an Owner and is encrypted with that Owner's encryption key.
where_stored: Locally on device in SQLite database. Encrypted blobs sent to stateless relays (self-hosted or cloud-hosted) that cannot read or understand the data. Relays store nothing from prior syncs—each comparison is stateless.
format_and_model: SQLite database with Kysely for typed SQL queries. Schema defined via Standard Schema validators (Zod, Valibot, ArkType compatible). Append-only schema evolution: can only add tables/columns, never remove or rename. CRDT-based conflict resolution with Range-Based Set Reconciliation (RBSR) using binary, fingerprint-based protocol. Soft deletes for synced tables (isDeleted flag). Unknown tables/columns stored in quarantine table until app updates.
multi_writer_and_merge: CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) enables conflict-free merges across multiple writers. Every change belongs to an Owner with that Owner's encryption key. Ownership model supports AppOwner (full access), ShardOwner (data partitioning), SharedOwner, SharedReadonlyOwner. No user-defined unique constraints allowed (distributed offline-first nature makes duplicates inevitable). Fingerprint-based reconciliation eliminates need for shared sync history, enabling stateless peer-to-peer sync.
realtime: Default WebSocket transport for synchronization. Range-based set reconciliation (RBSR) scales logarithmically: ~3 round-trips for 1M rows, ~4 for 1B rows. Binary, size-bounded messages (~100 bytes compresses 31 timestamps; ~272 bytes for 16 fingerprints representing entire database). Insertion rate: ~60,000 timestamps per second. Stateless sync compares fingerprints rather than histories.
search_retrieval: SQLite queries via Kysely typed SQL interface. Reactive queries with React Suspense support. Framework integrations for React, Vue, Svelte. Temporal syncing and logical sharding via ShardOwner primitives. No full-text search or advanced indexing explicitly documented.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Evolu is designed as a generic local-first sync engine for application data. No specific support for LLM agent sessions, conversation history, code versioning, or prompt linking. Could be used as underlying storage for such systems but provides no domain-specific abstractions.
privacy_security: End-to-end encryption with key derived from cryptographically strong secret (can use BIP-0039 mnemonic representation). Post-quantum safe encryption claimed. Relays are 'deliberately blind by design'—cannot understand shape or meaning of data. Soft deletes preserve deletion history enabling time-travel recovery. Owner-based encryption ensures data segments are independently encrypted per ownership boundary. No mention of audit logging, redaction, or secrets management.
lesson_for_parinn: Range-Based Set Reconciliation (RBSR) with fingerprint-based comparison scales conflict-free sync to billions of records with constant protocol overhead and stateless relay design. This avoids maintaining sync history per client, enabling truly scalable multi-peer replication. Quarantine table approach for forward-compatible schema evolution during rolling updates is applicable to ParleyInn's append-only constraint model.
sources: https://www.evolu.dev/ — Main website and platform overview
https://evolu.dev/docs/local-first — Local-first platform documentation with sync, encryption, deletion, storage format details
https://evolu.dev/docs/schema — Schema definition and data model constraints
https://evolu.dev/blog/evolu-8-is-released (September 1, 2026) — Evolu 8 architectural redesign with storage, sync, schema, and ownership changes
https://evolu.dev/blog/scaling-local-first-software (May 24, 2025) — Scale characteristics: RBSR performance, user count handling, complexity management
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evoluhq/evolu/main/README.md — Repository README with framework support and development infrastructure
https://github.com/evoluhq/evolu/issues — Open issues including relay improvements and scalability concerns
https://github.com/evoluhq/evolu/discussions — Community discussions on features and use cases

name: Exceeds Ink (Exceeds AI, Inc.), the `exceeds-ink` CLI
category: Commercial git-notes AI-provenance attestation, with local capture and an optional hosted or self-hosted analytics collector
status: beta. The product page labels it "Ink · public preview" and its governance features "in beta" (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). The public installer repo was seeded 2026-04-13. It has 85 release tags, the highest is v0.1.55, and the `latest` installer branch was last synced 2026-08-26 (git ls-remote and clone of https://github.com/Exceeds-AI/exceeds-ink-downloads). The signed manifest for v0.1.55 lists builds for macOS arm64/x86_64, Linux gnu/musl and Windows MSVC, plus a VS Code/Cursor VSIX (https://github.com/Exceeds-AI/exceeds-ink-downloads/releases/download/v0.1.55/release-manifest.json). Those Rust target triples are consistent with the "Rust binary" claim. Nothing is archived or superseded.
what_is_stored:
Two layers.

(1) In git, one JSON "attestation" note per commit. The vendor's published example has these fields: schema "authorship/3.0.0", commit, tool (e.g. cursor), model, session (e.g. "sess_7xKp2mNq"), turn, interaction_mode (plan|ask|agent|edit|headless), timestamp, lines {ai:[...], human:[...], unknown_lines:[...]}, token_cost {input, output, model_cost_usd} and session_hash "sha256:..." (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/). The vendor says notes hold "session hash references rather than inline transcripts" (same source). The example session_hash, e3b0c44298fc..., is the SHA-256 of the empty string, so the example is only illustrative.

(2) Off git, every captured event (prompts, diffs, mode switches, tool invocations, per-turn tokens and cost) goes into a local SQLite database "before any optional remote delivery" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/; https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). The product page markets it as recording "every prompt, diff, and dollar" (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). Depending on the privacy rung, aggregates, redacted prompts or verbatim transcripts are sent to a collector (see privacy).

The full schema is not published, and the vendor's own posts disagree. One shows a single tool/model/session per note with flat line-number arrays and no file paths (code-level-ai-provenance). Another says "a lines array where each entry carries tool, model, session_id, interaction_mode, and timestamp" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). A third says "every line carries its tool, model, session, turn..." (https://blog.exceeds.ai/git-ai-track-ai-code/). How multi-file commits are represented cannot be verified.
where_stored: Git notes under the custom ref refs/notes/exceeds-ink (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/), plus a local SQLite DB on the developer machine. Optional remote delivery goes to a collector over OTLP HTTP (default https://ink.exceeds.ai/api/v1/otlp) and a "compat" ingest endpoint (default https://ink.exceeds.ai/api/v1/ingest). Both endpoints are hard-coded in the public installer, whose README calls the target "the public Exceeds Vercel collector" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Exceeds-AI/exceeds-ink-downloads/latest/install.sh; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Exceeds-AI/exceeds-ink-downloads/latest/README.md). The vendor offers three deployments: local only, self-hosted ("Bring your own Postgres") or Exceeds-hosted (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink; https://blog.exceeds.ai/ai-code-detector-provenance-tracking/). An "in-SCM deployment option" is also claimed (https://blog.exceeds.ai/git-ai-track-ai-code/). The binary installs to ~/.exceeds-ink/bin by default (install.sh).
format_and_model:
The model is a per-commit JSON attestation as a git note, keyed by commit SHA. The schema string is "authorship/3.0.0" and the vendor calls it versioned and stable (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). The same string is the version of the open Git AI Standard v3.0.0, but Ink's published example does not follow that standard. The standard requires the ref refs/notes/ai, a text attestation section, a `---` divider and JSON metadata with a `schema_version` key (https://github.com/git-ai-project/git-ai/blob/main/specs/git_ai_standard_v3.0.0.md). Ink uses refs/notes/exceeds-ink and a pure-JSON body with a `schema` key. Whether the real binary emits Git-AI-compatible bodies cannot be verified.

Capture runs through repo-local git hooks installed by `exceeds-ink init`: prepare-commit-msg, post-commit and post-rewrite (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). Per-tool "checkpoint materializers" resolve edit evidence against the working tree at commit time. The Claude Code adapter reads PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook events, the Cursor adapter reads Cursor's state DB, Codex is captured through a headless adapter, and Copilot/Windsurf use telemetry plus "code-pattern analysis" (same source). Lines that cannot be attributed are recorded as unknown_lines rather than counted as AI or human (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/).

The vendor also says Ink "does not modify commit messages", yet it installs prepare-commit-msg, and the purpose of that hook is not documented (https://blog.exceeds.ai/git-ai-track-ai-code/). The installer also sets up a VS Code/Cursor extension and "tool integrations" (install.sh; https://ink.exceeds.ai/tos).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Little is documented. Each developer machine writes notes for its own commits into the shared ref. The vendor tells users to add notes refspecs, either `+refs/notes/exceeds-ink:refs/notes/exceeds-ink` or `fetch = +refs/notes/*:refs/notes/*`, because git does not push or fetch notes by default (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). The post says the fetch refspec "handles clone and push", which is not how git fetch refspecs work. The product page lists a "Notes Pushed per Day" metric, which implies Ink pushes notes (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). Nothing published covers concurrent pushes to the same notes ref (non-fast-forward rejection, `git notes merge` strategy).

On history rewrites, the post-rewrite hook calls `exceeds-ink rewrite` to copy notes from old SHAs to new ones after a rebase or amend (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). For squash merges the vendor says to "configure the merge driver to consolidate notes... Exceeds Ink handles this automatically" (same source). That is unverified and doubtful for server-side squashes on GitHub or GitLab, where no client hook runs. The product page lists a "Rebase/Squash Recovery" metric (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink), which hints at some later reconciliation step whose mechanism is not described. Separately, the vendor criticises Git AI's async daemon for a push race. Those claims about Git AI were not checked here.
realtime:
Not real-time between agents. Notes are written locally at commit time. The vendor's timing claims contradict each other: "finalization runs through a spawned post-commit subprocess, so git commit returns immediately", yet "the note is written before the commit is reachable for push" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/git-ai-track-ai-code/). No pre-push hook is listed, so the no-race claim cannot be verified.

Telemetry to the collector is near-real-time at best. The product page says "Data starts flowing within about 15 minutes" (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). A blog FAQ says "first insights ... within sixty minutes" and that new commits are attributed "in real time from the moment hooks are active" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/). The page also tracks a "Rollup Sync Latency" metric (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). Nothing propagates live context between machines or sessions.
search_retrieval:
CLI commands: `exceeds-ink blame <file>` for per-line attribution, `exceeds-ink trace`, `exceeds-ink status [--all-tools]` and `exceeds-ink verify` (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/; https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). Plain git also works: `git notes --ref=exceeds-ink show <SHA>` (cursor post). GitHub's web UI does not show notes (same source).

Beyond the CLI there are web dashboards (spend, model mix, conversion funnel, mode mix), PR-view line attribution in the Exceeds platform, data-warehouse export, and use of notes as input to OPA or CI policy checks (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/; https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). "MCP and API" are listed as "Coming Soon" (https://www.exceeds.ai/). No full-text or semantic search over transcripts is documented. Agents cannot recall their own history through it, apart from the "ink-prompting-coach" SKILL.md and slash command pushed into Claude Code or Cursor (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, and this is the core purpose. Each commit note carries a tool/agent session ID, turn number, model, interaction mode and token cost, plus line-level AI/human/unknown attribution (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/). A session_hash points to the transcript, which stays in the local SQLite store or, at higher rungs, at the collector. The transcript itself never goes into git (same source).

Marketing goes further, claiming "every line tagged with agent, model, prompt" and "every line you ship, traced to the prompt that wrote it" (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). For Claude Code, the turn mapping comes from PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook events (https://blog.exceeds.ai/cursor-provenance-git-notes/). Resolving a hash to a transcript requires Ink's local DB or the dashboard. The note alone cannot recover the prompt.
scale: No Ink-specific performance figures are published (hook latency, note size, DB growth). Platform-level marketing says "benchmarked on 356K+ engineers across 53.9B lines of code and 16M commits" (https://www.exceeds.ai/). It names one customer with 300 engineers (https://blog.exceeds.ai/git-ai-track-ai-code/) and claims "lighter-weight detection" for "approximately 50 AI tools" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/). The binary is about 10 MB (same source). Pricing: Ink is free for individuals and a $10/seat/month team add-on on the Pro plan (https://www.exceeds.ai/). None of this is independently verified.
privacy_security:
There are four privacy rungs, settable per team (https://blog.exceeds.ai/code-level-ai-provenance/):
- Local only: nothing leaves the machine.
- Aggregate only: spend and tool inventory, no prompts. Elsewhere this is described as one environment variable that "keeps transcripts off the wire" (https://blog.exceeds.ai/ai-code-detector-provenance-tracking/).
- Abstracted replay: "AI-redacted prompts and suppressed transcripts", using LLM-based redaction "before persistence".
- Full identified replay: verbatim content, captured with explicit engineer approval.
Where redaction runs is ambiguous. The product page says "server-side prompt redaction" (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink), while the blogs say "before any prompt content is persisted". The vendor says git notes hold only session-hash references "regardless of the rung" (code-level post). Notes still expose session IDs, model, timestamps and costs to anyone with repo access, and whether the hash is salted or keyed is not documented.

Ingest is signed with HMAC-SHA256 using a revocable per-machine token (https://www.exceeds.ai/ink). Other controls listed are per-repo allowlists, retention windows and outbound-host blocking (governance beta) (same source).

Supply chain: the installer checks an RSA-SHA256-signed release manifest against an embedded public key, then the SHA-256 of each asset, including a signed VSIX (install.sh).

Caveats:
- The installer default is not local-only. It runs `exceeds-ink setup` and `install --all` against the public collector, pairs the machine through web.exceeds.ai, and requires accepting the ToS (install.sh; README). The MDM mode auto-initialises repos, so per-repo opt-in is not always how it works (install.sh).
- The ToS says Ink "is not intended for collecting secrets, credentials, or private keys", but no secret scanning is documented (https://ink.exceeds.ai/tos).
- No encryption at rest for the local SQLite DB is documented.
- SOC 2 Type II was "working toward" as of July 2026 (https://blog.exceeds.ai/ai-code-detector-provenance-tracking/).
- The Trust Center (https://trust.exceeds.ai) renders only with JavaScript and could not be read.
- The services privacy policy is generic and says nothing specific about Ink (https://www.exceeds.ai/legal/services-privacy).
license: Proprietary, closed source. The public repo is "a distribution mirror. The private source of truth lives in the main exceeds-ink repository" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Exceeds-AI/exceeds-ink-downloads/latest/README.md). There is no LICENSE file in the mirror (404 for LICENSE and LICENSE.md), and installing requires accepting the Exceeds Ink ToS (https://ink.exceeds.ai/tos). No source code or open schema specification was found.
lesson_for_parinn:
Put a reference in git, never the content, and make that reference safe. Ink's one design choice worth copying: the shared, permanent, fork-replicated git channel carries only a small per-commit note (session ID, turn, digest, plus a stated "unknown" bucket), while transcripts stay in a local SQLite store that is pulled on demand. If ParleyInn uses git at all, it should push only a notes ref that maps each commit to a ParleyInn session ID and record-chain head hash. The hash-chained record should travel separately and be recalled pull-only, which matches I2 and I4.

Do better than Ink in three places:
1. Use a keyed or salted digest (e.g. HMAC with a per-project key), or an opaque random ID, instead of a bare SHA-256 of content. A bare hash lets anyone holding a guessed transcript confirm it.
2. Make attribution gaps explicit and counted, like unknown_lines, never silently folded into another bucket (I6).
3. Publish a versioned schema under ParleyInn's own namespace, with a gate test that enforces it. Ink's three posts disagree on its schema, and it reuses Git AI's "authorship/3.0.0" version string under a different ref, so neither consumers nor auditors can rely on it.

Also, do not claim "written before push" without a pre-push gate. Ink's detached post-commit subprocess cannot guarantee that ordering.
confidence: medium. Whether the product exists, how it is distributed, its version history, that it is closed source, its hooks, the notes ref name, and its collector endpoints and signing are verified from the installer and release artifacts. Everything about the note schema, rewrite and squash handling, timing, redaction and privacy rungs comes only from the vendor CEO's marketing posts, which contradict each other in places. No independent technical discussion was found: the web-search budget ran out, and none of the pages fetched link to one. The binary was not inspected.

name: Factory Droid CLI and Factory web/app (cloud session sync, Sessions API, Droid Computers)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Full agent session transcripts: user, assistant and tool messages, which can carry text, images and file attachments, plus per-session settings (model, reasoning effort), stats, tags and names (https://docs.factory.com/api-reference/sessions.md, https://docs.factory.com/droid-cli/cli-reference.md). Saved Spec Mode specs are written to ~/.factory/specs (specSaveDir) and worktrees go under ~/.factory/worktrees (https://docs.factory.com/docs/droid-cli/settings). Separately, opt-in OpenTelemetry metrics and spans count files modified or read, lines changed, commits created and PRs created per session.id (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/telemetry/data-reference.md).
where_stored: Two copies. (1) A local store: hook input gives transcript_path as "/Users/.../.factory/projects/.../session.jsonl", so it is per-project JSONL under ~/.factory/projects, a layout like Claude Code's (https://docs.factory.com/harness/hooks.md). The ~/.factory/sessions path named in the discovery note did not show up in the docs I read. (2) Factory's cloud (app.factory.ai): cloudSessionSync (boolean, default true) "Mirror CLI sessions to Factory web" (https://docs.factory.com/docs/droid-cli/settings). An org-managed sessionRetentionDays (14 to 365) sets "how long synced session history is retained before deletion" (same page). Airgapped deployments keep everything inside the customer network (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/privacy-and-data-flows.md). Sessions can also run on Factory-managed or bring-your-own persistent "Droid Computers" (https://docs.factory.com/droid-computers/overview.md).
format_and_model: Locally there is one JSONL file per session (the file name session.jsonl comes from the hook docs example). The per-line schema is not documented, so I could not verify it. The cloud side is a REST Sessions API: create, retrieve, update, delete (a soft delete, restorable within the retention period) and interrupt. Sessions are either running or idle. Messages have a messageId and a role of user, assistant or tool. A computerId parameter scopes calls to a machine (https://docs.factory.com/api-reference/sessions.md). Session ancestry is copy-based: --fork and /fork copy a session into a new one, and /compress "compress[es] session and move[s] to new one with summary" (https://docs.factory.com/droid-cli/cli-reference.md). There is no hash chain, signing or append-only guarantee in the docs.
multi_writer_and_merge: One writer per session. Divergence is handled by forking (copying) and never by merging. I found no documented merge of two session histories (https://docs.factory.com/droid-cli/cli-reference.md). Sharing between users or devices goes through the central Factory web mirror and the Sessions API, not through peer replication. Whether two clients can drive one session at the same time is undocumented.
realtime: Partly. Sync to Factory web is described as mirroring, but the docs give no sync latency or protocol. The Factory App shows live connection status for Droid Computers ("connecting / connected / error") and they can be reached from the App or Slack on different devices (https://docs.factory.com/droid-computers/overview.md). Locally, droid exec can stream output as stream-json or stream-jsonrpc (https://docs.factory.com/droid-cli/cli-reference.md). The docs I fetched name no SSE or webhook stream for session events.
search_retrieval: `droid search "query"` searches local sessions (messages, documents, tool results). /sessions lists and picks past sessions and has an Archived tab. `droid --resume [id]` resumes the last-modified session by default, and `droid exec -s <id>` resumes in headless mode (https://docs.factory.com/droid-cli/cli-reference.md). The Sessions API can filter messages by role (https://docs.factory.com/api-reference/sessions.md). The search engine and index format are undocumented.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Nothing is written into git: no notes, trailers or refs. For remote delegations, the Factory Droid GitHub App opens PRs and "Factory is the pull request author, not the teammate who requested the work" (https://docs.factory.com/remote-delegations/index.md). Telemetry keys code metrics to session.id (droid.git.commits, droid.git.pull_requests, droid.code.lines_modified, and droid.repo.metadata with one record per workspace) (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/telemetry/data-reference.md). The privacy page says aggregate mode strips commit.hash, pr.number and pr.url, which implies the default per-user mode carries them (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/telemetry/privacy.md). Worktrees are managed under ~/.factory/worktrees.
scale: No scale claims for session storage were found. The only bounds are the retention range of 14 to 365 days and a 32,000-character truncation per telemetry content attribute (https://docs.factory.com/docs/droid-cli/settings, https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/telemetry/privacy.md).
privacy_security: Cloud mirroring is on by default and set to false to keep sessions local (https://docs.factory.com/docs/droid-cli/settings). Synced history is deleted after the org's sessionRetentionDays. The data-flow page says file I/O stays local and content leaves the machine only inside LLM requests, but it does not cover the cloud session mirror. Factory keeps "limited operational logs and metrics", and airgapped deployments send Factory no runtime data (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/privacy-and-data-flows.md). Droid Shield detects secrets with patterns plus an entropy ("randomness") check, and version 2.0 adds two fine-tuned classifier models. It only blocks git commits and pushes made through Droid. The docs do not say it redacts transcripts or synced sessions (https://docs.factory.com/autonomy-and-safety/droid-shield.md). Message content in telemetry is off by default and is exported "raw, with no redaction". Org settings win on a most-restrictive basis, and spans never reach Factory's collector (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/telemetry/privacy.md). I found no documentation of encryption at rest for the local JSONL or the cloud mirror; the security page defers to a Trust Center (https://docs.factory.com/enterprise/security.md). The docs also do not say whether recalled history is treated as untrusted.
license: Proprietary commercial product. I found no open-source license for the CLI in the docs.
lesson_for_parinn: Factory shows the common commercial pattern: a local JSONL transcript under the home directory, mirrored by default to a vendor cloud that is the only place sharing and retention happen. Its secret scanner guards git pushes and not the transcripts it uploads, and the docs I read say nothing about encrypting either the local JSONL or the cloud mirror. ParleyInn should keep the opposite defaults. Sharing should be opt-in and go through a transport ParleyInn's core does not own. Redaction should run on the record before it is replicated anywhere (I6), not only at the git boundary. Divergent sessions should be modelled explicitly: Factory has only fork-by-copy and /compress-to-new-session. ParleyInn's hash chain can record fork and compaction lineage (parent session id plus chain head) so a forked or compressed session stays verifiable back to its origin.

name: FAVA Trails (Federated Agents Versioned Audit Trail), by Machine Wisdom AI
category: git-native agent memory (Jujutsu): a Python MCP server for curated, governed shared memory. It does not capture session transcripts.
status: shipped. v0.7.0 went to PyPI and GitHub on 2026-09-13. The repo is active, with commits to main through 2026-09-29 (HEAD 6678c4d, read for this sheet). Unreleased changes switch the Trust Gate default to OpenRouter Decisions. The repo is not archived and has 26 stars, 5 forks and 456 commits (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails, https://pypi.org/pypi/fava-trails/json, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). It is written in Python >=3.11, not Go.
where_stored:
Working-tree files in a separate data git repo (the "Fuel" repo), which is distinct from the code repo and from the engine package. It runs Jujutsu (jj >= 0.28.0) in colocated mode on top of git, and the default path is ~/.fava-trails. Sharing across machines is optional and goes through any git remote the operator already runs, such as GitHub. FAVA never creates hosted repos or changes remotes itself (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails#cross-machine-sync, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/jj-compatibility.md).

Local JJ metadata, not versioned, holds two working files:
- a governance before-image journal at .jj/fava-governance-transaction.json;
- a cross-process lock at .jj/fava-governance.lock.
Source: https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/transactions.py
multi_writer_and_merge:
**On one machine.**
- Each MCP process has one operator-set identity (FAVA_TRAILS_AGENT_ID). A caller-supplied agent_id must match it.
- Within a process, an asyncio lock per repo root serializes push, fetch and gc.
- Across processes, governance writes take a non-blocking flock. A busy lock is a retryable error. A write-ahead before-image journal keeps readers on the old complete state until VCS persistence succeeds (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/transactions.py, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/governed-recall.md).
- Before each commit, the server refuses dirty paths outside the trail's scope ("cross-trail pollution"), unexpected dirty files, case-colliding paths and executable-bit changes.

**Across machines.** All machines use one shared git remote and a single main bookmark. The FAQ states there are no per-agent branches: "one repo-wide current JJ change" (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/fava_trails_faq.md).

Publishing:
- With push_strategy: immediate, the server runs `jj bookmark set main -r @-` then `jj git push --bookmark main` after every successful write. Push failures are non-fatal warnings, with no retry found in the code.
- With manual, the bootstrap default, an operator pushes by hand.
- Plain `git push` is forbidden after colocation.
Sources: https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails#cross-machine-sync, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/vcs/jj_backend.py

Pulling: peers call the `sync` tool, which never pushes. It runs `git fetch --all` and then `jj rebase -d main@origin`. It refuses to start on a dirty working copy or case collisions, and returns not_configured when no remote exists.

**Merges and conflicts.** Thought files have unique ULID names, so concurrent new saves merge cleanly. Conflicts come from in-place mutations: file moves on promotion and superseded_by backlinks.
- On conflict, sync restores the pre-sync JJ operation with `jj op restore` and returns a summary ("Pull Daemon safety: abort on conflict").
- Non-operators get only a fixed message, and "Existing conflicts require operator repair" (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/trail.py, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/governed-recall.md).
- JJ is configured with snapshot-style conflict markers.

The FAQ's claim that contradictory beliefs are kept "as structured data" rather than halting is weaker in the shipped code, which aborts the sync instead. The docs also say concurrent replacements "cannot silently overwrite an already approved successor".
realtime:
No. Propagation is pull-based and eventually consistent: a writer must push, and readers must call `sync`.
- The "Pull Daemon" for automatic sync, with a design target of about 30 s, is planned and not shipped (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/fava_trails_faq.md).
- The only automatic loop is the optional `fava-trails-tunnel` gateway (for ChatGPT via OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel). Its `--sync-interval-seconds` starts a recurring fetch/rebase worker and defaults to 0, meaning off. `--sync-on-start` is fail-closed (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails#chatgpt-tunnel-freshness, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/secure-mcp-tunnel.md).
- There is no push notification, websocket or p2p channel.
- The product site's summary describes sync() as "publishing to shared repositories", which contradicts the README's "sync … does not push". This came through a fetched summary of https://fava-trails.org/ and was not verified verbatim.
search_retrieval:
**How recall matches.** `recall` is lexical and documented as not semantic. It lowercases the query, splits it on whitespace, and requires every token to appear as a substring (AND) of a string built from:
- content and thought_id;
- source_type and agent_id;
- metadata project, branch and tags.
metadata.extra is not searched. There is no ranking, stemming or phrase search (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/retrieval-baseline.md).

**Cost.** Each request scans and parses every thoughts/**/*.md file in-process to build a snapshot (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/transactions.py, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/trail.py).

**Filters and extras.**
- Scope filters on project, branch and tags.
- Multi-scope globs through trail_names.
- Optional one-hop relationship expansion.
- Exact lookup by ULID with get_thought.
- Optional on_recall hooks, such as ACE playbook reranking.

**Visibility modes.**
- governed (the default): approved records with no approved successor.
- authoring: the configured agent's own drafts and proposals.
- history: an operator endpoint only.
Source: https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/governed-recall.md

**Other tools.** Diff and history go through operator-only diff, rollback and op-log tools. A local, read-only Astro "Rich Views" dashboard is available. A semantic or full-text index is only under discovery (issue #59, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/issues/59), with no embeddings product selected.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weakly, and only by convention. The data repo is separate from the code repo, and no capture hook records prompts, transcripts or commit SHAs. The available links are:
- A `.fava-trails.yaml` committed in the code repo names the default scope. FAVA_TRAILS_SCOPE can override it per worktree (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/AGENTS_USAGE_INSTRUCTIONS.md).
- Agents are told to fill metadata.project and metadata.branch, and to detect the branch with `git branch --show-current`. Both are free-text fields.
- Runtime context such as session_id, host and cwd is recommended for metadata.extra, but that field is not searched and is excluded from Trust Gate egress.
- intent_ref can point to the ULID of an intent document.
- The usage guide has agents call recall at session start and propose_truth on task completion.
The thought-to-code link is therefore textual metadata, not a verifiable reference.
scale:
No benchmarks are published. The FAQ calls its numbers "design targets only": draft save under 50 ms on local disk, and recall cost that "depends on corpus size (full scan … in-process today)" (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/fava_trails_faq.md).

Hard bounds in code and docs:
- The `/healthz` readiness probe walks at most 100,000 scope-tree entries within 2 s, and parses one thought of up to 512 KiB (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails#chatgpt-tunnel-freshness).
- GC runs every 500 snapshots or 3600 s (jj util gc plus `git gc --prune=now`).

Adoption: the 0.7.0 changelog says "This release does not report measured user adoption". The project is small: 26 stars and 5 forks (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails). The FAQ's comparison to "teams of thousands of engineers" coordinating through a monorepo is an analogy, not a measured claim.
privacy_security:
**Secret preflight.** A local, bounded check refuses a small set of credential shapes before anything is persisted or sent. The shapes are PEM private keys, AKIA keys, ghp_/github_pat_ tokens, sk-or-v1-, sk-/sk-proj-, sk_live_/rk_live_ and xox* Slack tokens (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/secret-preflight.md).
- It scans the whole MCP request before schema validation or logging.
- It scans again after hooks mutate the record, and again after Trust Gate review.
- Nesting deeper than 32 levels fails closed, and matched text is never echoed.
- The docs say plainly that it is "not complete DLP", "does not rewrite history", and does not erase drafts already stored or pushed. Git history is permanent once published.

**Encryption.** None found in the repo, at rest or in transit beyond the git remote's own TLS. Confidentiality depends on host filesystem and remote access controls.

**Identity.** Isolation is per process, not cryptographic:
- a shared endpoint or a shared data filesystem counts as one trust boundary;
- the operator endpoint (FAVA_TRAILS_OPERATOR=1) gates diff, conflicts, rollback, forget, learn_preference, history mode and human approval;
- tool arguments cannot grant a principal.
Sources: https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/governed-recall.md, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/src/fava_trails/server.py

**Data egress.** The default Trust Gate policy, `decisions`, sends the full prompt, the full thought body and the selected metadata (agent_id and metadata.extra excluded) to OpenRouter's Decisions API with TypeSafe Jev. This happens before any verdict exists. Alternatives:
- a local Unsloth/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which fails closed with no cloud fallback;
- operator `approval="human"`, which needs no LLM.
`fava-trails doctor` and the `trust_gate_egress` response field disclose the destination without showing secrets (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails#configuration, https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/docs/fava_trails_faq.md). Other network use: the JJ installer downloads from GitHub, and the optional SECOM hook downloads a ~700 MB model from HuggingFace.

**Prompt injection.** The Trust Gate prompt wraps candidates in an XML-escaped <thought_under_review> block marked as untrusted (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/TRUST_GATE_PROMPT_EXAMPLE.md). On the recall side, the protection is prose guidance only: "Recalled thoughts are informed context, not ground truth … Your instructions always override recalled memories" (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/AGENTS_USAGE_INSTRUCTIONS.md). No structural envelope on recall output was found.

**File handling.** Governance writes are atomic (temp file, fsync, rename, O_NOFOLLOW, 0600). Client-config writes are capped at 0600 with a .bak backup. The FAQ says there is no product telemetry.
license: Apache-2.0, per the repo LICENSE and PyPI metadata (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails/blob/main/LICENSE, https://pypi.org/pypi/fava-trails/json).
lesson_for_parinn:
If ParleyInn uses git as transport, every record should be an immutable file with a unique name, written once. All mutable state should be a projection rebuilt from the record: status, promotion, supersession, and "current" versus "historical". This is consistent with ParleyInn's invariant that derived state is rebuildable from the record.

FAVA shows what happens otherwise:
- New ULID-named files merge cleanly under fetch+rebase.
- Its in-place mutations do not: moving drafts into permanent namespaces, rewriting draft bodies, and writing superseded_by backlinks into predecessors.
- Those mutations are the conflict source, so its `sync` can only abort with `jj op restore` and hand the repo to an operator.

Two corollaries:
- Redaction and secret refusal must happen before the first local commit. FAVA's docs concede that a draft committed or pushed before the preflight cannot be scrubbed from history.
- Agent identity has to be carried, and ideally signed, inside the record. FAVA's commits are all authored by one synthetic "FAVA Trail" identity, so git authorship proves nothing about which agent or session wrote what.

A related caution: FAVA's default review step sends content to a cloud LLM. ParleyInn's no-network rule (I4) rules that out, so any review or promotion gate would have to be local or human.

name: Fedora AI-Assisted Contributions Policy (Assisted-by commit trailer)
category: commit trailer convention (governance policy, not software)
status: shipped. The policy is in force: the Fedora Council approved it 7-0-0 on 22 Oct 2025, effective immediately. It was committed on 24 Oct 2025 (commit 823e93b6). The only later commit, 6fdcc1be on 15 Jan 2026, added the line "v1.0, 2025-10-24" and dropped a page-authors attribute. The normative text has not changed since. Note: the docs.fedoraproject.org page sits behind an Anubis bot wall and returned an access-denied page to automated fetching. The text was verified from the AsciiDoc source on forge.fedoraproject.org (council/docs, file council/modules/ROOT/pages/policy/ai-contribution-policy.adoc).
what_is_stored:
Only a disclosure that AI was used, as free text, normally a tool or model name. The policy's own examples are "Assisted-by: generic LLM chatbot" and "Assisted-by: ChatGPTv5". Nothing else is defined: no prompts, no transcripts, no session ids, no model versions in any fixed form, no record of which lines the AI produced.

When disclosure is required:
- MUST: "when the significant part of the contribution is taken from a tool without changes".
- SHOULD: other AI uses, "where it might be useful".
- Not needed: grammar, spelling or clarity fixes.

The stated purpose is to help Fedora "evaluate their impact, build new best practices and adjust existing processes".

The rest of the policy is about accountability, not storage: the contributor "is always the author and is fully accountable". AI must not be "the sole or final arbiter" of a substantive judgment or of a person's standing. Large-scale AI initiatives need separate Council approval.
where_stored:
Wherever authorship is normally recorded ("Disclosures are made where authorship is normally indicated"):
- Work tracked in git: inside the commit message itself, as an `Assisted-by:` trailer (the recommended method).
- Everything else: document preambles, design-file metadata, translation notes, or the Fedora Wiki category Category:AI_Assistance_Used.

There is no separate store, ref, notes namespace or database.
format_and_model:
A standard git trailer: a "key: value" line in the last paragraph of the commit message, after a blank line, parsed by git interpret-trailers (keys are ASCII letters, digits and hyphens; values may fold over several lines).

The value has no fixed form. It is free text naming the tool, and the examples above do not even agree on a shape.

It can be queried with `git log --format='%(trailers:key=Assisted-by)'`, which matches keys case-insensitively.

The data model is one trailer, or several, per commit. It is part of the commit object, so it is covered by the commit hash and by any signature.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Inherits git's model: each commit carries its own trailers, so no shared state exists to merge. A rebase, squash or cherry-pick keeps the message only if the person doing it keeps it.

Squash-merging in a forge can drop or concatenate trailers. The policy does not address this (not covered in the sources).

git's own handling of repeated trailers is set by trailer.ifexists; the default, addIfDifferentNeighbor, skips adding a key-value pair when the same one sits right next to it.
realtime: Not applicable. A disclosure exists only once a commit is made and pushed. Nothing is streamed or synchronised.
search_retrieval:
Only what git offers: `git log --grep` or `%(trailers:key=Assisted-by)` over history, plus forge commit search.

Fedora defines no index, dashboard or aggregation tooling. The Council meeting summary mentions no tooling or tracking of disclosures.

The wiki side can be browsed through the MediaWiki category Category:AI_Assistance_Used.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weakly, at commit granularity only. The trailer ties a commit to a tool name. It does not link to any agent session, prompt, transcript or conversation id, and it does not mark which hunks were generated.

No mechanism lets anyone check whether a disclosure is accurate or complete. It is self-reported and depends on the honour system plus reviewers. Suspected violations go to the Fedora Council through private tickets.
scale: No scale claims. The policy covers all Fedora contributions tracked in git (packages, docs, infrastructure) and non-git ones such as wiki, design and translation work. It says nothing about adoption rates or volume.
privacy_security:
Minimal by design: only a tool name enters public, permanent git history, so prompts and session content never leak. The policy says nothing about redaction, encryption or secrets, because nothing sensitive is stored. Being in the commit object, the trailer is tamper-evident through the commit hash and any GPG or SSH signature. It cannot be removed later without rewriting history.

Trust lies in accountability rather than technology. The human contributor vouches for quality, license compliance and utility. AI may assist reviewers but cannot be the final arbiter.
lesson_for_parinn:
ParleyInn should split the public pointer from the private record. The public part matches the convention projects are standardising on: a small, signable trailer in the commit message (Assisted-by: <agent>/<model>, plus an opaque ParleyInn session or record hash). The full session history stays in ParleyInn's own append-only, hash-chained store and never goes into git history.

Fedora shows that open-source projects will accept only a minimal, free-text disclosure in public history. Its value has no fixed form and cannot be verified. A ParleyInn-written trailer could close both gaps:
- Use a fixed form: one key, a structured value, and an optional record digest.
- Make the trailer verifiable against the local hash chain without publishing prompts. This keeps I2: no untrusted content flows in, and recalled content stays enveloped.
- Never require network access, which keeps I4.

ParleyInn should also expect trailers to be lost in squash, rebase or cherry-pick. So the link from session to commit should live on the ParleyInn side, recording which commit SHAs a session produced. The trailer is a hint, not the source of truth.
license: Not stated in the policy file. Fedora Docs content is generally CC BY-SA 4.0, but that was not verified for this page.

name: Fly.io Sprites
category: persistent agent sandbox with checkpoints (hosted microVM, not a VCS)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: A persistent 100 GB ext4 root filesystem per Sprite, which is a Firecracker Linux microVM with root access (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/, https://fly.io/learn/fly-vs-modal/). Checkpoints capture the writable filesystem overlay above the base image: files, packages, config and on-disk databases such as SQLite. They do NOT capture running processes, memory or open network connections (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). Nothing stores agent sessions, prompts or transcripts as structured records. Whatever an agent such as Claude Code writes to disk (for example ~/.claude session JSONL) ends up in the disk snapshot as plain bytes. That is my inference from 'checkpoint = whole disk'; Fly does not document it. Fly also stores per-account metadata in a separate SQLite database for each account (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/), and stores Connector credentials encrypted in the org database (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/connectors).
where_stored: Server/cloud. The authoritative state is S3-compatible object storage. A sparse 100 GB NVMe volume attached to each Sprite is only a read-through cache of immutable chunks ('nothing in that NVMe volume should matter'). Fly writes that 'the durable state of a Sprite is simply a URL' (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Pricing separates hot storage (about $0.50/GB-month) from cold storage (about $0.02/GB-month) (https://fly.io/sprites). An 'S3 Block Device' backend, which shows object storage to the kernel as a block device carrying ext4 with block-level snapshots, is in early access (https://fly.io/sprites).
format_and_model: The storage stack follows the JuiceFS model: Fly runs 'a very hacked-up JuiceFS, with a rewritten SQLite metadata backend'. Data is split into immutable chunks held in object storage. Metadata, the map of which chunks make up the filesystem, lives in local SQLite and is kept durable by Litestream replication to object storage (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Checkpoints are copy-on-write snapshots that only shuffle metadata, so they are incremental and billed by blocks retained (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). The model is a linear version list per Sprite: manual checkpoints v0, v1, v2... with an optional comment each, plus hidden 'auto-' checkpoints that are pruned over time. Restore rolls the same Sprite back in place; it is asynchronous and destructive, restarts the inner environment and ends active sessions. You cannot delete the active checkpoint (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). User code runs in an inner container. Orchestration, the storage stack, logs and the service manager run in the VM's root namespace ('inside-out orchestration'), so a restore does not reboot the VM (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Fly's own comparison page says manual checkpoints 'do not rot' (https://fly.io/learn/fly-vs-modal/). At launch (Jan 2026) a third-party write-up described rolling back to the 'last 5 checkpoints' under /.sprite/checkpoints; current docs do not repeat that limit, so it may be outdated (https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jan/9/sprites-dev/).
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable in the VCS sense. Each Sprite is a single-writer machine with a linear checkpoint history. Sprites cannot branch, merge or reconcile divergent states. Native 'fork a new Sprite from a checkpoint' does not exist yet. A June 30, 2026 community feature request calls it a popular ask (about 20 similar threads), and Fly staff replied only 'We'll have more to share soon' (https://community.fly.io/t/feature-request-native-fork-sprite-from-checkpoint/28191). The workaround is to copy the overlay out and back in on the client side. Users report this is slow, over a minute, and hits stream timeouts for an overlay of about 723 MB (same source). Several agents can share state only through external systems such as git or HTTP; I could not verify any built-in mechanism.
realtime: This is not a real-time sync or replication system for users. Litestream streams metadata continuously to object storage, so durability is near-continuous, but that is internal (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Fly says checkpoint creation takes about 300 ms (sprites.dev, per https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jan/9/sprites-dev/) or about one second (https://fly.io/sprites). Restore is asynchronous (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). Sprites sleep when idle and wake on an incoming HTTP request to their URL (https://fly.io/sprites). Public-URL routing goes through Corrosion, Fly's gossip service-discovery system, which 'propagates across our fleet instantly' (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/).
search_retrieval: There is no content search. Retrieval means listing checkpoints by version ID and comment ('sprite checkpoint list [--include-auto]', GET /v1/checkpoints over the management socket) and then restoring a whole snapshot in place (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). A REST API (api.sprites.dev/v1) and SDKs for JS, Go, Python and Elixir exist (https://fly.io/sprites). Nothing indexes or searches inside snapshots.
links_sessions_to_code: Only implicitly. A checkpoint freezes the agent's working files and its on-disk session logs together, so restoring one rewinds both. Fly says the preinstalled Claude Code 'will checkpoint aggressively for you without asking' and that Claude, Gemini and Codex are taught to checkpoint and restore (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Checkpoint comments could serve as a hand-written link. No explicit record ties a prompt or turn to a checkpoint or a commit, and none is documented. Claude Code runs there in --dangerously-skip-permissions mode by default (same source).
scale: No storage volume or fleet numbers are published. Plan limits: 100 concurrent or warm Sprites on the Hero tier, and creation rates from 10/min (pay-as-you-go) up to 240/min (Mythic) (https://fly.io/sprites). Creation takes 1–2 s from pre-warmed pools of standard-image Sprites (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/). Each Sprite has 100 GB of disk, billed by blocks written that differ from the base image (https://fly.io/sprites, https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints). Sprites launched on January 9, 2026 (https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jan/9/sprites-dev/).
privacy_security: Isolation: 'Every Fly.io Sprite is a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, on every tier' (https://fly.io/learn/fly-vs-modal/). Egress: unrestricted by default. An optional DNS-based allowlist sits read-only inside the Sprite at /.sprite/policy/network.json. Disallowed domains get DNS REFUSED, raw-IP connections are blocked unless resolved through an allowed domain, private IPs are always blocked, and policy changes reload live (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/networking). Ingress: Sprite URLs are org-only by default and can be made fully public with no authentication (same source). Secrets: Connectors keep OAuth or API tokens encrypted in the org database and never return them through the API. A Sprite calls api.sprites.dev/v1/gateway/<provider>/<connection_id>/<path>; the gateway checks the Sprite's identity and deny-by-default policies (block rules before allow rules) and attaches the credential, so the Sprite never holds a long-lived secret (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/connectors). Encryption at rest of Sprite chunks and checkpoints in object storage: I could not verify it for Sprites. Fly's general security page covers LUKS for Fly Machines volumes and databases (https://fly.io/docs/security/security-at-fly-io/), but Sprites use a different storage stack. I found no documented redaction of disk or snapshot contents. Restore is destructive, with no backup of the state it overwrites (https://docs.fly.io/sprites/concepts/checkpoints).
license: Proprietary hosted service. Fly mentions work on an open-source local Sprite runtime, but I could not verify a release (https://fly.io/blog/design-and-implementation/).
lesson_for_parinn: Sprites shows that a durable agent record can be 'immutable content-addressed chunks in dumb object storage plus a small SQLite metadata log replicated by Litestream'. In that design, checkpoint and restore cost only metadata, and the local disk is a disposable cache. That suits ParleyInn on ephemeral cloud sandboxes: an append-only, hash-chained segment set that any blob or git transport can carry, with derived indexes rebuilt from it (I10). ParleyInn's core can stay offline (I4) while a separate shipper moves segments. Sprites also marks the limits to avoid. Its history is a single-writer linear chain with destructive in-place restore: no fork (still an open request as of June 2026) and no merge. It captures sessions only as opaque disk bytes, with no content search and no redaction. ParleyInn should keep session records as first-class, append-only, mergeable logs that are never overwritten by a restore. Its records should exist independently of the sandbox's disk snapshot, which can roll them back or lose them. A per-session ID should tie a turn to a commit or checkpoint, which Sprites lacks. A second lesson is the Connectors pattern: credentials stay outside the sandbox behind a policy-checking gateway. It suggests that whatever transports ParleyInn history across machines should hold the signing or push keys, not the agent's sandbox.

name: Fossil SCM
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Fossil stores append-only version control artifacts in a single SQLite database: code check-ins (commits), wiki pages, ticket/issue changes, forum posts, technotes (blog entries), attachments, and control artifacts (tags/properties). All content is content-addressed via SHA1 hash and organized in a Directed Acyclic Graph (Merkle DAG) structure similar to Git. Artifacts are stored as delta-compressed and zlib-compressed blobs.
where_stored: Single SQLite database file (*.fossil extension). All artifacts, metadata, user accounts, permissions, and settings coexist in the same database. Each repository is one self-contained file. Repositories can be cloned to create distributed copies. Auxiliary files (unversioned) can be stored separately.
format_and_model: Structural artifacts are UTF-8 text with card-based format: each card type (B, C, D, F, N, P, Q, R, T, U, Z for manifests; similar for other artifact types) occupies one line with space-separated arguments. Cards are lexicographically ordered and checksummed (MD5). Manifest format supports baseline/delta encoding: baseline manifests record complete file lists, delta manifests record only changes. Artifacts can be PGP clearsigned. Stored as blobs in SQLite using zlib compression and delta compression for bandwidth efficiency (80:1 compression observed on long-lived projects like SQLite source).
multi_writer_and_merge: Fully distributed DVCS supporting concurrent development. Default 'autosync' mode automatically pushes commits to and pulls from a configured server, preventing forks. In manual mode, developers use explicit 'fossil push', 'fossil pull', and 'fossil merge' commands. Forks detected automatically; leaf selection based on timestamp to pick the most recent when multiple branches exist. Merges are explicit (fossil merge HASH) and applied to working directory before committing, allowing testing and verification. Cherry-pick (--cherrypick) and backout (--backout) also supported. Synchronization uses bandwidth-efficient HTTPS or SSH protocol.
realtime: Not designed for real-time. Fossil is pull-based: agents must actively sync to see changes from other writers. No built-in webhook or pubsub mechanism for live notifications of new commits. Can work offline and sync later; autosync mode reduces but does not eliminate latency. Suitable for loosely-coupled distributed teams, not for tight real-time coordination like shared editing or live agent session updates.
search_retrieval: Optional full-text search (FTS) via built-in Fossil search feature, disabled by default to save CPU/IO. When enabled, search indexes code files, wiki pages, tickets, and forum posts. Search accessible via web UI and command-line.
