Built-in web interface provides timeline, file browser, diff viewer, and artifact inspection. No SQL query interface; retrieval is through Fossil commands (fossil artifact, fossil log, fossil blame) or web UI.
links_sessions_to_code: No native support. Fossil has no concept of 'agent sessions' or 'prompts'. Could create custom unversioned artifacts or wiki pages to document agent context, but no structured link type exists. Forum posts can reference check-ins by hash (cross-referencing auto-detected), but agent-to-code linking would require external system or convention-based metadata (e.g., commit messages containing session IDs).
scale: Tested and proven: Fossil repository of SQLite project has 77,492 check-ins with 80:1 compression ratio (was 320MB under CVS, now ~40MB in Fossil). Single check-in typically uses 3-4KB network bandwidth. Fossil executable is a single self-contained binary (~15-20MB compiled). Runs on resource-constrained hardware: documented to work on $5/month VPS and Raspberry Pi. No special scaling infrastructure required; SQLite handles ACID transactions. Not tested for millions of artifacts or extreme concurrency, but well-established for mid-size to large open-source projects (SQLite, Fossil itself use it).
privacy_security: Artifacts can be PGP clearsigned (optional, not default). No encryption at rest in database. User passwords stored as hashes. Repository file contains auxiliary sensitive data: password hashes, email addresses, user account info. 'fossil scrub' command removes sensitive data before sharing repository file. All content syncs to clones (distributedly tamper-proof via Merkle DAG: any tampering detected by hash mismatch). User capability system for granular permissions (read/write code, tickets, wiki, forum, admin). No redaction mechanism; once written, artifacts cannot be unwritten (only new artifacts can override old ones via tags). No built-in secrets management or encryption key handling.
lesson_for_parinn: Fossil demonstrates that a single SQLite database can efficiently store and distribute diverse artifact types (code, metadata, discussions) with strong integrity guarantees via Merkle DAG. However, for ParleyInn's security model (I2: untrusted content must not reach the model, I6: no silent failures), Fossil's approach has three gaps: (1) no encryption at rest means secrets risk exfiltration if the .fossil file is stolen, (2) no mechanism to redact or selectively forget sensitive session content, (3) sync-on-demand (not real-time) makes it hard to ensure all agents see consistent, pinned constraints after compaction. For ParleyInn, consider Fossil's architecture as inspiration for atomic transactions and Merkle verification, but add: encryption at rest (AES-GCM on blobs), ability to rewrite/remove artifacts under strict control (contrary to append-only principle), and a pubsub or notification layer so agents can immediately react to constraint updates or security revocations.
sources: https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/fileformat.wiki — Artifact format specification (manifests, control artifacts, wiki, tickets, forum, attachments)
https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/concepts.wiki — Distributed version control concepts, workflows (autosync vs manual), merging
https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/branching.wiki — Branching, forking, merging, tagging mechanics and DAG structure
https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/forum.wiki — Forum feature, permissions, capabilities, email alerts
https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/stats.wiki — Performance metrics: SQLite repository 80:1 compression, bandwidth per check-in
https://fossil-scm.org/home/doc/trunk/www/mirrortogithub.md — GitHub mirroring: fossil git export, one-way export limitations
Latest version observed: Fossil 2.28 (2026-03-11) running at fossil-scm.org; local server version 2.29 (2026-10-01)

name: Gas Town
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Gas Town stores seven categories of persistent state: (1) **Work beads** — issues, tasks, features, molecules stored in Dolt SQL. (2) **Agent identity and lifecycle** — agent bead records (Mayor, Deacon, Polecats, Witness, Refinery, Crew) with persistent identity, session history, and state tracking. (3) **Convoy coordination** — grouped work units spanning multiple rigs. (4) **Mail** — inter-agent messages, delivered via beads with `issue_type='message'`, threaded via dependencies. (5) **Merge requests** — MR beads created when polecats run `gt done`, tracked through the Refinery merge queue. (6) **Operational metrics** — session lifecycle, agent state changes, tool invocations, nudges, slings (recorded via OpenTelemetry). (7) **Git history** — full commit graph in Dolt, with cleanup via rebase/gc (CREATE → LIVE → CLOSE → DECAY → COMPACT → FLATTEN lifecycle). Ephemeral patrol data (wisps) are deleted after 24h; permanent data survives indefinitely with history compaction.
where_stored: Three-tier storage hierarchy: (1) **Dolt SQL Server** — primary store, one server per town on port 3307, data in `~/.dolt-data/`. Each rig gets a separate database (`hq` for town, `<rigprefix>` for rig). Auto-started by `gt daemon`, queries via MySQL protocol. (2) **Git worktrees** — agents (Polecats, Refinery, Crew) work in git worktrees (not full clones) rooted at `mayor/rig`, enabling fast spawn and shared object storage. Beads data lives in canonical `mayor/rig/.beads`, redirected from worktrees via `.beads/redirect` file. (3) **JSONL ledger backup** — permanent record of completed work. The JSONL Dog exports scrubbed snapshots every 15 minutes to a git-backed archive (`~/gt/.jsonl-backups/`), providing disaster-recovery durability. Git remotes can also hold code branches.
format_and_model: **Beads** — rows in Dolt SQL `issues` table. Schema v6: `id` (VARCHAR primary key, format `prefix-5alphanumeric`), `title`, `description`, `status`, `issue_type`, `assignee`, `hook_bead`, `role_bead`, `agent_state`, `metadata` (JSON), plus `created_at`/`updated_at`/`closed_at`. Relationships via separate `dependencies` table (type: blocks, parent-child, thread). Labels via `labels` table. **Dolt** — git-like SQL database with versioning; each row mutation becomes a durable Dolt commit. `dolt_history_*` tables provide row-level history. **JSONL** — exported snapshots in JSON Lines format, one bead per line, pushed to git for durability. **Git** — Commit graph is the permanent record; rebase/gc compaction happens daily. **Telemetry** — OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) structured logs (resource attributes: `gt.role`, `gt.rig`, `gt.agent`, `gt.session`, `gt.run_id`), metrics (counters for spawns, merges, formula instantiations).
multi_writer_and_merge: **All-on-Main strategy**: Every agent (Polecats, Refinery, Witness, Deacon, Crew) writes directly to the `main` branch of their rig's Dolt database with no branching. Concurrency managed through **transaction discipline**: all writes wrap `BEGIN` / `UPDATE issues SET ...` / `CALL DOLT_COMMIT('-Am', 'message')` / `COMMIT` atomically. This eliminates the former branch-per-worker strategy and ensures immediate cross-agent visibility — no visibility gaps. Dolt auto-commits are on by default; agents can batch writes by temporarily disabling auto-commit within a transaction. **Conflict resolution**: Dolt's default merge strategy is `newest` (most recent `updated_at` wins for scalar fields); arrays (labels) use `union` merge; counters use `max`. Agents never merge from separate branches; all mutations are immediate on `main`. Multi-statement `bd` commands batch their writes inside a single transaction. **Write sequencing**: No WAL, no optimistic locking; Dolt's SQL server serializes transactions at the MySQL protocol level.
realtime: Yes. **Three real-time channels**: (1) **Mail system** — messages delivered as beads with threading; agents poll inbox via `gt mail read` or receive nudges. (2) **Nudges** — direct tmux messages via `gt nudge`, bypassing mail queue. (3) **Activity monitoring** — `gt feed` TUI reads beads and renders live agent activity, Convoy status, event stream. (4) **OpenTelemetry events** — structured logs streamed to OTLP backend (defaults to VictoriaLogs); agents subscribe to real-time feeds of session lifecycle, prime operations, bd calls, state changes. (5) **Witness patrol** — per-rig Witness runs continuous health checks (configurable frequency) to detect stuck polecats, triggering nudges or escalations. (6) **Deacon daemon** — cross-rig supervisor running patrol cycles every heartbeat (~3 min), monitoring all rigs. No message queue (work is on hooks, not in a buffer). Agent sessions are tmux panes; output is captured on-demand via `CapturePane` (not streamed). Dolt commits are immediately visible to all readers.
search_retrieval: **SQL queries** — agents query beads via `bd show <id>`, `bd list --filter`, or raw SQL via `gt dolt sql`. Filters support `--status`, `--assignee`, `--label`, `--type`. **Dolt-specific**: `AS OF` queries for time-travel (e.g., 'what did this bead look like yesterday?'), `dolt_diff()` to see changes between points, `dolt_history_*` tables for full row-level history. **Full-text search** — Beads supports FTS5 on `title` and `description` (planned; not yet shipped in Gas Town). **Query API** — Beads provides a query DSL (`BeadsQuery`) that translates to SQL; agents can use `bd list --query 'status=open AND assignee=polecat-alpha'`. **Routes** — `routes.jsonl` file maps ID prefixes to rig locations; `bd show hq-mayor` automatically routes to town beads, `bd show gt-abc12` to the gastown rig. **Reconstruction**: Since Dolt stores full history, any state at any point in time is queryable via `AS OF <commit>`. Beads compaction (REBASE) removes intermediate history but preserves the final result.
links_sessions_to_code: **Multi-layered linkage**: (1) **Bead ID** — each work unit is identified by a bead ID (e.g., `gt-abc12`). Beads can reference git branches and commits via metadata JSON field. (2) **Git branches** — Polecats create feature branches per task; the branch name is tied to the bead ID via naming convention (e.g., `polecat/abc12-<timestamp>`). When a Polecat runs `gt done`, it pushes the branch and creates an MR bead. (3) **Worktrees** — each agent's worktree is located in a predictable path based on agent type/name and rig (e.g., `gastown/polecats/toast/<rigname>`), enabling correlation. (4) **Agent beads** — Polecats, Crew, Witness, Refinery each have a persistent agent bead (e.g., `gt-gastown-polecat-toast`, `gt-gastown-crew-alice`). The agent bead carries `hook_bead` (currently assigned work) and `role_bead` (agent role definition). (5) **OpenTelemetry correlation** — Every operation emits events with `gt.agent`, `gt.rig`, `gt.work_bead`, `gt.work_mol` resource attributes (PR #2199 adds `gt.run_id` for cross-event correlation). Agents query their session history via `gt seance --talk <session-id>`. (6) **Mail threading** — Messages link to beads via dependencies (type='thread'), enabling agents to ask predecessors about decisions on a specific bead. (7) **Formulas and molecules** — Molecules (multi-step workflows) are tracked as beads, with `mol_type` and `metadata` identifying the formula source and step sequence. No automatic session-to-session transcript persistence (agents read conversations via `--resume`); Gas Town tracks *work* not *conversation*.
scale: **Claimed**: Gas Town is designed to coordinate 20–30 parallel Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini agents (README line 15 and discovery note). **Tested**: No explicit public test report; changelog mentions 'scale comfortably to 20-30 agents' but cites test references like 'Clown Show #13' and 'Leviathan tests' which are not public. **Scaling mechanisms**: (1) **Dolt server** — single server per town serves all rig databases via SQL; no sharding. (2) **Scheduler** — `gt config set scheduler.max_polecats 5` gates concurrent agent spawn to prevent API rate limit exhaustion; default is immediate dispatch. (3) **Witnesses and Deacon** — patrol agents run independently per-rig (Witness) and cross-rig (Deacon), avoiding centralized bottleneck. (4) **Convoy batching** — `gt convoy create` groups related beads and assigns them as a unit, reducing per-bead overhead. (5) **Worktree efficiency** — agents use git worktrees (not full clones), enabling fast spawn and shared object storage. **Known constraints**: Dolt's commit graph grows indefinitely (not rows, but commits); rebase compaction is required daily. JSONL export Dog runs every 15 minutes; OTLP export may add latency if backend is slow.
privacy_security: **No encryption** — Dolt data in `~/.dolt-data/` is unencrypted on disk. Mail beads, agent state, work history are readable by any process with filesystem access to the town root. **No secrets management** — Gas Town does not encrypt or redact secrets. Agents can read and execute shell commands; credentials in env vars or `.env` files are visible to agents running in the same tmux session. No credential isolation. **No redaction** — OTEL logs and JSONL exports carry full message text and tool input/output (unless sampling is applied externally). **Agent isolation**: Workers run in separate tmux sessions but share filesystem (same user account). Polecats run in worktrees under the town user; filesystem permissions are standard Unix. **Git permission**: Agents can push to configured remotes; no per-agent branch restrictions. **JSONL backup**: The JSONL Dog exports 'scrubbed snapshots' every 15 minutes, but scrubbing is not documented (status ambiguous). **Recommended**: Run Gas Town in isolated environments for untrusted code; review agent output before pushing to production. Use appropriate git remote permissions.
lesson_for_parinn: **Lesson: Git worktrees are a lightweight, durable persistence layer for agent work state.** Gas Town uses git worktrees (not full clones) as the canonical workspace for agents, enabling fast spawn and shared object storage. Each agent's work is a git branch rooted at a shared canonical clone (`mayor/rig`), automatically giving ParleyInn's agents: (1) **zero-copy branch isolation** — fast spawn, no disk duplication. (2) **implicit undo** — `git reset` or `git checkout` to recover any prior state. (3) **natural sharing** — all branches in the same object database are instantly visible to all agents. (4) **merge-ready** — worktree branches can be rebased/merged with standard git tooling. **Secondary lesson**: **Dolt provides multi-writer coordination without branching.** Gas Town's all-on-main strategy (transaction discipline, atomic commits) eliminates the coordination overhead of per-writer branches. For ParleyInn, this suggests: write-in-place (not branches) on a central Dolt server may be preferable to distributed git branches for fine-grained session snapshots, especially when cross-agent visibility is a priority. However, Dolt's commit graph (not rows) is the storage cost; history compaction (rebase/gc) is not optional at scale. **Tertiary lesson**: **Beads (issue tracking) decouples work tracking from code changes.** Gas Town tracks agent work as beads (issues) in a separate Dolt database from code repos, enabling: agents to query and update work status without touching git, work to be assigned/claimed independently of branches, and machines/agents to be swapped without re-cloning. For ParleyInn, this pattern suggests storing session metadata (agent identity, work item, decision log) in a separate Dolt or SQL database alongside git, rather than in git notes or custom refs. **ParleyInn-specific consideration**: Gas Town does not encrypt session history or redact secrets; for agent security, ParleyInn should add crypto-shredding (rotate keys, re-export) when agents log out or sessions end. ParleyInn's append-only invariant could benefit from Dolt's rebase-based compaction (keep the final state, discard intermediate commits) rather than pure append-only-forever.

name: Gemini CLI
status: archived
what_is_stored: Complete conversation history including: user prompts and model responses, all tool executions with inputs and outputs, token usage statistics (input, output, cached, thoughts, tool tokens), assistant thoughts and reasoning summaries, workspace directories added during session, memory scratchpad with workflow metadata (workflow summary, tool sequence, touched paths, validation status), session metadata (sessionId, projectHash, startTime, lastUpdated, summary, kind: main or subagent)
where_stored: Local filesystem at ~/.gemini/tmp/<project_hash>/chats/ where <project_hash> is a SHA-256 hash of the project's root directory. Sessions are stored as JSONL files named session-<number>.json. Project hash is managed via a ProjectRegistry stored at ~/.gemini/tmp/projects.json. Global runtime directory can be ~/.gemini or ~/.cache/.gemini depending on sandbox mode.
format_and_model: JSON Lines (JSONL) format. Data model uses TypeScript interfaces: ConversationRecord as the root containing sessionId, projectHash, startTime, lastUpdated, messages array, and optional summary/memoryScratchpad/directories/kind. Messages are typed MessageRecord union: BaseMessageRecord (id, timestamp, content as PartListUnion, optional displayContent) + ConversationRecordExtra (type: 'user'|'info'|'error'|'warning'|'gemini' with optional toolCalls array, thoughts array, tokens summary, model name). Supports append-only mutations via MessagePatchRecord ($patch), MessageRecord (new message), MetadataUpdateRecord ($set), and RewindRecord ($rewindTo) for checkpoint rewinding.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single-writer per active session; each CLI invocation opens its session exclusively. Sessions can be resumed from other CLI instances via --resume flag, which loads the entire ConversationRecord. Supports manual checkpoints via /resume save <name> / /resume resume <name> for named branch points within a session. Append-only JSONL structure with patch records (MessagePatchRecord, MetadataUpdateRecord) enables non-destructive history evolution. No distributed merge conflict resolution; sessions are project-local.
realtime: Automatic background saving during interaction. Sessions are recorded automatically as the model responds, tool outputs are captured, and token stats are updated. No explicit flush required; each message and tool call appears to be persisted immediately to the session file.
search_retrieval: Sessions listed by project with --list-sessions flag showing session index, first user message (display name, truncated to 100 chars), last updated time, session UUID. Interactive session browser accessible via /resume slash command with: scrollable list of past sessions, preview of session date/message count/first prompt, /keystroke to search sessions by ID or content, Enter to resume, Esc to exit. Can resume latest session via --resume, by index number via --resume 1, or by full UUID via --resume <uuid>.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Sessions are project-specific, keyed by project root directory hash. Workspace directories can be added via /dir add and stored in the session's directories field. Sessions track which project they belong to via projectHash. Different projects automatically use different session histories.
privacy_security: Sessions stored locally in user's home directory (~/.gemini/tmp/), not encrypted by default. Sessions can be manually deleted via --delete-session <index|uuid> or via Session Browser (x key). Automatic cleanup configured via settings.json: enabled/disabled flag, maxAge duration (default 30d), maxCount (default unlimited), minRetention safety limit (default 1d). When a session is deleted, all associated data (implementation plans, task trackers, tool outputs, activity logs) is also removed. No built-in redaction shown in documentation; full conversation history including tool inputs/outputs retained.
lesson_for_parinn: Gemini CLI's JSONL append-only format with patch records (MessagePatchRecord, MetadataUpdateRecord) and checkpoint support (RewindRecord for /resume save/resume) provides a practical pattern for immutable session history with non-destructive updates. Project-scoping by directory hash avoids collisions across worktrees and machines. However, no distributed merge strategy or multi-writer coordination is evident; ParleyInn must add those for multi-agent shared history. The automatic background saving works because a single CLI instance owns each session; ParleyInn's distributed hash-chained design with mandatory pull-only recall (I2) must avoid the silent-overwrite risk that single-writer-per-session sidesteps. The 50-message and 50KB-per-tool-output limits suggest ParleyInn should define bounds on replay size and redaction rules upfront.

name: Gemini CLI checkpointing (/restore, shadow git and conversation JSON)
category: Agent CLI checkpoint (shadow git snapshot plus conversation JSON)
status: shipped. It is in google-gemini/gemini-cli main as of commit c9096a8 (2026-10-01), package version 0.64.0-nightly.20260929. It is off by default. The --checkpointing CLI flag was removed in 0.11.0, so settings.json (general.checkpointing.enabled) is now the only way to turn it on. A newer, separate /rewind feature overlaps with it.
what_is_stored: Each checkpoint has two parts. (1) A git commit in a shadow repo that holds the whole project working tree, minus anything the user's .gitignore excludes, as it stood just before the tool ran. (2) A JSON file with these fields: `history` (the UI history items), `clientHistory` (the full Gemini API Content[] conversation: role plus parts), `toolCall` {name, args} for the pending call, `commitHash` (the shadow commit) and `messageId` (the prompt_id). Only the edit tools trigger a checkpoint. EDIT_TOOL_NAMES = {replace/edit, write_file}, and the file is written while the call is in AwaitingApproval. A call is skipped (and the skip is logged) when its args have no `file_path`. Shell-tool side effects are not snapshotted per call, though they show up in the next snapshot because `git add .` stages the whole tree. Sources: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/utils/checkpointUtils.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/cli/src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/tools/tool-names.ts
where_stored: Everything stays on the local disk, outside the project's own repo. The shadow repo is a separate git dir at ~/.gemini/history/<id>/.git. Git is run with GIT_DIR pointed there and GIT_WORK_TREE set to the project root, so the user's .git is never touched. The JSON files go in ~/.gemini/tmp/<id>/checkpoints/<ISO-timestamp>-<basename>-<tool>.json. The docs still say <project_hash>, but current code has moved to a human-readable slug "shortId" taken from a lock-protected registry at ~/.gemini/projects.json (proper-lockfile). Old sha256(projectRoot) directories are migrated to the slug on startup. Sources: https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/checkpointing/ https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/config/storage.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/config/projectRegistry.ts
format_and_model: Snapshots are plain git objects. The shadow repo is initialised with branch main and an empty initial commit, and each snapshot is a linear commit with the message "Snapshot for <tool>" and the fixed author "Gemini CLI <gemini-cli@google.com>". gpgsign is off and commits use --no-verify. If nothing changed, the current HEAD is reused, so several checkpoints can share one commit. The conversation is a pretty-printed JSON file per checkpoint and holds the whole conversation, not a delta. That makes the record O(n^2) in conversation length: each checkpoint copies everything that came before it. The JSON points to the code state only through `commitHash`. There is no hash chain, no append-only log and no schema version field. On load the file is checked with zod (getToolCallDataSchema). Restore runs `git restore --source <hash> .` and then `git clean -f -d` against the real project tree, reloads both histories, and offers the original tool call again. Sources: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/services/gitService.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/commands/restore.ts
multi_writer_and_merge: It is single-user and single-machine, with no merge. Within one process, createFileSnapshot runs `add . / status / commit` under an in-process path lock keyed on the realpath of the project root. A code comment says this lock exists because two concurrent snapshots "fold each other's files" into one commit. Edit tools are also forced to run sequentially in the scheduler. I found no cross-process lock on the shadow repo, so two gemini sessions in the same directory share one shadow repo and one checkpoints folder, and only git's own index.lock stands between them. That is inferred from the code and I have not tested it. The registry file mapping project paths to ids is cross-process locked with proper-lockfile. Each git worktree path gets its own id and shadow repo, because ids are keyed by path. Sources: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/services/gitService.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/scheduler/scheduler.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/config/projectRegistry.ts
realtime: Does not apply. Checkpoints are written locally and synchronously before each edit tool runs, and nothing is shared or streamed to other agents or machines. https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/checkpointing/
search_retrieval: None beyond listing. `/restore` with no argument lists checkpoint filenames (timestamp, file basename, tool name), and `/restore <name>` loads one. There is no full-text search over conversations. The commit can be read with ordinary git log/diff against the shadow GIT_DIR, but that is not a documented interface. If the commit has been garbage-collected or the repo rebuilt, restore fails with "could not be found ... garbage collected". https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/checkpointing/ https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/commands/restore.ts
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, tightly but only locally. Each JSON checkpoint ties the full conversation, the pending tool call and the prompt_id to one shadow-repo commit hash, and restore rolls back files and conversation together. The link lives entirely outside the user's real git history: no trailers, notes or refs go into the project repo, so the session-to-code link cannot be pushed or shared and does not survive a move to another machine. The related /rewind command reverts only changes made by the AI edit tools. It does not undo manual edits or shell (`!`) changes. Sources: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/utils/checkpointUtils.ts https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/cli/rewind.md
scale: The project makes no scale claims. Every snapshot stages the whole working tree with `git add .`, and since the shadow repo copies the user's .gitignore, untracked but un-ignored files are captured too. The JSON files duplicate the full conversation each time. I found no retention, pruning or GC of checkpoint JSON or shadow commits in the code: grepping the code for uses of the checkpoints and history directories found only write and restore paths. Absence of cleanup is therefore unverified but likely. Sources: https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/checkpointing/ https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/services/gitService.ts
privacy_security: Data is local only ("stored locally on your machine"). Nothing is redacted or encrypted at rest. The full conversation and tool args are written as plaintext JSON, and any secret files the user has not gitignored are committed into the shadow repo. The git process is hardened: GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM point to a private gitconfig and an empty system file, GIT_DIR and GIT_WORK_TREE from the environment are not inherited, the environment passes through sanitizeEnvironment with variable redaction, and commits use --no-verify, so the user's hooks, signing and aliases do not run. However, simple-git's "unsafe" option guards are all switched off for the shadow repo (allowUnsafe* = true). On the destructive side, restore runs `git clean -f -d` on the real project tree, which deletes untracked, non-ignored files created after the snapshot. Restored conversation goes straight back into model context, so recalled content is treated as trusted. Sources: https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/checkpointing/ https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/services/gitService.ts
lesson_for_parinn: The idea to keep: a separate GIT_DIR outside the project, with a sanitized environment, a private gitconfig and no hooks. That gives cheap, content-addressed code snapshots without touching the user's repo, and ParleyInn can store a session event's code state as a single commit/tree hash. Two weaknesses to avoid. First, the conversation is stored as full copies per checkpoint, joined to code only by a commit hash that GC can orphan. ParleyInn should keep the conversation as its append-only, hash-chained delta log, have each event carry the tree hash, and pin those commits with a ref so GC cannot strand a record (I6, I10). Second, restoring history straight into the model is a trusted path. ParleyInn's I2 requires that recalled history stay enveloped and pull-only. Smaller points: gate any git-clean-style restore behind an explicit, audited operation; never snapshot un-ignored secret files without redaction; and put a cross-process lock on any shared shadow store, because Gemini's lock is in-process only and ParleyInn expects many agents and worktrees.

confidence: high. This is based on the official docs and a source read of main at commit c9096a8 (2026-10-01). Two points rest on code reading and are untested: the lack of a cross-process lock on the shadow repo, and the lack of retention or GC.

name: Gerrit NoteDb
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Code review metadata: changes (pull requests), comments (inline and global), votes, approvals, patch sets, account data, group information. All modifications stored as append-only sequence of Git commits. Per-change metadata includes global fields (status, votes) and revision-specific comments.
where_stored: Git refs within the same repository as code. Metadata: refs/changes/45/12345/meta (NoteDb notes branch per change). Patch set code: refs/changes/45/12345/{PATCHSET_NUMBER}. Account/group data: All-Users repository. Inline comments stored in NoteMap (Git tree structure) with commit SHA-1 as key.
format_and_model: Append-only event log using Git commits. Global metadata (votes, status changes) stored in commit messages on meta refs. Inline comments stored as JSON in NoteMap indexed by commit SHA-1. Comment JSON schema includes: uuid, filename, patchSetId, lineNbr, author (id), writtenOn (ISO 8601 timestamp), side (1 or -1 for parent), message, range (startLine, startChar, endLine, endChar), revId (patch set commit), serverId (UUID of origin Gerrit server), unresolved flag. Data model built on JGit NoteMap abstraction for key-value trees in git.
multi_writer_and_merge: Append-mostly event log with no strict multi-writer guarantees. Metadata stored as immutable Git commits appended to meta refs. Meta refs may be rewritten, but default assumption is all operations are logged. Supports online and offline migration from ReviewDb (Gerrit 2.x). Replication plugin enables automatic push to multiple systems (warm-standby, mirroring, load balancing). Per-change ref isolation (refs/changes/NN/NNNNN/meta) allows independent replication and updates per change. Multi-writer coordination relies on Git's underlying ref update semantics (atomic per-ref); no explicit conflict resolution documented for simultaneous writes from multiple Gerrit servers, though serverId field suggests federation-aware design.
realtime: Not real-time. Changes updated asynchronously via Git commits. Lucene search index updated separately from metadata writes. No built-in streaming or event notification beyond git ref updates and standard replication plugin. Changes propagate to replicas via push operations, not continuous streaming.
search_retrieval: Lucene-based full-text and field search, separate from storage. Supports complex search operators (status, project, author, topic, change-id, commit, file path, etc.). Search index built from NoteDb metadata. Search decoupled from write path: metadata committed first, index updated asynchronously. No mention of real-time indexing or consistency guarantees between storage and search index.
links_sessions_to_code: Limited. Each comment includes serverId field (UUID) to track which Gerrit server wrote it, enabling identification of origin. Comments linked to patch sets via commit SHA-1 (revId field). Change metadata maintains referential integrity with code via patchset commit SHAs. No explicit support for agent sessions, prompts, or multi-agent session tracking. Design assumes single code review system (one or more Gerrit servers), not multiple independent agents.
privacy_security: No built-in encryption or secrets management. Data stored in plain text within git repository. Access control enforced at Gerrit application layer (existing ACL model), not at storage layer. Redaction of comments is possible (tools exist to delete zombie comments) but not automatic. No field-level encryption or secret masking documented. Sensitive data (auth tokens, etc.) should not be stored in review metadata. Backups include full metadata history (auditability), creating privacy implications for data deletion.
lesson_for_parinn: Seven lessons: (1) Append-only event sequences in git refs successfully handle high-volume metadata at scale (Google-scale Gerrit sites). (2) Separation of storage from search/indexing allows independent optimization and scaling. (3) Metadata consistency with code achievable when both stored in same git repository (single source of truth). (4) Per-change refs (refs/changes/NN/NNNNN/meta) provide isolation and enable fine-grained replication control—applicable pattern for isolating agent session streams. (5) ServerId field pattern enables tracking origin in federated multi-server scenarios. (6) Git's native ref semantics (atomic per-ref) sufficient for serializing updates to single change, but multi-change coordination across writers not explicitly addressed. (7) Gerrit's move from mutable SQL (ReviewDb) to immutable git-based storage shows strong appeal of event-based immutability for audit and consistency, but NoteDb's lack of explicit multi-agent coordination or conflict resolution is a gap ParleyInn must address.

name: Git AI (git-ai)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Line-level attribution data linking each code line to originating agent, model, and prompt; message-level attribution to source conversations; token usage counts; session history; prompt context tied to generated code; code rework metrics and PR impact analysis
where_stored: Git notes under refs/notes/ai namespace for line-level attribution in commits; prompts stored securely outside Git; enterprise platform stores additional metadata (token accounting, session context, dashboards) in cloud or self-hosted database
format_and_model: Git-native approach using standard git notes (refs/notes/ai). Agents call 'git ai checkpoint' to record changes. System converts lightweight local checkpoints into authorship logs attached to commits. Line-level attribution format: maps each line to agent identifier, model name, and prompt reference. No custom binary formats; integrates directly with git without hooks or command wrapping (zero-overhead design).
multi_writer_and_merge: Supports multiple AI agents (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf) writing simultaneously. Preserves attributions automatically through complex git operations: rebases, merges, squashes, cherry-picks, resets. Git notes are rewritten automatically across history rewrites to maintain accuracy. Handles merge conflicts in notes by preserving agent identity per line.
realtime: Open source version: local-first, offline-capable with checkpoint mechanism. Detects agent changes in real-time as code is written. Enterprise platform version: real-time insights dashboard with token accounting, session tracking, and SDLC-wide visibility. No background processes or keyloggers in either version.
search_retrieval: AI-aware blame command traces code lineage and attribution through multiple commits. Message-level attribution allows developers to query agents about code they generated and access source conversations. Platform provides per-PR, per-contributor, per-team, and per-repo filtering and search. Custom dashboards and data export available in enterprise tier.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Session history feature allows developers to 'ask agents about the code they created.' Each line is linked to specific agent session, conversation context (message-level attribution), and exact prompt that generated it. Session metadata stored and retrievable. Harness engineering platform provides comprehensive session tracking and incident correlation.
privacy_security: Prompts stored securely outside Git (not in repository history, preventing accidental exposure). Local-first open source version requires no login or cloud connectivity. Enterprise version offers self-hosting option. No heuristic-based detection—only explicit agent reporting ensures accuracy. No keyloggers or background processes. Auditing and counting of all operations. Supports data export and custom redaction policies in enterprise tier.
scale: Open source CLI available free to teams of any size. Enterprise platform designed for scale: serves hundreds of engineering teams including Fortune 100 companies. Supports unlimited agents, contributors, teams, and repositories. Performance is O(commit size), not O(repository size).
lesson_for_parinn: Git AI demonstrates that git notes (refs/notes/*) can serve as a viable, open standard for storing agent-generated metadata alongside commits while preserving lineage through complex git operations. Key insights: (1) Separation of prompt/session data from git history protects against accidental exposure while maintaining auditability. (2) Explicit agent reporting (not detection) is more accurate and verifiable. (3) Git's native facilities handle multi-writer scenarios and history rewrites automatically. (4) Zero-overhead integration achieved by leveraging git notes instead of hooks or command wrapping. (5) Message-level attribution linking code back to source conversations provides richer context than code-to-agent alone. For ParleyInn: storing agent session history and prompts in git notes under refs/notes/agent/* alongside hash-chained storage could leverage git's native merge handling while keeping sensitive prompt data in separate secure storage.
sources: https://usegitai.com/about (company background, founded July 4, 2025 by Aidan Cunniffe and Sasha Varlamov, acquired by OpenAI September 11, 2026)

name: Git Prompt Story (QuesmaOrg/git-prompt-story)
status: beta. It exists and was shipped through Homebrew and `go install`, with tags up to v0.9.0 (2026-01-04). The GitHub description still reads "Store LLM prompts in git notes. (DEV release, not for public yet)", with 5 stars, 0 forks and 214 commits. The last commit on the default branch is 524e633 from 2026-01-17. The repo is not archived, but nothing has landed in the roughly 8.5 months before October 2026, so it looks dormant. That is inferred from commit dates; I could not confirm whether it was abandoned on purpose.
what_is_stored: 1) A small JSON manifest per commit: {v:1, start_work, sessions:[{tool:"claude-code", id, path, created, modified}]}. 2) Whole Claude Code session JSONL files, copied as-is from ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-path>/<id>.jsonl but scrubbed first. The `toolUseResult` field is dropped (README says this saves about 37%) and Read-tool outputs are replaced with <REDACTED> (about 8%). 3) A trailer line appended to the commit message: "Prompt-Story: Used Claude Code (N prompts)" or "Prompt-Story: none [version]". 4) An optional `annotate-cloud` command pulls Claude Code cloud sessions from api.anthropic.com /v1/sessions/{id}/events, using the OAuth token in the macOS keychain, and converts them into the same format. Only Claude Code is supported. Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI are listed as planned, and Cursor work sits on unmerged branches (cursor-support, feature/cursor-support).
where_stored: Custom git refs inside the project repo. refs/notes/prompt-story is an ordinary git-notes ref, with the manifest as the note on each commit. refs/notes/prompt-story-transcripts is not a notes ref and not a commit chain. It points straight at a bare tree object (claude-code/<session-id>.jsonl), rebuilt with `git mktree` and moved with `git update-ref`, so it keeps no history of its own. A pending note blob SHA is staged in .git/PENDING-PROMPT-STORY between the prepare-commit-msg and post-commit hooks. A debug log goes to .git/prompt-story-debug.log. A GitHub Action can also publish rendered HTML transcripts to GitHub Pages.
format_and_model: Many-to-many links between commits and sessions. Each commit's note lists the session IDs and transcript paths it touched. Each transcript is stored once per session ID, as a git blob, so it is deduplicated by session. The manifest references a transcript by path (refs/notes/prompt-story-transcripts/claude-code/<id>.jsonl), not by blob SHA. Each new commit re-hashes the whole current session file and replaces the tree entry for that ID. So an older commit's note resolves to the newest, longest snapshot of the session, not the content as it was at commit time. The viewer and CI summary rebuild the per-commit slice at read time by filtering JSONL events to the window from start_work to the commit time. start_work comes from the reflog (previous commit or last branch switch). Sessions are picked at commit time by file mtime, by the cwd and timestamp on the first line, and by whether the session has user messages in that window. README design notes: "Whole sessions: transcripts stored as-is, no slicing. Parsing happens in viewer." Schema version field: v=1.
multi_writer_and_merge: Weak, and lossy across machines. Merging happens only for history rewrites. A post-rewrite hook moves notes from old SHAs to new ones, and when commits are squashed it unions their sessions, deduplicated by session ID, keeping the earliest start_work. Nothing merges concurrent writers. The pre-push hook force-pushes both refs (+refs/notes/prompt-story and +refs/notes/prompt-story-transcripts) to whatever remote is being pushed. A code comment admits notes "can diverge when ... Multiple machines work on same repo without syncing notes" and calls force-push "safe since notes are metadata". In practice, a second machine or worktree that pushes overwrites the first one's notes and transcripts on the remote: last writer wins. Because the transcripts ref is a bare tree with no parent commits, git cannot run a three-way merge on it, and there is no fetch-and-merge step (no use of `git notes merge`). The README recommends force-pushing after a local redaction as well.
realtime: None. Capture happens only at `git commit`, through the prepare-commit-msg and post-commit hooks. Sharing happens only at `git push`, through the pre-push hook or a manual push of the refs. Sessions in progress are not streamed, and work that is never committed is never captured.
search_retrieval: No index and no full-text search. You retrieve by commit or range: `git-prompt-story show <commit|A..B>` opens a Bubble Tea TUI that browses sessions and can redact, and `git-prompt-story pr preview/summary A..B` renders Markdown or HTML. A GitHub Action posts a PR comment and can optionally deploy full HTML transcripts to Pages. Raw access works with plain git (`git notes --ref=prompt-story show`, `git cat-file -p refs/notes/prompt-story-transcripts:claude-code/<id>.jsonl`). The README calls prompts "searchable", but no search feature exists in the code.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Linking to commits is the whole point. Each commit gets a git note listing its sessions plus a Prompt-Story trailer in the message, and the PR view aggregates sessions over a commit range. Notes survive amend, rebase and squash through the post-rewrite hook. Since 2026-01-17, `pr summary` warns when a commit has a trailer but its note is missing. The link is by session and time window, not by blob hash. It does not pin the exact transcript bytes or attribute individual lines or hunks.
scale: The project makes no scale claims. Its only storage figures are the reductions from dropping toolUseResult (~37%) and Read outputs (~8%). Structurally, every commit that touches a long-lived session re-stores that session's entire scrubbed JSONL as a new blob. Old blobs drop out of the tree and become unreachable locally, but they can linger in clones and on remotes. Tree rebuilding is O(sessions) on each commit, run through shell-outs to git. No benchmarks are published.
privacy_security: Notes stay local until pushed, and pushing is automatic when the hooks are installed with --auto-push. Scrubbing runs before storage and is on by default: regex recognizers cover user home paths, DB/URL credentials, emails, credit cards, AWS/Stripe/GitHub/Anthropic/OpenAI/OpenRouter/Google/Discord/NPM/SendGrid/Twilio/Slack keys, Bearer tokens, cookies, password= and *_TOKEN= assignments, and PEM private keys. Read-tool outputs are removed by default, but Bash, Edit and Write outputs are kept. Scrubbing can be turned off with GIT_PROMPT_STORY_NO_SCRUB=1 or --no-scrub. Manual redaction in the TUI replaces messages with "<REDACTED BY USER>", and you then force-push. That does not purge blobs already fetched by others or cached by the forge. There is no encryption, signing, integrity chain or access control beyond repo permissions; notes are as public as the repo. Recalled transcripts are not treated as untrusted (no prompt-injection handling), because the content is aimed at human reviewers, not fed back to models. Unlike ParleyInn's I4, the tool shells out to git (`os/exec`), and `annotate-cloud` makes network calls with the user's Claude OAuth token read from the keychain.
lesson_for_parinn: Do not copy the "metadata, so force-push is fine" stance. Git Prompt Story silently loses notes from other machines because it force-pushes a parentless tree ref, and its commit notes point at a mutable path rather than a content hash. If ParleyInn uses git as a transport, three things follow. Each writer (agent, machine or sandbox) gets its own commit-chained ref, for example refs/parinn/<writer-id>, and refs are only fast-forwarded, never overwritten. Any commit-to-session link records the exact record hash or chain head at commit time, so the slice is pinned and verifiable rather than recomputed from timestamps. Redaction is a new appended tombstone event that is itself audited (I6), not a history rewrite plus force-push, which cannot really remove data from other people's clones anyway.
license: Apache-2.0 (GitHub license badge and README).
confidence: high. Facts come from cloning the repo at HEAD 524e633 (2026-01-17) and reading its source, plus the live GitHub page for the description, stars and commit count. Two points are inferred: that the project is dormant (no commits since January 2026) and that the blog post is the project's announcement. The prompts-source-code link in the README now redirects to the 2026-01-09 post "Vibe Coding Needs Git Blame" by Piotr Migdał.

name: Git reftable ref backend
status: shipped (opt-in since Git 2.45; still not the default. git-scm.com lists Git 2.56.0, released 2026-09-28, as the latest release, and the Git 3.0 BreakingChanges doc still says "There is no planned release date for this breaking version yet". Whether 2.56 changed the default was not checked line by line; BreakingChanges says the switch comes with 3.0.)
what_is_stored: Only git references (name -> object id, or symref target) and their reflogs (old_id, new_id, committer name/email/timestamp/tz, message). It holds no blobs, trees, commits or any session content: those stay in the object database. Deletions are tombstone records, so the "files" backend's full packed-refs rewrite is not needed (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable ; https://git-scm.com/docs/BreakingChanges).
where_stored: Local repository files under $GIT_DIR/reftable/. That is a stack of binary tables named ${min_update_index}-${max_update_index}-${random}.ref (or .log for log-only tables), ordered by $GIT_DIR/reftable/tables.list. Readers read the tables newest-first (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable). It is a local storage backend only. The sources describe no reftable-specific wire protocol. Fetch and push still use the ordinary git protocol, and remotes may use either backend (an inference from the sources, which describe reftable purely as on-disk storage).
format_and_model: The model is a sorted key-value table stack, a log-structured-merge design. Each table holds ref blocks ('r'), optional obj blocks ('o') that map abbreviated object ids back to ref blocks for reverse lookup, zlib-deflated log blocks ('g'), index blocks ('i') and a footer. Ref names are sorted and prefix-compressed. Restart points every 16-64 records allow binary search inside a block, up to 65,535 restarts per block. The block size is configurable (4k/8k/64k suggested, max 16,777,215 bytes), and a ref name cannot span blocks. Every transaction gets a unique 64-bit update_index. Reflog keys are ref_name '\0' reverse_int64(update_index), so the newest entries come first. Directory/file conflicts such as refs/heads/foo plus refs/heads/foo/bar are representable. You enable it with `git init --ref-format=reftable`, init.defaultRefFormat or GIT_DEFAULT_REF_FORMAT. `git refs migrate --ref-format=reftable` converts existing repos (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable ; https://git-scm.com/docs/git-init ; https://git-scm.com/docs/git-refs ; https://github.blog/open-source/git/highlights-from-git-2-45/).
multi_writer_and_merge: Writes are serialized locally: one writer at a time holds tables.list.lock. The writer reads the stack and picks update_index = max+1. It then writes a new table, renames it into place, appends it to tables.list.lock and renames that over tables.list. A multi-ref transaction is therefore atomic. The files backend, by contrast, "may see in-between states" (https://git-scm.com/docs/BreakingChanges). Readers take consistent snapshots by reading tables.list and retrying if a listed file has vanished. Geometric compaction runs after every write. It locks only the tables it merges and then swaps tables.list atomically, so reads and compaction do not block on writers (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable ; https://about.gitlab.com/blog/what-s-new-in-git-2-51-0/). There is no merge semantics for ref values. Concurrent remote writers still meet git's usual compare-and-swap / non-fast-forward rejection at push time, and reftable does not change that. Limits: `git refs migrate` "cannot migrate repositories that have worktrees", and it cannot block concurrent writes during migration (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-refs).
realtime: Not applicable. It is a local on-disk format with no notification or streaming mechanism. It only makes the per-update cost of ref writes small: transactions are O(size of update), not O(total refs) (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable). Any real-time sharing would still have to poll or push via normal git transport.
search_retrieval: Lookup by exact ref name is near constant-time, and prefix enumeration of a whole namespace (e.g. refs/tags/) is efficient. Optional obj blocks give reverse lookup from object id to refs. Reflogs for a ref are returned newest-first. Measured on Android's 866k refs with a cold cache: lookup by name 409,660 usec -> 33.9 usec, by SHA-1 412,536 usec -> 323.2 usec, full scan 402 ms -> 112 ms (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable). There is no content or full-text search: it indexes ref names and ids only.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Reftable is a generic ref store with no concept of agent sessions or prompts. It matters only indirectly: a design that maps each session (or event stream) to a ref, as Gerrit does with refs/changes/* and GitHub with refs/pull/*, is exactly the workload reftable was designed for. The spec says it "assumes the vast majority of references are single object names valued with common prefixes, such as Gerrit Code Review's refs/changes/ namespace, GitHub's refs/pulls/ namespace" (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable).
scale: From the spec, packed-refs vs reftable size: Android (866k refs) 62.2M -> 36.1M, Rails (31k refs) 1.8M -> 1.1M. Reflog: 149,932 entries 173M -> 5M, about 37 bytes per entry vs 1,209 (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable). Git 2.51 batched ref updates into one transaction for fetch and push. With 10,000 refs, git-fetch got a 22x speedup on reftable vs 1.25x on files, and git-push 18x vs 1.21x (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/what-s-new-in-git-2-51-0/). Note that the 22x figure is from Git 2.51, not 2.48 as the discovery note said. The 2.48 article reports only a 7% speedup from iterator reuse plus reflog support in `git refs migrate` (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/whats-new-in-git-2-48-0/). BreakingChanges says writing many refs is faster than the files backend "by multiple orders of magnitude" (https://git-scm.com/docs/BreakingChanges).
privacy_security: None. Tables and reflogs are plaintext binary, with no encryption, redaction or secret handling. The reflog stores committer identity, timestamps and free-text messages. Tombstones make deletion logical until compaction or reflog expiry removes the data, so crypto-shredding or GDPR-style erasure is not something the format provides. Integrity rests on git's object ids. The tables carry no hash chain or signatures of their own; the spec describes integrity checks for the file format only, such as footer CRC (https://git-scm.com/docs/reftable). Not verified: whether GitHub or Forgejo run reftable server-side. JGit, libgit2 and Gitoxide support is named as a prerequisite for making it the default (https://git-scm.com/docs/BreakingChanges), and their current support status was not verified.
lesson_for_parinn: If ParleyInn ever maps sessions or events onto git refs (refs/parinn/sessions/<id>, or notes-style), reftable removes the local cost of many refs: atomic multi-ref transactions, O(update) writes, tombstone deletes and fast prefix enumeration. But it does nothing for transport, realtime delivery, encryption or erasure. Hosts and other git implementations may still use the files backend, and `git refs migrate` refuses repos with worktrees, which is ParleyInn's core multi-worktree setup. So treat one-ref-per-session as a sync and export convenience, not the system of record. ParleyInn's own append-only store can borrow the design directly: an immutable table stack plus an atomically renamed manifest (tables.list), a monotonic update_index per transaction, newest-first log keys and geometric compaction. Those fit I10's "rebuildable from the record" and need no network (I4).
license: Part of git (GPL-2.0), and the reftable library sits in git's tree. Not separately verified in this session.

name: git-bug
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Distributed issue tracker storing bugs/issues, comments, identities (authors), and complete operation history. Organizes changes as sequences of edit operations (Operation-based CRDT), not final states. Supports labels, status changes, comment editing, and identity management with partial public key support.
where_stored: Git objects stored as blobs, trees, and commits in the repository, not as files in the working tree. References stored under refs/<namespace>/<id> pointing to commit chains. Each entity's complete history forms a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph). One common blob used for Lamport clock metadata entries to minimize network transfer.
format_and_model: JSON-serialized OperationPacks containing arrays of Operations. Each Operation has: type, author ID, Unix timestamp, Lamport clock value, cryptographic nonce for entropy, and operation-specific data (message, status value, etc.). OperationPacks grouped by session/author. Entities identified by SHA hash of first operation. Full formal specification documented in spec (git-bug spec).
multi_writer_and_merge: Fully distributed with git push/pull for synchronization. Concurrent edits resolved via DAG merging: loads all commits and OperationPacks, validates Lamport clocks respect DAG structure, applies deterministic ordering (Lamport clock if not concurrent, else lexicographic OperationPack ID). Parent commits cannot have higher or equal Lamport clock than children—violations are rejected. Secondary ordering unbiased and hard to abuse.
realtime: Not real-time by default. Works offline with explicit push/pull commands for synchronization (git-bug push/pull). Web UI with GraphQL API runs on localhost with no background sync. CLI, Terminal UI (gocui), and Web UI all available. Synchronization is pull-only for reading, push for writing.
search_retrieval: Query language with filters: status (open/closed), author, participant, actor, label, title, and missing features. Text search in bug titles and comments. Sorting by ID, creation time, edit time. Fast in-memory cache layer with BugExcerpt and IdentityExcerpt for quick indexing/filtering without loading full entities. Repository locking prevents concurrent git-bug operations; normal git operations unaffected.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not link sessions to code. Bridges to GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Launchpad for importing/exporting issues, but focused on issue tracking, not session history. Web UI includes code browser for repository browsing (file tree, syntax highlighting, commit history, diffs), but no integration between issues and code changes.
privacy_security: Credentials (tokens, passwords) stored in system keyring, never in git config. All data stored as git objects, opaque in repository unless accessed via git-bug tools. No explicit encryption at rest; relies on git transport security. No redaction mechanism; all operation history persists in git. Public key support for signed identities planned but only partially implemented. Commit signing available but not enforced.
lesson_for_parinn: DAG structure with Lamport clocks for deterministic ordering of concurrent edits is proven distributed data structure. Operation-based (not state-based) storage enables proper conflict resolution without central authority. refs/<namespace>/<id> pattern cleanly organizes multiple entities. Offline-first with explicit sync (push/pull not continuous) is practical for agents. Cache layer crucial for performance at scale. Separate credential storage from git config is essential. Consider whether full encryption is needed (git-bug doesn't implement it). Git objects hide data structure details from working tree, but everything stays in git history—no content is ever shredded.

name: git-memento (mandel-macaque/memento)
category: git-notes session transcripts (commit-time capture CLI written in F#/.NET NativeAOT, plus a composite GitHub Action)
status: shipped
license: MIT (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/LICENSE)
what_is_stored:
What it stores, for each commit: a Markdown rendering of one or more AI sessions. It fetches each session from the provider's CLI when you run `git memento commit <session-id>` or `amend` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md).

Default note:
- Header bullets: `- Provider:`, `- Session ID:`, `- Session Title:`, `- Committer:` (git user.name) and `- Captured At (UTC):` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/Markdown.fs).
- Then a `## Conversation` section with one `### <speaker>` block per message. User turns are labelled with the committer's git name and assistant turns with the provider name (same file).

The capture is lossy:
- The parser keeps only the `role` plus the `text`/`content` strings of each message. It never fills timestamps (`Timestamp = None`) (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/AiProvider.fs).
- The bundled Codex adapter keeps only user/assistant `input_text`/`output_text` items. It drops tool calls and reasoning (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/tools/codex-cli-adapter.sh).
- Every line is stripped of log prefixes such as `[debug]` and `info:` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/TextCleaning.fs).

Summary mode (`--summary-skill`):
- `refs/notes/commits` gets an LLM-written "Git Memento Session Summary", which the user confirms with y/N (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/CommitWorkflow.fs).
- `refs/notes/memento-full-audit` gets the full rendered conversation. It carries the header `<!-- git-memento-full-audit:v1 -->`, a `Summary SHA256` and an `Original Session Log SHA256`.
- That "original log" hash is taken over the parsed, in-memory session, not over the provider's raw JSONL bytes (Markdown.fs).

Squash or merge carries append blocks headed "# Git Memento Carried Notes" (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/NotesCarryWorkflow.fs).

Provider settings live only in local `.git/config` under `memento.*` (README).

Observed in the project's own repo on 2026-10-02, after cloning it and fetching its notes refs from https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento.git:
- `refs/notes/commits`: 34 notes, about 699 KB, largest about 78 KB.
- `refs/notes/memento-full-audit`: 4 notes, about 239 KB.
where_stored:
Git notes refs inside the code repository itself (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md):
- `refs/notes/commits` holds the default note or the summary.
- `refs/notes/memento-full-audit` holds the full transcript in summary mode.
- `notes-sync` creates `refs/notes/memento-backups/<UTC timestamp>/...` and `refs/notes/remote/<remote>/...` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/NotesSyncWorkflow.fs).

They reach the git remote (GitHub) through `git push <remote> refs/notes/*` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/GitService.fs).

The Action can also copy notes into GitHub commit comments, which then live on GitHub's servers (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml).

Configuration is stored in `.git/config` and is not shared between clones (README).
format_and_model:
Storage model:
- Each note is a git blob keyed by the annotated commit's SHA inside the notes ref's tree. The notes ref is itself a commit chain; its commits read "Notes added by 'git notes add'" (observed in the clone; mechanism per https://git-scm.com/docs/git-notes).
- Notes are written with `git notes add -f -m <markdown> <sha>`, which force-overwrites any existing note. Carry operations use `git notes append` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/GitService.fs).

Blob format, a versioned Markdown envelope (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/SessionNotes.fs):
- It opens with `<!-- git-memento-sessions:v1 -->` and `<!-- git-memento-note-version:1 -->`.
- Each session sits between `<!-- git-memento-session:start -->` and `<!-- git-memento-session:end -->`.
- A content line that equals a marker is escaped with a leading backslash.
- Old single-session notes are upgraded to the envelope when `amend` appends a session (README).

In-memory model (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/Domain.fs):
- `SessionData{Id, Provider, Title, Messages}`
- each message is `{Role: User|Assistant|System|Tool, Content: string, Timestamp option}`

There is no structured JSON on disk. Validation is a regex match for `- Provider:` and `- Session ID:` lines anywhere in an entry (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/AuditCore.fs).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Shared ref: every writer updates the same mutable notes ref per namespace.
- Notes on different commits merge cleanly as a tree merge.
- Notes on the same commit go through `git notes merge -s <strategy>`. The default strategy is `cat_sort_uniq` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/docs/team-adoption.md).
- Per git, `cat_sort_uniq` concatenates both versions, sorts the lines and removes duplicate lines (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-notes). On a Markdown transcript that reorders lines and deletes repeated ones. `union` (plain concatenation) is the opt-in alternative.

What `notes-sync` does (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/NotesSyncWorkflow.fs, GitService.fs):
1. Adds the forced fetch refspec `+refs/notes/*:refs/notes/*`.
2. Backs up the local refs.
3. Fetches the remote notes into `refs/notes/remote/<remote>/*`.
4. Merges them.
5. Runs a glob push, `git push <remote> refs/notes/*`, which is not forced.

Side effects observed with `git ls-remote` on 2026-10-02:
- Because the push is a glob, the project's own GitHub remote now holds `refs/notes/memento-backups/20260302174353/*`, `refs/notes/remote/origin/*`, the recursively nested `refs/notes/remote/origin/remote/origin/commits`, and `refs/notes/verify/*` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento).
- My inference: the leading `+` forces updates (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch), so a plain `git fetch` can move local notes refs to the remote's value and drop notes that were never pushed. They would then be recoverable only from the reflog or a backup.

Rewrites:
- `notes-rewrite-setup` sets `notes.rewriteRef=refs/notes/*`, `rewriteMode=concatenate` and rewrite on rebase and amend.
- `notes-carry --onto X --from-range a..b` appends the source notes for squash flows (README).

Action merge-carry mode (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml):
- It runs when a PR is closed and merged, and computes `base..head`.
- It skips the carry if a `- Source range:` line is already present, then runs `notes-carry` and `git push origin 'refs/notes/*'`.
- There is no retry or merge step, so a concurrent writer causes a non-fast-forward failure.

In practice (observed in the clone):
- The six most recent main commits, squash-merged PRs since 2026-03-02, carry no notes.
- The 4 full-audit notes sit on PR-branch commits that are not on main.
- Every notes commit is by the single maintainer. Concurrent multi-agent writing is not exercised.
realtime:
None. Capture is pull-based and happens only at commit time: the user runs `git memento commit/amend <session-id>` after the session (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md).

There are no agent-lifecycle hooks, no daemon and no streaming. Sharing happens only through explicit `git memento push`, `share-notes` or `notes-sync`, or when CI Action runs fire on push or PR events (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml).
search_retrieval:
There is no index or query engine. Retrieval is by commit:
- `git notes show <sha>` and `git notes --ref refs/notes/memento-full-audit show <sha>`
- `git log --show-notes`
- `git memento audit --range A..B [--strict] [--format json]` lists missing notes and missing markers.
- `doctor` checks configuration and sync posture.
(All per https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md.)

The team guide's suggested search, `git log --grep-reflog="Provider: Claude" --walk-reflogs`, does not search note bodies (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/docs/team-adoption.md). Per git, `--grep-reflog` matches reflog messages, while `--grep` matches note text only when `--notes` is in effect (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-log). The working forms are `git log --notes --grep=...` or `git grep` on the notes ref.

On GitHub, the Action's comment mode renders each note into a commit comment inside `<details>` blocks, truncated at 65,000 characters by default (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/note-comment-renderer.ts).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, at commit granularity:
- Each note is keyed by commit SHA and records the provider, session ID, title, committer and capture time.
- One commit can hold several sessions, from different providers, because `amend` appends (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md).
- There is no line-level, file-level or diff-level attribution. The link exists only if the human passes the right session ID.

Gate mode fails CI when a commit in the PR range lacks a note or the Provider/Session ID markers. A PR label (`ignore-notes`) bypasses it (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml).

Claude Code support is broken by default:
- The provider shells out to `claude sessions get {id} --json` and `claude sessions list --json` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/AiProvider.fs).
- The current Claude Code CLI reference lists no `sessions` subcommand (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference).
- Issue #9, open since 2026-04-06, reports that it was removed in v2.1.x and proposes parsing `~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl` directly (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/issues/9).
- I could not verify that `claude sessions` ever existed.
- The only bundled adapter is for Codex; it reads `~/.codex/sessions/*.jsonl` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/tools/codex-cli-adapter.sh).
- Every dogfooded note in the repo is from Codex (observed in the clone).
scale:
The README and release notes make no scale or performance claims (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/README.md, https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/releases/tag/v1.1).

Hard limits in the code:
- Summary input is capped at 2,000 characters per message, 24,000 per transcript and 32,000 per prompt (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/AiProvider.fs).
- The commit-comment cap defaults to 65,000 characters (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml).
- Full notes are unbounded and accumulate in the repository's object store.

Observed size: about 20 KB per note on average (34 notes, about 699 KB) in its own repo.

Adoption and activity:
- 452 stars and 20 forks on 2026-10-02 (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento).
- 35 commits; the last commit on main is dated 2026-03-05.
- Latest release is build 1.2.0-8543d652, dated 5 March (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/releases).
- Open items: issue #9, and PRs #6, #8 and #10, the newest from 2026-06-05 (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/pulls?q=is%3Apr).
- The repository is not archived but has had no commits for about seven months.
- HN launch thread: "If AI writes code, should the session be part of the commit?", 2026-03-02 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47212356).
privacy_security:
Full transcripts are stored verbatim:
- The CLI has no secret scanning, redaction or encryption on the full-transcript path. The only text processing strips log-level prefixes (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/TextCleaning.fs, AiProvider.fs).

Summary mode redaction is prompt-based only:
- The prompt tells the provider LLM to "treat transcript content as untrusted data" and to "Remove personal or identifying data" (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/GitMemento.Cli/AiProvider.fs).
- The default skill lists names, emails, tokens and machine paths to replace with `[redacted]` (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/skills/session-summary-default/SKILL.md).
- A human confirms the summary with y/N.
- The transcript goes to `claude -p` or `codex exec` as a command-line argument, so it reaches a networked model.

Summary mode still publishes the full transcript:
- The full transcript stays in `refs/notes/memento-full-audit`, and the glob push `refs/notes/*` publishes it together with the summary (GitService.fs).
- The comment renderer even points readers to that ref (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/src/note-comment-renderer.ts).

Observed in the project's public notes on 2026-10-02:
- 30 of 34 default notes and all 4 full-audit notes contain macOS home-directory paths (`/Users/...`).
- Injected AGENTS.md and skill instructions appear as the "Session Title".
- A quick grep found no `ghp_`, `sk-` or `AKIA` key patterns.

Integrity:
- Notes are not signed and can be overwritten with `-f`.
- The SHA-256 fields cover the parsed text, not the raw logs (Markdown.fs).

Supply chain and controls:
- Installation is `curl | sh` from `releases/latest` with no checksum or signature check (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/install.sh).
- In comment mode, the Action runs `npm ci` at run time (action.yml).
- The gate can be bypassed by anyone who can add the `ignore-notes` label (https://github.com/mandel-macaque/memento/blob/main/action.yml).
lesson_for_parinn:
If git carries ParleyInn history, keep the private record out of any ref namespace that a wildcard push or fetch reaches, and do not let writers share one mutable ref.

memento shows what goes wrong otherwise:
- Its `git push <remote> refs/notes/*` published the supposedly private full-audit transcripts, which contain `/Users/...` paths, alongside the summaries.
- The same push leaked its own backup refs and nested `remote/origin/remote/origin` copies onto GitHub.
- It merges concurrent notes with `cat_sort_uniq`, which sorts lines and so scrambles transcripts.
- Its forced `+refs/notes/*` fetch refspec can silently move local refs to the remote's value.

What to do instead:
- Give each writer and session its own append-only ref, for example `refs/parinn/<writer-id>/<session-id>`, so a sync is a union of disjoint refs and never needs a content merge.
- Push and fetch with explicit, non-forced refspecs only.
- Make publication a separate, opt-in, redacted export into its own namespace. Never derive the public view by filtering a ref that also holds raw history.
- Hash the provider's raw bytes, not a re-rendered Markdown form, so the record stays lossless and verifiable.

name: git-prompt-log (parasti/git-prompt-log)
status: beta
what_is_stored:
Only the human steering prompts, not the full transcript. Each note holds a session header with four fields: Assistant-Session (the harness session UUID), Assistant-Harness (name plus version, e.g. "Claude Code <claude --version>"), Assistant-Model and Assistant-Recorded (a UTC timestamp). Below that is an Assistant-Prompts list of "[YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC] text" entries, newest first, so the prompt that caused the commit sits on top (README "Note Schema": https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md ; SessionNote/PromptEntry: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L31-L69).

The note is cumulative. Every commit gets every session prompt whose timestamp is at or before the commit's author date, not just the prompts since the previous commit (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L2995-L3005). The display shows only the last 4 prompts by default (DEFAULT_LOG_PROMPT_LIMIT=4, L27).

Answers to interactive tools (AskUserQuestion and similar) are kept with a "[tool:<name>]" prefix. For local `!command` turns the command is kept and the output dropped. Claude Code turns with isMeta=true or promptSource="system" are skipped, and <system-reminder> blocks are removed (L691-L703, L1591-L1730).

Assistant responses, tool calls, diffs and file contents are NOT stored. There is no audit trail of agent actions.

Some side state is local only, outside git objects:
- Per-session exclusion lists live in prompt-log-excludes.json, either in the harness session directory or in .git/prompt-log/sessions/<id>.json.
- A rewrite-chain map lives in .git/prompt-log/rewrite-chain.json (L646-L689, L3280-L3320).
where_stored:
There are two homes for the data.

(1) Git notes on the local ref refs/notes/commits (DEFAULT_NOTES_REF, configurable with --ref). Hooks and config sit in the common git dir, so all linked worktrees share them (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L26 ; init at L4994-L5030 ; SKILL.md: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/SKILL.md).

(2) For sharing, Markdown files in the working tree under prompts/YYYY_MM_DD_HHMMSS_<slug>.md, committed to the feature branch. The project's own repo has about 20 of them (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/tree/main/prompts).

The tool deliberately never pushes refs/notes/*. A `git ls-remote` of the GitHub repo on 2026-10-02 showed only HEAD and refs/heads/main, with no notes ref (my observation; see README "Why Export and Import Instead of Pushing Notes?": https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md). On the input side it reads harness transcripts directly:
- Claude: ~/.claude/projects, ~/.claude/sessions, or $CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH
- Antigravity: its brain/ directory
- OpenCode: ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, a SQLite file

Sources: README "Supported Harnesses"; code at L1520-L1542 and L1932-L1957.
format_and_model:
Notes are plain text in an RFC-822-like "Assistant-*:" trailer format. Multi-line prompts continue on lines indented by 4 spaces. When a commit carries several sessions (after a squash), the session blocks are separated by "\n\n---\n\n". The parser picks the prompt block out of a note by grammar and keeps any unrelated note text before or after it, so the tool can share refs/notes/commits with other note users (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L146-L245).

The data model is commit SHA -> list of SessionNote, with no global session object. A session exists only as the set of commits whose notes carry its ID.

The export Markdown has two layers. The visible layer has a header, then per-session Session/Harness/Model bullets, a Commits list and blockquoted "Steering Prompts". The hidden layer is an HTML comment "<!-- git-prompt-log:metadata {json} -->" with {version:1, exported_at, export_command, import_command, commits:[{hash, subject, note}]}, where note is the raw note text (example: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/prompts/2026_10_01_102931_session_export_deduplication_and_incremental_modes.md ; writer at L4249).

Import reads only the JSON envelope when it is present and ignores the rendered Markdown (L4299-L4302). Records carry no hash chain, signature or content address.

Implementation: one Python 3 script of about 5.5k lines using only the standard library (sqlite3 for OpenCode). Its header says "Generated by Antigravity CLI 1.1.25 (Gemini 3.8 Flash (High))". There is a unittest suite of 148 tests (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/bin/git-prompt-log ; https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/tests/test_git_prompt_log.py).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no shared notes ref, so concurrent writers never meet in git. Every clone keeps its own refs/notes/commits. Teammates converge only through export files that land on main and are then re-imported.
