The README says pushing notes causes non-fast-forward races and `git notes merge` pain, and that the export/import design avoids this (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md).

Merging is done by one function, merge_session_notes (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L247-L301):
- Notes are grouped by session_id.
- Within a group, prompts are unioned and deduplicated on the key (timestamp, stripped text), then sorted newest first. Harness, model and recorded_at come from the most recent note.
- Distinct sessions stay as separate blocks, ordered by their first prompt.

This works like a grow-only set. It is idempotent and order-insensitive for adds. It has no tombstones: exclusions (`session drop`) live in local JSON and are applied as filters, not stored in notes. My inference from the code is that re-importing an old export could bring dropped prompts back.

Rewrites are handled in three places:
- `init` sets notes.rewrite.rebase/amend=true and notes.rewriteRef. It also installs a post-rewrite hook that reads "old new" pairs and merges the notes of all old SHAs into the new SHA (L4994-L5030, L3331-L3400).
- Multi-step rewrites, such as `rebase --exec 'git commit --amend'`, reach the hook as separate calls. The tool chains them through intermediate SHAs using a persisted edge map that is discarded after 3600 s (L3271-L3330).
- Forge-side squash or rebase merges create SHAs the hook never sees. For those, `import` re-attaches each note: first by exact hash if it is an ancestor of HEAD, otherwise by exact commit-subject match among only the last 50 commits, otherwise to HEAD when the file has a single entry (L4317-L4345).

Within one machine, writes use `git notes add -f`, so the last writer wins per commit (L374-L388).
realtime:
None. Notes are written synchronously by the post-commit hook, which runs only when agent environment variables are present (CLAUDECODE=1, CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, AGY_SESSION_ID, OPENCODE_*), or by a manual `record` (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L3238-L3270 ; L1490-L1501).

Sharing is batch only: export to a file, commit it, push it, merge the PR, then import (README Pull Requests section: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md). Nothing streams, watches, syncs or serves anything. Prompts typed before a commit are invisible to others until that whole cycle completes.
search_retrieval:
There is no index or full-text search. Retrieval works by commit:
- `git prompt-log` / `log` wraps `git log` as a stream, interleaves formatted prompt blocks, and forwards native options (-n, -p, --stat, --graph, ranges).
- `show <rev>` prints one commit's note.
- `timeline [range]` and `session --commits` merge session prompts and branch commits into one chronological timeline.
- `session list-sessions` lists candidate harness sessions for the repo or worktree.
- Plain `git log` shows the notes natively.

(README "Inspecting Commits & Prompt History": https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md.) The bundled agent skill finds earlier exports with a plain `grep -l <session_id> prompts/*.md` (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/SKILL.md). Nothing is recalled into the model automatically. It is a human and PR-review tool.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes. Linking sessions to code is the tool's whole purpose. Each commit's note names the session ID, harness and model, and lists the prompts that came before it in time. Attribution uses the commit's author date by default, so rebased or amended commits still match the original prompts. Commits with no earlier prompts are skipped during range recording. A 120-second clock-skew window applies only for a single commit (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L2984-L3022).

Session-to-repo association:
- Claude transcripts are matched to the repo when the path contains a repo identifier or when the transcript's first recorded "cwd" lies under any `git worktree list` path (L1544-L1589 ; design doc: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-07-claude-compatibility-design.md).
- Antigravity and OpenCode subagent sessions are resolved to their root session (L1146, L1999).
- Commits that only touch prompts/ (export commits) are excluded from attribution (L3226-L3236).

The link runs one way only, from commit to session. Prompts from sessions that never commit are never recorded.
scale:
No scale claims or benchmarks. From the code I infer two pressures:
- Notes are cumulative per session, so storage grows roughly with prompts × commits in a long session. Exports deduplicate when rendering, but the JSON envelope repeats the full cumulative note for every commit, as the example export shows (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/prompts/2026_10_01_102931_session_export_deduplication_and_incremental_modes.md).
- Import's subject fallback scans only the last 50 commits (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L4334).

Adoption on 2026-10-02: 0 stars, 0 forks, 121 commits, no topics and no releases shown. The repo was created 2026-09-04 and last pushed 2026-10-01, by a single author (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log ; https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/commits/main).
privacy_security:
The privacy rationale is explicit. refs/notes/commits covers the whole repo and would leak prompts from private branches and experiments if pushed. So sharing happens through an export scoped to a branch range, by default upstream..HEAD or origin/main..HEAD (README: https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/main/README.md ; https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log/blob/49cb75c68f2d9e2f19734dea56792b41859ffeda/bin/git-prompt-log#L3461-L3478).

Redaction is opt-in. It uses regex rules "pattern => replacement" in git config `prompt-log.redact`, or a --redact flag, with a literal fallback when the regex is invalid. Rules apply on record (so notes are sanitised on disk), on display and on export. No rules ship by default, so nothing is redacted out of the box: no secret scanner, no entropy check (README "Auto-Redaction"; L478-L552). Default exclusions drop only trivial prompts (yes / ok / do it / resume), and per-session `drop` hides chosen prompts (L395-L442, README).

There is no encryption, no signing, no integrity check and no hash chain. Prompts sit as plaintext in .git and, after export, in the public repository history. Once committed, redaction cannot be undone.

Trust gap: import trusts the hidden HTML-comment JSON, not the Markdown a reviewer actually reads (L4299-L4302). A PR could therefore show innocuous prompts while carrying different "provenance" that gets imported into notes. Imported notes are also unauthenticated, so anyone can forge attribution. This is my inference from the code; the project does not discuss it.

Prompt text goes unescaped into PR Markdown blockquotes. The post-commit hook also invokes the harness binary (`claude --version`) through subprocess (L1510-L1518). Nothing ever feeds recalled prompts back to a model, so there is no injection path into agents.
lesson_for_parinn:
Pick the replication unit to match the privacy boundary, and make what humans review the same bytes that machines ingest.

git-prompt-log rightly refuses to push a repo-wide notes ref. That ref is all-or-nothing and would leak private-branch prompts, so it ships an export scoped to a branch inside the PR. It also handles forge squash merges by re-anchoring on subject. But import trusts a hidden JSON comment rather than the visible text, and nothing is signed or hash-chained. Provenance can therefore be forged, and a reviewed export can differ from what gets ingested.

For ParleyInn this argues for three things if git is ever a transport:
- Publish only an explicitly selected, redacted slice per branch or PR, never a global ref.
- Make the exported artifact self-verifying: content-addressed records plus the hash-chain head, so an importer can check integrity and append-only order and treat everything else as untrusted data (I2/I6).
- Anchor records to stable session and event IDs rather than commit SHAs or subjects, because forge rewrites orphan SHA-keyed notes.

Also adopt its rewrite-chain technique (chaining old->new SHAs across a multi-step rebase) for any commit linkage ParleyInn keeps.
license: None. The repository root has no LICENSE or COPYING file at commit 49cb75c, and the GitHub page shows no license (https://github.com/parasti/git-prompt-log). Default copyright applies, so the code cannot legally be reused or vendored.

name: git-remote-gcrypt
category: encrypted git transport (git remote helper, gcrypt:: URLs)
status: shipped. Maintained but slow-moving, not archived. The last release is 1.5, from 21 Aug 2022, and Debian unstable, testing and stable all carry 1.5-1. A 1.6-1 entry is still UNRELEASED in the changelog: it adds a gitception integration test and README clarifications (Dec 2024). The most recent commit is "replace deprecated keyring options" (authored 27 Jul 2026, committed 15 Aug 2026). The GitHub repo is an automated mirror; the primary repo is git.spwhitton.name/git-remote-gcrypt, and patches go to a mailing list, not GitHub PRs.
what_is_stored: An entire git repository: all refs and all objects, as ordinary git packfiles. Nothing specific to agents or sessions. The remote holds two kinds of file. (1) One manifest, GPG signed and encrypted to the participants (EncSign). It lists every ref as '<sha-1> <ref>' lines, every packfile as 'pack :SHA256:<hash> <symmetric key>', 'keep :<hash> <generation>' repack bookkeeping lines, the Remote ID ('repo :id:...'), and preserved-but-unused 'extn' extension lines. (2) Opaque packfile blobs, each a git pack encrypted symmetrically with its own fresh random key. Locally, the remote's Remote ID is cached in git config (remote.<name>.gcrypt-id) and a have_packs list is kept under the local git dir.
where_stored: On a remote that does not need to be trusted, in one of two layouts. (a) A plain directory of files, reached as a local path, over rsync:// (rsync over ssh) or sftp:// (via curl), or over rclone:// (experimental, 'early adoptors only'). (b) Any git URL, called 'gitception'. There the same files become blobs in a tree on one branch of a normal git repo (default master, or the one named in a URL fragment like #next), and that branch is overwritten on every push. Locally the bridge uses the ref refs/gcrypt/gitception.
format_and_model: The design is content-addressed, encrypted packs plus a single signed root manifest. Write: each new packfile P becomes P' = Encrypt(Ki, P), using gpg -c with --force-mdc and no compression and a random key Ki of 63 bytes. P' is stored under the filename Hi = SHA-256(P'). Then EncSign(refs || pack list || Remote ID) is written to the manifest. Read: decrypt the manifest and check its signature, warn if the Remote ID changed, fetch each Hi, check that the hash matches, decrypt with Ki, and hand the pack to git. The manifest has a fixed filename, a constant hex string (91bd0c09...aa0a). For file backends a URL fragment instead names it by SHA-224 of the fragment. A new pack is uploaded first and the manifest after it, so the manifest is the single commit point. Once there are more than 25 packs (Repack_limit), or when GCRYPT_FULL_REPACK is set, the remote is repacked: old packs are merged into a new one and then deleted, which can mean re-uploading the whole history. The helper is a single POSIX shell script of about 970 lines that drives gpg and git.
multi_writer_and_merge: Weak, and the README says so. Every pushing user needs the public keys of all collaborators and the same participant config, because each push re-encrypts the manifest to the configured participants. There is no locking and no compare-and-swap on the manifest. Known issue: 'Every git push effectively has --force. Be sure to pull before pushing.' Concurrent or stale pushers silently clobber each other's refs. The cause is in the remote-helper protocol: git checks fast-forward only after the helper has already pushed. Joey Hess proposed a fix in Debian bug #877464 msg 32: cache refs at 'list for-push' and reject non-fast-forwards with merge-base. It is unimplemented as of the last maintainer note in April 2024. The mitigation is the opt-in setting gcrypt.require-explicit-force-push=true, which refuses pushes that lack --force or '+'. That stops accidental pushes but does not detect races. Merging itself is ordinary git merging, done locally after a pull. Two writers who upload the manifest at once leave the last write winning, and the losing writer's pack becomes an orphan.
realtime: None. Sync is explicit git push and fetch, in batches. With gitception and sftp every push re-uploads the whole repository history, and a repack can happen 'without warning' and re-upload everything. The README says these backends are 'inappropriate for most repositories', suitable only for small cases like credential stores. Even rsync and local are batch only. There are no notifications, no subscriptions, and no incremental streaming.
search_retrieval: None on the server side: the host sees only ciphertext. All search happens after a full fetch, decrypt and unpack into a local git repo, using normal git tools. 'git-remote-gcrypt --check url' reports whether a URL is a gcrypt repo and can be decrypted (exit 0, 1 or 100), but it too has to fetch the contents.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. This is a generic transport for whole git repos and knows nothing about agents, prompts or sessions. If session history were committed to a git repo, gcrypt would encrypt it in transit and at rest, but would add no link or provenance of its own.
scale: The README makes no numeric claims, and its warnings point the other way. gitception and sftp push cost grows with total history size until 'continued usage of git-remote-gcrypt is impractical'. Periodic full repacks (more than 25 packs) re-upload all history and 'might fail over a poor link'. rsync:// and local scale better but do not work with GitHub, GitLab or Gitolite. Each fetch downloads and decrypts every pack the client lacks.
privacy_security:
Strengths:
- Confidentiality covers everything, including ref names and commit metadata.
- Each pack has its own random symmetric key, kept only inside the manifest encrypted to participants. Each pack is checked by SHA-256 against its filename before decryption.
- The manifest is signed. With gcrypt.participants set, only signatures from those keys are accepted. Unset ('simple'), it encrypts to your default key and accepts any valid signature.
- Recipient key IDs are hidden by default (gpg -R); gcrypt.publish-participants turns that off.
- Algorithm choices are left to the user's GPG config. A random Remote ID warns if the remote is replaced or re-created.
- Temp files go in a randomly named directory under TMPDIR, not secured on MSYS/MinGW per the code.

Gaps (my reading of the code and docs, not stated by upstream):
- No rollback or freshness protection. Nothing like a monotonic counter or signed timestamp exists, so a malicious host could probably serve an older, validly signed manifest.
- The constant manifest filename marks the remote as gcrypt.
- Pack sizes, pack count and push timing leak.
- Membership is managed only by re-encrypting the manifest. Old packs and keys stay readable to anyone who once held them, so there is no forward secrecy and removing someone does not revoke access.
- No redaction or secret scanning: it encrypts whatever git holds.

It relies on GnuPG (1.4 or 2) and external rsync, curl or rclone.
lesson_for_parinn:
Two lessons.

What to copy: the 'encrypted content-addressed blobs plus one signed root manifest' pattern lets a dumb, untrusted store (a git branch, sftp, rsync, an object store) carry confidential, authenticated history. The host only ever does opaque GET, PUT and DELETE. That fits I4 if the transport sits outside ParleyInn's core.

What to avoid: gcrypt shows what goes wrong when a single mutable manifest is rewritten with no compare-and-swap:
- silent last-writer-wins clobbering, with every push effectively forced
- whole-history re-uploads on repack
- no rollback protection

ParleyInn's many-writer, append-only hash chain should instead:
- give each writer its own append-only segments, signed and encrypted, named by hash and never rewritten or repacked
- carry a per-writer sequence number or chain head in each signed segment, so a replica can detect rollback, gaps and forks rather than overwrite
- merge on the read side, not by force-pushing a shared root

Key handling should also allow per-segment or per-epoch keys, so removing a member or crypto-shredding is possible. gcrypt's single participant list cannot do that.
license: GPL-3 (or GPL-2+), per README.rst 'License' section and the script header; COPYING is the GPL text

name: git-remote-gcrypt and git-crypt
status: shipped
what_is_stored: git-remote-gcrypt: entire repository (objects, refs, history) encrypted as packfiles with symmetric keys. git-crypt: selectively encrypted files within a normal git repository (at rest in git objects and working tree).
where_stored: git-remote-gcrypt: local filesystem, rsync-accessible SSH targets, SFTP, plain git repositories (via git backend), or rclone-configured remotes. Manifest file (signed, GPG-encrypted summary) stored per backend. git-crypt: encrypted files stored as normal git objects in any git host (GitHub, Forgejo, GitLab, self-hosted); symmetric keys and metadata in .git-crypt/ directory within repo.
format_and_model: git-remote-gcrypt: custom binary format. Each packfile P encrypted with random symmetric key Ki (AES-256-CBC, Packkey_bytes=63 random bytes) → P'. Packfile hash Hi = SHA256(P') (configurable to SHA512/384/224). Manifest contains branch refs (B), packfile list with hashes and keys (L), Remote ID (R). Manifest = EncSign(GPG, B || L || R). Data model: pull manifest, verify GPG signature, retrieve packfiles by hash, decrypt with stored keys, pass to git. git-crypt: AES-256 in CTR mode with synthetic IV derived from SHA-1 HMAC of file content (deterministic encryption). Encryption at clean filter (commit), decryption at smudge filter (checkout). Files specified by .gitattributes patterns. Symmetric key stored in .git-crypt/keys/default or .git-crypt/keys/KEYNAME.
multi_writer_and_merge: git-remote-gcrypt: Participants configured as space-separated GPG key IDs per remote. Each push regenerates manifest encrypted to all participants. Manifest must be re-encrypted by each pusher with all participant keys. Known issue: 'every git push effectively has --force' — last writer wins, no automatic conflict resolution. Full repository repack triggered every N pushes (default 25), requiring re-upload of entire history. Collaboration requires all writers to have current participant list and all collaborators' public keys. No key revocation. git-crypt: Full git merge semantics preserved. Multiple keys supported (default + named alternatives per .gitattributes). Key sharing via GPG per user per key. No del-gpg-user command — access revocation not supported. Encrypted files not compressible; each change stores full file. Merge conflicts in encrypted files require manual resolution on decrypted content.
realtime: git-remote-gcrypt: Manifest must be fetched before each operation. No streaming; git backend and SFTP backend require uploading entire history per push (performance degrades as repo grows). Rsync backend more efficient (delta). Repack times unpredictable and can cause sudden multi-minute delays. No real-time collaboration semantics; store-and-forward only. git-crypt: Transparent to git; filter operations run on checkout/commit. No additional latency beyond git filter overhead. Filter-based design does not block on network. Works with all git workflows (push, pull, fetch, clone) without modification.
search_retrieval: git-remote-gcrypt: No search facility. Must retrieve entire repository, decrypt locally, then search. URL detection: git-remote-gcrypt --check URL exits 0 if repo exists and decryptable, 1 if gcrypt but not decryptable, 100 if not gcrypt. git-crypt: Cannot search encrypted file contents without decryption. File metadata visible (names NOT encrypted, commit messages NOT encrypted, symlink targets NOT encrypted, file sizes visible). Can detect file changes via identical ciphertext. Refs and history fully searchable.
links_sessions_to_code: Neither system has built-in awareness of agent sessions or prompts. Both are pure encryption/transport layers with no session model. To link sessions to code, ParleyInn must implement a layer above these systems (e.g., commit message convention, separate metadata branch, or external mapping). git-remote-gcrypt's Remote ID per repository could assist in identifying repository contexts, but contains no session semantics. git-crypt's .git-crypt/ directory could host session metadata, but this is not supported natively.
privacy_security: git-remote-gcrypt: All packfile contents encrypted (confidentiality). Manifest signed and encrypted (authentication + confidentiality). GPG key IDs can be obscured with -R flag (default: on). Symmetric keys stored in manifest (unencrypted in memory, encrypted in manifest). No file metadata encryption (refs, branch names, commit messages, object sizes visible). Remote ID is public. Symmetric key generation relies on GPG/system randomness; no key rotation support. Cryptographic strength depends on GPG key strength and symmetric key entropy. git-crypt: File contents encrypted with AES-256-CTR (NIST-approved, semantically secure under DCPA per authors). IV derived from SHA-1 HMAC (deterministic; leaks no information beyond identical-file detection). Determinism required for git to detect changes but allows fingerprinting. File metadata NOT encrypted (names, commit messages, sizes, symlink targets, gitlinks visible). .gitattributes not encrypted (attacker can disable encryption by mutating it; requires repo integrity protection via GPG tags). Symmetric keys stored unencrypted in .git-crypt/ (must protect .git-crypt/ directory separately). No key rotation. Not suitable for encrypted patches (determinism breaks git-apply). GPG trust model: requires GPG web-of-trust or explicit key trust per user.
lesson_for_parinn: Both systems prioritize encryption at the storage/transport layer rather than the application layer, leaving metadata and structure unencrypted. Neither system preserves agent session semantics or enables searching encrypted history without full decryption. For ParleyInn: (1) metadata (session IDs, agent names, timestamps, tree context) should be encrypted separately or require a custom layer, not left in plaintext refs; (2) key rotation and access revocation will require explicit design outside git (neither git-remote-gcrypt nor git-crypt support it); (3) deterministic encryption (git-crypt model) leaks information-theoretic equivalence and enables correlation attacks, so if ParleyInn adopts it, consider ephemeral IVs or content-hiding strategies; (4) multi-agent collaboration in ParleyInn requires solving the 'every push is force' problem (git-remote-gcrypt) or the 'no revocation' problem (both), suggesting ParleyInn must layer additional merge/conflict semantics on top; (5) neither system provides search or indexing of encrypted content, so ParleyInn's pull-only recall design aligns better with their threat model than a query interface.
sources: https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt (primary source repository, README.md and crypto.hpp examined 2026-10-02)
git-remote-gcrypt README.rst: Repository format section, Manifest file section, Configuration section, Performance notes
git-crypt README.md: Security section (AES-256 CTR mode, synthetic IV, DCPA semantics), Limitations section (metadata not encrypted, determinism, key revocation, no patch support)
git-crypt crypto.hpp header (cryptographic primitives: Aes_ctr_encryptor, Hmac_sha1_state, AES key length, CTR mode)
git-crypt NEWS.md (version history v0.1–v0.8.0, OpenSSL 3 support 2025-09-23)
git-remote-gcrypt shell script source (Packkey_bytes, Hashtype, EncSign logic, Manifestfile, participant encryption, repack logic)
git-crypt doc/multiple_keys.md (multi-key design, per-file key selection via .gitattributes)
license: git-remote-gcrypt: GPLv3 (or v2+); git-crypt: GPLv3 with OpenSSL exception clause
scale: git-remote-gcrypt: not recommended for large histories (pushes slow as repo grows, especially with git/sftp backends due to full repack). Stated suitable only for small credential stores or unusual cases. rsync backend scales better but incompatible with hosting services (GitHub, GitLab, Gitolite). git-crypt: scales as normal git; encrypted files trade compression for per-file overhead (each change stores full file). Suitable for mixed public/private repos where most content is unencrypted.

name: GitAgent (open-gitagent/gitagent; formerly "gitclaw". Lyzr's agent runtime, distinct from the OpenGAP spec repo)
category: git-native agent definition and memory (agent runtime that keeps its state as committed working-tree files)
status: shipped. The repo is active and not archived. The latest commit is ed59584, dated 2026-08-20 (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent). npm @open-gitagent/gitagent 2.2.0 was published 2026-08-20T11:37Z (https://registry.npmjs.org/@open-gitagent/gitagent). The repo is the former "gitclaw" runtime, renamed in PR #43 on 2026-05-24 (commit d32e526), and github.com/open-gitagent/gitclaw now serves this repo (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitclaw). The original GitAgent *standard*, the CLI plus SPECIFICATION.md, moved to https://github.com/open-gitagent/opengap ("OpenGAP", about 2,964 stars). Its README says it was "originally @open-gitagent/gitagent", but its spec badge still links to open-gitagent/gitagent paths, which are now stale. The discovery note's 711 stars and 135 forks match the org page (https://github.com/open-gitagent).
what_is_stored:
Three kinds of data.

(1) The agent definition, as files in the repo: agent.yaml (model, tools, runtime, extends/dependencies, compliance, mcp_servers, plugins), SOUL.md, RULES.md, DUTIES.md, AGENTS.md, and the directories skills/, tools/*.yaml, hooks/hooks.yaml, workflows/, knowledge/index.yaml, config/, compliance/, plugins/ and schedules/ (README "Architecture", https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent; Documentation.md, https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/Documentation.md).

(2) Memory, which is committed:
- The working layer is memory/MEMORY.md. It is free-form Markdown that the model writes in full on every `memory save` (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/tools/memory.ts).
- Extra layers can be configured in memory/memory.yaml.
- Lines past max_lines move to memory/archive/YYYY-MM.md.
- The docs also list memory/mood.md, memory/photos/ and memory/journal/<date>.md. The docs say the voice agent "automatically detects and saves personal information" such as names, locations and relationships (Documentation.md, Memory System section).
- Learned skills are written to skills/<name>/SKILL.md and git-committed by the skill-learner tool (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/tools/skill-learner.ts).

(3) Runtime state in a gitignored .gitagent/ directory:
- chat-history/<branch>.jsonl holds {ts, msg} UI/voice messages. It skips audio deltas, thinking and partial transcripts (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/chat-history.ts).
- chat-summary-<branch>.md holds an LLM summary of at most 200 words.
- audit.jsonl is opt-in through compliance.recordkeeping.audit_logging. It records session_start/end, tool_use with its args, and errors (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/audit.ts).
- learning/tasks.json and schedule-logs/ also live here.

What it does not store: the CLI/SDK agent loop's full prompts, completions and tool results are not durably kept as a verbatim transcript. OpenTelemetry spans carry token counts and costs and "never contain the prompt or completion text" (README, Telemetry).
where_stored:
Working-tree files committed to git in the agent repo itself.

- **Local-repo mode:** the agent repo is the target code repo. Work happens on a branch named `gitagent/session-<8 hex>`, which is pushed to the GitHub remote at session end (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/session.ts).
- **Sandbox mode:** an e2b VM is driven through the optional `gitmachine` peer dependency, which commits inside the VM (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/sandbox.ts).
- **Logs and summaries:** these sit in the local, gitignored .gitagent/ directory. The spec's "Runtime State" section says `.gitagent/` is gitignored (https://github.com/open-gitagent/opengap/blob/main/spec/SPECIFICATION.md).
- **Telemetry:** optional, exported to an OTLP collector.

A blog post in the repo frames the repo as "the database, the audit log, the memory store, and the deployment artifact simultaneously" (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/docs/serverless-blog.md). That post's claim that "audit logs are append-only" and git-tracked does not match the code: audit.jsonl lives in the gitignored .gitagent/ directory.
format_and_model:
Plain Markdown and YAML files plus JSONL logs. The memory model is a single mutable snapshot document, not an event log.

- **Save:** each save overwrites MEMORY.md with model-supplied content, runs `git add`, then `git commit -m <model-supplied message>`. The tool schema asks for a message saying "why this memory changed" (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/tools/shared.ts). History therefore lives only in git's commit DAG of whole-file rewrites.
- **Archive:** the archive is append-only Markdown with "_Archived: <ISO>_" separators.
- **Missing structure:** there are no per-entry IDs, no schema for memory content and no hashing beyond git's own objects.
- **Spec settings not implemented:** the spec's memory.yaml example declares update_triggers (on_session_end, on_explicit_save) and an archive_policy (max_entries 1000, compress_after 90d) (spec §12). memory.ts declares an archive_policy type but nothing reads it, and nothing in src reads update_triggers. Only the max_lines overflow is implemented (src/tools/memory.ts).
- **Inheritance:** memory/ is "isolated per agent (not inherited)" when an agent uses `extends` (spec §15).
- **Rust port:** the "ira" port in the same repo has a memory tool that writes the same file and commits it through argv git (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/rust/gitagent-rs/src/sdk/tools.rs).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Essentially not designed for multiple writers.

- **One branch per session:** each local-repo session creates its own `gitagent/session-<random 4-byte hex>` branch. Resuming checks the branch out and does a plain `git pull origin <branch>`. Finalize runs `git add -A`, commits and pushes, with no fetch or rebase first.
- **No merge help:** there is no merge driver or conflict handling (no merge or rebase logic in src). Merging session branches back to the default branch is left to humans, for example through PRs. Because MEMORY.md is rewritten whole on each save, concurrent edits from two branches will collide as textual conflicts.
- **Same-branch pushes:** two writers pushing the same branch get a non-fast-forward rejection. The Rust port ignores push failure with `.ok()` (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/rust/gitagent-rs/src/sdk/session.rs).
- **Destructive reuse:** reusing an existing clone runs `git reset --hard origin/<default>` (src/session.ts).
- **In-process races:** gaps.md G25 found that parallel tool execution raced memory saves and git commits ("index.lock, corrupt files, lost writes"). Hardening batch 1 (commit f2e89e9, 2026-08-10) made mutating tools sequential (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/gaps.md; https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/commit/f2e89e9d66feb1fcd6f489201a8987eb5cdae042).
realtime: None across agents. State reaches other machines only when the session's `finally` path commits and pushes at session end ("commits any state changes to git, pushes them to the remote, and exits", https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/docs/serverless-blog.md). Within one process, the SDK streams delta, tool_use and tool_result events to the embedder, and the web UI has a live log tab (README SDK section). OpenTelemetry spans and metrics stream to a collector but exclude content. Two agents do not share memory live; one sees another's memory only after a clone or pull of the pushed branch.
search_retrieval:
There is no index, full-text search or embeddings. Retrieval works in four ways:
- **Memory tool:** `memory load` returns the whole working-layer file (src/tools/memory.ts).
- **Git history:** the system prompt tells the model to use the `cli` tool for "git log, git diff, git show" to inspect memory history (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/loader.ts).
- **Context builders:** in the voice and agent paths, MEMORY.md, the branch chat summary and the last 30 chat messages are truncated by a chars/4 token estimate and pasted into the system instructions. The caps are about 1,200 tokens of memory and 800 of chat (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/context.ts).
- **Knowledge:** knowledge/index.yaml supplies tags and priority hints. Documents marked always_load are injected inline, and the rest are listed for the read tool (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/src/knowledge.ts).
links_sessions_to_code:
Only implicitly, by sharing a branch.

- **Same branch for code and memory:** in local-repo mode, code edits and memory commits land on the same `gitagent/session-<id>` branch. The final commit message is "gitagent: auto-commit (<branch>)" in TS, or "gitagent: session <branch>" in the Rust port (src/session.ts; rust/gitagent-rs/src/sdk/session.rs).
- **No trace in commits:** prompts, transcripts and tool traces are not attached to commits. There are no git notes, no trailers and no session ID in the commit itself.
- **Audit log not linked:** the audit log carries a session_id but is gitignored and unlinked to commit SHAs (src/audit.ts).
- **Concrete example:** the framework's own history interleaves an agent memory commit, "Created Flappy Bird game with webcam overlay and opened in Safari" (commit a1a7f82, which changed memory/MEMORY.md), plus many auto "Scaffold gitclaw agent" commits on main (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/commit/a1a7f82). Memory commits mix into code history unless a separate repo or branch is used.
scale:
There are no throughput or size claims for memory.

- **Spec limits:** the spec caps MEMORY.md at "200 line max" (spec §2).
- **Cost claims:** the blog claims zero idle cost, saying it is "free entirely" on GitHub Actions for most usage (docs/serverless-blog.md).
- **Known growth problems:** the project's own gap review (scoped to v2.1.0) says chat-history JSONL "grows unbounded with full-file sync reads on the hot path". It also says MEMORY.md load is uncapped and save re-sends the whole file (G27), and that synchronous execSync git blocks the event loop for every tenant (G23) (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/blob/main/gaps.md).
- **Adoption:** 711 stars and 135 forks on the runtime repo (https://github.com/open-gitagent).
privacy_security:
**No redaction or encryption.** The TS src has no redaction, masking or encryption code (code search of src at ed59584). Memory, which the docs say includes auto-captured personal details, is committed in clear text and pushed to the git remote.

**Gitignore is not guaranteed.** `.gitagent/` is added to an existing .gitignore, and first-run scaffolding writes one. However, ensureGitagentDir does nothing when no .gitignore exists (src/loader.ts), and local-repo mode then runs `git add -A` (src/session.ts). From the code, audit and chat logs could therefore be committed and pushed in a target repo that lacks a .gitignore. This is an inference from reading the code and has not been tested.

**PAT handling.** The PAT sits in the remote URL (https://<token>@github.com/...) during a session and is scrubbed on finalize. G17 noted the PAT was visible to `ps` on the clone command line and pushed before the scrub. Batch 2 moved finalize into `finally` (https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent/commit/85a3b19909a6bc4af7543304acea1d66e9f7e280).

**The project's own security review.** gaps.md says the "agents as repos" premise makes agent.yaml, extends, plugins and mcp_servers attacker input. It lists these findings:
- G1: load-time shell-injection RCE.
- G2: API-key exfiltration through `model@baseUrl`.
- G3: plugin and MCP auto-spawn.
- G4: `${VAR}` interpolation leaks secrets.
- G5: hooks fail open.
- G6: no filesystem jail.
- G7: audit is opt-in, agent-writable and records secret args unredacted.
- G27: shell injection through the memory commit message.

**Status at HEAD ed59584.** The batches fixed G1 for extends/dependencies, plus G8, G9, G12, G17, G18, G20, G21 and G25. Three findings remain open in the code:
- memory.ts still builds a shell string, escaping only double quotes.
- session.ts still interpolates `--session` into execSync.
- hooks.ts still returns "allow" when a hook fails.

The Rust port uses argv git calls "so the load-time RCE the TS version shipped with ... can't happen here" (rust/gitagent-rs/src/sdk/session.rs).

**Prompt injection through stored content.** Stored memory and chat are injected into system instructions without an envelope (src/context.ts), so persisted content is an automatic channel back into the prompt.

**Telemetry** excludes prompt and completion text (README).
lesson_for_parinn:
Do not make history a set of mutable files in the code branch's working tree.

GitAgent shows what you get from that design: "git log your memory" comes for free. It also shows the costs:
- **Rewritable history:** the model rewrites MEMORY.md whole, so content can be silently dropped or rewritten, and it is archived only by line overflow. That breaks append-only and lossless guarantees.
- **No merging:** session branches plus a whole-file Markdown document produce textual conflicts, with no merge semantics.
- **No real-time sharing:** sync happens only at push time, at session end.
- **Noise in code history:** memory commits land in the code history (a1a7f82).
- **Leaks:** whether logs reach the remote depends on a .gitignore that may not exist.
- **Prompt injection:** stored memory is pasted back into the system prompt with no envelope.
- **Command-construction bugs:** shelling out to git with interpolated strings produced the RCE and injection bugs the project's own review flagged (G1, G27).

If ParleyInn uses git at all, it should be only as a transport for immutable, content-addressed, hash-chained event segments on a dedicated ref or separate repo. Merging should be a set union of events, never a textual merge of a document. Any "memory view" should be a derived projection rebuilt from the record (I10). Recall should stay pull-only and enveloped (I2). The core never runs a `git` subprocess (I4 forbids os/exec).
license: MIT (LICENSE file and package.json "license": "MIT"; https://github.com/open-gitagent/gitagent). The OpenGAP spec repo is also MIT (https://github.com/open-gitagent/opengap).

name: GitButler Claude Code hooks ("but claude pre-tool/post-tool/stop") and Agents tab
url: https://docs.gitbutler.com/features/ai-integration/claude-code-hooks (returns 404 as of Oct 2026; the last source is in the gitbutler-docs repo at commit c6f6f89^, content/docs/features/ai-integration/claude-code-hooks.mdx)
category: session-to-branch commit automation (removed). Its successor is agent-driven version control through the `but` CLI plus an installed agent skill.
status: archived. The feature was removed, but GitButler itself is still shipping. Timeline: the Agents tab shipped in GitButler 0.16 on 2025-09-11/12 (https://blog.gitbutler.com/gitbutler-0-16, https://blog.gitbutler.com/agents-tab). The Agents tab docs were removed on 2026-01-21 in gitbutler-docs commit f3bd442, whose message reads "Adding Coding Agents docs while removing the agents tab idea" (https://github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler-docs/commit/f3bd4422028546582c8da71f7d68152cf1412f1b). The code went in gitbutler commit 1dbe2bdb, authored 2026-05-17 and shown on GitHub as May 19: "Remove agent/codegen integration ... Deleted the but-claude and but-cursor Rust crates, along with all associated frontend components", with -17,869 lines (https://github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler/commit/1dbe2bdbe88e6c79da228a8fa080985340a27f3a). The hooks, Cursor hooks and MCP-server docs were removed on 2026-06-02 in commit c6f6f89, "Remove superseded AI integration docs" (https://github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler-docs/commit/c6f6f89f1041d88009537bb98c132520f63907b3). The current docs instead describe `but agent setup`, a wizard that installs a GitButler skill and writes instruction text, after which agents call `but` commands themselves (https://docs.gitbutler.com/ai-agents/overview, https://docs.gitbutler.com/commands/but-agent). The current command list has no `but claude` subcommand.
what_is_stored:
Git received only code commits; the hooks never stored the session transcript in git. But the user's prompt did reach git: by default each auto-commit message was the prompt followed by the transcript's summary record (`format!("{prompt}\n\n{change_summary}")` in crates/but-action/src/simple.rs). When an OpenAI-configured LLM provider was available, that message was then reworded, and single-commit unpushed branches were renamed, from the same prompt and summary (crates/but-claude/src/hooks/mod.rs at 1dbe2bdb^). The removed docs say: "GitButler will commit all the changes and write a more sophisticated commit message based on what you had prompted your agent".

Outside git, a per-repository SQLite database held the following tables (crates/but-db/src/table/claude.rs; the migrations are still at HEAD):
- claude_sessions: id, current_id, a session_ids JSON array, in_gui, and approved/denied permission lists.
- claude_messages: id, session_id, created_at, content_type and content. In the Agents tab, content held the raw Claude Code SDK streaming JSON, user inputs, system messages, and "GitButler" updates such as CommitCreated with stack_id, branch name and commit ids (MessagePayload in crates/but-claude/src/lib.rs).
- claude_permission_requests: tool_name, input, decision.
- File write locks, one row per path and owner session.
- Session-to-stack assignment rules.
- ButlerAction records: external_prompt, external_summary, handler, source=ClaudeCode(session_id), snapshot_before and snapshot_after as oplog git object ids, outcome and error (crates/but-action/src/action.rs).

In hook mode, Claude Code's own transcript stayed in ~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<session>.jsonl. GitButler only read it, at the transcript_path the hook passed in (crates/but-claude/src/claude_transcript.rs).
where_stored: Code commits went onto GitButler virtual or stacked branches in the user's own git repository, with oplog snapshots before and after each auto-commit. Session metadata and messages went into a local SQLite file at <git_dir>/gitbutler/but.sqlite by default; the location can be overridden by the git config key gitbutler.storagePath (but-db FILE_NAME="but.sqlite"; crates/but-project-handle/src/storage_path.rs). Transcripts stayed in Claude Code's local ~/.claude directory. Nothing was pushed apart from the code branches the user pushed, and there was no server-side session store.
format_and_model:
Hooks were Claude Code command hooks:
- PreToolUse with matcher Edit|MultiEdit|Write ran `but claude pre-tool`. It parsed the hook JSON (session_id, transcript_path, tool_input.file_path) and took a per-file write lock in SQLite, retrying every 1 s for up to 30 s.
- PostToolUse with the same matcher ran `but claude post-tool`. It used tool_response.structuredPatch hunk headers to assign the matching uncommitted hunks to the session's stack.
- Stop with an empty matcher ran `but claude stop`. If the worktree had changes and auto-commit was on, it created or got the session's stack and committed every hunk assigned to that stack.

Data model: one Claude session maps to one GitButler stack (a virtual branch) through an assignment rule (session_id to stack_id). A missing stack is recreated under a "canned" branch name. Hook config and behaviour come from the removed docs page (gitbutler-docs c6f6f89^) and crates/but-claude/src/hooks/mod.rs and hooks/file_lock.rs at gitbutler 1dbe2bdb^. The Agents tab wrapped Claude Code through GitButler's fork of claude-agent-sdk-rs (crates/but-claude/Cargo.toml) and stored the streamed messages as JSON text rows in SQLite.
multi_writer_and_merge:
This was designed for several concurrent Claude sessions in one working directory, with no worktrees: "if you have three sessions of Claude Code running at the same time ... GitButler will be assigning each change to the correct branch automatically" (removed hooks doc). Coordination was a SQLite file lock per path plus hunk-level assignment. It was local to one machine, so there was no cross-machine merge of session state.

The removed Agents tab doc admits a limitation: "If two agents modify lines in a file right next to each other, the hunk can only be assigned to one lane". Conflicts were left to manual moves afterwards. The current docs warn that parallel GitButler branches "are not runtime isolation" and share the filesystem and build state (https://docs.gitbutler.com/ai-agents/parallel-agents).
realtime: Local and synchronous only. The hooks ran inline with each Edit/Write tool call. The Agents tab streamed SDK output into its UI and showed live per-branch token and cost estimates (https://blog.gitbutler.com/agents-tab). Nothing was shared between machines or users in real time. Sharing happened only through ordinary git pushes of the resulting branches.
search_retrieval: None documented. There was no search over sessions or prompts. Retrieval meant listing messages per session_id from SQLite (list_messages_by_session in crates/but-claude/src/db.rs), reading git log or commit messages, which contained the prompt, or using the oplog/timeline to inspect and undo snapshots (https://docs.gitbutler.com/ai-agents/review-agent-work). The Agents tab had a "Clear Context" button per branch. No full-text index was found in the source examined.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, by three mechanisms:
1. An assignment rule binds each Claude session_id to one stack, i.e. one branch, so all of that session's hunks land there.
2. Each auto-commit message embeds the user's prompt verbatim plus Claude's summary, optionally rewritten by an LLM.
3. A ButlerAction row records the prompt, summary and source=ClaudeCode(session_id), and links the action to the oplog snapshot object ids before and after it.

There is no git trailer or note carrying the session id. The session-to-commit link lived only in local SQLite, as CommitCreated messages and ButlerActions, so it did not travel with a push. Only the prompt text inside the commit message travelled with the push. Sources: crates/but-action/src/simple.rs and action.rs, crates/but-claude/src/hooks/mod.rs at 1dbe2bdb^.
scale: No scale claims were made for the hooks or the Agents tab, beyond running "multiple agents working on multiple parallel branches simultaneously" in one directory (https://blog.gitbutler.com/agents-tab). The current agent workflow cites GitButler's own benchmark at vcbench.dev: about 80% fewer commands and about 60% faster than plain git at similar reliability (https://docs.gitbutler.com/ai-agents/overview). That claim is about the CLI and skill workflow, not about session storage.
privacy_security:
No redaction, encryption or secret scanning was found in the hook path.

- Prompts and transcript summaries were copied verbatim into git commit messages. These are immutable once pushed and cannot be redacted without rewriting history.
- When an LLM provider was configured, the prompt and summary were also sent to it to reword commit messages and branch names (LLMProvider::default_openai in crates/but-claude/src/hooks/mod.rs; but-llm reads credentials from the environment).
- The SQLite database was a plaintext file inside .git/gitbutler.
- The Agents tab offered a "YOLO mode" that dangerously allows all permissions, off by default (removed agents-tab.mdx at gitbutler-docs f3bd442^).

Failure behaviour: if a hook errored, the output carried continue:false, which stops Claude rather than failing open (OutputClaudeJson in hooks/mod.rs). A pre-tool lock held by another session for more than 30 s produced exactly that error.

A real-world leak example: GitButler's own removal commit 1dbe2bdb carries a pasted Claude Code compaction summary in its message, including a developer's local transcript path (/Users/.../.claude/projects/...jsonl) and internal CI details (https://github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler/commit/1dbe2bdbe88e6c79da228a8fa080985340a27f3a). This shows how session content slips into permanent git history once tooling or habits put it in commit messages.

GitButler has no stated privacy policy for agent session data. Its blog posts are silent on it.
lesson_for_parinn:
The session-to-branch link held up while it was kept as local, out-of-band metadata: a session-to-stack rule plus action records pointing at oplog snapshot ids. The parts that leaked or proved fragile were the parts that pushed session content into git.
- Writing the raw prompt into commit messages created an unredactable, push-propagated copy of untrusted text. GitButler's own repository shows a pasted transcript summary and a local ~/.claude path in a commit message.
- The vendor-coupled hook/SDK integration, including fail-closed hooks (continue:false on error, 30 s lock waits), was deleted outright after about 8 months.

For ParleyInn:
- Link sessions to code by reference, through commit or snapshot ids recorded in ParleyInn's own hash-chained record, and never by writing prompts or transcript text into commit messages, trailers or branch names.
- Keep any git-facing hook thin and fail-open (I9).
- Never auto-send recorded prompts to an LLM, for example to reword commits (I2, I4).
license: GitButler is source-available under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1-MIT), which converts to MIT after two years. I did not re-check the LICENSE file for this sheet, so treat this as unverified here (https://github.com/gitbutlerapp/gitbutler).

name: GitButler: Claude Code hooks (2025, now apparently removed) and its successor `but agentlog` on git-meta
category: VCS client that runs parallel agent sessions. It also captures agent transcripts into git-native metadata refs (git-meta).
status: archived. The hook feature was shipped in 2025 and now looks superseded. The blog post announcing it is dated 2025-07-22 (article:published_time meta tag). The Agents Tab followed on 2025-09-11. Its docs pages (features/ai-integration/claude-code-hooks, features/agents-tab, ai-overview) now return HTTP 404. At gitbutlerapp/gitbutler main commit 28dcf96 (2026-10-02) the `but` CLI has no `claude` subcommand, and there is no but-claude crate. Only leftovers remain, such as the claude_sessions/claude_messages SQLite tables in but-db. The removal is inferred from the source tree and the 404s. I found no removal announcement. The successor for prompt and transcript history is `but agentlog`, crate but-agentlog. It is in main but is a hidden command (`#[clap(name = "agentlog", hide = true)]`), so treat it as beta or experimental. The current public docs (ai-agents/*) describe skills plus CLI steering, with one branch per session. They do not mention hooks or transcripts.
what_is_stored:
2025 hook feature: Claude Code hooks passed the session ID to GitButler. GitButler then created one virtual branch per session and assigned that session's edits to it. When a chat round ended, it made one commit holding the original prompt. A background step could rewrite the commit message with AI, using the prompt and the changed files. The Agents Tab (2025-09) also put the prompts into commit messages. It showed token use and cost per branch, but the post does not say where those were stored.

Current `but agentlog`: it captures the full agent transcript, from Claude Code or Codex JSONL. A hook payload supplies transcript_path. Each record is stored with:
- source index, record hash, timestamp, kind and role
- the redacted text; tool results are capped at 4 KiB, head plus tail with a [TRUNCATED] marker
- tool name, tool kind, redacted tool_input, exit code and outcome
- SHA-256 fingerprints of the repo-relative file paths edited
- the redacted raw provider envelope (`source_record`)

It also stores turn summaries and details. Schemas are gitbutler.agent-session.v1 and gitbutler.agent-session-turn.v1. A turn records capture_kind (backfill or incremental) and previous_turn_key. It also records an environment snapshot: worktree files, stacks, branches, commits with change IDs and file hashes, and reviews. Further keys hold source metadata (agent, provider, model, tool version) and the targets the session touched (branch, review/PR, change ID). Lookup index sets are keyed by sha256 of the target.
where_stored:
2025 hooks: prompts lived in ordinary git commits, on GitButler virtual/stacked branches in the working repo. Session state sat in GitButler's local SQLite (tables claude_sessions, claude_messages, claude_permission_requests in but-db).

Current agentlog: storage is git-meta. The working store is a SQLite database inside .git. Large values go to git blobs. Exchange is done by serializing to a commit on custom refs: refs/meta/local/main locally, fetched into refs/meta/remotes/main. The ref can go to the same remote as the code or to a separate meta repo. All agentlog keys sit on the `project` target.

Local-only sessions use the `local:` key prefix, which the git-meta serializer never writes into any tree. Sessions become published only through `but agentlog publish`, or when git config `gitbutler.agentlog-share-default=true`. A file lock, `agentlog-capture.lock`, in GitButler's storage dir serializes local captures.
format_and_model:
git-meta model: (target, key, value) tuples. Targets are commit, change-id, path, branch or project. Values are string, list or set. The serialized tree layout is `{target-type}/{target-value-with-fanout}/{key-segments}/__value`. A list becomes a `__list/` subtree with one blob per entry, named `<ms-timestamp>-<hash>`. Deletions are explicit tombstones; missing data never implies deletion. Metadata history is linear. Prune commits, marked by a commit trailer, cut the tip tree back to a working set, and older values can be recovered by walking history. The license is MIT.

agentlog key layout, on the project target:
- `gitbutler:agent-sessions` (set)
- `gitbutler:agent-session:<session_key>:{schema, updated-at, sources, source:<source_key>:*, transcript (list of JSON records), record-hashes (set), turns (list of JSON summaries), turn:<turn_key> (JSON), associated-targets}`
- `gitbutler:agentlog-index:v1:<kind>:sha256-<target>` (sets of {session_key, turn_key})

session_key = sha256("agent\0" + provider session_id, or the transcript path), truncated to 128 bits. turn_key = sha256(session_key, source_key, the record hashes). Each turn links to previous_turn_key, giving a content-derived but unsigned chain. Records are deduplicated by sha256 of each raw JSONL line, so re-reading the whole transcript on every hook is idempotent.
multi_writer_and_merge:
2025 hooks: there were many concurrent Claude sessions in one working directory. GitButler's hunk assignment split their edits into per-session virtual branches. Merging the code was ordinary git branch work.

agentlog/git-meta: each machine writes to its local SQLite and serializes to its own refs/meta/local/main. Sync (`sync_metadata`) does a pull/materialize, then `push_once`. On a non-fast-forward it calls `resolve_push_conflict` and retries, up to 5 attempts. That resolution merges the remote tree into the local one in memory, then fast-forwards. Appends from different writers merge cleanly as a union of tree entries, because each list entry is a separate, uniquely named file. Sets merge as unions. If both sides changed the same string key, the 'ours' strategy keeps the local value at the tip, and the other value survives only in history. When two writers each start a fresh history, a baseless 2-way merge favours local. A force-push rewrite (for example to purge a secret) is absorbed by the same no-merge-base path.
realtime:
This is not real-time, but it is near-line.
- 2025 hooks: changes were committed when the Stop hook fired, at the end of each chat round.
- agentlog: each hook invocation captures the new transcript records synchronously into local SQLite. When the session is published, the hook also spawns a detached background `but agentlog sync` (pull plus push). Other machines only see the data after their own pull.
- There is no push notification or streaming. I could not verify which Claude Code hook events `but agent setup` registers for agentlog. The `hook` command accepts any payload that carries transcript_path.
search_retrieval:
There is no full-text search. Retrieval is target-centric through `but agentlog skim [branch|review|change <key>]`. It discovers the applied GitButler branch automatically and lists every related session and turn in chronological order, abbreviated with previews and tool counts. `but agentlog show <session-key> [--turn <turn-key>] --limit N` drills into bounded record windows. Both commands have `--json` output that returns handles.

Index sets map hashed branch, review and change keys to (session, turn) hits. The code comments call them rebuildable lookup data that readers verify against the turn details. A packaged agent skill (SKILL.md) tells agents to skim before acting and to drill down only when needed.

On the git-meta side the author benchmarks a tree diff: finding 1k new values on a ref with metadata for 1M commits took under 1 s. Reconstructing all keys across 10k metadata commits with 550k targets took about 15 s.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, strongly, at two levels.
1. 2025 hooks: one virtual branch per Claude session and one commit per chat round, with the generating prompt in the commit message. Prompt history lived directly in the code's git history.
2. agentlog: each turn stores observed targets and an environment snapshot. These include branch keys, review/PR keys, change IDs, commit IDs, file hashes, and fingerprints of the edited paths. Index sets let a branch, PR or change be resolved back to the sessions and turns that touched it. The skill warns agents to treat these matches as 'related evidence, not ownership'.
scale:
git-meta README claims:
- a tree-diff update over metadata for 1M commits found 1k new values in under 1 s
- full key reconstruction over 10k metadata commits and about 550k targets took about 15 s, with 120 prune commits

It also cites an anecdote of an unnamed project as the motivation. That project, with 400 files and 2k commits, gathered over 2.5 GB of transcripts in three months, and its packfile grew from 5 MB to 500 MB. A blobless clone of the same history would be under 2 MB. Mitigations are blobless/promisor fetches plus pruning commits.

agentlog bounds its stored size by capping tool results at 4 KiB. I found no agentlog-specific scale numbers.
privacy_security:
agentlog: transcripts stay local-only by default. Keys carry the `local:` prefix, which git-meta never serializes. Sharing is an explicit `but agentlog publish <branch|review|change>`, which has a dry-run, unless the repo sets gitbutler.agentlog-share-default.

Redaction runs heuristically before storage (redaction.rs):
- named-secret patterns: api_key, token, password, secret, cookie, authorization and similar
- sensitive JSON keys are blanked wholesale, including anything ending in token, secret, password, apikey or path, plus id, uuid, branch, cwd and worktree
- high-entropy strings of 20+ characters are replaced with [REDACTED:entropy]; the entropy threshold is 4.0, or 3.0 for hex
- absolute paths become [REDACTED:path]
- edited file paths are stored only as SHA-256 fingerprints

There is no encryption and no signing of metadata commits. git-meta allows routing keys to separate refs or remotes (`route`/`exclude` filter rules) for private versus public metadata. Hard deletion of a leaked secret requires a force-push rewrite.

Recalled transcript text is handed to agents through the skim/show skill with no untrusted-content envelope, so stored history becomes agent context. ParleyInn's I2 forbids exactly that pattern.

The 2025 hook feature sent prompts to an AI model to rewrite commit messages. Prompts landed in commit messages in plain text, with no documented redaction.

GitButler itself is FSL-1.1-MIT (source-available, converting to MIT later).
lesson_for_parinn: git-meta's exchange layout is a ready answer to 'git as transport for many writers'. ParleyInn can keep its own local append-only store and only serialize to a custom ref (refs/meta/... or refs/parinn/...) in a separate step. Each event becomes its own blob, named by timestamp plus content hash, under a list tree. Concurrent appends from any number of worktrees, sandboxes or machines then merge as a pure union of tree entries, and push becomes retry-merge-until-fast-forward. ParleyInn's core never touches the network: it writes refs, and ordinary git or Forgejo push/fetch, or a separate meta remote, moves them. Two parts of that design are worth copying: the hard 'local: is never serialized' rule, and an explicit publish step. Two gaps should be closed rather than copied. First, the hash chain should cover record content and be signed: agentlog's previous_turn_key is unsigned, and 'ours' can silently overwrite mutable string keys. Second, recalled transcripts must be enveloped as untrusted. agentlog's skim feeds them straight back to agents.
license: GitButler client: FSL-1.1-MIT (Functional Source License, converting to MIT). The git-meta spec and reference library: MIT.
sources: https://docs.gitbutler.com/features/ai-integration/claude-code-hooks (HTTP 404 on 2026-10-02. The PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop -> `but claude pre-tool|post-tool|stop` configuration is known only from the search-engine snippet of this page)
confidence: medium. Confidence is high for the agentlog and git-meta storage, merge and redaction facts, which were read directly from source at the cited commits. It is medium for the claim that the 2025 hook and Agents Tab features were removed. That claim rests on the 404 docs and on their absence from the current source tree; no announcement was found. Which hook events agentlog registers was not verified.

name: GitHub Agent HQ / Mission Control (third-party Claude and Codex agents on GitHub), plus the Copilot session-sync and /chronicle layer it depends on
category: Forge-hosted multi-agent platform (proprietary SaaS control plane over GitHub repos, Actions compute and a hosted session-log store)
status: Shipped, mostly still in preview. Agent HQ was announced at GitHub Universe on 2025-10-28. Third-party Claude and Codex agents entered public preview on 2026-02-04 for Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise, and reached Business and Pro on 2026-02-26. The third-party agents docs still say "public preview". The Agent tasks REST API is in public preview (API version 2026-03-10). Session sync and /chronicle went GA on 2026-06-02. Google, Cognition and xAI agents were announced on 2025-10-28; I could not confirm that any of them shipped.
what_is_stored: (1) Cloud agent sessions. Session logs show "Copilot's internal reasoning and the tools it used to understand your repository, make changes, and validate its work", plus token usage and session length. The code itself lands as commits on a branch and one PR per task. (2) Task and session metadata, exposed by the Agent tasks REST API. A task has id, state (queued/in_progress/completed/failed/idle/waiting_for_user/timed_out/cancelled), sessions[], artifacts[] (provider github, type pull or branch), creator, repository, custom_agent, created/updated/archived_at. A session has id, state, prompt, model, usage {type, amount}, error, head_ref, base_ref and timestamps. (3) Local sessions from Copilot CLI, VS Code, JetBrains and the Copilot app. These hold prompts, responses, tools used and file changes. VS Code also records conversation turns, file paths from tool calls, PR and issue references, and metadata: repo, branch, working directory, timestamps, agent. (4) Audit log events for the partner GitHub Apps ("anthropic code agent", "openai code agent"). For third-party Claude and Codex sessions, the docs only say there is a "View session" overview with "detailed activity logs". I could not find any public statement on where those transcripts are stored, or whether Anthropic or OpenAI also keep them.
where_stored: Split across tiers. Code goes to ordinary git branches and PRs on GitHub; the cloud agent only works with GitHub-hosted repos. Transcripts and logs live in GitHub's own hosted service, not in git: no notes, no refs, no files in the repo. Local sessions go to files under ~/.copilot/session-state/ (the "complete record of each session"), indexed in a local SQLite "session store". They sync to the user's GitHub account by default. Third-party agents run on GitHub infrastructure and use Actions minutes. One secondary source says code processed by Codex "flows through OpenAI's infrastructure"; no primary doc confirms or denies that.
format_and_model: Public format: REST/JSON task and session objects (fields listed above), with no transcript or log endpoint. The task API returns only the prompt text, not the log. The format of hosted session logs is undocumented; they are rendered as a UI timeline. Locally there are raw per-session files plus a SQLite index that is a derived projection: "/chronicle reindex" rebuilds the session store from the files on disk. Commits made by the cloud agent are authored by Copilot, with the requesting human as co-author.
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no shared, multi-writer transcript. Each session has one writer (the agent) and one owner. Parallel agents are kept apart by giving each task its own branch: the agent "can only push to a single branch", a new copilot/ branch per task, and one PR per task. Integration happens through normal PR review and merge; Agent HQ announced "one-click merge conflict resolution". People influence a running session by steering, which is follow-up prompts, but "Steering is not available for third-party coding agents". Cloud sessions can be archived but not deleted. Only local sessions can be deleted.
realtime: Yes, for watching progress: you can "follow progress in real time or review completed sessions" from the Agents tab, the agents panel, VS Code's Agent sessions view, Mobile and the CLI. Local sessions sync to the GitHub account, but the docs give no latency figure or real-time guarantee. I found no streaming API for logs. The REST API only lets you poll task and session state.
search_retrieval: /chronicle (GA 2026-06-02) answers natural-language questions and keyword or file-path searches over synced sessions from Copilot CLI, cloud agent, code review, VS Code, JetBrains and the Copilot app. Subcommands include standup, tips, search, improve and reindex. The search mechanism (FTS, embeddings or LLM) is not documented. The docs do not say whether third-party Claude and Codex sessions can be searched by /chronicle. Shared local sessions do not show up in other users' search results.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, through a URL rather than a git object: "the commit message for each agent-authored commit includes a link to the agent session logs". Each task has a 1:1 task-branch-PR mapping, artifacts[] in the API ties a task to a pull or branch, and each session records head_ref and base_ref. Local session metadata records repo, branch, working directory and touched file paths. Following the link requires GitHub's hosted log store, so the git history alone is not enough.
scale: No quantitative scale claims found. Limits that are stated: a cloud agent session runs at most 59 minutes (hard limit); one repository and one branch per task; one premium request per third-party session during the preview. The REST API is pitched for fanning out refactors and migrations across many repositories.
privacy_security: Cloud agent protections, which third-party agents share ("the same security protections, mitigations, and limitations as Copilot cloud agent"): an internet firewall that "restricts ... access to the internet"; pushing only to its own copilot/ branch; only users with write access can trigger it; Actions workflows do not run until a human clicks "Approve and run workflows"; hidden characters, such as HTML comments in issues, are filtered out before user input reaches the agent; CodeQL, secret scanning and an Advisory Database check run on the agent's output; session logs and audit events are available to admins. Session sync: local sessions are unshared and private by default, while cloud agent sessions are shared by default. VS Code strips "secrets such as tokens, API keys, and credentials ... before data leaves your machine". Repos can be excluded by exact name or glob (chat.sessionSync.excludeRepositories). Admins can turn sync off by policy (CopilotSessionSync; "Store local sessions in the Cloud"). I found no documentation on encryption at rest, retention periods, or how much third-party transcript data Anthropic or OpenAI keep.
license: Proprietary SaaS (GitHub/Microsoft), included in paid Copilot plans. Not open source.
lesson_for_parinn: The largest forge did not put agent transcripts in git. Code stays in git and transcripts go to a hosted store. A local store keeps raw per-session files as the record plus a SQLite index that /chronicle reindex can rebuild, which is ParleyInn's I10 pattern. Agent commits carry a pointer back to the session in their message. ParleyInn should copy that shape without the hosted dependency: write a stable session or chain-head id into commit trailers, kept as an opaque id rather than a URL so I4 holds offline, and keep the hash-chained record out of the working tree. GitHub's sync also gives ParleyInn concrete defaults for any future sync or export: redact before data leaves the machine, private by default, per-repo exclude globs, and an admin kill switch. GitHub's agents cannot be steered and the log format is undocumented, so a portable, verifiable record format is a gap ParleyInn can fill.
confidence: medium-high for Copilot cloud agent, session sync and /chronicle (from primary docs); low for where third-party Claude and Codex transcripts are stored, how long they are kept, and whether the partners also hold them, since no primary source says.

name: GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw, GitHub Next / Microsoft Research)
category: hosted agent run logs on GitHub Actions (plus git-branch and Actions-cache agent memory)
status: beta. GitHub's changelog announced a technical preview on 2026-02-13 under the MIT license (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-02-13-github-agentic-workflows-are-now-in-technical-preview/). The newest release, v0.90.1 on 2026-09-30, is marked pre-release (https://github.com/github/gh-aw/releases). The README warns "Use it with caution, and at your own risk" and says releases >=0.83.3 and <0.85.4 were retired over a vulnerability (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/gh-aw/main/README.md). The primary docs are verified at github.github.com/gh-aw. The skills.sh page in the discovery note mirrors .github/skills/debugging-workflows/SKILL.md in the github/gh-aw repo, and I fetched that file from raw.githubusercontent.com.
what_is_stored:
Each run of an agent is saved as GitHub Actions artifacts. They are not git objects. According to the current artifacts reference (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/artifacts/):
- "activation": aw_info.json (engine config and workflow metadata), prompt.txt (the generated prompt sent to the agent), github_rate_limits.jsonl.
- "agent": the agent's execution logs, agent_output.json (safe-output requests), agent_usage.json (token usage) and otel.jsonl (OpenTelemetry spans).
- "firewall-audit-logs": api-proxy-logs/token-usage.jsonl, squid-logs/access.log, audit.jsonl, policy-manifest.json.
- "detection": detection.log, or detection_result.json from the external engine.
- "usage": a compact summary.
- Optional: safe-outputs-items (safe-output-items.jsonl, temporary-id-map.json, safe-output-errors.json), evals.jsonl, experiment state.json, SARIF.
- Legacy standalone artifacts (safe-output, agent-output, aw-info, prompt) are now bundled into the ones above.

The debugging skill's older table lists what `gh aw logs` downloads per run: aw_info.json, safe_output.jsonl, agent_output/, agent-stdio.log, aw.patch ("Git patch of changes made during execution"), workflow-logs/ and summary.json (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/gh-aw/main/.github/skills/debugging-workflows/SKILL.md).

Separately, agents can keep persistent "memory" in two places:
- repo-memory: files committed to a git branch (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/).
- cache-memory: files kept in the GitHub Actions cache (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/).

Neither the docs nor the skill describe the full raw Claude Code session transcript (for example the JSONL) as a first-class stored artifact. Beyond the stdio and engine logs, I could not verify whether it is kept.
where_stored:
The main store is server/cloud: GitHub Actions artifacts and job logs. GitHub's default retention for these is 90 days, and it can be changed (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/remove-workflow-artifacts).

`gh aw logs` caches downloads locally in .github/aw/logs/run-{id}/ (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/setup/cli/).

Memory has two backends:
- repo-memory lives on a custom git branch, `memory/{id}` (default `memory/default`), with unlimited retention.
- cache-memory lives in the GitHub Actions cache: branch-scoped, evicted after 7 days unused, 10GB per repository with LRU eviction.

Sources: https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/ and https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/
format_and_model:
Data is a set of flat files per run, keyed by the Actions run ID. Most records are JSON or JSONL (aw_info.json, agent_output.json, otel.jsonl, token-usage.jsonl, audit.jsonl), plus plain logs (agent-stdio.log, squid access.log), prompt.txt and a git patch (aw.patch) (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/artifacts/).

`gh aw logs --json` gives structured output with lineage under `.episodes[]` and `.edges[]`. `--cached-jsonl` writes schema-versioned run records, one JSON value per line (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/setup/cli/).

repo-memory holds arbitrary files on a git branch, with optional extension allow-lists and optional JSON pretty-printing. Defaults are 100KB per file (configurable up to 1MB), 100 files and a 10KB patch per run (up to 1MB). Agents change it only through safe-output tools such as `ledger_append` (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/).

cache-memory by default allows only .json, .jsonl, .txt, .md and .csv files (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/).

There is no hash chain or signature over the run record.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Run artifacts are immutable and written once per run, so runs never need to be merged.

repo-memory is shared by many concurrent writers. The docs say: "each run commits with a compare-and-swap on the remote branch head and, if another run wins the race, re-reads the head, rebases its change with JSONL union merging, and retries with exponential backoff." For .jsonl files, "rows written by concurrent runs are all kept; other file types keep the local version" (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/). That means non-JSONL files are last-writer-wins.

cache-memory is branch-scoped. A restore prefers the same branch, then falls back to the default branch. Cache keys include the integrity level and a hash of the guard policy, so lower-integrity runs cannot poison higher-integrity caches (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/).
realtime: None. Artifacts are uploaded when jobs finish, and `gh aw logs` / `gh aw audit` pull them after the run (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/setup/cli/). repo-memory is committed and pushed only after the workflow completes, and only if threat detection passes (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/). The docs mention an OpenTelemetry integration for token and spend tracking (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/), but I could not verify live streaming of the session.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is through `gh aw logs`, which filters by count, date range, engine and repo, can convert logs to markdown, emits JSON, reads run IDs from stdin, and can train drain3 anomaly weights. `gh aw audit <run>` produces a per-run report (prompt analysis, MCP health, safe outputs, firewall, metrics). `gh aw audit A B` diffs runs to catch regressions in network domains, tools and tokens. Both cache locally for faster repeat runs (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/setup/cli/).

There is no full-text or semantic search across history. Retrieval is per run, and scale comes from local caching.

repo-memory files are mounted into later runs at /tmp/gh-aw/repo-memory-{id}/, and cache-memory at /tmp/gh-aw/cache-memory/ (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/, https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/).
links_sessions_to_code:
Partly. Each run keeps aw.patch, the git diff it produced (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/gh-aw/main/.github/skills/debugging-workflows/SKILL.md). Issues and PRs created through safe outputs carry a hidden marker `<!-- gh-aw-workflow-id: WORKFLOW_NAME -->` and an attribution footer, which can be turned off with `footer: false` (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/safe-outputs/).

So the link runs from a PR to a workflow, and then to an Actions run whose artifacts expire. Commits get no trailers or git notes that point at a durable session record, and I could not verify any per-commit link to a prompt.
privacy_security:
Security is defense in depth (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/introduction/architecture/):
- The agent job has read-only permissions. Its write requests are buffered as artifacts (agent_output.json), checked by a separate detection job ("same AI engine ... security-focused system prompt"), and only then applied by separate jobs with scoped write permissions.
- The Agent Workflow Firewall containerizes the agent and forces HTTP/HTTPS through a Squid proxy with a domain allow-list. An API proxy keeps credentials away from the agent.
- Integrity filtering drops content below `min-integrity`.
- Before upload, artifacts are scanned for secrets using "safe string matching (not regex)", and matches are masked as the first 3 characters followed by asterisks.

Safe outputs also sanitize text with domain and GitHub-reference allow-lists and mention limits (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/safe-outputs/).
