For memory:
- cache-memory strips execute bits and disallowed file types from restored files.
- repo-memory validators run in both the agent job and the push job, and get no write tokens.
- Both docs say "Do not store sensitive data ... It follows repository permissions" (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/, https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/).

Prompts and outputs are kept as artifacts that anyone with repository read access can download. I found no encryption at rest beyond GitHub's own.
scale:
No throughput claims. The documented limits are:
- cache-memory: 10GB per repository, 7-day eviction.
- repo-memory: 100KB per file by default (max 1MB), 100 files, a 10KB patch per run by default (max 1MB), unlimited retention.
- Actions artifacts: 90 days by default.

Sources: https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/cache-memory/, https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/repo-memory/, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/remove-workflow-artifacts. The local log cache is said to make repeat analysis "10-100x faster" (https://github.github.com/gh-aw/setup/cli/).
license: MIT (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-02-13-github-agentic-workflows-are-now-in-technical-preview/)
lesson_for_parinn:
gh-aw stores two kinds of data in two places:
- Bulky, short-lived run telemetry (prompt, stdio, OTel spans, firewall logs, patch) goes to non-git artifacts that expire after 90 days.
- Small, durable shared memory goes to a dedicated git branch (memory/{id}). It is written by many concurrent sandboxes through compare-and-swap on the branch head plus JSONL union merge, but only after validation and threat detection, and only through a privileged job the agent cannot drive directly. The agent can only request appends (`ledger_append`).

For ParleyInn:
1. A git ref is a workable sync point for append-only JSONL written by many ephemeral sandboxes: compare-and-swap push, then rebase, then a line-union merge.
2. Both the docs and the size caps (100KB per file, 10KB patches) show git suits small curated records, not full transcripts.
3. Union merge plus "local wins" for other files breaks any hash chain. ParleyInn would need per-writer chains (one file or ref per agent) merged as a set rather than rebased.
4. Validation and redaction should run before data leaves the sandbox. Treat anything restored from shared memory as untrusted input, the way gh-aw strips files and filters by integrity level on restore, which matches ParleyInn's I2.

name: GitHub Copilot CLI (cloud sandboxes, session sync and /chronicle)
category: CLI agent with cloud session state
status: The CLI itself has shipped: changelog version 1.0.91 is dated 2026-10-01 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/copilot-cli/main/changelog.md). Cloud and local sandboxes are beta. The docs say they are "in public preview and subject to change". Cloud sandboxing is "currently an experimental feature" and needs `copilot --cloud --experimental`. Organisations have it disabled by default (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes).
what_is_stored: Docs define session data as "prompts and responses, tools used, and changes made to files" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Each local session directory holds an event log (`events.jsonl`) plus "workspace artifacts (plans, checkpoints, tracked files)". These are what make `--resume`/`--continue` work (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). Since 0.0.422 (2026-03-05), usage metrics (requests, tokens, code changes) are also written to events.jsonl at session end. Since 1.0.85 (2026-09-16), automatic compaction saves a checkpoint, visible in /session checkpoints (changelog URL above). A separate SQLite session store keeps a subset of the data for cross-session work: "checkpoint indexing and search" (config-dir reference). For a cloud sandbox, stopping the session snapshots the whole environment: "your files, environment variables, and in-progress work are restored" on resume. Deleting the session removes both the environment and the snapshot (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL).
where_stored:
Several places, depending on the session:
- **Local disk.** `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/` holds the complete record. `~/.copilot/session-store.db` holds the SQLite index. Also `command-history-state/`, and `logs/process-{timestamp}-{pid}.log` (config-dir reference). This confirms the local path the discovery note had marked unverified.
- **GitHub account (synced copy).** Local CLI sessions are synced to the user's GitHub account by default. That copy "is stored separately" and deleting local files does not touch it (session-data URL; config-dir reference).
- **Cloud sandbox sessions.** These run on GitHub-hosted infrastructure "built on Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, with GitHub providing the identity, policy, and billing layer". State persists as a snapshot billed at $0.005 per GiB-month (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL).
- **Cloud agent sessions.** These run in an ephemeral environment. The environment is destroyed afterwards, but "the session log remains available on GitHub.com" (session-data URL).

Nothing is stored in git, git notes or custom refs.
format_and_model:
Each session is an append-only JSONL event log keyed by session ID (UUIDs appear in the docs' examples), with a derived SQLite index beside it.

- **The index is rebuildable.** `/chronicle reindex` "rebuilds the session store from the files under ~/.copilot/session-state/". The docs describe session.store.db as "re-created automatically" if deleted (session-data URL; config-dir reference).
- **The event schema is not published.** I found no public schema for `events.jsonl` and no evidence of hash-chaining or signing.
- **Import exists, but its spec does not.** 1.0.85 added "session and memory import commands for the semantic JSONL interchange format". I found no published spec for that format (changelog).
- **Writes are periodic, not per event.** Data is written to the session directory "periodically during a session, and also when the session ends", and the store is "populated incrementally" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/chronicle).
- **Exports.** `/share` (alias `/export`) produces a GitHub.com link, a private gist, Markdown (`copilot-session-SESSIONID.md`) or interactive HTML (chronicle URL).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no documented multi-writer model and no merge. Every session has one owner and lives in its own directory. The docs hint at process-level exclusivity: `/session delete-all` skips "Sessions that are in use by another process" (chronicle URL).

- **Cross-device continuity is not merging.** For cloud sandboxes, the session runs in one GitHub-hosted environment that any device can attach to (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL). For local sessions, a one-way sync to the user's account is the mechanism.
- **Worktrees.** The CLI creates them with `/worktree`, `/move` and `--worktree`. Each worktree starts a new session; session logs are not merged across worktrees (changelog). Linked worktrees resolve to the main repo root only for permissions (config-dir reference).
- **Sharing.** A shared session is view-only for recipients and is not merged into their own history (session-data URL).
realtime: Partly real-time. Remote control arrived in 1.0.25 (2026-04-13): `--remote` or `/remote` let another device steer a running CLI session. Managed settings can disable it or require SSO (changelog; `remoteControl` in the config-dir reference). The `remote` setting "Controls session syncing and remote access" and `remoteExport` exports sessions when sync is available (config-dir reference). The Sessions tab marks remote (cloud) rows online or offline (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-command-reference). Cloud sandbox sessions can be picked up "on any device, regardless of where the session was originally started" (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL). Local persistence is periodic and at session end, not per event (chronicle URL). The docs give no sync latency or transport protocol; changelog entries mention uploads to "Mission Control".
search_retrieval:
Retrieval comes in three forms:
- **Resume.** `--continue` picks the most recent session. `--resume [ID]` and `/resume` open a picker or jump to an ID. Resume "loads the full conversation history" (chronicle URL).
- **Search and insights.** `/chronicle search` "searches all of your session content (not just summaries)" with direct content search. Other subcommands produce standup reports, tips, cost-tips and suggested edits to the instructions file (chronicle URL).
- **Free-form questions.** The CLI answers questions about past sessions automatically from the session store. The docs say "full-text search across your session history", and by default it searches all repos and branches; only `improve` is limited to the current repo (chronicle URL).

The session store is SQLite (config-dir reference). The docs do not say which full-text engine or embedding method it uses. Recalled data goes to the model: "Copilot may send relevant session data, such as prompts, context, and responses, to the AI model" (session-data URL).
links_sessions_to_code: The link to code is loose and inferred, with no commit trailers or per-commit provenance. Session directories hold checkpoints and tracked files, and the rewind picker shows working-tree diff stats at each checkpoint (config-dir reference; changelog 1.0.60-era entries). `/chronicle standup` groups work by branch and checks the status of linked PRs and issues, which suggests branch and repo are recorded as session metadata (chronicle URL). The cloud agent (a separate product) works on one branch, writes the commits and keeps viewable logs, and the CLI can bring a cloud agent session down to the local machine (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent; https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/use-copilot-cli). I found no documented commit trailer, git note or mapping from session to commit.
scale:
The docs make no numeric scale claims. The changelog shows the vendor working on large histories:
- "Reduce metadata scanning time for large local session histories" (1.0.83)
- "Resume very large local sessions" (1.0.82)
- resume reads history "once at startup" (1.0.78)
- infinite sessions via compaction checkpoints (0.0.385, 2026-01-19)

Automatic compaction starts at 80% of the token limit (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/use-copilot-cli). Cloud sandboxes support running "multiple tasks in parallel", with no stated limits (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL).
privacy_security:
**Sync and access**
- Sync is on by default. Local sessions are "synced to your GitHub account" by default; `remote: "off"` keeps data local (session-data URL; config-dir reference).
- For Business and Enterprise users, sync needs the "Store local sessions in the Cloud" policy set to at least "View from cloud". Unconfigured means local only.
- Synced data is private to the user by default. Admins "enabling syncing does not give them access to your session data".
- Cloud agent sessions are shared with everyone who has repo access, by default (session-data URL).

**Secrets**
- `mcp-secrets/` is a fallback store when the keychain is unavailable (config-dir reference).
- 1.0.51 (2026-05-20) added a warning when token storage falls back to plain-text config.
- 1.0.51 also extended secret scanning to "commit messages and PR descriptions, redacting secrets before they are published".
- 1.0.66 mentions unspecified "secret filtering".
- 1.0.87 (2026-09-21) stopped writing secrets exported in the launching shell to debug logs.
- Sources: changelog.

**Isolation and network**
- Cloud sandboxes are ephemeral Linux environments and inherit cloud agent policy, including firewall rules.
- Local sandboxing uses MXC (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux, BaseContainer on Windows). It is lighter-weight isolation, not a VM.
- The CLI's built-in file tools are not OS-sandboxed; they honour the policy only "on a best-effort basis" (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL).

**Not stated in the docs**
- encryption at rest for session-state, the SQLite store or synced copies
- retention periods
- whether events.jsonl is redacted before sync
- any untrusted-content handling when recalled history is fed back to the model
lesson_for_parinn:
Copilot CLI confirms the split ParleyInn already plans, and shows the defaults ParleyInn should reverse.

**What it confirms:**
- **Shape of the store.** The source of truth is a per-session append-only `events.jsonl`. `session-store.db` is a disposable SQLite index rebuilt with `/chronicle reindex`, which matches I10.
- **No git for history.** Session history moves through a vendor account sync, not through git. A cloud sandbox gets continuity from a whole-VM snapshot, not by sending the history anywhere.

**What ParleyInn should reverse:**
- **Sync default.** Copilot syncs by default; ParleyInn should sync only on opt-in, through a separate transport that is not the core (I4).
- **Integrity.** Copilot neither documents a schema nor hash-chains or signs its JSONL; ParleyInn should hash-chain, sign and export the log in a documented format.
- **Recall.** Copilot pipes recalled history to the model with no documented envelope; ParleyInn should keep recall pull-only and enveloped (I2).
- **Portability.** A snapshot only helps inside one vendor's sandbox, so ParleyInn needs an export path for ephemeral sandboxes.

**Worth copying:** the explicit rebuild command that also re-syncs.
license: Proprietary. The github/copilot-cli repository publishes the changelog, but this research did not verify a license for the CLI itself. Its use requires a Copilot subscription, and cloud sandboxes are billed per use (about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes URL).

name: GitHub Copilot CLI session store / chronicle (session-state + session-store.db + GitHub session sync)
status: shipped. /chronicle and syncing local sessions to the GitHub account were announced GA on 2026-06-02 (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-02-gain-insights-across-your-agent-sessions-with-chronicle/). Live remote control and real-time streaming of CLI sessions to GitHub was in public preview as of 2026-04-13 (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-13-remote-control-cli-sessions-on-web-and-mobile-in-public-preview/). I found nothing saying the remote-control feature has since gone GA.
what_is_stored: GitHub says session data "can include prompts and responses, tools used, and changes made to files" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Each session has three parts. (1) events.jsonl, an event log per session. (2) "Workspace artifacts (plans, checkpoints, tracked files)" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). (3) workspace.yaml with git context: root, repository, branch and revision (https://docs.rs/toolpath-copilot). The VS Code docs for the same shared session store list what gets indexed: session metadata (repository, branch, working directory, timestamps, agent), conversation turns, file paths from tool calls, and external references such as PR numbers, issue numbers and commit SHAs (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/session-insights). The synced copy on GitHub also holds sessions from Copilot cloud agent, code review, VS Code and the Copilot app (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/chronicle).
where_stored: Local working files outside the repo, plus a local DB, plus GitHub's servers. Locally: ~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/ holds the full record, and the location can be overridden with COPILOT_HOME. ~/.copilot/session-store.db is a SQLite database "used by the CLI for cross-session data such as checkpoint indexing and search" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). In the cloud: by default, sessions sync to the user's GitHub account. That copy is stored separately, so deleting local files does not touch it (same source). Sessions show up in the repository's Agents tab (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-02-gain-insights-across-your-agent-sessions-with-chronicle/). Nothing goes into git itself: no commits, notes or refs. History is held in GitHub's application storage, not in the repository.
format_and_model: Each session is a directory keyed by session ID. Inside it, events.jsonl is an append-only event stream, plus workspace.yaml and a checkpoints/ folder of file snapshots. The events.jsonl format is officially undocumented. One crate (toolpath-copilot) reverse-engineered it and checked it against copilotVersion 1.0.67. It found one JSON envelope per line, with event types such as session.start, tool.execution_*, assistant.message (carrying reasoningText and outputTokens) and system.message. Types such as subagent.*, skill.invoked, hook.*, abort and session.shutdown appear in its spec but are unverified (https://docs.rs/toolpath-copilot). The SQLite session store holds a subset of the record. It is a derived index that can be rebuilt from session-state with `/chronicle reindex` (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). Its schema and FTS details are not published (could not verify). The sync wire format and how GitHub stores data server-side are not documented.
multi_writer_and_merge: Each session has one writer, and one session lives on one machine. Sessions from different machines and tools never merge into each other. They are collected side by side under the user's GitHub account and queried together, from the CLI, VS Code, JetBrains, the Copilot app and github.com (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/chronicle). No conflict-resolution or merge mechanism is documented, and none appears to be needed because session IDs never collide. VS Code's docs say plainly that they don't detail cross-device merging (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/session-insights). Interrupted sessions can be restored after a crash, but this is opt-in through COPILOT_ENABLE_INTERRUPTED_SESSION_RESTORE=1 (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/cli-command-reference). Sharing is per session and view-only: a GitHub link, a secret gist, or a Markdown or HTML export (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/chronicle).
realtime: Two separate paths. (a) Session sync to the GitHub account, on by default. GitHub does not document how fast or often it uploads (could not verify). (b) Remote control, public preview since April 2026: "Copilot streams your CLI session activity to GitHub in real time." You can watch and steer the session from the web or GitHub Mobile, and actions sync both ways. Each remote session is visible only to the user who started it (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-13-remote-control-cli-sessions-on-web-and-mobile-in-public-preview/). The `remote` setting ("on" by default, or "off") turns off both remote control and remote session data (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). There is no real-time multi-user sharing of one session.
search_retrieval: `/chronicle search` does a direct keyword or content search, unlike free-form questions that rely on semantic understanding (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/chronicle). Other subcommands: standup (a work report, which can include recent local sessions), tips, cost-tips (token usage), improve (suggests custom instructions, limited to the current repo), and reindex. Free-form questions about past work automatically pull in session data. All subcommands except improve look across every repository by default (same source). Sessions can be resumed with --continue, --resume or /resume <id>. The picker sorts by relevance, last used, created or name (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/cli-command-reference). The search runs over the SQLite session store. Whether queries on other surfaces hit the synced cloud copy or a local index is not documented in detail.
links_sessions_to_code: Only loosely, by metadata. workspace.yaml records repo root, repository, branch and revision when the session starts (https://docs.rs/toolpath-copilot). The index records file paths touched by tool calls, plus PR numbers, issue numbers and commit SHAs mentioned in a session (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/session-insights). Synced sessions appear in the repository's Agents tab (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-02-gain-insights-across-your-agent-sessions-with-chronicle/). Checkpoints snapshot files. Nothing is written into commits, trailers or git notes. The link is held on GitHub's side, so it would not survive pushing the code to Forgejo or any other forge.
scale: No scale claims are published: no limits on session count, store size or query latency (could not verify).
privacy_security: Sync is on by default. Users opt out with "remoteExport": false (or remote: "off") in the CLI settings JSON (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-config-dir-reference). For Business and Enterprise users, the "Store local sessions in the Cloud" policy must be at least "View from cloud" for sync to work. GitHub says synced data is tied to the personal account and visible only to that user by default, and that admins who enable sync do not gain access to it. Cloud-agent sessions, by contrast, are shared by default with anyone who has access to the repository, and they can be archived but not deleted (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Secret redaction is documented only in the VS Code docs: "Secrets such as tokens, API keys, passwords, and connection strings are filtered before data is synced." VS Code also has repo exclusion through chat.sessionSync.excludeRepositories, which takes owner/repo names or globs (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/session-insights). I could not verify that the CLI's own docs say the same about redaction, and the CLI has no documented per-repo exclusion. Encryption at rest, retention and data residency are not documented. The local session-state files are plaintext. If no credential store is found, the auth token is written in plaintext under ~/.copilot/ (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/cli-command-reference). Deleting locally with /session delete, delete-all or prune does not delete the synced copy, which has to be removed separately (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/chronicle). Secret gists are not available to Enterprise Managed Users or under data residency (same source). Nothing is documented about treating recalled history as untrusted: chronicle feeds past sessions straight back into the model and into suggested custom instructions (`improve`), with no envelope or trust boundary described.
lesson_for_parinn: The layout to copy is a canonical record per session plus an index you can throw away. An append-only events.jsonl in each session directory is the source of truth. A SQLite store is explicitly derived and can be rebuilt with `/chronicle reindex`. That maps directly onto ParleyInn's I10, and it shows sessions from many machines can be collected side by side without merging: one writer per session ID, so there are no conflicts to resolve. What ParleyInn should do differently: (1) Never sync by default, and never send data to a forge account. Copilot uploads to GitHub unless the user opts out, which conflicts with I4. ParleyInn should leave transport to an external, explicitly opt-in mechanism. (2) Strip secrets before any record leaves the machine, and enforce per-repo exclusion in the core. Copilot documents both only for VS Code. (3) Keep code links forge-neutral, recorded as repo, branch, revision and commit SHAs inside the record, not as a GitHub-side Agents-tab association. (4) Treat chronicle's `improve` loop, where past sessions turn into custom instructions, as exactly the injection channel I2 forbids. Any similar feature in ParleyInn must stay pull-only and enveloped.
confidence: high for paths, files, the reindexable SQLite store, default sync, the opt-out keys, the enterprise policy, the chronicle subcommands and sharing options. Medium for the events.jsonl and workspace.yaml internals, which come from reverse engineering, and for secret filtering, which is documented only on the VS Code side. Unverified: sync wire format, server-side storage, encryption, retention and scale.
license: Proprietary. Copilot CLI is a closed-source GitHub product, and the session file formats are undocumented. No license applies to the storage format (https://docs.rs/toolpath-copilot notes the format is undocumented).

name: GitHub Copilot cloud (coding) agent: Agent-Logs-Url commit trailer and hosted session logs
status: shipped
what_is_stored: In git: only a pointer. Since 2026-03-20 every commit the agent makes carries an `Agent-Logs-Url` trailer in its message, described as "a permanent link from agent-authored commits back to the agent session logs." Because it is a trailer, it shows in plain `git log` (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-03-20-trace-any-copilot-coding-agent-commit-to-its-session-logs, https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/track-copilot-sessions). Commits are authored by Copilot, the requesting developer is marked as co-author (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/risks-and-mitigations), and since 2026-04-03 they are signed and show as Verified (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-03-copilot-cloud-agent-signs-its-commits/). On GitHub: the full session log, which holds "Copilot's internal reasoning and the tools it used to understand your repository, make changes, and validate its work". That includes setup steps such as MCP server start, bash commands with their output, test and linter results from the ephemeral environment, token usage and session length (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/coding-agent/using-the-copilot-coding-agent-logs). Session metadata, from the gh CLI's client struct: id, name, user_id, agent_id, state, owner_id, repo_id, resource_type/resource_id (the linked PR), created/last_updated/completed_at, event_url/event_type (what triggered it), premium_requests, workflow_run_id and an error code and message (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). I could not find the exact URL pattern of the trailer value in a primary source.
where_stored: The logs live on GitHub's servers in the Copilot API service, not in git. The gh CLI reads them from `{capiBaseURL}/agents/sessions/{id}/logs` and lists sessions from `/agents/sessions` (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). The git repository holds only the trailer URL plus the signature. The agent runs in an ephemeral GitHub Actions-backed environment (the session has a workflow_run_id).
format_and_model: The log is a server-sent-events-style text stream. Each line is `data: <json>`, and the JSON is an OpenAI-compatible `chat.completion.chunk` object: id, choices[].delta.content, role, tool_calls[] with function name and JSON arguments such as run_setup, bash and view, finish_reason, created in ms and model. Clients render it into a transcript and skip entries of any other object type (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/log.go, test fixtures at https://github.com/cli/cli/tree/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/testdata). Data model: session 1:1 task, linked to one PR, many commits, each commit pointing back by trailer. There is no hash chain and no content addressing of the log itself. Integrity rests on GitHub signing the commits, not the logs. The changelog does not say which key or mechanism signs the commits (unverifiable from https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-03-copilot-cloud-agent-signs-its-commits/).
multi_writer_and_merge: This does not apply in the usual sense. Each session has one writer: the agent, which "only has the ability to push to a single branch" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/risks-and-mitigations). Several sessions can run at once on different branches and PRs. Users steer through PR comments and chat, but view-only recipients "cannot steer or modify the session" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/coding-agent/using-the-copilot-coding-agent-logs). The logs never need merging because they are never in git. A git rebase or squash that rewrites the commit message can drop the trailer. That is my inference: GitHub documents no protection against it.
realtime: You can watch a session live in the agents panel and the PR timeline, and Copilot Chat "reflects its status" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/track-copilot-sessions). From the terminal, `gh agent-task view <id|pr> --log --follow` follows live. Under the hood it polls: it re-fetches the whole log every 5 s (defaultLogPollInterval) and prints only the new suffix, so there is no push stream (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/view/view.go, gh 2.89.0).
search_retrieval: Retrieval works by navigation, not search. Routes in: the trailer URL from git log, the PR timeline, the agents panel at https://github.com/copilot/agents, and `gh agent-task list` and `view` with --json fields such as id, state, pullRequestNumber, repository and user (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/view/view.go). I found no documented full-text search over log contents and no documented export format. The docs page does not specify either (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/coding-agent/using-the-copilot-coding-agent-logs). Cross-repo commit search for the trailer string was not possible from this sandbox, so how widely it appears in public commits is unverified.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and this is the core of the feature. The link runs both ways: commit to session through the `Agent-Logs-Url` trailer, and session to PR through resource_type/resource_id in the session record. `gh agent-task view` accepts a session id, a PR number, a PR URL or a branch (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/view/view.go). The prompt (issue, PR comment or chat) is captured as the session's triggering event (event_url/event_type) and appears in the log.
privacy_security: Access: cloud agent sessions are shared by default with anyone who has repo access. Local (IDE/CLI) sessions are unshared by default and can be shared view-only. Cloud sessions "can be archived but not deleted" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/using-github-copilot/coding-agent/using-the-copilot-coding-agent-logs). I found no documented retention period. Only users with write access can trigger the agent. Its internet access is restricted by a firewall. "Hidden characters" are filtered from inputs to blunt prompt injection. Untrusted user events are ignored by default. CodeQL, advisory-database checks and secret scanning run on its output, workflows do not run until a human reviews, and audit events are recorded (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/risks-and-mitigations). I found no documented redaction of secrets inside session logs. Encryption at rest is not described for logs specifically (unverifiable). Logs are readable only through authenticated GitHub/Copilot APIs. The trailer URL is public in the commit message, but the content behind it is access-controlled.
scale: GitHub publishes no scale claims for the logs. The feature is available to Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business and Enterprise subscribers, and Business and Enterprise need an admin to enable it (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-03-20-trace-any-copilot-coding-agent-commit-to-its-session-logs).
license: Proprietary GitHub service. The gh CLI client code that reads the logs is MIT (https://github.com/cli/cli).
lesson_for_parinn: Put a small, signed pointer in git and keep the heavy, sensitive transcript outside it. Sharing then becomes access-controlled, deletion stays possible, and history never needs merging. GitHub's version still has gaps that ParleyInn can close. Its trailer is a mutable HTTPS URL to a server that holds an unhashed, unredacted log: if the link dies the record is lost, and nothing proves the log the trailer points to is the one that produced the commit. ParleyInn should emit a commit trailer such as `ParleyInn-Session: <session-id>@<head-hash-of-chain>`. Being content-addressed, it binds the commit to an exact prefix of the append-only, hash-chained record and stays verifiable offline (I10). It works with any transport (git ref, file sync, forge), so the core never needs the network (I4). ParleyInn should also treat anything fetched through such a link as untrusted, enveloped recall rather than restore content (I2). A second, smaller lesson: GitHub's "live" log is 5 s polling of the full log plus a suffix diff. An append-only record with offsets makes incremental tailing cheap and exact.

name: GitHub Copilot cloud agent (formerly Copilot coding agent)
status: shipped. GA on 2025-09-25 as "Copilot coding agent" (https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-copilot-coding-agent-is-now-generally-available/), first announced 2025-05-19 (https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-meet-the-new-coding-agent/). The docs now call it "Copilot cloud agent", but the URL path still says coding-agent. A dotnet/runtime commit from Feb 2026 still says "Copilot coding agent", so the rename came after that (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/commit/1c7b5c49466a1a2ca6a3c2bba12dbfe80159fab4). I could not find a rename changelog to cite. Several adjacent pieces are still public preview: the Agent tasks REST API, `gh agent-task`, Copilot Memory, and third-party agents (Claude, Codex).
what_is_stored: Per task, GitHub keeps one or more agent sessions (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). Each session has a session log that shows "Copilot's internal reasoning and the tools it used to understand your repository, make changes, and validate its work". The log also shows setup-step progress, token usage and session length (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions, https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment). It also includes security-validation results and public-code matches (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations, https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/responsible-use/agents). The task and session metadata the API returns covers: prompt, head_ref and base_ref, model, state, usage (AI credits or premium requests), error, timestamps, and artifacts (a PR id or a branch) (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). The git side holds signed commits on a copilot/* branch plus a PR. Observed on public repos, not stated in docs: the PR body embeds the original prompt, including the issue text and comments, inside a "<!-- START COPILOT ORIGINAL PROMPT -->" block. A squash-merge then carries that block into git history (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/commit/1c7b5c49466a1a2ca6a3c2bba12dbfe80159fab4). Two related stores sit nearby. Copilot Memory (preview) keeps repository facts with citations to code, plus per-user preferences (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory). Synced sessions from Copilot CLI and the Copilot app feed the same history you can query (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data).
where_stored: Server/cloud (GitHub.com), with the work products in git. The agent runs in an ephemeral GitHub Actions environment that "is destroyed when the session ends, but the session log remains available on GitHub.com" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Logs are reached through the Agents panel or page and the repository's "Agents" tab (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions). gh CLI source shows log content served by the Copilot API at GET {copilot-api}/agents/sessions/{id}/logs. The client finds the base URL through GraphQL viewer.copilotEndpoints.api (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/capi.go). Code, commits and the PR live in the GitHub repository on a copilot/ branch (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations). No session data is written into the repository except commit trailers and PR text. For comparison, Copilot CLI and the app keep the full local record under ~/.copilot/session-state/, a SQLite index at ~/.copilot/session-store.db, and sync to the GitHub account by default (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/chronicle).
format_and_model: The documented model, from the public-preview REST API version 2026-03-10: a Task {id, name, creator, creator_type, user_collaborators, owner, repository, state ∈ queued|in_progress|completed|failed|idle|waiting_for_user|timed_out|cancelled, session_count, artifacts[{provider: github, type: pull|branch, data}], archived_at, custom_agent} has many Sessions {id, task_id, state, prompt, head_ref, base_ref, model, usage{type, amount}, error, created/updated/completed_at}. The endpoints let you list, start and get tasks; none returns log content (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). The log format is undocumented. Per the gh CLI parser it is newline-separated "data: {json}" lines, SSE-style. The entries that matter are OpenAI-style "chat.completion.chunk" objects with choices[].delta {role, content, reasoning_text, tool_calls[{id, function{name, arguments}}]} and finish_reason (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/log.go). The raw session object also carries workflow_run_id, resource_type/resource_id (the PR), event_type and premium_requests (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). On the git side, commits carry an "Agent-Logs-Url: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/sessions/<uuid>" trailer plus Co-authored-by trailers (observed: https://github.com/christaegger-dot/Tardoc_Soziale-Arbeit-KJPP/commit/8fffcab23e7a98977c876765f854fe5b70ef2403). Setup is configured in .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml, hooks in .github/hooks/*.json, version 1 (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/hooks).
multi_writer_and_merge: There is one agent per session, and each task touches one repository and one branch. Copilot "can open exactly one pull request to address each task" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent). The agent can push only to its own copilot/ branch, or to the PR's branch when someone mentions @copilot on that PR. It "cannot directly run git push or other Git commands" and stays subject to branch protections (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations). A task can hold several sessions (session_count, sessions[]) (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks), and gh warns that one PR may have several tasks (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_agent-task_view). Humans can steer a running session with follow-up messages, which take effect after the current tool call. Teammates in Teams or Slack can also steer (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions, https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent). Concurrent work is reconciled only through normal git/PR merging; the agent itself can resolve merge conflicts (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent). No log-level merge exists: each session log is a single-writer stream held by GitHub.
realtime: The UI is live: you "monitor an agent's progress in real time" and can steer or stop. Stopping ends the Actions run and keeps commits already pushed (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions). Copilot Chat shows the status of a running session (same source). `gh agent-task view --log --follow` (preview) works by polling, not streaming. Every 5 seconds it re-fetches the whole log and renders only the new suffix, comparing by string prefix, and stops at finish_reason "stop" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/log.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/view/view.go). This works only because the log is append-only. The REST API offers state polling only; I found no documented webhook or push stream for session-log events (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). Not verified beyond these pages.
search_retrieval: You can ask natural-language questions of your own history in Copilot Chat (VS Code, JetBrains, the Copilot app, GitHub.com). It "searches across your synced sessions from Copilot CLI, Copilot cloud agent, and Copilot code review". You can query only sessions you started, and shared sessions are not indexed for other users (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions). Answering these queries "may send relevant session data, such as prompts, context, and responses, to the AI model" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Copilot Chat can also answer "what changed, what was validated, and why" about an agent PR from its session logs (track-copilot-sessions). The REST API filters tasks by state and is_archived (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). On the CLI side, `/chronicle search` does direct full-text search, and `/chronicle reindex` rebuilds the SQLite index from session files (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/chronicle). Copilot Memory checks each stored fact's code citations against the current branch before use. Unused entries expire after 28 days (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory). For cloud sessions there is no documented bulk export. The REST API returns metadata only, and gh `--log` reads raw logs through an undocumented preview endpoint.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and strongly. "Each commit message includes a link to the session logs". Commits are authored by Copilot, with the person who started the task as co-author, and are signed so they show as "Verified" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions). The responsible-use card calls this "a permanent link from any agent-authored commit to the full session logs" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/responsible-use/agents). The concrete form is an "Agent-Logs-Url: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/sessions/<uuid>" git trailer. It survives a squash-merge only when the squash message keeps the commit bodies (observed: https://github.com/christaegger-dot/Tardoc_Soziale-Arbeit-KJPP/commit/8fffcab23e7a98977c876765f854fe5b70ef2403). A squash built from the PR body drops it but keeps the embedded original-prompt block (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/commit/1c7b5c49466a1a2ca6a3c2bba12dbfe80159fab4). Both observations rest on single examples. Task artifacts link tasks to PR ids and branches (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). Session URLs also take the form github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/N/agent-sessions/<uuid> (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_agent-task_view).
scale: Hard limits per task: 59 minutes (`timeout-minutes` can only lower it), one repository, one branch, one PR. Only GitHub-hosted repositories are supported (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent). The runtime is a GitHub Actions runner, optionally a larger or self-hosted ephemeral one; Ubuntu x64 or Windows only (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment). The pages I read gave no official adoption or throughput figures; the GA changelog has none either (https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-copilot-coding-agent-is-now-generally-available/). As a rough, unofficial signal only: GitHub commit search for "Agent-Logs-Url" on 2026-10-02 reported about 747k public matches, with the incomplete_results flag set. Usage metrics APIs report PRs created and merged by the agent and median time to merge (about-coding-agent page).
privacy_security: Who can trigger: only users with write access, and "comments from users without write access are never presented to the agent". Hidden characters and HTML comments are filtered out of issue and PR input to blunt prompt injection. Draft PRs need a human to merge. The requester cannot approve. Actions workflows wait for "Approve and run workflows". An unattributed agent PR needs one extra approval. Generated code goes through CodeQL, secret scanning and Advisory Database checks. Session logs and audit events are available to admins (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations). The egress firewall is on by default with a recommended allowlist. It covers only processes the agent starts through its Bash tool, not MCP servers or setup steps, and the docs say it "may" be bypassed (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-firewall). Secrets: the agent gets only dedicated "Agents" secrets and variables, never Actions secrets. COPILOT_MCP_* values go only to MCP servers. "Secret values are masked in Copilot cloud agent session logs" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/configure-secrets-and-variables). Retention and visibility: cloud sessions "can be archived but not deleted" and are shared by default with anyone who has repository access (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/track-copilot-sessions). The session-data controls table marks Delete as not supported for cloud sessions (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). I found no stated retention period and no statement on at-rest encryption for session logs in these pages (unverified). The verbatim original prompt in the PR body can carry untrusted issue text into git history (dotnet commit above).
license: Proprietary GitHub SaaS, billed through paid Copilot plans, GitHub Actions minutes and AI credits (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/coding-agent/about-coding-agent). The gh CLI client (`gh agent-task`) is open source (https://github.com/cli/cli). I believe it is MIT-licensed but did not re-check that here.
lesson_for_parinn: Use a commit trailer as the pointer from code to session, but make the trailer verifiable and keep the record outside git and the forge. GitHub's Agent-Logs-Url trailer, sitting on signed commits, is a cheap link that survives forges. But it points at a log only GitHub holds: it cannot be deleted, has no documented export, and disappears when a squash is built from the PR body. Meanwhile the PR body copies the raw prompt, untrusted issue comments included, into history. ParleyInn should write a trailer that holds only an identifier, such as `ParleyInn-Session: <session-id>@<chain-head-hash>`, with no prompt text (I2). That lets any clone check the commit against its local hash-chained record and lets the record travel without the forge (I4). ParleyInn should also expose an offset- or hash-resumable tail. gh's `--follow` re-downloads the whole append-only log every 5 seconds and diffs by prefix. That works only because the log is append-only, and a hash chain gives ParleyInn the same property with integrity included.

name: GitHub Copilot cloud agent session logs (formerly "Copilot coding agent"), plus the gh agent-task CLI and the Agent tasks REST API
status: shipped
what_is_stored: One log per agent session. The docs say a log holds "Copilot's internal reasoning and the tools it used to understand your repository, make changes, and validate its work", including the tests and linters it ran. The session view also shows token usage and session length (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents). Setup-step output (copilot-setup-steps.yml) appears in the log (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/customize-the-agent-environment). So do security-validation details from CodeQL, the Advisory Database and secret scanning (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations) and public-code matches (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/responsible-use/agents). The session record the gh CLI reads has these fields: id (UUID), name, user_id, agent_id, logs, state, owner_id, repo_id, resource_type/resource_id/resource_global_id (the linked PR), created/last_updated/completed_at, event_type/event_url (the trigger), premium_requests, workflow_run_id (the GitHub Actions run) and error {code, message} (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). The public REST API adds task-level metadata. A task holds sessions[]. Each session carries prompt, head_ref, base_ref, model, usage {ai_credits or premium_requests} and state, and the task carries artifacts (pull or branch) (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). Since 2026 the same "session data" umbrella also covers synced local sessions from Copilot CLI and the Copilot app. Those hold prompts, responses, tool use and file changes (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data).
where_stored: On GitHub's servers, not in the repository. The agent runs in an ephemeral, GitHub Actions-powered environment that "is destroyed when the session ends, but the session log remains available on GitHub.com" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). The gh CLI fetches logs from the Copilot API service (CAPI), not from the git repo or the REST v3 API. The base URL is resolved through the GraphQL field viewer.copilotEndpoints.api, which can be tenant-specific for data-residency hosts (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/capi.go). The logs come from GET {capi}/agents/sessions/{id}/logs (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). That endpoint is internal and undocumented; the public REST API in public preview (/agents/repos/{owner}/{repo}/tasks, /agents/tasks/{id}) exposes no log endpoint (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). The web URL form is https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/sessions/<uuid>, seen in commit trailers. gh also accepts .../pull/N/agent-sessions/<uuid> (gh agent-task --help, gh 2.89.0). Cloud-agent sessions can be archived but not deleted. No retention period is documented, and I could not verify one (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents).
format_and_model: The raw log is a text body of Server-Sent-Events-style lines, "data: {json}", one OpenAI-style "chat.completion.chunk" object per line: choices[].delta with role, content and tool_calls[{function{name, arguments}, id}], plus finish_reason, created (epoch ms) and object. Tool results, such as Bash output or file views, are embedded as content (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/testdata/log-1-input.txt). The gh renderer keeps only entries whose object equals chat.completion.chunk and skips the rest (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/log.go). So the log is a model-stream transcript, not a typed event schema, and the format is not publicly specified. The data model is hierarchical: task, then sessions (session_count), then one log per session. A task links to artifacts of type pull or branch, and a session links to one Actions workflow run (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks; https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). States are queued, in_progress, completed, failed, idle, waiting_for_user, timed_out and cancelled. No hashing, signing or integrity chain over the log is documented.
multi_writer_and_merge: Each session has a single writer, the agent, which works on one branch and opens at most one PR per task. It cannot touch multiple repos in one run (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/about-cloud-agent). Humans can add to a running session by "steering": a follow-up prompt that "Copilot implements ... after it finishes its current tool call". In Teams and Slack, several teammates can steer one session (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents; https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/about-cloud-agent). Several sessions on one PR stay separate logs, and gh warns that "there may be multiple tasks for a given pull request that require disambiguation" (gh agent-task --help). Logs have no merge semantics. Only the code converges, through normal git and PR review. The agent cannot run git push itself; GitHub does "simple push operations" to a copilot/ branch for it (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations).
realtime: The docs say you can "Monitor an agent's progress in real time" in the agents panel or on github.com/copilot/agents (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents). The CLI is not push-based: `gh agent-task view --log --follow` and `gh agent-task create --follow` poll every 5 s (defaultLogPollInterval). Each poll refetches the whole log, then renders the suffix after the previously seen prefix. That design assumes the log only ever grows (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/view/view.go; https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/shared/log.go). Correction to the discovery note: `--log` is a flag of `gh agent-task view`, not `list` (gh 2.89.0 help; the CLI is in preview). There is a hard limit of 59 minutes per session (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/about-cloud-agent).
search_retrieval: You retrieve a session by its UUID, PR number, PR URL or branch through gh (https://cli.github.com/manual, local gh 2.89.0 help). The gh list command shows the viewer's latest sessions, sorted last_updated_at desc, 50 per page (https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/pkg/cmd/agent-task/capi/sessions.go). The REST API filters tasks by state, since, creator_id and is_archived, sorts by created_at or updated_at, and pages up to 100 per page; it returns metadata only (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). Content search runs through the model. Copilot Chat in VS Code, JetBrains, the Copilot app or GitHub.com answers natural-language questions across your synced sessions from CLI, cloud agent and code review, but "You can only query sessions that you started". Shared sessions are not indexed for other users' queries (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents). Copilot Chat also answers questions about a PR "by drawing on the session logs" (same page). For the CLI, a local SQLite session store (~/.copilot/session-store.db) is derived from ~/.copilot/session-state/. It supports `/chronicle search` full-text search and can be rebuilt with `/chronicle reindex` (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/chronicle).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, mainly one way, from code to session. The docs say agent commits are authored by Copilot, with the initiating user as co-author, and that "Each commit message includes a link to the session logs". Commits are signed and show as Verified (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/use-copilot-agents/manage-and-track-agents). In practice the link is a git trailer, `Agent-Logs-Url: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/sessions/<uuid>`. Examples: https://github.com/cli/cli/commit/cdda57e3601d2ce94ebae101d0dfa4983479ee6d and https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/commit/7fd6a92cef38f0ab4796bae53716f510d3d4c8b3. The trailer survived a rebase by a human committer and a squash-merge body (https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/commit/569a48d847236e7ed8d2b46ca57af8af7f768b36). I checked this myself by cloning the two repos and fetching recent PR heads. Only 3 of 24 commits authored by copilot-swe-agent[bot] since Jan 2026 carried the trailer, and none of the 8 from Jul–Sep 2026 did (example: https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/commit/7bfe9ae7a4dcea0334e18be1f38206eae9f2ad08), although those commits were PGP-signed by GitHub. The docs' "each commit" claim is therefore not reliable as of Oct 2026. Local Copilot app/CLI commits carry a different trailer, `Copilot-Session: <uuid>` (https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server/commit/a7d2b3b55740b5a7d701da853a28dda03c1dc6c3; observed only, undocumented). From session to code: the session record holds the PR resource id and the workflow_run_id, and the REST task lists its pull or branch artifacts. The org audit log's pull_request.create event carries agent_session_id (https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/audit-log-events-for-your-organization).
privacy_security: Visibility: cloud-agent sessions are "shared by default", meaning visible to anyone with access to the repo. They can be archived but not deleted. Synced local sessions are private by default, and enabling sync "does not give [admins] access to your session data" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). An anonymous fetch of a public-repo session URL returned HTTP 404 (my test), so you probably need to be signed in. I could not verify who exactly can see sessions on public repos. Secrets: the agent sees only the dedicated "Agents" secrets and variables, not Actions, Codespaces or Dependabot secrets. COPILOT_MCP_-prefixed values go only to MCP servers, and "Secret values are masked in Copilot cloud agent session logs" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/customize-copilot/customize-cloud-agent/configure-secrets-and-variables). No redaction of other sensitive content in logs is documented. Containment: an internet firewall with an allowlist, push to a single copilot/ branch only, no direct git commands, human approval before Actions workflows run, and a ban on the requester approving their own agent PR (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/risks-and-mitigations). Prompt-injection defenses act on input only: hidden characters and HTML comments are filtered, and comments from users without write access are never shown to the agent (same page). However, querying sessions or /chronicle "may send relevant session data, such as prompts, context, and responses, to the AI model" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/security-governance-and-network-settings/session-data). Recorded history, which includes raw tool output, can therefore flow back into a model. No envelope or untrusted-content marking is documented. Encryption at rest specific to session logs is not documented. Audit log events cover agent config changes (copilot.swe_agent_*) and agent_session_id on PR creation (https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/audit-log-events-for-your-organization).
scale: GitHub publishes no volume or storage numbers for session logs. I found none in the docs or in the GA announcement (https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-copilot-coding-agent-is-now-generally-available/). The documented limits are a 59-minute hard cap per session, one repo and one branch per session (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/cloud-agent/about-cloud-agent), and a REST page size of at most 100 (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/agent-tasks/agent-tasks). The product went GA for all paid Copilot plans on 2025-09-25, and the agents panel launched on 2025-08-19 (https://github.blog/changelog/2025-08-19-agents-panel-launch-copilot-coding-agent-tasks-anywhere-on-github-com/).
license: Proprietary GitHub service; no license applies. The gh CLI client that reads the logs is MIT-licensed open source (https://github.com/cli/cli).
lesson_for_parinn: A commit-trailer back-link from code to session is useful but cannot be relied on, so ParleyInn's record has to be the source of truth for the session-to-commit link. Two observations support this. First, GitHub promises a session link in every agent commit, yet only 3 of 24 recent agent commits in two GitHub-owned repos carried `Agent-Logs-Url`. Second, where the trailer was present, it survived rebase and squash only because of how the message was concatenated. ParleyInn should record the commits a session produced inside its own hash-chained record, for example the HEAD before and after each tool call that ran git. That way the session-to-code index can always be rebuilt from the record (I10). A trailer (e.g. `ParleyInn-Session: <session-id>`) should be an optional hint carrying a host-independent id, not a forge URL like `github.com/OWNER/REPO/sessions/<uuid>`, which breaks off-forge and on Forgejo. A second, smaller point: GitHub stores the raw model stream (OpenAI chunk JSON) and tails it by refetching the whole log every 5 s. ParleyInn's append-only chain can offer cursor-based tailing that verifies each new entry. Also, unlike Copilot Chat, which answers "by drawing on the session logs" without any documented envelope, ParleyInn must keep recalled tool output enveloped as untrusted (I2).

name: GitHub Copilot Memory (agentic memory, also called cross-agent memory)
category: hosted repo-scoped memory (a proprietary SaaS feature of GitHub Copilot)
status: beta. It is still public preview in early October 2026. The docs say it is "currently in public preview and is subject to change" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory). The preview began 2026-01-15 (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-01-15-agentic-memory-for-github-copilot-is-in-public-preview/). A changelog entry on 2026-09-25 still says "public preview" (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-25-agentic-autofix-now-uses-copilot-memory).
what_is_stored:
It stores short facts that the model writes itself. It does not store session transcripts, prompts or tool traces. There are two kinds (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory):
(1) Repository-level facts: coding conventions, architectural decisions, build commands and project-specific rules. Each fact carries citations to the code that supports it.
(2) User-level preferences: "implied or stated personal preferences" about how a user works with Copilot. Their citations "may include direct user quotes". This kind is newer than the January launch posts, which described only repository-scoped memory (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Since 2026-09-25, agentic autofix also stores the patterns it used to fix security alerts as memories (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-25-agentic-autofix-now-uses-copilot-memory).
Facts can also be captured from pull requests that were closed without merging (docs above).
Nothing in the record says which session, prompt or commit produced a memory. Of provenance, only the citations and a "reason" field are documented.
where_stored:
On GitHub's servers, in a backend GitHub does not document. The blog calls it "the memory database" (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Memories are not files in the repository, git notes or refs. The only places they show up are web UIs: Repository Settings > Copilot > Memory for repo facts, and github.com/settings/copilot/memory for preferences (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/copilot-memory/manage-for-yourself).
User preferences are stored against the user's active "billing entity", meaning the organization or enterprise that grants the license, and are retrieved only for that entity (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
The docs give no data-residency or region information.
I found no REST endpoint for memories. A docs search of the REST reference turned up user management, cloud agent management, usage metrics and content exclusion endpoints, but nothing for memory (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/copilot/copilot-user-management). Treat this as unverified.
format_and_model:
Each memory is a flat record created by the tool call `store_memory`. The engineering blog shows its shape:
{subject, fact, citations: ["path:line", ...], reason}
For example: citations ["src/client/sdk/constants.ts:12", "server/routes/api.go:8", "docs/api-reference.md:37"] (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Each memory also has an implicit timestamp, which drives recency retrieval and the 28-day expiry, and a scope key: a repository, or a user plus billing entity.
- Citations are path:line strings. The published example has no commit SHA or branch, and verification is "against the current branch" (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
- There is no versioning, no history and no edit chain. A correction is stored as a new memory.
- Unused entries are deleted after 28 days. The timer "may reset" when Copilot validates and uses an entry (same docs).
- The full internal schema and storage format are not published.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Many agents write into one shared pool per repository: cloud (coding) agent, code review, CLI and agentic autofix (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
Only users with write access who have Memory enabled can trigger new repo facts. Anyone with read access can have them used in their tasks (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
There is no merge or conflict resolution. GitHub explicitly rejected an offline curation service that would deduplicate entries, resolve conflicts and track branch status, citing "significant engineering complexity and LLM costs" (blog above). Instead:
- conflicting or stale facts are resolved at read time, by the reading agent checking the citations;
- if the code contradicts a memory, the agent "is encouraged to store a corrected version";
- if a memory checks out, the agent re-stores it to refresh its timestamp (blog above).
This makes the pool append-and-supersede with last-writer-wins. Old entries are not deleted. They simply stop being refreshed and expire.
Branches are not modeled: one pool serves all branches, and citation checks filter it.
Repo owners can delete facts by hand (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/copilot-memory/manage-for-yourself). On Business and Enterprise plans, admins can export or delete user preferences in bulk or per user (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
Policy is enabled per user. If a user's license comes from more than one organization, the most restrictive setting applies (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/copilot-memory/manage-as-administrator).
realtime:
Partly real time. A memory stored by one agent becomes available when the next session starts: "When an agent starts a new session, we retrieve the most recent memories for the target repository and include them in the prompt" (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Nothing documents pushing memories into a session that is already running.
Verification is "real-time" or just-in-time: "a small number of simple read operations, adding no significant latency" (same blog).
Propagation delay is not documented.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by recency only. The most recent memories for the repository are injected into the prompt when a session starts. There is no search tool yet. A "search tool and weighted prioritization" are listed as future work (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Before using a memory, the agent is prompted to check its cited locations. Facts are used only after they validate (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
Which memories each feature reads:
- Code review uses repo facts only, never user preferences.
- The CLI uses repo facts plus the preferences of the user who started it (same docs).
The cap on how many memories are injected is not documented.
links_sessions_to_code: Only weakly. Memories link facts to code through path:line citations, which are re-checked against the current branch. They do not link agent sessions or prompts to code or commits. No session ID, PR ID or commit SHA is documented on a memory record, and transcripts are not kept (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/). Cloud agent session logs live elsewhere in Copilot, separate from Memory (not covered by these sources).
scale:
GitHub has published no figures for memory counts, storage size or throughput. It cites "GitHub's scale" as the reason it skipped offline curation (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
Published evaluation results (same blog):
- Code review: precision up 3% and recall up 4% on a deliberately noisy memory pool.
- A/B tests: coding agent PR merge rate 90% vs 83%; positive feedback on code review comments 77% vs 75%; both p < 0.00001.
Availability: all paid Copilot plans. On by default for individual paid plans. Off by default for organization and enterprise plans, where an admin must enable the policy (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/copilot-memory/manage-as-administrator).
privacy_security:
Access control:
- Memories are scoped to a repository, and "memories about a repository stay within that repository" (https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/).
- Only users with write access can trigger repo facts. Read access is needed to use them.
- User preferences are owned by the billing entity and can be viewed, exported and deleted by Business and Enterprise admins (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-memory).
Prompt-injection defense:
- The only documented defense is citation verification. GitHub seeded repositories with adversarial memories whose citations pointed to irrelevant or nonexistent code. It reports that agents "consistently verified citations, discovered contradictions, and updated incorrect memories", and calls the defense robust (blog above).
- Verification is LLM-judged ("the agent is prompted to verify"), not deterministic.
- Memories go into the prompt automatically. They are not marked or enveloped as untrusted data in any documented way.
- User preferences rely on the model's "best judgment" and have no code check (docs above).
- Facts taken from PRs closed without merging can enter the pool, so untrusted or abandoned contributions are a path in. They are only filtered by validation (docs above).
Not documented: encryption at rest, secret scanning or redaction of memory content, and data residency.
Management is UI-only: owners review and delete facts, users delete their own preferences. Unused entries expire after 28 days.
lesson_for_parinn:
Borrow "citations checked just in time" as a provenance aid, but do not treat it as a trust boundary.
Copilot shows two useful ideas:
- Derived knowledge (facts, pins) is worth storing with anchors back to code. Validating those anchors at read time removes the need for offline curation or merge logic. For ParleyInn, an anchor should be path plus line plus commit SHA plus content hash. Path plus line alone, which is all the published example carries, cannot be checked deterministically.
- Recency retrieval with a 28-day expiry is enough for a v1 memory feature.
But Copilot's model is the opposite of ParleyInn's invariants:
- Memories are lossy summaries, not an append-only record, so they conflict with ParleyInn's lossless record and rebuildable projections (I10).
- They are pushed into the prompt automatically, and their only safeguard is the model's judgment. That breaks I2: no automatic path from untrusted content to the model. A memory captured from an unmerged PR by a write-access user reaches every reader's prompt.
- They are stored on a hosted, opaque server outside git, which conflicts with I4 (no network) and with portability.
So for ParleyInn: keep the record lossless and local. Treat any summary derived from it as untrusted, and give it to the model only on pull, inside an envelope. Use citation checks only as a signal for ranking or staleness, never to authorize content.
Copilot also shows the price of storing memories outside the repository: no history, no audit trail and no export of repo facts.
confidence: high for the documented behaviour: scope, permissions, 28-day expiry, the record fields, recency retrieval and citation verification all come straight from GitHub's docs and engineering blog. Low for anything about the backend, encryption, data residency or limits, which are undocumented. The engineering blog's real URL is github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/building-an-agentic-memory-system-for-github-copilot/, published 2026-01-15, not the 2026-01-09 path given in the discovery note.
license: Proprietary. It is a feature of GitHub Copilot's paid plans, and no source code is published.

name: GitHub Copilot Workspace
category: Forge-hosted agent (web-based, transitioned from experimental to production)
status: archived
what_is_stored: Task definitions (natural language intent), specifications (current and proposed code states), implementation plans (files to modify with step-by-step changes), generated code implementations, session state (undo/redo history, UI state, file contents), session metadata, sharing links, and file references. Each session encapsulates one task's journey from specification through implementation.
where_stored: Cloud-hosted on GitHub's servers (not in git repositories). Sessions persist in a cloud database accessible via REST API. Synced bidirectionally with VS Code extension via real-time API calls. Codespaces provide isolated compute environments. Historical user-manual documentation archived 2025-09-02, last experimental update 2025-09-01.
format_and_model: Web application (React-based frontend) with RESTful JSON API backend. Session model is hierarchical: Task → Topic → Specification (current + proposed) → Plan (files with steps) → Implementation (generated files). OAuth 2.0 for GitHub authentication. Real-time state synchronization protocol between web server and VS Code extension. File contents transmitted as text/binary diffs.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single-writer per active session with no detected multi-writer capability. Shared sessions created as snapshot copies (not live references), eliminating merge conflicts. VS Code extension provides bidirectional sync with web server as authoritative store. No visible support for concurrent editing or branch-and-merge of session states.
realtime: Yes. Sessions auto-save. VS Code extension syncs file changes to web within seconds (stated 'within a few seconds'). Live dashboard updates. Real-time undo/redo. Codespaces provide just-in-time compute with terminal access. No polling delays; appears to use websockets or similar for live updates.
search_retrieval: Dashboard at copilot-workspace.githubnext.com (historical URL, now integrated into GitHub web UI) shows session list sorted by repository. VS Code extension browses sessions by repository, displays recent/bookmarked/completed sessions. Search appears to filter by repo name. Implementation uses unspecified backend (likely Elasticsearch); search terms not documented in user manual.
links_sessions_to_code: Tightly integrated with GitHub. Sessions originate from GitHub issues, pull requests, or ad-hoc repository selection. Can publish results directly: create pull requests, commit to branches, or add comments to issues/PRs. Uses GitHub OAuth for authentication and authorization. Deep links allow bookmarking sessions from code context.
scale: Claimed to work with 'many existing large repositories,' but with size limitations on repository analysis. Repository-specific content selection (LLM + traditional code search) manages scope. Known limitation: 'some repositories are so large that even listing their files is challenging.' No explicit claim of handling 1M-file repositories or beyond.
privacy_security: GitHub OAuth eliminates credential storage. Commits generated in sessions not signed (documented as known limitation to be addressed). Content selection avoids unnecessary file exposure by ranking relevant files. Codespaces provide sandbox isolation with no host system access. Harmful content reporting channel: copilot-safety@github.com. No documented encryption at rest or secrets redaction; relies on GitHub's platform security. Session deletion capability available. No documented data retention policies or compliance certifications (PII handling, etc.).
lesson_for_parinn: Architectural divergence: Copilot Workspace stores session history and state on cloud servers separate from git, enabling real-time sync and stateful UI features (undo/redo). ParleyInn's design goal to store session history in git (or git + forge) trades real-time sync capability for security-first offline auditability and no cloud dependency. The snapshot-sharing pattern (copies vs. live refs) shows one approach to avoiding merge conflicts in agent sessions; ParleyInn's append-only immutable history with pull-only recall may achieve similar safety differently.
sources: https://github.com/githubnext/copilot-workspace-user-manual/blob/main/changes.md (changelog entry 2024-12-06: graduated from GitHub Next to main GitHub product)

name: Gitify Prompt (gauravkrp/git-for-prompts, npm package gitify-prompt)
status: beta
what_is_stored:
One JSON record per Claude Code invocation. It holds a random 16-hex session id, the tool name ("claude-code"), startTime, and the git author {name, email} from git config. It also holds messages[] of {role, content, timestamp} and filesModified[] of {absolute path, timestamp}.
