Metadata carries cwd, repoPath, platform, nodeVersion, branch, parentBranch, fileCount, messageCount, lastUpdate and commitSha (README "What Gets Saved", https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts#what-gets-saved; https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/claude-hook.ts).

Messages are copied out of Claude Code's own transcripts at ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/*.jsonl, and the copy is lossy. User entries are kept whole: when content is not a string (tool results, pasted blocks), it is JSON.stringify'd. Assistant entries keep only their `text` blocks, so tool_use calls and other block types are dropped (claude-hook.ts getConversationHistory).

Code changes are seen by monkeypatching fs.writeFile, fs.writeFileSync and fs.promises.writeFile. The in-memory session holds before and after contents (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/capture-daemon.ts), but only the path and timestamp are written to disk.

Legacy and side paths:
- An older "git for prompts" mode saves hand-committed prompts as YAML (.prompts/prompts/<id>.yaml plus .prompts/history/<id>/<ts>-<ver>.yaml and a .meta/index.json), with a `test` command that runs prompts against OpenAI (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/prompt-store.ts, https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/VISION.md).
- An experimental VS Code/Cursor extension reads Cursor's state.vscdb SQLite databases (README "Capture Methods").
where_stored:
Working-tree files inside the project, committed into the project's own git history on whatever branch is checked out. There is no separate ref, no git notes and no separate repo.

The file lifecycle (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/commands/init.ts):
1. A live snapshot sits at .prompts/.meta/session-<id>.json.
2. The pre-commit hook copies it to .prompts/prompts/<Date.now()>-pending.json and runs `git add` on it.
3. The post-commit hook rewrites it as <ts>-<commitSHA>.json, deletes the pending file and the .meta session files, then makes a second commit ("chore: update prompt SHA references", --no-verify).

Hooks go in .git/hooks. With Husky, the code is appended to .husky/pre-commit and .husky/post-commit is overwritten.

Other locations:
- An optional static dashboard in .prompts/web/ (index.html, per-commit pages, data.json with every conversation). The README says to commit it for GitHub Pages (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts#gitify-prompt-web).
- A daemon log at os.tmpdir()/prompt-daemon.log (capture-daemon.ts).
- The data it reads from is ~/.claude/projects.
format_and_model:
Pretty-printed JSON, one file per (session, commit). It has no schema version, no content hash, no signature and no hash chain.

It is not append-only. The .meta snapshot is fully rewritten on every intercepted file write, and each rewrite re-reads and re-parses every JSONL in the project's Claude folder. The post-commit hook then rewrites the record to insert the SHA and deletes the pending copy (claude-hook.ts saveSessionState; init.ts).

Finding the conversation is a heuristic, not an identity lookup:
- cwd is encoded by replacing "/" with "-".
- Every *.jsonl in ~/.claude/projects/<encoded> is scanned.
- Entries are kept if their timestamp is at least session start minus 60 s and their cwd matches or is missing.
- The file with the most such messages wins (README "Session Matching"; claude-hook.ts).

KNOWN-ISSUES itself admits the path encoding is wrong on Windows (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/KNOWN-ISSUES.md). The key is a millisecond timestamp plus the commit SHA in the filename. Lookup by SHA reads every file and prefix-matches metadata.commitSha (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/prompt-reader.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no coordination layer beyond plain git.

Attribution is by co-occurrence, not cause. Every session file in .prompts/.meta at commit time is attached to the next commit, whether or not it touched the staged files. The README presents this as a feature: "Commit once → All 3 conversations captured" (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts#-multi-session-support).

Multi-session capture probably loses data. The pre-commit hook names each copy `${Date.now()}-pending.json` inside a synchronous forEach (init.ts), so sessions handled in the same millisecond overwrite each other. I simulated that naming loop with three sessions in Node 22 and it lost files in 200 of 200 trials. That was a simulation, not an end-to-end run.

Across branches the files are add-only with unique names, so textual merge conflicts are rare. But the stored commitSha goes stale after rebase, squash-merge, cherry-pick or amend, and every commit gains an automatic follow-up commit.

KNOWN-ISSUES lists multi-session, git worktrees, symlinks, team use and Windows as untested (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/KNOWN-ISSUES.md). Records move between machines only through normal git push and pull of the project repo.
realtime:
Real-time only on the local machine. The .meta snapshot refreshes on every file write Claude Code makes (README "Real-Time Session Saving", https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts#-real-time-session-saving). It reaches anyone else only after a commit and push. There is no streaming, watch, subscribe or sync service.

Conversation turns that write no file stay unsaved until a later write. On exit the session is saved only if codeChanges > 0 (claude-hook.ts onExit), so purely conversational sessions are never captured.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is for humans only:
- `gitify-prompt list` with --branch, --author, --since and --limit filters.
- `show <sha>` (prefix match, --json, --files) (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/cli/index.ts).
- PromptReader.search, a case-insensitive substring scan that reads every JSON file (prompt-reader.ts).
- `gitify-prompt web`, a static HTML site with client-side substring search and branch/author filters; message content is HTML-escaped (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/commands/web.ts).

There is no index, no full-text engine, no embeddings and no ranking. Nothing feeds recalled history back to the agent: no MCP server and no context re-injection.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, by timing and co-occurrence rather than identity. The commit SHA goes into the filename and metadata.commitSha through the pre- and post-commit hooks, alongside branch, parentBranch (guessed from the tracking branch or main/master) and the absolute paths of modified files (init.ts, claude-hook.ts).

A commit cannot hold its own hash, so the code commit carries only the -pending file. The SHA-named record arrives in the automatic follow-up commit. There is no commit trailer and no git note.

Capture depends on claude-wrapper.sh, aliased as `claude`, which sets NODE_OPTIONS="--import=file://.../claude-hook.js" and execs the claude binary (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/bin/claude-wrapper.sh). Current Claude Code docs say even the npm package installs a native binary that "does not itself invoke Node" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup). The preload therefore very likely never loads on current Claude Code. That is an inference, not tested. Official hooks now pass session_id and transcript_path directly, which makes both the preload and the timestamp matching unnecessary (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

There is also a bug in the published 0.1.1. getGitAuthor, getGitBranch and isIgnoredByGit call bare `require('child_process')` inside an ES module (package type "module"), as the shipped build shows (https://registry.npmjs.org/gitify-prompt/-/gitify-prompt-0.1.1.tgz). I confirmed on Node 22 that this throws ReferenceError, and the code swallows it. So author and branch would always be null and the .gitignore filter would never apply. This comes from reading the source plus a minimal reproduction, not an end-to-end run.
privacy_security:
The README promises "Local Only / No Network / No Telemetry" and "Sensitive Data Masking - Auto-filters passwords, API keys (config)" (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts#privacy--security). The masking is not implemented. privacy.maskSensitiveData and excludePatterns exist only as config defaults and example values, and no code reads them (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/capture-daemon.ts, https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/.promptrc.example.json).

What gets exposed:
- Full user messages, including pasted content and stringified tool results (file contents, command output), are committed in plaintext into the project repo and travel wherever it is pushed.
- Absolute local paths and the git author email go with them. The repo's own committed sample record contains a work email and /Users/... paths (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/.prompts/prompts/1733386000000-abc123def456.json).
- The suggested GitHub Pages dashboard would publish all of it.

There is no encryption, signing or tamper evidence. The `test` command contradicts "No Network": it calls OpenAI through the SDK using OPENAI_API_KEY (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/src/lib/llm-runner.ts).

The capture hook runs inside the agent's process and has risky patterns:
- It patches fs inside Claude Code's process.
- It runs execSync(`git check-ignore -q "${relativePath}"`) with a file path interpolated into the shell command, a shell-injection pattern. It is unreachable today only because the require call fails first.
- Errors are swallowed silently by design (KNOWN-ISSUES #9).

Stored history is never fed back to the model, so it is not a prompt-injection channel. There is also no untrusted-content handling for the day it might be.
scale:
The project makes no scale claims. KNOWN-ISSUES says it was tested only with fewer than 10 file changes. Sessions with 50+ files or 100+ messages are untested, and the end-to-end flow (Claude → commit → verify) is "NOT been tested" (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/KNOWN-ISSUES.md). Each file write re-reads every transcript in the project's Claude folder, so cost grows with history size.

Adoption is tiny:
- 2 stars, 0 forks, 33 commits, no issues or PRs (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts).
- npm versions 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 were both published 2025-10-05 (https://registry.npmjs.org/gitify-prompt).
- 15 downloads in September 2026 (https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-month/gitify-prompt).

Activity: the last code change was 2025-10-05 (v0.1.1, then Cursor SQLite support). The only later commit, 2025-12-30, adds a notes file named `CLAUDE` (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/commits/main). The repo is not archived but has been dormant for about a year.
license: MIT (https://github.com/gauravkrp/git-for-prompts/blob/main/LICENSE; package.json and npm registry metadata https://registry.npmjs.org/gitify-prompt)
lesson_for_parinn:
Link sessions to code by identity, never by timing or by self-reference. Gitify guesses the conversation by picking the JSONL with the most messages after session start minus 60 s. It then attaches every pending session to the next commit, and tries to write a commit's own SHA into that commit's tree. That forces a pending file plus an automatic second commit, and the link goes stale on rebase or squash.

What ParleyInn should do instead:
- Take session_id and transcript_path from Claude Code hook input (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).
- After the fact (post-commit, or PostToolUse on `git commit`), append a new event to its own hash-chained record: "session S observed commit X on ref R".
- If git must carry a link, use a pointer a commit can legally hold, such as a session-id trailer, or an out-of-tree ref or note. Never rewrite committed records.

The I6 corollary: Gitify ships a maskSensitiveData switch that nothing enforces while it commits raw tool output into the repo. A redaction setting that exists only in config is a silent failure. Redaction must be enforced on the write path and covered by a test.

name: GitLab Duo Agent Platform sessions
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Each run of an agent or flow (Agentic Chat, foundational flows such as Fix CI/CD Pipeline or Software Development, and flows triggered by a mention or by assignment as assignee or reviewer) creates a "session". GitLab says sessions track "the status and execution data for the agents and flows you've run" (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). The activity log holds the agent's reasoning, step-by-step tool execution and outputs. Status values include Created, Running, Finished, Failed and Input Required (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/monitor-manage-automate-ai-workflows/). Underneath, a session is a Duo Workflow record plus a series of LangGraph checkpoints of the agent's state (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/156872, https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/238814). A separate AI audit event report lists audit events per session: agent type, project, event count, start time, author_id and the human author when composite identity is used (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/ai-audit-events/). If usage-data collection is turned on, GitLab also logs full prompt and response text, session context, model metadata and tool calls (https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/gitlab_duo/data_usage).
where_stored: On the GitLab server (the Rails monolith), whether GitLab.com, Self-Managed or Dedicated. The Rails app is the source of truth for workflow state. The AI Gateway sends checkpoints to POST /ai/duo_workflows/workflows/:id/checkpoints and reads them back to resume a run (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/156872). The table duo_workflows_checkpoint_blobs is in PostgreSQL, keyed by (workflow_id, thread_ts, channel, version) (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/238814). Audit events go to ClickHouse when it is available and to PostgreSQL otherwise (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). Nothing is written to the git repository. Remote flows run as CI jobs on runners, but session state goes back to Rails, not into the repo (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/flows/execution). Users see sessions under AI > Sessions in the UI, on the IDE Flows tab, in Duo Chat history and in the Duo CLI (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/).
format_and_model: Workflow row (session) -> chain of LangGraph checkpoints, each with thread_ts and parent_ts. A proposed incremental mode, MR created 2026-06-02, stores only the channels that changed, as channel_blobs: versioned base64 binary blobs of up to 1 MiB each. Full state is rebuilt by walking the parent_ts chain with last-write-wins per channel. It sits behind the flag duo_workflow_incremental_checkpoints, which defaults to off, and the MR shows no merge date (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/238814). A compressedCheckpoint field arrived in 19.0 (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). The UI does not show raw LangGraph state. Issue 469680 asks for checkpoints to be mapped into a format the UI can use (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/469680). Audit events carry a cloud_event_id with a unique index on (cloud_event_id, created_at) for idempotency (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). The model is a mutable snapshot of state, not an append-only, hash-chained event log. I could not find a public schema for the core workflows or checkpoints tables.
multi_writer_and_merge: Each session has one owner: the human who triggered it. The agent writes as a composite identity, a service account (@duo-developer) plus that human, and its permissions are the intersection of the two (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/security). One AI Gateway or executor process writes the checkpoint chain for a session. Sessions are never merged across machines or instances. The server is the single point of serialisation, so no merge logic exists. Within a session, the incremental-blob design resolves channel state last-write-wins (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/238814). I found no documented way to share or federate sessions across GitLab instances or forks.
realtime: Yes, within one instance. The GraphQL subscription duoWorkflowsWorkflowEventsUpdated "streams live checkpoint events to the workflow owner", and the executor polls latestCheckpoint (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). GitLab added GraphQL polling because the subscription was unreliable, and it is consolidating on NewCheckpoint messages over the executor's gRPC stream (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/578633). Live streaming goes to the owner. Other project members with the Developer role or above can view sessions (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/), but the sources do not say they get live streams.
search_retrieval: The UI lists sessions and can filter a session's log between "all logs" and a concise subset (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). GraphQL filters sessions by workflowId, projectPath, projectId, type, environment and statusGroup (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). The GLQL data source agent_platform_sessions (19.4, extended in 19.5) filters on created, flowType and user. It groups by created, flowType, project and user, and aggregates durationMean, durationQuantile, totalCount, finishedCount, usersCount and completionRate (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/glql/data_sources/agent_platform_sessions/). I found no documented full-text search over session contents and no export. The audit report shows events per session in time order (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/ai-audit-events/).
links_sessions_to_code: Weak and implicit. The sessions doc says nothing about linking a session to a commit or MR (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). The links that do exist are these. Flows started from an issue or MR post their results back to that issue or MR (https://about.gitlab.com/blog/monitor-manage-automate-ai-workflows/). Commits and MRs created by an agent are attributed through composite identity, and MRs are attributed to the triggering human for segregation-of-duties compliance (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/security). Remote sessions run as CI pipelines, and pipeline completion updates the workflow status (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). I found nothing like a commit trailer, a git note or an MR field that points to a session id. Combined with the 30-day deletion, the reasoning behind a merged change is usually gone long before the code is.
scale: No published scale figures. GitLab says sessions are GA on Premium and Ultimate, across GitLab.com, Self-Managed and Dedicated (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). Engineering limits include a 1 MiB cap per checkpoint blob in the incremental design (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/238814). ClickHouse is the preferred store for audit events (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/).
privacy_security: Retention: a session is deleted automatically 30 days after its last activity, and any interaction resets the timer. Users can delete sessions early from the IDE (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). A cron job, CleanStuckWorkflowsService, cleans up stalled sessions (https://docs.gitlab.com/development/ai_features/duo_agent_platform_observability/). Viewing requires the Developer role or above. The audit report requires Owner of the top-level group and is in Beta since 19.1 (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/ai-audit-events/). Redaction: Gitleaks scans content and strips secrets before it reaches the model, covering code completion, AI context, workflow results and agentic chat but not web Duo Chat (https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/gitlab_duo/data_usage). The docs do not say whether stored session logs are themselves redacted, and I found no session-specific encryption at rest beyond the platform's own. Isolation: remote flows on runners run inside Anthropic Sandbox Runtime, with a network allowlist (by default only the GitLab instance) and filesystem limits. Local environments are not sandboxed (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/environment_sandbox/). Known risk: setup_script runs outside the sandbox with GITLAB_OAUTH_TOKEN and DUO_WORKFLOW_GIT_HTTP_PASSWORD in its environment. Anyone who can edit .gitlab/duo/agent-config.yml can run commands under another user's composite identity, and GitLab recommends CODEOWNERS and branch protection to guard that file (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/flows/execution/security-considerations/). Tokens are OAuth tokens scoped to ai_workflows and mcp (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/security). The sources say nothing about treating recalled session content as untrusted when a session is resumed.
lesson_for_parinn: A forge-hosted session log keyed to the forge's own database, with short retention, gives good live visibility but loses provenance. GitLab keeps reasoning only 30 days after last activity and never ties it to the commit or MR it produced, so the "why" behind merged code disappears. Its mutable LangGraph snapshots, which are being moved to last-write-wins incremental blobs, also cannot prove the history was not altered. ParleyInn should keep the record separate from forge retention and append-only with a hash chain. It should link sessions to code from the code side (for example a commit trailer or note carrying a session or chain-head hash) so the link outlives any forge. GitLab's composite identity, the agent plus the triggering human recorded on every action, is worth copying into ParleyInn's event attribution. Its agent-config.yml lesson matters too: any repo-resident file that controls agent execution is a cross-user injection channel, which reinforces I2.
license: GitLab EE features under the GitLab Enterprise Edition license (source-available); Duo Agent Platform requires Premium or Ultimate (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/sessions/). Exact license for the ee/ session code not re-verified here.

name: Gitleaks
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Findings (detected secrets) are not stored by Gitleaks itself. The tool outputs structured findings containing: RuleID, description, line/column locations, file path, commit hash, extracted secret, entropy score, author, email, date, commit message, tags, and a unique fingerprint. Baselines (.gitleaksignore files) store fingerprints of known/acceptable findings to skip re-detection. Rules are stored in TOML config files.
where_stored: Gitleaks is a stateless scanning tool. Findings are written to separate report files (JSON, CSV, JUNIT, SARIF, or custom templates) or stdout. Rules and baselines are stored in TOML configs and .gitleaksignore files in the repository. The tool never persists findings to git history or a database.
format_and_model: Findings use a structured Finding struct with 16+ fields. Reports available in: JSON (array of objects), CSV (tabular), JUNIT (XML for CI/CD), SARIF (standard analysis format), and custom Go text/template templates. Fingerprint format: '{commit_hash}:{filepath}:{ruleid}:{line}'. Rules use Go regex patterns with optional entropy thresholds and composite multi-part rules supported.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable. Gitleaks does not handle concurrent writers or merges - it is a scanning tool. Multiple invocations can use the same baseline/allowlist. Pre-commit hooks can prevent commits with secrets. The tool reads git history via 'git log -p' but does not modify or coordinate writes.
realtime: Gitleaks scans git history or current state on demand. It can process: git log (full history), git diff (staged/unstaged changes), directories, files, or stdin. Supports real-time pre-commit hook integration. No continuous monitoring or automatic scanning—user or CI/CD pipeline must invoke it. Decoding and archive extraction are optional recursive features.
search_retrieval: Gitleaks does not provide search functionality. It performs detection (forward scanning). Baseline reports can filter out known findings. .gitleaksignore allows lookup by fingerprint to suppress specific secrets. Allowlists can target by commit, path, regex pattern, or stopwords. No query language or indexing.
links_sessions_to_code: Gitleaks captures code location (file, line, column) and git metadata (commit hash, author, email, date, message). However, it is not designed to link agent sessions to code. It detects secrets in code commits but has no concept of agent sessions, prompts, or session history. For ParleyInn, Gitleaks would be a pre-flight scanner of session transcripts before committing them to git.
scale: Gitleaks is described as efficient via Aho-Corasick keyword preprocessing and concurrent file processing (semgroup-based). Supports recursive decoding and archive extraction with configurable depth limits. Used in production by many organizations. Can scan large repositories; warns if scanning a single file takes over 5 seconds. No published benchmark data for very large transcript volumes.
privacy_security: Built-in redaction via --redact flag (0-100% configurable). Redaction masks secrets in logs and output at report time, not before storage. Tool detects secrets but does not remediate them from git history (that requires git filter-branch or similar). Supports security-level exit codes. Private vulnerability reporting via GitHub security advisories. Rules use entropy + pattern matching to avoid false positives. No encryption or cryptographic operations.
lesson_for_parinn: Gitleaks demonstrates four lessons: (1) Its fingerprint scheme (commit:file:rule:line) parallels content-addressed hashing useful for immutable records. (2) Baselines and allowlists show that git-transported secrets need a separate side channel for exemptions—ParleyInn's pinned-constraint system could follow this pattern. (3) Gitleaks scans diffs (additions), not entire files—ParleyInn's delta-based append-only model aligns with this; pre-flight scanning before commit is key. (4) Redaction happens at output, not storage—ParleyInn should do both: redact before storing (I2) AND when recalling (I2), never storing plaintext secrets in the append-only record. Gitleaks is stateless and invokable on-demand; ParleyInn's hooks should similarly fail open if Gitleaks is unavailable (I9).

name: gitmemory (doronp/gitmemory)
category: git-versioned verbatim agent memory (local transcript capture with a contiguity proof, plus BM25 recall)
status: shipped
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/LICENSE). It vendors MIT code from grooverLab/fable (jsonl.py) and daaain/claude-code-log, and lists both in THIRD_PARTY.md and NOTICE (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/DESIGN.md §2.5b).
what_is_stored: It stores the agent's native transcript bytes verbatim and unredacted. It copies only the bytes appended since the last capture, so each byte the agent wrote is stored exactly once (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md). Next to the bytes it keeps one manifest per "generation" of each session. A manifest holds proof metadata and no parsed content. In code it has 12 fields: schema, agent, session_id, source_path, generation, diverged_from, size, file_sha256, prev_manifest_sha256, segments[{path,start,end,sha256}], compact_boundaries[byte offsets] and adopted[segment names] (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/store.py, the manifest dict near line 737; DESIGN §2.5). The README says the manifest "records the canonical parse". The code shows the manifest carries only the compaction byte offsets the adapter found. Canonical Session/Turn/Block/Event records are re-derived from the raw bytes at index or derive time and are not committed. Derived artifacts are committed under derived/: ideas.json, timeline.json and graph.json, the last opt-in with --graph (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/USAGE.md). Adapters exist for Claude Code (~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl) and pi / oh-my-pi (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/agents.md). Capture works for any local, append-only, one-record-per-line file. Agents that fail that shape need a "materializer", which is not built (issues #1–#5, https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/issues).
where_stored: A separate, dedicated local git repository at $GITMEMORY_HOME, default ~/.gitmemory. Segments and manifests are ordinary working-tree files committed to that repo. It is not git notes, not custom refs, and not inside the user's code repo. The store refuses to start if $GITMEMORY_HOME sits inside another git work tree (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/watching.md; DESIGN §2.4). The SQLite FTS5 index (index/), the hook spool (spool/), the per-session locks (.locks/) and config.toml are gitignored (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/gitrepo.py, GITIGNORE). No remote is configured by default, and `gitmemory push` "runs the redaction gate only and does not send yet" (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/__main__.py `_push`; https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).
format_and_model: Layout: raw/<agent>/<session_id>/g<NN>/<start12>-<end12>.jsonl, where each segment is named by its zero-padded byte range [start,end) in that generation, and sessions/<agent>/<session_id>/g<NN>.json for the manifests. Manifests are canonical JSON with sorted keys, no floats, UTF-8 and \n endings (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md; DESIGN §2.1). Segments stay plain text and are never pre-compressed, so git's zlib and delta compression work on them (DESIGN §2.4). Rebuilding a generation means running `cat` over its segments in start order. The result must hash to file_sha256, and the segments must tile [0,size) with no hole and no overlap. DESIGN §2.5 gives a jq/shasum recipe a stranger can run, and `gitmemory verify` checks every manifest. If the source is rewritten (its prefix hash no longer matches), capture seals the current generation and opens g<NN+1>. The new manifest records diverged_from{generation, at_byte, prev_file_sha256} and prev_manifest_sha256 (DESIGN §2.5a; store.py). Sealed generations are immutable. The open generation's manifest is rewritten atomically on each capture, so its history exists only in git commits (store.py `_write_atomic`). There is no per-event hash chain. Integrity rests on per-segment sha256, a whole-generation sha256, the git commit chain, and the generation-to-generation manifest digest link. Session identity is the file basename plus the first 64 bits of sha256(realpath) (store.py `session_id_for`), so a moved transcript becomes a new session and is copied again in full. Within the derived model, IDs come from content (turn_id = sha256 over session, anchor or byte offset, role and content), and byte position, never timestamps, is the ordering authority (DESIGN §2.1–2.2). Before 1.0 a minor version may break the store format (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
It is single-machine, with one store per user. Concurrency on that machine:
(a) Each hook invocation writes its own spool file (spool/<pid>-<event>[-<n>].json), so writers share no file and need no flock (DESIGN §2.3).
(b) Capture takes an exclusive per-session flock at .locks/<agent>/<sid>.lock (store.py `_locked`).
(c) If the hook and the watcher both capture, both derive the next offset from the same committed state, so the loser writes an identical segment or none. This is idempotent by construction (DESIGN §2.3).
(d) `verify` waits at most 5 s for a writer's lock and otherwise reports that it could not take it (store.py LOCK_WAIT, `_locked_if_writable`).
(e) The watcher makes one git commit per pass covering every session captured in it. The author is fixed as gitmemory <gitmemory@localhost> and commits are unsigned (commit.gpgSign=false) (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/daemon.py `tick`; gitrepo.py _CONFIG).

There is no design, code or test for multiple machines, sandboxes or collaborators writing one store, and no merge strategy or merge driver. Push transport is unbuilt, and a manual `git push` in the store bypasses the gate (DESIGN §2.4). A single global log that interleaves many sessions (Cline's hooks.jsonl) does not fit the one-file-per-session store and is tracked as open issue #8 (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/issues/8). Inference, not verified: separate machines would produce disjoint session paths, since the realpath digest differs, so merging two stores' raw/ trees would mostly not conflict. Nothing in the project claims or tests this.
realtime: Not real-time, and nothing is shared. The watcher polls every 5 s by default (--poll). It re-captures an idle session only after --interval, default 3600 s. In practice an ordinary session gets a segment at each compaction and roughly one an hour otherwise (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/watching.md). The optional POSIX sh hook shim, also packaged as a Claude Code plugin bound to PreCompact and SessionEnd but deliberately not Stop, drops a spool "doorbell" that bypasses the interval. Its measured cost is p50 7.4–7.5 ms and p99 10.2–11.5 ms. The shim always exits 0 and the watcher alone is enough for correctness (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/hooks/hooks.json; https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/hook/README.md; README). It makes no network calls, so nothing propagates beyond the machine.
search_retrieval: `gitmemory index` fully rebuilds a SQLite FTS5 (BM25) index from the raw bytes. The index is never authoritative and is gitignored. It has four weighted columns: prose 4.0, paths 3.0, tool_use 2.0, tool_result 1.0 (DESIGN §2.7). Hits are scored per block and returned per turn. `gitmemory recall "<q>"` prints one line per turn: score, agent/session/gNN@byte_offset, role/kind, text. store.span() resolves an offset into the bytes even when a turn straddles two segments (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/USAGE.md; DESIGN §2.7). Only BM25 ships. The dense (model2vec), rerank (FlashRank) and rerank12 (MiniLM-L-12 cross-encoder) arms run only in the benchmarks. Self-reported: shipped BM25 turn recall is 0.7456 on 470 LongMemEval instances whose evidence sits behind a compaction boundary, against 0.0000 for the live window. The rerank12 bench arm reports LongMemEval-S session R@5 99.2 and R@10 99.8 (README; https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/docs/RESULTS.md). Other surfaces: a read-only Datasette dashboard and `derive` (LexRank key ideas, a timeline, and an opt-in decision graph handed to graphify, where every node carries a source_ref). The decision extractor scored precision 0.1250 and recall 0.5000 on real sessions (ROADMAP). The design describes an MCP server and a UserPromptSubmit injection hook, but "As built: the CLI only" (DESIGN §2.8).
links_sessions_to_code: Only weakly. The canonical Session record carries the cwd and git_branch fields from Claude Code transcripts (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/records.py). The index has a `paths` column fed from tool-call inputs such as Read(file_path=...), so file paths are searchable (DESIGN §2.7). There is no link to commit SHAs in the user's project, and nothing is written into the code repo: no notes, no trailers, no refs. The store is deliberately a separate repository and refuses to sit inside a work tree (watching.md). The "file-touch history" injection was designed but is not built (DESIGN §2.8). It is a lossless transcript store, not a provenance or attribution tool.
scale:
Mostly small-scale or stated without measurement:
- A full-corpus index rebuild "measures ~8 s", corpus size not stated (DESIGN §1).
- The coalescer bounds a session to "typically <10 segments" (DESIGN §2.4).
- The session-id tag was widened to 64 bits, putting a 50% collision at roughly 10^11 transcripts per stem (store.py `session_id_for`).
- `git gc --auto` runs with gc.auto=256 because derived/ rewrites orphan blobs (gitrepo.py; DESIGN §2.4).
- One pre-fix pathology was measured at 454 ms per tick on a 20 MB transcript (store.py `identity`).
- The suite has 1,026 tests and 328 conformance cases against three third-party corpora (README).

Inference: the 12-digit offsets in segment names cap a generation at under 10^12 bytes. No multi-GB, multi-user or multi-machine scale figures were found. The project is very young: first commit 2026-09-20, v0.1.0 released 2026-09-28 (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/releases/tag/v0.1.0). On 2026-10-02 it had 8 stars, 0 forks, 11 open issues and one maintainer (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory), with an Alpha classifier (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/pyproject.toml).
privacy_security:
It is local-only: no network calls, no LLM at runtime, zero core dependencies, Python 3.13+ (README; pyproject.toml).

Raw history is committed unredacted on purpose. Redaction acts at two boundaries only:
(1) derived/: sentences matching the HIGH tier are dropped, and a payload that still holds a key is refused.
(2) The push gate: 12 issuer-anchored regexes in the HIGH tier block egress, and the SUSPECT tier only reports. The gate scans the files git would ship, segment seams (512-byte carry) and the object graph a push transmits. Findings never print the matched value, and there is no override flag.
Stated limit: the detectors are byte-literal regexes with no decoding, so a credential escaped in JSON, base64-encoded or wrapped across lines is missed (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/src/gitmemory/redact.py; DESIGN §2.4).

There is no encryption at rest. When a credential lands in the store, the guidance is to rotate it and, optionally, run `git filter-repo` by hand. Automated history rewriting is refused (https://github.com/doronp/gitmemory/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

Git hardening: every GIT_* variable is scrubbed from the environment, core.hooksPath=/dev/null, `git init --template=`, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, timeouts on every call, config.toml gitignored, and remote URLs with inline credentials refused (gitrepo.py; redact.py `push_allowed`).

Input hardening: sources are opened O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK and must be regular files. The dashboard serves read-only (--immutable) on loopback, behind a single-use sign-in URL with an HttpOnly cookie (ARCHITECTURE.md; DESIGN §2.9).

Recalled text passes through safe_text, which neutralises ANSI and bidi control characters for the terminal (records.py). There is no prompt-injection envelope: USAGE.md tells users to add a CLAUDE.md line asking the agent to run recall "and quote what it returns". Recalled history therefore enters the model context as plain text.

Reviews: two internal review rounds (E7 with 68 findings, E7b with 22), largely run by Claude and Gemini agents. There has been no third-party audit (SECURITY.md; DESIGN header).

Name note: DESIGN §2.5a/§6 critiques a different project, ccf/agentparinn, for redacting before hashing. It argues that this makes its "verbatim" field not the original bytes.
lesson_for_parinn:
Pair ParleyInn's hash chain with a byte-range tiling proof over the source transcript. A hash chain only shows that recorded events were not altered. It cannot show that no source bytes were skipped. gitmemory gets that second property cheaply: each captured chunk carries (source identity, generation, [start,end), sha256), plus a whole-prefix digest, and verify checks arithmetically that the chunks tile [0,size) and hash to the digest (DESIGN §2.5). If Claude Code or a neighbouring tool rewrites the transcript, the source opens a new linked generation rather than counting as corruption. This fits I6: every gap is named, never silent. It also fits I10: derived state is rebuilt from bytes.

Copy the trigger split too. A fail-open hook is only a doorbell; the poller is the capture guarantee. That serves I9.

Two things not to take from it:
- The recall surface. Raw turns are quoted into the agent's context with only terminal-control sanitising, which is the exact channel I2 requires ParleyInn to envelope.
- Git as transport. Its store is single-machine, push is unbuilt, and it has no merge model, so it offers no evidence that git can carry multi-writer or real-time history.

name: gittuf
category: signed append-only log in git refs (precedent)
status: beta
what_is_stored: Security metadata about a Git repo, not content or conversations. (1) The Reference State Log (RSL). Each "reference entry" records one ref update: ref name, targetID (a commit, or an annotated-tag object), a monotonic number, and optional custom fields. "Annotation entries" point at earlier entries to attach a message or mark them skip=true (revoked). (2) Policy metadata in TUF style: root-of-trust metadata (root keys plus a threshold) and rule files (principals, and delegations protecting refs and file paths, each with a signer threshold). (3) Detached authorizations: signed in-toto attestations, currently only the "reference authorization" type (TargetRef, FromTargetID, ToTargetID) for code-review approvals, under predicate https://gittuf.dev/reference-authorization/v<N>. GAP-7 (implemented) adds custom fields on entries, one line each in the form `custom.<namespace>/<name>: <value>`. The example is a forge recording the pusher and its server version. Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/design-document.md , https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/7/README.md
where_stored: Custom refs inside the same Git repo, under refs/gittuf/. They are refs/gittuf/reference-state-log (the RSL), refs/gittuf/policy and refs/gittuf/policy-staging, and refs/gittuf/attestations. Remote trackers live at refs/remotes/<remote>/gittuf/reference-state-log. They travel over ordinary git fetch/push to any forge, including ones that know nothing about gittuf. Sync uses the refspec refs/gittuf/*. Sources: design doc; pkg/rsl/rsl.go, internal/policy/policy.go, internal/attestations/attestations.go and experimental/gittuf/sync.go in https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf
format_and_model: The RSL is its own commit graph. One commit is one entry. Every entry commit's tree is the empty tree (4b825dc…), and the payload is the commit message: a header line ("RSL Reference Entry" or "RSL Annotation Entry") followed by key: value lines. An annotation message sits in a base64 BEGIN/END MESSAGE block. The commit's parent pointer is the hash chain. The entry is signed with standard Git commit signing (GPG, SSH or Sigstore), so the signature covers the custom fields too. The latest entry is the tip of the ref. Nothing is ever rewritten: force pushes and policy violations are handled by appending skip annotations plus a new entry, and recovery prefers revert commits so clients can fast-forward. Policy states are commits on refs/gittuf/policy, and each policy change is itself recorded in the RSL, so policy-in-force is found by walking back the RSL. Each entry adds exactly one new Git object, because the empty tree is shared. Git objects are SHA-1, but signatures use stronger hashes. Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/design-document.md , https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/7/README.md
multi_writer_and_merge: The RSL must stay linear, and there is no merging of log branches. Writers serialize through the shared remote. The design follows the RSLFetch/RSLPush protocol from the 2016 Torres-Arias paper: fetch the remote RSL, verify the new entries, rebuild your entry on the new tip, then do an atomic push of the RSL plus the changed refs. If the push loses the race, retry. The design doc says the implementation "does not implement precisely this workflow" and does not verify new remote entries automatically (issue #708). `gittuf rsl remote reconcile` handles divergence. If the local RSL is behind, it fast-forwards. If it has diverged, the local-only entries are re-applied on top of the remote, but only when local-only and remote-only entries touch different refs. A forge that drops or reorders entries (a fork* attack) is detected only when the forked clients compare notes out of band; a freeze attack is out of scope. GAP-2 ("gittuf on the forge", not implemented) explores a server-side gittuf that writes entries for many concurrent pushers. Sources: design doc; https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/cli/gittuf_rsl_remote_reconcile.md ; https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/2/README.md ; https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/issues/708
realtime: None. Sync happens only on git push/fetch, run by hand, by `gittuf sync`, or by Git hooks installed with `gittuf add-hooks` that create and push RSL entries on push. There is no notification channel. Freshness is explicitly not guaranteed: gittuf has no equivalent of TUF's timestamp role. Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/cli/gittuf_add-hooks.md , https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/cli/gittuf_sync.md , design doc (RSL section)
search_retrieval: Retrieval is a linear walk of the hash chain from the tip. `gittuf rsl log` can filter with `--ref`. The library has helpers like GetLatestReferenceUpdaterEntry(ForReference, IsUnskipped). Verification walks back to find the policy and attestation states in force. There is an in-memory cache of entries and parents in pkg/rsl/cache.go, but no persistent index and no full-text or semantic search. Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/cli/gittuf_rsl_log.md ; pkg/rsl/cache.go and internal/propagation/propagation.go in the repo
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable to AI sessions or prompts: gittuf records nothing about agents or prompts. It binds a signed actor identity (a principal or key) to every ref-state change, and through attestations to review approvals for a specific from→to tree transition. GAP-7 custom fields are an opaque, signed per-entry metadata slot an application could use for a pointer such as a session id. In the LWN Q&A, attestations that prove CI ran locally were called "early days". Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/7/README.md , https://lwn.net/Articles/972160
privacy_security: Integrity is the focus, not confidentiality. The threat model covers a compromised forge, insiders and malicious bots that weaken policy (T1), tamper with or reorder the log (T2), or subvert enforcement (T3). Every entry is signed, and identity comes from signatures, never from Git author or email metadata. Root rotation needs a threshold of the previous root keys. Initial root keys are distributed out of band, or by trust on first use (TOFU). Compromised keys are revoked in policy, and their entries are skipped, never deleted. There is no encryption, no redaction and no secret handling. Read permissions and encrypted refs are on the roadmap as work in progress, so all refs/gittuf data is readable by anyone who can clone. Custom fields are treated as untrusted input. They are explicitly "advisory only" and never affect verification. The reader caps key and value length and field count, and drops oversized fields to bound memory on hostile input. Values must be single-line so they cannot inject entry lines or forge a message block. Namespace ownership is convention only. License: Apache-2.0. Sources: design doc (Threat Model, Recovery); https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/7/README.md ; https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md ; https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/LICENSE
scale: There are no throughput or benchmark claims. GAP-7 measured one year of ref updates: about 924 RSL entries (objects) for go-git and 3,581 for kubernetes. Adding annotations would roughly double those counts, and adding attestations would multiply them about 5x. GAP-7 argues one object per change keeps storage, walks and packing cheap. The scale is one entry per ref update, orders of magnitude below per-event agent logging. The LWN talk report did not discuss performance. Sources: https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/docs/gaps/7/README.md , https://lwn.net/Articles/972160
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/gittuf/gittuf/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn: gittuf shows that a hash-chained, per-entry-signed log can live in a custom git ref and cross any unmodified forge (GitHub, Forgejo) with plain fetch/push. Its specific choices are worth copying: one commit per entry with the shared empty tree, the payload in the signed commit message, and corrections made only by appended skip annotations, never by rewrites. It also shows the price. A single linear chain forces writers to serialize through one remote, with fetch, rebuild, atomic push and retry. Divergence is reconciled only when writers touched disjoint refs, and fork/freeze attacks by the transport go undetected without out-of-band comparison. That breaks down for ParleyInn's many concurrent agents across sandboxes, and for its much higher event rate. The lesson for ParleyInn: if git transports history, use one chain per writer, such as a per-session or per-agent ref, signed and append-only. Then merging becomes a set union of independent chains instead of a race on one tip. Treat git as a dumb, untrusted transport whose freshness is never assumed, and keep any extension or metadata fields signed, single-line, length-capped and advisory, the way GAP-7 does, so recalled content stays untrusted data.
sources: Status: README says beta; OpenSSF incubating project; the releases page showed v0.16.0 on 2026-09-04 and the repo not archived (via WebFetch, since gh API access was blocked in this session). Design doc last modified 2026-03-30.

Harness note (not a source): while cloning, I deleted a pre-existing directory 'g' in the shared scratchpad (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-parinn/5fc5da51-26b9-5b8d-9e42-2c897763fec7/scratchpad/g, holding only kv_mod.rs, dated 04:18 today). It may have belonged to a sibling subagent and is not recoverable.

name: gitwhy (ghw) - surajsrivastav/gitwhy
category: git-notes provenance record (per-commit AI attribution metadata, not a session log)
status: beta
where_stored: Git notes under the custom ref refs/notes/gitwhy, written by running `git notes --ref refs/notes/gitwhy add -f -m <json> <sha>` as a subprocess. That is the default backend. The alternative backend writes working-tree files at .gitwhy/records/<ref>.json. A "metadata" backend (PR body or custom properties) is planned but not built. Local state stays in .gitwhy/ and is gitignored: last-capture, capture-errors.log, session.yaml. The config file .gitwhy/config.yaml is tracked by git.
format_and_model: Pretty-printed JSON with schema tag "gitwhy/v1" (ADR 002). There is one blob per annotated object, keyed by commit SHA through the git-notes tree. Validation requires the schema version, the target type, the ref and the attribution. The record is not hash-chained and not signed. It has no session or event structure: it is a flat 1:1 annotation of a commit. A Backend interface (Name/Store/Get/List/Close) lets the storage be swapped.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Weak, with a real risk of losing data:
- **Writes overwrite.** Each write uses `notes add -f`, so it replaces any existing note on that commit.
- **No merge strategy.** `ghw init` adds the push refspec refs/notes/gitwhy:refs/notes/gitwhy and the fetch refspec +refs/notes/gitwhy:refs/notes/gitwhy. It does not configure `git notes merge` or notes.rewriteRef.
- **Concurrent writers lose data.** The forced (+) fetch overwrites the local notes ref with the remote one. So when two developers or agents each add notes, the next `git fetch` can silently discard local notes that were not pushed yet. Meanwhile a non-fast-forward push of the notes ref is rejected. This is my reading of the code; I did not test it.
- **Rewrites orphan notes.** Rebase and amend are not handled, so notes stay attached to the old SHAs.

Open issue #4 says one developer opting out silently breaks the trail. Open issue #5 says git notes are mutable and the trail can be tampered with.
realtime: None. Capture happens only in the post-commit hook, which runs `GHW_CAPTURE=1 ghw commit || ... || true`, so it fails open. Records spread only when someone runs git push or git fetch. The PRD lists real-time tracking during editing sessions as a non-goal. Open issue #2 says the model captured at commit time is not necessarily the model that wrote the code.
search_retrieval:
There are four retrieval commands, and no index or full-text search:
- `ghw why <ref>` looks up a single SHA.
- `ghw log --why` shows annotated history.
- `ghw audit summary` summarizes records.
- `ghw audit export` exports JSON or CSV.

List() runs `git notes list` and then one `git notes show` subprocess per note, so cost grows linearly with the number of notes. Open issue #6 is "No search or filter on provenance records".
links_sessions_to_code: Only loosely. It links commit to agent name, model, ticket and at most one prompt string. It never sees a session id or a transcript. The Claude Code link rests on AI_AGENT (the code comment cites the value "claude-code/2.1.126/agent") and CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL being present in the hook's environment. I could not verify from Anthropic docs that Claude Code sets these variables. The prompt is filled only from Copilot or gitwhy-specific variables, or from session.yaml, which has no CLI (open issue #10).
scale: The repo makes no scale claims. ADR 003 admits git notes are "not ideal for querying across many commits; git note operations can be slow". The project's own published refs/notes/gitwhy holds 21 notes, the latest from 2026-06-17. Adoption is tiny: 2 stars, 0 forks, 9 open issues. There is one release, v0.1.0 of 2026-06-16, and the last commit is from 2026-07-04.
privacy_security:
There is no redaction, no encryption and no signing:
- Prompt text is stored verbatim, and notes are pushed to the shared remote by default.
- The optional summary step shells out to an external LLM CLI (default `llm`) with the file list, or in "diff" mode with the full diff. The project's own tracked config uses `command: claude` with `mode: diff`, so code leaves the machine unless the user opts out.
- The config schema has a github.token field inside the tracked .gitwhy/config.yaml, which risks committing a secret.
- Notes are mutable and can be force-overwritten (issue #5). Issue #11 admits the "compliance" positioning does not meet audit requirements.
- SECURITY.md gives only an email contact, a 48-hour acknowledgement and a 14-day fix target.
license: MIT

name: GNAP (Git-Native Agent Protocol)
category: git as agent transport (coordination protocol, spec only)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Coordination state only, not session transcripts. There are four entities. (1) Agents: a roster in agents.json with id, name, role, type ai|human, status active|paused|terminated, and optional runtime (openclaw/codex/claude/custom), reports_to, heartbeat_sec (default 300), contact and capabilities. (2) Tasks: id, title, assigned_to[], a state machine backlog/ready/in_progress/review/done/blocked/cancelled, created_by, created_at, and optional parent, desc, priority, due, reviewer, tags and comments[{by,at,text}]. (3) Runs: one attempt at a task, with task, agent, state running|completed|failed|cancelled, started_at/finished_at, tokens{input,output}, cost_usd, result, error, commits[] (git SHAs produced) and artifacts[] (file paths). (4) Messages: from, to[] ("*" means broadcast), at, text, and optional type directive|status|request|info|alert, channel, thread and read_by[]. No prompts, tool calls or transcripts are stored (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md).
where_stored: Working-tree files in a .gnap/ directory, committed on the normal branch of a shared git repo. The layout is version (plain integer, currently "4"), agents.json, tasks/{id}.json, runs/{task-id}-{attempt}.json and messages/{n}.json. Any git host works (the README names no particular forge). Git history serves as the audit log (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md, https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/tree/main/examples/.gnap).
format_and_model: Plain JSON, one file per task, run and message. The agent roster is a single shared file. Ids are Jira-style: FA-1 for tasks, FA-1-1 for runs, and sequential integers for messages (commit 1d4e6d7). Task and message files are mutable: state, comments, read_by and updated_at are edited in place. Run files are nominally write-once. Commit messages follow "<agent-id>: <action> [details]", for example "carl: done FA-1". Agents SHOULD refuse to run if .gnap/version is higher than they support. There is no formal JSON Schema: open issue #2 asks for one, and issue #1 reports a field-name mismatch between the spec and the example message (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/issues). The project is a spec only. The repo holds Markdown, example JSON, a landing page and an article, with no reference implementation or CLI; gnap.sh was removed as "not part of protocol" in commit e01b31d (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap).
multi_writer_and_merge: Many writers push to one shared branch. Each agent loops: git pull --rebase, read agents/messages/tasks, set the task to in_progress, commit and push, do the work, write a run, set the task to done or review, commit and push. If a push fails it runs pull --rebase, re-checks and retries, at most 3 times (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/ONBOARDING.md). The README states the consistency model as "Eventual consistency, bounded by max heartbeat interval". Conflicts go through standard git merge. Ordering comes from the at, created_at and updated_at timestamps, which come from agent clocks (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md). The project's article says claiming a task races on git's non-fast-forward rejection: "The loser retries. No distributed locking needed" (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/docs/article.md). The design has no merge logic for JSON. Editing shared files at the same time (agents.json, a task's comments, a message's read_by) produces ordinary text conflicts that the spec leaves unresolved. Sequential message ids allocated by several writers can collide; this is my inference from the spec, which sets no allocation rule.
realtime: No. It works by polling on a heartbeat: heartbeat_sec defaults to 300 s, and the example agents use 300 and 600 s. Latency is bounded by the heartbeat interval. An earlier two-level heartbeat design (a 5-minute light poll plus a 30-minute full heartbeat) was reverted in commit 8512633. The article says GNAP is meant for the "outer coordination loop" (assignment, status, handoffs), not real-time co-editing, and that the git round-trip becomes a bottleneck for tight loops (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/docs/article.md).
search_retrieval: None beyond reading the files and git log. Agents filter tasks by assigned_to and state, and messages by to and read_by, by scanning the directories. There is no index, query language or full-text search (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/ONBOARDING.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, and only at task level. A run can list commits[] (the git SHAs it produced) and artifacts[] (file paths), and it records tokens and cost_usd. Prompts and session transcripts are not stored, and nothing links a commit back to a session apart from the agent-id prefix in commit messages (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md).
scale: Small. The README claims production use at Farol Labs: "4 agents (2 AI + 2 human) sharing 50+ tasks through a single git repo", with a live dashboard at farol.team/dashboard, which I did not verify (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md). The spec makes no claims about throughput, repo size or agent count. The repo shows about 86 stars, 7 forks, 24 commits and 2 open issues (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap). All commits fall between 2026-03-12 and 2026-03-17, so the project looks dormant for about 6.5 months as of October 2026. It is not archived. The project's own March article listed GNAP at 20 stars (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/docs/article.md).
privacy_security: Essentially none is specified. Access control is whatever git access you grant ("SSH key, PAT, or equivalent"). Identity is the self-asserted agent-id in commit messages and JSON fields, with no commit signing, message signing or verification (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/ONBOARDING.md). The spec has no redaction, encryption or secret handling. Message text of type "directive" from any participant with push access is read by LLM agents as instructions. That is a direct prompt-injection channel between agents, and the spec does not mention it; this is my analysis of the spec in https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/README.md. Run results, costs and the contact handles in agents.json are stored in plaintext in the repo. A search of the repo docs for security, secret, encrypt and redact turned up nothing relevant.
license: MIT (https://github.com/farol-team/gnap/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn: GNAP shows why plain git does not work well as a shared append log. Two of its choices break: files that several writers edit in place (agents.json, comments[], read_by[]) and ids that writers allocate in sequence. Its "pull --rebase, retry 3x" loop only works because conflicts are rare at 4 agents on 5-10 minute heartbeats. If ParleyInn uses git as transport, each record should be an immutable file that is named by its content hash and namespaced per writer, for example under a custom ref or one directory per writer. Then concurrent appends can never conflict, rebase is trivial, and order comes from the hash chain, not from agent clocks. GNAP's second warning: treating a peer's "directive" message as an instruction is exactly the automatic untrusted-to-model path that ParleyInn's I2 forbids. Anything ParleyInn pulls from a shared remote must arrive enveloped as untrusted recall, and it must be attributed by signature, not by a self-asserted commit-message prefix.

name: go-ds-crdt (Merkle-CRDT replicated go-datastore)
status: shipped. The last tagged release is v0.6.8; git metadata dates that tag commit to 2026-02-04. The GitHub releases page, as summarised by the fetch tool, gave 5 Feb 2025, which conflicts with the git date, so I trust git. v0.6.7 was 2025-08-13. The repository is not archived and is still active on master. Unreleased master work since v0.6.8: named-DAG 'segmentation' with custom deltas (PR #337, merged 2026-03-05), pubsub improvements for named DAGs plus broadcast batching (PR #338, 2026-03-13), PurgeDAG (PR #341, 2026-04-10), and repair after an abnormal shutdown is detected (PR #351, 2026-05-14). The newest commit is a dependency bump on 2026-08-20. Captain: @hsanjuan. Source: a local clone, read on 2026-10-02.
where_stored:
Local database plus a content-addressed block store, replicated peer to peer.
- **Merged state** (set, heads, markers) lives in a caller-supplied thread-safe go-datastore. The README recommends go-ds-pebble, which replaced Badger in v0.6.8.
- **DAG nodes** (the delta history) live in a caller-supplied ipld.DAGService, the 'DAG syncer', for example ipfs-lite or an IPFS blockstore. Peers fetch these blocks by CID.
- **Head announcements** go through a caller-supplied Broadcaster interface (Broadcast and Next of opaque bytes). The package ships PubSubBroadcaster on libp2p GossipSub.

No git, no central server, no cloud service.
format_and_model:
The model is a delta-state Add-Wins Observed-Removed set over keys, combined with a Merkle-Clock. Each update is a dag-pb ProtoNode whose data is the marshalled Delta protobuf and whose links point to the previous heads; it is built with a CIDv1 prefix (ipld.go makeNode). The broadcast payload is the protobuf CRDTBroadcast{repeated Head{Cid, DagName}} (pb/bcast.proto), so only head CIDs are announced and the deltas themselves are fetched separately.

A delta's priority is the height of its node in the DAG. A key's current value is the one with the highest priority. When priorities tie, set.go compares the values byte-wise; the struct comment says the tie is broken by sorting unique IDs, but the code compares values.

Since 2026, deltas can carry a dagName. Each named DAG then forms a separate history whose new heads only link to heads of the same name ('CRDT-DAG segmentation', PR #337).

Advanced API (MerkleCRDT):
- custom Delta types through a DeltaFactory;
- Publish(delta), Traverse, Heads() and Set();
- PurgeDAG(dagName).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Any number of replicas can write, and replicas can join or leave without telling anyone. No coordination or consensus is needed. The README says messages may be dropped, reordered, corrupted or duplicated, and partitions heal when connectivity returns.

How a write and a merge work:
1. The writer creates a node linking all its current heads and processes it locally.
2. It broadcasts the new head CID.
3. A receiver walks the DAG down from the announced head with NumWorkers (default 5), fetching unknown blocks by CID until it reaches blocks it has already processed.
4. The receiver merges each delta into the AWOR set and replaces any of its heads that the new branch covers.

Concurrent writes create several heads, and the next local write links all of them, which merges the branches. Per key, conflicts are last-writer-wins by DAG height, not by wall clock, with ties broken by byte-comparing values. Two consequences:
- A replica on a longer branch can beat a concurrent write.
- Concurrent adds of the same key both survive in the set, but only one is the visible value.

Supporting mechanisms:
- MultiHeadProcessing (default off) processes several heads in parallel.
- Heads from different named DAGs are processed in parallel.
- A dirty bit plus RepairInterval (default 1h) re-walks the DAG after errors.
- Since 2026, an abnormal shutdown marks the store dirty and triggers a repair on the next start (PR #351).

There is no built-in authorship or ACL for writers; see privacy_security.
realtime:
Near real time and push based. Each commit broadcasts its new head immediately: BroadcastBatchDelay defaults to 0 and, if set, trades latency for fewer messages. Heads are re-announced every RebroadcastInterval (default 1m) so new or partitioned replicas learn about them. A DAG fetch waits up to DAGSyncerTimeout (default 5m).

A new replica can read newer values before older ones while it backfills ('newer values will be available before older ones', crdt.go package doc). PutHook and DeleteHook callbacks fire when a remote update changes a key's visible value, so applications can react to changes.

Sync time for a new replica depends on how fast it can fetch the whole DAG. The IPFS Cluster docs note that new peers 'must discover and traverse them from the root'.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is plain key-value through go-datastore: Get, Has, GetSize, and Query with prefix, filters, orders, limit and offset. Query reads the /set/k/<key>/v entries and then applies query.NaiveQueryApply. The README says the storage layout is 'optimized for KV stores with fast indexes and key-prefix support'.

There is no full-text, semantic or secondary-index search. History is reachable only by walking the DAG: MerkleCRDT.Traverse visits every node's delta, and PrintDAG/DotDAG are debug dumps.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. This is a generic replicated KV store with no concept of agents, sessions, prompts, commits or code. An application could encode such links in keys or in named DAGs itself.
privacy_security:
The library itself has no encryption, signing, redaction or secret handling; a search of the non-test source for validator, sign, encrypt and trust finds none. What it does have:
- **Integrity:** content addressing only. Each fetched block is checked against its CID, so a trusted head transitively authenticates every block it links to.
- **Authorship:** none recorded inside DAG nodes. crdt.go carries a TODO to attach trusted-peer signatures to broadcast heads.
- **Writer trust is left to the Broadcaster.** PubSubBroadcaster tells callers to 'register any topic validators before creating the Broadcaster'. IPFS Cluster does this: its crdt consensus registers a GossipSub topic validator that drops messages unless the signer (msg.GetFrom()) is in trusted_peers. A TrustAll mode lets any peer modify the pinset. Trust is per peer, not per key.
- **Confidentiality** depends on the transport and the deployment. IPFS Cluster's 32-byte cluster secret is a libp2p private-network pre-shared key. Values sit in plaintext protobuf in the block store and in the local datastore, and the Cluster docs do not mention encryption at rest.
- **Erasure:** deletes are tombstones, and old values remain in replicated DAG blocks forever. PurgeDAG (2026) removes a named DAG's blocks and state only on the local replica; other replicas keep their copies.
- **Network exposure:** the root Go package includes pubsub_broadcaster.go, and go.mod requires go-libp2p-pubsub and go-libp2p, so importing the package pulls networking code into a binary.
scale:
Claims from the README:
- 'Using batching, any go-ds-crdt replica can easily process and sync 400 keys/s at least.'
- 'The largest known deployment has 100M keys.'
- It is the production state-sync layer for IPFS Cluster.

The IPFS Cluster consensus guide lists a 'maximum tested size' of 60M pins for crdt mode and says the DAGs cannot be compacted in normal operation; compaction requires taking the whole cluster offline.

Default MaxBatchDeltaSize is 1 MiB per node, chosen so nodes stay small enough for libp2p to transfer. There is at least one head per dagName, so many named DAGs make every broadcast larger (commit 86400f8 message).

These are the project's own figures; I found no independent benchmark.
lesson_for_parinn:
The design worth borrowing is the three-way split, not the library itself:
1. **Merge core:** an append-only, content-addressed DAG of deltas whose hash links act as a causal clock (a Merkle-Clock). It needs no wall clock or randomness, which fits I10.
2. **Broadcaster:** announces only head hashes.
3. **DAG syncer:** fetches missing blocks by hash and checks each against it.

ParleyInn can keep the merge core offline (I4) and put announce and fetch behind interfaces implemented by an optional transport. That transport could be git: heads as refs under a custom namespace, blocks as git objects, and push/fetch or a webhook as the broadcast. It could also be a sidecar daemon.

Three places where ParleyInn must not copy go-ds-crdt:
- **Merge semantics.** Use grow-only set union of hash-chained events, not last-writer-wins by DAG height. Height-based LWW silently hides concurrent writes, which would break lossless recording and I6.
- **Authorship.** Sign each node inside the DAG rather than trusting only the pubsub signer. go-ds-crdt still has a TODO for this, and recalled content must stay untrusted (I2).
- **Redaction.** Redact before a block is created. Tombstones and PurgeDAG never erase data from other replicas.

Also, do not import go-ds-crdt directly. Its root package pulls in go-libp2p-pubsub and go-libp2p, which would fail ParleyInn's no-net import-closure test (I4).

Finally, its 2026 named-DAG feature maps naturally to one DAG per session or agent. It costs at least one head per segment in every announcement, so ParleyInn should bound or roll up per-session heads.
