confidence: high. Data model, merge, storage layout, defaults and security facts come from source code read in a local clone of master at commit 1108fa0 (2026-08-20). Release dates come from git tag metadata; the releases page, as summarised by the fetch tool, gave conflicting years. Scale figures are the project's own claims and were not independently checked. ipfscluster.io returned HTTP 503, so I read the same docs from the website's source repository on GitHub. The star count (about 489) comes from a page fetch and was not verified.

name: golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog (tamper-evident log library behind the Go checksum database, sum.golang.org)
status: shipped. It is maintained and not archived. Latest module release is v0.41.0 (published Aug 24, 2026, BSD-3-Clause). It needs `go 1.26.0`, which matches ParleyInn's go.mod (pkg.go.dev page, and the x/mod go.mod at tag v0.41.0). cmd/go vendors it at src/cmd/vendor/golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog. Current users of the package include Sunlight, Torchwood, Let's Encrypt Boulder and transparency-dev/witness (pkg.go.dev imported-by tab). Tessera v1.0.4 and Sunlight also require x/mod v0.41.0 in their go.mod. It is not superseded, but the newer C2SP tlog-tiles spec generalises its tile format, and Torchwood adds tlog-tiles helpers on top of it (see format field).
what_is_stored:
The package stores nothing and does no I/O of its own. It does the Merkle-tree math for an append-only log.
- Hashes. A record hash is SHA-256(0x00||data) and an interior node is SHA-256(0x01||left||right), as in RFC 6962 section 2.1. The empty-tree hash was fixed to RFC 6962 in 2024.
- Write path. `StoredHashes(n, data, r)` returns the 1 to (1+log2 n) hashes to persist when record n is appended, averaging just under two per record.
- Read path. `TreeHash` computes the root. `ProveRecord`/`CheckRecord` handle inclusion proofs (RFC 6962 "audit path"), and `ProveTree`/`CheckTree` handle consistency proofs between an older and a newer tree size.
- Tiles. `Tile`, `NewTiles`, `ReadTileData` and `TileHashReader` serve and authenticate fixed-height tiles.
- Tree and record text. A `Tree{N, Hash}` describes a signed tree head. `FormatTree`/`ParseTree` and `FormatRecord`/`ParseRecord` give sumdb's text encodings.
The record payload itself is the caller's to store. In sum.golang.org each record is go.sum-style lines (module, version, h1: hash). Sources: pkg.go.dev doc; tlog.go, note.go and tile.go at v0.41.0; design doc 25530.
where_stored:
Wherever the caller puts it. The library talks to storage only through interfaces:
- `HashReader.ReadHashes([]int64)`, for hashes addressed by a dense "stored hash index" (`StoredHashIndex(level, n)`, Crosby and Wallach ordering). This suits a single append-only hash file of about 2N hashes.
- `TileReader` (`ReadTiles` and `SaveTiles`), usually an on-disk cache or a remote tile server.
Russ Cox's design describes three append-only files: record data, record index and hashes. The sibling package golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/storage defines a transactional key-value `Storage` interface for a server. sum.golang.org serves tiles over HTTPS at /tile/8/L/NNN; a fetched full tile is 8192 bytes. Clients cache under $GOPATH/pkg/mod/download/cache/sumdb. Sources: tlog.go, tile.go, storage.go; research.swtch.com/tlog; design 25530; direct fetch of https://sum.golang.org/tile/8/0/000.
format_and_model:
The model is a single, totally ordered, append-only sequence of records numbered 0..N-1, committed by an RFC 6962 Merkle tree. A log with N not a power of two is split into complete power-of-two subtrees.
- Tiles. A tile at height H (1 to 30) and level L lists W of 2^H consecutive hashes at tree level H*L. Level L=-1 means a "data" tile holding raw records. Path form is tile/H/L/x001/x234/067[.p/W], three digits per path element to keep directories small.
- Tree head (sumdb text format). Three lines: "go.sum database tree", then N, then a base64 hash. It is wrapped in a signed note; the sibling package sumdb/note supports only Ed25519. A live example from https://sum.golang.org/latest: N=66338570 followed by a "— sum.golang.org <sig>" line.
- Records (sumdb text format). The record id line, then text, then a blank line. Text must be UTF-8 with no control characters except newline and no blank lines. `RecordHash` itself accepts arbitrary bytes.
- Proofs. `[]Hash` of length O(log N).
- Relation to C2SP tlog-tiles. tlog-tiles uses the same RFC 6962 hashing but fixes height at 8 and drops H from the path (tile/L/N). Its entry bundles are uint16 length-prefixed binary, not sumdb text. Its checkpoints follow c2sp.org/tlog-checkpoint, with an origin line instead of "go.sum database tree".
- Interop. x/mod's `Tile.Path()` emits sumdb-style paths. filippo.io/torchwood v0.10.0 (BSD-3) adds `TilePath`/`ParseTilePath` for tlog-tiles, entry-bundle helpers, checkpoint verification, subtree proofs and a `HashReaderOverlay`.
Sources: tile.go, note.go, c2sp.org/tlog-tiles, pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The design is single-sequencer with no merge semantics. `StoredHashes(n, ...)` must be called for consecutive n, so appends must be serialised by one writer. The sumdb storage interface offers `ReadWrite` transactions that retry, for the server side.
Two logs that grow differently from a shared prefix are, by definition, a fork. `CheckTree` fails on the consistency proof, and the go command "will complain loudly" if it ever sees inconsistent signed tree heads (design 25530). There is no way to reconcile two branches into one tree. Multi-party trust is built outside this package:
- witnesses and cosigning (c2sp.org/tlog-witness; Torchwood's litewitness);
- multiple mirror URL prefixes serving identical content (tlog-tiles).
For ParleyInn, this means each concurrent writer (agent, worktree, sandbox) needs its own log, or there must be one sequencer. Git-style merging of trees is impossible by design. Sources: tlog.go, storage.go, design 25530, c2sp.org/tlog-tiles, github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood.
realtime:
None in the library. It is synchronous math over caller-supplied readers, with no push or subscription.
In deployments, clients poll. sum.golang.org serves /latest; in tlog-tiles the /checkpoint endpoint is mutable and "SHOULD prevent caching beyond a few seconds", while tiles and entry bundles are immutable and cacheable for a long time. I could not verify how often sum.golang.org signs a new tree head.
For ParleyInn's coding rules: `HashReader.ReadHashes` and `TileReader.ReadTiles` take no `context.Context`, so a blocking backend cannot be cancelled through the API. Torchwood's `TileReader` adds context. Sources: tile.go, c2sp.org/tlog-tiles, pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by record index only. You fetch the record or data tile for index n, then prove it against a trusted tree head with `ProveRecord`/`CheckRecord`, and prove one head extends another with `ProveTree`/`CheckTree`. Both proofs are O(log N).
Russ Cox estimates that a proof in a log of about 100M records with height-8 tiles needs about three tiles, 24 kB. Any key-to-index lookup is outside tlog: sumdb's /lookup/M@V goes through a separate `ServerOps.Lookup` index in sumdb/server.go. There is no full-text or semantic search. Auditors can iterate the whole log tile by tile. Sources: research.swtch.com/tlog, tlog.go, server.go at v0.41.0.
links_sessions_to_code:
No. It has no concept of agent sessions, prompts or commits.
The closest analogue is sumdb's use: each record binds a module path and version to an h1: hash of the module source tree and its go.mod. That is content-addressed provenance for code releases, not session linkage (design 25530). Any session-to-commit link would live in ParleyInn's own record payload, with tlog committing to it.
privacy_security:
Integrity only. There is no encryption, redaction or secret handling.
- Domain separation. RFC 6962 0x00/0x01 prefixes separate leaf hashes from node hashes. Its proofs are tested against real Certificate Transparency proofs; ct_test.go is a network test and not part of the built package.
- Verify before persist. `TileHashReader` authenticates every fetched tile against the trusted tree hash or its parent tile before returning hashes. The `TileReader` contract says downloaded tiles "should be considered suspect" and must not be persisted until `SaveTiles` is called.
- CVE-2026-56865 / GO-2026-6179 (fix committed 2026-08-13, released in v0.40.0). Before the fix, `TileHashReader` skipped authenticating up to two tiles. A malicious proxy could return attacker-chosen hashes and get them persisted through `SaveTiles`. The fix adds a test that tampers with every index for tree sizes 1 to 100.
- CVE-2026-56864 / GO-2026-6180 (also fixed in v0.40.0). A sibling flaw in sumdb `Client.Lookup` returned unauthenticated hashes. The go toolchain is fixed in 1.25.13, 1.26.6 and 1.27.0-rc.3. Any embedder must pin x/mod >= v0.40.0.
- Network isolation (ParleyInn I4). I checked the import closure with `go list -deps` on v0.41.0 under go1.26.0. It is stdlib only (crypto/sha256, encoding/base64, fmt, math/bits, strconv, strings, unicode/utf8, bytes) and contains no net, net/http or os/exec. The parent package golang.org/x/mod/sumdb does import net/http, so ParleyInn must import only sumdb/tlog (and optionally sumdb/note).
- Privacy. Logs and proofs reveal record hashes. A hash of low-entropy plaintext can be brute-forced, so commit to salted or encrypted bytes if privacy matters. The design doc notes that querying sumdb leaks module paths, mitigated by proxies or GONOSUMDB.
- Removal. tlog-tiles "pruning" hides old entries without changing hashes. True deletion breaks the tree.
- Panics. `TileForIndex` panics on height <= 0, and internal "bad math" panics exist. These must be recovered at ParleyInn's entry points (ENG-04).
Sources: tile.go, ct_test.go, fix commit 96f62ae, vuln.go.dev entries, local go list run, server.go, design 25530, c2sp.org/tlog-tiles.
lesson_for_parinn:
Adopt tlog's Merkle layer next to the existing hash chain, not in place of it.

The problem it solves: a linear chain needs O(N) work to show that an old event is still in the current head, or that a new head extends an old one.

How it would fit:
- Compute `RecordHash` over each canonical event's bytes.
- Append the output of `StoredHashes` to a sidecar hash file indexed by `StoredHashIndex`. The file is fully rebuildable from the record, so I10 holds and the code reads no clock or randomness.
- This gives O(log N) inclusion proofs for recall envelopes, and consistency proofs (`CheckTree`) between signed checkpoints exchanged by machines and sandboxes.
- A rewritten or forked replica then fails verification mechanically.

Constraints to design in:
1. tlog has no merge. Give each writer (session, worktree, sandbox) its own tree and checkpoint, and federate by exchanging checkpoints and tiles. Witness cosigning is optional. Do not try git-style merges of one tree.
2. Import only golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog, pinned to >= v0.40.0 (CVE-2026-56865). Add a depguard rule banning golang.org/x/mod/sumdb, which imports net/http. Wrap the context-free `HashReader` behind a ctx-aware local reader.
3. Copy its verify-before-persist rule into I2. Never cache or index peer-supplied tiles or entries until they are authenticated against a trusted head.
4. Copy the CVE fix's exhaustive tamper test (every index, every tree size 1 to 100) as a fuzz target. Proof-authentication code is subtle, and even the Go team shipped a bypass for years.
5. Hash salted or encrypted event bytes rather than plaintext, so a later redaction (crypto-shredding) keeps all proofs valid and leaves no brute-forceable leaf hashes.

Adding it means one new direct dependency (BSD-3-Clause, needs an ADR under ENG-18).

name: Google ADK SessionService
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Session identification (app name, user ID, unique session ID), ordered Event objects (user messages, agent responses, tool invocations, LLM responses), Session State (working memory, temporary conversational data), metadata (timestamps, state change audit trail). Events form an append-only sequence; state evolves through event-applied deltas. Sessions can accumulate thousands of events without per-record size limits through automatic segmentation.
where_stored: Multiple backend options: InMemorySessionService (application memory, no persistence), FirestoreSessionService (Google Cloud Firestore, serverless), VertexAiSessionService (Vertex AI Agent Platform managed infrastructure), SqliteSessionService (SQLite), PostgresSessionService (PostgreSQL), MongoSessionService (MongoDB), Neo4jSessionService (Neo4j), RedisSessionService (Redis). Each backend handles underlying persistence differently while maintaining the same SessionService interface contract.
format_and_model: Event-sourcing architecture. Events are the basic unit of communication capturing interactions (user input, agent output, tool invocation). Each event carries optional state_delta—changes to session state committed atomically with the event. State is represented as maps and updated through cumulative delta application. Session key combines application name, user ID, and session ID for multi-user, multi-app deployments. Segment model automatically opens new records when a segment fills, enabling transparent handling of long histories. Java/Kotlin API returns RxJava3 reactive types (Single, Maybe, Completable).
multi_writer_and_merge: Atomic appends ensure each event and its state delta commit in one write. No explicit merge mechanism—consistency guaranteed through sequential append ordering. Idempotent design allows replayed writes to update the same slot without duplicating turns, enabling safe retries under network failures. Concurrent access handled through atomic operations (stress-tested with 64 parallel writers adding 1,000 events each per tutorial). Different backends use different mechanisms (Firestore transactions, row-level locking for SQL backends via locks, atomic Aerospike operations). No cross-session merge semantics exist.
realtime: Streaming support for real-time text through event filtering patterns. Partial events enable real-time UI updates during agent responses. No explicit pub/sub or subscription mechanism documented. Event retrieval through pagination and filtering provides near-real-time visibility into session history. Reactive API design (RxJava3 Single/Maybe/Completable) supports asynchronous, non-blocking operations suitable for streaming agent applications.
search_retrieval: getSession(sessionKey, optional config) retrieves a specific session with optional event filtering. listEvents(sessionKey) lists events within a session. Timestamp-based filtering supported (RFC 3339 format, e.g., timestamp>='2025-01-31T11:30:00-04:00'). Pagination via PageToken and PageSize (default 100 events). Ordering support via comma-separated field lists in ascending order. list_sessions method lists all sessions for a given app/user combination. No full-text search across event content or cross-session querying documented.
links_sessions_to_code: Limited direct code linking. Sessions serve as conversation containers maintaining history of agent interactions. ADK SkillToolset enables progressive disclosure of agent capabilities through skill factories and dynamic code loading, but sessions do not directly store source code references or prompt text. Tools are Python functions exposed to agents, but tool definitions are separate from session events. Session history records what agents did (tool invocations) but not how they decided it (prompt reasoning).
privacy_security: VertexAiSessionService supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), VPC Service Controls, and IAM-based access control. Data residency options available for compliance. No explicit PII redaction or scrubbing mechanisms documented for ADK SessionService. No mention of automated secret detection or removal from session history. Security relies on backend infrastructure security (Firestore firewall rules, Cloud IAM policies, VPC isolation). No audit logging or immutability guarantees at the ADK layer; delegated to backend systems.
lesson_for_parinn: The segmentation strategy is instructive for ParleyInn's long-running session problem. Rather than enforcing history into a single immutable record, ADK SessionService auto-segments into multiple records as they grow, transparent to the calling code. This enables efficient retrieval of recent events (numRecentEvents parameter) without loading entire session histories into memory, critical for agents with thousands of turns. For ParleyInn, this suggests: (1) considering segmentation strategies for append-only logs to avoid prohibitive read latencies on old content, (2) supporting selective history loading (recent N events) for model context without full replay, (3) the atomic append + idempotent design provides a proven pattern for durability under multi-writer distributed scenarios with retries—ParleyInn's security-first, append-only model could benefit from ADK's verification that atomic operations and sequential ordering alone suffice without explicit distributed locking.

name: Google Antigravity (Artifacts)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Structured deliverables created by agents: implementation plans (Markdown), code diffs, architecture diagrams, images, and browser recordings. Session history stored as conversation transcripts (JSONL and SQLite). Agent state, workspace configurations, and build artifacts.
where_stored: Local directories: ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/ (CLI), ~/.gemini/antigravity/brain/ (desktop 2.0), ~/.gemini/antigravity-ide/brain/ (legacy IDE). Within those: history.jsonl (master file for resume), conversations/ (SQLite .db per session), brain/ subdirectory (static files, logs, transcripts). Optional cloud sync via Google Cloud Storage and enterprise GCP integration.
format_and_model: Artifacts: Markdown (.md) with embedded JSON metadata. Conversation history: JSONL format (history.jsonl), SQLite databases (.db) for structured session data, Protocol Buffer (.pb) format on some platforms. Audio/video: MP3, WAV, OGG, M4A supported. Artifact model: interactive, versioned documents with human-in-the-loop review via sidebar (2.0) or terminal review panel (CLI).
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple agents operate in isolated Git worktrees (one per subagent in 2.0), providing isolated context windows and file system separation. Reconciliation of multi-agent work happens at merge time with mandatory human code review. No real-time synchronization of parallel writes; agents are not blocked but their changes are isolated until integration.
realtime: Streaming support for agent output and internal model reasoning. Real-time monitoring via Manager View (desktop 2.0) shows multiple agents working simultaneously. Visual feedback through sidebar artifacts (plans, diffs, recordings) updates asynchronously during agent work. Human can provide inline text feedback during execution. Scheduled tasks support via cron syntax (2.0) for background operations without real-time supervision.
search_retrieval: Artifacts are viewable and reviewable through UI (sidebar in 2.0, terminal panel in CLI) but no full-text search capability documented across artifact database. Conversation retrieval via history.jsonl indexed file and session IDs. The /resume command references history.jsonl to restore sessions. Limited evidence of search/retrieval API; primarily navigational UI-based access.
links_sessions_to_code: Git VCS integration tracks all repository changes (not just agent edits) on current branch. Isolated git worktrees link each agent session to a separate working directory in the same repository. VCS diff tracker (2.0) shows staged/unstaged changes relative to origin/main with commit message generation. Agent edits viewable in sidebar alongside other changes. Artifacts include code diffs linked to specific repository state. Extension extensions.worktreeConfig used to mark worktree-aware repos (though causes compatibility issues with some agents).
privacy_security: Credentials API (preview): agents see placeholders, not secrets; proxy inserts real tokens only for approved domains, blocking exfiltration attempts. Known vulnerabilities: prompt injection via 1-pixel font or code comments can bypass .gitignore and exfiltrate .env credentials; browser tool default allow-list includes webhook.site as exfiltration vector. Mitigations: use non-production credentials with spending limits; Credentials API hides secrets from model context. Local-first storage reduces cloud exposure but sync to GCP introduces shared tenancy risks. No documented encryption at rest for local brain/ directories.
lesson_for_parinn: Antigravity's separation of structured artifacts from raw execution logs proves valuable for verifiable agent output. Key lessons: (1) Local-first storage with optional cloud sync balances accessibility and control—ParleyInn should default to local append-only record. (2) Worktree isolation per agent is essential for safety when multiple agents access the same repository—extends cleanly to ParleyInn's multi-agent, multi-machine model. (3) Credentials management requires proxy architecture so untrusted recalled content (model context) never sees real secrets—directly applicable to ParleyInn's 'recall is pull-only' invariant (I2). (4) Git integration for session/code linking is practical but requires careful handling of .git/config state and worktree extensions—ParleyInn using git as transport should document these compatibility concerns. (5) Artifacts as human-reviewable deliverables decouple agent autonomy from transparency, enabling asynchronous feedback loops that do not require real-time synchronization.

name: Google Jules (Jules REST API v1alpha, Jules Tools CLI)
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
Google stores every task as a Session. A Session holds the prompt, a title (generated if you leave it out), its state, its sourceContext, its outputs, createTime and updateTime, an archived flag, and a url pointing to the web app. The states are QUEUED, PLANNING, AWAITING_PLAN_APPROVAL, AWAITING_USER_FEEDBACK, IN_PROGRESS, PAUSED, FAILED and COMPLETED. Each Session holds an ordered list of Activities. Every Activity has an originator ("user", "agent" or "system"), a description and a createTime. It has exactly one event field set:
- planGenerated: a Plan with id, createTime and steps, each step having id, index, title and description
- planApproved: a planId
- userMessaged: the userMessage text
- agentMessaged: the agentMessage text
- progressUpdated: title and description
- sessionCompleted
- sessionFailed: a reason

An Activity can also carry Artifacts of three kinds:
- changeSet: a source plus a gitPatch made of baseCommitId, unidiffPatch and suggestedCommitMessage
- bashOutput: the command, the combined stdout and stderr, and the exitCode
- media: a mimeType and base64 data

Session outputs are a pullRequest (url, title, description, baseRef, headRef) and/or a changeSet. Sources: https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/types and the live discovery document, revision 20260929: https://jules.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1alpha

The service stores more than this. Per-repository "Memory" of user preferences and corrections exists since 30 Sep 2025. Environment snapshots built from setup scripts exist since 5 Aug 2025. Per-source environment variables exist, toggled by sourceContext.environmentVariablesEnabled. Per-task VM logs exist. Sources: https://jules.google/docs/changelog/, https://jules.google/docs/environment/, https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/

None of these internal stores (memory, snapshots, environment variables) is exposed through the API. The discovery document's proto comment "next_id: 19" hints that the Session has more internal fields than the 13 it exposes. That is my inference, not documented.
where_stored:
Google's servers and cloud, inside the Jules service. Transcripts, plans, bash output and memory never go into the repository.

Code results go to GitHub only on request. "Publish branch" or "Publish PR" in the web app pushes them (https://jules.google/docs/code/). So does automationMode AUTO_CREATE_PR in the API, which pushes to sourceContext.workingBranch or to a generated branch name (discovery document).

Patches can be pulled to a local checkout with `jules remote pull --session <id>`, documented at https://jules.google/docs/cli/reference. The changelog says the CLI can "pull work-in-progress code from an active Jules session and apply it to your local machine" (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).

Each task runs in its own short-lived Ubuntu VM, which "maintains its own logs, environment setup, and code changes" (https://jules.google/docs/environment/, https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/).

Only GitHub is supported. The docs say "In the future, Jules will work with more version control systems" (https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/).
format_and_model:
The API is a Google-style resource-oriented REST/JSON API (protobuf-backed). Base URL: https://jules.googleapis.com/v1alpha/. Auth: the x-goog-api-key header. The resource tree is sources/{source}, sessions/{session} and sessions/{session}/activities/{activity}.

Clients cannot edit or patch an Activity; only list and get exist. The API never exposes an update for Activities, so to API clients the history is effectively append-only. Clients add events only indirectly:
- sessions:sendMessage records a user message
- sessions:approvePlan records a plan approval

Other Session methods are create, get, list, delete, archive and unarchive. Each Activity is a discriminated union: exactly one event field is populated.

Code changes travel as plain unified diffs anchored to a baseCommitId. They are not git objects or commits.

The API is labelled alpha: "experimental", with specs and keys that may change (https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/). The docs pages lag behind the discovery document. The pages omit archive/unarchive, workingBranch, environmentVariablesEnabled, SessionOutput.changeSet and PullRequest.baseRef/headRef. The discovery document (revision 20260929) has all of them: https://jules.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1alpha
multi_writer_and_merge:
The record has no multi-writer support and no merge.

Each session belongs to one Google account. A per-user API key from jules.google.com/settings authenticates calls (https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/authentication). Only two parties write to a session's history:
- the user, via the web chat, the CLI or the API sendMessage and approvePlan calls
- the agent

The server orders their activities. Users can message Jules or pause it mid-task (https://jules.google/docs/running-tasks/).

Parallel work means separate sessions. `jules remote new --parallel N` starts N sessions on the same task (https://jules.google/docs/cli/reference). Concurrency limits are 3, 15 and 60 tasks by tier (https://jules.google/docs/usage-limits/).

Sessions never merge history. Code reconciliation happens entirely in GitHub, through branches and pull requests. The CI Fixer (19 Feb 2026) pushes follow-up fixes to PRs that Jules created.

Commit authorship has three modes: Jules alone, Jules co-authored with you, or you alone. The setting applies org-wide (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).

I found no documentation of team sharing of sessions or of multi-user access to one session.
realtime:
There is no real-time push; the API is polling only. No streaming, webhooks or push notifications are documented (https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/activities).

Incremental sync uses the AIP-160 filter on ListActivities, which "only supports filtering by create_time". Example: create_time > "2024-09-04T10:00:00Z" (discovery document). The 26 Jan 2026 changelog added this so clients "only fetch new activities over the network" (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/). The docs example instead uses a bare ?createTime=$TIMESTAMP parameter, which disagrees with the discovery document.

Live viewing is possible only in Jules' own clients:
- the web app (Session.url)
- the CLI/TUI dashboard (https://jules.google/docs/cli/reference)
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by ID and listing only; the API has no full-text or semantic search.
- ListSessions: pageSize up to 100, default 30. Its filter only accepts archived, and the default returns non-archived sessions.
- ListActivities: pageSize up to 100, default 50. Its filter only accepts create_time.
- ListSources: filters by name only.
- Get exists for a single session, activity or source.

Sources: discovery document https://jules.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1alpha, https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/sessions

Since 26 Jan 2026 the API can download a session's whole change set as a git patch (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).

Repository Memory is retrieved internally by the agent. Its retrieval mechanism and any user view or edit are undocumented (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).
links_sessions_to_code:
The links run from session to code, and are all held on Google's side:
- sourceContext.source (sources/github-{owner}-{repo}) plus githubRepoContext.startingBranch fix where a session starts.
- An optional workingBranch names the push target.
- Every changeSet artifact carries the baseCommitId its unidiff applies to.
- outputs.pullRequest records the PR url, baseRef and headRef.

Sources: https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/types, discovery document.

The reverse direction, from code back to session, is weak:
- Commits from a published branch show Jules as author, or co-author depending on the attribution mode (https://jules.google/docs/code/, https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).
- The GitHub-issue trigger (label an issue "jules") makes Jules comment on the issue with the PR link (https://jules.google/docs/running-tasks/).

I could not verify whether PR bodies or commit messages embed the session URL or ID, or the prompt and plan. The docs do not say (https://jules.google/docs/code/). The official GitHub Action's README does not mention recording session IDs either (https://github.com/google-labs-code/jules-action).

The full transcript never lands in git.
scale:
No claims about storage or throughput scale. The published limits are:
- daily tasks (rolling 24 h): 15, 100 and 300 (free, Pro, Ultra)
- concurrent tasks: 3, 15 and 60 (https://jules.google/docs/usage-limits/)
- API page sizes: at most 100 (discovery document)

A Planning Critic for auto-approved plans claims a 9.5% cut in task failures (26 Jan 2026, https://jules.google/docs/changelog/).

The product left beta and launched publicly on 6 Aug 2025 (https://blog.google/technology/google-labs/jules-now-available/).

Timeline:
- REST API: 3 Oct 2025
- Jules Tools CLI: 2 Oct 2025
- latest changelog entry: 9 Mar 2026 (Gemini 3.1 Pro); none since (https://jules.google/docs/changelog/)
- discovery document revision: 20260929, so the API is still being maintained
privacy_security:
What is documented:
- "Jules does not train on private repository content" (https://jules.google/docs/faq/).
- Code runs in "a secure, cloud-based virtual machine (VM) with internet access". Users "are responsible for the code you run" and should keep secrets and untrusted packages out of repos (https://jules.google/docs/faq/).
- VMs are short-lived and isolated per task (https://jules.google/docs/environment/, https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/).
- Deleted tasks "are removed permanently" (https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/). The API also has DELETE and archive/unarchive (discovery document).
- The API key is shown once and must not be committed (https://jules.google/docs/api/reference/authentication). The discovery document also declares the OAuth scope cloud-platform, while the docs describe API keys only.
- GitHub access goes through the "Google Labs Jules" app with per-repo selection (https://jules.google/docs/tasks-repos/).

What is not documented on the Jules docs: retention periods, encryption at rest, redaction of secrets in stored bash output or transcripts, how per-source environment variables are stored, and memory deletion.

The Jules privacy page (https://jules.google.com/privacy) is a client-side app that returned "not yet available in your region" to my fetch, so I could not verify it. The site footer links to the general Google Privacy Policy (https://policies.google.com/privacy).

Stored agentMessage and bashOutput are raw strings with no trust labelling. A consumer has to treat them as untrusted.
license: Jules is a proprietary hosted Google service under Google Terms of Service (https://policies.google.com/terms, linked from https://jules.google/). The CLI ships on npm as @google/jules (https://jules.google/docs/cli/reference). I did not verify the licenses of the CLI or of google-labs-code/jules-action.
lesson_for_parinn:
Jules shows a split ParleyInn should copy. History lives in its own store as a typed, append-only event union. Every record has exactly one event kind and an originator (user, agent or system), and code-bearing artifacts are anchored as (baseCommitId, unidiffPatch, suggestedCommitMessage). Git carries only outcomes: branches, PRs and commit attribution.

For ParleyInn:
1. Give each record a code anchor: the base commit plus a patch digest. Any session event can then be tied to, and replayed against, an exact commit without transcripts entering the repo.
2. Make incremental sync work by cursor. Jules uses a create_time filter. ParleyInn should use its hash-chain sequence number or head hash instead of wall-clock time. That fits I10, and it lets an ephemeral sandbox pull just "what's new since X" without trusting server clocks.

The counter-lesson is Jules' weak point: vendor custody, a polling-only API, no reverse link from commit to session, and raw untrusted agentMessage and bashOutput strings. Any Jules importer must sit outside ParleyInn's network-free core (I4). It must ingest those fields only as enveloped, untrusted data, never as TrustedText (I2).

name: goose (Agentic AI Foundation / Linux Foundation; formerly block/goose)
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
Each session gets a metadata row and an ordered list of messages. The metadata covers id, name, description, working_dir, timestamps, session_type, provider and model config, goose_mode, recipe JSON and recipe values, extension_data JSON, token and cost totals, parent_session_id (for subagents), project_id and archived_at. Each message holds role and content_json (the full content blocks: text, thinking, tool requests and tool results). There is also a per-call usage ledger (model, tokens, cost, is_compaction flag). The logs guide confirms the database holds "Tool calls and results (IDs, arguments, responses, success/failure status)" (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/logs). Schema source: https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose/src/session/session_manager.rs (create_schema, around L1028-1100).

The record can be changed after the fact. replace_conversation deletes every message row of a session and re-inserts the conversation. Rewind and fork delete messages after a given point (truncate_conversation). Message metadata and tool_meta are updated in place. Deleting a session hard-deletes its rows (same file, around L1967-2003, L2288-2312, L2620-2660, L2790-2830). The docs also say a delete "cannot be undone".

Compaction itself does not delete anything. Original messages are flagged agentVisible=false and stay visible to the user. A summary message is added that is agent-only (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose/src/context_mgmt/mod.rs, around L137-148; flags defined in crates/goose-provider-types/src/conversation/message.rs, MessageMetadata).

Separate stores: CLI command history is a text file at ~/.config/goose/history.txt. System logs live in ~/.local/state/goose/logs/, and CLI log folders are deleted after two weeks (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/logs).
where_stored:
One local SQLite database per user, in WAL mode. Paths are ~/.local/share/goose/sessions/sessions.db on Unix and %APPDATA%\Block\goose\data\sessions\sessions.db on Windows (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/logs).

Before v1.10.0 each session was its own .jsonl file. Those files are imported automatically on upgrade and then left on disk unmanaged (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/sessions/session-management).

Session history is not kept in git, on a server or in the cloud. The only way it leaves the machine is a manual export file (JSON, YAML, Markdown or HTML).
format_and_model:
Relational SQLite accessed through sqlx, schema version 16 (CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 16 in session_manager.rs). Tables:
- sessions: TEXT primary key plus metadata columns. JSON blobs sit in TEXT columns: extension_data, recipe_json, model_config_json.
- messages: INTEGER AUTOINCREMENT id, a message_id string ("msg_<session>_<uuidv4>" when none is supplied), session_id foreign key, role, content_json, created_timestamp, metadata_json. Messages are ordered by (created_timestamp, id), and add_message never lets a new message sort ahead of the ones already stored.
- usage_ledger.
- schema_version.
- Provider inventory tables.
- Migration 10 also creates threads and thread_messages tables for upgraded databases. The fresh schema does not include them (observed in source).

Session IDs are local, per-day counters, YYYYMMDD_<N>. The counter is computed as MAX+1 over the local database inside a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction (session_manager.rs, around L1630-1650; docs: "Session IDs use the format YYYYMMDD_<COUNT>").

Export: the JSON export is the serialized Session struct, conversation included. Markdown and YAML exports are also available (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/documentation/docs/guides/goose-cli-commands.md, "session export").

Import: accepts native goose JSON, and also converts Claude Code .jsonl (~/.claude/projects/...), Codex rollouts and Pi .jsonl into goose JSON (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose/src/session/import_formats/mod.rs). The docs say import is Desktop-only. The CLI source, however, has an Import subcommand for "JSON or a Claude Code / Codex / Pi .jsonl" (crates/goose-cli/src/cli.rs L579). Docs and code disagree here.
multi_writer_and_merge:
On one machine, several writers share one file. The CLI, the Desktop app's backend, the ACP server and the scheduler all open the same sessions.db. Every write runs in a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction with WAL and a 30 s busy_timeout (session_manager.rs, around L950-955). A code comment records a fixed race: two processes creating the schema on first run hit "table already exists". The fix is BEGIN IMMEDIATE plus IF NOT EXISTS (around L995-1010). Desktop and CLI therefore see the same history; the docs note "Deleting a session from goose Desktop will also delete it from the CLI".

Across machines there is no merge at all. The only path is export to JSON, then import. "Importing creates a new session with a new ID rather than overwriting existing sessions" (session-management doc). The ID must be re-minted because IDs are local counters that would collide. There is no dedupe, no conflict resolution, no provenance link back to the source session, and no hash chain. Copy and fork likewise create a new session and copy the messages (copy_session, fork).
realtime:
No real-time sync or replication of history exists.

Roaming agents (crate goose-roaming) are experimental. They are "not included in released goose binaries" and need a source build with the roaming feature. A remote ACP client can drive a host's agent live over iroh QUIC, peer to peer, falling back to goose-managed or n0 relays. All history stays in the host's sessions.db. Roaming "adds no session semantics", and live multi-viewer co-driving of one session is explicitly deferred.

Sources: https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/roaming-agents and https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose-roaming/README.md.

On a single machine, no change-notification mechanism is documented. Clients re-read the shared database.
search_retrieval:
Cross-session recall comes from the "chatrecall" platform extension, which is off by default (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/mcp/chatrecall-mcp). It has two modes:
- Keyword mode: the query is split on whitespace, and each word becomes LOWER(json_extract(content.value,'$.text')) LIKE '%word%', OR-joined. Only agent-visible text blocks are searched, excluding turn-context blocks. Results are ordered by timestamp descending, with a default limit of 10 and a maximum of 50. Optional filters are a date range, excluding the current session, and session_type.
- Session-id mode: returns the first and last 3 messages of a session.

There is no FTS5 index, no BM25 ranking and no embeddings (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose/src/session/chat_history_search.rs; crates/goose/src/agents/platform_extensions/chatrecall.rs).

Other retrieval: `goose session list` can filter by working dir, limit results and output JSON, and the docs suggest querying sessions.db directly with sqlite3.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weakly. Each session stores working_dir, an optional project_id and recipe info. Tool calls and results, including file edits and shell commands, sit inside content_json. Compaction's StructuredSummary can carry FileActivity, meaning which files were touched (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose-context-management/README.md).

I found no git linkage: no commit SHA, branch, trailer, git note or worktree identity. A grep of session_manager.rs for git or branch fields came back empty.
privacy_security:
Local-first. The docs say goose logs "are never sent to external servers or third parties" (https://goose-docs.ai/docs/guides/logs). PostHog telemetry is opt-in: it sends only if the user explicitly enabled it, and GOOSE_TELEMETRY_OFF forces it off (crates/goose/src/posthog.rs). I did not verify the exact telemetry payload.

At rest:
- sessions.db is plaintext SQLite with no encryption.
- On Unix the sessions directory is chmod 0700 at creation (session_manager.rs, around L940-947).
- Session content gets no secret redaction. Tool outputs are stored verbatim, and the JSON export contains everything.
- The Markdown export truncates long tool output for readability, which is not a security measure.
- Provider secrets live in the OS keyring or a separate secrets file (crates/goose/src/config/base.rs), not in sessions.

Prompt-injection handling:
- A scanner and an optional adversary.md inspector review tool calls; the adversary inspector fails open (crates/goose/src/security/).
- Recalled history is returned to the model as a plain tool result, annotated audience=assistant, with no untrusted-content envelope (chatrecall.rs).

Roaming has a written trust audit. Identity is one ed25519 key per node, kept in a 0600 file. Access uses a mutual public-key allowlist that fails closed. Revocation is live, within about 2 s. Relays see only metadata. The audit also states plainly that "Accepting a key is equivalent to granting shell access", and there is no per-peer action audit log (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/b9db895a771dbed15d854b241c4cf77e6f89a538/crates/goose-roaming/SECURITY.md).
scale: I found no documented scale claims or benchmarks for session storage. The design is one SQLite file per user. Schema v16 added a composite index on messages(session_id, created_timestamp, id) for ordered reads. Project-level numbers, not storage scale: about 54.9k GitHub stars, 15+ LLM providers and 70+ MCP extensions per the README (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn:
Do not mint record identity from a local counter. goose's YYYYMMDD_N session IDs are allocated with MAX+1 in the local database. As a result, the only way to move history between machines, JSON export then import, has to create a new session with a new ID. Provenance, dedupe and idempotent re-import are all lost, so two machines can never converge on one history.

For ParleyInn to move history over git or any other transport across worktrees, sandboxes and machines, every event needs a globally unique, content-derived identity: a hash-chain link plus an origin or agent ID. Then merging is an idempotent union of append-only logs, never a re-keyed copy.

Two goose patterns are worth keeping. Compaction-by-visibility-flag (agentVisible=false while the user still sees the message) keeps the record lossless. A single local SQLite file with WAL and BEGIN IMMEDIATE works well as the per-machine writer arbiter.

Two goose behaviours to avoid. Its rewind and replace operations delete rows, which ParleyInn's I10 forbids. Its chatrecall returns past text unenveloped, which is exactly the channel ParleyInn's I2 closes.

name: Goose session export / import, with the encrypted Nostr share link (aaif-goose/goose, formerly block/goose)
status: archived
what_is_stored:
STATUS IN SHORT: Goose itself is active (Apache-2.0, Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation; https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose). The Nostr share feature was added on 2026-05-13 (PR #8922), first shipped in v1.35.0 (2026-05-21), and was last present in v1.52.0 (2026-09-22). On 2026-09-30 it was removed from main by "Remove Nostr session sharing from goose core" (PR #12453, closes issue #12169). The next release (main is at 1.53.0) will not have `--nostr`. Plain JSON export and import stay. The mankier man pages show the v1.35 to v1.52 CLI. Verified by cloning the repo and running `git tag --contains` on both commits.

WHAT IS STORED: (1) Locally, a full Goose session. The `sessions` row holds id, name, description, working_dir, project_id, parent_session_id, session_type, token and cost counters, provider_name, model_config_json, recipe_json, extension_data JSON and goose_mode. The `messages` table holds role, content_json (text, tool calls and results, thinking), timestamps and metadata. There are also `usage_ledger` and `threads` tables (schema v16). (2) Export writes that whole Session struct, pretty-printed with serde_json, as JSON or YAML. Markdown is a readable rendering that trims long tool output. main also lists html. The JSON includes the conversation, working_dir, the recipe and extension_data. extension_data contains `enabled_extensions.v0`, the list of extension configs, which includes the command and arguments for stdio MCP servers. (3) With `--nostr`, exactly that JSON was encrypted and published as one Nostr event. Nothing else was stored remotely.
where_stored: Local: one embedded SQLite DB at $XDG_DATA_HOME/goose/sessions/sessions.db, default ~/.local/share/goose/sessions/sessions.db, or %APPDATA%\Block\goose\data\sessions\sessions.db on Windows. It has used SQLite since v1.10.0 (2025-10-14). Older per-session .jsonl files are imported once and then left on disk unmanaged. Export goes to stdout or a file. Nostr share (v1.35 to v1.52): public Nostr relays. Defaults were wss://relay.damus.io, wss://relay.primal.net, wss://nos.lol and wss://relay.nostr.band. They can be overridden with the GOOSE_NOSTR_RELAYS config key or repeated `--relay` flags. The event was a single kind-30278 event (in the addressable 30000-39999 range). Nothing is stored in git.
format_and_model:
Native model: a session row plus an ordered list of message rows. Messages use MCP/rmcp content types: text, tool request and response, thinking and redacted thinking. Export is that model serialized as one JSON or YAML document, with no per-event hashing, signing or chaining. The Nostr share (nostr_share.rs at v1.52.0) worked like this:
- It generated a fresh throwaway signing keypair for each share (Keys::generate) and a separate random encryption SecretKey.
- It encrypted the JSON with NIP-44 v2 (secp256k1 ECDH to its own public key, then HKDF, ChaCha20 and HMAC-SHA256), which in effect is symmetric encryption under a key carried in the link.
- It built the event with content = ciphertext, tag d = "goose-session-<uuidv7>" and tag client = "goose".
- It printed `goose://sessions/nostr?nevent=<bech32 NIP-19 event pointer with author, kind and relay hints>&key=<hex secret key>`.
- Import parses the link, fetches the event by id and kind 30278 from the relay hints (8s connect and 10s fetch timeouts), decrypts it, then runs the normal JSON import.
Import format detection sniffs the first line. Accepted inputs are Goose JSON, Claude Code JSONL (lines with sessionId plus type or uuid), Codex rollouts (session_meta first line) and Pi JSONL (session header). The Claude Code importer is lossy: it keeps user, assistant (including thinking) and ai-title lines and drops attachments, queue operations and hook lines. NIP-44's spec currently allows plaintexts up to 2^32-1 bytes using a 6-byte length prefix. Relay event-size limits were not checked and are unverified.
multi_writer_and_merge: On one machine, several Goose processes (CLI, desktop, ACP server) share sessions.db. It runs in WAL mode with a 30s busy_timeout, and schema creation uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE so concurrent first starts do not race. The store is mutable, not append-only: replace_conversation deletes and reinserts all of a session's messages, truncation deletes messages after a timestamp, and content_json and metadata are updated in place. There is no cross-machine sync and no merge. Import always creates a new session with a new id and never merges into an existing one. Fork and copy duplicate a session. A Nostr share was a one-shot snapshot. It was never updated: although the kind is addressable, each share used a new key and d-tag. Two people sharing the same session produce two independent copies.
realtime: No. Export and share are manual, point-in-time snapshots. Nostr was used only as a store-and-fetch drop box (publish once, fetch by event id). There were no subscriptions, live updates or streaming of a running session. A desktop fix (PR #9918) only deduplicated double-fired deep-link imports.
search_retrieval: Local only. The Chat Recall / cross-session search runs a case-insensitive `LOWER(json_extract(content.value,'$.text')) LIKE ?` over message JSON, with an optional date range and session-type filter. The default limit is 10, and the docs say results are capped at the 10 most recent matching messages. There is no FTS index and no embeddings. Indexes cover session_id, timestamps, message_id, updated_at, session_type and parent. The docs also suggest raw sqlite3 queries. Shared Nostr sessions are unsearchable: content is encrypted, and you can only fetch by the exact event id plus key from the link.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. A session records working_dir and an optional project_id, plus parent_session_id for subagents and forks. There are no commit SHAs, branches, diffs or git trailers in the schema. On resume, Goose warns if the current directory differs from the session's working_dir. Imports from Claude Code, Codex and Pi carry over cwd as working_dir only.
privacy_security:
Local data is plaintext SQLite. The docs promise logs and sessions are never sent to external servers. Export does no secret redaction: the full transcript, tool outputs, working_dir, recipe and extension configs go out verbatim. Markdown only truncates long tool output for readability. Nostr share properties:
- Relays see only ciphertext. The NIP-44 padding still leaks approximate size, plus the timestamp, a `client=goose` tag and a d-tag. The publisher's IP is visible to relays.
- The decryption key travels in the link's query string. The desktop warned: "Anyone with this link can fetch and decrypt the session. Treat it like a secret."
- In #8922's review, a bot flagged that full URLs, key included, were being logged. Maintainers called that "overdramatic", so it was dismissed. This comes from the PR page summary.
- The signing key was thrown away. As a result the sharer can never send a NIP-09 deletion and cannot revoke the event; relays may keep it indefinitely.
- An enterprise switch, GOOSE_DISABLE_NOSTR_SHARING=true (PR #10044), hid only the desktop UI. The CLI path did not check it.
- The nostr crate had a NIP-44 decrypt panic, RUSTSEC-2026-0216 (CVSS 7.5, a denial of service on crafted payloads). It was patched by a bump to 0.44.6 (PR #10733).
- Issue #12169's stated reasons for removal: a heavyweight transport for what it does; throwaway keys embedded in links mean core cannot check that an imported session is authentic; there is no useful UI point at import to involve the user in trust decisions; transport belongs to client implementers; and the dependency burden.
- Imports do sanitize Unicode tag characters (NFC normalization plus stripping) in imported tool output, against hidden-text injection.
- My own code reading, not tested end to end: import copies extension_data verbatim, and `goose session --resume` restores extensions from it (EnabledExtensionsState::for_session, then the stdio launcher). The only gate on stdio commands is an OSV malware lookup for npx/uvx packages. So an imported or shared session can carry stdio extension commands, a list of commands to run, that start when the session is resumed. I did not confirm whether any prompt intervenes.
scale: No scale claims found. It is single-user and local, with one SQLite file per user. A Nostr share is one event per session snapshot, and relay size limits are unverified. The repo itself: about 54.9k stars and 5,767 commits on main, per the GitHub page fetched 2026-10-02.
license: Apache-2.0
lesson_for_parinn:
Treat any transport for shared history as a carrier of untrusted, unauthenticated data, and make the payload pure data. Goose's maintainers retired Nostr sharing within about 4.5 months. They gave four reasons: the throwaway per-share keys meant an imported session could not be authenticated, a bearer key in a URL cannot be revoked (and was logged), there was no useful trust point in the UI at import, and the dependency weight was not worth it. Also, the exported JSON was not just transcript: it included settings that run things on resume (extension commands and recipes). For ParleyInn, applied in requirement terms:
(1) Any export or import format should hold only enveloped, append-only events with hash-chain and signature metadata, so authenticity is checked against a known writer key before anything is accepted. It should never carry settings that execute or change behavior (I2).
(2) Keep sharing transport out of the core, which already must not touch the network (I4). Expose a deterministic, verifiable bundle and leave relays, git remotes or Nostr to an outside, opt-in tool.
(3) Make revocation and redaction a first-class part of the design before sharing ships: a published ciphertext with a lost signing key can never be deleted.
(4) Make importing a Claude Code JSONL transcript lossless and audited. Goose silently drops attachment and hook lines, which would break I6 for ParleyInn.

name: Grace (Scott Arbeit) - "Version Control for the AI Era"
category: Cloud-native, centralized, event-sourced VCS with agent-work capture (work items, prompts, summaries, continuous review)
status: beta
what_is_stored: File versions, DirectoryVersions, References and Branches, plus repo, org and owner entities. Work items (title, Markdown description, status, links to references, promotion sets and artifacts). Attachments of type summary, prompt or notes. Promotion sets and queues, validation results, review notes and checkpoints, policy snapshots, approvals and webhooks. Reference kinds are Save, Checkpoint, Commit and Promotion. `grace watch` turns every on-disk save into an uploaded file plus a Save reference. Agent capture has four commands. `grace agent bootstrap` writes a local identity: an agent GUID, a display name and a source (default "cli"). `grace agent work start/stop/status` opens a session tied to a work item. `grace agent add-summary --prompt-file --prompt-origin` uploads the summary text and optionally the prompt text as artifacts linked to the work item. Full agent transcripts and tool calls are not captured; only what the agent or user chooses to submit is stored. Active agent-session records are held in server memory (ConcurrentDictionary) and are explicitly "process-local across restart". The durable trace is the AgentWorkStarted, AgentWorkStopped, AgentSummaryAdded and AgentBootstrapped automation events and the work-item artifacts. Note: the README still lists `grace agent bootstrap` as a roadmap item ("give coding agents context"). In the code as of 2026-09-11 it only bootstraps identity, not prompt context.
where_stored: On a server/cloud backend, not in git. Orleans virtual actors persist their state to Azure Cosmos DB (dev default container name "grace-events"). File content and artifacts (including prompt and summary attachments) go to Azure Blob Storage. Event streams go out over Azure Service Bus. SignalR, backed by Redis, provides live client coordination. Aspire orchestrates the stack, with emulators for local development. Each working copy also has a `.grace/` directory holding `.grace/objects` (files renamed with their SHA-256), a local Grace Status file, an IPC file and a SQLite local-state DB. AWS and other clouds are aspirational, not implemented.
format_and_model: Event sourcing per actor. Each Orleans grain (Branch, Reference, Repository, WorkItem, Artifact, PromotionSet, Review, DirectoryVersion and others) persists an `IPersistentState<List<XxxEvent>>`: the entity's whole event list is its grain state. Projections are precomputed and cached from those lists. EventMetadata carries Timestamp (NodaTime Instant), CorrelationId, Principal, ClientType and a Properties dictionary. No per-event hash chaining or signing was found. Automation events use an AutomationEventEnvelope {EventId Guid, EventType, EventTime, CorrelationId, Owner/Org/RepositoryId, ActorId, DataJson}. Content model: DirectoryVersions and files carry both BLAKE3 and SHA-256 version hashes as data fields, not primary keys. Keys are GUIDs (DirectoryVersionId and similar), chosen so hash algorithms can change without a Git-style SHA-1 migration. Large files use manifest-backed content-addressed storage (ADR-0001): clients split content into ContentBlocks, upload only missing blocks and finalize a FileManifest. Domain code is F# with Orleans serializers. The CLI emits a JSON envelope (GraceReturnValue<T> / GraceError) under `--output Json`.
multi_writer_and_merge: Centralized and multitenant: Orleans actors serialize writes per entity, so there is no distributed merge of history. Grace "doesn't do merges, it does promotions". In the default "single-step" branching, a child branch may be promoted only to its parent and must first be based on the parent's latest version; the parent then points at the child's version. `grace watch` auto-rebases a branch when its parent is promoted. A promotion queue with promotion sets, integration candidates, gates and attestations resolves conflicts "according to rules and confidence levels you set". Agent sessions allow one active session per (repository, agent) key. A conflicting start is rejected; operation IDs make retries idempotent replays. In V1, renames are captured as a delete plus an add, with no rename identity.
realtime: Yes, central to the design. `grace watch` uses a FileSystemWatcher to upload changed files, recompute directory versions and create a Save reference, "generally within a second of the file being saved". It holds a SignalR connection per branch: same-branch reference notifications wake Watch, which replays server-ordered Commit, Checkpoint and Save events after a stored opaque cursor. Watch advances that cursor only after durable local completion. Service Bus streams and signed outbound webhooks let external consumers react to committed facts. The README pitches watching and reviewing agent work "in real-time from your computer". It needs a reachable Grace Server; there is no offline or peer-to-peer mode.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by ID. Work items are fetched by GUID or number (`grace workitem show 42`), attachments with `attachments list/show --latest/download`, plus `grace diff commit|promotion|checkpoint`, `grace status`, and JSON output with a `--select` projection. There is no work-item list or search yet. The design doc marks repository list and search (DEC-009) as an open decision, organization-wide search as deferred, and full-text search of comment content as deferred. No semantic or full-text search over prompts or summaries was found.
links_sessions_to_code: Partly, and only through explicit, cooperative CLI calls. An agent session is bound to a WorkItemIdOrNumber and a PromotionSetId. The work item links to References (code versions), promotion sets and artifacts (summary, prompt, notes). Review reports attach to promotion candidates. The link runs session -> work item -> reference/promotion set, not per prompt -> per file change. Saves from `grace watch` are timestamped but not tied to a specific prompt or turn. Capture depends on the agent being told to run `grace agent bootstrap` / `work start` / `add-summary`; there is no hook into Claude Code or other agents' transcripts.
scale: Claims only, no published benchmarks: "multitenant, built for massive repositories, insane numbers of developers and agents, and ludicrous amounts of code and binary files of any size", and Cosmos DB "at ludicrous scale and speed". The one concrete data point is anecdotal: the largest tested status file was about 53 MB, deserialized in "low two-digit milliseconds". The roadmap lists "Repeatable performance benchmarking" as not yet done. The README warns alpha with breaking changes, "not ready for or intended for production".
privacy_security: Alpha. SECURITY.md says hardening "may not yet cover all threat models". Vulnerabilities are reported through public GitHub issues with a Security label; there is no private channel. Auth uses personal access tokens and test auth for local development; managed identity is the pre-production path for cross-account blob SAS. Redaction exists only for operational surfaces: webhook and approval URLs are redacted in logs and CLI JSON, and `grace doctor` has redaction notes. Webhook deliveries are signed (signature, timestamp, payload hash, delivery id). Nothing redacts or secret-scans uploaded prompts, summaries or auto-saved files: `grace watch` uploads every non-ignored file on save, so secrets in the working tree reach cloud storage unless `.graceignore` excludes them. No Grace-level client-side or end-to-end encryption is documented (at-rest encryption would be whatever Azure provides by default; not verified in the docs). Attachments have logical delete with a recovery window of LogicalDeleteDays (default 30), and Save and Checkpoint references expire per SaveDays and CheckpointDays. The author calls using the event stream (for example, save frequency) to monitor developers "stupid" and floats mitigations: keep saves off the shared Service Bus, or disable auto-save per repo. He leaves the design to the community. Stored prompts are not treated as untrusted; review prompts and models are user-configured and run server-side.
lesson_for_parinn: Grace is one of the few VCSes that models agent work explicitly, and even it captures only curated artifacts: an opt-in prompt file and a summary linked to a work item, which in turn links to code references. It keeps live agent-session state process-local and throws it away on restart, so the lossless transcript is missing. That gap is what ParleyInn fills, and it suggests a clean interop seam: ParleyInn keeps the full append-only, hash-chained session record locally, and exports only a derived, redacted digest that can be attached to a work item, PR or Grace reference. That digest would be a summary, the prompt, and the record's head hash plus the content hashes of the code it touched. The full record is never pushed. Two smaller patterns are worth copying. First, keep hashes as data fields next to stable IDs, not as primary keys, so the hash algorithm can change later; Grace already carries BLAKE3 and SHA-256 side by side. Second, give every mutating call a client-generated operation ID so retries from flaky sandboxes replay idempotently. Avoid Grace's auto-upload-on-save without a redaction step: it would breach ParleyInn's no-network and untrusted-content invariants.
