name: Graft
status: beta
what_is_stored: Sparse, append-only collections of fixed-size 4 KiB pages organized into Volumes. Each Volume can represent entire databases, data subsets, or arbitrary sparse/partially replicated datasets. Pages are indexed starting at 1, with sparse indexing (not every PageIdx must be filled).
where_stored: Dual-storage architecture: (1) Local FjallStorage using LSM-tree based storage with partitions for tags, volumes, logs, and pages; (2) Remote object storage (S3-compatible, filesystem, or in-memory) storing commits at paths `/logs/{LogId}/commits/{LSN}` and segments at `/segments/{SegmentId}`. Segments are Zstd-compressed frames (up to 64 pages per frame).
format_and_model: Transactional storage engine using Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs—monotonically increasing per-volume transaction ids), immutable Snapshots (logical views at a point-in-time), Commits (transaction records with commit hashes), and Segments (compressed collections of pages). Pages use 128-bit Graft Identifiers (GIDs) with embedded timestamp and random components, encoded as 24-character base58 strings. SQLite extension via VFS integration (libgraft_ext) supports any SQLite version after 3.44.0.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple concurrent writers within a single process supported via read-your-writes semantics on staged segments. Commit serialization enforced through optimistic concurrency control with global write lock. Cross-process access NOT supported. Conflict/divergence detection: when both local and remote logs have uncommitted changes, a `VolumeDiverged` error is returned requiring manual intervention—automatic merge not yet implemented (planned future feature for non-overlapping transactions using optimistic snapshot isolation).
realtime: Not true real-time. Background autosync available (configurable interval in seconds via `PRAGMA graft_autosync`). Writes are pushed/pulled on demand or on configured schedule. No event subscriptions or webhooks mentioned.
search_retrieval: Lazy page loading on-demand. When a reader requests a page, Graft searches the snapshot to find the segment containing it, then fetches that segment's frame from remote storage if not already cached locally. No full-text search or structured query capabilities beyond SQLite (when used as SQLite backend).
links_sessions_to_code: No. Graft is a general-purpose transactional storage engine for lazy partial replication. It has no built-in support for linking agent sessions, prompts, or code changes. Potential use case for such linkage would require application-level implementation.
privacy_security: No built-in encryption or redaction documented. All data in object storage and local storage stored unencrypted. No mention of secrets handling, access control, or audit logging. No vulnerability disclosure policy found. Still alpha-quality software—security review pending per README recommendation to contact maintainer before production use.
lesson_for_parinn: Divergence detection as a safety boundary: Graft demonstrates that partial replication with strong consistency can avoid silent merges through strict divergence detection. When writers on both local and remote have uncommitted changes, Graft fails loudly rather than attempting automatic resolution. This principle aligns with ParleyInn's I2 invariant (no automatic path from untrusted content to model) and I9 invariant (fail open except where continuing breaks other invariants). The key insight: treat divergence as a protocol error, not a feature. Graft's optimistic concurrency control with serialized commits also provides a model for ensuring monotonic progress without deadlock—relevant for ParleyInn's multi-agent, multi-worktree model.

name: Graphiti (getzep/graphiti), plus the Zep Cloud context
category: temporal knowledge graph memory (LLM-extracted graph over ingested 'episodes')
status: shipped. Graphiti is active: graphiti-core v0.30.2 went up on PyPI on 2026-09-08 (https://pypi.org/pypi/graphiti-core/json) and the MCP server has its own tag, mcp-v1.1.0 (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/releases). Zep Community Edition is deprecated: it gets no more updates or support, and its repo stays open under Apache-2.0 (https://blog.getzep.com/announcing-a-new-direction-for-zeps-open-source-strategy/). The help.getzep.com/ce-deprecation-notice URL returned a 404 when fetched on 2026-10-02. getzep/zep is now 'Zep Cloud: Examples & Integrations', 'not Zep's product' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/zep/main/README.md). Zep Cloud is a proprietary managed service. Graphiti's Kuzu backend is deprecated and will be removed (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
what_is_stored:
Four layers, per the README (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti):
(1) Episodes (EpisodicNode). The raw ingested data, kept verbatim as provenance, 'the ground truth stream'. Fields: content, source (EpisodeType message / json / text), source_description, valid_at (the reference time), entity_edges and episode_metadata (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/graphiti_core/nodes.py).
(2) Entity nodes. A name, a name_embedding, an LLM-written summary that changes over time, and typed attributes.
(3) Entity edges, which are the 'facts'. Each holds a relation name, a natural-language fact string, a fact_embedding, the list of episode UUIDs that support it, valid_at / invalid_at (event time), created_at / expired_at (system time), reference_time and attributes (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/graphiti_core/edges.py).
(4) Community nodes, which are cluster summaries, and Saga nodes, which hold running summaries of ordered episode chains. Structural edges: EpisodicEdge (MENTIONS), HasEpisodeEdge, NextEpisodeEdge and CommunityEdge.
Developers can define custom entity and edge types as Pydantic models.
where_stored:
An external graph database the user runs. Supported: Neo4j 5.26+, FalkorDB 1.1.2+ (falkordblite is the embedded variant), and Amazon Neptune Database or Neptune Analytics with OpenSearch Serverless for full-text search. Kuzu 0.11.2 still works but is deprecated (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti; https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/releases).
The MCP server defaults to FalkorDB in one Docker container. On FalkorDB each group_id gets its own graph (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server).
Zep Cloud runs on a proprietary 'Context Graph Engine', fully managed or in the customer's VPC (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
Nothing lives in git or in the working tree.
format_and_model:
A property graph with a bi-temporal fact model. Every node and edge carries a uuid4 and a group_id ('partition of the graph') (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/graphiti_core/edges.py).
On ingest, the LLM extracts entities and edges from each episode using prompts such as extract_nodes, extract_edges, dedupe_nodes and dedupe_edges (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/graphiti_core/prompts). It then resolves them against what the graph already holds.
When a new fact contradicts an old one, the old edge is not deleted. Its invalid_at / expired_at fields are set ('automatic fact invalidation'), which preserves history and supports point-in-time queries (https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/overview).
Episodes stay verbatim, but entities, edges and summaries are derived by the LLM and are non-deterministic. Neither the derived graph nor the episodes are append-only or hash-chained: delete_episode cascade-deletes the facts that episode alone created, and clear_graph wipes a group (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server).
The Zep paper describes the architecture as episode, semantic-entity and community subgraphs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no merge model. Writers share one database, and the database's transactions are the only coordination.
The library runs ingestion concurrently, bounded by SEMAPHORE_LIMIT (default 10, set low to avoid LLM 429 errors) (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
The MCP server serializes episodes per group_id, but only inside one process: QueueService keeps an in-memory asyncio.Queue per group_id and one worker per queue (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/mcp_server/src/services/queue_service.py). Two MCP processes writing the same group are not serialized against each other. The worker also only logs a failed episode with logger.error and moves on, so the failure is never surfaced to the caller.
Agents merge facts semantically, not structurally: LLM dedupe plus temporal invalidation. There is no CRDT, vector clock or causal ordering beyond reference_time and NextEpisode links.
I could not find official guidance on concurrent writers to one group across processes or machines. One third-party wrapper, Gralkor, serializes Graphiti construction per group_id (https://jido-gralkor.hexdocs.pm/Gralkor.GraphitiPool.html).
realtime:
Ingest is incremental: 'new data integrates immediately without batch recomputation' (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
The MCP server's add_memory queues the episode and returns. Processing is asynchronous, so a fact is searchable only after the LLM extraction finishes (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server).
There is no push, subscription or change feed to other readers. Real-time sharing means every agent points at the same database server.
search_retrieval:
Hybrid search: embedding similarity, BM25 full-text and graph traversal (BFS, or search centred on a node via center_node_uuid). Results are fused, optionally reranked (RRF, MMR, node distance or a cross-encoder) and are 'typically sub-second' (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti; https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/overview).
MCP tools: search_nodes (filter by entity type), search_memory_facts (filters on valid_at / invalid_at date ranges), get_episodes, get_episode_entities (traces provenance from an episode to the facts it produced), get_entity_edge, summarize_saga and build_communities (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server).
Retrieval returns derived facts and summaries by default, not verbatim history. Raw episodes come back only through get_episodes and provenance lookups.
links_sessions_to_code:
Not natively. Graphiti has no notion of a repo, commit, file or diff.
The MCP server documents Cursor integration, with a cursor_rules.md that tells the agent to store preferences and procedures in memory, and it works with Claude and other MCP clients (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server). The agent itself decides what to save, as text or JSON episodes.
Session-to-code linkage exists only if the agent writes it into episode text or episode_metadata, or uses a group_id per repo or project. Built-in entity types include 'Procedure' and 'Organization', but nothing code-specific (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/mcp_server/README.md).
scale:
Graphiti's README claims 'parallel processing' and 'sub-second' query latency. It also says retrieval performance 'depends on your setup' (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
Zep Cloud claims 'sub-200ms performance at scale' and an engine 'built for millions of context graphs' (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
The Zep paper (arXiv 2501.13956, January 2025) reports 94.8% on DMR against MemGPT's 93.4%, and on LongMemEval up to 18.5% higher accuracy with about 90% lower latency than baselines (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956). These are vendor-authored benchmarks and I did not verify them independently.
Ingest throughput is bounded by LLM calls per episode, not by the database (the SEMAPHORE_LIMIT guidance, https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
Repo popularity is about 31.4k stars per the WebFetch summary of the GitHub page. The GitHub API was not reachable from this session, so that number is unverified.
privacy_security:
Graphiti (open source):
- No redaction, secret scanning or encryption layer of its own. Security depends on the graph database, and the MCP docs give no authentication or access-control guidance for the HTTP endpoint (https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/mcp-server).
- Every episode's raw content is sent to an external LLM and embedding provider for extraction: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, Azure, or local models through OpenAI-compatible endpoints (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti/tree/main/mcp_server). That is a network data flow by design.
- Telemetry is opt-out PostHog analytics with an anonymous UUID stored in ~/.cache/graphiti/telemetry_anon_id. It does not send episode, node or edge content. Disable it with GRAPHITI_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti).
- Recalled facts are LLM-written text returned to the agent with no untrusted-content envelope. Stored text, including text injected from tool output, can come back as prompt content.
- SECURITY.md routes vulnerability reports through GitHub private reporting, and only the latest 0.x release is supported (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/getzep/graphiti/main/SECURITY.md).

Zep Cloud: SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA BAA for Enterprise, encryption at rest with customer-managed AWS KMS keys, and a VPC deployment option (https://help.getzep.com/security-compliance).
lesson_for_parinn:
Keep the verbatim, append-only record as the source of truth, and treat any LLM-derived graph as a separate projection that can be thrown away and rebuilt.

Graphiti gets the provenance idea right. Every fact carries the episode UUIDs behind it, and supersession is recorded with valid_at / invalid_at and created_at / expired_at instead of overwriting. ParleyInn could use that bi-temporal 'invalidate, don't delete' shape for pinned constraints that change over time, and the episode-to-fact provenance link for recall.

It also shows what to avoid:
- The derived layer is non-deterministic, because LLM extraction breaks I10 rebuildability.
- Ingest needs a network LLM, which breaks I4.
- Recalled facts come back un-enveloped, which breaks I2.
- Episodes can be cascade-deleted.
- The MCP queue serializes writers per group only inside one process and only logs failures, which breaks I6. Multi-machine writers get no ordering guarantee.

ParleyInn should get per-writer ordering from its hash chain, not from an in-process queue, and should count and audit every failed ingest.
license: Graphiti: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/getzep/graphiti). Zep CE: Apache-2.0, unmaintained (https://blog.getzep.com/announcing-a-new-direction-for-zeps-open-source-strategy/). Zep Cloud: proprietary commercial service.

name: GrayCodeAI/trace (two unrelated codebases have used this one module path: (A) v0.1.0 to v0.1.4, June to July 2026, a session-capture library derived from Entire's CLI; (B) the current repo since late September 2026, a self-hosted Git forge with signed agent history)
category: git orphan-branch capture (A, superseded) / self-hosted forge with signed agent-history refs (B, current alpha)
status: B (the forge) is alpha: version 0.0.1, not yet released, 6 commits, 0 stars. Its latest proxy pseudo-version is v0.0.0-20260929181201-2badf3c616bd. A (the session-capture library) is superseded. The tags v0.1.0 to v0.1.4 survive only in the Go module proxy, and the current repo replaced that content. Its stated purpose ("Git-native engineering context, provenance, checkpoint, and continuity") seems to have moved to the sibling repo GrayCodeAI/across. across is local alpha with all agent adapters marked UNIMPLEMENTED. That A moved to across is my inference; no source states it.
what_is_stored:
A (v0.1.4) stored full transcripts as full.jsonl per session, plus user prompts and responses, files touched, token usage and USD cost. It also stored per-checkpoint metadata.json. Temporary shadow branches held whole-worktree snapshots, used for rewind and fork. Supported agents: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Factory Droid, Copilot CLI and Cursor (Cursor without rewind).
B (current) stores deliberately less: structured agent sessions and checkpoints with a description and summary, agent name, ref and linked commit. Its hook adapters (Codex notify, Claude Code Stop, Gemini AfterAgent, Cursor stop) record by default only a fixed completion label, hashed session and turn IDs, and the Git HEAD observed at hook time. The last assistant message is stored only on opt-in (-include-assistant-summary). B never stores raw prompts or tool transcripts. Alongside sessions, B is a whole forge: bare repos, users.json with token hashes, issues and PRs, webhooks, an audit log, LFS, packages, CI logs and a search index.
where_stored:
A: inside the user's own repo. Committed checkpoints went on the orphan branch trace/checkpoints/v1. In-progress state went on local shadow branches named trace/<commit[:7]>-<worktreeHash[:6]>. The working branch got no commits. Config lived in .trace/settings.json and settings.local.json.
B: on a server node's local data directory (data/repos/OWNER/NAME.git, data/*.json, data/search-index). This is a set of JSON files with no central database. On opt-in, signed snapshots are published to a protected per-node Git ref under refs/trace/agent-bundles/ in a private repo, or exported as signed JSON bundle files. The client-side capture config and outbox live in .git/trace-agent-capture.json, outside the working tree.
format_and_model:
A: the trace/checkpoints/v1 tree is sharded by checkpoint ID: a 2-character shard directory, then the rest of the ID, then a session index (0, 1, ...). Each session directory holds metadata.json (CommittedMetadata) and full.jsonl. The checkpoint root holds metadata.json (CheckpointSummary, with aggregated stats and paths to each session's files). Commit subjects read "Checkpoint: <id>". Writes used go-git loose objects. Checkpoint commits were signed best-effort with the user's GPG or SSH git key and fell back to unsigned on failure. The design is an Entire derivative: the module imports github.com/entireio/auth-go, and its docs mirror Entire's shadow-branch model and its condensation step at commit time.
B: sessions are records with numbered checkpoints, each linked to a commit SHA. The export unit is a versioned JSON bundle signed with the node's persistent Ed25519 key (data/node/identity_ed25519). Git publication puts that same snapshot on a per-node ref, adding a new snapshot commit only when sessions changed. Event IDs are hashed provider IDs, so replays are idempotent.
multi_writer_and_merge:
A: concurrent sessions on the same base commit share one shadow branch and their checkpoints interleave, each under its own .trace/metadata/<session-id>/. Condensation merges files_touched and aggregates stats across sessions into a single checkpoint. When the base commit changes, the shadow branch is renamed. The docs found say nothing about cross-machine merges of trace/checkpoints/v1.
B is single-writer by design: one authoritative node per repository, with manual failover. Each node signs only its own history. Imports are append-only: they reject a changed signature, a wrong node ID, missing commits, or a modified earlier checkpoint. Re-import is idempotent and a later bundle can add checkpoints. Imported sessions are read-only, and an export never re-signs another node's sessions. A future milestone would give each writer its own ref namespace (refs/trace/writers/<key>/...) with owner-reviewed promotion. Mirrors stop syncing on divergent or deleted refs until an admin accepts the exact signed object ID.
realtime: Neither version is real-time. A wrote locally and condensed at git commit; the user pushed the branch. B: hooks queue events in a local outbox until the observed HEAD exists on the server, then flush on the next hook or on `trace agent sync`. Mirror and bundle sync is pull-only and scheduled externally. Automatic cross-node session sync is listed as future work.
search_retrieval: A: the README promises a searchable record of sessions, plus rewind, resume and fork from checkpoints. B: literal (non-semantic) search across code, commit messages and structured session summaries. Session results are capped at 100 matches and 280-character excerpts. Workspace search spans repositories, respects read grants, and pages 10 repositories at a time. The browser view is /repos/OWNER/NAME/agents, and the JSON API includes agent-sessions and the bundle endpoints.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, in both. A tied each checkpoint to the user commit that triggered condensation and made per-checkpoint worktree snapshots so code could be rewound. B links every checkpoint to a commit SHA and refuses an import whose target commits are missing. The README states that a hook event records only the HEAD it observed and "does not prove that Codex authored that commit". Authorship verification is not implemented.
privacy_security:
A redacted on condensation, always on: entropy above 4.5, Betterleaks patterns, credentialed URIs, database DSNs and bounded KEY=VALUE credentials, each replaced with REDACTED. Shadow branches were NOT redacted, and users were warned not to push them. Fields named signature or ending in id were skipped. Anyone with repo access could read the full transcripts, including the whole world for a public repo. The module also depended on posthog-go (telemetry) and Entire's auth client.
B minimizes data by default (hashes and labels only, no prompts or transcripts). Its redaction is basic: it masks token, password, secret and authorization assignments and is documented as limited. Git publication is refused for public, mirrored or archived repos, and a repo cannot be made public while an agent ref exists. The docs note that unpublishing does not erase objects already fetched. There is no encryption at rest; the architecture doc says private repos need a separate key-distribution design. Other controls: token hashes only, an Ed25519 node identity pinned on first contact, signed webhooks with SSRF guards, a sandboxing CSP on raw files and Pages, rate limits, TOTP, OIDC and SCIM. Release binaries are unsigned (SHA-256 checksums only).
scale: B gives no performance claims; its only figures are hard caps: code search 100 matches and 512 KiB, index skips files over 2 MiB and stops at 64 MiB of text, commit search scans the newest 1,000 commits. A documented one scale failure: go-git loose objects past the gc.auto threshold (about 6,700) let a background `git gc --auto` prune checkpoint objects still referenced by the worktree index (KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md).
license: MIT for both versions (Copyright 2026 GrayCode AI). B has one direct dependency, golang.org/x/crypto. A had about 30 direct dependencies, including go-git v6 alpha, entireio/auth-go, betterleaks and posthog-go.
lesson_for_parinn:
This project's own pivot points one way. It began by pushing full transcripts on an orphan branch in the code repo: an Entire-style design with unredacted local shadow branches and best-effort redaction and signing. It ended with signed, append-only, per-writer snapshots. Each node signs only its own history and imports are verified against an expected node ID and the target commits. Publication goes to a protected ref only in private repos, is refused for public ones, and is opt-in. Lessons for ParleyInn:
- If git is used as a transport, publish per-writer, append-only signed segments under a per-writer ref namespace (like refs/trace/writers/<key>/), never one shared branch that has to be merged.
- Make import reject any rewrite of history already accepted. This matches ParleyInn's hash chain.
- Never re-sign another writer's records.
- Treat publish-to-git as an explicit, refusable act gated on repo visibility. A deleted ref does not un-leak objects already fetched.
- Avoid go-git loose objects for high-frequency writes (the gc.auto pruning bug in A).
- Keep the capture hook's outbox local and idempotent, keyed by hashed provider IDs, so it fails open (I9) and replays without duplicates.
confidence: medium. High for what each codebase documents, which comes from primary files: the v0.1.4 module zip from the Go proxy and the current main branch. Medium-low on lineage. The tags v0.1.0 to v0.1.4 (June 2 to July 11, 2026) and the 2026-09-29 pseudo-version resolve to the same repo URL, but the current CHANGELOG calls 0.0.1 the "first public version", previously developed privately as MeshGit and Refweave. Nothing found says what happened to the v0.1.x code, so the repo name was reused for a different product. The 2026-09-26 creation date could not be checked: the GitHub API was not reachable from this session. That A was derived from Entire's CLI rests on its import of entireio/auth-go and its matching design, not on any attribution statement. Also not verified: whether anyone uses either version, and the code behind B's README claims.

name: Grov (npm package "grov")
category: Memory layer with team sync. It is a local HTTP proxy or MCP server that uses an LLM to pull structured "memories" out of agent sessions and serves them from a SaaS backend (Supabase plus pgvector).
status: beta, probably dormant. The newest commit on main is 2026-01-28 ("Improve seo"), seen in a clone made on 2026-10-02. npm dist-tag latest is 0.6.19, last modified 2026-01-28, package first created 2025-11-29 (https://registry.npmjs.org/grov). package.json in the repo says 0.6.20, which is not on npm. There have been no commits for about 8 months. I could not check the archived flag or the star count (about 191 in the discovery note) because the GitHub API was blocked in this session. From this sandbox, https://grov.dev returned HTTP 522 (Cloudflare origin timeout) and https://app.grov.dev failed the TLS handshake. That suggests the hosted service may be down, but the sandbox proxy could also cause these errors, so this is unverified.
where_stored: Locally, a SQLite file at ~/.grov/memory.db (better-sqlite3, WAL mode). The directory is created 0700 and the file is chmod 0600 (src/core/store/database.ts). Login tokens go in ~/.grov/credentials.json with 0600 permissions (blog: landing/src/content/blog/team-sync.mdx). With team sync on, memories are upserted to the hosted API at app.grov.dev, backed by Supabase Postgres with pgvector. The privacy page says Supabase data is in the EU and hosting is on Google Cloud EU West 1 (landing/src/pages/privacy.astro). It does not use git: no git storage, refs or notes.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The server is the single source of truth. It does not use CRDTs or git merges.
- Before upload, the client asks the API's /match endpoint for a similar existing memory, scored with hybrid search.
- If there is no match, it inserts. If there is a match, an LLM call (shouldUpdateMemory, Claude Haiku on the user's key) chooses UPDATE or SKIP and lists which old decisions are superseded.
- prepareSyncPayload then marks those decisions active=false with superseded_by, appends new ones, adds an evolution step, and cuts the arrays to their caps (src/core/cloud/cloud-sync.ts).
- Inserts are idempotent: upsert with onConflict 'team_id,client_task_id' (api/src/routes/memories.ts; blog team-sync.mdx).
- Updates overwrite the row by memory_id. Concurrent writers get last-writer-wins, with no version check visible in the code.
- "Memory branches" are labels on memories, not git branches. Merging a branch is a bulk UPDATE that sets branch='main', source_branch and merged_at on memories and chunks. Unmerge reverses it. Only branch admins can do either (api/src/routes/branches.ts).
- The local SQLite store has one writer per machine. Uploads run fire-and-forget in batches of 10, with 3 retries and exponential backoff. The blog describes the failure path as "Silent fail - local capture still works" (team-sync.mdx).
Source: https://github.com/TonyStef/Grov/blob/main/api/src/routes/branches.ts
realtime: Near-real-time push, pull on demand. The README says "Memories sync to your team in real-time": the client uploads when a task finishes or a context threshold is hit. Other agents only see a memory when their proxy calls fetchTeamMemories at the start of a prompt (status=complete, limit 3) (src/integrations/proxy/handlers/preprocess.ts). There is no streaming of in-progress sessions. The only Supabase realtime channel in the code is for the dashboard's plan task list (dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/plans/[id]/_components/task-list.tsx). In the code I read, injection reads only from the cloud. Local SQLite is used by `grov status`, and the comment in src/core/store/tasks.ts says "For CLOUD injection, use fetchTeamMemories()". So without sync, captured memories are not re-injected. That contradicts the "local by default" framing.
search_retrieval:
Hybrid search runs on the server through the Supabase RPC hybrid_search_memories. It combines a pgvector similarity score on the query embedding (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) with a lexical score, and adds a boost when the current files overlap files_touched. The API returns semantic_score, lexical_score, combined_score and file_boost_applied (api/src/lib/search.ts, api/src/lib/embeddings.ts). Semantic search is off if the server has no OPENAI_API_KEY. The dashboard also offers ilike filters on original_query and goal (api/src/routes/memories.ts).

To the agent, retrieval works in two steps. The proxy injects a short preview of up to 3 memories by 8-character ID. The tool description then tells the model to call grov_expand({ids}) before any other tool (src/integrations/proxy/injection/memory-injection.ts; src/integrations/mcp/tools/expand.ts, preview.ts). The local SQLite store has no FTS index.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Memories carry project_path and files_touched; file paths drive the retrieval boost. Schemas include a linked_commit column (local and server) and a file_reasoning table with anchor, line range and code_hash. However, I found nothing in src/ that fills linked_commit: no git invocation and no child_process use outside the store and sync passthrough (grep over src/). Commit linkage is therefore schema-only as far as I can tell. That part is unverified beyond reading the code.
privacy_security:
Local protections:
- ~/.grov is created 0700 and memory.db is set 0600.
- LIKE patterns are escaped.
- Search input to the server is sanitized against PostgREST filter injection (api/src/routes/memories.ts).
- Login is a GitHub OAuth device flow; JWTs use a secret of at least 32 characters (api/src/lib/jwt.ts).

Gaps:
- Session content is not redacted before it goes to Anthropic for extraction or to the cloud. I found no redaction or secret-scrubbing code in src/, api/src or shared/src. scripts/scan-secrets.sh is only a pre-commit hook for the Grov repo itself.
- The proxy on localhost:8080 sees all Claude Code traffic.
- The README tells users to put ANTHROPIC_API_KEY permanently in their shell profile.
- Extraction and drift checks call Claude Haiku. Server-side embeddings call OpenAI, but the privacy page lists Supabase, GCP, Anthropic and Stripe and not OpenAI (landing/src/pages/privacy.astro).
- The privacy page claims TLS in transit and encryption "at rest" (provider-level). There is no end-to-end or client-side encryption.
- Extended-cache mode sends keep-alive API calls on the user's behalf, and is opt-in.

Prompt injection: retrieved team content is framed as fully trusted. The injected block says "[TEAM KNOWLEDGE BASE - SOURCE OF TRUTH] This knowledge is verified and authoritative. Trust it." The tool description says "KB = Source of Truth = verified. Do NOT 'verify' in code" and "Decisions in KB = ALREADY MADE. Do NOT re-evaluate them" (src/integrations/proxy/injection/memory-injection.ts lines ~240-290). Any teammate's session, or text an LLM extracted from attacker-influenced content, therefore becomes authoritative instruction-like context in every other teammate's agent. Security contact: security@grov.dev (SECURITY.md).
lesson_for_parinn:
Grov is the counter-example for I2 and I1. It turns other agents' sessions into LLM-summarised, edited-in-place records, sends them through a server, and injects them as "verified, authoritative, do NOT verify in code". That is an automatic path from untrusted content (any teammate's transcript, after model summarisation) to every other agent's prompt. The upload path fails silently, and the edits overwrite history.

For ParleyInn:
- When records are shared across agents or machines, keep content from other writers in the untrusted, pull-only, enveloped recall lane.
- Never let sync quietly promote shared content into restore blocks or authority-claiming framing. Promotion to TrustedText must stay a local, explicit, audited act.
- Record supersession ("decision X replaced by Y") as new appended events in the hash chain. Grov instead sets an active=false flag and truncates arrays, which loses provenance.
- Make sync failures counted, audited events (I6), not a silent fire-and-forget.
- Grov's useful idea is a file-overlap boost on retrieval (files_touched matched against the files in the current prompt). It is cheap and deterministic, and ParleyInn could reproduce it locally from the record without embeddings or network access.
license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file; package.json "license": "Apache-2.0"). The hosted backend is SaaS, but its source (api/, dashboard/) is in the same repo.
confidence: high for storage, data model, sync, search and injection behaviour, all read directly from source at commit d4d8cda (2026-01-28). Low for the current status of the hosted service, the star count and the archived flag, which I could not verify from this session.

name: Happy (Happy Coder), by slopus
category: E2E encrypted real-time relay. It is a remote-control and sync layer for Claude Code, Codex and other ACP agents, with mobile, web and macOS clients.
status: shipped
license: MIT (LICENSE, 'Copyright (c) 2026 Happy Coder Contributors'). The hosted relay is a free service. The app has a paid tier through RevenueCat, used for voice, according to PRIVACY.md.
what_is_stored:
On the relay, each account has Postgres rows of these kinds (prisma/schema.prisma):
- Session: plaintext tag, seq, active and timestamps. It also holds encrypted 'metadata', which covers cwd path, host, homeDir, machineId, gitBranch, claudeSessionId, summary, lifecycle state and fork parent/message id. It holds an encrypted 'agentState' with pending and completed permission requests (tool name, args, decision), and a wrapped per-session dataEncryptionKey.
- SessionMessage: append-only rows of {id, sessionId, localId, seq, content:{t:'encrypted',c:base64}}.
- Machine: encrypted metadata and daemonState.
- Project: plaintext externalId plus encrypted name.
- Artifact: encrypted header and body.
- UserKVStore: the key is plaintext 'for indexing'; the value is encrypted.
- Also AccessKey, push tokens, and UsageReport, which keeps token counts and cost as plaintext JSON.
- Uploads and attachments go to S3 as sessions/<id>/attachments/<id>.enc.
- GitHub OAuth tokens and OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini vendor tokens are encrypted on the server, not end to end.

The message payload is not a raw transcript. It is a mapped 'session protocol' projection with these event types: text (including thinking), service, tool-call-start (name, title, description, args), tool-call-end, file ref, turn-start/turn-end, and subagent start/stop.
- In the current Claude and Codex mappers, tool-call-end carries only the call id, so tool outputs are not uploaded. The app's parser does accept an optional 'result' field.
- Claude 'system' records are dropped. 'summary' records only update metadata.
- The lossless Claude JSONL stays in ~/.claude/projects on the machine. In local mode Happy tails it.

On the machine, ~/.happy holds settings.json, access.key (bearer token, the account content public key and a random machineKey), daemon.state.json and logs.
where_stored: On a server you can host yourself; git is not involved. The hosted relay runs Node (Fastify and Socket.IO) on Postgres via Prisma, with Redis and S3/MinIO, on Kubernetes. The CLI default is api.cluster-fluster.com, and the server README names happy-api.slopus.com. To self-host, there is a single container with embedded PGlite, local filesystem uploads and an in-memory event bus, or `happy server` from the happy-server-self-host npm package. Local state lives in ~/.happy. The canonical Claude transcript remains in ~/.claude/projects/<cwd-slug>/<id>.jsonl.
format_and_model:
The wire format is JSON over HTTP (/v1–/v3) plus Socket.IO at /v1/updates. Encrypted fields travel as base64.

Two cipher variants exist:
- Legacy: tweetnacl secretbox (XSalsa20-Poly1305) with a single shared 32-byte secret, laid out as [nonce24|ct].
- Current 'dataKey': AES-256-GCM with a random 32-byte DEK per session or machine, laid out as [ver=0|nonce12|ct|tag16]. Each DEK is wrapped with tweetnacl box from an ephemeral keypair to the account's content public key, laid out as [ver|ephPub32|nonce24|ct].

The key hierarchy is a master secret held only on mobile (base32 backup code). HKDF ('Happy EnCoder', ['content']) derives the content keypair from it, and that keypair wraps the DEKs.

The message model is a flat event stream. Each envelope is {id: cuid2, time: ms, role: user|agent, turn: cuid2, subagent?: cuid2, ev:{t:...}}. Provider tool ids are deliberately kept out of the envelope. Ordering has two counters: a per-account monotonic update seq (Account.seq) and a per-session message seq. Mutable objects carry integer versions. Schemas are shared through the @slopus/happy-wire npm package (Zod).
multi_writer_and_merge:
The server is the only sequencer, and there is no merge.
- Any writer can append to a session: the CLI session process, the app or the happy-agent CLI. They POST /v3/sessions/:id/messages in batches of up to 100, and each message needs a localId. The unique (sessionId, localId) pair makes retries idempotent.
- Inside a DB transaction the server increments Session.seq and hands out contiguous seqs. Total order is therefore arrival order at the relay.
- Mutable state uses optimistic concurrency. This covers session metadata and agentState, machine metadata and daemonState, artifact header and body, access keys and KV. Writes send expectedVersion and get back 'version-mismatch' with the current value, and the client resolves the conflict.
- Only one side controls the agent at a time. The session switches between 'local' mode (terminal) and 'remote' mode (phone), restarting the agent, and a keypress takes control back; there is a controlledByUser flag.
- An offline CLI queues an outbox and flushes the newest batches first.
- Forks create a new session with parentSessionId and forkedFromMessageId.
- There is no CRDT, no reconciliation of divergent histories, and no way to share a session across accounts. Sharing with friends by re-wrapping the DEK is documented as 'Future'.
realtime:
Yes, this is the product's main purpose.
- Socket.IO connections have user, session or machine scope and join rooms like user:<id>:session:<sid>.
- Persistent 'update' events carry a seq and are stored. 'ephemeral' events (presence, thinking, usage, machine-status) are not stored.
- On reconnect, clients re-fetch over REST. connectionStateRecovery is commented out.
- Point-to-point RPC rides the same socket. Methods are routed by rooms rpc:<userId>:<method>, with a 10 s grace for a reconnecting daemon, a 30 s ack timeout and a 1 s presence poll.
- Multi-replica fan-out uses the Socket.IO Redis streams adapter. multi-process.md says production still ships replicas: 1.
- Push notifications go through Expo.
- History stays readable on the phone after the terminal exits, because the relay stores the encrypted blobs.
search_retrieval:
The server cannot search, because content is opaque to it. Retrieval works like this:
- The session list is paged with a cursor and changedSince.
- Messages are paged with after_seq or before_seq, up to 500 per page.
- `happy-agent history <id> --limit N` reads the same pages.
- The ripgrep and difftastic RPCs search the live working tree on the machine, not past sessions.

I found no full-text or semantic search across session history in the server or app code I inspected. That is from a limited grep, not an exhaustive audit.
links_sessions_to_code:
The link to code is weak and nothing is written to git.
- Encrypted session metadata records cwd path, host, machineId, the git branch (`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` at start), claudeSessionId and the worktree name.
- A Project with an opaque externalId groups the checkouts of one project.
- Git status and diffs are pulled live from the app through encrypted RPC 'bash' calls (git status/diff parsers in happy-app) and are not persisted.
- The app can create worktrees on the machine via `git worktree add -b`.
- No commit SHA is recorded and there are no git notes or trailers, so there is no durable session-to-commit link.
scale: I found no quantitative scale claims. The server README says 'Distributed Ready - Built to scale horizontally when needed'. multi-process.md says the multi-replica code is on main but production runs replicas: 1. API limits are 100 messages per POST and 500 per GET page. On adoption, GitHub shows 24.0k stars, 2.0k forks and 2,513 commits; the last commit I saw was 2026-09-27; the CLI npm package 'happy' is at v1.2.5. Some docs are stale: the docs site still calls the server '900' or '1,293 lines' and points to slopus/happy-server, which was archived on Feb 14, 2026 and merged into the monorepo.
privacy_security:
Encryption covers this:
- Content is encrypted client-side, and the server only sees blobs.
- The master secret never leaves the phone.
- A CLI machine gets only the content public key plus a random machineKey. It creates a fresh DEK for each session and wraps it to that public key, and the DEK stays in memory. A compromised CLI can therefore read only its own sessions, not other machines' history (security.mdx compromise table).
- Login is a signed challenge with no passwords. The server issues bearer tokens via privacy-kit from HANDY_MASTER_SECRET.
- Retention is indefinite until the user deletes; deleted data is removed within 30 days (PRIVACY.md).

What is not end-to-end encrypted:
- GitHub and vendor API tokens, which are encrypted on the server under HANDY_MASTER_SECRET.
- Optional voice. ElevenLabs receives session history, paths and pending tool args in plaintext.
- Plaintext metadata: ids, timestamps, seq, session tag, KV keys, project externalId, token and cost usage, profile and username, and the account public key.
- PostHog analytics, under an ID derived from the master secret.

The CLI applies no secret redaction before encrypting and relies on encryption alone.

My own findings from reading the code at commit 4cf54d1:
1. AES-GCM is used with no associated data, and there is no hash chain or signature across messages. Ciphertexts are not bound to session id, seq or RPC method. A malicious relay could drop, reorder or replay messages, or replay a captured encrypted 'bash' RPC request, and no client would notice.
2. The RPC surface (bash, readFile, writeFile, listDirectory, ripgrep, difftastic) is remote execution by design. It is gated only by holding the session key.
3. how-it-works.mdx says the server stores only a hash of the public key. authRoutes.ts actually stores the hex-encoded public key in Account.publicKey.
4. access.key is written with the default file mode, with no explicit 0600.
lesson_for_parinn:
Happy shows that a blind relay with per-session DEKs wrapped to an account public key works in practice for real-time sync across devices. It also gives a useful write-only split: a machine or cloud sandbox can append encrypted records but cannot decrypt anyone else's history. ParleyInn should copy that for ephemeral sandboxes.

Happy also shows that confidentiality is not integrity. Its ciphertexts carry no associated data and no chain, so the relay still decides order and could drop, reorder or replay records without anyone noticing. Its stored copy is also a lossy projection that leaves out tool outputs, not the record itself.

For any ParleyInn transport, whether git remote, relay or object store, and always outside the network-free core:
- Ship the same hash-chained records as the local store, not a projection.
- Seal each record with AEAD whose associated data binds (session id, seq, prev-hash), and sign it.
- Then the transport is just an untrusted pipe. Gaps, reordering and replay become detectable, and the lossless canonical record stays local.

name: Harbor ATIF (Agent Trajectory Interchange Format)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: One agent run (a "trajectory") as a single JSON document. The RFC defines a trajectory as everything that happened in the run: user and system messages, agent replies, explicit reasoning (`reasoning_content`), tool calls (`tool_call_id`, `function_name`, JSON `arguments`), observations that link back to the call through `source_call_id`, and per-step metrics. The metrics cover prompt, completion and cached tokens, `cost_usd`, optional `prompt_token_ids`/`completion_token_ids`/`logprobs` for RL, and `llm_call_count`. At the root the document also holds agent name, version and model, optional OpenAI-style `tool_definitions`, `final_metrics`, `notes`, and open `extra` objects at every level. Images (v1.6) and audio (v1.8) are not inlined: they are referenced by path or URL (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/rfcs/0001-trajectory-format.md). The format also defines markers for compaction and copied context. `is_copied_context` flags steps carried across a summarization boundary. A system step with `extra.context_management` {type: compaction|pruning|injection, boundary: replace|append|truncate} declares what the context window holds after that point (RFC section VII). Sandbox files are not stored: "Neither restores sandbox files" (https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/jobs/loading-trajectories).
where_stored: Plain files in a working tree. In a Harbor trial directory the trajectory is `agent/trajectory.json`, with media in sibling `images/` and `audio/` directories (https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/agents/atif; RFC image and audio storage conventions). Agents that declare `capabilities.atif` write it to their log dir. The Claude Code adapter converts the native session JSONL after the run (`populate_context_post_run` in https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/agents/installed/claude_code.py). Two optional copies can exist. (1) Harbor Hub, via `harbor upload` or `harbor run --upload`: the trajectory goes to a Supabase storage bucket at `trials/<id>/trajectory.json`, with rows in a DB (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/upload/uploader.py, .../upload/storage.py, https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/harbor-hub/upload). (2) Arize Phoenix, which imports trajectories as OTel/OpenInference spans (https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/release-notes/04-2026/04-03-2026-atif-trajectory-upload.md). Nothing is stored in git: no notes, refs or branches.
format_and_model: JSON, versioned by a `schema_version` string. ATIF-v1.0 through v1.8 are accepted, and the Pydantic default is "ATIF-v1.8" (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/models/trajectories/trajectory.py). The RFC lists v1.8 as current (April 2026). The docs page still says v1.7, and the Claude Code converter still emits "ATIF-v1.7". The data model is a document snapshot, not an event log. The root object holds an ordered `steps[]`, and `step_id` must be dense and sequential from 1. Each step's `source` is one of system, user or agent. Tool calls are matched to observation results by id, and the validator enforces sequential ids and valid tool-call references. Unknown fields are rejected (`extra: forbid`), and anything custom goes in `extra` (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/models/trajectories/step.py). Subagents can be embedded (`subagent_trajectories[]`, resolved by a unique `trajectory_id`) or referenced as files (`trajectory_path`, which may be a file path, S3 URL or DB reference). `session_id` is run-scoped, may be shared, and is informational only. Change v1.7 is breaking for refs carrying only a `session_id`. Long runs split across files through `continued_trajectory_ref` (RFC section II). The format has no hash, signature or checksum fields; a grep of the models turns up none. The reference implementation is Pydantic models plus a CLI validator (`python -m harbor.utils.trajectory_validator`). The repo is Apache-2.0 at harbor-framework/harbor (version 0.23.0 in pyproject.toml, HEAD bf991e4, 2026-10-01). The docs show 33 built-in agents that produce ATIF (claude-code, codex, gemini-cli, openhands, cursor-cli, copilot-cli, goose, opencode, pi and others). Only claude-code and codex can load one (https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/agents/pre-integrated-agents).
multi_writer_and_merge: Not designed for this. Each trajectory has one producer, and the file is rewritten whole rather than appended to. Merges, CRDTs and concurrent writers are not defined. Multi-agent runs are composed rather than merged. A parent either embeds complete, independently valid child trajectories or points at their files. Several documents may share a `session_id` (parent, subagents, continuation segments), and only `trajectory_id` is unique (RFC). Phoenix reassembles sessions split across files when their `session_id`s end in `-cont-N`. It also derives trace and span IDs from `session_id` with SHA-256, so uploading the same trajectory again is idempotent (Phoenix release note). Harbor Hub upload is idempotent per trial: if a storage object "already exists" the upload is skipped, and a rerun of `harbor upload` fills in missing trials (uploader.py, storage.py). Seeding works by conversion and has no merge step: `atif_to_native_trajectory` mints a new Claude Code JSONL with fresh uuid/parentUuid links and message ids, and drops system steps (claude_code.py). Loading is also refused when a simulated user_agent is configured (loading-trajectories doc).
realtime: The format is batch: the authoritative ATIF is written after the run. Harbor fakes a live view when the environment has streaming enabled. Every 2 s (`POLL_INTERVAL_SEC = 2`) it connects to the sandbox over SSH, tars the agent's native `*.jsonl` session logs, runs the full native-to-ATIF conversion again, and atomically swaps in a new `trajectory.json` via a temp file and rename. A failed download leaves the previous copy in place (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/trial/sync_trajectory.py). So "live" means a fresh full snapshot each poll, not a stream of new events. `harbor run --upload` sends each trial to the Hub as it finishes, not step by step (uploader.py comments; upload doc). Phoenix import is an offline upload done with the Python client (arize-phoenix-client 2.3.0+).
search_retrieval: ATIF itself defines no index and no query. Retrieval is by file path, by `trajectory_id`/`trajectory_path` for subagents, or by trial id from the Hub (`harbor trial download <trial-id> --trajectory`, https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/harbor-hub/download). The local results viewer shows `agent/trajectory.json` in a Trajectory tab. Its search and filters cover job and task metadata, not trajectory content (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/viewer/server.py). After import into Phoenix, trajectories are AGENT-rooted traces with LLM and TOOL sibling spans carrying OpenInference attributes (tokens, cost, model, tool definitions, reasoning), so they can be queried with Phoenix's tooling (Phoenix release note). Harbor's RewardKit LLM judge also reads ATIF and forwards its media to the judge model (CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Only weakly. ATIF has no fields for a repo, commit, diff or file change. The Claude Code converter puts the native session's `cwd` and `gitBranch` values into `agent.extra.cwds` / `agent.extra.git_branches` and step `extra.cwd` (claude_code.py). Going the other way, the native session it writes back has `cwd: "/app"` and `gitBranch: ""` hard-coded. Harbor links a trajectory to its trial, task and dataset (config.json, result.json, verifier output in the same trial directory), not to the code commits the agent produced. As the docs put it, loading a trajectory "restores portable conversation content", not sandbox files (loading-trajectories doc).
privacy_security: The format has no redaction, encryption, integrity or provenance fields. The Claude Code converter drops genuine Anthropic `redacted_thinking` ciphertext rather than copying it into the message text. It decodes OpenRouter's plain-text abuse of the same envelope (claude_code.py, around line 837). Harbor's secret redaction covers env vars and logged commands. `redact_sensitive_value` keeps the first 4 and last 3 characters, and sensitive env values are turned into `${KEY}` templates when persisted (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/src/harbor/utils/env.py; base.py `_redact_command`). I found no scrubbing of trajectory message or observation content, so secrets an agent printed stay in `trajectory.json`. This is inferred from grepping the source, not stated in the docs. Live sync downloads "only transcripts, never config/credentials" (sync_trajectory.py). Hub upload uses an allow-list of trial entries so stray files and secrets in the job dir are left out, but the whole `agent/` directory, trajectory included, is uploaded (uploader.py). Uploads are private by default. `--public` or `--share <org>` changes that, and sharing a job "automatically shares all trials and trajectories" (https://docs.harborframework.com/core-concepts/harbor-hub/sharing). Two places treat trajectory files as untrusted. RewardKit confines media paths to the trajectory's own directory and rejects URL media, because "the agent under evaluation writes that file". Prompt templates now run in Jinja's sandbox (CHANGELOG.md). The import path does not. ATIF-to-native conversion writes observation content verbatim as Claude Code `tool_result` blocks, and `claude --resume` then replays them to the model as history, with no trust envelope (claude_code.py `atif_to_native_trajectory`).
scale: ATIF has no scale claims. Harbor says it runs "thousands of environments in parallel" on providers such as Daytona and Modal (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/README.md). Each trajectory is one JSON document, loaded whole into Pydantic models for validation and conversion, and the live view re-converts the full document every 2 s. Large or long runs therefore depend on document size, plus optional token-id and logprob arrays that grow with token count. Splitting long runs is only possible through `continued_trajectory_ref` and subagent files. I found no published size or throughput figures, so none can be verified.
lesson_for_parinn: Use ATIF as an export projection that ParleyInn writes, and never as an import path into the model. Concretely: (1) Write an ATIF exporter as a rebuildable projection of the hash-chained record (I10). It would give ParleyInn interop with Phoenix/OpenInference, RL and SFT pipelines, and Harbor's viewer. Its `is_copied_context` flag and `context_management` boundary markers already match ParleyInn's compaction and restore events. The exporter must not fill missing timestamps from the clock, which Harbor's converter does with `datetime.now()`. (2) Never seed a session from imported ATIF the way Harbor's `atif_to_native_trajectory` does. That function writes observation text verbatim as `tool_result` blocks that `claude --resume` replays to the model, which is exactly the automatic untrusted-to-model path that I2 forbids. An ATIF import into ParleyInn should land as untrusted records, reachable only through enveloped pull recall. Media `path` values should be confined to the import's directory, as RewardKit does, because ATIF allows absolute paths and URLs. (3) ATIF has no hashes, signatures or append semantics, and Harbor's live mode rewrites whole snapshots. ParleyInn should keep its append-only event log as the source of truth and record the ATIF schema version per export, because v1.7 broke subagent refs and Phoenix supports only v1.0 to v1.6.
sources: https://github.com/harbor-ai/agent-trajectory-format (cited by the Phoenix note; returns HTTP 404, unverifiable)

name: Hermes Agent memory (Nous Research)
status: shipped
license: MIT (GitHub repo page shows LICENSE as MIT; https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent). I could not get the SPDX field from the GitHub API because this session has no API access to the repo.
what_is_stored: Hermes stores two layers. (1) Curated memory: MEMORY.md holds the agent's own notes, capped at 2,200 characters (about 800 tokens). USER.md holds a user profile, capped at 1,375 characters (about 500 tokens). The agent writes both through a `memory` tool with add, replace and remove actions. Replace and remove find their target by substring match on `old_text`, and the tool has no read action. Source: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory. (2) Full session history: every CLI and messaging-gateway session is stored. The `sessions` table holds id, source, user_id, model, title, timestamps, token counts, a parent session ID and cwd. The `messages` table holds role, content, tool_calls, tool_name and token_count. Source: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions. The README also lists auto-created skills ("Autonomous skill creation after complex tasks") as part of the learning loop (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent).
where_stored: Local files and a local database. Curated memory lives in ~/.hermes/memories/, or ~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/memories/ per profile. Session history lives in a SQLite database at ~/.hermes/state.db (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory). Optional external memory providers are plugins and may be hosted services: OpenViking, Mem0, Holographic, RetainDB, ByteRover and Supermemory are bundled, and Honcho and Hindsight come from the plugin catalog (same URL). Hermes uses no git storage and has no built-in sync. The README mentions no sync mechanism (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent).
format_and_model: Memory is plain Markdown entries with hard character budgets. When a write would go over the budget, the tool returns an error rather than silently dropping anything, and the agent consolidates entries in the same turn before retrying. At session start the memory is injected into the system prompt as a frozen snapshot: "captured once at session start and never changes mid-session", which keeps the LLM prefix cache valid. Writes reach disk immediately but stay invisible until the next session (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory). Sessions are relational SQLite rows (sessions, messages) plus a messages_fts FTS5 virtual table. Titles are unique when not NULL. When context is compressed, Hermes starts a new continuation session linked by a parent session ID and auto-titles it ("my project #2"). Sessions export as JSONL (default), Markdown, HTML or Quarto (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). The docs describe a mutable record with pruning, not an append-only or hash-chained one.
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no merge model. state.db uses SQLite WAL mode: "concurrent readers and a single writer", which serializes the gateway's multi-platform writers inside one host (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). The memory docs warn explicitly: "Don't point two agent processes at the same Hermes home directory ... two writers sharing one home will compound each other's entries into state neither of them (nor you) authored" (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory). v0.21.3 (2026-09-14) fixed long-lived processes leaking duplicate state.db writer handles, which could corrupt sessions. v0.21.4 added `hermes sessions set-journal-mode` (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/releases). Profiles separate state by giving each one its own directory; they do not merge.
realtime: Within one host, the gateway serves Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal and CLI from a single process, with "cross-platform conversation continuity" (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent). Curated memory is deliberately not real-time inside a session: the frozen snapshot only refreshes at the next session start. I found no documentation of real-time sharing across machines.
search_retrieval: Curated memory is pushed into the system prompt automatically at session start. History is pulled on demand by the `session_search` tool, which runs SQLite FTS5 queries (about 20ms per query and about 1ms to scroll, per the docs). Per the sessions docs it "makes no LLM calls and returns views of actual messages from the DB rather than generating summaries" (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). The README still says "FTS5 session search with LLM summarization" (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), so the README looks out of date against the docs and I treat the docs as current. v0.21.4 (2026-09-21) added after/before time bounds and an OR-relaxed retry when recall is poor (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/releases). External providers add their own semantic retrieval; I did not verify how each one works.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Each session records its working directory ("its git repo root or project dir") in sessions.cwd, which allows resuming and filtering by workspace (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). I found no linkage to commits, diffs, branches or files changed, and nothing written into git.
scale: Memory is bounded by design: about 1,300 tokens in total across MEMORY.md and USER.md. Session search claims about 20ms per FTS5 query (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory). By default, ended sessions are auto-pruned after `sessions.retention_days` = 90, and active sessions are never pruned (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). As adoption context, the repo page shows about 250.7k stars, and v0.21.4 alone merged 1,812 PRs (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent, https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/releases). The docs make no claims about database size.
privacy_security: Memory entries are scanned before they are accepted, because they get injected into the system prompt. The scan blocks prompt-injection, credential-exfiltration and SSH-backdoor patterns and invisible Unicode (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/memory). This is a heuristic denylist on the write path, and recalled content is not enveloped. Session export supports `--redact` to remove API keys, tokens and credentials, but only from exported content. The docs do not say that stored transcripts are redacted at write time (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions). The docs I read do not mention encryption at rest, and I could not verify any. External providers can send memory to third-party services.
lesson_for_parinn: Copy the split, not the trust model. Hermes keeps two separate channels: a tiny, hard-capped curated memory that is pushed once per session as a frozen snapshot (which preserves the prompt cache), and a full transcript store that the model can only pull through FTS5 search, with no LLM summarization in the path. This matches ParleyInn's pinned-constraints restore plus pull-only recall, and suggests a budget error with no silent drop (I6) and an FTS index rebuildable from the record (I10). Hermes also shows what ParleyInn must avoid. It relies on a regex scanner to make agent-written memory safe for the system prompt. It makes the same agent the writer of what gets auto-injected. It cannot handle two writers on one home directory, so its own docs forbid it, because auto-written memory "compounds into state neither of them authored". For many agents across worktrees, ParleyInn needs per-writer provenance and an explicit trust boundary (only TrustedText auto-injected, I2), not a shared mutable file.

name: hex/claude-sessions ("cs", a session manager for Claude Code)
category: session docs under git (model-written Markdown session notebooks in a local git repo per session, plus crash-recovery shadow refs)
status: shipped. The project is active: 2,168 commits since 2025-11-24, 147 tags, and the latest release is v2026.10.1 (commit 1f2b3c4, 2026-10-01). It is MIT-licensed. The GitHub page shows 44 stars and 5 forks and no archived flag. Facts here come from a clone of main at that commit. The REST API was blocked from this sandbox, and the web-search budget had run out, so no third-party discussion was found or checked.
what_is_stored:
The core is a set of model-written Markdown notes, kept per session. cs does not store a lossless transcript.
- `.cs/README.md` holds YAML frontmatter (status, created, tags, aliases), the objective and the outcome. The objective is the first substantive prompt, cut to about 100 characters.
- `.cs/memory/narrative.<actor>.md` is an append-only lab notebook, one per actor. A Stop hook asks Claude to append to it about every 5 minutes.
- `.cs/memory/` also holds Claude Code's native auto-memory files and the `MEMORY.md` index. cs redirects them there with `CLAUDE_COWORK_MEMORY_PATH_OVERRIDE`.
- `.cs/summary.md` is written by `/wrap` and `/summary`.
- `.cs/checkpoints/*.md` are labelled snapshots. Each holds the short HEAD sha, up to 20 lines of `git status --porcelain` and a full copy of the narrative.
- `.cs/handoffs/*.md` are rotation handoffs. Each records the parent conversation UUID, purpose, next step and a status of unconsumed, consumed, discarded or superseded.
- `.cs/narrative-archive/<actor>/<through-date>-<blob8>.md` are rotated narrative sections, moved verbatim.
- `.cs/timeline.jsonl` is an event log with events `started`, `ended`, `checkpoint`, `rotated`, `narrative_rotated`, `worktree-retired` and `feature-integrated`.
- Per-machine encrypted secret exports are kept as `.cs/secrets.<user@host>.age`.

Machine-local state lives in the gitignored `.cs/local/`:
- `session.log` records every Bash command Claude runs, cut to 200 characters.
- `state` holds the conversation UUID to resume.
- Also here: the mailbox (one JSON file per message), the queue, notifications, traces, and status-line numbers (context % and rate limits).

Raw Claude Code transcripts stay where Claude Code writes them: `~/.claude/projects`, or `.cs/claude-config` in an encrypted session. cs only reads them, for token accounting in `cs -usage`.
where_stored:
Working-tree files inside a local git repo, one per session.
- Sessions live at `~/.claude-sessions/<name>/`, or under `CS_SESSIONS_ROOT`.
- `cs -adopt` instead puts `.cs/` into an existing project in place, symlinks it from the sessions root, and runs `git init` only when the project has no repo.
- Crash-recovery snapshots go to a per-conversation shadow ref, `refs/worktree/cs/session/<conversation-uuid>`. Git keeps `refs/worktree/*` per worktree and never pushes it. A clean SessionEnd deletes that ref. Refs from crashed conversations older than 14 days are garbage-collected.
- Encrypted sessions (macOS only) symlink `.cs/{memory,plans,claude-config,private}` into an hdiutil AES-256 sparse bundle stored at `~/.local/share/cs/vaults/<name>.sparsebundle`.

Nothing is stored on a server. Cross-machine sharing is a manual `git push` or `git pull` of the session directory.
format_and_model:
Plain files, no database.
- **Markdown narratives:** the model appends `## ` sections. The written rule is append-only: a correction is a new dated note, never an edit.
- **timeline.jsonl:** one `jq -nc` object per line, e.g. `{ts, event:"started", source, session_id, branch}` or `{ts, event:"rotated", from, to, reason: handoff|rebind|declined-resume|resume-failed, handoff?}`.
- **Autosave:** a PostToolUse hook runs on every Write or Edit. It stages the whole tree into a temporary index with `git add -A`, excluding vault mounts and link targets, then `git write-tree`, then `git commit-tree`, chained onto the previous autosave. The message is `autosave: <time>` with a `cs-base: <HEAD sha>` trailer, and `git update-ref` moves the ref. HEAD and branches are never touched.
- **Narrative rotation:** `cs -narrative rotate` runs once a file passes 224 KiB and keeps a 112 KiB tail. It removes exactly one interior run of sections, and the tail stays byte-identical. The removed bytes go to an immutable chunk named by date and the first 8 hex digits of `git hash-object`, so the name is content-addressed.
- **Integrity:** there is no hash chain, signature or tamper evidence on the record itself.
- **Data model:** a session is a directory, it owns many conversations (UUIDs), and the chain of conversations is rebuilt from `rotated` events.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writes are split by writer and merged with git merge drivers set in `.gitattributes`.
- **Per-actor files:** each actor gets its own narrative file, so co-developers never edit the same file. The actor slug comes from `$CS_ACTOR`, then `.cs/local/identity`, then git `user.email`, then `user.name`.
- **merge=union:** `narrative.*.md` and `timeline.jsonl` use it, so appends from both sides are interleaved rather than conflicting. Line order across writers is therefore not guaranteed.
- **merge=ours:** `MEMORY.md` uses it, and each actor's pointer line is re-added on the next launch. This driver is per-clone git config that every `cs` launch installs, so a fresh clone falls back to an ordinary text merge until its first launch.
- **Default merge:** the README, the summary and shared memory facts can genuinely conflict, and a person resolves them by hand.
- **Measured union-merge hazards:** the rotation spec reports that renaming the file, or truncating it to EOF, makes the whole old body come back after a merge. That is why rotation must remove one interior hunk only. Archive chunks are content-addressed, so two machines archiving the same sections produce an identical file.
- **Same machine:** a PID lock plus a ps-based guard block two launches of the same conversation.
- **Autosave refs:** each conversation has its own ref, created and deleted with compare-and-swap `update-ref` calls. This followed a 2026-07-22 incident in which a single shared `refs/worktree/cs/auto` produced false crash prompts and one conversation stripped another's protection.
- **Feature worktrees:** `<base>@<feature>` sessions are git worktrees on branch `cs/<feature>`. `/finish` merges in a temporary detached worktree, runs the repo's gates, fast-forwards the base, and folds the worktree's timeline and narrative into the base.
- **History:** auto-commit and push sync (`cs -sync`, `auto_sync`) and SSH remote sessions were removed in v2026.6.9 (2026-06-24). The changelog gives the reason: cs had been writing "Session update" commits into adopted projects' real branches. cs now never commits user work. It commits only its own scaffolding, narrative rotations and migrations, staging named paths only.
realtime:
Real time on one machine only.
- **Liveness:** a session counts as live when its PID lock is held or when the status line refreshed `.cs/local/context-pct` within the last 900 seconds.
- **Mail:** `cs -msg` delivers a message by writing a file and renaming it into the recipient's `mail/new/`. The recipient wakes either at its next turn boundary (Stop hook) or through Claude Code's FileChanged watch. Wakes are capped at 5 between prompts.
- **Across machines:** the docs say outright that there is no network or cross-machine presence. Sharing between machines is asynchronous, by git push and pull. Attribution of who did what comes from git history (`cs -who`, plus a resume digest built from a watermark).
search_retrieval:
There is no index.
- `cs -search <query>` runs a case-insensitive `grep -in` over each session's `.cs/README.md`, `.cs/memory/*.md` and the narrative archives. It skips archived sessions unless given `--include-archived`.
- The session picker does fuzzy matching on names plus `#tag` filters.
- On resume the model reads its own narrative in full. It reads a teammate's narrative only from the line the digest names, and it greps the archives on demand.
- The `scope-prompt` hook pushes up to 8,000 bytes per prompt: matching tracked files, recent commits and the working-tree diff.
- The sessions root can be opened as an Obsidian vault and queried with Dataview over the frontmatter.
- Raw transcripts are not searchable through cs.
links_sessions_to_code:
Loosely. The session directory is the code repo, either the session's own or an adopted project. The links that exist:
- `timeline.jsonl` events record the conversation UUID and the current git branch.
- Checkpoints record the HEAD short sha and the dirty files.
- Autosave snapshot commits carry a `cs-base: <HEAD>` trailer. Crash recovery uses it to refuse a blanket restore once HEAD has moved.
- `feature-integrated` events record the sha that was merged.
- Handoffs record the parent conversation UUID.

What is missing: user commits get no trailer naming the session or conversation, and no prompt-to-diff mapping is kept. The first prompt survives only as a truncated objective line.
scale:
No claims about agent count or throughput. Figures that appear in the sources:
- **Narrative growth:** the rotation spec measured files of 802 KB / 8,062 lines and 776 KB / 13,133 lines, and a third session reported 3.7 MB. At about 200K tokens per file, the spec says no conversation can read one whole, and that drove the rotation design.
- **Rotation budget:** 224 KiB, chosen to stay under the Read tool's 256 KiB ceiling, with a 112 KiB tail kept.
- **Mail:** bodies up to 64 KB; at most 5 bodies are inlined into context.
- **Scope injection:** capped at 8,000 bytes, with a 1,500 ms budget.
- **Vault bundle:** grows up to 50 GB.
- **Autosave cost:** the whole tree is restaged on every Write or Edit, so cost grows with tree size.
privacy_security:
**Local file protection**
- `.cs/` is mode 0700, re-applied on every open.
- `.cs/local/` is gitignored, and a launch guard refuses to run if it ever becomes tracked.
- An executable `pre-open` hook lives only in uncommitted `.cs/local/`, so a cloned session cannot make cs run code. The docs warn that file-sync tools such as rsync or Dropbox do copy it.

**Secrets**
- Stored in the macOS Keychain, or in an AES-256-CBC file with PBKDF2 at 100k iterations. That file is keyed by a machine salt unless `CS_SECRETS_PASSWORD` is set.
- Values are read on stdin. `cs -secrets set` refuses placeholder values. Export for sync is per machine, using age recipients.

**Redaction:** none is mechanical.
- The bash log records commands verbatim, cut to 200 characters; it is machine-local.
- The rotate skill is told, in prompt instructions, to strip credentials and sensitive personal detail from handoffs, because handoffs are committed.

**Encrypted sessions (macOS only)**
- An hdiutil AES-256 volume holds memory, plans, Claude Code's config dir (so transcripts never reach `~/.claude`) and cs's private files.
- While the volume is locked, cs writes nothing in plaintext in its place.
- Autosave excludes vault paths so their blobs never land in `.git/objects`.
- Plaintext metadata hides handoff and checkpoint names.
- The docs list what still leaks: backups, `summary.md`, `brief.md` and git history.

**Prompt injection**
- Cross-session mail is pushed into context automatically on every prompt. Each body is wrapped in a `<cs_mail id=<random>>` tag with matching close tag, plus a warning not to follow instructions inside unless the user asks, and control characters are stripped.
- Who sent a message is unauthenticated, by design.
- Other injected text, such as sibling objectives, git author names and commit subjects, gets the same control-character scrub.
- `cs -doctor` lists every hook that injects into the model's context, with the switch that turns it off.

**Network:** cs is not network-free.
- Self-update downloads from GitHub Releases and checks SHA-256, plus minisign when it is installed.
- The status line fetches Fable usage from `api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage` using Claude Code's credential.
- The optional `ctrl+g` prompt rewriter sends the prompt to Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or xAI.
- The optional council integration sends a digest to third-party models, after asking the user.
lesson_for_parinn:
Split the record by writer, make segments immutable, and keep it off the user's code branch. cs learned all three the hard way.
- **Union merge loses order and can bring text back.** Its shared append-only files merge with `merge=union`, which interleaves lines in no fixed order. The project measured that renaming or truncating such a file brings the old body back after a merge, so it now forbids those rewrites by protocol. A hash-chained log merged that way would break its chain. ParleyInn should give each writer (agent or conversation) its own hash chain in its own file or ref, and derive the cross-writer order rather than merging text.
- **Immutable, content-addressed segments merge for free.** Two machines archiving the same data produce the identical file, so no merge driver is needed. cs's narrative archive chunks work this way.
- **Recovery state needs one ref per writer, updated by compare-and-swap.** A single shared shadow ref produced false crash prompts and let one conversation delete another's protection, until cs moved to per-conversation `refs/worktree/...` refs with compare-and-swap `update-ref`.
- **Automatic git transport into the project repo did not survive.** cs removed auto-commit and push sync in v2026.6.9 because it polluted adopted projects' real branches. If ParleyInn uses git as transport, it should push under its own ref namespace or a separate repo, and only on explicit action.

name: Hindsight (Vectorize)
category: long-term memory service (LLM-extracted semantic memory, server-side, PostgreSQL)
status: shipped
license: MIT, Copyright (c) 2025 Vectorize AI, Inc. (repo LICENSE, https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight/blob/main/LICENSE). Hindsight Cloud is a hosted commercial service on top of it (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/coding-agents).
what_is_stored: LLM-derived memory, not a lossless log. Retain sends content to an LLM that pulls out facts, entities, relationships and time data, then embeds them (README, https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight). The source text is kept in a `documents` row (id, bank_id, original_text, content_hash). Extracted `memory_units` hold text, a pgvector embedding, context, event_date, occurred_start/end, mentioned_at, a JSONB metadata field and a fact_type of world, experience or observation. Observations are beliefs that consolidation merges and backs with evidence. Other tables: `entities` (canonical_name, first/last_seen, mention_count), `unit_entities`, `entity_cooccurrences`, `memory_links` and `banks` (disposition, background) (hindsight-api-slim/hindsight_api/models.py, https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight/blob/main/hindsight-api-slim/hindsight_api/models.py). Link types are temporal, semantic, entity, causes, caused_by, enables and prevents, with weight 0..1; retain now writes only caused_by (same file). On top sit mental models and knowledge pages, which are standing synthesized answers (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/mental-models).
