For coding agents, the plugin stores agent conversation transcripts plus the repo's git history: commit messages by default, or messages and full per-commit diffs with gitIngest="full" (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/coding-agents).
where_stored: On a server, in a database. PostgreSQL 15+ with pgvector 0.5+. Oracle AI Database is an enterprise alternative with "full feature parity". The docs say outright there is "no storage abstraction" (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/storage). For local dev, pg0 is an embedded PostgreSQL binary with pgvector. With no HINDSIGHT_API_DATABASE_URL set, it starts on port 5555 with data in ~/.hindsight/pg0/ (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/0.7/developer/storage, https://github.com/vectorize-io/pg0). Deployment modes for the coding-agents plugin: Hindsight Cloud (the default), a self-hosted server, or a local `hindsight-embed` daemon at 127.0.0.1:9077 that all agents and repos on the machine share (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/coding-agents). Nothing is stored in git or in the working tree. The plugin deliberately has no repo-carried config.
format_and_model: Relational, vector and graph data in Postgres: tables plus JSONB, pgvector HNSW indexes, tsvector/GIN full-text indexes (optional ParadeDB pg_search for BM25), and graph queries through recursive CTEs (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/storage, https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/configuration). Migrations use Alembic, about 110 revisions in the clone I read (repo path hindsight-api-slim/hindsight_api/alembic). Memory is partitioned into "banks", one per user, agent or project. Bank ids are free-form strings; the coding-agents default is `coding-agent::{gitProject}`. Tenants map to PostgreSQL schemas through a TenantExtension (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/extensions). Access is through a REST API (/v1/{tenant}/banks/{bank_id}/...), an MCP server per bank, Python, Node.js and Go SDKs, a CLI, and an LLM wrapper (README). Current version is 0.10.2 (hindsight-api/pyproject.toml; https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight/releases/tag/v0.10.2). The latest main commit I saw is dated 2026-10-02.
multi_writer_and_merge: This is a central server with one database, so it does no distributed merge. Several writers just call the same API. Idempotency depends on the caller-supplied document_id. update_mode="replace" (the default) deletes the old document and all its derived memories, then re-extracts. update_mode="append" concatenates the new content and re-extracts only the changed chunks. Without a document_id, each request gets a random UUID and re-ingesting creates duplicates (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain). So history is mutable and gets overwritten: re-retaining a conversation replaces its memories. Background consolidation merges facts into deduplicated observations "that refine rather than overwrite" (README). observationScopes picks whether all agents on a repo build one shared set of beliefs or keep them apart per tag or source (coding-agents doc). Several agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI, Copilot CLI and about 15 more) share one bank per repo by default. Banks can be merged on purpose through mapPathToBank, e.g. two repos into `team::product` (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/coding-agents). Background workers claim rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (hindsight-api-slim/hindsight_api/engine/maintenance.py). There is no hash chain, no signature, and no conflict model beyond last write wins per document_id.
realtime: Near real time, through the server. Every agent's Stop hook writes the session back after each turn, and UserPromptSubmit or the first prompt injects recalled or reflected context. Extraction is asynchronous, so new facts show up after LLM processing finishes, typically 0.5–2 s per batch, longer in async mode (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/performance). Async retain can use provider Batch APIs, which allow up to 24 h windows (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain). Push notifications come as per-bank webhooks (retain.completed, consolidation.completed, memory_defense.triggered). They are queued in the same DB transaction as the write, so delivery is at least once. HMAC-SHA256 signatures are available, plus a timestamped V2 signature for replay protection (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/webhooks). I found no streaming or subscription API for clients beyond webhooks.
search_retrieval: Recall (called TEMPR) runs four strategies in parallel: semantic (pgvector), keyword (BM25 via tsvector or pg_search), graph traversal over entity, temporal and causal links, and temporal filtering. It fuses them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, reranks with a cross-encoder, applies boosts, then truncates to a token budget (low/mid/high budget plus max_tokens) (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/retrieval). Reflect is an LLM synthesis over recalled memories and mental models (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect). The plugin's default auto-inject is a low-budget reflect on the session's first prompt; if that fails it falls back to knowledge-page search, then recall (coding-agents doc). This is relevance-ranked retrieval of extracted facts. It cannot replay exact history.
links_sessions_to_code: Partly. Sessions link to a repo, but not to commits. The coding-agents plugin keys banks by git project, seeds a cold bank from the most recent 300 commits (autoSeed, seedLimit), and keeps it current as HEAD moves. Commit messages go in as one document that is re-upserted; with "full", diffs go in per commit. It also re-runs a structural "survey" every 20 commits (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/coding-agents). Transcripts are attributed to a repo only when the session itself records its cwd (Claude Code entries, Codex session_meta). It does not guess from Claude's dash-encoded project folder names, because `/` and `.` both encode to `-` and a guess could file someone else's conversation into your bank (same doc). Provenance travels as optional retainTags and retainMetadata (e.g. project:{gitProject}). The old Claude Code plugin recorded only session_id, message_count and retained_at, with no project id. That plugin is now superseded (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/claude-code). I found no link from a memory to a specific commit SHA, file or line.
privacy_security: Memory Defense is off by default and opt-in per bank. The open-source version implements the `sensitive_data` rule with 45 regex patterns: AI, cloud, VCS and payment keys, DB URLs, PEM keys, JWTs, credit cards and US SSNs. A redact action stores `[REDACTED:type]` in both the memory units and the document body; a block action drops the item and returns 422 if every item is blocked. Existing memories are not rescanned (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/memory-defense). The policy schema also names prompt_injection, protected_key, immutable_key, size_anomaly and a quarantine action (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks). The docs say the OSS build implements only sensitive_data, so I could not verify prompt-injection detection in OSS. A partial block returns 200 and blocked items are "silently dropped" from the result, though recorded in security_events (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/retain). Audit logging is disabled by default and can be toggled per bank (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/configuration). Auth uses a TenantExtension. The built-in option is one API key from an env var on the public schema; per-user schema isolation needs the external StaticKeys or Supabase extensions (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/extensions). The README promises "strict bank isolation". I found no app-level encryption at rest in the docs; that is left to Postgres or the host. All content goes to an external LLM for extraction unless you configure a local model (Ollama, llama.cpp). Recalled memory is injected automatically into the agent's context through additionalContext (claude-code doc). The core docs do not wrap it as untrusted; only some integrations (e.g. Right Agent) do (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/sdks/integrations/right-agent). Fail-closed privacy features: optInOnly / optInPaths, and a cloned repo cannot turn memory on because no repo-carried config is read (coding-agents doc). SECURITY.md patches the latest version only and promises a 48 h response (https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight/blob/main/SECURITY.md).
scale: Claims: state-of-the-art accuracy on LongMemEval as of January 2026, said to be independently reproduced by Virginia Tech and The Washington Post (README; paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12818). I did not verify the reproduction claim. Performance docs give recall at 100–600 ms, reflect at 800–3000 ms, retain at 0.5–2 s per batch, and vector search at 10–50 ms on 100K+ facts (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/performance). Multi-tenant ops figure: migration resweep measured at 20k tenant schemas (https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/configuration). GitHub showed about 44.5k stars when I fetched the page; GitHub API access was blocked here, so this is unverified via the API.
lesson_for_parinn: Hindsight shows the opposite trade-off to ParleyInn's, and ParleyInn should keep both layers apart. Hindsight's record of truth is mutable and LLM-derived. A replace upsert by document_id deletes earlier memories, redaction happens before storage, and recall output is auto-injected as context. So it cannot replay what an agent actually saw, and stored text is an automatic path to the model. ParleyInn should keep the append-only, hash-chained lossless log as the only source of truth. Any Hindsight-style fact, entity or graph index should be a rebuildable projection (I10), recalled only on request inside an envelope (I2), and never the record itself. Two concrete Hindsight practices are worth copying. First, attribute a session to a repo only from the cwd the transcript itself records, never from Claude's lossy dash-encoded project folder names. Second, fail closed with no repo-carried config, so a cloned repo cannot turn on capture or point it at a shared store. Also avoid its "silently dropped" partial-block behavior: under I6, every block or redaction must be audited and counted, not optional or off by default.

name: Hugging Face Agent Traces (Hub trace viewer, Session Traces Format, Storage Buckets)
category: hosted trace datasets (git-backed dataset repos or non-versioned Xet buckets)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Raw agent session JSONL files, uploaded unchanged. The docs name three supported harnesses and their local directories: Claude Code (~/.claude/projects), Codex (~/.codex/sessions) and Pi (~/.pi/agent/sessions). Custom harnesses can write the Session Trace Simple Format (STS) instead (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/agent-traces, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/session-traces-format). The docs warn that these files "can include prompts, tool inputs, command output, local paths, screenshots, secrets, private code, and personal data" (agent-traces page). The `datasets` JSON loader also detects droid, hermes and openclaw traces (https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/blob/main/src/datasets/packaged_modules/json/json.py). In a Dataset repo, Data Studio turns each file into one derived row with these columns: harness, session_id, prompt (the first user message), messages, tools and metadata (SFT conversion through the third-party `teich` package), sent_at, num_user_messages, num_tool_calls, trace (the whole raw file as Json) and file_path (same json.py; teich: https://pypi.org/project/teich/). Data Studio also auto-converts the first 5GB of a dataset to Parquet on the refs/convert/parquet branch (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/data-studio).
where_stored:
Server/cloud on the Hugging Face Hub, in one of two places.
(a) A Dataset repo. Dataset repos are git repositories backed by the Xet chunk store, with full history and pull requests (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/repositories, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets).
(b) A Storage Bucket. This is S3-like object storage on Xet. It is "non-versioned and mutable" and has no commits, branches or tags. You reach it through hf://buckets/ paths, the hf CLI, the Python API, an S3-compatible API or a filesystem mount. Bucket data lives in US or EU regions (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/webhooks, https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/storage-buckets-security).
The local source of truth stays in the harness's own session directory.
format_and_model:
JSONL throughout. One file is one session and one viewer row; hermes files are the exception and can hold several sessions (json.py comment).

Detection is by schema markers in the `datasets` JSON loader:
- {type: string, message: Json} means Claude Code, Pi or openclaw
- {type, payload} means Codex
- {type, id, version, cwd} means droid
- {id, source, model, system_prompt, messages} means hermes

The harness is inferred from the first event's `type`:
- user, assistant or system → claude_code
- session or message → pi
- session_meta, turn_context, response_item or event_msg → codex
- session_start → droid

The session id comes from Claude's `sessionId`, Codex's `payload.id`, or the Pi/droid header `id` (https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/blob/main/src/datasets/packaged_modules/json/json.py, added in https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/pull/8113).

STS format:
- The first line is a header: {"type":"session","harness":<id, required>,"id":<required>,"name":<optional>}. Any extra metadata "is allowed and ignored".
- Every following line is {"type":"message","message":{role: user|assistant|system|tool, content, reasoningContent?, toolCalls?: [{id, function:{name, arguments (JSON string)}}], toolCallId?, timestamp? (epoch ms), model?}}.
- The viewer pairs each tool result with its call through toolCallId. The only harness id the docs list as recognized is `llama.app`. Pi's own session format is accepted as an alternative if a `harness` field is added (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/session-traces-format).

STS has no schema-version field, no hashes, no signatures and no event ids beyond tool-call ids.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no content-level merge anywhere.

Dataset repos:
- `hf upload` / upload_folder create commits server-side over HTTP. Large folders are split automatically into several commits, and uploads resume by skipping files already committed (https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/upload).
- CommitOperationAdd overwrites an existing path.
- create_commit takes an optional `parent_commit` for optimistic concurrency. The commit "will fail if `revision` does not point to `parent_commit`", which is "especially useful if the repo is updated / committed to concurrently" (https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/package_reference/hf_api).
- Pull requests use refs/pr/N.
- HF's recommended pattern for concurrent replicas is unique (UUID) file names, so writers never overwrite each other (CommitScheduler section of the upload guide). Claude Code sessions are one file per session UUID, so independent machines rarely collide on a path. Two writers uploading the same growing file would overwrite each other; this is inferred, not stated.

Buckets:
- Overwrite-in-place, no versions, and deletes are "immediate and permanent" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets).
- batch_bucket_files is "non-transactional", so a failure can leave a partial result and raise BucketBatchError (https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/buckets).
- `hf buckets sync` goes one way per invocation. It compares size and mtime by default and only adds or updates unless --delete is passed.
- The docs describe no conditional writes or conflict detection, so the behaviour is effectively last-writer-wins (inferred).
- The docs show writing each agent to its own prefix (…/codex).

The third-party pi-share-hf supports several machines for the same project through incremental workspace state (https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf).
realtime:
Not real-time on dataset repos. Each upload is a git commit. For live traces HF recommends either a Storage Bucket or a CommitScheduler set to commit every N minutes, with at least 5 minutes advised. It explains that "you don't want to version every update of your data because it'll make the git repository unusable" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/datasets-ingesting, https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/upload).

`hf buckets sync` is a one-shot command. The CLI reference lists no --watch, interval or daemon option (https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/package_reference/cli). "Keep syncing as new sessions land" therefore means re-running it, for example from cron or a hook. Buckets accept high-rate updates. HfFileSystem append mode with flush() uploads only new data because of Xet deduplication; the default blocksize is 5 MiB and can be lowered (datasets-ingesting).

Consumers can follow changes in two ways:
- Bucket webhooks: `repo.content` events carrying `updatedFiles` (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/webhooks).
- Live follow, documented 2026-09-17 (https://github.com/huggingface/hub-docs/pull/2786): a server-sent-events stream at GET /api/buckets/<owner>/<bucket>/events. It emits ready, changes, reset and reconnect events. Changes are coalesced and give path, op (add/update/delete), size, xetHash, uploadedAt and mtime, but no file content. Only about the last 15 minutes can be replayed. Streams are recycled about every 20 minutes and pinged every 30 seconds (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets).
search_retrieval:
Dataset repos, in Data Studio:
- A paged table of 100 rows; clicking a row opens the trace viewer, which shows the "session timeline, prompts, assistant messages, tool calls, and results" (agent-traces page).
- Case-insensitive word search across string columns, nested values included.
- Filter by value.
- A DuckDB SQL Console over the auto-converted Parquet, also available as `hf datasets sql`.
- For JSONL datasets over 5GB, only the first 5GB is shown and searchable.
- For private datasets the viewer needs PRO, Team or Enterprise (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/data-studio).

Buckets: you navigate to a .jsonl file and open it; listing is by prefix. No full-text search over buckets is documented (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets).

Programmatic: datasets.load_dataset returns the agent-trace features (json.py).

Discovery across the Hub: the format:agent-traces filter (https://huggingface.co/datasets?format=format%3Aagent-traces).

No semantic or vector search is documented.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Traces live in a dataset or bucket separate from the project's code repository. Neither the agent-traces docs nor the STS spec define fields for repo, commit, branch or diff; extra header metadata is allowed but ignored (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/session-traces-format). Any cwd or branch fields in the raw harness lines are kept verbatim inside the `trace` column but not interpreted. The loader uses `cwd` only to tell openclaw from Pi (json.py). A dataset repo's git history versions the trace files themselves, not the code they describe. The only cross-link the docs mention is model-card `buckets:` metadata, which links a model to a bucket, not to code (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/storage-buckets).
privacy_security:
Redaction:
- The upload path does no redaction; raw JSONL goes up unchanged. The docs tell users to "Review and redact traces before publishing them publicly, or keep the dataset or bucket private" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/agent-traces).
- The Hub runs TruffleHog "on each push" and emails the owner only about verified secrets. This is detection after upload, not blocking (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security-secrets). Whether bucket writes are scanned is not documented, so this cannot be verified.
- For Pi, the docs point to the third-party pi-share-hf (https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf). It redacts exact secret values taken from an env file, secret files or literals, and deliberately avoids generic regexes ("Exact values are high precision. Generic token regexes are noisy"). It then runs TruffleHog and blocks a session on any finding: verified, unverified or unknown. An LLM review follows, and only sessions that pass all checks are uploaded to a dataset along with a manifest.jsonl. It can also strip images.

Platform security:
- Buckets are encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS. Access is controlled through SSO, RBAC via Resource Groups and scoped tokens. Organizations get audit logs. Data residency is US or EU. HF holds SOC 2 Type 2 and states GDPR compliance (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/storage-buckets-security).
- Encryption is server-side only. No client-side or end-to-end encryption is documented, so HF can read the content.
- Xet deduplication is permission-scoped: "you can only read chunks which are required to reproduce files you have access to" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/xet/security).

Erasure:
- Bucket deletes are permanent, which helps erasure.
- In a dataset repo, a leaked secret stays in git history until the history is squashed, an irreversible step (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/storage-limits).

The ecosystem's stated purpose is sharing traces as training data (teich SFT conversion). The docs do not discuss prompt-injection risk from recalled traces.
scale:
Xet:
- Content-defined chunking at about 64KB (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/xet/deduplication).
- Repos "up to Terabyte-scale" (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/repositories).

Git-repo guidance, which does not apply to buckets (https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/storage-limits):
- Under 100k files per repo and under 10k entries per folder.
- Under 200GB per file, with a 500GB hard limit.
- About 50–100 files per commit.
- The experience "starts to degrade after a few thousand commits" because "a git repository is not meant to work as a database with a lot of writes".

Storage pricing (same page): 100GB of private storage free for free accounts, then $18/TB/month private pay-as-you-go. No per-bucket size limit is stated.

Data Studio previews and searches only the first 5GB of a dataset.

Observed usage:
- Example dataset TeichAI/DeepSeek-v4-Pro-Agent: 4,006 JSONL session files, about 280MB (https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeichAI/DeepSeek-v4-Pro-Agent).
- The format:agent-traces filter listed 503 datasets on 2026-10-02. That count came from a model-extracted page summary, so treat it as approximate.
license: The Hub service and the trace viewer UI are proprietary; I found no open-source viewer, which is unverified rather than confirmed. The detection and parsing code is in `datasets` (Apache-2.0, per its LICENSE file; https://github.com/huggingface/datasets). Format tagging is in dataset-viewer (Apache-2.0 per its SPDX headers; https://github.com/huggingface/dataset-viewer). teich is Apache-2.0 (https://pypi.org/project/teich/). I did not find a license line in pi-share-hf's README. I did not check the license of huggingface_hub (the hf CLI) in this session.
lesson_for_parinn:
HF has run this exact workload: raw Claude Code JSONL, many machines, kept syncing. Its own docs say git is the wrong live store. "A git repository is not meant to work as a database with a lot of writes", the experience degrades "after a few thousand commits", and live traces should go to a non-versioned bucket or be batched into commits at least 5 minutes apart.

What HF chose instead gives up everything ParleyInn needs:
- Buckets have no history and overwrite in place.
- Sync decides what to upload by size and mtime only.
- Batch writes are non-transactional.
- Live-follow replay covers only about 15 minutes.
- Integrity, ordering and redaction are left to the user.

Concrete lesson:
- Keep the canonical record in ParleyInn's own append-only, hash-chained log.
- Treat any git or hosted remote only as a batched export or transport target.
- Write one immutable file per session id, which conflict-free multi-writer needs without merges, and include the hash-chain head so the remote can be verified without being trusted.
- Never write one commit per event.
- Put a pi-share-hf-style gate in front of any export: exact-value secret redaction, a scanner that blocks on any finding, then review. HF itself only warns and emails after the push, and leaked secrets stay in dataset git history until an irreversible squash.

Cheap interop win: emit STS-format JSONL so ParleyInn sessions open in the HF viewer. Note that STS carries no integrity fields of its own.

name: Hypercore (Holepunch / Pear stack)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Hypercore stores arbitrary binary blocks in a single append-only log. Each block can be at most 15 MB (MAX_SUGGESTED_BLOCK_SIZE). Next to the blocks it keeps the Merkle tree nodes, bitfield pages that record which blocks are held locally, auth and manifest data, sessions, and a key-value "User Data" store that stays local (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore, https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore-storage). Blocks can be decoded as json, utf-8, binary or any compact-encoding codec (README valueEncoding). User Data "is persisted locally and is not replicated". Autobase uses it to keep encryption keys (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore). Hypercore has no built-in notion of agent sessions, prompts or code. It is a general-purpose log.
where_stored: A local DB on each peer, replicated peer to peer. Since the Hypercore 11 line the storage engine is hypercore-storage, "Built on RocksDB", and the README says "random-access-storage is no longer supported" (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore-storage, https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore). Corestore manages many cores in one store (https://github.com/holepunchto/corestore). Peers sync over Hyperswarm/HyperDHT connections encrypted with Noise. There is no central server, although a relay node can be named for when hole-punching fails (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hyperswarm). The Pears docs still describe per-core oplog/tree/blocks/bitfield files (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hypercore). That looks like the older v10 layout and disagrees with the current README.
format_and_model:
- **Data model:** a log of blocks addressed by index. It exposes length, byteLength, fork, signedLength and contiguousLength (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore).
- **Integrity:** a BLAKE2b Merkle tree, using a flat-tree layout (flat-tree is a dependency per the npm metadata at https://registry.npmjs.org/hypercore/latest). Ed25519 signatures cover the tree roots. signable() encodes key + treeHash + length + fork (README).
- **Identity:** the core's public key is a hash of its manifest. The manifest holds version, hash: 'blake2b' ("Only Blake2b is supported currently"), allowPatch, quorum, signers [{signature: 'ed25519', namespace, publicKey}], prologue, linked and userData. Changing any manifest field changes the key (README).
- **Discovery key:** derived from the public key. It lets peers find each other "without leaking the core key" (README).
- **Rewrites:** truncate(newLength) rolls back and bumps a fork id, which "should be monotonely incrementing" (README).
- **Version and compatibility:** Hypercore 10 is "LTS, meaning the storage format and wire protocol is forward compatible with future versions" (README). The current npm release is hypercore 11.37.1, published 2026-09-28, MIT licensed. hypercore-storage is 3.3.1 under Apache-2.0 (https://registry.npmjs.org/hypercore, https://registry.npmjs.org/hypercore-storage).
- **Language:** JavaScript only, running on Node or Bare.
- **Ports:** a Rust port exists, datrs/hypercore 0.17.0-alpha.1 (Aug 2026), with a wire-protocol crate that targets LTS v10 (https://crates.io/crates/hypercore, https://docs.rs/crate/hypercore-protocol/0.7.2). No Go implementation of the protocol was found. A pkg.go.dev search turned up only undocumented go-hypercore fragments (bitfield, flattree, merkle) with no stated protocol compliance (https://pkg.go.dev/search?q=hypercore&m=package).
multi_writer_and_merge:
A core is single-writer by default: one keypair appends. The manifest can list several signers with a quorum, so signedLength is "signed by a quorum", but that is joint signing of one log, not concurrent writing (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore).

Real multi-writer comes from Autobase (7.28.2, Sep 2026, Apache-2.0):
- Each writer has its own core, and blocks carry explicit causal references that form a DAG.
- A deterministic linearisation guarantees "nodes never precede nodes they reference", and ordering "is eventually consistent".
- An apply() function folds the linearised nodes into views, usually Hypercores or Hyperbees.
- When new causal information arrives, Autobase "undoes and reapplies" view changes. Views must therefore derive only from their store argument.
- Indexers set a quorum-signed checkpoint, after which the order no longer changes.

Sources: https://github.com/holepunchto/autobase, https://registry.npmjs.org/autobase. There is no textual merge or conflict UI. Merge semantics are whatever the app's apply() does.
realtime:
Yes. Real time is a core design goal: "sharing large datasets and realtime streams" (README).
- `core.get(i)` waits for a block to download, with timeout, wait:false and onwait options.
- `update()` fetches the newest signed length from peers.
- `createReadStream({ live: true })` stays open and emits new blocks as peers append them.
- Replication is sparse: download(range) fetches only selected blocks, and every block is checked against the signed tree when it arrives.

Sources: https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore, https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hypercore. Peers find each other through 32-byte topics on HyperDHT and connect with hole-punching, with optional relayThrough (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hyperswarm).
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by block index, by index range, or by byte offset through `seek(byteOffset)`. `proof()` and `verifyFullyRemote()` support verified reads of single blocks (README). Sorted key/range lookups come from Hyperbee, "An append-only B-tree running on a Hypercore", whose latest release is 2.27.3 (https://github.com/holepunchto/hyperbee). There is no full-text, semantic or vector search anywhere in the stack, so any index has to be built as a derived view.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. Hypercore is a generic log substrate and has no concept of agent sessions, prompts, commits or worktrees. Linking sessions to code would be up to the application, for example by writing commit SHAs into blocks or Hyperbee keys. No such integration was found.
privacy_security:
- **Integrity:** Ed25519-signed BLAKE2b Merkle trees let any peer verify every block it receives, even from untrusted peers (README).
- **Read access:** holding the core key is enough to read and verify. The discovery key used on the DHT is derived from it and does not reveal it (README).
- **Transport:** connections are Noise-encrypted secret-streams. `createProtocolStream` creates "an encrypted noise stream". Hyperswarm adds a firewall callback to reject peers (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore, https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hyperswarm).
- **At rest and against replicas:** optional block encryption uses `encryption: { key }` or a pluggable HypercoreEncryption provider with key ids and rotation through a getEncryptionKey(id) hook. Encrypted blocks are padded (https://github.com/holepunchto/hypercore-encryption, README).
- **Redaction:** none. Blocks are immutable once replicated. clear() only drops local copies, and truncate() forks the log but cannot recall data peers already hold (README).
- **Secrets:** there is no secret scanning. Writer secret keys and Autobase encryption keys sit in local storage and User Data (README).
- **Exposure:** the DHT shows peer IP addresses and which discovery keys a peer announces. The docs do not discuss metadata privacy (https://docs.pears.com/building-blocks/hyperswarm says nothing on it, so this cannot be verified from primary sources).
scale: The only documented limit is the 15 MB maximum suggested block size (README). The design aims at "large datasets" through sparse replication and O(log n) Merkle proofs (README). The stack underpins Holepunch's Keet and the Pear runtime (https://docs.pears.com/). No published numbers on log length, peer counts or throughput were found, so scale claims cannot be verified.
license: MIT for hypercore, hyperswarm, hyperbee and corestore. Apache-2.0 for hypercore-storage, autobase and hypercore-encryption (npm registry metadata, e.g. https://registry.npmjs.org/hypercore).
lesson_for_parinn:
Give each writer its own signed log, and verify with a Merkle tree rather than a plain hash chain.

Hypercore keeps every log single-writer, so each agent or session would own its own core. Merging happens only in a deterministic derived view. Autobase does this: it linearises a causal DAG and replays apply() when the order changes, which matches ParleyInn's I10 "everything derived is rebuildable".

Signing Merkle roots plus an explicit, monotonic fork counter gives two things a linear hash chain does not:
- O(log n) verified reads of a single event, which allows sparse or partial replication to sandboxes.
- Rewrites that are visible rather than silent.

Hypercore also uses three separate keys, and ParleyInn could do the same: one to verify and read (the public key), one to find peers (the derived discovery key), and one to decrypt (the block encryption key).

Hypercore itself cannot be embedded. It is JavaScript-only, there is no Go port, and it is network-native, which conflicts with I4. At most it could serve as an out-of-process transport sidecar. ParleyInn should copy its data-structure ideas, not take it on as a dependency.

name: IETF SCITT (RFC 9943)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Signed statements (COSE_Sign1 structures) about supply chain artifacts. Statements can contain SBOMs, security analysis reports, vulnerability disclosures, build metadata, deployment records, malware scan results, patch logs, or any content an issuer wishes to publish. Each statement is identified by issuer (iss claim) and subject (sub claim, the artifact). Statement payloads are opaque to the transparency service and may be encrypted.
where_stored: Transparency Services (TS) maintain Verifiable Data Structures (VDS)—append-only, cryptographically verifiable logs. Multiple TS instances can each maintain their own VDS. A single signed statement may be registered with multiple TS. The VDS itself is typically backed by trusted hardware, consensus protocols, or cryptographic evidence. Statement payload storage is decoupled from VDS metadata; VDS may store only cryptographic hashes rather than full statements (via adjacent services).
format_and_model: Signed Statements: COSE_Sign1 messages (RFC 9052) with CBOR (RFC 8949) encoding. Message structures defined in CDDL (RFC 8610). Statements use CWT Claims (RFC 8392) in protected header for issuer and subject identity. Receipts: COSE_Sign1 structures (RFC 9942) containing Verifiable Data Structure Proofs (VDP)—currently RFC9162_SHA256 (similar to Certificate Transparency's Merkle tree). Extensible to other VDS types and proof formats. Application media types: application/scitt-statement+cose, application/scitt-receipt+cose.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single-issuer statements: each statement is signed by one issuer with a non-repudiable signature. Multiple issuers can make different, conflicting, or affirmative statements about the same artifact (same sub claim). Statements are recorded in a linear, irrevocable order by the TS (append-only). Non-equivocation property ensures all proofs from the TS derive from a single VDS with a unique ordered sequence—no forks. Multiple receipts may be attached to one signed statement if registered with multiple TS. Merges: not applicable; the model is append-only, not merge-based.
realtime: Not specified in architecture. Registration is asynchronous: client submits signed statement, TS evaluates registration policy, adds to VDS, produces receipt. Timing and notification mechanisms are TS-implementation-specific and out-of-scope of RFC 9943. Relying parties retrieve transparent statements and proofs at their own pace (pull model).
search_retrieval: Search/retrieval mechanisms are out-of-scope in RFC 9943. VDS provides: (1) Inclusion proofs—receipts prove a statement is at a specific position in the VDS, verifiable without contacting TS; (2) Consistency proofs—prove the VDS is append-only between two points. Relying parties can replay the entire VDS to audit. Adjacent services (APIs, databases, object storage) may expose query interfaces for finding statements by subject, issuer, or metadata; these are implementation-defined.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. SCITT is designed for supply chain artifacts (compiled binaries, source code components, SBOMs, vulnerability reports, build records) and their provenance. It does not address AI agent sessions, prompts, or session history linkage. However, supply chain statements could reference code artifacts (by hash, package name, version) to establish traceability.
privacy_security: Privacy: TS is trusted with confidentiality of submitted signed statements. Issuers and clients responsible for assessing TS's privacy/security posture before submission. Statements may contain sensitive data; PII and confidential information must be carefully reviewed. Metadata analysis possible (order of submissions may reveal patterns). VDS can operate in privacy-preserving mode using only cryptographic hashes of statements in the log, with payloads stored separately. Security: Mandatory registration checks verify COSE signatures cryptographically using trust anchors (X.509 roots, OIDC providers, etc.). Registration Policies enforced at registration time and made transparent (stored as statements themselves). Key management: TS public key must be known by relying parties. Signature algorithm agility supported via COSE. Revocation and key compromise handled via new registration policies and statements.
lesson_for_parinn: SCITT demonstrates a production-grade standard for append-only, non-equivocal statement transparency with cryptographic receipts. Key lessons for ParleyInn: (1) Non-equivocation—consistent proofs to all relying parties despite multiple TS instances and auditors. Use of Merkle trees ensures universal verifiability without online TS access (similar to CT). (2) Receipts as minimal proofs—prove statement inclusion without revealing the statement itself, allowing external storage. (3) Registration policies as first-class statements—policies themselves versioned and traceable, enabling auditability of policy changes. (4) Single-issuer but multi-statement design—unlike consensus ledgers, SCITT trusts a single TS operator for ordering, simplifying security model. For ParleyInn: could adopt COSE signing for agent session records, SCITT-like receipts from a consensus VDS to prove non-equivocation, and store payloads in git while VDS anchors them cryptographically.

name: immudb (Codenotary)
status: shipped. Latest stable release is v1.11.2, dated 3 Sep 2026 on the releases page. The tag points at master HEAD bfdce03 (2 Sep 2026), so the project is active and not archived. v1.11.1 came out on 26 Jun 2026 and v1.11.0 on 23 Apr 2026. A v2.0.0-RC1 pre-release from 20 May 2025 has only the changelog line "v2 version" and no v2 GA has followed. The discovery note's v1.9.5 is stale: it dates from 16 Sep 2024, although the README quickstart still shows it. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/releases and https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/CHANGELOG.md
what_is_stored: General-purpose tamper-evident data. It is not agent-specific. You can add new versions of a record but never change or delete it in place. The same store works three ways: as a key-value store, as JSON documents in versioned collections, and as SQL tables. Each transaction holds a list of key/value/metadata entries plus a header: timestamp, version, tx metadata, entry count, EH, BlTxID, BlRoot and the Alh hash. KV metadata has three attributes: deleted (a logical tombstone), expiresAt and nonIndexable. Size limits differ by layer. The embedded store defaults to MaxTxEntries=1024, MaxKeyLen=1024 and MaxValueLen=4096 bytes. The server raises MaxValueLen to 32 MB. With the opt-in --audit-log flag, the server also stores one JSON event per gRPC operation under the key prefix "audit:" (fields ts, user, ip, db, method, type, ok, err, dur_ms, sid). Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/kv_metadata.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/options.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/pkg/server/db_options.go, https://immudb.io/docs/develop/document/datamodel/
where_stored:
A local data directory of append-only files. Per database, the store creates:
- a transaction log ("tx")
- a commit log ("commit")
- N value logs ("val_0".."val_N")
- the appendable hash tree in "aht/"
- the B-tree index in "index/", or "index_<prefix>" for multi-index SQL

The file names are visible in embedded/store/immustore.go. Optionally, the data can live on S3 or an S3-compatible service such as MinIO, read with range fetches. It runs as a server (gRPC on port 3322, metrics on 9497, plus PostgreSQL wire protocol v3) or fully in-process as a Go library. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/immustore.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/docs/EMBEDDING.md
format_and_model:
Custom binary chunked append-only logs, hashed with SHA-256. This is not git and not human-readable. The verification model works in three layers:
1. Each entry digest is SHA-256 over the metadata length, the metadata, the key length, the key and SHA-256(value). Values are committed by hash (EntrySpecDigest_v1).
2. The entry digests in one transaction form a per-tx Merkle tree whose root is EH.
3. The tx hash is Alh = H(TxID, previous Alh, innerHash). innerHash covers the timestamp, version, metadata, entry count, EH and the main Merkle tree state at commit (BlTxID, BlRoot).

So the Alh values form a linear hash chain, and each Alh is also appended as a leaf to one persistent main Merkle tree per database. Proofs are "DualProofs": a Merkle part for history up to BlTxID, which is logarithmic, plus a linear part. Since v1.3.2 the linear part is limited to one entry. Indexing uses an extended B-tree (tbtree), synchronous or asynchronous. The README lists ACID with snapshot isolation (it writes "SSI") and calls the store schema-free. SQL and document layers sit on top of the KV store, using key prefixes and multi-indexing. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/docs/security/PROOFS.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/verification.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/docs/EMBEDDING.md
multi_writer_and_merge:
One writer per database, with no merge model. Inside one process, many goroutines can write at once (MVCC/snapshot isolation; MaxConcurrency defaults to 30). Across processes, the embedding guide says a data directory "must be opened by one process at a time". immudb takes no lock file and no flock, so a second process opening the same directory succeeds, and the result is "silent corruption". The guide also points to a flock example at contrib/immuledger, but no contrib/ directory exists at tag v1.11.2 (checked in a clone).

Replication is primary to replica only:
- Asynchronous replicas pull committed transactions through the ExportTx gRPC stream. Replicas "are read only and any direct write operation will be rejected", and replicas can be chained.
- Synchronous replication waits for a majority quorum of replicas. If the quorum is lost, the primary "goes into a hung state". Failover is manual promotion, and "the primary node [must] be always predefined". There is no multi-primary.

History is one total order: each Alh chains to the previous one. Two independently written stores therefore cannot be merged. Each would have to stay a separate database (a server holds many) or be re-appended as new transactions. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/docs/EMBEDDING.md, https://immudb.io/docs/production/replication/, https://immudb.io/docs/production/sync-replication/, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/options.go
realtime: Partly. Inside a process, a reader can block until a transaction ID commits or is indexed (WaitForTx and WaitForIndexingUpto in embedded/store, backed by embedded/watchers). Replicas follow the primary over a streaming gRPC export (exportTx / streamExportTx), and sync replication confirms a commit only after a quorum has it. In schema.proto at v1.11.2 I found no general subscribe, watch or change-feed RPC for ordinary clients (grep). Clients get chunked streams for get, set, scan and history, but no push notification of new transactions. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/embedded/store/immustore.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/pkg/api/schema/schema.proto, https://immudb.io/docs/production/sync-replication/
search_retrieval:
Exact and structured lookups only:
- KV: Get, prefix Scan, ZScan over sorted sets, History of a key (shows deletions) and TxScan.
- Verified reads: VerifiableGet or SQL verification functions, for example immudb_verify_row, immudb_verify_tx and immudb_history.
- Time travel: SINCE/UNTIL TX ranges and DIFF OF queries, which return INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE per row between two transactions.
- SQL: joins, CTEs, window functions and LIKE/ILIKE.

Indexes are B-tree only. The README lists GIN/GiST as unsupported. There is no full-text or semantic search. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/pkg/api/schema/schema.proto, https://immudb.io/docs/develop/deleting/
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. immudb is a generic database with no notion of agent sessions, prompts, commits or worktrees. The "sid" field in its audit log is immudb's own client session ID. The README does list users who store CI/CD recipes and build artifacts tamper-proof, but there is no git integration. Source: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md
scale: The README claims immudb "can handle millions of writes per second". Its embedded-store benchmark inserts 1M entries on a 4-core E3-1275v6 machine with SSD, using batches of 1000: 1.2M/s with 20 workers, 1.8M/s with 50 and 1.6M/s with 100. In Hacker News discussion 29702974, user yencabulator criticised such figures because they rely on batched inserts. The README also claims 157M Docker Hub pulls and sharding as its partition method. I found no independently verified production size figures. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=29702974
privacy_security:
Integrity:
- Tamper evidence comes from the SHA-256 Alh chain plus the Merkle tree. The client keeps the last trusted state (Go file cache, Python/Java/C# state holders) and checks every verified read or write against it.
- The server can sign states with an ECDSA key (--signingKey), and an auditor process re-checks consistency. Since v1.11.1 the auditor has an opt-in --audit-verify-values flag that re-reads committed values and checks their SHA-256.
- Past proof bug: the "linear-fake" issue let a server show different transaction contents to different clients, because the middle of the linear proof was not checked. It was mitigated by a LinearAdvance proof and by keeping linear proofs at length 1, true for transactions committed by servers v1.3.2 and later.
- The HN thread points out the limits: a client that writes legitimately can still move the store to any state, and rollback detection depends on state kept outside the database.

Deletion and erasure:
- DELETE is logical: a tombstone, still visible through History and the embedded store. expiresAt is also logical.
- Physical erasure exists only through retention/truncation, which "only deletes data that is stored in the value log, leaving the proofs and schema configuration data intact". This works because entries commit to value hashes.

Encryption and secrets:
- In the v1.11.2 source I found no encryption at rest for local data. The only encryption options are S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or aws:kms) for remote storage.
- There is no redaction or secret scanning.

Defaults and hardening:
- TLS is off by default (TLSConfig nil). The default admin account is immudb with password immudb. The PG wire server warns that it uses cleartext passwords without TLS.
- Recent hardening: archive-restore path-traversal checks, sessions invalidated when a user's permissions change, and token files written with mode 0600.

For ParleyInn's I4: `go list -deps` at v1.11.2 shows that even the leanest embed (embedded/store) pulls in net, net/http and crypto/tls, through Prometheus client_golang (expvar, expfmt). pkg/database also links google.golang.org/grpc. Importing these packages is not the same as opening sockets, but it would fail ParleyInn's depguard and import-closure gate.

Sources: https://immudb.io/docs/management/state/, https://immudb.io/docs/production/retention/, https://immudb.io/docs/develop/deleting/, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/tree/v1.11.2/docs/security/vulnerabilities/linear-fake, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/pkg/server/options.go, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/README.md, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=29702974
license:
Business Source License 1.1, which is source-available, for immudb 1.9DOM.2 and later (from 29 Dec 2023).
- Licensor: Codenotary, Inc.
- Additional Use Grant: production use is allowed unless you offer immudb to third parties "on a hosted or embedded basis" in a paid "competitive offering" that significantly overlaps Codenotary's paid versions. Free products and internal use are explicitly not competitive.
- Change License: Apache 2.0, effective four years after each version is published.

Releases up to v1.9DOM.1 (16 Nov 2023) are Apache-2.0. An HN post titled "Immudb changes license to BSL just before holidays" (item 38807459, 29 Dec 2023) marks the switch; the item page itself returned 403, so it is known only from the HN search API listing. MariaDB's BSL FAQ describes BSL as "a new alternative to closed source or open core licensing models". BSL 1.1 would fail a permissive SPDX allow-list such as ParleyInn's ENG-18 gate. Its OSI status was not fetched here. Sources: https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.11.2/LICENSE, https://github.com/codenotary/immudb/blob/v1.9DOM.1/LICENSE, https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=immudb&tags=story, https://mariadb.com/bsl-faq-mariadb/
lesson_for_parinn:
Commit to the hash of each payload, not the payload, and keep payloads in a separate value log. Wrap the hash chain in an append-only Merkle tree.

How immudb does it: an entry digest is H(metadata, key, SHA-256(value)), and transactions chain through Alh = H(TxID, prevAlh, innerHash). Retention can therefore physically delete value-log bytes while every proof still verifies. The Merkle tree over the Alh values gives logarithmic inclusion and consistency proofs between any two heads.

What ParleyInn should copy:
- Hash records as H(header || SHA-256(body)), so a redacted or GDPR-erased body leaves a verifiable tombstone instead of a broken chain (I6 and I10 stay intact).
- Persist the last trusted head outside the store, so a rollback or a forked replica is detectable.
- Verify every element a consistency proof consumes; immudb's "linear-fake" bug came from checking only the endpoints.

What ParleyInn should not copy:
- immudb's embedded mode takes no directory lock. ParleyInn must flock its log itself.
- It is single-primary with a total order and no merge. Many worktrees, sandboxes or machines need one log per writer, with cross-log proofs rather than one shared chain.
- Taking immudb as a dependency is ruled out anyway: the BSL license fails the allow-list, and its import closure includes net/http.

name: in-toto agent-decision/v0.1 predicate RFC (in-toto/attestation issue #554)
category: provenance spec (proposal): a proposed in-toto attestation predicate type for AI agent authorization decisions
status: announced. This is an open RFC issue with nothing merged. The issue is titled "RFC: agent-decision/v0.1 predicate for AI agent policy decisions". GitHub user 0xff4c1d opened it on 2026-05-19 and gives the affiliation "Auxidus Technologies". When fetched on 2026-10-02 it was open, had no labels, and no comments or linked PRs were visible (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554). A shallow clone of in-toto/attestation main (HEAD fd2609c, 2026-09-14) has no agent-decision file in spec/predicates/. The vetted-predicates list also does not mention it (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/main/spec/predicates/README.md). For it to be accepted, someone would have to open a PR from the predicate template, ideally with a protobuf definition, and the maintainers would review it at a meeting (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/blob/main/docs/new_predicate_guidelines.md#vetting-process). None of that has happened yet.
what_is_stored:
One signed statement per authorization decision an AI agent makes about tool use. Five predicate fields are required:
- agent_id: a stable agent instance identifier.
- principal: {subject, optional spiffe_id}.
- policy_evaluations[]: each entry is {policy, decision allow|deny, reason, optional policy_ids}.
- tool_calls[]: each entry is {name, args_hash}, where args_hash is "sha256:<hex>" of the tool arguments. The raw arguments are not stored.
- decided_at: an RFC 3339 timestamp.

Two fields are optional: evaluation_results[] ({name, passed} gate results, e.g. a "cedar-ifc-gate") and trace_parent (a W3C Trace Context traceparent).

In the example, the statement subject[] is the tool name ("write_file") with a sha256 digest, and that digest is all zeros. The record holds no prompts, model outputs, conversation transcript, model identity, or code diff (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554). The motivation section cites EU AI Act Article 12 record-keeping for regulated deployers (issue #554). Article 12 itself requires automatic event logging over the lifetime of high-risk AI systems, for risk identification, post-market monitoring and operational monitoring (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/12/).
where_stored: The spec does not say. It only defines a payload format. The deployer chooses where to store and transport the signed statements: a file, an OCI registry, a transparency log, and so on. Nothing in the RFC mentions git, a database or a server (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554). Section 1 of the issue's open questions asks whether the predicate URI should live at https://auxidus.dev/attestation/agent-decision/v0.1 or at an in-toto.io alias. auxidus.dev did not resolve in DNS when fetched from this environment on 2026-10-02, so the URI currently points nowhere I could verify.
format_and_model:
An in-toto Statement v1 ("_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1"), carrying subject[], predicateType and predicate, wrapped as a DSSE payload. The planned repo layout is docs/predicates/agent-decision/v0.1/README.md plus a JSON Schema file named agent-decision-v0.1.json. The RFC says a reference implementation exists: an "auxidus_evidence::dsse" module that signs DSSE envelopes with Ed25519. The issue says the predicate's semantics follow a "human-review/v0.1" predicate. The v0.1 roadmap lists SPIFFE-bound principals, cosign compatibility and OpenTelemetry traceparent (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).

Three claims could not be verified:
- The reference implementation: the author's GitHub profile shows only two unrelated forks (https://github.com/0xff4c1d). A GitHub repository search for "auxidus" finds only 2019 C# libraries (https://github.com/search?q=auxidus&type=repositories).
- The human-review/v0.1 predicate: it does not appear anywhere in the in-toto/attestation repo (checked by grep of the clone at fd2609c).
- The JSON Schema: no schema file has been published.

The data model is flat and has one record per decision. It defines no chaining, sequence number, session id or reference to an earlier record.
multi_writer_and_merge: Does not apply. Each statement stands alone and is signed by whoever produces it. The model has no shared log, no ordering and no merge rule. The only fields that could tie records together across writers are agent_id, principal and the optional trace_parent (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).
realtime: Not addressed. A statement is produced at decision time (decided_at), but the RFC defines no streaming, transport or subscription mechanism (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).
search_retrieval: Not addressed by the predicate. Retrieval would rely on generic in-toto and Sigstore tooling, or on correlation through trace_parent with an OpenTelemetry backend. The RFC specifies no index or query surface (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).
links_sessions_to_code: Weak. A record links an agent and principal to tool names and hashes of the tool arguments. It does not link to a session, prompt, commit, file content or diff. The subject is a tool name with a digest, and in the example that digest is all zeros. Section 3 of the issue's open questions defers linking to SLSA and OIDC identities to v0.2. A trace_parent could correlate decisions with one distributed trace or agent run (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).
scale: No scale claims in the RFC (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554).
privacy_security:
- Tool arguments are recorded only as SHA-256 hashes (args_hash) to keep raw arguments out of the record. Section 2 of the issue's open questions asks whether to keep this or embed redacted arguments instead.
- The hashes are unsalted. Low-entropy arguments, such as short paths or small JSON objects, could be recovered by brute-force guessing, and the RFC does not mention this risk (my analysis, not stated in the RFC).
- Integrity and authenticity come from a DSSE signature, Ed25519 in the claimed reference implementation.
- The spec defines no encryption, secret scanning, key management or revocation.
- The reason field is free text, and any viewer could read it as instructions. The RFC does not discuss this.
Source for all points about the RFC's content: https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/issues/554.
license: Not stated for the predicate. If it were merged, it would fall under the in-toto/attestation repository's license (Apache-2.0 per the repo). I did not re-check that license for this report. The claimed reference implementation has no license I could verify.
lesson_for_parinn:
ParleyInn should borrow the envelope but not the data model. A DSSE-wrapped in-toto Statement v1 with a custom predicateType is a cheap, standard, offline-verifiable way to export signed ParleyInn records. It fits I4 because signing and verifying need no network. A predicate is also how auditors citing EU AI Act Art. 12 increasingly expect agent evidence to look.

The RFC also shows what ParleyInn must add on top:
- A record field that chains to the previous record's hash and gives a session id or sequence number. Isolated signed statements cannot prove that nothing was dropped (ParleyInn's I6).
- A salted or keyed hash, or pointers to encrypted content, instead of a bare sha256 of the arguments. Otherwise the arguments can be recovered by guessing.
- Free-text fields such as reason treated as untrusted on recall (I2).

So an "agent-decision"-style export should be a view projected from ParleyInn's own append-only record, not the record itself. ParleyInn should not depend on this predicate URI until it is merged and hosted. As of 2026-10-02, the issue is unmerged and the auxidus.dev namespace does not resolve.
confidence: medium. The issue's existence and content are confirmed from the GitHub page, and the predicate is confirmed not merged as of repo HEAD on 2026-09-14. The reference implementation, the human-review/v0.1 predicate it cites, and the auxidus.dev namespace could not be verified. The issue's comment thread could not be read through the API: GitHub API access to this repo is not enabled for this session. The web page showed no comments.

name: in-toto AI Agent Action predicate (in-toto/attestation PR #588), type URI https://in-toto.io/attestation/ai-agent-action/v0.1
category: provenance spec (draft in-toto predicate) plus reference MCP audit gateway
status: announced (open PR, not merged; last activity 2026-09-30; spec v0.1.0, listed under community contributions, not vetted). The type URI returns 404 because nothing is merged yet.
what_is_stored: Metadata about one MCP tool call per record, as seen by an intermediary (gateway, proxy or sidecar) between the AI client and the tool server. Stored fields: id, type, timestamp, method, toolName, namespace, upstream server, principal, durationMs, success, errorCode/errorClass, previousHash, SHA-256 content digests of the JSON-RPC params and of result/error, attestorVersion, configHash (hash of the policy config), and optional decisionContextDigest, extensions/extensionsDigest, aiInvocation (model, sessionId, turnId, invocationReason) and parties (provenance). By default it stores no tool arguments or outputs, only their digests. There are two more record types on the same chain: checkpoint (sequence, recordCount, head hash) and chain_break (reason, priorHead, priorSequence, priorRecordCount). It does not store prompts, model output, transcripts or file contents. One caveat about the reference gateway (elang2/mcp-audit-gateway v0.8.2, HEAD 6d90b7e): its `wrap` mode builds entries that hold the raw tool `args` inline (src/wrap/proxy.ts createEntry). That differs from the spec's digest-only default.
where_stored: The spec covers format, not storage. The canonical artifact is an append-only JSONL audit file written by the intermediary. In the reference gateway that file is ~/.mcp-audit/audit.jsonl, with the HMAC key in ~/.mcp-audit/key.hex in wrap mode. Each record can be wrapped as an in-toto v1 Statement in a DSSE envelope, for any attestation store. Checkpoints are meant to be copied by the consumer to a store the attestor cannot overwrite: a transparency log, a separate cloud account or an HSM. Git is not used.
format_and_model: There are three layers. (1) Record: one JSONL line per record whose bytes MUST equal the RFC 8785 JCS form of the parsed record, including its `attestation` member. Verifiers recompute that form and reject any byte mismatch. Only safe integers are allowed: no floats, no exponents, nothing at or above 2^53. Strict I-JSON applies: no duplicate members at any depth, well-formed UTF-16/UTF-8, nesting depth at most 128. (2) Signing form: an ordered tuple-array of [field, value] pairs with a fixed field list per record type. Absent base fields are null. Structured values use M/L type tags. The tuple is signed with HMAC-SHA256 or Ed25519, and the signature is stored as fixed-length lowercase hex in `attestation`. (3) Statement: an in-toto v1 Statement whose subject digest is the chain hash of the chain's root record, so a policy can target a whole chain. A DSSE signature covers the Statement. Chain hash = SHA-256 of the record's JCS bytes, carried by the next record as previousHash. The first record carries the literal "genesis", which may appear only once. Each previousHash value may appear on exactly one record, and verifiers MUST reconstruct the chain by a strict walk from the root to detect forks. Checkpoints and chain_breaks sit on the chain themselves, so deleting one breaks linkage. A chain_break with priorHead null starts a new segment with a new identifier, and a deployment that claims resistance to a compromised attestor MUST forbid it. Content digests use JCS plus SHA-256 over the params member, and over the result or error member. The conformance corpus is astrogilda/aee-conformance (README now says probityai/agent-evidence-vectors), Apache-2.0. The spec pins release v0.8.0: 53 vectors, 37 accept and 16 reject, vendoring spec commit 8783c6b. Corpus main and v0.14.1 through v0.16.0 have 62 vectors (41 accept, 21 reject) tracking a5dd509. The '61 vectors' figure comes only from the PR conversation summary and does not match any tag I checked.
multi_writer_and_merge: The model is one chain per attestor (intermediary). There is no multi-writer merge. Forks are defined as an attack: two records sharing one previousHash are rejected fail-closed, as are duplicate ids and a second genesis. Several agents or servers are handled by having one gateway serialize the calls (namespace or upstream fields route between servers), or by keeping separate chains with separate subject identifiers. Chains continue across log rotation, and a crash becomes an explicit signed chain_break. There is no cross-chain ordering, no CRDT and no reconciliation.
realtime: Records are written per tool call as the response passes through the proxy. The reference CLI has `mcp-audit tail` for a live stream and OpenTelemetry export in gateway mode. The spec defines no replication or sharing protocol. Integrity against tail truncation is only as fresh as the last checkpoint the consumer has externalized; the spec's example suggests a checkpoint every 100 records or every 60 s.
search_retrieval: Not specified. Verification is by chain walk (`mcp-audit verify <log>`) and by in-toto policy evaluation over Statements, targeted by subject digest, the chain identifier. There is no indexing, full-text search or query API.
links_sessions_to_code: Only weakly. agent.sessionId, turnId and model are optional fields that the client asserts and the gateway cannot verify; the spec says to treat them as claims. The subject is the audit chain, not a code artifact: there is no commit, tree or file digest binding. The worked example records a github/create_pull_request call, and the only link to code is the content digest of the call's params. The spec pitches the records as joining 'AI supply chain' attestations next to build and provenance predicates, but defines no join key to commits.
privacy_security: Privacy works by digesting: arguments and outputs are bound by SHA-256 of their JCS form and not stored inline, unless an implementation chooses otherwise. Extensions can be kept out of storage by setting extensionsDigest at emission time; stripping a payload after signing is forbidden because it breaks the chain. There is no encryption and no secret redaction scheme, and the reference README says nothing on redaction. The threat model is detailed: field provenance via `parties` (witness vs asserter); tail truncation is only detectable against externalized checkpoints, which detect but cannot attribute; chain fork; planted chain_break; duplicate-member parser differentials; log shippers that re-serialize JSON. HMAC MUST NOT be used to claim non-repudiation; Ed25519 is required for attestor accountability. Content digests are unsalted SHA-256 of canonical JSON, so low-entropy payloads could be confirmed by guessing. That last point is my inference; the spec does not discuss it.
scale: No scale claims. The only figure is the overflow headroom: at one record per ms and one checkpoint per 100 records, the safe-integer sequence lasts about 29 million years. The reference gateway is a single-process Node.js proxy writing one JSONL file.
license: The spec PR goes into in-toto/attestation, which is Apache-2.0 (license from my general knowledge of the repo; I did not re-check it in this session). Reference gateway: MIT, with Apache-2.0 test fixtures. Conformance corpus: Apache-2.0.
lesson_for_parinn: If a record is hashed, its stored bytes must be the canonical form, and the verifier must recompute that form and reject on mismatch. ParleyInn should take three things from this spec. (a) Store each event as exactly its JCS (RFC 8785) bytes, no floats, strict I-JSON, and fail closed on any reserialization drift. Otherwise a log shipper, git smudge/clean filter or sync layer that re-emits JSON silently breaks verification. This matters a lot if git or any transport touches the record. (b) Make fork, truncation and restart first-class: each previousHash may appear on only one record (strict walk, not a set-membership check), checkpoints sit on the chain and are copied to a store the writer cannot overwrite, and a crash produces a signed chain_break rather than a silent new genesis. (c) Tag each field as witnessed or asserted (the `parties` model), which fits I2's trusted/untrusted split. The same spec shows the limit for ParleyInn's goal: its single-attestor chain treats concurrent writers as forks. Many agents, worktrees and sandboxes therefore need one chain per writer plus a separate cross-chain ordering or merge layer. Do not try to merge into one chain.

name: IPFS (Kubo/Boxo) and IPLD
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Immutable, content-addressed blocks organized as Merkle DAGs; files chunked into blocks and structured as trees via UnixFS; mutable references to immutable content via IPNS (self-certifying names). Data is stored as individual blocks, each addressed by its cryptographic hash (CID: Content Identifier). For files: UnixFS wraps file/directory metadata, chunking strategy (leaf hashes of chunks + tree structure). For mutable updates: IPNS records (public key + signature + pointer to content CID + TTL/expiry) distributed via DHT or PubSub.
where_stored: Local filesystem blockstore by default at $IPFS_PATH/blocks (directory hierarchy based on multihash prefixes); supports pluggable backends: RocksDB, LevelDB, AWS S3, Arweave, filesystem-based (blockstore-fs), filestore (direct reference to original file location). Distributed across peer nodes in the IPFS network. No central server; each Kubo node maintains its own blocks and advertises provider records to DHT.
format_and_model: IPLD (InterPlanetary Linked Data) unified data model with support for multiple codecs: DAG-CBOR (binary, CBOR RFC 8949 with additional constraints), DAG-JSON (JSON variant), and others. UnixFS (protocol-buffers format) for files/directories: data format specifies file types, sizes, permissions, timestamps; importer builds DAGs via chunking and layout (balanced or trickle); exporter retrieves via in-order traversal. CID format: combines multihash (algorithm ID), multicodec (data interpretation), and multibase (string encoding). Deterministic serialization for hash consistency.
multi_writer_and_merge: No native multi-writer support. IPNS provides mutable pointers: each IPNS name is derived from a public key's hash; signed records point to content CIDs and can be updated. Updates trade consistency (favor availability via PubSub or consistency via DHT). Conflict resolution is left to application layer; some projects (OrbitDB, Ceramic, Lit Protocol) layer CRDTs or vector clocks on top. Multiple writers to same IPNS name must coordinate or use higher-level protocols (e.g., git-like merge semantics built by application).
realtime: PubSub system available (experimental flag): topic-based publish-subscribe. Publishers send messages classified by topic; subscribers receive only their topics. Messages routed through connected peers—if peers A, B, C all subscribe and A→B→C, then A receives C's messages through B. API: pubsub.subscribe(topic, handler), pubsub.publish(topic, data), pubsub.ls(), pubsub.peers(topic). Favors availability over consistency when used for IPNS record distribution. Not suitable for strict ordering or guaranteed delivery; latency depends on network topology.
search_retrieval: Content retrieved by CID (cryptographic hash). Discovery: Kubo maintains provider records in a distributed hash table (DHT) or via PubSub. When you request a CID, Kubo queries the DHT for provider peers holding that block. Retrieval uses Bitswap protocol for negotiating block exchanges. No full-text search built-in; applications must index content externally. HTTP gateways support trustless retrieval (verification of content hash before trust). Routing can be delegated to HTTP Routing V1 services.
links_sessions_to_code: No native session tracking. IPFS is general-purpose content storage. Potential approach: encode agent session history as content-addressed blocks (each session event as a block, linked via CID hash chain); use IPNS names for mutable session references; store session index as root CID. However, no explicit support for agent metadata, prompt recovery, or session binding. Kubo RPC API (HTTP) could expose session storage endpoints; Boxo library provides building blocks for custom implementations. Researchers have explored agent storage on IPFS (https://fast.io/resources/decentralized-ai-agent-storage.md) but no standard pattern; implementation left to application.
privacy_security: Transport-layer encryption between IPFS nodes (TLS/noise protocol). Content itself is public: anyone with a CID can download and view the content. Metadata leakage: node PeerIDs are publicly discoverable; content IDs (CIDs) and provider records visible on DHT; third parties can monitor which CIDs are requested by monitoring DHT and PubSub. No built-in content encryption. Recommended mitigations: encrypt data before uploading (application-level), disable re-providing (prevent metadata leakage via provider records), use private IPFS network with swarm key (restricts DHT and peer discovery). Projects like Ceramic, Lit Protocol, OrbitDB add encryption layers. Quantum-resistant encryption concern: IPFS content persists; CBOR/hash algorithms subject to future cryptanalysis.
lesson_for_parinn: Content addressing via cryptographic hashes provides tamper resistance and deduplication like git, but IPFS is decentralized and network-dependent, violating ParleyInn's I4 invariant (no network calls in shipped code). IPFS's default public visibility of content IDs conflicts with I2 (no automatic path from untrusted content to model)—ParleyInn's approach of pull-only, enveloped recall is safer. IPFS has no native multi-writer conflict resolution; ParleyInn's append-only, single-writer, hash-chained record is simpler and easier to audit. CID format is more complex than git's simple content hash + object type. IPNS trades consistency for availability, while ParleyInn requires deterministic, pin-able history. Real-time PubSub conflicts with I4 and I10 (no randomness/clock). If ParleyInn adopts content addressing, keep it local-only (no DHT, no network), encrypt session records by default (not optional), and avoid mutable references (IPNS)—instead, link sessions via immutable CID chains, like a git reflog but on-disk only.

name: iroh (n0-computer / number0), with the iroh-blobs, iroh-gossip and iroh-docs protocols
status: shipped. Core iroh 1.0.0 came out 15 Jun 2026 and 1.3.0 on 28 Sep 2026 (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh/releases; crates.io lists 1.3.0 as max stable, published 2026-09-28: https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh). The data protocols are still pre-1.0. iroh-docs 0.101.0, iroh-gossip 0.101.0 and iroh-blobs 0.103.0 were all published 15 Jun 2026 (crates.io API: https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh-docs, https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh-gossip, https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh-blobs). The iroh-blobs README says "this version of iroh-blobs is not yet considered production quality. For now, if you need production quality, use iroh-blobs 0.35" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-blobs). The official FFI covers only the 1.0 transport surface and excludes blobs, docs and gossip (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-ffi). The Go binding is community-run and marked "Highly Experimental" (https://git.coopcloud.tech/decentral1se/iroh-go). Not archived.
what_is_stored:
Core iroh stores no application data. It is a transport: endpoints dial an Ed25519 public key (EndpointId) instead of an IP, hole-punch when they can, and fall back to relays otherwise (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh, https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy). Relays are stateless and "don't store your application data" (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays). Each endpoint does publish a small signed record (public key plus home relay) to dns.iroh.link by default (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy).

The optional protocols store data:
- iroh-blobs: opaque byte blobs addressed by their BLAKE3 root hash, plus HashSeq/collection blobs that list other hashes, plus tags that keep blobs alive (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/blobs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-blobs).
- iroh-docs: replicas (documents) made of signed entries keyed by (namespace, author, key). An entry's value is only the content's 32-byte BLAKE3 hash, its size and a timestamp. "The content data itself is not stored or transferred through a replica"; the bytes live in iroh-blobs (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs).
- iroh-gossip: stores nothing durable. It broadcasts ephemeral messages per 32-byte topic (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-gossip).
where_stored:
Local DB plus files on each peer, replicated peer to peer. No server holds the data.
- iroh-docs: persists "the whole store with all replicas to a single file" in redb, an embedded key-value store. In-memory mode is also available (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs).
- iroh-blobs FsStore: a writable directory. A database actor keeps per-hash metadata, tags, and small files' data and outboards inline; larger blobs are stored as files (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-blobs/blob/main/src/store/fs.rs).
- Relays (n0 public relays, Iroh Services shared or dedicated relays, or self-hosted iroh-relay) only forward encrypted packets (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays).
format_and_model:
Transport: QUIC through n0's own "noq" stack, with ALPN-routed protocols on a Router. Identity is an Ed25519 key, and TLS 1.3 uses raw public keys (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh, https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-post-quantum-handshakes).

iroh-blobs:
- Content-addressed by BLAKE3. Transfers use BLAKE3 verified streaming with 1 KiB chunks, which adds about 6% outboard overhead, and allow verifiable byte-range requests (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/blobs).
- A collection or HashSeq is 32-byte hashes concatenated with no separator. By convention element 0 is an application-defined metadata blob. Collections are "the only means of relating blobs" and cannot be queried as nested graphs (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/blobs).

iroh-docs:
- A multi-dimensional key-value store. Each entry is signed by two keys: the namespace key (write capability; its public key is the NamespaceId) and an author key (proof of authorship) (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs).
- A Record is {len, BLAKE3 hash, timestamp in microseconds since the Unix epoch}. Records order by timestamp, then by hash (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
