- Serialized with serde/postcard (postcard is a declared dependency in iroh-docs Cargo.toml: https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/Cargo.toml).
- Docs calls itself "built on CRDTs" (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents).

The model is mutable per key. It is not an append-only log and has no hash chain.
multi_writer_and_merge:
iroh-docs is the only multi-writer piece.
- Write access: anyone holding the namespace secret can write. A Write-mode DocTicket hands that secret to peers (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents).
- Authors: any number of author keys can write. Entries are keyed by (namespace, author, key), so one author cannot overwrite another author's entries (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs).
- Merge rule: per (author, key) it is last-writer-wins by the writer's wall-clock timestamp, with ties broken by content hash. An insert fails if "a newer entry exists for either this entry's key or a prefix of the key". Remote entries are rejected if their signatures are bad or their timestamp is more than 10 minutes ahead of the receiver's clock (MAX_TIMESTAMP_FUTURE_SHIFT) (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- Deletes: delete_prefix writes an empty tombstone that clears all of that author's entries under the prefix (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- Sync: replicas converge by range-based set reconciliation (Meyer 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13567). Peers recursively compare fingerprints of key ranges; peers already in sync exchange a single fingerprint (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents).
- Concurrent sync: when two peers dial each other at once, the winning direction is decided by comparing endpoint ids (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/state.rs).
- Blobs are immutable, so they never need a merge.
- Gossip has no merge semantics.
realtime:
Yes. The transport carries QUIC bidirectional streams and datagrams. 1.3.0 added batched datagram send and receive (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-1-3-0).
- iroh-gossip broadcasts live to topic subscribers over HyParView/PlumTree epidemic broadcast trees. The default maximum message size is 4096 bytes and the configurable minimum is 512 (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-gossip/blob/main/src/proto.rs).
- iroh-docs uses gossip to "carr[y] live sync notifications, so peers learn about new entries as they appear rather than only on reconnect". doc.subscribe() streams LiveEvent::InsertRemote and ContentReady events (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents).
- Connectivity claims: "roughly 9 out of 10" network conditions allow a direct path (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays), and 95–99% direct connection rates are claimed (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-language-support).
search_retrieval:
Core iroh: none, since it is only a transport.
- iroh-docs queries by exact key, key prefix, author, and "single latest per key" (Query API). Each entry returns a hash, and the bytes are then fetched from the blob store (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- iroh-blobs fetches by hash and supports verified byte-range requests (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/blobs).
- No full-text, semantic or BM25 search is documented in any iroh component.
links_sessions_to_code:
No. iroh has no notion of agent sessions, prompts, commits or code.

The agent-related use is Block's Buzz (post dated 22 Sep 2026). It uses iroh only for "Authenticated QUIC connections and direct network paths" (ALPN buzz/mesh/1, QUIC streams for tunnels, datagrams for huddle audio). The same table assigns "Membership, signed status, discovery, and workspace history" to the central Buzz relay and session ownership to a Redis CAS lease (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/buzz-agent-workspaces). So iroh does not store or sync agent history even in its agent showcase.

Mesh LLM, another AI use, pools GPUs for inference (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/mesh-llm).
privacy_security:
Transport encryption:
- Every connection is end-to-end encrypted with TLS 1.3 over QUIC, authenticated by Ed25519 raw public keys (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy, https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-post-quantum-handshakes).
- Hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange is available but opt-in, behind the tls-aws-lc-rs and prefer-post-quantum feature flags. Signatures are not yet post-quantum (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-post-quantum-handshakes).

What leaves the machine or is visible:
- Relays cannot read content but see who connects, which pairs talk, when, and how much (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy).
- The default N0 preset publishes a signed record to n0's dns.iroh.link. Internal IPs are filtered out by default (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy).
- A direct connection reveals each side's public IP to the peer. Tor and Nym transports exist as mitigations; relay-only mode is listed as upcoming (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy).

Relay access control:
- Shared and dedicated relays authenticate by default with expiring, endpoint-bound tokens derived locally from a project API key. Revocation takes effect live (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays).
- Self-hosted relays can use an allow-list or a shared password. Public relays are open to anyone (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/security-privacy).
- Security fixes shipped in 1.0.2 (iroh-relay) and 1.1.0 (https://www.iroh.computer/blog).

Data-layer gaps (my reading of the source and docs):
- iroh-docs read access is a bearer capability. A Read ticket carries the NamespaceId, and the default engine accepts a sync request for any namespace it is syncing, with no per-peer ACL (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/state.rs).
- No at-rest encryption, redaction or secret scanning is documented for iroh-docs or iroh-blobs. Content sits in plain redb and files (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs).
- Gossip messages carry delivered_from, the forwarding neighbor, which "is not the same as the original author". Apps must sign payloads themselves to authenticate who wrote them (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-gossip/blob/main/src/api.rs).
- The FsStore warns that writes from the last seconds before an unclean shutdown may be missing unless Store::shutdown is called (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-blobs/blob/main/src/store/fs.rs).
scale:
- n0's public relays saw "more than 200 million endpoints created, in the last 30 days alone" (iroh 1.0 announcement, https://www.iroh.computer/blog/v1).
- iroh-blobs transfers scale "from kilobytes to terabytes" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh).
- One gossip topic for all peers "scales to a few thousand peers" (https://docs.iroh.computer/connecting/gossip).
- iroh-docs reconciliation is cheap when peers are already in sync: one fingerprint (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/documents).
- Vendor cost example: 2,000 devices at 10 GB/month cost about $100 with iroh versus about $1,742 on centralized AWS (https://www.iroh.computer/).
- About 2.9M crate downloads for iroh (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh) and 12.6k GitHub stars (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh).
- Runs on an ESP32 with 4 MiB of flash as of 1.2.0 (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-1-3-0).
- I found no published benchmarks for iroh-docs with millions of entries or many concurrent writers.
license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual) for iroh, iroh-docs, iroh-blobs, iroh-gossip and iroh-ffi (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-ffi). The community iroh-go binding uses the same dual license (https://git.coopcloud.tech/decentral1se/iroh-go). Hosted relays and metrics are a paid Iroh Services offering (https://docs.iroh.computer/concepts/relays).
lesson_for_parinn:
iroh-docs models multi-writer replication well, but ParleyInn should borrow the model and not adopt the transport in-process.

What to borrow: the reconciliation model. Give each writer its own signing key, sign every entry, store only BLAKE3 hashes in the index and keep content-addressed blobs separate, and replicate with range-based set reconciliation. That fits ParleyInn's per-agent, hash-chained, append-only logs especially well. If keys are (agent key, sequence number) and entries are immutable, set union is the whole merge.

What to avoid:
- iroh-docs's last-writer-wins by writer wall clock, its rejection of entries more than 10 minutes in the future, and delete_prefix tombstones. All three are mutable, clock-dependent semantics that conflict with lossless I10 rebuilds.
- Treating a namespace id as secret. It is a bearer read capability, and docs and blobs are stored and served in plaintext. ParleyInn must encrypt at the application layer before anything is replicated, and treat every replicated entry as untrusted (I2).

Integration practicalities:
- I4 bars network code from the core, so a p2p transport would have to be a separate opt-in sync sidecar.
- iroh's Go route today is a cgo, musl, Linux-only experimental community binding pinned to iroh 1.0.3, and it excludes blobs, docs and gossip. Practical use from Go therefore means a Rust sidecar or reimplementing the reconciliation protocol in Go.
- By default, endpoints also contact n0's DNS server and public relays.

name: iroh-docs (n0-computer)
status: shipped. The crate is maintained but still versioned 0.x, so no 1.0 stability promise. It is not archived. The latest release is 0.101.0, published 2026-06-15 against iroh 1.0, iroh-blobs 0.103 and iroh-gossip 0.101 (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh-docs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The newest main commit I cloned is 8cfeacb from 2026-08-19, "fix: Improve API around untrusted range bounds (#119)". The project moved into its own repo with iroh 0.28 in November 2024 (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-0-28-let-them-have-crates). iroh itself reached 1.0 on 2026-06-15 (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/v1). That post does not say whether docs is covered by 1.0 guarantees. n0 also runs a separate Willow implementation, iroh-willow, with Meadowcap and Confidential Sync (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-willow). That repo is a possible successor direction, but n0 has not said so.
license: MIT OR Apache-2.0, at the user's choice (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/README.md).
what_is_stored:
Only signed metadata entries. Content bytes live elsewhere. Each entry is identified by (NamespaceId, AuthorId, key). The key is arbitrary bytes. The value is a Record holding the 32-byte BLAKE3 hash of the content, the content length, and a u64 timestamp in microseconds since the Unix epoch. The README says "The content data itself is not stored or transferred through a replica" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/README.md, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs). The content bytes live in iroh-blobs, a content-addressed store (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/kv-crdts).

The redb file also holds other local state, defined in https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store/fs/tables.rs:
- Author secret keys, in the authors-1 table
- Namespace capabilities, in the namespaces-2 table. For writable replicas this is the namespace secret key.
- The latest entry per author
- A key index
- The peers that were useful per document, with timestamps
- A postcard-encoded download policy per document

Sessions, prompts and agent concepts are not modelled. It is a generic key-value store.
where_stored: A local embedded database. The persistent store is redb, which keeps all replicas in a single file; an in-memory store is the alternative (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/README.md). Content blobs sit in a separate iroh-blobs store, either memory or filesystem. Replicas travel peer to peer over iroh QUIC connections under the ALPN "/iroh-sync/1" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/net.rs), with no central server. Writes go into an open redb write transaction that is committed once it is older than MAX_COMMIT_DELAY = 500 ms (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/actor.rs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store/fs.rs). I infer from this code that a returned insert is not yet durably committed. Open issue #78 reports entries surviving a crash while their blob data is missing (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/issues/78).
format_and_model:
A multi-dimensional key-value CRDT, which n0 documents as a "KV CRDT" (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/kv-crdts).

Identity and signing:
- A SignedEntry is an Entry {RecordIdentifier = namespace(32) || author(32) || key, Record} plus two Ed25519 signatures over the canonical encoding.
- One signature comes from the namespace secret, which is the write capability; the other comes from the author key, which proves authorship (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- A code TODO notes that the signature input lacks a domain-separation prefix: "this should probably include a namespace prefix".
- Capability is either Write(NamespaceSecret) or Read(NamespaceId).

Records table layout: (NamespaceId, AuthorId, Key) maps to (timestamp, namespace_sig, author_sig, len, hash) (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store/fs/tables.rs).

Wire format: postcard messages in 4-byte length-prefixed frames, capped at MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE = 1 GiB (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/net/codec.rs). A DocTicket holds a Capability plus a list of EndpointAddr peers (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/ticket.rs).

History is not kept. The model is last-writer-wins per (author, key) and the store is not append-only: superseded entries are deleted from the store. The comment in ranger.rs says "The deleted entries are simply dropped right now" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/ranger.rs).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Any number of authors may write, provided each holds the namespace secret. Replicas merge by computing a set union with range-based set reconciliation, after Aljoscha Meyer's paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13567). Sets are recursively partitioned and per-range fingerprints are compared. Here the fingerprint is the XOR of each entry's BLAKE3(namespace, author, key, timestamp, hash) (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/ranger.rs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).

Conflict rule, following the Willow spec:
- Record ordering compares timestamp first, then content hash.
- A new entry is inserted only if it is strictly greater than every existing entry with the same key or a key that is a prefix of it.
- After the insert, any entries keyed under it that are not newer are removed.
- So an empty entry at a prefix acts as a prefix-delete tombstone (delete_prefix).
- Entries are keyed by author, so different authors writing the same key coexist. A single_latest_per_key query picks a winner at read time (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store.rs).

Validation:
- The namespace must match.
- Both signatures must verify for entries arriving from remote peers.
- The timestamp may be at most 10 minutes ahead of local wall-clock time (MAX_TIMESTAMP_FUTURE_SHIFT).

Two weaknesses:
- Invalid remote entries are dropped. In sync the validate callback returns is_ok(), and in gossip the drop is logged only at debug level ("ignoring entry received via gossip") (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/gossip.rs).
- Open issue #120 (2026-09-09) shows that because merging trusts timestamps the writer declares, no safe skew bound exists. A writer stamping now+9m59s can keep control of a key indefinitely while honest writes are silently shadowed (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/issues/120).
realtime:
Yes, live sync is available.
- On join, the engine subscribes to an iroh-gossip topic named after the NamespaceId (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/gossip.rs).
- Every local insert is broadcast as Op::Put(SignedEntry). ContentReady and SyncReport messages are broadcast too (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/live.rs).
- Set-reconciliation sync runs with neighbors to catch up.
- doc.subscribe() streams these events: InsertLocal, InsertRemote, ContentReady, PendingContentReady, NeighborUp, NeighborDown and SyncFinished (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine.rs, https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/kv-crdts).
- Content blobs are fetched afterwards through iroh-blobs, gated by a per-document DownloadPolicy that includes or excludes keys by filter (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store.rs).
- Peers find each other through iroh endpoint discovery and relays (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/README.md).
- No latency figures are published.
search_retrieval:
Structured queries only. There is no full-text or semantic search. Queries can filter by exact key, key prefix and author. There are two query kinds:
- Query::all, sorted by author then key, or by key then author, ascending or descending.
- Query::single_latest_per_key, where the key filter applies before grouping and the author filter after it.

Queries take limit and offset, and can include empty tombstone entries (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store.rs). Content is read separately by hash from iroh-blobs. Any content indexing is up to the application.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. iroh-docs is a general-purpose key-value sync layer with no idea of agent sessions, prompts, commits or worktrees. An application would have to encode such links in keys and values. I found no agent-session use of iroh-docs in n0's materials. The iroh blog's September 2026 Buzz post covers p2p agent and compute workspaces built on iroh, but does not say iroh-docs is used (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/buzz-agent-workspaces).
scale:
No numbers are published.
- The README claims a replica holds "an unlimited number of Entries" (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/README.md).
- The docs say peers that are fully in sync "only need to exchange a single fingerprint to confirm it" (https://docs.iroh.computer/protocols/kv-crdts).
- The paper claims local computation is a logarithmic factor faster than earlier work (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13567).

Open issues point at limits rather than claims:
- #59 "Optimize document store and sync algorithm"
- #65 "Iroh aborts under high load"
- #56 non-symmetric sync
- #77 leaking doc handles

All four are listed at https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/issues. The repo has about 74 stars (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs). crates.io shows about 167k total downloads (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/iroh-docs).
privacy_security:
Strengths:
- Integrity: every entry carries Ed25519 signatures from both the namespace and the author, and both are checked on remote entries. Content is BLAKE3-addressed (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- Transport: iroh QUIC with TLS 1.3 and raw public keys (RFC 7250), so peers are authenticated by their endpoint key (https://www.iroh.computer/blog/iroh-0-34-0-raw-public-keys).

Gaps:
- Read access: the read capability is simply knowing the NamespaceId. An incoming sync request is rejected only as NotFound (namespace not open locally), AlreadySyncing or InternalServerError. There is no per-peer allow-list (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/state.rs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/net.rs).
- Tickets: a DocTicket for a writable document contains the namespace secret itself (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/ticket.rs).
- At rest: no encryption is used. Author secrets and namespace secrets are written as raw 32-byte values into the redb file (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store/fs/tables.rs, https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/store/fs.rs). I found no use of encryption anywhere in the source.
- No redaction or secret scanning is provided.
- Write access cannot be revoked short of moving to a new namespace. Confidential sync and fine-grained capabilities are what iroh-willow/Meadowcap targets, not iroh-docs (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-willow).
- Timestamp trust allows key capture by a single writer (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/issues/120).
- Rejected entries are not surfaced (https://github.com/n0-computer/iroh-docs/blob/main/src/engine/gossip.rs).
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy the shape of iroh-docs but not its merge rule.

What to copy:
- Small, doubly signed metadata entries that point to content by BLAKE3 hash.
- Reconcile those entries by fingerprinted range set union.
- Fetch content lazily under a receiver-side download policy. That fits ParleyInn's pull-only recall (I2) and keeps metadata sync cheap across machines and sandboxes.

What not to copy: iroh-docs is mutable last-writer-wins. Writer-declared wall-clock timestamps decide the winner, superseded entries are dropped, and rejected remote entries vanish into a debug log. That breaks I6 and I10, and enables key capture (issue #120).

For ParleyInn:
- Make every synced entry immutable, keyed by (author, chain position, hash), so the set union is the merge and nothing is ever superseded.
- Derive order from the hash chain, never from clocks.
- Audit and count every rejected or invalid remote entry.
- Keep transport out of the network-free core (I4). ParleyInn would only export and import such sets through an external sync agent. iroh-docs is Rust-only, so a Go binding is not available off the shelf. I did not verify any iroh-docs FFI.

name: JetBrains Junie (CLI, IDE plugin, GitHub Action, GitLab CI/CD)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: There are three kinds of stored data. (1) Plans. Plan Mode does read-only analysis and writes a structured design document before any code changes. Its sections are requirements, technical design, testing and delivery steps, and simple tasks get fewer sections (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-plan-mode.html). JetBrains describes plans in .junie/plans as editable and committable "living task documentation" (https://blog.jetbrains.com/junie/2026/06/junie-coding-agent-out-of-beta?map=1). (2) Full session context. The CLI docs say Junie "stores the full session context, including LLM usage data and the history of user prompts and agent responses, for all your saved sessions". Each session has an events.jsonl file, a continuously updated transcript.md beside it, and a subagents folder holding subagent transcripts (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html). (3) Configuration and guidance: ~/.junie/config.json and <project>/.junie/config.json, .junie/AGENTS.md guidelines, allowlist.json for permitted commands, sandbox.json, and model, skill, command, agent and extension folders (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/parameters.html, https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-on-github.html, https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html). In CI, the GitHub Action keeps "working files, caches, and session artifacts" in a runner work directory (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-on-github.html). The action returns only branch_name, commit_sha, pr_url, junie_title and junie_summary, plus a branch, PR and comments.
where_stored: Plans are working-tree files under <repo>/.junie/plans and travel in git only if the user commits them. Session logs (events.jsonl, transcript.md, subagents/) are local files. The docs do not say whether they live under ~/.junie (JUNIE_HOME, default ~/.junie) or the project's .junie directory, so the exact path is unverified (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html, https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/parameters.html). Caches go to a configurable --cache-dir. On GitHub Actions everything sits in junie_work_dir, default /tmp/junie-work, on the runner (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-on-github.html). On GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners that directory disappears after the job. That is inferred from GitHub runner behaviour, not stated by JetBrains. Durable CI output is only the git branch or PR and the issue or PR comments. GitLab works the same way: a dedicated container project runs the pipeline, and the outputs are an MR and a comment (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-gitlab-ci-cd.html). Remote mode streams a live session through a JetBrains web app, at https://junie.jetbrains.com/remote/<session-id>. The docs do not say whether that service keeps any data (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-remote-mode.html).
format_and_model: Plans are Markdown documents with tabbed sections (requirements, technical design, testing, delivery steps) (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-plan-mode.html). The plan file naming scheme is not documented. Sessions are an append-style JSON Lines event log (events.jsonl) with a derived Markdown rendering (transcript.md), and subagents get nested transcripts (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html). Each session has an ID and a junie://sessions/<id> link, used with --session-id or --resume (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/parameters.html). The event schema is not published, and I found nothing about hash chaining or integrity protection. Config files are JSON.
multi_writer_and_merge: No session-level multi-writer or merge model is documented. Plans are ordinary files, so concurrent edits fall back to git's normal text merge with no Junie-specific merge driver (none documented). GitLab CI/CD can run several tasks at once but excludes parallel runs on the same MR branch (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-gitlab-ci-cd.html). That is serialization per branch, not merging. Session logs are local to one process. Remote mode allows "only one web client" per session at a time (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-remote-mode.html).
realtime: Remote mode keeps the agent on the user's machine. It "opens a secure tunnel to the Junie web app and streams the session into a web UI". Prompts, approval replies and plan refinements from the web UI go back to the same running process. Only one web client can connect at a time, and the session stops if the machine sleeps (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-remote-mode.html). There is no real-time sharing between agents or machines. In CI, progress shows up only as PR, MR or issue comments.
search_retrieval: The /history command opens Task history to "search session history, switch between live sessions, or resume a saved session from a previous run". Ctrl+O opens the current or subagent transcript.md (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html). The search method (full-text or otherwise) and any cross-session recall by the agent are not documented. A JetBrains community thread reports IDE chat history lost after clicking Start New Task, which suggests the older IDE-side history was fragile (https://intellij-support.jetbrains.com/hc/en-us/community/posts/30638248669714). That is anecdotal and may predate GA.
links_sessions_to_code: The links are weak and indirect. A committed plan in .junie/plans sits in the same commits as the code it describes, so git history links the design intent to the change, but only when the user chooses to commit it (https://blog.jetbrains.com/junie/2026/06/junie-coding-agent-out-of-beta?map=1). In CI, the link is the branch, PR or MR plus the summary comment, and the action outputs commit_sha, pr_url and junie_summary (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-on-github.html). I found no documented trailer, git note or ref that ties a commit to its session's events.jsonl. The full prompt and response history stays local and is not linked to commits.
scale: There are no storage or scale claims. The only scale-like figure is a benchmark: on SWE-rebench Junie scored "61.6% resolved and a 72.7% pass@5" (https://blog.jetbrains.com/junie/2026/06/junie-coding-agent-out-of-beta?map=1). GitLab CI/CD can handle several tasks at once, but no more than one per MR branch (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-gitlab-ci-cd.html).
privacy_security:
- **Ignore files:** .aiignore entries (and .gitignore or .cursorignore) keep files away from Junie and AI Assistant (https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai/data-retention.html, https://jetbrains.com/help/ai/enterprise-privacy.html).
- **Retention:** JetBrains says it keeps no customer data unless the user opts in to detailed data collection (zero data retention) and does not train on customer data (https://www.jetbrains.com/help/ai/data-retention.html).
- **Models:** BYOK and local models through LiteLLM, LM Studio or Ollama mean "prompts and code never shared externally" (https://blog.jetbrains.com/junie/2026/06/junie-coding-agent-out-of-beta?map=1).
- **Command control:** allowlist.json limits which commands may run, sandbox.json sets sandbox policy, and the CLI asks for project trust (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli.html, https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-headless.html).
- **CI secrets:** in GitHub Actions, API keys are masked in workflow logs. The action needs contents, pull-requests and issues write permissions (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-on-github.html).
- **Not found:** nothing documented about redacting secrets in events.jsonl or transcript.md, encrypting the local session store, or treating stored content as untrusted. Committed plans can carry whatever the model wrote into them.
- **Remote mode:** the docs do not cover tunnel encryption or relay retention (https://junie.jetbrains.com/docs/junie-cli-remote-mode.html).
- **License:** the client is proprietary, and the public GitHub repo holds installers and configuration under "All rights reserved" (https://github.com/JetBrains/junie).
lesson_for_parinn: Junie splits session data into two tiers, and ParleyInn should adopt the split while closing the gap it leaves. The raw session (events.jsonl plus a derived transcript.md) stays local and unlinked, and a small curated artifact (the plan) is what travels in git. In ephemeral CI the raw tier is thrown away with /tmp/junie-work, so only the PR, the summary comment and an optional plan survive. For ParleyInn this means two things. First, the curated tier (pinned constraints, plans, summaries) can move over git, while the full append-only record needs a separate, deliberate export from ephemeral sandboxes, or it is lost exactly where agents run unattended. Second, a committed, model-written plan is untrusted content that later sessions will read back. ParleyInn should give such committed artifacts a stable session ID and hash anchor, and recall them only inside an envelope, never splice them into a restore block (I2). Junie publishes neither a format nor a security model for this.
license: Proprietary client under the JetBrains AI Service Terms of Service. The public repo github.com/JetBrains/junie holds installers and configuration, marked "All rights reserved".

name: JetBrains Local History (IntelliJ Platform "LVCS")
status: shipped
what_is_stored: An automatic, per-machine change log of project files. The docs say it "automatically records your project's state as you edit code, run tests, deploy applications" and keeps revisions "for all meaningful changes made both from the IDE and externally". Some revisions get automatic labels on events such as running tests, deploying and committing, and users can add their own labels with File | Local History | Put Label (docs). In the open-source implementation (platform/lvcs-impl in intellij-community, read at commit 377916a, 2026-10-02) the unit of record is a ChangeSet: id, timestamp, an optional name, an optional ActivityId and a list of Changes. Change types are Create file or directory, Content, Rename, Move, Delete, read-only status, PutLabel and PutSystemLabel. A ContentChange does not hold the file bytes. It holds an int content id that points into the IDE's shared VFS content store (PersistentFS.storeUnlinkedContent / acquireContent). Unsaved editor documents are captured too (registerUnsavedDocuments, bytesFromDocument). Which files are tracked: files under a project content or library root that are not excluded or ignored. workspace.xml, *.iws and *.class are always skipped. Files outside every open project, such as scratch or external files, are tracked unless they match the IDE's ignored-file patterns (IdeaGateway.isVersioned). No prompts, chat or agent transcripts are stored.
where_stored: Local DB/cache on one machine. The change log lives in the IDE system/cache directory as PathManager.getSystemDir()/LocalHistory/changes (a record table plus a data file). The docs give the base paths: Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\JetBrains\<product><version>, macOS ~/Library/Caches/JetBrains/<product><version>, Linux ~/.cache/JetBrains/<product><version>. File contents sit outside that folder, in the IDE-wide VFS content storage, and are referenced by id. If the persistent storage cannot be created, it falls back to an in-memory store. There is one store per IDE installation, shared by all projects. A label is scoped to a project by p.getLocationHash(). Nothing is kept in git, in the working tree or on a server.
format_and_model: Proprietary binary format, documented by the source only. LocalHistoryStorage extends the platform AbstractStorage. Its records table header holds a version (VERSION = 7), the last id and the VFS creation timestamp. Each record has prev/next pointers and a timestamp, which makes a doubly linked list of serialized ChangeSet blocks (DataOutput varints and strings, ChangeSet VERSION = 1). The model is an append-only operation log of filesystem deltas plus labels. A past state is rebuilt by walking changes backwards from the current tree (RootEntry/DirectoryEntry/FileEntry and revisions). Nothing is hash-chained and nothing is signed. If the format version or the VFS timestamp does not match, the store is dropped and rebuilt empty, for example after the VFS cache is rebuilt or the IDE is upgraded. The docs warn that Local History "is cleared when you install a new version" and that "revisions are not guaranteed to persist". Retention: the default is 5 "working days (days when the file was modified)". It is set under Settings > Advanced Settings or with -DlocalHistory.daysToKeep, and 0 disables the feature. Purge works from the oldest record. It sums the active time between changes and counts gaps over 12 hours as one day (findFirstObsoleteBlock, DEFAULT_INTERVAL_BETWEEN_ACTIVITIES = 12h). A background coroutine flushes every 1 second.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer only. One IDE process owns the store and serializes writes through synchronized methods and storage locks. All writers inside that process share one log: editor typing, refactorings, VCS operations and external filesystem changes picked up by a VFS refresh (CommonActivity.ExternalChange). LocalHistory.startAction groups file changes into one named action. The docs say it "does not support shared access, it is stored locally and intended only for personal use". There is no sync, replication or merge. The only way to share is to export a revision as a patch file.
realtime: Yes on one machine, no across machines. Changes are recorded as VFS and document events happen. The write cache is flushed every second. An experimental Activity tool window (registry key lvcs.show.activity.view) shows actions live. Nothing streams to other machines or users.
search_retrieval: From the GUI, File | Local History | Show History works on a file, folder, selection or project. It shows a revision list and a diff viewer. The dialog has a search bar that finds revisions by file content (docs). Users can revert a whole file ("Revert Selected and Later Changes"), copy fragments back with the chevron buttons, restore deleted files from the parent folder's history and create a patch. The plugin API (LocalHistory.kt) offers: putEventLabel/putSystemLabel, which return a label id; isLabelValid, which checks a label was not purged; suspend revertToLabel(project, labelId, file), which restores a file or tree to a label; and getByteContent(file, timestampCondition). There is no CLI, no external query interface and no full-text index outside the IDE.
links_sessions_to_code: No prompt or session linkage. The closest hook is ActivityId(providerId, kind), marked @ApiStatus.Experimental. An action or event label can carry it to "identify which IDE activity created changes" and to change how that activity is shown. Only providers built into the open platform (Command, ExternalChange, UserLabel) appear in the open-source code. The API's label-then-revertToLabel pair has the shape of an agent checkpoint/rollback primitive. I found no public JetBrains document saying that AI Assistant, Junie or JetBrains Air tag edits with an ActivityId or use Local History for rollback. Those products are closed source, so AI or agent attribution cannot be verified. An agent running outside the IDE (for example Claude Code in a terminal) shows up only as an anonymous "External change" captured by the VFS refresh. That last point is an inference from the ExternalChange activity and the VFS refresh path, not a documented claim.
scale: No published scale claims. Scale is bounded by design: 5 working days by default, one machine, every project in one IDE install. The source has a TODO to move to mmapped storage for "less freezes, and also more reliability" (PersistentChangeListStorage.kt). I found no documented file-size limit.
privacy_security: No redaction, no secret filtering and no encryption. Neither the docs nor the code mention any. Contents are kept in clear in the IDE cache and VFS content store under the user's cache directory, protected only by OS file permissions. Any non-excluded file under a content root is captured, plus files outside projects unless they match IDE ignore patterns. So secrets in files such as .env can be retained for the retention window. Whether a VCS-ignored file counts as "excluded" depends on IDE project settings. That is an inference from isVersioned, not documented. Deletion happens by retention purge, by setting retention to 0 (or the lvcs.disable.local.history system property) or by deleting the cache. Corruption handling: the store is dropped and recreated, with a log error and an "Local history is broken" notification, so history is lost by design. Local History is disabled in headless mode.
lesson_for_parinn: Treat Local History as a counter-example for durability and a model for capture. It records everything automatically, including external changes and unsaved buffers, with zero user effort, and its label-then-revertToLabel API is a clean checkpoint primitive. But it is a disposable cache. It is wiped when the format version or VFS timestamp changes, it is silently capped at 5 active days and it is dropped wholesale on corruption. It cannot attribute edits from an outside agent, which arrive as anonymous "external change". ParleyInn should copy two things. First, automatic event-level capture grouped into named actions with a provider/kind activity id. Second, cheap content-addressed blob references kept apart from a small operation log. ParleyInn should reverse three things. Its record must be the durable source of truth, never a cache that gets rebuilt empty (I10 runs the other way: projections are rebuilt from the record, not the record from the filesystem). Corruption or purge must be audited and counted, never silently reset (I6). Every change must carry an explicit session, agent and tool-call identity at write time, because attribution cannot be recovered later from filesystem events.
license: Apache-2.0 (the IntelliJ Platform LVCS modules in intellij-community). The AI Assistant, Junie and Air integrations are proprietary and closed source.

name: Jujutsu (jj) operation log
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
Two kinds of object, "operations" and "views". A view is "a snapshot of how the repo looked at the end of the operation". It holds where each bookmark, tag and Git ref pointed, the set of head commits, and the working-copy commit of each workspace (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/). In the schema a View holds head_ids, wc_commit_ids keyed by workspace, bookmarks, local_tags, remote_views and per-workspace git_heads. Its git_refs field is "Only a subset of the refs. For example, does not include refs/notes/" (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/protos/simple_op_store.proto).

An Operation holds view_id, its parent operation ids, commit_predecessors (the evolution history, since jj 0.30) and OperationMetadata. The metadata has start and end timestamps (ms plus timezone offset), description, hostname, username, is_snapshot, workspace_name and a free-form attributes map (same proto file).

The CLI fills attributes with one key, "args": the full shell-quoted jj command line (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/cli/src/cli_util.rs). Library callers can set any key with Transaction::set_attribute (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/transaction.rs).

File contents are never in op objects. Ops point to commits in the commit backend. Almost every jj command first snapshots the working copy into a commit, which is "recorded as an operation" (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/working-copy/).

Nothing about agents, prompts or conversations is stored.
where_stored:
A local directory store under .jj/repo/, separate from git:
- op_store/operations/<hex> and op_store/views/<hex>, one file per object (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/simple_op_store.rs)
- op_heads/heads/<hex>, empty files whose names are the current head ids (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/concurrency/)

Commits and files go into a git repo: colocated .git by default, or hidden at .jj/repo/store/git (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/git-compatibility/). They are kept from git gc by refs/jj/keep/* (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/architecture/). Change ids and predecessors sit in a StackedTable in .jj/repo/store/extra/ (same page). Since jj 0.30 a change-id header is also written into git commits (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/git-compatibility/).

The op log never reaches a git remote. The README says "only commits and files are stored in Git; bookmarks (branches) and other higher-level metadata are stored in custom storage outside of Git" (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/README.md).

Backends are pluggable, chosen by .jj/repo/op_store/type and op_heads/type (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/architecture/). Google runs an internal DB-backed jj server that stores "repos (operation logs)" in the cloud. An open-source server and daemon are only on the roadmap (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/roadmap/).
format_and_model:
The model is a Merkle DAG that mirrors git: "each commit object is instead an 'operation' and each tree object is instead a 'view'". The log "is normally linear" and branches only when operations diverge (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/concurrency/).

Objects are proto3 protobuf, one file per object (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/protos/simple_op_store.proto). The id is BLAKE2b-512 of a structured content hash of the object, not of the serialized bytes. Each file is written to a temp file and then persisted under its hex id (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/simple_op_store.rs, https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/core/src/content_hash.rs). Because parent ids are inside the hashed content, the ops form a hash chain.

To commit, jj adds the new head file and then removes the old one: "Writing the new file is what makes the operation visible… This scheme ensures that transactions are atomic" (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/concurrency/). Op and working-copy state files have been fsynced on save since 0.33.0 (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/CHANGELOG.md).

History is not immutable. `jj op abandon ..<op>` drops ancestors and reparents descendants onto the root. `jj util gc` then prunes unreachable ops and objects older than 2 weeks by default (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/cli-reference/). Reparenting changes the content of the descendant ops, so their hash ids change too. That is an inference from the content addressing.

The project is pre-1.0. The README marks concurrent replication as experimental, with possible "backwards incompatible storage changes" (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/README.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
The design is lock-free by intent. A command loads the repo at the latest operation and does not see concurrent writes. When it finishes, it writes its op with the start op as parent, and it "cannot fail to commit (except for disk failures and such)". Detecting divergence is left to the next command (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/concurrency/).

When jj finds several op heads it does "a 3-way merge of the view objects based on their common ancestor". Conflicts are recorded in the view instead of raising an error, e.g. bookmark main "moved from A to B or C" via RefTarget adds and removes. The repo stays usable, though commands that resolve a conflicted bookmark fail (same page). Concurrent rewrites of one commit show up as divergent changes (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/).

The op-heads lock only stops processes from merging the same heads twice: "It is not needed for correctness" (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/op_heads_store.rs).

Several machines can write over a shared filesystem "as long as the file system guarantees that a write is only visible once previous writes are visible" (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/). Syncing with rsync, Dropbox or NFS is documented, with caveats (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/technical/concurrency/):
- The git backend is "not entirely lock-free". Issue #2193 is still open: the change-id index relies on locks, and the fix is `jj debug reindex` (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/issues/2193).
- Colocated repos are less tested and "might conceivably lose some bookmark pointers".

A race that caused divergent ops in colocated repos was fixed in 0.36.0 (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/CHANGELOG.md).

Workspaces are several working copies sharing one repo and one op log. A workspace goes "stale" when another workspace rewrites its commit, and `jj workspace update-stale` fixes it (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/working-copy/).

The global flag `--no-integrate-operation` (0.41.0) lets background tools record ops without changing repo state; `jj op integrate` merges such ops in later (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/CHANGELOG.md, https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/cli-reference/).

There is no command to exchange op logs between separate clones. Clones collaborate through git push and fetch of commits and bookmarks only (README, as above).
realtime:
Not real-time.
- jj runs no daemon. The working copy is snapshotted only when some jj command runs, so an agent crash before any jj call loses unsnapshotted edits (https://www.panozzaj.com/blog/2025/11/22/avoid-losing-work-with-jujutsu-jj-for-ai-coding-agents/).
- The documented way to react to new ops is to watch .jj/repo/op_heads/heads with watchexec (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/faq/).
- Ops are not pushed or pulled at all.
- Google's internal server and caching daemon are proprietary. The open-source version is a roadmap item with no date (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/roadmap/).
search_retrieval:
Commands (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/cli-reference/):
- `jj op log` takes -n, --reversed, -T template, -d/--op-diff, -p and --show-changes-in <revset>.
- `jj op show` and `jj op diff` show one op or the difference between two.
- Ops are addressed with `@`, `x-` (parents) and `x+` (children) (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/).

Time travel:
- `--at-op` loads the whole repo at any past op for read-only commands, without snapshotting (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/).
- The revset function `at_operation(op, x)` evaluates a commit query at a past op (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/). Unreleased main lets it target sibling, concurrent ops (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/CHANGELOG.md).
- `jj evolog` shows how one change evolved.

Machine output: the Operation template type is Serialize, so `jj op log -T 'json(self)'` emits JSON (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/templates/).

There is no full-text index or search over op metadata or content. Filtering is by template plus external grep.
links_sessions_to_code:
Not natively. The op log records repository operations, not agents, prompts or sessions (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/operation-log/). Each op does carry a timestamp, workspace name, hostname, username and the exact jj command line. Every snapshot is an op, so the log is a fine-grained timeline of agent edits that can be joined to sessions by time and workspace. That join is an inference, not a jj feature.

The attributes map could carry a session id, but only through jj-lib's Transaction::set_attribute. The CLI sets only "args" (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/cli/src/cli_util.rs).

Community practice:
- Claude Code SessionStart and PreCompact hooks run `jj status` to force a snapshot (https://www.panozzaj.com/blog/2025/11/22/avoid-losing-work-with-jujutsu-jj-for-ai-coding-agents/).
- FAVA Trails, an agent-memory MCP server, uses jj in colocated mode as its storage engine (https://github.com/MachineWisdomAI/fava-trails).
- jj is promoted as agent-friendly by Amplify Partners, an ERSC investor (https://www.amplifypartners.com/blog-posts/will-agents-like-git-any-more-than-we-do).
- jj's creator joined ERSC as CTO on 2026-09-01 and remains a core maintainer (https://ersc.io/blog/martin-joins-ersc).
scale:
jj publishes no scale or benchmark figures for the op log. It stores one file per op or view object. The git-compatibility page still says there is "no garbage collection and repacking of Jujutsu's own data structures yet" (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/git-compatibility/). That page may be stale: `jj util gc` does prune unreachable ops (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/cli-reference/).

Large deployments are known only secondhand:
- Google runs an internal DB-backed jj server (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/roadmap/).
- Amplify, an investor and so a secondary source, says jj "is being standardized across Google's internal version control stack" (https://www.amplifypartners.com/blog-posts/will-agents-like-git-any-more-than-we-do).

In colocated repos with very many refs, the automatic git import makes every command slower (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/git-compatibility/).
privacy_security:
No encryption at rest and no secret redaction before storage.

Op metadata stores username, hostname and the full command line (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/cli/src/cli_util.rs). So anything passed as an argument, such as `-m` text, is kept verbatim in the op log.

Identity is self-asserted. It comes from the config keys operation.username and operation.hostname (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/lib/src/settings.rs). Ops are unsigned. Only commits can be signed, with GPG or SSH (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/config/).

The builtin_op_log_redacted and builtin_log_redacted templates redact only display output, for sharing bug reports: attributes print as "(redacted)" and workspace names are hashed. The stored data is unchanged (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/cli/src/config/templates.toml).

New files are auto-tracked and snapshotted (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/working-copy/). A secret file that is not gitignored therefore ends up in commit history until `jj op abandon` plus gc. That is an inference from the docs.

Untrusted repo state: since 0.38.0, per-repo config lives outside the repo (~/.config/jj/repos/<config-id>) because a shared repo's config.toml could run arbitrary commands, the "zip file problem" (https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/design/secure-config/, https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/CHANGELOG.md).

Vulnerability policy: reports through GitHub advisories, with a 90-day disclosure timeline (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/SECURITY.md).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/blob/0cb02a837f28459cd698734264c9fcd3712ec0d1/LICENSE; reaffirmed in https://ersc.io/blog/martin-joins-ersc). Latest release v0.45.1, 2026-09-03; main is active (commit 0cb02a8 on 2026-10-01). The repo moved to the jj-vcs org in Dec 2024. Docs moved from jj-vcs.github.io, which now returns 301, to docs.jj-vcs.dev.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy jj's write protocol for many writers. Make each record an immutable, content-addressed object whose hash covers its parent ids. Mark heads with empty files named by the head id. Let any writer commit without a lock. Treat several heads as data: the next reader merges them deterministically and records conflicts explicitly ("A to B or C"). This survives worktrees, sandboxes and file-syncing transports, and fits ParleyInn's I10 rebuild-from-record rule. jj documents rsync, Dropbox and NFS as experimental and has one open locking bug, #2193, on the git backend.

Do not copy jj where it falls short of ParleyInn's guarantees:
- Hash chaining alone is not append-only. `jj op abandon` plus gc rewrites and prunes history.
- Metadata is unsigned and self-asserted.
- Raw command lines are stored, and redaction happens only at display time.
- The op log never crosses a git remote. A git-backed tool kept its own history out of git, and its creators' answer for sharing is a DB-backed server, not git.

ParleyInn needs signatures or an external anchor for tamper evidence, and redaction before write.

name: Keyhive + Beelay (Ink & Switch)
category: E2EE local-first sync with access control
status: announced
what_is_stored: Automerge CRDT documents with encrypted content; hierarchical membership graphs representing access control relationships; group key material from BeeKEM (continuous group key agreement); causal history of document changes; authenticated message envelopes with signatures and timestamps
where_stored: Local complete replicas on each device; encrypted-at-rest using hierarchical key material based on document causality; data organized in Sedimentree structures (hierarchical compression of commit history); primary implementation in Rust with WebAssembly bindings for JavaScript/browsers
format_and_model: CRDT-based (Automerge documents); three-layer architecture: (1) convergent capabilities for permission delegation using public keys, (2) group management CRDT for organizational structures, (3) end-to-end encryption with causal keys; Sedimentree hierarchical tree structure where older commits compress into progressively larger chunks based on commit hash trailing zeros; authenticated message envelopes with Ed25519 signatures
multi_writer_and_merge: CRDT-based automatic conflict resolution through Automerge; BeeKEM handles concurrent group membership updates by preserving conflict keys (storing multiple encrypted values until resolved); supports thousands of members in logarithmic complexity; handles network partitions and fork scenarios with cross-fork security property
realtime: Yes. Beelay is an RPC protocol designed for real-time sync over any transport providing confidentiality (HTTPS, WebSockets, etc.). Uses Rateless Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables (RIBLT) for efficient set reconciliation. Three-stage synchronization: membership graph sync, document collection sync, individual document sync. Pipelined round trips optimize single-document changes to approximately 2 network round trips
search_retrieval: Not documented. Document retrieval appears to be based on document IDs and membership graphs; no full-text search functionality is described in available materials
links_sessions_to_code: Not designed for this purpose. Keyhive/Beelay target real-time collaborative editing of shared documents (Automerge CRDT), not agent session history. However, the architecture could theoretically be adapted: capability-based access control with encrypted audit logs could serve as infrastructure for agent session recording with cryptographic permission enforcement
privacy_security: End-to-end encryption with causal keys (individual operations not encrypted; ranges of changes compressed then encrypted); forward secrecy (compromised user cannot access group secrets from prior operations); post-compromise security (secrets created after compromise remain protected); cross-fork security (novel property preventing decentralized fork attacks); Ed25519 signatures bind messages to specific recipients; timestamp validation with clock-skew tolerance prevents replay attacks; servers see only ciphertext, cannot decrypt plaintext; pre-alpha code not yet security audited; no formal credentials binding redaction or secret handling
lesson_for_parinn: Keyhive demonstrates that capability-based access control can function in local-first systems without central servers by using cryptographic self-certification: permissions travel with data via signed public-key envelopes. The causal ordering model (rather than linear timestamps) handles decentralized scenarios including network partitions and concurrent updates. For ParleyInn's session history: access control could be enforced cryptographically at the envelope level rather than relying on server validation, enabling offline permission checks and supporting multi-device agent teams across ephemeral environments

name: Kilo Code checkpoints (snapshot system in the new Kilo CLI/VS Code extension, an opencode-derived codebase)
status: shipped. Snapshots are on by default in the current extension and CLI. The monorepo github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode is MIT-licensed and active: HEAD 622ed1f was committed 2026-10-01. The legacy extension's shadow-git checkpoints, inherited from Roo/Cline, are superseded.
what_is_stored: Two layers. (1) Workspace state: a full git tree of the worktree at each agent step boundary. One snapshot is taken before model generation and one after the tool calls run, so a single user message can produce several snapshot pairs. Each snapshot is a git tree object made by `git add --all --sparse` followed by `git write-tree`; no commit object is created. Files are excluded when they match the project's .gitignore, and the project's info/exclude is copied in. Untracked files larger than 2 MiB are skipped (`limit = 2 * 1024 * 1024` in packages/opencode/src/snapshot/index.ts). Diffs shown in the UI are capped at 256 KiB (MAX_DIFF_SIZE). (2) Session linkage: the tree hashes are written into the session record. The assistant message schema carries `snapshot: {start?, end?, files?[]}` (packages/schema/src/session-message.ts). The session row carries a `revert` JSON state with a workspace status: restored, snapshots-disabled, unavailable or not-a-git-repo (packages/core/src/session/sql.ts). Not stored: external edits made outside a Kilo task, and gitignored files such as .env.
where_stored: Two local stores. The snapshot repo is a separate bare-style git dir per user and machine, at ~/.local/share/kilo/snapshot/<project-id>/<Hash.fast(worktree)>/ (Global.Path.data). It is used with `--git-dir <that dir> --work-tree <project>`, so the project's own .git is never written. Session and message data, including the hashes, live in a local SQLite database through drizzle (SessionTable, MessageTable and PartTable with JSON `data` columns). Nothing goes to a remote by default. A session `share_url` column exists for Kilo's separate cloud share feature.
format_and_model: Native git object store. Each snapshot is an unparented tree id with no commit, no message and no author. Reachability is kept by refs/kilo/snapshots/<epoch-ms>/<treehash> (pin) and refs/kilo/materialize/<hash>. A seed step can borrow the project's committed objects through objects/info/alternates. It writes a private, normalized copy of the project index so the first snapshot hashes only dirty files, and it uses a temporary ref in the source repo. After a quiet period, `git repack -a -d` copies borrowed objects into the snapshot repo, which then drops the alternates dependency. Git is invoked with core.autocrlf=false, core.longpaths=true, core.symlinks=true and core.quotepath=false. Restore runs `read-tree <hash>` and then `checkout-index -a -f`. Patch-level revert also exists: the files changed between two trees are restored one by one. The conversation is a relational model: session → message → part, as JSON in SQLite. Reverting truncates the visible conversation at a user message, and Redo / Redo All step forward again.
multi_writer_and_merge: No merge, ever. Snapshots are linear points per worktree. Concurrency control is local only: an in-process semaphore per gitdir plus a file lock (EffectFlock, key `snapshot:<gitdir>`; packages/opencode/src/kilocode/snapshot/lock.ts) serializes snapshot, gc and repack. Separate worktrees hash to separate snapshot repos, so parallel agents in different worktrees never share one. Nothing replicates the snapshot repo across machines.
realtime: Snapshots are written synchronously at each model-call boundary inside a turn. Nothing streams to other machines or viewers. Maintenance runs on a schedule: gc happens hourly, refs older than 7 days are pruned, and then `git gc --prune=7.days` runs.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by tree hash only. The UI exposes per-message diffs (diffFull/diffFile between two trees), Revert to here, Redo and Redo All. There is no content search over snapshots. Session search, if any, runs over SQLite and is unrelated to the snapshot repo.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, tightly but only locally. Every assistant message stores start and end tree hashes plus the list of changed files, so the exact workspace state before and after each step is addressable from the conversation. The link points one way, from session to tree. The snapshot repo holds no record of which session or prompt produced a tree; the ref name carries only a timestamp and the hash. Nothing links to the project's real commit history, because snapshot trees are not commits and never reach the user's repo or remote.
scale: No numeric claims are published. The code is visibly tuned for very large repos: a single-pathspec bulk add for root snapshots and for more than 1,000 candidates avoids quadratic pathspec matching, the private index copy keeps stat data, and seeding stats files in parallel straight through libuv. The docs warn that very large binary files degrade performance. Retention is bounded at 7 days of pinned refs.
privacy_security: No redaction and no encryption. The snapshot repo holds full plaintext copies of every non-ignored file under the user's data directory. Secrets are kept out only when .gitignore already excludes them (the docs cite .env, node_modules/ and dist/), so an untracked, unignored secrets file under 2 MiB is captured. Retention is the only mitigation: 7-day prune plus gc. Per the docs, deleting a session removes its conversation history permanently, across every project on that machine. Kilo credentials live separately in ~/.local/share/kilo/auth.json, according to a Kilo blog post. Git must be installed, because Kilo shells out to the git binary.
license: MIT (Kilo-Org/kilocode LICENSE, "Copyright (c) 2026 Kilo Code")
lesson_for_parinn: Store code state as content-addressed git tree ids inside the session record, not as commits or branches in the user's repo. Kilo's split is the right shape for ParleyInn: an out-of-tree object store keyed by project and worktree, with the session log holding only `snapshot.start` and `snapshot.end` hashes per step. Restore stays exact and the user's history stays untouched. ParleyInn should make three changes. (a) Put the session and step id in the pin, for example a ref or a hash-chained record entry, so the link also runs from tree to session and survives an index rebuild (I10). (b) Do not reuse .gitignore as the secret policy. Kilo silently captures any untracked, unignored secret file under 2 MiB, and it skips large files with only a log line. ParleyInn needs explicit redaction, and every skipped or redacted path must be audited and counted (I6). (c) Do the snapshotting with in-process git object writing rather than shelling out to `git` (I4 forbids os/exec). Kilo's alternates-then-repack trick is still worth borrowing for a cheap first snapshot of large repos.
confidence: high for storage layout, git mechanics and session linkage, which I read in source at commit 622ed1f (2026-10-01) and which matches the official docs. Medium for the legacy shadow-git comparison, which rests on the Kilo docs and blog comments only. I could not verify scale figures, because none are published.

name: Kilo Code Memory Bank (deprecated)
status: archived
what_is_stored: Project documentation that the LLM writes and edits by hand. It holds no session records. The removed docs page (last version deleted in commit 56751c52d, 2026-02-03) lists five core files. brief.md is written by the user ("Kilo Code will not edit this file directly"). product.md covers why the project exists and the UX goals. context.md covers "current work focus and recent changes", active decisions and next steps, and is "the most frequently updated file". architecture.md covers design decisions, patterns and component relationships. tech.md covers the stack, setup, constraints and dependencies. An optional tasks.md holds repeatable workflows (files to touch, steps, gotchas), written by "add task" / "store this as a task". Users could add free-form files too. The bank stores no transcripts, prompts, tool calls, timestamps or session ids, and the LLM rewrites the files in place, so earlier state is lost unless git kept it. Deprecated in favor of AGENTS.md. The docs say "Existing memory bank rules will continue to work." Kilo has since shipped a separate opt-in "Kilo Memory" feature that is explicitly "Not the deprecated Memory Bank". It stores project.md, environment.md, corrections.md and session digests outside the repo; see lesson_for_parinn.
where_stored: Working-tree files in the project repo: .kilocode/rules/memory-bank/ (original). The current deprecation notice also names .kilo/rules/memory-bank/. A user-created .kilocode/rules/memory-bank-instructions.md holds the instructions that tell the model how to maintain the bank. The bank is committed (or not) like any other file. The successor Kilo Memory instead lives outside the repo at ~/.local/share/kilo/memory/<project-slug>-<sha1-12>/ (XDG_DATA_HOME respected), and linked git worktrees share one folder.
format_and_model: Plain, unstructured Markdown with no schema, front matter, ids or versioning. The design is prompt-only. The bank is "built on Kilo Code's Custom Rules feature": every file under .kilocode/rules/ is put into the system prompt as a rule. A rules file tells the model, at the start of every task, to read ALL the bank files, begin its reply with "[Memory Bank: Active]" or "[Memory Bank: Missing]", and summarize the project. Your own grep of the current legacy extension source (src/ and docs/ at HEAD, not a full-repo search) found no references to the memory bank, so no dedicated loader, parser or index shows up there. The data model is mutable snapshot documents. The docs rule that on inconsistency the model should "prioritize information from brief.md as the source of truth".
multi_writer_and_merge: No specific mechanism. The files are ordinary tracked files, so concurrent agents or developers merge through normal git merges of free-form prose. context.md is rewritten often, which makes it a likely conflict point; that is an inference, not documented. The docs only say each project has its own bank and that manual edits "will be respected". The newer AGENTS.md docs present version control as the team-consistency mechanism ("Lives in your repository alongside your code").
realtime: None. The bank is read at task start, and updates happen only when the model decides to make them or the user says "update memory bank". The user-facing workflow for full context windows is: "update memory bank", then start a new task. Changes reach other agents or machines only through git push/pull.
search_retrieval: None. All files are loaded in full into context at the start of every task (the docs admit it "does consume some of your context window"). No index, keyword or semantic search, or on-demand recall exists. "update memory bank" makes the model "Review ALL project files" again, which the docs call "resource-intensive". The successor Kilo Memory adds what the bank lacked: a compact injected index plus a pull-only kilo_memory_recall tool with search, typed, digest and catalog modes. Its matching is keyword-based ("not semantic"), it has a "/memory rebuild" for the index, and it falls back to kilo_local_recall for full transcripts.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Sessions, prompts and commits are not linked. context.md holds a prose "recent changes" note, and git history of the bank files is the only implicit link to code. tasks.md lists file paths for recurring tasks, but as prose, not structured links. Kilo Memory session digests carry a session id (session=<id>) but, per its docs, no commit linkage.
scale: No numeric scale claims. The docs say "Testing shows that while Memory Bank uses more tokens initially, it dramatically reduces the total number of interactions", but cite no data (unverifiable). They warn that lightweight models handle the full-repo analysis poorly and advise "Keep memory bank files concise". Scale is bounded by the context window, since every file loads on every task.
privacy_security: None in the memory bank. There is no redaction, secret filtering, encryption or access control; the files sit in the repo and may be committed and pushed. The files are injected as system-prompt rules, so anything in them, including text the model or a contributor wrote from untrusted input, is treated as trusted instruction: a persistent prompt-injection channel. One documented side effect is that the bank's status-line instruction leaked into unrelated outputs. Kilo's commit-message generator prompt had to say "DO NOT include any memory bank status indicators like \"[Memory Bank: Active]\"" (src/shared/support-prompt.ts, changed in 56751c52d). The successor Kilo Memory adds regex and URL-userinfo secret redaction (packages/kilo-memory/src/capture/redact.ts: sk-, ghp_, AKIA, JWT, PEM keys, key=value assignments). It frames memory as "context, not instruction", ranking below current messages, repo files and AGENTS.md. Its docs warn that auto-save "sends best-effort-redacted turn context to your configured model provider". Its audit log has been removed and remains only as a no-op "Compatibility facade for the removed memory audit log" (storage/audit.ts).
license: Apache-2.0 for the legacy Kilo Code extension (inherited from Roo Code/Cline). This was not re-verified in this pass, so treat it as unconfirmed. The successor @kilocode/kilo-memory package declares "license": "MIT" in its package.json.
lesson_for_parinn: Do not inject a summary the model edits as trusted instruction. The memory bank put LLM-rewritten Markdown into the system prompt as rules on every task. That gave prompt injection a permanent home (against I2). It overwrote history in place (no append-only record, against I10). It also leaked its own control strings into unrelated outputs: the commit-message prompt had to filter "[Memory Bank: Active]". Kilo dropped it and the replacement went the way ParleyInn already does: memory outside the repo, a small injected index plus pull-only recall, "context, not instruction" framing, and redaction before writes. The replacement also removed its audit log; ParleyInn's I6 should keep that. So: keep pinned constraints few, human-authored and verbatim (like brief.md, which the model may not edit). Keep everything the agent writes as untrusted, enveloped recall data. Never let a model-maintained file reach the restore block. One more point for the git question: a prose file every agent rewrites is the worst case for git merges (one hot file, no ids). Append-only per-event records merge cleanly; mutable summaries do not.

name: Kilo Sessions (Kilo Code session history, cloud sync, remote mode and share/fork)
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
The docs list four things a session keeps: the repository, the conversation ("your prompts and the agent's replies"), task metadata, and "Optional Git context (for example, the repo URL and a lightweight snapshot of state)" (https://kilo.ai/docs/collaborate/sessions-sharing). The source code is more specific.

Cloud sync stream: the client sends a typed list of items (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/opencode/src/kilo-sessions/ingest-queue.ts):
- kilo_meta {platform, orgId, gitUrl, gitBranch}
- session (title, directory, summary diffs, cost and token counters)
- message
- part
- model
- session_diff (cumulative per-file diffs; Kilo's FileDiff schema can carry patch, before and after content, see https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/opencode/src/snapshot/index.ts)
- session_open and session_close
- session_status (idle, busy, question, permission, retry, scheduled)
- session_pr_link {platform, prUrl, prNumber}
- agent_notification

Every PartUpdated event is forwarded without filtering by type, so tool calls with their inputs and outputs are included (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/opencode/src/kilo-sessions/kilo-sessions.ts).

Local SQLite tables (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/core/src/session/sql.ts):
- session, message, part, todo
- session_share (id, secret, url)
- event and event_sequence, keyed by aggregate_id plus seq

Local snapshots: a separate "shadow" git directory per worktree supports undo and revert. It is pruned after 7 days and is not synced (snapshot/index.ts above).

Mobile attachments and Cloud Agent environment profiles (env vars, encrypted secrets, setup commands) live in the cloud (https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cloud-agent).
where_stored:
Local copy:
- A SQLite file, kilo.db, on the machine where Kilo runs: ~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db, or on the remote host under VS Code Remote SSH. It uses WAL mode, and `kilo db path` prints the location (https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/agents/session-history).
- Shadow git snapshot directories at <data>/snapshot/<project-id>/<hash(worktree)>.

Cloud copy, on Kilo Cloud, which runs on Cloudflare:
- Each session is one Durable Object, SessionIngestDO, keyed by user and session. Items go in its SQLite table ingest_items. Items larger than about 1.94 MiB spill to an R2 bucket (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/cloud/blob/3de933dd85070e9d15c41d8ff3af6c91ca856fd4/services/session-ingest/src/db/sqlite-schema.ts and https://github.com/Kilo-Org/cloud/blob/3de933dd85070e9d15c41d8ff3af6c91ca856fd4/services/session-ingest/src/util/ingest-limits.ts).
- A PostgreSQL table, cli_sessions_v2, reached through Hyperdrive, holds the index row: title, git_url, git_branch and public_id (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/cloud/blob/3de933dd85070e9d15c41d8ff3af6c91ca856fd4/services/session-ingest/src/services/session-share-token.ts).
- The endpoint is ingest.kilosessions.ai (kilo-sessions.ts).
- The privacy policy says data is hosted in the US (https://kilo.ai/privacy).

Git is not used as a store. Cloud Agents only commit and push code to a session branch in the user's GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository (https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cloud-agent).
format_and_model:
Local data model: relational, defined with Drizzle (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/core/src/session/sql.ts):
- A session row with JSON columns (summary_diffs, metadata, revert, permission, model) and a parent_id for child sessions.
- message and part rows, each holding a JSON `data` blob.
- IDs like ses_..., ordered ascending.

Export and import format: JSON {info, messages:[{info, parts}]}, via `kilo export <id>` and `kilo import <file|url>` (https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cli). Import rejects duplicate IDs, dangling or circular parent links, and dangling compaction tails (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/kilo-gateway/src/cloud-sessions.ts).

Wire format: POST {data:[items]} to <ingest>/api/session/:id/ingest?v=2 with a bearer token (ingest-queue.ts).

Cloud data model: not a log. It keeps the latest value per entity identity:
- 'session', 'message/<id>', '<messageID>/<partID>', 'session_diff', 'kilo_meta', and so on.
- Writes are upserts (onConflictDoUpdate).
- There is no hash chain and no append-only guarantee (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/cloud/blob/3de933dd85070e9d15c41d8ff3af6c91ca856fd4/services/session-ingest/src/dos/SessionIngestDO.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Each session has one authoritative writer: the host running the agent, which is the CLI, the IDE extension (backed by the CLI) or a Cloud Agent container.

Client side (ingest-queue.ts):
- Updates are coalesced per entity key; the newest wins.
- Each session flushes at most about once per second.
- Failures on 408, 409, 425, 429 and 5xx are retried with exponential backoff capped at 60 s.
- Requeued retries use a 'fill' mode that never overwrites newer data.

Server side: each item is upserted, guarded by a server-assigned ingested_at (Date.now() at staging). Older updates are skipped, so the rule is last-writer-wins per entity (SessionIngestDO.ts, stage-and-enqueue.ts).

Remote mode: web and mobile clients do not write directly. They send relay commands to the CLI, such as send_message, permission_respond, question_reply, create_session, drop_queued_message and exit_cli (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/opencode/src/kilo-sessions/remote-sender.ts). Renames sync in both directions (https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cloud-agent).

Divergent histories are never merged. Collaboration means sharing a link and having each person fork it; forking "creates a new session in your account, with its own ID", and "you'll each have independent progress and costs" (https://kilo.ai/docs/collaborate/sessions-sharing). Moving a session between cloud and local is a clone or import that assigns new IDs (`--cloud-fork --session`, `kilo import`). Cumulative diffs are carried across a fork (https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode/blob/622ed1f5ae5af2d864908a0bb759b0c9121d406c/packages/opencode/src/kilocode/session-portability/cumulative-diff.ts).
