name: Marmot v2
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Row-level change data captured from distributed SQLite databases. Each node stores complete replicated databases in SQLite WAL mode. CDC records encode changed rows as msgpack-serialized EncodedCapturedRow structs with statement metadata. Transaction metadata (version timestamps, locks, apply markers) stored in Pebble KV. Vector index derivatives (IVF/PQ clusters, rowmaps, block metadata) are local non-replicated artifacts per node.
where_stored: Working tree files: SQLite .db files (WAL mode) + .db-wal + .db-shm journals in configured data_dir. Separate git repo: N/A. Pebble KV store alongside SQLite for transaction intent locks and row-version metadata. CDC segment log files stored in Pebble. Vector index artifacts stored as local .vecseg generations next to databases (not replicated).
format_and_model: Data: SQLite (WAL mode, standard wire format). CDC: msgpack binary encoding for rows, then stored as segments with deterministic record boundaries. Metadata: Pebble B+tree for transaction state and row versions (table, key, HLC timestamp, node ID, tombstone flag). Network: Protocol Buffers over gRPC for cluster gossip/replication. Client wire: MySQL protocol for SQL access. Vector indexes: Residual PQ8 quantization with IVF clustering, compacted int8 overlays.
multi_writer_and_merge: Leaderless multi-master: any node accepts writes. Replication via 2PC (Two-Phase Commit) with tunable consistency: ONE (1 ack, fast), QUORUM (majority, default), ALL (all nodes, durable). Conflict resolution: per-row Last-Write-Wins on HLC commit timestamp; higher node ID breaks ties. Concurrent writes to same row conflict at PREPARE phase—only one commits. Replayed changes from anti-entropy converge identically across nodes regardless of arrival order via per-row LWW.
realtime: SWIM-style gossip protocol for cluster membership, failure detection, and schema version exchange. Anti-entropy background process runs every 30s (configurable), pulling live commit logs from each peer database. 2PC replication can be tuned: ONE returns ~5ms (one node), QUORUM ~22-40ms (majority on local 3-node), ALL slower. Network partitions: minority side fails writes (no quorum), majority side succeeds; partition heal via anti-entropy + per-row LWW merges divergent data.
search_retrieval: Full MySQL SQL compatibility: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP TABLE), transactions, savepoints, vector search. Vector search: vec_match(embedding, query_vec, k) for ANN candidate set, vec_distance(embedding, query_vec) for exact reranking. Metadata queries: SHOW DATABASES/TABLES, INFORMATION_SCHEMA, type-converted for MySQL compatibility. Direct SQLite file read on local node for maximum performance. All replication deterministic (row data, not SQL replay).
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Marmot v2 is a distributed database replication layer, not an agent session manager. Could serve as backend for agent session storage if integrated externally (rows would be CDC-replicated across nodes), but no built-in session lifecycle or workflow semantics.
privacy_security: Pre-Shared Key (PSK) authentication required for all gRPC cluster communication (gossip, replication, snapshots). Cluster secret empty = auth disabled (warning logged). Row versioning prevents silent data loss: applies only rows newer than local version. DDL cluster-wide locking (30s lease) prevents concurrent schema mutations. CDC encoding is deterministic (no SQL parsing, no injection vector). No untrusted input ever reaches queries: all changes are replayed row data.
lesson_for_parinn: CDC-based row replication (msgpack EncodedCapturedRow) ensures deterministic consistency without SQL parsing differences between SQLite nodes. Per-row HLC versioning + node ID tiebreaker enables truly leaderless operation without Raft. Gossip + anti-entropy (background log pulls with exactly-once via applied markers) recovers from split-brain + node failures automatically. Combining CDC + version numbers replaces consensus complexity. Can store immutable append-only records as tables; row-level timestamps + node versioning give natural history tracking.

name: Mastra observational memory
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Compressed conversation observations and message history. Raw messages stored until 30k token threshold, then compressor agent creates observations. When observations reach 40k tokens, reflector agent removes irrelevant ones. Stores three-date metadata per observation (creation date, referenced date, relative date). Also maintains conversation message history, working memory (persistent structured user data like preferences/goals), and semantic recall indices.
where_stored: Text-based formatted entries persisted to pluggable storage backends. Mastra supports 25+ storage adapters: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, libSQL, DynamoDB, Cloudflare D1/KV, Google Cloud Spanner, ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, Redis, LanceDB, and others. Stored in databases user selects; self-hosted deployments keep all data locally.
format_and_model: Text-based formatted entries, not structured objects. Two-level bulleted lists, emoji-based prioritization (🔴 critical, 🟡 moderate, 🟢 info), titles, timestamps, and inline dates. Three-date model for temporal reasoning. Achieves 3-6x compression ratio on conversational data, 5-40x on tool-call-heavy workloads. Formatted as append-only log with dated sections.
multi_writer_and_merge: No information provided. Research describes single-agent synchronous operation: 'conversation blocks while the Observer processes messages.' No documented support for concurrent writes, conflict resolution, or multi-agent shared memory coordination.
realtime: Synchronous single-agent operation with blocking: observation runs when 30k token threshold hit, blocking the conversation. Uses prompt caching for stable, cacheable context window. No multi-agent real-time synchronization documented. Cost reduction through caching (4-10x vs uncached) but not through real-time streaming.
search_retrieval: No dynamic per-turn retrieval. Maintains completely stable, prompt-cacheable context window with all observations preserved. Retrieved observations based on relative date computation. No vector search or similarity-based retrieval mentioned; uses formatted text structure for organization.
links_sessions_to_code: Not found. No GitHub or git integration documented for linking agent sessions to code repositories. Integrations mentioned (Jira, GitLab, incident.io) are for workflow/issue management, not session-to-code linkage.
privacy_security: PII redaction via configurable PIIDetector (email, phone, credit-card, SSN). SensitiveDataFilter for trace redaction. Data remains in user infrastructure with self-hosting. EU region deployment option. SOC 2 Type II certified. Standard Contractual Clauses for EU. Public subprocessor list with 30-day notice. Data not used for training. No automatic path from untrusted content to model (must be configured explicitly).
lesson_for_parinn: Text-based append-only observation logs avoid knowledge graphs and structured objects, similar to ParleyInn's trust model. However, Mastra's system is single-agent-per-memory context with synchronous, blocking compression. ParleyInn must support multiple agents concurrently accessing shared session history across machines and ephemeral sandboxes. Mastra does not address distributed writes, conflict resolution, or multi-writer merge semantics—critical for ParleyInn's requirement (I10) that everything be rebuildable from the record. Mastra's prompt caching strategy optimizes LLM token efficiency, but ParleyInn's pull-only recall model and red-tape pinning constraints differ fundamentally.

name: Matrix Protocol
category: Federated signed event DAG with optional linear variant
status: shipped
what_is_stored: JSON events representing transient messages and persistent state (membership, room metadata) organized in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) per room. Each event is immutable once persisted; only redaction (sanitization) is allowed. Events contain type, sender, timestamp, content, cryptographic signatures from originating and hub servers, and hash references to parent events.
where_stored: Events are persisted in local database stores on homeservers (Synapse reference implementation uses PostgreSQL or SQLite). Events are replicated across all federated homeservers participating in a room. Each homeserver maintains a copy of the full event history for its rooms. In Linearized Matrix variant, a hub server maintains the authoritative linear history while participant servers relay through it.
format_and_model: Events are JSON objects serialized using Canonical JSON (RFC 8785). Standard event format includes fields: room_id, type, sender, origin_server_ts, content, hashes (content hash via SHA-256, reference hash for event ID), signatures (ed25519 keys), auth_events, prev_events. Event IDs are derived from reference hashes in format $<base64-reference-hash>, creating cryptographic binding between event identity and content. Maximum event size is 65,536 bytes. State events use type+state_key tuple for deduplication. Linearized Matrix variant uses doubly-linked list structure instead of DAG.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple homeservers can write events to the same room; writes are broadcast via Persistent Data Units (PDUs) in HTTPS transactions (max 50 PDUs per transaction). When event branches merge in the DAG, deterministic state resolution algorithms (version-specific) automatically resolve conflicting state without central coordination. Each event carries prev_events references establishing causal ordering via a depth field ensuring strict partial ordering. Authorization rules are consistently enforced across all participating servers to maintain semantic equivalence. Linearized Matrix simplifies this by routing all writes through a hub server which maintains linear history and broadcasts to participant servers.
realtime: Real-time synchronization via /sync endpoint allows clients to retrieve incremental updates about rooms, messages, and user presence. Servers track session state and push incremental updates rather than requiring full refetch. Event broadcasts between homeservers use PDU transactions over HTTPS. Synchronization supports both lightweight clients fetching on-demand and heavyweight clients maintaining full local state.
search_retrieval: Server-side search via /search endpoint with room event filtering, result ordering, pagination, and grouping. Direct history retrieval via /rooms/{roomId}/messages endpoint with backward/forward pagination. Event context via /rooms/{roomId}/context/{eventId} showing surrounding messages. Specific event lookup via /rooms/{roomId}/event/{eventId} and timestamp-to-event conversion. Supports varying client storage and connectivity profiles through multiple retrieval mechanisms.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Matrix is designed for user conversations and community communication, not for agent session tracking or code linkage. Rooms are identified by opaque IDs and human-readable aliases; no native concept of linking to agent sessions or code repositories. Could be adapted for this purpose but would require custom event types and application-layer logic outside the protocol.
privacy_security: End-to-end encryption via Olm (one-to-one, m.olm.v1.curve25519-aes-sha2) and Megolm (group, m.megolm.v1.aes-sha2) with server-side key backups using m.megolm_backup.v1.curve25519-aes-sha2. Device key management with one-time and fallback keys. Device verification through Short Authentication Strings (SAS), QR codes, or cross-signing. Event redaction for moderation and sensitive data removal. Cryptographic signatures (ed25519) on all events from sender and hub servers prevent tampering. Events validated through format, signature, hash, and authorization checks before persistence. Lineage checked through prev_events field. No automatic encryption at storage layer (homeserver databases may be plaintext unless operator deploys encrypted storage). Content hashes and reference hashes prevent fork attacks where a hub could send different event copies with same ID.
lesson_for_parinn: Matrix demonstrates that cryptographic content hashing works well for immutable append-only event logs and prevents fork attacks. The DAG-based causal ordering through prev_events and depth fields provides ordering guarantees useful for multi-writer scenarios, though the full state resolution algorithm adds significant complexity. Linearized Matrix variant proves the DAG can be simplified to a doubly-linked list through a hub model, reducing operational complexity. However, Matrix's federation model (rooms replicated to all participating servers) differs fundamentally from ParleyInn's use case (agent session history across worktrees and machines in a single logical session). Matrix prioritizes conversation-centric security (E2EE for user privacy); ParleyInn needs history-level security (redaction, immutability, no prompt injection from untrusted recall). Matrix's event model is document-shaped (JSON); ParleyInn may benefit from schema-enforced structures for agent session state. Lesson: cryptographic event IDs and content hashes prevent tampering, but applying federated room replication to agent sessions requires careful adaptation of the federation model.

name: MCP Agent Mail (Python original; Rust rewrite mcp_agent_mail_rust now the main line)
category: agent mail / inter-agent messaging (MCP server with a git-backed audit archive and a SQLite index)
status: shipped. Both repos are active. The Python repo had commits up to 2026-09-29 (https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail/commits/main). The Rust rewrite released v0.3.36 on 2026-09-16 (https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail_rust/releases). Its README calls itself "The Rust rewrite of the original Python project" and says "The Rust implementation is authoritative" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail_rust/main/README.md). The Python version is not marked archived, but it is no longer the main line. The Python README still says "Under active development".
what_is_stored:
It stores only coordination data that agents choose to send. It does not store session transcripts. Stored items are:
- Agent profiles: a generated adjective+noun name, program, model, task description and contact policy.
- Messages: subject, GFM Markdown body, to/cc/bcc, thread_id, importance and ack_required. Each message is stored once as a canonical copy, once in the sender's outbox and once in each recipient's inbox.
- Per-recipient read and ack timestamps (SQLite only).
- Advisory file reservations (leases): glob, exclusive or shared, TTL and reason.
- Cross-project contact links, project sibling suggestions, build slots (Rust), and attachments. Images are converted to WebP and stored by sha1 hash.
Sources: README "Core ideas", "On-disk layout" and "Data model (SQLite)" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail/main/README.md).
where_stored:
Two local stores under STORAGE_ROOT, both separate from the code repo.

1) A local git archive.
- Python default: ~/.mcp_agent_mail_git_mailbox_repo (README config table).
- Rust default: $XDG_DATA_HOME/mcp-agent-mail/git_mailbox_repo. The legacy path is still used if it already exists (Rust README "Storage Layout").

2) A SQLite database, storage.sqlite3, inside STORAGE_ROOT.

Correction to the discovery note: in the Python code there is one git repo at STORAGE_ROOT, not one per project. Each project is a subdirectory projects/<slug>/. ensure_archive_root() runs Repo.init on the root, and ensure_archive() returns repo_root/"projects"/slug with the same Repo object (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail/main/src/mcp_agent_mail/storage.py, lines ~1417-1476). The Python README's "per-project Git repo" wording is loose; its own text mentions "the shared archive repo". The Rust README diagram does show a .git directory under each projects/{slug}/.

The archive is never pushed to a remote. Agents on other machines reach the single HTTP server instead. The only things that push to GitHub/Cloudflare Pages are the optional static "share" export bundles (README "Static Mailbox Export").
format_and_model:
Git tree per project:
- agents/<Name>/profile.json
- agents/<Name>/inbox/YYYY/MM/<id>.md and outbox/YYYY/MM/<id>.md
- messages/YYYY/MM/<id>.md
- optional messages/threads/<thread-id>.md digest
- file_reservations/<sha1-of-path>.json
- attachments/<xx>/<sha1>.webp

Messages are GFM Markdown with JSON frontmatter between `---json` fences. Frontmatter fields: id, thread_id, project, project_slug, from, to, cc, created, importance, ack_required, attachments.

SQLite tables: projects, agents, messages, message_recipients(read_ts, ack_ts), file_reservations, agent_links, project_sibling_suggestions. Python also has fts_messages (FTS5), kept current by triggers. Message ids are integers from SQLite. There is no hash chaining or content addressing of messages; only attachments are stored by sha1.

Rust stores all timestamps as i64 microseconds.

Sources: README "Message file format", "Data model (SQLite)"; Rust README "Key Design Decisions".
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is a single writer. Every agent goes through one server process, so git merges never happen.

Python:
- A per-project .archive.lock guards file writes.
- A .commit.lock serializes git index and commit operations.
- Files are written first, then committed together. One send_message gives one commit that holds the canonical, outbox and inbox copies.
- An in-process _CommitQueue batches commits that touch different paths (max_batch_size 10).
- index.lock errors are retried with backoff.
- Lock files carry .owner.json metadata so stale locks can be detected (storage.py header and lines 74-140).

Rust:
- The write path changes SQLite first, then writes git artifacts through a write-behind queue and an async commit coalescer. In the recorded stress test, 100 concurrent writes became 11 commits.
- It uses git plumbing commits so the normal path avoids index.lock.
- The README says: "Concurrent writes are queued, not hand-merged ... There is no workflow where two agents create a Git merge conflict".
- A database generation token stops a rebuilt database from overwriting older reservation artifacts.

Sources: Rust README "Consistency and Recovery Model" and "Write Path".

Coordination with code edits uses advisory leases, not locks. Reservations are always granted and come back with a list of conflicts. An optional pre-commit / pre-push hook in the code repo blocks commits that touch another agent's exclusive reservation (README "File Reservations and the optional pre-commit guard").
realtime:
There is no push delivery to agents. Delivery is polling.
- Agents call fetch_inbox or read resource://inbox/{agent}. unread_only=true cuts the token cost of polling.
- The installers add a Claude Code / Gemini / Codex PostToolUse hook, check_inbox.sh. It curls the server after Bash tool calls and prints a reminder about unread mail, at most once every 2 minutes (README "Automatic inbox reminders").
- The Rust TUI, robot CLI and web UI read a /mail/ws-state snapshot by polling (Rust README).

The git archive is not a real-time transport. It is a local audit ledger. Real-time sharing comes from the central HTTP server, which listens on port 8765 by default.
search_retrieval:
Python: search_messages runs SQLite FTS5 with bm25 over subject and body, limited to messages the calling agent can see. The web UI falls back to LIKE. Query syntax supports subject:, body:, quoted phrases and AND/OR/NOT.

summarize_thread pulls out participants, key points and actions. Its optional llm_mode calls an LLM through litellm (commit "perf(llm): defer litellm import", Aug 2026). That call goes over the network.

Rust: "Search V3" uses frankensearch. A lexical tier is the default. Semantic and hybrid search (Model2Vec plus a reranker) sit behind a build-time "hybrid" feature flag. In Rust, FTS5 is kept only as a legacy artifact (Rust README "Search Architecture").

Retrieval also goes through MCP resources: inbox, outbox, thread, and views such as ack-overdue and urgent-unread. A "product bus" combines search and inbox across linked projects.

Static share bundles ship a SQLite snapshot and do FTS in the browser.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only loosely. Agent sessions and prompts are not recorded. Links to code come from these:
- A convention of using a Beads issue id (bd-###) as the thread_id, the reservation reason and, optionally, in commit messages.
- whois(include_recent_commits) and resource://mailbox-with-commits. These attach commit metadata from the mail archive.
- Reservation globs over code paths, enforced by the pre-commit/pre-push guard. AGENT_NAME names the committing agent.
- Project identity worked out from the code repo. In order of precedence: a committed .agent-mail-project-id marker, .agent-mail.yaml, .git/agent-mail/project-id, the origin URL plus default branch, a hash of the git common dir, or a hash of the directory. This applies with WORKTREES_ENABLED or GIT_IDENTITY_ENABLED; the default is off (README "identity modes").

Sources: README sections on Beads integration and the guard.
scale:
The project's own claims, not independently checked:
- Walkthrough: 7 agents sent more than 1,000 messages over two days.
- Rust stress campaign: 100 concurrent writes became 11 commits (9.1x batching) with 0 lock errors. 60 threads on a pool of 15 at a sustained 50 RPS for 30 s gave 0 timeouts. The README says these are "retained results ... not a guarantee".
- It names three failure modes the Python version hit under real multi-agent load: git lock contention, SQLite pool exhaustion, and cascading failures.

Sources: Rust README "Rust vs. Python: Stress Test Results". The Rust README also cites the Python repo at 1,700+ stars.

Quotas exist but default to unlimited (QUOTA_ATTACHMENTS_LIMIT_BYTES, QUOTA_INBOX_LIMIT_COUNT).
privacy_security:
Server and access:
- HTTP server with a static bearer token or JWT+JWKS, plus RBAC on MCP POSTs.
- A localhost-unauthenticated mode for development.
- Optional token-bucket rate limiting.
- Per-agent registration tokens (Rust v0.3.35 requires them for lifecycle tools over HTTP).
- Contact policies (open, auto, contacts_only, block_all) gate who may message whom, including across projects.

Content handling:
- Inbox copies redact the bcc list (storage.py, issue #186).
- Absolute attachment paths are off by default. The README warns that enabling them makes send a file-read primitive.
- Web UI HTML is sanitized with Bleach.

Identity: self-asserted by default. Rust has an opt-in Ed25519 "Registration Proof Gate" that fails closed and has replay-protected nonces.

Not found: any encryption at rest of the git archive or SQLite database, and any secret scrubbing at write time.

Redaction exists only on the export path. Share bundles have a "standard" preset that regex-scrubs GitHub, Slack and OpenAI keys, bearer tokens and JWTs, and a "strict" preset that drops all bodies and attachments. Bundles get SHA-256 manifests, optional Ed25519 signing, and optional age encryption. Rust doctor support-bundles leave out message bodies.

Prompt-injection posture: message bodies from other agents go into an agent's context through fetch_inbox with no untrusted-content envelope described. "Human Overseer" messages add a preamble telling agents to put the instruction first. Contrast ParleyInn's I2.

Rust releases are minisign-signed, and the Rust crates use #![forbid(unsafe_code)].

License: "MIT License (with OpenAI/Anthropic Rider)". It grants no rights to OpenAI, Anthropic or their affiliates, or to anyone acting on their behalf, and it defines "use" to include analyzing and indexing (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail/main/LICENSE). The author accepts no outside contributions.
license: MIT with an added OpenAI/Anthropic rider. The rider withholds all rights from OpenAI, Anthropic, their affiliates and their agents or contractors. It is not OSI-approved as written. ParleyInn should not copy code; at most it can take design ideas, and the rider also makes that sensitive (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Dicklesworthstone/mcp_agent_mail/main/LICENSE).
lesson_for_parinn:
The lesson is to treat git as a write-behind audit ledger behind a single writer, not as the real-time bus or the merge layer.

Agent Mail puts SQLite in charge of live state and serializes all writers through one process. It then writes git files from that state through a commit coalescer. Its own record shows why: with one commit per message, the Python version ran into git lock contention, and the Rust rewrite cut commits about 9x.

For ParleyInn this suggests:
1. Keep the hash-chained append log as the source of truth, with one writer per log. Render git artifacts asynchronously and in batches, never one commit per event.
2. Never rely on git merges for concurrent writers.
3. Make the index rebuildable from the ledger. This mirrors Agent Mail's `doctor reconstruct` and matches I10.

Agent Mail gets real-time cross-machine sharing only from a central HTTP server, which ParleyInn's core cannot run (I4). It also pipes peer messages straight into model context with an authority preamble, which is the injection channel I2 forbids. Any ParleyInn sharing layer would need to put a transport outside the core and keep recalled peer content enveloped and pull-only.

name: MCP GitHub Memory Server ("gitmem", panosAthDBX)
status: beta: an early hobby project, not archived, no releases. I cloned it on 2026-10-02 and found 7 commits on one branch (main). Six are dated 15-17 Nov 2025 and the latest, eb9fffc, is dated 25 Jun 2026. The README calls it "Current (v1.0)", but every crate is version 0.1.0, and parts of the SPEC are missing from the code (details below). I could not read the star count myself because the GitHub API was blocked for this session. The figure of 0 stars comes from the discovery note.
what_is_stored: Curated "memories" and notes that the agent writes on purpose. It does not record sessions or transcripts. Each record has an id ("mem_"+UUIDv4), a version counter, a type (fact, preference, profile, reminder, note or policy), a title, content, tags (including an automatic "project:<id>" tag), an optional score, a TTL, created/updated/deleted timestamps (deleted acts as a soft-delete tombstone), encryption metadata, compat metadata, and an optional source block. The source block holds agent, session, origin and app, plus file_uri, relative_path, checksum_sha256, mtime and front_matter for files brought in from linked folders such as Obsidian vaults. It exposes the Basic Memory tool set (write_note, search_notes, build_context and others) plus its own memory.* tools. Sources: crates/core/src/model.rs and SPEC §4 and §8 (https://github.com/panosAthDBX/mcp-github-memory-server/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md), README (https://github.com/panosAthDBX/mcp-github-memory-server/blob/main/README.md).
where_stored: A git working tree on local disk. Files go under memories/<project>/YYYY/MM/DD/<id>.json, with a per-project MANIFEST plus link registry under meta/. That tree is pushed to a device-specific branch, devices/<HOSTNAME> by default and overridable with GITMEM_DEVICE_BRANCH, in a GitHub (or any git) remote. The search index (milli-core on LMDB) lives only on the local machine. There is also a local-filesystem backend with the same layout and no git, and an in-memory backend for tests. The code: path_for_memory, default_device_branch and do_push in crates/storage/github/src/lib.rs. A file:// remote is handled by copying the directory tree, not by git.
format_and_model: One pretty-printed JSON file per memory, chosen so merges are easier (SPEC §4). The model is mutable records: an update rewrites the file in place and bumps the version, and deletes are soft (deleted_at) or hard. Nothing is append-only and there is no hash chain inside the records. Git history is the only audit trail, and it is coarse. The code's git_commit() is a stub that only appends a line to .git/COMMITS. A real commit (libgit2, signed as "gitmem <gitmem@example.com>", message "chore(mem): sync push") is created only at push time and stages all of memories/ and meta/ at once. So the per-memory Conventional Commit messages described in the SPEC ("feat(mem): add <title> [mem:<id>]") are not implemented. SPEC §22 calls for per-field vector clocks, but the Memory struct has none.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The design (SPEC §5.1 and §11): one branch per device, merged into main by fast-forward or a PR; a field-level three-way JSON merge; irreconcilable cases written to conflicts/<id>/<ts>.json and opened as a PR. The code does much less:
(1) Push uses the force refspec "+refs/heads/X:refs/heads/X", so each device overwrites its own remote branch.
(2) Pull fetches that same device branch, unconditionally points the local ref at the remote commit, checks it out and rebuilds the manifest. That is not a merge.
(3) Nothing merges device branches into main, and there is no PR automation; both are on the v1.1 roadmap.
(4) "Conflict" handling is an optimistic local check: an update whose version or updated_at is not newer than the copy on disk is rejected, and before.json and after.json are written under conflicts/<id>/<ts>/.
(5) Several MCP processes on one machine coordinate through file locks: a per-project meta/<project>/LOCK, a non-blocking .git/gitmem-sync.lock, and a /tmp/gitmem-push.lock (LOCKING_ANALYSIS.md, MULTI_INSTANCE_FIX.md).
In practice, devices are kept apart by branch and do not converge. Sharing across devices or agents is left to a manual git merge.
realtime: No. A write returns right away and marks the project dirty. A background tokio worker checks every 10 seconds and then commits and, if auto_push is on, force-pushes. A push failure is logged and retried; it does not fail the write (BACKGROUND_SYNC_FIX.md; spawn_sync_worker in crates/server/src/lib.rs). Pulling happens only when the user calls memory.sync or the CLI's sync. There is no periodic pull and no webhook listener; webhooks with ETag polling are in the SPEC and on the v1.1 roadmap. Linked external folders are polled, by default every 30 s with jitter. A WebSocket transport is described for remote MCP access, but that is for clients, not for sync.
search_retrieval: A local full-text index in milli-core (Meilisearch's engine on LMDB) with BM25 ranking, filters on type, tags and time range, TTL enforced at query time, and sorting by relevance, recency or score. A real Tantivy engine is available behind the real_tantivy feature (crates/index/tantivy/Cargo.toml). Indexing is asynchronous through an unbounded queue, with a warning above 5000 queued items. The index is rebuilt from the files and is never committed. Basic Memory-style build_context and recent_activity are also offered. Embeddings and hybrid search are roadmap items (v1.2). When encryption is on, title and content are emptied before indexing, so only metadata is searchable (redact_encrypted_for_index in crates/server/src/lib.rs).
links_sessions_to_code: Barely. Memory.source.session is a free-form optional string (the SPEC example uses a timestamp), next to agent, origin and app. There is no link to commits, worktrees, files under edit or prompts. The memory repo is separate from the code repo. The only file linkage is the linked-folder import, which records file_uri, relative_path and a sha256 of each imported Markdown file.
scale: These are targets from the README and SPEC, not published results: save p50 under 5 ms locally and under 50 ms with GitHub batch push; search p95 under 50 ms on 50k memories; import above 1k writes/s to the local index; Git pushes in batches of 500 files; under 50 MiB memory when idle; a recent-ID manifest capped at 1024 entries; max_memory_size of 80 KiB per record in the sample config. A criterion bench exists (crates/benchmarks), but the repo contains no benchmark results. One JSON file per memory in a date-sharded tree means the file count grows with every record.
privacy_security:
Optional age X25519 encryption with multiple recipients, applied only to title and content and stored as base64 ciphertext in the JSON. Tags, type, timestamps, source and project names stay in plaintext in git. Passphrase mode is rejected (crates/crypto/src/lib.rs). GitHub credentials come from an environment token (a classic PAT with repo scope, as the README's quickstart shows), username/password, SSH agent, or a git credential helper. The SPEC also promises GitHub App short-lived tokens and the OS keychain.
The README and SPEC promise "PII redaction: configurable content filters", but I found no such code: a grep for redact and pii finds only the index-blanking function above. There is no secret scanning and no handling of stored text as untrusted when it is recalled into a prompt. The server makes network calls itself (libgit2 push/fetch, optional WebSocket bind on 0.0.0.0:8177). Force-push means a compromised or buggy device can rewrite its own branch's history.
license: Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual), declared in Cargo.toml and README. The README links LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT files, but neither is in the repository tree at eb9fffc.
lesson_for_parinn: A branch per device (devices/<host>) avoids push races but never converges, and this project shows why. Without a deterministic merge, each machine just force-pushes its own island. The SPEC's field-level three-way JSON merge, vector clocks and conflict PRs never shipped, because merging mutable JSON records is the hard part. ParleyInn's append-only, content-addressed events are a better fit for git. If ParleyInn adds a git transport, it should keep each writer's append-only ref, never force-pushed and checked by fast-forward, and build the merged view as a deterministic union keyed by event hash, not as a git merge of mutable files. That keeps I10, since the view is rebuildable from the record. It also means the transport never has to resolve conflicts. A second lesson: an optional sync that is batched, never blocks the write path and runs off-thread (a 10-second dirty-flush with retry) is the right pattern for I9. But gitmem keeps libgit2 networking inside the server, whereas ParleyInn's I4 requires that networking to live in a separate process outside the core. Also, encrypting only title and content still leaks tags, project names and timestamps into the git remote, so ParleyInn should encrypt the whole event envelope if history ever leaves the machine.
confidence: high (from a clone and code read at commit eb9fffc on 2026-10-02). The star count and wider adoption are unverified: the GitHub API was blocked and I found no outside discussion.

name: MCP Memory Service (doobidoo/mcp-memory-service)
category: memory MCP server (local DB + cloud sync)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Distilled "memories", not raw session logs. A memory is a text item with a content hash, tags, memory_type, a JSON metadata blob and created/updated timestamps. Lineage columns arrived in migration 011: parent_id, version, confidence, last_accessed, superseded_by. Each memory has an embedding. Around the memories sit a knowledge-graph edge table (memory_graph) and a derived belief store. Each belief has a status and keeps provenance as the hashes of the memories it came from. Memories reach the store four ways: (1) explicit memory_store calls; (2) memory_store_session, which saves a whole list of conversation turns as one memory and always adds a session:<id> tag; (3) Claude Code hooks, where SessionEnd stores a session summary tagged with the project, language and frameworks; (4) an opt-in SessionEnd harvest that reads the Claude Code transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/ and keeps only extracted decisions, bugs, conventions, learnings and context. Consolidation compresses and forgets old memories, so history is deliberately lossy. Since v11.14.0 (2026-09-25) a memory can also carry the agent_id of its author.
where_stored: Local DB plus an optional cloud copy. The sqlite_vec backend is a local SQLite file using the vec0 virtual table plus an FTS5 trigram index. The cloudflare backend keeps rows in Cloudflare D1, vectors in Vectorize, and content over 1 MB in R2. The milvus backend uses Milvus Lite, self-hosted Milvus or Zilliz Cloud. The hybrid backend, which the project recommends for production, writes to local SQLite-vec first and replicates in the background to D1 and Vectorize. The knowledge graph is answered from the local SQLite primary only. I found no code that replicates memory_graph to Cloudflare (zero references in cloudflare.py and hybrid.py), so graph edges look local-only. OAuth state goes in memory by default or in a separate SQLite oauth.db. Nothing is stored in git. Repo history: the project lived on Codeberg from June to September 2026 and moved back to GitHub on 2026-09-05; the Codeberg archive stays readable.
format_and_model: Relational rows and vectors. The local SQLite table is memories(id INTEGER PK, content_hash TEXT UNIQUE, content, tags TEXT, memory_type, metadata TEXT (JSON), created_at REAL, updated_at REAL, *_iso TEXT, deleted_at REAL), extended by migration 011 with parent_id, version, confidence, last_accessed and superseded_by. Embeddings live in a separate vec0 table with cosine distance and a store partition key ('default', 'docs' and so on). The D1 schema is similar, with tags normalised into tags and memory_tags tables plus vector_id, content_size and r2_key columns. Identity is content-addressed: content_hash = SHA-256(content.strip().lower()), deliberately ignoring tags and metadata. Two writers storing the same text therefore produce one record. Dedup has two layers: an exact-hash check that is always on, and a semantic near-duplicate check that can be skipped. Passing conversation_id bypasses dedup. In hybrid mode, content longer than 800 characters is chunked for Cloudflare. Local embeddings use ONNX all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The Cloudflare side embeds through Workers AI with @cf/baai/bge-base-en-v1.5, so the two indexes use different embedding models. Records are mutable rows (update, soft-delete, supersede). There is no append-only log and no hash chain. Export and import use JSON.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writers on one machine share one SQLite file through WAL mode and busy_timeout. Larger setups run a single HTTP server that every client talks to, and that server is the serialisation point. Across machines, hybrid replication works like this:
(a) Each local write goes into an in-memory asyncio queue (up to 2000 operations, batches of 100, 3 retries). A loop drains it about every 5 s into D1 and Vectorize.
(b) New memories are pulled from the cloud at startup, on a manual force-pull, and in an hourly drift scan. The startup pull uses a hash-set difference: it fetches cloud hashes and pulls the missing ones by hash.
(c) The drift scan (MCP_HYBRID_DRIFT_CHECK_INTERVAL, default 3600 s, at most 100 memories per batch) settles metadata conflicts by last-writer-wins on updated_at, with 1 s tolerance ("newer timestamp wins"). It depends on clocks, can silently drop concurrent edits, and its batch size caps how much one pass catches up.
(d) Deletes are soft: deleted_at marks a tombstone. A locally tombstoned hash is pushed to the cloud as a delete, never re-pulled. Tombstones are purged daily once older than TOMBSTONE_RETENTION_DAYS (default 30), so a device offline longer than that can bring deleted memories back.
(e) MCP_HYBRID_SYNC_OWNER (http, mcp or both) chooses which process on a host runs the sync. The docs recommend http to avoid two sync queues.
Content conflicts in meaning, such as a value swap, go to an optional NLI contradiction and quarantine path (memory_conflicts, memory_resolve, get_quarantined_memories), not into replication. Correction to the discovery note: at HEAD the 300 s "periodic sync" only retries failed operations, probes health and gates the hourly drift and capacity checks. Pushes go out about every 5 s, but routine cloud-to-local pulls happen at startup, on demand or hourly, not every 5 minutes in both directions.
realtime: Partly real-time. Within one server, GET /api/events (SSE) emits memory_stored and memory_deleted events, so agents sharing that server can react at once. Hybrid also broadcasts sync-progress and sync-completed events. Across devices, a local write reaches Cloudflare within seconds (the queue drains about every 5 s). Another device sees it only after a restart, a manual force-pull, or the next drift scan (hourly by default, configurable down to 60 s). Default cross-device latency is therefore up to about an hour, not instant. The cloudflare-only backend skips the lag because every client reads the same D1 database.
search_retrieval: memory_search has four modes: semantic (the default, cosine kNN over vec0), exact (substring match), hybrid and ranked. For hybrid, config/search.py describes BM25 over an FTS5 trigram index fused with vector scores: weighted average by default with keyword 0.3 and semantic 0.7, or Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60. The MCP tool's own description, by contrast, calls hybrid "semantic plus quality scoring", so the docs disagree. Searches can filter by natural-language time (time_expr such as "last week"), by after/before dates, and by tags with ANY or ALL matching. A quality_boost re-ranks by a quality score, which can come from an LLM. Since v11.14 an opt-in agent_id filter matches metadata.agent_id or the agent:<id> tag. There is also a store partition, a knowledge graph with typed edges (causes, fixes, contradicts), entity extraction (@mentions, #tags, URLs, file paths), and memory_explore / memory_detail. In hybrid mode reads always hit local SQLite; the claimed latency is about 5 ms. Cloudflare Vectorize caps a query at 50 neighbours, so tag-filtered recall can come back incomplete; since v11.14.0 the result carries a recall_may_be_incomplete flag. Published retrieval-only benchmark: LongMemEval-S R@5 86.0% and R@10 93.0% with session-level ingestion, on v10.34.0.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, through tags and heuristics. No commit SHAs or file diffs are stored on a memory. At SessionStart the Claude Code hook detects the project from cwd and runs `git log` (14-day lookback, at most 20 commits, plus changelog entries) only to steer which memories it retrieves and how it scores them. It then injects the selected memories into the session automatically. SessionEnd stores a summary tagged with the project name, language and frameworks, plus project_context metadata. The harvest endpoint maps a session to its project through the cwd-derived ~/.claude/projects/<-path-with-dashes> directory name. Sessions are identified by session:<id> tags or the metadata session_id. Entity extraction can link file paths it finds in memory text. Overall the store is a project-tagged knowledge base, not a record of which prompt produced which change.
privacy_security:
Hardening present:
- The server binds to 127.0.0.1 by default.
- HTTP auth uses an API key or OAuth 2.1 with Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591): JWT access tokens, default lifetime 60 min, refresh tokens only with offline_access, scopes read, write and admin.
- OAuth state persists in SQLite with atomic one-time code consumption.
- A log-redaction filter keeps API keys out of uvicorn access logs.
- Log-injection guards have been added module by module.
- Several GHSA advisories are fixed, e.g. GHSA-7w86-2vmv-fqwm, an unauthenticated /mcp/health route that leaked storage statistics, fixed in v11.14.0.
Gaps:
- I found no redaction of secrets in stored content; captured transcripts and summaries are stored as written.
- I found no encryption at rest in the code (no SQLCipher or Fernet). SECURITY.md says at-rest and backup encryption is the user's responsibility, which contradicts the "Optional encryption at rest" line in docs/architecture.md.
- In hybrid or cloudflare mode, content is stored in plaintext in the user's Cloudflare D1 and R2 and is sent to Workers AI for embedding. So the README's "memory never leaves your infrastructure" holds only for local-only backends.
- SECURITY.md warns the Cloudflare API token "has full account access".
- Access control is all-or-nothing by scope: there is no per-user or per-tenant isolation. Agent identity is a tag or metadata label, not an authorization boundary.
- Hooks inject retrieved memories into Claude Code context automatically at session start (optionally after compaction too). I found no untrusted-content envelope or prompt-injection mitigation in the hooks or docs (grep for "untrusted" and "prompt injection" found nothing).
- The harvest classifier can send transcript-derived text to external LLMs (Groq or Gemini) when use_llm=true, which is opt-in.
- Some hook settings allow disabling TLS verification (allowSelfSignedCerts).
lesson_for_parinn: The local-first, async-replicated shape is right (about 5 ms local reads, a durable outbound queue, offline tolerance, sync owned by one process). But the merge semantics show what to avoid for an append-only record. Mutable rows plus last-writer-wins on updated_at, and tombstones that expire after 30 days, lose concurrent edits, depend on clocks, and can bring deleted data back on a device that was offline too long. Content-addressed dedup on normalized text silently merges two agents' identical lines into one record. ParleyInn should instead replicate immutable, hash-chained events keyed by (writer id, sequence), so merging is a set union with no conflict resolution. It should treat a delete or redaction as a new audited event, never as a row mutation that expires. It should list missing entries by hash difference, which is the one thing this project does well in its startup pull. Two further lessons: keep embeddings and every other derived index rebuildable locally, never computed by the remote store; and never auto-inject recalled memories the way these SessionStart hooks do, since that is exactly the stored-content-to-prompt path ParleyInn's I2 forbids.
license: Apache-2.0
scale: Self-described limits: SQLite-vec is comfortable at about 100K to 1M memories, and Milvus is recommended beyond that. Cloudflare limits the code enforces: 10 GB per D1 database, 5M vectors per Vectorize index, 10 KB metadata per vector, a 50-neighbour query ceiling, warnings at 80% and 95% capacity. The claimed latency is about 5 ms for local reads. The hybrid queue holds 2000 operations by default. Retrieval quality is published as LongMemEval-S R@5 86.0% with session-level ingestion on v10.34.0. I could not verify any production deployment sizes; the project website points to "deployments people run in production" but I did not check it. The project is very active (v11.14.0 on 2026-09-25, a commit on 2026-10-02), maintained by one person, with about 2k GitHub stars according to the repo page at the time of fetch.
