name: MCP reference Memory server ("Knowledge Graph Memory Server", npm @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory, part of modelcontextprotocol/servers)
category: knowledge graph memory MCP (reference or educational implementation, local single-file store)
status: shipped. It is an active reference server, not archived. It is still listed under "Reference Servers" in the repo README, separately from the "Archived" list (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/README.md). The latest npm release is 2026.8.31, published 2026-08-31 (https://registry.npmjs.org/@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory). That release already has atomic writes and the MCP Resource subscription; I checked by inspecting its dist/index.js in the npm tarball. Several fixes merged to main on 2026-09-02 were not in any published npm version as of 2026-10-02: the in-process mutation lock (#4555), on-load schema validation (#4717), the 2048-char search query cap (#4662), in-batch duplicate skipping (#4383), dangling-relation rejection (#4477) and ~ expansion (#4447). Source: git log of src/memory, https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/commits/main/src/memory. The repo README says these servers are "reference implementations ... educational examples ... not as production-ready solutions" (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/README.md).
what_is_stored: It stores a user-curated knowledge graph that the model writes through tools. There are three kinds of record. (1) Entities: a unique name, an entityType and an observations string[]. (2) Directed relations: from, to and relationType, written "in active voice". (3) Observations: atomic free-text strings attached to an entity (README: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/memory/README.md). It does not store transcripts, prompts, tool calls, timestamps, authors, session ids or any provenance. It holds only the current state of the graph, with no history, because deletes physically remove lines (index.ts: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/memory/index.ts). The README's example system prompt aims it at personal facts about the user: identity, behaviours, preferences, goals, and relationships up to 3 degrees. It does not target coding-session history.
where_stored: It is one local file. The default is memory.jsonl in the package's own dist directory, next to index.js. MEMORY_FILE_PATH overrides it: absolute paths are used as-is and relative paths resolve against the package directory. A legacy memory.json is auto-renamed to memory.jsonl (index.ts ensureMemoryFilePath, https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/memory/index.ts). The Docker setup keeps it in a named volume mounted over /app/dist (`-v claude-memory:/app/dist`). The README warns that an old index.js in that volume can clash with a new image (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/memory/README.md). Inference from the code, not documented: with the default npx launch the file sits inside the npx package cache, so clearing the cache or changing versions can lose it. It uses no server, cloud, git or other database.
format_and_model: JSONL with one JSON object per line. Each line is either {"type":"entity","name","entityType","observations":[...]} or {"type":"relation","from","to","relationType"}. Entities are written first, then relations, with a trailing newline (saveGraph in index.ts; trailing-newline fix #3653). The name is the identity: create_entities silently skips names that already exist, and observations are deduplicated by exact string equality. Deleting an entity also deletes every relation that touches it. The file is not an append-only log, despite the JSONL format. Every mutation loads and parses the whole file, mutates it in memory, and rewrites the whole file. Since #4642 (merged 2026-08-28) the rewrite goes to a random-named temp file in the same directory and is then rename(2)-d over the target, so a crash cannot leave a truncated file (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/4642). On main only, load-time validation skips malformed or invalid lines with a stderr warning (#4717, https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/4717). There is no schema version, no versioning, no index, no hashes and no signatures (index.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no merge model; the last writer wins over the whole file. Issue #1819 (opened 2025-05-17) reported that several memory tool calls from one LLM turn raced and corrupted the JSON (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/issues/1819). It was fixed on main only on 2026-09-02 by #4555, an in-process async promise-queue mutex around the six mutation methods (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/4555). That fix had not shipped in npm 2026.8.31. The lock is explicitly in-process ("Adds an in-process async mutex", commit d73f99e). Inference from the code: there is no flock or advisory lock and no file watch. Each MCP client spawns its own stdio server process, so two agents or sessions pointing MEMORY_FILE_PATH at the same file still lose each other's updates silently. Atomic rename prevents torn files but not lost updates. There is no cross-machine sync, and no CRDT, git or merge-driver story.
realtime: This is limited to one client per process. Since #3323 (merged 2026-06-16, in npm 2026.8.31) the whole graph is exposed as the MCP Resource memory://knowledge-graph. The server declares resources.subscribe, and the mutation tools emit notifications/resources/updated to a client that subscribed (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/3323; README Resources section). The transport is stdio only (StdioServerTransport in index.ts). Inference from the code: it does not watch the file, so another process's writes are never noticed. There is no cross-agent or cross-machine real-time sharing.
search_retrieval: There are four read paths. read_graph returns the entire graph with no pagination. search_nodes does a case-insensitive substring match over entity name, entityType and observations, and returns the matching entities plus every relation touching them. open_nodes fetches entities by exact name and returns the relations that touch them. The resource read returns the full graph (index.ts; README). The code itself calls searchNodes a "Very basic search function". Each call is a linear scan after re-reading and re-parsing the whole file. There is no ranking, BM25, embeddings, index or temporal filtering. On main only, the query is capped at 2048 chars because "an oversized query costs an O(graph) scan per call" (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/pull/4662). Results go back to the model as raw pretty-printed JSON text plus structuredContent.
links_sessions_to_code: It does not apply. There is no concept of a session, prompt, commit, file, repository or worktree. Records carry no timestamps or source attribution (data model in index.ts). Any link to code would only exist as free-text observations the model chose to write.
scale: No scale claims are documented. Every operation is O(file size): mutations parse the full file and rewrite it, and read_graph and the resource return the whole graph to the model's context (index.ts). The 2048-char query cap (main only) is the only bound in the code. The repo says these servers are educational, not production-ready (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/README.md). I found no published benchmarks.
privacy_security: It has no redaction, encryption, secret scanning, access control or audit log (index.ts, README). The file is plaintext JSON. Inference from the code: the temp file is created by fs.writeFile with the default mode (0666 filtered by umask) and then renamed over the target. So every save replaces the inode, and any tighter permissions a user set on memory.jsonl are lost. Recalled observations go back verbatim as tool-result text with no provenance or trust labelling. The README's example system prompt tells the model to "Always begin your chat by ... retrieve all relevant information from your knowledge graph". Anything stored once, whether a planted instruction or text quoted from an untrusted page, is therefore re-injected at the start of every later session. That makes it a persistent prompt-injection and memory-poisoning channel; this is my analysis, not a documented threat model. The repo README leaves security to deployers: "Developers should evaluate their own security requirements and implement appropriate safeguards" (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/README.md). The server itself makes no network calls, since its only imports are the MCP SDK, zod, fs, path, os and crypto (index.ts). Docker hardening is limited to running node:22-alpine with production dependencies (Dockerfile).
license: The repository is part-way through moving from MIT to Apache-2.0. New contributions are Apache-2.0, documentation is CC-BY-4.0, and MIT-licensed contributions whose authors have not given relicensing consent stay MIT (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/LICENSE). package.json says "SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE", while the memory README still says MIT (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/memory/README.md).
lesson_for_parinn: A per-process mutex is not multi-writer safety, and a mutable file with whole-file rewrites loses history and updates without telling anyone. MCP stdio starts one server process per client, so every agent pointed at a shared store is a separate OS-level writer. The reference server needed about 15 months (#1819, May 2025, to #4555, Sept 2026) to serialise even writes inside one process. It still loses updates across processes, with no error or count. That is exactly the silent failure that ParleyInn's I6 forbids. ParleyInn should do three things. (a) Make the record append-only, with per-writer hash chains, so concurrent writers add records instead of overwriting state. Then merging is a union of chains, not last-writer-wins. (b) Either give every store one owning writer (a daemon or lock holder) or take an OS-level lock. Put a real multi-process writer test in the requirement matrix, not only concurrent goroutines. (c) Create files with explicit 0600 permissions and keep them across any rename-based compaction. Second lesson: the server's own suggested prompt auto-recalls raw stored strings at the start of every chat. That is the automatic untrusted-to-model path that I2 bans. It confirms ParleyInn's choice of pull-only, enveloped recall that carries provenance.

name: mcp-knowledge-graph (shaneholloman), npm package "mcp-knowledge-graph", MCP server named "Aim-Memory-Bank" in the README examples
category: knowledge graph memory MCP server: a single-file TypeScript stdio server, forked from the official MCP reference "memory" server
status: shipped. v1.4.0 was tagged on 2026-05-29. The last commit, "chore: housekeeping" (9f6268c), landed on 2026-05-30. Before that, releases came in bursts: Dec 2024, Apr-May 2025, Aug 2025, Dec 2025 and May 2026. The repo is not archived. GitHub marks it as a fork and showed about 891 stars, 102 forks and 3 open issues when fetched. Issues #22 (cross-project contamination) and #23/#24 (MCP spec-conformance reports from a bot) have no maintainer reply. The npm page returned HTTP 403, so I could not check the published version or download counts there.
what_is_stored: Facts the agent chooses to save through tool calls, kept as a typed knowledge graph. The data model has two kinds of item. An entity has a name (the unique key), an entityType and an array of observation strings. A relation has from, to and relationType. Every write is an explicit model tool call: aim_memory_store, aim_memory_add_facts, aim_memory_link, aim_memory_forget, aim_memory_remove_facts or aim_memory_unlink. Nothing is captured automatically. There are no transcripts, prompts, tool calls, timestamps, authors, session ids or provenance. Nothing records when or by whom a fact was added, and deletes are hard deletes with no history.
where_stored:
Plain JSONL files on the local filesystem.

How the location is chosen:
1. Auto mode walks up at most 5 directories from the process cwd. It stops at the first directory holding any of .aim, .git, package.json, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml or go.mod.
2. If that directory contains a .aim/ folder, the server uses <root>/.aim/memory.jsonl, or memory-<context>.jsonl for a named database.
3. Otherwise it falls back to the global --memory-path directory. With no --memory-path at all, the base directory is the package's own dist/ folder (__dirname), which under npx is the package cache.
4. A per-call location parameter of project or global overrides auto mode.

The README presents project-local .aim/ as storage that lives in the project tree. It never says to commit it. The tool's own .gitignore ignores *.jsonl, yet the repo force-tracks two sample .aim files. For syncing across machines, the author recommends pointing --memory-path at a Dropbox folder and says he does this himself.
format_and_model:
UTF-8 JSONL with one JSON object per line.

- Line 1 is always the ownership marker {"type":"_aim","source":"mcp-knowledge-graph"}.
- The lines after it are {"type":"entity","name","entityType","observations":[...]} or {"type":"relation","from","to","relationType"}.
- Observations are stored as an array inside each entity's line.
- Files are written with no trailing newline (lines.join("\n")).

Each database is a separate file, memory.jsonl ("default"/master) or memory-<context>.jsonl. The context name must match ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$ and must not be "." or "..".

On load, every line after the marker is parsed with JSON.parse and no error handling, so one malformed line makes the whole database unreadable. Load does not remove duplicate names. Contrary to its tool description, a relation is accepted even when its endpoint entities do not exist (createRelations has no check). The data model is the upstream MCP reference memory server's, with renamed tools and multi-file support added.
multi_writer_and_merge:
None, and it is unsafe. Every mutation reads the whole file, changes it in memory and rewrites the whole file with fs.writeFile. There is no lock, no temp-file-plus-rename, no append and no version check.

I tested this against v1.4.0 (built locally, Node 22.22, with a temporary memory directory):
- 8 server processes each issued 10 concurrent aim_memory_store calls into one memory.jsonl. All 80 calls returned success, but only 5, 7 and 6 entities survived across three runs.
- One process with 20 concurrent calls kept only 1 entity in each of two runs.

So lost updates are silent, both across processes (one per agent session) and inside a single process.

The repo has no merge logic. Git merges of a committed .aim file would be line-based (my inference, not tested). Different entities on different lines may merge cleanly. Concurrent fact additions to the same entity edit the same line and conflict. After a merge, duplicate entity lines are kept as they are. The Dropbox sync the author recommends has the same last-writer-wins behaviour at file level.
realtime: None. There is no watcher, subscription, notification or sync protocol. Each tool call re-reads the file from disk, so another writer's changes appear on the next call if they survived the race. Any sharing across machines is left to external file sync, such as Dropbox per the README.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is brute force over the whole file on every call. aim_memory_search lowercases the query and does a substring match against name, entityType and each observation. It returns the matching entities and only the relations whose two ends are both among the matches. There is no ranking, no full-text index, no embeddings and no graph traversal. aim_memory_get fetches entities by exact name. aim_memory_read_all dumps the entire database. Output is JSON by default, or a "pretty" text form. aim_memory_list_stores lists the .jsonl files in the project and global directories.
links_sessions_to_code:
No. Entries carry no session id, prompt, commit SHA, file path, branch or timestamp. The only link to code is that the store is picked by project-root detection, the nearest of .git, package.json and similar markers within 5 levels, and only used if .aim/ exists in that root.

This detection is brittle, as issue #17 reports. My inference about other layouts, which I did not test: in a monorepo, a subpackage's package.json stops the walk before a root-level .aim. A git worktree has its own .git file, so each worktree needs its own .aim, which means separate, diverging stores. Issue #22 (open) reports that when no marker is found, memories silently fall back to a shared global store and mix across projects.
scale: The project makes no scale claims. Every operation loads and rewrites the full file, and search is a linear substring scan. read_all returns everything, so the cost to the model's context grows with the store. Issue #20 (closed) separately complains that the tool definitions alone use too much context. Pre-1.4.0 the code had no tests at all; v1.4.0 added only path-safety tests.
privacy_security:
Security handling is minimal:
- **No redaction, secret scanning, encryption or access control.** Files are plaintext JSONL, and stored facts go back to the model verbatim as tool-result text, with no trust label or envelope.
- **Ownership marker:** the _aim first line makes the server refuse to read or write a file that lacks it, so it does not clobber unrelated JSONL files.
- **v1.4.0 fixes (commit 61cccd2):** a path-traversal bug (CWE-22, issue #21) where a context such as "../x" could create files outside the store. The fix adds an allow-list check on context names and a path.relative check that the resolved path stays inside the store directory. The same commit stopped error messages from echoing the absolute storage path (CWE-209).
- **Open problems:** silent fallback to a shared global store leaks data across projects (issue #22, no maintainer reply). Without --memory-path, data lands in the npx package directory.
- **README advice:** auto-approve the read tools, and sync memories through Dropbox, which puts the plaintext on a third-party cloud.
- **Other:** it depends on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk pinned at 1.0.1. An automated conformance sweep reported version-negotiation failures against newer MCP spec revisions (issue #23).
lesson_for_parinn:
Two lessons, both checked against the code:

1. **Mark your own files.** The first-line _aim marker is a cheap guard worth copying in hardened form. ParleyInn can open each segment with a versioned, signed or hash-anchored header naming the store, and refuse to read or extend any file without it.
2. **Never let a store pick its own location or rewrite in place.** Whole-file rewrites lost 74 of 80 successful concurrent writes without a single error, which is exactly what I6 (no silent failures) forbids. When no project marker is found, writes silently fall back to a shared global store (issue #22).

ParleyInn should therefore:
- write append-only with fsync, one writer per segment (or a lock), and atomic rename for anything that is rewritten;
- resolve the store location explicitly, record it in the audit log and fail closed on ambiguity;
- give each worktree or session its own segment, merged by a union of hash-chained events. That avoids line-level git merges of a mutable "current state" file, which conflict whenever two sessions edit the same entity line.
license: MIT (LICENSE file and package.json)

name: Mem0 (OSS SDK + self-hosted server) / OpenMemory MCP (archived) / new OpenMemory session porter
category: long-term memory service (extracted-fact memory layer); OpenMemory MCP now archived and the OpenMemory name reused for a cross-harness session porter
status: shipped (mem0 SDK v2.2.1, released 2026-09-25; repo active, last commit 2026-10-01). OpenMemory MCP server: archived. It was sunset (issue #4923), removed from the monorepo on 2026-07-29 (PR #6530) and kept as a read-only snapshot in mem0ai/openmemory/openmemory-archive. The mem0ai/openmemory repo now holds a different beta product: a session porter between Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.
what_is_stored: Mem0 does not keep transcripts. An LLM pass turns incoming messages into short natural-language "memories" (facts). Each memory has an embedding plus a payload: text, an md5 hash used for dedup, created_at/updated_at, the identity scope (user_id / agent_id / run_id / actor_id), role and metadata. v2.0.0 (2026-04-14) made extraction ADD-only: no more UPDATE/DELETE events, memories pile up and are tied together through linked_memory_ids. spaCy-extracted entities go into a second vector collection, '{collection}_entities', which replaces the external graph stores. Those stores (Neo4j, Memgraph, Kuzu, AGE, Neptune) were removed from the OSS SDK. A SQLite history table logs each memory change (id, memory_id, old_memory, new_memory, event, created_at, updated_at, is_deleted, actor_id, role). A SQLite messages table keeps a rolling window of raw messages, 10 per session scope (id, session_scope, role, content, name, created_at); older raw turns are dropped. Memories can be flagged immutable and given an expiration_date. The archived OpenMemory MCP added Postgres/SQLite tables for users, apps, memories, categories, access_controls, archive_policies, memory_status_history and memory_access_logs. The new OpenMemory porter stores a PortableSession IR, text turns only. It drops tool_use, tool_result and thinking blocks and keeps only a count of them (droppedTurns).
where_stored: OSS SDK is local-first. The default vector store is Qdrant (VectorStoreConfig provider default 'qdrant'), embedded at path /tmp/qdrant with on_disk=False by default. History and messages go to SQLite at ~/.mem0/history.db (or $MEM0_DIR). There are adapters for about 20 other vector stores (PGVector, Milvus, Pinecone, OpenSearch, Turbopuffer, S3 Vectors, Oracle and more). The self-hosted server/ is FastAPI + PostgreSQL/pgvector, deployed with docker-compose. The hosted Mem0 Platform (app.mem0.ai, /v3 API) is a separate cloud offering. The archived OpenMemory MCP was a local Docker stack: Qdrant plus SQLite at sqlite:///./openmemory.db (or Postgres), a dashboard on localhost:3000 and the MCP API on localhost:8765. The new OpenMemory porter writes straight into each harness's native store (for example ~/.claude/projects/<encoded cwd>/) and keeps a JSON ledger at $XDG_DATA_HOME/openmemory/ledger.json. No git anywhere.
format_and_model: Vector points: embedding plus a JSON payload, in a mutable vector DB. History is a relational SQLite table, an audit log of before/after text per memory event. It is not hash-chained or tamper-evident. Retrieval scope is a tenancy tuple of user_id/agent_id/run_id/actor_id. Since v2.0.18 the session scope key percent-escapes those ids, and since v2.0.13/v2.0.16 metadata can no longer overwrite or inject the identity fields. Porter IR: zod schema PortableSession v1.0.0 {sourceHarness, sourceSessionId (idempotency key), sourcePath, cwd, title, createdAt, updatedAt, turns[{role, text, timestamp, model}], droppedTurns, sourceMetadata (gitBranch, version, tokens...)}. Ledger records are keyed by (sourceHarness, sourceSessionId, destHarness), with sourceRevision = the turn count at export time.
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no merge model. Several writers share one backing vector DB plus SQLite, or one server/Platform tenant. Contention is left to the database, and the SDK's SQLiteManager serializes access with an in-process threading.Lock. The old 2-call pipeline used an LLM to decide ADD/UPDATE/DELETE. v2 is append-only at the memory level, so concurrent writers just add facts, and conflicts or duplicates go unreconciled apart from md5-hash dedup and entity linking. Nothing like CRDTs, vector clocks or cross-machine sync exists for the OSS store. The porter serializes ledger writes only within one process (a promise-chain withLock). It deliberately keys idempotency on native session ids rather than content hashes, because sessions grow on continuation and a content hash would re-import them as duplicates.
realtime: The SDK is synchronous request/response, with an optional async_mode/AsyncMemory. Platform User Profiles are generated as async jobs. There is no push or subscription stream. OpenMemory MCP served MCP over SSE on localhost, so clients on the same machine shared a store immediately, but it had no cloud sync. Porter realtime 'autosync' between harnesses is a roadmap item ('coming soon'), not shipped.
search_retrieval: v2 search is hybrid. The score fuses semantic similarity, BM25 keyword match (native keyword_search() in 15 vector-store adapters), an entity boost and temporal boosts. Defaults: threshold 0.1, top_k 20, rerank off. Optional rerankers are Cohere, HuggingFace, SentenceTransformer cross-encoder, Zero Entropy and an LLM reranker (gpt-5-mini). Filters on the identity scope and metadata support eq/ne/gt/gte/lt/lte/in/nin. OpenMemory MCP exposed the tools add_memories, search_memory, list_memories and delete_all_memories. Recall returns paraphrased LLM-extracted facts, not exact history.
links_sessions_to_code: Mem0 core: no. run_id/agent_id give session and agent scoping, but nothing links a memory to a commit, file or repository. The new OpenMemory porter is the closest to ParleyInn. It treats cwd as authoritative and keeps gitBranch in sourceMetadata. Its worktree.ts remaps a git-worktree cwd (Conductor or hand-made `git worktree add`) back to the parent repository, first via a local `git rev-parse` and then via Conductor's SQLite db for deleted worktrees. The original path is kept in sourceMetadata.originalCwd for audit. It does not link sessions to commits.
scale: Vendor benchmark claims in the README: the April 2026 algorithm scores LoCoMo 92.5 (about 7.0K tokens, p50 0.88s) and LongMemEval 94.4 (6.8K tokens, 1.09s). BEAM scores are 64.1 at 1M tokens and 48.6 at 10M tokens. These are vendor-reported and not independently verified. The repo has about 66.5k GitHub stars. Storage scale depends on the chosen vector DB. delete_all paginates in batches of 1000 (v2.0.15). No published numbers exist for events per second or store size.
privacy_security: The OSS core is not network-free. Extraction and embedding call an external LLM by default (OpenAI; v2 default model gpt-5-mini) unless Ollama, vLLM or similar is configured. PostHog telemetry is on by default (MEM0_TELEMETRY defaults to True, events sent to us.i.posthog.com); hot-path events are sampled at 10% and opt-out is via environment variable. Redaction applies only to secrets in the telemetry config payload, not to stored memories. There is no PII or secret scrubbing of content and no at-rest encryption in the SDK; history.db and Qdrant files are plaintext. Recalled memories carry no trust labeling, so stored text returns verbatim into prompts, which is an injection channel by design. Security fixes in the changelog: FAISS pickle-deserialization RCE closed (v2.0.0), Upstash filter injection validated (v2.0.16), metadata can no longer move memories across tenant scopes (v2.0.13/v2.0.16), and the litellm auto-pip-install was removed (v2.0.19). The self-hosted server has auth on by default (JWT for the dashboard, X-API-Key for programs, revocable per-user keys). The archived OpenMemory MCP had access_controls and memory_access_logs tables. A 2025 SDK changelog entry mentions 'SOC2 and HIPAA compliance documentation' for the Platform; the claim itself was not verified. The porter is local-only and runs git through child_process.
lesson_for_parinn: Two lessons, both supporting ParleyInn's lossless, untrusted-recall stance. (1) Mem0 deliberately keeps only LLM-paraphrased facts plus a 10-message raw window. It had to move from LLM-decided UPDATE/DELETE to ADD-only accumulation in v2 because rewriting memories in place was unreliable. ParleyInn should keep the immutable raw record as the source of truth and treat any extracted facts as a rebuildable projection (I10), never the store. Recall must stay enveloped, because Mem0 shows how extracted text flows back into prompts with no trust boundary. (2) Mem0's own OpenMemory MCP was archived in 2026, and the name was reused for a Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode session porter. That suggests real demand is for portable session history across coding harnesses rather than fact memory. The porter's design choices are worth copying: idempotency keyed on the native session id, not a content hash, because sessions grow; worktree cwd remapped to the parent repository with the original kept for audit; dropped content counted, not silently lost. Its v1 IR discards tool calls and thinking, which ParleyInn should not do.
license: Apache-2.0 (mem0 SDK, server, archived OpenMemory MCP). The new mem0ai/openmemory porter CLI is MIT ('Copyright (c) 2026 Howard Gil').

name: Memori (Memori Labs, formerly GibsonAI/memori)
category: SQL-native memory layer (LLM-client wrapper that extracts facts and knowledge-graph triples into a relational DB or a hosted cloud)
status: shipped. Active: the main branch's last commit is 2026-09-17 (commit 574b1ea, seen in a shallow clone). pyproject.toml on main says 3.3.7. The newest dated CHANGELOG entry is 3.3.6 (2026-05-27). Python SDK plus a TypeScript SDK (memori-ts). Memori Cloud launched 2026-03-02 (https://memorilabs.ai/blog/launching-memori-cloud/). The README reports about 17k stars (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori). I could not check the GibsonAI/memori redirect from here: the GitHub API was not enabled for this session and a plain curl got a proxy 403.
what_is_stored: Two layers. (1) The raw conversation. Each LLM call through a wrapped client (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, xAI; also LangChain, Agno, Pydantic AI) is written to memori_conversation_message (role, type, content) under memori_conversation (with an LLM-written summary), memori_session, memori_entity (the user) and memori_process (the agent). (2) Derived "Advanced Augmentation" memories. memori_entity_fact holds the fact text, an embedding BLOB, num_times, date_last_time and a uniq dedupe key. memori_process_attribute holds process attributes. memori_subject, memori_predicate and memori_object feed memori_knowledge_graph triples, each with a frequency count. memori_entity_fact_mention links a fact to the conversation it came from. Source: https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/storage/migrations/_sqlite.py. The marketing lists the categories as attributes, events, facts, people, preferences, relationships, rules and skills (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori). Nothing about code, files, commits or diffs is stored.
where_stored: Either your own database ("BYODB") or a hosted server (Memori Cloud). BYODB supports SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, MongoDB, CockroachDB, OceanBase and TiDB (including TiDB Zero auto-provisioning), plus Neon, Supabase and RDS/Aurora (https://www.memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/support/faq, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/tree/main/memori/storage/migrations). Even in BYODB mode, Advanced Augmentation sends the selected conversation messages and conversation summary to Memori's hosted API (https://api.memorilabs.ai, route sdk/augmentation) and writes the returned facts and triples into the local DB. Entity and process ids are SHA-256 hashed before sending; message content is not (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/memory/augmentation/augmentations/memori/_augmentation.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/_network.py). Memori's architecture doc says BYODB "stores all data in your database with no external dependencies" (https://memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/concepts/architecture/). That is true for where data rests, not for where it is processed.
format_and_model: Relational, mutable rows with integer autoincrement ids plus UUIDs, created and updated timestamps, and ON DELETE CASCADE foreign keys. Schema versions live in a migrations dict per dialect, tracked in memori_schema_version. The attribution hierarchy is entity, then process, then session, then conversation, then message. Derived facts are deduplicated per entity with UNIQUE(entity_id, uniq) and reinforced by incrementing num_times and date_last_time, not by appending. Triples are UNIQUE(entity_id, subject, predicate, object). Embeddings come from a local fastembed/ONNX model in the Rust core (default all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and are stored as BLOBs (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/_config.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). There is no hash chain, signing or append-only guarantee, and rows can be updated and deleted.
multi_writer_and_merge: There is no merge model. It relies on the shared database's own transactions and on unique-key upserts. Many app processes can write to one Postgres or MySQL, and duplicate facts collapse on the uniq key with a frequency bump. Inside one process, augmentation runs as asyncio tasks capped by a semaphore (50 workers by default) and writes through a bounded DB-writer queue (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/memory/augmentation/_runtime.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/memory/augmentation/_db_writer.py). Offline or divergent replicas (SQLite on two machines) are not reconciled. There is no sync protocol, CRDT or conflict resolution; sharing means pointing every writer at the same server DB or at Memori Cloud. The project's own MCP guidance warns about memory mixing across projects unless entity and process ids are scoped per workspace (CHANGELOG 3.3.6, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
realtime: Capture is synchronous, on the LLM call path. Augmentation (fact and triple extraction) runs asynchronously in the background after the turn (https://memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/concepts/architecture/). Other writers see new facts as soon as they are committed to the shared DB or Cloud. There is no push, subscription or change-feed mechanism; readers just query again on the next recall.
search_retrieval: Hybrid dense plus lexical retrieval over the facts of one entity. Dense: cosine similarity via FAISS on the Python path, or the Rust core's similarity search, over the embedding BLOBs loaded from the DB. Lexical: BM25 computed in Python or Rust over the candidate pool, with dense/lexical weights chosen per query. A relevance threshold then applies (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/search/_faiss.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/search/_lexical.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/search/_core.py). The docs mention ranking and decay (https://memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/concepts/architecture/). Recall is automatic: facts above the threshold, plus their linked conversation summaries, are appended to the system prompt inside a <memori_context> block that begins "Only use the relevant context if it is relevant to the user's query" (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/llm/pipelines/recall_injection.py). There is also an explicit Memori.recall(query) API and agent-callable tools via MCP. Benchmark claim: 87% on LoCoMo at about 721 tokens per query (2.8% of full context), per the README and arXiv 2603.19935 (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19935). This is a vendor-reported result I did not check.
links_sessions_to_code: No link to code. Sessions are tied to an entity (user), a process (agent) and a session id, not to repositories, commits, files or diffs. The Claude Code integration is a Bash-invoked skill (SKILL.md plus a Bun TypeScript CLI) that talks to Memori Cloud. It runs recall before each response and advanced-augmentation after each turn. It derives the project id from basename($CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR) and the session id from $CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/integrations/claude-code/README.md). A workspace folder name is the only link to code.
scale: Vendor claims only: "up to 98% lower inference costs" for Memori Cloud (https://memorilabs.ai/blog/launching-memori-cloud/), and 2.8% of the full-context token footprint and a 67% reduction versus Zep on LoCoMo (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori). I found no published numbers on rows, throughput or concurrent writers. Dense search loads candidate embeddings per entity into memory for FAISS or Rust scoring, not into an in-database ANN index (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/search/_faiss.py), so recall cost grows with each entity's fact count. That is my inference from the code, not a measured result. The free API key gives 5,000 Advanced Augmentation calls per month (https://www.memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/support/faq).
privacy_security: Weak for ParleyInn's threat model. (a) The data egress is not documented. The FAQ says the open-source version works without an API key, which "only unlocks higher Advanced Augmentation quotas" (https://www.memorilabs.ai/docs/memori-byodb/support/faq). But the SDK sends conversation messages to api.memorilabs.ai even in BYODB, using a production API key hardcoded in memori/_network.py when the user supplies none (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/_network.py). (b) I found no redaction of message content and no encryption at rest beyond what the database provides. Redaction exists only for API keys in debug logs and DSNs in provisioning output (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/_logging.py, https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/memori/provisioning/_utils.py). (c) Recalled content is injected into the system prompt automatically, with no trust labeling beyond a soft instruction. Stored or extracted text therefore becomes a standing prompt-injection channel (recall_injection.py, linked above). (d) The Claude Code skill keeps MEMORI_API_KEY in .claude/settings.local.json or a .env file, and the agent may write MEMORI_ENTITY_ID there itself (integrations/claude-code/README.md). (e) SECURITY.md routes reports to GitHub private vulnerability reporting (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori/blob/main/SECURITY.md). The Cloud launch post makes no compliance claims such as SOC 2, retention or encryption (https://memorilabs.ai/blog/launching-memori-cloud/).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/MemoriLabs/Memori)
lesson_for_parinn: Keep the lossless record and the derived memory as separate things, and never let the derived layer leave the machine or reach the prompt on its own. Memori shows both failure modes. Its "bring your own database" story still ships raw turns to a vendor API for extraction, because the useful part (fact and triple extraction) is a hosted LLM service hidden behind a quota. It also pushes recalled facts into the system prompt automatically. Its plain SQL schema of entity, process, session and conversation, with a fact-to-conversation mention table, is a useful pattern for provenance. ParleyInn can copy that shape as a rebuildable projection over its hash-chained log, keyed to worktree, commit and session rather than user, but must keep three rules: extraction is local or explicitly opt-in, deduplicated and reinforced rows are never the source of truth, and recall stays pull-only and enveloped (I2, I4, I10). Also, a shared server database is not a sync protocol. Memori has no story for offline or ephemeral writers merging later, which is exactly the problem ParleyInn has to solve.

name: Memoria (MatrixOrigin / MatrixOne)
category: versioned agent memory (curated memory store with database-native git-like versioning, MCP server)
status: shipped. It is under active development. The latest tagged release is v0.5.2 (2026-09-11), and the last commits I saw are dated 2026-09-28 (#258, #260), so the project is not archived. A hosted service exists at thememoria.ai. Memoria is also the memory component of MatrixOrigin's Astra agent. I could not confirm the star count (~607) because the GitHub API was blocked from this session.
what_is_stored:
Memoria stores curated memories, not transcripts. Each memory is one short fact written through an MCP tool call such as memory_store(content, type). There are five types: semantic (project facts and decisions), profile (user preferences), procedural (workflows), working (temporary task context) and episodic (session summaries). Episodic summaries come from POST /v1/sessions/{id}/summary. That endpoint calls an LLM to produce either topic/action/outcome text or 3-5 bullet points, and it keeps source_event_ids that point back to the memory rows it summarised. POST /v1/observe takes conversation messages and stores memories extracted from them. Each user database also holds:
- an entity/graph layer (mem_entities, memory_graph_nodes/edges)
- an edit log (mem_edit_log: operation, JSON payload, reason, snapshot_before, created_by)
- retrieval feedback, access stats and tool-usage/API-call logs
- branch and snapshot registries
Full turn-by-turn session transcripts are not stored.
where_stored:
A server-side database, either Memoria Cloud or a self-hosted MatrixOne SQL database (MySQL wire protocol, port 6001, run with Docker Compose or K8s). There are two deployment modes:
- **Remote:** the local memoria CLI acts as a stdio MCP bridge and calls the hosted REST API with a Bearer token.
- **Embedded/self-hosted:** the MCP server talks SQL straight to MatrixOne.
Data layout: one shared control-plane database holds the user registry, API keys, distributed locks, async tasks and plugins. Each user gets a separate database, mem_u_<hash(user_id)>, and each group gets mem_grp_<hex>. Nothing is kept in git or in working-tree files. The only files written into the repo are steering rules (.claude/rules/*.md) and the .mcp.json config.
format_and_model:
Relational rows. In mem_memories:
- memory_id is the primary key
- user_id, author_id, subject_id, memory_type
- content is a TEXT column with an ngram FULLTEXT index
- embedding is a vecf32(dim) column; the dimension is fixed in the schema when the database is first set up, and the docs default to BAAI/bge-m3 at 1024
- session_id, source_event_ids (JSON), extra_metadata (JSON)
- is_active plus superseded_by (corrections are soft supersession, not in-place edits)
- trust_tier (default T1) and initial_confidence, with exponential confidence decay C0*exp(-age/half_life)
- observed_at, created_at and updated_at as DATETIME(6)
Versioning comes from MatrixOne's copy-on-write/MVCC storage:
- snapshots are CREATE SNAPSHOT ... FOR DATABASE
- branches are separate br_* tables created with DATA BRANCH CREATE TABLE ... FROM, zero-copy
- rollback restores the data tables from a snapshot; the snapshot/branch registries and active-branch state are deliberately left as they are
The records are mutable rows with no hash chain. The audit trail is the edit log plus snapshots, not a tamper-evident log. The data model is a set of mutable rows, not an append-only event log. Implemented in Rust (crates memoria-core, -storage, -git, -service, -api, -mcp, -cli). Apache-2.0.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writers are clients of one central database, so there is no replica merge. Branch merge is MatrixOne's `data branch merge <branch> into <main> when conflict skip`: rows are inserted by primary key and conflicting keys are skipped. Two finer-grained options exist:
- **Cherry-pick:** `data branch pick ... keys(...)` or `between snapshot A and B`, with a fail, skip or accept strategy.
- **Selective apply:** an LCA-based diff classifies rows as added, updated, removed or conflict (the same memory_id changed on both sides, with superseded_by pairs tracked), and the user chooses which branch-side conflicts to accept.
Group mode (spec dated 2026-04-12) adds a shared database per team:
- Native merge is blocked there, and main is read-only except through selective apply.
- The spec rules out field-level or three-way merge.
- Each member keeps their own active-branch pointer.
- author_id records who created a memory; correctors appear only in the edit log.
For multi-instance API servers, coordination goes through DB-based distributed locks with TTL and leader election.
realtime: Shared state is immediate for every agent pointed at the same backend, because all writes go to one central database. Writes are synchronous REST/SQL calls. I found no push, subscription or streaming of changes to other agents. Other agents see new memories on their next retrieve or search call. Async tasks such as summaries are polled through GET /v1/tasks/{id}. Real-time sharing works only while online and connected to the server; there is no offline or local-first mode.
search_retrieval: Hybrid retrieval: a vector search over the embedding column with l2_distance, combined with MatrixOne FULLTEXT `MATCH(content) AGAINST(... IN BOOLEAN MODE)` using an ngram parser. Results can be filtered by memory_types, subject_id and session scope (prefer/only). A retrieval-params tuning and feedback loop records useful/irrelevant/outdated/wrong signals. Background governance runs on cooldowns: quarantine of low-confidence memories (1h), contradiction detection (30min) and reflect/synthesis (2h). Structured queries arrived in v0.5.0. Embeddings can come from an OpenAI-compatible API (the docker-compose default), a local model, or a mock (the config.rs default). Retrieval is pull-only through MCP tools. Steering rules installed into .claude/rules tell Claude to call memory_retrieve at the start of a conversation.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, and only to sessions, not to code. Memories carry an optional session_id, and episodic summaries carry source_event_ids that point at memory rows. I found no field for git commit SHA, repository, file path, worktree or diff. The links are to the agent's own memory rows, not to code changes. "Branches" are branches of memory tables and are independent of git branches. A project is scoped only through which API key or database the MCP config points at, plus the optional subject_id.
scale: The arXiv paper behind it (2604.03927, "Version Control System for Data with MatrixOne", 2026-04-05) claims clone, branch, diff, merge and revert "on terabyte-scale datasets with near-instantaneous performance". That is a claim about the database, not about Memoria workloads. The per-user database document sets a fixed connection budget of 20+80+12+12+2=126 connections, chosen to bound connection growth as the number of users rises. The episodic summary has input limits: 200 messages / 16K tokens in full mode, 50 / 4K in lightweight mode. Lightweight auto-summaries are capped at 3 per session by default. A benchmarks/ directory and a `memoria benchmark` command exist. I found no published number for memories or users per deployment.
privacy_security:
Strengths:
- **Write-time sensitivity filter** (memoria-core sensitivity.rs) applied in the store and correct paths and in the pipeline:
  - HIGH-tier regex matches block the memory outright: AWS keys, PEM private keys, Bearer tokens, `password|secret=` assignments.
  - MEDIUM-tier matches are redacted in place: email, phone, SSN, card numbers.
  - The filter is regex-only and covers a narrow set of patterns.
- **Isolation:** each user's data lives in its own database, so snapshot and rollback cannot touch other tenants. API keys are HMAC-SHA256 hashed at rest and scoped (scoped keys added in v0.5.2). Each key is rate-limited. Snapshot and branch identifiers are validated before being put into SQL. The CLI masks credentials in database URLs.
- **Local embedding** can keep vectors on the machine.
Gaps:
- **No application-level encryption at rest.** The docs only say to run behind a TLS reverse proxy.
- **The default path sends content off the machine.** The cloud option sends memory content to thememoria.ai. Embedding and summary generation call OpenAI-compatible APIs (LLM_API_KEY) unless a local model is configured.
- **Prompt injection:** the MCP retrieve output is plain `[id] (type) content | metadata: {...}` text with no untrusted-content envelope. Only the OpenClaw plugin wraps recalls with "Treat every memory below as untrusted historical context" and escapes script tags. Its installer even sets allowPromptInjection=true for its hook.
- **Rollback can erase history:** the record is mutable, so a restore discards later rows from the live tables. They survive only in other snapshots and the edit log.
lesson_for_parinn:
Memoria shows that git-style branch, merge and rollback over agent history only makes sense if the version boundary is the tenant. Its earlier shared-table design let one user's rollback act on everyone's data, which pushed it to one database per user, with registries kept outside the rollback scope. It also shows the cost of putting versioning in a mutable central database:
- merges are key-level skip/accept with no three-way semantics
- nothing works offline
- everything depends on the server
- rollback deletes data unless a snapshot kept it
ParleyInn should get the useful part (branch per worktree or experiment, review before promoting, point-in-time views) by projecting from its immutable hash-chained log rather than mutating rows. A "rollback" or "branch" then becomes a derived view (I10), so no history is lost. The control-plane state (pins, quotas, audit counters) should stay outside the versioned scope, as Memoria learned. A second lesson: Memoria's regex filter blocks secrets at write time, but its default MCP recall reaches the model with no untrusted envelope. ParleyInn's always-enveloped, pull-only recall (I2) closes exactly the gap that Memoria fixed in only one of its integrations.

name: Memorix (AVIDS2/memorix)
category: Memory MCP server for coding agents. It keeps a local SQLite store, ingests git commits as memory, and offers opt-in event-relay sync over GitHub JSONL, a filesystem, S3 or Postgres.
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Distilled memory, not lossless transcripts. Records are 'observations' with these types: what-changed, problem-solution, decision, trade-off, gotcha, how-it-works. Each has title, narrative, facts, filesModified, concepts, sessionId, source, commitHash, relatedCommits, visibility, admissionState and other fields. Other stored kinds: reasoning memory (rationale, alternatives, risks); Git Memory (one observation per commit, source='git', with the commit hash); session rows (id, project, start/end, summary, agent); curated long-term memory that moves candidate -> qualified -> approved; knowledge-graph entities and relations; mini-skills; team coordination state (agents, tasks, messages, file locks); CodeGraph symbol and file snapshots; and opt-in media assets kept by SHA-256 (README, ARCHITECTURE.md, src/store/sqlite-db.ts). Hook capture covers prompts, tool events, edits, the session lifecycle and compaction. It passes through a significance and admission filter first. The README says a compaction checkpoint 'is lifecycle evidence, not durable memory or a transcript backup', so raw session history is not kept verbatim (README; docs/hooks-architecture.md).
where_stored: Local DB. The canonical store is SQLite at ~/.memorix/data/memorix.db (MEMORIX_DATA_DIR overrides it), in WAL mode. Derived indexes can be rebuilt: Orama in memory for small stores, a persistent SQLite FTS5 index, and an optional LanceDB vector shadow index. Global config lives in ~/.memorix/config.toml and project overrides in <git-root>/memorix.toml. Secrets come from environment variables or a .env file. Sync is opt-in and off by default. It writes immutable per-device JSONL event batches to one of four relays: (a) a private GitHub repo on branch 'memorix-sync' (the default), at events/project-<sha256(projectId)[:32]>/<deviceId>/<20-digit seq>.jsonl, written through the GitHub Contents API with one commit per batch; (b) a filesystem directory (MEMORIX_SYNC_FS_ROOT); (c) S3 objects under projects/<ns>/batches/<device>/<seq>.jsonl; or (d) a Postgres table memorix_sync_batches(namespace, device_id, sequence, payload jsonb). It never uploads memorix.db, -wal or -shm. Snapshots (snapshots/<hash>/<id>.json.zst) are in the design doc, but phase 3 is still future work (docs/MULTI-DEVICE-SYNC-RESEARCH.md; src/sync/adapters/*.ts).
format_and_model: Relational SQLite tables. Observations keep JSON arrays in TEXT columns, and integer ids are local to each replica (meta.next_id). Project identity comes from the normalized git 'origin' URL (for example 'user/repo'), or 'local/<dirname>' when there is no remote. Clones and worktrees of the same repo therefore share one project ID (src/project/detector.ts). The sync envelope is a ChangeBatch {formatVersion:3, namespace, projectId, deviceId, sequence, producedAt, entries[]}. Each entry is a ChangeEntry {syncKey, kind: upsert|tombstone, version {revision, writer, at}, contentHash = SHA-256 of the canonical row, row?}. The syncKey is 't:<projectId>:<topicKey>' for topic-keyed rows and 'u:<originDevice>:<originId>' otherwise. Additive tables hold the sync state: sync_row_state, sync_meta, sync_conflicts and sync_outbox (src/sync/types.ts, src/sync/journal.ts). Batches are capped at 750,000 bytes and pulls are paged 100 batches at a time (src/sync/engine.ts). The record is not append-only and has no hash chain. Rows are updated in place and deleted, while sync tracks tombstones. The relay holds an append-only event log per device until an explicit compaction.
multi_writer_and_merge: On one machine: SQLite WAL allows one writer per file, SQLITE_BUSY is retried with bounded backoff, and the docs recommend one local HTTP service as the database owner when several agents run (ARCHITECTURE.md, Persistence Contract). Across devices: merge is row-level last-writer-wins. Each row has a logical clock (revision, writer): a per-row Lamport counter with the device id as a deterministic tiebreak. It is a strict total order, so replaying batches in any order converges. The wall-clock 'at' is informational and never compared. Tombstones are durable, versioned states, so a stale upsert cannot bring back a newer delete. When two writes share a revision but come from different writers, the losing version is kept in sync_conflicts as evidence. A replay with the same version but different content is rejected (src/sync/merge.ts, src/sync/engine.ts). An earlier lifecycle-rank rule made the merge depend on order, so it was removed in favor of provable convergence (MULTI-DEVICE-SYNC-RESEARCH.md §4.3). Each device writes only its own files, keyed by (deviceId, sequence), and pushes are idempotent: a 409/422 from GitHub with an identical blob counts as success. A copied data directory is caught by a fingerprint check (platform|hostname|homedir) and must run 'memorix sync store device rotate' before it can publish (src/sync/store-port.ts). The scope is one user's several machines. The docs state 'No claim of conflict-free collaboration between different users.' The design and code came from contributor PR #277, merged 2026-09-07, and shipped in 1.9.0.
realtime: No real-time sync. Store sync is manual: 'memorix sync store status|push|pull|repair'. Background or interval sync is listed as future work (MULTI-DEVICE-SYNC-RESEARCH.md, phase 4). The only live sharing is a local HTTP MCP service on localhost:3211 that several agents on one host can share, with team tasks, messages and 10-minute TTL file locks (TEAM.md). Older research rated GitHub 'Not real-time, merge conflicts / Too slow for live coordination' and kept coordination state local to one HTTP server (docs/CLOUD_SYNC_AND_MULTI_AGENT_RESEARCH.md).
search_retrieval: Search is project-scoped by default, with scope="global" to search across projects. The path runs: SQLite FTS5 lexical candidates, then optional vector candidates (LanceDB HNSW+SQ, trained above 10k vectors), then optional CodeGraph or knowledge candidates, then rank fusion, then an optional rerank of the short list, then compact IDs with details on demand. Ranking is intent-aware: 'what changed' boosts Git Memory and 'why' boosts reasoning. Disclosure is progressive across search, timeline and detail. 'memorix context' builds a bounded task 'Workset' brief, and 'resume' adds the latest session summary plus at most three durable anchors and one compaction checkpoint. Embedding and LLM formation are optional, and keyword search remains the fallback (README; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md; docs/PERFORMANCE.md).
links_sessions_to_code: Partially, and indirectly. A post-commit hook ('memorix git-hook' runs 'memorix ingest commit --auto') stores each commit that passes the noise filter as an observation with source='git', commitHash, changed files and a derived narrative. The ingested record carries no sessionId, so commits are not tied to the agent session that produced them automatically (src/cli/commands/ingest-commit.ts). Agent-written observations carry a sessionId and filesModified. Reasoning records can cite commits through a manual 'relatedCommits' field, and the compact view shows 'Cited commits' (docs/GIT_MEMORY.md; src/compact/engine.ts). Nothing is written into git itself: no notes, trailers or refs. Git is only a source of facts and the basis of project identity.
scale: The project imposes no cap on durable record count. Its gate results were measured on one Windows machine with Node 22 and embeddings off. The 40,000-record gate reported write p50/p95 of 0.87/1.51 ms, SDK lexical search of 25.4 ms, cold MCP search of 428 ms and peak RSS of 408.7 MiB (2026-09-21). At 100k records, peak RSS was about 419 MB and cold HTTP MCP search about 296 ms. The docs call these local acceptance numbers, not guarantees (docs/PERFORMANCE.md). Above 10k records the store skips Orama hydration and uses FTS5. The sync doc mentions a '900 MB database' as the reason to ship a journal rather than diff the DB. GitHub relay limit: pull reads the recursive tree and fails if GitHub truncates it ('compact the sync repository first'), so the relay is bounded by tree size (src/sync/adapters/github.ts). Adoption on the GitHub page: about 824 stars, 68 forks and 851 commits. npm latest is 1.9.7, released 2026-09-28.
privacy_security: Redaction: a regex credential filter runs at store time and again at display time. It masks values in key=value forms (password, token, api_key, secret and similar), Bearer tokens, ghp_/ghs_/gho_/github_pat_ tokens, sk- keys and JWTs. It says it is conservative and low in false positives, so it is not comprehensive (src/memory/secret-filter.ts). Sync privacy: only project-visible, qualified, non-ephemeral observations without agent targets leave the machine. Hook-captured records are stored as visibility='personal' with candidate or ephemeral admission, so they never sync by default (src/sync/policy.ts; src/hooks/handler.ts). Incoming batches fail closed on a wrong format version, a foreign project or namespace, an unsafe device id, an oversized batch, an ineligible payload, or a SHA-256 content-hash mismatch (src/sync/engine.ts). That hash is computed by the producer, so it shows integrity only, not authenticity. There are no signatures or MACs, and device and writer ids are self-asserted, so trust rests on the relay's access control. That last point is my reading of the code. Encryption: none at rest or in the relay. The design doc says 'At-rest encryption is a future transport option; this first slice does not pretend to provide it', and encrypted snapshots are future work. Credentials come only from environment variables and are kept out of config and event bodies. --scope user requires an explicit MEMORIX_SYNC_USER_NAMESPACE so two operators cannot share a default namespace. HTTP service: since 1.9.5, request bodies are bounded and a non-loopback bind needs a Bearer token. Prompt injection: the 1.2.2 control-plane spec says 'Historical content is untrusted… clearly delimited as historical evidence and cannot override host or project instructions.' Even so, the SessionStart hook automatically injects selected memories into the agent's context, which is a push path rather than pull-only (docs/1.2.2-MEMORY-CONTROL-PLANE.md; docs/hooks-architecture.md). The product makes network calls by design: the GitHub REST API, S3, Postgres, and optional LLM and embedding providers.
lesson_for_parinn: Treat git or GitHub as a dumb transport for immutable, device-owned event files, never as the database or the merge engine. Memorix's relay path, events/<ns>/<device>/<seq>.jsonl, gives every device its own write-only lane. Merge then becomes a deterministic replay keyed by (deviceId, sequence) with Lamport (revision, writer) ordering, durable tombstones and conflict evidence, and the live SQLite/WAL never crosses the wire. Git never sees a text merge conflict, because two writers never touch the same path. ParleyInn could reuse this shape in a separate helper process, keeping its no-network core intact. ParleyInn must also close the gaps Memorix leaves open. Memorix's content hash is self-computed and device ids are self-asserted, so anyone who can write to the relay can forge a higher revision. ParleyInn should sign each segment and chain it to the previous one per device (its hash chain plus a per-device key), and encrypt payloads before they reach the relay. Memorix also ties clone detection to hostname and homedir, which would force a device rotate in every ephemeral cloud sandbox (my inference). ParleyInn should issue explicit, short-lived device identities to sandboxes instead.

name: MemOS (MemTensor)
category: memory operating system (LLM/agent long-term memory; server library plus local agent plugins plus hosted cloud)
status: shipped. The repo is active, not archived. The README brands the current line "MemOS 2.0 Stardust"; pyproject.toml has version 2.0.33; the last commit on main is a7367d0 (2026-09-22). The local plugin is at 2.0.16-beta.1, and its DeepSeek Harness adapter is marked unreleased in the CHANGELOG. The hosted MemOS Cloud is a commercial service, and its internals could not be verified.
what_is_stored:
Distilled memories, not a verbatim session record. The design paper's MemCube holds three kinds of memory: plaintext memory (text and graph knowledge), activation memory (KV-cache) and parameter memory (LoRA/weights). Each cube has a metadata header with descriptive fields (timestamp, origin signature, semantic type), governance fields (access control, lifespan, priority, compliance tags) and usage fields. The paper also describes "full provenance metadata, including creation source, invocation lineage, and mutation logs" (arXiv 2507.03724).

In the shipped server code, a textual memory item carries: user_id, session_id, status (activated/resolving/archived/deleted), a version number, a history list of archived versions (update_type conflict/duplicate/extract/feedback, archived_memory_id), evolve_to links, memory_type (WorkingMemory, LongTermMemory, UserMemory, ToolTrajectoryMemory, SkillMemory, PreferenceMemory, RawFileMemory and others), visibility (private/public/session), tags, confidence, an embedding, and sources (SourceMessage provenance: role, chat_time, message_id, snippet, doc_path).

The local plugin stores four layers in SQLite: sessions; episodes; L1 traces (one row per turn: user_text, agent_text, tool_calls_json, reflection, reward values, float32 embeddings); L2 policies; L3 world models; and skills. It also keeps feedback, decision_repairs and an audit_events table.
where_stored:
Server or cloud deployment: a graph database. The factory supports neo4j, neo4j-community, polardb and postgres. AGENTS.md and the docs still list NebulaGraph ("nebular"), but no Nebula backend exists in src/memos/graph_dbs at commit a7367d0, so treat Nebula support as stale or removed. A vector database (Qdrant or Milvus) sits alongside it. Users and cube ownership live in MySQL or SQLite via SQLAlchemy, and the scheduler queue runs on Redis. A MemCube can be dumped to and loaded from a directory (config.json plus memory files).

Local plugin: a single SQLite file at ~/.openclaw/memos-plugin/data/memos.db, ~/.hermes/memos-plugin/data/memos.db, or $DSH_HOME/memos-plugin/data/memos.db. Skill packages go under skills/ and rotating logs under logs/ (audit.log, llm.jsonl, events.jsonl).

MemOS Cloud: a hosted API with keys prefixed mpg-.

None of these deployments use git as storage.
format_and_model:
Python (Pydantic) models stored as graph nodes and edges with properties, plus vectors. Tree-structured textual memory is reorganised by an LLM (GraphStructureReorganizer, RelationAndReasoningDetector) that builds relation edges.

In-place versioning: when new content conflicts with or duplicates an existing node, the node's version number goes up. The old content is pushed into the node's history list, and a full copy is kept as a separate node with status=archived. The model is therefore mutable and LLM-curated, not append-only, and nothing is hash-chained.

Local plugin: relational SQLite tables with JSON columns and BLOB embeddings, plus an FTS5 index, migrated by schema_migrations. Only audit_events, and its mirror logs/audit.log, are declared append-only, and only by convention ("no UPDATE or DELETE should ever be issued").
multi_writer_and_merge:
Server: many users and agents write through one central REST service. A cube has an owner, a users list and an access check (owner or member); the paper describes a "ternary permission model" with private, shared and read-only policies. Concurrency is left to the backing database. A "merge" is semantic: an LLM decides whether new memory conflicts with, duplicates or extends existing nodes, then rewrites or archives them. There is no CRDT, no vector clock and no deterministic replay.

Local plugin: a single writer per agent home. An optional "hub" for team sharing is disabled by default (hub.enabled). A client pushes skills, plus L1 trace excerpts if the user opts in, to a LAN/VPN hub server protected by team and user tokens, and pulls peers' skills. Imported content lands in a separate hub.imported_skills table, is never merged into local L2, L3 or skills, and is lifted into retrieval only at query time. Unpublishing spreads to subscribers as tombstones on their next poll.
realtime: Ingestion is asynchronous: MemScheduler queues work, on Redis in the server deployment, and the README claims millisecond-latency writes. Memory is injected at every turn start. The local plugin's viewer streams events over HTTP plus SSE (default 127.0.0.1:18801). Hub sync between instances works by polling; there is no live replication.
search_retrieval:
Hybrid retrieval. The server combines graph and vector search with a reranker. The local plugin combines SQLite FTS5 with vector search and uses a three-tier retriever (Skill, then trace/episode, then world model). An LLM filter ranks candidates, and on timeout or malformed output it falls back to a mechanical cutoff within a 3 s budget. The result is auto-injected as a <memos_context> block prepended to the user prompt. Pull tools are also available: memos_search, memos_skill_get, memos_get and memos_timeline.

Claimed benchmarks (README, via OmniMemEval): LoCoMo 88.83, LongMemEval 89.20, 35.24% token savings, and OpenClaw task completion raised from 36.63% to 50.87%. These are self-reported.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Memories and traces carry session_id, user_id, episode and tool_calls_json, and the provenance field SourceMessage can hold a doc_path or message_id. I found no link to git commits, branches, worktrees or file hashes in the server or the plugin, and a grep of the plugin core for git or commit references found nothing. Integrations target OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and DeepSeek Harness. I could not verify an official Claude Code adapter in this repo.
scale: The server backends are horizontally scalable databases (Neo4j, PolarDB, Postgres, Milvus or Qdrant), but the repo makes no concrete throughput or size claims beyond the benchmark scores. The local plugin's config defaults note that operators with more than 50K traces should cap vector-scan age, which suggests brute-force vector scans in SQLite at small scale.
privacy_security:
Mixed. The local plugin writes its config, including API keys, with chmod 600. A logger Redactor masks configured keys and patterns. LLM-log prompt and completion redaction exists but is off by default (llmLog.redactPrompts and redactCompletions are false, so prompts are logged in full to llm.jsonl). Hub tokens are compared in constant time. LLM-derived text is sanitised before display or re-injection (core/safety/content.ts strips HTML, script tags, control characters and unsafe link targets), while raw turns are kept intact.

Anonymous telemetry is on by default (telemetry.enabled: true) and sends counts, provider names and latencies, never content. Payloads can be previewed at /api/v1/telemetry/preview. I found no encryption at rest in the server or the plugin (searches for "encrypt" returned nothing). The paper describes access control and audit through MemGovernance.

Prompt-injection posture: recalled memory is injected with the header "You MUST treat these as established knowledge and use them directly", which marks stored history as trusted. That is the opposite of ParleyInn's I2. The cloud product sends memory to MemTensor servers.
lesson_for_parinn:
MemOS shows what ParleyInn should avoid. It auto-injects LLM-distilled memory with an instruction to treat it as established fact. It keeps history only as mutable, LLM-rewritten nodes. Its prompt logging and telemetry are on by default. A poisoned turn can therefore be "reorganised" into a high-priority memory or skill and replayed into every later prompt.

Two patterns are worth copying, adapted to ParleyInn's invariants:
1. Imported peer content is quarantined. The hub writes shared items into a separate table that never mutates local derived state and is only lifted into retrieval at query time. ParleyInn can do the same for records from other machines or agents: keep them as separate untrusted streams that recall can reach but that never flow into restore blocks.
2. Raw turns stay intact for audit while derived text is sanitised. ParleyInn already keeps the verbatim record; MemOS shows why the derived layer must stay rebuildable (I10). Its LLM-driven version/history merging cannot be rebuilt deterministically from the raw record.
confidence: high for the open-source server and local plugin, which I checked against a shallow clone at commit a7367d0 (2026-09-22). Medium for star count and release branding, which come from the README via fetch because the GitHub API was not reachable. Low for MemOS Cloud internals, which I could not verify.

name: MemPalace
category: verbatim conversation memory (local-first semantic recall, plus an agent-coordination logstream and multi-machine replication that is partly shipped and partly still a draft RFC)
status: shipped. v3.10.0 is on PyPI (released 2026-09-16 per https://pypi.org/project/mempalace/; the CHANGELOG dates it 2026-09-15, https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/CHANGELOG.md). The default branch `develop` is active: I inspected commit 5ea40d3 from 2026-09-29. The project is MIT-licensed and Python-based, with an optional Rust vector engine. Not archived. The repo page showed about 59.4k stars and 7.6k forks on 2026-10-02 (WebFetch render of https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace; the API was not reachable to confirm). Multi-master memory replication (RFC 004 steps 1 and 2a) exists only on the unmerged branch `feat/replicated-palace` (last commit 2026-09-21). Only the logstream replication from step 0 is on develop.
what_is_stored:
(1) **Drawers.** Verbatim text chunks from mined sources: Claude Code / Codex JSONL transcripts from ~/.claude/projects, project files, and diaries. "It does not summarize, extract, or paraphrase" (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/README.md). Conversations are chunked one exchange pair (user turn plus AI reply) per drawer (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/convo_miner.py). Project files use roughly 800-character chunks (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/CLOSETS.md). `mempalace sweep` stores one verbatim drawer per user/assistant message (README). The hooks capture raw tool output too, such as Bash results and build errors (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/hooks/README.md). Each drawer carries metadata: wing, room, source_file, chunk_index, filed_at, authored_at plus authored_at_source, content_date plus content_date_source, last_modified and id_recipe (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/authored-at.md, CHANGELOG 3.10.0).
(2) **Closets.** Compact pointer lines of the form `topic|entities|→drawer_ids`, built for project and diary mines only, never for conversations (docs/CLOSETS.md).
(3) **Temporal knowledge graph.** Entities, triples with valid_from/valid_to, and attributes (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/schema.sql).
(4) **Hallways and tunnels.** Entity co-occurrence links held in JSON files (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/hallways.py).
(5) **Agent diaries and logstream.** Coordination events (task.request, patch.ready, ack…) and verbatim artifacts such as unified-diff patches, logs and JSON (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/rfcs/003-agent-logstream-coordination.md).
(6) **Write-ahead audit log.** A JSONL log of write operations with content and query fields redacted (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/wal.py).
where_stored:
On the local machine. The directory is ~/.mempalace for existing installs, or ~/.config/mempalace / $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mempalace for new installs since 3.10.0 (CHANGELOG 3.10.0). It holds the palace, config.json and the cached embedding model (README). Inside it:
- the vector store, ChromaDB by default (`chroma.sqlite3` plus HNSW segments, collections `mempalace_drawers` and `mempalace_closets`; docs/CLOSETS.md)
- `knowledge_graph.db` (SQLite; docs/schema.sql)
- `logstream.sqlite3` (RFC 003)
- `replica.json` (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/replica.py)
- `peers.json` (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/logsync.py)
- `wal/write_log.jsonl` (wal.py)
- `hook_state/` (hooks/README.md)

**Optional server backends:** Qdrant, Milvus or Postgres+pgvector (README). There is also a central "team server" mode in which the verbatim memory lives on a host you operate (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/website/guide/remote-server.md).

**Not stored in git.** Git is used only for gitignore-aware ingest/prune (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/sync.py) and as "final source control", which the logstream explicitly does not replace (RFC 003 Non-Goals).
format_and_model:
The model is a "method of loci" hierarchy:
- wings (people or projects)
- rooms (topics)
- halls (fact, event and other categories)
- closets (index pointers)
- drawers (verbatim chunks)
- tunnels (cross-wing links) and hallways (within-wing entity links)

Sources: README; https://mempalaceofficial.com/concepts/the-palace.html; docs/CLOSETS.md.

**Drawer ids** are truncated SHA-256 hashes (24 hex characters) of length-prefixed, delimited parts. The current recipe is v3: `(source_file, chunk_index)` for mined files, and `(wing, room, content)` for MCP-added drawers. So ids are not content-addressed, and re-mining rewrites content in place (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/ids.py; RFC 004 §6.3). A planned v4 recipe would make ids `drawer_<hash(content)>`, with organization moved into ops (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/rfcs/004-replicated-palace.md).

**Knowledge graph:** SQLite tables `entities`, `triples(subject, predicate, object, valid_from, valid_to, confidence, source_closet, source_file)` and `attributes` (docs/schema.sql).

**Logstream:** SQLite `events` (id, type, stream, room, topic, from_agent, to_agent, correlation_id, branch, base_commit, status, body, created_at, metadata_json), `artifacts` (kind, sha256, size_bytes, content) and `event_artifacts`. Limits are a 256 KiB body and 4 MiB per artifact (RFC 003).

**Branch-only op-log** (`oplog.sqlite3`, feat/replicated-palace): `ops(op_id 'op_<origin>_<counter>', origin_replica, origin_seq, hlc, author_agent, authored_at, kind, payload, subject_id)`. It is append-only in WAL mode, with a closed set of op kinds (drawer.add/revise/tombstone, org.*, kg.*, registry.*, event.append, artifact.put). There is no prev-hash chain and no per-op signature (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/feat/replicated-palace/mempalace/oplog.py).

**HLC strings** are `<unix_ms:13>-<counter:6hex>-<replica_id>`, sortable as TEXT (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/hlc.py).
multi_writer_and_merge:
**Shipped today: a single writer per palace.** One `mempalace serve` hub "holds the palace's writer lease and safely serializes concurrent writes from every client — never point two server processes at the same palace". Local stdio MCP processes auto-proxy each request to a live hub. Remote agents connect over HTTPS with a bearer token (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/website/guide/shared-brain.md). An opt-in daemon write-routing policy (direct, prefer or require) decides whether hooks and CLI writes go through the daemon (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/write-routing-policy.md). Read-only searches open in SQLite WAL reader mode and no longer contend for the lease (CHANGELOG 3.10.0). The opt-in `pgvector_shared_namespace` lets several machines read and write the same Postgres tables (CHANGELOG 3.10.0).

**Logstream (shipped, RFC 004 step 0): multi-master.**
- Each replica stamps events with `origin_replica` plus an HLC.
- Peers pull missing per-origin ranges by version vector, sending artifacts first, then fold them idempotently.
- There is no push path and no coordinator.
- The transport is HTTPS with per-peer bearer tokens kept in `peers.json` (logsync.py; https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/transport.py).
- Cursors use local arrival order (rowid), not HLC, so late remote events are not skipped (hlc.py).

**Memory replication (designed, branch only, RFC 004).** Each human has one personal palace, fully replicated to N devices. The merge rules are:
- drawer revisions form a grow-only set with the head picked by HLC
- tombstones hide content but never delete it
- organization is last-writer-wins by HLC, and every merge must be "surfaced to the user, never silent"
- KG assertions form a grow-only set, and interval close takes the minimum valid_to
- artifacts form a grow-only set keyed by sha256

Duplicate task claims across a partition resolve by earliest HLC. Indexes are never synced; each machine rebuilds them ("sync the facts, derive the senses"). The RFC rejects automerge/yjs, cr-sqlite and file-level sync of live SQLite ("corrupts"). Multi-user merge and authorization are explicit non-goals (RFC 004).
realtime:
**Memory capture is batched, not real time.** The Claude Code Stop hook mines the transcript every 15 human messages and then blocks the AI so it saves topics and decisions. The PreCompact hook mines before compaction. The SessionEnd hook backgrounds a final mine (hooks/README.md). RFC 004 sets budgets of hooks under 500 ms and startup injection under 100 ms (RFC 004 R0).

**Coordination is near real time:**
- `mempalace_event_wait` long-polls for up to 5 minutes
