- `GET /logstream/stream` serves Server-Sent Events with bearer auth, `Last-Event-ID` resume and 15 s heartbeats (RFC 003 status line)
- a `mempalace logstream watch` CLI is available (shared-brain.md)

**Cross-machine sync is pull-based anti-entropy.** The RFC requires snapshot-then-tail on every connect so no op is missed (RFC 004 §5.4). The push half of the transport is `NotImplementedError` on develop (transport.py).
search_retrieval:
Semantic vector search over drawers, with an embedding model running locally. The default is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (about 80 MB); embeddinggemma-300m (about 300 MB) is an option, and so is any OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint (README).

**Hybrid ranking** combines vector and SQLite FTS5 BM25 scores, weighted 0.6/0.4 by default and configurable. Ties break on authored_at (CHANGELOG 3.10.0; docs/authored-at.md). A closet match can boost a drawer's rank but never gates results (docs/CLOSETS.md). Searches can be scoped by wing and room metadata filters; the project retracted its "+34% palace boost" claim because that is ordinary metadata filtering (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/docs/HISTORY.md).

**Query sanitizer.** It strips system-prompt contamination from queries. Its own docstring claims recall drops to 1.0% without it and to about 70–80% at worst with it (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/query_sanitizer.py).

**Other surfaces:**
- KG queries and timeline (README)
- 45 MCP tools, or a 3-tool "light" server using Palace Query Language, e.g. `FIND "oauth" IN backend/auth LIMIT 5` (CHANGELOG 3.10.0)
- `wake-up`, a 4-layer stack. L0 identity and L1 "Essential Story" (the most recent drawers, about 600–900 tokens) are always loaded into the session. L2 and L3 load on demand (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/layers.py).

**Published benchmarks** (retrieval recall, not QA accuracy):
- LongMemEval R@5: 96.6% raw, 98.4% hybrid on a held-out set, ≥99% with an LLM rerank
- LoCoMo R@10: 88.9% hybrid
- MemBench R@5: 80.3%

Sources: README; corrections history in docs/HISTORY.md and https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/issues/875.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only loosely.
- **Project-level link.** Conversation drawers map to a wing derived from the transcript's `cwd`, and worktree paths collapse into the parent project's wing (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/mempalace/convo_scanner.py; CHANGELOG 3.10.0). Project files are mined as drawers with source_file and line metadata (docs/CLOSETS.md).
- **No commit link for drawers.** Drawers carry no commit or branch id.
- **Coordination events do carry code links.** Logstream events have optional `branch` and `base_commit` fields and verbatim patch artifacts (RFC 003). `mempalace task create` requires an immutable hex base commit id and rejects mutable branch or tag refs (CHANGELOG 3.9.0).
- **Hallways** link file paths and symbols that co-occur in drawers, including paths parsed from `git diff`, and keep each file's qualified path (CHANGELOG Unreleased).
- **No commit trailers or git notes** are written.
privacy_security:
**Network posture.** The core is local: "Nothing leaves your machine unless you opt in", and the core benchmark path needs no API key (README). That is not a ParleyInn-style no-network rule. Shipped features include:
- an HTTP MCP hub
- peer sync over HTTPS
- opt-in PyPI release checks
- remote embedding endpoints
- an external-LLM consent gate for `rooms propose` / `kg normalize`, which since this release judges IP addresses rather than hostname prefixes (README; CHANGELOG Unreleased)

**Access control:**
- The bearer token is auto-generated only for non-loopback binds. A loopback bind behind a proxy has no token unless one is set ("one trap worth calling out"), and the docs warn never to expose the logstream unauthenticated (shared-brain.md).
- Peer bearer tokens sit in `peers.json` in the palace directory, giving an N-squared token model (transport.py).
- Config and WAL directories are 0700 and files 0600; WAL entries redact content and query fields (wal.py, config.py).

**Content handling:**
- There is no secret scanning or redaction of mined content. Transcripts, including raw tool output, are stored verbatim, and the shared-brain rules only ask agents "Don't file secrets or tokens" (hooks/README.md; shared-brain.md). This comes from my grep of the miners at 5ea40d3, which found no redaction code; it is not a project statement.
- No at-rest encryption ships. RFC 004 §10 makes it mandatory for replication: Tier 0 is full-disk encryption, and Tier 1 is a SQLCipher-style per-palace data key wrapped by the OS keystore and never synced.
- No prompt-injection defense for recalled content turned up in the same grep. Recall is quoted verbatim, and L1 wake-up auto-injects stored drawers into context (layers.py; CHANGELOG 3.10.0 notes a DeepSeek-harness plugin putting wake-up in the system prompt).

**Designed trust model.** Mesh membership is "the only ACL", with no per-op signature check in Layer 2 (RFC 004 §10.1).

**Supply chain.** There are documented impostor-site and malware incidents, plus an early shell-injection fix in the hooks (docs/HISTORY.md).
scale:
**Retrieval benchmarks:**
- LongMemEval: 500 questions, reproduced in under 5 minutes on an M2 Ultra (docs/HISTORY.md)
- LoCoMo: 1,986 questions
- MemBench: 8,500 items

**Field sizes in the CHANGELOG:**
- a 126k-drawer Qdrant palace (list_drawers drops from 275 s to one scroll)
- a 160k-drawer Qdrant palace (`status` drops from 1 m 46 s to 3.4 s)
- a wing with 79,135 hallway records rebuilt down to 66,927

Wake-up costs about 600–900 tokens (layers.py). There are no published figures for the native Rust engine ("measure on your own data"; README). There is no stated multi-machine scale claim. RFC 004 targets one human with N full replicas and excludes phone-class partial replicas in v1.
license: MIT (https://github.com/MemPalace/mempalace/blob/develop/LICENSE; https://pypi.org/project/mempalace/)
lesson_for_parinn:
MemPalace's replication design gives ParleyInn a template for real-time multi-machine sharing without git merges. Each replica keeps its own append-only, strictly ordered log keyed (origin, seq). Peers exchange version vectors and pull the missing per-origin ranges: snapshot first, then tail, with the cursor based on local arrival order rather than timestamps. Ops are applied idempotently, merge is a union, and vector/FTS indexes are never synced but rebuilt locally ("sync the facts, derive the senses"). This maps one-to-one onto ParleyInn's I10, and onto one git ref, or one log, per writer. The project explicitly rejects file-level sync of live SQLite and generic CRDT engines.

ParleyInn should not copy the trust model. MemPalace authenticates only the channel (bearer token, later mesh membership) and has no per-op signature or hash chain. An op relayed through a third replica or the planned E2EE courier therefore carries no verifiable provenance, and any member can rewrite or forge another origin's history. MemPalace also stores raw tool output verbatim with no secret redaction, and auto-injects recalled drawers at wake-up.

ParleyInn should keep per-origin logs but make each one hash-chained and signed by the origin's key. That lets provenance survive any transport, including git, a relay or a courier. Redaction should happen before append, and recall should stay pull-only and enveloped.

name: Mesa (Mesa Systems, Inc.), the versioned filesystem MesaFS, plus its open-source spin-off Agent Blame
category: versioned filesystem for agents (hosted VCS/storage service built on Jujutsu)
status: beta. Early access per the homepage (https://mesa.dev). The launch post of 2026-04-28 calls it private beta (https://mesa.dev/blog/introducing-mesa-filesystem-for-agents). The pricing page lists a Free tier, a Scale tier and an Enterprise tier, so it is commercially available but still pre-GA. The core server and filesystem are proprietary. Only the SDKs (Apache-2.0) and some tools are public (https://github.com/mesa-dot-dev).
what_is_stored: Arbitrary files in "repositories", together with full version history: code, documents, spreadsheets, images, datasets, models (https://mesa.dev). The "What is Mesa?" post says the targets are agent artifacts: "Agent memories unique to users, projects, and organizations", shared team skills, generated code and data files. It also says agent traces are captured "within the version tree itself" (https://mesa.dev/blog/what-is-mesa). Mesa does not store conversation transcripts as a first-class record type. Session data is only whatever the agent writes as files, plus change metadata (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/usage-patterns/overview.md).
where_stored: On Mesa's server or cloud: a hosted multi-tenant service, or Enterprise BYOC/self-hosted in the customer's own AWS, GCP or Azure VPC (https://mesa.dev). Clients mount it with FUSE on Linux, or with an in-process "app mount" in Node.js. Reads and writes go to Mesa's API, with local caching and prefetching (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/filesystem.md). Paths matched by .mesaignore stay in ephemeral local storage and "disappear on restart" (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/mesafs/advanced/mesaignore.md). Optionally syncs with GitHub; the homepage also names GitLab and Bitbucket (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/integrations/github/sync.md, https://mesa.dev).
format_and_model:
Jujutsu (jj) data model with a custom storage backend. The docs say Mesa is "based on Jujutsu VCS which allows for full Git-compatibility" (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/versioning). The blog says "JJ is a meta-vcs ... allows us to bring our own implementation" (https://mesa.dev/blog/what-is-mesa).

- A Change is a uniquely identified unit of edits, roughly a commit, and changes form a DAG.
- A Bookmark is a mutable pointer to a change that does not advance automatically, roughly a branch; main is the default.
- There is no staging area: edits are "automatically persisted" into the current change.
- Conflicts are first-class objects stored in history (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/versioning).

Access is through the REST API (an OpenAPI spec is published), TypeScript and Python SDKs, a CLI, and a Git interface for egress. Webhooks emit events (https://docs.mesa.dev/llms.txt). The public docs do not give the on-disk format, hash algorithm or object-store layout.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The homepage claims "unlimited concurrent writers without file locks" (https://mesa.dev). Isolation is per change: two mounts on the same change see each other's edits, and you isolate them by giving each writer its own change with `mesa new` (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/filesystem.md).

Racing edits within the same second do not resolve as last-writer-wins: "MesaFS keeps both sides" and writes jj-style conflict markers. You resolve a conflict by editing the file again (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/mesafs/advanced/realtime.md). Merging bookmarks either fast-forwards or creates a merge change. Conflicts are "non-blocking" and can be resolved later or ignored (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/versioning). "a conflict is always preserved in the historical record" (https://mesa.dev/blog/what-is-mesa).

GitHub sync runs one direction per call (pull or push), is fast-forward only, skips refs that have diverged, and does not sync deletions (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/integrations/github/sync.md).
realtime: Yes. The realtime "room" is a change. Active mounts on the same change see remote edits "within seconds", so latency is seconds, not sub-second (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/mesafs/advanced/realtime.md). Two machines mounting the same bookmark get "identical views" (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/filesystem.md). Apps can subscribe to file changes with fs.subscribe(), and webhooks cover repo and sync events (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/mesafs/advanced/realtime.md). The blog says "every single part of our filesystem and version control server works in realtime" (https://mesa.dev/blog/what-is-mesa). The transport (websocket or polling) is not documented.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by path through the filesystem, plus API calls for content.get, changes.list/get, diffs.get and bookmark listing, with pagination limits of up to 500 per page (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/reference/limits.md). Files materialize sparsely and on demand; the homepage claims under 1 s to mount a 10 GB repo (https://mesa.dev). The blog claims "efficient embeddings built into our version history" with "semantic search as well as graph traversal APIs" (https://mesa.dev/blog/what-is-mesa). I could not find a search endpoint in the published API page list (https://docs.mesa.dev/llms.txt), so semantic search is unverified as a shipped feature.
links_sessions_to_code:
Partly, and only by convention. The docs recommend these patterns (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/usage-patterns/overview.md):
- "Timeline-per-session": one bookmark per session, `session/<session-id>`.
- "Checkpoint-per-prompt": a new change after each user input.
- The change message references the user prompt and the author field names the agent, which the docs call "a clear audit trail".

Mesa does not enforce or structure any of this.

The separate open-source tool Agent Blame (https://github.com/mesa-dot-dev/agentblame) attributes code lines:
- It hooks Claude Code, Cursor and OpenCode edits.
- It stores added lines with SHA-256 hashes (exact and normalized) in a local SQLite database.
- A post-commit hook matches the commit diff against those lines, with confidence 1.0 for exact and 0.95 for normalized matches.
- It writes file path, line range, provider, model and confidence into git notes. A GitHub Action handles squash and rebase.
- It needs no backend (https://mesa.dev/blog/agentblame-deep-dive).

Prompts and transcripts are not stored in the notes.
privacy_security:
Homepage claims (https://mesa.dev):
- AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.3 in transit. These are server-side; there is no client-side or end-to-end encryption.
- SOC 2 Type II.
- Access logging and fine-grained ACLs per branch or path.
- BYOC or self-hosting in the customer's VPC.

Authentication (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/concepts/authentication.md):
- Long-lived private keys never leave the customer. The SDK signs short-lived JWT access tokens locally, and Mesa stores only the public key.
- Tokens default to a 15-minute TTL, with a maximum of 4 hours and no auto-refresh.
- A token's authority is exactly the repositories declared in its mount "layout", each read-only or read-write. Tokens cannot mint other tokens or create repositories.

What is missing:
- Secret redaction or scanning is not documented. The only exclusion mechanism is .mesaignore, which keeps matching paths from ever being uploaded (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/mesafs/advanced/mesaignore.md).
- Nothing treats recalled content as untrusted or defends against prompt injection.
- The model requires network access to Mesa's service.
scale:
Homepage claims, unverified (https://mesa.dev):
- Sub-50 ms MesaFS reads and writes; p95 under 100 ms for API reads.
- Under 1 s to mount a 10 GB repo.
- Millisecond forks.
- Unlimited concurrent writers.
- Large-file deduplication.

The docs claim support for "thousands of ephemeral agents" reading and writing concurrently (https://docs.mesa.dev). Documented API limits (https://docs.mesa.dev/content/reference/limits.md):
- 128 KB inline data per file operation and 16 MB per call.
- 10,000 file operations per call.
- Diffs: 1 MB maximum blob and 3,000 files maximum.

No total repository size limit or rate limit is published. Free tier: 50 GB storage and 1,000 repos. Scale tier: $0.20/GB-month storage (https://mesa.dev).
license: Proprietary hosted service. The public SDK mirrors (github.com/mesa-dot-dev/sdks) and saguaro are Apache-2.0. The agentblame repo is public, but the org listing does not show its license; unverified (https://github.com/mesa-dot-dev).
lesson_for_parinn:
Two lessons.

1. Mesa makes concurrent writes safe by refusing last-writer-wins. Racing edits become conflict objects that keep both sides in permanent history and never block the writer. Isolation is per writer: each writer works on its own change, and the shared bookmark is only a pointer. ParleyInn's multi-agent sharing can copy the same shape with one hash-chained, append-only log per writer (agent, worktree or sandbox). Sharing and merging then means interleaving or referencing other writers' chains. It never means rewriting any of them, so divergence becomes a recorded fact instead of a sync failure. Mesa itself fails ParleyInn's I4 and I2: it is a network service with server-side-only encryption and no handling of untrusted content. It is a transport and data-model reference, not a candidate backend for the core.

2. Mesa's Agent Blame shows a backend-free way to tie sessions to code. It hashes agent-added lines at hook time into a local store, matches them against the diff at commit, and writes only small metadata (provider, model, line range, confidence) into git notes. ParleyInn could keep transcripts local and publish only content hashes or record IDs into git notes. That links sessions to code wherever the repo travels without putting untrusted transcript text into git.
confidence: medium. Everything here comes from Mesa's own homepage, docs and blog; no independent reviews were found. The web search budget was used up, so third-party discussion was not checked. The scale, SOC 2 and semantic-search claims are vendor claims I could not verify.

name: Microsoft Agent Framework
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Session state (key-value bags in AgentSession), conversation message history (chat messages with role metadata), message groups (system, user, assistant text, tool calls, summaries), file memory (optional session-scoped or shared), todo tracking state, tool approval decisions, operating mode state, and user preferences. No automatic encryption or redaction of stored content.
where_stored: In-memory by default (not persistent). Optional service-managed history via Azure OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Responses, or Microsoft Foundry. Custom storage via pluggable ChatHistoryProvider (in-memory, database, file-backed) and AgentFileStore. Messages serialized to JSON format. No built-in git integration, though custom history providers can write to any backend.
format_and_model: Chat messages as structured JSON (role, content fields), message groups with metadata (GroupKind: system, user, assistant_text, tool_call, summary). Sessions serializable via session.to_dict()/AgentSession.from_dict() (Python), JSON.Marshal/Unmarshal (Go), agent.SerializeSession/DeserializeSession (C#). Per-service-call history persistence writes after each model call in tool-calling loops.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer per session implied by service_session_id scoping. No explicit multi-writer or merge conflict resolution. Multi-tenant applications must validate service session ID ownership before resuming (documented warning: do not treat service_session_id as authorization boundary). Session reuse with different agents/configurations may cause invalid context. No version control-style merging; sessions are tied to single agent configuration.
realtime: Streaming responses supported via async generators. Middleware can intercept real-time updates at agent, function, and chat levels. Background agents support asynchronous task delegation with continuation tokens. Per-call history persistence enables handling long tool-calling loops without blocking.
search_retrieval: File memory search via file_access_grep (case-insensitive regex, 10-second budget). In-memory history retention via sliding window or truncation compaction. No full-text search on archived message history. Compaction strategies (TruncationStrategy, SlidingWindowStrategy, SummarizationStrategy, ToolResultCompactionStrategy) manage history size; summarization delegates to a separate LLM for context preservation.
links_sessions_to_code: Implicit: file memory providers store agent-managed notes; file access providers (optional) give agents read/write to working files with grep search. Background agents delegate tasks to child agents. No explicit version control or git integration for session history. Tool approval state is session-tied for governance.
privacy_security: Middleware pattern enables custom security validation (e.g., blocking sensitive queries before execution). Service session ID ownership validation required in multi-tenant. Data flows to third-party model providers per user's model choice (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.); user is responsible for reviewing third-party data handling. Responsible AI guidance recommends implementing metaprompts, content filters, safety systems. No built-in encryption at rest or in transit; user must implement credential management (avoid DefaultAzureCredential in production; use specific credentials like ManagedIdentityCredential). Tool arguments/results sent to summarizer client (if used) are untrusted and may contain sensitive data.
lesson_for_parinn: 1) Session serialization pattern (to_dict/from_dict) and clear separation of serializable state from transient context. 2) Importance of scoping service IDs per tenant/user and validating ownership on resume (ParleyInn's I2 parallel: untrusted content never reaches model without explicit envelope). 3) Compaction strategies preserve context without full history (ParleyInn could apply similar tiered strategies for long-running multi-agent sessions). 4) Middleware/context-provider pattern for cross-cutting concerns like redaction, auditing, security checks (aligns with ParleyInn's I6 audit requirement and I2 trusted-text boundary). 5) Per-call history persistence during tool loops enables recovery at finer granularity than session-end checkpoints.

name: NATS JetStream (persistence layer of nats-server)
status: shipped. The latest stable release is nats-server v2.15.0, published 17 Sep 2026. v2.15.1-RC.1 and v2.14.8-RC.1 followed on 28 Sep (https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/releases; date and year confirmed at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2/server). The repo is active, not archived, with about 20.8k stars (https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server). NATS joined the CNCF at Incubating level on 15 Mar 2018 (https://www.cncf.io/projects/nats/). In May 2025 Synadia and the CNCF settled a governance dispute: the trademarks went to the Linux Foundation, the license stays Apache-2.0, and the repos stay with the CNCF (https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2025/05/01/cncf-and-synadia-align-on-securing-the-future-of-the-nats-io-project/).
what_is_stored:
Opaque messages. Each one has a subject, optional NATS headers and a byte payload, and a stream captures it when its subject matches the stream's subject filters (e.g. `orders.>`). The server assigns each message a stream sequence number and a timestamp. Sequence numbers only ever go up, even after a purge (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams, https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/altering-stream-state).

The server also stores consumer state, meaning durable cursors and ack positions kept on disk under the consumer's name (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/reading-back).

Two abstractions are built on streams:
- **Key Value:** a bucket is a stream named `KV_<bucket>` on subjects `$KV.<bucket>.>`. Put appends a message, get reads the last message for a subject, and watch opens a consumer (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/key-value-store). History is capped at 64 revisions per key (`KeyValueMaxHistory = 64`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats.go/main/jetstream/kv.go).
- **Object Store:** stream `OBJ_<bucket>`, with chunks on `$O.<bucket>.C.<nuid>` and metadata on `$O.<bucket>.M.<name>`. The default chunk is 128 KiB and each object carries a SHA-256 digest (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats.go/main/jetstream/object.go).

There is nothing agent-specific or code-specific. Any session semantics would live in ParleyInn's subjects and payloads.
where_stored:
Server side, on the nats-server host. A stream uses either file storage (the default, under the configured `store_dir`) or memory storage (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams, https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/encryption_at_rest).

On disk, each stream has a `msgs/` directory of `.blk` block files, at most 8 MB each, plus an `obs/` directory for consumer state (constants `msgDir`, `blkSuffix`, `consumerDir`, `maxBlockSize` in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/filestore.go).

Streams can be replicated over RAFT to R=1, 3 or 5 servers; 5 is the maximum (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/surviving-node-loss; `StreamMaxReplicas = 5` in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/stream.go). Leaf-node servers at the edge can hold their own JetStream domain and sync to a hub with mirrors or sources (https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/leafnodes).

On embedding:
- Running the server inside a Go process is technically possible. `server.NewServer`, the `DontListen` option and `(*Server).InProcessConn()` exist; the doc comment on the last reads "returns an in-process connection to the server, avoiding the need to use a TCP listener" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/server.go, https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2/server).
- That same server package imports `net`, `net/http` and `_ "net/http/pprof"` directly (server.go import block). Linking it into ParleyInn's core would therefore break the I4 import-closure rule.
format_and_model:
The data model is an append-only, totally ordered log per stream. A message is a subject plus headers plus an opaque payload. Consumers are server-side views of the log: durable or ephemeral, push or pull, with explicit acks (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream, https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/reading-back).

**Retention:** Limits, Interest or WorkQueue. Limits cover MaxMsgs, MaxBytes, MaxAge and maximum message size. The discard policy is Old or New (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams).

**On-disk record:** binary, little-endian. The layout is `total_len(4) sequence(8) timestamp(8) subj_len(2) subj [hdr_len(4) hdr] msg hash(8)`; the high bit of total_len marks a record with headers (comment and code in `writeMsgRecordLocked`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/filestore.go).
- The 8-byte trailer is a HighwayHash-64 checksum.
- Its key is derived with SHA-256 from the stream name or a per-block key (`key := sha256.Sum256([]byte(cfg.Name))`). That key is not secret, so the checksum detects corruption but does not authenticate. Each record is checked on its own; records are not hash-chained.

**System headers** steer the server: Nats-Msg-Id, Nats-Expected-Stream, Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence, Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence, Nats-Expected-Last-Msg-Id, Nats-Rollup, Nats-TTL, Nats-Incr, Nats-Batch-Id/Sequence/Commit and Nats-Schedule-* (constants in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/stream.go).

**Payload size:** the default maximum is 1 MiB, and the server warns above 8 MiB (`MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE`, `MAX_PAYLOAD_MAX_SIZE` in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/const.go).
multi_writer_and_merge:
**Writes:** any number of publishers can write to a stream. Every write goes through the RAFT leader, which assigns the sequence number. It returns a PubAck only once a majority of replicas hold the message. If quorum is lost, writes block (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/surviving-node-loss). There is no merge or conflict resolution: the order is whatever the leader serialises.

**Coordination tools:**
- Optimistic concurrency through the Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence and Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence headers. The docs advise: "If the order itself matters, set `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` on each publish" (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing).
- Idempotent publish through Nats-Msg-Id, deduplicated inside a window (2 minutes in the docs example, https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/streams).
- Atomic batches through Nats-Batch-*. A batch holds up to 1,000 messages by default, a stream allows at most 50 batches in flight, and a batch idle for 10 s is dropped "with no error reply". Batches need `AllowAtomicPublish` (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing).
- KV compare-and-swap on the expected revision (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/key-value-store).

**Combining streams:**
- A **mirror** is a read-only copy of one upstream that keeps the same sequence numbers, timestamps and subjects.
- **Sources** merge several upstreams into one stream. Order is kept within each upstream, but "across upstreams there's no ordering guarantee, and the aggregate gives them fresh sequence numbers". Both work across accounts and JetStream domains (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/mirrors-and-sources).
realtime:
Yes, this is NATS's core strength.
- Consumers can start from the beginning, the latest message, a given sequence or a given time, then keep receiving live messages.
- Unacked messages are redelivered, which gives at-least-once delivery (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream).
- Replay runs either instantly or at the original pace (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/reading-back).
- KV watch delivers a snapshot of every key and then live changes (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream/key-value-store).
- The project claims "sub-millisecond latency" (https://nats.io/).
- Direct Get "is not read-after-write coherent" (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/get-direct).
- Leaf nodes connect outbound only and carry only subjects that someone on the other side is interested in. That suits egress-only sandboxes (https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/leafnodes).
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by sequence, time, subject or subject wildcard only.
- **Direct Get** fetches by sequence, the last message on a subject, or a batch or range. Any replica or mirror can answer (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/get-direct).
- **Consumers** filter by subject and set a start sequence or time (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/reading-back).
- **KV** reads the latest value or the history per key.
- There is no full-text, content or semantic search, and no index over payloads (none is described at https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/get-direct). ParleyInn would keep its own local index, such as SQLite FTS.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. JetStream has no notion of git, commits, repositories, agent sessions or prompts. Any link to code would have to be encoded by ParleyInn in subject names (e.g. `parinn.<repo>.<session>`) and payload fields. There is no first-party source to cite for this, because nothing of the kind exists in the docs reviewed.
privacy_security:
**Transport and access control:**
- TLS protects each link type independently: client, cluster, leaf node and gateway.
- Accounts give multi-tenant isolation, and per-subject publish and subscribe permissions control access.
- Authentication options are config users, tokens, NKeys, TLS certificates, decentralised operator/account JWTs (Ed25519) and auth callout (https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/security).

**Encryption at rest:**
- It is one server-wide setting. It "encrypts stream data and metadata on disk with an AEAD cipher": ChaCha20-Poly1305 by default, AES-GCM optionally.
- The key belongs to the server and should be passed in through an environment variable. Rotation uses `prev_key`. "A wrong at-rest key hides streams; it doesn't destroy them" (https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/encryption_at_rest).
- No client-side or end-to-end payload encryption is described. The server operator can read the plaintext.

**Deletion controls:** `SecureDeleteMsg` overwrites bytes. `DenyPurge` is permanent once set (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/altering-stream-state).

**Redaction:** there is no redaction or secret scrubbing of message content (none mentioned at https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/security).

**Tamper evidence:** none. The per-record checksum uses a key derived from the stream name, as described under format (filestore.go).

**Audit:** Trail of Bits, April 2025, funded through OSTIF. The scope included TLS, encryption at rest and the parser. It reported 10 findings (3 Medium, 1 Low, 6 Informational), all resolved or accepted before publication (https://ostif.org/nats-audit-complete/).

**Durability caveats:**
- File storage syncs to disk every 2 minutes by default (`defaultSyncInterval = 2 * time.Minute`; the `SyncAlways` option exists, filestore.go). The docs warn that "File storage doesn't sync every write to disk right away" (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/surviving-node-loss).
- Jepsen tested 2.12.1 (8 Dec 2025). It found that acknowledged writes can be lost to power failure under lazy fsync. Bit flips or truncation in `.blk` or snapshot files on a minority of nodes lost acknowledged writes; in one run 679,153 of 1,367,069 acked writes went missing. Replicas also diverged (https://jepsen.io/analyses/nats-2.12.1).
- Issue #7549 (single-bit errors in .blk files cause loss of acknowledged writes) was still open with a stale label when fetched on 2 Oct 2026 (https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/issues/7549).
- Whether v2.15 fixes the other Jepsen issues could not be verified.
scale:
No throughput figure is published on nats.io. The homepage claims "sub-millisecond latency", "400M+ Downloads", "1K+ Contributors" and "45+ Client Libraries" (https://nats.io/).

Hard limits found in the source and docs:
- **Replicas:** at most 5 (stream.go).
- **Block files:** 8 MB maximum (filestore.go).
- **Payload:** 1 MiB by default, with a warning above 8 MiB (const.go).
- **Disk store:** `JetStreamMaxStoreDefault` is 1 TB (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/server/jetstream.go).
- **KV history:** 64 revisions per key (kv.go).
- **Atomic batches:** 1,000 messages by default, 50 in flight per stream (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing).

v2.15.0 adds a "Desired State Metalayer" for safer moves and scaling of streams, plus persisted source indexes that avoid backward scans on restart (https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/releases).
lesson_for_parinn:
JetStream's per-subject optimistic append fits ParleyInn as an optional relay protocol run in a separate process. The transport should only move ParleyInn's own self-verifying chain, never define it.

**How the protocol would work:**
- Publish each session's events on their own subject.
- Set Nats-Msg-Id to the event hash, so a retry is idempotent.
- Set Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence to the last sequence the relay acknowledged. This gives one writer per session a strict order with no merge logic (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing).

**What the relay cannot be trusted for, and why:**
- Sources renumber merged streams (https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/mirrors-and-sources).
- The on-disk checksum is a HighwayHash with a key derived from the stream name, which gives no tamper evidence (filestore.go).
- Jepsen showed that acknowledged writes can vanish with lazy fsync or bit flips (https://jepsen.io/analyses/nats-2.12.1).

So ParleyInn must carry its own sequence number, previous-hash and signature inside the payload, verify the chain on receipt, and treat everything it pulls as untrusted (I2).

**Constraints on deployment and content:**
- The server must not be embedded. The server package imports net/http and net/http/pprof (server.go), which would fail the I4 import-closure test.
- Encryption at rest is server-held and nothing is redacted, so ParleyInn must redact and, across trust boundaries, encrypt payloads before they leave the machine.
- Leaf nodes connect outbound only, which fits egress-only cloud sandboxes (https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/leafnodes).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server, https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2/server). Direct Go dependencies include klauspost/compress, minio/highwayhash, nats-io/jwt, nkeys, nuid, nats.go, google/go-tpm and golang.org/x/crypto (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nats-io/nats-server/main/go.mod).

name: ngit / GRASP / gitworkshop.dev (Git collaboration over Nostr, NIP-34)
category: Decentralized forge (Nostr-based forge layer over ordinary git servers)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Everything a forge holds except the git objects. Nostr events carry: repository announcements (kind 30617: name, clone URLs, relays, maintainers, earliest-unique-commit), repository state, meaning the signed refs and HEAD (kind 30618), patches as git format-patch text (1617), pull requests that point at a tip commit plus clone URLs (1618), PR updates (1619), issues (1621), NIP-22 comments (1111), and open/merged/closed/draft status events (1630-1633), per NIP-34 (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md). v3 adds more event types: user GRASP server lists (10317), NIP-44-encrypted private-repo relay lists (10318), maintainer, moderator and lead role history, CI control and result events (9840-9844, plus 39842 for progress), NIP-82 software releases, OCI container tag maps (30624) and NIP-5A static-site manifests (CHANGELOG v3.0.0, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md; ci-trust.md, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/ci-trust.md). Git objects (commits, trees, blobs) sit on ordinary git servers. Release assets, site files, container blobs and CI artifacts go to Blossom blob servers (README, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli). The CI page says signed per-job log tails appear in results, with a link to the full log for each job (https://ngit.dev/ci). Nothing about agent sessions, prompts or transcripts is stored.
where_stored: Three places plus a local cache. (1) Nostr relays hold the events. The relays named in the repository's announcement are authoritative for collaboration data. v3 fetches state and collaboration events only from those repo relays; user, fallback and indexer relays are used only for discovery and profiles (CHANGELOG v3.0.0). (2) Ordinary git Smart-HTTP servers hold the objects, for example self-hosted servers, GitHub or Codeberg. These servers are interchangeable caches, not the authority (https://ngit.dev/how-it-works). The usual host is a GRASP server ("Git Relays Authorised via Signed-Nostr Proofs"), which bundles a Nostr relay with a Git Smart-HTTP server at /<npub>/<identifier>.git and creates the repository automatically from a signed announcement (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01). (3) Blossom servers hold content-addressed blobs. (4) Locally, ngit keeps an LMDB event cache, nostr-cache.lmdb, in the git common directory, plus a global cache that NGIT_CACHE_DIR can relocate. The global cache falls back to memory in sandboxed or ephemeral agent environments (README; https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/event-cache.md). gitworkshop.dev is only a browser client and owns no data: "Nothing in ngit depends on it being up" (https://ngit.dev/how-it-works). The GitHub repository looks like a mirror. The README sends contributors to gitworkshop.dev and nostr://danconwaydev.com/ngit, and the ecosystem page gives the source as https://ngit.dev/ngit.git (https://ngit.dev/ecosystem/).
format_and_model: Every record is a NIP-01 JSON event: id = sha256 of the serialized [pubkey, created_at, kind, tags, content], with a BIP-340 Schnorr secp256k1 signature, so each event is self-authenticating (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md). There are two storage classes. (a) Regular events (patches, PRs, issues, comments, statuses) are immutable and form threads through e/E/a/q tags. A patch series chains through NIP-10 reply tags, and revisions point back to the root patch (NIP-34). (b) Addressable events in the 30000-39999 range, such as the 30617 announcement and the 30618 ref state, are keyed by (kind, pubkey, d-tag). NIP-01 says "only the latest event MUST be stored by relays, older versions MAY be discarded", so ref history on relays is lossy, not append-only (NIP-01). The 30618 state event is a flat tag list of [refs/heads/x, <sha>] entries plus HEAD. Repository identity is the coordinate 30617:<pubkey>:<d>, and the earliest-unique-commit "r" tag groups forks of one project. The model separates the small, mutable, signed state (refs, on relays) from large, immutable, content-addressed data (objects, on git servers) (https://ngit.dev/how-it-works). PR git data is pushed to refs/nostr/<event-id> on GRASP servers (GRASP-01). ngit itself is Rust, MIT-licensed; v3.0.3 was released 2026-09-21 (CHANGELOG; https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/LICENSE.md).
multi_writer_and_merge: Writing is permissionless: anyone can send patches, PRs, issues or comments to any repository (NIP-34). Branch and tag authority belongs to a recursive maintainer set. Each maintainer publishes their own 30618 state event. ngit treats the "canonical latest event for the repository across maintainers" as current: latest created_at wins, and on equal timestamps the lowest event id wins, as NIP-01 specifies (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/event-created-at-ordering.md). Nostr timestamps have one-second resolution, so a same-second replacement could randomly lose to the older event. ngit works around this by grinding a nonce until the new event gets a favourable id (bounded at 100,000 attempts) or by pushing the timestamp forward, which can produce future-dated events (same doc). A GRASP server accepts a git push only when it "match[es] the latest repo state announcement on the relay, respecting the recursive maintainer set" (GRASP-01). Since v3, listing someone as maintainer is only an invitation; they gain authority once they accept. There is an explicit lead, non-pushing moderators, and role history, so past status changes stay valid after someone leaves (https://ngit.dev/maintainers). Status events count only if they come from the author or a maintainer, and the newest valid one wins (NIP-34). Content merges are plain git. `ngit pr merge` does a local no-ff merge; the push then enforces authority and publishes a 1631 merged status (CHANGELOG v3.0.0). When synchronized refs diverge, v3 prints "an actionable merge recipe" rather than auto-merging. To keep state and data consistent, push sources are frozen before planning (v3.0.2), and the state event is broadcast only after a git server accepts the data and a relay accepts the event (CHANGELOG). On the server side, GRASP keeps state, announcement and PR events in "purgatory" and does not serve them until the git data arrives; they are discarded after 30 minutes (GRASP-01).
realtime: The transport can push in real time, but the CLI does not. Nostr relays keep a REQ subscription open after EOSE and push new matching events over the websocket (NIP-01). GRASP-02 servers must sync events from the other repo relays "using both historic and live sync mechanisms", but sync git data only "no less than every 1h". That gives up to an hour of object lag between replicas, although clients can fetch objects from any listed server (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/02). The ngit CLI pulls: repository commands and git fetch or push refresh from relays, and agents are told to use --offline once the cache is warm (https://ngit.dev/agents/). CI progress events are short-lived, with NIP-40 expiry of 30 minutes or less (ci-trust.md). Whether GitWorkshop shows live updates was not checked.
search_retrieval: Retrieval uses NIP-01 tag filters on relays: #a for the repository coordinate, #r for the earliest-unique-commit or a commit id, #E for a PR root, and #c for a commit. For example, CI attaches to a PR through an #E filter and to a commit through #c (ci-trust.md; NIP-34). Discovery uses ngit-indexer, a relay that gathers repository announcements from across Nostr (https://ngit.dev/ecosystem/), together with NIP-05 or NIP-AD web addresses and NIP-65 outbox relay discovery (CHANGELOG v3.0.0). GRASP-03 servers sync a repository's whole conversation history, so clients "can ask any one of those servers for the complete collaboration history" (https://ngit.dev/roadmap). Local reads come from the LMDB cache with --offline, and `--json` gives stable machine output (https://ngit.dev/agents/). The docs I read describe no full-text or semantic search over code or discussion. Code browsing happens in web clients such as GitWorkshop, viewsource.win and Treegaze (https://ngit.dev/ecosystem/).
links_sessions_to_code: No. Nothing records agent sessions, prompts or transcripts, and nothing links them to commits. The agent-facing pieces are limited to: (1) `ngit skill install`, which drops a versioned SKILL.md and reference guides into the Codex and Claude discovery paths and adds a pointer to an existing AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md (README; https://ngit.dev/agents/); (2) a --json automation contract and llms.txt and Markdown doc endpoints (https://ngit.dev/agents/); (3) v3 moved nsec keys out of git config into the OS keychain, citing a changed threat model: "coding agents and other tools now routinely read Git config" (CHANGELOG v3.0.0). Links that do exist are commit-level: status events record the merge commit and applied commits, and issue-resolution statuses record the triggering commit and PR (NIP-34; CHANGELOG v3.0.0). The ecosystem page lists Buzz (Block), "a self-hostable workspace where people and agents collaborate" that uses NIP-34 events, and Shakespeare, an AI app builder that keeps generated code in GRASP repos (https://ngit.dev/ecosystem/). I did not verify whether either records agent sessions.
scale: No numbers on adoption, repositories, users or servers were found. The v3 launch page has none (https://ngit.dev/v3), and gitworkshop.dev/repos renders client-side, so it could not be checked. The design limits I found: patches should stay under 60 KB per event, and larger changes should use PRs that point at git data (NIP-34); GRASP-02 syncs git data at least hourly; PR refs are garbage-collected after 20 minutes if no matching event arrives; purgatory discards after 30 minutes (GRASP-01/06); GRASP-08 credentials must be within 60 seconds of server time (GRASP-08). For maturity, the ecosystem lists several GRASP implementations: ngit-grasp (reference, stable 3.0.4), Pyramid and n34-relay ("not yet feature-complete"). ngit-relay is retired, superseded by ngit-grasp (https://ngit.dev/ecosystem/; https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp). CI currently runs on one operator's own host using `act`, Linux only (https://ngit.dev/ci).
privacy_security: Public by default, and permanent in practice. Every event is signed and copied to many relays. Deletion is only a NIP-09 request ("Relays SHOULD delete..."), and clients may already hold copies (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/09.md). There is no redaction or secret-scrubbing for event content or pushed objects. Private repositories (GRASP-08, new in v3) rely on access control, not encryption. The relay requires NIP-42 auth from a whitelisted npub. Git HTTP requires a repository-scoped NIP-98 kind-27235 credential. The service-wide whitelist "controls access only; authorized users and the server can copy and republish all events and git data". Only the user's list of private relays (kind 10318) is NIP-44 encrypted (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/08). The docs say plainly: "private mode provides access control rather than end-to-end encryption" (https://ngit.dev/repositories/private). Private-repo events must go only to the repo relays, never to users' outbox, inbox or fallback relays (GRASP-08). Keys live in the OS credential store, or in a 0600 plaintext file as fallback. The stated threat is incidental disclosure through git config read by agents, not a targeted filesystem attacker (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/credential-storage.md). CI secrets are encrypted to the coordinator, optionally sealed to a maintainer's remote signer, and injected only when a confirmed maintainer authored the trigger. Third-party PRs run with empty secrets (https://ngit.dev/ci). The CI trust model is "evidence, not scores", so that "a signature is never silently presented as maintainer endorsement"; quoted events are re-fetched and re-verified rather than trusted (ci-trust.md). Optional Tor support exists for .onion relays and clone URLs (CHANGELOG v3.0.0).
license: MIT for ngit (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/LICENSE.md). The ngit.dev home page says ngit-grasp, ngit-ci, GitWorkshop and GRASP are also MIT (https://ngit.dev); I did not check each repository's license file. The bundled agent skill is CC-BY-SA-4.0 (skills/ngit/SKILL.md in the repo).
lesson_for_parinn: Split a small signed head from the bulk data, and refuse to publish or serve the head until the data it names is present. ngit puts the authoritative ref state in small signed events and treats git servers as interchangeable caches of content-addressed objects. It broadcasts state only after a git server has accepted the objects, and a GRASP server holds incoming state in "purgatory" until the git data arrives (https://ngit.dev/how-it-works; https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01). For ParleyInn this is a sound replication design with no network code in the core. Make the hash-chained record head (a signed tip hash) the only mutable pointer. Store sealed segments content-addressed on dumb, replaceable stores (a git remote, a GRASP server, an object store or a USB stick), and ship the transport as a separate remote-helper binary, the way git-remote-nostr is, so the core keeps I4. Three ngit pitfalls to avoid. (a) It orders writers by one-second wall-clock created_at plus lowest-id tie-break, which forces id grinding and future-dated events (event-created-at-ordering.md). ParleyInn should order by explicit parent hashes, which also keeps I10 free of clock reads. (b) Relays keep only the latest addressable state event (NIP-01), so the record must not live in a replaceable slot. (c) "Private" in GRASP-08 means access control, not encryption, and deletion is only a request (GRASP-08; NIP-09). Session transcripts must therefore be encrypted and redacted client-side before any such transport. Recalled events stay untrusted even when the signature is valid, in line with ngit's own CI rule that a signature is evidence, not endorsement (ci-trust.md).

name: Nimbalyst (successor to Crystal)
category: Visual agent workspace with worktrees. It is an Electron desktop app for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Copilot CLI, with iOS and Android companion apps, a Cloudflare sync relay and an optional Cloudflare sandbox runner.
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
Repo paths below are relative to https://github.com/Nimbalyst/nimbalyst/blob/main/. I read a shallow clone of main at commit 9f13b27, dated 2026-09-30, which is release v0.79.1 (CHANGELOG.md).

(1) Raw agent transcripts. Every provider SDK chunk (user prompts, assistant output, tool_use, tool_result, subagent spawns) goes into the table ai_agent_messages. Each row holds session_id, created_at, source, direction (input/output), content, JSON metadata, a hidden flag, provider_message_id, and searchable_text plus message_kind, which are extracted when the row is written. The docs call this table 'the sole persisted source of truth'. Canonical events are derived in memory from it, kept for at most 16 sessions (MRU), and never written to disk (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).

The log is not a faithful copy of what the provider sent:
- Claude Code chunks are slimmed on write. The tool_use_result sidecar and the ~12 KB thinking 'signature' are dropped, about 60% of the bytes. Transient chunk types (hook_started, tool_progress, rate_limit_event and others) are not stored (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- An optional retention pass tombstones aged tool output in place. It never touches user prompts, assistant text, tool_use calls or compact_boundary rows (packages/electron/src/main/database/toolOutputRetentionPass.ts; CHANGELOG.md, 'an option to discard old tool output').

(2) Session metadata in ai_sessions: provider, model, title, session_type (session, workstream or blitz), parent_session_id, worktree_id, provider_session_id, draft_input (docs/DATABASE_SCHEMA.md).

(3) Links from sessions to code:
- session_files: edited/referenced/read.
- ai_tool_call_file_edits: maps tool calls to file edits.
- session_commits: maps a commit SHA to a session.
- pull_requests: per worktree, migration 0009.
- worktrees: id, path, branch, base_branch.
All are in packages/electron/src/main/database/sqlite/schemas/.

(4) Document edit history as compressed BYTEA snapshots in document_history (docs/DATABASE_SCHEMA.md).

(5) Plain content files in the user's repo: markdown docs, plans and tracker items, slash-command workflows, and Crew persona files under nimbalyst-local/ (README.md, 'Plain files on disk… everything in your git repo'; docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.md).

Discovery note resolved: transcripts are NOT in the git repo. They live in the local app database.
where_stored:
Mainly a local database. The docs give two different locations:
- Repo docs: ~/Library/Application Support/@nimbalyst/electron/pglite-db/ on macOS (packages/electron/DATABASE.md).
- User docs: ~/Library/Application Support/Nimbalyst on macOS, %APPDATA%\Nimbalyst on Windows, ~/.config/Nimbalyst on Linux. They say new installs use SQLite and older installs stay on PGLite until migrated, with backups every 12 h and on quit, two rolling copies kept (https://docs.nimbalyst.com/open-safe-private-secure/session-and-window-state-storage.md).

The code runs on two backends: PGLite (Postgres in WASM, the original) and better-sqlite3 (the migration target), chosen per workspace (packages/electron/DATABASE.md).

Second, an optional cloud relay and cache: Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects and SQLite at wss://sync.nimbalyst.com. It has per-user index rooms and per-session rooms, and it is described as 'a cache; these limits do not delete desktop history'. Retention there is 30 days for the index and 14 days for transcripts (packages/collab-protocol/src/sessionRetention.ts; design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md). The server code is in a separate repo, nimbalyst-collab (LICENSING.md; docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md). https://github.com/Nimbalyst/nimbalyst-collab returns 404, so the server is not publicly auditable.

Third, the working tree of the git repo, for content files only (README.md).

Shared session links are uploaded to Cloudflare R2 (design/Collaboration/session-share-cloudflare-hosting.md). Nimbalyst does not keep a copy of Claude Code's resume history. Resume relies on the SDK's own history files (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).
format_and_model:
Local storage:
- Relational tables. The transcript is append-by-convention rows of provider-native JSON (TEXT content plus a JSON metadata column), one row per SDK chunk, ordered by an autoincrement id within session_id (schemas/0001_initial.sql).
- Per-provider pure parsers (ClaudeCodeRawParser, CodexRawParser, CopilotRawParser, OpenCodeRawParser and others) turn raw rows into canonical event descriptors in memory. A projector turns those into a view model (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- Before June 2026, canonical events were persisted in ai_transcript_events. A forward-only migration (0005) dropped that table, with no rollback path (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- Sessions form a two-layer hierarchy (workstream, then session). The rule 'worktree IS the workstream' applies: a worktree can hold many sessions, and a session belongs to at most one worktree, through ai_sessions.worktree_id (docs/DATABASE_SCHEMA.md; docs/WORKTREES.md).
- The session_commits primary key is (commit_sha, session_id), with attribution 'exact' in v1 (schemas/0031_session_commits.sql).

Wire format:
- Personal sync uses the CollabV3 append-only message protocol. Each EncryptedMessage is {id (ULID), sequence (monotonic per session), createdAt, source, direction, encryptedContent (AES-256-GCM), iv, metadata: {}} (packages/collab-protocol/src/personal.ts).
- Team documents and trackers are Yjs Y.Docs relayed by Durable Objects (docs/COLLABORATION_GUIDE.md).
- Team conversations are an append-only event log in a ConversationRoom (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md).

No hash chain or Merkle structure turned up in client code. A grep for prev_hash, hash chain and merkle in packages/{electron,runtime,collab-protocol}/src found nothing.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Code: each session is isolated in an opt-in git worktree. Worktrees are created at ../{project}_worktrees/ on a branch named worktree/<adjective-noun>, through simple-git (docs/WORKTREES.md; https://docs.nimbalyst.com/developer-features/worktrees.md). Merging is a normal git merge or rebase that the user starts from the panel, and rebase auto-stashes uncommitted changes (https://docs.nimbalyst.com/developer-features/worktrees.md). GitRefWatcher watches .git/refs and .git/index, so commits made by any tool are detected (docs/GIT_INTEGRATION.md).

Transcripts:
- In practice each session has one executing host: desktop, the headless Node runner, or a Cloudflare sandbox. Other devices mirror the session. Remote sandbox mirrors 'never create executable local session rows' (packages/cloudflare-sandbox/README.md).
- The phone does not run agents. It writes encrypted queuedPrompts into the session index, and the desktop picks them up and executes them (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md; https://docs.nimbalyst.com/mobile/mobile-app.md).
- The server orders messages with a per-session sequence. Duplicates are removed with a stable sync ID, a SHA-256 over session, timestamp, direction and the first 100 characters of content (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- On startup, delta sync compares message counts per session (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- Optional import of external Claude Code and Codex sessions (OFF by default) tails JSONL under ~/.claude/projects with per-file cursors. It deduplicates on provider message IDs, and a stale cursor fails closed (packages/electron/src/main/services/externalSessions/ExternalSessionPersistence.ts; docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.md).

Team content: merged by Yjs CRDT, with deterministic seeding so that two first-openers do not duplicate elements (docs/COLLABORATION_GUIDE.md).

Local database: the SQLite backend serializes writes through a WriteCoordinator, and PGLite uses a single worker with a PID lock (packages/electron/DATABASE.md).
realtime:
Yes.
- Desktop: after each raw write, processNewMessages parses the rows past an in-memory watermark and sends transcript:event over IPC to the UI (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- Across devices: WebSockets to Durable Object rooms. The index room stays connected, and session rooms open on demand. A client may hold at most 10 session sockets, and a socket idle for 5 minutes can be evicted. When all 10 are busy, a new socket is refused and must be surfaced to the caller (packages/runtime/src/sync/sessionConnectionAdmission.ts). Other devices receive message_broadcast, metadata_broadcast and index_broadcast. Device presence is re-announced every 30 s (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md).
- Team docs target cross-instance edits within about 200 ms. Awareness (cursors) is throttled to about 2 Hz, and snapshot compaction runs after about 200 updates (docs/COLLABORATION_GUIDE.md).
- Push notifications go through APNs (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md; https://docs.nimbalyst.com/mobile/mobile-app.md).
- Sync is optional. On failure the app reverts to local-only and queues operations to retry (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md).
search_retrieval:
Local full-text search over the raw table:
- SQLite: FTS5 external-content index ai_agent_messages_fts on searchable_text. The initial schema uses the porter unicode61 tokenizer.
- PGLite: partial GIN index on to_tsvector('english', searchable_text).
Sources: docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md; schemas/0001_initial.sql.

Cross-session queries such as 'list all user prompts' filter on message_kind='user' (docs/TRANSCRIPT_ARCHITECTURE.md).

UI: Cmd+L session quick open, where Shift+Tab searches message contents (docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.md).

Agent-side recall: a session-context MCP server offers get_session_summary, get_workstream_overview, list_recent_sessions and get_workstream_edited_files (packages/electron/src/main/mcp/sessionContextServer.ts). A grep of that file found no untrusted-content marking or enveloping of recalled text.

The optional Nimbalyst Memory extension adds hybrid semantic plus keyword search. Indexing AI sessions there is off by default (docs/FEATURE_INVENTORY.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, but only in the local database. Nothing is written into git.
- session_files records files a session edited, referenced or read (docs/DATABASE_SCHEMA.md).
- ai_tool_call_file_edits ties a message or tool call to a file edit, with match_score and match_reason (schemas/0001_initial.sql).
- session_commits records which session produced a commit. It is filled from commit-proposal widget responses ('"action":"committed"'), plus a resumable backfill over the '~2M-row' message log. It is keyed on commit_sha alone, because sessions in worktrees commit under the worktree path while users browse the log from the main checkout. It feeds the Session column of the Git Log panel (packages/electron/src/main/services/SessionCommitService.ts; schemas/0031_session_commits.sql).
- Pull requests are linked per worktree (schemas/0009_worktree_pr_linkage.sql).

A grep found no commit trailers, git notes or custom refs, so the provenance does not travel with the repo to other machines.
scale:
Project and repo:
- About 1.8k GitHub stars, 281 forks and 6,208 commits on main, as seen on https://github.com/Nimbalyst/nimbalyst at fetch time.
- Very active: v0.79.0 shipped 2026-09-29 and v0.79.1 on 2026-09-30 (CHANGELOG.md).
- Crystal, the predecessor, has 3.1k stars and was deprecated in February 2026 in favour of Nimbalyst. Its repo is deprecated but not archived (https://github.com/stravu/crystal).

Operational figures, all self-reported in the docs and not independently verified:
- ai_agent_messages 'can be >1M rows'. A startup backfill full-scanned ~1.3M rows and blocked the single SQLite worker for 30–39 s (packages/electron/DATABASE.md).
- '~2M-row' message log (schemas/0031_session_commits.sql).
- A '5.6 GB database on one measured install', of which pruning tool output reclaimed about 1 GB (CHANGELOG.md).
- About 90% of SessionRoom bytes were tool_result payloads (packages/runtime/src/sync/syncContentTruncator.ts).
privacy_security:
Personal and mobile sync (end-to-end encrypted):
- Messages, titles, project IDs and queued prompts are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, one random 96-bit IV per message.
- The key comes from PBKDF2-SHA256 with 100k iterations over a 32-byte random seed, salted with 'nimbalyst:{personalMemberId}'.
- The seed is stored through Electron safeStorage and the OS keychain. It moves to the phone only by QR code.
- The server still sees timestamps, source, direction, sequence, provider and model (design/MobileSync/SYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md; packages/runtime/src/sync/encryptionKey.ts; packages/collab-protocol/src/personal.ts; https://docs.nimbalyst.com/mobile/mobile-app.md).
- Push alert titles and Live Activity state leave in plaintext, because APNs has to render them (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md).
- Changing a single character of the salt silently orphans all existing data, so test vectors pin it (encryptionKey.ts).

Team content (not zero-knowledge):
- A per-team AES-256-GCM DEK is held by the server and wrapped with HKDF(baseKEK). Content is plaintext on the wire inside TLS. The client-side E2E team lane was deleted (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md; https://docs.nimbalyst.com/team-collaboration/overview.md).
- Known gap: an open WebSocket never re-authenticates, so a member who is downgraded keeps write access on sockets already open (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md, gap G1).

Shared session links:
- The exported HTML is encrypted, the key sits in the URL fragment, and the default TTL is 7 days (packages/electron/src/main/ipc/ShareHandlers.ts). The older design doc said shares were plaintext, which the code now supersedes (design/Collaboration/session-share-cloudflare-hosting.md).

Redaction:
- I found no secret redaction of transcript content.
- Provider API keys are scrubbed from the environment of spawned agent processes (packages/runtime/src/ai/server/providerApiKeyScrub usages).
- Bug reports get a scrub plus an AI redaction pass. Analytics (PostHog) exclude file and chat content (https://docs.nimbalyst.com/open-safe-private-secure/privacy.md).
- I found no at-rest encryption of the local transcript database (unverified). The local collab document replica is AES-256-GCM encrypted (docs/IDENTITY_AUTH_AND_ROOMS.md).

Prompt injection: the docs only say that permission modes guard against it (https://docs.nimbalyst.com/open-safe-private-secure/permissions-and-safety.md).

The app talks to the network heavily (sync, Stytch auth, R2, Cloudflare sandbox).
license: MIT for the repo (LICENSE; LICENSING.md). The collab sync server behind wss://sync.nimbalyst.com is a separate project. LICENSING.md states no license for it, and its repo is not public (404).
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy the shape of Nimbalyst's transport but not its losses.

What to copy is the PersonalSessionRoom shape for ParleyInn's real-time sharing:
- one append-only stream per session, end-to-end encrypted
- the relay sees only (ULID, seq, ts, source, direction, ciphertext)
- duplicates removed by a content-derived ID
- the relay explicitly treated as a cache, never the record

What not to copy is that the record is lossy wherever it lives:
- Tool output is cut to 4 KiB before upload.
- Relay transcripts expire after 14 days.
- The local 'append-only' log is changed in place: chunks are slimmed on write, and maintenance passes UPDATE and DELETE rows.
- The session-to-commit ledger exists only in one machine's database.

For an ephemeral sandbox, which 'does not restore prior execution state', this probably leaves the truncated relay copy as the only survivor once the container dies. That is my inference, not something the docs state.

So ParleyInn should:
- Ship full events from sandboxes, or record every elision, retention tombstone or slimming step as a new hash-chained event, never as an UPDATE (I6, I10).
- Carry the session-to-commit link with the record, keyed on commit SHA alone. Nimbalyst found that the workspace path breaks across worktrees.
- Pin key-derivation parameters with test vectors, as Nimbalyst does.

name: noa / libnoa (celestia-island)
category: agent-native VCS alongside git (Rust; CLI `noa`, server `noa-server`, library crate `libnoa`)
status: beta. It is active but early and pre-1.0. The latest crates.io release is 0.4.0 (2026-07-15), after 0.1.0 (2026-06-05), 0.1.1, 0.3.0 (2026-06-08) and 0.3.2 (2026-07-08); the crate has had about 951 downloads (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/libnoa). The master Cargo.toml already reads 0.4.1, which is not yet published. The last commit is dac001c on 2026-09-26, and the repository is not archived. The discovery note named v0.3.0 as current, but that is superseded. I could not check the star count, because the GitHub API was blocked for this session.
what_is_stored: Noa stores no conversations or prompts. Each agent workspace has its own append-only log of file operations. A log entry holds seq, op, path, blob_id, from_path, conflict ours/theirs ids, snapshot_id, a timestamp in microseconds and an optional message. The ops are write, delete, rename, snapshot, merge and resolve (src/log/mod.rs). Beside the logs it keeps SHA-256 content-addressed blobs and trees, plus snapshots. A snapshot records id, tree_hash, parents, workspace, author, timestamp and message. It also keeps refs, workspace records (head, seq, base) and a PR store on the server. The PR store holds model, token and cost metadata (src/snapshot/mod.rs, docs/en/designs/pr-platform.md). Agent session data reaches noa only as a summary of model ids and token counts, which it reads from entelecheia chat logs (src/coauthor/session.rs).
where_stored: Noa data lives in its own directory inside the repository, not in git objects. If .git exists, it runs in a mode it calls 'parasitic' and uses <root>/.git/noa. Otherwise it uses <root>/.noa, which it adds to .gitignore automatically (src/repo.rs resolve_noa_dir, manage_gitignore). The directory holds an embedded redb database (noa.redb), an agent-logs/ folder with one JSONL file per workspace (mode 0600), and HEAD/ORIG_HEAD pointer files. Optionally, snapshot trees and blobs can be pushed to S3/MinIO, IPFS (with pinning), SFTP or FTP, or to a self-hosted noa-server over an HTTP API (src/object/*, src/cli/storage_cmd.rs, src/server/mod.rs). A .gitattributes line `noa-remote=<url>` records where this 'agent iteration data' is hosted (src/repo.rs manage_gitattributes).
format_and_model: Logs are one serde_json LogEntry per line, appended and fsynced. The log lines are not hash-chained. Readers skip corrupted lines with only a tracing warning (src/log/format.rs). compact_to(seq) rewrites the file without older entries, so in practice the log is append-only with truncation (src/log/file_impl.rs). Blobs and trees are SHA-256 content-addressed. Records in redb are serialized with rmp-serde (MessagePack). A snapshot id is 'noa_' plus the SHA-256 of the plain concatenation of tree_hash, parent ids, workspace, author and message, with an optional timestamp variant. The fields have no length prefixes or separators, so the hash input is ambiguous. Parent links form a git-like DAG of snapshots. I found no command that verifies the chain or checks integrity (src/snapshot/mod.rs). Exporting to git writes only the HEAD snapshot's tree into the working tree. It then runs `git add -A` and commits one '[noa export] snapshot <id> from workspace <ws>' commit with the system git CLI (src/git/export.rs). Fine-grained agent history never goes into git.
multi_writer_and_merge: Each agent writes to its own named workspace and log, which isolates writers. Merging is a recursive three-way merge at file level: it compares blob ids against a base tree, with no line-level merge. A conflict must be resolved explicitly with Ours or Theirs (src/merge/mod.rs, src/merge/conflict.rs). On a self-hosted noa-server, a PR merge runs the same machinery on the server. It writes the merged tree as a new snapshot or returns MergeConflict with the conflicting paths (docs/en/designs/pr-platform.md). There is a hard limit on concurrency: redb takes an exclusive file lock, so concurrent CLI processes cannot share one repository. Agents must share one long-lived process or use the noa-server HTTP API (examples/multi-agent/run.py docstring). Git push and pull shell out to `git push` and `git pull`, and pull re-imports git into noa (src/cli/pushpull.rs). PRs can target GitHub (REST) or the self-hosted backend; GitLab and Gitea are planned for v2.
realtime: Only local, and limited. A Unix-socket JSON-RPC 2.0 SyncServer accepts up to 32 connections and 16 MiB messages, with a token handshake, a 1-hour session TTL and a socket at mode 0600 (src/sync/server.rs). It exchanges batches of SyncEvent (log entries) in push or pull direction for one workspace (src/sync/events.rs, src/sync/mod.rs). The handshake also proposes a branch to an agent host, for example entelecheia/agent-session-{uuid} (src/sync/handshake.rs). There is no cross-machine live replication. Remote exchange is request/response over HTTP or object storage, and the git path is batch push/pull. A WebSocket 'Sync.PrUpdate' notification is only planned (pr-platform.md section 10).
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by id and sequence number only. You can read a log since seq N (read_since), list snapshots, workspaces and refs, diff snapshots, and fetch a blob or tree by hash over /api/v1 (src/log/mod.rs, src/snapshot/diff.rs, src/server/mod.rs). It has a TUI with virtual scrolling and a web UI that shows snapshots, workspaces and PRs. I found no full-text, semantic or BM25 search.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, through commit and PR trailers rather than stored transcripts. The coauthor module scans the newest entelecheia chat logs (~/.config/entelecheia/chat_logs/chat#*.log, or ENTELECHEIA_CHAT_LOG_DIR). It sums tokens per model and detects 'YOLO' mode. It then writes trailers like 'Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.8 (↑ 12k ↓ 3k) <anthropic.com@celestia.world>' (src/coauthor/mod.rs, src/coauthor/session.rs, src/coauthor/provider.rs). PR records carry model, input_tokens, output_tokens and cost_usd. On GitHub these go into the PR body as a fenced block (pr-platform.md sections 4 and 6.1). A snapshot's author field is usually the agent id. Prompts and tool calls are never stored or linked. Support for Claude Code covers naming the provider only; there is no hook or transcript ingestion.
scale: The project makes no published scale claims or benchmarks. The docs hold only a README, a translated intro and one PR-platform design doc (docs/en). Practical limits visible in the code: one exclusive redb lock per repository; a 50 MiB HTTP body limit and a per-IP rate limiter on noa-server; 16 MiB sync messages; max_seq recovery that reads the last 64 KiB of the log (src/server/mod.rs, src/sync/server.rs, src/log/file_impl.rs). The codebase is about 16.9k lines of Rust under src/.
privacy_security: Implemented controls: logs at mode 0600 and the sync socket at 0600; constant-time token comparison; a random sync token unless NOA_SYNC_TOKEN is set. noa-server rejects all API requests when NOA_API_TOKEN is unset and has a per-IP rate limiter. Path-traversal checks run on sync and export. Git URLs are validated: ext:: is blocked, as are a leading '-' and control characters. Only the env-var name of the PR token is persisted (src/sync/*, src/server/mod.rs, src/git/export.rs, pr-platform.md section 11). Gaps: I found no encryption at rest or in transit beyond TLS to remote stores, and no redaction or secret scanning. A grep for encrypt, redact and secret finds only credential fields. S3/MinIO access_key and secret_key are stored in the repository config (src/config.rs). NOA_GIT_USER and NOA_GIT_PASS are spliced into the https URL passed as an argv to `git push` and `git pull`, which exposes them in the process list (src/cli/pushpull.rs inject_git_creds). Export runs `git add -A` and warns that uncommitted working-tree changes will be swept into the commit (src/git/export.rs). Log corruption is skipped silently. The crate ships HTTP clients for S3, IPFS, FTP, SFTP and GitHub, so it is network-heavy by design. Licence: SySL-1.0, a custom 'Synthetic Source License' for AI-generated code that requires disclosing AI generation and the models used. It is not OSI-approved (LICENSE, https://sysl.celestia.world).
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy noa's split, not its integrity model. It keeps high-volume agent iteration data out of git entirely, in .git/noa/ (which survives clones and needs no .gitignore entry) or an ignored .noa/. Git sees only curated, squashed results, and a .gitattributes 'noa-remote=' pointer says where the rich history is hosted. That is a cheap pattern for ParleyInn's 'git is transport for code, not the session record' question. Noa also shows the pitfalls ParleyInn's invariants already rule out, and each could become a test case:
- Its JSONL log is not hash-chained, can be compacted (truncated), and skips corrupt lines silently (against I6).
- Its snapshot ids hash fields concatenated without length prefixes, so the inputs are ambiguous. ParleyInn's chain hash should use length-prefixed or canonical framing.
- Its exclusive redb lock blocks concurrent writers in different processes. ParleyInn's many-agents-per-worktree case needs a WAL or a per-writer segment design, not one locked embedded database.
