name: Nostr NIP-34 ("git stuff") with ngit / git-remote-nostr and GRASP servers
status: shipped. Spec: NIP-34 is merged but still marked `draft` `optional`. It was first merged 2024-03-05; the last change on master was 2026-07-26 (#2423), and the copy checked was at master 0046368, dated 2026-09-27 (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md, https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/commits/master/34.md). The multi-maintainer roles that ngit v3 implements (M/m/o tags, invitation plus acceptance) are still an open upstream PR, #2324, opened 2026-04-25 (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2324, https://ngit.dev/protocol/nip-34/specification). Implementation: ngit v3.0.3 was released 2026-09-21, and v3.0.0 on 2026-09-08 alongside ngit-grasp v3, GitWorkshop v4 and ngit-ci 0.1 (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md, https://ngit.dev/v3). The project is active and not archived. The README points PRs and issues to nostr://danconwaydev.com/ngit and gitworkshop.dev, so the GitHub repository seems to be a mirror (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli).
what_is_stored:
Forge metadata only. The git objects themselves are not stored in Nostr events.
NIP-34 defines these signed event kinds (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md):
- 30617, repository announcement: name, description, web, clone, relays, an `r` tag with the earliest-unique-commit marker "euc", maintainers, a `u` tag for a subordinate fork, and `t` labels.
- 30618, repository state: one `refs/heads|tags/<name>` = `<commit-id>` tag per ref, plus HEAD.
- 1617, patch: the content is `git format-patch` output. Optional tags `commit`, `parent-commit`, `commit-pgp-sig` and `committer` let the applied commit keep the same id.
- 1618, pull request: markdown body, a `c` tag for the tip commit, at least one `clone` URL, and optional `merge-base` and `branch-name`.
- 1619, PR update: a new tip.
- 1621, issue: markdown with subject and labels.
- Replies use NIP-22 comments (kind 1111).
- 1630–1633, status: Open, Applied/Merged/Resolved, Closed, Draft. A merge status can carry `merge-commit` or `applied-as-commits`.
- 10317, the user's list of GRASP servers.
ngit v3 also publishes:
- encrypted private-relay lists (kind 10318)
- CI requests and results
- NIP-82 software releases
- OCI tag maps (kind 30624)
- nsite manifests
Sources: https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli.
In the project's own words, nostr carries "repository identification and discovery", "state (ie. git refs)", and "proposals (PRs), issues and related discussion", while "a git server is still required for data storage" (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli).
where_stored:
Next to git, not inside it.
- Signed events live on Nostr relays: independently run WebSocket servers. Each repository names its relays in the `relays` tag (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).
- Git objects live on ordinary git servers such as GitHub, Codeberg, self-hosted servers, or GRASP servers. The docs say the git server "is no longer authoritative, it's a cache" (https://ngit.dev/how-it-works).
- A GRASP server ("Git Relays Authorised via Signed-Nostr Proofs") bundles a NIP-01 relay at / with unauthenticated Git Smart HTTP at /<npub>/<identifier>.git. It accepts pushes only when they match the latest signed 30618 state from the recursive maintainer set. PR tips are pushed to refs/nostr/<event-id> (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp, https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01).
- Locally, ngit keeps repository events in `.git/nostr-cache.lmdb` (an LMDB store; earlier versions used SQLite) plus a global cache that `NGIT_CACHE_DIR` can relocate. The README names "a sandbox or ephemeral agent environment" as a use for that variable, and falls back to an in-memory cache (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/event-cache.md, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli).
- Contributor PRs show up as local `pr/<branch>` branches (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli).
- Signing keys go in the OS keyring, with a 0600 file as fallback (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/credential-storage.md).
format_and_model:
Every record is a NIP-01 JSON event: {id, pubkey, created_at (seconds), kind, tags[][], content, sig}. The id is the sha256 of the serialized event, and the signature is BIP-340 Schnorr over secp256k1, so events are content-addressed and self-authenticating (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md).

There are two storage classes:
1. Regular events, which are immutable: patches, PRs, PR updates, issues, comments and statuses.
2. Addressable events (kinds 30000–39999, keyed by kind+pubkey+d), used for announcements (30617) and state (30618). For these, "only the latest event MUST be stored by relays, older versions MAY be discarded" (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md).

Threading is by event-id references rather than a hash chain:
- Patches in a series carry a NIP-10 `e` reply to the previous patch.
- Revisions reply to the root patch.
- Everything for a repository carries an `a` tag ("30617:<owner-pubkey>:<repo-id>") and an `r` tag with the repository's earliest-unique-commit id. That commit "identif[ies] it among forks and group[s] it with other repositories hosted elsewhere" (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).

Large changes use a PR instead of a patch: "Patches SHOULD be used if each event is under 60kb, otherwise PRs SHOULD be used." A PR points at a commit that can be fetched from the `clone` URLs (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).

The `nostr://<npub|nip05>/[<relay-hint>/]<identifier>` URL is resolved by the git remote helper git-remote-nostr (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writes are permissionless for contributions and maintainer-gated for state.
- Anyone can publish patches, PRs, issues and comments to any repository (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).
- Status: "The most recent Status event (by created_at date) from either the issue/patch author or a maintainer is considered valid" (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md).
- Each maintainer publishes their own 30617 and 30618. When these are merged across members, "standard addressable event rules apply (greatest created_at, lowest event id as tie-break), except relays and clone tags SHOULD be unioned." That is last-writer-wins on second-resolution timestamps (https://ngit.dev/protocol/nip-34/specification, PR #2324).
- Authority is a recursive, reciprocal graph: listing someone is only an invitation until they sign an acceptance. A lead maintainer coordinates the roster. When authority cannot be resolved, clients fail closed rather than guess (https://ngit.dev/protocol/nip-34/maintainers, https://ngit.dev/maintainers/going-deeper).
- ngit makes ordering deterministic in two ways (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/event-created-at-ordering.md):
  - It grinds a nonce tag until the replacement has a lower event id, or advances the timestamp by one second.
  - It gives proposal revisions strictly later timestamps.
- The same doc admits the limit: "Ordering is relative to the observed predecessor, not a distributed lock: concurrent writers with stale caches can still race."
- Actual code merges happen in git. ngit gives "an actionable merge recipe when synchronized refs have diverged" (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md).
- GRASP servers hold state events in "purgatory" until the matching git data arrives, and discard them after 30 minutes (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01).
realtime:
Near-real-time at the protocol level, pull-based in the CLI.
- Relays push live events to WebSocket subscriptions (NIP-01 REQ/filters) (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md).
- GRASP-02 servers must sync events from the other listed relays "using both historic and live sync mechanisms." They must sync missing git data from the other clone URLs at least hourly, and must fetch PR git data at least hourly (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/02).
- GRASP-03 also syncs conversation history about accepted issues, patches and PRs from authors' outbox relays (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/03).
- ngit itself refreshes on git fetch or ngit commands. Agents are told to use the network for the first read in a session and `--offline` against the LMDB cache after that (https://ngit.dev/agents/).
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by structured filter, not full text.
- NIP-01 filters cover ids, authors, kinds, `#<tag>` values, since/until and limit (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md).
- NIP-34 adds tags specifically so clients can subscribe by repository:
  - `a` coordinate
  - `r` with the earliest-unique-commit id ("so clients can subscribe to all patches sent to a local git repo")
  - `r` with the current commit id ("so clients can find existing patches for a specific commit")
  - `r` with merge or applied commit ids on status events
  (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md)
- ngit offers list and view commands (`ngit pr list --json`, `ngit issue view nevent1… --comments --json --offline`) that read the local cache, and returns `nevent1…` ids for follow-up calls (https://ngit.dev/agents/).
- GRASP-03 lets a client ask a single repository server for the complete collaboration history (https://ngit.dev/roadmap).
- NIP-34 defines no full-text or semantic search, and I found no documented search feature in ngit.
links_sessions_to_code:
No agent-session or prompt provenance.
NIP-34 links collaboration records to code only through commit ids:
- the earliest-unique-commit `r` tag
- the PR tip in the `c` tag
- `commit` and `parent-commit` on patches
- `merge-commit` and `applied-as-commits` on status 1631
(https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md)
ngit is agent-aware but does not record sessions:
- `ngit skill install` writes a SKILL.md for Codex and Claude, plus a pointer in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.
- Commands have stable `--json` output.
- The docs site publishes llms.txt.
- `NGIT_CACHE_DIR` supports ephemeral agent sandboxes.
(https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli, https://ngit.dev/agents/)
I found nothing that stores the prompts or transcripts behind a patch or PR.
scale:
No adoption or throughput figures are published. The v3 launch page gives no counts of repositories, users, relays or GRASP servers (https://ngit.dev/v3). The size limits that are documented:
- the 60kb-per-event guideline for patches; larger changes go through git servers as PRs (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md)
- GRASP servers MAY reject pushes or events by size, quota, PoW, payment or web-of-trust (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01, https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/06)
- the `nostr.http-io-timeout-ms` setting for "large GRASP pushes" (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli)
Durability depends on relays: older addressable versions "MAY be discarded" (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md), and ngit says cache recovery "cannot recover events that are no longer available from any relay" (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/architecture/event-cache.md).
privacy_security:
Integrity: every event is Schnorr-signed and content-addressed (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/01.md). GRASP accepts git pushes only when they match signed maintainer state (https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/01).

Confidentiality: events are public broadcast by default. NIP-34 has no redaction or secret scanning, and a patch carries raw `git format-patch` text (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/34.md). Deletion is only a request: relays "SHOULD delete or stop publishing" the referenced events (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/09.md).

Private repositories (GRASP-08, ngit v3):
- A service-wide whitelist of npubs.
- NIP-42 authentication is required on the relay.
- A repository-scoped NIP-98 HTTP credential (kind 27235, created_at within 60 seconds) is required on git endpoints.
- Events go only to the repository's own relays.
- The kind 10318 list of private relays is encrypted with NIP-44.
- The spec admits the limit: "authorized users and the server can copy and republish all events and git data they receive."
(https://ngit.dev/protocol/grasp/specification/08, https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/44.md)
The private-repository guide is explicit that this "provides access control rather than end-to-end encryption" (https://ngit.dev/repositories/private).

Keys: v3 moved the nsec out of git config into the OS keyring because "coding agents and other tools now routinely read Git config" (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/credential-storage.md).

Network: ngit can route `.onion` traffic through Tor (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli/blob/master/docs/onion.md).

Trust: adding a maintainer delegates trust recursively to the people they accept (https://ngit.dev/maintainers/going-deeper).
lesson_for_parinn:
The main lesson is to split small, signed, content-addressed records from bulk data, and key every record to the repository's earliest-unique-commit id and to specific commit ids, the way NIP-34's `r` and `euc` tags do. That way, records for the same project group across forks, worktrees and machines without living inside git, and git servers stay interchangeable caches. There are three caveats:
1. Do not copy NIP-34's replaceable, last-writer-wins model for anything that must be lossless. Addressable 30617 and 30618 events let relays discard history and rely on second-resolution timestamps with lowest-id tie-breaks, and ngit admits stale writers can still race. ParleyInn should publish only immutable, append-only events and derive current state from them (I10).
2. Public-by-default relay broadcast is incompatible with ParleyInn's threat model. Even GRASP-08 is access control, not encryption. Any shared transport should carry only ciphertext (or redacted records) and should sit in an adapter outside ParleyInn's network-free core (I4).
3. ngit moved keys out of git config because agents read it. ParleyInn should keep signing keys and secrets outside every file an agent can read.
license: NIPs, including NIP-34, are public domain (https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/README.md). ngit is MIT (https://github.com/DanConwayDev/ngit-cli). The bundled agent SKILL.md is CC-BY-SA-4.0 according to its front matter in the repository's skills/ngit/SKILL.md. The ngit.dev footer reads "MIT licensed", but I did not separately confirm the licenses of ngit-grasp or the GRASP spec.

name: NTM (Named Tmux Manager)
category: tmux control plane for agent swarms (local orchestrator with durable state, audit and recovery)
status: shipped. Under active development: VERSION file reads 1.36.1, and the latest main commit 15e4dd5 is dated 2026-10-02, from a shallow clone made today. Nothing is archived or superseded.
what_is_stored: NTM does not store agent transcripts. It stores orchestration state around them. (1) Prompt history: every `ntm send`, with id, ts, session, target panes, agent types, the full prompt text, source (cli, palette or replay), template, success, error and duration (internal/history/entry.go). (2) A tamper-evident audit log of send, response, error and state_change events, with actor user, agent or system, plus target, payload and metadata (internal/audit/logger.go). (3) An analytics event stream. (4) Checkpoints: tmux layout, pane scrollback captures, each agent's recorded launch command (model, persona, reasoning effort, account-profile reference), bead-to-agent assignments, and git state (branch, HEAD SHA, dirty flag, a `git status` text file and a `git diff` patch file) (internal/checkpoint/types.go). (5) Timelines of session or agent state. (6) Handoffs: the goal, current task, decisions and next steps, auto-injected into the next spawn. (7) Pipeline step outputs and delivery receipts. (8) A SQLite runtime projection: sessions, attention journal, incidents and watermarks. (9) Policy and approvals. Agent Mail, Beads (.beads/issues.jsonl) and CASS stay external sources of truth that NTM does not own (docs/robot-sqlite-schema.md, section 2.1).
where_stored: All storage is local files plus a local SQLite database. Nothing lives in git or on a server. The discovery note's claim that 'checkpoints and audit trails live in project-local .ntm/' is only partly right, because code defaults put most durable state under XDG directories. Locations: history in ~/.local/share/ntm/history.jsonl. Audit in ~/.local/share/ntm/audit/<session>-<pid>-<date>.jsonl. Timelines in ~/.local/share/ntm/timelines. Checkpoints default to ~/.local/share/ntm/checkpoints/<session>/<id>/, though the README also lists .ntm/checkpoints/ as a project asset. Events in ~/.config/ntm/analytics/events.jsonl. Runtime DB in ~/.config/ntm/state.db. Policy in ~/.ntm/policy.yaml. The project-local .ntm/ holds handoffs/*.yaml, pipelines/, workflows/, personas.toml, recipes.toml, config.toml, rate_limits.json, pids/ and ensemble-cache. Checkpoints can be exported to and imported from tar.gz or zip archives for moving between machines.
format_and_model: Most stores are append-only JSONL files with one JSON object per line. Each audit entry carries sequence_num, prev_hash and checksum, where checksum is SHA-256 over the JSON-marshalled entry with the checksum field emptied. VerifyIntegrity walks a file and fails with 'hash chain broken at sequence N'. A checkpoint is a directory: metadata.json, session.json, a panes/ directory of scrollback, and git status and patch files. It carries a format Version field and has an integrity check (integrity.go). Handoffs are YAML files named YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM_<desc>.yaml and rotate after a per-directory cap. Runtime state is SQLite through pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite v1.56.0, with migrations and robot_<domain>_<purpose> tables. The schema doc treats the tables as a recomputable projection of external truth (tmux, beads, mail), with only the attention journal, incidents and watermarks durable.
multi_writer_and_merge: NTM has no merge model and no cross-machine replication. Writers coordinate through file locks: history and events have unix and windows lock files and a multiprocess logger test. A known fork bug in the audit hash chain was fixed by sharding. Two ntm processes on one session file each appended seq N+1 with the same prev hash, which left verification permanently red. Now every OS process owns its own file, named <session>-<pid>-<date>.jsonl, and its own chain. A code comment says 'a hash chain requires a single writer by construction', and that a lock could not fix it because entries are buffered until flush. Readers then union these files by session prefix. There is no cross-file ordering or merged chain. Coordination between agents, such as file reservations and messaging, is handed to the external Agent Mail server. Optional per-agent git worktrees give filesystem isolation, but NTM says worktrees do not replace reservations.
realtime: Real time is local only. `ntm serve` exposes REST, SSE and WebSocket streams plus an OpenAPI spec, and `--robot-*` JSON gives snapshots and watches. By default it binds to 127.0.0.1 with a localhost CORS allowlist. It refuses to bind a non-local host without --auth-mode and credentials (internal/serve/server.go). Remote tmux sessions are supported, but NTM keeps no history replicated across machines. It skips local handoffs for remote sessions rather than trust a matching path.
search_retrieval: `ntm history search "<text>"` searches prompt history. `ntm timeline list/show`, `ntm audit show` and `ntm changes/conflicts` read the other stores. Transcript or memory search is handed to CASS (`ntm --robot-cass-search="..."`). Retrieval is automatic on spawn: the latest readable handoff is injected before the user prompt, within a bounded budget, falling back to an older file if the newest is corrupt. It can be turned off with --no-recovery or recovery.auto_inject_on_spawn=false. I found no built-in full-text index beyond the CLI search. Whether history search is substring or indexed was not verified.
links_sessions_to_code: The link is weak and happens at checkpoint level only. Each checkpoint records branch, HEAD commit, the dirty flag, and status and diff patch files, and restore can target a different worktree with --directory. Prompts themselves are not tied to commits, and nothing is written into git (no notes, refs or trailers). The Beads integration commits .beads/issues.jsonl to the repo, and ideation can stamp `--plan-version=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)` as an audit token. Each agent pane can get its own git worktree.
scale: Its own verification doc is candid. The synthetic load harness runs exactly 100 panes and 500 events, with no real tmux or agent CLIs. It says any claim above 100 panes needs the harness raised and a committed run, and it notes that an earlier cited benchmark 'never existed'. I found no storage-size or event-volume benchmarks.
privacy_security: Redaction uses the regex engine internal/redaction (docs/REDACTION_SPEC.md). It detects provider API keys, GitHub, AWS and bearer tokens, passwords and private keys, uses category-aware placeholders that do not leak length, and requires O(n) patterns. Audit payloads go through redaction, ModeRedact by default. History and events have redact hooks. Checkpoint export has `--redact-secrets`. Encryption at rest is opt-in and off by default (docs/ENCRYPTION_SPEC.md). It uses AES-GCM in internal/encryption, a key from an env var, a file or a command such as the macOS keychain, a keyring with active_key_id for rotation, and it fails loudly on a missing key. It covers prompt history, event logs, checkpoint exports and support bundles. Audit files are written 0600, though the audit directory is created 0755. The REST server refuses to bind off-localhost without auth, and docs/claude-credential-isolation.md covers isolating Claude credentials per pane. A safety policy plus approvals gate destructive commands such as `git reset --hard`. One gap for ParleyInn's threat model: the auto-injected handoff YAML, which agents or summaries write, reaches the model on spawn with no untrusted-content envelope that I could find in internal/handoff/reader.go. Recalled state is treated as trusted.
license: MIT with an added 'OpenAI/Anthropic Rider' (LICENSE header, https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm/blob/main/LICENSE). The rider makes it not plain OSI MIT, and it should be reviewed before any reuse. I did not read the rider text in full.
lesson_for_parinn: NTM learned in production that one hash chain cannot have concurrent writers. Two ntm processes appending to one session file forked the chain, which made 'tamper detected' indistinguishable from normal concurrent use. Their fix shards the chain per writer as <session>-<pid>-<date>.jsonl, but readers then have no merged order or cross-writer integrity. ParleyInn should design for this from day one: one chain per writer (agent, process, machine or sandbox), with an explicit join record or merge-commit-style checkpoint that hashes the heads of several writer chains. That keeps verification green under concurrency, and it maps cleanly onto git refs or a sync transport later. A second, negative lesson: NTM auto-injects recovered handoffs into new agents as trusted text. That is exactly the path ParleyInn's I2 forbids, so ParleyInn's restore must stay restricted to TrustedText and keep recall enveloped.

name: Oak (Oakspace Inc., "Oak VCS")
category: Agent-native hosted VCS: a new, non-git version control system with a hosted forge (oak.space) and an Apache-2.0 Rust core and CLI
status: beta
license: Core library and CLI (crates oakvcs-core and oakvcs-cli, repo oak/oak) are Apache-2.0 (https://oak.space/oak/oak README "License: Apache-2.0"; crates.io lists Apache-2.0 for every oakvcs-core version: https://crates.io/crates/oakvcs-core). The hosted server (oak/oakspace, named in the Aug 3 2026 dev log at https://oak.space/blog) does not appear to be public: https://oak.space/oak/oakspace returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-02. Treat the server as closed source. The hosted service is under its own Terms and AUP (footer links on https://oak.space).
what_is_stored: Source code and binary assets, versioned as content-addressed objects. There are four object kinds. (1) Blobs: file contents, BLAKE3-hashed. Files at or above LARGE_FILE_THRESHOLD = 10 MB are split into FastCDC chunks (min 256 KB, avg 1 MB, max 4 MB), and each chunk is BLAKE3-hashed on its plaintext and zstd-compressed at rest when that helps (core/src/chunking.rs and core/src/lib.rs in https://oak.space/oak/oak; summary in https://oak.space/docs under "For VCS nerds"). (2) Trees/manifests: (path, blob_hash, mode) entries. (3) Commits: branch_name, parent_hash, merge_parent_hash, manifest_hash, author, optional message, timestamp. (4) Branches: name, description, parent_branch, open/closed status, close reason (core/src/protocol.rs, SQLite migrations). Feature-branch commits carry no message. The branch description is the narrative and becomes the squash-commit message on main (https://oak.space/docs Concepts). The server also stores CI workflows, runs, logs and encrypted secrets; path-permission policy (.oak/PERMISSIONS, a file in the repo); org audit events; webhooks; per-repo "Ideas" boards ("prompts-to-do-work" cards that agents create and humans claim); branch read receipts; and feedback items (https://oak.space/docs API reference; https://oak.space/blog). It does NOT store agent transcripts, prompts or session logs (see links_sessions_to_code).
where_stored: Client side: a single SQLite database per repo at <repo>/.oak/oak.db, holding manifests, blobs, commits and a stat cache (cli/src/resolve.rs and core/src/sqlite.rs in https://oak.space/oak/oak; "the manifests, blobs, and commits live in a single local database file", https://oak.space/docs For VCS nerds). Lazy mounts keep a local overlay and cache per mount (default under ~/oaktree) and expose files through FSKit (macOS 26+), FUSE (Linux) or ProjFS (Windows) (https://oak.space/docs Lazy mounts). Server side: hosted at oak.space, where "main only exists on the server" (https://oak.space). The web/API server is "a single Rust binary (Axum) deployed on a Linux host in Oregon" (https://oak.space/docs). Per the dev log, metadata is in Postgres, CI runs in Cloudflare Sandboxes driven by Durable Objects, and the CI cache is in R2 (https://oak.space/blog). A code comment in core/src/chunking.rs refers to "presigned R2 GET, CDN" for chunk bytes. I could not verify the server's storage layout beyond these statements because the server is not public. Self-host: `oak serve` is "a minimal self-hosted Oak server backed by SQLite ... one SQLite file per repo, with no organizations and no auth model" (https://oak.space/docs CLI reference). Storage is deduplicated per organization: "Blobs and chunks are shared across every repo within the same organization" (https://oak.space/docs Organizations).
format_and_model:
This is a custom format, not git objects. Hashing is BLAKE3 throughout, so it is a Merkle DAG. Docs describe "Manifests and commits, like Mercurial ... no tree objects ... flat manifest" (https://oak.space/docs For VCS nerds). The current source differs: core/src/tree.rs says "Each Tree contains its DIRECT children ... subtrees that don't change between commits are shared by hash reference", and Manifest::new computes the hash "as the root tree hash of the equivalent nested tree". So the docs page is behind the code. Trees are stored as one zstd blob per tree in SQLite (migration 0008_trees_content.sql). The v1 commit hash is BLAKE3 over "branch_name
parent
merge_parent
manifest
author
message
timestamp_rfc3339" (core/src/hash_format.rs). An older 6-field preimage without merge_parent is still accepted to verify commits from around April 2026. A "dormant" v2 format with domain-prefixed preimages (oak-blob\0, oak-tree\0, oak-chunk\0, oak-commit\0), length-prefixed fields and the files list is implemented. It sits behind a repo flag that "cannot be enabled by any command yet" (oak/oak commit 1213b6e8, listed at https://oak.space/oak/oak). Branches are first-class, with an explicit parent branch. Commits record the branch name inside the hash. Squash commits on main keep a pointer to the pre-squash branch tip ("The squash commit keeps a pointer back to the original branch tip", https://oak.space/docs). A newer local "change_sets / change_captures" table holds "append-only" capture occurrences of immutable working-tree change objects with provenance (origin, source_branch, base_commit_hash, captured_at) (core/src/migrations/sqlite/0014_change_captures.sql). The wire protocol is a JSON HTTP API: push, pull, blobs/check, chunks/check, chunks/batch and chunks/{hash} (https://oak.space/docs API reference). Git interop: `oak clone <git-url>` and `oak init` replay git history onto main. Submodules are skipped, octopus merges keep only 2 parents, and only one line of history (HEAD) is imported (https://oak.space/docs Importing from Git). `oak export <dest>` replays Oak history into a fresh git repo and preserves author and timestamp. A read-only git Smart-HTTP endpoint serves main. I verified this on 2026-10-02: `git ls-remote https://oak.space/oak/oak.git` advertised only HEAD and refs/heads/main. A clone held exactly 1 commit, a snapshot with no history, dated 2026-09-27. The receive-pack (push) endpoint returned HTTP 403.
multi_writer_and_merge: The writer model is centralized, with branch-per-session. `oak init` and `oak clone` put every writer on a personal feature branch off main. "One branch per session ... Branches are cheap by design." Each agent task gets its own lazy mount on its own virtual branch, so parallel agents "can't step on each other, and none of them can touch main" (https://oak.space/docs Working with agents and Example session). Direct pushes to main are refused, except for the first push of an empty repo. The only merge is a server-side squash of the branch onto its parent: POST /{owner}/{name}/branches/{br}/merge. This returns HTTP 412 while CI for the branch head is red or in flight, and ?force=1 overrides it (https://oak.space/docs API reference). Conflicts surface on the feature branch during `oak pull`, which merges the newer main into the branch. Conflicts use line-level markers, and `oak conflict status|show|take --json` exists so an agent can resolve them. `oak merge --dry-run` predicts a merge locally. `--merge-preview` adds "four-tree merge-safety detection" that flags merges which would silently revert target-branch work (https://oak.space/docs; https://oak.space/blog). `oak branch triage --remote --json` scores many agent branches as mergeable, closable or ambiguous without a checkout (https://oak.space/docs Example session). `oak push -f` can overwrite diverged remote branch history (CLI reference). Branch rename is "temporarily disabled (returns 503) pending a storage-integrity fix", because renaming rewrote a hashed field (https://oak.space/docs API reference; https://oak.space/blog). The docs say "merging is a human decision". The recommended flow is that agents push and stop.
realtime: There is no real-time co-editing or live replication of working state. Edits stay in a local mount overlay: "nothing leaves your machine until you push" (https://oak.space/docs Lazy mounts). Sync is explicit push and pull. Lazy mounts hydrate file contents on demand on first read ("fetched manifest · 2.4MB · 0 blobs ... files hydrate on read", https://oak.space). Server-side push signals exist. Webhooks fire on branch.created, push and merge, signed with X-Oak-Signature-256. CI logs and GitHub-import progress stream over Server-Sent Events. "Pushed branches show up live on the repo's branches page in the web UI as they land" (https://oak.space/docs API reference and Example session; https://oak.space/blog). `oak mount list --json` reports each local mount's dirty and unpushed counts.
search_retrieval: Search is limited to VCS-level queries. `oak log -S TERM` and `oak log -G PATTERN` give git-style pickaxe search over diffs. The log and diff pagers have in-viewer search (https://oak.space/docs CLI reference). File bytes at any commit are retrievable via GET /{owner}/{name}/raw/{commit}/{path} and tree listings via /tree/{commit} (https://oak.space/docs API reference). Checkout-free review and diff for agents: `oak branch diff|review --remote --json`, with a contribution, tree or net-merge mode and byte budgets (`--max-bytes`, `--changed-files-limit`). Bounded "recall-oriented" JSON comes from `oak status --json --compact` and `oak agent state --json` (https://oak.space/docs CLI reference). Docs and API reference show no full-text code search, semantic search or history index. Whether the web UI has code search could not be verified.
links_sessions_to_code: Only structurally. The unit of work is "one branch per session", and the branch description, typically written by the agent via `oak desc` or `oak finish --desc-file`, becomes the squash message on main (https://oak.space/docs). Oak records no session ID, prompt, transcript or model metadata in commits. Commit fields are only branch_name, parents, manifest, author, message and timestamp (core/src/hash_format.rs and core/src/protocol.rs in https://oak.space/oak/oak). The CLI includes Claude Code WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove hook handlers, so `claude --worktree` and subagent `isolation: "worktree"` get an `oak mount` on its own virtual branch instead of a git worktree (cli/src/commands/mount/worktree.rs, which cites https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#worktreecreate). The hook's stdin JSON includes session_id and transcript_path, but Oak's input struct keeps only worktree_path and base_ref and drops the session linkage (same file). `oak space new` scaffolds AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.json, and `oak skill install` installs an oak-vcs Agent Skill into .claude/skills/ (https://oak.space/docs). The Ideas board API stores "prompts-to-do-work" cards that agents create and humans claim, but the docs describe no link from cards to resulting commits (https://oak.space/docs API reference). A "software factory" orchestration layer for dispatching agents exists behind a flag and is "Not on yet" (https://oak.space/blog). Oak explicitly does not run agents and "makes no AI calls on your behalf" (https://oak.space).
scale: These are vendor claims from its own harness. Up to "−95%" p50 latency versus git on snapshots, for example "many small files · 50k initial snapshot: git 29,723 ms vs oak 1,412 ms". Oak is slower than git on cold init (+188%), process spawn (+143%) and cold dirty status on 50k files (+82%) (https://oak.space; harness at https://oak.space/oak/benchmarks, whose README says public claims "must cite raw JSONL, tuned Git baselines, runner identity, sample counts"). "A 20 GB monorepo is editable in seconds" via lazy mounts (https://oak.space/docs). The launch post claimed "50% fewer VCS-related tokens and 90% faster per operation" (https://oak.space/blog, June 22 2026). Beta quotas: 100 GB storage per org, unlimited repos, branches and members, and 3,000 CI minutes per month. Intended future pricing is $10/month for an individual and $30/seat/month for a team, with 100 GB storage and 100 GB egress per seat pooled (https://oak.space/pricing). Correction to the discovery note: Oak is currently free with "nothing to buy". The "$10 Pro plan" appears only in the homepage schema.org JSON-LD and as a stated future intention. No independent benchmarks or customer-scale figures were found. Adoption looks small: oakvcs-core shows 302 crates.io downloads (https://crates.io/crates/oakvcs-core, checked 2026-10-02). The team is two people, Zach Geier and Adam Morse (https://oak.space).
privacy_security: Repo content is not encrypted end to end or client side. Chunks are stored zstd-compressed and addressed by plaintext hash, and the server must read content to serve web views, raw endpoints and the git snapshot (core/src/chunking.rs; https://oak.space/docs). CI secrets are "encrypted at rest, injected into every step's environment at dispatch, and redacted out of streamed logs" (https://oak.space/docs), using ChaCha20-Poly1305 (https://oak.space/blog). Secret values are write-only through the API (https://oak.space/docs). Docs mention no secret scanning or redaction of committed content. Path permissions live in .oak/PERMISSIONS, read from the main tip, and work fail-closed. They are enforced at the content layer: "a restricted file's name and size stay visible, but its bytes are withheld", because the client re-verifies manifest hashes and the server "can't redact entries" (https://oak.space/docs Path permissions). Auth uses bearer API keys (oak_...) shown once, GitHub OAuth, and session tokens. `oak login` stores credentials in the OS keychain (https://oak.space/docs). However, a source comment says the repo's .oak/oak.db "can hold the user's API token (persisted on oak clone / oak create)", hence a 0600 chmod (core/src/sqlite.rs in https://oak.space/oak/oak). The GitHub import App asks only for read access and uses short-lived per-repo tokens (https://oak.space/docs). Integrity hardening: hash verification on insert, immutable hashed fields, tree entry names validated against \n, NUL, / and .. to close "the confirmed preimage-injection bug where a file named 'a\nb.txt' produced a tree that round-tripped into different entries", and rejection of control characters in authors and branch names (https://oak.space/blog; oak/oak commit 1213b6e8). CLI releases carry SHA-256 and minisign signatures and use two-phase staged promotion (https://oak.space/docs API reference). Other measures are a CSRF guard and 404 instead of 403 for private-repo existence (https://oak.space/blog). Oak "does not train on your code" and makes no AI calls (https://oak.space). `oak serve` has no auth model, and a non-loopback bind requires --token (https://oak.space/docs). CI runners have outbound internet and run as root in fresh containers (https://oak.space/docs).
lesson_for_parinn: Fix the hash-chain preimage before the first record ships. Oak's commit hash is BLAKE3 over newline-joined fields, and that one choice caused three integrity bugs in under six months. First, a filename containing \n produced an ambiguous preimage. Second, branch_name was a hashed but mutable field, so branch rename produced commits that "fail verification on clone"; rename is still disabled. Third, Postgres timestamp truncation "quietly chang[ed] a hash". The domain-separated, length-prefixed v2 format that fixes all three still cannot be switched on, because v1 hashes are already in the wild (https://oak.space/blog; core/src/hash_format.rs in https://oak.space/oak/oak). For ParleyInn's append-only, hash-chained session record, this means four things. Use a domain-tagged, length-prefixed canonical encoding with a format version from day one. Put only immutable fields in the hashed envelope, and keep labels like branch or worktree names in derived, rebuildable projections (I10). Fix timestamp precision in the canonical form. Verify at insert and pin golden vectors (Oak's own fix). Secondary lesson: Oak already sits in Claude Code's WorktreeCreate hook and receives session_id and transcript_path, then throws them away (cli/src/commands/mount/worktree.rs). Neither Oak nor git keeps the session-to-branch-to-commit link, so ParleyInn should record it as an event in its own record. ParleyInn should not expect the VCS to carry it. Oak's pointer from each squash commit to the pre-squash tip is a stable anchor for that link.

name: OKF Agent Memory (okf-memory/okf-agent-memory, CLI `okf`)
category: git-native agent memory (curated knowledge base, not session history)
status: shipped (pre-1.0, active: v0.1.0 on 2026-09-05, v0.5.0 on 2026-10-01; not archived)
what_is_stored: Curated, distilled project knowledge only. It stores no session transcripts, by design. There are two layers ("Dual-Memory Agent Architecture", DMAA). (1) A push layer: a compact codex of about 100-150 tokens in AGENTS.md, written in its "Agent Action Grammar" micro-syntax and loaded at session start. (2) A pull layer: an OKF v0.2 knowledge bundle under knowledge/. It holds "concepts" (Decision, Fact, Requirement, Convention, Runbook and others; the type set is open), plus index.md files for progressive disclosure and a dated log.md change log. The convention says the corpus "is not a transcript of conversations and it is not an internal chain-of-thought store", and the bundled skill says "Conversations: Never" (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/docs/spec/CONVENTION.md, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/.agents/skills/okf-memory/remember.md). The security guide forbids persisting secrets, PII, raw chain-of-thought, tool-call logs and large stack traces (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/docs/security/SECURITY.md). Since v0.5.0 it also stores vendored third-party bundles pulled from a registry, pinned in okf.lock with SHA-256 checksums (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/docs/releases/v0.5.0.md).
where_stored: Working-tree files in the project's git repo: ./knowledge/ and AGENTS.md, committed and reviewed like code. Plus scope layers on the local filesystem: .okf/vendor/<bundle>/ for vendor bundles (priority 70), ~/.okf/ for the user layer (50) and /etc/okf/ for the system layer (10). The project layer (100) shadows all of these (README, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory#readme). Optional since v0.4.0: an encrypted, content-addressed "blind" vault on a self-hostable OKF Hub HTTP server (`okf hub serve`), with vault config in .okf-vault.json (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/architecture/zero-knowledge-vault-sync.md). There is no database, and the tool does not run git itself. Users commit with ordinary git; I found no git or exec calls in pkg/ or internal/.
format_and_model: Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, following Google's Open Knowledge Format v0.2. Its only required field is `type`. Recommended fields are title, description, resource and tags. Optional trust and lifecycle fields are `sources`, `generated` {by, at}, `verified` [ {by, at} ], `status` (draft/stable/deprecated) and `stale_after` (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md). OKF Agent Memory adds two extensions. `governance` takes constraint, hold or context: constraint is a mandatory guardrail and hold freezes edits to the referenced paths. `code_refs` is a list of paths or globs (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/architecture/governance-model.md). A concept's id is its path relative to the bundle. Relationships are markdown links, and the validator checks the link graph, broken links and drift. Concepts are mutable documents updated in place, not an append-only log; history lives in git and log.md. Trust tiers: an agent writes `generated: {by: agent/...}` and must never write `verified`, which is reserved for humans; `okf validate --strict` flags invalid actor schemas. The vault model resembles git but is separate. A Commit holds {version, parent_commit, tree_hash, timestamp, author{client_id, agent}, message}. A Tree maps each path to {blob_hash, size, plaintext_hash, modified_at}. Each blob is an AES-256-GCM envelope [version byte | 12-byte nonce | ciphertext | 16-byte tag], stored under the key sha256(envelope) (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/vault/commit.go, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/vault/tree.go).
multi_writer_and_merge: Through git, multiple writers rely on ordinary branches, pull requests and textual merges. The tool adds no merge driver, and the convention explicitly lists "concurrency and multi-agent editing" and "merge/conflict handling" as open questions for v0.2 (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/docs/spec/CONVENTION.md#25-open-questions-for-v02). Locally, a write goes to a temp file and is then atomically renamed into place. The concept file, the parent index.md and log.md are updated in separate steps. A crash-consistency test covers the case where the concept file exists but the index and log lag behind. I saw no file locking between concurrent local agents (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/okf/mutate.go, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/okf/crash_consistency_test.go). Through the Hub, the vault head advances by compare-and-swap (`POST /commit` with expected_previous_head, which returns HTTP 409 on a mismatch). The client then runs a three-way reconcile over whole files, matched by plaintext_hash, between base, local and remote trees. Changes to different files merge automatically. When both sides change the same file, the remote version stays at the original path and the local one is saved as `<name>.conflict-local.md`. log.md conflicts are merged semantically: entries are unioned under their date headings and deduplicated. Retries use exponential backoff (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/sync/reconcile.go, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/sync/log_merge.go, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/sync/engine.go).
realtime: None. Sharing happens through git push and pull, or explicit `okf hub push|pull|sync` commands. I found no push notifications, websockets or watch mode in pkg/sync (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/tree/main/pkg/sync).
search_retrieval: Local, lexical, in-memory BM25 with Unicode-aware tokenization and deterministic tie-breaking by concept id; no embeddings (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/architecture/search-tokenization.md). It is exposed through the CLI (search, show, validate, create, update) and a stdio MCP server with okf_search, okf_show, okf_validate, okf_create, okf_update and okf_relate (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/pkg/okf/mcp.go). Agents are told to search before writing and to drill down from index files rather than bulk-scan. `okf search --for-path <file>` returns the concepts whose code_refs govern a source file. Searches span scopes, ranking by layer priority first and BM25 score second, and can be filtered with `--scope` (v0.5.0 notes). The bundle is loaded from disk on every MCP call; there is no persistent index.
links_sessions_to_code: It links knowledge to code, not sessions to code. `code_refs` binds a concept to source paths or globs. `--for-path` surfaces the constraints and holds on a file before an agent edits it, and the validator warns when a non-glob code_ref points to a path that does not exist (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/architecture/governance-model.md). Provenance records the agent family (for example `generated.by: agent/codex`) and a timestamp, and vault commits carry client_id and agent. Nothing ties a concept to a session id, a prompt or a commit SHA; the only link is the git commit that carries the file.
scale: Only the project's own claims, not independently checked: search under 300 µs, about 4 ms to parse and validate a corpus of 50+ concepts, under 4 ms cold start and under 15 MB RSS (README benchmark table). A third-party write-up stresses that these are "project-provided benchmarks" that "have not been independently validated" (https://www.remio.ai/post/okf-agent-memory-hit-hacker-news-but-git-native-memory-still-has-to-prove-itself). The project claims nothing for corpora of thousands of concepts. Because every call reparses the whole bundle, cost grows linearly with corpus size. GitHub showed about 742 stars and 58 forks on 2026-10-02 (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory). The HN thread "OKF Agent Memory – Git-native persistent memory for AI coding agents" reached 81 points and 23 comments around 2026-09-06 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49581240, mirrored at https://hn.nuxt.dev/item/49581240); an early snapshot showed 11 points.
privacy_security: There is no automated redaction or secret scanning. A grep of the Go sources for redact or secret-pattern code found nothing. Keeping secrets and PII out relies on policy and the agent's own judgment, the git audit trail, PR review and git filter-repo after the fact (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/docs/security/SECURITY.md). Tool arguments are treated as untrusted input. Paths are confined with canonical-root checks against `..` traversal and symlink escapes. Root-reserved files cannot be overwritten. Newlines and `---` are rejected in scalar frontmatter fields, so an agent cannot smuggle in a forged `verified: human`. Bidirectional-override characters are banned in ids, and MCP argument sizes are capped (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/architecture/security-boundaries.md, https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/knowledge/convention/mcp-agent-safety.md). Memory poisoning is addressed only by labelling `sources` and by human review. When okf_show returns a recalled concept, it is raw JSON with no wrapper marking it as untrusted (pkg/okf/mcp.go). `governance: constraint` concepts are meant to be "injected as a hard constraint", and that applies to vendored registry bundles as well. Files are written 0644. Encryption covers only Hub sync: client-side AES-256-GCM, with keys derived by Argon2id (64 MiB, t=3, p=4) from a password plus a 128-bit Secret Key printed as an "Emergency Kit". The server sees only sha256-addressed ciphertext and Bearer tokens (zero-knowledge-vault-sync.md). The repo itself is plaintext in git. The core binary does use the network: net/http in pkg/sync, pkg/registry and internal/cli/hub.go. The badge says "Zero Deps", but go.mod requires golang.org/x/crypto (https://github.com/okf-memory/okf-agent-memory/blob/main/go.mod).
lesson_for_parinn: Keep two tiers apart. A small, reviewable, human-curated tier rides in git; the raw record stays out of git. In OKF, distilled decisions carry provenance (`generated` vs `verified`, `code_refs`) and travel with the repo. Raw transcripts are refused precisely because git plus PR review cannot carry them, and file-level merges degrade into `.conflict-local.md` forks. ParleyInn could take the same split: hold the append-only hash-chained session record in its own store, and export only promoted, human-verified constraints as git-native files. An agent may write `generated`, but `verified` stays human-only and is rejected at parse time. OKF also shows what to avoid. Its recalled and vendored content can carry `governance: constraint` authority, and okf_show returns it unwrapped. ParleyInn's I2 forbids exactly this, so any git-imported memory must stay enveloped and pull-only. Only locally verified pins can be promoted to TrustedText.

name: Omnara (pivoted; relaunched 2 Sep 2026 as an open-source managed-agents platform)
category: Managed-agents platform: hosted or self-hosted agent runtime, control plane and durable event log. It used to be a mobile/web remote control for Claude Code and Codex; that product line has been superseded.
status: shipped. The relaunched product is live. It runs as Omnara Cloud at app.omnara.com and can also be self-hosted under Apache-2.0. The repo is very active: the last commits are dated 2026-10-01, the changelog's latest entry is dated 2026-09-30, and SECURITY.md says there is no stable release yet ('fixes are applied to the latest version on main'). The earlier product, a mobile wrapper around the Claude Code CLI (YC S25), is unmaintained and superseded. That history comes only from secondary sources.
what_is_stored:
Omnara stores the agent loop that it runs itself, not transcripts from Claude Code. Each agent has one ordered timeline of events, and an event is one of four kinds:
- agent_input: a message, an interaction answer, a cancel, or a config change
- model_output: one completed model response, with stop_reason and the tool calls it requested
- tool_result: succeeded, failed, denied or canceled, linked by tool_call_id
- context_checkpoint: an LLM-written summary used for compaction, recording summarized_through_event_sequence

Events are grouped into turns. Content blocks (text, reasoning, structured_data, tool-call data, media_ref) are stored in separate rows. File bytes (attachments, tool outputs) are never inlined: they go to a blob store as artifacts (art_...) and the event points at them through media_ref.

The same Postgres database also holds:
- organizations, projects, RBAC actors and grants
- agent configs and profiles, machines and pools
- skills, MCP connections, model calls with provider cost, cron triggers, webhooks
- envelope-encrypted secrets

Streaming deltas (partial text and tool-call arguments) and tool_call_update lifecycle frames are explicitly not saved. Sources: README; docs/events/streaming.mdx; docs/events/artifacts.mdx; migrations/000004, 000005, 000006.
where_stored:
On a server, in the cloud or self-hosted:
- PostgreSQL is the system of record: 'all persistent data … organizations, projects, agents, events, machines, secrets'.
- Redis carries SSE notifications and rate limits only; it is not durable history.
- S3-compatible blob storage holds artifact bytes. RustFS is the dev default; the bucket is set with OMNARA_BLOB_S3_*.
- A small daemon, omnarad, runs on each machine (installed under ~/.omnarad) and only executes tool calls. It dials out to the control plane over HTTPS and WebSocket.

Nothing is stored in git, and nothing lives in the working tree. Source: docs/self-hosting/architecture.mdx.
format_and_model:
The data model is relational, a normalized Postgres schema managed by goose migrations (48 so far) and sqlc.

agent_events table:
- columns: id uuidv7, agent_id, turn_id, sequence bigint, event_kind, idempotency_key, plus exactly one FK to agent_inputs, model_outputs, tool_call_results or context_checkpoints. A CHECK enforces the one-of rule.
- unique keys: UNIQUE(agent_id, sequence) gives a dense per-agent order; UNIQUE(agent_id, idempotency_key) gives idempotent appends.
- immutability: a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger raises 'agent_events are immutable' (SQLSTATE 25006).
- agent_inputs carries a state machine (received, resolved, rejected, canceled). A trigger makes terminal states and identity/intent fields immutable.

Other tables:
- agent_turns: turn_sequence, with deferred FKs that require an opening event.
- content_blocks: owner, ordinal, block_kind, text_content, structured_data jsonb, artifact_id.
- context_checkpoints: summary text, summarized_through_event_sequence.

Public IDs are prefixed strings (evt_, trn_, art_, agt_, sec_). On the API side, the OpenAPI spec is served under /api/v1, and events are read as JSON pages keyed by sequence or streamed over SSE, where the SSE id equals the sequence.

There is no hash chain or content addressing on events. The only hashes in the schema are token and password hashes. Sources: migrations/000004_events_messages_turns.sql, 000005, 000006; api/openapi/openapi.yaml.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is a single writer per agent and no merging.

- Stateless workers 'claim ready agent work'.
- The agent_runtime_locks table has UNIQUE(agent_id) plus a lease (renewed_at, lease_expires_at, cancel_requested_at), so only one worker drives an agent at a time.
- A maintenance process reaps expired locks and times out stuck work.
- Ordering comes from the per-agent dense sequence and Postgres transactions ('state is committed atomically to Postgres').
- Concurrent human inputs are not merged. They are queued as agent_inputs with delivery_mode queued, steering or immediate and an input_rank, then admitted into the timeline in order.
- Several machines can be attached to one agent, but they only run tools; they never write history.
- Subagents get their own separate timelines.

There is no cross-agent or cross-instance merge, and no replication or federation between deployments. Sources: migrations/000004 (agent_runtime_locks, agent_inputs); docs/self-hosting/architecture.mdx; docs/events/streaming.mdx.
realtime:
Yes, server-push over SSE: GET /agents/{id}/events/stream.

- Saved events carry their sequence as the SSE id.
- Heartbeats arrive every 10 seconds.
- A client resumes with Last-Event-ID or after_sequence and catches up on every saved event since then.
- Optional stream_deltas=true adds model_output_delta previews, which are not durable and not replayed.
- tool_call_update frames may arrive out of order and are not replayed; after a reconnect, clients re-query GET /tool-calls.
- A parent's stream carries its subagents' tool_call_update frames but not their timelines.
- Redis fans out the notifications.
- Event webhooks have existed since 2026-09-24, and there is a first-party Slack connector.

The TypeScript SDK's openAgentEventStream reconnects automatically. Sources: docs/events/streaming.mdx; docs/changelog.mdx.
search_retrieval:
Search is minimal.
- The API pages through events by sequence (after_sequence or before_sequence, limit up to 500) and lists turns newest first.
- tool-calls and interactions can be listed, optionally with subagents included.
- I found no full-text or semantic search over history: no tsvector or pgvector in the migrations, and none documented.
- The README's answer for deep retrieval is SQL: self-hosted users can 'query agent history directly in Postgres for analytics, evals, prompt analysis, and training datasets'.
- For the model, long contexts are handled by context_checkpoint summaries (internal/compaction), not by retrieval. The original events stay in the immutable log.

Sources: docs/events/streaming.mdx; README; migrations/.
links_sessions_to_code:
No, not natively. History is keyed by org, project, agent, turn and event. Nothing in the data model ties a turn to a commit, branch, repository or diff.

Git appears only as a tool inside sandboxes:
- git and gh are preinstalled on managed pools.
- A GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable authenticates both.
- One built-in tool example runs 'git log -1 --format=%H'.

Any link to code therefore exists only as text inside tool_call results. Omnara also does not ingest Claude Code session transcripts. It runs its own agent loop against model APIs: Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions, and OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Ollama and Bedrock endpoints. Sources: docs/machines/pools.mdx; docs/tools/built-in.mdx; README.
privacy_security:
Secrets:
- Secrets are envelope-encrypted. The scheme constant is 'aes-256-gcm-envelope-v1': a per-secret data key wrapped by a key-encryption key (KEK) from a key ring set in OMNARA_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEYS and OMNARA_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_ACTIVE_KEY_ID, with associated data. Dev mode ships an insecure 'dev-local' key.
- Read endpoints never return secret values.
- Rotating a secret versions it while keeping the same sec_ ID.
- Secrets have narrow owners (org, project or user), and projects need explicit grants to use them.

Access control:
- RBAC applies at org and project level for both users and API keys.
- Auth tokens are stored only as hashes. OIDC and device OAuth are supported.
- Skill downloads go through HMAC-signed, machine-bound capabilities.
- The codebase has ssrf, urlpolicy and outboundhttp packages, and a tool-permission and approval system.

Logs:
- internal/log/scrub.go applies regex redaction to logs only: bearer tokens, key=value secrets and URL query strings.

Gaps relative to ParleyInn:
- Conversation content (content_blocks.text_content and structured_data) is stored as plaintext in Postgres. I found no field-level encryption of history and no redaction of secrets in event content.
- There is no tamper evidence beyond DB triggers, which a DB superuser can bypass.
- Recalled history goes back into model context unenveloped as normal conversation, with no injection-isolation model.
- The README warns that local defaults are insecure.

Sources: internal/secrets/secrets.go; docs/organization/secrets.mdx; docs/self-hosting/configuration.mdx; migrations/000001, 000006; internal/log/scrub.go.
scale:
No numeric scale claims about history size or throughput. The architecture claims are qualitative:
- workers 'are stateless and scale horizontally' (worker xN)
- agents recover from crashes, restarts and machine disconnects
- an agent can use no machines or several at once

Resource limits can be overridden per org (migration 000019). As of the README at clone time (2026-10-02), the repo has about 2.9k stars, 231 forks and 533 commits. Sources: docs/self-hosting/architecture.mdx; README; GitHub repo page.
license: Apache-2.0 for the repo and self-hosting; Omnara Cloud is a commercial hosted service (https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara/blob/main/LICENSE, README).
lesson_for_parinn:
Enforce the record's append-only shape at the storage layer, but do not mistake that for integrity.

What to copy:
- A dense per-agent sequence with UNIQUE(agent_id, sequence) and UNIQUE(agent_id, idempotency_key) makes appends safe to retry.
- A one-of CHECK on event_kind keeps each event well-formed.
- Immutability triggers on events.
- Leased single-writer locks per timeline.
- Compaction summaries stored as just another event kind (context_checkpoint with summarized_through_event_sequence). The originals stay intact, which is the same lossless shape ParleyInn wants.
- SSE with the sequence used as Last-Event-ID, so readers resume exactly. Non-durable previews are kept explicitly separate from the saved record.

Where Omnara stops short, and what ParleyInn should add:
- Its guarantees end at the database operator. Triggers can be dropped and content sits in plaintext.
- ParleyInn should keep the same sequence and idempotency contract but make it travel with the data: hash-chain each event over (prev_hash, sequence, canonical bytes) so any transport (git, a sync server, a p2p log) can verify order and completeness without trusting the store.
- Encrypt content at rest per agent, which would also allow crypto-shredding.
- Treat summaries and recalled events as untrusted, enveloped data rather than ordinary conversation.
- Omnara has no session-to-commit link and no cross-deployment merge. ParleyInn has to design both explicitly if it wants many machines and worktrees.
confidence: high for the current product's storage model, which was verified directly from the cloned repo's SQL migrations, docs and Go source at commit 546a691 (2026-10-01). Low to medium for the pre-pivot history: the CLI-wrapper deprecation and YC S25 details come only from secondary aggregator pages and the YC listing, and I could not check the old repo state, because gh API access to the repo was refused in this session.

name: Ona (formerly Gitpod)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Agent execution sessions and history; pull requests created by agents; audit trails of all operations; environment configurations (Dev Container specs); automation logs and failure reports; session metadata (pins, search indexes, conversation history); model access control settings; run parameters and outputs
where_stored: Hybrid: (1) Customer VPCs on AWS, GCP, or Azure host the actual agent execution environments (isolated VMs, not containers, each with its own kernel and memory space); (2) Git repositories (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) store the PRs and code changes agents produce; (3) Ona platform backend stores session metadata, audit logs, and configuration; (4) Source control integrations provide the primary record of completed work
format_and_model: Dev Container specification (OCI-compatible) for environment definitions; automations.yaml for automation configuration; Protocol Buffer JSON for RPC API communication; Claude (Anthropic LLM) as the agent model; agents communicate with Ona platform via Connect RPC API at https://app.ona.com/api; execution model is event-driven (PR events, schedules, webhooks, manual triggers)
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple agents can run in parallel across different repositories or the same repository on different branches. PR merge handling relies on Git's standard mechanisms (conflicts resolved at merge time in target repository). Session data itself does not support concurrent writes—each automation run is isolated. Agents do not directly merge session history; instead, they produce PRs which are merged or rejected by code review processes.
realtime: Supports live conversation controls (queue follow-up prompts while agent executes); session sidebar search by environment/branch/project; keyboard shortcuts for switching between pinned sessions; webhook triggers enable real-time automation on PR events; agent outputs (logs, reports) stream to UI as they complete; does not provide real-time multi-user collaboration on active agent sessions
search_retrieval: Sidebar search by environment, branch, and project; session history searchable by keywords and metadata; comprehensive audit trails queryable via API; Connect RPC API (gitpod.v1.EnvironmentService/ListEnvironments, etc.) enables programmatic access to sessions; GitHub/Git provides search on code and PR history; reports and failure logs included in automation output and audit trail
links_sessions_to_code: Strong linking: agents execute in ephemeral environments tied to Git branches; all agent-produced work ends up as PRs in the target repository with links back to the automation run; audit trails include references to commits and PRs generated; environments are branch-aware; engineers can take over the exact environment an agent used for manual intervention or debugging
privacy_security: Data isolation: VPC-hosted execution (no shared infrastructure); kernel-level enforcement via Veto (monitors syscalls, file access, network packets, executable hashes before execution); short-lived, scoped tokens tied to organization + project + user (prevents privilege escalation); policy-as-code for hard constraints; OIDC token integration for credential handling; service account support with inherited access control; port authentication with creator-only, org-member, or public access levels; SOC 2 compliance claimed; secrets propagated via secure channels; model access control prevents overrides by inherited tokens
lesson_for_parinn: Ona demonstrates that (1) using actual VMs instead of containers enables stronger kernel-level auditing and policy enforcement without agent circumvention; (2) storing completed work (PRs) in standard Git repositories provides durable, auditable records with minimal custom code and leverages existing tools (GitHub, etc.); (3) separating session metadata and audit logs from code history allows independent retention and access policies; (4) scoping all credentials to specific contexts (org/project/user) prevents privilege creep; (5) ephemeral environments reduce the surface area for state leakage between agent runs; (6) tight integration with code review workflows (PRs) naturally surfaces agent work for human oversight

name: oobo (ooboai/oobo)
category: orphan-branch commit enrichment (git-native AI provenance and attribution store, Rust CLI, optional hosted recall)
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
One 'anchor' per commit, plus per-session and per-turn provenance. Two corrections to the discovery note. First, v2.0.0 (2026-06-21) removed the local SQLite database: "the entire src/db/ module is removed", with state only on the orphan branch or in a file-based hook buffer (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). rusqlite remains only to read other tools' databases such as Cursor and OpenCode (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/Cargo.toml). Second, transcript publishing is on by default, not opt-in: the code default is "on" (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/config.rs) and the official docs say "`on` (default)" (https://docs.oobo.ai/concepts.md). The mintlify.wiki page says Off is the default and describes the v1 layout, so it is stale (https://mintlify.wiki/ooboai/oobo/concepts/transparency).

The anchor JSON holds: commit hash, branch, author, author_type (agent/assisted/human/automated), contributors, message, files changed, added/deleted counts, and per-file changes. Each file change carries ai/human/mixed attribution, agent, and line_attributions ranges in committed-file coordinates. The anchor also holds ai/human added/deleted totals, ai_percentage, session_ids, summary/intent/reasoning, transparency_mode, cross-session file_interactions (writer/reader/both) and turn refs with tree_hash (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/core/anchor.rs).

The v2 AnchorRecord adds three things:
- session_refs: pointers, never embedded copies.
- session_links: per-session model, input/output/cache tokens (native, or tiktoken estimates flagged is_estimated), duration, tool usage, bash commands, thinking time, compactions, files touched.
- A 'coverage manifest': which tools had live hooks, which hook events were seen, and which files had capture gaps.

Provenance layer: session.json stubs, plus immutable turns/NNNNNN/turn.json and edits.json. turn.json holds tokens, model, a sanitized prompt preview called 'trigger', timestamps, tool names and a capture_gap flag; edits.json holds per-file pre/post blob hashes. Conversation layer, written only when transparency is on: per-turn transcript.json (a sanitized slice of the native transcript) and tool_calls.json. Index files: anchors-by-time.jsonl, sessions-by-time.jsonl and a global sessions.jsonl (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs).

Local only:
- Full turn snapshots: commits with the workspace tree and a JSON message, under refs/oobo/turns/v1, used by `oobo goto` (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/turns.rs).
- Active-session hook buffer at ~/.oobo/tmp/hook-buffer/<sid>.json (https://docs.oobo.ai/privacy.md).
- Commit spool at <git-common-dir>/oobo/spool.jsonl (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/spool.rs).

Sessions are read from 15 tools (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md).
where_stored:
Shared data lives on the git orphan branch refs/heads/oobo/anchors/v2 in the code repo; oobo/anchors/v1 is read-only legacy, and v1 writes were removed in 2.0.0 (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The branch is pushed to `origin` by default, or to another named remote or a full URL set in .oobo/config [anchors].remote, for example a separate private anchors repo (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md). oobo dogfoods that: its own repo pushes anchors to the private git@github.com:ooboai/oobocli-anchors.git with transparency=off (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/.oobo/config).

Local-only items:
- Hidden refs refs/oobo/turns/v1/..., never pushed (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/turns.rs).
- Files in ~/.oobo/ (config, hook buffer) and the project's .oobo/ (config, a 0600 secrets file, a turn cache) (https://docs.oobo.ai/privacy.md).

An optional hosted backend (api.oobo.ai, or a self-hosted one) has no git access of its own. It ingests anchors by reading the branch through the GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket APIs when push webhooks fire (https://docs.oobo.ai/backend-api.md).
format_and_model:
Pretty-printed JSON files in a sharded tree on the orphan branch. v2 layout: repos/<repo_key>/anchors/<sha[0:2]>/<sha[2:]>/{anchor.json,timeline.json}; repos/<repo_key>/provenance/<sid shard>/{session.json,turns/NNNNNN/{turn.json,edits.json}}; repos/<repo_key>/index/*.jsonl ('ts\tsha' lines); sessions/<sid shard>/{session.json,turns/NNNNNN/{transcript.json,tool_calls.json}}; and index/sessions.jsonl.

Design rules stated in the code:
- Ids are used to address records; timestamps only order them.
- Prefix fan-out keeps tree nodes small.
- turns/NNNNNN/ directories are immutable; session.json is the only mutable file.
- A conversation is stored exactly once, in the session's 'home store'. Other repos the session edited get provenance stubs with a home_location pointer.

Keys: repo_key is a slug of the project id plus an FNV hash (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs). session_uid is a UUIDv5 over "{tool}:{native_session_id}" in a fixed oobo namespace, so different machines converge on the same id. turn_uid is a UUIDv5 over the pair (native_session_id, native_turn_index), so it cannot collide across resume seams (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/core/identity.rs).

Every write is a new commit on the branch, built with plumbing: hash-object, then update-index on a temp index, write-tree, commit-tree, and a compare-and-swap (CAS) update-ref. oobo shells out to the git binary to do this (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/mod.rs). There is no signing and no application-level hash chain; integrity rests on git's object hashes alone.

Docs drift: the official backend-api page describes the 'v2' layout as XX/<38-hex>/metadata.json with numbered session folders (1/transcript.json). That is the v1 shape and does not match the v2 code (https://docs.oobo.ai/backend-api.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Local writes use a CAS update-ref (old value expected), retried up to 3 times with jitter. Temp index files are scoped by PID and nanoseconds, and first branch creation uses a null-OID CAS (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/mod.rs). Immutable turn writes are skipped if the path already exists, so re-runs do nothing (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs).

Push runs `git push --no-verify <remote> oobo/anchors/v2` and retries up to 5 times. After a non-fast-forward rejection it fetches into a PID-namespaced temp ref, refs/oobo/fetch-tmp/<pid>, to avoid FETCH_HEAD races, then reconciles. If one tip is an ancestor of the other, it fast-forwards. Otherwise it runs replay_local_files, which builds one new commit on top of the remote tip:
- Local-only files are added.
- Files present on both sides with different content: remote wins, with two exceptions.
- session.json is merged per field: sets are unioned, counters take the max, scalars are last-writer-wins by updated_at.
- *.jsonl indexes are merged by deduplicated line union.

Local commits are never merged in, so their history is discarded and a divergent local anchor.json rewrite (for example a backfill) silently loses to the remote copy. In effect the branch is a convergent key-value snapshot, not an append-only log. A failed push leaves a 'pending' marker in the git common dir, and the next push retries it (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/sync.rs). These race fixes landed in 0.1.10, 'eliminating data loss when multiple users or agents push concurrently' (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

Worktrees: the spool and temp indexes live in the shared git common dir, and turn refs are keyed by a worktree id (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/turns.rs). The hook buffer uses atomic read-modify-write under advisory file locks (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). `oobo session share` copies a session's conversation turns into another repo's store, idempotently (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/commands/sessions.rs).
realtime:
Not real time.

Locally: agent lifecycle hooks (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Kiro, Continue, Droid) capture turns as they happen (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md). On commit, the post-commit hook only appends a line to the spool. A detached worker drains the spool asynchronously, which keeps the git path near zero cost (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/spool.rs).

Sharing: data only leaves the machine when the user runs git push. The pre-push hook drains the spool and then pushes the anchor branch (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/cli.rs). Other machines hydrate on clone or through the post-merge hook, which runs fetch_and_reconcile (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/proxy.rs).

The docs state: "There is no background sync, no outbox, no cloud upload pipeline" (https://docs.oobo.ai/privacy.md). The hosted backend updates on push webhooks (https://docs.oobo.ai/backend-api.md).
search_retrieval:
Lookups are O(1) by key through `git show branch:path`, falling back to the origin remote-tracking ref on a fresh clone. Bulk reads use one ls-tree plus one cat-file --batch (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs).

Local `oobo recall` is naive. It loads every anchor and scores it by the fraction of query terms found as substrings of the anchor's intent and commit message. It does not search transcripts (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/commands/recall.rs).

`oobo search` is semantic search over code, not sessions: hybrid BM25 plus vector search via the sonar-core crate, indexed locally (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md).

With an API key, remote recall hits POST /anchors/search, which returns full-text ('fts') and 'memory' hits plus an LLM-synthesized answer (https://docs.oobo.ai/backend-api.md). The benchmark methodology lists OpenAI text-embedding-3-large and pgvector (https://docs.oobo.ai/benchmarks.md).

MCP: the local tools are search and find_related; the cloud tools recall, get_context and ask are also served at agentic.oobo.ai/mcp (https://docs.oobo.ai/mcp.md). Other retrieval: `oobo blame` adds a per-line AI column, and `oobo goto`/`back` restore the workspace tree from turn snapshots (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes; this is the product's purpose.

Commit-to-session links are either explicit (from hooks) or inferred: a time window (±5 minutes is documented) plus file overlap (https://docs.oobo.ai/backend-api.md, https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). Since 2.0, an idle live session no longer counts as authorship without per-commit evidence (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

'Claim-on-commit' ties captured edits to the commit by content:
1. Exact match of the committed blob against a captured post_blob.
2. Otherwise, the best overlap of added lines (a hunk-level match).
3. Ties go to the most recent edit by timestamp and sequence number.

There is no time window: an edit stays claimable as long as its session state exists (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/attribution/claim.rs).
