The provenance engine maps line → edit → turn → trigger (a sanitized prompt preview) → session. It labels lines it cannot explain as 'Uncaptured', never as human by default, and keeps a record of overwritten work (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/provenance/mod.rs).

Attribution gives each (commit, session) pair a non-overlapping window of turns (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/attribution/mod.rs). After a rebase or cherry-pick, the post-rewrite hook re-keys anchors to the new SHAs by matching tree hashes (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
privacy_security:
Everything written to the branch passes through one Publisher gate: sanitize_for_public, which redacts secrets and then rewrites project-root paths as relative and the home directory as ~/ (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs).

For anchor, provenance and session records the gate blocks: if redaction changed the text, the write is refused (SecretBlocked). For conversation transcripts it redacts and writes anyway, never blocking (same source).

Redaction is weaker than the 'gitleaks' label suggests (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/redact/mod.rs):
- The gitleaks binary is used only if installed. oobo writes the text to a plaintext file in the system temp dir and runs `gitleaks dir` on it.
- Four built-in regexes always run (key=value tokens, AKIA keys, bearer/authorization headers, sk_/pk_live keys).

Other measures:
- Gitignored paths are filtered out of files_touched since 1.1.2, after a leak that required scrubbing the branch history (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
- API keys live in .oobo/secrets with 0600 permissions; config files are chmod 0600 (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/README.md).

Gaps:
- No encryption at rest or on the branch. Anyone with read access to the anchor remote can read the anchors and, with transparency on (the default), the redacted transcripts (https://docs.oobo.ai/concepts.md). On a public origin that makes them public, unless a separate private anchor remote is configured.
- Turn snapshots stay local by design (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/turns.rs).
- 'No telemetry' is claimed; network calls are git push, API calls only when a key is set, and `oobo update` (https://docs.oobo.ai/privacy.md).
- Recalled content is not treated as untrusted: I found no envelope or injection handling in the source. The MCP docs even recommend a rule making agents call get_context at the start of every task, which is an automatic path from stored history into the prompt (https://docs.oobo.ai/mcp.md).
scale:
No storage-scale or throughput claims were found.

Built-in bounds:
- Tree fan-out by 2-character prefix (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/src/git/orphan/v2/mod.rs).
- Hook-event and tool-call vectors capped at 200 per turn (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
- 1.0 claimed 626 tests (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

My inference from the code (not measured):
- Each write is a full git commit, and each append rewrites the whole JSONL index blob, so index writes grow linearly with history.
- Local recall reads every anchor per query.

Marketing claims are about memory effectiveness, not storage, and are not independently verified: '60% more bugs fixed' on SWE-bench (2294 tasks, 12 Python repos, Claude Sonnet 4) (https://docs.oobo.ai/benchmarks.md).

Adoption: about 43 stars, 9 forks, 202 commits, 9 open issues (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo). Latest tag v2.0.0; last commit on main 2026-07-08, so the repo has been quiet for about 3 months but is not archived (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
license: Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual) (https://github.com/ooboai/oobo/blob/133cb05e0343abf41de393557e244b5ace62786b/Cargo.toml)
lesson_for_parinn:
oobo's v2 layout shows git can carry multi-writer agent history without merge conflicts, provided the shared tree is designed for it. Paths are derived from ids (sha or UUIDv5 session_uid, with prefix fan-out), turn directories are write-once, and the two merge rules beyond that (per-field merge of session.json, line union of JSONL) are explicit. Its weak spots mark where ParleyInn must go further.

1. Reconcile resolves divergent files as 'remote wins' and drops local commits, so the branch is not an append-only audit record. ParleyInn should publish only content-addressed, write-once segments, each named by its hash. Then any two trees merge by plain union, and ParleyInn verifies its own hash chain instead of trusting branch history.
2. Transcripts go to `origin` by default, and redaction depends on an optional external gitleaks plus 4 regexes. ParleyInn should keep transcripts off any shared ref unless the user opts in. It should redact in-process (I4 forbids os/exec) and copy oobo's block-on-detection mode for metadata, counting and auditing every block (I6).
3. oobo moves data only inside git's own push and fetch hooks. ParleyInn can do the same: hand push and fetch to the user's git rather than opening sockets itself, which keeps I4 intact.
4. oobo returns stored history to agents without treating it as untrusted. ParleyInn's pull-only, enveloped recall (I2) addresses exactly that gap.

name: Opaline CLI (formerly Rudel; canonical repo now opalinehq/cli, old obsessiondb/rudel URL redirects)
category: Team transcript upload + analytics. A hosted SaaS (opaline.so, Opaline Labs, Inc.) fed by an MIT-licensed Node/TypeScript CLI that installs agent hooks.
status: shipped. The hosted service is live. The CLI is at v0.11.0 on npm as `opaline`, `@opalinehq/cli` and `rudel`, all published 2026-10-01 (https://registry.npmjs.org/opaline). The Rudel name is superseded. Rebrand order: `@opalinehq/cli` on 2026-08-25 (commit e55f55e), `opaline` became the primary install on 2026-09-13 (#476), docs introduced Opaline on 2026-09-19 (#485). The Opaline Product Hunt launch was 2026-09-24. The self-hostable server was public until 2026-08-25. That day's rebrand commit deleted 1,149 files: apps/api, apps/web, the ClickHouse/Postgres schemas, Dockerfile, docker-compose and docs/self-hosting.md. CI had disabled the public production deploy the day before (#460). The public repo is now CLI-only, so self-hosting the current product is not possible from public code. Only the git history keeps the older server. The discovery note's 'nua (fka Rudel)' name could not be verified: the Product Hunt page now lists Opaline, Trading Cards by Rudel and Rudel, with no 'nua'. My web-search budget ran out before I could check further.
what_is_stored: Hosted side: the full, verbatim agent transcripts (Claude Code JSONL and Codex rollouts) plus every sub-agent transcript. Per session it adds sessionId, source, projectPath, git remote, branch, HEAD SHA, package name/type, an optional task tag (research/new_feature/bug_fix/...), organizationId and filter_version (contracts/ingest.ts). Separately the hooks send 'repository evidence'. That covers git state: status porcelain v2, index, untracked and ignored lists, worktree list, sanitized working and staged diffs, and recent commit metadata. It also includes the contents of CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (including nested and local variants), SKILL.md, agent-definition .md and agent/MCP config files. Other skill resources go only as path, size, SHA-256 and git provenance. A filtered transcript revision completes the set (docs/data-handling.md, git-collector.ts). The privacy policy also lists account data and usage logs, including IP, OS and CLI version. Separately, PostHog product analytics records only counts and outcomes, never transcript content. Local side (~/.rudel, kept for compatibility, overridable with OPALINE_CONFIG_DIR): credentials.json, retry queues and failed-upload lists, logs, project-to-workspace mappings, per-session transcript-revision manifests, a pending-evidence spool with bounded quotas, repository-evidence-pause.json, and a pinned runtime copy of the CLI in ~/.rudel/runtime.
where_stored: Server/cloud (hosted, proprietary). The last public server design (Aug 2026) kept transcripts in ClickHouse tables `rudel.claude_sessions` and `codex_sessions` on an S3 storage policy, plus analytics materialized views. Postgres held auth and the session_ownership bookkeeping. The Bun API ran on Fly.io (docs/self-hosting.md and base-sessions.ts at e2e5884). The current CLI uploads through presigned Cloudflare R2 multipart URLs ('r2_multipart_v1'; 'repository_evidence_v1' for evidence) when the server advertises that, otherwise through a legacy oRPC /rpc ingest. Today's server-side storage engine is not publicly documented, so it is unverifiable. Client side: plain files under ~/.rudel. Nothing is written into the git repository: the CLI only runs read-only git commands (rev-parse, status, ls-files, diff, log, worktree list). It uses no git notes, refs or trailers.
multi_writer_and_merge:
No merge. The model is a central server with first-writer ownership and snapshot replacement. Each developer's CLI uploads its own sessions into a shared org workspace. Server-side (last public API, router.ts and session-ownership.service.ts at e2e5884):
- The first user to upload a sessionId within an org reserves ownership in the Postgres `session_ownership` table. Another member's upload of the same id fails with SESSION_OWNERSHIP_CONFLICT.
- Re-uploads replace the whole snapshot. ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest row by ingested_at.
- An upload smaller than the stored one (fewer bytes or assistant lines) is refused with SESSION_UPLOAD_SHRINK_REJECTED unless force_replace is set or the filter version changed.
- The server hashes the exact stored bytes plus filter version, so an old unfiltered upload and a new pre-filtered one converge instead of duplicating.
- A usage receipt uses a reserved generation as compare-and-set so an older writer cannot certify a newer snapshot.
Client-side: per-session revision files are guarded by lock files (25 ms poll, 30 s stale), and repository config edits use a config lock. Worktrees are grouped under one repository identity: git-common-dir resolution, plus local-repository and local-worktree SHA-256 ids and an installation UUID. Already-uploaded sessions are skipped through a remote cache.
realtime: Near-real-time for Codex, batch for Claude Code. Claude Code: only the SessionEnd and SessionStart hooks are registered, in user-level settings (HOOK_EVENTS in claude-code/settings.ts). The transcript uploads at session end. SessionStart only captures start-of-session repository evidence. Codex: the `notify` hook fires on every agent-turn-complete. Each turn uploads the current transcript snapshot (non-terminal) and a 'checkpoint' evidence capture (hooks/codex/turn-complete.ts). Hook evidence work has a shared 20 s budget. Failed deliveries back off 5, 15, 60, then at most 240 minutes, and `opaline upload --retry` drains them. Nothing streams events to other agents or clients. Teammates see sessions only after upload, in the web app. There is a browser-to-terminal pairing (`--code`, valid 10 minutes) for live setup and upload status only.
search_retrieval: Human-facing web app only. You browse sessions by repository, follow the conversation and tool calls, and see model, token and API-cost analytics (README; opaline.so). In the last public server, analytics came from ClickHouse materialized views computed on insert: session analytics, error patterns, a success score, skill uses and language signals (packages/ch-schema at e2e5884). The public API had no full-text transcript search; the only `search` parameter found filters the admin user list. The team also shipped a `chcli` agent skill for ad-hoc ClickHouse queries (commit 2175df6, Feb 2026). There is no agent-facing recall path (no MCP server or CLI query that feeds history back to the model). Whether the current hosted app has transcript search is unverifiable.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, one way: session to code, kept server-side, never written into git.
- Every upload records the normalized git remote (credentials stripped), branch, HEAD SHA, repository root and package name (lib/git-info.ts).
- Evidence captures add base and head commit, staged and working diffs, recent commits (hash, parents, author, dates, refs, subject), worktree list, status, and GitHub provider identity (host, owner, name, numeric repositoryId, nodeId).
- Each capture links to a transcript watermark (byte offset and event ordinal) and records whether it happened before or after the session's first action. Captures chain through parentContextId.
This ties a code state to a point in a prompt stream. Commits do not point back to sessions: no git notes, trailers or refs.
scale:
No throughput or benchmark claims. Data points:
- The Show HN dataset was the team's own 1,573 sessions, 15M+ tokens and 270K+ interactions over about 3 months, from a team of about 6 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47350416).
- Hard limits: 128 MiB per ingest, 512 sub-agents, 64 MiB per evidence object, 4,096 objects and 8 MiB multipart parts.
- Capture bounds: at most 256 blobs and 2 MiB of content, a manifest of at most 2,000 entries and 256 KiB, streamed filtering capped at 32 MiB and 256 streams.
- The old ClickHouse schema had a 365-day TTL.
On HN a commenter (vidarh) called the ClickHouse/Neon/Fly stack over-engineered for that data size.
privacy_security:
Redaction:
- Client-side, deterministic, best-effort. 18 rules derived from gitleaks v8.30.1 (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS, GCP, GitHub, GitLab, npm, Slack, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, private keys) replace matches with `[REDACTED:<rule>]` (secret-filter/generated-rules.ts and filter.ts).
- Filtering covers main and sub-agent transcripts and evidence metadata (paths, filenames, skill names).
- The upload fails closed when redaction exceeds 20% of the payload (MAX_REDACTION_RATIO 0.2), does not converge, or would break JSON integrity.
- Every record is stamped with filter_version, and pending evidence from an older filter version is quarantined, not sent.
- The old README conceded misses: `DB_PASSWORD=hunter2`, unprefixed tokens, split, base64 or paraphrased secrets, screenshots, double-escaped JSON. It said 7 of the 18 rules need a trailing delimiter. The last public API re-ran the filter server-side; whether the current server does is unverifiable.
- Credential-like paths, including .env.example, .env.sample and .env.template, and the CLI config dir are excluded from evidence and patches.
Encryption:
- None client-side. Transcripts reach the vendor in plaintext over TLS.
- Plain-HTTP API or upload endpoints need explicit opt-ins (OPALINE_ALLOW_INSECURE_API_BASE / _ENDPOINT).
- The API token sits in a plaintext JSON file (~/.rudel/credentials.json, mode 0600, directory 0700). No OS keychain.
- No encryption-at-rest statement in the README or privacy policy.
Hosted terms (https://opaline.so/privacy):
- Opaline Labs, Inc., San Francisco. Data may be processed in the US and other countries.
- Sessions are kept until the customer deletes them; residual copies remain in backups.
- Session content is not used to train general models.
- Repo toggles are opt-in per repository. Turning a repo OFF stops future uploads but does not delete past ones.
- CLI analytics go to PostHog and can be opted out with DO_NOT_TRACK=1.
- The /subprocessors URL returned 404.
Security policy: private GitHub advisories, 48 h acknowledgement, latest version only.
Trust boundary: no prompt-injection or untrusted-content handling, because nothing is re-injected into agents.
license: MIT for the CLI and npm packages (opaline, @opalinehq/cli, rudel). The hosted service is proprietary. The server, web and schema code was MIT while it was in the repo (Feb to Aug 2026). It survives in git history but is no longer maintained publicly.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy Opaline's transcript-revision watermark when ParleyInn imports Claude Code JSONL into its hash-chained record. Treat the source file as untrusted and possibly rewritten. On each hook:
- Take only whole lines, up to the last newline.
- Record {byteOffset, prefixSha256, recordCount}, per-chunk sha256s and parentRevisionId. revisionId is the SHA-256 of the canonical manifest.
- Before appending, re-hash the old prefix. If the source shrank, the prefix changed, or the actor/session scope changed, start a new generation linked to the old chain. Never splice or overwrite.
Pair this with the server-side rule that a smaller snapshot is refused unless explicitly forced. Together they keep the record lossless across compaction and transcript rewrites, and fit I6 if ParleyInn audits each reset or refusal as an event. A secondary lesson: stamp the redaction-filter version on every stored record, and quarantine older-version pending data rather than sending it. Opaline also shows the cautionary path. Verbatim upload to a vendor was the top objection on HN, and the self-hostable server was later removed from the public repo. That supports ParleyInn's choice to keep the core offline and make any sharing an opt-in transport rather than a SaaS.
confidence: high for the client: storage, hooks, redaction and the revision model come from reading the CLI source at HEAD 7ef8e97 (2026-10-01) and its full 505-commit history. Medium for the hosted backend: its design is known only from the server code removed on 2026-08-25, and current server storage, encryption at rest and search are unverifiable. Low for the 'nua' name, which could not be confirmed.

name: OpenAI Agents SDK Sessions
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Conversation history items: user messages, assistant responses, tool calls and results. Items are stored as TResponseInputItem objects, a standardized container for conversation turns. Each item carries metadata required to resume an agent mid-conversation. The system preserves full conversation history chronologically for context restoration.
where_stored: Multiple pluggable backends: (1) SQLiteSession: file-based (:memory: in-memory) with JSON serialization, (2) AsyncSQLiteSession: async variant using aiosqlite, (3) AdvancedSQLiteSession: enhanced with branching and usage analytics, (4) RedisSession: distributed memory with low-latency access across workers, (5) SQLAlchemySession: SQLAlchemy ORM for PostgreSQL, MySQL, other production databases, (6) MongoDBSession: horizontally scalable with logical-batch documents, (7) DaprSession: cloud-native via Dapr runtime (30+ backend databases), (8) OpenAIConversationsSession: server-managed via OpenAI Conversations API, (9) EncryptedSession: transparent encryption wrapper over any backend.
format_and_model: SQLite: Two-table schema (agent_sessions, agent_messages). Sessions table: session_id (TEXT PRIMARY KEY), created_at, updated_at. Messages table: id (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT), session_id, message_data (TEXT, JSON-serialized TResponseInputItem). Uses WAL journaling mode for concurrency. MongoDB: Logical-batch documents in messages collection with monotonic seq counter field; sessions collection tracks metadata. Items serialized as JSON. OpenAI Conversations API: Server-managed via REST API, items returned as structured objects. Redis: JSON-serialized items stored with watch-based transaction markers. Format is protocol-agnostic: all implementations serialize to JSON, deserialize to TResponseInputItem at retrieval.
multi_writer_and_merge: SQLiteSession: Thread-level RLock serializes concurrent access. File-backed databases use process-level locks; in-memory assumes single process. Transactions with explicit rollback on failure. MongoDBSession: Atomic increment of a seq counter on session metadata document guarantees strictly monotonic insertion order safe across multiple writers and processes. Each message batch carries the final item's seq; this prevents out-of-order delivery even when document inserts race. RedisSession: WATCH/EXEC transaction pattern with retry logic on WatchError. Conflicts trigger automatic retry (configurable). SQLAlchemySession: Database-level transaction isolation; serializable or repeatable-read modes possible depending on backend. All async implementations support concurrent reads and serialized writes via locking or database transactions.
realtime: Async/await throughout; all session methods return Awaitable. No polling required. RedisSession provides 'low-latency' performance suitable for distributed workers. OpenAIConversationsSession lazily initializes conversation on first API call. AdvancedSQLiteSession supports branching (multiple conversation branches from a single session). No server push or webhook notifications; agent retrieves history on demand before each run. Each runner.run() call fetches full session history (or limit), appends new turn, persists atomically.
search_retrieval: get_items(limit) retrieves conversation history, optionally capped to most recent N items. No built-in full-text search. pop_item() removes and returns most recent item for correction workflows. get_items(limit=None) retrieves all items. No filtering by message type, timestamp range, or content. SQLiteSession and subclasses support efficient limit queries via SQL. EncryptedSession must scan and decrypt all items to find valid unexpired ones; max_scan_items parameter bounds cumulative decryption cost per get_items call. No indexing on content or metadata beyond session_id and insertion order.
links_sessions_to_code: Sessions maintain conversation state but do not store code, file references, or commit hashes. Runner.run(agent, input, session=session) passes the session to the agent; history is prepended to the input. Sessions are agent-execution records, not connected to repository state or development workflows. Tools called by the agent may read/write code; those interactions are captured as tool calls in session history but the code itself is not stored. OpenAI Conversations API sessions are similarly execution-focused: no built-in linking to a codebase, project, or version control.
privacy_security: EncryptedSession provides transparent encryption using Fernet (symmetric) with per-session key derivation (HKDF-SHA256). Master key provisioned externally; a high-entropy key is required. TTL-based expiration: expired items silently skipped on retrieval (default 600 seconds). Expired records remain in store until manually cleaned. No built-in redaction of sensitive content (API keys, credentials, personal data) from conversation items; applications must sanitize before add_items. SQLiteSession assumes application-level trust: database file permissions must restrict access. No row-level security or authentication. OpenAIConversationsSession delegates to OpenAI-managed API; relies on OpenAI's transport security (HTTPS) and API authentication. EncryptedSession can wrap any backend, including OpenAIConversationsSession. No key rotation mechanism built-in; requires application code. Clock skew tolerance: TTL validation uses system clock; NTP synchronization across servers recommended.
lesson_for_parinn: The pluggable Session protocol (interface-based, not inheritance-required) decouples history storage from agent execution. ParleyInn can adopt this pattern: define a core protocol (get_items, add_items, pop_item, clear_session) and ship multiple backends (SQLite, Git, custom). MongoDB's approach to multi-writer ordering (atomic seq counter) is superior to timestamps for distributed scenarios; ParleyInn's append-only record could use a hash-chained sequence number instead of relying on insertion order. EncryptedSession as a wrapper layer (not a monolithic feature) allows encryption to compose with any backend, reducing duplication. Async/await throughout enables efficient multi-agent deployments. The decision not to store code or link to repositories lets sessions remain portable and replayable across machines. For ParleyInn: keep sessions decoupled from the codebase they instrument; store references to commits or files only if the agent chooses to record them as part of a tool call or decision log.

name: OpenAI Codex CLI Rollout Files
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Complete append-only transcripts of every agent session invocation. Stores thread lifecycle events (started/completed), turn boundaries, per-turn token usage (input, output, cached, reasoning), and per-action item events capturing agent messages, internal reasoning, command executions with exit codes and stdout/stderr, file diffs, MCP tool calls with arguments and results, web search queries and summaries, plan creation and transitions, user approval/rejection decisions, and errors/failures. Each event is a self-contained JSON object.
where_stored: Local filesystem at ~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<UTC-timestamp>-<session-uuid>.jsonl. Date-partitioned directory structure. Files are plain JSONL (JSON Lines, one JSON object per line). Optional zstd compression available but breaks resume functionality. No cloud default, local-first architecture.
format_and_model: JSONL (JSON Lines): append-only, line-delimited JSON. Event model: thread.started → [turn.started → [item.completed+]+ → turn.completed]+ → session end. Core event types: thread.started (contains thread_id UUID), turn.started/completed (with usage metrics: input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_tokens), item.completed (type: agent_message, reasoning, command_execution, file_change, mcp_tool_call, web_search, plan_update, approval_decision), turn.failed/error. Session ID is server-side generated UUID; timestamp in filename is UTC.
multi_writer_and_merge: No explicit multi-writer merge documented in primary sources. Each session generates a single JSONL file per invocation. Codex CLI supports /fork and /side commands for conversation branching, creating separate sessions with independent rollout files. Session state for resumed sessions includes approval history, preventing re-asking for previously approved changes. No distributed merge semantics described; appears to be single-writer per session with fork as the branching mechanism.
realtime: Sessions write events incrementally to disk during execution. Files are accessible and readable while session is running. Can be streamed with jq or tail in real time. No batching or buffering documented. Resume capability requires reading the entire rollout file to reconstruct conversational state.
search_retrieval: Plain Unix tools (jq, grep, awk) work directly on JSONL. Community tool ccusage aggregates sessions by directory/date, shows per-model breakdowns, cached token counts, and cost. codex debug trace-reduce command condenses traces into summaries of tool/code-mode/session/subagent boundaries. codex resume <SESSION_ID> retrieves and restores session from rollout file. No full-text search or database indexing documented.
links_sessions_to_code: file_change events contain diffs applied via apply_patch. command_execution records shell commands run, exit codes, stdout/stderr. Plan mode transitions (plan_update events) link to work tasks. approval_decision events show which changes were approved. Agent messages and reasoning capture intent. Filename and thread_id provide stable session identifiers. No direct source-control (git) integration documented in rollout format.
privacy_security: Optional --ephemeral flag prevents writing rollout files to disk. User prompts can be redacted via config (log_user_prompt = false in OpenTelemetry section). Local storage only, no automatic transmission to cloud. Optional OpenTelemetry export available for centralized observability with SigNoz/Jaeger/Grafana/Datadog. No built-in encryption at rest documented; stored in plaintext on filesystem. Compression with zstd possible but unsupported for resume. Redaction and content filtering deferred to client-side config.
lesson_for_parinn: Codex CLI demonstrates that append-only JSONL + date-partitioned local storage + session resume from rollout files is a proven, production pattern. Strengths: simplicity (plain JSON amenable to Unix tools and standard querying), portability, and local-first security posture. Event-based model (thread, turn, item) with discrete event types supports flexible querying without schema migration. Approval decisions as first-class events are essential for auditability and session resumption without re-prompting. Session ID generation and stable identification crucial for multi-agent scenarios. Session branching via /fork/side creates independent rollout files—no complex merge semantics needed. Lessons: (1) plain JSONL + Unix tools scales far enough to avoid database overhead; (2) date-partitioning enables retention policies and archival without schema coupling; (3) local-first + optional cloud export (OpenTelemetry) separates safety from observability, respecting I2/I4 equivalent invariants; (4) approval history must persist in rollout for true auditability; (5) long-term disk management (archive, compress) should be deliberate, not automatic, to preserve resume guarantees.
sources: https://codex.danielvaughan.com/2026/04/29/codex-cli-rollout-files-session-recording-replay-audit-trails/ (primary source: rollout file format, anatomy, inspection, replay, audit trails)
https://www.amazon.com/dp/1808348893 (Agentic Coding with OpenAI Codex CLI by Daniel Vaughan—confirms Codex CLI as real product, published format)
https://codex.danielvaughan.com/ (blog index—confirms active ecosystem, multiple articles covering audit, resumption, multi-agent coordination as of October 2026)

name: OpenAI Codex cloud ("Codex Cloud", plus the older "Codex Cloud (Legacy)")
status: shipped. There are two versions. (1) The current Codex Cloud runs each task in a VM started from a reusable, published "cloud environment". It was announced in the DevDay 2026 notes (dated September 29, 2026) and in the What's new entry for Sep 28–Oct 2, 2026 (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/whats-new/devday-2026, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/whats-new). (2) Codex Cloud (Legacy) uses containers built from the `universal` image. It still serves Code Review and the Linear and GitHub integrations, and OpenAI says: "We plan to deprecate this experience" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environment). The old URL developers.openai.com/codex/cloud now returns a 308 redirect to learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud, and developers.openai.com/codex/cloud/environments redirects to /docs/environments/cloud-environment (checked by fetch on 2026-10-02).
where_stored: On OpenAI-managed servers, in the ChatGPT backend. The CLI calls endpoints such as `/backend-api/wham/tasks`, `/wham/tasks/{id}`, `/wham/tasks/{id}/turns/{turn}/sibling_turns` and `/wham/environments/by-repo/github/{owner}/{repo}` (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/backend-client/src/client.rs, https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/env_detect.rs). Execution state lives in per-task VMs (current) or containers (legacy) on OpenAI infrastructure. Nothing is stored in git by Codex itself. Code reaches GitHub only when the user commits or opens a PR, or applies the diff locally (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud).
format_and_model:
The backend schema is proprietary and unpublished. The open-source client's own comment says "The generated OpenAPI models are pretty bad", so it hand-rolls them (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/backend-client/src/types.rs). The data is JSON over HTTPS.
- Model: Task → Turns (user turn, assistant turn, diff turn). Each turn holds typed items (`message` with content fragments, `output_diff`, `pre_apply_patch`). Best-of-N attempts are sibling turns, ordered by `attempt_placement`.
- Diffs are plain `diff --git` unified-diff text.
- Creating a task sends `{new_task:{environment_id, branch, run_environment_in_qa_mode}, input_items:[...], metadata:{best_of_n}}` (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks-client/src/http.rs).
- `codex cloud list --json` returns `tasks[]` (id, url, title, status, updated_at, environment_id, environment_label, summary, is_review, attempt_total) plus a `cursor` (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli#cli-codex-cloud).
- The record is mutable server state. Nothing in the docs suggests a content-addressed or hash-chained log.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no shared writable session. Each task gets its own isolated workspace from the published environment. "Access to the setup doesn't grant access to someone else's task or permission to edit the environment." Republishing an environment affects only new tasks: "existing tasks retain their own state" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments). In Slack or Teams, "another participant's request doesn't automatically continue your task" (same page).
Within one task, best-of-N runs 1–4 parallel attempts as sibling turns, and the user picks one (`--attempts 1-4`; `codex cloud apply/diff --attempt N`) (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli, https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/cli.rs).
All merging is left to git:
- The user commits or opens a PR.
- `codex apply` / `codex cloud apply` runs `git apply`, with a preflight dry run that reports `conflict_paths` and `skipped_paths`, and "exits non-zero if `git apply` fails (for example, due to conflicts)" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli, https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks-client/src/api.rs).
- `@codex fix ...` on a PR starts a legacy cloud chat that "can push a fix back to the branch when it has permission" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/third-party/github).
realtime: Tasks run asynchronously and "can keep working while your computer is asleep". You can reopen the same task to continue on web, mobile or desktop (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments). The CLI checks status by polling REST endpoints (list, status, diff) (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/cli.rs). Live co-editing by several users, or a public event stream for cloud tasks, is not documented. Hosted safety monitoring "runs asynchronously and can pause a task", and a pause "can arrive after the activity that triggered it" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-approvals-security).
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is shallow:
- `codex cloud list` filters by environment, takes `--limit` 1–20 and a `--cursor`, and can output `--json`.
- `codex cloud status`, `codex cloud diff` and `codex apply` work on a single task (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli, https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/cli.rs).
- The client can fetch a task's prompt, its assistant messages and its sibling attempts (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks-client/src/api.rs).
No full-text or semantic search over cloud task history is documented, and neither is a user-facing transcript export. Enterprise audit export goes through the Compliance API as JSONL (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/compliance-api).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, on the server side, but nothing is written into git. Each task is tied to:
- an environment (a set of GitHub repos) and a git branch. Legacy mode checks out "the selected branch or commit SHA" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environment).
- a unified diff as its output, and `external_pull_requests` in the task details (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/backend-client/tests/fixtures/task_details_with_diff.json).
The CLI picks an environment automatically by mapping the local GitHub origin through a by-repo endpoint (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/env_detect.rs). On PRs, `@codex review` posts a GitHub review, and other `@codex` mentions start a legacy cloud chat "using your pull request as context". Security Review findings link to "the associated Codex task" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/third-party/github).
Not verified: whether Codex-created commits or PR bodies carry a back-link, trailer or note pointing to the task or transcript. No primary source describes this.
scale: Default VM size per task: Plus has 2 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM and 8 GiB disk. Pro, Business and Enterprise have 4 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM and 32 GiB disk. Larger VMs are available for Enterprise (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments). Other limits: best-of-N up to 4 attempts; the list page holds at most 20; saved state lasts 7 days; the legacy cache lasts 12 h (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environment). Not available: GitLab and self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server in the new cloud environments, and computer or browser use (same page). No user, task-volume or throughput figures could be verified. The original 2025 announcement (openai.com/index/introducing-codex) returned 403 and could not be read.
privacy_security:
- Sign-in and access: Codex cloud requires ChatGPT sign-in, and MFA is mandatory for email/password accounts (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth). It is off by default for Enterprise workspaces. It respects the repository permissions of the connected source system and does not inherit local device policy (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/admin-setup).
- Network: internet access is configured per environment, with an allowlist ("Package managers" preset, custom domains, or unrestricted). All outbound traffic goes through an HTTP/HTTPS proxy. The egress IP ranges are shared across customers (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environment).
- Secrets: a network secret reaches programs only as a placeholder. The proxy substitutes the real value for allowed HTTPS:443 destinations and "doesn't put the raw credential in a local process or file". A Personal vault keeps per-user values out of shared environments (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments). In legacy mode, secrets get "an additional layer of encryption", are decrypted only for task execution, and "are removed before the agent phase starts" (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environment).
- Cloud identity and VPN: OIDC gives short-lived cloud credentials (Enterprise, by request). Tailscale VPN uses reusable, ephemeral keys (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/cloud-environments).
- Prompt injection: the docs warn about it explicitly, with a worked example of exfiltration through a malicious GitHub issue, and suggest limiting HTTP methods to GET/HEAD/OPTIONS (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud/internet-access).
- Adjacent product, not Codex Cloud itself: the Work Cloud security page says Work Cloud "uses the Codex task-execution harness". For Business, Enterprise and Edu it states encryption in transit and at rest, no training on business data by default, EKM coverage of supported hosted execution snapshots, and that hosted execution state "follow[s] a separate lifecycle" from conversations (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/chatgpt-work-cloud-security).
- Not documented: any redaction of transcripts or worklogs. Codex-specific transcript retention could not be verified.
license: The hosted service is proprietary. The Codex CLI, including the `codex cloud` / cloud-tasks client crates, is open source under Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/LICENSE). The `openai/codex-universal` reference Docker image is public on GitHub, but no LICENSE file was found at its root (https://github.com/openai/codex-universal), so its license is unverified.
lesson_for_parinn:
Codex Cloud sends only the code result (a unified diff) to git, through a PR or through `git apply` with a preflight conflict check. The session itself stays in a closed server store: prompts, the worklog and sibling attempts. The sandbox state that produced it disappears 7 days after last use, and the docs say "Saved state doesn't replace source control". Once the VM expires, nothing in the repository lets you recover or verify how the code was produced.

The concrete lesson for ParleyInn:
- Keep the session record off the code branch, in its own append-only store, but bind the two in both directions. Write a verifiable pointer (record or segment id plus the chain-head hash) into the commit or PR the session produced.
- In an ephemeral sandbox, flush the hash-chained segment out before teardown instead of trusting the sandbox to keep it.
- Model best-of-N or parallel attempts as sibling branches under one turn, the way Codex's `sibling_turn_ids` and `attempt_placement` do, and never as overwrites.
- Copy the network-secret placeholder pattern. When the agent process only ever sees placeholders, secrets never enter the recorded history, which is better than redacting them afterwards.

name: OpenAI Conversations API (Responses API store)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Conversation objects containing message arrays with user and assistant roles, tool calls and outputs, response objects with phase information, and reasoning items (encrypted by default for reasoning models). Responses API responses can optionally include encrypted reasoning content for multi-turn stateless use.
where_stored: OpenAI cloud infrastructure. Responses are stored server-side; conversation objects are persisted indefinitely. Response objects have configurable retention via the `store` parameter (default: 30 days). Encryption applied to reasoning items by default.
format_and_model: Messages in structured array format: {"role": "user|assistant", "content": "text"}. Response objects include phase information. Responses API supports reasoning models with encrypted reasoning tokens. No published schema available for internal storage format.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multi-writer scenarios not explicitly addressed in public documentation. Agents API manages 'Saved session configuration, turns, and items' centrally. Responses API supports response chaining via `previous_response_id` parameter to fork conversations at specific response points, but no collaborative merge semantics documented.
realtime: WebSocket support for Realtime API enables 'repeated response.create events' over persistent connections with 'connection-local cache' for low-latency continuation. Agents API maintains session state for multi-turn interactions. No documented support for concurrent modifications to the same conversation.
search_retrieval: Responses are 'viewable in the dashboard logs page or retrieved via the API' but no search or query functionality documented. Retrieval is by response ID or conversation ID. No full-text search, filtering, or semantic retrieval capabilities mentioned.
links_sessions_to_code: Agents API, SDK sessions, Responses conversations, and sandboxes are separate resources. No documented linking between stored conversation state and external code repositories, worktrees, or development contexts. Agents can reference tools but conversation history is not linked to code artifacts.
privacy_security: API key authentication via HTTP Bearer token. Reasoning items encrypted by default. Encrypted reasoning content enables stateless multi-turn use when `store: false` is set. Enterprise features available but specific details not publicly documented. Zero data retention program option mentioned but not detailed. No encryption keys disclosed; key management handled by OpenAI.
lesson_for_parinn: OpenAI's 30-day default retention for responses (with opt-out) contrasts with ParleyInn's append-only indefinite record. ParleyInn should enforce I2 (untrusted content never reaches model) by keeping conversation state server-side and pull-only like OpenAI, but enable query/search since ParleyInn owns the record. The `previous_response_id` branching mechanism shows how to avoid merge: fork conversations atomically rather than merge parallel writes. For multi-agent scenarios, ParleyInn could mandate exclusive read-before-write sessions per agent or use response chaining instead of concurrent writes.
sources: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state (primary source for conversation state management and retention)
https://developers.openai.com/docs/guides/agents (Agent runtime storage: Agents API maintains saved session configuration, turns, and items)
https://github.com/openai/openai-python (Python SDK reference implementation, examples directory)
https://github.com/openai/openai-go (Go SDK documentation confirming Responses API, multi-turn conversations, streaming, tool calling support)
https://status.openai.com (confirms APIs operational as of October 2026: Responses, Agents, Chat Completions at 100% uptime)

name: OpenAI Symphony
category: Issue-board-driven autonomous agent runs (orchestrator/scheduler for Codex, not a history store)
status: shipped (engineering preview). Public since 28 April 2026 (https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/28/openai-symphony-codex-orchestration-linear/). Releases v0.0.1 (18 July), v0.0.2 (24 July) and v0.0.3 (15 September 2026), plus a rolling nightly build (https://github.com/openai/symphony/releases). HEAD of main is be10a1b, dated 2026-09-15, from a shallow clone. The README calls it "a low-key engineering preview for testing in trusted environments" (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/README.md). The Elixir code is "prototype software intended for evaluation only" (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/README.md). OpenAI does not plan to maintain it as a standalone product and treats it as a reference implementation (Help Net Security, link above). The repo is not archived.
what_is_stored:
Symphony keeps almost nothing durable. The spec says scheduler state is "intentionally in-memory" and that "restart recovery is tracker-driven and filesystem-driven (without a durable orchestrator DB)" (SPEC.md §2.1, §7.4, §14.3, https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/SPEC.md). What exists:
(1) In-memory orchestrator state (§4.1.8): running map, claimed set, retry entries, completed set, token totals and the latest rate-limit snapshot. The live-session record (§4.1.6) holds session_id = <thread_id>-<turn_id>, the Codex PID, the last event and a summarized last message, token counters and turn_count. The blocked or needs-approval map is also memory-only and is cleared on restart (elixir/README.md).
(2) Per-issue workspace directories on disk. They are reused across runs and kept after successful runs (§9.1). What goes in them is set by hooks, typically a `git clone` (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/WORKFLOW.md).
(3) Operational logs: key=value lines carrying issue_id, issue_identifier and session_id (§13.1, https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/docs/logging.md).
(4) The policy itself: the repo-owned WORKFLOW.md, which is YAML front matter plus a Liquid prompt template (§5).
Durable run history is pushed outward by prompt convention, not by orchestrator code. The agent keeps a single "## Codex Workpad" comment on the Linear issue (plan, acceptance criteria, validation notes, handoff), edited in place. It attaches the PR URL to the issue and keeps code on git branches and PRs (elixir/WORKFLOW.md). Symphony does not store Codex conversation transcripts. Where the Codex app-server keeps thread history is not documented in Symphony's sources, so I could not verify it.
where_stored:
- Scheduler state: process memory in the BEAM orchestrator.
- Workspaces: local filesystem under workspace.root. With the SSH worker extension, workspace.root is on the remote host (SPEC Appendix A).
- Logs: an OTP rotating disk_log at ./log/symphony.log, 10 MB x 5 files by default, root changeable with --logs-root (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/lib/symphony_elixir/log_file.ex).
- Durable work record: the external issue tracker (Linear, GitHub Issues, Jira Cloud, Asana or GitLab adapters; elixir/README.md) and the git host (branches and PRs).
- No database. Ecto appears in mix.exs but the source uses it only for config schema validation, not persistence (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/mix.exs).
format_and_model:
The domain model (SPEC §4) has these entities: Issue, Workflow Definition, Service Config, Workspace, Run Attempt, Live Session, Retry Entry and Orchestrator Runtime State.
- Issue fields: id, identifier, title, description, priority, state, branch_name, url, labels, blocked_by, dispatchable, timestamps and an opaque native_ref.
- Internal claim states: Unclaimed, Claimed, Running, RetryQueued, Released.
- Run-attempt phases: PreparingWorkspace through Succeeded, Failed, TimedOut, Stalled, CanceledByReconciliation (§7).
- Workspace key: the sanitized issue identifier ([A-Za-z0-9._-]), plus a hash suffix of at least 64 bits when sanitizing changed it (§4.2).
- Logs: single-line key=value text.
- Observability API: JSON at /api/v1/state, /api/v1/<identifier> and /api/v1/refresh (§13.7).
- Workpad: free-form Markdown in a tracker comment, not a structured or append-only log.
- Workflow: Markdown with YAML front matter, hot-reloaded on change (§6.2).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is one authoritative orchestrator per deployment. "The orchestrator serializes state mutations through one authority to avoid duplicate dispatch" (SPEC §7.4). Claims live only in memory. The spec has no design for several orchestrators sharing one board. My inference: two instances on the same board would race, because nothing writes a lock to the tracker. Concurrency is bounded per process: a global limit, per-state limits and a per-SSH-host cap (§8.3, Appendix A).
Each issue gets its own isolated workspace, so agents don't share a working tree. Code merging goes through ordinary git and the PR flow, driven by the agent's repo skills (pull, push, land under .codex/skills). The workflow tells the agent to sync with origin/main before editing and to land approved PRs (elixir/WORKFLOW.md).
The tracker workpad comment is edited in place by a single agent per issue. Last write wins, and there is no merge semantics. The linear_graphql tool adds "no idempotency key, retry, scope guard, or rate-limit policy" (elixir/README.md).
realtime: This is polling, not push. The tracker is polled every polling.interval_ms (5000 ms in the sample WORKFLOW.md), and each tick reconciles running issues first, then dispatches (§8.1). Codex app-server events stream to the orchestrator over stdio (§10.3), locally or over SSH. The optional Phoenix LiveView dashboard shows live runtime state, and so does the JSON API (§13.7, elixir/README.md). Changing an issue's state in the tracker stops its run on the next reconcile (§14.4). Nothing replicates session history between machines in real time.
search_retrieval:
There is no search or recall feature. Retrieval options are:
- The JSON debug endpoint per issue identifier.
- Grepping the key=value logs by issue_id, issue_identifier or session_id. The logging guide's stated goal is "Make logs searchable by issue and session" (elixir/docs/logging.md).
- Reading the tracker workpad comment and the PR.
Continuity between turns comes from the Codex thread: continuation turns go to the same live thread, and the task prompt is not re-sent (§7.1). After a restart or retry, continuity comes only from the preserved workspace and the workpad. The prompt tells the agent to "Resume from the current workspace state" (elixir/WORKFLOW.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
The links are weak and indirect. Logs tie session_id (Codex thread-turn) to issue_id and issue_identifier (§13.1). The issue ties to code because the agent attaches the PR URL to the tracker issue and records commit and validation summaries in the workpad comment (elixir/WORKFLOW.md). Issue.branch_name passes tracker branch metadata into the prompt (§4.1.1). The before_remove hook closes open PRs for the workspace's branch when the issue is cleaned up (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/elixir/lib/mix/tasks/workspace.before_remove.ex).
No prompt or transcript is stored with, or hashed into, commits, git notes or PRs. The PR body format is enforced by a pr_body.check task, but it holds proof of work, not session history.
privacy_security:
Each implementation sets its own trust boundary (SPEC §15.1). The reference implementation is aimed at trusted environments.
Secrets (§15.3):
- Config supports $VAR indirection.
- Tokens must not be logged, and secrets are checked for presence without being printed.
- Tracker tools such as linear_graphql, github_api, jira_rest, asana_api and gitlab_api run host-side with the adapter credential. The Codex child gets the results, never the raw token.
- Adapters declare their secret env names so those can be stripped from the child's environment.
Filesystem safety (§9.5, §15.2): the agent's cwd must equal the per-issue workspace, the workspace must stay under its root, and directory names are sanitized.
Hooks are fully trusted shell scripts, must have timeouts, and their output should be truncated in logs (§15.4).
Defaults: the Elixir README describes rejecting approval and elicitation requests plus a workspace-write sandbox. The repo's own sample WORKFLOW.md, however, runs approval_policy: never, inherits the full shell environment and allows network access.
§15.5 warns that tracker data, repo contents and tool arguments may be untrusted and lists optional hardening steps.
Raw tracker tools are not limited to the configured project: the linear_graphql tool "can access whatever the configured Linear token can access" (elixir/README.md).
Not present: redaction of log or workpad content, encryption at rest, and integrity protection or tamper evidence for any record.
scale:
- Per process: default max_turns 20, and the sample WORKFLOW.md sets max_concurrent_agents 10. Optional SSH worker pools spread runs across hosts (elixir/README.md, SPEC Appendix A).
- Usage claim: some OpenAI teams saw "a 500% increase in landed pull requests during the first three weeks" (Help Net Security, citing OpenAI). I could not fetch the primary OpenAI post (https://openai.com/index/open-source-codex-orchestration-symphony/), which returned 403, so that figure is unverified beyond secondary coverage.
- Popularity: about 27.5k GitHub stars and 2.9k forks as of early October 2026 (repo page).
- Non-goals include a multi-tenant control plane and a distributed job scheduler (§2.2).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/openai/symphony/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn:
Symphony shows the gap ParleyInn fills, and it uses a pattern ParleyInn should copy.
The gap: Symphony deliberately has no durable record. Scheduler state is memory-only and rebuilt on restart by reconciling against outside sources of truth (tracker state plus preserved workspaces). The only lasting narrative of a run is a mutable, last-write-wins Markdown "workpad" comment in a third-party SaaS tracker, plus a PR. Nothing is append-only, hash-chained, redacted or treated as untrusted, and continuity across workers or hosts is a cold restart.
Concrete lessons:
(a) Key ParleyInn records by the same join tuple Symphony already logs: tracker issue identifier, then sanitized workspace key, then session_id (<thread_id>-<turn_id>). A local ParleyInn record could then sit under an orchestrator like Symphony and give it exact recall of history across restarts and SSH hosts, which the tracker-driven rebuild cannot.
(b) Copy the "host-side tool, child never sees the credential" boundary, and the rule that derived state must be rebuildable from an authoritative source. Unlike Symphony, that source should be ParleyInn's own local append-only record, never a networked tracker. Symphony needs network access and its workpad sits in Linear, both of which I4 rules out for ParleyInn's core.
(c) Don't treat a tracker comment or PR body as the history channel. It is mutable, writable by anyone with tracker access, and it flows straight back into the next agent prompt. That is exactly the untrusted-content-to-model path that I2 forbids.

name: OpenClaw memory (memory-core plugin, builtin SQLite engine)
status: shipped
license: MIT, copyright OpenClaw Foundation (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw). The repo page showed about 391k stars, about 104k commits and 5,000+ open issues when fetched in October 2026 (same URL). The repo page did not show the latest release date, so that is unverified.
what_is_stored:
Memory is files that people and the agent can both edit. The docs say "The model only remembers what gets saved to disk; there is no hidden state" (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory). The files are:
- MEMORY.md: curated long-term facts.
- USER.md: optional user profile.
- memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md or memory/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md: daily notes. Today's and yesterday's notes load automatically on /new or /reset.
- DREAMS.md: a consolidation diary meant only for human review.
- memory/imports/<source>/: memory imported from Codex, Claude Code (~/.claude/projects/*/memory/*.md) or Hermes. It is indexed for search but never merged into MEMORY.md (same URL).

Session transcripts are stored separately as JSONL (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace). The architecture page sorts all of this into five tiers (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture):
- Instructions: written by humans only.
- Curated core: MEMORY.md and USER.md.
- Episodic: daily notes and transcripts.
- Prospective: standing intents, kept in SQLite.
- Review: DREAMS.md, never injected into the model.

An SQLite index sits beside the files. It holds chunks, embeddings, FTS5 data and provenance columns (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin).
where_stored:
Working-tree files in the agent workspace, ~/.openclaw/workspace by default. OPENCLAW_WORKSPACE_DIR, OPENCLAW_PROFILE or per-agent config can move it (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace).

Local state lives under ~/.openclaw/. Each agent has an SQLite database at ~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin). Two pages give different transcript paths:
- ~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/sessions/*.jsonl (https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security/secrets-and-storage)
- under agents/<agentId>/agent/ (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace)

Optional index backends: Honcho and LanceDB (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory). Everything stays on the user's hardware (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw). The default embedding provider is OpenAI, though, so chunk text is sent to a remote API unless the user picks a local provider or provider "none" (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-search).

For backup the docs say to put the workspace in a private git repo, and never to commit ~/.openclaw (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace).
format_and_model:
Memory files are plain Markdown. Daily logs are append-style, one file per day. MEMORY.md is curated and gets rewritten by the "dreaming" consolidation. Entries can carry inline HTML-comment metadata, for example `<!-- trigger: a, b --> <!-- importance: 9 -->` (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture).

Transcripts are JSONL. The index is an SQLite database at agent schema 23. It stores:
- chunks of 400 tokens with 80 tokens of overlap
- an FTS5/BM25 table with stable integer chunk IDs
- full-precision float64 vectors as BLOBs, plus a float32 sqlite-vec index
- provenance columns, kept apart from the Markdown text (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin)

Provenance has these fields (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture):
- origin class, from the closed set owner, agent, untrusted, system
- session kind: interactive, cron, heartbeat or sub-agent
- timestamps
- supersession keys

The files are the source of truth and the index can be rebuilt from them with `openclaw memory index --force` (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory). Nothing in the sources describes hash-chaining or tamper evidence. Daily files are append-style by convention only; the system does not enforce it.
multi_writer_and_merge:
This is a single-host design. The only documented merge mechanism is optimistic concurrency when MEMORY.md is consolidated (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture):
- A content hash is taken while the new version is built and checked again before an atomic rename.
- If an editor or a parallel session changed the file in between, the rewrite aborts and an append-only fallback runs instead.
- The pre-image is kept and a summary is appended to DREAMS.md. The docs call the remaining race "milliseconds wide and recoverable".

Several agents can share a workspace. When they do, promotion uses the smallest bootstrap budget among them (same URL).

Sync across machines is left to the user's own private git repo. Moving to a new machine means cloning that repo and, optionally, copying the SQLite database to keep session history (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace). The sources describe no CRDT, no merge driver and no handling of concurrent edits across machines.
realtime: Local only. The index watches the files through native filesystem events with a 1.5 s debounce. Where native events are unavailable it polls, at intervals of no less than 30 s, and searches also pick up changes incrementally (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin). Nothing replicates memory between machines or users in real time; the git backup is manual and asynchronous (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace).
search_retrieval:
The agent has these tools (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory):
- memory_search: hybrid search.
- memory_get: reads a file or a line range.
- intent: standing intents.
- sessions_search and sessions_history: transcript search, with visibility checked on every request.

Ranking is hybrid relevance (vector plus BM25) times a recency decay with a 30-day half-life, times an importance multiplier. Diversity comes from MMR with lambda 0.7 and Jaccard overlap, over up to 400 candidate chunks. MEMORY.md, USER.md and undated files are "evergreen" and do not decay (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-search). Ranked search makes no model call at query time. Trigger-phrase prefiltering uses a threshold of about 0.72, and at most 3 trigger entries are injected per turn (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture).

Transcript indexing is opt-in: set experimental.sessionMemory and add "sessions" to sources. Its scope is set by tools.sessions.visibility, one of agent, tree or self (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-search). Vector queries run in a read-only sqlite-vec subprocess and fall back to in-process cosine similarity. After a 30 s deadline, search returns whatever keyword results are ready (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin).

Before compaction, a silent "memory flush" turn asks the agent to write important context to the memory files (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory).
links_sessions_to_code: Only weakly. When a session runs inside a git repository, memory annotations record the project identity as the normalized `origin` remote. Each session keeps up to 4 recently active repo keys in LRU order, and these are not persisted. Project scope affects ranking and trigger eligibility but does not partition the files (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture). Nothing in the sources links prompts or sessions to commits, diffs or file lines.
scale:
No published scale claims or benchmarks. Documented limits and knobs:
- 400-token chunks, 400 MMR candidates, a 30 s tool deadline (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-search, https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin)
- at most 2 sqlite-vec subprocesses per database (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-builtin)
- bootstrap token budgets; when MEMORY.md exceeds its budget, a truncated copy is injected (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory)

The project itself is very large (about 391k stars) but that says nothing about memory scale (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw).
privacy_security:
Session boundaries:
- MEMORY.md should load only "in the main, private session (not shared/group contexts)" (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent-workspace).
- Curated files are auto-injected only in sessions that pass a provenance check. Episodic memory is never auto-injected and is reachable only by explicit search (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture).

Poisoning defenses (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-architecture):
- Origin labels live in SQLite columns the model cannot forge and are never parsed from prose.
- Content with origin untrusted or system is structurally excluded from promotion into curated memory, before any prompt is built.
- Taint spreads per turn: a tool result from a network source marks the whole turn untrusted until the next user message.
- Content that was injected is marked so it cannot be re-extracted as new memory, which stops recall loops.
- The docs cite benchmarks finding that agents do better the less they retrieve automatically.

Deletion and admission (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-provenance):
- `memory forget` takes explicit session IDs, requires a mandatory dry run, and records the sessions as forgotten so they are not re-ingested.
- It does not remove original transcripts, paraphrases, backups or untracked memories.
- An admission policy can stop future ingestion from sources such as gmail, email and webhook.

Secrets and encryption (https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security/secrets-and-storage):
- Pattern-based log and transcript redaction is always on, with custom patterns via logging.redactPatterns.
- Transcripts may still contain "pasted secrets, file contents, command output".
- Recommended permissions are 700 on ~/.openclaw and 600 on the config file.
- There is no built-in encryption at rest; the docs recommend full-disk encryption.

Network: embeddings default to a remote provider (OpenAI) (https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/memory-search).
lesson_for_parinn:
Keep trust labels as structured index columns the model cannot write, never as text inside the content, and gate on them before any ranking or prompt assembly. OpenClaw sets an origin class (owner, agent, untrusted, system) and a session kind as SQLite columns at index time. Taint spreads to the whole turn when a tool result comes from the network, and untrusted rows are dropped before scoring, so no amount of recall frequency can promote them. ParleyInn could do the same with a closed-set origin field on each record that only ParleyInn writes, and make "untrusted never reaches a restore block" a structural filter rather than a heuristic.

OpenClaw also shows the weak spot. Its consolidation rewrites MEMORY.md in place under a content-hash check, falls back to append when that check fails, and syncs across machines through a hand-managed private git repo. That gives no tamper evidence and no multi-writer merge. ParleyInn's hash-chained, append-only log fills exactly that gap.

One more point: OpenClaw's default embedding provider is a remote API, which would break I4. ParleyInn's search must default to keyword-only (FTS5/BM25), with any embeddings local and opt-in.

name: OpenCode /share (session share links)
status: shipped
license: MIT for the client and the share server: LICENSE plus packages/enterprise in https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode (I cloned sst/opencode; its README now links to anomalyco/opencode). The hosted service at opncd.ai is SaaS. The org-account "/api/shares" backend is not in the repo, so its license and code cannot be checked.
what_is_stored: A public, mutable snapshot of one session. It is a flat JSON array of tagged items: "session" (title, version, timestamps, summary, projectID and the absolute local `directory` path), every "message" (role, model and provider, tokens, cost, agent, path, error), every "part" (text, reasoning, file, patch, compaction, step-start/finish and tool parts with full `state.input` and `state.output`, for example bash commands with their output, file reads and edits), a "session_diff" (per-file patches; an older share I sampled had full `before`/`after` file contents), and a "model" list (model metadata: api, capabilities, cost, limits; `headers` and `options` were empty in that sample). Sources: share-next.ts Data union and full() https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/share/share-next.ts ; the docs say it includes "Full conversation history, All messages and responses, Session metadata" https://opencode.ai/docs/share/ . I checked the field list by fetching the repo's own test fixture share https://opncd.ai/api/share/Jsj3hNIW/data on 2026-10-02, looking only at field names: 2,165 items, 8.15 MB. On the client, a `session_share` table keeps (session_id, share id, secret, url) https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/core/src/share/sql.ts .
where_stored: Local first: sessions live in a SQLite database, opencode.db (WAL), under the XDG data dir (~/.local/share/opencode) https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/core/src/database/database.ts . The troubleshooting docs still describe the older per-project JSON storage/ folders https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/web/src/content/docs/troubleshooting.mdx . A shared copy goes to a server/cloud object store. In the current version ("ShareNext") the default base URL is https://opncd.ai, which `enterprise.url` overrides. That host is a SolidStart app on Cloudflare backed by an R2 bucket ("EnterpriseStorage"), with keys share/<id>.json and share_snapshot/<id>.json https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/infra/enterprise.ts https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/enterprise/src/core/storage.ts . A user logged into an org account is routed instead to that account's URL at /api/shares, with a Bearer token and an x-org-id header (share-next.ts lines 205-222). That backend is closed or not in the repo. The legacy generation still serves old shares: api.opencode.ai, a Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per share plus R2, viewed at opencode.ai/s/<id> https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/function/src/api.ts . I confirmed by curl on 2026-10-02 that both legacy endpoints still return data.
format_and_model: An entity-snapshot model, not an event log. Each item is {type, data}, keyed by "session", "message/<msgID>", "part/<msgID>/<partID>", "session_diff" or "model". The server keeps one JSON array per share. Each sync reads that array, merges the incoming items into a Map by key (last write wins per key), sorts by key, and rewrites the whole object to R2 (Share.sync/merge) https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/enterprise/src/core/share.ts . An earlier server format kept share_event/<id>/... objects plus a share_compaction snapshot. That format is now read only, as a migration fallback (`legacy()` in the same file). The share id is the last 8 characters of the session id (`sessionID.slice(-8)`). The session id is "ses_" plus 12 hex characters of time and counter, plus random base62 https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/schema/src/identifier.ts . Write access is a random UUID secret returned at create time. The server returns the URL `https://<host>/share/<id>` https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/enterprise/src/routes/api/%5B...path%5D.ts . The docs still say `opncd.ai/s/<share-id>`, but on 2026-10-02 opncd.ai/s/<id> rendered a "Not Found" page (HTTP 200) while /share/<id> worked. The repo's own test labels /s/ the "legacy format" https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/test/cli/import.test.ts .
multi_writer_and_merge: There is one writer by design: whoever holds the per-share secret, stored in the local session_share table, can sync or delete. The client queues updates per session, dedupes them by entity key and flushes once after a 1 s delay (share-next.ts line 142). On the server, merging is a whole-entity overwrite per key. There is no CRDT, no versioning, and no ETag or conditional write on the read-modify-write of the R2 snapshot. From the code I infer that concurrent syncs for the same share can lose updates. Each sync also rewrites the entire snapshot, so the bytes written grow roughly with the square of session length. Nothing exists for many agents or many machines writing one shared history. Collaboration means read-only viewing. `opencode import <url>` copies a share into another user's local database as a separate session, and the fork never syncs back https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/import.ts .
realtime: The client side is near real time. In manual or auto mode, after a share is created, the client watches Session.Updated, Message.Updated, PartUpdated and Session.Diff events and pushes debounced batches about 1 s apart; Session.Deleted triggers unshare (share-next.ts lines 180-200). The current opncd.ai viewer is not live. It is a server-rendered snapshot with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=86400` and session_status hard-coded to "idle". It embeds the full snapshot inline (8.16 MB page for the fixture) https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/enterprise/src/routes/share/%5BshareID%5D.tsx . The legacy generation was live: each publish went to a per-share Durable Object, which fanned it out to viewers over a WebSocket (/share_poll) with auto-reconnect (api.ts lines 16-66, 165-175; packages/web/src/components/Share.tsx). The enterprise docs say shared data "is cached on the edge near your users" https://opencode.ai/docs/enterprise/ .
search_retrieval: There is no search. Retrieval is by share id only: GET /api/share/<id>/data returns the whole flat array, CORS * and CDN-cached. An unknown id returns HTTP 200 with [] (verified by curl on 2026-10-02). Pages carry robots noindex/nofollow. `opencode import <share-url|file.json>` rebuilds the session, messages and parts into the local SQLite database https://opencode.ai/docs/cli/ https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/import.ts .
links_sessions_to_code: Only loosely, through URLs in GitHub text, not through commits. (1) The share carries session_diff file patches and any patch or edit tool parts. (2) The OpenCode GitHub Action shares by default on public repos and not on private ones unless `share: true`. It appends "[opencode session](https://opencode.ai/s/<id>) | [github run](...)" plus a social-card image to its issue and PR comments https://opencode.ai/docs/github/ https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/github.handler.ts (lines 515-519, 1356-1365). (3) `opencode pr <n>` checks out the PR, regex-scans the PR body for `https://opncd.ai/s/<id>`, imports that session and resumes it https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/pr.ts . The URL formats disagree across the code: the Action posts opencode.ai/s/, pr.ts matches only opncd.ai/s/, and import's parser accepts only /share/. From reading the code, I infer this chain probably breaks for current links; I did not test it end to end. No commit trailers, git notes or SHAs tie a session to code.
scale: I found no official scale claims. Observed on 2026-10-02: one share was 2,165 entities and 8.15 MB of JSON stored as a single object and served as one 8.16 MB page. That points to a design aimed at viewing single sessions, not at large or long-lived histories.
privacy_security: Anyone with the link can read a share; the docs note says "Shared conversations are publicly accessible to anyone with the link" https://opencode.ai/docs/share/ . The id is 8 base62 characters derived from the session id (about 47 bits, slightly modulo-biased), so anyone who knows a session id knows its share URL. Write and delete use a UUID secret compared with `!==`, not constant-time (share.ts lines 137, 164). A support endpoint allows admin removal with SUPPORT_API_KEY. Nothing is redacted on /share: tool outputs, file contents, diffs and the absolute local directory path are uploaded as is. `opencode export --sanitize` does exist, but it replaces whole text fields with [redacted:...] placeholders and is not used by /share https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/export.ts . There is no client-side or end-to-end encryption, only TLS in transit. Encryption at rest depends on Cloudflare R2, which I did not verify. The docs' answer is "Only share conversations that don't contain sensitive information". /unshare deletes the R2 objects, but CDN caching (s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=86400) means copies can outlive the deletion for a while (inferred from the headers). Controls: `"share": "manual"|"auto"|"disabled"` in opencode.json, which can be committed to enforce a team policy (schema https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/1ddb0873aee50d209d1a8d7f91b89c5daf692d49/packages/core/src/v1/config/config.ts ); env OPENCODE_DISABLE_SHARE and OPENCODE_AUTO_SHARE; `enterprise.url` to point at another server. The share page claims "Restricted to users authenticated through SSO only" and "Self-hosted" options. The enterprise docs say self-hosting share pages "is currently on our roadmap" and recommend disabling sharing https://opencode.ai/docs/enterprise/ . I could not verify the SSO restriction in public code, because the org /api/shares backend is not in the repo. Separately, `opencode import`/`opencode pr` pull remote, untrusted session JSON straight into a local session the agent then resumes, with no sanitisation. That is a prompt-injection path.
lesson_for_parinn: Treat a share as a derived, redacted projection pushed one way, never as the record, and never as a source to resume from. OpenCode overwrites a mutable last-write-wins JSON snapshot on a CDN and cannot recall it once cached. It uploads unredacted tool output, and its import/pr path turns someone else's share into model context. For ParleyInn, sharing should be opt-in per session (manual by default, with a `disabled` policy committed in the repo, as opencode.json allows). It should be built from the hash-chained log through the same redaction pipeline (I6 audited), sent as content-addressed, idempotent events rather than whole-snapshot rewrites, and any imported share should come back as pull-only, enveloped, untrusted recall (I2), never as a resumable session. The idea worth copying is OpenCode's stable per-entity keys (session, message/<id>, part/<msg>/<id>) for at-least-once sync.

name: OpenCode snapshots and sessions (anomalyco/opencode, formerly sst/opencode)
category: agent CLI snapshot (separate git object DB) plus local session store
status: shipped
