what_is_stored: Two separate stores. (1) Snapshots are full git trees of the session's active directory: tracked files plus non-ignored untracked files up to 2 MiB each. They are taken before each model call and again when the step succeeds or fails (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/). In the source, snapshot.track() runs at stream start, step-start and step-finish. The returned tree hash is written into the step-start and step-finish message parts (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts). The 2 MiB cap is `limit = 2 * 1024 * 1024` in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/snapshot/index.ts. (2) Sessions store a lot. Session rows hold title, slug, parent_id for subagent sessions, workspace_id, version, share_url, diff summaries, token counts, a revert state, the permission ruleset, agent and model. Messages and parts are JSON blobs. There are also todos, shares, projects and accounts (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/core/src/session/sql.ts, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/storage/schema.ts). Older builds also wrote session_diff and tool-output files (https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/22110).
where_stored: All local, under the XDG data dir (~/.local/share/opencode). Snapshots live in a separate bare git dir at <data>/snapshot/<projectID>/<hash(worktree)>, driven with --git-dir/--work-tree against the user's worktree (snapshot/index.ts, line ~71). The source says this "does not create commits, move branches, or intentionally change your repository's index" (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/). It sets objects/info/alternates to the user repo's object store and seeds its index from the repo's index, so blob hashes are reused on huge repos (snapshot/index.ts, lines ~195-231). Sessions are in SQLite in current code: drizzle sqliteTable definitions, located with `opencode db path` (https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/oh-my-opencode@4.18.2/dist/skills/coding-agent-sessions/references/opencode.md). Earlier versions used one JSON file per entity: storage/session/<projectID>/<sessionID>.json, message/<sessionID>/<msgID>.json, part/<msgID>/<partID>.json, session_diff/<sessionID>.json, share/, project/ (https://forums.basehub.com/anomalyco/opencode/15). A JSON Storage module with migrations still ships (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/storage/storage.ts). I could not find the exact version or date of the JSON-to-SQLite cutover.
format_and_model: Snapshot: a git tree object made by `git add --all` plus `write-tree`. No commits and no refs. A step is identified by its tree hash. Patch = names changed between two trees (`diff --cached --name-only`). Restore and revert check out paths from a tree. Revert touches only paths attributed to assistant steps after the chosen boundary, and deletes files those steps created (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/; snapshot/index.ts interface: track/patch/restore/revert/diff/diffFull). Sessions: relational SQLite with session -> message -> part, cascade deletes, and message.data/part.data as JSON text columns (core/session/sql.ts). It is a mutable CRUD store: rows are updated in place, and the revert state is a column on the session. There is no append-only log and no hash chain.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single machine only. Within one process, a semaphore per gitdir serializes snapshot git operations (`lock(state.gitdir).withPermits(1)`, snapshot/index.ts line ~165). There is one snapshot gitdir per project and worktree pair (Hash.fast(ctx.worktree)), so separate worktrees don't collide. There is no merge of session history between machines or users. Snapshot trees are never pushed and have no refs, so they cannot be fetched or merged with git. I found no documented cross-machine sync of the local SQLite store.
realtime: Local: snapshots are taken synchronously around each model step. Remote: only through opt-in sharing. /share, or share:"auto", syncs the conversation to OpenCode's servers at opncd.ai/s/<id>. The default is manual, and sharing can be set to "disabled" (https://opencode.ai/docs/share/). In code, the share module subscribes to session, message, part, session_diff and model events. It merges updates per session in a queue keyed by item and flushes after a 1 s delay as a POST to <baseUrl>/api/.../<shareID>/sync carrying a per-share secret. baseUrl defaults to https://opncd.ai or the enterprise URL (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/share/share-next.ts). The flow is one-way, viewer only; there is no co-editing.
search_retrieval: No built-in full-text search over history was found in the docs I read. Retrieval means listing or continuing sessions (`opencode session list --format json`) or running SQL directly against the db at `opencode db path` (https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/oh-my-opencode@4.18.2/dist/skills/coding-agent-sessions/references/opencode.md). Snapshot diffs are retrieved by tree hash (diff/diffFull in snapshot/index.ts) for /undo, /redo and UI diffs (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, closely but locally. Every step-start and step-finish part records a snapshot tree hash, and patch parts list the files changed in the step. That gives an exact step-to-file-state mapping used for /undo, /redo and per-session diff summaries (processor.ts; https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/). It is not linked to real commits: snapshots never create commits or refs, so nothing reaches the project's git history or a remote. The link is lost once trees are pruned or the machine is gone.
scale: Snapshots: an hourly cleanup loop runs `git gc --prune=7.days` on the snapshot gitdir (snapshot/index.ts: `const prune = "7.days"`, `Schedule.spaced(Duration.hours(1))`). Unreferenced trees therefore become collectable after about 7 days. Large-repo tuning includes feature.manyFiles, index.version 4, untrackedCache and object alternates, with chromium named in a comment (snapshot/index.ts lines ~195-336). Sessions: no automatic retention. One user measured ~5.1 GB after ~5 months: part/ ~966 MB in 30,122 files, session_diff/ ~989 MB, message/ ~497 MB, or about 500 MB/month. They asked for `opencode session prune`, and the issue was closed as not planned on 2026-04-12 (https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/22110). Unverified: whether the SQLite move changed that growth rate.
privacy_security: Nothing is encrypted at rest. Plain SQLite or JSON plus git objects sit in the user's data dir. I found no redaction or secret scrubbing in the snapshot or share paths I read. Snapshots copy every non-ignored file up to 2 MiB, including untracked .env-like files unless they are gitignored (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/). Sharing uploads the full history to opncd.ai. The docs only advise users to "only share conversations that don't contain sensitive information" and to unshare later. Shared data persists until removed. Enterprise can disable sharing, require SSO, or self-host (https://opencode.ai/docs/share/). Recalled history is not treated as untrusted; it is replayed as normal conversation context (inferred from the session model; no explicit doc found). The docs warn that snapshots are "a convenience, not a transaction or backup" and cannot undo shell or database side effects (https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots/).
lesson_for_parinn: A shadow git dir driven with --git-dir/--work-tree, sharing blobs with the user repo through objects/info/alternates, gives cheap code state per step without touching the user's index, refs or remotes. ParleyInn could record a tree hash in each hash-chained step event and get exact session-to-code linkage without writing to the repo. Two cautions from OpenCode: trees with no refs are lost to gc (OpenCode prunes after 7 days), so ParleyInn must pin what its record references (a private ref namespace, or a bundle) to keep I10 rebuildability. And ParleyInn needs retention and size accounting from day one: OpenCode's unbounded ~500 MB/month store, with a prune request closed as not planned, is the failure to avoid. Under I4, ParleyInn should do this through a git library or plumbing behind an interface, not os/exec.
license: MIT (repository license; not re-verified via API in this session because GitHub API access to anomalyco/opencode was not enabled)
confidence: high for snapshot mechanics (read from source on dev branch and official docs); medium for session storage format (source shows SQLite via drizzle, but the cutover version/date and the current growth profile are unverified)

name: OpenFab (openfab/generation in-toto predicate)
status: beta. The Phase-0 MVP code is public. The README calls the build 'v0.3', while Cargo.toml says 0.1.0. The predicate itself is a draft: v0.1, rev 0.1.5. History runs from 2026-06-10 to 2026-09-29: 131 commits by 2 authors ('csheargm' and an 'OpenFab Builder' identity), last commit 13fd0a8. It has about 6 stars and 0 forks. Registration upstream is still a proposal. in-toto/attestation issue #604 was opened 2026-09-30 by csheargm and is open with no visible comments. An earlier OpenSSF TAC discussion, ossf/tac #628 (opened 2026-06-30 by chrisxie-fw), showed as closed in one fetch; I could not verify why it closed or what was decided. Signing through Sigstore, Rekor and Fulcio is planned as a 'production swap' and is not implemented.
what_is_stored:
Per generated release (one spec id plus version), OpenFab stores:
(1) A signed attestation, `<spec-id>-v<version>.att.json`, holding an in-toto Statement v1. Its subject is the SHA-256 of the sorted 'path:sha256' lines of the changed files. Its predicate (type https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1) holds:
- spec_ref
- builder {id, base}
- agent {did:key, base, model, optional id 'AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION', optional tools}
- prompt_sha256: a hash only, never the prompt text
- params
- generated[] entries {path, lines 'N' or 'A-B', sha256, author ai|human}. Ranges for one path must not overlap.
- materials[] {uri, sha256?}
- acceptance_passed
- acceptance[]: the frozen shell checks, re-runnable
- timestamp
- signoffs[] {did, name, timestamp}
(2) A CycloneDX-style SBOM, `<spec-id>-v<version>.sbom.json`.
(3) Generated source files plus commit trailers.
(4) Local run-state per run under .openfab/runs/<id>/, never committed: run.json, spec.yaml, timeline.md (the decision log), events.jsonl, status.json and prompt.txt (the full prompt in plaintext).
(5) Local identity seeds and allowlists: .openfab/identity/*.seed, .openfab/maintainers/<name>.seed, .openfab/allow/{maintainers,fab}.json.

The reference implementation does not do what the spec and the discovery note describe for authorship:
- It emits whole-file ranges ('1-N') tagged only 'ai' (spec_cycle.rs, around line 403).
- add_signoff never adds 'human' ranges, although a code comment says sign-off adds the human tag later.
- The TODO admits that `attest` records author: ai with no per-line mix.

So per-range ai/human attribution is specified but not produced in practice.
where_stored:
Split between the working tree in git and local files.
- Committed: the attestation and SBOM go in the repo's provenance/ directory, on a forge branch: `openfab/<spec>-v<ver>` for releases, `openfab/draft/<run>` for unsigned drafts. They are committed together with the generated code and opened as a pull request on GitHub, Forgejo, Gitea, GitCode or a local git 'forge'.
- Not committed: everything under .openfab/ (runs, prompts, timelines, seeds, allowlists) is control-plane state that is never committed. ops.rs export text says 'LOCAL RUN-STATE (OpenFab's own notes — NOT committed to the artifact repo)'. The local forge's `git clean` excludes .openfab.
- Commit trailers link each commit to its attestation: Spec, Assisted-by, OpenFab-Base, OpenFab-Attestation=<payload_sha256>, OpenFab-Acceptance.
- No git notes, no custom refs and no separate store.
format_and_model:
The file is JSON and the envelope is 'DSSE-style', not DSSE. The file holds {payload_type, payload_sha256, statement (in the clear), signatures[{keyid: did:key, sig: base64 ed25519, algo, role: fab|human-signoff}]}. There is no PAE and no base64 payload; v0.2 intends to adopt real DSSE as a breaking change.

The signed bytes follow normative canonical JSON, equal to RFC 8785 JCS:
- keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit
- integers only, within the I-JSON safe range
- empty arrays and absent optional fields omitted
- verifiers must build preimages from the received statement bytes and refuse duplicate keys

Signature coverage:
- The fab signature and payload_sha256 cover the statement with signoffs removed.
- The n-th human-signoff signature covers the statement with signoffs truncated to the first n records, its own included.
- Record n's did must equal the n-th signoff keyid.
- N-of-M counts distinct verified keys.

The rev 0.1.4 coverage rule broke older sign-off signatures. Conformance is pinned two ways: a golden canonical vector (756 bytes, sha256 7051cb70…) and four signed vectors in docs/vectors/ with published test keys, cross-verified in CI between the Rust and browser (WebCrypto) implementations.

did:key is ed25519: 'z' + base58btc(0xed01 || pubkey), so verification needs no keystore.

The JSON Schema file lags the prose spec: its $id uses openfab.ai rather than open-fab.ai, and it omits acceptance[] and agent.id/tools.

The data model is versioned snapshots. Each version is its own attestation, and there is no cryptographic chaining yet: parent_attestation_sha256 is a v0.2 TODO, and lineage lives only as parent_run in local run.json.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Designed for a single writer, with gated human approval on top.
- One fab key signs at build time.
- Each sign-off loads the attestation from the run branch, appends a record plus signature, rewrites the same JSON file, and commits it with an 'OpenFab-Signoff: <did>' trailer.
- Because the n-th signature covers the first n records, the order of sign-offs is part of what is signed. Two maintainers signing on different clones would both append record n to the same array, producing a textual git conflict and signatures that are invalid after any reorder. I found no merge driver, rebase or reconcile logic.
- Within one host, the web server holds a global lock that serializes git-touching operations (run, feedback, signoff).
- Concurrent runs are kept apart only by per-spec-version branches and file names.
- In the MVP all maintainer seeds live under .openfab/maintainers/ on the machine running OpenFab, so N-of-M is not key-separated across people. The documented production swap is Sigstore OIDC for human identities.
- Merging into main happens locally for local forges, or through the forge's own UI or API once the gate opens.
realtime:
Not real-time across machines.
- Locally, a background thread appends timeline events to .openfab/runs/<id>/events.jsonl and status.json, and the web UI polls GET …/events?since=N.
- Between machines, history is shared only by git push and pull requests.
- The TODO lists swarm coordination transport (WebRTC, a relay, or forge issues as a message bus) as an open question.
search_retrieval:
Minimal. Retrieval is by file:
- `openfab verify-file --att provenance/<x>.att.json` verifies offline, without .openfab run-state.
- jq can read the JSON.
- list_runs scans .openfab/runs/*/run.json.
- An 'audit' view runs git log over a run branch and parses the provenance trailers.

There is no index, full-text search or query API over attestations or timelines.
links_sessions_to_code:
Partly, and by hash only.
- Code to attestation: the attestation binds per-file sha256 digests and a source-bundle digest.
- Commit to attestation: the commit points at it through the 'OpenFab-Attestation: <payload_sha256>' trailer. The attestation carries no commit SHA, which is deliberate so it stays forge-agnostic.
- Trailer cross-check: since rev 0.1.5, a verifier that is given Assisted-by trailers MUST check that they match agent.id and agent.tools.
- Prompt: linked only as an unsalted prompt_sha256. The text stays in local prompt.txt, and the spec says it 'can be linked by content-hash' if disclosure is needed.
- No transcript: no agent session id, turn log or Claude Code transcript reference is recorded. The project's own position is 'a manifest, not a transcript'.

Code caveat: when a spec has several task cards, the loop in spec_cycle.rs overwrites `prompt` and `model` on each card. prompt_sha256 and model therefore reflect only the last card.
scale: No scale claims and no benchmarks. This is a Phase-0 MVP: about 8.6k lines of Rust, '51+' tests per the README, and a web UI. Storage is one small JSON attestation per spec version. Each sign-off re-canonicalizes the whole statement. The TODO notes there is no test harness for the web UI and that native bases and live forges are untested against real servers.
privacy_security:
Strengths:
- Prompt text is deliberately kept out of the signed artifact; the reason given is that prompts carry secrets, PII or proprietary context.
- Verification works offline from did:key.
- Received bytes are authoritative and duplicate JSON keys are refused.
- An integer-only value domain avoids cross-language parse differences.
- Embedded acceptance checks are treated as untrusted executable content. The default verify never runs them; `--run-checks` is an explicit opt-in. The spec states that a valid signature does not make a check safe to run.

Weaknesses:
- prompt_sha256 is a bare, unsalted SHA-256, so it can confirm guesses of short or templated prompts.
- There is no redaction pass and no encryption at rest. prompt.txt, timelines and seeds are plaintext files.
- Seeds are raw 32-byte files written with std::fs::write, which uses default permissions rather than enforcing 0600.
- .openfab/identity and .openfab/maintainers are gitignored in OpenFab's own repo. I found no code that adds a .gitignore to target repos, so a user's own `git add -A` could commit seeds. OpenFab itself commits only explicit paths.
- All maintainer keys sit on one host in the MVP.
- The sandbox is a 'gated-host-subprocess': command-prefix allowlist and substring denylist from policy/trust.json plus a timeout, not a container (Podman or gVisor are listed as production).
- No transparency log yet (no Rekor).
license: Apache-2.0
lesson_for_parinn:
If ParleyInn ever writes anything about a session into git, copy OpenFab's 'manifest, not transcript' split and fix its two weak spots.
- What to copy: commit only a small signed record next to the code, bound to file digests and pointed to by a greppable commit trailer. Keep the transcript in ParleyInn's local store.
- Weak spot 1: OpenFab publishes a bare SHA-256 of the prompt, which confirms guesses. ParleyInn should use a keyed or salted commitment, such as an HMAC under a per-project key.
- Weak spot 2: OpenFab appends order-dependent sign-offs to one shared JSON array, which conflicts as soon as two clones write. ParleyInn should write one immutable file per record, or per-writer segments, so concurrent writers never touch the same bytes.
- Also worth borrowing: OpenFab's normative byte rules (JCS canonical form, integer-only values, duplicate keys refused, verify from received bytes) and its 'n-th signature covers the first n records' coverage rule, as a template for specifying ParleyInn's hash chain.

name: OpenHands (Software Agent SDK + Agent Server, Agent Canvas, OpenHands Cloud/Enterprise)
status: shipped. The SDK V1 and Agent Server are live in the MIT repo OpenHands/software-agent-sdk; the clone I read was last committed 2026-10-01 (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk). Agent Canvas is shipped but labelled beta. It now occupies the OpenHands/OpenHands repo and its README badge says 'status-beta' (https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands). OpenHands Cloud is a commercial SaaS and Enterprise is a commercial self-hosted product (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/enterprise-vs-oss.md). Superseded pieces: V0's single trajectory.json is replaced by per-event files (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence.md). The V0 REST API (/api/conversations) is marked deprecated with removal scheduled for 2026-04-01 (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/cloud/cloud-api.md). The Socket.IO 'oh_event' WebSocket page is V0-era (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/developers/websocket-connection.md). docs.all-hands.dev answers HTTP 308 and redirects to docs.openhands.dev (I checked with curl -I).
what_is_stored:
One record per conversation, event-sourced (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.03690v2):
(1) A base-state snapshot holding agent config (LLM settings, tools, MCP servers), execution status, iteration count, stats (tokens and cost), workspace context, activated skills, secrets, custom agent_state, tags and a tree HEAD pointer (leaf_event_id) (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence.md; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/state.py).
(2) Every event: user and agent messages, the system prompt with tool schemas, tool calls (ActionEvent, which carries thought, reasoning and a security-risk rating), tool observations and errors, user rejections, pause events, state-update events, and condensation requests and results (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/events.md).
Compaction does not delete anything. A Condensation event lists forgotten_event_ids plus a summary, and only the LLM 'View' drops those events (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/condenser.md).
The Agent Server also keeps meta.json and an owner_lease.json per conversation, and bash events under workspace/bash_events with optional retention (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/config.py).
Separate opt-in 'persistent memory' lives in Markdown: MEMORY.md plus YYYY-MM-DD.md logs in ~/.openhands/memory/ and <workspace>/.openhands/memory/ (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/persistent-memory.md).
Workspace files are not part of the record. On Enterprise they are deleted along with the sandbox, while the transcript is always kept (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
where_stored:
Plain working-tree-style files on the backend host's local filesystem, not in git.
- SDK: under persistence_dir/<conversation-id>/, with workspace/conversations/ as the default (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence.md).
- Agent Server: under conversations_path, default workspace/conversations (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/config.py).
- CLI: under ~/.openhands/conversations (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/cli/resume.md). That page still shows a single conversation.json per conversation, which contradicts the SDK layout; I treat it as stale but did not verify.
- Agent Canvas is only a browser client. 'Agent Server stores conversation history', and Canvas stores only backend connection info (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/architecture.md). Archive flags live in the browser's localStorage and do not sync across machines (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md).
- Cloud/Enterprise: inside the managed backend. Enterprise needs PostgreSQL databases (openhands, runtime_api_db, automations and others) (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/external-postgres.md). It has conversation_metadata and conversation_cost_events tables, and MinIO object storage is configurable (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/release-notes.md). Which store holds Cloud event payloads is not publicly documented: unverifiable.
- Git is used only by 'Git Sync' for automation definitions (automation.yaml plus an expanded tarball/), never for conversations (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/git-sync.md).
format_and_model:
Event sourcing with a snapshot.
- base_state.json is the whole Pydantic ConversationState minus events. It is rewritten on every public-field change, detected through __setattr__ (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence.md), and written with atomic_write_text (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/io/local.py).
- Events are files named events/event-{idx:05d}-{event_id}.json. The index is padded to at least 5 digits with no upper limit. Each file holds one Pydantic model, serialized with model_dump_json(exclude_none=True) (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/persistence_const.py; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/event_store.py).
- Base Event fields: frozen model with id (uuid4), timestamp (datetime.now().isoformat(), naive local time), source (user|agent|environment) and parent_id (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/base.py).
- The docs say explicitly that source (who produced an event) is independent of LLM role: 'Do not infer event origin from LLM role' (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/events.md).
- History is a tree, not a line. Events that share a parent_id are sibling branches, and leaf_event_id is a movable HEAD. navigate_to() re-roots the active branch while 'all branches stay on disk'. Legacy events with no parent fall back to a linear chain (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/event_store.py; .../impl/local_conversation.py).
- Forks are new conversations that deep-copy events, optionally only up to from_event_id, and record forked_from_event_id (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-fork.md; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/models.py).
- Sidecar files: .eventlog.lock and .eventlog-len-N.marker.
- No content hashes, hash chain or signatures. The index scan stops at the first gap and only logs a warning (event_store.py).
- Exports: Markdown or HTML transcripts named conversation-<id>.md/.html, built in the browser (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md). A trajectory zip of the conversation directory (file_router.py). An example converts events to OpenAI Chat or Responses messages (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
The design is single-writer per conversation, and there is no merge.
- In process: a FIFO lock serializes state updates and event appends (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md).
- Across processes: EventLog.append takes a flock on events/.eventlog.lock with a 30 s timeout. It re-syncs from disk when the length marker shows another writer appended, and rejects duplicate event IDs and unknown parents. The docstring warns that 'file locking via flock() does NOT work reliably on NFS mounts or network filesystems' (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/event_store.py).
- Across Agent Server instances: owner_lease.json records owner_instance_id, a monotonically increasing generation and expires_at (default TTL 45 s), plus host and pid so a dead owner can be taken over and 'stale owners can be fenced off' (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/conversation_lease.py).
- base_state.json is last-writer-wins.
- Divergence happens only through branches or forks. A fork is independent after creation and the source is never modified (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-fork.md). No merge-back operation is documented.
- Child conversations launched with launch_child_conversation stay linked to the parent and return their result to it. Local children get an isolated worktree or share the parent's workspace (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md).
- On Enterprise, several conversations can share one sandbox, which means shared files and credentials, but each keeps its own history (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
- Git Sync (automations only) is bidirectional, and pending local changes win for that cycle (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/git-sync.md).
realtime:
Server-push streaming from the one backend that owns a conversation. The log itself is not replicated.
- RemoteConversation streams events over WebSocket from the Agent Server (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md).
- The endpoint is /sockets/events/{conversation_id}. resend_mode 'all' replays history on connect and 'since' replays events after after_timestamp. Auth is a first frame {"type":"auth","session_api_key":...}; passing the key as a query parameter is deprecated. A PubSub fans events out to many subscribers (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/sockets.py; .../pub_sub.py).
- Canvas shows a live activity chip for the running action (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md).
- On Cloud/Enterprise, clients read events through REST and reconcile status after missed events from the app-conversation record (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
- Persist latency is reported as 0.20 ms median and 0.31 ms P95 per event (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.03690v2).
- Nothing syncs history between separate backends. Switching backends switches which conversations you see (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/backends.md).
search_retrieval:
Structured filters and listing only. No full-text index or semantic search is documented.
- Per-conversation event search: GET .../events/search filters by kind, source, case-insensitive body text and a timestamp range, with up to 100 results per page. A count endpoint exists. There are also conversation search and count routes (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/event_router.py; .../conversation_router.py).
- Cloud/Enterprise V1: GET /api/v1/app-conversations/search, GET /api/v1/conversation/{id}/events/search, and a trajectory download at /api/v1/app-conversations/{id}/download (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md). Enterprise 0.74.0 fixed exports that were capped at 10,000 events (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/release-notes.md).
- In memory, EventLog keeps an id-to-index map and loads event files lazily (event_store.py).
- The CLI's --resume lists the 15 most recent conversations with a preview of the first message (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/cli/resume.md).
- Persistent memory injects only MEMORY.md. Daily logs are read on demand with the agent's file tools (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/persistent-memory.md).
- Optional OpenTelemetry traces group runs by conversation ID in Laminar, Honeycomb and similar tools (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/observability.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Weakly. Code linkage comes from workspace and git context, not from the record.
- The system prompt tells the agent to add 'Co-authored-by: openhands <openhands@all-hands.dev>' to commits. The trailer does not carry a conversation ID (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/context/prompts/sections/static.py).
- The Agent Server can give each conversation a dedicated git worktree under conversation_worktree_root, default /tmp/conversation-worktrees (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/config.py).
- The workspace archive endpoint returns a 'git-delta' patch against a base ref, with X-Archive-Base-Commit, Head-Commit, Branch and Repo-Remote headers 'so consumers can replay the patch' (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/file_router.py).
- Cloud conversations start with selected_repository and selected_branch. Enterprise exposes /git/changes and /git/diff per conversation (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
- Canvas has a Commits drawer showing commits and uncommitted changes for the conversation's workspace (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md).
- Nothing writes conversation history into git: no notes, refs or branches.
scale:
Claims from the SDK tech report (MLSys 2026, arXiv 2511.03690 v2, 2026-04-22) (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.03690v2):
- per-event persist: 0.20 ms median, 0.31 ms P95
- crash recovery: 7.4 ms median, 14.9 ms P95, 32.1 ms max at 358 events
- storage per conversation: 380 KB median, 3.4 MB max
- 61% fewer system-attributable failures, from 78.0 to 30.0 per 1k conversations, over a 15-day production comparison
- 433 SWE-Bench Verified conversations totalling 39,870 events
Product limits:
- Enterprise caps a running session at 12 hours, and it is force-paused after that. Configurable idle and deletion timers then pause the sandbox and, later, permanently delete the conversation and its storage (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
- Enterprise markets 'unlimited parallel agent conversations' (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/enterprise-vs-oss.md).
No figures are published for the number of conversations per backend or for multi-host throughput: unverifiable.
privacy_security:
Secrets at rest (base_state.json):
- With a cipher configured, secrets are Fernet-encrypted. The key is the SHA-256 of OH_SECRET_KEY, falling back to the session API key. Without a cipher they are written as '**********' and lost on restore, with a logged warning. Decryption failures quietly become None (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/utils/cipher.py; .../conversation/state.py; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/config.py).
Secrets in output:
- Known secret values are replaced with '<secret-hidden>' in command output, using a streaming masker that handles values split across chunks. This only catches registered secrets, so an unregistered credential appearing in tool output would be stored in plaintext. That last point is my inference from the value-based design (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/secret_registry.py; https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/secrets.md).
- No at-rest encryption of event files is documented.
Exports:
- The trajectory zip redacts LLM credential fields and any Fernet token on the way out (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/_secret_redaction.py).
- Canvas builds Markdown and HTML exports locally in the browser (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/conversations.md).
Memory injection:
- Persistent memory is injected into the system prompt automatically but wrapped in <UNTRUSTED_CONTENT>, with a warning that it may contain prompt injection. It is capped at about 6,000 characters and excluded from base_state.json (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/persistent-memory.md).
Access, telemetry and tracing:
- The Agent Server authenticates with session API keys.
- Telemetry is consent-gated through OH_TELEMETRY_CONSENT, with exporters none, posthog or http (config.py).
- OpenTelemetry tracing captures prompts and tool I/O to third-party backends when enabled (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/observability.md).
Enterprise:
- When a sandbox is cleaned up, an internal workspace archive is kept for 'debugging, support, and audit trails' and users cannot access it (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/conversations-and-sandboxes.md).
Git Sync (automations):
- Optional per-file encryption, which the docs admit breaks code review and diffs. The access token is encrypted at rest. A private repo is advised (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/git-sync.md).
license: MIT for the SDK, Agent Server and Agent Canvas, per the LICENSE files in both repos (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/LICENSE, https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/blob/main/LICENSE). OpenHands Cloud is a commercial SaaS and Enterprise is commercial (https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise/enterprise-vs-oss.md).
lesson_for_parinn:
Take OpenHands' record shape and leave out its gaps.

The shape worth copying: one append-only directory per session, holding one immutable event per file plus a rebuildable snapshot. Branches are parent_id pointers with a movable HEAD inside the record. Forks deep-copy and record forked_from_event_id. Compaction is a Condensation event, so the log stays lossless and only the view loses detail. Each session has exactly one writer, enforced by a lease with a generation number for fencing. Together these give git-like branching without putting history in git.

The gaps:
- No hash chain. The scan silently truncates at an index gap.
- Timestamps are naive local time.
- Cross-process safety rests on flock, which the code itself says is unreliable on NFS.
- Untrusted memory is auto-injected into the system prompt with only a textual <UNTRUSTED_CONTENT> warning. ParleyInn's I2 forbids exactly this.

OpenHands is deeply tied to GitHub, yet it uses git only for small, reviewable automation definitions, and even there the optional encryption kills diffs. It moves session history over a backend event store with REST/WebSocket and lease fencing. That supports keeping ParleyInn's session record out of git and using git at most as an export or transport for small artifacts.

name: OpenHands conversation EventLog (software-agent-sdk + agent-server)
status: shipped. The SDK is at openhands-sdk 1.50.1 per pyproject on main, with the last commit on 2026-10-02 (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk). The backend now lives in the SDK's agent-server. The OpenHands/OpenHands repo is now the "Agent Canvas" frontend, labelled beta (https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands). Older docs that describe a monolithic OpenHands server persisting events are superseded by this split.
what_is_stored:
Each conversation has two parts:
- A typed event stream. Every event is a pydantic `Event` with `id`, `timestamp`, `source` (agent, user or environment) and `parent_id` (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/event/base.py). Event kinds include MessageEvent, ActionEvent and Observation events, which can be filtered by kind (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/event_router.py).
- A mutable `base_state.json` snapshot. It holds the agent config, execution status, stats, metadata, the secret registry, agent_state and `leaf_event_id`, the HEAD of the active branch (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence ; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/state.py).

Large environment observations go to an `observations/` subdirectory (state.py, `env_observation_persistence_dir`). The docs list what is persisted as "Message History, Agent Configuration, Execution State, Tool Outputs, Statistics, Workspace Context, Activated Skills, Secrets, Agent State" (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence).

Agents running over ACP, including claude-agent-acp (Claude Code) and Gemini CLI, are recorded in the same EventLog (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/agent/acp_agent.py).
where_stored:
Local filesystem, one directory per conversation, behind a pluggable `FileStore` interface (implementations: LocalFileStore, InMemoryFileStore, plus a cache layer) (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/tree/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/io).
- Layout: `<persistence_dir>/<conversation_id>/base_state.json` plus `events/event-{idx:05d}-{event_id}.json`, and the sidecar files `.eventlog.lock` and `.eventlog-len-N.marker` (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/persistence_const.py ; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/event_store.py).
- The agent-server default is `workspace/conversations/<uuid hex>/` (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/config.py).
- Without a persistence_dir the SDK falls back to an in-memory store and warns that the data will not persist (state.py).

OpenHands Cloud exports a conversation as a zip "containing all events and metadata" via `GET /api/v1/app-conversations/{id}/download` (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/cloud/api-reference/conversations/export-conversation.md). Cloud's server-side backing store could not be verified, because the cloud backend code is not in the public repos I checked.
format_and_model:
Event sourcing, one JSON file per event, written by pydantic `model_dump_json(exclude_none=True)`. LocalFileStore writes text files atomically (event_store.py, io/local.py).
- Index: the zero-padded sequence in the file name is the log index, and the UUID is the event id. On open, the log rebuilds its index by listing the directory. It stops at the first gap in the sequence and logs a warning for gaps and duplicate ids (event_store.py `_scan_and_build_index`).
- Docs: EventLog is an "Immutable append-only store with efficient queries", built on "Event sourcing with indexing" (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md).
- Tree history: events carry `parent_id`, so the log is a tree. Navigating or forking moves `leaf_event_id` (HEAD) in base_state.json. Abandoned branches stay on disk, and the active view is `path_to_root(leaf)` (state.py, event_store.py).
- Legacy events without `parent_id` are read as a linear chain, so old logs need no rewrite.
- Integrity: there is no hash chain, signature or MAC on events. Immutability is a convention: nothing in the code stops a file from being edited in place.
- Update paths: there are two, "state-only updates" (base_state.json is rewritten on every public field change via `__setattr__`) and "event-based updates" (append) (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md ; https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/convo-persistence).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Single directory, many local writers, no merge.
- Append: each append takes a file lock (`filelock`, flock-based) on `events/.eventlog.lock` with a 30 s timeout. A count-in-filename marker lets a writer rule out a concurrent append with one `exists()` call. Otherwise it rescans the disk and syncs before assigning the next index (event_store.py).
- Rejected appends: an append is rejected if the event id already exists or its parent_id is unknown.
- Network filesystems: the code says flock "does NOT work reliably on NFS mounts or network filesystems" and that shared-storage deployments need "alternative coordination mechanisms" (event_store.py docstring).
- In-process: a FIFO lock gives "ordered, atomic updates" and "Read operations never block writes" (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md).
- Across agent-server instances: a lease file holding owner, monotonically increasing generation and expiry fences stale owners after a takeover, with guarded writes (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/conversation_lease.py).
- Divergent copies: there is no way to merge two copies of a conversation from different machines. Branching inside one log is supported, but it is not distributed merge.
realtime:
Yes, but only for a live conversation on one server, and not as replication of the store.
- RemoteConversation uses a "WebSocket event stream" (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md). The agent-server exposes `/sockets/events/{conversation_id}` (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/sockets.py).
- WebSocket auth prefers sending the key in the first message, "keeps tokens out of URLs" (sockets.py).
- Callbacks fire after a commit succeeds (conversation.md).
- Persistence uses "Debounced writes, incremental events" (conversation.md).
search_retrieval: Retrieval works by index, by event id, or by walking `path_to_root(leaf, limit)` for a recent window (event_store.py). The agent-server endpoint `GET .../events/search` filters by kind, source, case-insensitive body substring and timestamp range, with sorting and paging up to 100 results. It is a linear scan over the EventLog, with no full-text or vector index. Reads skip the state lock because "events are append-only and immutable once written" (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/event_router.py ; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/event_service.py). Cross-conversation search was not found.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak, and only at the conversation level:
- Settings carry `selected_repository` (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/settings/model.py).
- The agent-server can give each conversation its own git worktree under `conversation_worktree_root` (default `/tmp/conversation-worktrees`) (config.py).

I found no per-event commit SHA, no git notes and no trailers. Nothing writes conversation history into the repository. The link from session to code goes through the workspace and the PRs the agent opens, not through stored metadata.
scale:
No published scale claims. Implementation notes:
- A file per event and a directory listing on open make cold start O(n) in event count.
- The docs cite incremental view maintenance as an optimization, while a branch switch rebuilds the view in O(n) (state.py comments, #3053).
- The LocalFileStore read cache is bounded by `cache_limit_size=max_iterations` (state.py).

No benchmarks were found.
privacy_security:
Secrets:
- The Secret Registry is "Memory-only with masked logging" (https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/conversation.md).
- Known secret values are replaced with `<secret-hidden>` in tool output and in non-tool-call LLM messages before they become events (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/secret_registry.py ; https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/agent/agent.py).
- In base_state.json, secrets are Fernet-encrypted only if a `Cipher` is passed. Without one they are redacted and lost on restore, with a logged warning (state.py `_save_base_state`).
- On trajectory zip export, the agent-server redacts LLM/AWS credential fields and any Fernet token, treating them as "recoverable secret material" (https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-agent-server/openhands/agent_server/_secret_redaction.py ; file_router.py `download-trajectory`).

Not covered:
- Event bodies are plaintext JSON on disk, with no encryption at rest beyond the filesystem's.
- Masking only catches registered secret values, so there is no pattern-based redaction of unknown secrets.
- No integrity protection.
- Recalled events are not treated as untrusted when they go back to the model: the event stream simply is the agent's context.
license: MIT (software-agent-sdk LICENSE, "Copyright (c) 2026 OpenHands contributors"): https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/LICENSE
lesson_for_parinn:
One immutable file per event, named `event-{idx}-{uuid}.json`, plus a separate mutable HEAD pointer (`leaf_event_id`) and `parent_id` links works well:
- Forks and rewinds never rewrite history.
- Legacy linear logs still load.
- A directory of write-once files syncs and exports trivially (zip, or git-friendly since files never change).

ParleyInn should copy the shape, not the trust model. OpenHands relies on flock, which it admits breaks on NFS. It has no hash chain, so an in-place edit cannot be detected, and it treats replayed events as trusted context. ParleyInn should:
- Hash-chain or sign each record (parent hash inside the content-addressed name).
- Make cross-machine sharing a merge of write-once files keyed by id, rather than a lock on shared storage.
- Mask secrets before the append (as OpenHands does with `<secret-hidden>`) and again at every export boundary (as its trajectory redactor does).

name: OpenInfra Foundation Policy for AI Generated Content (Assisted-By / Generated-By commit labels)
category: commit trailer convention (governance policy, not software)
status: shipped. Policy version 0.11.2 (8 July 2025) is still the live text as fetched on 2026-10-02. A March 2026 board-list proposal to add Synthesized-By:, AI-Specification: and AI-Workflow: trailers was not adopted as of this fetch, and a board AI policy working group was formed in April 2026.
what_is_stored: Two kinds of record. (1) Free-text commit trailers. "Assisted-By:" covers predictive, autocomplete or assistive use and minor edits made from a prompt. "Generated-By:" is for patches where "a substantial portion" was produced by a generative tool. Both sit next to the existing DCO "Signed-Off-By:", which "is a statement that you take responsibility for the entire contents of the commit, including any parts that were generated or assisted by AI tools" (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). (2) A prose explanation "in comments or the commit message" of "any prompts or background context the reviewers might need to fully understand the change and how much of the change was generated by the tool" (same URL). No session transcript, prompt log or tool-call record is kept. Version 0.11 (24 June 2025) removed the example commit message from the policy, according to its change history (same URL). Project rules add to this. Nova's contributor docs fix the trailer value as "<tool-name> [model-version]": the tool name is required and the model is optional but recommended. Nova also forbids Co-Authored-By: for AI because it "identifies human co-authors and carries a DCO implication". Its example: "Assisted-By: my-agent my-model-v1 / Signed-off-by: Jane Smith <jane@example.com> / Change-Id: I..." (https://docs.openstack.org/nova/latest/contributor/commit-messages.html). Cinder and Cyborg have similar commit-message pages (https://docs.openstack.org/cinder/latest/contributor/commit-messages.html), but I did not check their wording.
where_stored: The git commit message: trailers plus body, carried with the commit through Gerrit review into the project's git history. The policy applies to "all contributions of content committed into source revision control systems by projects housed under the OpenInfra Foundation" (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). It defines no git notes, refs or side store.
format_and_model: RFC-822-style "Key: value" git trailers in the commit footer, which git interpret-trailers can parse. Data model: per commit, zero or more Assisted-By / Generated-By lines, each naming a tool. Policy v0.11.1 "added clarifications about combining labels" (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). Nova allows one trailer per tool when several tools materially contributed (https://docs.openstack.org/nova/latest/contributor/commit-messages.html). The categories are a human judgement (predictive, generative, assistive) with no machine-checkable threshold. Reviewers are told that if a change "is substantially re-worked by human changes during the code review process, consider whether it makes sense to remove the 'Generated-By' or 'Assisted-By' label prior to committing" (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). So the label is mutable until merge and can be dropped. Rejected proposal (12 Mar 2026, E. Glynn): add "Synthesized-By:", "AI-Specification: docs/specs/my-feature-design.md" (spec file committed in the patch) and "AI-Workflow: handwritten spec, looped generate-evaluate-refine" (https://lists.openinfra.org/archives/list/foundation-board@lists.openinfra.org/thread/B6RFW55FEH2632VD7IEDPCR67TBF7XZQ/).
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable as a storage mechanism. Concurrency is ordinary git/Gerrit: one commit per change, amended through patch sets, with labels decided by the submitter and possibly removed by reviewers before merge (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). No merge semantics exist for the metadata beyond the commit itself.
realtime: None. Provenance shows up only when a patch is pushed for review and becomes permanent at merge.
search_retrieval: Nothing is specified. Retrieval is whatever git offers for trailers (git log --grep, interpret-trailers, %(trailers) formats) or Gerrit/OpenDev search. Julia Kreger wrote that the original goal was for AI-enabled items "to be identifiable, and then on some level quantified should we ever need to" (https://lists.openinfra.org/archives/list/foundation-board@lists.openinfra.org/thread/B6RFW55FEH2632VD7IEDPCR67TBF7XZQ/). That makes coarse counting the intended query, not recall.
links_sessions_to_code: Only loosely, and by hand. The commit names the tool and optionally the model (Nova format). It asks for a human-written summary of prompts and context in the commit body, with no pointer to a session ID, transcript or hash. The March 2026 AI-Specification: proposal would have linked a commit to a spec file committed alongside it, still not to a session. Thierry Carrez pushed back: "at the end of the line, a human vouches for the contribution", and Synthesized-By adds little "compared with 'Assisted-By: a bunch of agent loops'". Kreger noted "pushback on a high level of verbosity from the contributors who utilize these tools" (https://lists.openinfra.org/archives/list/foundation-board@lists.openinfra.org/thread/B6RFW55FEH2632VD7IEDPCR67TBF7XZQ/).
scale: No scale claims for the convention. It applies to all OpenInfra-hosted projects (OpenStack, Kata Containers, StarlingX and others). OpenInfra became a directed fund of the Linux Foundation effective 23 July 2025, and its projects keep their existing technical processes (https://openinfra.org/blog/openinfra-joins-linux-foundation). Kreger gives one data point: an AI-assisted change of more than 6000 lines in Ironic had to be split up to fit reviewer capacity (https://lists.openinfra.org/archives/list/foundation-board@lists.openinfra.org/thread/B6RFW55FEH2632VD7IEDPCR67TBF7XZQ/).
privacy_security: No guidance on redacting prompts or on secrets, PII or encryption. Contributors are asked to paste prompt and context summaries into permanent public commit history without any caution about sensitive content (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/). Its security stance is about trust in the output instead: "Treat such code as if it came from an untrusted source", reviewers apply "heightened scrutiny", and contributors must check nothing is "inherently harmful, malicious, or outright incorrect". It also notes some tools "source context from the contents of a project being worked upon", raising EULA and licensing awareness. Its other concerns are licensing (Apache 2.0 or OSI-compatible output, enabling public-code-match filters) and DCO responsibility (same URL).
lesson_for_parinn: OpenInfra shows that the norm for open-source projects is a short commit-trailer claim that a human vouches for ("Assisted-By: <tool> [model]" plus Signed-off-by), not shipping session history inside git. The people who maintain the convention keep rejecting extra verbosity, and it gives no guidance on redaction. ParleyInn should therefore keep its hash-chained session record out of the commit and out of public history. At most it should emit an opt-in trailer that matches this vocabulary: Assisted-By/Generated-By with tool and model, never Co-Authored-By. That trailer can carry an opaque, non-reversible reference (e.g. a session-chain head hash) a maintainer can resolve locally, so the code-to-session link exists without publishing prompts. Two consequences follow. The policy lets the label be removed after human rework, so ParleyInn must treat commit trailers as untrustworthy, lossy hints and never as the authoritative record. Any prompt summary ParleyInn proposes for a commit body must pass through its redaction path first, because this convention sends that text straight into permanent public history.
license: The policy is a foundation governance document, and its page states no license. Governed projects use Apache 2.0 or other OSI-approved licenses (https://openinfra.org/legal/ai-policy/).

name: OpenSSF TAC issue #628: proposal to standardise the openfab/generation AI-authorship (AI-BOM) in-toto predicate
category: standards discussion (in-toto attestation predicate for AI-generated code provenance)
status: archived
what_is_stored: The issue itself stores nothing. It is a discussion thread. Its title is "Proposal for discussion: a standard 'AI authorship' attestation predicate for AI-generated code provenance". chrisxie-fw opened it on 30 June 2026, and the page shows it as Closed. It asks one question: "Is there interest in an 'AI authorship / AI-BOM' attestation predicate as a community-governed standard?" (https://github.com/ossf/tac/issues/628). The proposed predicate, openfab/generation v0.1 (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1), is a per-artifact manifest. Its fields are: spec_ref; builder {id, base}; agent {did, base, model, optional id in AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION form, optional tools}; prompt_sha256 (only the hash, because "the prompt text is deliberately not included"); params; generated[], with entries {path, lines "A-B", sha256, author: "ai"|"human"}, where ranges for one path MUST NOT overlap (rev 0.1.5) and author means generation origin, not legal authorship; materials[] {uri, sha256?}; acceptance_passed (the producer's self-report); acceptance[] {id, check (shell command), must_pass, passed}; timestamp (RFC 3339); and signoffs[] {did, name, timestamp} (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). The spec calls itself "a manifest, not a transcript". It leaves out per-iteration history, and each version gets its own attestation (same URL). Who closed the issue, when and why could not be verified. The fetched page showed no comments or timeline, and GitHub API access to ossf/tac was blocked in this session. Even so, the issue clearly drew substantive review: spec rev 0.1.4 credits "six community findings from the OpenSSF TAC review of this draft (issue 628)" (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1).
where_stored: The predicate spec does not say where attestations live. Distribution is left to deployment policy (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). The reference implementation (OpenFab, written in Rust, Apache-2.0) commits them inside the repository as plain JSON files in the working tree, at provenance/<spec>-vN.att.json. It also keeps a human-readable decision log at .openfab/runs/<id>/timeline.md (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab). Commit trailers carry a second, lighter layer: implementations SHOULD emit "Assisted-by: <agent.id>" trailers, and a verifier MUST cross-check them against the attestation (rev 0.1.5) (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). No git notes, custom refs, OCI registry or transparency log are used in the current version. Sigstore/Rekor is named as the planned production replacement for the signing layer (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab).
format_and_model: The predicate sits inside an in-toto Statement v1 ({_type, subject[{name, digest.sha256}], predicateType "https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1", predicate}). That statement is wrapped in a "DSSE-style" envelope that is not real DSSE, because it has no PAE: {payload_type "application/vnd.in-toto+json", payload_sha256, statement, signatures[{keyid did:key, sig, algo ed25519, role fab|human-signoff}]}. The canonical encoding matches RFC 8785 (JCS) for conforming documents: keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit, I-JSON safe integers only, no floats, and empty or absent optional fields omitted. Signature coverage works in layers. The fab signature and payload_sha256 cover the statement with predicate.signoffs removed. The n-th human-signoff signature covers the statement with signoffs truncated to the first n records. Published golden test vectors exist (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). The data model is one immutable document per artifact version. There is no event log and no chain across versions (same URL).
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple writers exist only as appended signatures. Humans add signoffs, and each signoff record must bind to exactly one signature (signoffs[n].did == signatures[n].keyid). N-of-M gates count "distinct verified signing keys, never records or signature array entries" (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). Signoffs are append-ordered by construction, because each signature commits to the prefix before it. The spec defines no merging of two attestations and no concurrent editing. A new version is a new attestation file (provenance/<spec>-vN.att.json) (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab). When two branches both write attestations, git file merge semantics apply. The spec does not address this case.
realtime: Does not apply. An attestation is produced once per generated artifact version and committed with it. Nothing is streamed or synchronised (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1).
search_retrieval: None is defined. Verification is the only read path. In the default attest-only mode, a verifier recomputes the subject and generated[].sha256 digests, checks the ed25519 signatures against did:key, and treats acceptance_passed as an unverified self-report. In the opt-in conformance mode, a verifier re-runs the embedded shell checks in isolation, but only with explicit operator consent (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). The OpenFab CLI provides verify and verify-file commands (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab).
links_sessions_to_code: Partly. It links a generation run to code by file path, line range and sha256, with an ai/human origin per range. It also records the agent DID, the model and the prompt's sha256 (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). The prompt text and the session transcript are deliberately excluded, so the link points one way: from the code to a fingerprint of the prompt. To resolve that fingerprint you need the local run state, which stays off-artifact. The Assisted-by: commit trailers tie the attestation to a git commit (same URL). OpenFab keeps agent instructions in a versioned openfab-agent.md file (https://todogroup.org/blog/2026-07-14-verifiable-provenance-ai-assisted-contributions/).
scale: No scale claims. The reference implementation has about 6 stars and 131 commits. It is active, with its latest commits on 29 Sep 2026 (rev 0.1.5) (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab, https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab/commits/main). The README reports v0.3 with "6 swappable bases" and a "4-forge matrix" (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab).
privacy_security: The prompt is hashed and never stored, specifically to avoid leaking secrets or PII and to keep artifacts small (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). There is no encryption and no redaction mechanism beyond that. Integrity rests on ed25519 signatures over did:key identities, with the fab key and the human keys kept separate. The signatures can be verified offline in the MVP, and Sigstore (cosign/fulcio/rekor) is the planned production path (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab). Rev 0.1.2 makes a notable security stance explicit. The acceptance checks are executable shell embedded in the attestation, and "a valid signature over a check establishes that it is the check that was signed—it does not establish that the check is safe to run". So execution is opt-in and isolated (https://open-fab.ai/attestation/generation/v0.1). Weaknesses: the envelope is DSSE-style without PAE, which is non-standard, and a prompt_sha256 of a short or guessable prompt could be brute-forced, because the hash has no salt. That second point is my own inference; the spec does not discuss it.
license: The OpenFab reference implementation is Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/Open-fab-ai/openfab). The spec page's license could not be verified.
lesson_for_parinn: Keep the shareable, git-committed provenance artefact separate from the lossless record. A small, signed, canonically encoded manifest can travel in the repository, as a working-tree JSON file plus a commit trailer such as Assisted-by:. It should hold only hashes: prompt_sha256, file and line-range digests, the model id, and distinct-key signoffs. The transcript itself stays in ParleyInn's local append-only store. If ParleyInn ever exports provenance to git or GitHub, it should emit an in-toto Statement v1 with JCS (RFC 8785) canonical JSON and real DSSE with PAE, and the commitment should be a salted or keyed hash, so a guessable prompt cannot be confirmed from a public attestation. Also adopt the spec's rule that signed content is not safe-to-execute content. That matches ParleyInn's I2 stance: anything recalled or imported, even when validly signed, stays untrusted and enveloped. The issue was closed with no visible adoption: no in-toto predicate (https://github.com/in-toto/attestation/tree/main/spec/predicates) and no OpenSSF outcome found. So ParleyInn should not bet on this predicate becoming a standard. If it exports anything, the format should be easy to map onto whatever AI-BOM predicate wins out.

name: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (agent spans)
status: beta. It is a live specification, but every GenAI span and attribute is still marked Development, not stable. Two things changed after the May 2026 discovery note. First, core semconv v1.42.0 deprecated all gen_ai.*, openai.* and mcp.* definitions in the core repo and moved them to a new repo, open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai. The old opentelemetry.io page at the URL given now only says the content has moved (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans/ ; https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases). Second, as of its 2026-09-30 commits, the new repo has made no release of its own: its CHANGELOG has only an 'Unreleased' section and the README's 'Schema URL' still reads TODO (checked in a local clone of the repo). The GitHub releases page as summarised showed 2024 dates for v1.41 to v1.44. That conflicts with Greptime's May 2026 dating of v1.41, so treat those exact dates as unverified. The spec does say outright that there is no stability timeline yet (https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions).
what_is_stored:
It defines no storage. It is a vocabulary for telemetry: span names, span kinds and attributes for agent and LLM operations. The agent spans are:
- create_agent (CLIENT)
- invoke_agent, as a CLIENT span for remote or hosted agents and an INTERNAL span for in-process frameworks
- invoke_workflow (INTERNAL)
- plan (INTERNAL)
- execute_tool, with refinements for load-skill, read-skill-resource and command execution (the Anthropic bash tool is cited as an example)

The generic spans cover inference (chat, generate_content, text_completion), embeddings, retrieval, fetch_response and memory. The memory operations are create_memory_store, search_memory, create_memory, update_memory, upsert_memory, delete_memory and delete_memory_store.

Metadata attributes include gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.agent.id and .name, gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type, gen_ai.skill.*, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.* token counts, and error.type.

Content attributes are all Opt-In: gen_ai.system_instructions, gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.tool.definitions, gen_ai.tool.call.arguments and gen_ai.tool.call.result. A new gen_ai.main_agent resource entity was added on 2026-09-30 (PR #270); it must carry a stable, provider-assigned id.

Sources: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md ; https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md ; https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/registry/entities/gen-ai.md
where_stored: Wherever the exporter sends the data. Spans leave the process through an OTel SDK exporter, usually OTLP, and go to a collector or a backend such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog or GreptimeDB (https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions). For production, the spec recommends a third option: put message content in external storage and keep only references on the span. That upload happens through an in-process hook or in the collector pipeline. The spec still has a TODO for how such references should be recorded (https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md#uploading-content-to-external-storage).
format_and_model:
The data model is the standard OTel trace model: a tree of spans linked by trace_id, span_id and parent, each with a kind, start and end time, status, attributes and events. The specs themselves are YAML models in the model/ folder, rendered to Markdown with OTel Weaver (v0.26.1 pinned).

Message content follows formal JSON Schemas: gen-ai-input-messages.json and gen-ai-output-messages.json. A ChatMessage has a role and a list of parts. The part types are TextPart, ToolCallRequestPart, ToolCallResponsePart, ServerToolCallPart, ServerToolCallResponsePart, BlobPart, FilePart, UriPart, ReasoningPart, CompactionPart and GenericPart. CompactionPart is notable for ParleyInn: it holds a provider id plus 'the unencrypted compacted conversation summary, when available'.

On events these values must be structured. On spans they may be a JSON string where the language SDK has no complex attribute values yet (OTEP 4485).

Sources: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/model/gen-ai/gen-ai-input-messages.json ; https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md#recording-content-on-attributes
multi_writer_and_merge:
The model has no merge step. The SDK generates trace and span IDs at random, and the W3C trace context links spans from many processes into one tree, so writers never conflict (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/trace/sdk/). Once a span has ended it is immutable: in OnEnd, 'modifying it is not allowed' (same source). Backends simply gather spans by trace_id.

gen_ai.conversation.id is how operations are tied to one session across traces. Instrumentations must use a real framework or provider conversation id, and 'a new UUID, a trace identifier, or a hash of request content SHOULD NOT be used as a fallback value' (https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md). There is no ordering guarantee and no hash chain.
realtime: Near real time, and lossy by design. A span is exported only after it ends. The batch processor exports every 5000 ms by default, in batches of up to 512, and once the queue of 2048 spans is full 'spans are dropped' (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/trace/sdk/). Sampling can also drop spans entirely. The spec does say that a content-upload hook should run 'regardless of the span sampling decision' (gen-ai-spans.md). The section on capturing streaming chunks is still a TODO.
search_retrieval: The standard defines none. Querying and retrieval are left to the backend: trace search by attributes such as gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.agent.name and gen_ai.operation.name. The spec does say some attributes should be set when a span is created so that samplers can use them. It also defines a retrieval span and memory spans, but those describe an agent calling a vector store or memory store. They do not retrieve telemetry.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only loosely. Sessions link through gen_ai.conversation.id, tool calls through gen_ai.tool.call.id, and skills through gen_ai.skill.name and gen_ai.skill.source.uri. The command-execution refinement covers shell and bash tools. There is no attribute for a git commit, repository, worktree or file diff.

Claude Code's own beta tracing emits claude_code.interaction, claude_code.llm_request and claude_code.tool spans. These carry some gen_ai.* attributes, including gen_ai.tool.call.id, plus session.id and prompt.id, but use Claude Code's own span names rather than invoke_agent or execute_tool (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage).
privacy_security:
Content is off by default. Instrumentations 'SHOULD NOT capture them by default, but SHOULD provide an option for users to opt in'. There are three patterns: 1) record nothing (the default), 2) record content on span attributes, recommended for pre-production, and 3) store content externally with references on the span, recommended for production because it 'enables separate access controls'.

The upload hook may modify spans and messages, which is where redaction can happen. Implementations may truncate message content while keeping the JSON structure. Many attributes, such as tool arguments and results, skill descriptions and skill URIs, carry a 'may contain sensitive information' warning, and credentials in a URI 'SHOULD be scrubbed'.

The spec itself defines no encryption, secret detection or integrity protection (https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md#capturing-instructions-inputs-and-outputs). Claude Code applies the same idea: prompts, responses, tool details and tool content are redacted unless the user sets OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS or OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage).
scale: The spec makes no throughput or volume claims; it only warns that content is 'often large' and can exceed backend attribute limits. Greptime cites survey figures on adoption, not scale (https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions). The new repo keeps Python reference scenarios for about 20 frameworks and providers, including CrewAI, DSPy, LlamaIndex, Bedrock, Azure, Google ADK and LiteLLM (reference/scenarios in the repo).
license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file in https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai)
lesson_for_parinn:
Use OTel GenAI as an export view of the record and never as the record itself. OTel spans can be dropped, sampled out and batched, they are not hash-chained, and content is off by default, so they cannot provide the lossless, auditable history behind I1/I6.

The model is still worth borrowing. ParleyInn could project its append-only record into invoke_agent, chat and execute_tool spans with gen_ai.conversation.id and gen_ai.tool.call.id, and reuse the ChatMessage/parts JSON Schema, including CompactionPart, as an interchange shape. That projection has to be offline and file-based, written for a separate exporter to pick up, because of I4. The spec's own production pattern also fits ParleyInn's I2 stance: keep sensitive content in a separate, access-controlled store and put only references on the spans. Exported content should never be fed back to the model.

Two cautions. Pin to a specific commit or version of the new repo: it has no release or schema URL yet, and attributes keep moving. Note too that the spec forbids inventing conversation ids, so ParleyInn's own session ids belong in a ParleyInn-namespaced attribute.

name: OrbitDB
status: shipped
license: MIT
what_is_stored: Append-only operation logs (OpLog) that serve as the foundation for multiple database types: Events (immutable log), Documents (JSON indexed by key), Key-Value stores, and Indexed Key-Value stores. Each database is entirely represented as an immutable, cryptographically verifiable Merkle-DAG of operations. Entries contain payloads, signatures, causal references, logical clocks, and identity hashes.
where_stored: IPFS block storage (via Helia) as the primary distributed store; entries are IPLD data structures (DAG-CBOR format) with content-addressable hashes. Local caching via LevelDB or other pluggable storage backends (MemoryStorage, LRUStorage, ComposedStorage). Identity data and access control policies stored as IPLD structures retrievable from IPFS.
format_and_model: IPLD/DAG-CBOR data structures. Merkle-DAG: each OpLog entry references previous entries forming a Directed Acyclic Graph establishing causal order. Entry structure: {v, id, key, sig, next[], refs[], clock{id, time}, payload{op, key, value}, identity}. Manifest format (IPLD): {name, type, accessController}. Database address: /orbitdb/{manifest_hash}. Logical clock model: Lamport clock with writer identity hash + monotonic time counter.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple writers identified by cryptographic public keys; each entry is cryptographically signed by its writer. Conflict resolution via deterministic Last-Write-Wins (LWW) sort function using logical clock: entries sorted first by logical time, then by writer identity hash. Ensures same total order across all peers despite concurrent writes. Concurrent updates from disconnected peers automatically merge deterministically when peers rejoin; no manual conflict resolution required. Access control via AccessController (IPFS-based immutable or OrbitDB-based mutable) determines write permissions.
realtime: Real-time synchronization via Libp2p Pubsub (default: gossipsub). Automatic peer discovery (mDNS, DHT, etc.). Event emitters for 'update' (new entry), 'join' (peer connected), and 'replicated' (replication complete). Eventually consistent model: updates propagate asynchronously; offline peers can write independently and merge later. No global clock or centralized sync coordinator.
search_retrieval: Iterator-based retrieval with optional filters (amount, gt/gte/lt/lte by hash). Can retrieve last N entries or entries in hash-based ranges. Documents indexed by key for retrieval. No full-text search built-in; custom indexing would require application layer. Entries retrievable individually by hash via IPFS.
links_sessions_to_code: Not directly. Identities are cryptographic public keys; each operation entry includes identity hash and signature. Access controllers can track which identities have write access. No built-in mechanism to link operations to external agent session IDs, prompts, or code commits. Could be extended via application-layer metadata in payloads or custom databases.
privacy_security: Cryptographic signatures verify writer identity and tamper-proof each entry (signature in entry itself). Optional encryption at two layers: payload encryption (data) and log entry encryption (replication), configurable independently. SimpleEncryption module provided but explicitly unaudited ('use at your own risk'). Custom encryption modules pluggable. Access controllers (IPFSAccessController immutable, OrbitDBAccessController mutable) enforce write permissions. No built-in redaction or secrets management; encrypted payloads are stored opaquely.
scale: Designed for distributed p2p scenarios with many replicas. Leverages IPFS deduplication and DHT scalability. Merkle-DAG structure enables efficient content verification without re-downloading.
