No explicit published benchmarks; claimed suitable for IoT, mobile devices, browsers, and decentralized apps. Storage backends are pluggable for speed/memory trade-offs. Logical clock avoids clock synchronization overhead.
lesson_for_parinn: Merkle-CRDTs provide tamper-proof, causally-ordered, append-only logs with cryptographic verification built in—directly addressing ParleyInn's I2 (untrusted content), I4 (no network calls in core), and I6 (auditability) invariants. Last-Write-Wins conflict resolution works for eventually-consistent p2p but may not suit strict session history ordering (ParleyInn prefers total order without tie-breaking). Logical clocks enable deterministic ordering across writers without external clock (supports I10: no clock/randomness in projection). Pluggable encryption and storage architecture is flexible. However, OrbitDB's focus on decentralized consensus differs from ParleyInn's agent-centric model: OrbitDB assumes equal peer authority, while ParleyInn requires pinned constraints re-injected post-compaction and strict history immutability for single-agent replay. OpLog's per-entry signatures could audit writer identity, but ParleyInn's I2 requires blocking untrusted content *before* model injection—OrbitDB returns entries for application verification, not pre-filtering at the boundary.

name: Orca (stablyai/orca)
category: Agentic development environment for parallel CLI coding agents: an Electron desktop app with one git worktree per task, a CLI, the orcad headless runtime, SSH worktrees, and iOS and Android companions paired over an end-to-end encrypted relay
status: shipped. The GitHub releases page lists v1.4.220 as latest, released Oct 4 2026. The commit read here, e2da3a1 of Oct 5 2026, still carries package.json version 1.4.214. The README says 'we ship daily'. The Android companion is a pre-release at 0.0.52. The repository page showed 85.4k stars, 5.5k forks and 12,737 commits on Oct 5 2026 (https://github.com/stablyai/orca, https://github.com/stablyai/orca/releases).
what_is_stored: Orca does not own agent transcripts. It runs third-party CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and about 30 others) in PTYs, one git worktree per task, and each harness keeps writing its own native file, even for chats held in Orca's own chat view (src/main/ai-vault-search/session-search-native-chat-indexing.test.ts). What Orca does store: (1) An agent-session journal for its structured chats. journal_rows(session_id, epoch, seq, ts, row_json) is 'every chat's append-only log', holding message, tool-call, diff, approval, question, status and turn items (src/main/native-chat/agent-session-journal/journal-database-schema.ts, src/shared/agent-session-journal-types.ts). Tool output and diff payloads keep a 16 KiB inline head plus a digest (journal-payload-bounds.ts). (2) The 'AI Vault' search index, an opt-in SQLite FTS5 copy of the user, assistant and tool text in each supported harness's transcripts (src/main/ai-vault-search/session-search-schema.ts). (3) Terminal history: 'verbatim screen and scrollback' per daemon session, as checkpoint.json, a framed binary output.log and meta.json, plus renderer scrollback snapshots (src/main/daemon/daemon-private-file-modes.ts, src/main/terminal-scrollback-snapshots.ts). (4) Profile state: settings, worktree metadata (display name, linked issue, PR or Linear ticket, createdWithAgent, lineage) and automation runs (src/shared/worktree/meta-types.ts, src/shared/persisted-state-types.ts). (5) The hook server's last agent status per pane, in last-status.json. (6) In the cloud relay, pairing and device credentials as hashes, placement and audit events. I found no relay table for message payloads (cloud/apps/relay/src/database.ts).
where_stored: Local, under Electron userData, except the mobile relay and push gateway. {userData}/agent-session-journal.db holds the journal and {userData}/ai-vault/session-search.sqlite the search index, with session-parse-cache.json beside it. Terminal history is in {userData}/terminal-history/{sessionId}/ (checkpoint.json, output.log, meta.json, legacy scrollback.bin), and renderer snapshots in {profileDir}/terminal-scrollback/v1-{sha256}.bin. Settings and worktree metadata are in {userData}/profiles/{id}/profile-state.db, which replaced orca-data.json; the JSON file is kept for import only. Hook status is in {userData}/agent-hooks/last-status.json (src/shared/profile-state-storage-paths.ts, src/main/ai-vault-search/session-search-database-path.ts, src/main/daemon/history-paths.ts, src/main/persistence/profile-state/legacy-json/README.md, src/main/agent-hooks/server/server-runtime-env.ts). Harness transcripts are read in place: ~/.claude/projects, $CODEX_HOME or ~/.codex/sessions, ~/.gemini/tmp, ~/.copilot/session-state, ~/.cursor/projects and the roots of about 20 more agents, inside WSL distros too (src/main/ai-vault/session-scanner-agent-sources.ts). On SSH worktrees and orcad hosts, the execution host keeps its own stores. Cloud: the relay and the push gateway use PostgreSQL in production and SQLite in tests, on GCE relay cells and a Cloud Run push service. The API and auth services live in the private stablyai/orca-cloud repository (cloud/README.md).
format_and_model: SQLite throughout, plus files for terminal history. The journal is append-only, keyed (session_id, epoch, seq), with each item as a JSON row (journal-database-schema.ts). An older layout kept one database per chat (journal-paths.ts). The search index is at schema version 6: sessions; files, which tracks dev, ino, byte_offset, mtime_ms and size_bytes for incremental tailing; messages; and messages_fts USING fts5(user_text, assistant_text, tool_text, identifiers) with a unicode61 tokenizer and detail=full, in WAL mode (session-search-schema.ts). It calls itself 'a cache over the transcripts, never a source': a schema bump or corruption drops and rebuilds it, rows are replaced on re-read, and retention purges them. Profile state is one JSON document per domain in profile_state_documents (profile-state-database-schema.ts). Terminal history is a framed binary log with magic OCKL plus a JSON checkpoint (terminal-history-log.ts). I found no hash chain or signature over journal rows.
multi_writer_and_merge: No merge of history. Each harness is the only writer of its own transcript. The execution host 'owns everything that touches execution', and the client 'is not authoritative for execution state' (docs/reference/ssh-execution-boundary.md). Each host keeps one agent-status store, and 'Mirroring is not merging: a client never writes its observations back to a host' (docs/reference/agent-status-store.md). The mobile app is a remote control, and 'the desktop is always the source of truth' (docs/site/content/docs/mobile.mdx). Orchestration state (runs, tasks, mailboxes) lives on the client, and the orca shim on a remote host proxies back to it. Orchestration federation pulls worker messages one way to the home runtime, with ack checkpoints, and treats 'Peer payloads [as] untrusted input' (src/main/runtime/orchestration/federation-sync.ts). Code comes together through git branches and PRs: fan a prompt across worktrees, then 'merge the winner' (README).
realtime: Yes, for status and control, not for history. Agents report through Orca-managed hooks to a loopback hook server. That feeds one status store per execution host, which the sidebar, `orca worktree ps`, the agent dashboard and the mobile app all read (docs/reference/agent-status-store.md). Terminals stream over SSH or, for phones, over the relay. The relay splices 'an opaque E2EE stream' between the outbound WebSockets of desktop and phone (cloud/packages/relay-contract/src/protocol-limits.ts, cloud/README.md). Notifications go through a push gateway to APNs and FCM. The search index reconciles every 20 s, with a full sweep every 15 cycles (session-search-indexer-options.ts).
search_retrieval: AI Vault session search, which is off by default: 'Off until the user turns it on' (src/shared/ai-vault-search-settings.ts). It runs FTS5 over user and assistant text in full and over tool output up to 3,072 characters per row. Queries take conversation or all scope, filters on agent, execution-host path and date, relevance or newest order, and opaque cursors fenced by an index generation (docs/reference/agent-session-search-contract.md). Search is per execution host; search across all computers is deferred. Hits carry agent, session id, title, cwd, branch, a snippet and, locally only, a resume command. Retention is historyDays, default null (all history) and at most 3,650, judged by transcript mtime (src/shared/ai-vault-search-settings.ts, session-search-retention-policy.ts). The CLI exposes it as `orca search`. Quick open searches worktrees, files, agents, commands and repo context (README).
links_sessions_to_code: Structurally, through the worktree: one task is one git worktree on its own branch (docs/site/content/docs/model/worktrees.mdx). Search rows keep cwd and branch per session, status rows carry worktreeId, and the journal keys chats by workspace_id. Worktree metadata records the linked issue, PR or Linear ticket and the agent the worktree was created with (src/shared/worktree/meta-types.ts). What Orca writes into git is plumbing: git config branch.NAME.base, a temporary refs/orca/rebase/UUID ref, and review-head refs under refs/orca/pull/ and refs/orca/merge-requests/ (src/main/git/worktree-add.ts, src/main/git/remote-rebase.ts, src/shared/review-head-tracking-ref.ts). It writes no git notes and no trailers. Its commit-message prompt says 'Do not include "Co-authored-by" or other git trailers' (src/shared/commit-message-prompt.ts), and AI-versus-human line attribution 'doesn't get committed to git' (docs/site/content/docs/review/attribution.mdx).
scale: The README pitches fanning 'one prompt across five agents'. I found no cap on worktrees or agents. Stated limits: a 5 MiB output.log and a 200,000,000-byte checkpoint per terminal session, with at most 10,000 restorable sessions (terminal-history-file-limits.ts, terminal-history-restorable-retention.ts). Renderer scrollback snapshots are capped at 5 MiB, of which 512 KiB is replayed (src/shared/terminal-scrollback-limits.ts). Search chunks messages at 8,000 characters, reads at most 256 KiB per message, commits at most 32 MiB of text at a time, and returns 20 results by default and 100 at most (session-search-message-rows.ts, session-search-index-writer.ts, src/shared/ai-vault-search-limit.ts). The search tuning used synthetic corpora of 10.5 MB (40 sessions) and 105 MB (docs/reference/agent-session-search-query-tuning.md). Adoption: 85.4k GitHub stars on Oct 5 2026.
privacy_security: Local stores are plaintext. Terminal history keeps verbatim screen and scrollback in files with modes 0700 and 0600 (src/main/daemon/daemon-private-file-modes.ts). The search index 'stores transcript content as written, with no redaction' (session-search-schema.ts). Paired relay, web and mobile clients get snippets, titles and cwd, but not file paths or resume commands (redactForTransport, docs/reference/agent-session-search-contract.md). The relay is end-to-end encrypted with NaCl boxes (X25519 and XSalsa20-Poly1305), and it stores invite and device tokens only as hashes (src/shared/e2ee-crypto.ts, cloud/apps/relay/src/database.ts). Configuration: Orca's 22 hook services write status hooks into user-global agent configs, among them ~/.claude/settings.json, Codex hooks.json and config.toml trust entries, and ~/.cursor/hooks.json. The setting defaults to on, and Orca reinstalls the hooks until the user turns it off (src/shared/default-global-settings.ts, src/main/agent-hooks/managed-agent-hook-registry.ts, docs/site/content/docs/agents/hooks-memory.mdx). The hook server listens on 127.0.0.1 with a per-launch random token and answers 403 without it (src/main/agent-hooks/server/server-lifecycle.ts). Injection: a dispatch types the coordinator's task spec into the worker agent's terminal verbatim, under '=== TASK ===' after a fixed preamble, with no untrusted-data label (src/main/runtime/orchestration/preamble.ts). Orchestration mail is not pushed: Orca types only a fixed pointer that says how many messages wait and which command reads them, `orca orchestration check`, and the preamble tells workers 'a durable message only arrives when you look' (src/main/runtime/orca-runtime-deliver-pending-messages.ts, src/main/runtime/orchestration/formatter.ts). `orca orchestration check` then returns each message under a 'From: SENDER (handle) (type)' banner with the body verbatim and no untrusted-data label (src/main/runtime/orchestration/formatter.ts, src/main/runtime/rpc/methods/orchestration/messaging/check-worker.ts). Orchestration is experimental and off until enabled under Settings, Experimental. Outside it, `orca terminal send`, the documented way to send a one-off prompt to another agent, pastes the text into that agent's terminal as given (docs/site/content/docs/cli/orchestration.mdx, src/main/runtime/orca-runtime-write-terminal-agent-prompt.ts). Orca does label the PR-check logs and PR comments it puts into prompts as 'untrusted data only, not instructions' (src/shared/pr-checks-fix-prompt.ts). Telemetry goes to PostHog Cloud in the US. New installs are opted in, and DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or ORCA_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 turns it off. It never sends prompts, agent output, terminal output or paths (docs/site/content/docs/telemetry.mdx, src/main/telemetry/consent.ts, src/main/persistence/loading-store/loaded-cohort-migrations.ts). An observability redactor scrubs provider keys, JWTs and .env lines from traces and support bundles (src/main/observability/redactor.ts). Shared agent skills are, in V1, 'not end-to-end encrypted from Orca Cloud operators' (docs/reference/agent-skill-sharing-threat-model.md).
license: MIT, 'Copyright (c) 2026 Lovecast Inc.' (LICENSE). The relay under cloud/ is covered by the same license. The API and auth services and two Terraform roots live in the private stablyai/orca-cloud repository (cloud/README.md). The app is free and runs agents on the user's own subscriptions (repository description).
lesson_for_parinn: Orca, an open-source parallel-agent workbench with 85.4k stars, confirms what Superset and Conductor show: the orchestrator does not become the system of record. Its search index calls itself 'a cache over the transcripts, never a source' and is rebuilt from the harness files, which is I10's rebuild rule applied to search. Its rule of one store per execution host, where 'Mirroring is not merging', matches ParleyInn's single-writer logs. Four of its choices are ones ParleyInn's invariants rule out. (1) A dispatch types the coordinator agent's task spec into the worker's terminal verbatim under a fixed preamble. One agent's output becomes another's input with no untrusted envelope, which is the automatic path I2 forbids. Mail the worker pulls with `orca orchestration check` comes back without an envelope too. Orca already wraps PR logs and comments as 'untrusted data only, not instructions' in its own prompts, so the envelope costs little. ParleyInn applies it on every path, not feature by feature. Orca's mailbox pointer, a fixed line that says how many messages wait and which command reads them, is close to ParleyInn's fixed templates that reference ids. (2) By default, Orca writes managed hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json and the configs of the other agents it supports, and reinstalls them at startup until they are turned off. I7 requires an explicit install that shows the change first. (3) The journal keeps only a 16 KiB head plus a digest of tool output and diffs, and the search index stores secrets as written. ParleyInn keeps the full event (I1) and redacts before storage. (4) New installs are opted in to PostHog telemetry until the user sets DO_NOT_TRACK or ORCA_TELEMETRY_DISABLED; I4 allows no telemetry at all. Orca's NaCl relay, which only splices ciphertext, is a working design for a phone view. Under I4 the same splice would have to run between nodes the owner enrolled (B2), not through a vendor relay.

name: Origin CLI (origin-cli, by Opsworks Co.; getorigin.io)
category: git-native session store (AI attribution, blame and memory layer), with an optional paid SaaS team layer
status: shipped. Development is active: the newest mirror commit is a012162, dated 2026-09-23, "sync CLI 0.20260922.2014 from opsworks-co/origin". The public repo is a one-way sync of a CLI that lives in a private monorepo, opsworks-co/origin. The Show HN post of 2026-03-24 gave github.com/dolobanko/origin-cli as the repo, so that URL is superseded by opsworks-co/origin-cli. The old URL returned 403 from this sandbox, so I could not confirm a redirect.
what_is_stored:
Origin stores six kinds of data.

1. Per-commit attribution: session id, model, prompt count, prompt summary, tokens, cost in USD, duration, and lines added and removed. Prompt text is included by default. The full last prompt is capped at 8KB, and up to 50 per-prompt texts at 1KB each.
2. Per session: metadata.json (metrics, git state, commits), prompts.md (every prompt, in order, as Markdown) and changes.json (version 2; maps each prompt to the files it touched, with diffs, editsJson, uncommitted diff, commit sha and tree sha).
3. Session memory: one rollup per session (summary, files, TODOs, decisions) plus one frozen record per commit. Decisions come from verbatim '[Origin: Decision]' markers or, optionally, from an LLM.
4. An LLM continuation brief, an opt-in LLM repo brief, and acceptance and survival data (how much agent output survived).
5. 'Shadow' snapshot commits of working-tree state, used by rewind.
6. Local state: per-session JSON, heartbeats, a hooks.log, a JSON prompt database, content-addressed blobs, and chunked transcripts (500KB chunks with a manifest).

Full raw transcripts go to the API in connected mode and to ~/.origin locally. The repo branch holds prompts and diffs rather than full transcripts. The README's claim that the branch holds 'transcripts' is looser than the documented three-file layout.
where_stored:
Mostly in custom git refs inside the project repo.

- Git notes: refs/notes/origin (attribution), refs/notes/origin-memory (memory: one JSON note on the repo's root commit), refs/notes/origin-memory-brief, refs/notes/origin-acceptance and refs/notes/origin-repo-brief.
- An orphan branch, origin-sessions, with the layout sessions/<id>/{metadata.json, prompts.md, changes.json} and trails/<id>.json. An opt-in 'refs' backend writes one ref per session at refs/origin/sessions/<id> instead.
- Shadow snapshots under refs/origin/shadow/.
- Staging refs refs/notes/origin-remote* for fetched notes.
- Local files under .git/origin-session-<tag>.json, .git/origin-handoff.json and ~/.origin/ (config, db/prompts.json, blobs, transcripts, sessions, heartbeats, todos).
- Optionally, a separate 'snapshotRepo' remote for the sessions branch.
- In connected mode, also the getorigin.io server (Origin API).
format_and_model:
- Notes are JSON blobs attached to commit SHAs through git notes. Attribution is keyed by commit. Memory is a single JSON payload on the root commit, keyed inside by sessionId and commitSha.
- The sessions branch is a plain git tree with one directory per session. Each write makes one commit, built with plumbing (a temporary GIT_INDEX_FILE, read-tree, commit-tree, update-ref). Commits can be GPG- or SSH-signed with signSnapshots.
- Commits made in a session can carry an 'Origin-Session' trailer (commitLinking defaults to always).
- The model is mutable, upsert-style metadata. There is no append-only event log and no hash chain beyond git's own commit DAG. Memory rollups are 'evolving', meaning they are upserted and regenerated.
- Capture comes from seven agent hook events (session-start, user-prompt-submit, stop, session-end, pre/post-tool-use) plus git hooks (post-commit, pre-push, post-rewrite, post-checkout, post-merge). It also detects agents that lack hooks.
- The CLI is written in TypeScript and runs on Node. Dependencies are the MCP SDK, commander, chalk, fzstd and sql.js.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Origin uses a different strategy for each ref.

1. Local concurrent writers on the origin-sessions branch: a compare-and-swap loop on update-ref, using the expected old tip, with jittered retry. The authors measured that only 1 of 16 sessions survived with 16 parallel agents before they added the CAS. Each write re-reads and rewrites the whole accumulated tree, so cost grows with history: 191ms at 100 sessions and 321ms at 2000. The opt-in per-session-ref backend stays flat at about 138ms because there is no contention.
2. Across clones, before a push: the remote origin-sessions tip is fetched and the two trees are unioned. The remote tree goes into a temporary index, the local tree is layered on top so local wins per path, and the result is a two-parent merge commit. The code records the earlier failure: the first clone to push won, and every other clone was silently rejected as non-fast-forward. On one machine 1,700 session commits never left.
3. Attribution and acceptance notes are fetched through the glob refspec '+refs/notes/origin*:refs/notes/origin-remote*' into staging refs. They are never forced onto live refs. They are then folded with 'git notes merge -s ours': the local note wins when both sides annotated the same commit, and distinct commits union. On a rejected push the CLI fetches, merges and retries once.
4. Memory is merged at the payload level, not with git notes merge, because a git-level strategy would drop one machine's sessions wholesale. Session rollups are keyed by sessionId and the newest write wins. Commit records are keyed by sha and the first write wins. The ref is then re-parented onto the remote tip, so the retry fast-forwards.
5. Rebase and amend: post-rewrite copies notes to the new SHAs. 'origin ci squash-merge' combines notes onto a squash commit.
6. Concurrent Claude Code sessions in one repo each get their own state file. Sub-agents in worktrees are tracked by observed writes per working tree.

Failures are mostly swallowed quietly ('best-effort', 'give up quietly').
realtime: Not real time through git. Pushes ride on the user's own git push (the pre-push hook) and on session end. Pulls come through ordinary git fetch or pull via the installed refspec. A post-merge hook folds staged notes into the live refs. Session start fetches as well, at most once per 10 minutes per repo, with a 6-second network ceiling. Real-time visibility exists only in connected (paid) mode: a heartbeat process pings the Origin API every 30 seconds, sessions are auto-ended after 15 minutes without updates, and the getorigin.io dashboard shows sessions live.
search_retrieval:
- 'origin search' runs full-text search over prompts, with filters for model, agent, repo and time ('--from 7d'). It searches, in order: the API (connected mode), local session JSON files, the refs/notes/origin notes, and the local JSON prompt database. That database is filled by 'origin db import', which walks the origin-sessions branch.
- 'origin ask', 'origin why <file>:<line>', 'origin prompts <file>' and 'origin blame' (an AI or human tag and the model for each line) resolve from code back to sessions and prompts, using notes on the commits that touched a file. They fall back to scanning the branch.
- An MCP server exposes get_repo_memory, get_file_context, get_session, list_sessions and other tools to agents.
- At session start, Origin injects a capped digest (sessions, 5 decisions, 5 TODOs) plus a 'memory pointer' that tells the agent how to query the rest. Truncation is marked explicitly.

There is no indexed engine: no FTS or BM25 is evident. The local database is a JSON file, despite the sql.js dependency.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and this is the core feature. Every AI-assisted commit gets a note keyed by its SHA, naming the session, model and prompts. An Origin-Session trailer goes into the commit message. changes.json maps each prompt index to its files, diff, commitSha and treeSha. Line-level blame ('origin blame', 'origin why') attributes each line to a prompt through edit replay. Shadow refs and 'origin rewind --to <sha>' restore the working tree to any per-prompt snapshot. Notes are carried through rebase, amend, stash and squash merges.
scale:
- The only measured figures are in session-store.ts: sessions-branch write latency of 191, 224 and 321ms at 100, 500 and 2000 existing sessions, against about 136 to 142ms for per-session refs.
- The code comments mention 16 parallel agents and 1,700 local session commits on one machine.
- Caps bound the size of each note: 8KB for the full prompt, 1KB for each prompt text, 50 prompts, 16KB for editsJson and 100 files read.
- Shadow refs are pruned only by an explicit 'origin clean --shadow-refs --force'. A ref must be more than 30 days old and appear in no saved evidence, and the deletion runs as one transaction against the expected old SHAs.
- No published claims about repo size or performance at scale. Not verifiable beyond the code comments.
privacy_security:
- Redaction: regexes and an entropy check cover AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Anthropic, Stripe, Slack and npm tokens, private keys, JWTs, database connection strings, Bearer tokens, and strings over 25 characters with Shannon entropy above 4.5. It is on by default (secretRedaction=true). It is applied to API payloads and to note contents.
- I could not trace redaction onto prompts.md and changes.json on the origin-sessions branch. The writer code (buildSessionWriteData and writeSessionFiles) does not call it. This is unverified, not proven; the docs describe the setting only as 'redact secrets before sending to API'.
- Defaults lean permissive. notesIncludePrompts defaults to true and pushStrategy to auto, so prompt text is pushed to the shared remote, where anyone with read access can fetch it. The scrub-notes source says 'new notes are metadata-only by default', which contradicts the shouldIncludePromptText default of true.
- Opt-out: notesIncludePrompts=false in .origin.json or ~/.origin/config.json suppresses prompt text and the branch and memory pushes. 'origin scrub-notes --push' removes prompt text after the fact, but it cannot purge git history that others have already fetched.
- No encryption at rest or in transit beyond the git transport.
- Optional GPG or SSH signing of Origin's own commits.
- Telemetry is opt-in.
- The README's claims of 'No server' and 'Nothing leaves your machine' hold only in standalone mode. The CLI does git fetch and push, and optional LLM features send a bounded bundle of repo content to Anthropic with the user's key, or to the server's key when connected.
- Memory and handoff text fetched from other clones is injected verbatim into the new agent's context at session start. The injection code shows no trust envelope or provenance marking, which makes it a cross-writer prompt-injection channel.
lesson_for_parinn:
Origin shows both what git gives for free and what it costs. Git provides clone portability, attribution keyed by SHA that survives rebase and squash, and staging refspecs for fetch. Nearly every multi-writer bug it hit came from a shared mutable ref:
- The sessions-branch CAS loop.
- Notes merged with -s ours.
- A single memory blob that needed a hand-written union.
- Pushes silently rejected as non-fast-forward, which stranded 1,700 commits.

If ParleyInn uses git as a transport, it should:
- Publish append-only, per-writer refs (one ref per session or per writer). Origin's own opt-in refs backend removed contention and kept write cost flat.
- Never write a single-blob or last-writer-wins payload.
- Fetch into staging refs and verify the hash chain before folding.
- Count and audit every rejected push or merge rather than swallowing it (I6).
- Treat anything fetched from other clones as untrusted data that is pulled and enveloped, never injected automatically. Origin injects teammates' memory into the agent's context verbatim (I2).
- Keep prompt text out of shared refs unless redaction is proven on every write path. Origin redacts notes but appears not to redact the branch files, and it pushes prompts by default.

name: Oxen.ai
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Large, unstructured datasets: images, audio, video, text files, tabular data (CSV/Parquet/JSONL), model weights, game assets, studio media. Designed for datasets ranging from millions of files to terabytes of data.
where_stored: Local filesystem via `.oxen/` directory, or remotely on oxen-server (self-hosted on Linux/macOS). Planned support for S3, GCS, Azure, Backblaze. Server stores all data under `$SYNC_DIR` with `.oxen/` hidden directories per repository.
format_and_model: Merkle tree structure for efficient change detection and file deduplication. Metadata stored in RocksDB (key-value); tabular data queried via DuckDB. File content stored as blobs, indexed by content hash. Directory metadata cached in merkle tree nodes. Commit objects contain message, parent commit ID, author, timestamp. Version history organized by commit hash with directory trees and file entries.
multi_writer_and_merge: Workspace system enables server-side editing without full clone (Editable=true workspace config). Three-way merge conflict detection using Least Common Ancestor (LCA) algorithm. MergeConflict struct tracks lca_entry, base_entry, merge_entry with file hash and commit ID. Collaborative editing through workspaces; merge operations structured but not automatic conflict resolution. No CRDTs or operational transform; conflicts raised to user.
realtime: Not fully real-time. Workspaces provide server-side editing without clone overhead, but synchronization is explicit via `oxen push/pull`. File streaming transfer for large datasets. Workspaces persist state on server, avoiding ephemeral checkout overhead. Operations are batch-oriented (add → commit → push) rather than continuous sync. HTTP API supports both CLI and server operations.
search_retrieval: DuckDB integration for native tabular data querying on CSV/Parquet/JSONL files. Metadata extractors for image/video/audio/text types, cached in merkle tree for fast access. File indexing by path and hash. Directory traversal via merkle tree. No full-text search built-in; relies on external tools for content search.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Oxen is a general-purpose data VCS, not specific to AI agent sessions or prompts. No built-in linking to code repositories or agent logs. Usable as storage layer for agent training data or session artifacts if wrapped by external system.
privacy_security: No built-in encryption at rest or in transit (beyond standard HTTPS). No secret redaction or data masking. No access control or permission system mentioned. Apache 2.0 licensed (permissive open source). File-level integrity via content hash. No mention of audit logging or compliance features. Self-hosted server ownership model allows private deployment.
lesson_for_parinn: Workspace abstraction separates server-side editing from local clones, valuable for ephemeral agent containers and CI/CD without full repo checkout. Merkle tree for history tracking is efficient, similar to ParleyInn's hash-chaining. Three-way merge with LCA detection handles concurrent edits without CRDTs—pragmatic for data (immutable files) but ParleyInn's append-only constraint is stricter. Layered storage (RocksDB for metadata + DuckDB for tabular) shows value of specialized DBs. However, Oxen treats content as untrusted by default (files are blobs); ParleyInn must go further: recalled history is untrusted until verified.
sources: File crates/liboxen/src/FileStructure.md (local and remote storage layout)
File crates/liboxen/src/storage/ (local and S3 backend abstraction)

name: Paperclip (paperclipai/paperclip)
category: Org-chart orchestration of agent teams. A Node.js/TypeScript control plane plus React UI that runs "companies" of heterogeneous coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw and others) as ticketed work.
status: shipped. Very active and not archived. The master HEAD I cloned was committed on 2026-10-02. The latest dated release notes are v2026.916.1, released 2026-09-21 (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/releases/v2026.916.1.md). The CLI and server package.json files say 0.3.1. GitHub showed about 96.1k stars, 16.3k forks and 4,732 commits on master when fetched (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip). A hosted "Paperclip Cloud" exists only as a waitlist (https://paperclip.ing/waitlist/, linked from the README).
what_is_stored:
Paperclip stores work-management state, not a lossless session transcript. All of the following live in about 143 Drizzle-defined PostgreSQL tables (packages/db/src/schema):
- Companies, agents, the org chart, goals, projects, issues (tasks), comments, documents, approvals, budgets and costs, routines, skills, secrets metadata, and an activity_log.
- heartbeat_runs: one row per agent wake. Columns include session_id_before and session_id_after, log_store/log_ref/log_bytes/log_sha256, and stdout_excerpt/stderr_excerpt (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/packages/db/src/schema/heartbeat_runs.ts).
- heartbeat_run_events: structured run-log events.
- agent_task_sessions: one row per (company, agent, adapter, taskKey), holding session_params_json and session_display_id. This lets an adapter resume the provider's own session, for example a Claude Code session id, on the next heartbeat (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/packages/db/src/schema/agent_task_sessions.ts).
- issue_work_products: PRs, deploys and similar outputs, with provider, external_id, url, source_trust and created_by_run_id (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/packages/db/src/schema/issue_work_products.ts).
- decision_training_examples: point-in-time snapshots of an issue, its comments and runs, exportable as JSONL (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/DATABASE.md).
Full stdout from each run goes to an NDJSON log file, not into the database (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/run-log-events.md). The README's own pitch is that "sessions persist across reboots" and that "supporting adapters resume saved sessions across runs" (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/README.md).
where_stored:
Server-side PostgreSQL in all modes (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/DATABASE.md):
- Embedded Postgres in ~/.paperclip/instances/default/db/ when DATABASE_URL is unset.
- Docker Postgres 17 locally.
- Hosted Postgres in production, for example Supabase.
Other locations:
- Run logs: NDJSON files on the server's local disk, under a basePath with path containment. Finished logs can optionally be mirrored to S3, and in-flight logs mirrored on a throttle, because cloud pods use emptyDir (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/server/src/services/run-log-store.ts).
- File bytes (attachments, assets): local disk or object storage.
- Secrets master key: ~/.paperclip/instances/default/secrets/master.key.
Database backups exclude uploads, workspace files and the master key (DATABASE.md). Company templates export as a markdown-first package: COMPANY.md, TEAM.md, AGENTS.md, PROJECT.md, TASK.md and SKILL.md, plus .paperclip.yaml sidecars (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/AGENTCOMPANIES_SPEC_INVENTORY.md). Git is not used as a store. Git is only the agents' workspace: worktrees and repo checkouts.
format_and_model:
The model is relational (Drizzle ORM) and company-scoped throughout.
- Issues have a single assignee (assigneeAgentId XOR assigneeUserId), parent/sub-issue structure and blocker edges. Statuses are backlog, todo, in_progress, blocked, in_review, done and cancelled, and each carries execution semantics (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/execution-semantics.md).
- activity_log rows carry actorType, actorId, action, entityType, entityId, agentId, runId, responsibleUserId, details (jsonb) and createdAt (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/packages/db/src/schema/activity_log.ts).
- Run events are JSONB. For the native runner, each event keeps the source instance, source event id, source sequence, schema version and a SHA-256 digest of the canonical source envelope. A lossless codec stores payloads containing NUL, which JSONB cannot hold, as a reserved escaped field (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/run-log-events.md).
- Native runs add an append-oriented evidence chain. completion_contracts, native_run_results, work_assessments, status_decisions and their effects use unique fingerprints, ordinals and idempotency keys, and composite foreign keys reject evidence that mixes owners (DATABASE.md).
I found no hash chain or signature across the activity log or the run log. The per-event digests and per-log SHA-256 are integrity checks on single items, not a tamper-evident chain.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no merge model: one Postgres is the single source of truth, and concurrency is handled with row locks and conditional updates.
- Atomic checkout is a single SQL UPDATE with `WHERE id = ? AND status IN (?) AND (assignee_agent_id IS NULL OR assignee_agent_id = :agentId)`. Zero rows updated returns 409 with the current owner (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/SPEC-implementation.md, section 10.4.1).
- checkoutRunId records which run owns execution rights. executionRunId records which run is actually live.
- Stale locks that point at terminal or missing runs self-heal or are cleared by a sweeper. Agents must treat a 409 as a real ownership conflict and stop rather than retry (execution-semantics.md section 5).
- Other mechanisms: SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE for identity and credential writes; controller leases with boot id, PID and database-clock expiry; per-run seq cursors allocated under a row lock. A byte-identical retry is idempotent, while a changed retry or a sequence gap fails closed (DATABASE.md, run-log-events.md).
- An explicit operator endpoint, POST /issues/:id/admin/force-release, writes an audit entry (SPEC-implementation.md).
- Agents never write the database directly. They call Paperclip's REST API from inside each heartbeat (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/docs/start/architecture.md).
realtime: Live within one server process only. publishLiveEvent emits on an in-process Node EventEmitter keyed by company, with a process-local incrementing id. That stream is pushed to the UI over a WebSocket (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/server/src/services/live-events.ts, https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/server/src/realtime/live-events-ws.ts). I found no Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY or broker for fanning events out across nodes. Agents are not streamed to continuously; they wake on heartbeats. A heartbeat is triggered by schedule, assignment, comments or feedback, or a manual invoke (docs/start/architecture.md). Run logs are tailed live from the local NDJSON file.
search_retrieval:
Lexical search inside Postgres only, deliberately with "no synonym service, embedding model or language-specific stemming" (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/SEARCH.md).
- What is searched: task ids, titles, descriptions, current comments and documents.
- Query handling: up to 8 terms, all required. Quoted phrases stay literal, and SQL wildcards are not expanded.
- Typo handling: conservative title-word typo correction only.
- Boundaries: company, visibility and deletion rules always apply.
- Stated targets: MRR ≥ 0.95 and nDCG@5 ≥ 0.90 on a synthetic adversarial corpus, and warm p95 ≤ 250 ms at 10k tasks and 30k comments. These are targets, not measured claims.
Memory is a separate, plugin-oriented survey ("memory landscape", dated 2026-03-17) covering mem0, memsearch and others. It describes a provider contract with provenance back to runs, issues and comments, not a built-in vector store (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/memory-landscape.md). Agents are given context on each wake, including goal ancestry and get_task_context.
links_sessions_to_code:
Indirectly, through tickets rather than commits.
- A heartbeat run links issue, agent, provider session ids before and after, and a log reference.
- Work products (for example a GitHub PR, with provider, external_id and url) link to the issue and to created_by_run_id.
- Projects bind GitHub repositories by GitHub's numeric repo id, and each task gets editable checkouts of those repositories (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/project-repositories.md).
- Isolated runs use git worktrees prepared on the server. SSH remote execution bundles the worktree over ssh and writes remote commits back "with no `git remote` configured" (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/docs/guides/board-operator/execution-workspaces-and-runtime-services.md).
- Managed GitHub operations can act as the responsible human user (README).
I found no mechanism that writes session ids, prompts or transcripts into git: no notes, no trailers, no refs.
scale:
No published production scale numbers. The only quantitative figures I found are design targets and quotas:
- Search: warm p95 ≤ 250 ms at 10k tasks and 30k comments, explicitly "not scale proof" (SEARCH.md).
- Runner API response snapshots: a 20 GiB per-company default quota.
- assets.byte_size widened to bigint for responses over 2 GiB (DATABASE.md).
- A pool size of 10 by default (DATABASE.md).
- A multi-company ("multi-organization") single deployment (README).
- Repository picker tests cover 40 repos per project (project-repositories.md).
The README pitches the "20 simultaneous Claude Code terminals" use case. Adoption is large by GitHub signals: about 96k stars (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip).
privacy_security:
Secrets:
- Secrets are stored as versioned rows with access events (secret_access_events).
- The default local_encrypted provider encrypts secret values at rest with a local 32-byte master key. The server tries to enforce 0600 on the key file but does not guarantee it.
- An AWS provider exists for hosted installs.
- A strict mode blocks inline sensitive env values, and a migration command moves them out (DATABASE.md).
- Company export scrubs secrets (README).
Redaction:
- Config read APIs redact secrets. Config revisions that contain redacted placeholders cannot be restored (SPEC-implementation.md).
- Error reports to Sentry are opt-in through a DSN. Before truncation they strip credential patterns, the user's home path, registered run-secret values and host credentials, and they never copy prompts, stdout, stderr or env (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/observability.md).
- Run-log events never contain bootstrap tickets, leases, keys or raw credentials (run-log-events.md).
- Deleting a comment replaces it in training snapshots with a content-free tombstone (DATABASE.md).
Prompt injection:
- An opt-in low_trust_review preset limits what an agent can read or change through the API. It "prevents raw untrusted output from being automatically promoted into higher-trust agent context", and new tasks carry quarantined source attribution.
- The docs state this is containment, not privacy: by default all work is visible to everyone inside the company (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/doc/LOW-TRUST-PRESETS.md).
- Work products carry source_trust metadata.
Gaps:
- I found no claim that ordinary content (issues, comments, run logs) is encrypted in the database. At-rest protection is left to the Postgres or disk layer.
- The project talks to the network by design: GitHub, connectors, MCP and sandbox providers.
- Vulnerabilities are reported through GitHub Security Advisories (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/SECURITY.md).
lesson_for_parinn:
ParleyInn should not adopt Paperclip's storage choice. A single central Postgres with in-process WebSocket fan-out is the opposite of ParleyInn's offline, no-network core, and Paperclip keeps no lossless or hash-chained transcript; it stores excerpts plus log files that may live only on local disk.

What ParleyInn should copy is Paperclip's append discipline at the point of write. Each event's source identity (instance, event id, source sequence, schema version, SHA-256 of the canonical envelope) is recorded under a per-run sequence cursor. A byte-identical retry returns the existing row, and a changed retry or a sequence gap fails closed instead of being merged.

That is the right contract for ParleyInn ingesting from many worktrees, machines and sandboxes. Each writer appends to its own sequenced, digest-checked stream, and synchronisation is replaying those streams idempotently, never three-way merging them. That holds whether the transport is git refs or something else.

Two smaller lessons:
- Paperclip's low_trust_review rule, never auto-promote raw untrusted output into higher-trust context, is the same idea as ParleyInn's I2. Paperclip makes it opt-in; ParleyInn should keep it as a default.
- Paperclip found JSONB cannot hold NUL bytes in tool output and needed a lossless codec. ParleyInn's "lossless" claim needs a test for this kind of byte-exactness.
license: MIT. The LICENSE file says "Copyright (c) 2025 Paperclip AI"; the GitHub page shows "MIT © 2026 Paperclip Labs, Inc" (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/blob/master/LICENSE, https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip).

name: pi coding agent (Earendil; formerly badlogic/pi-mono)
category: session tree + gist sharing (local JSONL tree per session; one-shot upload to share)
status: shipped. The coding-agent CLI is at package version 1.0.0 on main as of commit 9b3c19d (2026-10-02). In May 2026 the repo moved from badlogic/pi-mono to earendil-works/pi, and the npm scope changed from @mariozechner/* to @earendil-works/* starting with 0.74.0. The old repo and packages are superseded and deprecated. The durable/server/protocol/client packages are labelled experimental.
what_is_stored:
Each session is one append-only log of typed entries. It opens with a header line holding version 3, the session UUID, an ISO timestamp, the cwd and, for forks or clones, a `parentSession` path. Entry types:
- `message`: AgentMessage records for user, assistant (with provider, model, usage/cost, stopReason, thinkingLevel), toolResult and system. System messages hold prompt `sections` and tools added or removed, so replaying them rebuilds the exact prompt and tool loadout.
- `model_change` and `thinking_level_change`.
- `usage`, for cost that is not part of the context.
- `compaction`: the summary, `firstKeptEntryId`, tokensBefore, a full system checkpoint, and details such as readFiles/modifiedFiles.
- `context_edit`: an append-only override that hides or replaces an earlier entry in future model context only. The raw entry is kept.
- `branch_summary`: an LLM summary of the branch that was left.
- `custom` (extension state, never shown to the model) and `custom_message` (extension text that is shown to the model).
- `label` (bookmarks) and `session_info` (the session name).

Compaction never deletes the original entries. Sources: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session-format.md and https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/sessions.md
where_stored:
Local files only: ~/.pi/agent/sessions/--<cwd with separators replaced by ->--/<timestamp>_<session-id>.jsonl. The location can be changed with --session-dir, PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR or the sessionDir setting, and --no-session runs ephemerally (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session-format.md, https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/sessions.md).

Sessions are not kept in git or on a server. They leave the machine only through explicit /share:
- Radius (Earendil's hosted service) gets the active branch as NDJSON, POSTed to /v1/artifacts with visibility=organization, when Radius auth is configured.
- Otherwise a secret GitHub gist gets the rendered HTML, created with `gh gist create --public=false`.

Source: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interactive/session-share.ts

The separate experimental pi-durable runtime stores to SQLite (WAL) or to a directory of append-only JSONL files (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/durable/README.md).
format_and_model:
JSONL, one JSON object per line. The entries form a tree through `id` (usually an 8-hex ID) and `parentId` (null for a root), so every branch lives in the same file. On load, the current leaf is taken to be the last entry in the file (`_buildIndex` in https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts).

`buildContextEntries()` walks from the leaf up to the root. It applies the latest compaction on that path, then the latest `context_edit` for each target. So the model context is a projection that can always be rebuilt from the raw log.

Three ways to branch:
- `/tree` branches inside the file.
- `/fork` creates a new file from an earlier user message.
- `/clone` copies the active branch into a new file, linked through `parentSession`.

Schema versions: v1 was linear, v2 added the tree, v3 renamed hookMessage to custom. Older files are migrated automatically on load, which rewrites the file in place (`migrateToCurrentVersion` then `_rewriteFile` in session-manager.ts).

Append-only is a convention, not a guarantee. Normal writes use appendFileSync, but migration, fork-in-place and initialising an empty file call `_rewriteFile` (open with "w"). There is no hashing, signing or tamper evidence. Sources: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session-format.md and https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts

Exports:
- HTML export includes all entries (`sm.getEntries()`), so the whole tree is browsable, and the viewer supports leafId/targetId deep links (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/export-html/index.ts).
- JSONL export and Radius share include only the current branch, re-parented into a linear chain, plus a trailing `pi.share` custom entry carrying the system prompt and tool schemas (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-export.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Single writer per file, no merge. I found no file lock in SessionManager, and it keeps the whole entry list in memory. Two processes on the same file would each append from their own in-memory state, and a rewrite would discard the other's appends (inferred from the session-manager.ts code; not documented).

Divergent work is handled by branching, not merging: `/tree` branches inside one file, `/fork` and `/clone` create new files. A branch_summary carries what was learned on the abandoned branch into the new one. There is no cross-machine sync or merge of sessions.

pi-durable says outright: "One process owns a storage at a time; there is no cross-process locking" (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/durable/README.md). The experimental pi-server talks about "Session writer ownership" held by one worker, while multiple clients attach as read/presentation views (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/server/README.md).
realtime:
Classic CLI: none. Sessions are local files, and sharing is a one-shot snapshot: a secret gist or Radius artifact that is not updated afterwards (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interactive/session-share.ts).

Experimental stack: real-time viewing does exist.
- pi-durable commits partial output at most every 100 ms. `watch()` streams the Chord operations of each commit to subscribers.
- A slow watcher is capped at 100 frames, then collapsed to a full snapshot. Late joiners get the current view with no replay.
- pi-protocol v8 carries this over length-prefixed CBOR frames on any ordered byte stream (Unix socket, WebSocket). Routing uses {serverId, sessionId, attachmentId}, and the attachment ID is there to reject stale frames.

Sources: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/durable/README.md, https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/protocol/README.md, https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/client/README.md
search_retrieval:
The /resume session picker searches each session's id, name, the concatenated text of all its messages, and its cwd. It supports fuzzy tokens, quoted phrases and `re:<regex>`, sorts by threaded, recent or relevance, and can filter to named sessions. Matching is a linear in-memory scan, with no index (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interactive/components/session-selector-search.ts).

Inside a session, /tree navigates to any entry, and labels act as bookmarks. `--continue` reopens the latest session for the current cwd. There is no full-text index, no cross-session recall tool for the model, and no semantic search. Sources: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/sessions.md and https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session-format.md
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak. Each session is tied to a working directory: the cwd is in the header and the storage folder is keyed by path. Compaction and branch-summary `details` record readFiles and modifiedFiles. There are no git commit SHAs or branch names in the format, and grep finds none in session-manager.ts.

An example extension (git-checkpoint.ts) runs `git stash create` at each turn so /fork can offer to restore code. Its entry-to-stash map lives only in memory and is not written to the session (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/git-checkpoint.ts).

Sharing does not touch the code repository. A gist is a separate git-backed object, not linked to commits or PRs.
scale: No published scale claims for session storage. Every session is fully loaded into memory and searched by linear scan. pi-durable mentions storage benchmarks (`npm run bench:storage`) but publishes no numbers (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/durable/README.md). I could not verify any figures for user counts or session sizes.
privacy_security:
Session JSONL is stored in plaintext with no encryption at rest and no secret redaction on write or on share. The docs only warn users to "Review exported or shared sessions first. They can contain prompts, model responses, tool arguments, command output, file contents" and credentials (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/sessions.md, https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/security.md).

Sharing:
- The gist is created with --public=false, i.e. a secret, unlisted gist that anyone with the URL can read.
- The viewer link is https://pi.dev/session/#<gistId>, configurable through PI_SHARE_VIEWER_URL. Putting the ID after `#` keeps it out of the pi.dev server request.
- Radius uploads use a bearer token with visibility=organization.

Sources: https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interactive/session-share.ts and https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/config.ts

Redaction appears only in /bug reports: sensitive JSON keys and URL query parameters become `<redacted>`, and the transcript is optional (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/bug-report.ts).

Trust model: prompt injection from AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md is declared out of scope. Context files load regardless of project trust, and the local user account is the trust boundary (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/SECURITY.md). The CLI shells out to `gh` and calls the network itself, the opposite of ParleyInn's I4.
license: MIT (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/LICENSE; https://pi.dev/news/2026/5/7/pi-has-a-new-home)
lesson_for_parinn:
Pi shows that one append-only log can hold both the "raw record" and the "model context". It needs an id/parentId tree for branches, plus overlay entries that only append: `compaction` with firstKeptEntryId, `context_edit` that hides or replaces a target entry, and `branch_summary`. Context is then a deterministic projection from the leaf to the root, and the original entries are never mutated. That maps directly onto ParleyInn's I10 (derived state rebuildable) and its lossless restore.

ParleyInn should take the overlay-entry model but close three gaps in pi:
1. Pi still rewrites files in place on migration and fork. ParleyInn should never do that: migrate by projection, and hash-chain each entry, including its parentId, so a tree branch is tamper-evident.
2. Pi's sharing is an unredacted snapshot pushed through `gh`. ParleyInn's equivalent should be an explicit export, run by a separate tool, of a redacted, enveloped branch. A secret gist is unlisted, not private.
3. Pi's experimental durable stack keeps exactly one writer per store and streams commit ops to read-only attachments. That fits multi-agent real-time sharing better than merging: one writer per session log, many subscribers, and branches instead of merges.

name: Pi coding agent sessions (earendil-works/pi, formerly badlogic/pi-mono), JSONL session tree with /tree, /fork, /clone, /export, /share
status: shipped
what_is_stored:
Every entry of a coding-agent conversation goes into one JSONL file per session. Line 1 is a header: {type:"session", version:3, id, timestamp, cwd, optional parentSession}. Every later line is a typed entry with id, parentId and an ISO timestamp. The entry types are:
- message: an AgentMessage with role system, user, assistant or toolResult. Assistant messages record provider, model, usage, stopReason and thinkingLevel. System messages store the prompt sections and tool declarations as patches (toolsAdded and toolsRemoved), so the prompt and tool loadout can be replayed.
- model_change and thinking_level_change.
- usage: for example cache_warm cost, kept out of the LLM context.
- compaction: summary, firstKeptEntryId, tokensBefore, a systemMessage checkpoint, and optional details {readFiles, modifiedFiles}.
- context_edit: an append-only omit or replace of an earlier entry, affecting only future context.
- branch_summary: an LLM summary of an abandoned branch, with fromId.
- custom: extension state, outside the context. custom_message: extension text that does enter the context.
- label: a user bookmark on targetId.
- session_info: the display name.
Compaction never deletes the original entries ("It does not delete the original session entries"). Abandoned branches stay in the file. The session ID is a UUIDv7. Entry IDs are the first 8 characters of a random UUID, checked for collisions only within the session loaded in memory.
where_stored:
Local filesystem, outside any repository:
- Default path: ~/.pi/agent/sessions/--<cwd with separators replaced by '-'>--/<ISO timestamp>_<session-id>.jsonl. So sessions are grouped by absolute working directory, and each git worktree path gets its own folder.
- The location can be overridden with --session-dir, PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR or the sessionDir setting. A project-level sessionDir is read even before project trust is resolved.
- --no-session gives an ephemeral run with nothing persisted.
Off-machine copies exist only when the user exports or shares:
- /export writes a local HTML or JSONL file.
- /share uploads a JSONL artifact to Radius (https://radius.pi.dev/v1/artifacts, visibility=organization) when Radius auth is configured. Otherwise it uses `gh gist create --public=false`, which makes a secret GitHub gist holding the HTML export, viewed at https://pi.dev/session/<gistId>.
- The separate pi-share-hf tool publishes redacted sessions to a Hugging Face dataset.
An experimental separate runtime, pi-durable, stores sessions as SQLite at ~/.pi/agent/experimental/durable-sessions/<cwd-hash>/<session>/session.sqlite. It is not the default store.
format_and_model:
The model is a tree inside an append-only JSON Lines log. Each entry points to its parent through parentId, and roots have parentId null. The "leaf" is the current position. On load, the leaf is the last entry in the file.
- /tree moves the leaf to an earlier entry in the same file and branches from there. When you leave a branch, Pi can attach a branch_summary to the branch you enter.
- /fork creates a new file from an earlier user message. /clone copies the active branch into a new file. Both write parentSession into the new header as an absolute path to the original file.
- Building the context walks leaf to root. It then applies the latest compaction (summary plus entries from firstKeptEntryId onward) and then the latest context_edit per target. Only the active branch is sent to the model.
- Format versions: v1 was linear, v2 added id/parentId, v3 renamed hookMessage to custom. Older files are migrated on load.
Exports differ by path:
- JSONL export, used by Radius share, writes only the active branch, re-parented into a linear chain. The tree is lost.
- HTML export, used by gist share, embeds all entries plus leafId as base64 JSON in a self-contained HTML viewer.
Not strictly append-only. The file is created lazily: the first write, with open flag "wx", happens once a user or assistant message exists. After that each entry is written with appendFileSync. A version migration, or loading an empty file, rewrites the whole file in place (open "w"). Malformed lines are skipped silently on load.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Model: one process writes one session. The docs say nothing about concurrent writers. Parallel agents normally write separate files: one per session, grouped per cwd.

From the source at commit 7fbbd5f, inferred and not documented:
- There is no file lock and no fsync.
- Entry IDs are collision-checked only against the in-memory map.
- Two processes appending to one file with O_APPEND would tend to produce sibling branches. That works because every entry names its parent, but nothing guarantees it.
- A migration rewrite (open "w") could clobber a concurrent writer.

There is no merge:
- /fork and /clone only diverge, linking back by absolute parentSession path, which is not portable across machines.
- The only reconvergence is the LLM-written branch_summary attached when switching branches. It is lossy and model-generated.
- There is no cross-machine sync or conflict resolution.

The experimental pi-durable store is also single-owner: "One process owns a storage at a time; there is no cross-process locking". Its experimental TUI adds a lock file that goes stale after 10 seconds.
realtime:
Local only:
- Once the file exists, each entry is appended as it is created, so another local reader could tail the file.
- JSON event-stream mode and RPC mode stream live progress events to stdout for a single process, including streaming deltas, tool execution and compaction. These events are in-flight state, not the session file.
- An experimental Radius WebSocket relay exists in source (subprotocols pi-session-relay.host.v1 and pi-session-relay.client.v1) for remote clients attaching to a running session. Its product status and semantics could not be verified from docs.
Shares are one-shot snapshots. Neither gist nor Radius stays live-synced, and there is no multi-machine replication of session files.
search_retrieval:
For humans, the /resume session picker searches:
- Fuzzy tokens, quoted phrases and `re:` regex.
- It matches against session id, name, the concatenated text of all messages, and cwd.
- Sort modes are threaded, recent and relevance, and results can be limited to named sessions.
- It is built by fully reading every session file at list time, up to 64 files concurrently. There is no persistent index, no FTS and no semantic search.
Inside a session:
- The /tree navigator browses branches.
- Label entries bookmark entries.
- /session shows the file path, ID, message count, tokens and cost.
For programs, the SDK SessionManager offers getTree, getBranch, getEntries and listAll.
I found no built-in model-facing tool for recalling past sessions in the docs I read. The model sees only the active branch, after compaction and context edits.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak:
- The header records the absolute cwd, which also picks the storage folder.
- Compaction and branch_summary details record readFiles and modifiedFiles lists.
- No git commit SHA, branch or diff is persisted. The git branch shown in the footer is display-only.
- Sessions are not stored in the repository and are not attached to commits or PRs.
pi-share-hf maps one project directory to one Hugging Face dataset, and its LLM review judges whether a session is about that OSS project. That is a project-level association, not a link to a commit.
privacy_security:
Local storage:
- Session files are plaintext JSONL with no encryption and no redaction in core.
- The docs warn sessions "can contain prompts, tool arguments, command output, file contents, and credentials exposed during the conversation" and tell users to review before exporting or sharing.
- From source: session files are created with the default umask, while auth.json is written with mode 0600 in a 0700 directory.
Sharing:
- Gist sharing uses a GitHub "secret" gist. GitHub states "Secret gists aren't private": anyone with the URL can view one.
- The gist HTML embeds the whole session tree, including abandoned branches.
- Radius sharing uploads the active branch with organization visibility. It appends a pi.share entry containing the full system prompt and tool schemas.
- The HTML export guards the viewer itself: markdown URLs go through a scheme allow-list, and attributes and tree metadata are escaped, with XSS tests.
- /bug reports include provider config without credential values, and transcript inclusion is optional.
Public datasets go through the pi-share-hf pipeline:
- Exact-value secret redaction from an env file (default ~/.zshrc) or --secret.
- --deny regex rejection.
- A TruffleHog scan of the redacted output, where any finding blocks upload.
- An LLM review of shareability.
- Manual reject and a dry-run upload.
Threat model:
- Prompt injection from files or output is explicitly outside Pi's security boundary.
- Context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) load regardless of project trust.
- Pi has no built-in sandbox or permission system.
scale: No scale claims are published for the session store. From source, discovery reads every session file in full (1 MiB read buffer, 64 files at a time), so listing cost grows with total history bytes. Project popularity: the GitHub repo page showed about 111k stars and 14.1k forks when fetched. @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent 1.0.0 was published to npm on 2026-10-01.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy Pi's core idea: keep each event's parent pointer inside an append-only log. A fork, a branch switch or a compaction then adds entries and never rewrites history, and a context_edit is a new event, not a mutation. But make the IDs content-addressed instead of random 8-hex: hash(parent hash + canonical payload), which also gives ParleyInn its hash chain. Then copies of the same session from worktrees, cloud sandboxes or machines combine by plain set union into one DAG, and divergent writers become sibling branches with no git merge.

Do not copy what Pi gets wrong for ParleyInn's invariants:
- In-place file rewrites on migration.
- Silently skipped malformed lines (a silent drop, against I6).
- Absolute-path parentSession and cwd-keyed folders, which cannot move between machines.
- Lossy LLM branch summaries used as the only reconvergence.
- One-click share of unredacted history to secret gists, which are reachable by URL.

Sharing should be an explicit, audited projection. Model it on pi-share-hf's pipeline: exact-secret redaction, scanner backstop, deny-list, review, manual reject. It should never be the raw log.
