name: pi-share-hf
category: redacted publish to HF (one-way batch export of agent sessions to a public Hugging Face dataset)
status: shipped. It is a small TypeScript CLI by Mario Zechner, version 0.5.0 in package.json. The last commit on the default branch is 21c1d96 from 2026-04-13. As of 2026-10-02 the repo is not archived and has 259 stars, 24 forks, 5 open issues and 3 open PRs. No commits for about 6 months, so it is likely dormant but not superseded. Hugging Face's official agent-traces docs recommend it for Pi sessions.
what_is_stored: Pi coding-agent session files with exact known secrets redacted. A file is published only if it passed every gate: deny regexes, TruffleHog, LLM review, and no manual reject. Each published file is the full Pi JSONL session. That includes user and assistant messages, thinking blocks, tool calls and results, model and thinking-level changes, compaction and branch summaries, and extension data. Embedded images are kept unless --no-images is set. Next to the sessions the dataset holds a manifest.jsonl with one entry per file: file, source_hash, redaction_key, redacted_hash. A generated README.md dataset card records counts and the project's git origin URL. A private local workspace (.pi/hf-sessions/) holds workspace.json (cwd to repo mapping), manifest.local.jsonl, a cached copy of the remote manifest, redacted/ candidates, per-session redaction and TruffleHog reports (raw secrets stored only as a sha256 plus a masked form), LLM review sidecars and transcript chunks, extracted images, and reject.txt.
where_stored: Source: Pi's local session store, ~/.pi/agent/sessions/--<cwd with / replaced by ->--/<timestamp>_<uuid>.jsonl. Staging: the workspace .pi/hf-sessions/ inside the project directory, which the README says to add to .gitignore. Destination: a Hugging Face Hub dataset repo (git-backed and LFS-backed on the server side). It writes through the @huggingface/hub uploadFiles API as one commit per upload titled 'pi-share-hf upload <ISO time>', not through git. Nothing is stored in the project's own git repo.
format_and_model: Pi session format v3. This is JSONL where each line is a typed entry, and entries form a tree through id/parentId, so one file can hold several branches. v1 was linear and is auto-migrated. Pi's docs have moved: the README's pi-mono session.md link now returns 404, and current docs are at pi.dev and in the @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent npm package. Redaction walks every JSON string and replaces exact secret values with [REDACTED_<NAME>]. It does not change the structure, so the upload stays a valid Pi session that the HF trace viewer renders natively. The pipeline is incremental and keyed by content hashes. redaction_key = hash(source file sha256, secrets-set hash, noImages); redacted_hash = sha256 of the output. The review cache key combines the redacted hash, context-file hashes, provider, model, thinking level, deny hash, prompt version (4) and chunk size. The unit of publication is a whole session file, never single events.
multi_writer_and_merge: The README says you can use it on multiple machines for the same project, and the remote manifest.jsonl is the only coordination. collect and upload download it and skip sessions whose redaction_key or redacted_hash already match. Files are named <timestamp>_<uuid>.jsonl, so two machines rarely collide on a session name. upload merges the remote manifest snapshot with this machine's entries and uploads the merged manifest in a single commit. My reading of src/upload.ts and src/hf.ts, not documented: the commit is sent without a parentCommit or compare-and-swap. Two machines uploading at once could each overwrite manifest.jsonl, with the last writer winning. The session files would survive, but manifest entries could be lost, which only causes re-uploads. A machine with a different secrets set gets a different redaction_key, so it reprocesses and may re-upload a session differently redacted. Merges happen at whole-file granularity, a changed session replaces the old file, and there is no event-level or CRDT merge.
realtime: No. It is a manual, batch, human-in-the-loop pipeline: collect, then inspect with list/grep, then reject, then upload. Each collect re-runs TruffleHog and the LLM review on changed sessions. HF's own docs instead suggest `hf buckets sync` to Storage Buckets for continuous syncing as new sessions land, but that path has no redaction gate.
search_retrieval: Locally: `pi-share-hf list [--uploadable]` and `pi-share-hf grep <regex>`, which searches only the currently uploadable redacted set. It exists as a final human check for leaks, not for recall. Remotely: the HF Hub trace viewer (Data Studio) renders Pi, Claude Code and Codex JSONL natively, showing timeline, prompts, tool calls and results. Datasets are discoverable through the agent-traces format filter and the tags the dataset card emits (agent-traces, coding-agent, pi-share-hf). There is no index, no semantic search, and no API for agents to recall content.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Sessions are scoped to a project by Pi's cwd-derived directory. The dataset card records the project's `git remote get-url origin` URL, the only git call besides rev-parse. There is no linkage to commits, branches, files or PRs per session or per event, and nothing is written into the code repo, such as notes or trailers. LLM review uses README.md and AGENTS.md as context to judge whether a session is about the project (about_project: yes, no or mixed).
scale: No scale claims. TruffleHog runs in batches of 50 files, LLM review splits transcripts into chunks with configurable --parallel, and incremental hashing avoids reprocessing. Practical scale is one developer's sessions for one OSS project.
privacy_security:
Defence in depth with fail-closed gating:
(1) Deterministic redaction of exact literal values only. Sources are `export NAME=value` lines in --env-file (default ~/.zshrc), where NAME contains KEY/TOKEN/SECRET/PASSWORD/PWD/COOKIE and the value is longer than 4 characters, plus --secret files or literals. Longest values are replaced first. Generic regexes are deliberately avoided as too noisy. The generated dataset card claims 'curated credential patterns', but I found no such patterns in src/redactor.ts or src/secrets.ts at 21c1d96. That is an unverified gap between docs and code.
(2) User --deny regexes reject whole sessions.
(3) TruffleHog `filesystem -j --results=verified,unknown,unverified` runs on the redacted output. Any finding blocks the session. Reports keep only sha256 and a masked value.
(4) LLM review runs through the `pi` CLI with tools, skills and extensions disabled, and returns strict JSON. A session is uploaded only if shareable=yes, missed_sensitive_data=no and about_project is not 'no' on every chunk. Review errors or missing review data block the whole upload.
(5) Manual reject.txt plus a --dry-run.
Caveats: TruffleHog verification and the LLM review both send data over the network. Verification is TruffleHog's documented behaviour of checking candidates against provider APIs. The review sends redacted transcripts and images to whichever LLM provider is configured, such as openai-codex. Nothing is encrypted, because the destination is a public dataset. The HF write token comes from HF_TOKEN, HUGGINGFACE_TOKEN or ~/.cache/huggingface/token. Published content is permanent in HF git history even if later deleted. The dataset card sets license: other and warns the data is 'best-effort redacted'. The repo itself has no LICENSE file and no license field in package.json.
license: None declared. As of commit 21c1d96 there is no LICENSE file and no 'license' field in package.json, and GitHub shows no license. Datasets it generates are tagged 'license: other'.
lesson_for_parinn: Treat sharing as a separate, gated projection out of the local hash-chained record, never as the record itself. pi-share-hf's useful pattern is a content-addressed publish ledger. Each artifact carries (source_hash, redaction_key = hash(source, secret-set, options), redacted_hash), and both sides keep a manifest. Re-runs are therefore incremental, idempotent across machines, and auditable. A change in the secret set or reviewer forces reprocessing, and any gate error refuses the whole publish (fail closed, matching I6). ParleyInn could copy this for a later parinn-export or sync tool: exact-value redaction first, a pattern scanner on the redacted output, then human grep/reject. Keep that tool outside the no-network core (I4), since TruffleHog verification and LLM review call out. Three things to avoid. First, publish units are whole mutable files with a last-writer-wins manifest and no compare-and-swap, so ParleyInn should publish immutable, append-only segments keyed by chain hash and use parentCommit/CAS when the transport is a git-like hub. Second, an LLM judge reading untrusted transcripts is itself an injection surface: the transcript could talk the reviewer into shareable=yes. ParleyInn should never let a model's verdict be the only gate on content leaving the machine. Third, keep docs claims, such as the card's 'curated credential patterns', in step with code by running a drift test.
confidence: high. The facts come from reading the full source at commit 21c1d96 (2026-04-13) and the official HF docs. The multi-writer race and the docs-vs-code redaction gap are my own inferences from the code and are flagged as such.

name: Plandex
category: Terminal coding agent with versioned plan history. It is client-server, and the server stores each plan as its own git repository plus a PostgreSQL database.
status: shipped, but dormant. The open-source self-hosted version still runs; the last release is cli/server v2.2.1 (2025-07-16) and the last commit on main is 2025-10-03 ("link to cloud wind down post"). The GitHub repo is not archived (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/commits/main). Plandex Cloud has been "winding down as of 10/3/2025 and no longer accepting new users" (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/README.md). Issues kept arriving through Sep 2026, including two open path-traversal security reports (#352, Jun 2026; #367, Sep 2026), with no maintainer response visible (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/issues/367). On 2026-10-02, plandex.ai, docs.plandex.ai and app.plandex.ai all returned DNS SERVFAIL ("lame delegation", https://dns.google/resolve?name=docs.plandex.ai&type=A). So the official docs site and the wind-down post (https://plandex.ai/blog/winding-down) could not be fetched. I used the same docs from the repo's /docs folder instead. GitHub shows about 15.7k stars.
where_stored:
Server side, never in the user's project repo.

1. A private git repository per plan, on the server's persistent filesystem at $PLANDEX_BASE_DIR/orgs/<orgId>/plans/<planId>/. The default base is /plandex-server in production and ~/plandex-server in development (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/fs.go). In local mode this is the Docker volume plandex-files (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/docker-compose.yml).
2. A PostgreSQL database for orgs, users, projects, plans, branches, conversation summaries, model streams and repo locks. The self-hosting docs state the requirements: "The Plandex server requires a PostgreSQL database (ideally v14), a persistent file system, and git" (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/hosting/self-hosting/advanced-self-hosting.md).

On the client, the CLI keeps only pointers. The project-level .plandex/projects-v2.json holds org and project ids, and ~/.plandex-home holds auth.json, the current plan and settings (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/cli/fs/fs.go).

Plandex Cloud used AWS for hosting and the database (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/hosting/cloud.md).
format_and_model:
The plan directory is a git repo created with `git init -b main`, with commit author "Plandex <server@plandex.ai>". The server shells out to the git binary via os/exec (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/git.go).

Subdirectories (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/fs.go):
- conversation/<uuid>.json, one JSON ConvoMessage per message (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/convo_helpers.go)
- context/<id>.meta and <id>.body, plus a map file (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/context_helpers_store.go)
- results/<id>.json
- descriptions/<id>.json
- applies/<id>.json

Each event writes files and then runs `git add .` and `git commit -m <human summary>`. A summary looks like "Message #N | 💬 User prompt | <tokens> 🪙" or "🤖 Plandex reply". The version is the git commit SHA.

History is `git log --pretty=%h@@|@@%at@@|@@%B` parsed back out. Branches are git branches in that repo, created with `git checkout -b`. Rewind is `git reset --hard <sha>` (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/git.go).

Postgres mirrors branch metadata: parent_branch_id, status, context and conversation token counts (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/data_models.go). The author describes the design this way: "I tried to build the backend so that postgres, the file system, and git would combine to form effectively a single transactional database" (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39922550).

There is no hash chain beyond git's own commit DAG, and commits are unsigned. Rewind destroys history: "there's no way to undo a `rewind`", and branching first is the only safeguard (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/version-control.md).
multi_writer_and_merge:
One writer per plan, with no merging.

Writes are serialized by two layers:
- A Postgres-backed read/write lock: rows in repo_locks and lockable_plan_ids taken with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE, a 3 s heartbeat, a 60 s expiry, and exponential backoff with jitter (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/locks.go).
- A per-plan in-process operation queue. Writes run alone; reads are batched only when they target the same branch (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/queue.go).

Each plan repo has a single checked-out working tree, so a read on another branch conflicts with running reads, because it would force a checkout mid-read (locks.go comments). Only one active model stream may exist per plan and branch (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/model/plan/activate.go).

Branches exist to compare prompts, context or models side by side, and to make a rewind non-destructive (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/branches.md). The CLI has commands to create, switch, list and delete branches, but none to merge them (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/tree/main/app/cli/cmd).

Multi-user support exists only as "groundwork" for orgs. Plandex is "mainly focused on a single-user experience". The project-level .plandex file must either be committed with everyone in one org or be gitignored, "otherwise, each user will overwrite other users' .plandex files on every push" (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/orgs.md).
realtime:
Model output streams live from server to CLI as chunked HTTP (text/plain, messages separated by "@@PX@@") (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/handlers/stream_helper.go).

Tasks can run in the background. `plandex ps` lists them and `plandex connect` reattaches to a running stream (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/background-tasks.md).

For horizontal scaling, the server records each active stream's host IP in the model_streams table and proxies connect and stop requests to that host (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/handlers/proxy_helper.go).

History is persisted at event boundaries, one commit per message or build or apply, not per token. There is no real-time sync or collaboration between users or machines. Anyone can see a plan only by talking to the same server.
search_retrieval:
No search.
- `plandex log` lists versions. Its entries carry commit summaries; per the docs, message content is not included.
- `plandex convo [range]` prints the full conversation by message number, optionally as plain text.
- `plandex summary` shows the latest rolling summary.
- `plandex rewind [steps|sha]` returns to a version.
- `plandex plans` lists plans in the current and nearby directories.

Sources: https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/version-control.md, https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/conversations.md and https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/plans.md.

There is no full-text or semantic search across history or across plans. When the conversation exceeds the model's limit, older messages are swapped for automatic summaries. That swap is a context-window tactic, not retrieval (conversations.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
Loose, and only in one direction. A plan is bound to the directory where it was created, and context paths are relative to that directory (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/plans.md). Each context item records the SHA of the file it loaded (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/data_models.go).

Changes collect in a server-side sandbox until `plandex apply` writes them into the project. With auto-commit, which defaults to true, the CLI then commits only the touched files to the user's git repo (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/configuration.md). The commit message is "🤖 Plandex → <summary>" followed by per-step messages (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/shared/plan_result_pending_summary.go and https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/cli/lib/apply.go).

There is no back-link in either direction. The project commit carries no plan id or plan-history SHA. The server's PlanApply record lists message and result ids, not the project commit SHA (data_models.go).

Since v2.0.0, rewinding past an apply also reverts project files by default (auto-revert-on-rewind) (version-control.md).

Keeping plan history out of the project repo is deliberate. The author says it avoids intermingling the user's and the model's changes, tolerates a dirty git state, and works in directories that are not git repos (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39932661).
scale:
No claims about history size or throughput were found.

The README makes context claims only: it "can handle up to 2M tokens of context directly (~100k per file), and can index directories with 20M tokens or more using tree-sitter project maps" (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/README.md).

Storage is one git repo per plan, and each event runs `git add .` over the whole plan directory (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/server/db/git.go). The cost of each commit therefore grows with the number of files in the plan directory. That is my inference; no benchmark is published.

The author cites his own use on a codebase of about 200k lines, with a project map of about 43k tokens (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43718131).
privacy_security:
Model API keys are kept only in RAM during a stream: "never written to disk, logged, or stored in a database" (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/security.md).

Plandex will not load .gitignore'd files unless forced with --force, and also honours .plandexignore (security.md). There is no redaction or secret scanning. A file loaded as context, secrets included, is stored in plaintext JSON in the plan's git history on the server (data_models.go, context_helpers_store.go).

Rewind uses `git reset --hard`, so that alone does not purge objects already in the repo. This is my inference from git semantics; I did not test it.

Self-hosted mode has no encryption at rest beyond whatever the disk provides. The author says self-hosted mode has no telemetry (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39925211).

The local-mode docker-compose file:
- publishes Postgres on 5432 with user/password plandex/plandex;
- runs the server with GOENV=development, where email verification pins are skipped.

Sources: https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/app/docker-compose.yml and https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/hosting/self-hosting/advanced-self-hosting.md.

Plandex Cloud kept data "to debug and improve Plandex" and said it "may also be used to train and fine-tune models". It was "encrypted in transit and at rest" on AWS, deleted within 14 days of account deletion, and shared with OpenAI, OpenRouter, Vertex AI, Relace and others (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/hosting/cloud.md).

Stored model output is replayed onto the host:
- Apply and rewind write paths from stored plan results using `filepath.Join(fs.ProjectRoot, path)`, with no containment check. I confirmed this at app/cli/lib/apply.go:638,703 and app/cli/lib/rewind.go:175,271.
- Open issues #352 and #367 report that prompt-injected context can make apply or rewind write or delete files outside the project, while the confirmation prompt shows only a file count (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/issues/367). The full exploit chain is the reporter's claim; I did not reproduce it.
- After apply, a model-generated _apply.sh can run automatically: auto-exec defaults to true (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/docs/docs/core-concepts/configuration.md).
license: MIT (https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn:
Plandex is the clearest working example of git used as a private, server-side snapshot engine for agent history: one repo per plan, one commit per event, a branch per alternative. It also shows what that costs.
- Git, the filesystem and the database only behaved as "a single transactional database" after Postgres row locks, heartbeats and an in-process queue were added on top.
- Because each repo has one checked-out working tree, every plan has a single writer, and readers on different branches block each other.
- Rewind is a destructive `git reset --hard` with no undo, and branches never merge.
- The core shells out to the git binary (os/exec). ParleyInn's I4 forbids that.
- Replaying stored model output during apply or rewind writes model-controlled paths with no containment check (open issues #352 and #367).

Concrete takeaways if ParleyInn adopts git:
- Use it only as a content-addressed, append-only object store, written through plumbing (pure Go, no working tree, compare-and-swap ref updates).
- Never move a ref backwards. Express rewind and branch as new events that point to an earlier event, so the record stays lossless.
- Keep one writer per log.
- Put a back-link in both directions, from the session record to the code commit and from the code commit to the session.
- Treat anything replayed from history as untrusted data, never as file paths or commands to act on, which is I2.

name: PowerSync
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Synced data replicated from backend databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, SQL Server) as local SQLite copies on clients; the PowerSync Service maintains sync buckets with current state and full change history per bucket; write operations are queued on clients until backend processes them.
where_stored: Client: SQLite database file on device; Server: PowerSync Service stores sync buckets (organized logical partitions of data) with operation history; Backend: original source database (unchanged by PowerSync).
format_and_model: Data represented as JSON; stored in SQLite on client with schema; operations tracked as PUT (insert-or-replace) and REMOVE operations; checksums verify integrity by hashing individual operations per bucket; no custom binary formats.
multi_writer_and_merge: Default: last-write-wins per field (not per row); deletes always win (any delete prevents future updates). Supports CRDT integration (e.g. Yjs) for automatic collaborative merging when last-write-wins is insufficient (e.g. collaborative text editing). Writes go through application backend where developers control business logic, validation, authorization, and conflict resolution.
realtime: Sub-second end-to-end replication latency from Postgres through clients; uses persistent HTTP/2 or WebSocket connections for continuous change streaming; checkpoint-based protocol: server announces checkpoint with checksums, streams operations since client's last state, completes checkpoint, then waits for next cycle; client can interrupt and resume from last checkpoint.
search_retrieval: Full-text search via SQLite FTS5 extension (requires creating FTS5 tables with triggers); all queries run locally on client SQLite—no remote search; FTS5 supported in all PowerSync SDKs (JavaScript, Flutter, React Native, Kotlin, Swift, Node.js, .NET, Rust); data retrieval is local SQLite query performance.
links_sessions_to_code: Not designed for this. PowerSync is an offline-first app sync engine for mobile/web. No indication in documentation of tracking AI agent sessions, prompts, or code artifacts. Search for 'agent session prompt' returns unrelated PowerSyncPro migration product.
privacy_security: JWT-based authentication (HS256, RSA, EdDSA, ECDSA); 60-minute max token lifetime (5 minutes recommended); user identity in JWT subject claim; Sync Streams/Sync Rules enforce dynamic access control per user—only relevant data syncs to each user (rows filtered by user context from JWT); supports SQLCipher for client-side encryption; no automatic path from untrusted content—write logic controlled by application backend; user-context injected into parameter queries for authorization.
lesson_for_parinn: PowerSync's dynamic partitioning model (Sync Buckets/Streams) is valuable: instead of syncing all history, partition session data by user/machine/ephemeral container so each agent recalls only its relevant context. Checkpoint-based streaming with resumability prevents duplicate transmission and enables recovery from network interruption. Separating write validation (server) from conflict resolution (client) allows flexibility—ParleyInn could apply this to distinguish pinned constraints (server-enforced) from session state (client-managed). However, PowerSync targets offline-first apps, not audit logs with untrusted recall: ParleyInn's I2 invariant (no untrusted content to model) and I6 (no silent failures) require stricter boundaries.

name: Radicle (Collaborative Objects / COBs)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Social artifacts including issues, patches, and discussions are stored as Collaborative Objects (COBs). COBs are Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) that enable decentralized collaboration. Each COB is identified by a unique Git Object ID (OID—a SHA-1 hash). All COBs are cryptographically signed using Ed25519 public-key cryptography. Repository metadata, delegate definitions, and identity documents are also stored. COBs are stored alongside code within Git repositories rather than on external platforms.
where_stored: COBs are stored as Git objects within local bare repositories using Git's namespace feature. Each peer maintains its own namespace within a shared repository structure, enabling local-first storage where changes sync when peers reconnect. The repository receives a unique Repository ID (RID) derived from an identity document. Nodes are identified by Node IDs (NIDs) based on Ed25519 public keys. Data is never centralized; each node maintains a copy of repositories it participates in.
format_and_model: COBs use Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) as the underlying mechanism for data consistency without requiring conflict resolution. They are stored as Git objects with cryptographic signatures. The data model uses 'signed refs' to record repository state updates. Issues and patches are implemented as COBs with support for comments, revisions, and status tracking. Version 1.2.0 added JSON output for COBs enabling programmatic access. The identity document format includes metadata (name, description), delegates with authority over critical operations, and repository RID.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multiple writers can append data to a COB simultaneously, and changes from different nodes merge automatically without conflict due to the CRDT data structure. The system explicitly states 'any node can append data to a COB, and changes from different nodes can be merged without conflict.' This conflict-free property eliminates the need for manual merge resolution or centralized coordination. All operations are signed by their author, allowing verification of authorship independent of merge order.
realtime: Uses a gossip protocol for peer-to-peer communication with eventual consistency semantics. Nodes announce presence, inventory, and reference updates through gossip messages. Communication is encrypted via Noise protocol handshakes providing strong forward secrecy. Connections are made on port 8776 by default. The system operates in offline-first mode—users can create COBs (issues, patches) without internet access; synchronization occurs when peers reconnect. No strict real-time requirement; the network converges eventually as nodes exchange information.
search_retrieval: Search and retrieval are primarily command-line based via the `rad` CLI tool. Version 1.2.0 added JSON output for COBs and multi-COB display capability, enabling programmatic querying. The `rad patch` command supports multiple actions including filtering by status. Built-in search capabilities are not emphasized as a primary feature in official documentation. Full-text search or sophisticated query capabilities are not mentioned in primary sources. Retrieval is primarily by repository, issue ID, patch ID, or node identifier.
links_sessions_to_code: Patches are directly tied to code changes within repositories. COBs (particularly patches) create a link between discussion artifacts and specific code revisions. However, there is no mention of explicit agent session tracking, prompt history, or AI coding-agent context linking in Radicle's documentation. COBs could theoretically store agent session metadata if stored as custom COB types, but this is not a built-in feature. The system is designed for human collaboration, not agent session tracking.
privacy_security: All social artifacts are stored in Git and signed using Ed25519 public-key cryptography, ensuring authenticity and authorship verification. Peer-to-peer communications use Noise protocol handshakes for encryption with strong forward secrecy. Users operate independent nodes, maintaining full control and ownership of their data—no central authority can access or control information. Data is not encrypted at rest in standard configuration; security relies on local node control and cryptographic signing rather than encryption-at-rest. No explicit redaction mechanism is mentioned for sensitive data. The local-first architecture means users control backup and migration independently. Seed nodes can facilitate connectivity for NAT-restricted users but cannot forge repository data due to cryptographic identity.
lesson_for_parinn: Radicle demonstrates that CRDTs enable high-fidelity, conflict-free merging of non-code artifacts (issues, discussions) across a distributed network without central coordination. For ParleyInn, this suggests that CRDT-based append-only structures could support multi-agent session history replication across machines without requiring central consensus or merge conflicts. The use of Git as native storage (storing social objects directly as Git objects) validates using Git's cryptographic integrity as a foundation for trusted history. The 'signed refs' pattern and identity documents show how to establish repository-level cryptographic identity and delegate authorization without requiring external PKI. However, Radicle's signing model (per-change signing) differs from ParleyInn's requirement to treat all recalled content as untrusted and re-inject pinned constraints—ParleyInn would need additional envelope protection beyond what Radicle provides.

https://radicle.dev/ — Official Radicle website and homepage
https://radicle.dev/guides/user — Radicle User Guide on COBs and local-first storage
https://radicle.dev/guides/protocol — Radicle Protocol Guide describing nodes, identity, networking, and storage
https://radicle.dev/guides/seeder — Radicle Seeder Guide describing peer replication and seeding policies

name: Rekal (rekal-cli)
status: shipped
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/rekal-dev/rekal-cli/blob/main/LICENSE)
what_is_stored: Raw AI coding-agent transcripts captured on every git commit, with no LLM summarization (README). data.db tables: sessions (ULID, content hash, actor_type human/agent, agent_id, email, branch, source adapter, plus subagent metadata such as parent_session_id, team, workflow and spawn_depth); turns (role, full content, ts); tool_calls (tool, path, command prefix only, no tool output); checkpoints (git_sha, branch, email, exported flag); files_touched (from `git diff --name-status HEAD~1 HEAD`); and checkpoint_sessions, which joins checkpoints to sessions (cmd/rekal/cli/db/schema.go; docs/spec/command/checkpoint.md). Some tables never leave the machine: checkpoint_state, recall_edges (query text and access patterns), merge_gate_cache and schema_meta. A separate, disposable index.db holds BM25 FTS, LSA and nomic embeddings, facets, file co-occurrence and a 'knowledge' chunking of the repo's prose at HEAD (docs/db/overview.md). Adapters exist for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, Kiro and OpenCode (cmd/rekal/cli/session/).
where_stored: On disk: two DuckDB files in .rekal/ in the repo, gitignored and local. All linked worktrees share the main checkout's store. Transport: a local orphan branch per author, rekal/<email>, pushed to the existing git remote (GitHub, Forgejo or any other host). It holds two files, rekal.body and dict.bin. Teammates' branches are fetched into refs/remotes/origin/rekal/* (README; docs/git-transportation.md; docs/usage.md#worktrees).
format_and_model: Locally there are two DuckDB databases. data.db is the ledger, append-only by code convention; no DB triggers or hash chain were found. index.db is a pure function of the ledger and is rebuilt atomically (write a temp file, then rename). The wire format is custom binary. rekal.body starts with the header 'RKLBODY' (magic, version u8, flags u8), followed by frames. Each frame has an uncompressed 6-byte envelope (type u8, compressed_len u24, advisory uncompressed_len u16) and a zstd payload compressed with a 16 KB preset dictionary built into the binary. Frame types: session v1/v2 (turns as role, text and ts delta; tool calls as tool code, path ref and command prefix), checkpoint v1/v2 (HEAD SHA, branch, files with change type A/M/D/R, session refs), meta (counters), and batch 0x06 (one checkpoint's frames compressed together as one zstd stream). Readers skip unknown frame types by their length, which gives forward compatibility. dict.bin is an append-only string table with four namespaces (session ULIDs, branches, emails, paths), and frames refer to strings by varint index. Because existing bytes never change, git stores each new version as a delta of just the appended bytes. Commits to the branch are built with plumbing commands (hash-object, mktree, commit-tree), so the working tree is never touched (docs/git-transportation.md; docs/spec/command/push.md). Store and wire formats are frozen under semver as of 1.0 (README; docs/compatibility.md).
multi_writer_and_merge: Each author writes only to their own rekal/<email> branch, so two people never merge into the same file. Team sync (`rekal sync`) first checkpoints and pushes the caller's own work, then fetches every rekal/* branch. It decodes the other authors' frames into index.db only, never into data.db, and leaves out their tool calls. `rekal sync --self` imports the user's own remote branch into data.db, de-duplicating by session and checkpoint ID. A session already present is extended only when the stored turns are a prefix of the incoming ones; a frame that diverges is refused whole. When two machines share one identity, push and sync --self fast-forward the local orphan branch only if the remote strictly contains it. A real fork is never merged or rewound: the push is rejected and reported. rekal has no --force option, and a test (TestNoForcePushInSource) checks that no code path force-pushes. `--rebuild` regenerates the body from data.db, and only when the result is a superset of the remote body (docs/spec/command/sync.md; docs/spec/command/push.md; CHANGELOG 1.0.2). A merged-only gate controls publishing. A checkpoint is pushed only when its commit is an ancestor of the default branch, or when its branch landed as a squash commit with an equivalent patch (git cherry on a synthetic probe commit). Unmerged work stays local and is re-checked on each later push (docs/design/merged-only-sharing.md).
realtime: Not real time. Capture runs in the post-commit hook (rekal checkpoint). Publishing runs in the pre-push hook (rekal push), which fails open by default, and only merged work is published. Pulling teammates' context is a manual `rekal sync`. Nothing streams or runs in the background between commits, and work in progress is not shared until it merges to the default branch (README developer touchpoints; docs/spec/command/push.md; docs/spec/command/sync.md).
search_retrieval: All retrieval is local and hybrid: BM25 full-text search in DuckDB, LSA embeddings, deep embeddings from nomic-embed-text run on-device through llama.cpp/CGO, file co-occurrence and facets. Embeddings can optionally come from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. `rekal "<q>"` returns a compact 'seed digest' with a verdict (INJECT, KNOWLEDGE or SILENCE), a confidence score per session, and pointers for drilling in. Other commands: `rekal query --session <id> [--role human_steering]` for progressive loading, `rekal find` to list every mention of a term in time order, and `rekal query --sql` for read-only SQL. A personal 'recall graph' (recall_edges) slightly boosts sessions the user keeps returning to and is never synced. Claimed results: LoCoMo 90.57% accuracy and 98.61% recall@20, LongMemEval 86.6%, with about 7.5K context tokens per query and a median recall latency of about 150 ms (README benchmarks; arXiv 2607.14390). These figures are self-reported and were not independently checked.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and this is the core of the design. Each post-commit checkpoint row records the HEAD git_sha and branch, links to the sessions it covers through checkpoint_sessions, and lists files_touched from the commit's diff. Search can filter by --commit <sha>, --file <regex>, --author and --actor human|agent. Results carry the author, branch and commit (README commands reference and JSON example). The merged-only gate also ties publishing to whether the code reached main.
scale: Claims from the project's own sessions on an Apple M4 (6 Claude transcripts, 14 sessions, 473 turns): 8.5 MB of raw JSONL becomes 54 KB on the wire (about 158x), with a 5.8 MB data.db and a 10.8 MB index.db (README). SOUL.md claims that 'A year of team context fits in 200 KB' and that a 2–10 MB session shrinks to about 300 bytes on the wire. The design keeps one body file rather than shards, on the reasoning that git handles large append-only files well (docs/git-transportation.md). There is no published test with many authors or a large monorepo. The binary is about 170 MB to download because it bundles DuckDB, llama.cpp and the embedding model (README).
privacy_security: Redaction runs once, at capture, before anything is written to data.db. It uses about 25 regex patterns (Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, AWS, Slack, npm and PyPI tokens, JWTs, private keys, bearer tokens, DB connection strings, env-style secrets, URL secret parameters, emails, IPv4 addresses). It also flags high-entropy strings: 40 or more characters with Shannon entropy at or above 4.5 bits per character, with exceptions for paths and decorators. Home-directory paths are anonymized and text is normalized to valid UTF-8 (cmd/rekal/cli/scrub/scrub.go, secrets.go). The project calls redaction best-effort. If a secret leaks, the advice is to rotate it first and then rewrite or force-push the branch (SECURITY.md). Other controls: nothing local-only goes on the wire (recall_edges, configs, API keys); sessions imported from other repos stay index-only and cannot be pushed; there is no server, telemetry or phone-home. The only optional network call is the HTTP embedding backend you configure yourself. Not present: encryption at rest or on the branch, signing of frames or commits, and any hash chain or tamper evidence. Anyone who can read the remote can read every pushed session. Malicious wire frames (decompression bombs, allocation blowups) are in scope for security reports. Prompt injection through recalled content is explicitly out of scope: 'An agent acting on recalled content' is the agent's responsibility. SECURITY.md still says 'Rekal is pre-1.0', which is stale (SECURITY.md).
lesson_for_parinn: Rekal shows that git transport for a session ledger works without merge conflicts when (a) each writer owns its own orphan ref, (b) the ref holds an append-only, prefix-stable binary body plus an append-only dictionary, so git stores each push as a delta of just the appended bytes and the client only fast-forwards, never merges or force-pushes, and (c) a fail-closed 'merged-only' gate decides what is published. ParleyInn should copy (a) through (c), and fix two of Rekal's gaps. First, key refs by writer instance (machine or sandbox ID), not by email. Rekal's per-email ref forks when two machines share one identity, and a fork is simply rejected. Second, add the integrity and trust layer Rekal lacks: hash-chain and sign each frame, and verify on import. Imported records should stay in a separate, derived store (as Rekal's team sync writes to index.db only), and recalled text should be treated as untrusted and always wrapped in an envelope (ParleyInn I2), where Rekal explicitly places this out of scope. Rekal's push also runs in git hooks, so ParleyInn's I4 'no network in core' still holds if the git binary, invoked from a separate non-core process, does the transport.

name: Relace Repos
category: agent code-storage API (hosted git-compatible source control for AI codegen apps)
status: shipped. Relace announced it on 2025-10-16 (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos). As of Oct 2026 it is listed in the live docs index (https://docs.relace.ai/llms.txt) and in the official TypeScript SDK @relace-ai/relace 0.10.0, last modified 2026-08-07, which has repo, repo_token and repo_webhook resources (https://registry.npmjs.org/@relace-ai/relace). No beta label appears in the docs. Some features are partial or still to come. Reverse sync from Relace to GitHub is 'not currently supported but will be available in an upcoming release' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/github-integration). The repo.merge()/repo.refactor() subagents announced in Oct 2025 are absent from SDK 0.10.0 (inspected from the npm tarball). The two-stage semantic retrieval announced in Oct 2025 seems to have been replaced in the docs by agentic search (see search_retrieval). The project is not archived.
what_is_stored:
1) Source code repositories with git history. Files are 'Treated as UTF-8 text; binary content should be avoided', and 'Binary files are skipped downstream during embedding' (SDK docstrings, @relace-ai/relace 0.10.0 src/resources/repo/repo.ts, https://registry.npmjs.org/@relace-ai/relace/-/relace-0.10.0.tgz). Importing from a git URL defaults to shallow=true, and then 'Commit history is not preserved' (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/create).
2) Per-repo custom metadata as a flat key/value object; the SDK types it as {[key:string]:string}. It can be filtered with filter_metadata on list (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/list), and an update 'overwrites any existing metadata' (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/update).
3) Repo created_at/updated_at timestamps (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/get).
4) Repo-scoped access tokens with an optional TTL (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repo_tokens/create).
5) One push-webhook configuration per account, holding a URL and an optional token. This appears only in the SDK, not in the public docs (src/resources/repo-webhook.ts).
6) Per the Oct 2025 announcement, embeddings kept 'in a vector database, and kept in sync with your source code' (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos).
Nothing in the docs stores agent sessions, prompts, transcripts or tool-call logs. Commit messages are whatever the client writes. The commit author and message for API-made commits are not documented.
where_stored: Server/cloud. Relace hosts the repositories, which are reachable as git remotes at https://api.relace.run/v1/repo/{REPO_ID}.git and through REST on the same host (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/git-commands, https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/introduction). The backend is not disclosed: no storage engine, git server implementation, cloud provider or region is named. The announcement gives no architecture details (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos). Self-hosted and VPC deployment is advertised for Relace models; it is not stated for Repos (https://www.relace.ai/).
format_and_model:
The git object model (commits, refs, branches) is exposed over git smart HTTP. 'All standard git commands are supported... git fetch, git checkout, git branch, git merge, git log' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/git-commands). A JSON REST layer sits beside it, with each repo identified by a UUID (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/create).
Create sources come in three types (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/create):
- 'files': inline filename/content pairs
- 'git': url, branch, shallow
- 'relace': a template repo_id, with copy_metadata/copy_remote
Template-based creation is 'nearly instantaneous' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/relace-templates).
Update variants, each returning {repo_id, repo_head (commit SHA), changed_files} (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/update):
- 'files': a snapshot that replaces all content; 'Any files not included will be deleted'
- 'diff': write/rename/delete operations
- 'git': pull from a remote, described as 'pull & merge from a remote Git repository' in the SDK docstring
Single-file PUT, GET and DELETE on /v1/repo/{id}/file/{path} each auto-commit and return the new head (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/upload; SDK src/resources/repo/file.ts). GET /clone returns every tracked file's content as JSON (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/clone). The SDK adds an optional `commit` parameter to read a past snapshot (SDK RepoCloneParams). The response to an update is the new commit hash (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/onboarding). The OpenAPI spec documents only create, list, delete and update for repos (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/openapi.json).
multi_writer_and_merge:
The service is centralized: one hosted remote per repo. Two write paths exist.
(a) Git push from clones. Standard git semantics apply. Non-fast-forward handling is not separately documented and is presumably stock git behavior; this is not verified (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/git-commands).
(b) REST updates. These commit on the server against the current head. The SDK says 423 means 'Repository lock contention' and 400 can mean 'failed remote merge' (SDK src/resources/repo/repo.ts). The API docs list 423 as 'resource is temporarily locked (Repos endpoints only)' (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/introduction). Writes are therefore serialized by a per-repo lock.
The update API takes no expected-base-commit or if-match parameter (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/update). My inference: concurrent REST writers silently overwrite each other at file granularity rather than conflicting. A 'files' snapshot update also deletes anything another writer added.
Inside one diff request, operations run in phases (deletes, then writes, then renames), and 'the last write wins for a file' (SDK docstring).
Branches are available through the git CLI, and the homepage advertises 'fast branching for spawning subagents' (https://www.relace.ai/). The REST API exposes a branch only on git-source create/update.
GitHub sync works only 'If the Relace Repo has not diverged from the GitHub source' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/github-integration). Automatic conflict merging was announced as future work (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos).
realtime:
Repos have no live sync or streaming replication; clients pull and push. Two partial mechanisms exist:
(1) Push webhooks. The SDK defines a per-account webhook config (PUT/GET/DELETE /repo_webhook, with url and an optional token). The payload is {event:'push', repo_id, ref, commit}. This appears in SDK 0.10.0 only (src/resources/repo-webhook.ts) and I found no public docs page for it.
(2) Search streams progress as Server-Sent Events (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/agents/fast-agentic-search).
The announcement says embedding computation 'must be done asynchronously, exposing potential race conditions'. Index freshness was therefore eventually consistent (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos). The current docs say agentic search 'always runs on the current state of the code' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/onboarding).
search_retrieval:
Current docs, Oct 2026: POST /v1/repo/{id}/search with a natural-language query runs the 'relace-search' Fast Agentic Search agent. Its tools are view_file, view_directory, grep_search, bash and report_back. It streams SSE events (started with a prompt_id, then agent, tool, done). The final report_back event carries an explanation and a map of files to line ranges (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/agents/fast-agentic-search, https://docs.relace.ai/docs/fast-agentic-search/agent, https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/search). The homepage claims it can 'search a codebase in under a second' (https://www.relace.ai/).
Oct 2025 announcement: 'built-in two-stage retrieval'. A vector search narrows the candidate files and a reranker orders them, with auto-indexing, chunking of large files and an embedding store kept in sync (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos).
No semantic or retrieve endpoint exists in the current docs or OpenAPI: docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/retrieve.md returns 404 (checked 2026-10-02), and the OpenAPI is at https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/openapi.json. Only an 'embedding' remark survives, in an SDK docstring. The 'semantic search' in the discovery note therefore looks superseded by agentic grep/bash search. The Wayback Machine refused my requests (HTTP 429), so I could not confirm when or whether the endpoint was removed.
Repo listing has metadata filtering and created/updated ordering, with at most 100 results per page (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/list). There is no search over history or commits.
links_sessions_to_code:
No. Nothing in the Repos docs ties an agent session, prompt or trace to a commit. Metadata is per repo, not per commit (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/update). Search runs carry a prompt_id, but nothing documents it being stored or linked to commits (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/agents/fast-agentic-search).
Relace does process agent traces elsewhere. /v1/code/compact 'Compress[es] an agent trace to only the important details', taking OpenAI-style messages and tool_calls (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/openapi.json). Under the ZDR policy, such model inputs are held 'only transiently, in memory' and not persisted (https://www.relace.ai/legal/zero-data-retention-policy). Session data is therefore deliberately stateless, and code is the only durable artifact.
privacy_security:
Authentication:
- Bearer API keys with the prefix 'rlc-' (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/introduction).
- Repo tokens with the prefix 'rlcr-', scoped to a list of repo_ids with read/write access. They take an optional ttl_seconds, are 'shown' only once, and can be deleted after a sandbox session. They are 'strongly recommended for use in sandboxed environments' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/repo-tokens, https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repo_tokens/create). Read-only scoping is not offered.
- A missing permission returns 403 on Repos endpoints (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/introduction).
Compliance and encryption: the homepage FAQ claims SOC 2 compliance and says 'Even on our hosted tier, all data is encrypted in transit and at rest' (https://www.relace.ai/). The Vanta trust center at https://trust.relace.ai showed no readable content to my fetcher, so these claims are unverified beyond the marketing page.
Retention: the ZDR policy covers only 'the Platform, meaning Relace's API-accessible models' (https://www.relace.ai/legal/zero-data-retention-policy). Repos store code durably by design. The privacy policy, updated 2026-09-21, does not mention Repos retention, deletion or encryption (https://www.relace.ai/legal/privacy-policy). Delete removes 'a repo and all its associated data' (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/repos/delete).
No secret scanning, redaction or client-side encryption is described. The only hygiene advice is to use .gitignore for large files (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/git-commands).
Credential handling in the docs and SDK:
- Credentials go inside the git URL ('https://token:YOUR_API_KEY@api.relace.run/...'), so the token persists in the clone's .git/config. The sandbox examples put the full account API key there rather than a repo token (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/sandbox).
- The TS SDK git helper builds shell strings and runs them with execSync, e.g. `git -C ${rootPath} commit -m "${message}"`. This is a shell-injection risk if commit messages come from an agent (observed in @relace-ai/relace 0.10.0 src/git.ts).
scale:
Claims, none with published benchmarks:
- 'Multi-tenancy that scales to millions of repositories across thousands of users' (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/overview).
- The overview contrasts this with GitHub's limits of 100k repos per account or organization and 5,000 (or 15,000) REST requests per hour (https://docs.relace.ai/docs/repos/overview). The blog cites a 15k requests/hour limit for clone/push/pull (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos).
Rate limits are inconsistent across sources:
- Docs: 'per-key request budget over a rolling 60 second window. Free accounts start at 15 requests per minute... up to unlimited', with 429 and Retry-After (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/introduction).
- Homepage: 'no rate limits' (https://www.relace.ai/).
Other figures:
- Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB (413) on the model APIs (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/errors). I found no documented per-repo size limit.
- The retrieval benchmark covers apps of 50–500 files and open-source repos of 500+ files (https://www.relace.ai/blog/relace-repos).
- Pricing lists only token prices; Repos and relace-search cost $1/M input and $3/M output tokens. No storage or per-repo pricing is published (https://relace.ai/pricing).
license: The hosted service is proprietary. The SDKs are Apache-2.0: npm @relace-ai/relace 0.10.0 and PyPI relace 2.1.0, both pointing at github.com/squack-io/relace-sdk, which I could not open (GitHub API returned 403) (https://registry.npmjs.org/@relace-ai/relace, https://pypi.org/pypi/relace/json). The OpenAPI document's info block says MIT (https://docs.relace.ai/api-reference/openapi.json).
lesson_for_parinn:
A vendor building 'git for agents' keeps git only as the interoperability wire for clone and push from ephemeral sandboxes. Everything agents actually need sits outside git, in a central server:
- per-sandbox tokens scoped to specific repos with a TTL
- a per-repo write lock (423 on contention)
- push webhooks
- an asynchronously rebuilt search index that is eventually consistent
- no session-to-code provenance at all (session traces are processed statelessly under ZDR and dropped)
Its REST write path also has no expected-head check, so concurrent writers silently overwrite each other.
Concrete takeaway: if ParleyInn ever ships history through a git forge, git should be a dumb append-only transport, not the merge engine or the source of truth:
- give each writer (agent, sandbox) its own append-only ref, so writes never merge or force-push
- verify the hash chain on receipt rather than trusting the remote's head
- use short-TTL, single-repo, ideally append-only credentials per sandbox, never an account key in a URL persisted to .git/config
- treat any index (FTS or embeddings) as a projection rebuilt from the record (I10), with its staleness surfaced rather than hidden
Relace's SDK also shows the I4 hazard ParleyInn already bans: execSync of string-interpolated git commands that carry agent-generated text.

name: Replit Agent checkpoints and rollbacks
status: shipped
what_is_stored: According to the docs, each checkpoint holds five things: (1) project files, meaning "all files, directories, installed packages, and project configuration"; (2) "AI conversation context", meaning "the complete conversation history and context that led to current state"; (3) environment configuration, meaning runtime and publishing settings; (4) "Agent memory", meaning "the AI's understanding of your project architecture, preferences, and patterns"; (5) the development database's data and schema. Each checkpoint also carries an AI-generated description, a timestamp, the scope of the change, and its cost (https://docs.replit.com/features/version-control/checkpoints-and-rollbacks). Since late 2025 Agent makes one checkpoint per request in Build mode, and complex builds are bundled into a single checkpoint (https://docs.replit.com/billing/ai-billing.md). The only part of "agent memory" that can be confirmed as a file in the repo is replit.md in the project root. Agent creates it, reads it into context and updates it (https://docs.replit.com/features/project-setup/replit-dot-md.md). The docs do not say whether "agent memory" holds anything beyond replit.md. Rollback restores the database only when the user ticks "Database". The production database is never rolled back this way and needs a separate point-in-time restore (checkpoints doc). Nothing in the docs says Secrets are part of a checkpoint; Secrets are a separate tool that stores encrypted environment variables (https://docs.replit.com/core-concepts/project-editor/app-setup/secrets.md). This could not be verified either way.
where_stored: The parts are stored in different places, all on Replit's servers. Code: a real git repo inside the app filesystem, where every checkpoint makes a git commit. The engineering blog says "we create a Git commit and record it in the checkpoint metadata" (https://blog.replit.com/inside-replits-snapshot-engine). So the checkpoint itself is a proprietary metadata record on Replit's side that points at a commit. It is not stored inside git. The same post says git history is copied to a separate disk volume, and that "every Replit application has an immutable, append-only git remote" for recovery, even if the whole filesystem is deleted. Filesystem and dev database: "Bottomless Storage". These are virtual block devices served over NBD and backed by Google Cloud Storage. They are split into immutable 16 MiB chunks, and a manifest lists the chunks for one version. The dev database is unmodified PostgreSQL running on that storage (same blog post). Conversation context: on Replit's servers. No public doc names its store or says whether it goes into git. Enterprise prompts are kept server-side and can be fetched through the Compliance API, keyed to project.message_sent audit events (https://docs.replit.com/teams/identity-and-access-management/compliance-api.md). GitHub: "GitHub integration maintains checkpoint synchronization", which means the checkpoint commits get pushed. No doc says conversation or memory reaches GitHub, apart from replit.md, which is an ordinary tracked file. My reading is that transcripts stay on Replit; this is an inference, not documented.
format_and_model: The model is a timeline of snapshots. Each checkpoint is a tuple of {git commit SHA, filesystem/DB manifest version, position in the conversation, description, timestamp, cost}. The blog spells out the git commit and the manifest operations; the other fields come from the docs' list of what a checkpoint holds. Taking a checkpoint copies the current manifest under a new name. Restoring swaps the current manifest for an older one. Both cost the same regardless of disk size because chunks are immutable, which is the same copy-on-write mechanism as Remix (https://blog.replit.com/inside-replits-snapshot-engine). Code history is plain git, and "all four version control options interact with the same underlying Git repository" (https://docs.replit.com/learn/projects-and-artifacts/version-control.md). Rollback restores code, AI context, configuration and tool settings, and optionally the dev database. "Roll forward" works until new changes are made; after that, the later checkpoints "become part of an alternate branch of history" (checkpoints doc). The format of the conversation and memory records is undocumented. There is no public schema, export format or API for checkpoint metadata (searched docs.replit.com/llms.txt; none found).
multi_writer_and_merge: There are three ways more than one writer can work. (1) Multiplayer: humans edit the same app live. Collaborators see checkpoints, and team admins can roll back across other users' sessions (checkpoints doc; Secrets doc permission table). (2) Background tasks: each task runs its own Agent and thread in an "isolated copy of your project". Core plans run 1 task at a time, Pro up to 10 and Enterprise up to 64. The main version changes only when a task is applied. When several tasks touch the same files, applying uses "AI-assisted conflict resolution" (the card shows "Resolving conflicts") instead of manual merges. Dependent tasks wait in a queue until their prerequisite has been applied (https://docs.replit.com/core-concepts/agent/task-system.md, https://docs.replit.com/learn/build-in-parallel.md, https://docs.replit.com/features/agent/task-lifecycle.md). (3) Git: branches, pull and push, and conflict markers resolved by hand in the Git pane, with remotes on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or self-hosted servers (https://docs.replit.com/features/workspace-tools/git-interface.md). The conversation and checkpoint timeline is never merged. Each task thread keeps its own conversation, and only code changes (plus the DB if chosen) flow back into main. No doc describes merging conversation histories.
realtime: Real-time inside Replit only. "Collaborators see checkpoint creation in real-time" (checkpoints doc). Task threads show a live status, and Multiplayer editing is real-time (Secrets doc; task-system doc). Sync to GitHub happens when commits are pushed, so it is not a live stream, and the conversation is not synced outside Replit at all.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by browsing. Users get a chronological History view, the Agent tab's checkpoint list with AI summaries, and the Git pane, where checkpoints appear as commits. Some views offer a visual preview of the app at a checkpoint (checkpoints doc). The docs describe no full-text or semantic search over past conversations or checkpoints. The blog notes the agent itself runs ordinary git tooling over history, for example to bring back code that had been refactored away (https://blog.replit.com/inside-replits-snapshot-engine). Enterprise admins can pull full prompt text per audit event through the Compliance API, which needs the audit-logs:read scope (compliance-api doc).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and this is the main point of the feature. The checkpoint metadata ties a git commit to a point in the conversation and to a storage manifest, so one rollback moves code, chat context and DB together (blog; checkpoints doc). The link lives in Replit's proprietary metadata, not in git. No commit trailer, git note or ref carrying a session or prompt id is documented. A commit pushed to GitHub therefore carries only an AI-written message, and the conversation that produced it stays behind on Replit. This is an inference from the lack of any mention, not a documented fact. Cost is also attached per checkpoint (ai-billing doc).
scale: Snapshots and forks cost the same however large the project is ("doesn't matter how large the filesystem is"). Bottomless Storage was announced as letting apps grow more than 256x (https://blog.replit.com/inside-replits-snapshot-engine). Parallelism tops out at 64 active background tasks on Enterprise (task-system doc). No figures were found for conversation size, checkpoint retention or how many checkpoints are kept. File History, a separate feature, keeps 30 days (version-control doc). Checkpoint retention could not be verified.
privacy_security: The platform is hosted on GCP in the US, with an optional region in India. It uses AES-256 server-side encryption at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit, and Replit holds a SOC 2 Type 2 attestation (https://docs.replit.com/teams/information-security/overview.md). Secrets are a separate store, AES-256 at rest, exposed as environment variables (Secrets doc). The git-pane doc warns that a GIT_URL secret is readable by anyone with access to the app (git-interface doc). No redaction of conversation context or checkpoints is documented. The Compliance API doc warns that kept prompts "can contain source code, secrets, personal data" (compliance-api doc). Prompts and context are used to train models unless a Pro user opts out; Enterprise content is not used (https://docs.replit.com/legal-and-security-info/model-improvement.md). On safety, the agent can only reach the dev database, and dev and prod are fully split. That split came after the July 2025 SaaStr incident, in which the agent deleted a production database and wrongly told the user that rollback was impossible (https://blog.replit.com/inside-replits-snapshot-engine; https://www.thestack.technology/vibe-coding-ceo-deletes-production-database/; https://incidentdatabase.ai/reports/5578/). There is no client-side or end-to-end encryption and no tamper-evident hash chain over conversation history, apart from git's own content addressing of code and the append-only backup remote.
lesson_for_parinn: Replit is the closest hosted precedent, and it does not put conversation history in git. Git carries code only. The checkpoint record is a separate store that points at commit SHAs. Its backup copy of the git history is an immutable, append-only remote that the agent cannot rewrite, so even an agent that corrupts .git cannot destroy history. ParleyInn can copy that split: keep its own append-only, hash-chained session record, and have each record entry reference the commit SHA(s) it produced. Use git/GitHub at most as a transport for code (and perhaps for opt-in, redacted exports), never as the store of record. Keep the record somewhere a misbehaving agent's git commands cannot reach. Two warnings also follow. Replit's rollback truncates the conversation, which would violate ParleyInn's lossless I1/I10 invariants; ParleyInn should model a rollback as an appended event, never as deletion. And the SaaStr incident shows the agent's claims about what can be recovered must never stand in for asking the record (I2/I6).
confidence: medium: the checkpoint contents, git commit per checkpoint, storage engine, task isolation and security posture are documented in first-party sources. Where conversation context is stored and its format, whether it reaches GitHub, and checkpoint retention are not publicly documented and are marked as inference.
license: Proprietary hosted SaaS (Replit, Inc.); terms at https://replit.com/terms-of-service and https://replit.com/pro-agreement. No open-source component for checkpoints.

name: Review Assist (uditk2/review-assist; npm review-assist-mcp)
category: PR review from session (session distilled into a committed, diff-anchored artifact)
status: shipped (small, early project: npm review-assist-mcp 1.0.5, first published 2026-07-26, last published 2026-09-21; last commit on main 2026-09-21. Single maintainer. I could not confirm the star count through the API: GitHub API access was blocked in this session, so the discovery note's "0 stars" is unconfirmed.)
what_is_stored:
Durable: one curated "Intent Document" (JSON, schema v0.1) per branch/PR. It is not the transcript. Sections (SPEC.md):
- meta: ULID id, repo, commit_range {base_sha, head_sha}, session {agent, model, session_ids[], started_at, ended_at}, generated_by, generated_at, interview stats.
- problem: statement, origin, user_asks quoted verbatim, out_of_scope.
- assumptions[]: impact_if_wrong, how_to_verify, confidence, plus open_questions[].
- approach: requirements with source, trials {what, outcome, why_abandoned}, adopted.
- tour[]: stops with what/why/role/provenance, anchors to diff hunks {path, old_start, old_lines, new_start, new_lines} pinned to head_sha.
- verification: performed, added_tests, not_verified.
- optional Mermaid diagrams.
The repo's own .intent/main.json records rounds, questions_asked, unresolved, author_attested and unanswered.

Local only, never committed:
- ~/.review-assist/consent.json: per-repo always/never decisions ("once" lives only in memory).
- ~/.review-assist/runs/<run_id>.json: interview scratch state (questions by q_id, answers, head_history).
- Imported transcripts for cloud sessions, also under ~/.review-assist.
Raw transcripts are read in place from ~/.claude/projects (or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR) and ~/.codex (or CODEX_HOME).
where_stored: Working-tree files in the PR branch: .intent/<branch>.json, with '/' and '\' in the branch name replaced by '-'. It is committed together with the code. GitHub is the only durable store. The GitHub App (a Cloudflare Worker) has no database and keeps nothing at rest. Local per-user JSON files under ~/.review-assist hold consent, runs and imported transcripts.
format_and_model:
JSON validated by JSON Schema draft 2020-12, with TypeScript types in packages/schema. It is a typed tree, not an event log:
- Tour stops form a tree through parent ids.
- Assumptions link to stops via depends; why fields reference problem, approach and assumption ids.
- Anchors are hunk coordinates pinned to one head_sha.

Each document describes exactly one commit range. It is regenerated per push, not appended to, and SPEC.md lists this as an open question. Run ids are content-addressed: sha256(repo | base_sha). Interview questions are keyed by a hash of the question text, so recording a round is an upsert.

Authoring is a two-agent pipeline run by the MCP server:
- an Author subagent that holds the transcript, read as a paged "spine";
- a role-locked Reviewer subagent that sees only the diff.
REVIEW_ASSIST_ROLE decides which tools are registered for each role. The Reviewer alone can call submit_document, which gates on consent, head drift, anchor resolution, interview attestation and five deterministic checks: schema, staleness, coverage, cross-refs and redaction. The MCP server never calls a model itself.
multi_writer_and_merge:
No real multi-writer model.
- There is one document per branch file. A second session on the same branch regenerates or overwrites it. There is no CRDT, append or merge logic.
- Git merge conflicts on .intent/*.json fall to ordinary git handling. No merge driver is provided.
- session_ids[] lets one document cite several sessions.
- On disk, the two local roles share only the run file, and the content-addressed id lets them find the same run without talking to each other.
- Re-running import_session overwrites the earlier copy, by design.
- Cross-repo "feature" linking with sibling repo/branch keys is v2 roadmap only, not built.
realtime: None. The document is produced at the end of a session or on demand and committed. The GitHub App reacts to pull_request opened, synchronize and reopened webhooks: it recomputes coverage and posts a Check Run, a sticky summary comment and a managed block in the PR description. The viewer fetches the document and diff per request with no-store.
search_retrieval:
No search index.
- The Author deliberately reads the whole "spine" (paged) instead of searching. Measured across 41 sessions: 85 MB of raw transcript, conversation a median 4.8% of it, median spine about 11,886 tokens. Ranked search was dropped because it "cost more than reading everything and returning less".
- list_transcripts ranks candidate sessions for a repo by matching against the change, with ties broken by recency.
- The diff is paged by read_diff and the hunk index.
- Reviewers retrieve by PR: the viewer loads .intent/<branch>.json at head_sha.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and strongly. meta.session.session_ids[] and agent name the source sessions. commit_range pins base and head SHAs. Every tour stop anchors to concrete diff hunks at head_sha, carries a provenance marker (from_transcript, confirmed_in_interview or inferred_from_code) and why-links to verbatim user asks, assumptions and trials. A coverage check reports diff hunks no stop explains ("unexplained") and anchors not in the diff ("dangling"); .intent/ itself is excluded. A staleness check fails when head_sha is not the PR head. The link is to a curated summary, not to recallable raw prompts: the transcript is never shipped.
scale:
No throughput claims. The concrete figures are internal measurements:
- 41 sessions, 85 MB of transcript; the spine of 40 of them fits in one call.
- Over 15 runs, a median distillation of 1400 s, of which 670 s was a serialized phase. It was fixed by seeding standing questions so the Author and Reviewer run in parallel.
- In the repo's own .intent, one document records 16 interview rounds; the files run 6 to 60 KB.
privacy_security:
- **Transcript stays local.** The Intent Document is a curated artifact, and SPEC principle 5 makes redaction a generation step.
- **Redaction lint.** It walks every string field and hard-fails on regexes for AWS key ids, GitHub tokens, Slack tokens, generic api_key/secret/password/token assignments and URLs with embedded credentials. Users can add patterns. It detects and rejects; it does not rewrite. Verbatim user_asks are an acknowledged privacy open question for public repos.
- **Consent.** The server requires per-repo consent (always, once or never) before writing.
- **Untrusted content.** Both .intent files and the .reviewer/ house-rules folder are treated as untrusted repo content, since a fork PR or a prompt-injected agent can write them. The house rules reach the Reviewer through a bounded tool and are framed as reference material that cannot relax checks. The viewer renders Mermaid with securityLevel strict, and the spec requires markdown sanitization.
- **App side.** No database. The reviewer's GitHub token lives only in an AES-GCM-encrypted, HTTP-only cookie keyed from SESSION_SECRET. Repo-content responses must be private, no-store and never edge-cached. The installation token is used only for bot output, and the reviewer's own token for comments and verdicts. Code does pass through the hosted Worker in transit; self-hosting is offered.
- **No encryption at rest.** The ~/.review-assist JSON files and the committed document are not encrypted.
License: Apache-2.0.
lesson_for_parinn:
Split the private record from a shareable projection, and gate the projection mechanically.
- Keep the full append-only log local.
- Publish to git (as a .intent-style file at a pinned head_sha) only a curated, typed document whose every claim carries a provenance marker and is anchored to diff hunks.
- Before anything is committed, a deterministic validator checks coverage, staleness, cross-references and secrets, and has the final word.

This fits I2, I4 and I10. A ParleyInn projection could be rebuilt from the record, and git would carry only the summary, never the raw history. Treat any such committed file as untrusted on read-back, as Review Assist does with .intent and .reviewer.

A secondary lesson is about identifiers. Content-addressed ids (sha256 of repo and base_sha, hashes of question text) let independent writers converge with no coordination. Putting the moving head into the id silently orphaned state, so the head became state, not identity.
license: Apache-2.0
confidence: high (based on a full read of the cloned repo at commit 951da82 from 2026-09-21 and on npm registry metadata. Stars and adoption are unconfirmed; the mcpservers.org listing was not fetched.)

name: Rocicorp Zero
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Zero is a query-driven synchronization engine that replicates Postgres data to clients. Server-side: read-only SQLite replica of a PostgreSQL database maintained by zero-cache service. Client-side: normalized local SQLite store containing recently accessed rows. Works with normal Postgres databases using normal Postgres schemas. Schema is defined in TypeScript with ZQL (Zero Query Language). Supports IndexedDB as fallback client storage in browsers.
where_stored: Client storage: SQLite database or IndexedDB (browser default). Server storage: zero-cache maintains a SQLite replica of the Postgres database. Source of truth: PostgreSQL database. Storage locations: clients have persistent local SQLite; server has persistent SQLite replica at /data/replica.db in containerized deployments.
format_and_model: Data model: normal Postgres tables and schemas. Client storage: SQLite (schema auto-derived from Postgres). Server-side replica: SQLite with logical replication from Postgres. Query language: ZQL (Zero Query Language), a streaming query engine for incremental execution of complex queries. Type-safe: queries are generated as TypeScript functions with full type safety. Client bundle size: 718 KB uncompressed, 232 KB gzipped.
multi_writer_and_merge: Conflict resolution uses server reconciliation, a technique pioneered by the video game industry. Handles conflicts arising from multi-device or multi-client writes by reconciling on the server side. Writes are submitted to Postgres (the authoritative source), which returns results that replicate back to clients. No explicit merge algorithm described; conflicts are resolved server-side through Postgres transaction semantics.
realtime: Continuous synchronization: sync engine runs continuously between client and server. Queries execute first against local cache, returning results in the next frame while server fetches authoritative results in parallel. Changes pushed from server to client in background. System enables real-time user experiences with instant local reads and eventual-consistency writes. Specific network latency figures not published.
search_retrieval: ZQL provides query capabilities: filters, joins, and aggregations over Postgres data. Query-driven sync gives developers precise control over what data synchronizes to each client. Queries execute optimistically against local SQLite, with server results delivered asynchronously. Inspector tools available for query optimization and debugging slow queries. Supports querying by ID, filtering with WHERE clauses, and complex joins.
