links_sessions_to_code: No: Zero is designed for application data synchronization (music, documents, lists, etc.), not for tracking agent sessions or linking prompts to code. Does not provide session history, prompt logging, or code attribution features. Not applicable for ParleyInn's use case of recording agent-session history.
privacy_security: Authentication: supports cookies (with CSRF protections - warns against SameSite=None) or JWT/Bearer tokens, forwarded to application endpoints. Permission model: delegated to application layer (filter-based read permissions, ownership checks for writes, role validation). Data privacy: by default stores in browser IndexedDB, shared across users on same device (mitigated by setting kvStore='mem' for in-memory storage). Can call zero.delete() to clear all synced data. No encryption at rest mentioned. Server reconciliation provides conflict handling but does not provide redaction or data masking.
lesson_for_parinn: Query-driven sync is a powerful pattern for selective synchronization: Zero controls what replicates via explicit query definitions rather than whole-table rules. Server reconciliation is a proven conflict-resolution strategy applicable to multi-agent scenarios. However, Zero's core design (mutable state, server-reconciled conflicts, application-delegated permissions) differs fundamentally from ParleyInn's requirements: ParleyInn needs append-only, cryptographically hash-chained records where history never becomes a prompt-injection channel. Zero would not serve as storage for agent session history because it prioritizes operational consistency and data freshness over auditability and immutability. The lesson: for agent-session history, query-driven patterns should inform selective recall (ParleyInn could expose queries for session retrieval) but the storage model itself must be immutable and append-only.
sources: https://zero.rocicorp.dev/docs/tutorial (tutorial describing data model and storage)
https://rocicorp.dev (company background, team, and product history)

name: Roo Code checkpoints (shadow-git snapshots in the Roo Code VS Code extension)
status: archived. The discovery note missed this. The docs page still shows a 2026-05-15 update and no discontinuation notice (https://roocodeinc.github.io/Roo-Code/features/checkpoints). But the repo README says "The Roo Code Extension was shut down on May 15th" and points users to ZooCode and Cline. GitHub shows "This repository was archived by the owner on May 15, 2026. It is now read-only" (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code). The last commit is b867ec9 on 2026-05-15, titled "Remove roocode.com web app (#12375)", taken from a sparse clone. So the docs date is simply the shutdown date. A community continuation exists, Zoo Code (https://github.com/Zoo-Code-Org/Zoo-Code), whose README says it continues the project after the Roo team "wound down" Roo Code. Whether Zoo Code keeps the checkpoint design unchanged was not checked.
what_is_stored:
Whole-workspace file snapshots, not diffs or prompts. Each checkpoint is a git commit of every non-excluded file in the workspace, made with `git add . --ignore-errors` and then `git commit`. The docs say it captures content changes, new files, deletions, renames and binary changes (docs page). The first commit is "initial commit" (--allow-empty). Each later commit message is "Task: <taskId>, Time: <epoch ms>". Commits are authored as "Roo Code <noreply@example.com>" with commit.gpgSign=false (ShadowCheckpointService.ts and core/checkpoints/index.ts at b867ec9).

When a checkpoint is taken:
- Before the first file-changing tool of each streamed assistant message: write_to_file, apply_diff, edit/search_and_replace, search_replace, edit_file, apply_patch, new_task, generate_image. A per-turn flag (currentStreamingDidCheckpoint) limits this to one per turn.
- On every user chat message, as an allow-empty checkpoint hidden from the UI (Task.ts handleWebviewAskResponse).
- Not before execute_command. Shell side effects only show up in the next snapshot.

The conversation itself is not in git. It lives beside the repo as JSON: ui_messages.json, api_conversation_history.json, task_metadata.json and history_item.json (src/shared/globalFileNames.ts).
where_stored:
A separate shadow git repo on the local disk, one per task, inside VS Code's extension globalStorage. The path is <globalStorageUri>/tasks/<taskId>/checkpoints/.git (RepoPerTaskCheckpointService.ts), for example ~/.config/Code/User/globalStorage/rooveterinaryinc.roo-cline/tasks/... (issue #3080). The repo's core.worktree points at the user's workspace, so it reads the real files without touching the user's .git.

Checkpoints always use globalStorageUri. The chat JSON files go through getTaskDirectoryPath, which honours the customStoragePath setting (src/utils/storage.ts). So the two halves of a task can end up in different places.

The code also deletes old per-workspace repos at globalStorage/checkpoints/<sha256(workspaceDir)[0:8]> that used one branch per task, named roo-<taskId>. Reading that as a leftover from an earlier one-repo-per-workspace design is my inference from the deleteTask code. No git remote is ever configured, so nothing is pushed.
format_and_model:
Plain git objects, driven through the simple-git npm library and the system git binary (Git must be installed, per the docs page).

Setup: `git init --template ""`, then core.worktree=<workspace>, commit.gpgSign=false, user.name/email set to fixed values.

Excludes: .git/info/exclude is written with built-in patterns (excludes.ts):
- build and dependency folders: node_modules/, dist/, build/, vendor/, .terraform/ and others
- media, archives and binaries
- databases and CSV: *.sql, *.db, *.csv, *.parquet
- logs and caches
- config files: *.env*, *.local, *.development, *.production
- any pattern marked filter=lfs in the workspace .gitattributes

The workspace .gitignore also applies, because the worktree is the workspace. Per the docs, .rooignore does NOT apply to checkpoints.

Data model: one linear chain of commits per task. The service keeps the list of hashes in memory (_checkpoints) and treats the first commit as the base hash. Each checkpoint fires an event with {fromHash, toHash}, and the hash is saved in the task's ui_messages.json as a "checkpoint_saved" message.

Diffs: four modes (from-init, checkpoint, to-current, full). They run `git diff --summary`, then `git show <hash>:<path>` for the before and after content, and open VS Code's multi-file changes view.

Restore: `git clean -f -d` followed by `git reset --hard <hash>`. Later hashes are dropped from the in-memory list.
- "Restore Files Only" keeps the chat.
- "Restore Files & Task" also rewinds the conversation to that message and records the deleted API cost as an api_req_deleted message (core/checkpoints/index.ts).

There is no hash chain or signing beyond git's own commit DAG.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Not supported. Each repo belongs to one task in one VS Code extension host on one machine. It has no remote, no branches, no merge and no sync. The only concurrency guard is a checkpointServiceInitializing flag while setup runs.

The service refuses to open an existing shadow repo whose core.worktree differs from the current workspace ("Checkpoints can only be used in the original workspace"). It turns checkpoints off entirely if a nested .git is found anywhere in the workspace (ShadowCheckpointService.ts).

My inference from the code, not documented: two tasks in the same workspace get separate repos over the same working tree. Restoring one task (clean plus reset --hard) can therefore overwrite edits made by the other, with no conflict detection.
realtime:
Commits are local and happen inline. The checkpoint save awaits the commit before the file-changing tool runs (presentAssistantMessage.ts checkpointSaveAndMark). The UI is told through in-process events (currentCheckpointUpdated). Nothing streams or syncs to other machines or agents.

Setup can be slow on big trees. Docs give an init timeout of 10–60 s, default 30 s, but the code default is 15 s (DEFAULT_CHECKPOINT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS in packages/types/src/global-settings.ts), a mismatch between docs and code. Users get a warning after 5 s. On timeout or any error, checkpoints are silently disabled for that task: enableCheckpoints=false (core/checkpoints/index.ts).
search_retrieval: Minimal. A user can only browse the checkpoint markers in the chat timeline, open a diff between two checkpoints or between one and the current workspace, and restore. History has no content search, no index, and no lookup across tasks or workspaces. The agent never reads past checkpoints as context.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, but only one way and only locally. The session log (ui_messages.json) stores "checkpoint_saved" entries carrying the commit hash and {from, to}. That ties a point in the chat to a snapshot of the working tree. The shadow commits carry only the task id and a timestamp in the message. They hold no prompt, model output or tool call, and nothing ties them to the user's real git history.

"Restore Files & Task" uses this link to roll the code and the conversation back together to the same message (core/checkpoints/index.ts, rewindToTimestamp).
scale:
No official scale claims. The issue tracker shows growth was a long-running problem:
- #3080 (opened 2025-05-01, v3.14.2): 40 GB+ of globalStorage after minutes of use, including several 3.2 GB duplicate packs per task (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/issues/3080).
- #8040 (2025-09-16): reports of "hundreds of GB ballooning to TBs", no retention cap or size limit, and .rooignore ignored. Still open when the repo was archived (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/issues/8040).
- #10801 (2026-01-17): asks for a way to delete only checkpoints because of hundreds of GB of untracked large files (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/issues/10801).

The cause is the design: one full repo per task means each new task stores the workspace from scratch, and nothing garbage-collects it.
privacy_security:
The store is plaintext on local disk, with no encryption and no redaction. Secrets are handled only by the filename deny-list above (*.env*, *.local and so on). Any other file that is not gitignored is copied into the shadow repo on every checkpoint, for example *.pem, credentials.json, or a config.yaml holding tokens (from the exclude list in excludes.ts). The docs say outright that files blocked by .rooignore but not by .gitignore are still checkpointed.

Hardening that does exist:
- refuses to run when the workspace is the home folder, ~/Desktop, ~/Documents or ~/Downloads
- strips GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY and related variables from the git environment, to stop redirection, e.g. in Dev Containers
- disables commit signing and repo templates
- never adds a remote

Restore runs `git clean -f -d` and `reset --hard` against the user's real working tree, which is destructive by design. Failures are logged to the console and the feature turns itself off rather than surfacing an error (sources: ShadowCheckpointService.ts, core/checkpoints/index.ts).
license: Apache-2.0 ("Apache 2.0 © 2026 Roo Code, Inc." in the README, https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code)
lesson_for_parinn:
A shadow git repo pointed at the workspace (core.worktree) is a cheap, network-free way to snapshot code. Linking a session to code by writing the snapshot hash into the session log ("checkpoint_saved" with from/to hashes) is the right shape. Roo's version failed in three ways ParleyInn must design out:
- Unbounded storage: one full repo per task, with no shared object store, retention or size budget, led to 40 GB-to-TB blowups.
- Unredacted copying: any non-ignored secret was copied into an unencrypted store.
- Silent failure: on any error it disabled itself without telling anyone, which breaks I6.

If ParleyInn records code state, it should reference tree or commit hashes in one shared, size-capped store with audited eviction, put redaction in front of anything copied, and treat the snapshot store as derived, local-only data that is never the transport. Roo also shows the vendor risk: the history lived only inside one product's globalStorage, and the product shut down on 2026-05-15.

name: Roo Code Cloud Task Sync and Task Sharing (Roo Code VS Code extension + app.roocode.com)
status: archived
what_is_stored:
STATUS FIRST: the service no longer exists. Roo Code shut down all of its products (the Extension, Cloud and Router) on 15 May 2026, announced on 20/21 April 2026 (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code-Docs/blob/a676c4173ae60348095efaebfd1292a9617622c0/docs/sunset.md). The extension repo is archived and read-only (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code). The cloud code was deleted from it on 11 May 2026 in "Remove Roo Code Cloud and evals" (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/commit/8922418600b5d820696d2b606bd00552c3bce2d4). The URL given in the brief now redirects, through roocodeinc.github.io/Roo-Code/roo-code-cloud/task-sharing, to the archived docs root. That page reads "The Roo Code Extension was shut down on May 15th" (https://roocodeinc.github.io/Roo-Code/). Share URLs such as https://app.roocode.com/share/abc123 now serve a page titled "Roo Code Cloud is shutting down", which says "The cloud dashboard is no longer available". Everything below comes from the last published doc sources and the pre-removal client source code.

WHAT WAS STORED: the task's UI message stream, an array of ClineMessage records, not the raw LLM request history. Each record has these fields: ts (milliseconds), type ask|say, an ask/say subtype, text, images, partial, reasoning, conversationHistoryIndex, a checkpoint record, contextCondense/contextTruncation data, isProtected and apiProtocol (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/types/src/message.ts). The 28 say kinds include tool, command_output, reasoning, mcp_server_response, checkpoint_saved and condense_context. So tool payloads and terminal output went to the cloud as well.

Every synced event also carried metadata: taskId, parentTaskId, apiProvider, modelId, mode, todo counts, repositoryUrl, repositoryName and defaultBranch (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/3d37e054dd5a962c71bc832edb5c53b12eed8f44/packages/types/src/telemetry.ts).

Sharing stored share-link records: a visibility of organization or public, an expiry, and the creator. The dashboard listed recent links and let users delete them (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code-Docs/blob/a676c4173ae60348095efaebfd1292a9617622c0/docs/roo-code-cloud/task-sharing.mdx).
where_stored:
Primary copy: local files in VS Code globalStorage, under tasks/<taskId>/. These are ui_messages.json, api_conversation_history.json, task_metadata.json and history_item.json (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/src/shared/globalFileNames.ts).

Cloud copy: the Roo Code Cloud server behind https://app.roocode.com, which is now offline. Its backend was closed source; no server code appears in the public repo.

Failed uploads waited in a retry queue persisted to VS Code workspaceState under the key "roo.retryQueue" (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/cloud/src/retry-queue/RetryQueue.ts).

Auth credentials were kept in VS Code SecretStorage (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/cloud/src/WebAuthService.ts).

Git and git notes were not used to hold or carry task history.
format_and_model:
JSON over HTTPS, piggybacked on the extension's telemetry pipeline. There was no dedicated sync protocol.

(1) Live sync. Each time a non-partial message was added, or first completed, the extension sent POST {apiUrl}/api/events with the body {type:"Task Message", properties:{...telemetry props, taskId, message: ClineMessage}}. The body was checked against a zod discriminated union before sending (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/3d37e054dd5a962c71bc832edb5c53b12eed8f44/packages/cloud/src/TelemetryClient.ts, https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/3d37e054dd5a962c71bc832edb5c53b12eed8f44/src/core/task/Task.ts).

(2) Backfill. POST /api/events/backfill sent multipart form data: taskId, a properties JSON object, and a file field "task.json" holding the whole ClineMessage[] array (same TelemetryClient.ts).

(3) Share. POST /api/extension/share with {taskId, visibility:"organization"|"public"} returned {success, shareUrl, error, isNewShare, manageUrl}. Test fixtures show URLs of the form https://app.roocode.com/share/<id> (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/cloud/src/CloudAPI.ts, https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/types/src/cloud.ts).

Data model: a task is identified by taskId. A message is identified only by its millisecond ts within the task. There are no sequence numbers, hashes or signatures.

Org policy lived in a versioned settings object. Its cloudSettings held recordTaskMessages, enableTaskSharing, allowPublicTaskSharing, taskShareExpirationDays (default 30), allowMembersViewAllTasks, and workspaceTaskVisibility (all, list-only, admins-and-creator, creator or full-lockdown) (cloud.ts above).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Single writer, one way only. The docs say Task Sync "sends tasks from your IDE to Roo Code Cloud, but not vice-versa" and "doesn't sync tasks across devices at the moment" (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code-Docs/blob/a676c4173ae60348095efaebfd1292a9617622c0/docs/roo-code-cloud/task-sync.mdx). Each task was written only by the extension instance running it. There is no merge model.

Client-side duplicate suppression was an in-memory Set of message ts values. On task resume the Set was rebuilt from all saved non-partial messages, so messages already sent were not resent (Task.ts above).

If the task had never synced, sharing failed with 404 / TaskNotFoundError. The client then uploaded the full message array and retried the share (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/cloud/src/CloudService.ts).

Cannot be verified: how the server reconciled per-message events with a later full backfill, or with resent events. The backend was closed source.

Roomote Control (Aug 2025 to Feb 2026) briefly added a cloud-to-IDE command path over a Socket.IO bridge: bridgeConfig returned socketBridgeUrl. It was removed from the extension on 19 Feb 2026 (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/commit/d00f1a2bb8f4a6f51afae4b74b1549a14002e691) and from the docs on 11 Feb 2026 (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code-Docs/commit/40230c92b29599d5e05ffaf302612b8deb237c4b).
realtime:
Near real time, one way. The extension sent each message as one HTTP POST as soon as it was final. Partial, streaming messages were never sent.

The docs describe the dashboard as showing "near real-time updates (polled every few seconds): messages, mode changes, and status". They also say "your IDE must be open and connected" for live updates (task-sync.mdx above).

On a 5xx, a 429 or a network error, a request went into a persisted FIFO retry queue. The queue held at most 100 requests, retried every 60 s with no retry limit, and silently evicted its oldest entry when full. Other 4xx errors were not retried (RetryQueue.ts and TelemetryClient.ts above).

No push channel remained after Roomote Control was removed.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval was through the web dashboard's cloud task history: "Review your cloud task history anytime, even when your IDE is closed" (task-sync.mdx above). Org admins controlled visibility of workspace tasks with the workspaceTaskVisibility setting (cloud.ts above).

No search API, full-text search, export API or programmatic recall interface is documented. Whether the dashboard had search cannot be verified.

Share viewers opened a server-rendered page at app.roocode.com/share/<id>. The docs say "There's no link tracking at the moment" (task-sharing.mdx above).
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak, repository level only. Every synced event carried repositoryUrl, repositoryName and defaultBranch from the workspace's git remote. The URL was stripped of credentials and converted from SSH to HTTPS before sending (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/3d37e054dd5a962c71bc832edb5c53b12eed8f44/src/core/webview/ClineProvider.ts, https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/3d37e054dd5a962c71bc832edb5c53b12eed8f44/src/utils/git.ts).

Nothing tied a task to a commit SHA, working branch or PR. Messages could carry checkpoint metadata from Roo's local shadow-git checkpoints, but no cloud-side link to the user's real commits is documented.

The separate Cloud Agents and GitHub integration product could open PRs, but that is outside Task Sync and Sharing.
scale:
No scale claims were found for Task Sync or Sharing. The only figure is product-wide: "3 million extension downloads" (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code-Docs/blob/a676c4173ae60348095efaebfd1292a9617622c0/docs/sunset.md).

Known limits from source and docs:
- the retry queue held at most 100 requests, with FIFO eviction (RetryQueue.ts above)
- each request timed out after 30 s (CloudAPI.ts above)
- the share dialog showed the last 3 links plus a "+N more" summary
- links expired after 30 days on personal accounts, or after 1 to 365 days set by the org, default 30 (task-sharing.mdx above)
privacy_security:
Access control:
- Tasks were "private by default". Each link was scoped to the organization (Team plan only) or public to anyone holding the URL.
- Links expired: 30 days on personal accounts, an org-set 1 to 365 days for orgs.
- Org admins could delete any org link; members could delete links they had created (task-sharing.mdx above).
- Org admins could turn sharing off (enableTaskSharing) and, from Dec 2025, turn off public sharing (allowPublicTaskSharing) (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/commit/3502f41e7563aa0e8c7f550c583852453acc3257).

Sync defaults: on by default for personal accounts (taskSyncEnabled ?? true). For org members it was controlled by recordTaskMessages, which the client read as false when the org had not set it (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/blob/22d845cecb57c9615963141b2bab0348c8ccff59/packages/cloud/src/CloudSettingsService.ts). The env var ROO_CODE_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 disabled the cloud client, including sync (TelemetryClient.ts above).

No client-side redaction, secret scrubbing or content encryption: a scan of the cloud package for redact, secret, mask, encrypt and sanitize found only the SecretStorage handling of auth credentials. Raw command output, tool payloads, reasoning and images went to the server over HTTPS with a Bearer session token. There was no end-to-end encryption.

The retry queue persisted each failed request's full options to workspaceState. That included the Authorization header and the message body, so a token and transcript fragments sat at rest in VS Code state (RetryQueue.ts and TelemetryClient.ts above).

Privacy promises were policy statements only: "never used for training or advertising" and "The Roo Code team doesn't have access to the contents of your tasks, unless explicitly authorized" (task-sync.mdx above). They cannot be verified technically.

What happened to synced data after the 15 May 2026 shutdown cannot be verified. The sunset notice covers refunds and archiving the repo but says nothing about deleting data (sunset.md above).

License: the extension client was Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code). The cloud backend was proprietary and never published.
lesson_for_parinn:
Make any shared or synced copy a verifiable replica of ParleyInn's local append-only log, on a transport the user controls. Never make it a best-effort side stream into a vendor service.

Roo's sync was fire-and-forget telemetry:
- one POST per message
- duplicates suppressed only by the message's millisecond timestamp
- a 100-entry retry queue that silently dropped its oldest entry when full and stored bearer tokens at rest
- a whole-file backfill only when a share happened to hit a 404

There were no sequence numbers or hashes, so neither side could prove a synced or shared task was complete. On 15 May 2026 every share link became a shutdown page; the local ui_messages.json was the only copy that survived.

For ParleyInn this means:
- give every session a monotonic seq and a hash chain, and sync as idempotent appends of verified ranges, so a receiver detects gaps instead of trusting timestamps
- audit and count every queue drop (I6)
- redact before anything leaves the machine, and keep credentials out of queues
- implement share as a signed, self-contained export bundle (pushed to a git ref or Forgejo the user owns), with expiry and visibility enforced by the holder, so history outlives any hosted service and recalled content stays enveloped and untrusted (I2)
license: The client (Roo Code VS Code extension, including packages/cloud) was Apache-2.0; the repo is archived. The Roo Code Cloud backend and dashboard were proprietary and closed source. The service was shut down on 15 May 2026.

name: Roo Code Memory Bank (GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank)
category: in-repo Markdown memory (prompt-driven, no runtime code)
status: archived (in practice: superseded and dormant. GitHub does not mark the repo archived, but its host tool Roo Code shut down on 2026-05-15)
what_is_stored: Hand-curated project summaries written by the LLM, not session transcripts. There are five Markdown files. productContext.md holds the goal, features and architecture. activeContext.md holds the current focus, recent changes and open questions. progress.md holds completed tasks, current tasks and next steps. decisionLog.md holds each decision with its rationale and implementation details. systemPatterns.md holds coding, architectural and testing patterns. The user may also add projectBrief.md at the project root. The architect strategy file defines the initial templates (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/modules/memory_bank_strategy_architect.yml). The README lists the files and their purposes (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank#-memory-bank-structure). The model adds content when it judges a change "significant". A manual "UMB" / "Update Memory Bank" command makes it review the whole chat history and fold clarifications into the files (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/modules/memory_bank_strategy_code.yml). No raw prompts, tool calls or outputs are kept, so the result is a lossy summary.
where_stored: Working-tree files in a memory-bank/ directory at the project root, next to projectBrief.md (README "File Organization": https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank#file-organization). The behaviour lives in per-mode custom instructions. Users paste the modules/memory_bank_strategy_*.yml files into Roo Code's Prompts settings. Older versions used .clinerules-* and later .roorules-* files at the project root (README Quick Start; commit history: https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/commits/main). No database, server or sync service exists. Whether memory-bank/ is committed to git is left to the user, and the docs give no guidance. The repo's own .gitignore excludes its /memory-bank (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/.gitignore).
format_and_model: Free-form Markdown with fixed section headings. The rules ask for a "[YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS] - [Summary]" line on each entry (strategy YAML, memory_bank_updates.*.format). There is no schema, no IDs, no links between entries and no validation. The model edits through Roo Code's file tools: insert_content to append, or apply_diff to change existing entries. decisionLog.md and progress.md are told to "*append* ... Never overwrite existing entries". productContext.md, activeContext.md and systemPatterns.md may be edited in place with apply_diff (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/modules/memory_bank_strategy_code.yml). So "append-only" is a request in the prompt; nothing enforces it. The rules give the model no clock tool, so the timestamps are whatever the model writes (my inference from reading the rules). The repo ships no runtime code, only YAML/Markdown instructions plus install.sh/cmd and insert-variable scripts (tree at HEAD 7672d44: https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/tree/7672d44b398dfe5e1db80df0f3c73fe642c504bc). The developer primer describes an "Event Monitor", "Update Queue", "Sync Manager" and "Conflict resolution" (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/developer-primer.md). None of these exists as code; they describe behaviour the model is asked to perform.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not designed for this. There is one agent and one chat. Several Roo modes write the same files in turn: Architect, Code and Debug have update rules, and Ask is told not to update (strategy YAMLs in https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/tree/main/modules). The UMB command sets override_file_restrictions: true and override_mode_restrictions: true, so a mode that normally cannot write Markdown may write the memory bank. There is no locking, no writer identity and no conflict model. The "multiple projects" section covers several memory-bank/ dirs in one workspace, where the user picks one per chat. It does not cover several writers (developer-primer.md). If a team commits memory-bank/ to git, merges are ordinary line-based text merges. Mutable summary files such as activeContext.md and productContext.md will conflict or silently diverge when two branches each rewrite them. I found no documentation or issue confirming team usage; GitHub's issues page timed out (HTTP 504) and the API was blocked in this session.
realtime: "Real-time" in the README (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank#key-components) means the model is told to "UPDATE MEMORY BANK THROUGHOUT THE CHAT SESSION, WHEN SIGNIFICANT CHANGES OCCUR" (strategy YAML). It does not mean a file watcher or sync between machines or agents. UMB is the manual fallback for an unexpected session end. Sharing beyond the local working tree depends entirely on the user's git workflow.
search_retrieval: No search at all. At the start of every session the model is told to "READ *ALL* MEMORY BANK FILES" in order (productContext, activeContext, systemPatterns, decisionLog, progress). It then prefixes every reply with "[MEMORY BANK: ACTIVE]" or "[MEMORY BANK: INACTIVE]" (if_memory_bank_exists in https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/modules/memory_bank_strategy_code.yml). So context cost grows with file size. The author's next project, RooFlow, lists "Reduced Token Consumption" as a key improvement over the Memory Bank (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/RooFlow). The successor Context Portal moved to SQLite with FTS5 and vector search. Its README says it is "More efficient for managing, searching, and updating context compared to simple text file-based memory banks" (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/context-portal).
links_sessions_to_code: No. Entries carry no session ID, prompt reference, commit hash or file/line anchor. At most the free text names files or tasks, as in the primer's examples of decisions about `auth/login.py` (developer-primer.md). The link to code is implicit: the files sit in the repo and change alongside it if the user commits them.
scale: No scale claims. The design reads every file at every session start and has no pruning, rotation or summarising of old entries, so it suits small, single-developer projects. It has 1.7k stars, 185 forks and 83 commits; the first commit was 2025-02-09 and the last was 2025-05-15, a FUNDING.yml change, with the last substantive change on 2025-05-12 (GitHub page fetched 2026-10-02: https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank; history: https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/commits/main).
privacy_security: No handling at all. There is no redaction, no secret scanning, no encryption and no access control in the rules or docs (all of modules/*.yml and developer-primer.md were read in full or grepped for secret/redact/encrypt/security). Anything the model summarises, including credentials mentioned in chat, lands in plain-text files that may be committed. The files are re-read into the prompt as trusted project context every session. Anyone who can change memory-bank/, for example through a pull request, a branch, a malicious dependency or tool output the agent summarised, therefore gets a persistent prompt-injection channel. The UMB flags widen this further by overriding file and mode restrictions. Supply chain: config/install.sh curls unpinned files from raw.githubusercontent.com/.../main with no checksum, then deletes itself (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/config/install.sh). At HEAD it still lists .roorules-test and .roomodes, which were deleted in commit e343b44, so with set -e and curl -f it would abort. The rule files also still refer to RooFlow's "Flow-Architect" mode, which shows drift. Context: Roo Code itself was "shut down on May 15th" and its repo was archived on 2026-05-15. Its README recommends the Zoo Code fork or Cline (https://github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code/main/README.md). The author's README banner points to Context Portal MCP, which stores context in SQLite at context_portal/context.db per workspace, offers Markdown export/import tools, and had its last commit on 2026-01-19 (https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/context-portal).
license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file and README footer: https://github.com/GreatScottyMac/roo-code-memory-bank/blob/main/LICENSE)
lesson_for_parinn: Do not confuse a curated summary with a record, and do not make a mutable file both the source of truth and the thing that gets injected. In the Memory Bank, "append-only", "real-time sync" and "conflict resolution" are only promises in the prompt. The model can rewrite activeContext.md with apply_diff, nothing chains or verifies the history, and every file is fed back verbatim as trusted context, so whoever can commit to memory-bank/ can steer the agent. The author abandoned Markdown files for a per-workspace SQLite store with FTS and vectors (Context Portal), keeping Markdown only as an export/import format. That supports ParleyInn's split. The canonical store should be a machine-written, hash-chained, append-only log enforced in code. Memory-bank-style views (decisions, progress, active context) should be projections rebuilt from that log (I10). They should reach the model only as enveloped, pull-only recall, never auto-injected, unless they are TrustedText (I2). If git ever carries ParleyInn history, use immutable per-event or per-session objects that two writers never edit in common, never shared mutable summary files that need text merges.

name: rqlite
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Complete SQLite relational database with full SQL support (tables, indexes, triggers, views, constraints). Supports FTS5 full-text search, JSON functions, and SQLite extensions. Every node in the cluster holds a full copy of the database.
where_stored: Local SQLite database files (data.db) plus Write-Ahead Log (WAL) files on each node's filesystem. Snapshots stored in a custom snapshot store with full snapshots (complete database.db) and incremental snapshots (WAL frames). Raft log stored in BoltDB (bbolt). Supports backup export to S3, Google Cloud Storage, and MinIO.
format_and_model: Wire protocol: Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for Raft commands and cluster communication over TCP. Snapshot format: Custom framed protobuf format with headers followed by database/WAL bytes. Data model: Full SQL relational model with transactions, constraints, and triggers. Internally: SQLite in WAL mode with SYNCHRONOUS=OFF in steady state (Raft provides durability), SYNCHRONOUS=FULL during checkpoints.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single leader model: only the leader accepts writes. All write requests are serialized through Raft consensus log and applied to all replicas deterministically in log order. No multi-writer capability or merge semantics. Followers are read-only but can forward write requests to leader. Non-voter read replicas receive replication but do not vote in elections.
realtime: Yes. Raft-based replication delivers committed writes to followers with millisecond latency under normal conditions. Change Data Capture (CDC) available to stream INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events to webhooks with at-least-once delivery semantics. Supports tunable read consistency: none (direct local, may be stale), weak (local leader check), linearizable (quorum heartbeat), strong (through Raft log).
search_retrieval: Full SQL query interface via HTTP API (/db/query endpoint). Supports all SQLite features including FTS5 full-text search, JSON functions, and user-loaded extensions. Queries support tunable consistency levels and can use prepared statements. No specialized session query API.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. rqlite is a general-purpose distributed relational database with no built-in agent session or context linking. No session metadata namespace. Would require application-layer schema to track agent sessions (e.g. sessions table with agent_id, context_id, timestamp columns).
privacy_security: TLS 1.2+ for encryption in transit. Role-based access control with user authentication. Per-statement authorization checks. No built-in automatic redaction or secrets filtering. No data-at-rest encryption (relies on filesystem/storage encryption). Operator can load SQLite extensions for custom security (e.g. encryption functions). No automatic key rotation or secret management.
lesson_for_parinn: rqlite demonstrates that Raft consensus with full replication works well for append-only semantics. Key insights: (1) Single leader simplifies concurrency but requires failover detection; (2) WAL-based incremental snapshots are efficient for large persistent state; (3) BoltDB for Raft log is a solid persistent queue; (4) CDC webhooks could stream session events but rqlite has no session-context model; (5) SQLite's WAL mode with SYNCHRONOUS=OFF + Raft consensus is a sound durability strategy; (6) For agent sessions, rqlite's strong leader would work well for session writes but lacks built-in session semantics. CDC could deliver events to external session indexers.

name: S2 (s2.dev, "Stream Store") and s2-lite
status: shipped. The S2 cloud service went GA on Feb 25, 2026 with a 99.99% availability SLO. s2-lite (MIT, self-hosted) shipped Jan 21, 2026 and is described as "newer". The product-updates page shows activity up to Sep 14, 2026 (https://s2.dev/docs/updates.md, https://s2.dev/docs/s2-lite.md). Neither project is archived. The older v1alpha gRPC API was retired on Apr 29, 2026 and replaced by the REST-first v1 API plus the S2S session protocol.
where_stored:
S2 cloud: server/cloud on AWS. Each cell's "channel" pods write a WAL of chunks to object storage, and over time batch those chunks into per-stream segments (https://s2.dev/docs/platform/architecture.md):
- Standard class: one S3 Standard bucket.
- Express class: a quorum of three S3 Express zonal buckets.
- Both are multi-AZ durable before the append is acknowledged.
- Locations include aws:us-west-2 and aws:eu-north-1, among others (https://s2.dev/docs/updates.md).

s2-lite: a single-node Rust binary that runs as the `s2 lite` CLI subcommand. It stores data in SlateDB, an LSM tree on object storage, in any S3-compatible bucket (S3, Tigris, R2), a local directory, or in-memory as an emulator. The WAL can live in a separate bucket or directory (https://github.com/s2-streamstore/s2 README, https://s2.dev/docs/s2-lite.md).

Neither one stores anything in git.
multi_writer_and_merge:
S2 orders writes on the server; it does not merge. Every append lands at the single tail. A batch is atomic, with up to 1000 records or 1 MiB (https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/appends).

Coordination primitives (https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/concurrency-control):
- Optimistic: `match_seq_num` returns 412 if the tail moved. Combined with retries, this gives "exactly-once" for a single writer.
- Pessimistic: a `fence` command record sets a token of up to 36 bytes. Appends carrying a stale token get 412.
- Fencing is "cooperative": "an append that does not specify a fencing token will still be allowed".
- A failed precondition poisons an append session.

Retry semantics: the SDKs default to retry policy "all", where "Duplicates are possible". The `noSideEffects` policy avoids this but leaves the caller to check whether the append happened. With multiple writers, the docs advise putting a writer ID and a per-writer idempotency key in each record and deduplicating later (https://s2.dev/docs/sdk/retries-timeouts.md).

Multi-agent pattern: one shared stream acts as a message bus that gives every agent the same order, and each agent keeps a private stream (https://s2.dev/docs/use-cases/agents.md). The 2025 blog post talks about cloning streams to branch and then merging results. I found no fork or clone endpoint in the API index, so I could not verify that as a server feature (https://s2.dev/blog/agent-sessions, https://s2.dev/docs/llms.txt).

Merging concurrent state is the application's job. Examples:
- LiveStore maps each storeId to one S2 stream of JSON events (https://s2.dev/docs/integrations/livestore).
- opbox and y-s2 put Yjs CRDT operations on S2 (https://opbox.dev).

For opbox, concurrent creation of the same filename yields a "(Conflict x7f2)" copy (https://opbox.dev).
realtime:
Yes, this is the core feature. Tailing works through read sessions (S2S), SSE, or long-poll with `?wait=<secs>` (https://s2.dev/docs/llms.txt, https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/reads).

Append acknowledgement takes up to 40 ms on Express and up to 400 ms on Standard (https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/appends). Tailing readers see records "single-digit milliseconds" after they land on Express, and otherwise within up to 200 ms.

Readers can resume after a disconnect from a sequence number, a timestamp or a tail offset. The resumable-stream helpers use the SSE `id:` field as the cursor (https://s2.dev/docs/integrations/anthropic).

s2-lite latency is the bucket's PUT latency plus the SlateDB flush interval, "typically a few hundred ms". Each stream has a streamer task that broadcasts acknowledged records to its followers (https://s2.dev/docs/s2-lite.md, README).
search_retrieval:
Positional only: read by sequence number, by timestamp, or by offset from the tail. Reads can be bounded by count, bytes or end timestamp. `check-tail` returns the current tail position, and stream names can be listed by prefix (https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/reads, https://s2.dev/docs/llms.txt).

There is no full-text, header or semantic search and no secondary index. Applications build their own projections from a replay. S2 Studio is a browser tool for reading and appending to streams, not a search tool (https://s2.dev/docs/updates.md).
links_sessions_to_code:
No. S2 is a generic stream store. The docs and blog never mention git, commits, coding agents or Claude Code. The only git reference is a metaphor, "`git checkout` for agents" (https://s2.dev/blog/agent-sessions, https://s2.dev/docs/use-cases/agents.md).

Any link from a session to code (commit SHA, worktree, repo) would have to live in record headers or bodies chosen by the application.
privacy_security:
Cloud service (https://s2.dev/docs/platform/security.md, https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/encryption.md, https://s2.dev/docs/concepts/access-tokens):
- TLS on all endpoints and on internal service-to-service traffic.
- Encryption at rest is provided by the underlying cloud services.
- Compliance: SOC 2 Type II since Dec 2025, plus a HIPAA BAA and a GDPR DPA on request.
- Networking: AWS PrivateLink and dedicated cells are available.

Optional per-stream encryption with a client-supplied key (Apr 23, 2026):
- Ciphers: AEGIS-256 (recommended) or AES-256-GCM. AES-GCM streams are capped at 2^32 records.
- The key travels in the `s2-encryption-key` header, and "S2 does not persist or log the encryption key".
- Headers and body are encrypted, and the stream ID is bound in as associated data so ciphertext cannot be replayed into another stream.
- Command records stay plaintext.
- This is server-side encryption with a key you supply on each request, not end-to-end: S2 sees plaintext while handling a request. Encryption on the client side is up to the application, as opbox does with a workspace key.
- Keys cannot be rotated in place. Rotation means cutting over to a new stream, and envelope encryption (KEK in a KMS, one DEK per stream) is recommended.

Access tokens:
- Bearer tokens, scoped by basin, stream or token prefix (or exact name) and by operation group or individual operation.
- Can be read-only, can carry an RFC 3339 expiry, and can be revoked.
- "Auto-prefixing" gives each token a hidden namespace.

s2-lite: does not support the access-token API (issue #28, "planned"). It must be gated by your own auth layer, and data stays inside your own perimeter and bucket (https://s2.dev/docs/s2-lite.md, README).

Not offered: no redaction or secret scanning. Payloads are opaque.

Integrity: the docs describe deterministic simulation testing (Turmoil, Antithesis) and linearizability checks with Porcupine (https://s2.dev/docs/platform/architecture.md). But nothing in the docs gives client-verifiable tamper evidence: there is no hash chain or signed log.

Records can disappear in three ways:
- the default 7-day retention;
- any token with write access can append a `trim` command, and trimming is eventually consistent;
- delete_on_empty, if enabled.
license: The s2-lite server, CLI and Rust SDK are MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 Bandar Systems Inc. and contributors (https://github.com/s2-streamstore/s2/blob/main/LICENSE). The Go SDK github.com/s2-streamstore/s2-sdk-go is MIT (https://github.com/s2-streamstore/s2-sdk-go). The cloud service is proprietary and managed; its API layer and ecosystem projects are MIT (https://s2.dev/docs/s2-lite.md).
lesson_for_parinn:
S2 is a strong fit as an optional, out-of-process relay for ParleyInn's append-only record, but not as the record itself. Map one ParleyInn session to one S2 stream (agents/{session-id}) and have a separate sidecar do the network work, so the core stays network-free (I4).

The sidecar appends each batch with `match_seq_num` equal to ParleyInn's own local sequence number. This keeps the stream linear and makes retries idempotent instead of producing duplicates, which the default "all" retry policy would otherwise do. With many writers, give each writer its own stream instead of sharing one tail, because fencing is only cooperative.

Three things S2 does not guarantee, so ParleyInn must:
1. **History can disappear.** The default 7-day retention, any write-capable token appending a `trim` command, and delete_on_empty can all remove records. ParleyInn should set retention to infinite, issue append-only tokens without trim rights where possible, and check its own hash chain on every pull, so a trimmed or dropped head shows up as an audited gap (I6) rather than silent loss.
2. **Server-side encryption is not end-to-end.** With the client-supplied key, S2 still sees plaintext during requests. If remote storage must not see content, encrypt before appending, as opbox does.
3. **Pulled records are untrusted.** Treat anything read back from S2 as untrusted input that is only ever returned inside an envelope (I2).

s2-lite (MIT, single binary, can run against a local directory or in memory) is a ready-made option for self-hosted or air-gapped sharing and for CI emulation. Its catch is that it has no access tokens yet, so it needs its own authentication in front.

name: Sapling SCM (Meta)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Commit history, file contents, branches, tags, commit metadata (author, message, timestamp), repository state, and stack-based workflow information. Sapling stores the same revision control data as Git but organizes it differently in its native format via the Mononoke server.
where_stored: In Git-compatible mode (open-source client): stored in standard Git format (.git directory). In native Sapling mode (used internally at Meta): stored on Mononoke, a distributed Rust-based server backend that remains proprietary and not yet publicly available. EdenFS virtual filesystem caches working directory data for massive repositories (experimental, unsupported publicly).
format_and_model: Git-compatible wire format when operating as a Git client. Native format uses Mononoke's distributed storage model. Employs a stack-based commit model inspired by Mercurial and Git, allowing developers to manage multiple commits as stacks for code review workflows. Segmented changelog enables efficient history queries by downloading high-level commit graph shape (megabytes) before lazily loading individual commits.
multi_writer_and_merge: Handles multi-writer scenarios through rebase-based workflows, not traditional merge-based. Demonstrated at Meta supporting thousands of developers working simultaneously on massive monorepos with tens of millions of files and commits. Stack-based commits allow independent development and iteration. Merge conflicts resolved through interactive rebase workflows. No explicit optimistic locking or CRDT-style conflict resolution mentioned.
realtime: Not designed for real-time collaboration. Employs lazy loading of commits, trees, and files to optimize bandwidth for large repositories (only necessary data downloaded to client). Assumes single-master architecture typical of Meta's monorepo design. Smartlog visualization updates as local history changes. No streaming or real-time multi-user synchronization features.
search_retrieval: Smartlog command provides intuitive visualization of local repository state and commit history. Interactive Smartlog (ISL) web UI offers visual navigation of commits and branches. VS Code integration available. Standard Git search available when in Git-compatible mode. No full-text search across repository contents or commits mentioned as a built-in feature.
links_sessions_to_code: Not designed for agent session tracking. Sapling is a version control system focused on code repository management, not session management. Does not provide built-in mechanisms to link Claude Code agent sessions to commits, code changes, or development actions. Would require external integration layer.
privacy_security: Recent releases (as of 2026) include security fixes for working with untrusted repositories. Supports standard Git-based authentication mechanisms. No explicit encryption at rest mentioned. No secret redaction or automatic credential removal documented. Security considerations documented for untrusted repo handling (though details not publicly available for Mononoke backend).
lesson_for_parinn: Sapling demonstrates that stack-based commit workflows scale better than traditional branching for large teams, suggesting ParleyInn should consider immutable, append-only records at the agent-action level rather than traditional commit-based granularity. Sapling's lazy loading pattern (download shape, then fetch details on demand) parallels efficient session history retrieval: pin constraints as metadata, store events append-only, recall pulls only needed history. The separation of client UX from storage backend (Git compatibility vs Mononoke) suggests ParleyInn benefits from defining a wire format independent of internal storage, allowing multiple backends. Most important: Sapling's design assumes single-master, always-online environments; ParleyInn must handle disconnected agents, ephemeral sandboxes, and resumed sessions, requiring different consistency guarantees than Sapling's rebase-heavy model.

name: Sculptor (Imbue)
category: Started as "per-agent containers with git sync". That model is now superseded. As of Sept 2026 Sculptor is a local desktop orchestrator for parallel agents. Each workspace is a git worktree (clone and in-place modes are experimental). Session history lives in a local SQLite event log. Running the whole backend in Docker or on a remote host is an optional experimental mode.
status: beta
license: MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 Imbue, Inc. (LICENSE.md). The repo was opened at commit d2ab02fe, "Epoch: open-source start of Sculptor", dated 2026-06-12. The repo's first-commit date was checked by a local clone; there is no web page to cite for it. The README says external contributions are limited for now.
what_is_stored:
Per workspace (SQLite tables): Project, Workspace, Task, SavedAgentMessage and Notification records, plus UserSettings.
- Project: name, file:// repo URL, setup command, system prompt.
- Workspace: branches, source_git_hash, setup logs, diff status.
- Task: agent config, starting git_hash, system prompt, model, resumable state such as the terminal session id, outcome and error.
- SavedAgentMessage holds the message log: user chat inputs, model switches, answers to the agent's questions, and ResponseBlock messages. ResponseBlock content includes text, ToolUseBlock (tool name and input) and ToolResultBlock. For Write/Edit/MultiEdit, the result carries a DiffToolContent with the git diff string and file path.
- The log also keeps context-summary and context-cleared events after compaction, request start/success/failure/stop, per-turn metrics (tokens, duration), warnings and crash records.
- Partial streaming chunks and plan-mode/ask-question events are ephemeral and not persisted.

Per task, a transcript.jsonl of the raw Claude stream is written. Claude Code's own session JSONL is used for `--resume`. Plans are files the agent writes under .claude/plans/. Code changes are not stored in the database; they live as git working-tree changes and commits on the workspace branch. The marketing page says every session is saved with "plans, chats, tool calls, and code changes".
where_stored:
All local files, nothing on a server:
- Database: ~/.sculptor/database.db (SQLite).
- Workspaces: ~/.sculptor/workspaces/<internal-id>/, with the working copy at code/.
- Raw transcript: <workspace_root>/artifacts/tasks/<task_id>/transcript.jsonl.
- Config, including the telemetry instance_id: ~/.sculptor/config.toml.
- Env secrets: ~/.sculptor/.env and the per-repo .sculptor/.env.
- Claude Code's own session JSONL: <CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or ~/.claude>/projects/<sanitized-path>/.

Code goes onto a git branch (default pattern `<user>/<slug>`) inside the user's own repo through a worktree, so no separate remote is needed. In experimental clone mode it sits in a separate clone whose remotes mirror the user's. History is not kept in git notes, custom refs or a separate repo. The only git object writes are temporary trees in a throwaway objects directory.
format_and_model:
SQLite through a SQLAlchemy subset (no ORM), with Alembic migrations that run at startup.

"Dual form" pattern: each model has an immutable snapshot table (`<table>`, primary key snapshot_id) that is the "source of truth". A materialized `<table>_latest` table holds the current state and is kept up to date by a BEFORE INSERT trigger that upserts on object_id. Some models opt out of the latest table: SavedAgentMessage has no _latest table (is_dual_table=False). Code comments say "Never update records in the snapshots table. (Only insert.)"

Models are frozen Pydantic classes. Records use prefixed, typed ObjectIDs. Polymorphic payloads are stored as discriminated JSON columns: Task.input_data, current_state and SavedAgentMessage.message. A JSON-schema snapshot (frozen_pydantic_schemas.json) plus test-enforced data migrations keep old rows readable.

No hash chain, no signatures, no content addressing in the log.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Code:
- Each workspace is its own branch. The user commits (an agent writes the message) and merges or opens a PR to the target branch.
- Several agents in one workspace share a single working copy with no locking. The docs warn that simultaneous edits to the same file "can produce conflicting changes".
- In clone mode, changes come back by pushing to a shared remote or to the on-disk repo.
- The Sept 2025 announcement promised automatic merge-conflict flagging and handing conflicts back to an agent. I could not confirm this in current docs.

Session database:
- Single-process writer by design. The trigger code says "we assume the sqlite database is not used by multiple processes at the same time. Do not introduce concurrent writers".
- Concurrent writers within that process use BEGIN IMMEDIATE with a 15 s busy timeout. "Monotonic" columns are merged with MAX() so a stale transaction cannot flip True back to False.
- No replication and no cross-machine merge of histories.
- The experimental container backend runs a second, separate backend and database. The docs note you enter your identity twice.
realtime:
Local only.
- The UI talks to a backend over HTTP/WebSocket on 127.0.0.1 and streams agent events live.
- Worktree branches are visible right away in the user's repo, so nothing needs syncing.
- Agents in one workspace see each other's file edits immediately.
- Old Pairing Mode: synced work "both ways" between the agent's container and the local repo, and "the agent sees your edits and comments in real time". It is gone from the current repo; a grep finds no Pairing Mode feature.
- No real-time sharing of session history across machines or users.
search_retrieval:
- Cmd+K command palette: filters workspaces, agents, files and commands.
- Past sessions can be reopened, and Claude sessions resume with `claude --resume <session_id>`. Integrated harness state (queued messages, pending questions, interrupted turns) survives restarts by replaying the persisted message log.
- No full-text or semantic search over past chats: no FTS5 or search index found in the source.
- "Forking agents from any point in session history" was listed as planned in Sept 2025; not verified as shipped.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weak, partly implicit links:
- Each task records `git_hash` (HEAD when the task was created) for diff computation. Each workspace records source_git_hash and source/target branches.
- Edit tool results store the diff text inside the message log.
- Each turn, a tree SHA of the working state (including untracked files) is computed. It uses a temporary GIT_INDEX_FILE and a throwaway GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY that are deleted later, so these snapshots are not persisted as refs.
- A hidden system prompt asks Claude to end commits with "Co-authored-by: Sculptor <sculptor@imbue.com>". This is a prompt instruction, not enforced, and carries no session or task id.
- No git notes, no session refs, no commit-to-session index.
scale: No scale claims found in the docs, blog or README. The only hint is a busy timeout raised to 15 s for "concurrent agent-startup contention" (SCU-536) in a single-process SQLite design. Main was at version 0.49.0.dev0 on 2026-09-18.
privacy_security:
Threat model (SECURITY.md): "expected to be run locally only".
- The loopback server uses a per-session token against browser pages, but any local process can reach the port.
- Opening a repo runs its setup command and its checked-in .sculptor/.env, so "treat 'open this repo' like 'run this repo'". Plugins run with full UI privileges.

Agent isolation:
- Claude Code is launched with `env IS_SANDBOX=1 ... --dangerously-skip-permissions`, so tools are auto-approved.
- In the default worktree mode it runs on the host: "Agents act with your access". Stronger isolation needs the experimental container backend.
- On macOS that backend needs CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN forwarded in, because keychain credentials are not reachable from the container.

Secrets:
- A Secret wrapper prints "[redacted]" in logs. Credentials in remote URLs are redacted, and the PTY shell environment is scrubbed.
- No redaction of transcripts or tool outputs before storage, and no encryption at rest of database.db or the transcripts, were found.

Telemetry:
- PostHog runs in the frontend only, with mask_all_text and attribute stripping. The person id is uuid5(namespace, email).
- Sentry error reporting; session replay is buffered and uploaded only with a user bug report.
- One opt-out switch turns both off.

Recalled history is not treated as untrusted. Past chat is replayed into the UI and Claude resumes its own JSONL directly.
lesson_for_parinn:
Sculptor is a real case of a product that dropped per-agent containers with two-way git sync. Imbue's stated reasons: per-agent isolation stopped agents from inspecting each other's work, users found it confusing, and Docker Desktop hurt performance. It moved isolation to the whole app.

What it settled on is a clean split. Git carries code: workspace branches live in the user's own repo, so there is nothing to sync. A local, insert-only SQLite event log with trigger-maintained "_latest" views carries the session record, and that record never travels.

ParleyInn should keep that split but fix two gaps Sculptor left:
1. Bind sessions to code inside the tamper-evident record. Write commit and tree hashes as chained events. Sculptor only stores the starting HEAD, discards its per-turn tree snapshots, and relies on a Co-authored-by trailer that the prompt asks for.
2. Design for multiple writers from day one. Sculptor's log explicitly forbids concurrent writer processes, which is exactly what multiple worktrees, machines and sandboxes need.

name: Semantica (semanticash/cli)
category: git-linked provenance (local-first AI attribution with optional hosted sync)
status: shipped. Active early-stage project: v0.7.2 was released 2026-09-16 and 0.7.3 is unreleased in the CHANGELOG. The last commit, 4119c9b, landed 2026-09-18. Tags run v0.7.0 to v0.7.2. The repo is not archived and is tiny by adoption (about 3 stars, 1 fork per the GitHub page). Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md and https://github.com/semanticash/cli
what_is_stored:
Per repo:
- Lineage records ("checkpoints"), one per commit, and commit-hash-to-checkpoint links.
- Agent sessions with provider, model, timestamps and parent linkage.
- Agent events: prompts, assistant output, tool calls, shell and file edits, subagent boundaries.
- Tool-delta evidence (bounded, context-free diff hunks captured around agent shell or tool calls).
- File manifests (the tracked tree of a commit, or the workspace including untracked non-ignored files).
- Transcript slices, final responses and per-turn "provenance bundles". A bundle is a manifest that references prompt and step blobs and records provider-reported token usage.
- Per-file and aggregate AI-attribution results (exact, formatted or modified line classes, plus provider-only lines). Optional LLM-generated "playbooks" (title, intent, outcome, learnings, friction, open_items, keywords).
- Hosted-sync and backfill state.
- In 0.7.3, Claude "observed input" evidence: requests, attachments and tool results.

Global (under SEMANTICA_HOME):
- Broker registry, capture offsets and global CAS staging.
- Turn observations: per-turn baseline and end snapshots across repos.
- Unresolved-mutation records that embed their referenced objects, with no size cap or expiry.

Commits get git trailers: Semantica-Checkpoint (always), plus optional Semantica-Attribution and Semantica-Diagnostics.

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/limitations.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/features.md
where_stored:
Local DB plus a local CAS in a `.semantica/` directory next to `.git`, which is auto-added to `.gitignore`. Contents:
- `lineage.db` (SQLite) and `objects/` (SHA-256 content-addressed blobs, zstd-compressed, 2-char sharding).
- `tool-snapshots.git`: a private bare git object store with per-worktree ref namespaces. It reads the user repo through a read-only alternate and never writes objects or refs into the user repo.
- `settings.json`, logs, commit-receipts and handoff.md.

Global state lives in ~/.semantica (SEMANTICA_HOME).

Nothing goes into git history, notes or side branches. The only git footprint is commit-message trailers, which are written by the commit-msg hook.

There is an optional hosted server (semantica.sh) for sync after `auth login` + `connect`. Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/README.md#data-model , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#storage
format_and_model:
Relational plus CAS. The SQLite schema is managed with golang-migrate and sqlc. Tables:
- repositories, checkpoints (with repo sequence, retry state and a processing lease), commit_links
- agent_sources, agent_sessions, agent_events, agent_event_evidence_links
- provenance_manifests, session_checkpoints, checkpoint_stats, remote_attribution_backfills

Blobs are immutable and SHA-256 addressed. Events are written via a broker after provider-specific parsers turn transcripts and hook stdin into canonical events.

The model is commit-centric:
- pre-commit writes a handoff file and a pending checkpoint.
- commit-msg appends trailers.
- post-commit promotes the handoff to a durable receipt, links the SHA and spawns a background worker. The worker builds the manifest, links sessions, scores attribution, then optionally syncs and generates a playbook.

The DB rows are mutable (leases, retry state, completion markers). It is not an append-only or hash-chained log. I found no prev-hash or signature chaining in internal/ (grep of the cloned source; my own inspection, not a project claim).

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/go.mod
multi_writer_and_merge:
Capture is explicitly per-machine. "Another developer or CI runner working on the same repo needs its own Semantica setup." There is no local-to-local merge or replication. Each clone's .semantica/ is independent and gitignored.

Within one machine:
- Many agents and providers write concurrently through the broker. It routes each event to the repo that owns the touched paths (deepest-match), across repos and nested repos.
- Workers serialize per repo with `.semantica/worker.lock`. Checkpoints are processed in repo sequence with durable leases. A terminally failed queue head blocks later records.
- Tool-snapshot windows are serialized by an OS-backed lock, and overlapping windows are grouped with a join horizon.
- Unresolved-event redelivery keeps the first record and rejects conflicting content under the same event ID.

Rebases and squashes that collapse lineage records reduce attribution precision. In turn observations, merges and rewrites produce an explicit gap.

Cross-machine aggregation exists only through the optional hosted service (shared workspaces with owner/admin access requests).

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/limitations.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#broker , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/hosted-reporting.md
realtime:
Capture is near-real-time locally, and sharing is not real-time. Provider hooks (prompt-submit, tool, stop) call `semantica capture`:
- On prompt-submit it saves a transcript offset.
- On stop it reads the transcript from that offset and routes the events.

A worker reconciliation pass is the secondary path. Attribution waits for a 30 s capture-readiness grace period (retries every 5 s). The optional launcher (launchd, systemd user units or Task Scheduler) drains every 30 min.

Hosted sync is best-effort after each commit with a 10 s timeout. It is commit-triggered, not streamed live to teammates.

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#capture , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/limitations.md#hosted-reporting
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by commit, checkpoint or session, not search:
- `semantica blame <ref>` and `explain <ref>` (with --json).
- `sessions [<id> --transcript]`, plus `list`, `show` and `transcripts`.

There is an MCP server with a single tool, `semantica_explain(ref)`, which returns explain JSON. Playbooks carry keyword fields, but I found no full-text or semantic search over history (no FTS5 in the source; my grep, unverified as a design statement).

`semantica handoff --write` assembles a redacted markdown bundle for a fresh agent session: recent prompts, the last response, touched files, recent commits and working-tree context.

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/internal/mcp/tools.go , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/help.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/features.md
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes. Linking sessions to code is the core purpose:
- Commits carry a `Semantica-Checkpoint: chk_...` trailer that maps to a lineage record. session_checkpoints link the sessions that influenced it.
- Line-level attribution matches committed lines to captured AI output (exact, whitespace-normalized or modified-hunk). v2 scoring aligns verified shell or tool deltas with committed lines.
- Provider-touch-only lines are kept separate and excluded from the headline AI %.
- When capture is incomplete, unmatched lines are labelled "Unattributed", not "Human".
- Turn bundles tie prompt, then steps, then repo changes. Observation-linked bundles carry `repository_association {basis: turn_observation, authorship: unknown}` so that co-occurrence is not claimed as causation.

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/evidence-contract.md
privacy_security:
Local data: raw local capture (prompts, transcripts, command output, blobs) is stored unredacted and unencrypted in .semantica/. The blob store creates directories with mode 0755 (internal/store/blobs/store.go, my inspection). Unresolved-mutation retention has no size cap or expiry.

Outbound content (hosted sync, LLM prompts for playbooks and suggestions, handoff.md) passes through embedded Gitleaks rules, which replace matches with [REDACTED]. Known path fields are normalized to repo-relative form. If redaction cannot complete, the upload fails closed. The project itself says redaction is "best-effort, not a guarantee". Other outbound filtering:
- Steps whose primary file is git-ignored are dropped from synced bundles.
- Claude observed_input is stripped before upload.

Isolation and credentials:
- Snapshot subprocesses strip git env vars that could redirect repo access, ignore inherited config and remove remotes, so a snapshot never contacts a remote.
- OAuth tokens go to the OS keyring. The fallback is ~/.config/semantica/credentials.json with mode 0600.

Network and prompt injection:
- The binary does talk to the network: hosted sync, device-flow auth, and `skills install` fetching SKILL.md from GitHub. It also shells out to agent CLIs for LLM features.
- There is no stated defense against recalled content acting as prompt injection. handoff.md and MCP explain output feed captured text back to agents with only secret redaction (no trust envelope documented).

Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/SECURITY.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/hosted-reporting.md#security-and-redaction , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#tool-snapshot-store-tool-snapshotsgit
scale:
The project makes no throughput or volume claims. The documented bounds are:
- Turn observations snapshot at most 8 repos concurrently within a shared 5 s hook budget.
- Claude transcript readers accept encoded inputs up to 8 MiB.
- Tool deltas are bounded by path, byte, line and diff-work limits, and fail closed over the limit.
- Local storage "can grow without a bound" because of unresolved retention.

I found no customer or usage figures, and the website lists none. Sources: https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture.md , https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md , https://www.semantica.sh
license: MIT (https://github.com/semanticash/cli/blob/main/LICENSE). The hosted service's terms are not documented in the repo.
lesson_for_parinn:
Semantica demonstrates a practical design point for ParleyInn: keep the full session record outside git history, and link it to git only through a stable ID in a commit trailer (Semantica-Checkpoint). The record itself lives in a gitignored local SQLite + SHA-256 CAS. Commits stay clean, rebases do not rewrite the record, and the trailer survives push to GitHub/Forgejo, so any clone can find the matching history.

Two more patterns are worth copying for ParleyInn's I6 and I9:
- Its private bare repo (tool-snapshots.git, with a read-only alternate to the user's object DB, scrubbed git env and config, and per-worktree ref namespaces) captures workspace deltas without touching the user repo or the network.
- Its evidence vocabulary refuses to over-claim: Unattributed rather than Human, authorship: unknown, explicit capture gaps.

It is also a warning. Raw local capture is unredacted and not hash-chained. Recalled content (handoff.md, MCP explain) goes back to agents with only secret redaction, and sharing is per-machine plus a hosted SaaS. ParleyInn should add the parts Semantica lacks: a hash-chained append-only record, trust-enveloped recall, and a network-free core with transport kept outside it.

name: Serena memories (oraios/serena)
category: in-repo Markdown memory (part of a coding-agent MCP toolkit)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Notes about a project that an agent or a human writes and curates. These are distilled knowledge, not session history. Onboarding fills them with the project's structure, build system, test setup and conventions (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html). A shipped `memory_maintenance` template tells agents to store only "stable, non-obvious project conventions". It rules out one-off task notes, volatile line-level details and "behavior likely to change soon" (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/resources/memory_maintenance.md). Memories do not hold transcripts, prompts, tool calls, session IDs, authorship or timestamps. A memory is just a name plus a Markdown body (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py). Each write is capped at `default_max_tool_answer_chars`, which defaults to 150,000 characters (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/repl/api/mem_api.py, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/config/serena_config.py). Serena commits its own memories to its own repo: 7 files, including critical_info.md, project_structure.md and task_completion.md, seen at commit d0f7f92 on 2026-09-30 (https://github.com/oraios/serena/tree/main/.serena/memories).
where_stored: Plain files in the working tree. Project memories live in `<project>/.serena/memories/`. Global memories live in `~/.serena/memories/global/`, under `$SERENA_HOME/memories/global` when SERENA_HOME is set (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/config/serena_config.py). A `project_serena_folder_location` template can move the per-project `.serena` folder out of the repo, e.g. `/projects-metadata/$projectFolderName/.serena` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/050_configuration.html). Serena writes a `.serena/.gitignore` that ignores only `/cache` and `/project.local.yml`, so memories are committed by default (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/project.py). The docs say project memories "can be committed, reviewed in PRs, and reverted like any other repository artifact". Global memories are not versioned; the docs suggest turning `~/.serena/memories/` into a git repo yourself (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html). Serena has no git integration, server or database of its own.
format_and_model:
One UTF-8 Markdown file per memory, with no front matter or schema. A memory's name maps to its path: `/` in a name creates a topic subdirectory (`modules/frontend` becomes `modules/frontend.md`), and the prefix `global/` sends it to the global directory (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py). Memories link to each other with `mem:NAME` inside backticks. Agents are told to start from a `mem:core` root memory and follow references down, which forms a graph (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/resources/memory_maintenance.md).

Operations are exposed as MCP tools and a REPL API: write, read, list (optionally by topic), edit (literal or regex replace), rename (rewrites every `mem:` reference) and delete. Delete is meant to run only with user permission (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/tools/memory_tools.py). CLI-only commands: `serena memories check` (referential integrity, with fuzzy suggestions of near-miss names), `auto-prefix-references` and `initialize` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_reference_analysis.py).

Regex `read_only_memory_patterns` and `ignored_memory_patterns` from the global and project config are merged additively (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html). Data model: a mutable, overwrite-in-place document store. Edits replace the whole file and nothing is appended. There is no history except what git provides.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Serena has no concurrency control or merge logic of its own.

- **Torn files:** writes go through `write_file_atomic`, which writes a temp file and then calls `os.replace`, so a crash cannot leave a half-written file. This fix is on unreleased main (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/util/file_system.py, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
- **Lost updates:** memories have no file lock. `edit_memory` reads, modifies and writes back without one, so two concurrent writers give last-writer-wins on the whole file (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py).
- **Duplicate instances:** issue #1235 (2026-03-27) reports that two MCP clients on one project start two Serena processes with "last-writer-wins with no merge", and says simultaneous `write_memory` calls give "undefined" results. The issue is closed, but the resolution is not visible (https://github.com/oraios/serena/issues/1235).
- **Across machines or branches:** merging is left to git's line-based text merge. There is no custom merge driver. Because `rename_memory` rewrites references in every memory that cites the old name, renames on two branches tend to conflict in many files (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py).
- **Write protection:** read-only patterns block writes only in "tool context", i.e. from the agent; the CLI and humans bypass them (same source).
- **Cloud sync:** a request for opt-in sync to R2, S3 or Azure, with SHA256 conflict detection, was closed as not planned (https://github.com/oraios/serena/issues/1328).
realtime: None. Serena has no watch, pub/sub, sync daemon or network transport for memories.
