Each read opens the file from disk, so another local process sees a change on its next call (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py). The list of memory names reaches the agent only when the project is activated (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/agent.py). Other machines or worktrees see changes only after a git commit and pull. A local dashboard can view and edit memories while Serena runs (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html).
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is deliberately search-free and pull-only.

- **Name list up front:** when a project is activated, the full list of project memory names is sent as JSON, with the instruction to read relevant ones later (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/agent.py).
- **Progressive disclosure:** the agent follows `mem:` references, starting from `mem:core` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html).
- **No search engine by design:** the design calls search noise because lexical and semantic retrieval both produce false positives and negatives, while "explicit, name-based references decided by the agent are deterministic". It explicitly rejects database-backed memory: SQLite, graph databases and vector stores (same source).
- **Fallbacks:** `list_memories(topic)` and the generic regex search tool. A bug where `search_for_pattern` refused to search a gitignored `.serena` folder was fixed in PR #1810 (https://github.com/oraios/serena/issues/1805).
- **Design principle 5:** "the harness does not inject memory content" (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html).
- **Opt-in exception:** an `embed_memory(name)` Jinja function inlines a memory's content into context, mode or project prompts, wrapped in `<memory name="...">` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/050_configuration.html). Serena's own `project.yml` uses `embed_memory("critical_info")` (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/.serena/project.yml).
links_sessions_to_code: No. Memories carry no session ID, prompt, transcript, commit SHA, file or line anchor, or author (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py). The only link to code is location: project memories sit in the same git tree, so they are committed, reviewed and reverted together with the code. Commit history therefore provides any provenance (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html). Unreleased main now creates session IDs inside Serena, used by `activate_project` and the REPL, but they are not attached to memories (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). Memory names can mirror code modules such as frontend/backend, but that is a naming convention only (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/resources/memory_maintenance.md).
scale:
The project makes no numeric scale claims. The docs say only that topic filtering lets an agent "explore even large numbers of memories in a structured way", and they suggest `ignored_memory_patterns` (e.g. `_archive/.*`, `_episodes/.*`) for projects that pile up archived memories (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html). Structural limits:
- Every activation sends the full name list, so prompt cost grows with the number of memories (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/agent.py).
- Each write is capped at 150k characters by default (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/config/serena_config.py).
- Listing walks the directory on every call; there is no index (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py).

For adoption scale, the repo page showed about 29.9k stars and 2.0k forks and was not archived (https://github.com/oraios/serena). I could not verify how large real deployments' memory sets are.
privacy_security:
- **No protection of content:** memory text is not redacted, scanned for secrets or encrypted. It is plaintext Markdown, readable by anyone with access to the repo or `~/.serena`, and public once committed to a public repo (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py).
- **Path sandboxing:**
  - `..` segments are forbidden (v1.2.0).
  - Absolute names and empty path segments are rejected (v1.6.0), closing a write to `/etc/cron.d/backdoor` (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).
  - A lexical containment check backs this up. Symlinked directories are followed on purpose so memories can be shared (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py).
- **Stated trust model:** Serena assumes the local machine, the LLM, the repository and the user config are all trusted. Sandboxing is "the only way to fully protect" (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/070_security.html).
- **Trusted projects (v1.6.0):** trust gates only `activation_command` and `ls_specific_settings`. The docs call it "a functionality boundary, not a containment boundary" (same source). Memories and `project.yml` `initial_prompt` are not trust-gated: the activation message renders `initial_prompt`, including any `embed_memory` content, with no trust check. Memory text is wrapped in a tag but not escaped (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/agent.py). A repo-supplied memory can therefore reach the model as instructions.
- **Open issue #1251 (2026-03-30):** reports "cross-project memory poisoning". One prompt injection could write lasting instructions into global memory that "load into every future conversation on that machine, across all projects". No maintainer response is visible (https://github.com/oraios/serena/issues/1251). The available mitigation is `read_only_memory_patterns`, e.g. `global/.*` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/045_memories.html).
- **Network:** Serena sends anonymous usage data (version, OS, backend, dashboard state, context) at every start; opt out with `SERENA_USAGE_REPORTING=false` (https://oraios.github.io/serena/01-about/070_privacy.html). Its network services listen on localhost by default (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/070_security.html).
lesson_for_parinn:
Committing agent memory to the repo works well for a small, curated, human-reviewed layer: the PR review is the trust gate, and the memory reverts together with the code. But Serena can only call this safe because it declares the repo and the LLM trusted (https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/070_security.html). Once memories travel through git, any PR author or poisoned session can plant text that a later agent reads as guidance. Issue #1251 shows the cross-project version through global memories (https://github.com/oraios/serena/issues/1251).

If ParleyInn uses git as a transport, it should:
- Treat every record pulled from git as untrusted data. Recall stays enveloped (I2) whatever the commit provenance.
- Never let git-sourced content become pinned TrustedText unless a known principal signs it.
- Avoid Serena's mutable whole-file overwrite with last-writer-wins (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/src/serena/memories/memory_manager.py). Each writer, agent or machine should own an append-only segment, so git merges are just unions of files and never text conflicts.

Worth borrowing: Serena's deterministic, name-based references plus a CLI integrity check (`serena memories check`) map well onto ParleyInn's pull-only recall. Agents could cite stable record or hash IDs instead of running fuzzy search.
license: Released versions up to v1.7.0 (2026-08-09) are MIT; PyPI lists serena-agent 1.7.0 as MIT (https://pypi.org/pypi/serena-agent/json, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). On main, still unreleased as of 2026-09-30, the Serena application, including the memory code, is relicensed to GPL-3.0-or-later. The SolidLSP library stays MIT, earlier releases stay MIT (tag `mit-final`), and contributions now require a CLA (https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/LICENSE, https://github.com/oraios/serena/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

name: Sigstore gitsign
status: shipped. Actively maintained: latest tags are v0.17.0 and v0.17.1 (both 2026-07-29), and the last commit on main is 2026-09-10. The project is still pre-1.0. Two parts are labelled experimental: offline Rekor mode and Rekor v2 (rekor-tiles) uploads. Not archived.
what_is_stored: Signatures only, not content. For each commit or tag, gitsign stores a CMS/PKCS7 signature (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#privacy). The signature covers CMS SignedAttrs: content type, sha256 of the git object body (author, committer, message, parents, tree) and signing time (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/bundle-cms.md). It also holds the ephemeral Fulcio leaf certificate, valid about 10 minutes. That certificate carries the OIDC identity: an email SAN, or for workloads a URI SAN plus OIDs naming the GitHub Actions workflow, repo, ref, SHA and event (https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/keyless-git-commit-signing-with-gitsign-and-github-actions, https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/committer-verification.md). In offline mode the signature also carries the Rekor TransparencyLogEntry (protobuf) and inclusion proof, plus an optional RFC 3161 TSA token (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/verification.md). Separately, a mostly undocumented subcommand, `gitsign attest`, stores in-toto attestations: the raw predicate JSON plus a DSSE envelope (internal/attest/attest.go in the repo; https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/cli/gitsign_attest.md). Gitsign stores no prompts, sessions or other agent data.
where_stored: Three places. (1) Inside the git object itself, in the commit or tag `gpgsig` header. This is git's x509 interface: gpg.format=x509, gpg.x509.program=gitsign (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#configuration). (2) In the Rekor transparency log on a server. By default this is the public rekor.sigstore.dev; a private Sigstore deployment can be used instead (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#private-sigstore). (3) For `gitsign attest`, under custom refs `refs/attestations/commits` and `refs/attestations/trees`. Each ref points at a parentless-rooted chain of commits whose tree is laid out as <target-sha>/<file> and <target-sha>/<file>.sig (repo source internal/attest/attest.go; constants CommitRef/TreeRef). Optional local state: gitsign-credential-cache keeps the ephemeral key and certificate in memory behind a Unix socket, keyed per working directory (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/cmd/gitsign-credential-cache/README.md).
format_and_model: The signature is an RFC 5652 CMS SignedData in PEM form inside the gpgsig header, with ECDSA P-256 keys (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#inspecting-the-git-commit-signature). The thing signed and logged is sha256(DER(SignedAttrs)), not the commit body. Gitsign checks the content binding separately: it compares sha256(git object) with the messageDigest attribute (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/bundle-cms.md). Rekor entries are HashedRekord records. In online mode the entry is the commit SHA hash plus the certificate. In offline mode it is a hash of the commit content, and the log entry is embedded as unauthenticated CMS attributes, so it sits outside the signature but is verified through the inclusion proof (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#privacy, https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/verification.md). Since sigstore-go became the default (enableSigstoreGo=true), gitsign converts losslessly between CMS and Sigstore bundle v0.3 without changing the on-disk format (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/bundle-cms.md). Attestations are in-toto Statements whose subject is {gitCommit|gitTree: sha}, with a predicate type URI, in DSSE envelopes that are also uploaded to Rekor (repo internal/attest/attest.go).
multi_writer_and_merge: For signatures, every writer signs its own commits with its own short-lived identity, and git handles merges as usual: a merge commit is just another signed object. Rebasing or amending changes the object and needs a fresh signature. The attestation ref is updated with a local compare-and-swap (CheckAndSetReference against the old ref value). The code has no fetch, push or merge logic, so concurrent writers on different machines would hit non-fast-forward conflicts on refs/attestations/* with no built-in resolution. That reading comes from source inspection of internal/attest and internal/commands/attest; no doc confirms it. Rekor serves as a global append-only, multi-writer log shared by all signers.
realtime: Not applicable for distribution: data moves only when you push or fetch git refs. Signing is synchronous and needs the network at commit time: an OIDC token, a Fulcio certificate and a Rekor upload. The README warns that commit.gpgsign=true 'will make git commit/tag reliant on internet' (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#configuration). Interactive use opens a browser unless a token provider is set (github-actions, spiffe, google-workload-identity, buildkite-agent, filesystem, device flow) (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#file-config).
search_retrieval: Minimal. `gitsign verify --certificate-identity=... --certificate-oidc-issuer=... <rev>` checks one revision. It validates the signature, the Rekor entry and the certificate claims. Plain `git verify-commit` cannot check identity claims (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#verifying-commits). Rekor can be searched by hash or log index; offline-mode entries are 'complex to query manually' (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/verification.md). Attestations are found by walking the refs/attestations tree by target SHA. There is no content search.
links_sessions_to_code: Not directly. Gitsign binds a commit to the OIDC identity that signed it, such as a human email or a CI workflow URI with repo, ref and event (https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/keyless-git-commit-signing-with-gitsign-and-github-actions). It does not record prompts or sessions. `gitsign attest --type <predicateURI> -f file` could attach an arbitrary JSON predicate, for example a session digest, to a commit or tree SHA under refs/attestations/* (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/docs/cli/gitsign_attest.md). The predicate is uploaded to Rekor inside the DSSE envelope, so it becomes public on the public instance. A web search surfaced a third-party tool ('Pedigree') said to store agent prompt and model hashes in git attestation refs. I could not verify it from a primary source (the page cited for it, https://tessl.io/patterns/quality-security/ai-code-provenance/, does not mention it).
scale: No scale claims for gitsign itself. Each signature adds a few KB of PEM per commit (sample in the README, https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#inspecting-the-git-commit-signature), and each commit costs one Rekor entry. Rekor v2 (tile-based) support exists but is experimental (rekorVersion=2) (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#file-config).
privacy_security: No long-lived keys. The ephemeral key and certificate live about 10 minutes, and gitsign 'aims to not store refresh tokens or other cryptographic material on disk' (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#faq). The README flags the main privacy risk itself: Fulcio certificates in the public Rekor log may contain user emails or repo identifiers, and the mitigation is a private Rekor (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#privacy). Chainguard adds that workflow, repo and branch names are exposed (https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/keyless-git-commit-signing-with-gitsign-and-github-actions). The log is append-only, so nothing in it can be redacted, and the content is never encrypted. Online mode logs only hashes; attestation payloads go into the log in full. The credential cache is optional, and its README warns that anyone with access to the socket can sign as you; it recommends not using it on shared systems or where ambient OIDC credentials exist (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign/blob/main/cmd/gitsign-credential-cache/README.md). The urlOpener setting runs no shell (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#file-config). GitHub still does not show gitsign signatures as Verified: the Sigstore root is not in GitHub's trust store, and expired certificates need Rekor-backed validation (https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign#why-doesnt-github-show-commits-as-verified). By contrast, GitHub's own Copilot cloud agent has shown its commits as Verified since 2026-04-03; its signing mechanism is not documented in the changelog entry (https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-03-copilot-cloud-agent-signs-its-commits/).
license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file in https://github.com/sigstore/gitsign)
lesson_for_parinn: Copy the shape of gitsign offline mode plus `attest`, not its network dependency. ParleyInn's core cannot call Fulcio or Rekor (I4). It can still sign hash-chain checkpoints through an external signer process, the way git delegates to gpg.x509.program, so identity and network live outside the core. The signature and its transparency or inclusion proof should be embedded next to the record, as offline mode does, so that verification works offline in sandboxes. Two cautions. First, gitsign's split between the signed core and unauthenticated proof attributes shows that only a narrow, canonical digest should be signed; the content binding is checked separately. Second, anything sent to a public append-only log is permanent and cannot be redacted. ParleyInn should therefore only ever publish hashes of session records, never content or identities, which is exactly the trap `gitsign attest` falls into by uploading full predicates. The refs/attestations/<sha>/ tree layout with compare-and-swap ref updates is a ready precedent for attaching session digests to commits. It ships no remote merge story, so ParleyInn would need its own append-only union merge for multi-machine writers.

name: Sigstore Rekor v2 (rekor-tiles)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Immutable, append-only transparency log for software supply chain metadata. Stores signed artifact metadata, signatures, certificates, and attestations. In v2, supports two primary entry types: hashedrekord (artifact signatures) and dsse (attestations); removed intoto, rekord, helm, tuf, alpine, cose, jar, and rfc3161 entry types from v1 for simplification.
where_stored: Tile-backed transparency log using Trillian Tessera. Multiple backend options: GCP (Cloud Spanner for sequencing + Google Cloud Storage for tiles), AWS (Aurora/RDS MySQL + S3), POSIX (filesystem). Tiles stored as static, immutable HTTP resources with long-lived caching headers. Each annual log shard (e.g., log2025-1, log2026-1) gets its own instance at unique URL (logYEAR-rev.rekor.sigstore.dev); old shards frozen as static tiles served from CDN.
format_and_model: RFC 6962 Merkle tree with SHA-256 hashing. Checkpoints served as signed tree heads (STH) at /<prefix>/checkpoint. Merkle tree organized into 256-hash tiles (8192 bytes each) at /<prefix>/tile/<L>/<N> where L is tree level, N is tile index. Entry bundles as length-prefixed sequences at /<prefix>/tile/entries/<N>, typically compressed via HTTP. Clients fetch needed tiles and entries in parallel, compute inclusion/consistency proofs locally.
multi_writer_and_merge: Centralized append-only log with single-writer model. Multiple clients submit entries, but sequencing is deterministic and non-concurrent. Cosign v2.6.0+ uses SigningConfig to submit entries. Batching implemented to enable higher throughput without increasing latency dramatically. No merge semantics; entries ordered sequentially in tree. Witnessed/consensus model being implemented via omniwitness.
realtime: Batching introduces latency: responses take several seconds before entries appear. Not truly real-time. New log shard created annually to manage size; old shards frozen and served statically, preventing queries against live data after rotation. Checkpoint rotations happen periodically; clients use TUF to discover new log instances and verify transitions.
search_retrieval: Search indexing removed from Rekor v2, being reimplemented as separate service. Current capabilities: SAN-based lookup via subject field (merged July 2026). MySQL-backed indexes for efficient retrieval in underlying infrastructure. Clients can retrieve tiles and entries, then compute any desired proof locally without additional server requests. No full-text search or complex query API.
links_sessions_to_code: Not designed to link agent sessions to code. Records artifacts (binaries, containers, SBOMs) and their signatures/certificates. No mechanism to associate entries with source code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, or agent session IDs. Timestamps on certificates allow verification when signature was created, but no traceability to development workflow or agent provenance.
privacy_security: No encryption of stored entries; transparency log requires public readability. 100KB attestation size limit enforced. Immutable, append-only, cryptographically tamper-evident via Merkle proofs. No redaction mechanism; users must avoid submitting sensitive data to public instance. Security properties rely on transparency and external auditing (omniwitness, independent monitors). Identity proved via OIDC; private keys never touch Sigstore servers. Threat model: detects misbehavior rather than preventing it.
lesson_for_parinn: Tile-based static logs enable efficient verification and CDN distribution without requiring clients to trust a central server for freshness. Frozen annual shards separate concerns: live writes to current shard, static verification of historical shards. Append-only with no concurrent write merging greatly simplifies integrity proofs. However, ParleyInn's multi-agent, multi-worktree use case requires different model: concurrent writes from independent agents, local storage without central sequencing, and session-to-code linkage—properties Rekor doesn't provide. Lesson: tile architecture is elegant for read-heavy transparency, but agent session history needs fine-grained concurrency control, local-first write ordering, and bidirectional traceability to source.
sources: https://blog.sigstore.dev/rekor-v2-ga/ — Official GA announcement October 2025, describes v2 redesign, tile-backed log, annual sharding
https://docs.sigstore.dev/ — Sigstore documentation covering Rekor, Cosign, Fulcio, OIDC integration
https://github.com/sigstore/rekor — Rekor GitHub repository, v1.5.4 latest (Aug 2026), v2 development ongoing
https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/releases — Release notes showing v1 maintenance mode, Cosign v2.6.0+ support for v2
https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles — Tile log specification (RFC-style), defines static HTTP API for transparency logs
https://github.com/sigstore/cosign — Cosign tool documentation and integration with Rekor
https://github.com/google/trillian — Trillian transparency log infrastructure; v2 uses Tessera successor
https://transparency.dev — Transparency log concepts and verifiable systems
https://docs.sigstore.dev/security/ — Sigstore threat model, OIDC integration, limitations, monitoring

name: Sigsum
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Cryptographic signatures (signed checksums) in an append-only merkle tree. Each entry is a signature with metadata: signer identity, timestamp, and the signed checksum/hash. The log maintains ordered entries numbered sequentially. All entries are immutable once committed.
where_stored: Sigsum uses Trillian as the merkle tree backend, which stores data in MySQL/MariaDB. The specification is database-agnostic but the reference implementation (log-go) uses Trillian with MariaDB. Logs are operated as network-accessible HTTP services (e.g. 'seasalp' operated by Glasklar Teknik AB). Witnesses store the latest checkpoint they've verified for each log. Checkpoints and proofs are transmitted over HTTP/HTTPS and optionally via Tor onion services.
format_and_model: Sigsum follows the tlog (transparency log) format standardized via C2SP (Community Cryptography Specification Project). Data model: append-only merkle tree with signed checkpoints. Log entries are ordered and identified by index. Merkle tree uses binary tree structure for inclusion and consistency proofs. Checkpoints are signed by the log server and include a tree root hash. Witnesses provide cosignatures on checkpoints (format: note signatures with Ed25519, per tlog-cosignature@v1.0.0 spec). Proof bundles contain signed entries, inclusion proofs (merkle path), and witness cosignatures (proof-bundle-format in development).
multi_writer_and_merges: Single-writer log model (per-log has one authoritative operator). Multiple witnesses (read-only monitors) verify consistency. Witness model uses m-of-n cosigning: clients configure a trust policy naming multiple witness public keys and requiring a quorum of cosignatures before trusting a log entry. Witnesses independently verify the log's append-only property by validating Merkle consistency proofs submitted by the log. No automatic merging; clients pull from a single log and aggregate witness confirmations. The bastion host protocol enables private log backends to communicate with public witnesses synchronously via a reverse-proxy gateway.
realtime: Near-real-time. Sigsum submissions are logged and signed immediately by the log server. Checkpoints are signed periodically (frequency depends on log operator). Witnesses verify and cosign new checkpoints as they become available. Monitors (users) can poll logs in real-time to detect when keys are used. No push notifications; pull-based polling model. Responses are HTTP-based and can complete within seconds.
search_retrieval: Limited search capability. No full-text search or complex queries. Retrieval is primarily by: (1) entry index in the log, (2) inclusion proof verification for a known entry, (3) consistency proof to verify log growth. Monitors periodically poll the entire log or query specific entries. Command-line tools (sigsum-go, sigsum-c, sigsum-rs) provide query and verification functions. Florian's sigmon monitor (github.com/florolf/sigmon) offers enhanced monitoring capabilities but implementation details not documented.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Sigsum is designed for signing keys and cryptographic checksums, not for linking agent sessions or prompts to code artifacts. It can verify that a specific key produced a signature (enabling key-compromise detection) but does not track agent sessions, code commits, or execution traces. Could theoretically be used to transparently log CI/CD signing events or release artifacts, but this is not a primary design goal.
privacy_security: Privacy: Tor onion addresses available for privacy-conscious access. All log contents are public by design. Security: Ed25519 cryptography. Relies on trust policies configured by users (public keys and quorum thresholds). Witness quorum prevents single-party log manipulation: attacker must control majority of witnesses AND log operator to create undetected false entries. No redaction mechanism documented. Treats untrusted content (from logs) conservatively: verification is pull-only, not automatic. No secrets/passwords stored; signatures are permanent records. Encryption: relies on TLS for transport; data is not encrypted at rest in logs (transparency requires auditability).
lesson_for_parinn: The witness quorum model (m-of-n cosigning for log integrity verification) demonstrates a practical approach to multi-party consensus without requiring a blockchain or distributed ledger. For ParleyInn, this suggests: (1) append-only records verified by independent witnesses can replace trusting a single log operator, (2) cryptographic checksums and proofs (inclusion, consistency) scale better than full content hashing, (3) offline-verifiable proofs (via witness signatures) allow clients to verify history without querying live services continuously, (4) separating the log server from witness nodes enables private backends (via bastion protocol) while maintaining public auditability—applicable to ParleyInn if agent sessions need independent attestation without exposing infrastructure.

name: SLSA source-tool (sourcetool, SLSA Source Track proof of concept)
status: beta. The README still says "Status: in development" and DESIGN.md calls it a "proof-of-concept". It is not archived and is actively maintained: the latest release is v0.7.0 (tagged 2026-07-08), and commits on main run to 2026-09-28. That includes #456, which promoted the source and tag provenance predicates from "v1-draft" to "v1"; readers still accept the draft types. The SLSA 1.2 Source Track spec page at slsa.dev shows "Status: Approved", so the spec is final while this tool is still a reference PoC. GitHub's metadata API was blocked in this session, so star counts and the archived flag could not be read there. Activity comes from a git clone.
what_is_stored: Supply-chain attestations about commits and tags. It stores no session, prompt or chat data. Per commit on a protected branch it stores two items. (1) Source Provenance records subject gitCommit, prev_commit, the enabled controls with a 'since' timestamp for each (CONTINUITY_ENFORCED, REVIEW_ENFORCED, TAG_HYGIENE, PROVENANCE_AVAILABLE, GH_REQUIRED_CHECK_*), actor, branch, created_on, activity_type (for example pr_merge) and repo_uri. (2) A SLSA Verification Summary Attestation (VSA) records verifiedLevels (for example SLSA_SOURCE_LEVEL_3, TAG_HYGIENE, ORG_SOURCE_TESTED), verificationResult, timeVerified, the policy URI, the verifier id and source_refs. For tags it stores Tag Provenance: tag name, actor, controls, created_on, and vsa_summaries copied from earlier VSAs for the tagged commit. A separate policy JSON per repo sets the target level and 'Since' dates. It lives in the external slsa-framework/source-policies repo, not in the user repo.
where_stored: git notes in the default ref refs/notes/commits of the protected repository itself. A note is keyed by the annotated commit SHA, at the tree path <sha> while unsharded or <2 chars>/<38 chars> once sharded. History is never rewritten. Optionally it also pushes to the GitHub Attestations API (--push=github). Policy sits in a separate public git repo (slsa-framework/source-policies). Readers default to notes ("--from=github,note" selects other sources).
format_and_model: Each note is a JSONL in-toto bundle with one signed attestation per line. Each line is a Sigstore bundle (mediaType application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json) with a Fulcio short-lived certificate wrapping a DSSE envelope. The envelope carries an in-toto Statement v1 whose subject digest is gitCommit. Predicate types are https://github.com/slsa-framework/source-tool/source-provenance/v1, .../tag-provenance/v1 and https://slsa.dev/verification_summary/v1. The data model is a hash-linked chain: each provenance names prev_commit, and the level is computed as a memoized recursion, MIN(controlLevel(commit), level(prevCommit)), back to the policy start. Offline auditors can walk the whole chain. Since #455/#456 (Sep 2026) the predicates are generated from slsa-framework/protos. Reads and writes go through the carabiner-dev/collector 'note' package, built on go-git.
multi_writer_and_merge: There is effectively a single writer: the reusable GitHub Actions workflow compute_slsa_source.yml (in slsa-framework/source-actions), triggered on each push to a protected branch. Its OIDC identity is the signing identity. The storer (carabiner-dev/collector) works as follows. It clones or fetches refs/notes/commits with a force refspec. It reads the commit's existing JSONL, appends new lines, writes a new notes commit whose parent is the old notes tip, and pushes refs/notes/commits:refs/notes/commits without force. A concurrent writer therefore gets a non-fast-forward rejection. I found no notes merge strategy (such as cat_sort_uniq) and no retry loop in the storer code I read; whether callers retry could not be verified. Merge commits in the source branch are 'not officially supported' and sit behind an experimental allow-merge-commits flag. A missing provenance (for example from a failed workflow run) is treated as a control gap and breaks the chain until the policy is updated. DESIGN.md lists this as an open reliability issue.
realtime: No. Attestations are written asynchronously by a CI workflow after each push. Consumers pull notes on demand (via git fetch of the notes ref or the GitHub contents API). There are no subscriptions or streaming.
search_retrieval: Point lookup by commit SHA only. One path is the GitHub contents API at path <aa>/<rest> on ref refs/notes/commits, falling back to the unsharded <sha> path (issue #215). The other is a go-git clone of the notes ref. CLI commands: 'sourcetool get', 'verify' (exits non-zero on failure, usable as a CI gate), 'audit' (walks the chain) and 'attest'. There is no full-text or cross-commit query.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply to agent sessions or prompts. It links attestations to code by commit SHA (the in-toto subject gitCommit) and to the previous commit via prev_commit, and to refs via branch, tag and source_refs. The mechanism is still a direct precedent for attaching a session record to the commit it produced.
scale: No published scale claims. It shards the notes tree into 2-character directories once sharding is detected (git's own fan-out convention). Retrieval is O(1) per commit via the contents API. The verification workflow reads only the prior commit's attestations, which keeps per-push cost constant. Full audits are linear in chain length.
privacy_security: Integrity relies on Sigstore keyless signing. The signing identity is the reusable workflow, so callers cannot forge attestations. Each line carries a Fulcio certificate and transparency material, verifiable with sigstore-go. Contemporaneity is guaranteed only by the workflow running on push. It trusts GitHub APIs (rulesets, repository activity) to tell the truth. An external public policy repo outside the user's control blocks the 'disable controls, change, re-enable' backsliding move. There is no encryption and no redaction: notes are public in public repos, and the actor login and repo URI are in cleartext. Note that git notes are not protected by branch rulesets in the same way. Anyone with push access can rewrite refs/notes/commits, so trust comes from verifying signatures, not from where the data lives. That last point is my inference and is not stated in the docs.
lesson_for_parinn: Separate where records travel from what they are trusted for. source-tool puts signed, self-verifying, hash-chained records (an in-toto/DSSE statement with subject gitCommit and prev_commit) in a single append-only JSONL note per commit on refs/notes/commits. It treats the git transport as untrusted and verifies every line on read. The same move lets ParleyInn export a signed digest of its session chain (session id, chain head hash, commit SHA) as a git note line without rewriting history. Two cautions. First, git notes give no real multi-writer merge: a non-force push of one notes ref means concurrent agents collide, and a missing record reads as a gap. ParleyInn should keep its own local append-only log as the source of truth, treat a notes or ref export as an optional, idempotent and auditable (I6) side channel with fetch-merge-retry, and never re-inject note content as trusted text (I2). Second, in ParleyInn the push itself would have to happen outside the core, because I4 forbids network access.
license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file in repo; SPDX headers in source files). The storage dependency carabiner-dev/collector is also Apache-2.0.

name: SmolForge (swyx/forge, CLI @smolai/forge)
category: agent-native git forge (hosted Git remote plus CI, sites and agent-transcript capture, built on Cloudflare)
status: beta
what_is_stored: Normalized coding-agent transcripts, one per (repo, session). Each one holds session_id, agent_type (claude-code, claude-cowork, codex, cursor, factory, devin, opencode, aider, continue, custom), an optional commit_sha, session start and end times, message_count, and an ordered list of messages. A message has a role (user, assistant or system; the docs also list developer), content ("plain text, markdown, or compact tool summary"), a timestamp, message_kind, tool_name and image_keys (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/guides/agent-transcripts; schema in migrations/0001_fresh_schema_01.sql of https://forge.smol.ai/swyx/forge). Screenshots shared with the agent are stored as images (https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt). A junction table, transcript_commits, maps message ranges to commits: start_ordering, end_ordering and segment_message_count per commit. The source repo's migrations show this, and the public API returns it. Fidelity is lossy. The CLI and the documented parsers keep text parts and drop the rest; the Codex parser skips encrypted reasoning blocks (packages/api/src/features/transcripts/parsers.ts). Without ?full=true, reads truncate assistant messages to 500 characters (https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt). Forks do not copy transcripts (https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt).
where_stored: Server/cloud. Transcripts and messages live in Cloudflare D1 (SQLite) tables. Images and Git objects live in Cloudflare R2, with Git objects keyed by repo plus SHA. Everything runs on Cloudflare Workers, with Durable Objects as repo locks (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/overview). Nothing transcript-related is written into the git repo itself. The only in-git artifact is the optional 'AI-Session: <id>' commit trailer, which is plain text in the commit message.
format_and_model: Clients upload over HTTP with a Bearer JWT or PAT; a transcripts:write scope exists. The endpoint is POST /api/repos/:owner/:repo/transcripts. The body is either a {session_id, agent_type, commit_sha?, messages[]} JSON or a raw 'jsonl' string, which the server auto-detects as Codex or Claude Code format and parses (https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt; apiRoutes.ts). Capture is client-side through `sf hooks install <owner/repo> --agent all --git post-commit,pre-push`. It writes .smolforge/hooks/upload-transcript.sh, native agent hooks and git hook backstops (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/guides/agent-transcripts). For Claude Code that is a PostToolUse hook with the matcher 'Bash(git commit*)' (packages/cli/src/hooks.ts). Codex is found through ~/.codex/sessions JSONL, Cursor through ~/.cursor/projects/.../agent-transcripts, Factory Droid through a SessionEnd hook using transcript_path, and Devin and OpenCode through best-effort sqlite3 extraction from their local DBs (same guide). The relational model is transcripts (UNIQUE(repo_id, session_id)) 1-N transcript_messages (ordering), plus transcript_commits(transcript_id, commit_sha, start/end_ordering). There is no hash chain, signature or append-only guarantee: rows are mutable and the remask endpoint rewrites stored content.
multi_writer_and_merge: This is a central server, so there is no merge. Any number of agents and machines push transcripts to one D1 database over HTTPS. Each upload is a whole-session snapshot keyed by session_id. The schema puts a UNIQUE(repo_id, session_id) constraint on transcripts. The upload handler does a plain INSERT, and I saw no upsert. So a second upload of the same session probably fails or needs separate handling (inferred from apiRoutes.ts; not tested). The docs say session_id "must be stable enough to deduplicate a real agent session in the UI" (agent-transcripts guide). Git pushes are serialized per repo by Durable Object locks: "Push operations use repo-level coordination to avoid concurrent write races" (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/overview). Sharing and syncing transcripts across users is not built yet: "transcript and skill sharing and syncing are next" (https://forge.smol.ai).
realtime: Not real time. Uploads happen in batches at git commit time (PostToolUse on git commit, post-commit or pre-push hooks) or at session end. No streaming, subscription or presence for transcripts is documented. The "bounded managed realtime" in the docs belongs to Forge Deploy-hosted apps, not transcripts (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/overview; https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt). Live transcript sharing is listed as "next" (https://forge.smol.ai).
search_retrieval: Retrieval is by key only: a paginated list per repo (?page&limit), get by session_id, and get by commit SHA. A by-commit read returns only that commit's message segment (https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt; apiRoutes.ts). There is no full-text or semantic search over transcripts. The only FTS5 table in the schema is gist_search (migrations/0002_fresh_schema_02.sql). The UI shows an expandable "AI Transcript" on commit pages and "commit chips" on sessions (agent-transcripts guide).
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Linking to code is the feature's main purpose. The docs describe putting an 'AI-Session: <session-id>' trailer in the commit message, noting that trailers "survive rebases, cherry-picks, and format-patch" (agent-transcripts guide). In the shipped server code, the actual linking works differently (packages/api/src/features/transcripts/segments.ts). It starts from the explicit commit_sha in the upload. It then scans message content for 40-hex SHAs and keeps those that resolve to commit objects in the repo's R2 store with a committer time inside a padded session window. Each kept SHA gets a contiguous message range, giving per-commit segments. I found no server code that parses the AI-Session trailer. The trailer appears only in the README, llms.txt and the docs' example hooks, where it is used client-side to find the session file. So the trailer is a convention for discovering sessions, not the server's join key (my reading of the code, not stated by the project). linked_commits keeps only SHAs "that still resolve in the repository object store", and reindexing drops stale chips (guide). A live example: a public Codex session with 679 messages, split into 9 commit segments (https://forge.smol.ai/api/repos/swyx/forge/transcripts?limit=2).
scale: No scale claims for transcripts. Architecturally it is one D1 row per message. The upload handler inserts messages one at a time in a loop, and segment scanning caps candidates at 100 SHAs (apiRoutes.ts, segments.ts). Observed: the swyx/forge repo has transcript ids around 1,000,014 and sessions of hundreds of messages (public API above), with 5 stars and refs_generation 1767 (https://forge.smol.ai/api/repos/swyx/forge). Rate limits and Deploy limits are documented separately; I did not review them.
privacy_security: Redaction is regex secret masking with built-in patterns: cfut_*, sk-*, ghp_*, AKIA*, credentialed URLs, *PASSWORD/SECRET/TOKEN/API_KEY= shell variables, contextual password phrases, and piped login passwords. Repo-specific regexes go in via /secret-masks, and a /transcripts/remask endpoint fixes already-stored leaks. "Masking is applied both when storing and when retrieving transcript content" (agent-transcripts guide; packages/api/src/utils/secretMask.ts). I found no encryption at rest beyond Cloudflare defaults, and the transcript code has no encryption: the only 'encrypt' hit is skipping Codex's encrypted reasoning. Access follows repo visibility (public, unlisted, private). Transcripts on public repos can be read without authentication; I verified this with an unauthenticated curl to https://forge.smol.ai/api/repos/swyx/forge/transcripts. The docs say "Public transcript reads mask configured secrets" (guide). Auth uses JWT (HMAC-SHA256) plus PBKDF2 and scoped PATs (https://forge.smol.ai/docs/overview; https://forge.smol.ai/llms.txt). The design has no notion of transcripts as untrusted content or prompt-injection risk. The hook scripts interpolate session ids into sqlite3 SQL strings (hooks.ts). Capture relies on the network: hooks curl the hosted API using a token kept in git config or env.
license: Unclear. The homepage says "Open source" and "Self-hostable" (https://forge.smol.ai), and the source can be cloned publicly from https://forge.smol.ai/swyx/forge.git (I verified with git ls-remote and a shallow clone; main is at eeaec1e, dated 2026-08-23). But the repo has no LICENSE file, the repo API reports license_spdx: null (https://forge.smol.ai/api/repos/swyx/forge), and the root package.json says "private": true. The CLI npm package @smolai/forge is MIT, latest 0.6.0 (https://registry.npmjs.org/@smolai/forge). The source is hosted on SmolForge itself, not GitHub, which explains why github.com/swyx/forge returns 404. Self-hosting means deploying to your own Cloudflare account (Workers, D1, R2, DO); I did not verify a non-Cloudflare self-host path. The repo's API description field currently, and oddly, reads "Clank: a real-time chat platform...", which looks like a stale or mistaken description.
lesson_for_parinn: Do not make a git trailer, or any SHA mentioned in text, the authoritative session-to-code link. SmolForge documents 'AI-Session' trailers, but its server actually joins on an uploaded commit_sha plus heuristic scanning of 40-hex SHAs in message text, filtered by commit timestamps. It then stores mutable per-commit message ranges that must be "reindexed" when commits stop resolving after rebase or GC. ParleyInn should keep the link inside its own hash-chained record: an event that names the commit SHA, the tree hash and the event-range hash at commit time, captured locally by a hook. ParleyInn can write a trailer only as an optional, derivable pointer, so linkage survives rebases and stays rebuildable from the record (I10). Two more lessons from this design. Whole-session uploads with regex masking applied at both write and read time, plus an after-the-fact 'remask' that rewrites stored rows, are incompatible with an append-only log. ParleyInn should redact before append and record each redaction as an audited event (I6). And public, unauthenticated transcript reads with no injection envelope are the anti-pattern I2 exists to prevent.

name: Sniffly
category: analytics reader (read-only dashboard over Claude Code JSONL transcripts, with an optional cloud share/gallery)
status: shipped, but dormant. The latest PyPI release is 0.1.5. The last commit on main is dated 2025-08-08 and only added the LICENSE file; the last functional release was 2025-07-27. The repo is not archived and shows about 1.3k stars, 119 forks, 7 open issues and 4 open PRs (GitHub page, fetched 2026-10-02). I saw no activity in roughly 14 months, so treat it as unmaintained but not officially abandoned.
what_is_stored: Sniffly stores no history of its own. It reads Claude Code's own session transcripts (*.jsonl under ~/.claude/projects/<cwd with / replaced by ->/) and derives three things from them. (1) A persisted disk cache per project: metadata.json (a "checksum" of size+mtime for each JSONL file, plus cached_at), stats.json (aggregates such as tokens, cost, tool use, error types, interruption rate and steps per command) and messages.json (the deduplicated message list). (2) An in-memory LRU cache (the L1 cache). (3) A config file at ~/.sniffly/config.json. If the user clicks Share, it also creates a static share document: sanitized statistics, chart configs, optionally the raw text of the user's prompts (user_commands), project_name, version, is_public and created_at. It may also add a public gallery index entry and a share-creation log line with a SHA-256 IP hash and the user agent.
where_stored: Source data stays in the local filesystem as Claude Code's own JSONL files, which Sniffly only reads. The derived cache is local JSON under ~/.sniffly/cache/<md5(log dir path)>/. Shares go to the cloud: the local client POSTs to https://sniffly.dev/api/shares, a Cloudflare Pages Function that writes shares/<id>.json, gallery-index.json and share-logs/<date>.jsonl into a Cloudflare R2 bucket. Git is not used anywhere.
format_and_model: Input is Claude Code JSONL. Each record is parsed into a normalized dict with fields such as type, timestamp, session_id, cwd, uuid, parent_uuid, leaf_uuid, message_id (assistant messages), tool uses and token usage. Compact summaries are a separate type. Processing has four steps: load all files, merge streaming fragments that share message.id, combine tool uses deduplicated by tool id, then deduplicate across sessions. The cross-session key is type:timestamp:content-preview:uuid and deliberately leaves out session_id, because resumed or continued conversations copy earlier messages into the new file. Output is plain JSON aggregates. There is no schema versioning beyond the package version, no hashing or chaining, and no event log of its own.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not applicable for local data: there is a single reader, and Claude Code is the only writer. The one "merge" problem it solves is the duplication inside Claude Code's own logs (streaming fragments and resumed sessions that re-emit history), handled by the content-key dedup above. Shares are write-once objects keyed by a random id. The gallery index and daily share log are updated server-side by read-modify-write of a single R2 object, with no locking or conditional put. Concurrent shares can therefore lose gallery or log entries (my inference from the code). I found nothing that merges data across machines or users.
realtime: No live streaming or file watching. The dashboard calls POST /api/refresh, which compares size+mtime of every JSONL file against metadata.json and re-processes only on a change. The repo documents about 5 ms for a no-change refresh and under 500 ms for the initial overview load (repo-structure.md). A cache warmer pre-processes the N most recent projects at startup (default 3). Shares are static snapshots and never update.
search_retrieval: Only the browser filters, over messages already loaded: a substring search box (lower-cased includes, debounced 300 ms) plus filters by message type, error/non-error and tool. Initially 500 messages load (messages_initial_load), and the date-range picker caps at 30 days by default. There is no index, no full-text engine, no semantic search and no API for an agent to recall history. It is a human-facing viewer only.
links_sessions_to_code: No link to code. It groups sessions by the project directory, decoded from the ~/.claude/projects folder name, and parses cwd. It does not use the gitBranch field, commits, diffs or file hashes: no reference to git or subprocess anywhere in the sniffly/ package. Prompts are linked to the assistant steps and tool calls that follow them (the "command walkthrough", steps per command), not to code changes.
scale: Claims in the test suite: more than 10,000 messages/s for normal processing and more than 15,000 messages/s for stats extraction, with 25,000–27,000 messages/s "typically" observed (tests/sniffly/test_performance.py docstring). Memory is bounded by cache_max_projects=5 and cache_max_mb_per_project=500 by default. It is a single-user, single-machine tool. I found no independent benchmark.
privacy_security: The README says "All data processing happens locally", "No telemetry", "Your conversations never leave your computer" and "Shared dashboards are opt-in only". The server binds to 127.0.0.1:8081 by default. There is no redaction of secrets or PII anywhere: grep finds no redaction logic, and the only "sanitization" before sharing is dropping overview.log_directory (the full path). With "Include Commands" checked, the raw text of the user's prompts goes to sniffly.dev in the clear, so pasted API keys or secrets are uploaded too. "Private" shares are only security-by-obscurity: share_id = str(uuid4())[:24], about 88 bits of randomness. Public shares go into a public gallery index. The upload endpoint has no authentication. Nothing is encrypted at rest beyond whatever R2 provides; the local cache is plaintext JSON. Share-creation logs keep an unsalted SHA-256 of the client IP plus the user agent. An unsalted IPv4 hash can be brute-forced, so that is pseudonymization, not anonymization (my assessment). The share viewer escapes prompt text with escapeHtml before using innerHTML for command rows and modals. I did not audit every innerHTML sink. The client code ships with a hard-coded developer path (/Users/chip/...) as the default for local fake-R2 storage, and with share_enabled=true by default.
license: MIT (LICENSE file, Copyright (c) 2025 Chip Huyen; added in commit a237d7e on 2025-08-08)
lesson_for_parinn: Claude Code's own JSONL is not an append-only, duplicate-free record. Streaming writes several entries per message.id, and resumed or continued sessions copy prior messages into new session files. Any reader, Sniffly included, must therefore dedup across sessions by content. Sniffly's key, type:timestamp:content-preview:uuid with session_id deliberately excluded, is a useful test oracle for that. ParleyInn should record each event once, under a stable identity (message.id/uuid plus a content hash), at capture time. Its hash chain should cover canonical events, not raw transcript lines, so that a resumed session does not fork or double-count history. The second lesson is a cautionary one: Sniffly's single "share" button turns a local-only tool into a network uploader of raw prompts. It has no redaction, the links are unauthenticated and "private" only by being hard to guess, and the gallery is updated by read-modify-write without locks. ParleyInn's own rules already point the right way here: no network in the core (I4), an audit entry for every redaction (I6), and any sharing done as an explicit, separate, redacting export, never as a default-on feature of the reader.
confidence: high. I read the source directly from a git clone of main at a237d7e. Star, fork and issue counts come from a GitHub page fetch; the unauthenticated GitHub API was blocked here, so those counts could not be cross-checked. The R2 race and the IP-hash brute-force risk are my inferences from the code, not documented behaviour.

name: Soft Serve (charmbracelet/soft-serve)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Plain git repositories (bare repos, one per repo, nested names allowed), Git LFS objects and LFS locks, plus server metadata: users, SSH public keys, repos (public/private, owner), collaborators with access levels, HTTP access tokens, settings (e.g. anon-access), webhooks and webhook delivery records (request/response headers, status and body). It stores no agent sessions, prompts or chat; anything ParleyInn-like would be ordinary git objects pushed to it. Sources: README feature list (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve), schema migration 0001 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/pkg/db/migrate/0001_create_tables_sqlite.up.sql), 0002_webhooks migration (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/tree/main/pkg/db/migrate), webhook delivery persistence (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/pkg/webhook/webhook.go).
where_stored: On the server's own filesystem, in a data directory. Bare repos live under repos/<name>.git with generated hooks (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/pkg/hooks/gen.go). The same directory holds SSH host keys, LFS data, config.yaml and a hooks dir (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/README.md). Metadata goes in SQLite (soft-serve.db, the default) or PostgreSQL, set by db.driver / db.data_source (README). It is a self-hosted single binary ('soft'), installed with `go install github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/cmd/soft@latest` (README).
format_and_model: Repository content uses the standard git object/ref model (loose objects and packfiles, refs), served over SSH, smart HTTP and git:// daemon. Git LFS works over both HTTP and SSH transfer with no extra setup (README). Relational metadata covers the tables settings, users, public_keys, repos, collabs, lfs_objects, lfs_locks and access_tokens, with webhooks and webhook_deliveries added in migration 0002 (migrations listed above). Access has four levels: no-access, read-only, read-write and admin-access. Anonymous access defaults to read-only for public repos (README). The Go module is github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve on Go 1.26.5. It depends on go-git v5 and aymanbagabas/git-module, charm.land/ssh and wish/v2, modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go) and lib/pq (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/go.mod). Important: the pack protocol itself is not handled in-process. pkg/git/service.go runs `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git")` with upload-pack/receive-pack and inherits os.Environ(), so the system git binary is a runtime dependency (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/pkg/git/service.go). The code is split into pkg/ packages (access, backend, config, cron, daemon, db, git, hooks, jobs, lfs, ssh, ssrf, store, sync, web, webhook...) (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/tree/main/pkg). These can be imported as Go packages, but no stable embedding API is documented. I found no README text on embedding, so that is unverified.
multi_writer_and_merge: Writes follow plain git semantics. Many users or keys can push. Concurrent pushes to one ref are serialized by git receive-pack's ref locking, and a non-fast-forward push is rejected unless forced. The server does no merging. Repos are created on demand when a user with write permission pushes to a name that does not exist (README). Collaborators are added per repo with an access level (README). Server-side hooks pre-receive, update, post-update and post-receive run globally and per repo. Each repo hook is a dispatcher that pipes stdin to every executable in <hook>.d/ and fails on the first non-zero exit, and a 'soft-serve' entry calls `soft hook <name>` (gen.go). An operator can therefore drop in a pre-receive/update script that enforces append-only refs, for example by rejecting deletions or non-fast-forward updates, or by validating a hash chain. Soft Serve does not ship such a policy itself, and I could not verify built-in branch protection. Repos can also be pull-mirrored from remote sources (README).
realtime: There is no real-time sync or push channel to git clients, so clients must fetch or poll. Outbound notification comes through repository webhooks for push, collaborator and branch/tag create/delete events (README). They are sent as JSON or form-encoded, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in X-SoftServe-Signature, and carry X-SoftServe-Event and X-SoftServe-Delivery (UUID) headers. Delivery is synchronous via secureHTTPClient.Do with no retry logic visible: failures are logged and recorded but not re-sent (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/main/pkg/webhook/webhook.go). post-receive hooks are the other local trigger. Mirror syncs run as scheduled jobs (pkg/cron, pkg/jobs exist per the pkg tree), but I did not verify the exact interval.
search_retrieval: Retrieval is limited to browsing. An SSH-accessible TUI and SSH commands browse repos, files and commits, and can print files with optional syntax highlighting and line numbers (README). There is no full-text or code search, and no indexing beyond git itself. Clients fetch history with normal git clone/fetch, including partial-clone filters (service.go sets uploadpack.allowFilter=true).
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. Soft Serve has no notion of agent sessions, prompts or AI provenance. Any link between sessions and code would have to be encoded by the client, for example as commits, notes or custom refs in the pushed repo.
privacy_security:
Authentication uses SSH public keys and HTTP user access tokens. The initial admin comes from SOFT_SERVE_INITIAL_ADMIN_KEYS, repos are public or private, and anonymous access can be allowed or disallowed (README). The README notes that new SHA-2 RSA keys are not supported, only old SHA-1 RSA ones. There is no encryption at rest, no redaction and no secret scanning: repo data, LFS objects and DB rows are stored in plaintext on the server (the README and schema show no such feature). The SSRF guard (pkg/ssrf) covers repo import, mirror and LFS endpoints, and webhooks go through a 'secureHTTPClient'. 2026 brought a heavy run of advisories (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/security/advisories):
- Critical authentication bypass, GHSA-pchf-49fh-w34r, Jan 21 2026.
- SSRF via the LFS endpoint in import, GHSA-3fvx-xrxq-8jvv, Mar 5 2026.
- Import cloning another user's private server-local repo, GHSA-xgxp-f695-6vrp, patched in v0.11.6 on Mar 19 2026 (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/security/advisories/GHSA-xgxp-f695-6vrp).
- Critical CVSS 9.9 flaw: any SSH-key user can become global admin, and collaborators can read webhook deliveries and HMAC signatures across repos. Affects v0.11.6 and earlier, fixed in v0.12.0 (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/security/advisories/GHSA-952g-9vq9-782q).
- A vulnerable x/crypto/ssh path, an IPv6-transition SSRF bypass and a cross-repo LFS lock metadata leak, all July-August 2026.
- HTTP LFS write-check bypass via ?service=git-upload-pack, fixed in v0.12.1 (Aug 4 2026).
- LFS object-ID path traversal (`../../../../etc/passwd`), fixed in v0.12.2 (Aug 7 2026), the latest release seen (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/releases).
The server also execs the system git with the inherited environment (service.go).
scale: The project makes no scale or performance claims, and I found none in the README. The design is a single process with SQLite by default and PostgreSQL optional. I found no documented clustering, HA or replication beyond pull mirrors. Adoption signal: about 7.2k stars, 245 forks and ~1,047 commits on the repo page, as read in Oct 2026 (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve).
lesson_for_parinn: Treat any git server, Soft Serve included, as an untrusted, dumb byte transport and never as the integrity or confidentiality boundary. In 2026 alone, Soft Serve shipped two critical authorization flaws (an auth bypass and any-key-to-global-admin escalation), a private-repo import leak and an LFS path traversal. So ParleyInn's sync daemon, a separate binary outside the no-network core and able to use os/exec (Soft Serve itself shells out to `git`), should push only client-side encrypted, hash-chained, signed segments. Clients verify the chain on fetch and reject forks. Server hooks can enforce append-only refs: a pre-receive/update script in Soft Serve's <hook>.d/ dispatcher that rejects ref deletion and non-fast-forward updates. That is defence in depth, not the guarantee. Because webhooks are synchronous and never retried, real-time sharing still needs a fetch-by-cursor catch-up path, with webhooks or post-receive used only as a wake-up hint.
license: MIT (https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve)

name: Sourcegraph Agentic Batch Changes (ABC)
category: Code-intelligence platform agent (server-side orchestrator that turns a described change into PRs/MRs across many repos, built on Sourcegraph Batch Changes + Deep Search)
status: shipped. Beta announced 2026-06-29 (Cloud; self-hosted with 7.5 on 2026-07-08; free during beta) per https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/agentic-batch-changes-beta. GA on 2026-09-14 per https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga, which also says self-hosted would follow with 8.0. The releases page lists self-hosted 8.0.0 on 2026-09-17 (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/releases). The public docs repo shows the history: first docs on 2026-06-30 (commit df30816), and the Beta callout was removed in the 'prepare ... for GA' commit ab14b15 on 2026-09-14 (https://github.com/sourcegraph/docs). The feature is on by default in site config (`batchChanges.agenticBatchChanges.enabled`), but it needs a Batch Changes license that includes 'AI Terms 2025' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/config/site-config).
what_is_stored:
All of this sits on the Sourcegraph instance.
(1) The agent conversation ('thread'): user messages, agent turns and tool results. Users with Agent Read can view it, and so can anyone on the instance who has the share link (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration). Long threads get compacted: oversized tool results are cut short with a note, and if a conversation still does not fit, the message fails and can be retried (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga). Claude Opus 5.5 runs both the agent and 'ABC compaction' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/ai/models). The docs do not say whether the full transcript is kept after compaction.
(2) The Plan: the repos in scope, what changes in each, a canary repo, and the branch, title and commit message for each changeset (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes). The agent turns it into a Batch Changes batch spec ('prepare_batch_spec'; 'no batch spec written by hand') (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga).
(3) Workspaces, one per repo or path, with cached results for each step and the step logs. Inner-loop Claude Code/Codex agents emit JSON event streams that are shown in readable form, and logs are kept for cached steps (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-07-13#inner-loop-agent-outputs).
(4) Changeset state, checks and activity, plus 'hook runs, attempt budgets, per-step logs, and commits pushed by hooks' (Automations tab). This includes CI logs fetched by hook steps (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga).
(5) Guidance (AGENTS.md-style text, cut off at 32 KiB) and skills, set at site, org or user level or loaded from a configured repo branch.
(6) User and global secrets.
(7) Container images the agent builds, which are 'hosted directly in Sourcegraph'.
(8) Audit log events under the `batchChangeAgents` entity.
(9) Topic keywords an LLM extracts from each batch spec, kept for telemetry (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/telemetry/private-metadata-allowlist).
The client tool src-cli also exposes 'workflow instance variables', with examples named prompt, checkpoints and approval, through the GraphQL mutation `updateAgenticWorkflowInstanceVariables` (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/cli/references/abc; src-cli cmd/src/abc_variables_set.go at https://github.com/sourcegraph/src-cli).
No retention policy for conversations is documented. The only related setting found is `batchChanges.changesetsRetention`, which covers detached changesets (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/config/site-config).
where_stored:
On a server: the customer's Sourcegraph instance, either Sourcegraph Cloud or self-hosted. The architecture doc puts Batch Changes state (batch specs, changeset specs, changesets) in the instance's Postgres 'frontend-db' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/architecture). Hook events go through a Postgres-backed worker queue; this is inferred from the metric domain `changeset_hook_event_jobs_worker_store` (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/self-hosted/observability/alerts). The docs never say outright which table or store holds the agent conversation, so 'instance Postgres' is an inference.
All code-changing work runs in short-lived, isolated containers on executors, one per repository, pulled from the `batches` and `batches-hooks` queues (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/self-hosted/executors/executors-config).
Git holds only the outputs: branches, commits and PRs/MRs on the code host, each carrying a backlink to the conversation. Guidance and skills can optionally be read from a git repo branch and are reloaded on every message (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration). Session history is never written to git.
format_and_model:
The model is declarative desired state, in the style of Kubernetes. A batch spec in YAML (`on`/search scope, `steps`, `changesetTemplate`) is expanded into ChangesetSpecs. The Batch Changes controller then reconciles them against the actual changesets on code hosts (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/batch-changes/design). ABC adds three step types (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration):
- 'coding agent steps' (Claude Code or Codex; Codex is the default)
- 'changeset hooks' that run on CI-failure or merge-conflict events
- buildImage steps
Each step runs in a container image. Changing an execution step invalidates the cache for that step and every later step, while edits to titles, descriptions or hooks reuse the cached results. Changesets are keyed by (repository, branch), so changing the branch creates a new changeset and closes or detaches the old one (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/writing-prompts).
The API is GraphQL. Object IDs are Relay-style; for example, base64 of 'AgenticWorkflowInstance:1'. Variable values are read as JSON literals when they parse, and as strings otherwise (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/cli/references/abc).
The conversation schema is not documented. Nothing is described as append-only or hash-chained. The plan can change at any time, including after publishing, though the agent 'prefers additions over edits to existing steps, so finished work stays valid' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/writing-prompts).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is one writer per session. Each agentic batch change has exactly one owner, and 'only the owner can send messages, approve actions, and publish'. Other users get read-only access through a shared read link. 'There is no co-ownership and no transfer'; if the owner is unavailable, someone starts a new agentic batch change (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration). Rotating the share token keeps the Plan state (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga).
Inside one session, workspaces run in parallel on executors. Changesets are matched by repo+branch. The published-changesets entitlement is 'reserved atomically per changeset' so that bulk or concurrent publishes cannot overrun it (GA changelog, same URL).
Conflicts with other writers happen on the code host. They are handled by an optional merge-conflict hook that hands the work to a coding agent (for example, to rebase). The agent cannot merge; a human merges on the host or with Sourcegraph's Merge button (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes).
Configuration is layered: guidance from site, then org, then user. Skills are combined by name (case-insensitive), and the last one loaded wins (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration).
Threads can reference other ABC threads and Deep Search conversations with @@ mentions (GA changelog). This is a reference, not shared writing.
There is no replication or sync between machines or instances.
realtime:
Within one instance, updates are near real time, but there is no collaborative sync:
- Execution logs stream live in the UI, and inner-loop coding-agent 'thinking and progress' streams in real time (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-07-13#inner-loop-agent-outputs).
- The web UI polls for other updates, at different intervals for 'active chat' and 'chat awaiting user input' (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga).
- CI-failure and merge-conflict signals arrive from the code host and trigger changeset hooks on the `batches-hooks` executor queue. Without an executor on that queue, hooks 'never run' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/self-hosted/executors/executors-config).
- The agents list puts agents waiting on input first. Users can ask 'what happened while I was away?' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes).
search_retrieval:
Before planning, the agent researches with Deep Search: one focused request, reading exact files directly, and reusing a Deep Search the user links (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration). Other ways in:
- @@ mentions of other ABC threads and of Deep Search conversations
- workspace and changeset filters and sorting, kept in the URL so shared links show the same view
- a changeset inspector with an Activity tab and an Automations tab (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga)
- the GraphQL API and the audit log
Full-text or semantic search across past agent transcripts is not documented. Deep Search, a separate product, returns a source list and can export a conversation to PDF as an audit trail. That is not documented for ABC threads (https://sourcegraph.com/blog/compliance-first-ai-proving-agent-provenance).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, explicitly and by default. Under `batchChanges.attributionMode` = `bodyAndTrailer` (the default), Sourcegraph appends a link to the originating batch change or agent conversation to the PR/MR description. It also adds a `Sourcegraph-Batch-Change` trailer to the commit message. `trailerOnly` drops the description link to cut down on notification noise, but 'the commit trailer always contains a link to the classic batch change or agent conversation that created the changeset'. An explicit `${{ batch_change_link }}` in a template is always honored (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/config/batch-changes; documented 2026-09-24 in sourcegraph/docs commit 8764324; https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration).
On the instance, each changeset also ties back to its workspace, step logs, hook runs and commits pushed by hooks (GA changelog). The link is a URL to an access-controlled server page. It is not a content hash.
scale:
Vendor claims:
- Classic Batch Changes: the largest single batch change merged more than 2,200 changesets, and customers have merged 'hundreds of thousands of changesets, tens of millions of lines' (https://sourcegraph.com/blog/introducing-agentic-batch-changes).
- Server-side execution 'has been tested to run a simple 45K changeset batch change' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/batch-changes/server-side).
- The design target is '10,000s of repositories' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/batch-changes/design).
- ABC beta: 'over a thousand' merged changesets per the GA changelog, but 'nearly a thousand' per the launch blog, so the sources disagree.
- Beta examples: about 80 repos scoped for a GitHub Actions vulnerability (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-09-14#agentic-batch-changes-ga), and Canva merging 50+ PRs (https://sourcegraph.com/blog/agentic-batch-changes-pricing).
- One outer-loop thread often made '500 changes ... zero inner-loop coding agents' (https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/2026-07-13#inner-loop-agent-outputs).
Limits: guidance is cut off at 32 KiB, and executor jobs default to a 30-minute maximum runtime (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/self-hosted/executors/executors-config). No figures are published for transcript or storage size.
privacy_security:
The agent acts as its owner. It reads with the owner's repository permissions and publishes with the owner's or a global Batch Changes credential. Branch protection and required checks still apply (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/configuration).
Secrets:
- A step refers to a secret by name. The value is injected at run time and 'redacts it from logs; the value never appears in the plan, in the conversation, or in anything the agent reads'.
- The agent never asks the user to paste a secret.
- A new or changed step that uses a secret needs explicit approval, scoped to this run, this agent, or all agents.
- Org-level secrets cannot be used.
- Executor secrets are 'encrypted if encryption is on, and always redacted in log outputs' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/executors/executor-secrets).
Encryption: column-level `encryption.keys` covers external services, user accounts, credentials and webhook logs. No key is documented for agent conversations (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/self-hosted/encryption).
Isolation: one container per repo on executors. A container sees only its repo and the secrets its steps name, and it cannot publish. Firecracker microVMs are optional; Docker and Kubernetes give weaker isolation (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/executors).
Network and images: web search is ON by default. Disabling it 'does not block outbound network access from executor containers'. Container registries can be allow-listed or deny-listed.
Audit log: `batchChangeAgents` events carry identifiers only, with 'no URLs, links, or tokens'.
Access: RBAC uses the Agent Read/Write permission pairs (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/access-control/batch-changes). The share link lets any user on the instance read the conversation.
Weak points:
- Pauses between rollout stages 'are part of the agent's instructions, not a server-enforced approval gate' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/agentic-batch-changes/writing-prompts).
- No defense is documented against prompt injection from repository content, CI logs or web results.
- Coding-agent steps get full MCP access under the user's identity.
- LLM traffic goes through the Sourcegraph Model Provider.
lesson_for_parinn:
Let git carry a pointer to the session, and keep the session itself out of git. ABC never puts the transcript in git. Instead, every commit it makes carries a `Sourcegraph-Batch-Change` trailer that links back to the conversation, and that trailer stays even when the PR-body link is turned off (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/config/batch-changes). ParleyInn can do the same without using the network. While a session is active, it can stamp commits with a trailer such as `ParleyInn-Session: <session-id>@<chain-head-hash>`. Any clone, worktree, fork or sandbox then links code to its exact place in the record. Unlike a URL, the hash can be checked against the append-only chain. And because only the hash moves through GitHub or Forgejo, no untrusted transcript text travels with the code (I2, I4).
ABC also shows the opposite case: its staged rollout pauses are only agent instructions, while secret-using steps are held for approval by the server. ParleyInn's gates, such as enveloped pull-only recall and restoring only `TrustedText`, should be enforced in code like the latter, never left to the prompt.
sources: https://github.com/sourcegraph/docs (git history of docs/agentic-batch-changes: df30816 2026-06-30, ab14b15 2026-09-14, 8764324 2026-09-24)
confidence: high for the documented behaviour, which comes from official docs, the changelog and the public docs-repo history. Medium for the storage internals: that the conversation lives in instance Postgres is inferred from the architecture doc and metric names, and the transcript schema and retention are undocumented. A search for independent technical discussion turned up only Sourcegraph job posts on HN (hn.algolia.com search).
license: Proprietary and commercial. It needs a Sourcegraph license that includes Batch Changes and 'AI Terms 2025' (https://sourcegraph.com/docs/admin/config/site-config). Pricing is by outcome, in credits per merged changeset; it was free during the beta (https://sourcegraph.com/blog/agentic-batch-changes-pricing). The src-cli client is Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/sourcegraph/src-cli). I could not check from here whether the server source is public, because the proxy blocked github.com pages.

name: Sourcegraph Deep Search
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Conversation threads (user questions and AI-generated answers), detailed search sources (search types performed, files read), generated analysis artifacts (CSV, JSON, SVG), and conversation metadata. Intermediate search results are processed in an isolated sandbox and not persisted separately.
where_stored: Conversations and metadata stored in Sourcegraph instance database (self-hosted or Sourcegraph Cloud). Generated artifacts (CSV, JSON, SVG files) stored in object storage (S3-compatible). Only external calls made to configured LLM provider (Sourcegraph Model Provider).
