format_and_model: REST API using gRPC-style resource naming (users/~self/conversations/{id}); JSON request/response format. Models: Sourcegraph Model Provider with Anthropic Claude and OpenAI LLMs selected by Sourcegraph. Responses streamed via Server-Sent Events (SSE) up to 5 minutes per request.
multi_writer_and_merge: Not documented. Each conversation belongs to a single user (users/~self context). Conversations are read-only after creation; follow-up questions extend the thread. No multi-writer collaboration model or merge strategy documented. Conversations can be shared by URL but sharing bypasses repository permission checks.
realtime: Real-time streaming via Server-Sent Events (SSE). Responses progress through agent iterations and stream incrementally as the agent works. Single request can remain open up to 5 minutes. Network timeout on reverse proxies must be >= 5 minutes or responses are cut off.
search_retrieval: Deep Search is a built-in agentic loop that uses Sourcegraph Code Search and Code Navigation as tools. Every response includes detailed sources showing exactly which searches were executed and which files were read. Agent iteratively refines understanding through repeated searches. Answers formatted in Markdown with links to relevant code locations.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes. Every Deep Search answer includes comprehensive source attribution listing specific searches, file paths, and line numbers contributing to each answer. User can trace answer provenance through listed sources and execute follow-up questions mentioning specific sources.
privacy_security: Conversations shared by URL do not enforce repository permissions - any instance user can view shared conversations regardless of code host access. Generated artifacts stored in object storage with metadata in conversation. Deep Search runs Lua scripts in a sandbox with no network, no filesystem, and read-only repository access using Sourcegraph APIs. All LLM calls routed through Sourcegraph Model Provider (enterprise-grade privacy model). Repo permissions checked at search time but not enforced on conversation retrieval.
lesson_for_parinn: Deep Search separates conversation storage from access control, which creates a security gap when conversations are shared - the shared URL does not check repository permissions at retrieval time. ParleyInn should ensure that session recalls are enveloped and always checked against current permissions at recall time, not just at storage time. Additionally, Deep Search's model of storing comprehensive sources for each answer (exact searches, file reads) without leaking raw search data to the LLM mirrors ParleyInn's approach of treating recalled history as untrusted unless specifically marked as TrustedText. The sandbox pattern for intermediate operations (Lua scripts that run searches but only return aggregated results to the LLM) is a useful pattern for ParleyInn's own sandboxing of transcript derivations.

name: Spec Kit (GitHub)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Specifications (feature descriptions in Markdown), implementation plans, task lists, and project metadata. Specs are organized by feature in a feature directory structure (e.g., specs/001-feature-name/). Core metadata stored in .specify/ directory includes: feature.json (active feature pointer), integration configuration, extension catalogs, constitution (project governance), and shared scripts/templates. Bug assessments stored in .specify/bugs/{slug}/, idea assessments in .specify/assessments/{slug}/, and memory artifacts in .specify/memory/. All artifacts are Markdown or YAML files.
where_stored: Working tree files in the project repository. Specifications live in feature directories (typically specs/{number}-{feature-slug}/) checked into version control alongside code. Configuration and metadata in .specify/ directory. Managed by Git (optional git extension adds feature branch automation with sequential/timestamp numbering). No separate server or cloud storage required—all files are versioned with code in the same repository. Git serves as the transport and versioning mechanism.
format_and_model: Markdown (primary) for all specifications, plans, tasks, constitutions, and artifacts. YAML for configuration files (.specify/extensions.yml, .specify/integration.json, .specify/feature.json). Python-based Specify CLI with template-driven generation. Data model: each feature is a directory containing spec.md (requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria), plan.md (technical architecture, implementation details), tasks.md (enumerated implementation tasks with dependencies and owners). Extensions provide bug.md (assessment cause, reproduction, fix scope, verification) and assessment artifacts (intake, research, define, shape, decide). Templates are Markdown with structured sections and front-matter.
multi_writer_and_merge: Native Git merge support. Multiple team members work on different feature branches (e.g., 001-feature-a, 002-feature-b). Branch numbering (sequential or timestamp) prevents collisions. Git handles merge conflicts when the same spec/plan/task is edited concurrently. Feature.json tracks active feature per developer/environment, allowing isolated work. No built-in locking or explicit multi-writer coordination—relies on Git's merge conflict resolution. Extensions can hook into before/after specification, planning, and implementation phases to orchestrate team workflows. No mention of operational transformation or CRDT-style conflict resolution; standard merge conflict markers apply.
realtime: No real-time collaboration. Synchronous multi-agent coordination happens through workflows (orchestration of commands with step sequencing) and hooks (before/after lifecycle events). Agents can invoke commands sequentially, write to shared specs, plan, and tasks artifacts, commit changes, and push branches. No live document synchronization, change streams, or awareness of concurrent edits. Updates are discrete commits pushed to Git repository. Extensions can implement polling/webhook patterns but toolkit itself provides no real-time sync mechanism. Each phase (specify → plan → tasks → implement → converge) is agent-driven, not concurrent.
search_retrieval: No built-in full-text search. Specs are discovered by feature directory structure and .specify/feature.json pointer. Commands resolve features from the active feature directory or explicit SPECIFY_FEATURE_DIRECTORY environment variable. Specifications are plain Markdown files, searchable via grep or IDE search. Task dependencies expressed in tasks.md as structured text (task references like T001, T002 with dependency syntax). GitHub extension can search existing issues when syncing tasks to GitHub. Catalog system allows discovery of community extensions/presets/workflows but is static, not live-indexed. No semantic search or retrieval-augmented generation integration mentioned.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, strongly linked. Each feature is a directory containing both specifications and implementation guidance. .specify/feature.json tracks the active feature for all agent commands. Implementations are scoped to the feature directory. Git branch names (via git extension) encode feature number and slug, linking version control commits to specifications. /speckit.taskstoissues command (GitHub extension) creates numbered GitHub issues (T001, T002, etc.) from tasks.md, linking specification tasks to issue tracking. Feature branch commits carry semantic meaning tied to the specification. No built-in session recording or transcript storage—the tool coordinates agent workflow through specifications and implementation plans, not through session capture.
privacy_security: Security model: specifications are files in the repository and subject to repository access controls (GitHub permissions for GitHub-hosted repos). No encryption of stored specifications or in-transit communication—security relies on Git repository access controls. Input redaction: assess extension's intake command explicitly mentions redacting secrets (tokens, passwords, API keys, cookies) from captured ideas and sanitizing credential-bearing URLs before persistence. Extension system: extensions can be installed from URLs or catalogs; direct URL installation shows security warning. Workflows with shell steps are flagged as untrusted code execution—users must audit workflow.yml content before installation. No mention of encryption at rest, field-level redaction during spec evolution, or automatic secret scanning. Secrets handling is manual and upstream-focused (don't capture them in the first place).
lesson_for_parinn: Specification-as-source-of-truth architecture: Spec Kit inverts the traditional code-first paradigm by making specifications the primary artifact, with code as derived output. Git as the storage and transport layer works well for team collaboration and version control. Lesson for ParleyInn: a spec-first approach with lightweight Markdown artifacts and Git versioning could complement a session-history storage model. Git's merge conflict resolution is native and well-understood by teams, but it is not designed for append-only history or session transcripts—concurrent writes create conflicts that require human intervention. For ParleyInn's goal of lossless session recording across multiple agents and machines, Git alone would require custom conflict resolution for interleaved agent actions. Spec Kit's feature-branch workflow is explicit and numbered, reducing collision risk, but scales linearly with feature count. The .specify/memory/ directory pattern for governance and constitution shows how to store metadata separately from specs, a useful pattern for session state. Spec Kit's redaction-at-input approach (don't capture secrets) is insufficient for ParleyInn's threat model where untrusted content must be isolated after recall—ParleyInn requires output redaction or encryption of sensitive session content.

name: SpecStory
status: shipped
what_is_stored: AI coding agent session transcripts including conversations, tool calls, reasoning traces, and shell command output captured from VS Code, GitHub Copilot Chat, Cursor, and CLI runs. Each session is a complete conversation history with context and decisions.
where_stored: Local-first: .specstory/history/ directory inside project root as plain-text Markdown files. Project metadata in .specstory/.project.json. Session index in .specstory/.history.json. Optional Cloud storage: uploaded to SpecStory Cloud for centralized search and sharing when authenticated. VS Code also maintains workspace and composer storage state internally.
format_and_model: Plain-text Markdown format. Each session file timestamped (e.g., 2026-01-22_19-20-56Z-fix-bug.md). In Cloud, stored as both Markdown (human-readable) and raw JSON (original conversation data). Markdown structure preserves tool calls, reasoning steps, and shell output. No explicit schema version control documented.
multi_writer_and_merge: Currently single-user per session: each developer syncs their own .specstory/history/ independently. Team collaboration on the roadmap (team workspaces, invitations, role-based access not yet shipped). Git-friendly: Markdown files merge via standard git branch/merge semantics. Multiple developers can commit sessions to same repo but no cross-session coordination or conflict resolution mechanisms documented.
realtime: Autosave enabled by default in VS Code extension: sessions captured continuously as user codes. CLI watch mode can sync automatically. No live real-time collaboration or shared editing; syncs are explicit one-way uploads from local to Cloud for subsequent search and retrieval.
search_retrieval: Cloud-based search available via SpecStory Cloud API after sync. Web interface for searching synced histories across projects. Local search via CLI tools (e.g., specstory-link-trail for URL extraction). No mention of full-text indexing, faceted search, or query language in available documentation.
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, via external tools: SpecStory Link Trail extracts WebFetch URLs from session history. Separate agent skills (commit-context, commit-history) link git commits back to agent sessions using git blame and memory_commit_lookup. No built-in session-to-commit linking; requires additional tooling.
privacy_security: Local-first architecture: no network access until explicit Cloud sync. SpecStory Guard pre-commit hook scans .specstory/history for secret patterns (API keys, tokens, private keys) and blocks commits if found. Anonymous usage analytics (opt-in control via specstory.helpUsImprove setting). No encryption at rest documented; Markdown files stored plaintext. No mention of field-level redaction or selective filtering of sensitive content before capture. Secrets handling is reactive (Guard detects) not preventive (no automatic scrubbing).
lesson_for_parinn: SpecStory demonstrates high user value of committed session transcripts alongside code for traceability and knowledge sharing, but surfaces ParleyInn's core security constraints: (1) transcript files committed to git become permanent (git rm doesn't erase history); (2) secrets leak through multi-writer scenarios and public forks; (3) committed transcripts can become LLM input vectors for injection attacks if not tightly controlled. ParleyInn's I2 (no untrusted content to model), I4 (no network), I6 (audit failures) and I10 (everything rebuildable) suggest storing only TrustedText in transcript records, enforcing pre-commit or build-time secret scanning, never auto-injecting recall into prompts, and maintaining append-only hash-chained record so compromise is detectable.

name: SQLite session extension (changesets / patchsets)
status: shipped. It has been part of the SQLite amalgamation since 3.13.0 (2016-05-18) but is off by default (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html). It is still actively developed. 3.51.0 (2025-11-04) added sqlite3changeset_apply_v3 and generated-column support. 3.53.0 (2026-04-09) added sqlite3changegroup_change_* for building changesets one change at a time. The newest release listed is 3.53.4 (2026-07-24) (https://www.sqlite.org/changes.html). The rebaser API is still marked experimental (https://www.sqlite.org/session/rebaser.html).
what_is_stored:
A changeset holds row-level changes to tables that have a declared PRIMARY KEY. It does not record SQL statements, timestamps, authors or transaction boundaries (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
- While a session is active it records only the primary key of each inserted row, and the primary key plus all original values of each updated or deleted row. When the changeset is extracted, it is built against the database's current contents (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html, https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3session_changeset.html).
- Changesets contain net effects only. A row inserted and then deleted inside one session disappears from the changeset entirely. A row deleted and then re-inserted becomes a single UPDATE (https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3session_changeset.html).
- Changeset contents by operation: an INSERT carries all new values; a DELETE carries all old values; an UPDATE carries the primary key, the new values of modified columns, and the old values of those columns.
- A patchset leaves out the old values. A DELETE carries only the primary key, and an UPDATE carries the primary key plus the new values (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
- Not captured: changes to virtual tables, and rows with a NULL in any primary key column (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
where_stored: Nowhere persistent of its own. While a session runs, its state lives in process memory (sqlite3session_memory_used exists to measure it; https://www.sqlite.org/session/funclist.html). sqlite3session_changeset or sqlite3session_patchset returns the result as an in-memory blob. The application decides where that blob goes: a file, a BLOB column, a git object, removable media. The extension has no network awareness and leaves distribution to the application (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
format_and_model:
A compact binary format that the source-code header documents (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/ext/session/sqlite3session.c, the "CHANGESET FORMAT" comment).
- Changes are grouped by table. Each group starts with a header: 0x54 'T' for a changeset or 0x50 'P' for a patchset, then a varint column count, one PK-flag byte per column, and the NUL-terminated table name.
- Each change is an op byte (INSERT 0x12, UPDATE 0x17, DELETE 0x09), an "indirect" flag byte, then old.* and/or new.* records in SQLite's record encoding. Columns that are unchanged or irrelevant are marked "undefined".
- Columns are matched by position, not by name. A target table is compatible if it has the same name, at least as many columns, and its primary key columns in the same positions. Extra trailing columns are ignored.
- Tables with no compatible match are skipped silently: the only signal is a SQLITE_SCHEMA warning through sqlite3_log, not an error (https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3changeset_apply.html).
- The model is a state diff between two database snapshots (a delta), not an event log.
- Operations: invert, which undoes a changeset (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html); concat and changegroup, which merge several changesets into one; iteration with sqlite3changeset_start/next/op/old/new; sqlite3session_diff, which diffs against an attached database; and _strm streaming variants of most functions (https://www.sqlite.org/session/funclist.html).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Merging means applying a changeset to another database whose starting data is compatible.
- **Atomicity:** sqlite3changeset_apply wraps the whole apply in a savepoint and rolls it back on error, unless SQLITE_CHANGESETAPPLY_NOSAVEPOINT is set (https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3changeset_apply.html).
- **Conflict types reported to the handler:** DATA (current values differ from the recorded old values), NOTFOUND (no row with that primary key), CONFLICT (an INSERT hits an existing primary key), CONSTRAINT and FOREIGN_KEY (same page).
- **Handler choices:** OMIT skips the change, REPLACE overwrites the row, ABORT rolls back everything (https://www.sqlite.org/session/c_changeset_abort.html). The handler may run SQL to implement custom resolution.
- **Patchsets detect fewer conflicts.** Without old values they cannot detect DATA conflicts (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
- **Filtering:** apply_v3 (3.51.0) moves the xFilter callback from once per table to once per change (https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3changeset_apply.html).
- **Rebasing:** apply_v2 can output a "rebase" blob of the OMIT/REPLACE decisions it made. The experimental sqlite3_rebaser then rewrites local changesets so other sites do not have to resolve the same conflicts again (https://www.sqlite.org/session/rebaser.html).
- **What it does not provide:** vector clocks, causal ordering or CRDT semantics. Convergence across more than two writers is the application's job.
realtime: No. Nothing pushes or notifies. Capture runs on the preupdate hook (it needs SQLITE_ENABLE_PREUPDATE_HOOK; https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html). A changeset exists only when the application asks for one, so near-real-time sharing would mean extracting one per transaction and shipping it through a separate transport.
search_retrieval: Not applicable. A changeset can only be walked sequentially with an iterator (sqlite3changeset_start/next/op/pk/old/new; https://www.sqlite.org/session/funclist.html). It has no index and no query support. Search happens in the target database after the apply, for example with FTS5.
links_sessions_to_code: No. This is a generic database-replication primitive. In SQLite, "session" means a change-tracking object, not an agent session. It has no concept of prompts, commits or code.
scale:
The official docs make no throughput or size claims. Two things bear on scale:
- Session memory grows with the number of distinct rows modified, because old values are kept for each one. sqlite3session_memory_used reports it, and the _strm variants exist for changesets too large to handle as one buffer (https://www.sqlite.org/session/funclist.html).
- Coalescing keeps a changeset as small as the net change, however many intermediate writes happened.

Benchmarks: I found none to verify.
privacy_security:
The extension does not redact, encrypt or authenticate anything.
- **No integrity or authentication.** The format has no checksum, MAC or signature: a grep of sqlite3session.c for checksum, crc and hmac found nothing (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sqlite/sqlite/master/ext/session/sqlite3session.c).
- **Untrusted input writes freely.** Applying a changeset writes to whatever compatible table it names, unless the xFilter callback blocks it (https://www.sqlite.org/session/sqlite3changeset_apply.html). An untrusted changeset can therefore modify any table whose name and primary key layout match.
- **Secrets survive redaction in changesets.** For an UPDATE, a changeset carries the original values of the modified columns. A redaction done as an UPDATE therefore ships the secret it removed in old.*. A DELETE carries the whole old row. Patchsets leave old values out (https://www.sqlite.org/sessionintro.html).
- **Encryption** is entirely up to the transport or storage, or an encrypting VFS on each end.
lesson_for_parinn:
Model the record as insert-only rows whose primary key is the event hash. Then a changeset reduces to a list of new rows. Applying it with OMIT on CONFLICT gives an offline, idempotent union merge that needs no network and works by file or sneakernet. That fits I4. Do not trust the format itself, for four reasons:
- It is a state diff, not a log. Coalescing silently drops insert-then-delete history, which conflicts with losslessness.
- It has no integrity or authentication. Wrap it in a signed envelope and re-verify the hash chain after every apply.
- Without a per-change xFilter (apply_v3, 3.51.0+), an imported changeset can write into projection or configuration tables. Allow-list the record tables, and rebuild projections from the record (I10) rather than importing them.
- An UPDATE-based redaction leaks the pre-redaction value in old.*, so never export changesets across a redaction.

Driver availability: zombiezen.com/go/sqlite v1.4.2 exposes Session, Changegroup and ApplyChangeset, but has no Rebaser (https://pkg.go.dev/zombiezen.com/go/sqlite). The pkg.go.dev page for ParleyInn's chosen driver, ncruces/go-sqlite3 v0.35.6, lists no session API (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/ncruces/go-sqlite3). Using this extension would mean a driver change or a custom build, so a ParleyInn-defined export of hash-addressed events is probably simpler and easier to audit.
license: Public domain, like all of SQLite (https://www.sqlite.org/copyright.html). I did not re-fetch that page in this session.

name: Stift (stift-sh/stift)
category: session sync service (file-level backup and restore of agent session directories, plus a skill/config registry)
status: beta. It exists and is actively developed: tags v0.2.0 through v0.4.0, last commit 2026-09-21, a hosted Stift Cloud with Free and Pro tiers, and a low-traction Product Hunt launch (6 upvotes, ranked #151). Correction to the discovery note: since commit 1865648 (2026-08-26, "remove the Go server") the self-hosted server is no longer "a single MIT binary with no database". It is now a TypeScript container that needs Postgres and an S3 bucket. The stift.sh landing page still describes the old pure-Go, no-database design, so it is stale.
what_is_stored: The raw native session files of each agent, copied verbatim. Claude Code: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl plus todo state. Codex: ~/.codex/sessions/.../rollout-*.jsonl. Gemini CLI: ~/.gemini/tmp/<project>/ (logs, chats, checkpoints). Cursor CLI: ~/.cursor/chats/... opencode: session, messages and parts from its storage dir. aider: .aider.chat.history.md. Users can add other agents with glob patterns. Stift also syncs agent config as versioned "units": skills, subagents, slash commands, CLAUDE.md. It never syncs settings*.json, .mcp.json, env files, dotfiles, symlinks or files over 5 MB.
where_stored: Server/cloud. Metadata lives in Postgres. Session archives and skill files are blobs in any S3-compatible bucket (S3, R2, MinIO). Clients keep local state in ~/.config/stift and ~/.cache/stift/sync-state.json. Hosting is either Stift Cloud (app.stift.sh) or self-hosted (ghcr.io/stift-sh/stift plus Postgres and MinIO via docker compose). No git storage is involved.
format_and_model: Each session is one tar.gz archive of the agent's files, stored at <org>/sessions/<id>.tar.gz. A Postgres row holds its metadata: org_id, id, user_id, key, agent, session_id, project, project_id, repo, host, title, base, file count, size, sha256, mod_time and timestamps. The unique key is agent|host|project|session_id, so the same session pushed from two hosts becomes two records. A re-push replaces the archive in place ("updated"), or is a no-op when the sha256 matches ("unchanged"). Sessions have no version history: the server keeps only the latest snapshot per key. Skills and config are different. They are content-addressed blobs (sha256, 5 MB max each) plus versioned JSON manifests with parent pointers and a head counter. The API is described in OpenAPI, with a generated Go client.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Stift never merges.
- Sessions: last writer wins within a key. Because the key includes the host, two machines never overwrite each other's copy. On pull, the client extracts the archive but never overwrites an existing local file without --force. Files that already exist are skipped and the conflict is logged, not applied.
- Skills: optimistic concurrency. Each push names the parent version it last synced. A push on top of an unseen version is rejected as stale (409); the user must pull first or pass --force. A unit changed on both sides is logged and left alone, and the daemon never forces.
- Multi-user: one org per server, with admin and member roles. Members may write project-scope and their own user-scope units; only admins write org scope. With JWT auth, multi-org is optional.
realtime: Near-real-time polling, not streaming. A per-user systemd or launchd daemon (or a detached process) runs every ~30s (STIFT_SYNC_INTERVAL). Each run pushes every changed session across all projects and pulls sessions for projects linked on that machine. Skills are pushed only after 2 minutes unchanged (STIFT_SKILLS_DEBOUNCE). Stift has no push notifications, websockets or event log.
search_retrieval: Metadata filtering only. GET /v1/sessions takes agent, project, host and q, where q is a case-insensitive LIKE over title, project and session_id. Stift never searches conversation content and offers no full-text or semantic search. Retrieval means downloading the whole tar.gz (HTTP Range is supported) and restoring it to the original project path, so the native agent can resume it. A web UI lists sessions and offers archive download. The public skill registry has its own name search.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, at project level only. Projects are matched across machines by git repo name: the last path segment of the remote, or the folder name when there is no remote. The project_id and repo fields are stored per session. Stift records no commit SHAs, branches, worktree state or per-prompt links to diffs. Sessions are restored verbatim to the same path, with no cross-machine path remapping; a log line says so.
scale:
No published scale claims or benchmarks. Hard limits:
- blobs up to 5 MB
- blob existence checks up to 10k shas per call
- a maximum upload size on archives
Admins can cap sessions, skills, storage and seats with STIFT_MAX_*. Cloud Free allows up to 100 sessions; Cloud Pro costs $4 per seat per month for unlimited sessions (pricing from the stift.sh landing page).
privacy_security: Minimal. On the server, API tokens (stf_ prefix) are stored SHA-256 hashed and shown once. The server speaks plain HTTP and the docs say to put TLS in front with a reverse proxy. Stift does no client-side or end-to-end encryption and does no redaction or secret scrubbing of transcripts. The README warns that archives "often include source code and may include secrets your agent saw", so users must protect the database and bucket themselves. The only secret hygiene is excluding settings*.json, .mcp.json, env files and dotfiles from config sync; session transcripts are uploaded as-is. Tar extraction rejects absolute paths and '..' traversal. The install script checks SHA-256 checksums but has no signature verification. The skill registry routes are unauthenticated by design and not rate-limited. Restored transcripts go straight back into the agent's native history, where the agent can resume and read them. Stift treats none of that content as untrusted.
lesson_for_parinn: Two things are worth copying: per-host keys, so writers never overwrite each other's copy, and never overwriting a live local file on restore, with the conflict logged instead. Two things to avoid. First, the server overwrites the whole tar.gz snapshot on each push and keeps no history or hash chain, so a corrupted or tampered push silently replaces the good copy. Second, it uploads unredacted transcripts in plaintext to a server, which is the exposure ParleyInn's I2/I4/I6 rule out. ParleyInn should carry the same per-agent native-path adapters and the git-remote project identity, but over an append-only, hash-chained event log. ParleyInn's core would only produce or consume that log; a separate opt-in transport would move it, already redacted and encrypted. That way sync stays a dumb, auditable replication of records, not a rewrite of state.
license: MIT (LICENSE: Copyright (c) 2026 Stift Authors). Stift Cloud is a paid hosted service.
confidence: high for the storage, sync and security behaviour, which I read from the cloned repo source and README at commit 60c77c1 (2026-09-21). Medium for the pricing and Cloud tiers, which come only from the stift.sh landing page; that page is stale on the architecture, so its other claims may be stale too. I could not verify GitHub stars or adoption numbers because the API was blocked from this session.

name: sudocode (sudocode-ai/sudocode)
category: git-native agent orchestration / issue tracking ("context-as-code" spec and issue graph, plus a local execution server)
status: shipped. npm `sudocode` latest is 1.2.0 (dist-tag dev 1.1.18-dev.0), and the registry's last-modified time is 2026-03-18 (https://registry.npmjs.org/sudocode). The newest commit on the default branch is 632de19, dated 2026-03-18 (shallow clone of https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode). That is about 6.5 months with no commits as of 2026-10-02, so the project looks dormant rather than active, and the discovery note's "Active" is likely stale. I could not check whether the repo is archived: the GitHub API was unreachable from this session.
what_is_stored:
Specs and issues are shared through git. Specs hold human intent: requirements and design. Issues hold agent tasks and plans. Each entity carries id, uuid, title, Markdown content, priority/status, parent, archived flags, timestamps, tags and typed relationships (blocks, related, parent-child, discovered-from, implements). Issues also embed a `feedback` array. Field lists come from the repo's own dogfood data in .sudocode/issues.jsonl and .sudocode/specs.jsonl and from types/src/schema.ts.

Agent runs stay local and are not committed. The `executions` table records issue_id, the prompt, agent_type, session_id, mode (worktree or local), target and work branch, before_commit and after_commit, worktree_path, status, model, summary, files_changed and parent_execution_id. The `execution_logs` table holds the full agent output, either as raw stream-json JSONL (`raw_logs`) or as normalized NDJSON (`normalized_entry`). It also keeps workflows, workflow_events, prompt_templates, issue_feedback and an events audit table with old/new JSON snapshots and an optional git_commit_sha (types/src/schema.ts).

So full transcripts are stored, which corrects the discovery note. But they live only in the gitignored SQLite cache and are not shared through git.
where_stored:
Committed to git, in the working tree: .sudocode/issues.jsonl and .sudocode/specs.jsonl. In the current repo they sit directly under .sudocode/, not in the issues/ and specs/ subfolders that the older docs/storage.md shows. Also committed: .sudocode/config.json ({"sourceOfTruth":"jsonl", telemetry projectId}) and .gitattributes (`.sudocode/*.jsonl merge=sudocode-jsonl`).

Gitignored, per .sudocode/.gitignore: cache.db* (SQLite, which holds the execution transcripts), the generated Markdown views issues/ and specs/, worktrees/, config.local.json, merge-driver.log and the telemetry buffer files.

User credentials live in ~/.config/sudocode/user_credentials.json, or under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (cli/src/auth/credentials.ts).

Sources: https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode/blob/main/.sudocode/.gitignore and https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode/blob/main/types/src/schema.ts
format_and_model:
There are three tiers. This design is credited to Steve Yegge's beads (docs/storage.md).
(1) JSONL is the source of truth: one full-snapshot JSON object per entity per line, rewritten in place rather than appended as events.
(2) Markdown with YAML frontmatter is the human editing view. It is generated and gitignored in this repo. A draft spec, docs/specs/markdown-source-of-truth.md, proposes letting Markdown be the source of truth, and the config key `sourceOfTruth` already exists (cli/src/config.ts).
(3) SQLite is the query cache: WAL mode, a polymorphic relationships table, ready_issues and blocked_issues views, and an events audit table.

How the tiers sync: CLI writes go to SQLite first, then a debounced export (5 s) writes JSONL. Markdown edits flow through a chokidar watcher with a 2 s debounce. After a git pull, JSONL is imported back into SQLite, and the importer creates synthetic events by diffing ("short history"). Rebuilding the full history from git log is listed as TODO.

IDs: human IDs such as ISSUE-001 and s-xxxx are paired with UUIDs, and merges dedupe by UUID. The repo's own dogfood data is 676 issues (2.5 MB) and 75 specs (1.1 MB).

Sources: https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode/blob/main/docs/storage.md and README "Dual Issue/Spec Representation"
multi_writer_and_merge:
Many writers coordinate through ordinary git branches and merges. The README describes "one logical database across multiple environments through git synchronization" and says "Git handles distribution while AI handles merge conflicts."

The concrete mechanism is a custom git merge driver for .sudocode/*.jsonl, installed by `sudocode init-merge-driver`. It registers `driver = sudocode merge-driver --base=%O --ours=%A --theirs=%B` (cli/src/cli/merge-commands.ts). The resolver in cli/src/merge-resolver.ts works like this:
- It dedupes entities by UUID.
- It converts entities to YAML and runs a three-way `git merge-file` over them (cli/src/git-merge.ts).
- Conflicting scalar fields go to the side with the later updated_at ("latest-wins"). Array fields such as tags and relationships are merged as a union.
- If one side deleted an entity and the other modified it, the modification wins.
- updated_at is stripped before the merge to avoid spurious conflicts.
- ID collisions (two different UUIDs with the same human ID) are renumbered.

Within one machine, a single SQLite cache in WAL mode serializes writers. There is no CRDT. Last-writer-wins by wall-clock timestamp can silently drop concurrent edits.
realtime:
Within one machine, yes. The local server has a WebSocket service and a workflow broadcast service (server/src/services/websocket.ts, workflow-broadcast-service.ts), and the UI lets you watch running agent trajectories live and send feedback to running agents (README).

Across machines, no. Sharing is batch: it happens only on git commit, push and pull, followed by a JSONL import. There is also a `remote` command that deploys a sudocode server to a remote sandbox through a "sudopod" provider using GitHub CLI and Claude auth (cli/src/remote/spawn-service.ts). It is not a sync channel.
search_retrieval:
Search is structured queries over the SQLite cache. The ready and blocked views give dependency-aware next-work queries, and graph traversal follows the relationships table. Text search is plain SQL LIKE over title and content (`searchIssues` in cli/src/operations/issues.ts). FTS5 appears only as a later phase in docs/storage.md. Spec feedback carries text anchors that are re-located by content search (cli/src/operations/feedback-anchors.ts).

Agents reach this through the CLI, an MCP server and a Claude Code plugin (README Quick Start). I found no search over execution transcripts and no semantic or vector search.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, and quite tightly, but only in the local cache. Each execution row ties together issue_id/issue_uuid, the agent's session_id, the prompt, the agent type and model, the branch and worktree, before_commit and after_commit SHAs, and files_changed (types/src/schema.ts). Workflows run issues in topological order on a temporary branch or worktree, with one commit per issue, so each code commit maps to an issue (README "Graph-Based Planning" and workflow section). Specs link to issues with [[ID]] references and `implements` relationships. The events table has an optional git_commit_sha.

What git shares is only the issue/spec graph and the agents' self-written breadcrumbs (issue content and feedback). The execution-to-commit linkage and the transcripts are not shared.
scale: The only scale numbers are design targets, not measurements. docs/storage.md projects 1,000 specs at about 1 MB of JSONL and 5 MB of SQLite, 10,000 issues at about 10 MB and 50 MB, a ready-work query under 10 ms, and JSONL-to-SQLite import under 1 s for 10k entries. In practice the project's own dogfood repo commits 676 issues and 75 specs, 3.6 MB of single-file JSONL that is rewritten on each export. I found no benchmarks or multi-team deployments.
privacy_security:
Weak for ParleyInn's threat model. I found no redaction or secret-scanning code: grep for redact and secret in cli/src and server/src turned up nothing relevant. I found no encryption at rest and no integrity chain or signatures. Everything agents write into issues or feedback is committed to git in plaintext and fed back to later agents as context, with no trust boundary or envelope, so it is an open prompt-injection channel.

Transcripts in cache.db are gitignored, which keeps them out of git by default, but they are stored unredacted.

Credentials are written with file mode 0600 inside a 0700 directory (cli/src/auth/credentials.ts).

The CLI has OTLP telemetry (cli/src/telemetry.ts). Events are buffered locally to .sudocode/telemetry-buffer.jsonl: command name, success, duration, optional SUDOCODE_SESSION_ID and attributes. They are flushed with fetch() to an endpoint read from config.local.json, and are skipped when no endpoint is set or `disabled` is true. I could not verify whether a default endpoint is provisioned, but the committed config.json does carry a telemetry projectId.

The whole tool runs a Node server and spawns agents, so it is not network-free.
lesson_for_parinn:
The useful split: sudocode puts small, mergeable, low-volume state (specs, issues, agent breadcrumbs) in git as UUID-keyed JSONL with a custom merge driver. Bulky, sensitive transcripts stay in a gitignored local SQLite cache. Git serves as a batch transport for curated summaries, not for raw session logs.

What ParleyInn should copy:
- the split itself
- UUID identity plus a merge driver registered through .gitattributes, so git merges never corrupt the JSONL
- recording before_commit and after_commit SHAs and the agent session_id on each run, to link sessions to code

What ParleyInn should avoid:
- rewriting full snapshots in place under wall-clock latest-wins. That loses concurrent edits silently and breaks ParleyInn's append-only, hash-chained record and its I6 no-silent-loss rule. ParleyInn should merge append-only event logs, ordered by the hash chain, as a set union.
- shared text flowing straight back into agent context with no trust boundary. Under ParleyInn's I2, anything pulled from git must stay untrusted and enveloped.
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/sudocode-ai/sudocode/blob/main/LICENSE)
confidence: high for storage layout, schema, merge driver and transcript handling, all read from source at commit 632de19. medium for project status: no commits since 2026-03-18, archive flag unverified, and docs.sudocode.ai was unreachable from this session.

name: Supermemory (supermemoryai/supermemory), including Supermemory local, the Supermemory MCP server, the claude-supermemory Claude Code plugin and SMFS
category: long-term memory service (hosted memory/RAG API, with an MCP server, coding-agent plugins and a self-hosted binary)
status: shipped. The hosted platform, the MCP server and the plugins are live. The repo is active: last commit 2026-10-01, about 31.1k stars, MIT license, not archived. The self-hosted 'Supermemory local' binary is shipped, but I could not find its engine source in the public repo.
what_is_stored: Supermemory stores derived facts, not a lossless log. Clients send 'documents': conversation transcripts, text, markdown, HTML, PDFs, images, audio/video, code, URLs and connector items. A learning model then turns these into 'memories' with typed relations (Updates, Extends, Derives), an isLatest flag for versioning, and a split between static and dynamic facts. From those it keeps an auto-maintained per-container user profile (profile.static / profile.dynamic) (how-it-works.mdx; architecture.md; README). The model decides what to keep and 'when to forget', and old facts are superseded. For Claude Code, the plugin's Stop hook reads the session JSONL transcript. It sends the new user and assistant turns since a per-session cursor, which is stored in ~/.supermemory-claude/trackers/<session>.txt. Thinking blocks are dropped and tool results are cut to 500 chars. The turns go up as one document per session (customId = Claude session_id) with metadata: type=session_turn, project, sm_project_id, sm_scope, sm_capture_mode, timestamp (capture.js, transcript.js). An entityContext prompt tells the extractor to keep decisions, conventions, architecture and setup. It also tells it to SKIP 'transient repo state git already tracks' (api.js). A 'signalExtraction' mode captures only turns near keywords such as remember, decision or bug (plugin README).
where_stored: Hosted: the Supermemory managed cloud, at api.supermemory.ai. The MCP endpoint mcp.supermemory.ai is a Cloudflare Worker with two SQLite-backed Durable Objects (SupermemoryMCP and SpaceState). It proxies to API_URL=https://api.supermemory.ai (apps/mcp/wrangler.jsonc). SpaceState keeps only per-user MCP state, such as the active container tag and upload sessions with hashed tokens (space-state.ts). The discovery URL docs.supermemory.ai/supermemory-mcp/technology now 301-redirects to a page with no architecture details. Where the core API stores its data is not disclosed beyond 'a custom ... graph database that we built internally'. Self-hosted: one local process listening on :6767. All state sits in $SUPERMEMORY_DATA_DIR (default ./.supermemory): 'graph engine data, auth secret, embedding model cache', plus uploaded files. Provider keys go in ~/.supermemory/env, 'saved encrypted'. The on-disk format of the embedded engine is undocumented. The plugin also keeps local cursor files. SMFS mounts keep a local SQLite cache. Git is not used for storage or transport.
format_and_model: The API is JSON over HTTPS: POST /v3/documents {content, containerTag, customId, metadata, entityContext}, plus /v4/search and /v4/profile. The plugin flattens a transcript into one text document using pseudo-chat markers: <|turn_start|>ts, <|start|>user<|message|>…<|end|>, <|start|>assistant:tool_result<|message|>Tool(status): …<|end|>, <|turn_end|>. The engine is described as a 'temporal vector-graph engine … fact-based temporal graph that has Vector, FTS, and graph built in'. Its pipeline runs queued → extracting → chunking (semantic) → embedding → indexing (relations) → done. Memories carry isStatic and isLatest flags and Updates/Extends/Derives edges. containerTag is the tenancy and scoping key. Re-sending under the same customId upserts and diffs against what is already stored. The client must keep the same prefix and must not mix full re-sends with deltas for one customId (rules.mdx, billing.mdx). Self-hosted embeddings default to local Xenova/bge-base-en-v1.5 (768d), with a 'dimension lock'. There is no hash chain or content addressing, and records are mutable.
multi_writer_and_merge: Merging is semantic, done by an LLM, not structural. Many writers can share one containerTag. For coding agents, the plugin derives repo_<name>__<sha256(normalized git remote)[:16]>, so all clones and worktrees of a repo, and Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, write one shared container. SUPERMEMORY_ISOLATE_WORKTREES=true switches the key to the worktree path. sm_scope metadata keeps personal and team memories filterable inside a container (plugin README, container-tag.js). There is no CRDT or causal ordering. The docs say supermemory works out 'what came first' from ingestion order within a containerTag, and advise sequential ingestion (rules.mdx). Contradictions are resolved by the extractor writing an Updates relation that sets isLatest on the newer fact (architecture.md). The plugin advances its cursor only after a save succeeds, so a failed save is retried next turn (transcript.js). The docs for SMFS bidirectional sync describe write-push and poll-pull, but they give no conflict-resolution policy (mount.mdx).
realtime: Near-real-time, not streaming. Adds return immediately with status 'queued' and are processed in the background. In self-hosted mode, ingestion is throttled by RAM limit and concurrency, while searches are never queued (configuration.mdx). The plugin captures on each Stop hook, which runs asynchronously with a 30s timeout, and recalls on UserPromptSubmit (hooks.json). Hosted connectors sync through 'real-time webhooks' (README). SMFS lets agents in different sandboxes see each other's writes 'within a sync interval', default 30s polling (mount.mdx). Searches are not pushed to subscribers.
search_retrieval: Hybrid search mixes RAG over document chunks with extracted memories in one query (searchMode hybrid/memories). Results are ranked by similarity, recency, static over dynamic, relation strength and metadata filters, with a chunkThreshold cut-off (README; architecture.md). The engine claims built-in vector, FTS and graph indexes. Profile calls run in about 50ms. MCP tools are memory, recall and context. The plugin injects the profile at SessionStart as <supermemory-context>. On each prompt it adds a 'reasoned recall' directive and can inject relevance-ranked <supermemory-recall> results automatically, and it auto-approves read-only supermemory MCP calls (session-start.js, recall-directive.js). SMFS offers 'semantic grep by default' plus a virtual profile.md. Exact replay of a past session is not offered: there is no lossless transcript retrieval and no expand-by-id.
links_sessions_to_code: Links are weak, by repo only. The container key comes from the normalized git origin remote, or the worktree path when that option is set. Each session is one document keyed by the Claude session_id, with project and sm_project_id metadata (container-tag.js, capture.js). No link is recorded to commits, branches, files or diffs. The extraction prompt explicitly drops git-tracked state, such as branch position and in-flight commits (api.js). A /supermemory:index command indexes the codebase's architecture and patterns as memories, and connectors can sync GitHub content.
privacy_security: Hosted: TLS in transit and 'AES-256 class' encryption at rest. Isolation is enforced by containerTag, with scoped API keys and orgs. SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, and HIPAA BAA on Scale and Enterprise. Customer content is never used for training. Erasure works by deleting a container's content (overview/security.mdx). The MCP server authenticates with OAuth. Self-hosted: one auto-generated API key, provider keys saved encrypted, 'no analytics'. It can run fully offline with Ollama, but it still calls a configured LLM provider unless pointed at a local one (configuration.mdx). Plugin gaps I verified in the source: there is no secret or PII redaction. cleanContent strips only <system-reminder> and <supermemory-context> blocks, and tool results are only truncated. Raw transcript turns, including user-pasted secrets and 500-char tool-output snippets, go to the API. Recalled memories are injected automatically into model context with no untrusted-content framing. Team-shared repo containers mean one contributor's captured text can reach another's prompt. Hooks fail open, with 3–4s timeouts.
scale: Benchmark claims: '#1 on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, ConvoMem' and '95% Recall@15 with 99.4% context reduction' (README). Latency: ~50ms user profiles and ~sub-300ms p50 search on the managed platform (README; security.mdx). It handles documents over 400k tokens, though smaller documents are recommended (rules.mdx). Hosted is 'globally distributed, scales elastically'. Self-hosted is 'one machine, one process', single org (local-vs-enterprise.mdx). These are vendor claims only. I found no independent verification and no figures for record counts or storage size.
license: MIT for the repo (SDKs, MCP worker, docs, UI) and for the claude-supermemory plugin. The docs call the self-hosted binary 'open source' and link to git.new/memory, which redirects to github.com/Dhravya/supermemory, the same repo. The engine and server source behind supermemory-server and the hosted API were not present in the public repo at commit bce2d0d, so this claim cannot be verified. The hosted service is proprietary SaaS.
lesson_for_parinn: Supermemory's Claude Code plugin is the design ParleyInn's invariants rule out. It keys a container on the git remote hash and uploads deltas from the transcript JSONL on each Stop hook, with a cursor that advances only after a successful save (both worth copying). But an LLM extractor then rewrites and supersedes the content. The result is pushed back into every teammate's prompt automatically, with no redaction and no untrusted framing. That makes shared memory a cross-user prompt-injection and secret-leak channel, and the original history is unrecoverable. ParleyInn should borrow the identity and delta-cursor mechanics: one record per session_id, a remote-hash repo key with an opt-in worktree split, and an at-least-once cursor. Two things should stay separate: the lossless hash-chained record as the source of truth, and any distilled summary as a rebuildable projection, recalled only on request (pull) and wrapped in an untrusted-content envelope.
confidence: high for the plugin, MCP worker and documented API behaviour, which I read from source at pinned commits. medium for engine internals and scale, which rest on vendor docs only. low for the self-hosted on-disk format and for the 'open source' claim about the engine, neither of which I could verify.

name: Superset (superset-sh/superset)
category: Agentic IDE / workspace orchestrator for parallel CLI coding agents (Electron desktop app, CLI, SDK, MCP server, iOS app, plus a hosted cloud backend)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Superset does not own or store agent conversation transcripts. It runs third-party CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and about 20 others) in PTYs, one git worktree per workspace (README; docs/agent-sessions.mdx). What it does store: (1) Local per-host SQLite 'host.db' (host-service) with tables terminal_sessions, terminal_agent_bindings, projects, workspaces, pull_requests, host_agent_configs, workspace_tags and others (packages/host-service/src/db/schema.ts). terminal_agent_bindings maps a Superset terminal to the agent's own session id. It also keeps lifecycle fields (lastEventType, endReason, used for resume decisions) and the harness-reported transcript_path. (2) An Electron-side local SQLite (packages/local-db, drizzle dialect sqlite) with projects, worktrees, workspaces, settings, tasks, browserHistory, downloads and screenshots. (3) Terminal output, held only in memory: a 64 KiB live FIFO and a 2 MB catch-up ring per session in host-service (packages/host-service/src/terminal). The pty-daemon writes a snapshot so sessions survive daemon handoff and restarts (packages/pty-daemon/src/SessionStore). (4) Cloud Postgres (Neon) for org data: organizations and users, tasks, automations, automationRuns, automationPromptVersions, submitted_prompts (prompt_text), and chat_sessions. chat_sessions holds metadata only: id, org, creator, workspace, title and timestamps. The table set also covers Pages and page comments, files and attachments, cloud workspaces and presence and activity, encrypted environment_secrets and agent_credentials, and GitHub installations and PRs (packages/db/src/schema/schema.ts). (5) Cloudflare R2 bucket 'superset-private' plus Durable Objects for Pages storage and realtime (apps/realtime/wrangler.jsonc). Session history itself stays in the agent's native store, such as ~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<id>.jsonl or ~/.codex/sessions/.... Superset reads that store on demand (docs/agent-session-handoff.md).
where_stored: Several tiers. Local SQLite host.db per host and organization, at /var/lib/superset/host.db inside cloud sandboxes (packages/shared/src/sandbox-contract.ts; packages/cli/src/lib/host/manifest.ts). Local Electron SQLite. Worktrees under ~/.superset/worktrees/ and sessions under ~/.superset/sessions/ (docs FAQ). Agent-native JSONL files under ~/.claude or ~/.codex. Cloud: Neon serverless Postgres via drizzle (packages/db/src/client.ts), Cloudflare Workers with SQLite-backed Durable Objects (OrgHub, PageHub, HostTunnel), R2, and Workers KV for relay placement (apps/realtime/wrangler.jsonc, apps/relay/wrangler.jsonc). Git holds only code: one worktree and branch per workspace. Git is not used for session history.
format_and_model: Relational, defined with Drizzle ORM. Postgres for the cloud with UUID primary keys and snake_case columns. SQLite for both local stores, with drizzle-kit migrations; host.db migrations check that no foreign-key violation is introduced (packages/host-service/src/db/db.ts). Mutable rows with updatedAt and $onUpdate. Nothing is append-only and nothing is hash-chained. Transcripts are not normalized into Superset's schema. Per-harness parsers (harness-sessions/<harness>.ts, with locate, parseTurns and hasSession) read the agent's JSONL lazily. Claude: user and assistant turns, no tool output. Codex: message items, skipping injected AGENTS.md and environment context. Reads widen from the last 4 MB tail, up to 128 MB (docs/agent-session-handoff.md). Terminal history is a byte ring buffer, not structured events.
multi_writer_and_merge: No merge of session history, because each agent harness is the only writer of its own transcript file. Multi-device works by remote control, not replication. A workspace lives on one host, and other devices reach it through a Cloudflare relay tunnel: the HostTunnel Durable Object with ticketed dials, keepalives and access caching (apps/relay/src/host-tunnel.ts; docs FAQ 'Devices'). Org-level shared state is a single central Postgres with last-write-wins rows. Code integration goes through git branches and PRs. The docs say worktrees 'do not sandbox processes or prevent merge conflicts' (README). Two agent tools for history: 'Fork session' calls the harness's native fork (claude --resume <id> --fork-session). 'Continue with another agent' copies up to 36,000 characters of transcript into a new agent's prompt (docs/agent-sessions.mdx).
realtime: Yes, for UI state, not for history. The OrgHub Durable Object, one per organization, holds hibernating WebSockets. It fans out invalidation nudges that the API sends after Postgres writes, coalesced over 500 ms. It merges presence by user and 'stores nothing but what is waiting on the next broadcast; the data itself stays in Postgres' (apps/realtime/src/org-hub.ts). PageHub provides shared key-value storage for published Pages. Terminals stream live over the relay to desktop, CLI and iOS clients (README, Remote Access). Agent status comes from lifecycle hooks Superset installs into each agent's config (docs/superset-model.mdx).
search_retrieval: No full-text or semantic search over session history was found. Retrieval is by id: 'superset agents read --workspace --terminal' returns the agent's saved transcript for Claude Code and Codex only, with no fallback to terminal output (docs/agent-sessions.mdx). The handoff tries three sources in order: the harness store, the PTY ring replay, then the visible screen. The command palette searches workspaces and actions, not content (README).
links_sessions_to_code: Indirectly. The workspace is the unit that joins them: one git worktree and branch per task, terminals bound to that workspace, and terminal_agent_bindings recording the workspaceId and the agent session id. PRs are tracked per workspace (workspace_pull_requests, pull_requests tables). No commit-level or line-level link from a prompt or transcript to a code change was found: no git notes, trailers or refs. The handoff prompt says that 'the workspace, not the transcript, is the source of truth' (docs/agent-sessions.mdx).
scale: The discovery note's '100+ parallel agents' claim does not appear in the current README or docs; I could not verify it. The docs speak of 'five agents running' and racing N workspaces (docs/superset-model.mdx). Engineering limits in the docs: 36,000-character handoff cap, 2 MB PTY catch-up ring, transcript reads capped at 128 MB, session-id scan stopped at 5,000 Claude project directories or 2,000 Codex directories (docs/agent-session-handoff.md). Cloud sandboxes: 4-hour idle timeout, golden snapshots of about 4 GB. They are gated to @superset.sh users and a PostHog flag (docs/cloud-sandbox-considerations.md). Very active: last commit on main was 2026-10-01, and a release ships nearly every day ('we ship daily', README).
privacy_security: Secrets: environment_secrets.encryptedValue and agent_credentials.encryptedValue in Postgres. Desktop auth tokens are AES-256-GCM encrypted (packages/trpc/src/lib/secret-box.ts; apps/desktop/src/lib/trpc/routers/auth/utils/crypto-storage.ts). Transcript trust: the hook endpoint is unauthenticated. A reported transcript_path is stored only if it is absolute, ends in .jsonl and lies under the user's home. It is checked again on read, and the first MB must contain the session id. It is cleared when the binding moves to another session (docs/agent-session-handoff.md). No redaction: the docs warn that a handoff 'removes terminal control codes but does not redact anything, so tokens, keys, or connection strings ... go with it' (docs/agent-sessions.mdx). Superset says it 'never touches model traffic' (docs/superset-model.mdx). Code leaves the machine with Remote Access (traffic goes through the relay), cloud workspaces and published Pages (docs FAQ, Privacy). Telemetry uses PostHog and Sentry (plans/20260427-posthog-v1-v2-dashboard.md; apps/docs sentry config). Vulnerabilities are reported through GitHub private advisories; only the latest release gets fixes (SECURITY.md). Handed-off transcripts are labelled 'read-only history' in the prompt, but this is prompt text only, with no structural envelope (docs/agent-sessions.mdx).
lesson_for_parinn: Superset shows that even a heavily funded, fast-moving multi-agent product treats the harness's own JSONL (~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<id>.jsonl) as the system of record. It reaches that file through a fragile, undocumented path layout: its own docs name Claude Code 2.1.282's dir-name encoding, javaHash truncation past 200 characters, and a different filename seen in some versions. It falls back to an ID-based scan. Two lessons follow. (1) ParleyInn should copy Superset's defensive locator. Prefer the hook-reported transcript_path, validate it against a trusted-root and session-id check, because hook input is unauthenticated. Fall back to layout, then to an id scan. Log a miss loudly, which fits I6. ParleyInn should then go further than Superset and ingest into its own append-only, hash-chained record, so history survives harness deletion, layout changes and ephemeral sandboxes. Superset loses it in all three cases. (2) Superset's handoff re-injects up to 36k characters of raw, unredacted transcript into a new agent's prompt, protected only by a 'read-only history' label. That is exactly the I2 hazard ParleyInn exists to close. ParleyInn should offer handoff and fork only as pull-only, enveloped and redacted recall. On transport, Superset does not replicate history. It reaches the one host that owns it through a relay tunnel and uses a central DB plus a realtime nudge fan-out only for metadata. That suggests ParleyInn can split a small, shared, realtime metadata/index plane from a host-owned record, with git reserved for code.
license: Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2), which is source-available, not OSI open source. It bars offering the software as a hosted service and bars circumventing license-key functionality (LICENSE.md).

name: swarm-tools (Swarm: Hive, Hivemind, Swarm Mail). npm packages opencode-swarm-plugin, swarm-mail, claude-code-swarm-plugin
category: multi-agent coordination + agent mail (plus git-synced task tracker and local semantic memory / cross-agent session search)
status: shipped, but feature work stopped in Feb 2026. Last npm releases were opencode-swarm-plugin 0.63.2 and swarm-mail 1.11.2 on 2026-02-06 (https://registry.npmjs.org/opencode-swarm-plugin, https://registry.npmjs.org/swarm-mail). The last feature commit was 2026-02-23. The most recent commits (2026-05-20) only harden CI and the supply chain. I checked that remote HEAD is b685253 using git ls-remote. I could not check the archived flag because the GitHub API was blocked in this session. As of Oct 2026, treat it as low-activity or maintenance mode, not 'active'.
what_is_stored: (1) An append-only event log of coordination events: agent_registered, message_sent, file_reserved, file_released, checkpoint, outcome (README, https://github.com/joelhooks/swarm-tools/blob/main/README.md). Materialized projections built from it: agents, messages, message_recipients, reservations, locks, cursors, eval_records, swarm_contexts, decision_traces (decision, rationale, alternatives, precedent cited, outcome event id, quality score) and entity_links (packages/swarm-mail/src/streams/libsql-schema.ts). (2) Hive 'cells' (beads-style issues), whose fields are id, title, description, status open/in_progress/blocked/closed/tombstone, priority, type, parent, dependencies, labels, comments and timestamps (packages/swarm-mail/src/hive/jsonl.ts). (3) Hivemind memories: free text plus tags, confidence and metadata, with embeddings, entities, relationships and memory links (packages/swarm-mail/src/db/schema/memory.ts). (4) A session index. Transcripts from other agents (OpenCode, Cursor, and per the ADR Claude, Aider and others) are parsed, split into one chunk per message, embedded and stored for search. This in-houses CASS (Cross-Agent Session Search) (docs/adr/010-cass-inhousing.md, packages/swarm-mail/src/sessions/README.md). (5) Learning data: outcome records (duration, errors, files touched, success), pattern maturity levels, and anti-patterns created automatically when failure rate exceeds 60% (README).
where_stored: Hybrid. System of record: a single global embedded libSQL/SQLite database at ~/.config/swarm-tools/swarm.db. Project-local DBs are now actively refused (packages/swarm-mail/src/streams/store.ts, libsql.convenience.ts). An older design resolved every git worktree to the main repo's .opencode/swarm.db so worktrees shared one store (packages/swarm-mail/src/db/WORKTREE.md). Git artifact: the working-tree files .hive/issues.jsonl and .hive/memories.jsonl are committed to the project repo. Optionally, per-session event JSONL is exported to .hive/sessions/{session_id}.jsonl (packages/swarm-mail/src/memory/sync.ts, sessions/session-export.ts). .hive/.gitignore excludes *.db, WAL and daemon files and keeps the JSONL. Embeddings are never written to git; they are regenerated on import when Ollama is available (memory/sync.ts).
format_and_model: Event sourcing on SQLite. The events table is (id INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT, type, project_key, timestamp, sequence GENERATED ALWAYS AS (id), data TEXT JSON), indexed by project/type/time. State lives in materialized tables derived from those events (libsql-schema.ts; the Drizzle schema in db/schema/streams.ts is described as the source of truth). There is no hash chain, signature or content addressing; ordering is a local autoincrement id. Git exports are one JSON object per line. Example memory line: {"id","information","metadata","tags","confidence","created_at"} (memory/sync.ts). It is written in TypeScript on Bun with Drizzle ORM and Effect (repo package.json files). Coordination primitives are named DurableMailbox, DurableLock and DurableDeferred, with patterns credited to Electric SQL durable streams (README).
multi_writer_and_merge: On one machine, all agents and worktrees write to the same SQLite file, and concurrency comes from SQLite/WAL. Exclusive file reservations (swarmmail_reserve) check for conflicts first and reject unless force is set. For exclusive paths they take DurableLocks, and the default TTL is 3600 s. Expired reservations are swept by expires_at (packages/swarm-mail/src/streams/agent-mail.ts, reservation-utils.ts). These are advisory: they bind only agents that call the tool. The Claude Code plugin adds a PreToolUse 'pre-edit' hook that can enforce them (packages/claude-code-swarm-plugin/hooks/hooks.json). Across machines there is no live replication; sharing happens only through git. hive_sync flushes dirty cells and memories to JSONL, then runs 'git add .hive/', 'git commit -m "chore: sync hive"', 'git pull --rebase' and 'git push' (packages/opencode-swarm-plugin/src/hive.ts ~L1600-1705). Conflicts are handled by a deterministic 3-way JSONL merge ported from steveyegge/beads. Its rules: tombstone wins unless expired (30-day TTL, 7-day minimum, 1 h clock-skew grace); title and description use latest updated_at; closed beats open; higher priority wins; notes are concatenated; dependencies are unioned. Records are keyed on id+created_at+created_by (packages/swarm-mail/src/hive/merge.ts). Caveat: the repo's .gitattributes registers merge=beads only for .beads/issues.jsonl, not .hive/, and I found no code that installs the driver. So in practice merges of .hive/ may fall back to rebase plus ID-dedup (hive.ts merges beads.base.jsonl by ID, with issues.jsonl winning). The event log itself is never merged across machines.
realtime: Within a machine, yes. An optional 'Durable Streams' Bun HTTP server on port 4483 exposes the event log over WebSocket at /ws, with subscribe-from-offset and 30 s heartbeats. It also offers SSE at /events and /streams/:projectKey?offset=N&live=true, resumable with Last-Event-ID cursors, plus GET /cells; the dashboard uses it (packages/swarm-mail/src/streams/durable-server.ts). The server passes no hostname, and Bun.serve defaults to 0.0.0.0 per Bun docs (https://bun.sh/docs/api/http). That is my inference, not tested. Across machines and sandboxes there is no real time; sync happens only on explicit hive_sync or /handoff git push.
search_retrieval: Hivemind semantic search uses Ollama embeddings: default mxbai-embed-large 1024-d, also nomic-embed-text, all-minilm and snowflake-arctic-embed. It falls back to SQLite FTS5 when Ollama is missing (README; packages/swarm-mail/src/sessions/README.md). The session index has a chokidar file watcher (500 ms debounce), staleness detection (mtime more than last_indexed + 300 s), pagination, and a viewer that returns exact line ranges of the source JSONL. The cass_search/view/expand tools were only partly wired as of the ADR (docs/adr/010-cass-inhousing.md). Auto-recall injects memories into prompts through hooks. After a Feb 2026 incident it was throttled: 30 s cooldown, minScore raised from 0.3 to 0.55, 3 results, 600-char content, and a blocklist of 19 system-message patterns (commit 2ad83e6, https://github.com/joelhooks/swarm-tools/commit/2ad83e6).
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly. Claude Code hooks record session start, subagent start and stop, user prompts, pre-edit, and track-tool PostToolUse into the event log (packages/claude-code-swarm-plugin/hooks/hooks.json). Outcome events record files touched (README). decision_traces link decisions to epic and cell ids and to an outcome event, and entity_links link decisions to typed entities (libsql-schema.ts). Hive cells are versioned beside the code in the same git repo, but there is no field linking a commit SHA to a session or prompt. Hive commits are generic 'chore: sync hive' commits, separate from code commits (hive.ts).
scale: No formal scale claims. Observed in the repo itself: .hive/issues.jsonl has 786 lines and .hive/memories.jsonl has 11,873 lines, checked in. The Feb 2026 commit reports purging 8,918 garbage memories (12,824 down to 2,905) after auto-recall fired about 608 times in an 8-hour session, injecting about 760K characters (commit 2ad83e6). A legacy migration file mentions 519 historical issues (packages/swarm-mail/src/migrations/legacy-hive-transformer.ts). Design target is single-developer, local.
privacy_security: Local-first with no external servers; embeddings come from local Ollama (README). Searching the source turned up no redaction, secret scanning or encryption at rest. The only hit for 'redact', 'secret' or 'encrypt' was an unrelated skill file. Concrete leakage evidence: the project's own committed .hive/memories.jsonl holds session-derived records with metadata such as absolute paths. 6,669 lines contain '/Users/'; for example, source_path /Users/joel/.config/swarm-tools/sessions/... appears in lines exported from session chunks. So git sync publishes raw session-derived content and local paths to whoever can read the repo. Recalled memories are injected automatically into prompts with no trust envelope; the fixes were relevance filters, not a trust boundary (commit 2ad83e6). The streams server has no authentication in the source I read and may bind to all interfaces (inference, see realtime). Supply-chain hardening was added in May 2026: npm provenance and vouch PR gating (commits b685253, 983652c, b0cd955; SECURITY_SUPPLY_CHAIN.md). License: MIT (package.json files).
lesson_for_parinn: Keep two layers apart: the fast local store is the system of record, and git only carries a curated, deterministically mergeable export. But don't copy what swarm-tools got wrong. Its git export is a raw dump of session-derived memories: unredacted, with absolute paths, committed to a public repo. Auto-recall pushed untrusted stored text into prompts until it flooded sessions (about 760K characters per 8 hours). Its merge driver is not even registered for the .hive path it uses. For ParleyInn this argues for three things. (a) Anything leaving the machine through git should pass redaction and an explicit export policy. Use a dedicated ref or a separate repo rather than working-tree JSONL in the project branch. (b) Git-borne records need per-writer append-only segments, since the order can't come from a local autoincrement id. Hash-chained segments merge by union, with no field-level last-writer-wins rules that rewrite history. (c) Recall stays pull-only and enveloped, which I2 already requires. The swarm-tools incident is a ready-made real-world case for I2 and I9. Its advisory file reservations with TTL, enforced by a PreToolUse hook, are a cheap coordination pattern worth noting, but they belong in a coordination layer outside ParleyInn's offline core.
confidence: high for storage, data model, merge rules and hooks (read directly from source at HEAD b685253). Medium for project status, because the archived flag could not be checked via API, and for the 0.0.0.0 bind, which is inferred from Bun defaults.
license: MIT (package.json of swarm-mail, opencode-swarm-plugin, swarm-tools packages; README footer)

name: SWE-agent Trajectory Format (.traj)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Per-instance trajectory files store complete agent-environment interaction traces: (1) trajectory array of steps, each containing action (shell command), observation (command output), response (LM raw output), thought (parsed reasoning), and state (JSON environment snapshot of open_file and working_dir); (2) history array recording all messages sent to/from LM including system prompt, user messages, and assistant responses for the entire conversation; (3) info object with exit_status and submission (git diff patch); (4) environment string naming the runtime context. Trajectories capture full problem-solving path for a single GitHub issue fix across 1-N steps.
where_stored: Local filesystem in trajectories/<username>/<experiment_name>/<instance_id>/<instance_id>.traj. Single JSON file per instance. When run-batch is used, trajectories organize under experiment folders containing multiple instance subdirectories. Trajectories are written at end of execution, not streamed. No central repository or server storage mechanism; designed for local disk or manual upload to git.
format_and_model: JSON text format. Data model: top-level object with keys [environment (string), trajectory (array of step objects), history (array of message objects), info (object with exit_status and submission fields)]. Each step in trajectory: {action: string, observation: string, response: string, thought: string, state: string-serialized JSON}. Each message in history: {message_type: string, role: string (system/assistant/user), content: string}. Per v1.1.0+, query field added to steps showing exact LM input at current step.
multi_writer_and_merge: No multi-writer support. Each instance generates one .traj file. Batch mode (sweagent run-batch) runs multiple independent instances in parallel (num_workers configurable), each writing its own isolated trajectory file. No merging, synchronization, or conflict resolution. No append-only guarantee across instances. Each worker writes independently to disk. No locking or coordination between parallel writers to same trajectory directory.
realtime: Not real-time. Trajectories written post-execution when instance completes. No streaming, no incremental writes during agent work. Agent executes to completion (success, error, or timeout), then trajectory is serialized to disk. Users cannot observe trajectory growth during execution; only polling the directory shows new files after completion.
search_retrieval: Two built-in tools: (1) CLI inspector (sweagent inspect / sweagent i) - terminal pager allowing step-by-step navigation with vim-like keybindings (h/l for steps, j/k for scroll, t for trajectory search, v to toggle detail, e to open in $EDITOR); (2) Web inspector (sweagent inspector / sweagent I) - browser-based viewer on localhost:8000 (configurable port) with trajectory list, step details, and benchmark evaluation results if results.json is present. No full-text search indexing, no query language. Search within inspector is type-ahead matching on trajectory filenames.
links_sessions_to_code: Indirect linkage. Trajectory metadata includes: (1) instance_id matching GitHub issue identifier (e.g., swe-agent/test-repo#1); (2) config.yaml alongside trajectory records exact repo URL, branch, and problem statement; (3) submission field in info contains git diff patch showing code changes produced. Trajectory does not embed git commit hashes, branch names, or tree objects. Links to code via: instance_id -> GitHub issue URL (in config) -> repository clone. Diff is separate artifact, not version-controlled in trajectory file itself.
scale_claims: Batch mode claims arbitrary scaling. Parallel worker count configurable with --num_workers (tested at 30+ parallel instances in documentation). Dataset sources: SWE-bench lite/full (>1000 instances), HuggingFace (custom datasets), file-based (JSONL/YAML/JSON). Per-instance cost limits and timeouts prevent runaway. No claimed limits on total trajectory count or storage. Single experiment can contain hundreds of instances. Documentation shows example with 30 parallel workers; no maximum stated.
privacy_security: No built-in encryption. Trajectories contain: full command execution history, LM reasoning (thoughts/responses), repository code snippets in observations, file system state, working directory paths. No redaction of secrets, API keys, or sensitive data mentioned in documentation. No distinction between trusted/untrusted content. Trajectories are plain JSON on disk, readable by any process with file access. GitHub API tokens and model API keys live in .env or environment, not in trajectories. Replay tool (sweagent run-replay) can re-execute trajectory commands with new system, potentially re-exposing secrets.
lesson_for_parinn: Trajectories prioritize ease of inspection and replay over secure recall: JSON is transparent and widely readable, but this creates a tradeoff - ParleyInn's invariant I2 (no automatic path from untrusted content to model) would require explicit gates before any trajectory field reaches a restore block. SWE-agent's history array (LM message chain) can become a prompt-injection vector if recalled without TrustedText wrapping. Lesson: (1) Flat-file per-instance design avoids coordination but scales poorly for multi-agent shared history; (2) JSON is debuggable but leaks all details - ParleyInn's redaction and encryption layers are not present here; (3) Replay is powerful but unsafe without integrity checking - trajectory files could be tampered post-write; (4) State snapshots (working_dir, open_file) are minimal - ParleyInn may need richer environment context (process state, mounted volumes) for multi-machine sessions. Trajectories work for single-instance research benchmarks, but multi-agent long-running contexts (ParleyInn's use case) require append-only durability, tamper evidence, and principled untrusted-content handling.

name: syncestra
status: beta
what_is_stored: A mirror of agent configuration and state directories. Claude Code's ~/.claude is the main case: sessions, skills, agents, commands, MCP configs, CLAUDE.md, settings.json, hooks, plugins and memory. Project code repos, node_modules, caches and *.log files are excluded on purpose. Session transcripts are the multi-hundred-MB, churny ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl files. These are stored as compressed shards through the 'archive' adapter rather than tracked raw. Other services are supported (OpenClaw, Hermes, docker volumes), and composed 'agents' are stored as subsets of backed-up items with a provenance sidecar. Source: the PyPI long description (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
where_stored: On the client side, a local separate-git-dir mirror under ~/.syncestra/repos/<service>. Remotely, a mandatory private GitHub repo. Branches are named <service>/<profile> (e.g. claude-code/personal) in the default 'one-repo-branches' model. Two other models exist: repo-per-service and repo-per-profile.
