Recipe files go on recipes/<home-service> branches. There is an alternative S3/Cloudflare R2 object backend with client-side age encryption (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/; the sdist file src/syncestra/backends/s3_backend.py in https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/0f/01/e2e9e962929ba70598fcf4d8821216166ee60ebfcc972def7a312cc6664f/syncestra-1.26.2.tar.gz).
format_and_model: The working tree is a plain file mirror of the source directory, committed to git with GitPython. One branch is a whole service/profile snapshot. There is no event log and no custom database; per the README, 'the local clone is the source of truth; the GitHub repo is the replica.' The archive adapter compresses the tree into sharded .zst (default) or .gz files. By default there is one shard per source file; the alternative is shard_by: session. An append to one transcript therefore rewrites only that shard and keeps git deltas small, and compression streams in fixed chunks so it does not OOM the host. Per the README, this was added after raw-tracking projects/ 'once caused a host OOM + a dead mirror'. On the S3/R2 backend, each object is an age envelope (x25519 via pyrage). Composed agents carry <dir>/.syncestra/provenance.json with per-item sha256 hashes. Config is ~/.syncestra/config.yaml, or env-only SYNCESTRA_* variables (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/; sdist src/syncestra/backends/age.py and composition/provenance.py).
multi_writer_and_merge: Convergence is last-write-wins keyed by GitHub commit time. The README says: 'no custom database, no profiles engine'. pull only fast-forwards when the remote is ahead. Divergent branches where LWW is unsafe return frozen exit code 1 (conflict). The newer 'merge' command is a file-level merge engine with three rules: union for additive list files like MEMORY.md, deep-merge for JSON/YAML, and LWW with a .conflict.<ts> sidecar for opaque or binary files. Losers are backed up rather than dropped, using atomic write plus backup plus verify-or-restore. For archived transcripts, pull is non-clobbering: it only reconstitutes absent files and never overwrites a transcript Claude is writing. Restore on the origin machine is an explicit, destructive command. Concurrent local processes serialize on a per-service flock at <state_dir>/locks/<service>.lock. The deploy docs warn not to enable the inbound timer for write-heavy state dirs, 'which fast-forward would clobber'. In effect, it is single-writer per branch, with profiles as namespaces rather than true multi-writer merging (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
realtime: Near-real-time push only. A watchman trigger is auto-installed on init (on by default) and debounces file changes for 3 s before pushing. A foreground watchdog mode is also available. It is single-flight and loops until the workdir is clean, so writes made during a push are not lost. Inbound sync is not live: the VPS deploy uses a nightly systemd timer at 04:00 Europe/London that runs push-then-pull. Other machines therefore see changes only when they pull (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
search_retrieval: No search or recall over session content. Retrieval means restoring files: pull, restore, clone (new-machine restore) and status. The MCP server (syncestra serve, FastMCP over stdio) exposes only sync operations: init, status, push, pull, sync, restore, profile, list and list_agents. It offers no query over transcripts. 'diff', 'checkpoint' and 'rewind' are listed as planned, not shipped (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
links_sessions_to_code: No. It deliberately excludes project code ('without backing up project code'). Transcripts keep only Claude Code's own projects/<path> layout. Nothing ties a session to commits, files or worktrees in the code repo (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
privacy_security: The private repo is the stated security boundary: 'secrets ride inside it, so private visibility is mandatory and enforced'. Repo auto-creation only calls POST /user/repos with private=True and refuses public repos (exit 5). The PAT comes only from an env var and is 'never logged'. A pre-commit secret gate scans every staged blob with detect-secrets plus built-in patterns, logs redacted snippets, and blocks the push with exit 5. For archived transcripts, scanning happens on uncompressed content before compression. The gate can be weakened three ways: the per-path secret_allowlist (findings are still logged), the global --allow-secrets flag, and the config-level remote.allow_secrets: true. The last one disables the gate for every push, including watch, and only logs a warning. The README says it is meant for ~/.claude mirrors whose settings.json 'legitimately contains real keys'. The S3/R2 backend age-encrypts each object client-side. The identity key is env-only (SYNCESTRA_AGE_IDENTITY), and decryption fails closed on tampering. The GitHub backend has no at-rest encryption beyond repo privacy. There is no hash chain, signing or tamper evidence on the git history. Recalled content is not treated as untrusted (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/; sdist src/syncestra/backends/age.py, s3_backend.py, adapters/secrets.py).
scale: No numeric scale claims. The only figure is that ~/.claude/projects transcripts are 'multi-hundred-MB .jsonl files that churn every turn'. Raw git tracking of them caused a host OOM and a dead mirror, which the archive adapter fixes with per-file shards and bounded-RAM streaming compression. Foreground watch recycles itself when RSS exceeds 1536 MiB (configurable). A convergence probe exits with code 7 if the mirror never gets a born HEAD with objects. It is aimed at one user across a few machines/VPSes, not teams (https://pypi.org/project/syncestra/).
license: MIT (PyPI metadata, https://pypi.org/pypi/syncestra/json)
lesson_for_parinn: If ParleyInn ever ships its record over git, it should not commit live transcript files raw. syncestra's own incident shows why: raw-tracking ~/.claude/projects caused a host OOM and a dead mirror. Its fix was to compress into one shard per source file, so an append rewrites only that shard. ParleyInn's append-only, hash-chained record fits this even better. Transport could ship immutable, compressed, content-addressed segment files: a closed segment never changes, and only the open tail is new. The scan-then-compress order is also worth copying. Two parts are anti-patterns for ParleyInn. First, the config-wide allow_secrets bypass, which only logs a warning. Second, last-write-wins by commit time, which silently loses concurrent writers on the same branch. ParleyInn's I6/I2 posture needs per-writer append-only streams that merge as a union, not LWW.
sources: https://github.com/assaads/syncestra (linked from PyPI; unreachable from this session: the GitHub add_repo check reported 'not found or no access', consistent with the discovery note's 404)
https://github.com/assaads/testvibe (referenced in the README; not verified)

name: Tangled (AT Protocol forge: appview + knots + spindles + Bobbin; Knot 2 Rust implementation)
category: Decentralized forge (git transport + AT Protocol social layer)
status: shipped. It is a public alpha: release tags run to v1.16.1-alpha, and the monorepo's last commit is 2026-10-01 (seen in a shallow clone of https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core). Knot 2 (Rust, version 2.0.0) is shipped but opt-in. You migrate to it with an offline tool, and the published container's :latest tag is still the Go knot, so Knot 2 has to be requested as :2 (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md, https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
what_is_stored:
Code: plain git repositories, with optional LFS, hosted on 'knots' (https://docs.tangled.org/, https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md).

Social data: AT Protocol records in each user's own PDS (https://blog.tangled.org/federation/, https://blog.tangled.org/vouching/). These include issues, pull requests, comments, stars, follows, vouches, labels, 'strings' (gist-like snippets), SSH public keys, repo records and artifacts.

Pull requests: each PR record holds an append-only array of 'rounds'. Every round is a gzipped text git-format-patch blob (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/pulls/pull.json).

Push events: knots emit sh.tangled.git.refUpdate events with ref, old/new SHA, committerDid, changedFiles and pushOptions (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/git/refUpdate.json).

Access control: since v1.15 the knot, not the PDS, is the source of truth for members and collaborators (https://docs.tangled.org/migrating-knots-and-spindles.html). Knot 2 also stores the repo registry and the blocklist.

Repo identity: each repository has its own DID since v1.13 (https://docs.tangled.org/migrating-knots-and-spindles.html).

CI: pipeline runs, logs and secrets are stored on 'spindles'. Since v1.16 the spindle owns pipeline history; the appview no longer keeps it (https://docs.tangled.org/migrating-knots-and-spindles.html, https://docs.tangled.org/spindles.html).

Agent data: none. No agent sessions, prompts or transcripts are stored.
where_stored:
Data is split across four kinds of place:
1. Self-hostable knot servers hold the git repos. Knot 2 has no SQLite: 'git is the only database, along with a secret-key-file'. Its ACL data lives in custom refs (refs/cobs/*). Knot-wide objects (members, blocklist, repo registry) sit in a per-knot bare 'meta-repo' at a sharded path. Per-repo collaborator objects sit inside each repo (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md, https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/backend.rs). The older Go knot used a SQLite database with a casbin ACL table (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
2. Users' PDSes, which are AT Protocol data repositories on a server or cloud host, hold the social records (https://blog.tangled.org/bobbin/).
3. Spindles hold CI data. Secrets go in SQLite by default or in OpenBao (https://docs.tangled.org/spindles.html).
4. Derived indexes:
   - the appview at tangled.org, with Bleve indexers for repos, issues and PRs (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/tree/master/appview/indexer)
   - a Zoekt code-search index (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/temp/search/searchCode.json)
   - knotmirror, a Postgres-backed repo indexer (https://blog.tangled.org/newsletter-01/)
   - Bobbin, a read-only API appview that keeps everything in RAM and has no permanent storage (https://docs.tangled.org/bobbin.html).
format_and_model:
Git objects: SHA-256 by default for new repos in Knot 2; SHA-1 in the Go knot or when chosen (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md).

Social records: AT Protocol lexicon records under the NSID prefix sh.tangled.*, keyed by TID. They are DAG-CBOR in the user's signed repo and are fetched over XRPC (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/pulls/pull.json). Issue and PR state are separate records (issue/state, pulls/state), and records point to each other with at-uri references.

Knot 2 'collaborative objects' (COBs). They resemble Radicle COBs:
- Each change is a git commit. Its tree holds one blob named 'payload', a DAG-CBOR-encoded change.
- Three extra commit headers carry metadata: cob-type (an NSID such as sh.tangled.knot.member), cob-author (a secp256k1 public key) and cob-sig (hex ECDSA).
- The signature covers a DAG-CBOR 'SignedChange' structure. It has a domain-separation context 'sh.tangled.knot.cob.change.v1' and binds home kind and id (repo DID or knot), tree OID, parents, type, author, timestamp and object id.
- The committer is a fixed 'knot <noreply@knot>' and the commit message is empty.
- An object's id is its root commit OID. Its ref is refs/cobs/<nsid>/<root-oid>.
- State checkpoints live at refs/cob-checkpoints/<nsid>/<oid>, as DAG-CBOR (format 3) with a SHA-1 digest.
- State is a deterministic fold over a causal order: topological, with ties broken by (timestamp, change id).
(https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/backend.rs, https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/change.rs, https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/graph.rs)

Two object histories exist (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/object.rs):
- 'Linear', where merges are rejected. The current member, collaborator and registry objects are all Linear (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cobs/src/grant.rs).
- 'Convergent', a DAG that allows merges.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Git code: ordinary git push, over SSH or (Knot 2) HTTPS, gated by the knot's ACL. Allowed are the owner, collaborators the owner added, and members a knot admin admitted; admission is closed by default (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md). Cross-knot contribution works like email patches: you push to your own knot and open a PR against a repo on another knot (https://blog.tangled.org/federation/).

Social records: each user writes only to their own PDS, so every record has exactly one writer. The appview or Bobbin aggregates across PDSes; there is no shared mutable record (https://blog.tangled.org/bobbin/). PR revisions are appended as new 'rounds'. The lexicon says appviews may reject records that do not treat this field as append-only (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/pulls/pull.json).

Knot-side COBs: concurrent writers on one knot are serialized two ways. A process lock guards the meta-repo (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-xrpc/src/members.rs). Ref updates are compare-and-swap on the tip, retried up to 16 times (MAX_CAS_RETRIES) (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/lib.rs). Linear objects fail with ForkedHistory or DivergedTip rather than merge. Convergent objects merge by deterministic causal ordering (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/backend.rs). Clients cannot push to refs/cobs/* or refs/hidden/*, and COB refs 'cannot be deleted' (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-messages/src/lib.rs).

Planned: the team is re-assessing whether issues and PRs should move onto the knot as the source of truth, with a pointer record left in the user's PDS (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md).
realtime:
Yes, event-driven throughout:
- Knots serve a WebSocket event stream at /events (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html). In Knot 2 it is an in-memory bounded ring buffer with monotonically increasing cursors and cursor-based replay; the oldest events are evicted past capacity, so the stream is not durable (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-events/src/lib.rs).
- Spindles subscribe to the AT Protocol Jetstream for sh.tangled.spindle.member and sh.tangled.repo records; the default is wss://jetstream1.us-west.bsky.network/subscribe. They also subscribe to knot events and stream CI logs over WebSocket (https://docs.tangled.org/spindles.html). CI logs can also be tailed over SSH (https://blog.tangled.org/ssh/).
- The appview and knots read the AT Protocol firehose (https://docs.tangled.org/migrating-knots-and-spindles.html).
- Webhooks cover push, rename and PR events. They are signed with HMAC-SHA256 and get 3 attempts with exponential backoff and a 30 s timeout (https://docs.tangled.org/webhooks.html).
- Bobbin backfills from a Hydrant aggregator over WebSocket starting at cursor 0. That takes about 30 s to 90 s when warm and up to about 20 min cold (https://blog.tangled.org/bobbin/).
search_retrieval:
- Records: the lexicon sh.tangled.search.query defines full-text search over records, filterable by nsid, author DID, repo DID and since/until (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/search/query.json). The appview runs Bleve indexers for repos, issues and pulls (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/tree/master/appview/indexer).
- Code: full-text code search is backed by Zoekt (org.tangled.temp.search.searchCode, still a 'temp' namespace) (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/temp/search/searchCode.json). 'All things search' was a 2026 roadmap item (https://blog.tangled.org/seed/).
- API reads: Bobbin serves list, count and get XRPC endpoints for repos, issues, pulls, comments, stars, follows, labels and pipelines (https://docs.tangled.org/bobbin.html).
- Knot 2 ACL: an index is rebuilt from the meta-repo at startup, and the knot accepts no connection until 'index ready' (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
links_sessions_to_code:
No. I found no agent, session or prompt linkage. The only LLM-related features are defensive:
- 'Vouching', a web of trust against 'LLM spam'. Vouches are public PDS records with a reason, and an evidence-trail feature (attach the merged PR to the vouch record) is planned (https://blog.tangled.org/vouching/).
- The seed announcement's vision of 'one dev and a hundred agents' (https://blog.tangled.org/seed/).
A text search of the monorepo's lexicons and source for LLM, agent and AI terms (commit 3f736f0) found nothing beyond these. The nearest hooks for linking are push options on refUpdate events and arbitrary sh.tangled.repo.artifact records (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/git/refUpdate.json, https://docs.tangled.org/spindles.html).
scale:
- Users and repos: over 7,000 users and over 5,000 repositories as of 2026-03-02 (https://blog.tangled.org/seed/).
- Social layer: Bobbin holds Tangled's entire AT Protocol dataset in about 100 to 200 MB of RAM, and its backfill target is 90 s or less (https://blog.tangled.org/bobbin/).
- Knot 2 COB limits: MAX_GRAPH_CHANGES is 100,000 per object for normal loads, and the rebuild limit scales with available memory (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-cob/src/backend.rs).
- Knot sizing: a knot can be single- or multi-tenant, from a Raspberry Pi up to a community server (https://docs.tangled.org/).
- Missing: I found no published throughput or event-rate numbers.
privacy_security:
Public by design:
- AT Protocol records such as vouches are public (https://blog.tangled.org/vouching/).
- The repo record lexicon has no visibility or private field (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/lexicons/repo/repo.json), and the docs describe anonymous clone (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
- I could not verify that private repos exist at all. The web search budget ran out, so this claim rests on the repo source only.

Redaction: none found, either for content or for logs.

Encryption at rest, Knot 2:
- The sealed key store is AES-256-GCM, keyed by HKDF-SHA256 from a 32-byte master key held in an environment variable (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-secrets/src/lib.rs).
- It holds the knot's and each repo's secp256k1 signing keys. Repo DIDs are derived from these keys; losing the master key means the knot can no longer prove ownership to atproto (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md).
- Migration writes repo-signing-keys.json 'in the clear', and operators are told to move it off the server (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
- COB signatures are made with the knot's key, not the human user's. The human appears only in the payload (for example added_by), so this is server attestation, not end-to-end signing (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/crates/knot-xrpc/src/members.rs).

Authentication:
- SSH keys are read live from each user's PDS on a one-hour lease (keyfill.ttl_secs) (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).
- Since v1.7, inter-service authentication replaced shared knot secrets (https://docs.tangled.org/migrating-knots-and-spindles.html).

Isolation (Go knot 'Secure Mode'): Linux Landlock plus a per-owner virtual UID for each git subprocess (https://docs.tangled.org/knot-self-hosting-guide.html).

CI secrets: stored in spindle SQLite or in OpenBao at spindle/repos/{sanitized_repo_path}/{key}. Workflow environment variables are visible to anyone who can view the repository (https://docs.tangled.org/spindles.html).

Hardening (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/blob/master/knot2/README.md, https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core/tree/master/knot2/crates/knot-cobs/fuzz):
- rate limiting with an explicit trusted-proxy list
- the host key is refused if group- or world-readable
- fuzz targets for COB refs, COB changes and DID documents
lesson_for_parinn:
Knot 2 is a working example of 'git is the only database' for append-only, multi-party records. ParleyInn could copy its pattern if git ever carries session history.

What to copy:
- Model each session or log as a COB-like chain of commits under a reserved ref namespace (refs/cobs/<type>/<root-oid>). The server refuses client pushes and deletion there.
- Put the payload in a single canonical DAG-CBOR blob. Put type, author and signature in commit headers. Sign a domain-separated context ('sh.tangled.knot.cob.change.v1') that binds home, parents, type, author and timestamp.
- Use CAS-on-tip with bounded retries for concurrent writers. Pick per type between a 'Linear' history (no merges, fail loudly) and a 'Convergent' one (DAG with deterministic causal-order fold).
- Treat every index as a projection rebuilt from git, and refuse traffic until it is ready. This fits ParleyInn's I10 (everything derived is rebuildable from the record) and I6 (no silent failures). Bobbin pushes the same idea further: a disk-less projection rebuilt from an event stream in about 90 s.

Where ParleyInn must go further than Tangled:
- Tangled's signatures are server keys, not the writer's own. ParleyInn should sign with per-agent or per-machine keys.
- Its event stream is a lossy in-memory ring. ParleyInn's real-time feed must be replayable from the record itself.
- Everything on the AT Protocol side is public. Session transcripts would need client-side encryption before they touch any forge or PDS, and Tangled offers no redaction to lean on.
confidence: high for architecture and code-level facts. They come from the official docs and from reading the monorepo source at commit 3f736f0 (2026-10-01). medium for hosted-service status and for whether private repos exist, which I could not confirm beyond the source because the web search budget ran out.
license: MIT. The license file says 'Copyright (c) 2025 Anirudh Oppiliappan, Akshay Oppiliappan and contributors' (https://tangled.org/tangled.org/core). Contributions need a DCO Signed-off-by line.

name: Task Master (claude-task-master, npm task-master-ai)
category: AI task manager (PRD-to-task planner, CLI + MCP server), with an optional Hamster cloud backend
status: shipped. Latest version is 0.43.1 (CHANGELOG.md top entry; git tags reach task-master-ai@0.43.0). The newest commit on main I found is c0c98d3, dated 2026-04-23 ("replace retired task-master.dev URLs"). That means no commits for about 5 months before early October 2026. The repo is not archived and shows about 28.1k stars, 163 open issues and 50 open PRs. Product and docs have moved under Hamster (tryhamster.com), which positions it as a funnel to its paid team cloud. Read it as maintained but slowing, not abandoned. I could not confirm npm publish dates because npmjs.com returned 403.
what_is_stored:
It stores plans, not transcripts.
(1) Tasks and subtasks. Fields are id, title, description, status (pending, in-progress, done, deferred and others), dependencies, priority, details, testStrategy and subtasks. An optional free-form `metadata` JSON field arrived in 0.43.0, for things like external IDs.
(2) Per-tag metadata: created, updated and description.
(3) PRDs and design docs in .taskmaster/docs/.
(4) AI complexity reports per tag in .taskmaster/reports/.
(5) Generated per-task text files (task_NNN_<tag>.txt).
(6) state.json: current tag, lastSwitched, branchTagMapping, upgrade-prompt telemetry and exportedTags (a tag mapped to a Hamster briefId/briefUrl).
(7) config.json for model and provider settings.
(8) loop-progress.txt, which carries context across iterations of the `loop` command that drives Claude.
(9) For the TDD autopilot workflow, workflow-state.json plus backups and an append-only activity.jsonl event log (one event per line: timestamp, type, phase and so on).
It does not store Claude Code transcripts, prompts or tool calls.
where_stored: Files in the working tree under <repo>/.taskmaster/ (tasks/tasks.json, docs/, reports/, state.json, config.json), meant to be committed to git. Workflow and session state lives outside the repo, in ~/.taskmaster/<sanitized-abs-path>/sessions/. The code comments say this is "to avoid git noise", and the directory naming copies Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects path sanitization. Team mode can instead switch storage to Hamster's cloud API (default https://tryhamster.com/api, Supabase auth). The storage factory has 'file', 'api' and 'auto' modes. In 'auto' it picks API storage when the user is logged in and has a brief selected.
format_and_model: tasks.json is one pretty-printed JSON object keyed by tag name: {"master": {"tasks": [...], "metadata": {...}}, "<tag>": {...}}. Task ids are small sequential integers within a tag. Subtask ids are written as parent.child, for example 5.2. Dependencies are id arrays, so tasks form a DAG, and validate-dependencies checks for cycles. Tags are the workstream or branch unit. Commands can move tasks across tags, with dependency-conflict handling. The hosted docs say each tag gets its own file (tasks_feature-auth.json). The current code (PathResolver) and the repo's own tasks.json use a single tasks.json keyed by tag instead, so the docs and the code disagree. activity.jsonl is plain NDJSON. Nothing is hashed, chained or signed.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Local processes: writes take a cross-process lock with proper-lockfile, and the legacy JS path has its own `<file>.lock` with stale-lock recovery. They go through steno for atomic writes. Each write rewrites the whole file, and the code says this is to prevent lost updates.
Across branches and machines: nothing beyond git. Sequential per-tag ids collide when two branches each add tasks. The official tutorial says to resolve tasks.json merge conflicts by hand or with an agent, renumbering your own tasks with `task-master move --from=10 --to=16`. There is no merge driver, no CRDT and no stable unique ids. Tags are offered as the way to isolate parallel work and avoid conflicts (`add-tag --from-branch`, plus branchTagMapping in state.json).
Team mode: Hamster's server is the single source of truth. Its conflict resolution is not documented.
realtime: Solo or file mode: not real time. Changes spread through git commits and pulls. Team mode, per Hamster's docs: "tasks are stored in the cloud and synced in real-time across all team members", and `tm list --watch` uses cloud sync instead of file watching. Teams are capped at 10 members by email. Separately, `loop --verbose` streams Claude's output live to the terminal, but it is not persisted.
search_retrieval: No search index and no full-text or semantic search over history. Retrieval goes through structured commands and MCP tools: list (filter by status or tag), show <id>, next (the highest-priority task whose dependencies are met), complexity-report. The MCP server has 36 tools, about 21k tokens of context by default, and you can load a subset with TASK_MASTER_TOOLS. The `research` command makes outbound LLM or Perplexity calls with task and file context. It is not retrieval over stored history.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, and only from task to commit. The TDD autopilot's default commit template adds "Task: <id>", "Phase: <red/green>" and "Tests: N passing" lines to commit messages, and branch names are generated from tasks. Tags can map to git branches. Nothing links agent sessions, prompts or transcripts to code. activity.jsonl records workflow phases, not conversation content.
scale: No published scale claims for data size. The only number is MCP context cost: 36 tools, about 21,000 tokens. The single-file JSON model is rewritten in full on every write, which suits hundreds of tasks, not event streams. Team mode is capped at 10 members. Adoption: about 28.1k GitHub stars and 2.6k forks.
privacy_security: No redaction, encryption or integrity protection for stored task data. tasks.json and the PRDs are plaintext in the repo. Provider API keys go only in .env or the MCP client's env block, and the docs reserve .env for keys only. The core is network-heavy by design. It calls many LLM providers and Perplexity research, and in team mode Hamster does all AI inference and stores tasks on its servers. state.json holds upgrade-prompt telemetry and Hamster brief URLs. There is no treatment of stored task text as untrusted. AI-written `details` fields are fed straight back to the agent through MCP or CLI output, so content in tasks.json, which can arrive by a git pull from anyone, is a prompt-injection path. Hamster's security and encryption practices are not documented on the team page.
lesson_for_parinn: Two lessons. First, keep whole-file JSON with sequential ids out of git for multi-writer data. Task Master's official answer to concurrent edits is to hand-renumber task ids after a tasks.json merge conflict. ParleyInn records should be append-only, one record per file or line, with content-addressed or ULID ids. Then branches and machines merge by set union, with no renumbering and no merge driver. Second, Task Master already splits state the way ParleyInn would. Shared, reviewable artifacts (plans and PRDs) go in the repo under .taskmaster/. Noisy per-machine session state (workflow-state.json, activity.jsonl) goes in ~/.taskmaster/<sanitized-path>/, keyed like Claude Code's own project dirs. Its "real-time across machines" story, though, only exists by giving up local-first and moving to a hosted server, which ParleyInn's I4 (no network) forbids. A git-carried, union-mergeable record plus an optional external relay is the gap ParleyInn could fill. Also, any recalled task or plan text pulled from a shared repo must be enveloped as untrusted (I2). Task Master injects it verbatim.
license: MIT with Commons Clause ("Task Master License"), copyright Eyal Toledano and Ralph Khreish. Not OSI open source: it bars selling the tool or offering it as a hosted service.

name: Temporal
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Workflow execution histories as append-only event sequences (WorkflowExecutionStarted, WorkflowTaskScheduled, WorkflowTaskCompleted, ActivityTaskScheduled, ActivityTaskCompleted, TimerFired, etc.), plus 'Mutable State' (in-memory cache + persistent summaries of current execution state: active activities, timers, child workflows, signals), and internal task queues (Transfer Task queue for immediate work, Timer Task queue for scheduled work).
where_stored: Pluggable persistence layer supporting Cassandra (primary), MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite. Self-hosted on-premise deployments or Temporal Cloud (managed SaaS). Primary schema tables: history_node (workflow history events with branching support), history_tree (branch metadata), executions (mutable state + tasks), tasks (activity/workflow task queues).
format_and_model: Protocol Buffers v3 for serialization of events, mutable state, and payloads. Event sourcing: workflow state reconstructable from history alone. Events stored in batches (serialized_event_batch) with encoding type. Mutable state stored as binary blob with configurable encoding. Supports schema evolution through proto versioning.
multi_writer_and_merge: Single writer per History Shard enforced via Ringpop membership protocol and RangeID monotonic generation number (fencing). State transitions are atomic transactions: History Events appended, Mutable State updated, and History Tasks created within single database transaction. Conflict resolution available for multi-region replicated workflows via branch management (branch_id in history_tree). No simultaneous writers to same shard; ownership is exclusive and coordinated cluster-wide.
realtime: Polling-based task delivery model: Workers continuously poll task queues (Matching Service) for work. Transfer Task queue processes immediately when created; Timer Task queue triggers at scheduled time. Queue processors asynchronously dequeue tasks via QueueProcessor goroutines. History Service appends events and creates tasks on RPC/timer events; tasks propagate to Matching Service via Transfer Task queue processor (typically milliseconds latency). No continuous streaming or subscriptions; pull-based architecture.
search_retrieval: Visibility layer provides search and filtering of workflow executions via Search Attributes (custom index fields). Pluggable visibility backends: Elasticsearch or database-backed (SQL/Cassandra). List Filters enable querying by standard attributes (status, start time, etc.) and custom Search Attributes. History Events retrieved via GetHistoryEvents RPC; events returned in order they were appended. Pagination supported for large histories.
links_sessions_to_code: Workflows are deterministic user code in supported SDKs (Go, Java, Python, TypeScript, Rust, .NET, C++). Workers execute workflow and activity code; they poll Matching Service task queues and respond with task results/commands. Workflow code can call Activities (user-defined work executed in user processes) or child workflows (nested Workflow Executions). SDK correlation: gRPC connection from Worker to History/Matching services, task execution metadata includes workflow_id + run_id + task type. No automatic tracing between agent sessions; must be manually tracked via workflow input/output or search attributes.
privacy_security: Encryption at rest available in Temporal Cloud and self-hosted deployments (configurable). Secrets management: SDK interceptors can redact sensitive data before storage. Network isolation: can run entirely on-premise with no external dependencies. TLS support for all gRPC connections. Audit logging of workflow state transitions. Temporal Cloud: role-based access control, namespaces for multi-tenancy, compliance certifications. Data payloads stored in workflow history as binary blobs; redaction must happen at SDK layer before persistence.
lesson_for_parinn: Event sourcing with append-only history is production-proven at scale (1.9T events/month). Key insights: (1) Separate execution log (history) from mutable state caches improves query latency without losing consistency. (2) Branching support via branch_id critical for reset/conflict resolution workflows. (3) Single-writer enforcement via fencing (RangeID) prevents concurrent write conflicts more elegantly than distributed locks. (4) Task queues as first-class abstraction for routing work enables scalable task dispatch independent from history storage. (5) Visibility/search is separate concern from execution engine, allowing independent scaling. (6) Transactional Outbox pattern ensures consistency between history and external systems without 2PC. For ParleyInn: consider whether branching (for agent reset/backtracking) and visibility search are requirements; if so, Temporal's separation of history + mutable state + visibility is a proven model.

name: Terragon (Terragon Labs), open-source snapshot terragon-oss
category: cloud background-agent orchestrator (hosted SaaS; now a dead service with a code snapshot)
status: archived. The hosted service shut down on 9 Feb 2026 and all sandboxes were terminated (https://www.terragonlabs.com/ ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/docs/content/docs/resources/shutdown.mdx). The README carries a snapshot notice dated 16 Jan 2026 saying the code is "as-is", with no maintenance (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/README.md). The last commit, 83142a1, is dated 10 Feb 2026 (seen in a clone of the repo). The shutdown doc gives the reason: the service did not reach "the level of traction needed". I could not confirm GitHub's "archived" repo flag because the GitHub API returned 403 to me. Launch evidence: a Show HN post on 4 Sep 2025 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45127766).
what_is_stored:
Four kinds of data.
(1) Per-task transcripts. A "thread" is a task. Each thread has one or more "thread_chat" rows, one per agent conversation, and each holds a normalized message log. Message types are user, agent (text and thinking), system, tool-call, tool-result, git-diff, stop, error, meta (system-init and result with cost, turns and session_id), thread-context and thread-context-result. Each chat also stores queued follow-up messages, the agent's sessionId, status, context length and permission mode (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/db/db-message.ts ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/db/schema.ts#L248-L262).
(2) The raw, native Claude Code session file. This is the ~/.claude/projects/<proj>/<sessionId>.jsonl file, copied out of the sandbox, for Claude Code only (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/claude-session-internal.ts).
(3) Code state. Each task's work goes to its own git branch and PR on GitHub. The thread row also keeps the latest full git diff text and diff stats (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/db/schema.ts#L265-L336).
(4) Account data: encrypted per-repo environment variables and MCP config, encrypted agent credentials (API keys and OAuth tokens), GitHub PR and check-run mirrors, automations, usage and credit events (same schema.ts). Attachments (images, PDFs, audio, text files) go to Cloudflare R2 (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/r2-file-upload.ts).
where_stored:
Three hosted places plus a GitHub remote.
- PostgreSQL through the Drizzle ORM holds threads, chats and the message JSONB (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/AGENTS.md).
- A private Cloudflare R2 bucket holds the Claude JSONL snapshots. Keys follow claude-sessions/<userId>/<threadId>/<sessionId>-<uuid>-<ts>.txt, with a 100 MB cap per file (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/r2-file-upload.ts#L78-L84 , #L145).
- GitHub branches and PRs hold the code.
- Sandboxes (E2B, Daytona, Docker) are ephemeral working copies. Each task's sandbox makes a blobless clone (`--filter=blob:none`) of the repo (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/sandbox/src/setup.ts#L146-L163).
- Redis is used for rate limiting (AGENTS.md).
Nothing about sessions is stored in git itself: no notes, no custom refs, no files in the working tree. The CLI writes a pulled transcript into the local ~/.claude/projects directory (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/cli/src/commands/pull.tsx#L96-L105).
format_and_model:
Relational rows with JSON columns.
- thread: one row per task. Columns include user_id, github_repo_full_name, repo_base_branch_name, current_branch_name, github_pr_number, github_issue_number, the sandbox id and provider, git_diff (text), git_diff_stats (jsonb), parent_thread_id, automation_id, disable_git_checkpointing and source_type/metadata. A version column records the layout: 0 means the chat lives inline on the thread row, 1 means a separate thread_chat table (schema.ts#L265-L336).
- thread_chat: id, thread_id, agent, agent_version, status, messages jsonb (DBMessage[]), queued_messages jsonb and session_id (schema.ts#L343-L369).
- Message ids: there is no per-message row. Messages are elements of one growing JSONB array per chat, with no sequence number and no hash. Tool calls and results carry tool ids and parent_tool_use_id (db-message.ts).
- claude_session_checkpoints: (thread_id, session_id) is unique and r2_key points at the latest uploaded JSONL. The pointer is upserted, so an older snapshot object is no longer referenced. I did not see a lifecycle rule for orphaned objects, so their fate is unverified (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/model/claude-session.ts).
- Git side: ordinary commits on a per-task branch. Commit messages are generated by an LLM from the diff, plus a Co-authored-by trailer naming the GitHub App bot (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/sandbox/src/commands/git-commit-and-push.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Transcripts have one writer: the task's owner.
- Every update is filtered by user_id. Other users get read-only views through the visibility setting (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/model/threads.ts#L424-L519).
- Within a thread, separate thread_chats let several agent conversations run side by side.
- Appends are server-side SQL, `messages = COALESCE(messages,'[]') || $new::jsonb`, inside a transaction. Postgres's row lock makes concurrent appends atomic, and their order is commit order. Merging is never needed because the server is the single point of serialization (threads.ts#L830-L947).
- The in-sandbox daemon buffers messages, groups them by threadChatId, and retries with backoff. On failure it puts unsent entries back at the head of the buffer, preserving order. There is no idempotency key, so a retry after a lost response could duplicate entries; this is an inference from the code, not a documented behavior (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/daemon/src/daemon.ts#L1008-L1158).
Code merges go through git.
- Each task gets a unique branch, and pushing to the default branch is refused.
- A rejected (non-fast-forward) push triggers git fetch, then `git rebase origin/<branch>`, then a second push. If the rebase hits conflicts it is aborted and the error is reported as CONFLICT (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/sandbox/src/commands/git-push-with-rebase.ts).
- On a failed push the server sends the agent a "retry-git-commit-and-push" system message so it can try to fix the problem itself (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/checkpoint-thread-internal.ts#L234-L258).
- "git fsck" runs before each push as an integrity check (git-commit-and-push.ts).
- Forking a task creates a new thread seeded with an LLM summary of the parent. It is a copy, not a merge (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/docs/content/docs/resources/release-notes.mdx#L43-L45).
realtime:
Yes, near-real-time, server-mediated, with notify-then-refetch.
1. The sandbox daemon debounces agent stdout messages, by default for 1000 ms (daemon.ts#L85).
2. It POSTs each batch to /api/daemon-event with an X-Daemon-Token header (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/daemon/src/runtime.ts#L179-L197 ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/app/api/daemon-event/route.ts).
3. The server appends to Postgres, then POSTs a small notice (ids plus a messagesUpdated flag) to a per-user PartyKit room. PartyKit runs as a stateless, hibernating WebSocket broadcaster (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/shared/src/broadcast-server.ts ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/broadcast/src/server.ts).
4. Browsers then refetch.
A separate PartyKit party streams an interactive terminal (PTY) into the sandbox (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/broadcast/src/sandbox.ts).
The raw JSONL is not real-time. It is uploaded only at checkpoint time, when a task finishes (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/checkpoint-thread.ts#L94-L101).
Sessions have no peer-to-peer or git-based real-time path.
search_retrieval:
No full-text or semantic search over transcripts. I found no tsvector, ILIKE or embedding code over messages; this was a grep of the snapshot.
- Indexes cover user_id combined with created_at, updated_at, status or archived, plus repo with PR number, parent thread, schedule and source type (schema.ts#L317-L335).
- Retrieval is by thread id. The `terry pull <taskId>` CLI fetches the thread over oRPC. The server reads the JSONL from R2 first; if it is missing, it reads it from the live sandbox and backfills R2 (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/claude-session.ts ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server/orpc/cli-router.ts#L73-L107).
- Context reuse works only by LLM summarization. /compact and fork turn the history into text, with tool results cut to 1000 characters, and summarize it with gpt-4.1-mini (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/compact.ts ; https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/lib/thread-to-msg-formatter.ts#L140-L160).
- An MCP server exposes task list, create and pull tools (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/docs/content/docs/integrations/cli.mdx).
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, but mostly from the session side, by repo, branch and PR name, not by commit SHA.
- The thread row records repo, base branch, current branch, PR number and issue number, plus a snapshot of the latest diff (schema.ts#L265-L336).
- github_pr maps (repo, number) to thread_id (schema.ts#L393-L420).
- At each checkpoint where the diff changed, a git-diff message is appended into the transcript (checkpoint-thread-internal.ts).
- From code back to the session, the only link is the PR body, which includes "Task: <app>/task/<threadId>" (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/agent/pull-request.ts#L161-L165). Since 9 Feb 2026 those links point at a service that no longer exists.
- Commits carry no session id or prompt, only an LLM-written message and a bot co-author trailer.
- For local handoff, `terry pull` checks out the task branch and writes the JSONL into ~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<sessionId>.jsonl so `claude --resume` works. Code travels via git and the transcript via object storage (pull.tsx#L53-L105).
scale: The repo and docs contain no quantitative scale claims, such as user counts, sessions or throughput, as far as I found. I could not check secondary sources because my web-search budget was used up. Built-in limits: a Claude JSONL upload is capped at 100 MB (r2-file-upload.ts#L78-L84); diffs fed to commit-message generation are cut off at 200,000 bytes (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/sandbox/src/utils.ts#L15). The design keeps each chat's whole history in one JSONB value that is rewritten on every append, which suggests long transcripts were costly. That is an inference, not a measured claim.
privacy_security:
Secrets are encrypted at rest; transcripts are not.
- Encrypted with AES-256-GCM: environment variables, the MCP config, agent API keys and OAuth tokens, and the GitHub OAuth token. Each value gets its own random salt and IV, and its key is derived by scrypt from a single master key (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/utils/src/encryption.ts ; schema.ts#L512-L545, #L1133-L1160).
- Transcripts (the messages JSONB and the R2 JSONL) have no application-level encryption and no redaction. I found no redact or mask code. sanitizeForJson only strips invalid characters such as null bytes (threads.ts#L855-L860).
- Attachment buckets (images, PDFs, audio, text) are configured as "public". The session JSONL bucket is "private" (r2-file-upload.ts).
- Sandbox credentials:
  - GitHub OAuth asks for the "repo" and "workflow" scopes (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/components/auth.tsx#L55).
  - The user's token is written in plain text to ~/.git-credentials (credential.helper store) inside each sandbox, where the agent can read it (setup.ts#L166-L201).
  - The daemon reads BYO Claude credentials from ~/.claude/.credentials.json inside the sandbox (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/packages/daemon/src/claude.ts).
  - In credit mode the platform's Anthropic key stays server-side behind /api/proxy/anthropic (daemon.ts#L633-L640).
- Daemon to server: the token is a Better Auth API key that expires after 1 day (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/agent/daemon.ts#L38).
- Visibility: private, link (any logged-in user with the link) or repo (gated on the viewer's GitHub repo permission). Admins can read every thread (threads.ts#L424-L519).
- Third-party processing: transcripts and diffs go to OpenAI gpt-4.1-mini for summaries and commit messages (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/generate-commit-message.ts#L15).
- Prompt injection:
  - Fork and compact summaries, which include tool output, are injected back into the agent as a plain user message: "Context from previous task: ..." (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/www/src/server-lib/thread-context.ts).
  - Slack and GitHub thread context is likewise formatted into prompts.
  - The docs admit the injection risk and rely on sandboxing, user scoping and author allow-lists for automations (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/apps/docs/content/docs/security-permissions.mdx).
- At shutdown users were told to "download any important data" before 9 Feb 2026 (shutdown.mdx).
license: Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/LICENSE). A separate TRADEMARKS.md bars using the Terragon name or branding for hosted forks (https://github.com/terragon-labs/terragon-oss/blob/83142a17f3970df3e14d1879234a603db6e4f615/TRADEMARKS.md).
lesson_for_parinn:
Git worked well for moving code between sandboxes, but the session record lived only in a hosted service, and when that service died the record died with it.
Terragon kept three copies with different owners: native Claude JSONL in R2 (whole-file snapshots with an overwritten pointer), a lossy normalized JSONB log in Postgres, and code on per-task GitHub branches. The only link back from code to session was a PR-body URL. Since the 9 Feb 2026 shutdown those PRs point at dead task pages, and the transcripts exist only if users exported them in time.
For ParleyInn this argues for three things:
1. Make the append-only, hash-chained record self-contained and portable: a file or object an agent's machine owns, which can be verified offline. Never make the record depend on a server.
2. Link record and code by commit SHA in both directions, never by a hosted URL.
3. Treat git or any server as a transport, not as the system of record.
Terragon also shows the I2 failure mode in practice. Its fork and compact features turned prior history, including tool output, into a model-written summary and injected it as plain user text. ParleyInn should keep recall pull-only and enveloped.
confidence: high. The storage, merge, real-time and security facts come from reading the snapshot source at commit 83142a1 and its bundled docs. Three points are lower: the absence of scale figures is unverified because I had no web search left; GitHub's archived flag is unconfirmed because the API returned 403; and the duplicate-on-retry behavior and JSONB append cost are inferences from the code.

name: torchwood (filippo.io/torchwood), including litewitness, witnessctl and litebastion
status: shipped. v0.10.0 was tagged on 2026-09-24 and is still pre-v1. The repo is active, not archived: commits landed on 2026-10-01, and NEWS.md lists an unreleased new mpt package (https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood ; https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood). I saw the commit dates and NEWS.md in a local clone of https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood. The GitHub API refused access in this session, so I could not check the repo's archived flag. The GitHub page fetched on 2026-10-02 showed no archive banner and about 30 stars and 18 forks.
what_is_stored:
torchwood holds no agent history. It is tooling for transparency logs (tlogs), and it stores three kinds of data.
(1) Client library: verified tlog tiles. These are Merkle hash tiles and data tiles, also called entry bundles. Entries are opaque byte records that some log server produced. The library also parses checkpoints (signed tree heads) and cosignatures (https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood#Client).
(2) litewitness: only per-log witness state. For each log origin it keeps the latest tree size and root hash, the log's verifier keys, and optional bastion addresses. It never stores log entries. Its SQLite schema has three tables: log(origin TEXT PRIMARY KEY, tree_size INTEGER, tree_hash TEXT base64), key(origin, key), and bastion(origin, bastion) (internal/witness/witness.go in https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood).
(3) Newer subpackages. prefix is an append-only compressed binary Merkle trie, a key-value accumulator over 32-byte keys and values, compatible with akd's whatsapp_v1. mpt is a Merkle Patricia Tree for publishing a provable history of a key-value database; it is unreleased. tesserax adapts tessera.LogReader to TileReader. All three are documented in their package doc comments in the repo and in NEWS.md (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/NEWS.md).
where_stored:
The client stores no state by default. Tiles come from a remote HTTP server (TileFetcher), from an fs.FS directory (TileFS, optionally with gzip data tiles), or from numbered zip archives such as 000.zip (TileArchiveFS). PermanentCache optionally writes verified, non-partial tiles to a local filesystem directory in the c2sp.org/tlog-tiles path layout (https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood#NewPermanentCache).
litewitness stores its state in a local SQLite file (-db, default litewitness.db). The file must sit on a filesystem that supports locking, not a network filesystem. Its private key is never stored by litewitness: it stays in a dedicated ssh-agent reached over a Unix socket (-ssh-agent), which can be backed by a key file, PKCS#11 or a hardware agent (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/cmd/litewitness/README.md).
None of it uses git.
format_and_model:
The data model is an append-only Merkle tree log in the RFC 6962 / Go sumdb style. The library builds on golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog and golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/note (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood).
- Wire and storage layout follow C2SP specs. Tiles are static files under tile/<level>/<index> (c2sp.org/tlog-tiles). Checkpoints are signed notes: an origin line, the tree size and a base64 root hash, then signature lines (c2sp.org/tlog-checkpoint, c2sp.org/signed-note). Witnesses add timestamped cosignatures, using Ed25519 or, since v0.10.0, ML-DSA-44 (c2sp.org/tlog-cosignature).
- Proofs are portable "spicy signatures" per c2sp.org/tlog-proof@v1: an entry, its inclusion proof and a cosigned checkpoint bundled together and verifiable offline (FormatProof, VerifyProof). v0.10.0 added subtree hashes and subtree proofs.
- Trust is expressed as a configurable Policy, for example ThresholdPolicy(2, OriginPolicy(origin), SingleVerifierPolicy(logKey)). A k-of-n witness quorum composes the same way. ParsePolicy reads a text format based on Sigsum policies that the docs mark EXPERIMENTAL.
- The default entry framing is the tlog-tiles format (ReadTileEntry). Sumdb framing is selectable with WithCutEntry(ReadSumDBEntry).
- Client.Entries returns a Go iterator of (index, entry) pairs, with each entry verified against a caller-verified tlog.Tree.
Sources: https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood ; https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles ; https://c2sp.org/tlog-checkpoint ; https://c2sp.org/tlog-cosignature ; https://c2sp.org/tlog-proof
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no merge. A tlog has exactly one sequencer, the log operator, and a fork counts as misbehaviour, not as something to reconcile.
Witnesses exist to detect split views. Under c2sp.org/tlog-witness, a log POSTs its new checkpoint to /add-checkpoint together with the old size it believes the witness holds and a consistency proof. If the old size does not match, litewitness answers HTTP 409 with its known size (Content-Type text/x.tlog.size), and the log retries with a proof from that size.
Concurrent requests are handled by a compare-and-swap in SQL rather than a transaction: UPDATE log SET tree_size=?, tree_hash=? WHERE origin=? AND tree_size=?. If the update changes 0 rows, the request returns a conflict, which prevents a rollback race. A source comment explains that this design avoids hiding a security property inside implicit connection reuse.
witnessctl deliberately cannot remove a log. Its README says removal "presents the risk of signing a split view if re-added"; to disable a log, you remove its keys instead. witnessctl can safely edit the database while litewitness is running.
Sources: https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/cmd/litewitness/README.md ; internal/witness/witness.go in https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood ; https://c2sp.org/tlog-witness
realtime:
litewitness is described as a "synchronous low-latency cosigning witness": it cosigns inline when the log submits a checkpoint. It can listen on HTTP, which needs external TLS termination, or with -no-listen it can serve only through outbound bastion connections (c2sp.org/https-bastion). That lets a witness behind NAT be reached without opening ports.
The client follows a log by polling, not by subscription. Entries waits up to the WithTimeout default of 5 minutes for each next entry and may stop before a partial data tile. Clients that tail a growing log are told to fetch the next checkpoint and resume from it.
Sources: https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/cmd/litewitness/README.md ; https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood#Client.Entries
search_retrieval:
Retrieval is by entry index only. Client.Entries and AllEntries iterate from a start index, and ReadTileEntry splits entries out of a data tile. Proof functions show that a record is included (CheckRecordInSubtree, VerifyProof) or that two trees are consistent.
There is no content search or full-text index. Key-based lookup with inclusion and non-inclusion proofs is offered only by the separate prefix and mpt key-value structures.
Sources: https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood ; package docs in https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/tree/main/prefix and /mpt
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. torchwood has no notion of agent sessions, prompts or commits. Entries are opaque bytes. The cmd/ tools around it target transparency for age keyservers and apt package repos (cmd/age-keyserver, cmd/apt-transport-tlog), not agent sessions (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/tree/main/cmd).
scale:
I found no explicit scale claims for torchwood itself. Its design is static tiles that are cacheable, served from a CDN, filesystem or zip, plus PermanentCache and WithConcurrencyLimit. That design inherits the scaling model of c2sp.org/tlog-tiles, which the static CT ecosystem uses for very large logs (https://c2sp.org/tlog-tiles ; https://c2sp.org/static-ct-api).
litewitness state is O(number of logs), a few rows per log. witnessctl pull-logs imports logs in bulk from the transparency-dev witness-network log lists (https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/cmd/litewitness/README.md).
Neither throughput nor latency figures are published, so I could not verify any.
privacy_security:
- There is no encryption and no redaction of log contents. Tlogs are public by design, and the README says the tlog-witness protocol "is not designed to keep the supported logs or their tree states secret".
- The witness private key never touches litewitness memory or disk. Signing goes through a dedicated ssh-agent socket, which enables PKCS#11 or hardware keys. The README states that litewitness has no access to secrets apart from client IP addresses, and those are always redacted from /logz.
- -obscurity mode turns off the /, /logz and /metrics endpoints so the set of known logs is harder to enumerate. -listen-metrics can split metrics onto their own listener.
- Since v0.10.0 the library supports post-quantum ML-DSA-44 cosignatures.
- Recent hardening commits (2026-10-01): origins must be 1 to 255 bytes, and consistency checks at size zero are now enforced.
- Like all tlog clients, it verifies everything against a caller-verified checkpoint and a signature policy before yielding data.
Sources: https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/cmd/litewitness/README.md ; https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood/blob/main/NEWS.md ; commit log of https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood
lesson_for_parinn:
ParleyInn should adopt the tlog formats, not invent its own chain format. Concretely:
- Lay out the append-only session record as c2sp.org/tlog-tiles: immutable static tiles plus a signed-note checkpoint per session log.
- Fork detection: each sandbox or machine cosigns, or simply remembers, the last checkpoint it saw. A replica that receives a checkpoint not consistent with its stored (size, hash) rejects it, using litewitness's compare-and-swap on tree_size and its 409 known-size reply as the pattern.
- Transport: because tiles are immutable files, any dumb channel can carry them without ParleyInn's core touching the network (invariant I4). That includes a git branch, a zip bundle (TileArchiveFS) or an fs.FS directory (TileFS). An integrity failure is then detectable rather than silently merged (I6).
- Witness keys: litewitness's model of keeping the signing key in an external ssh-agent and keeping no secrets in the service is a good model for ParleyInn's key handling.
- Caveat 1: torchwood's TileFetcher speaks HTTP. ParleyInn's shipped core could import only the offline parts (TileFS, checkpoint, proof and policy verification) or reimplement them over golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog. Even then, depguard and the import-closure test would have to prove that net/http stays out.
- Caveat 2: torchwood is pre-v1, and its policy format is explicitly experimental. As a direct dependency it would need an ADR under ENG-18 and ENG-26.
- Caveat 3: tlogs are single-writer, so many agents would need one log per writer, with the logs cross-referenced, rather than merges.
license: BSD-3-Clause (https://pkg.go.dev/filippo.io/torchwood). It has 13 direct dependencies, including zombiezen.com/go/sqlite (backed by modernc.org/sqlite), tessera, sigsum-go, prometheus client_golang and golang.org/x/net, according to go.mod in https://github.com/FiloSottile/torchwood.

name: Traces (traces.com), Lab 0324, Inc.
category: hosted share network + git notes (pointer-only commit linkage); proprietary SaaS with local CLI and SQLite cache
status: shipped
license: Proprietary. The CLI is closed source. The npm package @traces-sh/traces (latest 0.6.36, modified 2026-10-01, 109 versions since 2026-01-28) has no license and no repository field, and ships only prebuilt platform binaries (https://registry.npmjs.org/@traces-sh/traces). The 'open source CLI' promised at launch (https://www.traces.com/blog/introducing-traces) has still not appeared: the traces-sh GitHub org has one public repo, mcp, under Apache-2.0 (https://github.com/traces-sh, https://github.com/traces-sh/mcp). Self-hosting and on-prem come only on the paid Custom plan (https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-for-teams). I could not find the @traces-sh/mcp package that the docs name on npm (registry returned 'Not found').
what_is_stored: Normalized coding-agent sessions ('traces'). Agent-specific adapters read each agent's native store (Claude Code JSONL, Cursor SQLite, Codex JSON, and others) and turn it into typed trace messages (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/supported-agents). Each trace has metadata: externalId, title, agentId, model, visibility, projectPath/projectName, gitRemoteUrl/gitBranch/gitRef, token usage, author, and subagent/resume relationships. It also carries a server-generated ai_analysis (summary, status, steps, badges, keywords) (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/traces). Messages have a role, textContent, an order (UInt32) and a timestamp. Each message holds parts: text, thinking, tool calls, tool results (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/messages, https://www.traces.com/docs/traces-web/exports). Local event types are user_message, agent_text, agent_thinking, tool_call, tool_result and error (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/search). Git holds only pointers: one line per trace, 'traces:<externalId> <sharedUrl>' (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks). Per the privacy policy, the server stores messages, tool calls and results, timestamps, agent and model ids, and project paths (https://www.traces.com/privacy). The service does not claim an append-only or hash-chained record. Writes are idempotent upserts keyed by caller-chosen IDs (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference).
where_stored:
Three places.
(1) Local SQLite cache. The docs mention 'local SQLite' (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks, https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/troubleshooting). The CLI binary embeds the path ~/.traces/traces.db (strings of npm tarball traces-linux-x64-0.6.36: https://registry.npmjs.org/@traces-sh/traces-linux-x64/-/traces-linux-x64-0.6.36.tgz). Per-worktree session state lives in traces-active.json inside the git dir (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/agent-hooks).
(2) The hosted server: API at https://actions.traces.com (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference) and hosted MCP at https://mcp.traces.com (https://www.traces.com/docs/mcp). The binary's staging endpoint is a *.convex.site host, so the backend appears to be Convex. That is inferred from the binary and not documented.
(3) Git: a custom notes ref, refs/notes/traces, pushed to the code remote (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or self-hosted) (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks, https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/cli-discovery).
Exports are ZIPs of JSONL that can optionally be pushed to a HuggingFace dataset (https://www.traces.com/docs/traces-web/exports).
format_and_model:
Server model: trace -> messages -> parts, keyed by stable external IDs that the integration supplies. Reusing an ID updates the same resource, which makes retries safe. Timestamps are milliseconds since epoch. Responses use a {ok,data}/{ok,error} JSON envelope. Routes: PUT /v1/traces/{externalId}, PUT /v1/traces/{id}/messages/{messageId}, POST /v1/traces/{id}/messages/batch, GET /v1/traces?gitRemoteUrl= (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference, https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/traces, https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/messages).
Export format: manifest.json plus traces.jsonl, messages.jsonl and parts.jsonl, at most 50 MB per file (https://www.traces.com/docs/traces-web/exports).
Git note format: plain text, one 'traces:<externalId>[ <sharedUrl>]' line per trace. The 'traces:' prefix avoids collisions with other note tools (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks). The binary also parses 'traces-detach:<id>' lines (binary observation, v0.6.36).
Client limits embedded in the binary: maxEventBytes 524288, maxBatchBytes 8 MiB, maxBatchItems 1000 (binary observation).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Git side (docs, plus the shipped hook code in v0.6.36):
- Notes are appended, never replaced, so several teammates can each attach a trace to the same commit (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks).
- Local writes run as a small transaction. The CLI copies refs/notes/traces to a temporary ref, refs/notes/transactions/traces/<pid>-<rand>-<n>. It runs 'git notes append' there, then compare-and-swaps the result with 'git update-ref refs/notes/traces <new> <old>', retrying up to 3 times.
- The pre-push hook has a 5 s budget. It fetches the remote notes into refs/notes/incoming/traces/<token> (using --refmap=), merges them with 'git notes merge --strategy=cat_sort_uniq', then runs 'git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null push <remote> refs/notes/traces'. If the push fails it re-merges once and retries. It always exits 0, so it never blocks the code push. The blog confirms that pre-push is the only piece that touches the remote (https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-git). The docs page instead lists 'pushes notes' as a post-commit step, which is an inconsistency.
- Older setups configured forced fetch refspecs (+refs/notes/traces:refs/notes/traces). Current setup removes them and adds notes.rewriteRef=refs/notes/traces, so notes follow amend and rebase (binary observation).
- pre-merge-commit and post-merge hooks attribute local merge commits and deliberately skip pulls (binary observation).
- For worktrees, dispatchers live in the common hooks dir and active-session state is kept per worktree (https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-git).
Server side: the server is the single authority. Concurrent writers converge through idempotent upserts by external ID. No CRDT or merge semantics are documented (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference). Organizations are namespaces, and a trace can be moved with 'traces transfer' (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/commands).
realtime:
Near-real-time through the hosted service, not through git.
- Agent hooks fire on session start, prompt submit and agent completion, and upload 'in the background as the agent works' (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/agent-hooks).
- 'traces share --follow' keeps syncing, and 'New messages appear in real time' (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/cli).
- 'traces refresh' uploads only new events under the same URL (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/cli).
- Git notes spread only when someone pushes. Discovery happens when the TUI reads refs/notes/traces from recent commits (https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-git).
- Write rate limit: 600 requests per minute per user (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference).
- 'traces resume' hands off to the same agent or a different one, either as an exact native resume (macOS only) or as a new session seeded from the trace with a 'Resumed from' link (https://www.traces.com/blog/handoffs, https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/commands).
search_retrieval:
Local search: 'traces search' runs case-insensitive regex (or --literal) over the local SQLite store, covering trace metadata and saved event text. By default it searches only user_message, agent_text and error events. Tool calls and results and thinking must be requested explicitly. Scan budgets (--scan-traces, --scan-events-per-trace) bound the work (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/search).
Bounded reading: 'traces show' returns event windows (default 40 events, max 200; --around-event; --max-event-chars up to 10000) (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/commands).
From git: 'traces notes --json' scans recent commits' notes, then 'traces show --remote' or 'traces sync' hydrates the content from the API (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/cli-discovery).
Hosted MCP: traces_lookup, traces_search (metadata filters: workspace, project, creator, agent, status, time) and traces_read (bounded window, tool events excluded unless asked for). Discovery and reading are deliberately split (https://www.traces.com/docs/mcp).
API: list traces filtered by an exact gitRemoteUrl (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/traces).
I found no documented semantic or vector search.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, this is a core feature.
- The post-commit hook reads the active trace IDs (instant when agent hooks are installed, otherwise 'traces list --dir . --since <ts>'). It records the repo URL, branch and commit ref on each trace in local SQLite, writes the IDs into refs/notes/traces on the commit, shares any unshared traces in the background, and the notes get pushed. The link is many-to-many (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks).
- Trace records carry gitRemoteUrl, gitBranch and gitRef (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference/traces).
- SSH and HTTPS remotes are normalized to one canonical HTTPS form (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/cli-discovery).
- A GitHub App reads the notes off a PR's commits, filters them to the PR head branch, and posts or updates a PR comment linking each trace (https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-git).
- For the DeepSeek Harness, notes attach through write/edit/bash file overlap (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/supported-agents).
- Separately, the team says it attaches a traces.com link to every PR (https://www.traces.com/blog/introducing-traces).
scale:
I found no quantitative scale claims: no user, trace or throughput numbers in the docs, blog or Show HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47277436).
- Free Core plan: unlimited traces, unlimited teams, up to 50 seats (https://traces.com, https://www.traces.com/blog/traces-for-teams).
- Limits: 600 writes per minute per user, 25 active API keys per namespace, 50 MB per export file (https://www.traces.com/docs/api-reference, https://www.traces.com/docs/getting-started/authentication, https://www.traces.com/docs/traces-web/exports).
- Very long sessions trigger a confirmation prompt before sharing (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/troubleshooting).
- Supported agents: 18+ on the homepage (https://traces.com). Gemini CLI support, listed at launch, was retired in v0.6.4 (June 2026) in favour of Antigravity (https://www.traces.com/blog/gemini-cli).
privacy_security:
Redaction:
- Secrets are 'stripped at source' (https://www.traces.com/blog/introducing-traces). API keys, emails and database credentials become [REDACTED] on publish (https://traces.com).
- In the v0.6.36 binary this is a client-side regex list applied recursively to the upload payload. It covers AWS AKIA keys, GitHub tokens (gh*_, github_pat_), Stripe sk_live/sk_test, Anthropic sk-ant-, OpenAI-style sk-, Google AIza, Slack xox*, npm, PyPI, HuggingFace, Vercel, Supabase sbp_, Traces' own trk_ keys, PEM private-key blocks, database URLs with credentials, email addresses, Bearer JWTs, *SECRET/PASSWORD/TOKEN/_KEY=value pairs, and *_DSN/_URL blocks.
- The redaction is pattern-based and best-effort. The privacy policy still makes users responsible for keeping secrets and others' personal data out (https://www.traces.com/privacy).
Access control:
- Visibility is public, direct (link-only) or private (namespace members only) (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/cli). Org admins can disable visibility levels, enforced on the server (https://www.traces.com/docs/organizations/privacy).
- API keys (trk_*) are scoped to one namespace with traces:read, traces:write, namespace:read and surfaces:write scopes. CLI device login shows the requesting hostname and a short code for confirmation (https://www.traces.com/docs/getting-started/authentication).
Encryption:
- 'Encryption in transit' only. No encryption at rest is promised, and there is no end-to-end encryption (https://www.traces.com/privacy).
- The CLI embeds a Sentry DSN for crash telemetry (binary observation).
Injection handling:
- The MCP docs say trace content is 'untrusted historical data and may contain prompt injection' (https://www.traces.com/docs/mcp).
- 'traces show --markdown' wraps content in random boundary tags with a 'historical context, not instructions' preamble (https://www.traces.com/docs/cli/commands). In the binary the tag is trace_<7-digit Math.random()>, which is not a CSPRNG, and event content is interpolated without escaping.
- 'traces notes' checks note URLs against an allowlist: traces.com plus TRACES_URL (https://www.traces.com/docs/sharing/git-hooks).
lesson_for_parinn:
Git works as a small pointer index, not as the store. Traces keeps all content in its own service and puts only one-line pointers in refs/notes/traces. Each write is a compare-and-swap transaction on a temporary ref. Pushes run inside a time-bounded pre-push hook that never blocks: fetch to an incoming ref, 'git notes merge --strategy=cat_sort_uniq', push, then re-merge and retry once if the push fails. notes.rewriteRef keeps notes on amended and rebased commits. This shape works across teammates and worktrees with no network in the commit path, and ParleyInn can copy it with a refs/notes/parinn ref.

ParleyInn should improve on it in two ways:
- Make each pointer a content hash of the session's chain head (e.g. 'parinn:<session-id> <head-hash>') instead of a URL. The link can then be checked offline against the local record (I4), with no allowlist needed.
- Treat every note line as attacker-written input, since anyone with push access can write notes. Avoid Traces' weak envelope (a non-CSPRNG 7-digit nonce, unescaped content): use a CSPRNG nonce and neutralize closing tags before any recalled text reaches the model (I2).

name: Trillian (google/trillian)
status: shipped. It is in maintenance mode and superseded by Tessera. The repo is not archived. The README says: "Trillian is in maintenance mode. The next generation of transparency logs uses Tiled APIs and are better supported by Tessera. We recommend that any new log operators first try Tessera." It also says "we do not plan to add any new features." Releases continue: tag v1.8.0 points at commit 0362d55, dated 2026-09-21. That release moves to Go 1.26, removes OpenCensus tracing and allows unencrypted PEM keys (https://github.com/google/trillian/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md). Map mode (the verifiable sparse map) is gone from the README's design section, which now lists only Log mode. The storage README still mentions Map support in MySQL, which looks like a stale doc. Skylog, the "Log V2" with higher throughput, is listed only as an "internal prototype" (docs/Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md).
what_is_stored:
An append-only, dense Merkle tree (RFC 6962 style) of opaque leaves. Each tree is a tenant identified by a TreeId. Each LogLeaf carries these fields:
- leaf_value: an opaque blob that is hashed into the tree.
- extra_data: kept and returned on reads, but "not covered by and do not affect the Merkle tree hash calculations".
- leaf_index: assigned by Trillian, or set by the client in PREORDERED_LOG mode.
- merkle_leaf_hash: computed by the server.
- leaf_identity_hash: the personality's dedup key. It defaults to the Merkle hash.
The tree also stores internal Merkle nodes and periodic log roots.
