A log root is a TLS-serialized LogRootV1 of tree_size, root_hash, timestamp_nanos, a deprecated revision field and metadata (trillian_log_api.proto and trillian.proto in https://github.com/google/trillian). Trillian holds no application semantics. A separate "personality" handles admission criteria, canonicalisation and the external API. Certificate Transparency in certificate-transparency-go is the main personality (README, https://github.com/google/trillian#personalities).
where_stored:
Server and cloud database behind a gRPC service: trillian_log_server plus trillian_log_signer, the sequencer. Pluggable SQL storage backends, per docs/Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md and storage/README.md:
- MySQL/MariaDB: GA.
- Google-internal Spanner: GA.
- CloudSpanner: Beta.
- PostgreSQL: Beta, used by Sectigo.
- CockroachDB: Alpha.
- In-memory: tests only.
The README names MySQL/MariaDB as the store needed for tests and production. It does not use git or local files.
format_and_model:
Data structure: a binary Merkle tree that fills from the left. Leaves are at level 0. Internal nodes are stored in SQL rows keyed by NodeID (storage/README.md).

API: protobuf messages over gRPC (trillian_log_api.proto):
- QueueLeaf
- AddSequencedLeaves (preordered mode)
- GetLeavesByRange
- GetInclusionProof and GetInclusionProofByHash
- GetConsistencyProof
- GetLatestSignedLogRoot, which can return a consistency proof
- GetEntryAndProof
- InitLog

Signatures: despite the name, SignedLogRoot is no longer signed by Trillian since PR #2452 (v1.4.0). The proto comment says signing "was intended to support a niche-use case but added significant complexity". The changelog adds "there should not be a trust boundary between Trillian and the personality" (trillian.proto; CHANGELOG.md v1.4.0). The personality signs tree heads, for example CT STHs.

Two hashes per leaf:
- The Merkle hash commits the full leaf, including the timestamp.
- The identity hash defines what counts as a duplicate (docs/TransparentLogging.md).

Leaf size: "fairly large" leaves are fine, but multi-GB leaves are not. The limit is about 10MB on CloudSpanner (TransparentLogging.md note 2).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Many clients can submit at once. QueueLeaf calls go to the gRPC server, which writes them to an unsequenced queue table. A single active sequencer per tree then assigns indices and integrates them. Mastership is chosen by an election service:
- etcd: GA.
- Chubby: GA, Google-internal.
- Kubernetes: Alpha.
(docs/Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md)

Duplicates are removed by leaf_identity_hash: a second submission of the same identity returns the existing leaf instead of a new entry (trillian_log_api.proto; TransparentLogging.md).

There is no merge, fork or branch concept. Each tree is one linear history with one writer, the sequencer. PREORDERED_LOG mode lets an external party fix the order, for example a CT mirror. That is the only way to bring in an ordering made elsewhere, and it still yields one linear log (README "Log mode"). Separate logs are separate trees. Nothing reconciles divergent histories. Divergence is treated as misbehaviour, detected through consistency proofs.
realtime:
Near-real-time but asynchronous. The signer polls the queue every 100ms by default (--sequencer_interval), with batch_size 1000 and 10 parallel sequencers (cmd/trillian_log_signer/main.go). A queued leaf is not in the tree until the next integration pass. Personalities give an inclusion promise (such as a CT SCT) before the inclusion proof exists (TransparentLogging.md, "Inclusion Proofs vs. Promises"). There is no push or subscribe API. Readers poll GetLatestSignedLogRoot and GetLeavesByRange.

Observed write throughput (Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md):
- CloudSpanner: 1000+ entries/s.
- MySQL: 400-500 entries/s.
search_retrieval:
Lookups only by position or hash:
- by index range (GetLeavesByRange)
- by Merkle leaf hash (GetInclusionProofByHash)
- by index with proof (GetEntryAndProof)
There is no content search, full-text search or query language. GetLeavesByHash and GetLeavesByIndex were removed in v1.4.0 (CHANGELOG.md). Any indexing is left to the personality or to external monitors.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. Trillian is a general verifiable log of opaque blobs and has no idea of agents, sessions, prompts or commits. The nearest analogue is the "Binary Transparency" example in TransparentLogging.md, which logs package hashes, not development provenance.
privacy_security:
Integrity is the only security goal: it gives tamper evidence through inclusion and consistency proofs. Confidentiality and redaction are not addressed.

- Encryption: no encryption at rest or of leaves. Transport TLS to PostgreSQL was added in v1.7.3 (CHANGELOG.md).
- Deletion: the docs warn that logged data "can't be removed without destroying the Log". The only escape (note 3) is to replace a leaf with a placeholder leaf type that holds just its Merkle hash. Monitors can see that substitution (TransparentLogging.md). The same doc names illegal or embargoed content as a risk for open logs. Its defence is strict admission criteria in the personality.
- Signing keys: PEM, PKCS#11 or Google-internal key management are listed (Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md), but root signing now sits with the personality.
- Secrets: no secret scanning or redaction.
- Access control: no ACLs in the core. ACLs, DoS protection and load-balancing are the personality's job (README).
- Network: it is a networked gRPC microservice plus an SQL database, the opposite of ParleyInn's no-network core (I4).
scale:
- CloudSpanner backend: "tested to tens of billions of entries and tens of log tenants".
- Google-internal Spanner: backs all of Google's Trillian deployments.
- MySQL: in production with at least one CT operator.
(docs/Feature_Implementation_Matrix.md)
The README says it is "used in production by multiple organizations, including many large-scale Certificate Transparency log operators". Tessera claims "far higher read-throughput and read-availability compared to Trillian v1" and lower TCO (https://github.com/transparency-dev/tessera).
license: Apache-2.0, per the LICENSE file in the repo. The GitHub API was not reachable from this session to confirm the SPDX id, but the LICENSE file is the Apache 2.0 text.
lesson_for_parinn:
Copy Trillian's data model, not its service.

1. Hash commitments in the chain, content beside it. Keep two hashes per record: a chain or Merkle hash over a commitment, and a separate identity or dedup hash. Keep the body outside the hash, like Trillian's extra_data, or commit only a hash of the body. Then redaction or crypto-shredding can swap a body for a hash-only placeholder without breaking the chain. Note 3 in TransparentLogging.md describes exactly that substitution, and it stays visible to verifiers. For ParleyInn this is how an append-only, hash-chained record can live with "delete this secret" (I6 audit, I2 untrusted content).
2. Order without merges. Use one sequencer per log plus consistency proofs between checkpoints, so many writers append without merges. Machines, worktrees and sandboxes would each keep their own linear log and publish checkpoints. Divergence is then detected, not merged.
3. Use the tiled successor for files, not a server. Trillian needs a gRPC server, a MySQL or Spanner database and an election service, which conflicts with I4. Its own maintainers now point to tiled logs: C2SP tlog-tiles via Tessera, which has a POSIX filesystem backend. Static tiles and signed-note checkpoints are plain files that git or any dumb transport can carry. That fits a no-network core that leaves transport to the user.
4. Sign in the application, not the log engine. Trillian v1.4 dropped root signing from the engine because a trust boundary inside it confused people. ParleyInn should likewise sign checkpoints at its own trust boundary, not inside the storage engine.

name: Trillian Tessera (transparency-dev/tessera)
status: shipped. The README calls it "generally available and production ready", and says it has been "production ready since the Beta release" (v0.2.0). v1.0.0 GA was tagged Sep 22 (2025, inferred). The latest tag is v1.0.4 (Jul 16, 2026, inferred: it fixes witness goroutine leaks and an AWS antispam bug). main had a commit on 2026-09-25, read from a shallow clone. It is actively maintained, not archived. Sigstore Rekor v2 runs on it in production (GA Oct 10, 2025). The MySQL driver was removed after v1.0.2. Trillian v1 is not archived but is positioned as legacy: "New ecosystems ... should strongly consider planning a migration to Tessera."
what_is_stored: Opaque application leaves ("entries") of up to 64 KiB each, or 256 KiB in Static-CT mode. Tessera also stores the RFC 6962 SHA-256 Merkle tree over those entries as tiles, and a signed checkpoint (tree size plus root hash, in signed-note format) that commits to the tree. Witness cosignatures are optional. It has no schema, metadata, timestamps or authorship per entry: anything like that must be encoded inside the leaf by the application (Tessera calls it the "personality"). On the POSIX driver, a private .state/ directory holds treeState (JSON size and root), lock files, GC state and a version file. Optional persistent antispam keeps a hash(entry) -> index map (BadgerDB on POSIX, the database on cloud drivers). That map is for best-effort dedup only.
where_stored: Pluggable storage, one log per location. POSIX filesystem: plain files under a directory, meant to be served read-only by any static HTTP server. GCP: GCS for tiles and Spanner for sequencing. AWS: S3 for tiles and MySQL/Aurora for sequencing; the README says any S3-compatible store plus MySQL-compatible database works on-prem. No git, no p2p. The library itself is embedded in your Go binary, with no separate service.
format_and_model:
C2SP tlog-tiles plus tlog-checkpoint. Paths:
- <prefix>/checkpoint: a mutable signed note. It must carry an Ed25519 log signature if the log is public or witnessed.
- <prefix>/tile/<L>/<N>[.p/<W>]: hash tiles. A full tile is exactly 256 hashes (8,192 bytes). N is split into x-prefixed 3-digit path segments, e.g. x001/x234/067. A .p/<W> suffix marks a partial tile.
- <prefix>/tile/entries/<N>[.p/<W>]: entry bundles, which are sequences of big-endian uint16 length-prefixed entries.

Tiles and bundles are immutable, so they can be cached long; the checkpoint cache should last only seconds. The data model is a single left-dense, append-only, totally ordered log. Indices are contiguous from 0 and never reused. Within one batch, the order in which indices are assigned is not guaranteed. Lifecycle modes are Appender, Migration Target, Quiescent (frozen), plus an experimental Mirror.

Writes go through three stages:
1. Add() returns a future that resolves to a durably assigned index (sequencing).
2. A background integration step extends the tree.
3. A periodic step signs and publishes a checkpoint, optionally after collecting enough witness cosignatures to meet a C2SP tlog-policy. If the policy is not met, nothing is published.

Each POSIX write goes to a temp file and is atomically renamed into place, with fsync for durability.
multi_writer_and_merge: Several writers share one log, but nothing merges divergent histories. Tessera requires that multiple personality instances can safely run concurrently against one storage instance; it is also a guard against accidental double launches. On POSIX, a process-local mutex plus a flock() on .state/treeState.lock serialises sequencing and integration, and .state/publish.lock covers checkpoints. This was tested on ext4, ZFS and CephFS with concurrent binaries. The docs warn that NFS and s3fs are "unlikely to result in long term happiness". The cloud drivers coordinate through a transactional database (Spanner, MySQL). There is no branch or merge model: one log means one total order. Running independent logs means sharding (separate logs; no built-in shared-resource support, issue #589). Migration copies an existing tlog-tiles log into another backend. Dedup across frontends is best-effort only; duplicates can land if they reach different frontends in close succession.
realtime: Near-real-time only, by polling. Entries are batched in memory and lost if the process dies before sequencing; batch size and age are set with WithBatching. Once sequenced, an entry is durable. Integration is meant to finish within "low single-digit seconds"; on POSIX it happens synchronously as each batch flushes. Checkpoints are republished on WithCheckpointInterval. PublicationAwaiter lets a writer block until a published checkpoint covers its entry. Readers poll the short-cache checkpoint and fetch the immutable tiles. There is no push or subscription feed. Measured POSIX time-to-integrate averages about 1.2 to 6 s under load.
search_retrieval: Lookup is by index only: fetch an entry bundle by tile path, verify it against tiles and the checkpoint, and build inclusion and consistency proofs through LogReader and client libraries. There is no content search, no full-text search and no secondary index. The antispam hash->index map is a dedup aid, not a query API. Sigstore dropped Rekor's search index when it moved to Tessera ("best-effort service") and plans a separate verifiable-index service. Any search layer has to be derived outside the log.
links_sessions_to_code: Not applicable. Tessera is a generic Merkle-log library and has no notion of agents, sessions, prompts, commits or code. Any such linkage would have to be encoded in leaf payloads by the application.
scale:
From the project's own docs: "All storage backends have been tested to meet the write-throughput of CT-scale loads." Reads scale through immutable, CDN-cacheable static tiles. Measured POSIX write rates:
- NVMe ZFS: about 10,000 writes/s with antispam
- SAS HDD mirror: about 2,900 writes/s without antispam, about 1,600 with
- e2-micro free-tier VM: more than 1,500 writes/s
- 4-node CephFS: more than 1,000 writes/s

GCP with 100 Spanner PUs and one frontend: more than 3,000 QPS without antispam, more than 800 with; 300 PUs with two frontends: more than 5,000 QPS with antispam. AWS numbers are "coming soon". The README warns that BadgerDB antispam on POSIX can OOM under heavy load without GOMEMLIMIT. Rekor v2 shards logs by year.
privacy_security:
The security model is integrity and transparency, not confidentiality:
- Tamper evidence comes from RFC 6962 SHA-256 Merkle tiles, a signed checkpoint (signer supplied via WithCheckpointSigner; Ed25519 is required for public or witnessed logs), and optional third-party witness cosigning under a C2SP tlog-policy, which detects split views and rewrites.
- No encryption at rest, no redaction, no secret scanning, no access control. The design assumes the log is publicly readable. POSIX files are written 0644 and directories 0755. .state/ "does not contain sensitive data".
- Entries are immutable. Removing one would change every root after it and break consistency proofs. Deleting a log means deleting all of it; garbage collection only removes obsolete partial tiles.

For a no-network core, this matters: in v1.0.x, both the root tessera package and storage/posix import net/http. The witness and mirror gateway and the POSIX Config.HTTPClient default to http.DefaultClient. I confirmed this with `go list -deps` on the 2026-09-25 main. Importing Tessera would therefore fail an import-closure ban on net and net/http, and it also pulls in OpenTelemetry. The module is Apache-2.0, with an OpenSSF Scorecard badge and a SECURITY.md.
license: Apache-2.0
lesson_for_parinn:
Adopt Tessera's on-disk formats, not the library:
- Laying the record out as C2SP tlog-tiles (immutable 256-wide hash tiles, length-prefixed entry bundles, temp-file plus atomic-rename writes, one signed-note checkpoint) gives a local, fsync-durable, tamper-evident file tree.
- That tree can be moved over any dumb transport (rsync, an object store, even git) and checked by consistency proofs instead of merges.
- Off-the-shelf tlog verifiers and witnesses could audit it.

Do not import tessera or storage/posix: both pull net/http and OpenTelemetry into the import closure, which would break I4. A small ParleyInn writer can use the pure transparency-dev/merkle hashing code, whose import closure should be checked separately, plus its own tile writer.

Two design choices follow from Tessera's model:
1. Give each writer (machine, sandbox, worktree) its own log and checkpoint, and federate across logs rather than merging. Tessera allows one total order per log, flock coordination only on a strongly POSIX filesystem, and no fork or merge.
2. Never put plaintext session content in the leaf. Leaves are immutable and meant to be public, so commit a hash of an encrypted or redactable event. Redaction then becomes key deletion (crypto-shredding) and does not break the chain.

name: Turso AgentFS
status: beta
license: MIT (README badge and "License: MIT"; the Rust crate's Cargo.toml says license = "MIT") — https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs , https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/rust/Cargo.toml
what_is_stored:
Each database holds three kinds of data (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/SPEC.md):

(1) A POSIX-like virtual filesystem: inodes, directory entries, file content in fixed 4096-byte chunks, symlinks, and since spec v0.4 also FIFOs, devices and sockets. Overlay mode adds whiteouts (deletion markers) and copy-up origin inode maps.

(2) A key-value store. Values are JSON strings with created_at and updated_at.

(3) A tool-call table: name, JSON parameters, JSON result, error, started_at, completed_at and duration_ms.

What it does NOT store:
- No model prompts, responses or conversation transcripts. They exist only if the developer writes them into fs or kv; the spec has no such table.
- No per-operation file history and no file versions. The fs tables hold only the current state. The README says "Every file operation, tool call, and state change is recorded" (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs), but no operation-log table exists. I verified this by listing every CREATE TABLE in the Rust, TypeScript, Python and Go SDKs (cloned main at commit 0a014eb, 2026-06-03). The only tables are fs_config, fs_inode, fs_dentry, fs_data, fs_symlink, fs_whiteout, fs_origin, fs_overlay_config, kv_store and tool_calls.
- "History" means copying the DB file. Official framing: "Snapshot an agent's state at any point with cp agent.db snapshot.db" (README). The FAQ says time-travel and forking come from SQLite's WAL.

Tool calls are not captured automatically:
- The CLI only reads tool_calls (`agentfs timeline`). Nothing in cli/src writes them, so SDK callers must call record() or start() themselves (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/cli/src/cmd/timeline.rs).
- The Claude Agent SDK example uses AgentFS only as a cache for PDF text (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/examples/claude-agent/research-assistant/src/agent.ts).
where_stored:
A local DB file in Turso's SQLite-compatible format, one file per agent or session, with optional sync to Turso Cloud.

Paths:
- `agentfs init <id>` / SDK `open({id})` create `.agentfs/<id>.db` (README; MANUAL "Files" section).
- The Go SDK README says `~/.agentfs/{id}.db` (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/README.md).
- `agentfs run` keeps its copy-on-write delta at `~/.agentfs/run/<session-or-uuid>/delta.db`, with a FUSE mountpoint `mnt` beside it (setup_run_directory in https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/cli/src/sandbox/linux.rs). The Sessions guide instead says `.agentfs/my-project.db` (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sessions); code and docs disagree.

Other stores:
- An in-memory ephemeral DB when no id is given (README).
- In-browser via WASM (https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs_browser — linked from the README; I did not read it).
- Cloudflare Durable Objects (examples/cloudflare).
- Optional remote copy in a Turso Cloud database (libsql://...) via `agentfs sync push/pull` (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sync).

Not git: git appears only as the agent's own tool inside the sandbox.
format_and_model:
Relational SQLite schema, "Agent Filesystem Specification" v0.4 (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/SPEC.md).

Tables:
- fs_config: immutable; chunk_size defaults to 4096; the SDKs also store schema_version.
- fs_inode: ino AUTOINCREMENT, mode, nlink, uid/gid, size, a/m/ctime plus _nsec columns, rdev.
- fs_dentry: parent_ino, name, ino; UNIQUE(parent_ino, name).
- fs_data: ino, chunk_index, BLOB.
- fs_symlink.
- fs_whiteout: path, parent_path, created_at.
- fs_origin: delta_ino to base_ino.
- kv_store: key PK, value JSON TEXT, created_at, updated_at; upsert via ON CONFLICT.
- tool_calls: id AUTOINCREMENT, name, parameters JSON, result JSON, error, started_at, completed_at, duration_ms.

Timestamps are Unix seconds. Tool durations are computed as (completed - started) * 1000, so they are whole seconds in disguise.

Spec vs. implementation:
- The spec calls tool_calls "an insert-only audit log": "Records MUST NOT be updated or deleted". It lists session_id, user_id, parent/child and token usage only as optional extensions.
- The Rust, TypeScript and Python SDKs diverge from this. They add a `status` column (default 'pending') with a nullable completed_at, INSERT a pending row, then UPDATE it on success or error (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/rust/src/toolcalls.rs; sdk/typescript/src/toolcalls.ts; sdk/python/agentfs_sdk/toolcalls.py).
- The Go SDK keeps the pending call in memory and INSERTs once. Its table has no status column, so the SDK schemas have drifted apart (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/schema.go, toolcalls.go).

Engines and drivers:
- Engine: Turso, the Rust SQLite rewrite (crate turso 0.4.4 with the "sync" feature) (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/rust/Cargo.toml).
- The Go SDK exists, contrary to the discovery note. It was added in 0.6.1 on 2026-02-18 (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), is importable as github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/sdk/go, and uses pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite v1.29.1 with go 1.21 (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/go.mod). The README's SDK list still names only TypeScript, Python and Rust.

Schema upgrades go through `agentfs migrate` (MANUAL).
multi_writer_and_merge:
On one host:
- Many processes share one session by opening the same DB through `agentfs run --session <name>`. "All terminals share the same copy-on-write filesystem. Changes made in one terminal are immediately visible in others" (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sessions).
- Writes are serialized by SQLite's single-writer model. The Rust SDK uses connection pooling, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` in the write path, and a busy timeout (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md, 0.4.0 and 0.6.0).
- A remote branch named `begin-concurrent` (MVCC multi-writer) exists but is unmerged (seen via git ls-remote; I did not inspect its contents).

Across machines:
- Sync is explicit push/pull against a Turso Cloud database (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sync).
- Turso's rule is "last push wins". On pull, "your local database is rolled back to the last synced state, remote changes are applied, your unpushed local changes are replayed on top", atomically (https://docs.turso.tech/sync/conflict-resolution).
- The AgentFS sync guide contradicts this slightly. It says last-write-wins, but also that a second machine's push "fails (conflict)" and must pull first.
- There is no file-level, tree-level or semantic merge, and no conflict surfacing beyond that.
- My inference, not verified: AUTOINCREMENT inode and tool_call ids created independently on two replicas could collide or be renumbered on replay.

Overlay sessions (one delta per base tree):
- `agentfs diff` lists created, modified and deleted files.
- Applying them back to the host is manual ("Apply changes to real filesystem (manually or via script)", sessions guide), or done by having the agent commit and push a git branch from inside the sandbox (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sandbox).

Future direction:
- A design post proposes pushing local changes to object storage as logical mutations and pulling remote ones as physical pages, with a coordinator. It is explicitly "a direction, not a finished system" (https://penberg.org/blog/disaggregated-agentfs.html, 2026-01-11).
realtime:
Local only.
- On one host: processes sharing a session DB or FUSE/NFS mount see changes immediately (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sessions). The docs pitch a second terminal for watching an agent (`watch ls`, `tail -f`) (same page).
- `agentfs serve nfs` (default 127.0.0.1:11111) and `agentfs serve mcp` expose a live DB to other clients (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/MANUAL.md).
- Across machines: there is no streaming, subscription or change-notification API. Sync is manual push/pull (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sync).
- Real-time multi-agent collaboration over object storage exists only as a proposal (https://penberg.org/blog/disaggregated-agentfs.html).
search_retrieval:
Plain SQL over the DB file with sqlite3 or tursodb (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/auditing).

Indexes:
- tool_calls(name)
- tool_calls(started_at)
- kv_store(created_at)
- fs_dentry(parent_ino, name)
- fs_whiteout(parent_path)

Source: https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/SPEC.md

Tools on top of SQL:
- CLI `agentfs timeline`: --filter by tool, --status pending/success/error, --limit, --format json (MANUAL).
- SDKs: path reads, readdir, KV prefix listing (`Keys(prefix)` in Go), tool-call GetByName, GetRecent and GetStats (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/README.md).
- The MCP server exposes read_file, write_file, readdir, kv_get and kv_list to a model (MANUAL).

No full-text (FTS), vector or semantic index is defined anywhere in the spec or the SDK schemas.

Docs error: the auditing guide's example queries use a table `toolcalls` and a column `path` on fs_inode, neither of which exists in the spec. The guide's SQL is illustrative, not accurate.
links_sessions_to_code:
Weakly, and only through the filesystem.

How it links:
- An overlay session is a copy-on-write delta over a base directory, usually a git clone. So the session DB contains exactly the files the agent created, changed or deleted, and `agentfs diff` lists them (https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs-overlay; https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/auditing).
- The docs suggest naming the session after the future git branch. The hand-off to code is the agent running "Create a branch ..., commit these changes, and push" from inside the sandbox (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sandbox).

What is missing:
- No prompt-to-file, tool-call-to-file or session-to-commit link.
- tool_calls has no session_id; the spec lists it only as an optional extension (SPEC.md).
- When you run `agentfs run claude`, Claude Code's own session transcripts are NOT captured. `~/.claude` and `~/.claude.json` are on the default allow-list, which bind-mounts them read-write to the real host, outside the overlay DB. That is DEFAULT_ALLOWED_DIRS plus the bind-mount logic in https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/cli/src/sandbox/linux.rs. The macOS defaults are in MANUAL.md ("Default allowed directories (macOS): ~/.claude ...").
scale:
No quantitative scale claims for agent count, history length or DB size.

What is published:
- The FUSE post times a git clone of 1,208 objects / 2.30 MiB at "real 0m2.053s". It claims "typical filesystem operations end up being just as fast as native filesystem operations", with extra overhead on non-cached reads and fsync() (https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs-fuse, 2025-12-08).
- Turso encryption is quoted at "as little as 6% read overhead and 14% write overhead" (https://docs.turso.tech/tursodb/encryption).
- Partial sync (lazy page fetch) exists for large filesystems (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sync).
- The design post concedes "SQLite has a single-writer model, which limits write concurrency" and names Turso MVCC as the planned mitigation (https://penberg.org/blog/disaggregated-agentfs.html).

Project activity:
- About 3.4k GitHub stars (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs).
- Beta since 0.6.0 (2026-02-05). Latest release 0.6.4 (2026-03-25) (CHANGELOG.md).
- Main's newest commit is 2026-06-03 ("Make clippy happy"), seen via git fetch. There has been no commit since, so the project looks quiet as of 2026-10-02.
- It is not archived; the GitHub page shows no archive banner.
- Hacker News traction was small, under 10 points per story (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46218308).
privacy_security:
Encryption at rest:
- Optional, via Turso page-level AEAD: AES-128/256-GCM and AEGIS variants. The key is passed hex-encoded with --key or AGENTFS_KEY (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/MANUAL.md).
- Turso encrypts each 4 KiB page with a unique nonce. The DB file and WAL are encrypted; the first 100 header bytes are not; keys are kept in memory (https://docs.turso.tech/tursodb/encryption).
- Encryption is flagged experimental in code (`experimental_encryption(true)`) (https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/rust/src/lib.rs).
- Local encryption and cloud sync are mutually exclusive: "Local encryption cannot be used with cloud sync" (MANUAL; also enforced in lib.rs).

Sync credentials: a Turso auth token in an env var. MANUAL says TURSO_DB_AUTH_TOKEN, the sync guide says TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN (https://docs.turso.tech/agentfs/guides/sync).

Redaction, secrets, integrity:
- None. Tool-call parameters and results are stored verbatim as JSON (SPEC.md).
- No hash chain, signature or other tamper evidence on the "audit trail".
- Three of four SDKs UPDATE audit rows despite the spec's insert-only rule (sdk/rust/src/toolcalls.rs).
- Agent ids are validated against path traversal (alphanumeric, '-' and '_' only) (lib.rs).

Sandbox isolation:
- Linux uses FUSE plus user and mount namespaces; macOS uses sandbox-exec with a generated profile ("kernel-enforced sandboxing without requiring any special privileges", https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs-overlay).
- A ptrace mode is experimental (MANUAL).
- The README FAQ calls the copy-on-write isolation "system-wide and cannot be bypassed". But the default allow-list leaves ~/.claude, ~/.codex, ~/.gemini, ~/.cache, ~/.local, ~/.npm and /tmp writable on the host (cli/src/sandbox/linux.rs; MANUAL).

Untrusted content: the MCP server hands file and KV contents to a model with no untrusted-content marking (MANUAL).
lesson_for_parinn:
Do not use a synced, mutable database as the record. Ship sealed, hash-addressed segments instead.

AgentFS shows two ways the record gets lost:

(1) Its "audit trail" is a normal table. The spec says insert-only, but three of four SDKs UPDATE rows, and nothing checks the rule.

(2) Moving data between machines uses Turso's row-level "last push wins" with rollback-and-replay. On top of that, encryption and sync cannot be used together.

Either path can silently overwrite or renumber history, and a reader cannot detect it. That breaks ParleyInn's lossless, append-only contract.

What ParleyInn should do:
- Treat the local SQLite DB only as a rebuildable projection (I10).
- Move history between worktrees, sandboxes and machines as immutable, already-encrypted segments named by their hash. Merging is then a set union of hash-linked events, never last-writer-wins. Transport can be git or anything else that copies files.
- Enforce append-only twice: with SQLite triggers that reject UPDATE and DELETE, and with chain verification on read. Both need a drift test, because AgentFS shows that a spec rule nobody checks drifts across writers.

Two smaller takeaways:
- Capture the session at the Claude Code hook level, not the filesystem. AgentFS's sandbox deliberately leaves ~/.claude (the transcripts) outside its DB.
- AgentFS's Go SDK picked pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite, a data point for ParleyInn's driver decision.

name: Turso Database (Rust rewrite of SQLite) and libSQL (its SQLite-fork predecessor)
status: shipped. The Turso engine works in production but is pre-1.0. The latest stable release is v0.8.1 (2026-09-29), and v0.8.2-pre.2 came out 2026-10-02. The Turso Sync layer was announced as beta in October 2025, and its current docs do not say whether it is still beta. libSQL is still maintained but superseded: new features go to Turso. libSQL embedded replicas are labelled 'legacy'.
what_is_stored: General-purpose relational data in SQLite format: tables, indexes, a WAL, and with MVCC a separate MVCC log. Nothing is specific to agents. Optional extras: (1) a change data capture table, `turso_cdc` by default. Each row holds change_id (monotonic), change_time (Unix epoch, not guaranteed increasing), change_type (1 insert, 0 update, -1 delete, 2 commit), table_name, rowid, before and after row images as BLOBs, an `updates` BLOB with column-level changes, and change_txn_id. Modes: id, before, after, full (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md). (2) Full-text indexes built on Tantivy, and vector columns (https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso). (3) For Turso Sync, local sync metadata alongside the database (https://docs.turso.tech/sync/usage).
where_stored: A local database file plus its WAL; this is in-process, embedded storage. An experimental `.tshm` sidecar lets several processes share the WAL (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md). The optional shared copy lives on a server: either Turso Cloud, which is proprietary SaaS, or a local `tursodb <db> --sync-server addr` that the docs present as for development and testing only, with no auth (https://docs.turso.tech/sync/local-sync-server). With libSQL, embedded replicas are local copies of a remote primary run by sqld or Turso Cloud (https://docs.turso.tech/features/embedded-replicas/introduction).
format_and_model: The file format is compatible with SQLite (it tracks SQLite 3.50.4), as are the SQL dialect and the C API. There is also experimental Postgres dialect and wire-protocol support. One engine, written in Rust, uses a VDBE bytecode virtual machine, io_uring async I/O, and DBSP incremental computation (https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso). MVCC is enabled with `PRAGMA journal_mode = mvcc`. It gives snapshot isolation, and a database written under MVCC must be checkpointed before a non-MVCC open can see the changes (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md). Sync uses a hybrid model. Local changes go up as logical row mutations read from the CDC table. Remote changes come down as physical pages, so the local replica matches the remote byte for byte. After each pull, local WAL changes are 'rebased' on top (https://turso.tech/blog/introducing-databases-anywhere-with-turso-sync). libSQL embedded replicas replicate 4 kB WAL frames (https://docs.turso.tech/features/embedded-replicas/introduction). License: MIT for both Turso (https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso) and libSQL (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/libsql/main/LICENSE.md).
multi_writer_and_merge: Inside one database, `BEGIN CONCURRENT` (MVCC only) lets transactions write at the same time. Write-write conflicts are detected per row: at commit, each row in the write set is checked for changes by another transaction (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md). Access from several processes is experimental (`--experimental-multiprocess-wal`, 'not production ready'), and the manual lists 'No multi-process access' as a core limitation (same source). Across replicas, Turso Sync uses explicit push() and pull(). The default conflict rule is Last-Push-Wins per row: 'the version that is pushed last will take precedence — regardless of the local commit time'. A `transform` hook can rewrite mutations before they are sent, for custom merges (https://turso.tech/blog/introducing-databases-anywhere-with-turso-sync, https://docs.turso.tech/sync/usage). The libSQL-era offline-writes private beta offered FAIL_ON_CONFLICT, DISCARD_LOCAL, REBASE_LOCAL and MANUAL_RESOLUTION modes (https://turso.tech/blog/introducing-offline-writes-for-turso). libSQL embedded replicas send writes to a single remote primary (https://docs.turso.tech/features/embedded-replicas/introduction). Nothing in the Turso sources is a CRDT or a true multi-master merge; there is a central server, and the last push overwrites.
realtime: Nothing syncs automatically. All reads and writes are local, and the app decides when to push() or pull(). Pull supports long-polling to cut down empty responses, so near-real-time fan-out works if a client keeps a long-poll open (https://docs.turso.tech/sync). libSQL embedded replicas can sync on a timer (`syncInterval`, in seconds) and give read-your-writes to the writing replica (https://docs.turso.tech/features/embedded-replicas/introduction). On one machine, CDC exposes changes immediately. Note: 'CDC records are visible even before a transaction commits' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md).
search_retrieval: Full SQL. Full-text search is built in on Tantivy: `CREATE INDEX ... USING fts`, with tokenizers default, raw, simple, whitespace and ngram, plus fts_match, fts_score (BM25), fts_highlight and OPTIMIZE INDEX. Vector types are vector32, vector64, vector32_sparse, vector8 and vector1bit, with cosine, L2, dot and Jaccard distances. Search is exact; approximate vector indexing is on the roadmap (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md, https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso). The FTS is Turso's own, not SQLite FTS5. The README promises SQLite compatibility, but I could not verify from these sources whether FTS5 is supported.
links_sessions_to_code: Does not apply. Turso is a general database engine with no idea of agent sessions, prompts, commits or worktrees.
privacy_security: Encryption at rest is experimental: run with `--experimental-encryption` and set `PRAGMA cipher` plus `PRAGMA hexkey`, or put them in the URI. Ciphers are AES-GCM 128/256, AEGIS-256 and AEGIS-128L with their X2 and X4 variants. The manual warns 'not production ready so do not use it for critical data right now' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md). libSQL embedded replicas accept an `encryptionKey`, and the application manages the key (https://docs.turso.tech/features/embedded-replicas/introduction). Turso Cloud sync uses fine-grained tokens and external auth through Clerk and Auth0 (https://turso.tech/blog/introducing-databases-anywhere-with-turso-sync). The local sync server has no auth at all (https://docs.turso.tech/sync/local-sync-server). The sources show no redaction or secret scanning. Supply-chain note for Go: the tursogo driver uses purego FFI to load prebuilt native libraries (no CGO), and its sync API (`NewTursoSyncDb`) talks HTTP to the server from inside that native code (https://docs.turso.tech/sdk/go/quickstart). As a result, a Go import-closure or depguard check cannot see the network-capable code.
scale: The README makes no numeric scale claims. It says the engine powers production apps at several organisations and advises keeping independent backups until 1.0 (https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso). The repo shows about 24.5k stars and 1.4k forks (https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso). Turso publishes a sync benchmark post (https://turso.tech/blog/sync-benchmark), which I did not read in detail. Limitations: multi-threading is not supported in the base implementation, it is UTF-8 only, and indexes on WITHOUT ROWID tables are not supported under MVCC (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tursodatabase/turso/main/docs/manual.md).
lesson_for_parinn: Turso's sync shows what an append-only record needs from a transport. It pushes row-level logical mutations taken from a CDC table, pulls physical pages, and settles conflicts by Last-Push-Wins per row. That rule is safe only for data that never needs a real merge. ParleyInn's hash-chained, append-only events with unique content-addressed IDs are exactly such data: rows are inserted and never updated, so LWW never fires, and pulled pages can be checked again against the chain. So a dumb, centrally ordered push/pull transport, including Turso Sync or git, will do for ParleyInn if every writer appends to its own per-session chain and nothing is ever updated in place. Two cautions. First, ParleyInn should verify hashes after every pull instead of trusting byte-for-byte page replication. Second, ParleyInn should keep any sync client outside its no-network core, as a separate opt-in process. tursogo's sync code is network-capable native code loaded through purego, which would get around the I4 import-closure test. Also, its CDC rows are visible before commit, so a projector that tails CDC must filter on COMMIT records to stay deterministic (I10).
confidence: medium-high. The core facts come from the README, the manual and the official docs. A few points could not be checked: the current beta or GA status of Sync, whether the release dates are exact (GitHub API access was refused in this session, so they come from the rendered releases page), and FTS5 compatibility.
license: MIT (Turso engine and libSQL). The Turso Cloud sync service is proprietary SaaS.

name: Vertex AI Agent Engine Memory Bank, renamed "Agent Platform Memory Bank" (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform) on April 22, 2026
url: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/memory-bank (the old URL https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-builder/agent-engine/memory-bank/overview now gives HTTP 301 to /gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale)
category: managed cloud memory service (LLM-curated long-term memory, closed source, Google Cloud)
status: shipped. Public preview was announced July 8, 2025 (https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/vertex-ai-memory-bank-in-public-preview?hl=en). GA with Sessions on December 17, 2025, and billing from February 11, 2026. I saw both facts only in search snippets of https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-builder/release-notes; that page now redirects, so I could not fetch the original entry. The rename on April 22, 2026 is verified: "Agent Engine is now Agent Runtime ... Memory Bank is now Agent Platform Memory Bank" (https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/release-notes). Later GA dates in the same release notes: global and multi-regional endpoints on June 17, 2026; IngestEvents GA in July 2026; memory profiles on July 15, 2026. The default generation model became Gemini 3.5 Flash on June 29, 2026. Nothing is archived or superseded; only the name changed.
what_is_stored: It does not store transcripts. It stores short facts that an LLM writes in natural language, and optionally structured "profiles". Each Memory has a name (projects/.../reasoningEngines/.../memories/...), a scope dict that is immutable, a `fact` string, topics, create, update and expire times, and typed metadata (string, double, bool or timestamp). Example: {"scope":{"agent_name":..,"user":..},"fact":"I use Memory Bank to manage my memories."} (overview page). Memory profiles are memories with memory_type STRUCTURED_PROFILE. They have a fixed schema, and each field is its own Memory (profiles page). MemoryRevision records are immutable snapshots, written on every create, update or delete. A revision holds the consolidated `fact`, plus `extracted_memories` (the intermediate extraction output) when the change came from GenerateMemories, and labels (revisions page). The raw conversation stays in the separate Sessions service as SessionEvents, or with the caller. Memory Bank keeps only what its extractor judges "meaningful" under the configured topics. The default topics are USER_PERSONAL_INFO, USER_PREFERENCES, KEY_CONVERSATION_DETAILS and EXPLICIT_INSTRUCTIONS. Extraction reads only text and files. "Function calls and responses are ignored" (generate-memories page). The docs say plainly that much is dropped: "Not all user-agent interactions result in memories being created or updated."
where_stored: Google Cloud server-side. Memories live in a Memory Bank instance, either under an Agent Runtime (reasoningEngines) resource or the newer projects.locations.memoryBanks resource. The location can be regional, multi-regional (us or eu) or global. Data at rest stays inside the chosen boundary. ML processing goes to the model endpoint's region and can fall back to global Gemini endpoints when no regional endpoint exists, for example for Gemini 3 models or Asia single regions (overview and setup pages). There is no local or offline mode. The client reaches it only over the network, through REST or the SDK.
format_and_model: Data model: scope → many Memory resources → many MemoryRevision children. The scope is an arbitrary key/value dict, matched exactly and independent of key order. A memory's scope is set at creation and "is immutable" (fetch-memories page). Revisions are kept by default with a 365-day TTL that can be configured or turned off. After a memory is deleted, its revisions stay readable for 48 hours, and RollbackMemory can restore the memory to a revision (revisions page). Memories have an optional TTL, which is off by default. Instance config sets the generation model (default gemini-3.5-flash), the embedding model (default text-embedding-005, with gemini-embedding-2 also supported), topics with few-shot examples per scope-key set, TTL, and revision settings (setup page). Wire format is protobuf/JSON over REST, and events use google.genai Content objects. Write paths: (1) GenerateMemories, a long-running operation that extracts with an LLM and then consolidates; (2) CreateMemory/UpdateMemory/DeleteMemory directly, the "memory-as-a-tool" path; (3) direct_memories_source, up to 5 pre-extracted facts consolidated in one call; (4) IngestEvents streams (generate-memories and ingest-events pages). It is not append-only and not hash-chained. The "current" Memory is mutated in place and the LLM may delete it.
multi_writer_and_merge: Merging is semantic and done by an LLM, not structural. In the consolidation step, Memory Bank looks up candidate memories in the same scope by similarity search. The LLM then marks each one CREATED, UPDATED or DELETED, deleting a memory when new information "was contradictory" (generate-memories and setup pages). By default the comparison uses only the latest revision; revisions_per_candidate_count widens it. metadata_merge_strategy can be MERGE (the default, last value wins per key), OVERWRITE, or REQUIRE_EXACT_MATCH, which limits consolidation to memories with the same metadata. IngestEvents deduplicates events by event_id within a stream (scope plus stream_id). The docs say nothing about ordering, locking, optimistic concurrency or conflict handling when several writers call GenerateMemories on the same scope at once. I found no ETag or version precondition in the guides. Any writer with memoryEditor rights on a scope can change or delete memories that came from another writer's sessions. The result depends on how the LLM handles each pair of facts, so it is not deterministic and cannot be replayed.
realtime: Near real-time at best, and asynchronous by design. GenerateMemories is a long-running operation that "can take a few seconds" (troubleshooting page). Production use is expected to set wait_for_completion=False. ADK's add_session_to_memory does not block. IngestEvents buffers events and generates on event_count, idle_duration or fixed_interval (each a multiple of 60 s), or on force_flush. Anything left pending is flushed 24 h after the last event (ingest-events page). A newly written fact is readable once its operation finishes. There is no push, subscribe or change-feed API for other agents.
search_retrieval: RetrieveMemories takes a scope and either returns everything in that scope (pages of up to 100) or runs a similarity search. The search embeds the query, ranks by Euclidean distance between embedding vectors of the facts and the query, returns top_k (default 3), and gives each result a distance score (fetch-memories page). Filters: metadata in disjunctive normal form via filter_groups, plus system-field filters in EBNF syntax over create_time, update_time, topics and `fact`, including a regex `fact=~".*allergies.*"`. RetrieveProfiles is a low-latency read of the structured schema. ListMemories ignores scope and is not recommended for low latency. There is no BM25 or keyword index, and no way to get the source transcript back exactly. In ADK, PreloadMemoryTool runs a search on every turn using the user's message as the query, and LoadMemoryTool lets the model run the search itself (ADK memory docs, https://adk.dev/sessions/memory/).
links_sessions_to_code: No. There is no concept of a repo, commit, file or code change. The only link is session to user: a GenerateMemories call with vertex_session_source defaults its scope to {"user_id": session.user_id} and can be limited to a time range of session events. ADK sets the scope to {app_name, user_id}, as seen in vertex_ai_memory_bank_service.py in google-adk 2.11.0. Callers can label revisions, for example {"data_source": "321"}, to point back to a source, and can attach metadata. They could store a commit SHA there, but nothing in the product interprets it (revisions and generate-memories pages).
privacy_security: Encryption, residency and compliance: CMEK, VPC Service Controls, data residency at rest, HIPAA, Access Transparency and Access Approval are all supported (security table at https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-builder/agent-engine/memory-bank/overview, which redirects to /gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale). CMEK cannot be used with the global endpoint (setup page). Access control: IAM roles memoryViewer, memoryEditor and memoryUser. IAM Conditions on the attribute aiplatform.googleapis.com/memoryScope, written in CEL, can restrict which principals read or write which scopes. Policies are capped at 1500 principals, and conditions do not apply to calls that span scopes, such as ListMemories and PurgeMemories (iam-conditions page). Redaction: there is no deterministic redaction. The extractor is "instructed to exclude sensitive or personal data, the system is not infallible ... assume that some sensitive or personal information may still be stored" (generate-memories page). Prompt injection: the overview has a section on "prompt injection and memory poisoning ... when false information is stored in Memory Bank. The agent may then operate on this false or malicious information in future sessions." The suggested mitigations are all outside the product: Model Armor, red-teaming and sandboxed execution. Memory Bank itself does not separate trusted from untrusted content. ADK's PreloadMemoryTool pastes retrieved facts into every request as role=user content inside a plain <PAST_CONVERSATIONS> tag, with no escaping or provenance. That is an automatic path from stored content into the prompt (preload_memory_tool.py, google-adk 2.11.0 wheel from PyPI). Contradiction-driven LLM deletion also lets a poisoned input erase true facts. Revisions and rollback are the only way to recover.
scale: No figures for corpus size or latency are published. The documented default quotas are 100 create/update/delete requests per minute (memory_bank_write_requests), 300 get/list/retrieve requests per minute (memory_bank_read_requests), and at most 100 Agent Runtime resources (https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/quotas). Generation uses Gemini under dynamic shared quota, so it can hit resource-exhausted errors; Provisioned Throughput is the recommended fix (troubleshooting page). Other limits: up to 5 direct memories per consolidation call, retrieve pages of 100, top_k default 3. The design is credited to an ACL 2025 Google Research paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.08026), per the launch blog. I did not read the paper.
license: Proprietary managed Google Cloud service, billed per use since February 2026 (date from search snippets of the old release notes; not fetched directly). The client SDKs (agentplatform / google-cloud-aiplatform) and ADK are open source, and ADK's PyPI wheel was inspected. The service itself is closed.
lesson_for_parinn: Memory Bank shows the opposite of ParleyInn's design, and that is the useful lesson. It loses detail and mutates state: the LLM extracts and consolidates in place, may delete facts that look contradictory, and keeps revisions only for 365 days. Google's own docs warn about memory poisoning. Yet the reference integration (ADK PreloadMemoryTool) still pastes top-k recalled facts into every turn as user-role text inside a bare <PAST_CONVERSATIONS> tag. Concrete takeaways: (1) Keep ParleyInn's raw, hash-chained event log as the only source of truth. Any LLM-made "memory" or profile should be a projection that can be rebuilt from it (I10), never a store that is edited in place. Memory Bank's revisions plus extracted_memories, and its rollback, are a weaker, expiring version of what the append-only log gives ParleyInn for free. (2) Do not ship a convenience like PreloadMemory. Recall stays pull-only and enveloped (I2), and anything that pushes text into a prompt automatically must be opt-in and carry only TrustedText. (3) Copy two good ideas: scope-keyed access control (IAM conditions on a scope map) and idempotent ingestion keyed by event_id with buffered flush triggers. Both suit many agents across worktrees and sandboxes writing to one store without a network-dependent core.

name: Vibe Kanban (BloopAI)
category: kanban for coding agents (orchestrator that runs Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Amp and others in per-task git worktrees)
status: shipped. The local app is still maintained after the sunset: the last commit on main is d5cbb53, dated 19 Sep 2026. Bloop announced the shutdown on 10 Apr 2026. The hosted cloud services (org kanban, relay) stayed up for 30 days and then went local-only. The blog says the project "will live on, open source and community maintained". The hosted cloud should be treated as superseded. I could not verify who maintains the project now or whether a community roadmap was published, because the web-search budget was used up.
what_is_stored:
The local SQLite tables (crates/db/migrations, 76 migrations) form a chain: projects/repos → workspaces → sessions → execution_processes → coding_agent_turns.
- workspaces: branch, container_ref (the worktree path), archived, pinned, worktree_deleted, and an optional task_id.
- sessions: executor and agent_working_dir. A session is one conversation thread inside a workspace.
- execution_processes: run_reason, the executor_action as JSON, status, exit_code, and a 'dropped' flag used for retries.
- coding_agent_turns: the prompt sent to the agent, a summary (the final assistant message), the agent's own agent_session_id and agent_message_id (used for resume), and a 'seen' flag.
- execution_process_repo_states: before_head_commit, after_head_commit and merge_commit per repo.
- Also merges, pull_requests, drafts, scratch, tags, images and attachments.
The full agent output is stored per process as JSONL LogMsg records. LogMsg is Stdout, Stderr, JsonPatch, SessionId, MessageId, Ready or Finished. These logs used to live in an SQLite table. A one-time migration moved them to flat files "to improve performance, data remains local".
Config, profiles, OAuth credentials, ed25519 trusted keys, the server signing key and relay-host credentials are JSON or key files in the same data directory.
The former cloud ran Postgres. It held organizations, projects, issues, comments, tags, notifications and a workspaces mirror. The mirror kept only metadata: local_workspace_id, the issue link, and files_changed / lines_added / lines_removed. It did not hold transcripts.
where_stored:
Local DB plus flat files.
- SQLite file: db.v2.sqlite under ProjectDirs("ai","bloop","vibe-kanban").data_dir(). That is ~/.local/share/vibe-kanban on Linux and ~/Library/Application Support/ai.bloop.vibe-kanban on macOS.
- Logs: <data_dir>/sessions/<session-uuid>/processes/<process-uuid>.jsonl.
- Git worktrees: /var/tmp/vibe-kanban/worktrees on Linux, or the OS temp dir on macOS and Windows. The base dir is configurable.
- Former cloud: Postgres 16 synced to clients with ElectricSQL 1.4.13, plus Azure Blob storage (Azurite in self-host) for attachments.
Nothing is written to git refs or notes. Git only holds the code and the branches the agents produce.
format_and_model:
Relational SQLite accessed through sqlx, with journal_mode=DELETE (not WAL) and versioned sqlx migrations. Rows are keyed by UUID and carry created_at/updated_at.
Transcripts are append-only JSONL. Each line is a serde-tagged LogMsg. Normalized conversation state travels as RFC 6902 JSON Patch entries inside the log stream. The parser is lossy: it skips unparsable lines and logs only the first three warnings. There are no hashes and no chaining.
Agent sessions are linked to code by commit SHAs (before/after/merge) per execution process per repo.
The cloud schema was relational Postgres. Tables were published to Electric with electric_sync_table() and REPLICA IDENTITY FULL.
multi_writer_and_merge:
Local is single-host, single-writer. One server process owns the SQLite file, and the migration pool allows up to 64 connections. There is no cross-machine merge of transcripts.
Parallel agents are isolated by git, not by the database. Each workspace gets its own branch and worktree. Sessions inside a workspace share files but not conversation context, and the docs warn that a new session does not inherit history. Integration happens through ordinary git merge, rebase or PR, and the merge commit is recorded in the merges and repo-state tables.
The former cloud used a central Postgres as the single source of truth. Electric streamed read-only shapes to clients, and writes went through the API. There was no CRDT or offline merge for issues.
realtime:
Local: the Rust server streams to the browser UI. It uses SSE events for stdout, stderr and json_patch, and WebSocket JSON-Patch streams for task, workspace and diff state.
Former cloud: ElectricSQL Postgres logical-replication shapes kept the team kanban live across members. A relay (WebRTC/WS tunnel with SPAKE2 pairing and ed25519 request signatures) let a phone reach a local host via cloud.vibekanban.com. Transcripts themselves were never shared in real time between users or machines, and with the cloud gone the relay path depends on self-hosting.
search_retrieval:
There is no FTS or semantic index on transcripts. I found no FTS5 or search tables in the migrations. Retrieval is navigational: open workspace → session → process logs, replayed from JSONL.
Composite indexes exist for performance only. Resume is delegated to the agent: Vibe Kanban stores the agent's own session_id/message_id and passes it back, for example to resume a Claude Code session. Cloud issue filtering was ordinary SQL over issues.
links_sessions_to_code:
Yes, and in some detail.
- Each issue/task can spawn workspaces, each on its own git branch and worktree.
- Each execution process records before_head_commit and after_head_commit per repo, plus merge_commit after a merge.
- Each coding_agent_turn stores the exact prompt and the final summary.
So one prompt maps to a commit range on a named branch, which in turn maps to a PR row in pull_requests / tracked PRs. Retries mark later processes 'dropped' and can reset to an earlier state.
The link lives only in the local DB, never in git. Once the DB is lost or the worktree is deleted (worktree_deleted flag), the provenance cannot be recovered from the repository.
scale: No published scale or performance numbers. The only hint is that logs were moved out of SQLite into flat JSONL files for performance. The README markets "10X more" out of coding agents but gives no benchmark. Usage was large enough that "the vast majority are free users" (shutdown blog), but no figures were given.
privacy_security:
- Local data is plaintext: the SQLite DB, the JSONL transcripts with full agent stdout and prompts, and config. There is no at-rest encryption.
- OAuth credentials go to credentials.json, created with mode 0600. I found no OS keychain use.
- I found no redaction or secret scrubbing of transcripts or prompts.
- Telemetry is opt-out-able (a Telemetry toggle in settings).
- Executors expose dangerous agent modes as config options, for example Claude bypassPermissions, Amp --dangerously-allow-all and Droid --skip-permissions-unsafe.
- Recalled history is not treated as untrusted. Prior summaries and prompts are replayed to agents and the UI with no envelope.
- Remote access used SPAKE2 pairing codes plus ed25519 signed requests (crates/trusted-key-auth). The cloud stored OAuth provider tokens encrypted (a migration adds encrypted_provider_tokens).
- License: Apache-2.0.
lesson_for_parinn:
The cloud shut down 30 days after the 10 Apr 2026 announcement. Shared kanban state survived only through a last-minute export feature, while the local SQLite and JSONL record, which had no server dependency, kept working. Vibe Kanban's most reusable idea is to record before and after HEAD SHAs per agent process per repo, tying each prompt to a commit range on a branch. It is also a warning. That link lives only in a per-machine SQLite file under ProjectDirs, while the worktrees sit in /var/tmp. So provenance cannot survive a lost machine or an ephemeral sandbox, and it can't be shared, which ParleyInn needs.
For ParleyInn:
- Record the same (before_sha, after_sha, branch, agent_session_id) tuple as a hash-chained event.
- Keep the core local-first and server-optional, so that no hosted sync or relay is ever on the critical path.
- Avoid Vibe Kanban's lossy JSONL parsing ("skip bad lines, warn three times"). It is exactly the silent drop ParleyInn's I6 forbids.
license: Apache-2.0

name: VibeStats (stephenleo/vibestats)
category: sync-to-git (aggregates only): a usage-analytics tool with a heatmap and dashboard, not a session-history store
status: shipped. v2.4.5 was released 2026-08-23 on crates.io and as git tag v2.4.5 (head commit 8f52350, 2026-08-23). The repo is not archived and was active through August 2026 (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/vibestats, https://docs.rs/crate/vibestats/latest). Adoption is small: crates.io shows 172 total downloads. The GitHub page, fetched through a summarizer, showed 1 star and 1 fork; I could not cross-check the star count.
what_is_stored:
Daily usage counters only. No transcript, prompt, response, tool input or file content is stored. Per machine, per harness (claude or codex) and per UTC day it keeps: sessions, active_minutes, input/output/cache_read/cache_creation tokens, a map of model to output tokens, longest_session_minutes, message_count and tool_uses (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md, https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/harnesses/mod.rs). A session is one JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects, dated by its first timestamp. Duration comes from turn_duration system entries. Tokens are de-duplicated by message.id plus requestId (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/harnesses/claude.rs). Codex data is parsed from ~/.codex/sessions rollout files (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/harnesses/codex.rs). The private repo also holds:
- registry.json: machine_id, OS hostname, status (active/retired/purged), last_seen.
- github/contributions.json: daily GitHub contribution counts, private ones included, fetched via GraphQL viewer.contributionsCollection. Only counts and dates are fetched, no repo names (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action/fetch_github_contributions.py).

Locally, ~/.config/vibestats holds config.toml (GitHub token, machine_id, repo name) and checkpoint.toml (throttle timestamp, auth_error flag, SHA-256 of the last pushed payload for each harness:date) (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md).
where_stored:
Three places, all in plain GitHub repos:
1. Working-tree files in a private GitHub repo named <user>/vibestats-data, which the installer creates with `gh repo create --private` (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh). It is written over HTTPS through the GitHub Contents REST API, not git push (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/github_api.rs).
2. A rolled-up file at <user>/<user>/vibestats/data.json in the user's public profile repo, plus SVG heatmaps and README markers. A daily GitHub Action commits these with git push (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action.yml).
3. The vibestats.dev/<user> dashboard has no server store. The browser fetches raw.githubusercontent.com/<user>/<user>/main/vibestats/data.json (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/site/src/pages/u.astro, https://vibestats.dev/docs/how-it-works).

Local state lives in ~/.config/vibestats, or %LOCALAPPDATA%\vibestats on Windows (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/README.md).
format_and_model:
Hive-style partition paths, with partition metadata in the path rather than the file: machines/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/harness=<h>/machine_id=<id>/data.json. Each file is one compact JSON object. The schema doc says the layout is chosen so Athena or BigQuery can read it with no transformation (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md).

The payload is serialized deterministically: struct fields in fixed order and a BTreeMap for models. A unit test pins the SHA-256 of a known payload so any byte-format drift fails the build. The hash is used only to skip unchanged uploads; it is not a chain (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/sync.rs).

The model is mutable state, not a log. Each (day, harness, machine) file is overwritten whenever its recomputed total changes. Every Contents API PUT makes a git commit titled "vibestats sync", so git history is the only implicit version trail (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/github_api.rs).

The public data.json is a single all-history document: generated_at, username, a days map keyed by YYYY-MM-DD, and github_contributions. Per-day totals are sums, except longest_session_minutes (max) and models (merge-sum). The schema doc estimates about 73 KB for 5 years (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md). Schema evolution relies on readers defaulting missing fields to 0 (`.get(field, 0)`).
multi_writer_and_merge:
Writers never share a data file, because each file's path includes machine_id and harness. Machines therefore never conflict on data, and there is no merge step. The daily Action (cron 02:00 UTC) recomputes everything statelessly: it globs every partition file, skips machines marked purged in registry.json, and sums them (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action/aggregate.py, https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/.github/workflows/aggregate.yml). The workflow uses a concurrency group (cancel-in-progress: false). Its own push back to the private repo retries with `git pull --rebase` (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action.yml).

The contributions snapshot uses a monotonic max-merge, so a stored count can only rise. The point is to survive GitHub retroactively hiding private contributions (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action/fetch_github_contributions.py).

Weak spots:
- **Shared registry.json.** It is updated by read-modify-write, carrying the blob sha as an optimistic lock (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh).
- **Same-machine races.** Each upload is a GET for the sha, then a PUT. Two hooks firing at once on one machine can race. GitHub documents 409 Conflict for this endpoint and says parallel use conflicts and must be serial (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/contents#create-or-update-file-contents). VibeStats retries only on 429, 5xx and transport errors, so a 409 fails at once. It is logged, the auth_error flag is set, the checkpoint hash is left unwritten, and the next sync retries (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/github_api.rs, https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/sync.rs).
- **Deletion is possible.** `vibestats machines remove --purge-history` deletes a machine's partition files through Contents API DELETE (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/commands/machines.rs).
realtime:
Near-real-time into the private repo, roughly daily for public output.

The installer adds `vibestats sync --quiet >/dev/null 2>&1 || true` to both the Claude Code Stop hook (async: true) and SessionStart. It does the same for Codex in ~/.codex/hooks.json (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh). Stop fires once per turn, not at session end (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks). Each sync recomputes today only and PUTs a file only if its SHA-256 changed (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/commands/sync.rs).

The planning documents call for a 5-minute throttle (NFR2) (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/prd.md). In v2.4.5, though, should_throttle() is called only in tests and the installed hook bypasses the session-start subcommand that held the throttle and catch-up logic (my reading of src/ at 8f52350). So the throttle does not appear to run, and every changed turn can cost a GET, a PUT and a commit.

The public data.json and SVGs refresh once a day at 02:00 UTC, or on manual workflow_dispatch. There is no push, streaming or subscription channel.
search_retrieval: Does not apply to content: there is none to search. Retrieval means reading the aggregated data.json, which a static Astro dashboard renders client-side (heatmap, KPIs, weekly per-model tokens) (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/site/src/pages/u.astro). The schema doc suggests querying the Hive layout with Athena or BigQuery external tables but ships no tooling for it (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md). The CLI offers only `status` and `machines list`.
links_sessions_to_code: No. It records no project path, repo, branch, commit SHA or prompt, and sessions are reduced to per-day counts (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md). The only nod to code is daily GitHub contribution counts (commits, PRs, issues, reviews) placed next to AI usage in the same data.json. That is a calendar correlation, not a session-to-commit link (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/action/fetch_github_contributions.py).
privacy_security:
Privacy rests on minimizing what is collected: "only small JSON aggregates ever leave your machine. No prompt or response content is stored or synced" (https://docs.rs/crate/vibestats/latest, https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/README.md). There is no redaction step, because content is never read beyond usage fields, and no encryption beyond GitHub's own: files are plaintext in a private repo.

The private/public boundary (NFR8/NFR9) is enforced only by the Action script: machine IDs, hostnames and paths stay in the private repo (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/prd.md). Even so, the per-day token, session, model and private-contribution counts are published publicly by design, on the profile repo and at vibestats.dev (https://vibestats.dev/docs/how-it-works). machine_id is the hostname plus the first 6 characters of /etc/machine-id or the macOS hardware UUID, and it sits in private-repo paths (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh).

Secrets:
- config.toml holds the user's full `gh auth token` in plaintext with mode 600 (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh).
- The VIBESTATS_TOKEN Actions secret also defaults to that full-scope OAuth token. A narrower fine-grained PAT is opt-in and offered only in interactive installs.
- Commit fd225e4 (#140) admits that earlier releases' PAT minting "failed on every install and silently fell through to `gh auth token`, so every VIBESTATS_TOKEN was really the user's full-scope OAuth token, not the narrow PAT the docs described" (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/commit/fd225e4). This contradicts the PRD's NFR7 claim that the machine token is scoped to vibestats-data Contents write.

Installation is `curl | bash` or `irm | iex`. Hook failures are hidden (`|| true`, output to /dev/null), so the hooks fail open (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/install.sh).
scale: Personal, single-user scale. The schema doc estimates about 73 KB of public data.json for 5 years (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/docs/schemas.md). The planning documents cite GitHub's 5,000 requests/hour authenticated limit and require backoff on 429. They rate overall scale "Low–Medium" (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/architecture.md). No multi-user, team or organization aggregation is offered. Write amplification grows with turns times changed days: one commit per changed file per sync (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/src/github_api.rs).
license: MIT (https://github.com/stephenleo/vibestats/blob/main/LICENSE, https://crates.io/crates/vibestats).
lesson_for_parinn:
Give every writer its own path and do all cross-writer merging in a deterministic, read-only recompute. VibeStats keys each file by (day, harness, machine_id), so many machines can sync through one GitHub repo without git merge conflicts. Its aggregator is a stateless pure function over all partitions, close to what ParleyInn's I10 asks for. VibeStats gets this cheaply only because it is lossy and mutable: it overwrites whole-day files and can purge them.

ParleyInn should keep the writer-sharded layout and swap the overwrite for immutable, append-only, hash-chained segments, one chain per writer (machine, sandbox or session). Then git or any dumb file transport is conflict-free by construction. A pure projection merges the chains, and a newer push can never silently replace older data.

Avoid VibeStats' other choices:
- **Synchronous network I/O in the agent's hook path.** It makes a GitHub Contents API call on every Stop turn, and its documented throttle does not run in v2.4.5. Under I4 that I/O belongs in a separate transport process, never inside ParleyInn's core.
- **Unchecked security claims.** The published token-scope claim (NFR7) went false in practice for releases until #140. ParleyInn's executable requirement matrix exists to catch exactly that.
- **Read-modify-write against the Contents API.** It returns 409 under parallel writers and creates one commit per PUT, so it is a poor real-time transport.

name: VS Code agent memory (built-in memory tool, GitHub Copilot Chat in VS Code)
status: shipped. The docs page was approved 9/30/2026 (DateApproved front matter in https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-docs/blob/main/docs/agents/run/memory.md). The implementation is in microsoft/vscode at extensions/copilot (main checked at a0601114ba4f, 2026-10-02). The old repo, microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat, is ARCHIVED. Its README says "This project has been moved into the main VS Code repository and this repository is now archived" (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat). Superseded: the archived code had an experimental path that sent /memories/repo/ to GitHub's cloud Copilot Memory service. That path is gone from current main, so repo memory is now local only (see multi_writer_and_merge).
what_is_stored:
Free-form notes the agent writes as it works, or writes when the user says "remember X". Three scopes (docs table, https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/memory):
- User, /memories/: preferences, patterns and frequent commands. Kept across all sessions and all workspaces.
- Repository, /memories/repo/: codebase conventions, project structure and build commands. Kept across sessions in one workspace.
- Session, /memories/session/: task context and in-progress plans for the current conversation. The Plan agent saves its plan at /memories/session/plan.md (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/planning).

What it does not store: transcripts, tool calls, prompts or diffs. The docs say memory "is separate from the conversation context that a session accumulates automatically" (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/concepts/agents#memory). It holds distilled notes only, not a record of the session.
where_stored:
Local DB? No: plain files in VS Code extension storage on the machine running the extension host. Source: memoryTool.tsx (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a0601114ba4fd6781f9ca13183e3ac3690c499b1/extensions/copilot/src/extension/tools/node/memoryTool.tsx). It sets MEMORY_BASE_DIR = 'memory-tool/memories'.
- User scope: <extension globalStorageUri>/memory-tool/memories/<file>
- Repo scope: <workspace storageUri>/memory-tool/memories/repo/<file>
- Session scope: <workspace storageUri>/memory-tool/memories/<sanitized chat-session id>/<file>

The concrete OS paths are my inference from VS Code's storage conventions and were not checked on disk: on Linux, ~/.config/Code/User/globalStorage/github.copilot-chat/... and .../workspaceStorage/<hash>/GitHub.copilot-chat/...

Also inference: in Remote-SSH, containers or Codespaces the extension host runs remotely, so "local" there means the remote machine. Nothing is written to the working tree, git notes, refs or a separate repo. The docs stress that repository memory "isn't a shared project file".
format_and_model:
A virtual file system under the /memories/ root, mapped onto real files. The model uses one tool, copilot_memory, with Anthropic-memory-tool-style commands: view (with view_range), create (fails if the file exists), str_replace (old_str must be unique), insert (at a line), delete (file or directory) and rename (not across scopes). Sources: package.json modelDescription (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a0601114ba4fd6781f9ca13183e3ac3690c499b1/extensions/copilot/package.json) and memoryTool.tsx.

Content is untyped text. The prompt nudges toward short Markdown bullets, one topic per file (e.g. debugging.md). There are no IDs, timestamps, hashes, provenance or schema. A companion tool, copilot_resolveMemoryFileUri, maps a memory path to its real URI (e.g. for artifacts).

The archived variant stored cloud repo memory as JSON {subject, fact, citations[], reason, category, source:{agent:'vscode'}}, keyed by GitHub owner/repo (agentMemoryService.ts at https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat/blob/5863f5a7088958050792b5dccbe8b46c6e13eccc/src/extension/tools/common/agentMemoryService.ts). Current main no longer has it.
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no multi-writer design. Writes are plain fileSystemService.writeFile calls. str_replace and insert read the file, change it and write it back with no lock and no version check. The only guards are create refusing an existing file and rename refusing an existing destination (memoryTool.tsx). My inference: two VS Code windows or sessions editing the same user-memory file means last writer wins, silently. There is no history, versioning or undo for memory files.
