Scoping keys on the VS Code workspace, not the git repo. My inference from the storageUri semantics: two worktrees or two clones of one repo get separate, unconnected repo memories. There is no sync. The docs mention none, and the code has no sync path. Extension globalStorage files are not covered by Settings Sync as far as I can verify (not documented either way).

Superseded design: in the archived repo (May 2026), with the experiment setting chat.copilotMemory.enabled (default false), /memories/repo/ writes went to GitHub's Copilot Memory service (CAPI) as create-only facts with server-side merge. Repo memory in that mode was shared across agents keyed by owner/repo (archived memoryTool.tsx and configurationService.ts lines 1004-1005). Current main routes /memories/repo/* "to local file-based repo memory" only.

The documented answer to sharing is human promotion. The docs give four steps: verify the memory against the code, move it into source-controlled docs or instructions, review it through the normal PR process, then delete the local copy (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/memory, https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/concepts/customization).
realtime: Not applicable. Memory is local only and is read at prompt-build time. Nothing propagates in real time between windows, machines or agents.
search_retrieval:
Retrieval works in two ways:
1. Automatic injection at the start of every session (memoryContextPrompt.tsx, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a0601114ba4fd6781f9ca13183e3ac3690c499b1/extensions/copilot/src/extension/tools/node/memoryContextPrompt.tsx):
   - All non-dot files in the user directory are joined in directory order, each under a "## <filename>" header. The result is cut to MAX_USER_MEMORY_LINES = 200 lines in total and placed in a <userMemory> tag. The docs say: "The first 200 lines are automatically loaded".
   - Session and repo files are listed by name only, in <sessionMemory> and <repoMemory> tags.
2. Agent-driven pull through the memory tool's view command, which lists directories and reads files with line numbers.

There is no full-text, semantic or ranked search, and no index. The user commands are "Chat: Show Memory Files" and "Chat: Clear All Memory Files". To edit or delete one file, the user asks the agent.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only weakly. Session memory directories are named after the sanitized chat-session id (extractSessionId in memoryTool.tsx). Repo memory hangs off the VS Code workspace storage. Nothing links a note to commits, files, line ranges, prompts or tool calls.

The archived cloud variant had a citations field ("Use the citations provided to verify the accuracy of any relevant memory before relying on it"), but that path is removed in current main. Session directories are swept once at tool construction: files whose mtime and recorded access time are older than 14 days are deleted (RETENTION_PERIOD_MS, memoryCleanupService.ts, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/a0601114ba4fd6781f9ca13183e3ac3690c499b1/extensions/copilot/src/extension/tools/common/memoryCleanupService.ts). So session notes stay on disk for up to about 14 days, even though the docs say they are cleared when the conversation ends.
scale: No scale claims. The only hard limit is the 200-line cap on auto-loaded user memory. The prompt tells the model to keep entries brief because "user memory is loaded into context automatically". Nothing is published on file counts, sizes or performance.
privacy_security:
What exists:
- Path containment. validatePath rejects any path not under /memories/, any path with '..' and any '.' segment. Session and repo URIs also get an isMemoryUri prefix check. User-scope paths rely on validatePath alone (memoryTool.tsx).
- Telemetry. The memoryContextRead event sends counts and lengths, not content (memoryContextPrompt.tsx).

What does not exist (not found in docs or code):
- No secret redaction or secret scanning on writes; a grep for secret, password, token and credential in the memory sources finds nothing relevant.
- No encryption at rest beyond whatever the OS provides.
- No per-file access control and no audit log.

Unframed auto-injection. User memory goes into every future prompt across all workspaces with no untrusted-content framing: the <userMemory> tag just says "The following are your persistent user memory notes". The agent writes memory by itself, possibly after reading untrusted repo content. My inference: that makes memory a persistent prompt-injection channel that crosses workspaces.

The removed cloud variant did frame recalled repo memories as possibly "obsolete or incorrect" and asked for citation checks. The docs carry no security guidance beyond keeping memory personal and unreviewed until it is promoted.
lesson_for_parinn:
Keep a local raw store separate from reviewed knowledge in git, and never auto-inject agent-written text. Microsoft tried routing repo memory to a cloud service keyed by GitHub owner/repo, then removed that path. It now tells users to move anything a team depends on into source-controlled, PR-reviewed files.

Meanwhile its 200-line auto-load re-injects notes the model wrote itself into every session in every workspace, with no envelope or provenance. That is exactly the gap I2 closes. It is the strongest argument for ParleyInn's rule: only human-pinned TrustedText reaches a restore block, and anything recalled is pull-only and enveloped.

Two concrete takeaways for ParleyInn:
- Key repository scope by repo identity (remote URL or root commit), not by editor workspace hash, so worktrees and clones share one history.
- Treat any optional sharing as an explicit, audited promotion step, not ambient sync.
license: The VS Code and Copilot Chat source, including the memory tool, is MIT-licensed (file headers: "Licensed under the MIT License", https://github.com/microsoft/vscode). Using it needs a GitHub Copilot subscription and Microsoft's product terms.

name: VS Code git.addAICoAuthor (AI Co-authored-by trailer)
status: shipped
license: MIT (the VS Code OSS source tree: the git extension and the workbench editTelemetry contribution). Per the file headers in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vscode/main/src/vs/workbench/contrib/editTelemetry/browser/aiContributionFeature.ts
what_is_stored: One fixed line of text, appended to the commit message: "Co-authored-by: Copilot <copilot@github.com>". Source: the AI_CO_AUTHOR_TRAILER constant in extensions/git/src/repository.ts, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vscode/main/extensions/git/src/repository.ts. Nothing else is persisted. The trailer does not record a prompt, chat session id, model, tool, line range, or percentage of AI code. It is a single yes/no attribution per commit. The data behind that yes/no is held only in memory and then thrown away. AiContributionFeature keeps a DocumentEditSourceTracker for each open document, in a ResourceMap. The tracker records which text ranges came from edits with source.category 'ai', and whether source.feature was 'chat' (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vscode/main/src/vs/workbench/contrib/editTelemetry/browser/aiContributionFeature.ts). Tracking state is cleared on commit, discard, revert, branch checkout and hard reset (the _aiEdits.clearAiContributions and clearAllAiContributions calls in repository.ts). A tracker is also disposed when its document stops being tracked.
where_stored: In the git commit object itself, as a standard trailer at the end of the commit message, after a blank line (repository.ts: `${trimmed}\n\n${AI_CO_AUTHOR_TRAILER}`). It is not stored in git notes, custom refs or a separate store. The per-document AI-edit provenance lives only in VS Code's in-memory workbench state and is never written to disk by this feature (aiContributionFeature.ts).
format_and_model: Git's RFC-822-style trailer convention (Co-authored-by: Name <email>), the one GitHub uses for co-author credit. The setting is git.addAICoAuthor: a string enum off | chatAndAgent | all, resource scope, default "off" (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vscode/main/extensions/git/package.json). With chatAndAgent, the trailer is added only when a tracked AI range came from chat or agent edits. With all, inline completions count too (package.nls.json descriptions and the _hasAiContributions level check). The check runs over the staged files, or over the working-tree files when committing with 'all' and nothing is staged. The trailer is skipped if it is already present, if chat.disableAIFeatures is true, or if the AI entitlement is 'hidden'. The last gate was added by PR #313931 (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/313931). Since 1.110, blame hovers also parse and show Co-authored-by trailers from any source (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_110; getCommitHover(..., coAuthors) in extensions/git/src/blame.ts).
multi_writer_and_merge: Not really applicable. Each developer's VS Code instance decides on its own whether its own commit gets the trailer. Because the trailer is part of the commit message, it travels with the commit through push, merge, cherry-pick and rebase, the same as any message text. Squash merges may drop it or concatenate it, depending on the forge. The feature only covers commits made from VS Code's own Source Control UI. The release notes say: "This setting does not modify commits made in external Git tools or the command line" (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_110). So CLI commits, other IDEs, and commits made by agents outside VS Code get no trailer, and coverage is inconsistent across writers.
realtime: No. The trailer is added synchronously at commit time and becomes visible to others only when the commit is pushed. The in-memory tracker updates live as edits happen, but it is local to one VS Code window and is never shared.
search_retrieval: Only through ordinary git tooling. Examples are `git log --grep='Co-authored-by: Copilot'` and `git interpret-trailers --parse`, plus forge co-author UIs. The only feature-specific retrieval is the blame hover in VS Code, which lists trailer co-authors (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_110). There is no index and no query API.
links_sessions_to_code: Weakly, at commit granularity. The trailer says some AI-originated text was in the files of this commit. It does not say which lines, which session, which prompt, or which model. AI line ranges are tracked in memory but are reduced to a boolean before commit and then discarded (aiContributionFeature.ts _hasAiContributions / _clearAiContributions). There is no pointer to a chat transcript. Commit and agent-session linkage is therefore absent.
scale: No scale claims. The per-commit cost is one in-memory check over the tracked documents. Unverified point: whether files closed before commit lose their AI provenance. The code disposes a tracker when its document leaves the annotatedDocuments set (aiContributionFeature.ts), which suggests they do, but I did not confirm when that set drops a document.
privacy_security: The trailer has no prompt or code content, so it leaks nothing beyond the fact that AI was used. That fact is permanent and public once pushed, and cannot be removed without rewriting history. The April 2026 incident is the key privacy/consent lesson. PR #310226 (merged 2026-04-16, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/310226) flipped the default from off to all. Users then reported the trailer on commits where Copilot was never used, even with chat.disableAIFeatures=true. It was also appended after the message was finalized, so users could not see or remove it in the editor (https://itsfoss.com/news/vs-code-credits-copilot-for-human-work/; HN discussion https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47991835). PR #313931, merged 2026-05-03 (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/313931), restored the off default. It also gated tracking behind the AI entitlement not being hidden, and made the git extension honour chat.disableAIFeatures. Current main still defaults to off (extensions/git/package.json). The VS Code 1.119 release notes (2026-05-06) do not mention the revert (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_119). itsfoss quotes Dmitriy Vasyura of the VS Code team: "There was no ill intent ... but rather a desire to support functionality that some customers expect." No redaction or encryption is involved. Nothing sensitive is stored, and the provenance data is never persisted.
lesson_for_parinn: Anything ParleyInn writes into shared, immutable git history (trailers, notes, refs) has to be explicit opt-in. It must be visible and editable before it lands, and computed from evidence ParleyInn can prove from its own record. The default must never be flipped silently. VS Code's flip to 'all' stamped false attribution on human-only commits that cannot be retracted without a history rewrite, and it caused a public backlash within weeks. This matches CLAUDE.md's rule: where usefulness and safety conflict, pick safety and make the convenience opt-in (and I6: no silent operations). There is a design point too. A boolean trailer computed from volatile in-memory state is a lossy, unauditable link. If ParleyInn links sessions to commits, it should do so in the other direction. The commit carries at most an opaque, content-free pointer, such as a session id or record hash. The hash-chained ParleyInn record holds the provenance, so the link can be checked and rebuilt (I10). It should not depend on a trailer whose truth cannot be re-derived after the fact.

name: VS Code Local History (Timeline view "Local History" source)
status: shipped. Introduced in VS Code 1.66 (March 2022). Still in current VS Code main: the setting defaults in workbench.contribution.ts were checked on 2026-10-02.
what_is_stored: Every save of an editor (a "stored file working copy") stores a complete copy of the file contents. It is not a diff. The 1.66 notes say "Each entry contains the complete file contents" (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_66), and the user-interface docs repeat it (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/userinterface#_local-file-history). Each entry also carries a small amount of metadata: an id, a timestamp (the file mtime at save), an optional "source" label, and an optional sourceDescription. The source can be "File Saved" (the default), "Undo / Redo", the label of the last non-typing undo element (for example a refactoring), or a rename/move (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/workbench/services/workingCopy/common/workingCopyHistoryService.ts, https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/workbench/services/workingCopy/common/workingCopyHistoryTracker.ts). A rename or move of a file carries its history entries over to the new path (moveEntries in the same file). Only saves made through VS Code are captured. Changes written to disk by another program, such as a CLI agent like Claude Code, a git checkout or another editor, are not recorded. The tracker hooks working-copy save events and file MOVE operations only (workingCopyHistoryTracker.ts). A third-party guide confirms it "only tracks files that you edit in VS Code" (https://bobbyhadz.com/blog/view-vscode-local-history). Defaults: enabled=true, maxFileSize=256 KB (larger files are skipped), maxFileEntries=50 per file (the oldest are discarded), mergeWindow=10 s (a save from the same source inside the window replaces the last entry), plus exclude globs (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/workbench/browser/workbench.contribution.ts). No prompts, chat or agent context is stored.
where_stored: A local database is not used on desktop. History lives as plain files in the user data folder: localHistoryHome = <appSettingsHome>/History (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/platform/environment/common/environmentService.ts). In practice that is ~/.config/Code/User/History on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/History on macOS and %APPDATA%\Code\User\History on Windows (third-party, https://bobbyhadz.com/blog/view-vscode-local-history). For remote workspaces it is stored in the remote machine's user data folder. In the browser without file-system access it is stored in IndexedDB (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_66). It is never in the working tree, git, or any server or cloud.
format_and_model: One folder per tracked resource, named hash(resourceURI.toString()) in hex. Inside are snapshot files named with 4 random alphanumeric characters plus the original extension, created by fileService.cloneFile, so each one is a byte-for-byte full copy. Also inside is an entries.json index of the form {version, resource, entries:[{id, timestamp, source?, sourceDescription?}]} (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/main/src/vs/workbench/services/workingCopy/common/workingCopyHistoryService.ts). The model is a per-file, timestamp-sorted list of snapshots that can be changed in place. It is not append-only. Entries can be replaced (the merge window), renamed (the source label can be edited), deleted one at a time or all together (workbench.action.localHistory.deleteAll), and dropped past the cap. There is no hashing, chaining or integrity check. When loading, the code rebuilds the list from the directory listing using file mtimes, then overlays metadata from entries.json. So a snapshot written before the index was flushed is still recovered (doResolveEntries / resolveEntriesFromDisk). History is per file. There is no snapshot of the whole workspace and no cross-file grouping.
multi_writer_and_merge: Designed for a single writer per machine. Saves are serialised within one VS Code process. A Limiter prevents parallel store() calls per model, and storeAll uses bounded parallelism (workingCopyHistoryService.ts). On desktop, entries.json is written on a debounced schedule and on shutdown. For remote workspaces it is flushed on every change "because the connection might drop anytime" (same file). There is no coordination between processes or machines, no sync, and no conflict resolution. Two VS Code windows on the same file are reconciled only by the snapshot-files-plus-index resolve logic. "Merge" here means only the time-window coalescing of saves from the same source, not merging histories. Whether Settings Sync carries local history could not be verified from the sources read.
realtime: Local and immediate. A new entry appears in the Timeline view on save through change events (onDidAddEntry / onDidReplaceEntry). There is no cross-device or cross-user real-time sharing (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_66).
search_retrieval: Browsing per file in the Timeline view, with a filter between Git and Local History sources (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/userinterface). Each entry offers: compare with the current file or the previous entry, restore, rename the label, and delete. Global commands: workbench.action.localHistory.create, workbench.action.localHistory.restoreViaPicker (a quick pick that can also find history of deleted files) and workbench.action.localHistory.deleteAll (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_66). There is no full-text search across snapshots and no query API. Retrieval is by file plus point in time.
links_sessions_to_code: No. Entries record only the save source label and a timestamp. No agent session, prompt or chat id is attached. Copilot chat "checkpoints" (chat.checkpoints.enabled) are a separate feature that snapshots affected files before each chat request. Their docs do not say where checkpoints are stored or whether they use Local History, and they describe checkpoints as "temporary" and not a replacement for Git (https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/chat-checkpoints). Edits made by an external agent such as the Claude Code CLI writing to disk are not captured at all (workingCopyHistoryTracker.ts).
scale: No scale claims. Growth is bounded by fixed caps: 50 entries per file and 256 KB per file by default, with a 10 s coalescing window. The oldest entries are deleted when the cap is exceeded (cleanUpEntries in workingCopyHistoryService.ts; defaults in workbench.contribution.ts). It is not designed for long-term or lossless retention.
privacy_security: Minimal. Snapshots are plaintext copies in the user profile, protected only by OS file permissions. There is no encryption, no redaction and no secret scanning. A .env file or credentials file saved in VS Code is copied verbatim into History/, and can outlive its deletion from the workspace, unless the user adds it to workbench.localHistory.exclude (an opt-out glob) or runs deleteAll (https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_66). The only protections are the size and count caps and the exclude globs. There is no integrity protection, so entries can be silently edited or deleted. History never leaves the machine, apart from being stored on the remote host for remote workspaces.
lesson_for_parinn: Three things to copy and one to avoid. Copy: (1) keep the record outside the working tree, in a per-user data home. (2) Write the payload before the index, and rebuild the index from the payload files when loading, which matches I10. (3) Flush right away when the store sits across an unreliable boundary. Avoid: Local History hooks the editor's save path, so anything that writes to disk outside it is invisible. That includes CLI agents, git checkouts and other tools. It also caps, coalesces, rewrites and deletes entries, and copies secrets in plaintext. So ParleyInn should capture at the agent-hook or event layer, not the editor or file-save layer. It should stay append-only with hash chaining instead of replace-on-merge-window. It should make any retention cap an explicit, audited operation (I6). It should redact or encrypt before persisting, rather than relying on opt-out exclude globs.
license: MIT for the Code - OSS source in microsoft/vscode. The Microsoft-branded VS Code binary ships under Microsoft's product license.

name: Warp cloud agents on the Warp Automation Platform (formerly "Oz"; the CLI, API and web app still use the Oz name)
category: Hosted agent platform (SaaS control plane; execution can be Warp-hosted or self-hosted)
status: shipped. Cloud agents, orchestration, handoff and session sharing are documented as current features, and cloud agents are included in the Build plan (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/faqs/). Brand note: the docs now say "Automation Platform (formerly Oz)" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/integrations/). The changelog renamed the "Oz agent UI" to "Warp Agent" on 2026-08-13 and "Oz Cloud API Keys" to "API keys" on 2026-08-27 (https://docs.warp.dev/changelog/2026/). The `oz` CLI, the "Oz Agent API" and oz.warp.dev still carry the name (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml). Sub-features at earlier stages: Agent Memory is a waitlisted research preview for design partners (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/agent-memory/). Warp Factories went to Early Access on 2026-08-27 (https://docs.warp.dev/changelog/2026/). Self-hosted data storage supports only AWS S3, with GCS and Azure "planned" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/data-storage/).
what_is_stored:
Each run is a task record. It holds inputs (the prompt plus trigger context such as a Slack message, PR metadata or CI logs), an optional environment, lifecycle state, and a persistent record: status, metadata and a session transcript with prompt, plan, commands, logs, outputs and follow-ups (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/).

Run data has three categories: transcripts (system messages, tool calls, tool results), artifacts (files, Computer Use screenshots, other binaries) and prompt attachments (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/data-storage/). Separately, Warp always keeps control-plane data: settings, agent and factory configuration, orchestration and lifecycle metadata, trigger and integration metadata, operational logs, and usage and billing (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/).

Also stored:
- Per-run timeline events (oz_run_created, oz_run_claimed, agent_started, oz_run_done, vm_shutdown and others).
- Typed artifacts: PLAN, PULL_REQUEST (url + branch), SCREENSHOT, FILE and EXTERNAL_REFERENCE.
- Token and cost usage.
- Immutable run metadata: at most 20 string keys (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml).

At the end of every session there is a workspace snapshot: git diffs of declared repos (tracked changes plus untracked, non-ignored files) and the verbatim contents of declared files (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/snapshots/).

For Claude Code runs, the open-source client captures Claude's native files and uploads them in a ClaudeTranscriptEnvelope {cwd, uuid, claude_version, entries, subagents, todos}. The files are ~/.claude/projects/<encoded_cwd>/<session_uuid>.jsonl, subagent JSONL files, and per-agent todo lists (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_transcript.rs).

Optional Agent Memory stores hold durable facts extracted from transcripts after each conversation ends (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/agent-memory/).
where_stored:
On a server / in the cloud. Run data (transcripts, artifacts, attachments) "lives in Warp-managed storage, independent of where runs execute" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/). Warp hosts on GCP (https://docs.warp.dev/enterprise/security-and-compliance/security-overview/). The client code names GCS objects as the transcript store (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_code.rs). Self-hosted workers must reach storage.googleapis.com to upload transcripts (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/self-hosting/security-and-networking/).

Customer-owned option: each of the three run-data categories can be mapped on its own to a customer AWS S3 bucket. Warp's control plane reaches it through a customer IAM role (sts:AssumeRole with an ExternalId) that allows only ListBucket and Get/Put/DeleteObject. Unmapped categories stay with Warp, and remapping does not migrate data (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/data-storage/).

Control-plane data and orchestration metadata always stay with Warp, even with self-hosted execution (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/).

Git is not used for session history. Git holds only code outputs (branches and PRs pushed by the agent) and acts as the diff format for workspace snapshots (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/snapshots/).
format_and_model:
Run model: a run has a run_id, state, prompt, source, creator and executor, plus session_id/session_link, trigger_url, conversation_id, parent_run_id, metadata and artifacts[] (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml).

The conversation is exposed two ways (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml):
- Normalized: GET /agent/runs/{id}/conversation returns a tree of ConversationSteps (nested steps for delegated work). Each step holds messages with role user/assistant/tool/system and typed content blocks: text, action, action_result and event. Action categories are command, files, search, integration, documents, computer, review and skill. Every block keeps the underlying transcript message_id.
- Raw: GET .../transcript returns a 302 to a time-limited download URL. The API supports it for third-party harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini). Some formats return 422 operation_not_supported on the normalized endpoint.

Claude Code raw form: a JSON envelope wrapping Claude's native JSONL entries verbatim. Resume rehydrates the files into ~/.claude, writes sessions-index.json and runs `claude --resume <uuid>`. A resume is rejected if cwd differs, because the JSONL entries embed cwd (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_transcript.rs).

Storage is mutable, not append-only. "Subsequent saves overwrite the same GCS objects keyed by this id" (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_code.rs). With S3 storage the transcript is updated after each turn (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/data-storage/).

Snapshot declarations are UTF-8 JSONL lines of the form {"version":1,"kind":"repo"|"file","path":"/abs"} (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/snapshots/).

No hashing, signing or tamper-evidence is documented anywhere in the Automation Platform docs (checked against https://docs.warp.dev/_llms-txt/automation-platform.txt).
multi_writer_and_merge:
There is no transcript merge. Each run, and each orchestration child, owns its own conversation, working directory and record. "Agents don't read each other's transcripts or live working trees". They coordinate only through a durable, server-backed message bus with one inbox per agent ID (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/orchestration/). Messages and run-state transitions share a global sequence number, so a parent never sees a child's SUCCEEDED before the message that produced the result. Orchestration is exactly one level deep (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/orchestration/).

Cloud-synced conversations store a snapshot at each sync point. If the same conversation is opened on two machines, "each continues independently ... changes on one machine do not sync to the other in real time". Continuing someone else's shared conversation creates a fork (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/cloud-conversations/).

Handoff:
- Local-to-cloud forks the conversation.
- Cloud-to-cloud appends to the same conversation and keeps the run ID.
- Workspace diffs are applied best-effort. Hunks that fail are reported and skipped.
- Runs that came from a local handoff can be continued only by their creator.
(https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/, https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/cloud-to-cloud/)

Code conflicts are left to the user: "you decide how agents should branch, coordinate, and resolve conflicts" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/faqs/).

Live shared sessions allow several concurrent editors with cursors and avatars, relayed through Warp's servers (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/session-sharing/).
realtime:
Yes, server-relayed and not peer-to-peer. Session sharing uploads scrollback and live output to Warp's servers, "so the session stays in sync" for all viewers. Viewers can follow from the app, a browser or a phone, and editors can steer (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/session-sharing/). Cloud runs can be followed live and followed up while the VM is still active (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/viewing-cloud-agent-runs/).

Self-hosted workers hold an outbound-only connection and need egress to app.warp.dev, rtc.app.warp.dev and sessions.app.warp.dev (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/self-hosting/security-and-networking/).

Orchestration lifecycle events and messages are pushed to parents without polling, and child status updates live in the UI (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/orchestration/).

Remote Control publishes a local Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode session for live remote steering (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/cli-agents/remote-control/).

Persistence is near real time but not streaming. Claude transcripts are saved periodically and at a final save point (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_code.rs). Local conversations sync "after each Agent interaction" (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/cloud-conversations/).
search_retrieval:
The runs list API supports (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml):
- filters by state, creator, executor, source, execution location, environment, skill, schedule, ancestor_run_id, metadata, artifact_type, and created/updated time ranges;
- fuzzy search `q` across run title, prompt and skill_spec only, not transcript content;
- pagination of up to 500 runs per page.

Other retrieval:
- Reverse lookup: GET /agent/run-by-external-reference?url= finds the run that reported a given EXTERNAL_REFERENCE URL (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml).
- The UI filters by source, day, creator and status (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/managing-cloud-agents/).
- Local and cloud conversations can be searched "by title or content" in the app (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/cloud-conversations/).
- Agent Memory runs a background search over memory stores and injects the results as context at task start. Agents can also pull more memories mid-run (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/agent-memory/).

No full-text or semantic search over raw transcripts through the API is documented.
links_sessions_to_code:
Partly, and at PR and branch level rather than commit level:
- Runs record PULL_REQUEST artifacts (PR url + branch) and a trigger_url (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml).
- Cloud-to-cloud handoff continues on the same Git branch (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/cloud-to-cloud/).
- Workspace snapshots are git diffs tied to the repos the run worked on (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/snapshots/).
- Linking a PR back to its session is manual: Warp's guide says to paste the session or run link into the PR description or a comment (https://docs.warp.dev/guides/agent-workflows/how-to-attach-agent-session-context-to-github-prs/).
- PR authorship shows provenance. User-triggered runs use the user's GitHub token. Agent-key runs with team GitHub authorization, and runs started by the GitHub integration, act as the "Warp Factories" GitHub App (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/, https://docs.warp.dev/platform/agents/).

No commit trailers, git notes or per-commit session IDs are documented. A search of the docs found none.
privacy_security:
Encryption and hosting: TLS 1.2+ in transit and AES-256 at rest; "known secret values are redacted at output boundaries"; run data is access-controlled by team roles (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/). SOC 2 Type II, hosted on GCP (https://docs.warp.dev/enterprise/security-and-compliance/security-overview/).

Managed secrets:
- Values are encrypted in the browser before upload and are never readable afterwards.
- They are scoped to a team or a person and injected as environment variables (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/secrets/).
- They are fetched just-in-time with a run-scoped token, and each delivery is audit-logged. Workload identity federation is available. Warp itself calls redaction "a backstop" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/).

Regex secret redaction for local terminal output is off by default. It is not applied to Session Sharing (https://docs.warp.dev/support-and-community/privacy-and-security/secret-redaction/). This conflicts with the security overview's claim that Warp "automatically detects and redacts" before data goes to LLMs (https://docs.warp.dev/enterprise/security-and-compliance/security-overview/). Treat the claim as unverified.

Snapshot `file` entries upload content verbatim. Warp warns users to keep secrets out of them (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/handoff/snapshots/).

Retention:
- Shared sessions expire after about one week.
- Account deletion jobs run every 24 hours.
(https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/session-sharing/)
- On the free plan, the oldest cloud conversations are removed when the plan limit is reached.
(https://docs.warp.dev/agents/local-agents/cloud-conversations/)

S3 mode: Warp uses customer SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS, uses presigned URLs so data does not pass through Warp's backend, and "never caches bucket contents". Warp still reads the data periodically, for example to run scorers (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/data-storage/).

LLM routing: Warp Agent inference goes to providers under ZDR. Claude Code calls Anthropic directly with the customer's key (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/architecture/).

Prompt-injection surface relevant to ParleyInn: lead-agent mailbox messages are injected into a Claude Code child's next-turn context through a hook's additional_context. They carry the preamble "Context type: user-level coordination messages" and are capped at 6000 characters by default (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp/blob/master/app/src/ai/agent_sdk/driver/harness/claude_code/parent_bridge.rs). Agent Memory automatically injects memories derived from transcripts (https://docs.warp.dev/agents/agent-memory/). Neither describes treating that content as untrusted.
scale:
No documented quantitative limits for history storage.
- Concurrency limits are "still being finalized" (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/faqs/).
- API limits: runs list up to 500 per page; metadata at most 20 keys of up to 256 bytes each (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml).
- Orchestration is one level deep (https://docs.warp.dev/platform/orchestration/).
- The Kubernetes worker's maxConcurrentTasks defaults to 0, meaning uncapped (https://docs.warp.dev/_llms-txt/automation-platform.txt).
- Marketing: Warp says it automates "about 30% of our tasks" through factories (https://www.warp.dev/blog/open-infrastructure-for-building-a-software-factory, 2026-08-18). One customer AI teammate "writes 35,000 lines of code each week" (https://www.warp.dev/oz).
- The headline counters on warp.dev/oz rendered as placeholder zeros, so fleet-size claims cannot be verified.
- The client repo has about 65k GitHub stars (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp).
license: Proprietary service and API: the OpenAPI spec declares license "Proprietary" (https://docs.warp.dev/openapi.yaml). The Warp client is open source: AGPL-3.0, except the warpui and warpui_core crates, which are MIT (https://github.com/warpdotdev/warp). The client includes the agent driver and harness code that captures and uploads transcripts. The control plane and storage backend are not published.
lesson_for_parinn:
Warp keeps session history out of git and splits it in two:
- A small, ordered control-plane index: runs, lifecycle events, and mailbox messages that share one global sequence number.
- Bulk run-data blobs (transcripts, artifacts, attachments), each category routable to a customer-owned bucket through a narrowly scoped credential.

Git carries only code state, as branches, PRs and snapshot diffs.

ParleyInn could adopt the split and the customer-owned sink. Two parts it should not copy:
- Warp overwrites one mutable GCS object per conversation on every save and drops resumable state when the final upload fails. ParleyInn should ship immutable, content-addressed, hash-chained segments, so a lost or concurrent write shows up as a gap or fork rather than silent last-writer-wins.
- Warp feeds mailbox messages and transcript-derived memories into Claude Code automatically through a hook's additional_context. That is exactly the automatic path from untrusted content to the model that ParleyInn's I2 forbids. Any cross-agent or cross-machine sharing in ParleyInn should stay pull-only and enveloped.

Warp's Claude Code capture shows that the native ~/.claude JSONL (main, subagents, todos) can be stored losslessly and replayed with `claude --resume`. Normalize cwd, though: Warp rejects a resume when the path differs.

name: Warp shared agent sessions (Agent Session Sharing, Cloud Conversations, Oz cloud-agent run links)
status: shipped
what_is_stored: Warp's docs describe three related features. (1) Agent Session Sharing, for local Warp agents and third-party CLI agents such as Claude Code. When you share, Warp uploads the session's scrollback and live output. Viewers see "Agent prompts, responses, thinking states, tool use, planning steps, and credit consumption" (https://docs.warp.dev/agent-platform/warp-agents/session-sharing). The PR guide adds terminal output, logs, command history, environment details and other scrollback (https://docs.warp.dev/guides/agent-workflows/how-to-attach-agent-session-context-to-github-prs/). (2) Cloud agent (Oz) runs. These hold "the prompt, plan, commands, logs, outputs, and follow-up messages where available", plus code changes, configuration changes and Computer Use (GUI and browser) artifacts (https://docs.warp.dev/agent-platform/cloud-agents/cloud-agents-session-sharing). (3) Cloud Conversations, an opt-in feature. It stores "a snapshot of the conversation state at each sync point" and the full conversation history (https://docs.warp.dev/agent-platform/warp-agents/cloud-conversations). The PR guide itself stores nothing. It is a suggested template for the PR description or a comment, with these fields: Goal, Agent context link, Changed files, Validation, Known risks, Reviewer asks (PR guide URL above).
where_stored: Warp's servers, which run on Google Cloud Platform (https://docs.warp.dev/enterprise/security-and-compliance/security-overview). The session is uploaded and a link is generated (session-sharing URL above). Git and GitHub hold only the URL, pasted by hand into a PR description or comment. No session content goes into the repo, git notes or refs.
format_and_model: Proprietary and undocumented. The docs model a shared session as a live terminal or agent session: scrollback plus a stream of agent blocks (prompt, response, thinking, tool use, plan), viewed in the Warp app, a web viewer or mobile. The docs do not specify a wire format, schema or export format. Cloud Conversations are point-in-time snapshots, not an event log. Opened on two machines, "each continues independently from that snapshot" (cloud-conversations URL above). There is no hash chain, signature or integrity model in the docs. Cannot verify any internal data model beyond this.
multi_writer_and_merge: Live sessions: one server-hosted session with many participants. "Multiple participants can join the same session from different machines, browsers, or environments... See each other's avatars and cursors... Edit together when granted access." Editors can send agent queries, type into the prompt, run commands, and start or switch conversations (session-sharing URL above). Writes are serialized through the single shared session, so nothing is merged. Cloud Conversations do not merge at all. Copies fork from the last snapshot and diverge (cloud-conversations URL above). There is no reconciliation of divergent histories.
realtime: Yes for live sharing. Updates go through Warp's servers, not peer to peer: "any new agent output or terminal activity appears for all viewers in real time" (session-sharing URL above). Cloud agent runs can be followed live and continued from the app or web (cloud-agents-session-sharing URL above). Cloud Conversations sync snapshots as you interact, but continuations are not bidirectional (cloud-conversations URL above).
search_retrieval: Cloud Conversations can be found "by title or content" inside Warp (cloud-conversations URL above). The docs point to a "Managing cloud agents" page for finding cloud runs by source, status, trigger or owner. Warp's docs describe no API for searching or exporting shared session content. Shared session links are retrieved only by URL. They cannot be found by searching from git or a PR, except as the pasted link.
links_sessions_to_code: Weak and manual. The link to a PR is a human-pasted URL in the PR description or a comment, wrapped in a template that lists changed files and validation (PR guide URL above). There is no commit-, file- or line-level attribution, and no automatic trailer or note. For cloud runs, the docs say that if the agent made a branch on the remote VM, "you'll need to clone that branch locally first" (cloud-agents-session-sharing URL above). Links into Slack, Linear, issues and incident reviews are also manual (https://docs.warp.dev/agent-platform/cloud-agents/viewing-cloud-agent-runs/).
privacy_security: Live shares expire: "Shared session data expires automatically about one week after you create the share. After that, the link can no longer be opened." Stopping a share ends live access at once (session-sharing URL above). Access tiers are view-only and edit, with edit requiring approval. Cloud Conversations links can be scoped to the team (the default), to specific emails, or to "Anyone with the link", which needs no authentication. Cloud Conversations are an opt-in Privacy setting that enterprise admins can disable. Deletion is permanent and immediate. Free plans evict the oldest conversations at a storage limit (cloud-conversations URL above). Secret Redaction is a local, regex-based filter with custom patterns, and it is off by default. It explicitly does NOT apply to Session Sharing: "treat a shared session like sharing your screen" (https://docs.warp.dev/support-and-community/privacy-security-and-licensing/secret-redaction). The PR guide tells users to check by hand for secrets, tokens and customer data before sharing. In transit Warp uses TLS 1.2+, at rest AES-256 (server-side, not end-to-end). Warp holds SOC 2 Type II and has zero-data-retention agreements with its LLM providers (security-overview URL above). The docs do not treat shared content as untrusted when it is re-fed to an agent.
scale: No scale claims specific to session sharing. The only company-level figure is second-hand. A third-party analysis says Oz launched on 10 February 2026, became multi-harness (Claude Code, Codex, Warp Agent) by May 2026, and that Warp claims over 700,000 developers (https://rywalker.com/research/warp-oz). Unverified against a primary Warp source.
license: The Warp client and service are proprietary and hosted. github.com/warpdotdev/warp appears to be the public issue tracker, not product source (seen through the mirror https://upd.dev/warpdotdev/warp/issues/8579). I could not verify whether any part of the sharing stack is open source.
lesson_for_parinn: A hosted link pasted into a PR does not give the PR a durable record. Warp's live shares stop opening after about one week, are not covered by secret redaction, and leave only a URL in the PR. A reviewer or auditor opening the PR months later finds a dead link and no content, hash or integrity proof. ParleyInn should treat any hosted or real-time view as a disposable transport, never as the record. What goes into the PR or commit (a trailer or git note) should be self-verifying. It should carry the session id and the hash-chain head at that commit, so whatever copy of the record still exists can be checked against it. Redaction should run before anything leaves the local store, so it covers every export and share path, and should never be a toggle that is off by default. Warp's fork-on-snapshot Cloud Conversations also show that multi-machine continuation needs an explicit model for histories that diverge.

name: whogitit (dotsetlabs/whogitit)
url: https://github.com/dotsetlabs/whogitit (404 on 2026-10-02); live copy: https://crates.io/crates/whogitit and source at https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/
category: git-notes line attribution (AI vs human, per commit, with prompts)
status: shipped. The project exists: crates.io lists versions 0.1.0 (2026-02-01), 0.2.0 (2026-02-02) and 1.0.0 (2026-02-26), MIT, by Greg King (nofunction99). Total downloads are about 127, which means very little use. The GitHub repository returns 404 today (checked by WebFetch on 2026-10-02, and add_repo reports no access), so it was deleted or made private. Whether anyone still develops it cannot be verified. Treat it as possibly abandoned. Its last published release is 1.0.0.
what_is_stored: One AIAttribution record per commit (SCHEMA_VERSION = 3, 'with edit context'). Each record holds: (1) session metadata: session_id (UUID), model {id, provider}, started_at (ISO 8601), prompt_count, used_plan_mode, subagent_count; (2) prompts[]: index, the full prompt text after redaction, timestamp, affected_files; (3) files[]: per-line attribution. Each line gets one of AI, AIModified, Human, Original or Unknown, plus the index of the prompt that produced it. The categories come from a three-way diff: original, then AI snapshot, then committed content. Commits can also get trailers: AI-Session (first 12 characters of the session id), AI-Model, AI-Lines, AI-Modified, Human-Lines and Co-Authored-By. It does not store the agent transcript, tool outputs or model responses. It keeps only the last user prompt for each edit, cut to 2000 characters by the hook. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/core/attribution.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/trailers.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/hooks/whogitit-capture.sh
where_stored: Git notes under the custom ref refs/notes/whogitit, one note per commit SHA, written through libgit2 (git2). Before the commit, data sits in .whogitit-pending.json at the repository root. That file is a JSON buffer, schema v3, mode 0600, and holds full before/after snapshots of every edited file. The hook keeps state under .whogitit/state. A local audit log lives in .whogitit/audit.jsonl. The audit log and pending buffer are never pushed. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/notes.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/capture/pending.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/audit.rs
format_and_model: Each note body is compact JSON (serde_json::to_string) and carries a version field. A schema mismatch only produces a warning. Size limits: a warning at 512 KiB per note and refusal at 4 MiB (NOTE_SIZE_WARN_BYTES / NOTE_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT_BYTES). Since 1.0.0, five CLI outputs (blame, prompt, show, summary, annotations) carry versioned JSON schemas with 'schema' and 'schema_version' fields. The model is commit-centric: attribution exists only for work that was committed. Uncommitted or abandoned agent work leaves no record. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/notes.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/CHANGELOG.md
multi_writer_and_merge: Weak. store_attribution calls repo.note(..., force=true), so a second write to the same commit overwrites the first. The code has no notes merge strategy (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/notes.rs). A post-rewrite hook copies notes across rebase and amend, and 'copy-notes' covers cherry-picks by hand (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/README.md). In one working tree, a flock on .whogitit-pending.lock serialises writers to the pending buffer, but only on Unix. Other platforms create a marker file with no real locking. When a new session id appears, the buffer is reset and uncommitted edits from the previous session are thrown away with a warning (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/capture/pending.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/capture/hook.rs). My inference, not stated in the docs: two machines pushing refs/notes/whogitit get ordinary non-fast-forward note-ref conflicts, and whogitit offers no way to reconcile them. Concurrent agents in one worktree lose data.
realtime: No. Notes are written at post-commit and travel only on git push and fetch. 'whogitit init' sets up fetching of the notes ref and a post-push hook that pushes it. CI fetches with git fetch origin refs/notes/whogitit:refs/notes/whogitit (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/README.md). Other agents cannot see anything before a commit is made and pushed.
search_retrieval: Lookups go from commit to line to prompt. There is no full-text search. Commands: blame <file> (per-line AI/human attribution), show <commit>, prompt <file:line> (the prompt that produced a line), summary over commit ranges (for PRs), status, export (JSON/CSV, date filters, prompts optional), a pager that annotates git diff, and annotations for the GitHub Checks API. Raw access: git notes --ref=whogitit show HEAD. Source: https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/README.md
links_sessions_to_code: Yes, and this is the tool's whole purpose. Claude Code PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks on Edit, Write and Bash snapshot each file before and after a tool call. The prompt comes from the Claude Code transcript_path: jq picks the last user message where toolUseResult is null, cut to 2000 characters. If that fails, the hook uses the tool's description field or a generic default. The post-commit step then runs the three-way analysis and binds session id, model, prompts and line ranges to the commit SHA. Trailers repeat a short session id inside the commit message. Setup writes the hook to ~/.claude/hooks/ and edits Claude Code settings.json. Other sources (https://tomevault.io/tome/dotsetlabs/whogitit) say Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Windsurf are also supported. I did not verify that in the source. Sources: https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/hooks/whogitit-capture.sh , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/README.md
scale: No numeric scale claims. The only hard limits are per-note sizes: 512 KiB warning, 4 MiB hard stop. 1.0.0 added 'retention preview --show <N>' for large repositories (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/CHANGELOG.md). The 1.0.0 crate is about 12.4k lines of Rust in 34 files, with about 127 downloads in total (https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/whogitit).
privacy_security: Prompts are redacted at capture time, before they are written to the pending buffer (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/capture/hook.rs , https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/capture/pending.rs). Redaction uses regexes only: 22 built-in patterns (API_KEY, EMAIL, PASSWORD, AWS_KEY, PRIVATE_KEY, BEARER_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, JWT, DB_CONNECTION, SSN, CREDIT_CARD, PHONE, NPM/PYPI/Stripe/Slack tokens and others). Matches are replaced with '[REDACTED]'. You can add custom named patterns, enable or disable built-ins, or turn redaction off. Each redaction event records the pattern name, the character range, a timestamp and a 10-character preview of the match (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/privacy/redaction.rs). Note that this preview can itself leak part of the secret into the audit trail. The local audit log (.whogitit/audit.jsonl, mode 0600) records Delete, Export, RetentionApply, ConfigChange and Redaction events. It is hash-chained: each event carries prev_hash and event_hash (SHA-256 truncated to 32 hex characters) and verify_chain() checks the chain (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/src/storage/audit.rs). Retention policies exist. Notes have no encryption: redacted prompts go in plaintext to every clone that fetches the ref. The pending buffer holds full file snapshots in plaintext, with 0600 permissions. Recalled prompts are not treated as untrusted. The hook fails open: it exits 0 on every error and logs to .whogitit/state/hook-errors.log (https://docs.rs/crate/whogitit/1.0.0/source/hooks/whogitit-capture.sh).
lesson_for_parinn: whogitit shows how far git notes can go as a transport for agent history: one overwrite-mode JSON blob per commit, capped at 4 MiB, written only at commit time, with no merge and a single-session pending buffer that drops work when a new session starts. That is fine for after-the-fact attribution. It cannot serve as a lossless, multi-writer, real-time record. ParleyInn should keep the authoritative hash-chained record outside git. Into git it should emit only a small derived pointer per commit, for example a trailer or note holding session id plus record chain-head hash and seq range, which can be rebuilt from the record (I10). Two things are worth borrowing: the post-rewrite note copy, and line-to-prompt blame as a projection. Do not copy its irreversible regex redaction at capture time. That conflicts with a lossless record. ParleyInn should redact on projection and export, and keep the redaction audit free of plaintext previews of the secret.
license: MIT (per crates.io metadata, https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/whogitit)
confidence: medium. The crate and its 1.0.0 source are confirmed on crates.io and docs.rs. Code details come from WebFetch summaries of the docs.rs source pages, plus a direct grep of the hook script. The GitHub repository is gone, so current development status and later versions cannot be verified. Two third-party claims are doubtful and unconfirmed: tomevault says 'requires Node 18+' and a pending-buffer 'version 2', but the 1.0.0 source is Rust and uses pending schema v3.

name: Willow Protocol + Meadowcap (Earthstar)
status: beta
what_is_stored: Arbitrary byte sequences organized by path (hierarchical, filesystem-like), timestamp, subspace (permission domain), and namespace (application isolation). Supports mutable data with human-meaningful names and modification times. Core data model is a key-value database where keys are paths and values are opaque binary blobs. Timestamps are logical, not wall-clock dependent for correctness but human-meaningful for users.
where_stored: Local hardware only—completely self-hosted, no network calls from protocol. Peers communicate via direct connection or optional relay servers. Supports local network auto-discovery and portable media (sneakernet via 'drops'). Relay servers are optional and transparent to the protocol.
format_and_model: Data organized as (namespace, subspace, path, timestamp) -> bytes. Willow is a meta-protocol; implementation details (encryption, serialization) are application-specific. Earthstar (v11) uses Willow specification. Paths have hierarchical structure; writing to a prefix (e.g., /a) when /a/b exists overwrites it (deletion). Timestamps determine versioning within a path; protocol remains correct even if timestamps are zero, but human semantics benefit from them.
multi_writer_and_merge: Multi-writer supported. Conflict resolution is 'last write wins' based on timestamp; application responsible for higher-level conflict handling. Prefix overwrites enable directory-level deletion. Meadowcap capability system allows delegable read/write grants per subspace, supporting both top-down (owned namespace) and bottom-up (communal namespace) permission models. Supports credential delegation and expiration.
realtime: Eventually consistent; no strict guarantees on propagation latency. In practice, real-time sync when peers online (used for real-time chat). Offline-first; peers can operate disconnected indefinitely and resync on reconnection. No clock dependency for correctness.
search_retrieval: Query by path, timestamp, subspace, or namespace. Can retrieve values newer than a given timestamp. Only most recent version of a document returned. No full-text search; filtering is application responsibility.
links_sessions_to_code: Not designed for agent session tracking. No built-in mechanism to link prompts, session history, or code artifacts. Could be adapted via subspace-based separation (each agent session as a subspace) but would require application-level design.
privacy_security: Meadowcap provides fine-grained, delegable read and write capabilities (no central authority required). Zero-knowledge proof protocol ensures peers can only exchange information about subspaces both have permission to read. Ed25519 verification. Read-only access grants possible. Credentials support expiration (though offline clients can circumvent by falsifying timestamps; application must re-timestamp on expiry). Encryption left to application (end-to-end encryptable). Deletion is supported via prefix overwrites but not guaranteed—uncooperative peers can retain deleted data; application must handle this risk (e.g., by re-timestamping).
lesson_for_parinn: Willow demonstrates that true mutable deletion (not append-only) scales in peer-to-peer systems via prefix-based overwriting and timestamp versioning. Decoupling sync primitives (3D range-based set reconciliation) from access control (Meadowcap) allows flexibility. Timestamps for human-meaningful versioning are viable in fully-offline systems without a global clock. For ParleyInn's append-only record with pinned constraints: the insight is that Meadowcap-style delegable capabilities could secure recall without central coordination, and Willow's namespace/subspace separation pattern maps cleanly to ParleyInn's requirement to isolate sessions and agents. However, Willow's mutable-deletion model conflicts with ParleyInn's immutability invariant (I8); ParleyInn's one-way redaction is more conservative.

name: workmux
category: worktree + tmux workflow for agents (Rust CLI and TUI that runs several agents side by side; not a history store)
status: shipped. Actively developed: v0.1.269 came out on 2026-09-30 and the latest main commit is e6500921 from the same day. Releases land every few days (CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The project is not archived. I could not check star counts because the GitHub API was not available in this session.
what_is_stored:
workmux keeps no conversation history. It stores only live coordination state and pointers.

(1) One JSON record per agent pane (AgentState):
- pane_key: backend, instance (for tmux, the socket path) and pane_id
- workdir
- status: working, waiting or done
- status_ts, activity_ts and updated_ts timestamps
- pane_title (Claude Code writes its session summary there)
- pane_pid and the foreground command, used to spot recycled panes and agents that have exited
- window_name and session_name
- boot_id, the multiplexer server's start time, used to tell a crash from a deliberate close
- agent_kind, such as "claude"
- agent_session_id, the agent's own session id taken from its hook payload

Source: src/state/types.rs, https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/src/state/types.rs

(2) settings.json: global dashboard and sidebar preferences such as sort mode, last pane visited and the last-done cycle state.

(3) runtime/<backend>__<instance>.json: short-lived state written by the sidebar daemon, such as the set of panes it considers interrupted.

(4) containers/<handle>/<name>: marker files that track sandbox containers.

(5) The task prompt, written in plain text to <worktree>/.workmux/PROMPT-<branch>.md (src/workflow/setup.rs).

(6) A log file, workmux.log. It records user prompts at info level when it asks an LLM to suggest a branch name (src/llm.rs).

(7) Configuration: ~/.config/workmux/config.yaml for the user and .workmux.yaml for each project (https://workmux.raine.dev/guide/configuration).

workmux never reads or copies agent transcripts. Its Pi integration says outright that it "does not read child session files" (docs/src/content/docs/guide/status-tracking.mdx).
where_stored:
Local files only.
- Agent state: $XDG_STATE_HOME/workmux/, by default ~/.local/state/workmux/, with agents/*.json, settings.json, runtime/, containers/ and workmux.log (doc comment in src/state/store.rs, https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/src/state/store.rs; src/logger.rs).
- Prompt files: in the worktree under .workmux/. workmux adds that folder to .git/info/exclude, so prompts stay out of git and are never committed.
- Live status: also kept as tmux window options (@workmux_status) inside the multiplexer server.

No git notes, refs, branches, separate repository, database or server. Git is used only for worktrees, branches and merges.
format_and_model:
Each record is a pretty JSON file named {backend}__{instance}__{pane_id}.json, with unsafe characters percent-encoded (for example tmux__default__%251.json). The record is keyed by multiplexer pane, not by agent session.

The model is a mutable snapshot, upsert-in-place: each hook event rewrites the whole file with a temp-file-plus-rename atomic write. Nothing is append-only and nothing is hash-chained, so no event history is kept.

Records from earlier multiplexer boots are compacted down to one recovery candidate per working directory. That candidate drives `workmux resurrect`, which reopens worktrees with each agent's resume arguments, for example Codex's last-session flag (https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/docs/src/content/docs/reference/commands/resurrect.md).

Serde defaults keep records written by older versions readable.
multi_writer_and_merge:
The writers are the hooks of several agents on one machine. They are serialized by an advisory flock on a lock file in the state directory (AgentStateLock wraps Flock<File> in src/state/store.rs).

Partial updates are merged field by field under that lock: a field the update leaves as None keeps its stored value. For tmux, a merge only happens when the pane PID and server boot match (persist_agent_update in src/state/mod.rs, https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/src/state/mod.rs).

A hook event that has no pane is bound to a pane through agent_session_id. v0.1.268 fixed a bug where unrelated Claude background sessions could overwrite an interactive pane's status (CHANGELOG).

The sidebar daemon writes to a separate runtime file so it never touches the per-agent files.

There is no sync between machines and no conflict resolution beyond last writer wins under the lock. Each multiplexer instance compacts only its own records.
realtime:
Real time on one machine only.
- Agent lifecycle hooks call `workmux set-window-status working|waiting|done` and `workmux register-agent`. These hooks exist for Claude Code (via a plugin), Codex, Gemini, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Grok and Antigravity. They update the tmux window title at once (status-tracking.mdx).
- The sidebar daemon flags an agent as "interrupted" when its pane output has not changed for 10 seconds while it is marked working.
- The dashboard reads the daemon's runtime file.
- A cache keyed on file revisions (dev, ino, len, mtime, ctime) avoids re-parsing files.

Nothing is shared across machines or sandboxes. Sandboxed agents send status to the host over local RPC authenticated with a per-session WM_RPC_TOKEN (https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/docs/src/content/docs/guide/sandbox/features.md).
search_retrieval:
None over content. Retrieval means navigation:
- the dashboard and sidebar list agents by status, recency, project or session
- `workmux last-done` jumps to the agent that most recently finished or is waiting
- `workmux last-agent` toggles back to the previous agent
- `workmux resurrect` restores worktrees after a crash
- the dashboard shows a live pane preview and a diff or patch view

There is no full-text or semantic search, and no history to search.
links_sessions_to_code:
Only loosely, and only while things run. Each agent record links:
- pane to working directory, which means the git worktree and branch
- pane to the agent's agent_session_id

The prompt that started a worktree is saved as .workmux/PROMPT-<branch>.md, but it is excluded from git and never tied to commits. `workmux merge` (rebase, squash, or merge) adds no trailers, notes or session references to commits (https://github.com/raine/workmux/blob/main/docs/src/content/docs/reference/commands/merge.md).

The dashboard can show pull request status, titles and the issues a pull request closes (v0.1.269). That links worktrees to pull requests, not sessions to commits.
scale:
No published scale claims. The design targets one developer running tens of parallel agents in one or a few tmux servers.

Recent changes target local performance:
- `sidebar.git_status: false` cuts background CPU use in large repositories (v0.1.269)
- a fix stopped tmux becoming unresponsive when many windows have sidebars (v0.1.265)

Source: CHANGELOG.
privacy_security:
No redaction and no encryption of its own state. The state files are plain JSON in the user's XDG state directory. Prompts are written in plain text into the worktree and are kept out of git only through .git/info/exclude. src/llm.rs logs the user prompt and system prompt at info level when generating branch names, so prompt text can reach workmux.log. Branch naming also sends the prompt to an external LLM tool (`llm` or a configured command), which is opt-in with -A (add.mdx).

Its real security work is in the optional sandbox (Lima VM or container) and its host-exec bridge (sandbox/features.md):
- the environment is sanitized, so host API keys are not inherited
- on macOS, Seatbelt denies access to ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.claude, ~/.config/gh, keychains and shell histories
- on Linux, bwrap mounts a tmpfs over secret folders and refuses to run if bwrap is missing (fail closed)
- ~/.gitconfig is not mounted; only user.name and user.email are injected
- network egress goes through a domain allow-list proxy that logs denials
- the setting dangerously_allow_unsandboxed_host_exec is global-only, so project config cannot weaken it

The docs warn that allow-listed build tools act as code interpreters and keep network access.

Status hooks fail open: hook commands are wrapped as `... || true`, and WORKMUX_DISABLE_SET_WINDOW_STATUS turns them off for nested agents.
lesson_for_parinn:
ParleyInn should key its records on the agent's own session id and the worktree path, not on tmux pane ids. It should take workmux's identity checks along with that.

workmux started with records keyed by multiplexer pane. It then had to add agent_session_id binding, pane-PID and boot-id checks against recycled panes, and per-boot compaction. Without them, hooks without a pane and Claude /bg sessions overwrote the wrong record; v0.1.268 fixed this.

What to adopt:
- the identity scheme: stable agent session id plus a stable host or boot discriminator
- a flock around writes, and temp-file-plus-rename atomic writes for mutable sidecars
- registration that records only verified live data

What to avoid: workmux's habit of putting prompts in a plain-text log and in files kept untracked only by .git/info/exclude. Both are silent leak channels that ParleyInn's I6 and redaction rules exist to close.

Separately, the workmux sandbox shows a host-side fail-closed policy that ParleyInn could point users to: secret folders hidden, settings that weaken security only allowed in global config, and a refusal to run without a sandbox.
